title: Detective Crusoe (Unfinished)
paragraphs: Diary Entry #1
Date: July 11th, 1935
I don’t like people, really. I’ve never liked people.
“So… How much do I have to pay you?”
Though, there’s no person that I hate more than Mr. Daynard. Mr. Daynard is a gruesome and unsightly man.

Even as he began to file through his pile of dollar bills, flashing a smug grin as an attempt at charm, I couldn’t help but feel disgusted by the sight of him. Mr. Daynard always has an oily look about him— and he especially had one tonight.
Tobacco juice smeared his lips. His hair appeared to have been slicked back with grease. His palms were sweaty.
It was impossible to go anywhere in his vicinity, without smelling the filthy scents that lingered around him.
“I don’t take money from mob bosses, Daynard,” I said. “How many people did that bust across the room cost you, by the way?”

Mr. Daynard’s marble bust— which Daynard mistakenly thought to have been designed in his likeness— sat across the room, staring at me in a chiseled expression of rage. While the real Daynard had minimal resemblance with it, he did share the bust’s rage.

“You know that’s not true,” Daynard said, sneering. “You and I— we’ve had a few scuffles throughout the duration of our relationship. But, even in the face of all the investigations, you’ve found that I’m clean!”
Mr. Daynard shoved his cigar into his mouth, letting charred bits of ash fall onto his coarse neck.
“You’re right, Daynard,” I said.
I felt my veins pulsate, and my fists clench. If it hadn’t been for the fact that my arm wasn’t feeling so weak at the time, I might’ve— well, I suppose I would’ve done nothing.
“I’m still not taking the money though— I’d prefer not to be under any bias. If you haven’t caught on yet, I’m an officer.”
“As if you haven’t made that clear enough…”
Mr. Daynard gave a grubby gesture to the badge on my chest. I felt the sudden wish to polish it off—the very fact that Mr. Daynard was staring at it made me feel as if the badge had filthened.
“Thanks for trying to help me out, anyhow,” he continued. “I can’t thank you enough for it. And, I really do hope that you take the money, eventually.”
He paused, to smirk.
“Even so, I’m not overly disappointed. I’ve lost enough money tonight…”

I opened my mouth to say something more. I couldn’t find anything to say. The atmosphere of Mr. Daynard’s entrance hall had left me feeling unnerved. Nicely decorated as it was, he had a bit too much detail put into it…
If there’s anything that I’ve learned in my investigative work, people always have something to hide. It’s people like Daynard—the most ostentatious of society—that tend to be the most corrupt.
I went for Daynard’s exit.
“I hope that you’ll be able to cover all of the property damages,” I said.
Before I left his house, for the police car waiting for me outside, I took a glance back to his wall— it had been defaced with red paint, and a wooden stake was pounded into it.
“Mob activity…” I muttered under my breath. “When will these cretins ever learn?”
Diary Entry #2
Date: July 15th, 1935
Miss Lucille Prestel
2056 Cannon Drive
Chicago, IL 60615
July 11th, 1935
Lieutenant Charles Jackson
850 W Addison St
Chicago, IL 60613
Dear Lieutenant Jackson,

as you’ve requested, I’ve sent you this letter as an account of what I remember taking place during the recent robbery, which occurred on my estate— Prestel Manor. I apologize for the prolonged wait, but I toiled over this manuscript without rest. I needed to perfectly convert my memory to text. I’m aware that you would’ve preferred for me to have told you the account in person during our past encounters. However, this was unfortunately the only way. Every time I speak of the event I feel as if my wits have been knocked right out of me.

I’m somewhat of a poet, so my prose should be amongst the most elegant you’ll ever read. I hold the belief that my writings are arguably the most refined of all literature. Since I know that you’ll find yourself envious of my jaded skills— even the strongest willed men feel envy—I’ll give you a tip as to how to recreate my excellence. Do as I did, and explore all five of our flattened Earth’s continents. Speak unto the stars, and let them answer you. Stare into the darkness, and try your hardest to listen to the voice of the ether. Only through doing that can you become as great as I.

Although, enough about myself. While I’m sure you wish for me to tell you of all my stunning adventures and journeys, I simply don’t have the time. After meeting you, I can attest that you’re a strapping young gentlemen of fifty— however, you’re not quite deserving of my greatest secrets, darling. Over the eighty-three years of my life, I’ve learned the beauty in brevity. That’s why I’m going to begin my wondrous account. I promise that you’ll be in awe. I showed it to my eighth husband’s ghost, and he adored it!
There was something strange during the night of the robbery... It was in the hair— I could feel it in my face. I should’ve brushed it before I went to bed, but I’d neglected to.
I could also feel the strangeness in my gut. It was rumbling and growling. While it might’ve only been because of hunger, I felt that there was something more to it— I think it was also my laxatives.

Whatever it was, I couldn’t take it anymore. I rolled out of my modest master bedroom and through my humble entrance hall. Creaks followed my footsteps, and I could’ve sworn that somebody was watching me. I looked around, and then saw that there was something watching me— a monkey skull.

I have a very grand collection of monkey skulls, and it’s a source of great pride. All of my pet monkeys have been kind enough to offer me this collection— but every time I see one of the skulls, the ether’s essence leaps out of my mouth. That night was no different. I wailed with a force that could’ve crumbled a mountain.

It was after I’d finished wailing that I discovered the wail wasn’t in vain. I heard footsteps begin to pound through the hall, and my favorite glasses and silverware crashed through my kitchen. The moment that this clatter reached my ears, I reacted with the agility of a lion. While people might state otherwise, I still have a very youthful vigor. My practice from on the moon’s jungles has yet to leave me.

As I ran toward the site of the sound, I could hardly feel the weight of my dressing gown. Once I’d made it to the area where the noise had come from, I pounced toward the culprit. He was dressed in extremely roguish garments. He had an oversized jacket, with a collar that covered his face. He also had a fedora pulled down over his eyes to complete the nonsensical getup. Because of this, the only feature that I could clearly catch was that he had a rounded, clean-shaven jaw. Just by the look of him, I could tell that he was a criminal.
Even with my Olympian speed, I was too slow to catch the man. He leapt from my grasp, and charged out of the room. Before I could yell for him to stop, he’d leapt out of my window and left in shards.
Studying the remains of my kitchen, I found that he’d pilfered my box of savings, and all of my legal documents. The very sight made my jaw slacken. This was all it took for me to call the police.

However, I would hate for you to believe that I went down without a fight. It was anything but that. I saw the man jump back from out of the broken window and back into the kitchen, displaying supernatural strength. However, it was no match for my own. We soon became caught in an enthralling battle. There was only one moment where I struggled. But, it passed quickly, and I soon had the man pinned to a wall. He was in my power, and I could’ve easily stopped him. The only reason that he—

“I can’t believe Lieutenant Jackson took this seriously,” I told myself, pushing the document across, to the other side of my desk. “But, why am I surprised? He had me go into Mr. Daynard’s house, after all.”
I paused, and then let out a chuckle.
“But, now this… This is the most ridiculous letter I’ve ever read.”

I’d been reading up on the Lieutenant’s case-file, concerning a string of recent crimes. Although, I seriously question the legitimacy of the case. Every document in it seems to either be falsified, or ambiguous. Miss Prestel’s latest letter was probably the strongest pieces of evidence yet— and that was saying a lot.
“What have I been worrying about?” I asked myself. “Crusoe can’t be back… How could I have ever let myself think he was?”
While there was comfort in knowing that the sightings of Crusoe were largely unfounded, the fresh robbery still retained an ominous atmosphere.

I’m not sure why I was so upset at the time, now that I look back on it… Crime is always an issue—even the return of Crusoe wouldn’t change that fact… Not that much, anyway. If I were to have been honest with myself, a few robberies are the least of my problems.

I’ve been trying to ignore it for the past few months, but the police have lost complete control over the skyrocketing crime rates—our handle on the law is slipping through our fingers, like grains of sand.

I looked the window of my moonlight smeared office, and saw a destitute street. It was littered with a grimy fog of trash, and a few flickering splays of light. There were even a few articles of clothing left on the ground. They moved in the wind, as if they were trying to flee from my sight.
“I should’ve moved to California…” I said, pulling at my silvering hair.

My eyes moved to the nameplate on my desk— Sergeant James Kyler. Those words used to glisten in a radiant gold. They’d dulled since then… Dust had covered the etchings. Years do that though. They leave the world to become but a fragmented memory of what it once was…
Memory…
My memory trailed back to the day I’d received the title of Sergeant, and the pride I’d felt.
“If only I could’ve seen where it was heading…” I whispered.
Memory and hindsight can be so treacherous…

I pulled out a pen and a sheet of paper from under my desk, and began to transcribe my observations concerning the Crusoe case. My breaths heaved, and my eyes started to lull. Though it wasn’t until the moonlight faded from my window, and the paper obscured, that sleep finally subdued me.

My jaw slackened, and my posture dipped into my desk. If my heart hadn’t been beating a dozen times a second, I would’ve fell dead. My heartbeat only rested for a moment, as the remaining sliver of silky moonlight dripped from the curtains of my office.

On a normal late night, I preferred for the moonlight to be drowned out— this allowed me to think without distraction. However, I welcomed the moonlight that night. It allowed me to see what I’d been ignoring. For the past few months, I’d been feeling my resolve begin to compromise. The world around me seemed to be doing the same. Poverty’s stroke was imbedded upon nearly every street in the city of Chicago. For a cop, an outbreak of poverty was one of the worst things to experience.
Poverty is the source of all crime, after all…
“If only it wasn’t so hard to detect for the past few years… Why has it taken until now for me to notice it?”
That’s a question that I can’t answer. For the past five years, there’s hardly been a Chicago street that wasn’t vacant or neglected.
I suppose that the reason I’ve ignored it all is because I’ve found a way to skirt by. I clung to my job, to the point that my clinging‘s intensity painted my knuckles white, and forced my eyes shut.

For a while, I thought that my clinging was the reason I’d kept my job. I reasoned that I’d worked hard enough for it. I thought that, by some act of pure skill, I was entitled to the right of keeping my career— everybody else had earned their misfortunes.
At least I was right about one thing— I was entitled.

Despite my ignorance, the problems were harder to dismiss. I can’t quite tell what it was that woke me up. Maybe it was the day that I went to the police department, and realized that half of the police force was missing. Maybe it was when I went to the store, and saw a vacuum. Maybe it was when I went to my apartment, and found my neighboring apartments to be empty.
Maybe it was the combination of all of this.

Whatever it was that woke me up, it was running me ragged, to the point that even sleep had become tiresome. Whenever I settled down in my bed for the night, my eyes wouldn’t shut. They’d stare up at the ceiling, for hours— and, they wouldn’t budge, no matter how hard I tried pulling them down.
Sometimes I’d wonder what I was looking at. Though, that wasn’t the right question. I should’ve asked myself what I was looking away from.
I can’t overstate this fact enough— I’ve always thought myself to be a good cop. Although, skyrocketing crime rates clearly say otherwise. I’ve kept my job only because nobody else has a job.
Nobody else has a job.
This sentence ticks in my brain, and it ticked in my brain then, with each tick of my office clock. A friend of mine recently lost a job— and I haven’t seen them since, because of it.
I looked at the clock, partially to check the time and partially to distract myself. It was 1:01.

I’ve been coming back to my office every night that I can’t sleep. A swamp of exhaustion has settled where my brain once was, but I can’t stop the habit. My mind is always going somewhere, but it never reaches where it’s going. It constantly drives me to act in the inky hours, and I always find myself looking for something— something that is never there. There have been some nights where I stay in my office the entire night, through to the daytime, and don’t leave until night falls again.
“Kyler!”

I snapped my head up from my paper, and looked around the room. Shadows still flooded it, and the moon’s milky wisp was still all that I could see. However, there was something else too, even if I couldn’t quite see it. I could sense another presence— another person, staring me down. For a moment, I nearly thought that I’d been dreaming. What I’d detected was something as slight as the breath of another— but it changed the room as much of an effect as the wind would have in a dustbowl.
My fingers edged near my flashlight.
“Well, no need to whip your head about,” the person chuckled. There was a bumbling slyness to it. It was coming from Lieutenant Jackson.
I’ve always thought that hate is a strong emotion. Respect towards authorities is a virtue that I’ve constantly tried to uphold. I make an exception when it comes to Lieutenant Jackson.

He’s the kind of person who likes to stick his nose in everything. The man has a special type of intuition that lets him know whenever there’s a conversation that he has no part in. If I didn’t know his middle name, I would guess that it’s, “Eavesdropping”.

In fact, dropping is a word that suits him in more ways than one. With nearly every step he takes, he looks like he’s about to trip and fall. Perhaps this is due to his sickly, lanky build. He has dark saggy eyes and a pale complexion. The only thing of color on him are tufts of strawberry hair, which poke out from under the hat that he constantly tucks over his head. From the way he wears himself, he’s indistinguishable from a walking corpse. Whenever I see him pass by, I can’t help but hold back a scowl. He’s inept in everything he does, he’s a terrible leader, and a disgrace to all Lieutenants. If there was anything about him that I feel confident in, it’s that he doesn’t deserve his title.
“What do you want, Jackson?”
“Well, you’re out of line— you’re to address me as Lieutenant Jackson.”
I grinned.

“I’d address you as Lieutenant if you were one— but you’re not,” I almost said. Looking back on the scene, I wish that I did. I wish that I’d torn my badge off my chest, and stormed out of the room. It would’ve served me better than what was to come out of my mouth.
“My apologies,” I said instead. “Why did you come into my office?”
“Uh… Well, I was wondering why you came to your office. You’ve been coming here early for the past week. I came here early, hoping to catch what you’re doing every night. What are you doing?”
“I come here to clear my head,” I said, plainly.

My plainness was but a guise. I was becoming anxious. Jackson was already studying the room around me, scoping it out for anything suspicious. Once I caught him distracted, I took Miss Prestel’s letter from the top of my desk, and shoved it into my back pocket.
“Huh…” Jackson said.

He hung on that word for a second too long. It was usually his way of saying that he didn’t believe a word of mine, but he didn’t feel that I was worth the time to interrogate. His eyes rolled to meet mine, and he savored the intimidation he held over me.
Huh… I thought to myself. The word huh says a lot more than I thought it did…
“Well, there’s no need for me to keep prying…” Jackson said.
That’s something else that I hate about him. He overuses the word well, well more than he should— something cruelly ironic, considering his unwell features.
“Well, there was another robbery at Lincoln Park,” Jackson said, leaning back and shoving his hands in his pockets.
“Well,” I said, mocking him. “That sounds like something we should be taking care of. Why didn’t you get to that subject sooner?”
“From what we can tell, Crusoe was there,” Jackson said, suddenly. “Detective Crusoe. We’ve had several eye-witness accounts, and they all point to him.”
He said the word Detective with a leer.
“What does that masquerading joke have to do with me?” I asked.
Sweat was pouring down my forehead, and I hardly knew why. Then I caught Jackson’s gaze. As sickly as he looks, Jackson can still muster an overpowering aura.

“It has everything to do with you— you know that. This is the third time this week that a crime correlated with the— Detective. And you’ve been coming to the police department each midnight— around the same time that Crusoe commits a crime. Are you going to tell me that there’s no correlation?”
“Correlation or not, I haven’t seen that man in years,” I said. “Everybody knows that. I’m surprised that he’s come back, but it has nothing to do with me.”

“That’s just it, Kyler. Nobody has seen him for years. If he was who you said he was, then why would he come back? The city has been ravaged by crime and poverty. Are you going to keep playing dumb, or are you going to talk?”
“I’ve been talking Lieutenant. Crusoe isn’t any of my business.”

“Fine then…” Jackson said, with a defeated look— something I long thought him incapable of making. “Well, Miss Prestel has finally sent me her witness account concerning the robbery. I can’t show it to you, because I misplaced it. Not that it matters, because it’s mostly full of absurdities— but, it’s provided enough new information to convince me that I need to make another investigation around her house. Most of our dogs were sick during the night of the robbery.
He tucked his hands into his pockets, and studied around my room once more. I knew that he was waiting for me to beg him to join. But, I wasn’t going to fall for his parlor tricks.

“Well I suppose that, if you really want, you could join me,” Jackson finally said, garnishing his words with a staged reluctance. “After all— you’ve been stuck in this office very often, as of late.”
Perhaps it was just me, but Lieutenant Jackson seemed to wield his every word like a dagger, steadily jabbing at me with them for long as he could. I simply did my best to ignore him.
As he walked off, he gave me one last glare.
I made a leer.
Diary Entry #3
Date: July 16th, 1935

I looked at the globe seated on my desk. Daylight drenched one side, but shadow dominated another. Absent-mindedly, I spun the globe around several times before stopping it to clasp two of my fingers onto a red pin. The pin which marked my city— my home.
I could hardly recognize it as my home though. The globe was obscured by the dimness of the room.
“Well, it’s time to get in the squad car,” Lieutenant Jackson said, intruding into my office.
I scowled. Thankfully, Jackson couldn’t see it, due to the veiled darkness of the room. This was perhaps the one benefit of me always keeping the shades drawn.
“We’re heading to Prestel Manor?” I asked.
“Where else?”
“As you said before, this will be your second inspection of the property… I never thought that you’d be in a rush to leave for there, this early…”
I looked down to my silver watch. It was eight in the morning.
There was something else on the watch too— a man with thick bags under his eyes, and a worn visage.
My reflection.
I really need to get more sleep… I thought to myself.

“I don’t expect to find much, but I suppose that we might as well give it a second look… We could use your second opinion,” said Lieutenant Jackson. “And, we need probably have this done first thing. Miss Prestel isn’t a person who understands the concept of brevity, and I have a busy schedule today.”
Jackson backed away into the doorway, before pausing to crack a smile.
“With that said, when I notified her of our coming arrival, she said she doesn’t want us to stay there too long. She, ‘prefers to keep company away.’ That fits with my agenda, I suppose…”
Jackson paused to grin.
“But, I’m not sure how she could feel that way, especially after the contents of her letter. I suppose that old age and the oversized house of hers made her become somewhat senile.”
Jackson let out a laugh, and I forced myself to join in. As our laughs evaporated, the journey from out of the aging police department and into our dated squad car was markedly silent.
“Well, you know, this reminds me of the Brad Duncan case…” Jackson said, once he’d gotten comfortable in the driver seat.

I still don’t know how he could’ve gotten comfortable in it. The whole car rattled once it was put into gear, and the seats were made of a stiff, torn fabric. It’s not just me who shares this sentiment either. Tin-can has become a nickname for it among much of the police department.
In retrospect, it was probably because he had to. A car-ride in silence would’ve only made things even more unbearable.
“Remember him?” asked Jackson. “Squinty-eyed… Had a wobbling gait. Not too bright?”
I remained unresponsive. Jackson was bursting into laughter though, even as he was backing out of the parking lot.

“I don’t think I’ve met such an idiot since! He thought that he’d been robbed, because his door had been left open, a few of his possessions were missing and his floor was covered in muddy footprints. But then… Then…”
Jackson was wheezing so hard that I decided to give him mercy.
“I remember… We found out that he’d just left the door open, and that the missing items and the muddy footprints were from his dog.”
“His dog! Yes! Right! Exactly!”

The rest of the car ride was like this. Lieutenant Jackson made uncomfortable jokes, jabs, and comments, while I forced myself to humor him. It was just short of torture. There were half a dozen times when I had the urge to cringe, but forced myself to stop.

I tried enjoying the scenery. I tried looking out into the street. Instead, I found myself staring into a dark and cloudy atmosphere. It was so thick that it looked something like a massive blot on the window. Fog and rain had poured on the city so relentlessly, that it had been left unrecognizable.
Can a diamond ever lose its beauty? I would’ve once answered that question with a no. Though, I’ve come to sympathize with a different view.
The streets steadily faded out, and the bleary silhouette of a slumping Victorian house was lit up by our headlights.
“We’re here,” Jackson said.
I watched as his face sloped downward, and he let out a slight sigh.

As he pulled into the Manor’s grove, and the surroundings became less obscured, I found it to be more elegant than I’d initially believed. Despite me knowing the Chicago streets as well as I knew my own apartment, the manor still had a new and enchanting look to it.

I’m sure that if I’d told Jackson what I felt, he would’ve disregarded me with a smothered chuckle. He wouldn’t have done so without reason, either. The manor had crumbling walls, a roof that was stained from chimney smoke, and a lengthy dirt driveway. Most of the manor’s bottom half was cloaked in a fog. Its pointed crown of a roof was folding in on itself, due to its aged and meagre architecture. I could even smell the manor’s thick mustiness, whilst I was sitting in the car. Yet, I somehow still let it take me back to a time when I was younger. There was something to it that gave me a jolt of energy.
I suppose that our opinions of things sometimes have a way of surprising us.

A woman strode out from the fog. She was clearly advanced in years, and had caked makeup over her face to hide it. To be frank, nearly every part of her was either doused in a cherry makeup, flowery garments, or a disgustingly sweet perfume.
“Welcome to Prestel Manor,” she said ceremoniously, as me and Jackson stepped out of our car. She beamed at the sight of Jackson, but construed her face at the sight of me.
“I’m Sergeant Kyler,” I said.
“More like unwelcome…” the woman muttered. “I’m Miss Prestel,” she said, putting on a false, cheery smile. “This is my manor, Prestel Manor, which has lasted throughout three generations.”
“That’s quite a long time!” Lieutenant Jackson said, gawping. “I wasn’t aware that this house was so old. From which side of your family did you inherit it?”
“Neither. I bought it. When I said, ‘three generations’, I was referring to the three generations of my pet monkeys. I’ve only had this house for thirty years, darling. Hardly enough time to—”
As I listened to her nonsense, I followed her up to her rickety porch. I could already tell that she was going to be quite the character.

“Let’s keep in mind that we’ve come to inspect the premises, not converse” I said to them, while staring at Miss Prestel’s fake diamond ornaments, which were draped across the overhang of her porch. In hindsight, it’s not a wonder that she was robbed.
“How did you happen to come into such a fortune, Miss Prestel?” I asked.

I asked this question presuming that knowledge on how she made her fortune might have an amount of relevance to the robbery at hand. However, after I asked the question, Mrs. Prestel gave me an aghast expression.
I still can’t quite tell what to make of it.

“It’s a strange thing, actually,” she said, awkwardly turning her head away for a moment. “I dabbled in a little bit of stock here, and a little bit of investments there… It was just a thing of savviness. It didn’t hurt that I did a little bit of exploration and treasure hunting in my younger years.”
Her servant swung the entrance doors open.
“This is my butler, Eustace Gretchen,” she said, as I and the Lieutenant thanked him. “I found him in my travels— oh what wild adventures I had.”

We were led past melancholy stuffed heads of monkeys that she kept nailed on her entrance hall, before being brought into her parlor. It was a small, square room— compared to the massiveness of the rest of her house, anyway— but she’d managed to stuff it to the brim. In the left corner, opposite to the entrance door, there was a couch. To the right of that, there was a coffee table that contained pictures of Miss Prestel and her several husbands. Along the walls, there were more pictures— most of them containing monkeys. Eerily, in each image of the monkeys, they were wearing the same outfit as one of Miss Prestel’s husbands.

Despite the parlor being full of pinks, purples, and blues, I still felt it was grungy. As Miss Prestel offered me a place in a purple chair with a swirl painted on it, I shook my head no. The very thought of taking seat in it felt unclean. I couldn’t help but wonder how she’d earned money for such a furnishing— undoubtedly by scraping through rich husbands, to pave her way to wealth. I wasn’t willing to rest on a chair that had been bought through such means.

“This is one of my favorite rooms,” Miss Prestel said, sitting at a pink, round table that had been placed at the center of it. “These images hold a sense of weight and meaning in my heart. I can’t quite say why, but they each make me feel as if I’m traveling back in time, to my happier days…”
I nodded.
“Is it true that you’ve had eight husbands, as your note declared?” I asked, trying to coddle her ego.
Miss Prestel frowned.
“No,” she said. “I had nine. But, I thought that you came here to study my case…”
“I was just curious… You inherited their wills each time they died, correct?”
“For most of them. But why do you—?”
“Do you think that any of their relatives have any sort of grudge against you? Perhaps a father or mother in law…”
“I already told you in my letter— I’m confident that the robber matched the gallivanting ‘Detective Crusoe’ figure. It’s unnecessary to try steering off into absurdities.”
Lieutenant Jackson nodded in agreement, and gruffly took one of the purple seats. He looked ridiculously out of place as he sat down in it, with the chair clashing with his dark uniform. I grinned.
“Well Sergeant, you’re overstepping your boundaries. If you wish to ask her questions, make sure that they’re relevant to the case at hand. Miss Prestel’s personal life can stay out of it.”
I stopped grinning.

Miss Prestel blushed, with her cheeks turning crimson— and my own cheeks turned the same color. I hadn’t expected such chastising from Lieutenant Jackson. Though, what hurt worse was that he was right.
I’ve gotten rusty, I thought to myself.

Jackson pulled out his notepad and a pen. As he did so, his pen opened with a crisp click, followed by the clucking of his tongue. This habit of his always found a way to get under my skin, but I managed to keep my jaw shut, and my eyes focused at the pink table.
“Well,” Jackson said, “where were you the day before you were robbed?”
“Right here in my home, all day. If you’d like proof, you can just ask my butler.”
“And this butler,” he continued, furiously writing in his notes, “Mr. Gretchen, as you call him? Where was he before the crime?”

“On weekdays, I pay Mr. Gretchen to sleep in my guest room, so that he’s here for me as needed throughout the night. However, with the crime having occurred on a weekend, he was at his house, near Roscoe Village.”
Jackson raised his eyebrows for a moment, but continued writing.
“Has he ever had any suspicious behavior before?” Jackson asked.
“No. Never! He’s served me for forty years. I—.”
“You said that you’ve only owned this house for thirty years,” I said.
“Yes, well… Mr. Gretchen has served me since before then. He’s a very loyal servant. The very suggestion of him attempting thievery is absurd.”
“Then, are there any other suspicious suspects surrounding the robbery?” Lieutenant Jackson asked. “Anybody who’s acted odd?”
While Miss Prestel might’ve been overjoyed to be in Jackson’s presence earlier, she looked somewhat disgusted now.
“I already told you both. The robber was Detective—.”

“It’s fine that you have your suspicions, ma’am,” Jackson said. “But we need to narrow things down to the facts. Supposing the robber really was Detective Crusoe, we’ll need to know all possible suspects— that’s the only way we’ll be able to figure out who this ‘Crusoe’ figure really is.”
Miss Prestel’s incredulity finally simmered.

“Well, I can’t think of anybody who might’ve been willing to rob me. The only thing that has been acting strange lately is my newest pet monkey— he doesn’t seem to be getting better from any of the help that my personal veterinarian has been giving him.”
“You have a personal veterinarian… could you please elaborate?”
Miss Prestel’s eyes fluttered, and she pushed her hair out of her face.

“He’s a wonderful and charming person. I have him come over to my house several times a week, to check on my monkey… And he’s so very kind to the creature. He goes by the name of, ‘Dr. Martin Smith’, and drives here in a funny little model T— I thought that people would’ve stopped driving those things by now. Oddly enough though— he stopped coming over and answering my calls a few days after the robbery.”
“How and when did you come to meet this, ‘Dr. Smith’?” Jackson asked.
He was now writing so fast that I thought his pen might break.
“He came to my door a month ago, asking me if I had any pets.”

“Thank you, Miss Prestel,” Lieutenant Jackson said, standing up from his chair. “I think that I’ve gained all the new information that I needed, as far as suspects go. Now, could you please give us a tour around your house. I’d like to get a better idea of how the crime might’ve been committed, and who might’ve been able to commit it.”

Miss Prestel nodded eagerly, and led us out of her parlor. Her elderly thumped on the floor, dragging us through her monotonous maze of oversized corridors and hallways. While there were several times where she claimed that she’d kept a, “unique and varied collection,” most of her decorations kept the trend of being adorned with some sort of monkey ornament, or bust. There were only a few items of hers that stood out from this trend— and they were usually images of her past husbands. However, one of them did retain a significance in my memory.

We passed a coffee table, with a brownie camera sitting on it. Just as I’d taken my last step away from it, the camera snapped a picture of my leg. Perhaps it had a loose spring, or perhaps the button was jammed. It probably wasn’t anything that I should’ve focused on. However, as a photo filtered through the two lips on the camera’s side, I was glued to it. I couldn’t take my eyes off the photo.
Could any of these fluke pictures have been taken at the crime scene? I wondered.
I was being too optimistic.
Any fluke picture that might’ve been taken probably would’ve been too dark and unclear to make out. Furthermore, even if such a picture could’ve been clear, Miss Prestel would’ve shown them to us.
That, or she hid them…
I quickly waved the idea off— but, that didn’t change the fact that I’d thought it. As Miss Prestel took us up her steps and into her bedroom chambers, my mind was only focused on that thought.
Our entire visit to Miss Prestel’s might’ve been meaningless.
“This was where I was sleeping when the terrible robbery took place,” Miss Prestel said, with a melodramatic wail. “When I heard the man come in, my heart leapt in shock.”
She showed us her bed.
“That was the very place I was in when it happened. It’s made of the finest silk, imported straight from China. I collected it during my journey to the—.”
I tuned her out and began studying the room for myself. There wasn’t much in there, besides her overabundant furnishings.
I let out a sigh, and brought my hands into my face.
The visit had become a little more than an excuse for Miss Prestel to show off her money.
“And this is where I leaped from my—,” Miss Prestel said, showing off her bed.
I cut her words off before she could finish.
“I think that I’ve seen enough. Could you please take me to your kitchen, where the crime was first committed?”
She gave a huff, and then rang a bell at the side of her bed. Within moments, Mr. Eustace Gretchen was standing in the entrance door.
“Could you be a dear and lead our guest to the kitchen?” Miss Prestel asked him. “He wishes to study how our robber might’ve broken in.”
I couldn’t help but gag when she described me as a, “guest.” It was as if she thought that she’d brought me over for one of her pitiful dinner parties.
However, I luckily was uprooted from my anger when Mr. Gretchen nodded, and began leading me out of the room. As I followed him, I heard Lieutenant Jackson’s voice faintly trail after me.
“I’ll be down with you in a minute. I just need to look over a few more things.”
I probably needed to hear that, in that moment. Some time away from Jackson is always a relief.
“Are you pleased with the madam’s house?” the butler asked me.
“Uh, Sure… Very much so. But, I really don’t have time to chat.”

Taking the message far better than I expected, Mr. Gretchen led me to the kitchen in a mere five minutes— a massive change in pace when compared with the twenty minutes that Miss Prestel would’ve taken.
“What happened to all of the glass?” I asked the butler, taking a glimpse of everything. “I thought that the robber had broken your window.”
A faint scowl formed between Mr. Gretchen’s brows, which he promptly erased.
“I was actually brought here from in the middle of my weekend to clean it up. The mess was a ghastly ordeal, and it became even more tedious when the window had to be replaced.”
I was about to ask him more— but a flare protruded through my vision before I could open my mouth to utter a word. There was a shard of glass on the ground.
I picked up. Though, it began to crumble in my hand.
“Gretchen, were there any other maimed items from the robbery?”

“Several actually… You wouldn’t believe it, but the window sill and the countertop were completely deformed afterward. We replaced the countertop and the window, and I tried repairing the deformed windowsill by putting on a sort of sealant… However, it hasn’t been quite the same.”
I did believe it.

I’d read the initial police reports. They had discussed some oddities concerning the broken window. There were suggestions that the deformity might’ve been caused by a sort of flame-thrower. Although, I knew better.
“Acid,” I muttered, under my breath. I let the dust in my hand fall to the floor, and Mr. Gretchen give me a look of dismay.
“You might want to consider giving this counter a deep scrubbing,” I said. “From what I can tell, it needs it.”
He didn’t seem to be listening— Gretchen was too focused on sweeping up some remaining bits of glass, along with the bit of dust that I’d dropped.
“Yes sir, very well sir,” he said, with an absent-minded glance in my direction.
I’d become focused in my own work as well.

Making a rough judgement of the counter’s height, I found that it was five feet in the air— high enough to keep anybody with a short stature from jumping on top of. It also had a somewhat flimsy build— but, I partially attribute that to the acid that was probably poured onto it.

My guess is that the person who’d escaped through it would’ve had to be light on their feet and agile to have made it through without injuring themselves. Moreover, if they had weighed more, they likely wouldn’t have had the need for the acid in the first place.
For a person who was willing to rob a house, they must’ve been fairly weak.

Backtracking to the accusations that the robber had been Detective Crusoe, I can’t help but laugh— the very thought of him leaping over five-foot hurdles comes across as humorous to me. While it would take me talking to somebody I trust deeply for me to admit, I know Crusoe very well— and his figure is far too robust to have performed such a stunt. Especially since he’s aged the same amount of years as I have since we’ve last met.

I now realize now that I’m much further along in this case than most of the police in the area. I know so much more about Crusoe than all of them combined. They don’t know what they’re looking for… They think that they know so much, but they haven’t gone around this city fifty times, like I have. They don’t know this place like the back of their head.
I do.

I was never able to inspect that kitchen as thoroughly as I might’ve liked to through. I was stopped when a shriek tore my eardrums. Thinking that something was horribly wrong, I charged out of the kitchen and up to the bedroom where I’d last seen Miss Prestel.
As I ran, I felt my body groan from the stress of it all, but it didn’t matter—I kept on running.

I made it to the room doubled over, and gulping as much air as my lungs could hold. To my surprise, I found the room to be just as I’d left it— with Jackson and Miss Prestel standing by the bed. They looked as shocked to see me as I was to see them.
“What happened?” I asked, still panting.

“Nothing,” said Jackson, looking slightly bemused. “Well… Nothing might be a bit of a stretch… We were just looking out the window saw a man running on the roof of the mansion. He was dressed in the typical Crusoe garb. But… how did you know that there was something wrong?”
I returned his expression.
“I heard a scream. Didn’t you scream at something, Miss Prestel?”
Her lips scrunched into her cheeks.

She said, “No dear… I’m not the sort of person who screams at danger. To be honest, I didn’t hear a thing. It could just be that I was too focused on the fleeing form of Detective Crusoe… But, maybe you’re hearing things?”
I nodded to her in understanding. Though, there was no part of me that understood.

There was no doubt in my mind that there had been a scream. My feet had felt the floor vibrate. My head was still throbbing from the sound of it. I found it stranger that they hadn’t heard it than the fact that I had.

Searching for any potential sources of the scream, I peered out the window— there was nothing in sight. I turned my head back and forth, from Johnathan to Miss Prestel. Neither of them compromised under my questioning gaze. Neither of them were willing to alter their stories.

In the corner of my eye, I thought I saw something flutter and take seat on the rain-smattered roof— Crusoe’s designated fedora. I whipped my head to the spot where it would’ve been, but I saw an owl take flight instead. It moved too fast for me to tell if it had taken the hat that I thought I’d seen. In fact, the only way I’d even been able to determine it was an owl was by the way it shrieked as it disappeared into the smoky clouds.
The only possible proof for whether the robber had really been Crusoe… And it was taken by a bird…
“Lieutenant, I think I’ve seen enough,” I said. “I’m ready to go.”
The ride back to the police department was silent. Though, this silence still managed to say everything that needed to be said.
“Why did you make such a fool of us?” I heard, in Lieutenant Jackson’s seethe.
I gave a cough, and leaned back in my seat, as if to say, “I knew exactly what I was doing.”
I didn’t though. Underneath my relaxed demeanor, I was tense. My mind raced as it tried to find answers. The Lieutenant’s disapproval was overwhelming.
The streets were obscured in a thick fog.
I used to see a thick cream amongst the fog. I used to see it as if the heavens had decided come down to anoint the streets. Now, I only ever see a map of gray.

I suppose the fog is the perfect allegory for life. Upon first looking at it, we see how mystifying and broad-reaching it is. However, the years pass, and we come to see it as it really is— constricting, random, and blurring. Past the fog, one’s destination could await them… And yet, some terrible accident— some unperceived undoing— could also await.
I guess that’s another reason why I can’t sleep at night. I’ve come to recognize that both destiny and travesty have drawn themselves closer and closer to me.
For some reason, I’d let Jackson bring me closer to travesty. I let him bring me back out into the field that morning.
I severely question whether that was the right choice.

I looked back across to Lieutenant Jackson. He had a scowl across his forehead, and a squint in his eyes.  I know that he just might’ve been straining to see through the intense cloud. But, I still think he was directing his anger onto me.

Droplets of water dripped on the side of my window. As each one slid down the window, a minute passed by on my clock. I know, because I counted each one. I eagerly watched time slip away, as I reminisced on my office, which stank of ink, polish, dust, and stacks of mildew papers.
Twenty-seven droplets of water had slid down my window by the time we reached the police station.
“What did you think?” I asked the Lieutenant, as I trailed behind him to his office.
“I’ve thought quite a lot of things… None of which I particularly wish to share with you,” he answered me, without even thinning his stride.

“I’m sorry about how some of the ways I acted were— amateurish,” I said, trying to appeal to him. “It’s just been awhile since I last worked on a case that was this personal. You have to understand— the topic of Crusoe is an uncomfortable one for me.”
“Well, if you’re going to be any help to this case, you need to get comfortable with it.”
He unlocked his office door. He went in.
I followed him.

The Lieutenant’s office is perhaps the single most consistent element within the police station. As far back as my memory can go, it had a soft coating of graininess, a floor that was cluttered with strewn papers, an untouched bookshelf that was covered in dust, and a desk, which was complete with a lamp that provided the only light in the room.

As my feet pattered against his carpet, the rain pattered against his window-pane with me. Despite his office’s sloppy textures, there was something uniform about it. It was one of those few places that I could go to, and be secure in the fact that nothing was being hidden from me.
Lieutenant Jackson was an insufferable slob— but he was always straightforward about it.
“What are you still doing here, Sergeant?” he asked.
Jackson had already slipped behind his desk. He glowered over me, leaning into his desk with his hands spread out to give him support
I went to speak, but felt my tongue go numb. My vocabulary had slipped from in between my teeth like water might slip through cupped hands.
“I wanted to tell you that I don’t think Crusoe could’ve committed the crime. I was studying the kitchen— and what I found didn’t support the claims.”
Jackson’s face softened— at least, in comparison to his usual gaunt look.
I began relaying everything that I’d studied of the crime-scene to him, and how it couldn’t have been caused by a flamethrower. For once, Jackson appeared legitimately impressed.

“It was after I studied these warped areas that I realized an older, thickly built man, like Detective Crusoe, couldn’t have made such a leap. It could’ve only been done by somebody who was skilled at doing hurdles and light on their feet.”
Jackson rested his chin on his fist, and grinned.

“I’ll admit— your skills are still sharp. For a man who has been out of practice for nearly a year, you haven’t even begun to rust… If I didn’t know any better, I would almost think that you hadn’t missed a single day since you decided to stop doing detective work.”
Jackson turn around in his chair, to face away from me.
“Keep it up Kyler. I can’t wait to see what other secrets you know.”
I nodded, but I still caught the underhanded undermining. There was an amount of toxicity behind his words.
There’s no doubt— Jackson still thinks that I’m still working with Detective Crusoe. If not, he thinks that I’m Detective Crusoe.

I’m disgusted by the very notion of being a suspect in Jackson’s mind. Yet, I can’t deny that I also feel flattered. Detective Crusoe has the best mind I’ve ever encountered when it comes to abductive reasoning.

“I know that it might be easy to think that Detective Crusoe is still at large. However, couldn’t it be possible that the man has merely decided to hang up the magnifying glass and trench coat? Like you said to me earlier today— poverty has hit everybody hard. Maybe Crusoe finally decided to stop playing his high-stakes version of dress-up, and began putting his focus onto other endeavors.”

“Kyler,” Jackson said, filtering through papers on his desk, “you and I know that Detective Crusoe is still out there. Whether he’s still performing acts of vigilantism is beside the point… He’s been associated with numerous murders and robberies, among other things. He supports acting outside the law, despite trying to enforce the law.

“Even if this new criminal isn’t him, and even if Detective Crusoe is being framed, the reason that somebody would even be able to frame Detective Crusoe is because of Crusoe’s history. No matter what, this current problem rests on his shoulders.”
Jackson furrowed his brow to look up at me, and let out a sigh.

“I know that he was once a man that you were a great friend with— but you need to let that memory go. It’s not the twenties anymore, when you had nothing to lose and the city had a lot less grit and cracks. Time is moving on, and you’re not moving with it. This Crusoe figure is nothing but a hypocrite. The world would be better off if he just turned himself in…”
I wanted to fight Jackson. Yet, his words still resonated with me
Crusoe had done a lot to hurt me, over the years. He’d blighted my name.
He’d stunted my career.
Although, there was something that the Lieutenant said that I couldn’t get past… I still haven’t gotten past it.
This current problem rests on his shoulders…
I wasn’t so sure about that.
While it’s tempting to blame something like this solely on Crusoe, I think it stretches further than that. This isn’t just Crusoe’s problem. This is everybody’s problem.

Though, if it’s everybody’s problem, is Crusoe truly to accountable for everything that he’s done? This is where my thoughts always trip on themselves. It’s the questions like these that make me want to give up entirely.
“Are we going to search for our lead— Dr. Martin Smith?” I asked Jackson.
He gave as gruff of a snort as his pencil-wide frame could muster.
“What else do you think that I’ve been doing all this time?”
He turned up the book that he’d been filing through—the white pages.

“I’ve looked through all of the names in this area that go under Smith, Martin,” he said. “But, none of them seem to be located anywhere near Prestel Manor. Moreover, none of them have any connections to a vet, like Miss Prestel had told us. Whoever this, ‘Martin Smith’ really is, he certainly knows how to make his business relatively hard to find…”
“Did Miss Prestel ever give you a description for this man?”

“Even if she did, we both know that it would’ve been tainted and exaggerated by her nonsensical fantasies… The only way we’ll be able to pinpoint this person is by tracking other crimes in the area that are like this one…”
“If he has any sense, he’ll quit while he’s ahead.”
Jackson looked me square in the eyes.
“If this man had any sort of sense, he wouldn’t have tried robbing an old lady in the first place.”

I smiled. He smiled back. The smug slyness was washed from his face, and I saw the man that I’d looked up to, over a decade ago. Despite some of the recent strains in our professional relationship, his words were strong enough to make me forget about all of them. I was reminded of the times when he and I had first worked together. Our work was defined by nothing less than thrill.
Things were far simpler then— blacks and whites didn’t bother masquerading as one other. Perhaps it’s just me, but it seems that time has made the world become darker.
Diary Entry #4
Date: July 19th, 1935
I met a beggar of the street today. Couldn’t give him anything, so he tried picking my pocket.
Fun.
I always wondered why people dare pull stupid things like that. Gotta think that one of them would’ve figured out not to mess with me by now.

I was sentimental again today, too, and don’t know why. I called up all my old friends. At least, I tried to. Nobody picked up the phone. However, I guess I shouldn’t have expected that much. There’s only five of them.

I hate Crusoe. I don’t think that this crime was his, but he definitely did his best to make me think that. He’s the most confusing person that I’ve ever met, really. One day, he was there… The next, he was gone. He’s never really been gone, though. He just tried to make me think that.
I hate him.

So far, none of the things that I collected from the crime scene have gone anywhere. The acid remnants were unrecognizable, and had already mostly been cleaned up. My physical approximation of the subject hasn’t gone anywhere either. And, as for Lieutenant Jackson? His focus has meandered elsewhere. This case isn’t going anywhere, and he knows it. He’s essentially given the entire investigation down to me.
The problem is that I don’t know enough. I wasn’t there on the night of the crime, so I have no idea if I have the right lead right now. I’m essentially just looking for a needle in a haystack.
I just hope that the Lieutenant ends up appreciating everything that I’ve done. Because, right now, I’m not sure if I’m going to be able to give him anything.
Diary Entry #5
Date: August 5th, 1935

It’s been weeks following my introduction to the Prestel case. Just found myself driving around Lincoln Park, for the eighteenth time. My eyes have begun scanning every miniscule detail that passes by. Hardly anything that escapes my sight anymore.

Read every aspect of this case, inside and out. Searched for the potential answers to questions at each junction. There isn’t an hour of the day when my mind doesn’t stop to dwell on the case. Always trying to find a solution that’s alluded me. The only way I could be doing more is by being in multiple places at once.

Despite being restless about all this, I’ve found that I’m only more energetic than before. The more that I work, the more I feel like I’m coming to the end. It gives me a sort of joy that comes with solving a puzzle. This all might be very exhausting, but I’m now reminded why I like a good detective case so much. I’ve even forgotten why I’ve come to loathe the job, up to this point.
That is, until I was scathingly reminded at the end of today— a Monday that has been full of more “moans” than “mons”. It all occurred after having returned to my apartment.
I was turning the knob of my door when I heard a man’s voice call after me. That’s rarely ever a good sign. I swiftly went into my apartment, and slammed the door behind me.
As I settled into my living room, there was a knock on the door. At first, I tried to ignore it. But, it continued, until it had risen to pounding.
The voice in the hallway had been familiar to me. I went to my door.
While I feared that the person at the door could’ve been a crook, I had a bit of self confidence in my abilities to ward him off.
“I’m a police officer,” I told myself, reassuringly. “I don’t have to worry about being able to defend myself. I know what I’m doing.”
I wouldn’t have been able to defend myself at that moment, should I have required it. I had no idea what I was doing.
Taking loud strides, which would’ve easily alerted the trespasser of my presence, I brought my eye to the peephole. I was greeted by the sight of an old friend.
“Hey, James,” he said, with his muffled echoes littering my apartment with old memories, “It’s me—Eddy. You know— Eddy Mulligan.”

Naturally, I opened the door. Eddy had been a good friend of mine throughout the duration of my high school years. He’d been one of those friends who livened you up when you felt exhausted. He was the sort of friend who bridged the gap between innocence and the rebellious trail to adulthood.

I would often skip classes with him, and explore the deep Chicago streets without a care in the world. The slippery wetness of the pavement threatened me, but I didn’t hear it. The buildings cracking concrete threatened to fall onto me, but I didn’t see it.

Like it is for most childhood friends, I can’t remember exactly what made us become friends. I can’t remember how we first met. I can’t remember what caused us to drift apart, either. We only see each other a few times a year now.
I suppose that our relationship deteriorated as our lives began to separate.
Perhaps that’s why I opened the door— a gesture of gratitude toward good memories.
Once he’d stepped inside I realized what a mistake I’d made. In retrospect, nostalgia never has offered me anything good.

I was greeted by a stranger who had taken over the body of Eddy. His hair was matted. His beard was even worse. He was dressed in tattered clothes that looked like they’d been pulled out of a garbage dump.

In fact, I think they were. He stank of trash. He clearly hadn’t showered in weeks, if not, months. At this point, I saw him no different than any of the other desperate hobos who I found on the street, vying for a job or a scrap of food.
I should’ve never let him in here, I thought anxiously.
My eyes widened. I watched him filthy my carpet with his crusty boots, and walk over to my fridge.
“So… What brought you over to this side of the neighborhood,” I asked him.
I walked over to my entrance, to relock the door of my apartment. Eddy hadn’t given the thought to try shutting it, and I could already hear my neighbor’s coarse yells and crashing glass.
“It’s been months since we last spoke,” I said.
“‘I was in the neighborhood’, as they say,” he explained, shoving a bit of my food into his mouth.
“Funny coincidence. I just phones you the other night, but you never answered.”
He didn’t seem to listen, and started shoving more of my food in his pockets.
“I have to say,” he continued, talking as he chewed, “I haven’t really realized until now, but you have a nice setup over here. Be proud of it. I’m practically living in the dump.”

He laughed. Although, he hadn’t fooled me. Even after years of infrequent meetups, I could detect jealousy and sadness in Eddy’s eyes from a mile away. If he’d been telling a joke, it had been the most somber joke I’d ever seen him tell.
“Yeah…” I said, not taking my eyes off him. I needed to make sure that he didn’t steal anything. “To be honest, I could’ve seen myself in a lot better of a place, ten years ago.”
He nodded, and looked around.
“I could’ve seen you in worse places, considering the way that we ran around this city when we were younger…” he said.
We both shared a laugh. Though, it still didn’t feel right. There was a hollowness to it, when compared to laughs that we’d shared in the past.
At least it was a real laugh this time.
“Yeah… We were wild back then. I’m glad that neither of us had a car. We would’ve crashed holes into just about every building that we drove by.”
He nodded, and grinned.
“You don’t have any time for that nonsense now though, do you?” he asked. “All busy and serious police work, eh?”
I looked at him quizzically.
“Is something wrong, Eddy?”
Eddy put down his food, and walked up to me. He was several inches shorter than me, but with the way he stood himself up, I was compelled to think otherwise.

“It’s not your absence that has been getting to me… It’s time that I got straight to the point,” he said, doing what I think was an awful job at getting straight to the point. “You see… Well it’s… Have you ever been put in a situation where you know something that none of your friends know, and they need to know it— but if you tell them what you know, then you risk losing something? Have you ever been in a situation like that?”
I told him that I hadn’t particularly experienced anything quite like that. I told him a lie.
“I need to tell you something, James… But you can’t tell anybody else that you got this from me.”
“I can keep a secret Eddy. If I couldn’t, then I would’ve sent you to prison a dozen times over.”
I smirked, and waited for him to laugh, but all I got was a slightly frustrated huff.
“I need you to give up the Crusoe case,” he told me.
My jaw dropped.
“How do you know that I’m working on the—.”
“It doesn’t matter,” he said. “All that matters is that you drop it. Stop working on it. Get your whole police station to dump it as fast as they can. And, if they don’t, quit your job.”
“What are you talking about? You can’t just barge in here and tell me all this, without any explanation!”
He gave a smirk.

“You have a nice place James. I’d hate to see you start living in the streets, with the rest of us bums. But, I don’t think it’s worth what’s coming for you. You’re in way over your head with this Crusoe guy— you might remember him as some nice guy who could fix all of your problems. Nowadays, he’ll definitely fix you up with something— but it’s going to be something that you regret.”

He walked over to my door, and began unlocking it. I was dumbfounded, but he didn’t even bother to make eye-contact with me. Screams and shouts flooded back into my ears, and my apartment’s dim lights began to leak out into the arms of the unsleeping city night.

“If unemployment is good enough for two-fifths of the population,” he said, taking one last bite in a roll of mine, before tossing it away, “Then it should be good enough for you. Thanks for the meal.”
As he shut the door, I watched his eyes turn to my windowsill. He stopped chewing.
I watched his pupils dilate.
“No…” I heard him say, in a muffled whisper. “Not here… Not now…”
I turned to the window, but all I saw was the shadow of the American flag, billowing atop rippling winds.
“What are you talking about?” I began to ask him. That is— I began to ask the only sliver left of him, disappearing behind the crack of my door.
“Goodbye,” a tendril of a voice said to me.

I can’t quite tell for sure if it had been Eddy’s voice. As I went to lock my door back up, I heard a coarse howl, followed by a crack of thunder. My lights flickered, and I watched my window flash in the swipe of God’s blade. The howl had caused a rift in the sky itself.
I don’t know how I knew it… But, somehow I knew that, had the voice who’d said goodbye been Eddy’s, it was the last time I’d ever hear it.
Every hair of mine stood on end.
I ran to the telephone, and called my Police Department to alert them of the situation.
“A police officer calling the police,” I said with a chuckle, as I nervously looked out the peephole of my door. “Never thought the day would come…”

To relieve myself while awaiting their arrival, I settled into my chair and turned on the radio. I was hundreds of miles away from the nation’s capital, but I could still hear the steady voice of F.D.R ringing through my ears. It was full of static, and I had no doubt that it was been recorded a couple of years prior. Though, as the confident and resolute words of the leader of the free-world sifted into my ears, I couldn’t help but feel a sense of comfort.
“There’s nothing to fear but fear itself.”
I mouthed those words, letting my breath reutter them. I almost felt as if I were casting some sort of spell onto myself— a way to assure myself that, no matter what, nothing would go wrong.

Then, I looked up to the American flag that had been hanging outside my window. Except, when I looked, there was no American flag. There was nothing at all. With a jolt of shock, I realized that the American flag couldn’t be seen from my window.
What had that billowing thing been?
I felt my body begin to quake, and the screams of Eddy echoed back into my ears.
“There’s nothing to fear but fear itself,” I said again.
If I’d hoped for those words to have driven the screams away, it didn’t work.

“You better have been right,” I said, looking at the radio. Despite Roosevelt’s words, I couldn’t help but speak in the same terrified whisper that I’d last heard Eddy speak in. Fear had succeeded to consume me. It was at this specific moment that I was reminded of the horrors of my career.
I now know what Eddy meant when he said that I should abandon it.

The Prestel case had been put aside to focus on the disappearance of Eddy Mulligan. Police cars arrived at my house fifteen minutes after I’d heard his shrill scream. In time since, I’ve wondered what might’ve become of me had they been fifteen minutes later, but I’ve preferred to avoid such thoughts— they’ve left me with continuous nightmares.

After arriving, my colleagues asked me the routine questions of where and when I’d last seen him, why he was here, and If I could give them any details that might prove to be of use. I did my best, but what I had to give wasn’t nearly as keen or insightful as I hoped it would’ve been. I came to the humiliating realization that useful words from a witness of a crime were just as valuable and hard to obtain— if not, more so— than a good police officer. There was an entire week where I and the rest of the force were investing more than five hours a day on this missing person’s case. I worked harder than any of them, since I was the one who’d watched it all take place— though, I knew that my work and research was hopeless.

I could still hear the scream ringing in my ears, days after Eddy had vanished. If he was kidnapped, there was no chance for the police to find him. If he was murdered, then the killer had done a tidy job of cleaning up after themselves. Perhaps too tidy.

I wasn’t one to believe in the supernatural— but, with everything I’d witnessed, I’d begun to consider it as a possible explanation far more than an officer as myself should have. Whenever I was honest with myself, this case had resulted in me being the most stumped that I’d ever been before.

All evidence seemed to point to this having been a kidnapping. Though, then why had Eddy screamed in such a way that his voice was unrecognizable? Had he been the one who screamed? If he’d been kidnapped, then why? Even if he hadn’t been murdered outside my apartment building, did he survive after he’d been kidnapped? Was he still waiting for somebody to come and rescue him?
My mind was like a spinning top, going in far more circles than one might think physically possible. I thought it to be unrelenting— however, this was a lie. Every top has its time of falling.

It seemed to me that, after Teddy’s disappearance, the sky itself cried. Its tears spilled onto the gravel, making the streets runny from its muddy mascara. The buildings and streets became blacker with the rain’s grime, looking as if it had dressed in the coating to morn. Inside, I felt the same as them. I caught myself beginning to wear darker attire— and when I forced myself not to, the rain made sure to darken my clothes anyway.
If Eddy hadn’t died, myself and the world around me made sure to treat the situation as if he had.
I came to work on a Wednesday, over a week after Eddy’s absence. Life felt as if it was barreling down on me, and I’d been trying with all of my abilities to barrel down on it.

Exhaustion filled my lungs, knives were in my chest, and my legs felt weak and numb. The disparity of everything had begun to take hold of me, and choke all of my energy from my throat. There was rarely an hour of the day where I didn’t feel my heart begin to flutter in terror. All that I could think about were all of the strange happenings that were going on around me, and how they seemed to be swirling inward, like sharks in an ocean. Eddy had used his last words with me to make me aware that the search for Crusoe was one that would leave me and my department in shambles.

I’m not sure why, but I hadn’t told anybody about the words Eddy spoke about. Sometimes I think that I should’ve— I could’ve decided to indirectly cause the future murders of several people in the decided to keep quiet.

It was on that Wednesday morning that the thought of having potentially cost several lives hit me like a truck. I’d come to the police department early that morning— at only three A.M. However, when I pulled into the parking lot, I found something that made my mouth go dry and my stomach churn in a sickening slush.

There was a man strapped to a lamppost— tied to it by a crude rope. I ran up to the man, and found him to be in healthy condition, save from a few bruises that were on his arms. Although, when I asked him what had happened, his jaw went stiff. I looked down at his arm, which had suddenly locked to the side of his body. That’s when I saw a note taped to it— not just any note either. It was a note that was distinctly written in the hand of Crusoe. There was no mistaking its skinny sprawl that seemed to smear across the page. Just the look of it beat me on the back of my head, and made me feel as if I’d taken just as many bruises as the man tied to the lamppost.
On it dribbled the ink of these words:
I figured that you’d be here early, Sergeant Kyler… You always are when you’re amidst a case.

As a token of my respect, here’s a gift for your hard work. I captured your man— Dr. Martin Smith. Or, should I say, “Martin Smiths”? He’s one of many, old comrade. These crime sprees and mysterious disappearances aren’t a work of mine, and they’re not— at least not entirely— a work of the pervasive poverty either. These crimes have been committed by a league of schemers.

I’m afraid that I neglected to provide you with any proof of this man being guilty, save my word that he gave his word. However, I was able to get him to squeal— via my methods of interrogation. And, after talking to me, I’m sure that he’ll be compelled to squeal for you as well. To be concise, I’ve given him a few, “incentives” to tell you the truth…

Though, supposing that he breaks my contract, I’ll be there to make sure that I enforce my conditions upon him. All you have to do to alert me is place a note on this lamppost— just like old times— and give me the date and time that you wish to meet me at— I’ll make sure to be in this parking lot accordingly. Like yourself, I won’t rest until all of these criminals are eradicated.

No matter what anybody says I’m not the outlaw that I’m being framed to be. Currently, I’m amidst a trail of clues that can only lead me to my vindication. This convict is a necessary piece, and I’ll require your help to make him run accordingly.
In the meantime, always be wary. Always be watching your back. Always be on my side.
Sincerely,
Detective Crusoe
P.S I have reason to believe that Eddy Mulligan is alive and well. Keep hope tight to your chest.

I stumbled in shock. A part of me must’ve misread the last sentence, because instead of holding hope tight to my chest, I merely felt my chest tighten. My heart began beating again, but the beat left me with more pain than I’ve ever felt before. It was as if dozens of needles had been shoved into my chest. The world around me began to spin, and I came to the realization of how fragile and exposed that I was— even at my own office, where I worked every day, Detective Crusoe was watching. He was returning to haunt me over the alliance that we’d made in the past.
For a moment, I still wanted to think that this was the fake Crusoe.
Somebody could’ve easily forged his handwriting and signature, I thought. And, Chicago is a big city… Maybe there just so happens to be a lot of people who bear similar handwriting.

It was but a lie that I’d constructed to comfort myself. All the proof was there— Crusoe had even gone so far as to place the note on a lamppost, just as he’d placed notes back when I and him were still allies, bent on freeing Chicago streets of all crime.
The only thing that I want the Chicago streets rid of now is Crusoe… I thought. I need to make sure that I act on to this desire.

Though, contrary to my initial belief, terror caused by Crusoe’s return wasn’t what made my chest pound. It wasn’t even the knowledge that Eddy Mulligan might still be alive, or that the criminal responsible for Miss Prestel’s robbery might’ve been captured.

It was the very fact that I held a thrill in the event of his reappearance that haunted me. I shouldn’t have felt gladdened by the fact that he was back— and yet, I did. I couldn’t quite defend why, or even how. Although, when looking upon the note, I was returned to a world that hadn’t crashed and burned into a pile of rubble. I was returned to a world that only had hope for improvement— a world where, “the American dream” was still alive and well.
Back then, a single man deciding to set out and make a difference, however outlandish his attempt to do so might seem, was a positive thing.

Despite all of these feelings of joy and nostalgia, I still knew that I was amongst a trash heap. Earth itself was moaning at the sloping state of everything. Its surface was filling with cracks and dust— and I was supposed to be among the people who were trying to fill in those cracks. With each hastening toward the memory of Crusoe, and each swell of the chest at the thought of his name, I was allowing myself into a place that I should’ve long since abandoned. It was a place that was the closest thing a person could have to an “illegal thought”.
I began untying the battered man from his restraining ropes, placing a pair of cuffs on his arms, behind his back, in their place.

He certainly wasn’t the sort of person who was nice to look at— he had a bit of a gnarled expression, a reddened rash checkered across his cheeks and forehead, and an overall filthy complexion. While there are some star-studded faces who walk the streets of California, making their way to movie-screens by their perfectly symmetrical features, it would’ve been borderline cruel to suggest that this man could do the same. Nearly everything about him was stretched in one wrong way or another. The only thing in his favor was that he looked somewhat young— around his early to mid-twenties. He also held a formidable build, with rippling muscles, runner’s legs, and cauliflower ears that could’ve only been achieved from several survived fights.
“I didn’t do anything!” he said, with an indignant shout. “I’m a good citizen! I haven’t done anything wrong! You can’t just arrest me!”

It might’ve just been exhaustion and a burst of anger that was shouting for him, and I should’ve been far more patient and smoother than I actually was— but, that doesn’t change the script that came out of my mouth.

“You say that you haven’t committed a crime,” I said, “But you can already tack resisting arrest onto the list. As for you not having done anything wrong, I have reason to suspect that you’re in league with the criminal vigilante, ‘Detective Crusoe’. To say that I can’t arrest you is the same as saying that a hound can’t chase after a squirrel— perhaps they shouldn’t, but once they’re set off, there’s no pulling them back.”

He writhed and struggled, and I found myself having to writhe and struggle with him— fighting wasn’t nearly as easy as it’d been when I’d began my career. I started listing off his rights, but he didn’t want to hear it. His forehead knocked me square in the nose, and he started trying to run off. I clung tightly to his cuffs, but, with the stream of blood coming from my nostrils, my grip began to slip as it would on something coated in grease.
“Stop,” I shouted to him, with my breath heaving louder than a vacuum. “You don’t realize what you’re doing.”

If my words had made any sort of difference, I certainly wasn’t able to detect it. Within ten seconds of my speaking, I practically found myself being dragged across the pavement. Any bit of myself that was still invested in the chase had been reduced to a mere sliver and was merely running off the egotistic side of myself that still believed I could overtake this man.

However, I can’t say that I don’t appreciate that stubborn, prideful sliver for the arrangement that it left me with. A fluke occurred where the man slipped on a puddle of misty rain and grime. Within moments, he was reduced to a crumpled heap that looked sorrier than I had when I’d been dragged.
I seized the opportunity and pulled him along by the collar. In my eyes, it was both an act of poetic justice and a way of showing just how far the tides had shifted.
There was something inside of me that wanted to say, “I don’t want to do this, son— but I have to…” However, I felt as if I couldn’t speak at all.
I should’ve been put into a better mood by this miniature triumph— there should’ve been some sense of pleasure that went off in my head. Instead, I felt troubled.
It shouldn’t have been that hard, I thought. I shouldn’t have beaten him by a trick of luck.

There was another layer to it that I was reluctant to recognize. In taking the convict, I’d in turn taken a bit of Crusoe’s advice. I’d let him manipulate me into working with him again— albeit, only indirectly.

In retrospect, that always had been an irritating aspect of Crusoe. He was amazing at pulling people around like marionettes, making them move to his will. The whole reason that we’d joined in the first place had been caused by a similar act of manipulating will, and strategizing ways to seat himself into a place of influence.

I felt the urge to back away when I saw Lieutenant Jackson’s nostrils flare at me. All of my muscles had lost their firmness, and gone weak. Any confidence that I’d had when arresting the man tied to the lamppost was gone.
“What made you think that arresting this man was ok?” Jackson said, yelling so loud that I wished I could be back in my bed, struggling to sleep.
“He was tied to our lamppost, bearing a sign of Detective Crusoe. What else was I supposed to do?”

“’What else was I supposed to do?’” Jackson repeated, with a scoff. “If I were to hear those words coming out of a newbie’s mouth, I’d whip them into their place… But out of the mouth of you? You’ve had years of experience, Kyler. This man was clearly either mugged by some punk, or by the actual Crusoe. You know exactly what you’re supposed to do in these sort of situations.”
Jackson dipped his head into his desk.

“We’re going to be the laughing stock of the entire Chicago police force…” he said, with a sigh. The creases on his forehead suddenly became more prominent than I’d ever remembered them being. It almost looked as if age had decided to build a roadway there. His position as head of the police station hadn’t been good to him. I suddenly lost a bit of my fear and jealousy, and felt a pity for him.

“I’m sorry, Jackson… But, didn’t you read the note? It was definitely by Detective Crusoe’s pen. And, if we interrogate his victim, we might actually be able to find out the answer to our case. My decision to arrest the victim might’ve been rash and unwarranted… But, I had the right purpose at heart.”

“Are you really sorry?” he asked me. “I know you well, Kyler— unlike a good portion of the police, you’re a good person. You came into the force with the intention of making the world a better place. However, the world is a lot more complicated than simple intention. I would’ve expected that you’d get passed your faith in Crusoe by now.

“Supposing that Crusoe has the best intentions at heart, you forget what he did to his victim— he pulled out all of his information by force. No good abductive mind does that, Kyler. No self-respecting cop does that either. I refuse to interrogate his victim. I’m sure that anything that comes out of their mouth won’t even be their words.”
“But, Crusoe has never failed in the—.”
I stopped myself before I finished the sentence.
“You’re not just going to abandon a good lead, are you?” I asked him. “We can’t just drop the charges without trying to get his side of the story. Besides— this man resisted arrest!”

“We can’t just drop the charges without looking like fools either. But we’re going to. I’m sure that somebody on this force is going to break my ruling, and ask this man a few questions— if the news is slow and the press gets their hands on this incident, then all sorts of stories will be going to the media. But like I said before— after reading Crusoe’s note, all I can say is that nothing the victim says can be taken as fact. And he’s not a ‘good lead’, Kyler. He’s a man, with his own family, his own life, and his own story. I prefer not to look at innocent people as if they’re just tools that we can manipulate to our digression.
“Did he resist arrest? Yes. But, considering the circumstances, you’re lucky that I’m not going to pin the entire incident on you.”
“What do you mean by that?”
“I’m taking full responsibility for everything that happened, Kyler.”
Suddenly, Jackson’s scrawny build had gained a vigorous regal spirit to it. I could hardly believe that this was the same man that I consistently silently ridiculed.
I might have my reservations against Kyler, I thought, but he’s a great man when it comes to being loyal to his own crew.
I thanked him earnestly, and then stood up to leave his office. However, his voice found a way to pull me back down into my seat.
