“While I’m against looking at innocent people as tools, I have quite a different view towards the criminal element,” he said, with his smug look returning to his face. “After this incident, I’ve realized just how much we need to put this Crusoe figure down. We can’t let him keep torturing the people of my city like this. But, he’s too fluid and graceful to trip up through any normal means— he has too many things plotted out and accounted for.”
“What are you getting at?” I asked him, wearily.

I already knew what he was getting at, and I grew more terrified every moment he drew closer to revealing it. Despite his reveal’s inevitability, its buildup remained a terrifying one for me. It was like escalating up an abandoned carnival’s rickety rollercoaster as it readied for its initial drop.
“I read the note of Crusoe’s, and, like yourself, I’m convinced that it’s really from him. I’m going to need you to call in the favor that he offered you. I plan on preparing an ambush for him.”
“I thought that you just spent these past ten minutes telling me not to manipulate people. You’re having second thoughts?”

“I’m having my priorities put into place. We can’t let this man continue to go around and act like he’s one of us. If stopping him means stepping over the line a bit, then that’s what we’re going to have to do.”
I stood up.
“I have a history with this man. We can talk again next week.”
“Good,” said Jackson, leaning back in his chair to create a false sense of ease, “I should have plenty of time to prepare then.”
I looked at him, and held back a scoff. I’d known Jackson long enough to where he couldn’t hide from me. I could tell that he was just as unsure as I was.
Opening the door to his office, I began to walk out.
“One last thing,” Jackson said, “I don’t want you to be that inevitable traitor on the force, who interrogates the victim against my will.”
I assured him that I wouldn’t. However, there wasn’t a power in the world that could’ve made my assuring true.
“What do you know about Detective Crusoe?” I asked with a leer.
I was staring down into the eyes of the criminal slime, who I’d just learned was named Job. Not that I cared. The only Job that I gave any care to was my job— making sure that justice was put out.

Job grimaced at me through the rusted bars of his prison cell. He had the grimy stink of poverty, and the look of a man who had crawled out of a mud pit. While I deeply wanted to believe otherwise, I knew that he was innocent of his crimes. My fury towards him came from the embarrassment that I was currently dealing with, my wish to usurp Lieutenant Jackson’s authority, and a confirmation bias that would stop at nothing for my two former thoughts to be validated.

Though, when I looked into the eyes of Job, I couldn’t help but see his undivided fury toward me. All it took was a look at him, and the spite between us locked onto our chests, and throttled our minds into positions that they wouldn’t have held, should we have not come into opposing positions.
“I already told you the extent of my knowledge on the situation,” Job said. “I don’t have any more to say on the matter.”
“I know that you’re not telling me the truth. There’s more to this story than the guise that you’ve chosen to put on.”

My hands clenched tighter around his iron bars. I began clenching them with such a ferocity that a part of me feared that I might rip them from their place. Job merely laughed at my exercise of superiority. Despite him being the one in the cage, he looked at me as if I were an amusing animal from in a zoo.

“Yes,” he said, mockingly, “continue your charade of strength. Continue your dance of hypocrisy. Continue displaying threats to me that would get me put under high security, should I have given those threats to you… After all, you control the law— right? You can stand on the top, while we all stand at the bottom…”
“As offensive as that statement might be, I couldn’t care less… Your personal view of me is wrong, and irrelevant to this conversation. All I’m here for is Crusoe.”

“You’re here for more than Crusoe, and my view of you is very relevant to the conversation… ‘The good man does not grieve that other people do not recognize his merits. His only anxiety is lest he should fail to recognize theirs.’

“That was a quote from Confucius— at least, I think it was… I can’t tell for certain, since I found it on an old scrap of paper in a trashcan. But, I don’t think that makes the words any less true. If you were really out to help people, why bother coming here to prove yourself? Why bother making a rebuttal to my senseless provocation? If you cared about the people around you, then you’d be spending time lamenting the fact that I’m unjustly in a prison cell for doing nothing more than walking down a street at night.”

I felt a harsh beating rise up in my chest, and I had a strong desire to put Job in his place. Yet, I also felt that I was getting nowhere with him, so I turned from his prison cell and started walking off.

I didn’t realize it then, but the main reason that I walked off had nothing to do with feeling that I was getting nowhere at all. I’d dealt with plenty of people who weren’t willing to comply during interrogations in the past— my slight break from my job hadn’t sanded my skills so smooth that I could no longer pass this obstacle.

No. The reason that I’d turned to leave was over Job’s words. They had a venomous bite to them. It was the very fact that I didn’t want to hear any more of his words that I felt that his words no longer had any merit to them.

“How ironic,” Job said snidely, as I went to leave. “You come here all high and mighty, only to be torn down by a few simple criticisms… You act like your will is so firm and unwavering. You act like your morals are above all others, and that they’re immune to the pettiness that seems to plague most of humanity. But, I see that you’re exponentially worse than many of the people to admit to their inherent flaws, and don’t pretend that they’re above others.”

I turned back around shocked. As angered as I was at his statements, I could no longer turn a blind eye to them. They had a challenging element— they contested everything that I’d come to believe, and put all of my logic into scrutiny. I no longer felt as if I were on a mission to validate Crusoe, but that I was now on a mission to validate myself.

The language used also had the impact that is found in one’s epiphany. When I heard it, I couldn’t help but see the flaws within myself. It forced me to look upon my ignorance and arrogance, which I’d constantly strived to convince myself was false. Even in trying to tell myself that it wasn’t real, and that the belief in such a thing was unfounded, I was only proving the point made by Job.

Still, I was stubborn. I didn’t want to believe that Job— a man who looked like the very embodiment of poverty— could’ve knocked me down from my intellectual high ground. I didn’t want to believe that he could’ve painted me into such a corner, and knocked me into a place that I thought that I would’ve been able to knock him into.

“I don’t want to hear you say any more of this,” I said, trying my best to act as if the words hadn’t phased me. “You’re acting as if I’d placed you in some archaic form of torture, and decided to scorn you and look down upon you. Though, it’s quite the opposite. I care about you— I care about the whole of society. As a police officer, that’s all I care about. Yes— power and authority is undeniably a pleasant thing to have. But, I’m motivated by something far greater than that. As odd as it seems, that’s why I had you arrested and put in prison. I felt that you were threatening yourself and society, and so I had you placed in a position where the justice system must now assess whether my belief was true.

“Perhaps you can take the stance that this is all about Crusoe, and perhaps you can take the stance that this is all about some sort of self-righteous vengeance and vindication. However, if that was so, then my end goal would be one that’s circular. And, somebody like you to be making such a claim as that might be considered hypocritical— especially since you’re the one that’s now keeping something that can help society secret. You’re wasting your time in refusing to supply me with needed evidence. Your argument is circular.”

After finishing my monologue, I was actually quite proud of myself. Looking back on it now, all that I can see is how smug and foolish that I was. My only defense is that hindsight almost always proves to be wiser than that of a present thinker.

Though, I did learn one thing from my rambling— the very act of doing so is how you know you’ve lost the argument. When one begins slinging insults about in order to justify one’s position, they no longer should be able to justify their position.

“Your argument is circular,” Job said, creating a circle between the end of my statement and the beginning of his. “You punish me to spare others of being punished, despite the fact that I never showed any sign that I needed to be punished in the first place. The only thing that validates your position is your personal thoughts— and your personal thoughts are wrong.

“I don’t know much about Crusoe, other than the fact that he’s a bully that thinks himself to be some sort of hero… Which is kind of funny, since it seems that you didn’t know that. Then again, I shouldn’t be surprised— after all, if you can’t see the flaw of arrogance in yourself, you wouldn’t be able to see it in others.”

I was dumbfounded by his statements— and was even more dumbfounded when I opened my mouth to speak, and found that I couldn’t utter a word in rebuttal. He had completely proven me wrong on every front.

Yet, I didn’t believe a word he said. I couldn’t believe a word he said. The very thought of doing so offered Job the victory— and, while I liked to think of myself as the bigger person, I was unwilling to allow him the win.
So, I left. I should’ve pursued him further. I should’ve looked deeper, and studied everything about him. Though, he won— he’d beaten me by making me think that he’d beaten me.
I now look back on that decision, and wonder what would’ve happened if I’d just continued asking him questions, then and there…

I’m aware that the world is a festering and decomposing soup of waste. I’m aware that the sludge that surrounds me is nothing that I can control. Though, as I look out my window, and see the world in its imperfections and vileness, I suddenly realize that I’m looking out the window— I’m not helping anything. I contribute to the problem.

Is it just myself, or is society a think that’s prone to self-corruption. Perhaps this is an immature and unfounded belief, and perhaps I look at the world with a cynical pair of eyes. Though, when I look at what civilization has accomplished, I oftentimes only see conquest— conquest, and oppression. Things that were put into place with the intention of helping oftentimes become the source of such oppression and conquest.

I’m not a scientific man— I don’t deeply understand the laws of physics, or have a strong affinity for new discovery. Though, I can’t help but feel that, with each discovery we make— with each grand progression— we also place ourselves into a bit of digression. We come to realize how insignificant and pitiful our existence really is. We come to terms with the fact that we’re actually more of a problem than a help. And, with every attempt we make to create such unrealistic ideals as, “peace,” “hope,” and, “freedom,” we slowly start to gnaw away at their definitions.

One might be able to argue that I’m looking too deeply engrossed in the negatives, and that my views aren’t positioned onto the positives enough. Though, the tendency to focus on negativity is the very nature of humanity— isn’t it? So, if my own negativity is being focused upon humanity’s negativity, is my additional negativity compounding onto the problem? Or, does my negativity multiplying other negativity somehow make a positive?

This is a question that’s been riddling me for the past day. I stare out my gray window, covered in the dust that caked on after years of me staying in the same place— the same rut. In a way, this dust haunts me. I can only see from inside the layer of dust— the rut that I’ve let myself fall into. My vision is completely clouded, but it’s entirely my fault. I’ve allowed the dust to smother me. I try to see past it— I think that’s the only way that I can solve my problem. Yet, as I try to see past it, the dust keeps falling, growing more mountainous.

I could use my duster to try cleaning it— but that itself has been covered in dust, and become irrelevant as I neglected it. If I try cleaning the window, it would take work, and potential wasted time— time that I could be using to find an alternate solution. The duster might also only make the mess even worse. Though, if I don’t clean it, the problem remains, and it clouds my vision— it keeps me from easily finding another solution.
So, I sit, breathing in the dust, and thinking that this could somehow solve my problem. Yet, the more dust that I breathe in, the more that I become part of the dust.

Life isn’t as grand of a thing as many prop it up to be. As human beings, we like to think that we’re amongst the greatest objects in the universe. Though, as Einstein has proven, something as simple as light is far beyond anything any of us were prepared to understand. It dwarfs our insignificant culture— our insignificant planet— and makes us into a sort of joke.
I laugh at jokes, and find joy in them— but all jokes require a bit of misery to them, in order for them to retain an element of humor.

We aspire for greatness, and then settle for mortality. We stack our Jenga blocks up to the sky, only for them to come crashing down atop our heads. We build vast inventions, machines, laws, governments, and cities. Though, they’re all distracting from the fact that we know so little, in spite of thoughts to the contrary.

We’re limited in the confines of our fleshy bodies. We believe that we can achieve immortality, yet still retain our current form. Little do we realize that our form is one of limitations and falsities, and that we’re digging ourselves into a pit. Little do we realize that the immortal things— the rocks, the stars, and the planets— are things that have no conscious. We fear death, but we fail to recognize that most of the things we observe in nature are most definitely dead by every definition— and they have far less to fear than us.

I don’t know why any of this matters to me… I don’t know why I even bother delving into this well of odd reasoning… Maybe I’m just partially insane, maybe the world’s cynical outlook has finally gotten to me, or maybe I’ve begun to see something that I’ve tried hiding from myself all my life. Whatever it is, I no longer believe that my career is a source of good. I’ve begun to suspect that I’m no different from the element that I fight against.

The day prior to me feeling these emotions and running thoughts, Job was broken out of prison during the night watch. The guards of the prison were suspected to have been working with him, and have broken him out through cohesion. Legitimacy of these claims were both invalidated and speculated. There was no substantial proof that the guards were in on the act, despite it strongly being suggested by the surrounding events.

Though, the ambiguity of the crime wasn’t what had made me feel so lost, and dazed. It was quite the opposite. I knew that the guards had committed the crime, or had at least played a part in it— they had no legitimate defenses, and the likelihood of Job escaping under their watch was extremely unlikely. What I was truly dazed and confused about was the complete denial of everything the justice system stood for. I’d thought for the force to be a somewhat infallible wall, over which crime couldn’t go. Although, this latest event had put me in my place. I’d thought that I was called on some mission to validate Crusoe’s innocence— but the world around me was crumbling.

Deep down inside, the very thing I hated the most was that everybody was right. I’d only just begun unraveling the mystery— the secret behind what might’ve been going on with the Prestel case and the kidnapping might’ve been right under my nose— and I’d let it slip by.
Jackson had warned me about this. Even Job, who’d clearly taken a firm stance against me, warned me that I was in over my head— that I was too proud for my own good.
I then knew that they were right, and the only question I had left is why I’d been so willing to accept my personal ignorance and arrogance, completely pushing aside any logic or reason.

Though, I secretly knew the answer to that, too. I just hadn’t been willing to admit it. I was proud, and I’d thought my personal ethics and morals to be above everybody else’s. To a degree, Job had been right— I had only taken my career as a police officer because it suited my ego best. In a way, it gave me a sense of power and superiority over others. I’d use it to display my authority.
At least, that’s what I’d thought until Job put me in my place.

I’d sent a letter directly to Miss Prestel the day that I’d spoken to Job— two days before Job had broken out of jail. I’d explained to her the current situation, and how progress had been stalled by the fact that we were busy with other cases, which we thought to be of greater concern.

She responded back with a letter that I found to be very insightful. She criticized me of having a double-sided code of ethics, and that I had an eschewed meaning of what it meant to be a cop— there was a point where she went so far to claim that, if I’d cared about her case, the police force would’ve already solved it.

As senile as I knew she was, and as wrong as I thought her to be, I couldn’t deny her of these words being truth. I believed them myself. I was an incompetent cop. It had been a month of me working on her case, amongst others— and I’d found that none of my research had brought me anywhere. In fact, a lot of it had stunted me, and pushed me further back from the truth.

There are some people who claim that the result of careful study and meticulous research is the truth— though, I combat that logic and say otherwise. If the laws of careful study applied to everything, then there probably wouldn’t be much crime remaining. In spite of police officers upholding their ability to properly assess scenarios, and deduce things, I’ve found that we know far less than we claim to. There have been many cases where I believed that I was getting somewhere, and that my constant studying was bringing me to a place of enlightenment— and yet, it had constantly and almost exclusively had all been a farce. More of my cases had ended in me coming up inconclusive than they had with me coming up with all of the answers.

One of the greatest questions in all of philosophy is who makes the watchmaker— who oversees the thing that must oversee? The answer to that always has been, and always is, that there isn’t one. Everybody in power is steering a ship without any steering, and directing everything through a sea of nothing— pretending that this sea of nothing was something.

Us police officers— us directors of authority— know just as much as the sea that surrounds us. We might pretend that we know that we’re doing, but we only pretend based on the faint glimmers of stars that we manage to grasp from out of this deep sea. We try to form a constellation. We try to paint a picture. Though, what nobody seems to realize is that constellations and pictures alike aren’t the great things of revelation that we often make them out to be. They’re merely randomized smears of imagination, spread across a canvas— a canvas that’s only called, “canvas” because that’s what we needed to call it when we first discovered it, in order to bend it to our wills and our desires.

There’s so much unknowing in what I do. There’s so much uncertainty and assumption that it’s no wonder that we need Judges to weed us out— it’s no wonder that many of us our corrupted by the confusion and much that encases us.
That encased me.

I wish that I had all of the answers— I wish that my head hadn’t been spinning and turning every which way, as if it were a carcass that was being wrestled about by a pack of wild wolves. I wish that everything could be solved so simply as the world makes it seem, with me asking the right questions, and with me getting the right answers. I wish that the morally right and the morally wrong had a clearer distinction than that of which I see in Crusoe and Job.

Yet, things can’t be so simple as these idle wishes. I know not why, but the will of things is that they can’t be changed unless an outside force is acted upon them. And, as somebody who isn’t on the outside but is very much trapped on the inside, how am I to change things?

There are thousands of instances of irony in life— the very word ironic is ironic, simply because I called it so. Though, the greatest irony is that I’m among the constellations of stars, looking out my window upon their canvas, staring into their expanse, clouded by Chicago’s cheap city lights, and smoggy air. A single star pokes out of these constellations, deciding to shine upon me, and to bust into my eye’s iris.

And, though, wish I may and wish I might, that star would never enact a single difference upon the earth. In spite of all of man’s superstitions, words, and claims to the contrary, the wish on the star would never make a difference. The star would fall from its peg in the sky before it would ever intercede in my personal and miniscule affairs.
Irony— a cop feeling as though he’s a criminal.

A day after my deep entrenchment in the philosophical ponderings of my purpose and usefulness in society, I came to realize that my purpose wasn’t one that could be answered so simply as by raising the question. That was because there was no known answer. I’d reasoned that, if there us, I wouldn’t have been looking for the answer in the first place. The whole world would’ve provided the answer for me.

So, I paced in circles around my apartment, considering hanging up my badge. I wasn’t quite sure why I thought of doing this— I wouldn’t have gained anything out of it, and neither would’ve the world around me. However, there was a slight relief in the thought of being able to toss everything away, and turn from things as if they’d never happened.

I’d come at a moral crossroads. Contact with Detective Crusoe was the only way that I’d be able to solve my problems— but, I couldn’t talk to Crusoe without compromising myself, and the instructions of Lieutenant Jackson. However, if I dared have Jackson know that I was willing to contact Crusoe— if I were to allow Jackson what he wanted— then I would compromise Crusoe’s will.

It had taken me a day to sift out this line of logic, but I knew that a kindergartener would’ve been able to surpass my line of reasoning within a day. The truth of the matter was, I was refraining from any sort of decision making, because I’d subsided into the realm of cowardice— I’d planted myself in a position where I had my loyalties conflicted, and I was going to have to pay for it.

“Why do you always do this to me?” I whispered under my breath as I pulled out a pen from my rickety old drawer, and tore out a piece of note paper. My hand was still shaky from my fit of indecision, and it showed on the paper. Though, once I’d wrote out the last line, I had a sense of weight let off my chest. I still didn’t know what I was going to do, but the very act of having written to Crusoe gave me, at the very least, and illusion of having gotten things figured out.
It read:
Dear Detective Crusoe,

I’ve become aware that strange activities are going on around me, and I no longer think that I’m capable of tackling the mystery through my own accord. The questions that revolve around me are as numerous as the stars in the sky— and are probably even more so. It’s simply not something that a single mind can take on by their own, and you’re the only person capable of giving me the mental boost that I need. As I’m sure we can both agree, you possess one of the greatest deductive minds known to the justice system— you’ve helped me out of so many mazes that I sometimes look at myself as the lab-rat, and you as the viewing scientist.

Perhaps I should’ve appealed to your advice sooner, and tried asking for your aid— and I know that you might hold a bit of bitterness towards me from my cutting of our past ties. But, you and I both know full well why I cut those ties, and why I have such hesitance towards the notion of retying them. While we once worked together fairly well in the past, you can’t possibly expect for me to be open to a continuation of our relationship after your immoral conduct— it’s simply ridiculous. And, you can’t hold my reluctance against me. If you happen to do so, then we will forever be on opposite sides of the law. We both uphold truth and justice, and I’m certain that I’ve given you your justice. If you act against my dubbed justice, then I’ll have no other choice but to put you in your place— just like you’ve done to countless others.

I want our meeting to be a cordial and kind one. I’m sure that both you and stand on equal ground when I state that we desire for this meeting to be similar to our past ones— where you humble me by showing me my ignorance, and where I rein you in, and keep you from going off the deep end of the law.

Now, before I end this, I just want to leave you with one question lingering in your mind— why is it that you decided to take the path that you did? If you weren’t ever guilty of your heinous act, like you’d once claimed, then why on earth did you ever disappear? And, if you disappeared, what compelled you to return?

I have nothing against you returning, save the fact that it was followed by a series of aodd crime sprees— in fact, I applaud it. Though, I can’t help but wonder what brought you back. Do you even know what brought you back?
But, if it was to help me— if it was to help the city around you— then you’ve done a great job at failing to do so in the greatest time of need.

I don’t wish to weigh you down with my tedious and depressing rantings. In fact, I hope that you’ve skipped my letter, and read to the end— my handwriting is so sloppy that it’s probably too hard to read this all the way through. Though, I just want you to remember— you’re supposed to be fighting on the side of the law. And, as long as that is so, I want you to act accordingly.

As professional and unemotional as our relationship has been, I do care about you— even if I’ve never seen your face, and even if I’ve never been given any reason to trust you, or see you as anything other than a masked criminal.

We might be on opposite sides of the law, but that doesn’t change my internal nature. While others might see you as some sort of deranged monster who deserves to be placed in some sort of cage, I see something different. I’ve come to see everybody as the deranged monster, including you and I. The only difference that you have amongst them is that you recognize the monster within yourself— and you’ve come to try and utilize it to do good.

Maybe I’m making baseless assumptions when I say that. However, out of all of humanity’s monstrosity’s and unspeakable acts, I believe that our greatest achievement is the compassion that we’re able to have amongst ourselves. It’s the ability to place our bodies into that of another that truly makes us into something admirable— something that just might make up for all of our errors.
Sincerely,
James

I reread this letter over and over again. I’d been the one who’d wrote it, and every word jotted onto the sloppy and thin sheet of paper had been dictated by the wells of my mind. Though, I couldn’t help but stumble through it, exploring each word as if it had been written by a stranger— as if it all had some foreign meaning to it that I hadn’t seen before.

This didn’t make sense, considering that, if anybody should’ve known it’s meaning, I should’ve. However, at the same time, my mind told me that it made perfect sense. The truth was, I didn’t know my intent was. I wanted to believe that I knew who’s side I was on when I wrote the words on my note to Crusoe. Nearly every ounce of my being wanted to be able to prove myself as a true friend to him. I’d put so much work into my words to him— I cringed at the thought of them being an illegitimate farce, crafted to ease my own mind.

Yet, that’s what they were. Reading the note over and over again, I could only perceive hollowness from within it. While I’d told myself that the note had been written for Crusoe’s benefit, it was, in a sense, more about me than anything else. There was no beauty or emotion behind it, outside of the comforting fiction that my min had built for me.

I left my house at noonday, when the fog had been reduced to a golden wisp. It acted as an unwanted cushion between my car and my sight of the road, but I didn’t care for very long. My mind wasn’t on the road, but where the road was taking me. In a way, I was the master of the streets. While I still hadn’t discovered a way to dictate the web of my mind and its intentions, I’d mastered the web of the ground. Every turn it took was simple and calculated— I would’ve been able to navigate it if I was sick as a dog.
I am sick as a dog, I thought as I rode down a hilly street, and felt my stomach lurch up through my throat, and my chest pang in a crushing pain.

If I was right in anything on that day, I’m certain that I was right in thinking that. I knew where I was going— but I didn’t know where I was going. I knew where my loyalties lied— but I didn’t know where they lied. I knew where my words told me I was— but I didn’t know where my words told me I was.

The only thing that I knew for certain was what I felt inside. The only thing a person can ever know for sure is the feelings that the world around them endows upon them. There’s never any telling if the world is real, or if any of the senses it gives are justified. There’s never any telling if the feelings that the experiences amongst the mess of experiences are true, or even if the interpretation of the experiences are correct— everything perceived is a sort of fiction. As people, we rely on the information provided by our minds and thoughts, hoping that these thoughts might help advise us in making sense of the world.

Even our own thoughts are unreliable, with them always changing and altering according to new knowledge, stimulus, and outside interaction. We like to think our brains to be infallible, but they’re clearly the most unreliable things in our existence— they’re the very reason that we’re such faulty beings.
Though, they’re also the only reason that we’re beings at all. We rely on our faulty evidence because that’s all we have to make judgements, and escape the prison that is our internal consciousness.

My feelings— the only thing in the world that I could truly rely upon to give me any guidance— were telling me that I didn’t know a thing, and that I was on the precipice of uncertainty and a dangerous decision. While my feelings might’ve been wrong and unjustified, and while they were worth nothing.

Once reaching my police department, I rode up to the lamppost. I felt a shudder down my spine as I pulled up to it— my memories of last time betrayed my resolve, and gave me uncomfortable images of Job having been tied to it. I once again began to question if my choice to side with Crusoe would be a right one— he’d committed too many atrocities in his day, acting against everything that I upheld and believed in. He was a man that I should’ve never considered working with, and was disgusted at the prospect of working with.

However, as I stepped out of my car, and placed the note on the rusting lamppost, I felt something entirely different. The straggling remains of morning’s long evaporated dew found its way up my nostrils, and I had better memories come to mind— memories of a time when I could hold a conversation with Crusoe, without fearing that he’d swoop down and attack me.
The words that I’d placed in the note came flowing back to me, and I remembered what a great man that Crusoe was.

Those memories had a feeling to them— a feeling that I couldn’t deny. As I walked back to the inside of my police department, within which my office resided, I contemplated and weighed the potentials of what I was going to do. Suddenly, everything became clear— clearer than it had felt in a while.
The pang in my chest had begun to subside.
Night’s cloak had been draped over the sky. For many people, the night is a place of quiet and solace. It’s a time when the lights go out, and slumber flows into the air. It’s not so in the city.

As I paced upon the pavement outside my police station, awaiting Crusoe’s arrival, I realized just how odd the night really was in the city. For many people, it might’ve appeared to be some mutated form of itself— a foreign creature, unbeknownst to most.

Whereas nights in a small town might be flooded with quiet, this night was clouded in the outbursts of clunky car engines and horns. There were also the occasional footsteps, and shouts that trickled into my ear.

This night also wasn’t limited by the natural laws of the night. Light darted everywhere, breaking through the bonds of the dark. It flowed from car headlights, dribbled down lampposts, and crept out from under thickly screened apartment windows. Some of the time, this light was so blinding that I found my vision becoming clouded with black spots.
The night needs to find a way to get in somehow, I thought.

There was a younger version of myself that had been overwhelmed by this overabundant stimulus. The sound of traffic horns might as well have been the wailing of a ghost. Though, I found that enough exposure to it had desensitized me, making me immune to its once terrifying effects. It was a strange thing. Similar to the city night itself, I couldn’t tell if my unnatural adjustment was one to appreciate or admonish. In a sense, the city had marked me, with its crude cement elements leaving its mark on me. Though, without the mark, I surely would’ve been swallowed whole by the city. I wouldn’t have been able to function.

I couldn’t quite tell what these thoughts were trying to get at. Perhaps it was just a distraction from the matter at hand. However, I can’t help but feel as if there were more to my thoughts than just that. While I’m inclined to believe that thoughts are but a randomized mechanization that only acts accordingly to outside interactions, I can’t help but feel that every thought it makes is trying to discover patterns— discover patterns and make clever connections.

I believe that my thoughts concerning my insensitivity to the city night also bled into another insensitivity that I was facing— I didn’t feel any kind of fear, or anticipation, or emotion of any kind concerning my meeting with Crusoe. My thrift-store watch, always half an hour off, ticked by— but I didn’t even bother to look at it.

In denial, I tried attributing this all to me being overwhelmed by emotion. Although, I knew this wasn’t true. The past few weeks’ events had frozen me, turning my insides into a sort of stone. Not that I could place all of the blame onto the past few weeks. My job was shriveling me up, turning my spirit into a raisin. In returning to my career, I’d only increased the rate of this shriveling.
“Boo.”
I jumped, and my heart leapt. Grabbing my chest, I felt a terrible ache. After catching my breath, and regathering my wits, I found Detective Crusoe standing next to the police station’s lamppost.

A glare passed between me and him. I’d become accustomed to glares— they were oftentimes an unavoidable part of interrogations— but, Crusoe’s glare was one that was unavoidable. It was irreconcilable. His eyes had a stony glint to them. They looked so much like flint that I was nearly convinced that I could’ve lit a match off of them— or, at the very least, get a spark.
To be frank, when I looked at him, I thought that I did see a spark come from off of his stark black pupils.

In my years of working with him, I’d tried to convince myself that Detective Crusoe was just a normal man, bound by the laws that every human being must learn to face. Though, just looking into his eyes was near unbearable— and looking at the rest of him was just about unearthly.

He was dressed in his usual brown trench coat and contrastingly black fedora. They both smelt of their familiar grimy oil— he’d fallen into a pit of crude oil during one of our cases together, and never managed to clean the smell out—but, I didn’t see it as just a smelly trench coat and fedora. Just like Merlin had his robes and wand, and Buck Rogers had his spacesuit and blaster, Crusoe had his odd getup. Irrational as it was, there was a type of majesty I saw in it.

Along with this, there was his stature and features. Rather than possessing an intimidating height, or gaunt features, he was actually quite stocky. He was only taller than me by a few inches. His chin was also rounded, and clean-shaven, being mostly indistinct from the rest of his face. There wasn’t much else past his chin that I could identify— his fedora cleverly covered most of his features.

In spite of all this, he was still one of the most intimidating things that I’d ever beheld. Even with my conditioning around him, no matter how many times I met him it was like I was meeting him for the first time, all over again.
“Twenty years of working with you, and you still haven’t stopped sneaking up on me…” I said, with an annoyance.
“Twenty years, and you haven’t stopped calling me for help…” Crusoe said in response, making sure to keep his voice gruff so as to mask its true nature.
I would’ve laughed, if it hadn’t been for the fact that his very presence begged an utmost seriousness.
“Only because you wouldn’t stop asking for me to call you…” I said, thinking that I had the upper hand in this debate. “Also
“Only because I knew that you’d always end back up under this lamppost talking to me again… Only because I knew that this city wasn’t getting anywhere with your twisted justice system.”
Detective Crusoe, in spite of all my misgivings toward him, had a way with words. He knew how to paint a persuasive picture, and make the most resolute of men rethink their ground.
“I didn’t call you here to be lectured by your twisted moral code…” I said, with annoyance.
“And, I didn’t come here to bicker,” he said. “You came here for a reason— you believe that this city is finally getting out of hand. I can help you with that.”
“What I believe isn’t yours to claim over me… I only came here because I thought you’d have an explanation for all of the odd crime sprees going on around us.”
“And I have an explanation… At least, a rough one,” Detective Crusoe said. “I’m sure that you’re familiar with Job— correct?”
I nodded. I couldn’t tell if he’d been able to see my nod through the darkness or not— if he had, I couldn’t see the response on his face.
“Job isn’t the only man that you’re after,” Crusoe said, with a confidence. “There is a league of men, all plotting and strategizing toward the same goal.”

He paused, as if waiting for my jaw to drop. My jaw didn’t. Everything he said was among the most mundane and inconsequential drivel that I’d heard in a while. I’d begun to have my regrets in having bothered to come to the lamppost at all.

“You already informed me of this in your letter to me,” I said, allowing my sarcastic disrespect to bleed into my voice. Crusoe clearly caught the idea, because I saw him begin to move uncomfortably, and loose a bit of his imposing posture.

Until now, I hadn’t seen this part of him. Whenever I’d spoken to him in the past, I didn’t think about the man who might’ve been underneath the clothes, and behind the illusion of Oz. In truth, I didn’t want to. Over all of the years that I’d worked with Crusoe, I could’ve torn the cloak and fedora off at any time. If I’d really been interested in doing my job, I would’ve been willing to cuff him to the lamppost that we’d constantly met up at.

“Ah yes… I forgot that I’d informed you on this already,” Crusoe said, backing into his tracks. “However, there’s much more to what’s going on than I previously revealed to you. I hadn’t been able to tell you everything, in fear of being found out and compromised.”
“And what is that?”

There was no answer— just Crusoe’s steely look, which attempted to scare me into submission. However, I no longer submitted to his attempts at making me fall into cowardice. I’d begun to see through his wizardry. He didn’t know anything.
He suddenly began to appear as he really was— an unknowledgeable hooligan who’d stuffed himself into a ridiculous outfit. He hardly looked different from a stuffed turkey.

“Here they are,” he finally said— and slips of paper, along with various keys, articles of clothing, fingerprints, and pictures flew from his hands. “And these are only the tip of what I’ve found. There’s so much more that surpasses it, you couldn’t even begin to imagine what my discoveries entail.”

This time, my jaw really did drop. I began lifting up all of the evidence. The letter contained the signature from a man by the name of, “Bob Murphy”, and several passages that asserted that some sort of kidnapping was to take place. The articles of clothing were lab-coats and trench-coats. There wasn’t much distinct about the pictures provided. One of them was extremely blurry, and contained the image of a woman walking down a hall. Another was a bit clearer, with it taking place in a dark alleyway. Although, in the background there was a man who was carrying some odd sort of trinket in hand— it almost appeared to be in the shape of a monkey. Apart from the pictures, the keys were probably the most out of place of all these objects— but I quickly assumed that Crusoe would provide explanation.

“I found the lab-coat in Job’s house,” Crusoe stated. “Job didn’t hold any profession that would’ve required him having a lab-coat— and it certainly isn’t anywhere near Halloween time… He also had keys in his house. They had fingerprints on them that perfectly matched Miss Prestel’s, and were able to open Miss Prestel’s door when I tested them… The only way that Job could’ve gotten these keys would’ve been by stealing them from Miss Prestel himself.”
I was dumbfounded. “But, Miss Prestel never said anything about misplacing her keys…”

“She’s an old lady, Kyler— I’m sure that the disappearance of her keys were misattributed to old age. Plus, I happened to use Job’s stolen keys to access Prestel Manor, and file through Miss Prestel’s bills— it just so happens that she recently had to pay a locksmith to make her new keys.”
I shook my head.
“Did you find fingerprints that matched Job’s on the keys?”

“No,” Detective Crusoe said, with a hesitance. “Job was extremely careful in making sure that nobody would be able to prove that he was the one that had stolen these keys. He must have worn gloves whenever handling them.”
A wave of doubt passed over me, but I ignored it.
“And, why haven’t you shown me this evidence until now?” I asked.
“I already told you— it was too easy for me to be compromised.”
For some reason, I didn’t entirely believe him. Maybe it was cynicism, or the fact that we hadn’t talked in so long— but, I just didn’t feel that anything Crusoe said was entirely trustworthy.

Then, I looked down at the trench-coats and hats. They didn’t have Crusoe’s distinct oily smell to them, but nearly everything else about them was a perfect copy of Crusoe’s. I was convinced that they’d even been made by the same tailor. Even the hat was the right color— black. This was something that had taken me weeks with Crusoe to discover. With these facts combined, I discernably knew that whoever had produced these, supposing they had been wearing them, knew Crusoe well, and was looking to frame him.

“Job must’ve had a busy day at the costume shop,” I said, yanking on the clothes to test their durability. They weren’t made of the cheap fabric that I’d hoped they might’ve been. Just by feeling them, I gained the sense that they were probably more durable to testing than Crusoe’s own clothes.
“I didn’t find these clothes at Job’s place.”

I nodded— I’d half-expected that he’d say this, since he had yet to provide me any explanation. However, this didn’t stop me from feeling a sense of shock in my gut when he revealed this to me. For some reason, I had a sort of belief ingrained inside of me, which made me believe that Crusoe was immune to having enemies that would watch his every move. The larger portion of me held the belief that all of Crusoe’s actions, outside of his interactions with me, were apart from the spying eye.
“Where’d you find them? Who would’ve gone to all the trouble of assembling these?”
I didn’t want to have to ask this question. However, I’d been doing a lot of things that I hadn’t wanted to do.
“Those are two very different questions…”
Crusoe offered this answer in a very mechanical and meticulous voice. It was as if he were measuring every word he spoke.
“I’d like the answer to the second question first, then.”

“What you’d like isn’t necessarily what you’ll get. What I’d like isn’t necessarily what I always get, either. If truth be told, I don’t have full truth to tell. I only have a full answer to your first question.”

I couldn’t discern if Detective Crusoe was trying to hide something from me, or if he had other motives that were beyond my sight. I looked around me, in a slight tremor. Something seeped into my bones, making them weak and flimsy. It was the thought of a spying sparrow, disguising as a problem only of morrow, that had sucked out my marrow.

“Then give me the answer to my first question,” I asked, in a haggard grunt. My impatience might’ve been unjustified, but I no longer cared for what was just or unjust. There was too much discomfort going on around me, and I no longer felt that I could afford the wasting of time.

“Eddy Mulligan had a lot more in his house than the police were able to turn up… I found these clothes hidden in between the walls, and the rafters. If they’re merely innocent, and Mulligan had no intention of masquerading as myself, then I’m unaware of why he went to the great lengths of sealing these clothes in wall cavities— it’s quite the sorry replacement for a closet.”

I’d been prepared for shock, but not this level of shock. None of this made any sense— Mulligan had been a good friend of mine, and we’d had no conversations until very recently. The very notion of him being a criminal, trying to frame Crusoe of committing criminal acts, seemed so out of character that I could no longer hear a word that Crusoe was saying.
“Crusoe… Were you there when I first started my investigation of Prestel Manor?”
For some reason, I couldn’t avoid asking the question. I needed to know if it had been Crusoe that had been spying on us, or Eddy.

“It might’ve been a tempting notion, and it was certainly something that would’ve given me a head start in this series of oddities. But, while I was aware of your proceedings, I didn’t take the time to interfere. The Prestel case seemed, until now, a somewhat trivial and irrelevant case. I’d been busy with other, more troubling matters at the time. Why do you ask?”

“There was somebody there,” I admitted. “A person had dressed up just like you, and perched on the roof of Prestel’s house. That is— they’d perched on the roof until Lieutenant Jackson caught sight of them.”

“That wasn’t me,” Crusoe said, with a certainty in his voice. I wasn’t sure why he had to reaffirm his position with such a severity— but, when he used the severity, it allowed my mental faculties no other option but to accept his words as fact. I knew Crusoe’s voice well enough to tell when he was lying or telling the truth. “Did you happen to catch sight of this pretender?”
Giving a sigh, I looked Crusoe square in his shadowed eyes.

“I didn’t… Crusoe, he was too fast. Only Jackson saw him. But, according to him, this person was a man— and they were fast and strong enough to run off the roof before I was able to come upstairs and catch him.”

Crusoe placed a gloved hand on his chin. When I watched him do so, I half thought that a part of his chin had disappeared— his gloves were so black, that they were almost indistinguishable from the rest of the night air.

“Whoever this person is,” Crusoe said, “be he Eddy Mulligan or otherwise, has me incredibly outmatched. At every turn— at every connection I try to make— it seems that there’s a new one that contradicts my theory. If this is done by a group of people, they’re among the smartest and tidiest people known to mankind. There just aren’t any discernable trails that make proper links…”

My mouth dropped in shock. I’d never seen Crusoe come to such a defeated state before. That is— not until now. I’d never even thought it to be possible that he’d admit to defeat. I’d forever categorized such an idea as an impossibility. If there was anything I’d learned about Crusoe, it was that he had a consistency to solving mysteries of every kind. He’d always seemed impervious to the limitations of a normal man.

Though, it seemed that tonight I’d seen far too much of the weak side of him. He’d become just a normal man, masquerading as something greater. His mind had just admitted to being outmatched. I felt like a fool, tricked by a fancy light show. I knew, in my heart of hearts, that Crusoe had made me out to be a puppet, leading me on as if I were cattle.

Though, I’d always been caught up in the show. Even in the times when I suspected that he was leading me on, I‘d always followed him gleefully. It had never mattered that he might’ve been playing me for a fool. If I were to be honest, I’d always had a part of myself that had suspected this— I’d merely ignored it. It was almost as if he were a magician, and I was the viewer. While I felt entitled to knowing the secret behind his tricks, I didn’t want to— I didn’t want to ruin the fun.

I felt a stinging pain crawl down my backside, biting at my spine. It hurt to think that my love of the fun in Crusoe was becoming too much of a hindrance. It hurt to know that I was but a pawn upon his chessboard— and Crusoe had just been checkmated.
“Put your hands in the air!” a voice cried out.
I stepped back from Crusoe, and allowed an officer to tackle him. My time was up. Crusoe had proven that he didn’t have the answers, and that he was just as clueless as the rest of us.

As Crusoe tried evading the officer’s attacks and making an escape, I bent down to retrieve all of the evidence that Crusoe had provided me. Each one of them seemed to be tainted in Crusoe’s mysterious spirit, with them even smelling of Crusoe’s kerosene slathered suit. As I carefully observed each one of them, using my gloves so as to avoid altering them with my own fingerprints, I felt as if the evidence cried out in anger against me. It beckoned to the vulnerable part of myself, telling it that I didn’t have the worthiness for it. I could’ve sworn that I felt it tearing at my chest. One of the pictures of Crusoe’s even gave me a papercut.
The pictures, I suddenly thought. I never gave him a chance to explain these to me.

It was at that moment that regrets began to seep in, and I no longer knew if I was doing the right thing. If I had, it didn’t feel like that at all anymore. Just by looking at Crusoe’s face, I knew that I’d sold a part of myself. His coal black eyes tugged at me, just like his evidence had. His blackness drained the color from my face, just like the sun drains the color from paint.

I wasn’t quite sure what, but it was in that moment that I felt as if something were missing. Maybe it was my youth that I felt slip away in that moment. Maybe it was a part of my nostalgia that had disappeared. Maybe, nothing left at all— maybe I simply was feeling something that had always been there, and it had only taken me until now to figure it out.

I had the sudden urge to tell my comrades to stop. Nothing in the world seemed more important than for me to utter those words. As I watched Crusoe struggle against the police, it was like watching the struggle of a friend. Yet, for some reason, I didn’t do anything to stop what was going on. I felt frozen in time. It was as if time had placed me in an invisible capsule, just so that it clearly could display everything that was going on before my eyes.

Gunshots filled the air. I could smell the stink of sulfur, as it rippled from the tips of pistols and into my nostrils. Shouts were everywhere. Crusoe had left two men with bloody noses, and another two flattened onto the pavement. In that instant, I realized that it was too late. If I were going to do anything at all, my chance to do so had already passed by.

There was more to it than just that. As much as I wanted to do something, there was still the larger part of me that didn’t. It seemed that the primal instinct to stay true to my group, over a single man, had betrayed the will of my conscience.
It overrode my conscience. It overrode everything— even my feelings.

All that you can ever trust is your feelings. While I didn’t want to have to betray Detective Crusoe, I’d decided that it was needed to have been done. It was necessary if I ever planned on getting anywhere in my case.

Crusoe is a criminal, and, in spite of our past relations, this was an inevitability, I thought to myself. There was no avoiding this. Even if I’d never taken this action myself, somebody else would’ve done it. Somebody needed to knock down Crusoe, and it had to be me.

As much as I said this to myself, and as much as I wanted to believe that I had taken the right course of action, I felt a scratching at the back of my mind. It told me that I’d made the wrong choice and that I’d taken the wrong path.

I knew that I’d made my decision based upon a feeling that I had, but now I felt something entirely different. What is somebody supposed to do when their feelings— their only way of getting in touch with the vast and complex universe that surrounds them— begins conflicting itself.
It was an inevitability that an inevitability would clash with my internal moral code. Though, that didn’t change how wrong it suddenly felt.

“Crusoe,” I finally said, finally allowing the flow of breath to return to my body, “I’m going to ask you one last time. What did you do all those years, when you were away from me— away from all of us? You’ve gotten rusty, old friend. So rusty, that your skills have been peeled away to something almost unrecognizable.”

Detective Crusoe didn’t give me an answer for the longest time. Instead, he continued busying himself in his purposeless struggle against the police. At this point, he’d already lost the fight. Now, he was only battling to instill his superiority, and resist the bondage of handcuffs.

One of the police shouted at me for distracting from the task at hand, and one of them even pushed me away. There were so many shouts in the air that, if I’d been talking to anybody other than Crusoe, I would’ve thought that he wouldn’t have heard him. Though, I was talking to Crusoe. And, while he acted as if I hadn’t said a word, I could tell just by the look in his eyes that he’d heard every word that I’d said— he was simply ignoring me.
Finally, he spat in my direction.

“I could ask you the very same questions,” he shouted at the top of his lungs. I heard his voice crack, and, for the first time in my long history, I caught a glimpse of his real voice. “You’re a traitor. You’re never going to be able to solve this case without my help! Don’t you see what they’re doing here?! They claim to give out justice, and they’re capturing a man who’s done nothing wrong!”

I wanted to tell him that he himself had captured people who’d seemed to have done nothing wrong. I wanted to tell him so many things, and to put him in his place. Yet, there was a prominence to everything that Crusoe did— there was an undeniable passion. When I looked into Crusoe’s mysterious eyes— possibly for the last time that I’d ever see mystery in them— I saw a man who was lost, and looking for a place in the world. The concept of bringing the truth to him sounded to heinous to act upon. Perhaps I was being too soft on the man. But then, how could something that felt so wrong possibly be the right thing to do?
“You’ve driven me to this point of desperation,” Crusoe said, making no sense whatsoever.
“What are you talking about, Crusoe?”

At this point, his face was planted into the pavement, he was under five men, and was at the complete mercy of everything around him. However, he strangely didn’t act that way. As the moon shone from out of the clouds, I caught a glimpse of Crusoe’s determined face.

“Just because you think I’ve gotten soft in old age doesn’t mean that I have to be,” Crusoe said, continuing the rambling of nonsense. “Allow me to prove to you that you have no idea of what you’re talking about— and that you never did.”

Then, a blast went off. Smoke was everywhere, and my eyes began to burn. Suddenly, all that I could see was a grayness. And then, even that began to fade into a blackness. Each breath my lungs pulled in was harder than the last. I groped around, hoping to find a way out of the blackness— but, there was no way out. It was everywhere. Finally, I stole a glance at my watch.
“Lieutenant Jackson,” I shouted, in a raspy grunt, “you ambushed Crusoe earlier than planned. You—.”
I didn’t get to finish that last bit. Though, if I could’ve, I would’ve said, “You need to follow through on every plan with Crusoe. You can’t act earlier than determined.”
I think I blacked out completely before I could say that last bit. Though, it didn’t matter— the words were just as powerful in my mind when they were unspoken as they were when they were spoken.

Crusoe had a way of getting what he wanted, even when it seemed like he didn’t— even when he didn’t have the ability to get what he wanted. That was perhaps the biggest charm of Crusoe. It was also his biggest weakness.

I awoke to find myself laying on the wetted pavement, looking up into the inked skyline. I wasn’t sure how long I’d been asleep, though it seemed that it hadn’t been long— I saw several bodies of fellow police officers sprawled around me, and the night still maintained its throne upon the air.
There were a few officers that were standing, and walking around. Though, they appeared to be just as bemused and confused as I was.

Trying my hardest to make out what had happened, I began pressing my fingers onto the wrists of all my fellow laying officers— they all still maintained a pulse, and a breath. Then, I started studying the ground around us, to make out what the toxic inhalant might’ve been. As I looked, I found that there was an odd sediment caked into the ground, in between miniscule pools of water. I pulled out my pocket knife, and used it to pick up a bit of this caked sediment. It wasn’t anything like mud— it had a rustiness to it— nor was it like a sand, salt, acid, or liquid.
What is it? I wondered.

All that I had to guess was that, whatever it was, it had been used as a way to non-lethally incapacitate all of us. The grayness that I’d seen before I’d blacked out had been a result of the fumes— we’d been disarmed via poison.

However, I couldn’t get past the how and why of this odd event. If it had been used as a way to disarm us, I knew for certain that Crusoe could’ve strategized a much safer way to do so. And, if it had been Crusoe’s way of giving out revenge, then why hadn’t he finished the job? Moreover, this was out of Crusoe’s character. He was many things— eccentric, cruel, brutal, and unforgiving. But, he wasn’t one to resort to any kind of potentially deadly weaponry in order to get his way. I couldn’t help but wonder what might have driven him to this point.
Desperation gnawed at the back of my head. Not only did the desperation ask me to find the answer— it also told me that it was the answer. At least, it was part of the answer.

My memory brought me back to the plague that had nested in my city— in my country. It was a plague that had refused to let up. Everybody was desperate now— even myself. And, I suddenly had the feeling that desperation had infected Crusoe too.
The most terrifying aspect of this was that, if Crusoe was willing to do all of that, what would he be willing to do in the future? How much worse might his interactions with the city become?

What I found that night was that I felt weaker and more helpless than I ever had in weeks… Though, it wasn’t due to the pounding in my chest, or the bodies of fellow officers sprawled around me. It was the fact that, no matter how I tried spinning it, I’d been wrong about Crusoe all along— I’d led everybody to a beast, thinking that it was harmless as a lamb.
I’d been wrong.

This fact alone was probably what tore at me the most. People were oftentimes wrong— especially these days— but, being the proud and haughty human being that I am, I always thought that I was immune to the limitations of incorrect information and decisions. I’d believed that I was unable to make the wrong conclusion, or assess something in a harmful way.

It was this lapse of judgement that truly made me feel weak. At the end of the day, when I looked at everything that surrounded me, it was the fact that I was so small that truly made me feel punitive, and even insignificant. Because, no matter how hard I tried, and no matter how many places I looked, I was never going to be able to make up for the blunder that I’d allowed.
Crusoe had been the only person I’d trusted. And, now he’d joined the expanding list of people who I couldn’t even be around.
“I just don’t understand,” I said, half to myself and half to the wind.
“Then, why don’t you move it and help us out Sergeant,” Another one of the officers said, lifting all of the people who were laying on the ground.

Recognizing my idleness, I hastily joined him. There were about seven cops still laying on the ground, all of them looking up with their eyes all being covered by a curtain of skin. I tried looking at them with a courage. However, such was a senseless pride on my part. When I actually tried looking at them I felt an immeasurable fear rise in my chest. At first, I was unsure of where this fear had come from.

Although, uncertainty is just a gauze— an excuse— to allow oneself to remain ignorant of obvious truths. I feared the men because I knew that their current state was of my doing. I’d placed them in their terrible positions of weakness…

When I saw their lifeless looks, I didn’t see the looks of men. I saw the looks of Crusoe instead. I saw the fact that, while I wanted to believe that the monster I was afraid of was outside of me, the monster was inside of me. It was me.

I was pulled out of this somewhat sulky reminiscing after I’d brought a third person under the canopy of some squad cars. Preparing to hop into one of them, I slipped a pair of keys out of my pocket. I could already hear the coming hum of a newly started engine.

Then, I heard the sound of a lighting match— and all dreams of turning on the car engine faded away. I tossed the keys into another officer’s palms, and then looked for where the familiar sound of a lighting match might’ve come from. After turning three-hundred and sixty degrees, and listening to the squad car drive off, I thought that I must’ve been imagining things. Though, then I felt a hand softly press against my shoulder— and, at that moment, I knew without a doubt what was going on.
“Kyler, it wasn’t your fault.”

It was the voice of Lieutenant Jackson, sounding as smarmy and self-important as ever. Though, for once, I wanted to hear his voice. I wanted to smell the terrible stench of tobacco and nicotine dripping from his lips. I felt lost, and his voice had found a way to bring me back to the shores of reality. It showed me that the simple and the quaint things of life still existed— that not everything had monstrous effects on the course of life.

“Things like this happen,” he continued. “I’ve seen you make bluffs and blunders on numerous cases in the past— it never stopped you then, and it shouldn’t stop you now. Most of us have a few tough cases. Maybe not as many as you’ve had, but still— my point stands…”

Suddenly, I realized that Lieutenant Jackson’s voice had endured five less years of time’s roughening than my own— and yet, he sounded far wiser than I thought I’d ever be able to achieve. For some random reason, I caught myself grinning. Usually, when speaking with Jackson, the only expression I could ever muster was a scowl.
“I could’ve pulled Crusoe’s mask off at any time I wanted…” I said, clenching my fist. “He was right there, in front of my face— he trusted me in that moment. And, I squandered it…”
“You can’t entirely blame yourself. I cut the time short.”
I chuckled.
“Yes, I caught that… We still have a few pieces of evidence that Crusoe never explained to me.”

“You haven’t caught on by now, have you Kyler? Maybe you’re just blinded, due to the fact that you are great friends with Crusoe. But, all of the evidence that he gave you was trash… It easily could’ve been faked.”
“But, he hasn’t given me false evidence in the past.”
“He hasn’t been in such a desperate time as now, either. He has an ego. He likes being the one who solves the case. And, I’m beginning to suspect that he’d even be willing to lie in order to do so…”
“But this picture of a guy carrying a monkey statue— you’re not even curious as to where Crusoe got this from?”

“Not really. Do you honestly expect me to believe that, in spite of the decades the Chicago police force has invested into solving these sorts of cases, a random guy from off the street with a magnifying glass and rubber gloves can outdo us?”
“Yes.”
I couldn’t believe that I’d said those words— I regretted them the moment that they came out. Though, I couldn’t deny that, somewhere inside myself, I believed them to be true.

Jackson thankfully didn’t take me serisously, and merely laughed. I watchd his head turn into the light of the slamppost, and the smoke from his cigarette waft into the night air. In a way, as the smoke left to join the clouds, I felt like Jackson left as well. He didn’t speak again until I saw another puff of smoke leap from his cigarette.
“Crusoe’s fumes must’ve gotten to your head…” he said, jokingly.

I’m not quite sure why, but I wasn’t able to take it as a joke in the moment. There was an odd part of me that had decided to take everything that Jackson said for verbatim. Looking back on it, I think it was due to just how confused and befuddled that night— I needed something to cling to, and believing that everything Jackson said was truth was one of the only things I had left.
Admittedly, lack of sleep also played a major role.
“What do you think Crusoe used on us, anyway?” I asked.
Jackson grinned, in his own gruff way.

“You’re begging answers from me, as if I were some kind of genie,” he said. “I’m not into forensics— there are other people that are far more informed in that subject than myself. Although, I will say this. Whatever the gas is, it’s something entirely new and unique to me. I’ve never heard of somebody using anything like it before… If Crusoe is the genius that we both believe him to be, then I definitely fear what he might end up using that special gas with. That, and I fear what else he might’ve been able to cook up.”
“Is that why you don’t trust him?”

“I’ll be blunt with you, Kyler– I find it hard to trust a man who hides behind a mask, and avoids answering for any of the questions that surround him. I would’ve thought that you would’ve joined me in this line of thinking by now— but, I start to suspect that your thoughts are oftentimes hindered by the fact that you once thought Crusoe to be a friend.”

I looked down to the ground, and watched a few drops of water plink onto the pavement. Though— they weren’t drops of water. They were droplets of sweat, sliding from off of my forehead. I felt my throat start to clog up— but I didn’t let that halt me in my conversation with Jackson.

“I’ve heard that same spiel over and over again,” I said, flippantly. “Everybody constantly goes around proclaiming that I made a mistake with Crusoe… But, have you ever thought that maybe everybody else might be making a mistake? I know that tonight was questionable— and, to be honest, it’s severely making me rethink my position, and consider Crusoe as a possible threat— but, I just can’t help but see Crusoe as an individual who’s misunderstood and misrepresented.”

The Lieutenant coughed— I couldn’t tell if it was from what I’d said, from his cigarette, or from something other. When I watched him wipe his mouth with his sleeve, my questions were no closer to being answered— he looked distant, and his smugness seemed to have peeled off. It was as if the distant, black expanse of the stars had sucked a part of him away.

“I simply wouldn’t call a man who dresses in cloaked attire and hides from everybody who tries talking to him is misunderstood… If Crusoe was the sort of person who wanted to be represented in a better light, then he’d come out into the light.”
“And why would he, when all of the police are after him?”
“And why are all of us after him, Kyler?”

Jackson walked further away from me, and leaned onto the lamppost where all of this had begun. Out of nowhere, I realized how old and tired he looked. It was if everything had finally found a way to wear him down— and he no longer had the willpower to fight against it. His gaunt features no longer looked loose and full of energy, but now withered, and sucked of a good portion of their life.
At that moment, I realized just how much more ancient and tired I must’ve looked.

“There are so many other cases that are far more important than this costumed wannabe,” Jackson said. “We’ve dealt with him for too long… I know that you see him as a friend, and you don’t understand what changed him. But, what you don’t realize is that Crusoe has been a vicious character all along. You’d simply used him as a crutch, unaware that the crutch had been covered in a corrosive mold.”
He put his hand to his forehead, and wiped off a layer of dust that had formed there.

“We can’t afford to have you continuing to waste away your talents in chasing after this fool… We need you to give out your best work, and rid the city of him. We’ve dealt with Crusoe for too long, and he’s no longer anywhere close to being relevant to our current times and troubles. He’s a relic— and, sometimes relics have to be forgotten in the papers of history. Don’t you understand?”

I understood completely, but that didn’t change the fact that I didn’t want to understand. It wouldn’t have mattered how eloquently Jackson had put it, or how heinous of a thing that Crusoe had done that night. I was too phased by my own ego to realize how much I’d actually have to sacrifice in order to achieve the most optimal state for the greater good.

My eyes went back down to the remaining clues that Crusoe had failed to explain to me. I knew that my internal feelings were irrational and unfounded— but I was suddenly determined to prove that Crusoe’s case wasn’t a fiction or a series of flukes.
“I can’t just give up my relations with Crusoe,” I said. “I feel as if you’re asking me to cut off my arm.”
“I’m asking you to cut off a leech.”

A breath came out of my mouth with a heaviness that I’d never thought possible. It became clear that a split had grown between me and Lieutenant Jackson— a split that I’d always recognized, but now suddenly no longer wanted to exist.
My eyes turned down to all of the remaining clues that Detective Crusoe had left me with.
“What if I could use these clues, and everything else that we have, to prove Crusoe’s innocence?” I asked. “Would that change your thoughts on him?”
Lieutenant Jackson gave an awkward pause that left me feeling disconcerted. Though, when I looked into his eyes, I saw that he was far more uncomfortable than I.
Then, he gave a sarcastic scoff, no doubt trying to hide his blurb of weakness.

“If you can prove that Crusoe is innocent, then I’ll vouch for you to trade positions with me,” he said. I could tell that he was only half-serious— yet, he seemed more serious than he was letting on, at the same time. “There’s nothing under the sun that can prove Crusoe’s innocence…”
“Are you saying that nothing can convince you?”

“I’m saying that, whatever could convince me, doesn’t exist. Do you realize how hard it is to prove a guilty man to be innocent? The only way for you to turn things around for Crusoe is to take all of the crimes he’s committed, and figure out a way to pin them on somebody else. But, even then, he’s a vigilante… We both witnessed it firsthand— he isn’t the kind of guy who we want roaming around our city, let alone trying to enforce his own personal form of justice.”
“I knew Crusoe— tonight was just a bad example.”
“He left the whole force unconscious, and some of them have to be hospitalized.”

Those words should’ve been enough to stop me— but, for some reason, I kept going. While there seemed to be nothing on earth that could convince Jackson I was telling the truth, nothing would convince me to stop fighting.

“He’s in the middle of trying to solve a crime for us… I don’t understand how you can so easily overlook that. Don’t you think that there might be a bit of a trustworthy person within Crusoe? What convinced you that he’s such a menace?”

“I was convinced that he was a menace the day that he betrayed you— betrayed all of us. And now, half of the crimes in this district are being linked to him. That’s not a coincidence Kyler. Like it or not, there’s somebody out there who calls himself Crusoe, and he’s not a good person. Just because somebody claims they want to help doesn’t mean they do…”
Jackson flicked his cigarette away, and began walking toward the street— his house wasn’t far from the police department, and he had the habit of walking between them.
“I’m going to prove that Crusoe is innocent!”
“You’d prove that you’re insane long before that would ever happen… Before you go on your crusade, make sure that everybody is safe at the hospital for me.”

The police force had been drained by the occurrence that had taken place between ourselves and Crusoe. Nobody was quite sure why, but it had produced a draining effect onto all of us. Whenever I walked by somebody down the hall of the police department, they no longer spoke to me. Even when I tried engaging them in conversation, they seemed hesitant and soft-spoken. I thought that this might’ve been in my head, but it went so far as there being sort of timidity to them. Whenever I looked into their faces, there was a distantness. I would make eye contact with some of them, but it was as if I were a ghost— they stared right through me.

Half of our force was gone for the next few days, with them all being treated with IVs. After speaking to the doctors though, I became aware that we were doomed to have them gone for far longer than anticipated. I was told that they’d been lucky to stay alive, and that some of them were having trouble breathing. I asked the hospital why this was, and what sort of chemical smoke might’ve been the cause.
There wasn’t any answer. They were just as clueless as myself.

On the subject of clueless, I also made sure to go to the forensics division, like Lieutenant Jackson had suggested to me. Ever since I’d done that, I found myself only feeling an enormous regret. Most of the people in there studied the sample I gave them, but said that it was nothing more than a simple dust powder— probably caused by the burnt butt of a cigarette, mixed with salts, sand, and dirt.

Angry with the fact that I looked like an idiot, I asked them to review the samples, and check it for any other potential causes. They didn’t even bother— told me to go somewhere else, and that I was wasting time that they could’ve been using on something far more productive.

I gave them what they wanted, even if it left me with an extremely bitter taste in my mouth. I decided that, if I was going to get things done and head somewhere, I was going to have to do it myself. I took the case into my own hands, omitting myself of any outside help.

A week was invested into trying to identify what might’ve been different about the samples. An entire week withered away, without me finding anywhere near anything. Eventually, I had to assume that I’d either picked a bad sample, or that the gas’s compounds had deteriorated.

I tried contacting Crusoe, but that of course didn’t work. He didn’t trust me any more than I trusted him. And, I’m sure that even if he did, he wasn’t going to be revealing his own secrets to me. If there was anything about Crusoe that I could be certain of, it was that he was the kind of person who wasn’t keen on giving. If I wanted something from him, I usually had to beg him for it, or strip it from him by force.
Though, I’ll give him this much— he wasn’t entirely wrong, and he wouldn’t still have his mask if he’d designed it any other way.

Moving on from the sample, I went to the evidence that Crusoe given me. Or, at least the closest thing that I had to evidence. I’d come to the conclusion that Crusoe had left me with nothing that could validate him as being a good person. However, he had left me with the clues— and, if I could prove that he’d been right with those, then I knew that I might subsequently be able to prove that Crusoe was innocent.

Another reason that I’d decided to turn the clues into a serious focus of mine was the fact that I’d been so busy with so many cases that I’d begun to ignore Miss Prestel’s. I assumed that, if I were able to find the meaning behind Crusoe’s clues, and they happened to be true, then I might be able to kill two birds with one stone and take care of Miss Prestel once and for all. I wasn’t going to be able to take care of Miss Prestel in any other way, that was for sure. For the past week, she’d made sure to send me a letter complaining about the tardiness of me finding a solution of her case. And, when Job had escaped, she’d made sure to give me no leniency on the blunder.
I’ll show her, I said to myself, when I finally cracked open Crusoe’s evidence. Job will be back behind bars, and she’ll be thanking the entire police force.

I was merely daydreaming. Deciphering the clues proved to be a far more menial task than I ever could’ve anticipated. It had taken me three days of reading and rereading Bob Murphy’s letter, and staring at the blurry photographs before I finally came to a conclusion—but even then, my conclusion was a fuzzy one.

My first attempt at getting of answer came when I started studying the photos. The first one I studied was the one with the man holding a monkey doll in an alleyway. Though, when my studies of it became inconclusive, I wetted the photograph, and then turned it face-down on a piece of paper. Once the ink of the image had bled onto the paper, I examined every etch and detail— most of it was blotchy and indistinct. But, I was able to make out the fact that the man’s shadow-drenched face had been bearded, and that he’d been dressed in a lighter-colored coat— probably a brown, or a yellow.
Perhaps the only piece of evidence that I found useful on it was a piece of graffiti that was on a nearby wall— it was an image of three lines, underlined by this series of numbers— 246.
