None of this helped me as much as I would’ve liked it to, though. If anything, it only made me more confused. I had thought that I was going to be coming upon a clear answer, only to find that what I thought to be a clear answer was actually just another question.
Is there anything significant to this graffiti? I wondered. Have I seen it anywhere before?

I didn’t dare to ask any more questions. Something that I’ve discovered about myself is that, when I begin to ask too many questions, my questions don’t stop coming. It’s like unlatching a rusted faucet— once it’s turned on, it’s hard to turn off.

However, I did have a strong feeling that I’d seen the graffiti somewhere. There was a familiar aspect to it— it gave me the same feeling that I would have when walking down a street and seeing a familiar face— only to find that the familiar face wasn’t so familiar after all, and that I had no idea where I’d seen the person before.

I was wrong when Id stated prior that uncertainty is just an excuse. IT goes far deeper than that.  Uncertainty is not only an excuse, but a blockade. It’s one of the main things that stops the human race from passing frontiers, risking to go over the border, attempting to study something unique, and daring to do things that nobody else had dared to do. Without uncertainty, the world would be a place that was far more diverse.
Though, then again, without uncertainty where is the mystery? Where is the itching for knowledge that propels us towards making something new?
Perhaps uncertainty is many things– a motivator, an excuse, a source of fear, and a hinderer.

Studying Crusoe’s evidence, I found myself experiencing all of these feelings from the uncertainty. However, some foreign part of myself refused to digest it. I had an internal resilience that pushed against the limits of my mind. A part of me believes that it was just due to the wish to be apart from the bondages of the world, and my own physical limitations. However, I’ve since begun to suspect that it was something far— something that I never could’ve guessed or dreamed of.

I jotted down notes about the studies that I’d conducted on the alleyway image, and then turned to look at the image of the woman walking down the hall. It was an extremely blurry image, and at first I wasn’t even sure if I was looking at a woman at all. It took me looking at the picture under one of my lamps to tell what I was seeing.

The picture was far brighter lit than the last, so that worked in its advantage. I was able to observe that the image took place in what looked like a hospital setting. There were pale, almost bluish, lights over head of the lady. The walls on each side of her were made of a pale brimstone, and there seemed to be a sort of stretcher far off from her. What was odd about this hospital was what I saw in the background— there seemed to be a loose pair of doctor uniforms at the end of the hall. But, they were a kind that hadn’t been used in years. It looked like it was coated in a blackening mold as well.

In spite of this decaying object, and the clear appearance of age in the hallway, the woman looked fresh and young— at least, that’s what her clothes suggested. When I looked to her skin, and her hair, it was too hard to discern anything. She was even giving a side-glance over her shoulder, exposing a bit f her profile— but it was still too unclear.
“If Crusoe hadn’t doctored this, he definitely should’ve given me a better commentary on it…” I whispered under my breath.

After having stared at the image, I started to feel far more clearheaded than I had in a long while. There was something alleviating about the picture of the woman. The connection to the hospital gave me a clarity that I’d been copiously searching for.

I’d come to the conclusion that the picture had been taken at some sort of abandoned hospital. However, which hospital was something that had persisted to gnash at me. I tried pairing the number from the other picture, 246, to see if it correlated with any hospitals that had been closed down. Though, I wasn’t able to find any matches on a map, nor anywhere else. I eventually brought the case over to Lieutenant Jackson, but of course he was no help. He informed me that I was working for a lost cause, and then shooed me off.

Still, that wasn’t enough to demoralize me and stop me from completing the task of which I thought to be right. I knew that there was something to the hospital lead, whether anybody thought that it was right or not.

What eventually brought me to a solid point of reference was when I started reading the back of the picture— it was labeled as having been printed at printing-shop— Jonah’s Printing Shop, according to the back of the picture. I knew that this lead was a pitiful one, and that it held no real importance. Still, this didn’t change the fact that it was all that I had to go by, and that I was desperate to find anything that might lead me to a solution.

Within an hour of finding this out, I had the address of the printing shop, and I was heading in my car towards the place. Traffic proved to be a blockade, but I managed to hurdle over it, and make it seem to be as insignificant as a flea. Another twenty minutes passed by, and I was already at the shop, preparing to go in and ask my questions.

I strode out of my squad car with a pride unlike any other that I’d felt in a long while. Though, it came to pass that when I started studying the printer’s building, my insides began to shrivel up. The building looked like it hadn’t seen maintenance in years, despite the fact that the sign said that it had only been established ten years ago. It had a grimy display window, crusty letters marking its stake, and a brick structure that looked as if it were one chisel away from toppling over.

This building was also squeezed tightly in between two other buildings, looking as if they were vying for dominance. Though, when I studied those buildings as well, it appeared that they were losing the battle. In fact, if I hadn’t known any better, I would’ve argued that the printer’s sickly decay had been contagious, and was spreading over to those buildings as well.

What made me feel most irksome in the presence of this building, however, had nothing to do with the building’s design at all, but the smell that it gave off. I have a habit of breathing as little as I can through my nose, when traveling through the city— you can never tell what awful scents you might pick up. Yet, this scent was so intrusive that it didn’t matter how I was trying to breathe through my mouth, instead of my nose. It was undoubtedly the same smell that accompanied rotting flesh. A few flies that flew passed my head confirmed this belief.
“Rats,” I said. “They have rats…”
If the owner of the shop had heard me, I’m sure that they would’ve driven me off the property. But, I didn’t care— the smell was too unbearable to go without being verbally identified.

I’d been to many places throughout my long career— some of them being just as grungy and revolting as this one. Though, if I’d ever come across a building that I would proclaim diseased, I don’t think that they could’ve been a better candidate for that title than this one.
In fact, I found it to be more than just diseased.
“This place must be cursed,” I said.

While even only a year ago I would’ve laughed at the thought of the supernatural, recent events had convinced me that perhaps it was far more around me than I liked to admit. I found that I’d become more open to curses— after over a year of trying to clean up Chicago, to no avail, using the word curse was oftentimes the best excuse that I’d been able to come up with for myself. I used to find it skeptical that supernaturalism typically went hand in hand with uncertainty— but, I’d begun to suspect that perhaps the reason they went hand in hand was because the supernatural was so uncertain. And this building had opened me up to that concept even more. Whether this notion of mine had been true or not, I knew this much— if I had opted to travel to the building at night, rather than in the evening, I wouldn’t have had the guts to walk in.

A bell chimed over my head as I walked into the printing shop, and I found the stench from at the doorstep to be even more penetrating to my nostrils. I was extremely tempted to leave, run down the street, and not return to this place. But, something had forced me to remain where I was, and keep looking in the room for answers.

Alongside the stink of dead rats, there was also a new smell of ink that accompanied it. I looked for where it might’ve been coming from, and found that there was a hidden room to the far side of the shop— it was behind an empty checkout desk, and shrouded in the sounds of noisy clacking and whirring.

AS I looked, I caught myself walking into a carousel. Thankfully, I managed to catch myself before I knocked it over. Not that it would’ve mattered if I had. It was completely rusted, and it appeared that it was about to unscrew from its stand anyway. There were metal carousels just like this one all around me too, full of old printing paper— and, overpriced printing paper at that. It all looked ancient, as if it hadn’t been touched by human hands before.

Turning my attention from that, I took a look at the floor underneath my feet— it was made of an older pine wood, which had clearly been laid down far before the mere decade the shop claimed to have been around. There were splinters all throughout it, and as I walked on it, I heard it creak with a brittleness, as if it were about to snap at any moment.
You would’ve thought that they would’ve replaced this by now, I thought to myself.

However, I knew the truth— I was only entertaining myself by pretending to be oblivious to it. This printing shop hadn’t made money since the Dust Bowl was born, and had probably been struggling even before then. It had the mark of desperation all about it. Every seam was splitting open, like its secret bits that it liked to hide were finally beginning to tear it apart from on the inside. This brought my mind to an image of a zoo that I’d remembered. I had a faint memory of a group of monkeys that had been in there once— one time, the monkey cages became too overcrowded, and one of the monkeys escaped.
The zoo was never able to get back on its feet after that incident— it allowing the animal to leak out had been its downfall.

That’s the reason why I’d looked down at the floor in the first place— I’d come to realize that you could learn a lot about a place, and the people who run it, by staring at the floor. After all— the floor is where nobody looks, but everybody walks upon. If a shop thinks it can get away with hiding its messes in plain sight, then you know just how little they think of you— and just how much they think that they’ll be able to get away with.

Just the sort of place that Crusoe would try printing a picture at, I thought, with a smirk. Of course he’d be trying to hide amongst the grime. Little does he realize how much hiding disadvantages what he’s able to do.

As I was thinking this, a door creaked open. Normally, I wasn’t able to hear the creaking of doors— my ears had been dulled so much by the sounds of gunshots and screams over the years, that hearing such acute things had become harder for me to do. However, this particular creak was so loud that I found my own ears beginning to howl in pain. I had to bring my hands to my ears, it hurt so much.
As I did this, I was immediately brought back to Miss Prestel’s house, when I heard the excruciating wail on the downstairs floor.
Had that been all that it was, I thought to myself. Just an unoiled door hinge?

I laughed to myself, and passed my association off as mere coincidence. Then, I heard a loud grunt from on my left side, coming from the same direction that the wailing door had. I turned around, and saw an angry looking man leaning over the previously unattended checkout desk.

While I might’ve been willing to laugh, this man clearly wasn’t in the mood to be humored. He took one look at my crisp police uniform, and then gave a scowl of disapproval. I’d become accustomed to people typically giving an expression of terror after glancing at my uniform. This new course of action knocked me completely off my feet, and I found myself stripped of all confidence and direction.
“What are you doing here?” the man asked, with his voice far removed from the typically cheery service.

I took a longer look at him. His face was coarse and leathery, along with having a haggard look to it. His lips were pale— I suspected from overexposure to some sort of chemicals from in the printing room— along with the rest of his face. The only thing that had color were his eyes and hair— both of which shared the color of gray. Unlike his eyes, however, his gray hairs still had a hint of brown in them. They were receding, and bordered by a line of gray, but that hint of color was still undeniably there. His stubble for a beard was an improvement, but still wasn’t that much more impressive of a sight. It looked as if the man had given up on shaving halfway through the job, and he had a greasy shirt that looked as if it hadn’t been changed in weeks. On this shirt, there was a plain title of the shop’s name, and the man’s name was printed onto a flimsy paper nametag— Jonah Gage. He had a tall and imposing height, but still maintained a heavy build. His arms were particularly broad and thick, so much so that they looked capable of knocking me to the ground.
His hands were probably my only advantage, if we were to get into a fight— they were smeared with ink and oil, and appeared to have been shriveled from years of working with the stuff.
“I was just here to ask a few questions about this picture I have— Jonah Gage is it?”
Opting to ignore me, Gage instead just offered a snide snort.
“You decided to dress up in that stuffy getup just to ask me a few questions? Give me a break… What are you actually looking for, officer?”

There was nothing about the man that I could truly find comfort in. No matter what light I looked at him in, he seemed to be able to find some new way to bring me into a squeamish state. Though, somehow, my lips and vocal chords managed to form the words that I needed to say.
“Answers… I’m looking for answers, and I think that you’re the only person that might have them for me.”

I tossed my pictures onto his desk. They floated down with a sort of angelic quality, arcing in and out from each other. It was as if they held some holy air about them. Compared to the shop around it, I found it almost impossible to believe that something so pretty and glossy could’ve been made somewhere so destitute.
Gage looked down at the pictures, with his eyes looking entirely unimpressed. However, his hands said otherwise, and they buried themselves into his chest, folding into the defense position.

“I don’t see what your point is…” Gage said, stiffly. “I printed a couple of pictures, and somebody paid me cash for it. Did you expect me to decline the offer? What does any of this have to do with me?”
“What I expect is for you to answer this question— who paid you for these pictures, and did they tell you anything about them before they did?”
“I’m not inclined to answer.”

At first, I felt like I was running in circles— even with my badge and my somewhat confident posture, it seemed that there was no swaying this man. However, then my nose gained an itch— and I remembered what ground of advantages that I did have over Gage.
Exaggeratedly, I took a large breath of air through my nostrils. Gage looked at me like I was insane, but I didn’t care— that was just the response that I’d wanted.
“You know a lot about this city, correct?” I asked.
Catching onto the fact that I was taking him through a sort of questionnaire, Gage became hesitant in giving a response. However, he eventually caved and said, “Yes.”
“So, I suspect that there are few people who walk in this part of the city that you don’t have any knowledge of or any connection with…”
This time, he didn’t answer me.
I took another whiff of air.

“I know that you’re not inclined to answer my question,” I said. “But, as for me— I’m inclined to believe that your shop is infested with rats, and many of them are dead and rotting. I’m not sure about you, but I think that you would’ve wanted to have taken care of this mess by now— you know, since you’re required by law to have paid an exterminator to take care of this mess… The fines for ignoring such laws are definitely hefty ones.”

This time, it was Gage who’d become squeamish. Although he had a different way of expressing it, such as by leaning backward, and by making his gaze move about the room, I knew without a doubt that he felt cornered.
Place a man where he’s weak, and he’ll always show his true colors… I thought.
Instantly, my mind went back to Crusoe. Thankfully, I managed to shove that thought away as quickly as possible.
“Answer my question. Or, would you like me to repeat myself?”
“Why not…” he said again, rolling his eyes.
I caught the roll of his eyes, however— and they weren’t rolling at all. It instead was the roll of the eyes that comes from a man who’s stalling, and searching for an escape.
“Who bought these pictures from you? And what are they pictures of? This is my last time asking you.”

At this point, I saw something within Gage shift— he had the look in his eyes of an animal that had finally been put in a place from which they couldn’t escape. Though, I was uncertain as to what decision he might make next— he could’ve either attacked me, in the same way that an animal could attack me, or he could’ve finally caved into my offer.
“She was really quiet,” Gage finally said. “She didn’t tell me her name. She didn’t even let me see her face.”
I had to keep my mouth from gaping— if there was anything that I hadn’t been expecting, it was probably the fact that Crusoe hadn’t bought these pictures.
“You’re sure that you’re not getting it confused?” I asked.
Gage looked incredulous.
“Of course I’m not getting it confused! I rarely ever get customers here, and when I do, I make sure to remember them as much as I can.”
I said nothing for a while, but couldn’t help but grin at that statement.
“How old did she look?”

“Couldn’t have been any older than forty— unless she dyed her hair. There wasn’t any gray in it. But, I didn’t catch much more than that. Like I said before, she didn’t tell me much… Her voice was too quiet to measure age with, and her face was too low to judge as well.”
“Did you happen to catch anything else?” I asked, being cautious not to pry too far— I felt lucky that I was getting this much out of him.

“Not much— I asked her what she wanted the pictures for, but she didn’t seem too willing to talk… I think that the hospital picture that you gave me was supposed to be from some attempt at exploration that she took, but I don’t know much else.”
I nodded.
“An attempt at exploring the hospital?” I said, making sure that I’d heard him right.

“Yeah,” he said. His eyes began to glaze over, looking as if he’d remembered something. “She’d said that she went there to check out the scenery— said that it was abandoned and that nobody went there anymore. I asked her the exact details of where she’d taken the picture at, but she didn’t seem quite as receptive when it came to that. She must’ve been trying to hide something from me, but I couldn’t tell quite what.”
“why do you think that she was trying to hide something from me?”
Gage’s own brand of squeamishness had returned.
He’s hiding something about somebody hiding something? I thought to myself with a smirk. That’s a new one…
“To be honest, I probably was a bit too abrasive with the amount of questions that I gave her,” he said. “I might’ve made her uncomfortable…”
I rolled my eyes.
I didn’t come here to be told about this man’s failed flirting attempts… I thought to myself.
“Where exactly do you think this hospital might be? And, did you get any specific details about it? Is there anything that I might like to know?”
“Considering the fact that you seem to want to know everything, I’d bet that there’s a lot you’d like to know… But, that doesn’t mean that I want to give it to you.”
“Come on, Gage… We’ve already been through what will happen if you don’t tell me what’s going on. Now, what do you think the hospital is? Do you have any ideas?”

“To be honest, I don’t know for sure,” Gage said. “But, considering that she came to my abandoned shop, of all places, I’m guessing that she was in the area… She was definitely a new face to me, so I’d assume that she wasn’t from here, and that she was just trying to get pictures of her visit.”
But why would Crusoe want this random woman’s pictures? I wondered.
“Spit it out already. What hospital is it?”

“It’s Harlem Grove Hospital… Well, it was Harlem Grove Hospital. Nowadays the sign reads, “Arlem Gove Pital” … Not nearly as catchy, but it does the job. Anyway, the hospital has been unmanned for years. Rumor has it, one of the doctors in there wasn’t following protocol, and it was found out that he was giving all of the patients diseases and sicknesses. Atop that, the owner mysteriously died from bronchitis, and then his broke son inherited the place… All of the sudden, nobody was going to that hospital anymore, and the place was shut down.”
“What sort of diseases were people catching…”

“I dunno— I hear stories that range from the common cold to polio. Personally, I don’t think that there’s all that much merit to them. People just like to pretend that they know something they don’t… What I believed really happened is that the owner died, and it was blamed on the hospital— after that, the blame kept spreading once the hospital was sold off. But, all that really happened was that the owner died of a freak accident, and his gambler of a son had to sell the place off…”

I made sure to place everything he said down in my notes. While I wasn’t sure if they would have any relevance, I felt a need to make sure that I was informed on every detail before I went searching through the hospital. I’d learned that, without a proper understanding of something’s history, that something becomes harder to understand and navigate.
“Is that all? Are there any dangers about the hospital— such as broken windows, locked doors, etc.”

“The doors can’t be opened,” Gage said. “To be honest, I don’t know a ton about the insides of the building— most of what I know is based on what other people know— and, what other people know about it isn’t necessarily true… But, I’ve heard that there’s broken glass strewn all throughout the halls, there’s graffiti spread throughout it, there are animals living in it, and there’s mold growing through it, all due to the place being unattended. Another thing is that there’s this weird rumor about ghosts wandering through there. Now, I don’t believe in ghosts, but I’d bet that there’s somebody living in the hospital who doesn’t like visitors— if you’re going to investigate the property I’d advise that you bring somebody with you. You also don’t want to go investigating through the east wing… I’m not sure why, but that’s what I’ve been told. I think the place is full of dangerous medical supplies or something…”
On my notepad I jotted down most of what he said, except for his latter words— I edited those to say, “Explore east wing.”
“Thanks for the information,” I said. “Now one last thing— I need you to tell me if you recognize the graffiti or number on the alleyway picture— the one with the man.”
Gage bent over and studied it.
“You know, I never did ask you how you got these pictures…” Gage said, making a suspicious gaze at the ceiling.
“You still haven’t answered my question.”
“I don’t know about the numbers, but the three random lines just look like tally marks… I don’t see anything unique about them… Probably just the work of random vandalizers.”
I pretended to be satisfied, but I could tell that he was lying to me— I saw a look of recognition in his eyes when he took a look at the graffiti. There was even a sense of terror and dread.
“Well, this was a good chat,” I said, taking the pictures from his desk and placing them in my pocket. Then, I handed him a five-dollar bill.
“It’s the best I can spare,” I said, “but you earned it. Take care, and use it on something nice. If I’m ever in need, this is definitely a place that I’ll have in mind.”
Gage nodded and grinned. Then, he scribbled something down on a piece of note paper and handed it to me.
“It’s my phone number,” he said. “If you ever have any more questions, just call me.”
In that moment, I saw a sincerity— all of our suspicions melted off, and I found ourselves on level ground.
“Yeah,” I said. “I’ll call sometime.”
The smell of ink left as I hopped back into my care. I wish that I could’ve said the same for the stink of rat.

After the conversation with Jonah Gage I found myself feeling a strange mixture of confusion and satisfaction that I hadn’t expected. On one hand, the conversation with the man had gone far smoother than I thought it would’ve— it was to the point that I found myself considering that he could’ve been a great colleague. On the other hand, I was extremely lost in what I felt I was supposed to do.

As if there’s a time when I don’t feel that way, I thought to myself, half-jokingly. Though, I was joking far less than I led myself on to believe. It was becoming far harder for me to discern what I was supposed to do, as well as to push against my natural inclination to go at it alone.

If I explore the hospital on my own, then I’ll be at risk of being attacked or kidnapped, like so many others have been… But, if I don’t, then I’ll be at risk of being compromised. I don’t want Lieutenant Jackson to know that I’ve been working on my case based off of Crusoe’s evidence, or that I’m planning on basing everything on hunch and assumption.

There are many things about myself that I find to either be peculiar, or impossible to rationalize with. One of those things are my very rationalization. The truth was, fear had found a way to sink its teeth into my mind— and, there was nothing but myself that could shake it off. At hearing that Crusoe’s pictures had come from a woman, my confidence level had fallen to an all-time low— at this point, it wasn’t that I didn’t know what to do. It was that I was afraid that, no matter what I did, it would be the wrong thing.
For a seasoned officer, I haven’t learned nearly enough in my time on the force. Some might argue that I’ve gotten slow, too skeptical, and not willing to take the necessary risks.
They’re right. At this point, I’m wondering if this is the sort of job that people at my age should really be bothering with. It’s a game— a young person’s game.

There was a time when I wasn’t afraid of making a mistake. If it so happened that I died on the police force, I wasn’t concerned— I trusted that everything would be alright in the end. I felt that I’d lived out my life to the fullest, and that there weren’t any squandered years.

In the time since, I’ve lost that sense. It’s kind of funny, in a twisted sort of way— when I had nothing to lose, I had far more to lose than I’d thought. Yet, as time went one, and I found myself beginning to think that I have everything to lose, I suddenly realized that I have far less to lose. My reliance on rationalization and self-preservation increased to such a high level that I never could’ve believed I would’ve had when I was younger.

Such is the great rigging that mortality has placed on our lives. When death seems so far and distant, one thinks that they can fight it with ease— one thinks that about everything that’s far and distant. Though, once you begin to feel death in your limbs— once it starts to bite at you, and take away possessions that you once greatly enjoyed— the fantasies that you once told yourself suddenly don’t apply anymore.

I used to ask myself how people can let themselves get old… I used to wonder what it was that tricked people into letting go of carelessness, and putting fear and trepidation in its place. Little did I know, that had always been the wrong question to ask.
The real question is this— why do young people act as if old age is never going to catch up with them?

Nobody can stop it. As time goes one, death intrudes upon you— it makes sure that you become acquainted with it, whether you wish for it or not. To be honest, I don’t entirely place any bitterness towards death— whether or not how I like its order of business, business is business. And, if it’s going to spend eternity with me, it might as well get to know me while I’m still alive.

Perhaps that’s why I haven’t given up on police work, even after death shoved its foot into the ajar door of my life. Perhaps it’s because death represents everything that I hold dear— it enforces a sort of law that, no matter how much people try to avoid it, nobody will ever be able to escape. It also is among, if not on top, of all the greatest mysteries to be unsolved by man. While I might have fear towards it, I also retain a sort of reverence for it.
The greatest mysteries, as beautiful as they might be, are also the most terrifying and foundation shaking.

Eventually, I came to the conclusion that there was nobody I could fully trust. And, even if there happened to be somebody who I could, I certainly wasn’t willing to put that person in harm’s way. The only people who seemed willing to sacrifice a good amount of their security for me were people who were too rare and valuable to risk.

So, I went from Jonah’s Printing Shop without saying a word to anybody. I acted as if nothing had taken place, and that I was still searching everywhere for answers. In truth, I was still searching— just not for the things that others thought I was. I was now searching for ideal dates to go explore the abandoned hospital, as well as other places that I might find clues…

Of course, I didn’t find anything. The best that I was able to come up with was conversation with Miss Prestel. I wrote her a letter in the morning, and the response suggested that she still felt quite a large amount of bitterness due to the way that our affairs had gone south, I didn’t care. In fact, I was slightly relieved by the fact that she seemed disgusted by the thought of conversation with me— it took one less worry off of my checklist of responsibilities.

Yes— responsibilities. While I was extremely engrossed by the case at hand, I also had a problem with the fact of dancing around my real life cares. My rent was a week overdue, since my police department was being paid in less optimal times, and my fridge had gone nearly empty. A sort of writhing desperation began crawling through my gut, choking me of some life.

I grew up being told that money didn’t grow on trees. Back then, I used to come up with some smart-aleck refutation in my mind— such as the fact that the paper money is made from comes from trees. Though, those days of ignorance are just a fading cloud of smoke now— I see the real truth. The world around me is so small, and insignificant. I’m living upon a cloud of people who think that they know what’s best. All of those who were able to find out the secret of money sucked it dry— and I‘m beginning to realize just how little there is for the rest of us.

Thankfully, my job didn’t allow me any major fears back then. While tons of people around me were falling into the category of unemployed, and while I knew that most of the jobs and careers were beginning to fade away, I didn’t fear for myself. Not even when I found my bread stretching thin, and my home doors threatening to lock up on me. I knew that my job was secure— and, for some twisted and construes reason, that gave me a sense of security.

Little did I realize that the reason I felt so secure was that I hadn’t seen poverty yet, at its lowest form. I hadn’t yet seen what it looked like to hit the bottom of the barrel, and then try to climb back out of it. There was so much hopelessness outside of my small magnifying glass that I called the city.

If I were to have been honest with myself, I was living in one of the safest pockets of Chicago. I didn’t know crime like many others did because I ignored crime— I tried to hide from it, and pretend that the world I lived in was safe and protected— that I was somehow making a sort of difference.

Another couple of days passed by, flickering off like a failing match’s flickering flames. My tedious chores had finally been plucked away. Typically, this would’ve given me a sense of relief and an optimistic sense of control. Control in a world that seems uncontrollable is oftentimes the most securing feeling that one can ever wish for. However, these feelings were almost foreign to me— dare I say, even forbidden.

I was in my squad car, driving towards the abandoned hospital that Jonah Gage had directed me for. Something in my head didn’t care about this— it was utterly turned off by the idea that everything was about to come to a close— that I was one step closer to finding answers.

To be frank, I didn’t understand this odd feeling at the time. I fully believed that I was fooling myself into feeling something that wasn’t fully there— that my fears were utterly unfounded. The sky above me was cloudless, and appeared to be a softer blue than I’d seen in the longest time. For the past month, all that I’d seen were stark grays and fat drops of oily water. It was if that terrible weather had decided to retreat. The clear sky allowed the sun to bounce off of everything, in an almost playful sort of way. All colors gained a strange new beauty, and I felt an odd but welcomed sense of relief. Even the wind, which had been tearing at me for the past few weeks, had finally allowed me a break.

Though, none of this changed how I felt inside. It might’ve just been from cynicism, but I’d grown used to seeing the worst storms follow the brightest of days. I didn’t care that everything had gone from gloom to a tranquil atmosphere. I had a feeling that the fog hadn’t retreated, but that it was taunting me. Even in its absence, I could feel its presence— I could feel the fear crawling up my back of its return.

After all, a clear day is an investigator’s dream— there isn’t a clue that can go unseen, or a single blemish on the road that will go unchecked. It allows near perfect perception, and even better insight into the hidden things— the things that the city doesn’t want you to see.
More than anything else, this is how the fog was able to taunt me— it was able to threaten a return. It was able to threaten taking all of that away.

I used to be a man who didn’t quiver in fear in the face of threats. I’m not sure how that part of me changed. It seemed that the cynical world around me had brought a new mind into the place where my old mind was. I was starting to feel as if I was no longer the same man that I was when I was younger, but something entirely new and different— almost a new creature.

Perhaps this was just because of everything going on around me. But, if it was because of everything going on around me, then that would still give victory to the adverse situations. It would still mean that struggles and trials had begun to alter me in some way.

I’d come to the point where there was nothing that I could place blame on. My age, and the passage of time had morphed me into a creature that was immune to excuses. Any path that I took to validate my innocence would only cause me to admit weakness and ignorance. Corners were all that my eyes could see. I was utterly stuck and trapped in the sludge of my own head.

To avoid these thoughts, my eyes turned from the road and to the streets surrounding me. There was an aspect to myself that felt I could avoid looking at my internal darkness by seeing the brightness that the world contained. That aspect was entirely ignorant. As my eyes began to scan the world, it met one of the sorriest sights that it had seen in a while— all that it saw was emptiness.

The day smelt of a warm wave. The sound of scraping chalk had turned to a mere ghost that echoed in my ears. Skipping kids, and whistling adults were nowhere to be seen. There was only one thing that managed to give me the hope that people were still dwelling in the emptiness— I found a few cars parked along the side of apartment buildings, marking the territory as its own. Broken bottles and graffiti also coated a few places, as if to give warning to people such as myself.
“It looks that I’m not the only one who’s suspicious of the bright weather,” I said to myself.

For some reason, this pulled me as far away from feelings of comfort that I could conceive. Everything had an oddly sinister overtone to it. I took a glance at the street again, and found its emptiness pull at me as if it were a vacuum. I n that moment, I suddenly wished that I had brought somebody along with me. I could barely stand the draining atmosphere.

A conclusion came to me in the midst of all this— there wasn’t an emptiness because this area of the city was vacant. I wouldn’t have been surprised if the narrowing and increasingly claustrophobic design was teeming with a population. What was going on was that everybody was compressed into the alleyways and the buildings. I could hear their whispers every so often— their scraping grunts and growls. Within the buildings, far beyond my sight, rats were everywhere. It was like Jonah’s Printing Shop, but worse— I couldn’t smell the dead rats anymore. Now, all that I could do was infer their existence.

I drove for a little while longer, wondering what might’ve driven people into the buildings with such a fear as they were displaying. However, it wasn’t long before I came to the conclusion that I’d simply been avoiding. People weren’t hiding from me, or the city, or reality— they were hiding from the light. Nobody wanted to be out, now that the weather was clear. Everything had been dark and gloomy for so long that a nastiness had festered in the hearts of these many people. They’d retreated to their homes for no other reason than to remain unseen— to hide from exposing themselves as they truly were.

Wanting to be disgusted with this notion, I tried thinking of ways that I would avoid ever reducing myself to such a low state. However, I couldn’t come up with anything. Truth be told, I wanted to hid e in the darkness myself. No, I didn’t just fear the return of the smog, like I told myself that I had— I also relished the idea. I wanted to hide in the darkness, so that I wouldn’t have to face reality— so that I could live in a world that was far easier to hide in, and see myself as a hero in. The thing about the light is that it reveals people as they truly are. Though, in the city, nobody is ever who they truly are. When you live your entire life hiding behind the curtain, and pretending to be somebody that you aren’t, then that’s what you become— somebody who always pretends. Once that opportunity to pretend is taken away, the only thing to fall back on is the instinct of hiding from the light, and looking for somewhere else to be yourself.

Little did I realize, the deeper that I went into the bright but empty city, the deeper that I tore at the elements I was made up of. I was not the sort of person who would help those in need, like I’d once pictured myself as. Rather, I helped those that my job required me to help. If I were honest, the world around me had allowed it so that human compassion was harder to give out. I saw everything as a tangled mess, steadily growing ever more tangled. I didn’t want to bother trying to untangle it, in fear of being entangled in the process. Though, such is the problem that ails all life— finding the balance between self-preservation, and the preservation of the whole of society. When preservation of society becomes the preservation of oneself, then something selfless starts to turn into something selfish— and then it becomes ever harder to complete the selfless acts that make society run so smoothly.
Why is it that the world has decided to dip so low, I wondered.

I was at the hospital by now, parked in front of its molded and decayed doorway. I didn’t care. All that I saw was something dead— something unimportant and insignificant to the grand scheme of things. In trying to solve the mystery, I realized that I was reaching into a darkness.

Is that darkness worth looking through? I asked myself. Or, should I be looking elsewhere for answers. After all, there’s far more that I don’t understand. There are far more questions that I should be asking myself, and focusing on. I can’t just ignore the fact that there are people all around me, wishing for me to succeed to find them answers. I can’t ignore the fact that the answers I find will never solve the problem.

I’ve started to have more and more questions about whether or not my job is the enlightening tool that I’d once looked at it to be. After all, everything that I see around myself suggests that there are far more messes than I’d like to confront. I’ve been ignoring the full truth of everything around me, which is that everything has a virus. That’s why I’ve seen the city grow, and then fall.  It has become infected, and like an infected cell, it’s now producing more of the virus. Eventually, the problem will be so pervasive, that I won’t even be able to do anything anymore. I will have to rely on others to solve the problems. I will become as helpless as those I try to help.

Yet, that puts me in a circle. In trying to help people, I give the problems a prolonged chance to grow. In my distraction, I can’t see the corruption that’s growing behind my back— and so, the corruption comes to a point where nothing can possibly cut it down. Then, I become the one who must be helped.
Here’s the real problem. If I’m the police, and I can’t stop it, then who’s supposed to police the police? Who’s supposed to clean up a mess that even the cleaners can’t clean?

I’m no god, and I’ve never perceived myself as one. Yet, I can’t help but feel that I’m responsible for the direction that everything takes. If the world starts to spiral into oblivion, am I not responsible?

“What am I supposed to do?” is the question that I keep coming to… I have a fuzzy idea of that now. I’m supposed to do what’s needed of me. However, that doesn’t answer the main question, which is this— where am I supposed to look for the solutions? Am I looking in the right places?

By the end of this internal monologue I felt such a weight in my gut that I barely had the willpower to step out of my squad car. The world around me was so cheery looking, and I had a guilt in myself from not being able to appreciate it. It was almost unnatural. Although, in a twisted sort of way, this unnatural look at things felt right. Without it, I wouldn’t have been able to question my actions, and wonder if what I was doing was really the right thing— I would’ve been able to act like everything was extremely simplistic and easy. Nothing would’ve been solved.

The hospital building was just as I’d expected it to be— vacant and extremely destitute. To a point, I thought that its atmosphere might’ve been what was causing all of my uncertainties and running thoughts.

It had a foreboding an overbearing size, taking up about a block, and having the height of an average apartment building. One of the greatest sources of discomfort that came from the sight of it, however, had nothing to do with its size, scale, or even its rotting design. It was the very fact that the place had once been a source of life. When people went to the hospital, they once thought that it was a place that might have been able to relieve them of their ailments. It was a beacon of hope that almost seemed untainted.

It was the very concept that something of hope could become so twisted— the fact that it was able to turn into the monstrous construction that it had— that made me feel an enormous terror inside myself.

I opened the entrance door to the hospital, and heard it groan with a creak that was like the dying cry of a bird. Inside the building, there was an inky blackness. Oddly enough, there was a reassuring element to it— I actually embraced the look of darkness, having been deprived of it for the entire day. In spite of this, I still pulled a bulky flashlight out of my pocket before proceeding into the hall.

In a way, I was able to swim through the darkness like a fish swims through water. I didn’t entirely know where I was going, but I was still able to make out a lot of what was going on. It was as if the darkness pulled me along with it— instead of me controlling it with my own will, the darkness controlled me with its will. Why this didn’t scare me, I don’t know. I think that it was because, inside of all of ourselves, we’re born with an instinctive fear of darkness. However, as we’re forced to live in it, we adapt. We come to a point where we can hardly be without it, and we’re almost reliant on it.

The halls held a beauty to them. They were adorned with the stripes of abandonment, having dings and scratches on every turn. Even the floor, made up of a cool gray tile, had managed to become dented and bruised. It appeared that the years had made the place soft. Though, softness was something that I’d come to embrace over my years of having to deal with the harshness of reality.

There was something reassuring about being able to walk into a place that was filled with messes and degeneration. Everywhere I turned, I felt that a clue was behind me, beckoning for me to come and study it. Normally, a detective might’ve been disoriented by such a place, and even made timid. The amount of information was overwhelming and indecisive. However, coming from off the empty streets, I was allowed a far more positive viewpoint on the matter. To me, the fact that I had any clues at all was enough to make me feel free again.

By seeing all of the worn down areas in the hospital, it became pretty easy for me to tell that the place had been used for shelter since it had been closed down. In some areas, there were blankets and clothes left behind, and in others I even found the rotting remains of food.
I pity the person who had to sleep here, I thought to myself, as I heard the floor creak beneath me. Who on earth would be so desperate as to come here?

At the moment of asking this question, I realized that I already knew the answer— only a criminal, with a devious and crafty outlook on everything, would’ve been willing to set up camp in such a place. I couldn’t imagine somebody being guided by any motivation apart from that.

There was about half an hour where I was just wandering about, looking for a place to settle my studies. Though, it seemed that there wasn’t any clear direction to look into. The hospital was so straightforward and simplistic in design that, if there had been anything suspicious in there, I wouldn’t have been able to tell. It was at this point that I’d seriously begun to regret not bringing anybody with me.

At every step, it seemed that the building was threatening to come down on me. While the stains on the walls had greeted me at the entrance, they now snarled at me. Some of them even managed to tear into my gut, making me feel utterly exposed and at the mercy of it. The blackness had gained an omnipotence that I didn’t dare to test.

The very thought of continuing began to send daggers in my back. My arms jerked, and groped about involuntarily. At first, I was unsure to why I was doing this, though it then became clear to me that the surrounding environment was forcing things onto me that I would’ve normally been able to view without having to confront. It was placing images into my head that I had nbo resistance for. It was if I were the place’s screen, and it was the projector— everything withing it was imposed onto me, and I was forced to look for a way to remove it from myself.
“I think that I’ve seen enough,” I said.
At that moment, my flashlight began to flicker, and my sight started to become vapid and almost nonexistent.
“I take it back!” I said, slapping the flashlight against the wall.

Thankfully, it turned back on— if a whole lot dimmer than it used to be. However, I knew that this marked the end of my security. I hadn’t packed any batteries, and if the light were to have gone out, I would be forever victim to the place.

Though, there was something that kept me going on. There was an air to the place. While the hospital might’ve started to seem far less hospitable than it had at the beginning of my journey, its initial mysteries remained in my head. It gave me a sort of drive and motivation. Even if there was nothing beyond what I could see, and even if I was wasting my time and my security, I wasn’t willing to leave without knowing for certain. I wasn’t willing to leave until I had satisfied the intuition in my chest.

My entire time in the hospital had been spent walking through the halls. There had been doors each side of them, some of them being wide open. Although, I’d opted to avoid them up to this point. There was a squeamish aspect within myself that didn’t wish to see the horrors that might await me. I’d thought that, behind one f those doors, I might’ve seen something that validated the darkness that surrounded me— something that would make me regret ever entering the rotted entrance doors. However, I flipped this notion on its head when I realized that, even if such things awaited behind the hospital room doors, I would regret my search if I didn’t begin looking.

Without rest, my eyes used every ounce of the flashlight to capture what was within the hospital bedrooms. Many of them were eerie, with torn apart beds, rusting metals, and dead remains of what the hospital once was. I felt an unexplainable squeamishness. If I could, I would’ve crawled out of my own skin and found a way to flee from the area.

However, my curiosity remained. There was an itch in y brain, telling me that somewhere beyond the foresight of my scope of vision there were the answers that I sought. Intuition had proven to be wrong for me time and time again. Though, there was something about the intuition this time. There was something in the way that it made me feel. Once again, I began to feel as if there was some supernatural force acting upon me, making sure that I was able to carry out the task that it had assigned me.

Whether it was God, fate, ghosts, or a figment of my own imagination, I’m not sure. However, it happened that after I’d explored the last room in the building I felt my instinct draw me to a room that I’d largely skimmed over. Unlike the others, it had seemed slightly cleaner, and there wasn’t nearly as much darkness in it— there were cracks in the wall that had allowed light to seep through.

Standing back in front of the door, I smelled the scent of perfume. It was slight and distant— like an old blanket, it had been unraveled to the point that all remaining was a single string. It was arguable that it had become so unrecognizable that it could be considered as something new entirely. For a moment, I even thought that the smell might’ve been entirely in my head.

The smell of perfume wasn’t the only thing that had faded to nearly nothing. The number five had been painted on the door at some point, before beginning to peel and age. Alongside it, it appeared that there were other numbers. However, they had long since faded— I could barely make up their features.

A sudden idea blasted into my head, forcing my head to jerk around. The neighboring doors contained the numbers, “25” and “57”. It was at this point that I came to a realization— the number of the door that I was standing in front of was, “256”— the very same number that had been on the photos that Crusoe had given to me.
Without having any hesitation, I opened the door and came bounding into the room. It didn’t matter to me that it seemed more vacant than the rest of the rooms. I knew what was going on.
“What are you keeping from me,” I whispered under my breath with a smirk.

My smirk didn’t last on my face for very long. Within a few minutes, I saw that there was nothing to be discovered or explored. The room was utterly barren when it came to clues.  I came to the point where I thought that my connections and intuitions had all been a result of mere fluke.

A wail resounded, snapping me up from these gloomy thoughts. I felt my chest pang, with the same pain that might be found in a hundred bruises. If only I could say that the wail was less painful. It had an odd sound to it— a mixture of scraping bone, the screech of a bat, and the cry of a human being. Just the very sound of it made me feel faint, and as if my lungs had been polluted by an abundance of fumes. My stomach lurched, and the world had begun to spiral.

Immediately, I started searching for where it might’ve come from— in that moment I was once again reminded of the wailing that I’d first heard in Miss Prestel’s mansion. The wail resounded three more times, and I continued to look without rest. Every spot in the room had been studied by my eyes, and there wasn’t a speck of dust that hadn’t been studied.

I heard the wail again, but I was still lost to what it might’ve meant. It had come to the point where it almost seemed like the wail was mocking me. It was as if it knew my position, and it had merely approached me top show that I had no hold over it— that no matter what I did, it was a lost cause.

It's in times like these when I wish that my hearing is far better than it is. For many detectives, their hearing is sharp enough to where they could hear a mouse scuttling across the floor. I oftentimes wonder what I wouldn’t give to have hearing like that.

By the thirtieth resounding, my brain had been ransacked with hundreds of possibilities— all of them being false. Though, there was one thing that I’d noticed amidst it all— I’d begun to sense a pattern in the wailing. It was coming in ten second intervals. That is, it came in ten second intervals until every fifth wailing. Those wailings came in five seconds and were typically the loudest of the bunch.

I looked at the floor. It was built from tiles, predominantly white and mixed with black. Every five rows contained all black tiles, while the main rows were a mixture of ten white tiles and three black ones.

Walking to the front door of the room, and standing on the center tile, I waited until the wailing stopped. There was probably a full minute that elapsed before it started back up again. Once it started back up, I turned left on the first wail, stepping on a tile. On the second wail I repeated this. I continued walking in this formation until the fifth wail— on that wail, I turned left.

I repeated this cycle, until the wailing stopped— and I found myself standing on a tile that had been next to a torn bed. Unscrewing one of the bed legs, I kept my focus on the tile and the wails that had since disappeared. Unlike the scent of perfume or the faded door numbers, I wasn’t going to let its sound slip away.

After removing the leg from the bed, I started using it as a crowbar and tried using it to remove the tile from the floor. Slowly but surely, the tile began to move around. At first, it was just a slight movement. Though, by the end of it, the tile had been thrown onto the ground, and a tunnel had been revealed from out of under it.

I had the temptation to jump in, but the tunnel’s black mouth had a way of crawling into my soul and stripping me of my confidence. I felt as if I had a vacuum in my gut, except it was becoming ever more empty. It was as if the longer I stared into the blackness, the more thoughts that slipped away from my mind. My very thoughts united with thoughts that were not my own, but a consciousness that was hidden within the hospital’s grimy depths. I felt so small and insignificant. Not only that, but I gained the feeling that I was trespassing in a place that I was not to trespass in— that I was exploring things that I was not meant to explore.

Feeling uncomfortable with this, I turned around from the dark hole. There was something to it that I couldn’t explain— but I couldn’t stare at it either, to find out answers. The longer that I stared at it, the more that I wanted to turn away. Even if there were answers tie how I felt, it was as if there was a spell over the tunnel— a sort of enchantment that kept me from being able to find such answers.

I started looking around the room for some sort of rope or ladder— I wasn’t willing to jump down the hole without any aid, nor was I willing to jump down without any sort of way of telling what awaited me.

However, then the wailing returned to my ears and I remembered that there must’ve been somebody or something that it had originated from— something that despereately needdd somebody to find out what it was.
Maybe I was insane in doing this, but I threw the bed sheets, pillows, an matress down the tunnel, and prepared to jump down. Though, right before I did, I laughed.
I was always told that I was the sort of person who never looked before they leaped… I thought to myself. I guess that they were right.

My deductive mind wanted to know how somebody could’ve built such a tunnel, or why somebody would even bother building a tunnel in such a desolate place as this. It wanted to know why this particular room had been the one that the graffiti correlated with, or why the lady had printed pictures of them.

However, all that mattered in the moment was that I knew the answer to the wailing and that I figured out how to leave the place forever. I could’ve listened to hundreds of different voices from in my head, but the one that I decided to listen to was the one that had told me to act without considering any other results.

Perhaps that’s what intuition truly is. It’s not some sort of magical force, or something from the heavens that’s directing you to your fate— it’s the decision to let a single voice from in your head to dominate your thoughts. It’s the decision to let everything else around you seep away— to have all of your senses completely disappear— and to have the one thought become the only thing that you sense.
I jumped

Wind rushed past my face, and my arms scraped across the harsh mortar walls that surrounded me. Darkness hugged around my eyes and chest, making me feel as if I were swimming around in an endless tank of blackness. Although, none of this mattered to me for some reason. The jump came as a thrill to me. Similar to an owl, I’d begun to find a sort of thrill in dwelling in the darkness. Similar to a bat, the deep caverns had become my home, rather than the blinding light that surrounded the world outside of me. Truly, the world outside of me had started to seem inconsequential. All that mattered was the hunt, and even that didn’t really matter. All that mattered was feeling alive.

My landing was a dull one— the cushions and mattress had broken my fall, making me feel hardly any of the impact. To my shock, this actually disappointed me to a degree. I felt my chest weakly flutter when my bracing proved to have been for nothing. It seemed that my glorious fall had proved to have been a short one, with it having lived and died with the same length that a spark does.

Now at the bottom of the pit, I realized how rash my decision had been. I was now left with no way back up. Even if I were to have found a way back up, I’d now left a way for somebody to detect my presence here.

However, for some reason, I didn’t find myself slapping myself in the face, or looking at my choice with disapproval. Rather, when I looked back at the decision to jump, I looked back at it in pride. There was something to the decision of jumping and acting on intuition. Perhaps more than the drop itself, I felt alive in that moment. I couldn’t quite understand it, but the feeling was undeniably there. Like a flower that grows without you planting it, the feeling of joy that I’d experienced was something that I couldn’t explain– but it was still very beautiful.

I suppose this helps show that the brilliance in life is in realizing that there is no brilliance in life— that everything we are is just a fragment of what has come before us. The joy that I felt might’ve been unexplainable— but that’s why it was something that contained so much joy. I was able to experience something that I thought I wasn’t allowed or able to experience. While it didn’t entirely make any sense, it didn’t have to.

I pulled the flashlight out of my pocket and began walking through the place that the tunnel had led me too. It was very damp, and full of fallen chunks of dirt and plumbing line. It appeared that the place I was in was some sort of abandoned sewage drain. It appeared to be ancient too, because its entirety was crumbling and decaying. Some parts of it had been entirely reduced to mud, and the only thing that seemed to be holding it together was the remainder of the hospital’s foundation.
“This place could collapse at any time,” I said, as I walked by a massive chunk of dirt that appeared to have fallen from the ceiling above.

As I said this, the whole place trembled. Debris started spraying from everywhere, even finding a way to travel up my nostrils. I looked from a shelter from the downpour, but soon found that there was no way out— I would have to suffer through it. Still, the trembling didn’t stop, and I felt it jolt up my bones, making me feel weak and helpless. It was as if I’d been hit by an oncoming train— all of my senses had begun to dull again, and I felt utterly lost.

At that same moment, my flashlight started to flicker, and my entire view of the place went with it. To help stop it, I smacked the flashlight against my thigh. However, I knew that this was just a temporary fix. If I didn’t find a way out of the sewage area soon, I would have to deal with groping through the darkness
“A little spelunking never heard anybody,” I said, once the shaking of the place had finally begun to cease.

I couldn’t convince myself. No matter how much a con artist might tell somebody that something fake is true, the con artist can never convince himself. I suppose that I was learning that sort of lesson the hard way. As much as I’d liked to tell myself that I could’ve ventured the hospital alone, I was abruptly beginning to see that such was not true— I was far too old to be undertaking the momentous task that I was. Moreover, I was steadily becoming aware of pricking needle that was injecting itself upon each nook of my spine. I wasn’t alone. Whether I was confronting a spirit, a native to the hospital, or some strange incarnation of my conscience that had decided to unveil itself in the worst possible place, I knew that I was being watched by it— and I knew that it was only a matter of time before I’d tested its patience far too much.

“I’d hate to have been the one who had to design this place,” I said to myself, trying to ease the feeling of an invisible, burning stare. “With all of this muck, it must’ve been a nightmare to design. Especially the tunnel— you’d think that somebody who is bedridden wouldn’t even have the energy to construct such a complex structure.”

I laughed to myself, and pretended that it was all a joke. I acted as if the place that I walked through was the product of some sort of childish fantasy— that it wasn’t something that could at all be taken seriously. However, I knew that something wasn’t right at all. There wouldn’t have been any need or a tunnel— especially in a hospital of all places.

I could hear the whispers that sprouted from long-dead, shifty dealings.  I could already see the locked doors, and the thickly knitted curtains. This hospital had so many tales to tell— so many secrets that were hidden amongst the rumpling of age. If only I had a way to decipher what everything might mean— what clues truly mattered.

When I was thinking about all this, I saw that the walls of the underground cavern were covered with the similar sort of graffiti that had been on the alleyway picture. Like an old cultic temple, it was riddled with all sorts of strange markings that suggested a sort of foreign symbolism— a language that had been lost in the depths of time.

The fallen rocks and dirt started to form more of a pattern. There were mounds made into the shape of pedestals. There were holes that clearly signified mud. Rats scurried about where long-decayed bones were. I would’ve checked to see the details of the bones— whether they were that of humans, or some other animal. However, the smothering cloak that surrounded me testified to the worst of the two. I didn’t have the nerve, nor the mettle to challenge it.

Deformity was in everything, to the point that such studying wouldn’t have mattered. I’d seen crookedness form in some of the most malevolent shapes within city depths. Though, this place was something new entirely.

After bashing my foot against a bit of metal, I bent down into the muddy ground and uncovered a bowl— and then several other bowls. They all had remains of some sort pf indiscernible mush in them. Not long after that, I found ropes tied into tight knots, and cuffs that were carved from wood. I also found a stethoscope that had been tied in a similar cuff shape.
What madman could’ve done this? I asked myself.

Although, that wasn’t even the real y question that was on my mind. When I looked at everything, absorbing it all with a complete focus, what I found was complete ugliness— and I couldn’t help but wonder how it had gone under everybody’s eyes unnoticed. I couldn’t help but ask myself how long it had gone on, or if it was still going on.

The wail returned, this time louder than ever. It was confined to my head this time around, but this didn’t change the fact that it hurt my eardrums, and made my chest pound with the same frailty that it had at first hearing it.
What happened to the person that was wailing?
Once again, I was trying to divert my attention. Although, this time, I caught myself.
Will what happened to them happen to me?

Maybe it was all in my head, but the moment that I thought this I swore that I watched my flashlight stop flickering. It appeared that its brightness had increased back to how it had been when I’d first put batteries in it.

Taking this as a sign, I looked up to where the flashlight was pointing— and I saw the remainders of a word on the wall across from me. I walked over there with a terror like no other. I’m not sure by what force it was, but I knew that there was something on the other side of the wall— something important.
Intuition had gotten me passed the door. Intuition had gotten me down the tunnel. Intuition had gotten me terrified.

The flashlight shone upon the wall with a radiance like no other, but this didn’t fool me. When the words on the wall were exposed, all that I could see was something revolting. There were names on it. One of them was the name of Job. The next was the name of.

There were other names on it too— plenty of names. They all contained people who were either missing, or involved in odd crimes. I saw a few that I didn’t know. However, it didn’t matter to me, because next to each name there was a symbol of a star— a star that represented everybody who’d been crossed off the list. Even Miss Prestel was on there.
“This doesn’t make any sense,” I said. “All of these people— all of these crimes are unrelated… They can’t all be run by the same person! This is nonsense.”

Disbelief was flooding through my brain, but none of it changed the names that were on the wall. There was nothing that could erase their marks. They were forever there— just like the hospital, they might’ve been a hideous blight. However, they were there, and there was no wiping them away.

The bottom of the list of names was the only thing that gave me any sort of relief. There were three names that I didn’t recognize there, and they all were lacking a star next to them. I immediately ripped out my notepad, and started scribbling everything down— the marked names, the strange observations I’d made, and the terrifying circumstances that had surrounded everything. However, what I wrote down with the most weight were the three names that hadn’t been crossed off— Margaret Rosemary, Bill Clyde, and Jack Crowley.
Why are they on this list? I wondered to myself.

I didn’t have the answers, but that was only the tip of what left me feeling lost and confused. Not only did I not know why these people were on the list, but I couldn’t understand why anybody was on the list. As somebody who constantly felt as if they knew what the answers were, feeling as if I didn’t have the answers was something that made me feel powerless.

I suppose I’m just going to have to get used to the feeling… Everything seems to be mysterious and uncertain these days… While I hate it, I suppose that nothing can be entirely obvious. That would make things too simple.

Even as I told myself this, I wasn’t accepting of it. I had a part within me that was unwilling to surrender or allow the surrounding circumstances to influence it. It was impervious to all outside influences.

Yet, this might’ve been just as harmful as it was good. I knew that, no matter what happened, I wasn’t going to give up until I found the answers. Although, if there were no answers, I knew that I would be forever at a loss.

As I idly sat in wonder about this, I heard the pattering of sloshing water. For a moment, it carried on with the guise of having been caused by more falling chunks of dirt. However, this falsehood didn’t last for very long. The sound of plunking water came ever closer, drawing in with the craftiness that a lion might use on its prey. I could sense an awkwardness in the air. Mud was caked everywhere— and yet, the sound was coming from the small pools of water. Somebody or something was playing me for a fool.
I moved my flashlight toward the spot where I’d last heard the plink of water, but all it exposed was a rippling pool.

“I know that you’re here!” I said to the echoing drops of water. “There’s no use hiding from me— I’ve caught plenty of people before and arrested them. There hasn’t been a case that I haven’t been able to crack.”
At this point, I was simply trying to appease myself. There was no other sign of another presence. From everything that I could observe, I was alone in the darkness and my delusions.

I clenched my jaw as I thought about this, swiftly turning my neck about so as to make sure there was nothing that I missed. As I did so, I felt my neck strain with the effects of whiplash. Stunted in my abilities, my hand shot toward it, clasping it with its best attempt at a comforting rub.

I was an idiot— such an idiot! I felt another hand clasp around my neck that was not my own. That single clasp was all that it took for the dark spires around me to send me into a spiral. Suddenly my breath halted, and the darkness became ever darker. I’m not sure how long the hand deprived me of breath, but all of my muscles weakened, to the point that my flashlight dropped out of my hand.
I’m not sure what came first after that— the flashlight going dead, or my mind going black. Whichever it was, unconsciousness has stowed the answer away from me…

There were many questions that came out of that journey to the hospital. Some were relevant, and others utterly irrelevant. However, the one question that remains untainted is to whom that mysterious hand belonged to.

After my vision went black and I regained my consciousness inside the hospital building— laying in front of the front door. For some reason, the hand hadn’t bothered to kill me, or capture me. For some reason, it had even put me in a favorable position.

However, that’s not to say that the hand couldn’t have been considered the hand of my enemy. It had stripped me of both my flashlight, the clues that I’d collected, and my notebook. It had even gone so far as to leave my arm horribly wounded, to the point that it seemed broken, and my head battered.

I was tempted to go back into the hospital, and study the place again for myself— to confront the person who’d dared attack me in the dark, while I was unprepared and undefended. However, I didn’t give into that notion due to me feeling sick inside. I was weak, and unable to keep up with the speed in which my thoughts were occurring. The longer that I stood in front of the hospital door, the longer that I felt my head go dizzy, and the pain in my arm grow to a sickening level.
“I need to go to the hospital,” I said, groping my arm. I now had no doubt that it had been shattered. “A good one this time around…”

Hospital beds are funny, in a way. On most beds, you can go and rest, letting your pillow absorb the fears of the day. Not so with hospital beds. When you’re sleeping on one, you’re never really sleeping— you’re just coasting through the hours until the doctor returns, along with your infliction.

As it turns out, not all resting places are ideal for rest… This might not be anything new, but it is new to me. When I really think about it, hospitals should be a place of comfort. Though, the only thoughts that come to mind for me is a sort of impending dread— a dark cloud that’s just waiting to unleash a downpour. I don’t mean to be pessimistic— however, I’m not really the type that’s all for positivity. I’ve learned in my vast experiences that you can’t rely on any place to nourish you back to health.

If only doctors could realize this much. When I came in, they looked at me with a face that contained a mixture of both joy and terror. It wasn’t until I looked through a hospital window and saw my reflection that I realized what they were both glad and terrified about— my face had been utterly battered, and my arm had a large purple bruise streaking down it. I looked far worse than I’d initially thought myself to be.

Perhaps this is just my observation, but doctors have just as much motivation to have hurt people as they do to have healthy people. After all, if the world lacked hurt people, then all hospitals would be out of a purpose. That’s why I wasn’t incredibly pleased when they directed me through their marble halls and placed me on a stretcher— nor was I pleased when their shouts began to fill my ears, and all that I could see were lights and nurses hovering over me.

If there’s any sort of relief of pain in this world, it certainly isn’t inside of the hospital. Rather, it’s outside of the hospital, when you can see the world again— when you can see that your pain is but a small thing in the vast expanse of everything else that’s going on around you…

An hour or two slipped by. They put a bandage around my head, and a cast around my arm. They placed an IV in my arm as well. When I asked them what the bandage was for., they informed me that they suspected I’d suffered from a concussion. I told them these measures were all absurd, but of course they didn’t listen to me— they felt that their expertise far surpassed any opinion of my own.

They were probably right too. I found myself drifting in and out of awareness, watching my surroundings blur and refocus as if they were tides on a morning beach. I wanted to keep my grip on reality, but that was one of my many mistakes. The harder that I forced myself to focus on everything, the more exhausted that I became. I eventually came to a point where I could keep my grip no longer— and I fell into a dark chasm that the nurses dubbed sleep.

However, as I stated before, sleep is foreign to the hospital. Such a thing is but a daydream. There are far too many noises, shouts, squeaking doors, and rumbling machines to ever truly experience rest.

“Curse you,” I whispered to the man who’d inflicted this on me. Even in my intoxicated state, I knew that they couldn’t hear me. Though, this mattered little. There was something to just uttering the words— to declaring them for even the air to hear— that made me feel that some sort of justice had been served. Even if it wasn’t visible to the eyes of anybody else, I knew that something had shifted.
With that, I felt my heartbeat slow. For a moment or two, I felt rest that I’d thought to be unattainable in a hospital.
“How are you?”

My eyes opened slowly, as if their lids were a large van being towed off by a truck. Normally, I would’ve groggily been upset by whoever woke me. However, here, being awake made me feel salvation— with the pain in my neck and the heaviness in my breath, sleep was the unconscious suffering of this pain. AT least while I was awake I could consciously reconcile with it.
I looked up and saw the familiar gaunt shape of Lieutenant Jackson.
“What are you doing here?” I said with a rasp.

“Trying to make sure that you didn’t put your foot in a place where you can’t take your foot out of,” he said, snidely as ever. “You just can’t go a week these days without stumbling into something, now can you?”
Sluggishly, I tried to look him in the eye. However, his eyes were planted on the floor.
“You shouldn’t have gone to that site on your own, Sergeant…”
“I was able to drive back here on my own. I was, at the very least, capable of taking care of myself for a little while.”
Jackson nodded. It was odd— he didn’t seem to have any prepared emotions to dish out. It was as if me becoming bedridden in the hospital had stripped him of his innately sarcastic persona.
“We need good men on the force,” Jackson said, continuing. “Don’t get too comfortable in here…”
“As long as you’re in the room with me, that shouldn’t be too hard…”
I thought that I saw Lieutenant Jackson offer a hint of a smile after I said this— but, it might’ve all been in my head.
“What happened?” he asked, after a moment of silence passed between us.
“That hospital had more in it than I expected it to have…”
Then, I ran him through everything that had happened. Oddly, I found that he seemed more disbelieving after I’d told him the story than he’d looked before I told it.
“Did you know that the doctors are suspecting that you may have suffered extreme brain injury?”
I laughed it off.
“I think that I could diagnose just about anybody with brain injury— it doesn’t mean that it’s true… I’m thinking a hundred miles a minute, Jackson.”
“I can see that…” But don’t you think that there’s a chance everything you observed might’ve been in your head… That you made it all up, after you recovered from your concussion…”
“I didn’t get a concussion, Jackson!” I said, with a shout.
My heart thumped terribly, and my body weakened, making me have to stop and calm myself down for a moment.
“Jackson, you didn’t see what I saw…”
“You were knocked out, and you don’t have any evidence for what you saw… It was all probably just a figment of your imagination.”
“there were the names of all of the victims to crimes…” I continued. “There were so many things connected to the police force mapped out in there.”
Lieutenant Jackson held back a laugh.

“You’re expecting me to believe that all of the crimes that we’ve been dealing with for the past two months are all staged— by somebody in an underground cave? You need to wake up and listen to yourself.”
I nodded in agreement with him, but I could hardly hear a word that he was saying. I knew that I knew the truth— nothing that he could say was going to shake me.

“I’ll tell you what…” Jackson said, with a chuckle. “You heal up, and get better. After that, you can go back to the hospital and find all of the evidence. If you found it once, you can find it again.”
