If it hadn’t been for the act that Jackson had gone to all the trouble of finding me in my hospital bed, and entertaining me, I would’ve scowled at him. The very thought of returning to that hospital made me lurch inside. Both he and I knew that I wasn’t going to be returning there.
“Please,” I said, giving him a pleading gaze. “You have to believe me. Nobody else will…”
“I believe that you saw something down there, Sergeant… I just don’t know how much of it was in your head.”
He turned around to leave, but he halted before he made it through the door.
“One other thing,” he said. Then, he pulled my notebook out of his pocket, and tossed it to me.

I held the notebook in my hand. Its leather spine brought me back to the dark, muddy tunnel. I could smell the stink of sewage again, and feel the trepidation in the air– my hand scribbling against its white sheets, putting down as many words as my hand and pen would allow me.
“How did you find this?” I asked him, with a snap.

I wasn’t sure if my words had come out too harshly, or if he was simply uncomforted by the question. Though, whatever it was, he didn’t answer me for a little while. He hung on my words for as long as he could, avoiding the utterance of clear words. All that came out of his mouth was a jumbled mess.
Finally, some coherence came from his tongue.

“We went to the abandoned site, to check the premises for the person that assaulted you. We couldn’t find anybody, or even a sign of anybody— other than yourself, of course. It seemed that the place has been completely deserted for years, which is strange when one considers your injuries. However, we did manage to find your notebook. It was left in the hospital hall, a good distance away from the door. If you’d had it on you the whole time, it definitely didn’t seem like it. We suspect that somebody had taken the notebook from you, like you said…”
“Were there any missing pages?” I asked.
Jackson’s brow furrowed.
“No,” he said, almost disappointed. “You can look in there for yourself. To be honest, we couldn’t find anything— not even a fingerprint. That is, other than your own.”
He was solemn for a moment, before breaking the awkward silence with a jolt of laughter.
“If you really did write things down, then the only explanation would have to be magic!”

He kept laughing, allowing me no room to speak. In fact, I think it was partially intentional— he didn’t want to hear what I had to say anymore. I could tell just by the way that he looked at me. An awkward curtain had been drawn between us. It made sure to hide any of the relationship that we’d previously been sprouting between each other.

Though, I can’t say that Jackson’s words weren’t extremely convincing. I flipped through the notebook myself. There were no notes, nor any sign of notes. If I really had written things down, it had magically disappeared.
Maybe I just thought I was writing things down. I thought to myself. It was really dark in there. It would’ve been pretty easy to make myself think that I was writing words down when I really wasn’t.
However, even those words couldn’t convince me. Something didn’t make sense, and nothing was adding up. That is, besides Jackson’s conclusion— I’d gone delusional.
“Thank you for this,” I told him.

Though, I was lying through my teeth. All that I could feel inside of myself was an incredible fear— a terror over battling with logic, and what I knew was true. Nothing was adding up for me. And yet, I knew that I couldn’t allow this to knock me to the ground. I was forced into an uncomfortable balance in between both viewpoints, constantly wondering which one I should turn to.
After all— if I couldn’t even trust myself, or what was going on around me, then what could I trust? Could I really trust anything?
Trust was becoming a constant dilemma for me. Although, it wasn’t as prominent as it was then.
As Jackson walked off, and gave the door a click of finality, I fell back into my pillow. A wave of concern fell over me.
“I’m not going to give up on where I’m going,” I finally said. “I don’t care that I can’t understand what’s going on… I’m going to keep looking for explanations. And, I’m going to find one.”
I didn’t know whether or not I could see my words as true or false. However, in that moment, they meant mountains to me.

It was about a fortnight before I was given my papers and completely discharged from the hospital. In that time, I entertained myself through torturous naps that were filled with discomfort, and overlong stares at the pale ceiling. What I found is that, when you look at something long enough, you start to see it as something it isn’t. Its simplistic features might morph into a face, or something else that you recognize. Though, in doing so, it becomes something nearly unrecognizable from what you first saw it as.

I suppose that the same could be said for my injuries. While I’d gone to the hospital in the mere desire to make sure that I hadn’t sustained any terrible damages, it turned out that there was much more going on than I’d originally thought. My charade of false invincibility was shattered in doing so— I no longer was able to feel secure in thinking that I could never be injured to a point of extreme weakness. Part of this was due to everything that I’d gone through. However, another part of it was due to an overwhelming pride that I held inside of myself. I’m not entirely sure where it came from— but, I started to feel that it might have been hindering me in more ways than I’d like to acknowledge.

I found that my thinking had started to slow. I felt sluggish. Every minute seemed to pass by with a greater rapidity than the last, and my ability to keep up with it was draining empty. It was as if the world had suddenly gained the speed of a cheetah, and my own speed had been reduced to that of a sloth.

Chicago’s skies and streets didn’t seem to feel any better than I did about the current state of things. Rain had returned to slather everything.  At night, when all there was to light everything were the kerosene street lamps, the roads started to look and smell like burning wax. Amongst the city’s drool, there was also a return of the roaches and rats. I couldn’t always see them, but whenever I tried leaving my apartment door for an evening stroll, I found that there were footsteps following my own. Every time my foot splashed against runny gravel, there was another splash echoing in my midst. It had reached a point where my apartment had become my bunker— my prison.
Just like the streets, I could only go so long before I began melting like a candle.

My investigations had once again come to a rearing halt, and everything had started to slow. I’d considered looking the people’s names who were written on the wall up— but, for one reason or another, I’d decided to push it aside. I simply couldn’t focus on any of it. I felt as if I was lost in a soup of work, and the thought of digging into more was heavying.

There were a few petty crimes that I meddled in, but nothing of consequence. The only things of importance were an identification of the chemicals I’d found on Miss Prestel’s window sill, as well as a letter that I made out to Miss Prestel subsequently. I informed her that I thought it important for me to search her premises for any missed clues. As expected, she was tardy with giving me a response.
I checked my mail every day— it was one of the few things that I was willing to leave my apartment for. Yet, there was no sign of anything. Only on Monday was there a letter for me.
It was a yellow letter, marked with a pretty stamp of a sun.
“Stamps these days,” I remarked.  “You’d think that, with their constantly increasing prices, they’d try minimizing the amount of money they spend to design them.”

In spite of my harsh reply, I was reeled in by the letter’s warm design. It reminded me of something distant— something long past. Even its smell, of a strange lavender perfume, offered me fuzzy memories that I couldn’t quite grasp. It wasn’t until I read who the letter came from that I realized why this was.
“Amelia Mulligan,” I said with a chuckle. However, that quickly faded into a frown.

Amelia Mulligan was the charismatic and outgoing sister of Eddy. Unlike her brother, she’d always been somebody who showed great potential— a rare sight in a high school. As time went on, she found a man, and left Chicago with him. It was one of those relationships that died down quick, never to be discussed again— similar to a plant that one neglects to water, and forgets entirely about. While both the planter and the plant might go on with their lives without the support of one another, far more changes than what seems. Without the reliance of one another, they fail to work as a unit.
I didn’t know why Amelia would’ve bothered to send me a letter at now of all times, but I already had my suspicions— and they weren’t comfortable to think about.

I went inside of my apartment and opened the letter. I felt a sense of wariness while doing so, but I also had an unexplainable sense of excitement. The mixture of both trepidation and anticipation was one that I didn’t have any clear feelings about. However, it still left me feeling a sense of fulfillment. I couldn’t explain why this was. Though, I did know that I liked it.
The moment that I opened the letter, I realized that my suspicions had been correct.
Dear Mr. Kyler,
It has years since we last spoke, and I’m sure that this letter might come as a surprise to you. However, you’re the only person that I could think to write a letter to.
As I’m sure you already know, my brother, Eddy Mulligan, has gone missing. If I’m not mistaken, I believe that you were a witness to this crime.

Now that it’s been nearly a month and there’s still no sign of him, I regret to state that he’s now legally dead. I, along with the rest of my family, will be gathering in Chicago to host a funeral for him. It’s the only thing that we can do to honor his memory.
You’re the only true friend of his that I actually knew. So, I incite you to join us. It will be taking place in St. Peter’s Cemetery, on Grover’s Road, August 15th…
Thank you for your time— both on his case, as well as us. I hope to see you again soon.
Sincerely,
Amelia

I’m not sure why, but I was both shocked and depressed by the contents of this letter. Even though I’d expected it to concern Eddy’s funeral, there was something about actually reading it that gave it a signature of finality. I now knew that, no matter what I did, Eddy’s gravestone was going to be planted in the ground. Even if I were to find Eddy, it wouldn’t change the fact that we’d spent hours mourning over him.

I’m typically a strong man— though, something in me snapped at the completion of the letter. I found myself stumbling to a chair, covered in tears. My face became red and blotchy. Despite this, I no longer cared. I no longer felt a thing. Even in my pain, all that I was willing to acknowledge and experience was the fact that my friend had died— and I was only just now beginning to see it.

This was probably an inevitable thing. After all, I wouldn’t have invested days into my research, and unearthed Crusoe again if I hadn’t thought that I had a shot at saving Eddy. Now, I knew that there was no chance. I knew that I was too weak to make any sort of difference. I knew that I’d been stuck in my head for far too long, to the point where it had clouded m entire experience of reality.

Frailty is a thing that most like to disregard. However, in the moment of sitting in the chair, with my face flooding with water, I started to see a side of myself that I often liked to avoid seeing— the side of myself that, no matter how strong it makes itself out to be, can never stand and face death without being reduced into something laughable. I’d begun to see a difference between myself and Crusoe—— one that I’d once thought to be my weakness, but now saw as a clear strength. No matter how many mistakes I made, and no matter how weak I proved myself to be, it only proved my humanity. It only reaffirmed what I actually was. Meanwhile, Crusoe would forever hold himself in a place of high esteem— thus setting himself apart from the rest of people, as well as the truth.

I’m not entirely sure why Crusoe came into my head immediately after I found out that the world had decided Eddy Mulligan was dead. Though, I think that it might have to do with how opposite they are. Despite being poor and clueless, Eddy Mulligan was honest about it all when he returned to me. He wasn’t afraid to speak the truth. He wasn’t afraid to give me a warning, even when it was at the risk of himself.

Detective Crusoe? He’s the sort of friend that will leave for years, and come back to make you regret letting them leave. I’m not even sure why I’ve entertained him, other than the fact that he has extensive inductive abilities. I’m starting to see why I don’t like Crusoe more clearly than I ever have— it’s because he’s constantly making mistakes, yet never admitting to them— constantly holding himself to a higher standard, although never doing any better than the rest of us.

Perhaps I’ve become to verbose in my dealings with past bitterness. However, if there’s anything that I’ve learned from Eddy’s death, and the letter that I received, it’s that writing things down has an effect on how you perceive the world. It can make dark things into light, and light things into dark. Words don’t have any magical power, but the person who speaks them must change in order to speak words. That’s why words are so strong. They have the ability to alter thoughts. And, thoughts are the directions for which we change the world.

Even the smallest alterations can cause such a massive shift. We can never see how the butterfly beating its wings brings change. Yet, the very fact that we’ve acknowledged how it can change things has changed our perception of things.

This is why I’m never going to forget Eddy Mulligan, even as his memory in everybody else’s mind fades away. I know that he stood for something precious. I can’t let that slip out of my fingers. I can’t let that disappear.

Heat chews at the back of my neck. As my neck bakes, it begins to turn red and raw— a contradictory phenomenon. One might think that the sun would cook its meal to make it less raw, not rawer. It’s shocking that it’s even capable of doing such a polarizing feat. Though, this shouldn’t surprise me. It seems that the sun likes breaking the laws of nature, and making me feel uncomfortable while doing it. Perhaps it only chews on me so that it can leave me with something to chew on.

I would look into the sky and curse, but that option isn’t allowed to me. The sun has made it so that I can’t look upon its deep, yellow figure without losing the ability to look altogether. There is something to it— the eyes find it to be both harrowing and refreshing at the same time.

My eyes finally turned away from its battle with the sky, and squinted to revive its view of the world around it. I couldn’t quite grasp why or how, but somehow heat found its way into my life. While I’d been trapped in the affairs of my business, it had slunk through the clouds and crashed onto the pavement. If it were but an affliction of the sun, then I couldn’t wrap my mind around how the sun hadn’t been so powerful before now.
It was as if the sun itself was trying to respect the memory of my passed off friend— it was as if its heat was emulating his speedy lifestyle. At least, that’s how my spotted sight perceived it.

Everywhere, the world was steaming and boiling. I felt as if I were drowning within a world of flames. This was an odd shift, considering how cold of a summer that the city had been enduring. Though, Chicago isn’t swayed by the will of the people. It’s a wild beast, which can only be tamed by its own will—not anybody else’s.

My feet grinded against the pavement, but its sound was quelled by the roars of cars rushing by. I frowned in annoyance, but quickly grinned— the noises had been far louder a decade ago, back before all of the cars started being sold off for cheap scrap metal.
So much has changed, I thought. It feels like that decade was but a day— and yet, it also feels like a lifetime.

On a normal day, I would’ve been driving with the rest of the whizzing cars, allowing their noise to become a sort of guiding tunnel, from which I traveled through. It felt far more freeing, and it made me feel as if I were somewhat above the city. However, today I walked through the city with the wish to feel one with it. I wanted to be able to absorb every crack on the sidewalk, drink up every crumbling bit of brick, and taste the vibrance in the air. As much time as I felt I might’ve been wasting, I wanted to feel as if I were living life to the fullest, and truly representing the memory of Eddy. I wanted to feel as a part of the world around me again. In the even to f realizing that Eddy was finally gone, there was a portion of me that realized how short life was, and how fragile everything is. All it might take is a few failed breaths to strip all that I know from my eyes. There was a terrifying element to knowing this, and a relieving element as well.
While I felt that Eddy was most likely gone, I also felt that I was a sort of remainder of him. In me, a part of him still lived on. I was trying to linger on that.

Surprisingly, I found that the sun didn’t really get to me. Unlike during my journey to the hospital, I felt free under it. Even with my arm in a cast, I had a sense of levitation. There was nothing that could hold me back— I could fly.

During all of these sensations, I’d almost forgotten where I was going to. However, all it took was standing in front of some rusted metal gates to be reminded again. The exuberant atmosphere of Prestel Manor was surrounding me again. It gave off an extremely unique feeling. Despite me standing in one-hundred-degree weather, I could’ve sworn that I felt cooler by the gate. It was as if they were able to reach inside of me, and cool me off.

Colors, smells, and even my own thoughts, all became more extreme in the presence of it all. The little boy inside of me was convinced that I was standing in a wonderland. Maybe it was because I was all alone, or maybe I was more receptive— however, Prestel Manor had gained a sense of magic about it that I hadn’t noticed the last time I was there. What used to appear as flamboyant now seemed strange… and mystical.

Miss Prestel had finally responded to my pleas of reinvestigating her household. This time around, I’d neglected to inform Lieutenant Jackson—while he’d offered me a hand of friendship, I still had feelings of distrust towards him.

As I stood in front of the gate on my own, waiting for Miss Prestel, I came to a mind-shattering realization of how alone I was in my work. I’m not sure what induced it, but I came to the full realization of how alone that I was all the time— and how much easier things might be if I were to allow the hand of friendship to come upon me, and alter the course of everything that I was doing.

There was a sudden moment where I felt as if I were trapped in a cage, and I was just running around in a hamster wheel. Running around, thinking that I was going somewhere, but really running nowhere at all.

I wiped my arm across my forehead. Sweat had begun streaking down it, out of my stress. My thoughts would’ve continued to focus on how alone I felt, even amongst the calls and coos of nature. However, the door of the gates of the manor started to screech before I could get that deep into thought.
“It’s nice to see you again sir,” I heard the butler say.

I turned to face him, and saw his familiar face. It’s odd how easy it is to remember faces, even if you’ve seen them only once. His graying hair, almond brown eyes, and chiseled but prune-like complexion made a striking call of memory to my mind. Maybe it’s just something that I’ve noticed because of being a detective. Though, I’ve begun to suspect that this is a strange aspect of human nature. Either way, I caught something in his face that hadn’t been there the first time that Id met him. His pale skin had gone extremely red, and his mouth was wide open, huffing and puffing. His nostrils were flaring also. His entire body had been poised into a position of exhaustion— it looked as if it had been overcome by an incredible force.
“It’s nice to see you too, Mr. Gretchen.”
He nodded curtly, and then turned to guide me down Miss Prestel’s driveway.

“The Mistress has been looking forward to your return,” he said, with a hint of sarcasm. “She says that she hadn’t expected you to come back, after your first visit… There was something about you being knowledgeable about everything you need to know…”
As he said this, I heard a few birds screech overhead, and I felt a slight tingle down my back.

“Yes well, there were a few things that we saw here that we never fully addressed,” I said. “There was some sort of acid on the windowsill, if you recall… There’s also a few things that I’d like to speak with you about…”
I watched Eustace’s face begin to look more tired.
“And what would that be, exactly?” he asked.

“I want to talk to you once we’re inside the manor… I don’t feel very comfortable out here. Not that it’s anything to get worked up about. I only want to ask you these questions because I feel that they’re things Miss Prestel would never honestly answer herself. She— she has the habit of exaggerating things in her letters, and during our chats.”
Mr. Gretchen chuckled.

“Oh, yes… She can become very exaggerative at times. However, I assure you that there’s nothing for you to be concerned about in here. Miss Prestel hasn’t suffered from any new incidents, and I’ve found that the place has become extremely quiet since your last visit. Perhaps it’s all in my head, but you act as a sort of crime repellant.”
Another bird screeched, and I felt my ears ring terribly again. My eyes snapped to the position of the noise’s origin, and found a crow in its place.
“When did you get those?” I asked. “I don’t remember them being here last time I was here.”
Mr. Gretchen’s face construed, but he kept walking.
“We’ve always had them…” he said. “If you recall, there was a loud screeching noise in the lower floor. That was because a crow had found its way in.”
But crows aren’t inherent to Illinois, I found myself thinking. Though, I didn’t say a word. I found that Mr. Gretchen was far more willing to talk when I put my prying comments to a minimal.

He laughed nervously, and then opened the door to the manor. I was surprised at how fast we’d gotten there— I could’ve sworn that the drive through the driveway, with Lieutenant Jackson, had been just as quick as the walk had been. It seemed that Mr. Gretchen had sped up the walk as much as he could, and he was even trying to rush through the conversation. For a moment, my thoughts turned inward, thinking that Mr. Gretchen was acting nervous due to something about me. although, I started to see how quickly he turned the knob to the door, and how he leaped into the room. There was something to him that was terrified by me. He was trying to get thing over with as quickly as possible.
“I’m sure that you’re familiar with these passages by now,” he said, gesturing to the massive hall.

I couldn’t have felt more opposed to Mr. Gretchen inference. The whole place still looked to be a labyrinth. In fact, it was even worse for me this time around. It had turned extremely stuffy and enclosed in the heat of the day. In a sense, I felt as if the house itself had begun to coil around m, and choke me of my breath. My head steadily began to ache and throb.
“How about the kitchen?” I said.
I could tell that Mr. Gretchen ad been preparing for me to lead the way.  Though, in spite of his reluctance to do so, he started walking through the halls to the kitchen.
“Where’s Miss Prestel?” I asked, as I passed a few of her odd monkey statues.
“In her chambers, probably still preparing herself,” he said. “You know how women are… Normally, she has my assistance, so that’s probably why she’s taking a bit longer than usual.”

On the spur of the moment, he clapped his hands together. Then, he pointed towards the kitchen. Unlike last time, it no longer smelled of chemicals, and the window had been completely repaired. The marble tile also looked cleaner than it had before.
“You’re amazing at keeping this place up,” I said, in an attempt to compliment him.

He made the face that normally would’ve been followed by a laugh— but no laugh came out. Instead he said, “Yes, you wouldn’t believe how much work Miss Prestel had me invest into cleaning up this house. She’s rather obsessed with making sure that her guests don’t walk through a mess…”
“Trust me, it’s far nicer than my apartment…”
I grinned, but he failed to grin back.
“So, I see that you repaired the window,” I said, attempting to change the subject.
His face lit up.
“Yes, I pit quite a lot of work into having the filthiness in the kitchen repaired… Your first impression of the place was extremely unjust towards its pure form.”
I couldn’t deny the truth in this. The whole place seemed to be just as cheery as the front yard had been. Although it was primarily colored with whites and silvers, it had a dazzling personality.
“So, I assume that you must have cleaned up all of the evidence that had once been here,” I said, looking up at the window.”
“The best that I could… I purposely clean up to make sure that the place is bleached to the eyes of people like you,” he said, jokingly.
This time, it was my turn to not laugh.

“Did you happen to find anything strange while you were cleaning?” I asked. “Such as odd residue? I’m particularly looking for something that looks like it might’ve come from a sort of gas. I suspect that your robber might’ve been using them.”
Gretchen shook his head.
“No sir… I found quite a lot of abandoned grime and dust, though I doubt that any of it could’ve been attributed to a gas.”
“I see…”
I didn’t entirely believe him— I was suspicious of Gretchen’s character. However, I was forced to believe that he was telling the truth.
“I have a few other questions for you,” I said. “As we both know, there was the acid on the window. Did you happen to find anything strange around there? I know that it was a curious occurrence…”
“Hard as I tried, I couldn’t find anything remotely unusual in the kitchen around the acid. However, I assume that you know this. It has been like this since you last arrived…”

“Right,” I said, compliantly. “Now, one of the chemicals used in the acid, from what the forensics department has been able to identify, is sodium hydroxide… Do you recognize it? It’s used in many cleaning supplies, and is extremely corrosive to the skin when at its most concentrated level.”
Mr. Gretchen scowled at me, but placed his hands behind his back just as they were clenching into fists.
“I think it’s rather rash to suggest that I had a hand in this,” he said, putting on a false smile.

“I never suggested that you were the one who did this,” I said. “If anybody is being rash, it’s you. I’m merely asking if you had any knowledge or prior experience with the chemicals. I want to know if there’s anything that I might want to look out for.”
“None that I’m aware of, sir.”

He was about to pull his hand back out as he said this, but then forced himself to keep it behind his back. As he did so, I saw a bit of skin stick out from under his gloves. It was extremely scarred and damaged looking. I was about to point it out, but I forced myself to neglect it.
“I have one last question,” I said.
Mr. Gretchen looked as though he were about to roll his eyes, but was restraining himself.
“And what might that question be?”
“I need you to tell me if Miss Prestel or you are familiar with any of these names…”
I then gave him the list of the three names that I’d remembered seeing on the hospital walls.
Mr. Gretchen laughed.

“I don’t know any of these people,” he said, in probably the most confident tone that he’d provided me during our entire conversation. “I’m not sure where you retrieved theses names from, but I don’t recognize any of them. Unless Miss Prestel is hosting gatherings under my nose, of which I’m not aware about.”
He laughed boisterously again.
“Well, thank you anyway,” I said, taking out my notepad and putting down everything that we’d discussed. “Now, I’d like to speak with Miss Prestel. Where is she?”
Mr. Gretchen’s laughter was instantly squelched.
“I’m not sure,” he said, nervously. Then, he ran towards the exit of the room. “Let me go check on her. She— she probably got tied up in her jewelry again! You can stay here.”

He broke into a run— surprising for a man who constantly held such a regal composure. However, I found the sight of him more humorous, than anything else. As he walked off, his attire chafed awkwardly, and he almost looked as if he were acting in a sped up waddle.

I sat there for about ten minutes, waiting for him to return with Miss Prestel. These ten minutes were extremely unbearable. Not just because of how stuffy the mansion had begun to feel, or because of the length of the wait, but because of the knife Mr. Gretchen had put in my plans. I’d strategized everything so that I would be able to talk with Miss Prestel in private, where Mr. Gretchen’s prying ears and eyes wouldn’t have any clout. However, I was certain that, when he returned with Miss Prestel, he’d also be returning to hear what I had to say. Therefore, I’d be able to say and ask far less of questions.

When the ten minutes had finally ended, Miss Prestel’s prune complexion came sticking out of the exit, and was followed by the rest of her. At first, I thought that I’d been wrong about Mr. Gretchen, and that he might come to respect my and Miss Prestel’s privacy. However, he followed soon after, and I was stuck in the room with the pair of them.
“Hello,” Miss Prestel said, croaking louder than ever. “Mr. Gretchen informs me that you wish to speak with me.”

Despite her having taken at least half an hour to prepare, Miss Prestel looked incredibly haggard. Makeup and perfume were smeared all across her face, with about the grace and thought that might be put into clown makeup. And, her clothes were no better— she adorned a dress of sorts that was shaped into a giant, rainbow-striped sphere. As she walked around in it, it looked as if she were an oversize bowling ball— a bowling ball that was as random, flamboyant, and disorienting as anything that might come out of a circus. The outfit was extreme, even for the extremeness that I’d come to associate Miss Prestel with.

“That’s correct. I’m happy to see you, face to face again,” I said. “I know that we’ve talked a lot in our letters, but I think that speaking in person is the best way for us to communicate with each other.
Miss Prestel’s bottom lip stuck out, and her eyes squinted.

“Our letters…” she said, racking her mind for a moment. “Ah yes— I think I have a faint memory of them. If you wanted to talk, you should’ve come sooner. I’ve invited you many times, my dear. If you worried that such might put me out, remember— a legend, such as myself, has no qualms with guests you know.”
I opened my mouth, to remind her that she’d actually insisted that I don’t come— however, I let the objection fall to the side. I quickly realized that it wasn’t something of consequence.
“I just wanted to know if you’ve been downtown recently— specifically Jonah’s printing shop.”
Her eyes lit up, as if they were miniature lightbulbs.
“I’m always heading downtown,” she said. “I love it there— the fancy lights, the wonderfully paved streets, all of the nice people, and the clean buildings… It’s the perfect place to be.”
I looked up at Mr. Gretchen, but he was despondent. I knew that my only chance at finding out the truth would be in continuing to decipher Miss Gretchen’s claims.
“So, you’ve been to Jonah’s Printing Shop?” I asked.
“Of course. Isn’t that the place where they… where they… where they print things?”

Clearly seeing that I wasn’t getting anywhere, I tried a different approach. Yanking out the pictures from my pocket, I said, “Do you happen to recognize any of these? They’re some names that I found in my investigations.”
Miss Prestel looked at them.
“Yes, I know these! They were all very close friends of mine, before they turned into treacherous scum...”
At this point, I knew that Miss Prestel was willing to say yes to anything. However, there was one last thing that I wanted to ask her about.
“Are these your pictures?”
I showed her the images of the woman in the hospital, and the man carrying the monkey-like statue.
“Yes, yes I do!” she said, ecstatically. “I took these thirty years ago!”
“Well then—  I suppose that I have no more questions to ask…” I said.
“Good on you!” Mrs. Prestel said. “You’re doing a fine job at solving the case of my robbery! Keep at it, sport, and you might just get to the answer.”
She patted me on the back as well as she could in her stiff outfit, and then tottered over to Mr. Gretchen.
I motioned to Gretchen that I had a final word to ask him about. He nodded, and then pulled Miss Prestel away, back toward her chambers.
As he came back, he had a far more receptive grin than I’d ever seen him with.
“What is your question?” he asked me, cheerily.
I looked down the hall where a monkey statue was.  Mr. Gretchen’s eyes followed.
“Do you know where she might’ve gotten the idea to keep all of these statues?” I asked. “I know that this might seem to be prying… However, I feel that it might be very relevant to the case at hand.”
Mr. Gretchen looked surprised, but retained his grin.

“I don’t actually know where she might’ve picked up the obsession,” he said. “I know that, in Miss Prestel’s middle age, she was obsessed with safaris to Africa, and becoming the next great explorer. Perhaps it’s linked to that? To be honest, she’s had an obsession with monkeys ever since I’ve been in her service, and I have yet to find a reason for it. Being the gentlemen that I am, I don’t pry in Miss Prestel’s personal life very often, unless she discloses it to me. Whatever the explanation is, I’m certain that it’s mostly innocent. You talked to her yourself— she doesn’t have a strong enough memory to tell you what a fly is, let alone the ability to hurt one.”
I chuckled.

“I guess you’re right in saying that,” I said. Then, I looked out the now-repaired window. “Well, I’m happy to have been able to talk to you and Miss Prestel again. It’s good to see that you’re doing well, in spite of our current struggles and the recent burglary. Hopefully this information will help me in the future.”

“Yes…” Mr. Gretchen said. “It was nice talking with you too. Hopefully you find the answer to our case so that our struggles subside. However, I don’t think that you’ll have to worry too much— with F.D.R now in office, we might just see all of our problems come to a halt.”

I smiled and agreed with him, before going on my way. As I was halfway down Miss Prestel’s front-yard path, I heard the door shut behind me with a both comforting and familiar click. However, just before I heard the door click, I looked behind myself and took one last look at the house. I could’ve sworn that I saw Mr. Gretchen staring at me through the remaining slit of the door, giving me an uncomfortably devious look. However, the door closed before I was able to tell if it was in my head or not.
With that in mind, I left Miss Prestel’s house with the same feeling that I’d had when I’d entered it— confliction and confusion.
I arrived at my street with my mind still in shambles. Somehow, the sun had managed to sink back into the horizon, and get over the troubles of the day. Yet, I wasn’t able to.

For a while, I thought that the confliction within my head was something that I’d be able to get over with during sleep. Although, now that I’d reached my street, my questions had started to solidify. I now realized, with extreme clarity, that there was no way for me to be able to save myself from the confines of my mind. At least, not until I figured out what I was supposed to do, and where the answers lied.
“Where do you answers lie?” I wondered. “And how do I know whether or not you’re a lie?”
I was distracted from this when I heard scraping feet tearing against the pavement. They weren’t just scraping feet— they were running feet.

Throughout my years, I’d learned that you can’t run in Chicago. If one decides to scrape their feet against their pavement, grasping towards their destination, the street will subsequently scrape against that person, grasping them into a new destination.

There is no rushing in Chicago. If one tries to, they’ll be knocked to their feet, and will be begging for mercy. Yet, these feet— while I couldn’t see the face of their owner— wouldn’t stop running. Their pace wouldn’t slow. I listened as their feet started scraping to the point that it sounded like one long scrape— but, it didn’t stop. It just kept going. I started to grow uncomfortable. My mind flashed through images of other criminals that I’d met— the noises of their own scraping feet. The scraping of Job.

I slowed down, and used the only sense that I could had— my ears. My street is among the cheaper ones, having only few lampposts, and no lampposts that actually functioned. I was compelled to pull out my flashlight, and to direct it towards the person who was running off— however, I knew that it would only give them awareness of my presence, and cause them to run off even faster.
I stood as still as I could, and listened to the rapid succession of scraping.

One second— the scraping seems indiscernible from the randomized mechanisms from a machine— another second— it’s becoming clearer now— another— it has the rubbery squeal of the sole of a shoe to it— another still— it’s become louder as I’ve listened to it. The pursuer is coming towards me!

As this last thought came into my mind, I dove forward. It could’ve been by chance or sheer luck, but the runner jumped over me, and kept going afterward. I couldn’t tell much about them, or where they were going. However, when I looked back after them, I managed to catch a bit of their body shape. They were tall, and thin— the perfect body type for a runner. Other than that, I had nothing else to go by.

I groaned as I pulled myself up from the pavement. The left side of my face felt as if it had been shoved into a fire pit, and the left side of my body felt as if it had one big bruise along it. Due to the fact that my right arm was stuck in a cast, I had to roll myself over, and then Pull myself back up with my left arm. I must’ve looked hilarious while doing this, but I felt completely miserable.

As I hobbled back to the house, my mind was busied with the curses that I was whispering under my breath. Though, the thing that I should’ve been focused on followed after me, until I’d made my way inside my apartment— what had the runner been running from?

Normally, I knew exactly what I was going to do when I got inside the door in my house. Though, tonight, I found that I was at a loss. I was leaning on my wall, staring at my telephone when I realized this. I didn’t know what to do, or if there were even anything that I was supposed to do.
“You’re one poor lost soul, Kyler…” I found myself saying to myself.
I gripped the telephone on the wall.
“I’m going to have to get rid of you pretty soon,” I said, with annoyance.

Prices had gone up, and my wage had gone down. Though, I didn’t have time to bother with focusing on any of it. My head felt as if it were being pulled in a million different places, like a piece of dough that a dough maker doesn’t know what to bake into.

“I can’t tell if I should be doing this anymore, or not…” I said to myself. “If this is supposed to be what I need to do, then I probably can’t do it anymore… I used to think that this all had a meaning in it— that serving out justice, finding right from wrong, and looking for the evidence that nobody else could find was a good thing. However, none of this matters, in the grand scheme of it all. That is, none of this matters, except to me…”
I sighed, and wiped my forehead.
“It’s making me superstitious of everything, and more tired than a man of my age should be. The streets are far too dark for somebody like me, who’s flickering out, will be able to light up.”

I put my hands in my pocket, and looked at a picture that was hanging on my wall— a picture of me, standing all alone in the dark, next to the lamppost by the police station. Crusoe had taken it, back when I and him were still working together.
“At least that lamppost is still working alright…” I said.

Though, then I took a closer look at the picture, and saw something disconcerting— the glass pane overtop the frame was cracked and broke, looking as if somebody had dropped it onto the floor and placed it back where it was on the wall. I ran over to it, and then saw that the picture wasn’t the only thing that had been damaged. The wall itself had damages on it— puncture marks, holes, big markings, and, scratches. My coffee table that had been near there was knocked over onto its side, and my chest on the other wall had its lock completely torn off.

I felt my heart race, to the point that I thought it might fling out of my chest. I had an urge to scream, but I didn’t know what to scream to or at. I was utterly lost and confused— I was the police officer. I had been robbed.

Realizing that there was nothing that I could do, I let my body slump until it had finally pressed against the floor— until my thoughts had pressed against the floor. My reasoning could go no further. ‘d been robbed, and I didn’t even know who it had been by. I didn’t even have the energy to bother looking for who it might’ve been by.
“This stuff just never stops,” I said, under my breath.

I could hear a clock on my wall, ticking slowly— and then slower. M heartrate slowed with the ticking of the clock. Everything slowed— every noise, ever sense in my body. Then, I suddenly felt it all begin to rush again, and an energy funneled through me and out of my mouth.
“It just never stops!” I yelled again, this time loud enough to awake my neighbors in the other rooms.
When I was done shouting, I found my fist in the wall to the left side of me, filled with a tent that was just as big as the dents next to my picture of Crusoe.

“I just don’t get it…” I whispered. “Nobody else seems to deal with this… I always am the one who gets the brunt of everything, always having to clean up after other people’s messes— I’m constantly looking for a plateau where it ends, but I honestly can’t tell where that might be. I’ve been looking for that plateau all my career, and it seems all but nonexistent.”

After venting this all out, I found myself laughing. It might’ve just been because of the constant barrage of everything coming to the point where I could no longer even battle it. However, I felt that it was even more than that. I was a police officer, who’d just been robbed. Though, I had no idea what to do about it. I was just as lost as anybody else might be in this situation, even with all of my experience in such matters.

“Is that what this is all about?” I asked, staring at the ceiling. “Am I just supposed to constantly come to the point where I think that I’ve mastered something, only to realize how clueless that I am about everything? Am I to be schooled in even the simplest aspects of my life, to the point where I can no longer hold any self-pride?
“I guess that I should’ve expected it all to come to this.”
I let out a wry chuckle.

I have always been curious why the older cops were always the ones who seemed to be the most clueless— the laziest of the bunch, I thought. Maybe I always saw it wrong. Now that I am the older cop, it’s just because you get tired… Your bones break easier, and they don’t heal as smoothly as they used to… The sunlight goes dimmer, the smaller things turn blurry, and your hearing starts to turn to deafness.

“I still can’t believe that this happened… It seems like complete nonsense. I wouldn’t have ever let something like this fly ten years ago. But, I guess it’s not just me who’s going deaf, either… Everybody is going deaf,” I said.

I wasn’t talking to myself anymore. In my thoughts, I’d decided to call up Lieutenant Jackson, and explain the situation. At first he laughed. Though, I soon found that he had more to relate to me with than I thought that he would’ve.

“Yes, I guess that we can sometimes become the butt of all jokes, can’t we?” Jackson said. “It becomes harder to get away with as much once you come to a point where you’re supposed to have more experience. Personally, I’ve always seen it as a good thing, and a bad thing…”

“But, don’t you agree with me? Don’t you think that everybody is starting to hear everybody else less. It seems to me that nobody matters to the other person anymore. Everybody is being treated the same way these days.”

“And, what would you expect?” Jackson asked. His voice was full of static, but I could still hear him as clear as day, even with my dying hearing. “Over the years, you stopped hearing all of the nonsense going on around you. Then, eventually people came to a point where they had to yell in your ear so that you could hear it. It might seem to you that the nonsense is worse than before. But, it’s only louder than before. And, honestly, that’s just because you can only hear the things that are louder now… We both can only hear the things that our louder…”

“Well, then what am I supposed to do now? I can’t tell the rest of the department, or they’ll laugh me off the force. Nobody else is getting robbed, or letting their own robber get away in plain sight.”

“First off, you need to keep you gun in your hand more often. You’ve gotten soft. Your ringing ears don’t like the sound of gunfire. They probably think that it’s too harsh and cruel— that it is no longer necessary to carry around all the time. Little do the y know how ill-informed that is— little do they know how much they’d regret such in the future. What you and your ears forgot is that gunfire is the only thing that really matters to people who don’t care for the rules of the law. If you ever want to stop a coward in their tracks, the only way to do it is by making a coward out of yourself— by doing the dirty deed that can undo their dirty deed.”

I wanted to refute everything that Jackson had said— I had the habit of wishing to disagree with his claims, due to his typically harsh viewpoint of things. However, there was nothing I could do to take down this particular claim of his. The more I thought about it, the more that I realized that he was right. As I looked out my window, as I found myself doing more often, I remembered all of the dangers that lay outside of it. It’s funny what a window can do— it can make one feel as if they’re not part of the world, and yet, as if they’re part of it anyway. It can make men feel— feel— feel like they’re above everything, and that it’s all just a game of chess for their eyes to feast upon. The dangers are disturbing and unwanted, of course. Though, they’re also far off— they’re things that can easily be dismissed.

Tonight, just like on the night that Jack died, I couldn’t have that same complacent view of everything. The night’s oily streak, on which the cars traveled down, now spoke a warning into my heart. I felt it become tattooed onto me— I couldn’t shake it off any easier than a cat could shake away a ball of catnip. Even as I did, I felt myself compelled to return to it— to chase after it again, and to play around with it, until I’d exhausted myself once more.
“Hey, Kyler? Are you there?”

I realized that I’d let my end of the phone go static. I felt my face redden, but thankfully there was nobody to see it— that was one good thing about communication of phones, no matter how inconvenient they might’ve been.
“Yeah, I’m here…” I said. “You know, that just got me thinking… The whole city is desperate. What if, in doing the dirty deed to reverse the dirty deed, we’re becoming the very thing that we fear.”
Jackson laughed me off— my ears pounded at the volume of his voice.
“Why, of course we’re becoming the very thing that we fear,” Jackson said.

I cringed, hoping to find a hint of sarcasm in what he said. However, there wasn’t any. I soon realized that everything he said was entirely sincere. Suddenly, in place of what I hoped would be sarcasm in Jacksons voice, I instead found a chasm.

“Kyler, that’s the whole point of the justice system,” he continued, acting as if every word he uttered had a complete obviousness to it. Rather, I instead felt dumbfounded at what he was saying— I felt both a respect and a disrespect toward him for the guts to say these words— words that I wouldn’t have had the courage to say, even if I’d been certain of them being the truth. “We’re supposed to offer the punishment for the crime. We’re supposed to put the order in the places without order. I’m sure that you understand… Even if you don’t like to admit it, we’re doing the same thing that criminals are doing to innocents— holding a gun to their head. Not to say that what we’re doing is wrong. Unlike them, the law is on our side. The only way to stop them from going off the deep end is by going off the deep end ourselves.”
I nodded in agreement, even though I wasn’t there to see him, and I didn’t even agree.
“I suppose you have a point there,” I said, dejectedly.

“It’s not as if we hold a gun to people’s heads unjustly,” Jackson continued, with a chuckle. “You’ve been at this for a couple more years than me, Kyler. You should realize this by now— we do what we do to protect the rights of those who are righteous. Without people like us, the whole city would spiral into chaos. Jonah’s speech had slowed, and become extremely weighed and calculated. I started to see that he rarely said a word without stopping to pause, and look around himself first. I knew that he was preparing to tell me the truth— but he was unwilling to do so. He was beating around the bush.
It was usually at this point that I

‘d begin using my interrogation tactics— my cruel threats, sticking into him like a knife might stick into a slab of meat. However, I wasn’t willing to use them on Jonah. Just like Jonah had a connection to Stephen, of which he didn’t want to betray, I’d found that I’d grown a connection with Jonah— however slight.

Sheets of rain began thundering outside, and leaking out of under the cracks of the store’s door. In the midst of Jonah’s speaking, I hadn’t really noticed. However, now that I was realizing how much time Jonah was wasting, the rainwater only testified to it. It hadn’t even looked like rain before I’d gone inside of the shop and yet, Jonah had found a way to keep me in, to the point where the entire atmosphere had changed outside.

“It all started becoming apparent when I started seeing things go missing,” Jonah went on. “This was when I really realized that something was up. One night, I woke up to a crash. Normally, I pass such things off as dreams— I grew up with illusory dreams all the time, when I was a kid, I’ve learned to ignore them. However, when I got up to use the bathroom, that’s when I found that it was far more than just my sleep issues that were causing problems— somebody had broken into the house, and tarnished it. Even stranger, the things that they’d tarnished weren’t things that were worth tarnishing. Picture frames, old sporting goods, a pair of shoes, a bedsheet— all of them were vandalized, in some shape or form. Personally, this is probably terrified me more than a normal robbery would’ve, since a normal robbery would’ve had far more rationality behind it— at least I would’ve been able to understand it. However, I get the creeping feeling that, whoever the robber had been, that’s the feeling they wanted to rip out of me. Moreover, when Stephen saw what had become of his house, he became more silent than usual— more disturbed looking than usual. His face had become reflective of the toughest parts of cement— crude, cracked, and unforgiving. The things that had vandalized must’ve had a personal significance to him. However, it didn’t stop there. A few nights later, when I slept there again, I found it vandalized again.”
“Is this when he disappeared? I’m sorry, but you’re feeding me information in an incredibly unorganized fashion…”

“He disappeared around this time— yes…” Jonah said. “He kept on talking to me about how rats were coming inside the house and ravishing everything— that they were big rats. I didn’t believe him of course, and I don’t think he thought that I believed him. Personally, I think that he just said this as a sort of code between me and him—  it was like a silent nod between ourselves. Of knowing. In the nights when his house was ravaged. I always had the sense that we had no way to escape the eyes of others. It seemed that there was no escape from it. So, being able to tell ourselves that it had all been caused by some invisible animal was far more comforting to acknowledge, even if it were clearly a lie…”
“I don’t understand how this is relevant…” I said, beginning to lose my patience.

“I’m sorry— it’s just, this was connected to the last words that I’d ever heard him say to me. I was lending him a new couch one night— well, not really a new couch. It was just my couch… My old couch… Not that it matters. I gave him the couch, so that he could replace his slashed couch… I hadn’t been to his house for a week when I was doing this. Then, I stayed there and chatted to him for an hour or so— mostly me doing the chatting, since Stephen had become something just short of a hermit, by that point. He tried his best to ignore my words, and pass them off as something that was unimportant. Though, I could tell as I was talking to him that I was getting through to him. I was telling him about the inking business, and just how effective it was— just how much money we could make together, and that we could reach our dreams in the business despite all of our misgivings with one another, and the hostility of the market. There were glimmers in him— moments where he entertained the dream, and acted as if it were something that we could’ve shared together.

“Of course, that’s all it had been. Him sharing a dream with me. The conversation eventually came to an end— I think it was with him eventually admitting that the inking business wasn’t as bright of a business that I was making it out to be, and that I was just sharing a tunnel dream with him. He wasn’t wrong, so there was nothing that I could really say about it to him. In this way, I felt a pit in my gut, and prepared to leave. It was before I left that he said something that I found to be very odd… Something about how, he was busy anyway— that he needed to go out and speak with the flying rats… It didn’t make any sense, but I laughed with him in jest anyway, and went on my way. Maybe I misheard him— maybe this was all in my head– but these were the last words I heard from him…

“Since then, I’ve heard similar stories from other people in this part of town— friends of theirs getting mixed up in the gutters, and then coming out with money. Though, this money never seems to last, and they eventually have all of their possessions vandalized. I used to always look at these cautionary tales as the rumors of a downtown area— those come about all the time, and they typically have no meaning. However, it was in this story of my own that I knew there was truth.

“For a little while after Stephen’s disappearance, I even found my own house getting trashed. I begin to suspect that this had more to do with Stephen than I realize— that there might’ve been something more to it than what I thought…”

IT was at this point that he finally came to a halt in his speech, and let his weariness cover his entire body. I could immediately tell that having him relay the story to me had drained a lot out of him, and that he had no more to say— if he had any knowledge, I doubted that it would’ve been anything vital to my case However, this didn’t change the hunger inside of me. I wanted more information. I felt as if the story he’d just told me was just beginning, and that I was on the precipice of a great discovery— though, I also knew my thoughts of him having any of the answers were cray, and unfounded. If he was to have had the answers, then he would’ve been able to fo8und the suspects himself. No— I was on my own in this. And, my questions were brewing to the max.
“Flying rats— those are honestly and truly Stephen’s last words?” I asked.

“Something like that,” Jonah said, not sounding to confident. “He kind of muttered them. And, it all went down a little over a year ago. Though, if my memory can be trusted at all, then that’s what he said. That’s all that I can really give you— what I can remember…”
I put my fingers through my hair, incredibly flustered. However, I knew that he was giving me all that he knew— and, this was all that really mattered.
“Alright then,” I said. “Thanks for that. And, these other people that have shared similar stories with you— do you happen to know any of their names?”

“No… Not really,” Jonah said, clearly trying to keep the names of his friends safe from my eyes. I knew that he didn’t want his people found it, and jailed. Though, I needed to know answers, So, even as he told me this, I remained in my place, as if he hadn’t said a word to me.
“You’re not going until I give you an answer— are you?” he asked me nervously.
“I just need the name of one person,” I said. “I can move out from there.”

Jonah scowled, and pursed his lips together. Although, just from my conversation with him, I could tell that he wouldn’t be able to do so for long. He was the kind of person who just didn’t know when to stop talking. His mouth was like a faucet. Even when he wasn’t supposed to be speaking, he was. He was probably one of the easiest people that I’d interrogated in a while.

“Margaret Rosemary,” he said. “I’m not going to say anything else about her, or let you know anything. In fact, if you try talking to her, don’t tell her that I gave you any information— I’d prefer to have my clients think that I’m not spilling any of their information out to people like you… But, if you do happen to talk to her, I’m sure that your ears will be a lot more interested than they were with my own story. She— she has something interesting to tell…”

I gave a nod— partially in commemoration of the nod that Jonah had described between himself and Stephen. I tried my best to keep my posture professional and regal, so as to not expose the fact that I really was surprised that he was leading me to the same place that I was already headed—  thankfully, I believe that he couldn’t see my struggle. I’d gotten very skill at the art of hiding within myself, over the years.
“Well, there’s only so long that I can sit in this shop without beginning to eel sickened by the smell…” I said, in jest.
“Yes, well— I’ve learned that it always serves me well to breathe through the mouth. I can never smell it, that way.”
We both shared a laugh— a laugh that we both shared despite ourselves, but a laugh all the same.

“What do you think this thing is…?” I asked, finally exposing my humanity— and my deeply imbedded terror. “I— I’ve never encountered anything quite like it before. Nobody just goes in a house, and leaves everything, other than your possessions, untouched… Why would it be targeting me?”

“Well… It could be a habit of some gangs…” Jonah said. “It’s probably the most logical of the explanations, if the most confusing. But, I feel that there might be quite a bit more of it at play, than simple gang activity… Rather, these incidents seem to be very meticulous, and personal. They target specific people, and act in very specific ways… Personally, I believe that it’s a fear tactic. But, even more so, I believe that they’re hiring some sort of vigilante to carry it out…”
“You mean— like a Crusoe?”
Jonah made a bitter face.

“Crusoe is a very dirty character, and is a big problem. But, I’d posit that, whoever his person is, they’re worse than Crusoe. The things that they’re capable of— it’s not normal. Most people could never hope to do what his person is doing. It requires a skill that’s far out of the reach of a normal man. Could it be that I’m exaggerating? Maybe… But, I don’t think so. Whoever is doing all of this, without being caught— without hardly even being detected— is somebody who requires a skill that even goes beyond what Crusoe can do.”

I didn’t believe these words for a second. In fact, they drove me out of his shop, and even compelled me to skip a formal goodbye. I simply couldn’t believe them. I knew, deep down inside of myself, that there was nothing— nobody— that could match the stature that Crusoe held. It was simply ridiculous nonsense. I’d seen Crusoe do so many things that were out of the grasp of most people. The idea that there could be another person who was like Crusoe— no, not even like him— somebody who surpassed him, was something that I couldn’t wrap my mind around.

“I don’t believe in magic,” I found myself whispering, on my way from Jonah’s printing shop and down the streets to my house. So, there are only three possibilities here… Jonah is pulling my leg, Crusoe has an equal, or I’ve been vandalized by Crusoe… And Crusoe is a criminal…”

I found myself become disturbed at the mere thought of it. A t saying my last words, I felt the world around me start to turn black as coal— my vision became spotty, and my head started to spiral into an impossible trance of illusory imaginations. I couldn’t even believe what I had just said to myself— that Crusoe could’ve been willing to stoop so low as to vandalize and threaten me. Yet, it was too true for me to ignore. In fact, when I thought about it, it all began to click into place. Crusoe had lost his entire career, and completely disappeared of the map. It was so clear to me— he must’ve been the one threatening me. It only made sense.

I soon found that I was torn between three ideals— Jonah being a liar, Crusoe being a liar, or Crusoe not being as skilled as I once thought he was. I found that I was unwilling to accept any of these— especially the latter, since this meant that I’d have to admit I might not have been in as controllable positon in the city as I once might’ve liked to believe. Though, I also found that, in spite of my unfavorable position, there was one thing that I could find favor in. The possibility that perhaps my vandalizer didn’t have the skills that Jonah claimed he possessed— that it was just slightly exaggerated— that it had all been a fluke, and that there was no true way of being as skilled as Crusoe was, without being Crusoe. However, this all disappeared when I went to my house... I was put back into my positon of terror. Not only that, but back into a position of weakness.

When I entered my apartment, it looked identical to how I’d left it earlier today— my books, being used to research the names I’d seen on the wall, were still in the same position. My breakfast was still on my kitchen counter, awaiting to be eaten. And, my dirty clothes were still on the floor, waiting for when I had the time to go to the laundromat.
If I don’t get those taken care of, I’m sure that I’m going to find myself wearing them soon, I said, in light of the fact that I’d exhausted most of my clean laundry.

However, my head was in a different place from where my mouth was. As I looked at my dirty clothes, I gained the eerie feeling of discomfort. One article of clothing was a coat— a coat that had fallen from a coatrack, which was sitting to the left of my pile. Normally, I would’ve dismissed such a thing. In fact, I was even slightly dismissive of it when I first saw it.
“I probably knocked it down on the way out of here, this morning,” I said. “I must’ve been so busy, that I didn’t notice when it fell to the ground.”

This was convincing enough— the coatrack was in the hall, on the way to my door. I had a habit of knocking it over each morning. However, I also had a habit of picking it back up, and putting it in its place.
I knew that it hadn’t been put back in its place. And, I hadn’t been in a rush.

I looked at my watch— it was nine. The same time that I’d gone to my house, the night before. Suddenly, I was compelled to walk through my house as quiet as I could. I knew that I’d already made my presence well-known— but, I also knew that trying to make up for my mistake was the only way that I’d be able to avoid it continuing to bite on me.
“You know what? What’s stopping me from taking care of this laundry right now?” I said, trying to sound as casual as possible.
I turned around, and opened and shut my door, taking great care to make it sound as if ‘d left the apartment.
It was all in superstition in paranoia. It was all needed.

Slinking through my apartment with the same measured steps and thoughts, I kept alert of everything. I fastened my eyes to every detail, so that I knew I wasn’t missing anything. Perfection still escaped me as I did this. Footsteps went too far, and made the floorboards creak. Certain muscles of mine became too tense, and cracked during some of my movements. Even my breathing— possibly the most essential thing that I needed to make sure that I had taken care of— was far too loud in the quiet of my apartment.

I felt as if my misgivings were practically as loud as that of a microphone. In fact, in comparison with the constant quiet and solace that encased me, I wouldn’t have been surprised If I’d discovered this to be true. My ears weren’t as sharp as they’d used to have been— it wouldn’t have been as hard for me to make a bumbling mistake as I might’ve liked to make myself believe.
It was probably only a matter of ten or so steps, in their sum. Though, the few mistakes that I’d made in these steps made me fear that there were much larger consequences than what I could perceive.

My living room slunk over me, with the unnoticed slickness that might be found in a cold piece of metal— one might be able to detect the coldness of the metal for a while, but if the metal is touched for long enough, it practically ceases to be there— it’s as if you’re touching air.

The same thing went for my living room. In passing through it so often, I didn’t even notice this time. However, my instincts did. They noticed far more than even the keenest of the detectives would’ve been able to— that is, except for Crusoe.

Despite not being able to actively sense anything odd about the room, I knew that the abnormalities were there— waiting for me to come up to them, and make myself known to it. It was just a matter of me finding it out, and making sure that I found it first.

I can’t let myself fall susceptible to their powers again, like I’d done under the hospital, I thought to myself. This time, I’m going to be the first one to make a move— the first one to throw the punch, and enact the attack.

In thinking this, I wasn’t just fighting against an invisible enemy. Rather, I was also fighting against my own personal limitations and insecurities— that of which I’d never been able to escape. I feared that I wouldn’t be able to escape them now, either. It was in this, that this was not just a normal test. It had become a way for me to prove myself to myself again— for me to gain faith in something that I’d begun to lose faith in— the fact that I was still skilled in what I did.

I listened to my breathing. It was stronger than ever now, and it moved at an unnaturally rapid pace. The most annoying and unsettling thing was, I couldn’t even feel the rapidity in my breathing anymore. I’d done all in my ability to make sure that my breathing had slowed down, and that it could no longer be a hindrance to me. However, it was still moving with a rate that matched the batting wings of a hummingbird.

A horror struck me, with the force of a heavily swung club. The heavy breathing wasn’t my own, or anything that I could control. The breathing was an alien one. My own chest was moving as slow as a snail— it was somebody else who had the fast breathing.

Immediately, I dived towards where I’d heard the sound of breathing. There was a shout— I couldn’t tell if it was from myself or the person, but it didn’t matter. I could see their flailing figure, even in the creamy-thick darkness of the room. I could sense their wish to take me down. I knew that I was going to get them first.
For a moment, it was just a grasp against a loose bit of their clothes. Then, my hand reached one of their limbs. I think that it was their wrist, but it might’ve been the elbow.

I writhed and cursed in anger as I felt them begin to escape my grasp, and pull me around the room with their superior strength. In spite of this, I managed to hang on. I believe that there was something within me— a sort of fighting spirit— that didn’t allow me to cave in, like most would’ve done in the situation.

“You broke into my house once,” I said, holding onto them as thoroughly as my left arm could. As I did so, I thought, with regret, how much more effective it would’ve been if I’d had access to my right arm. Thankfully, this thought only lasted a moment before they were redirected back to the important subject at hand— making sure that the criminal didn’t escape unpunished.

I was wrong in thinking that I had a sort of invincibility, however, I found myself shunted to the floor, like I’d been many times over, and left to only watch as the figure escaped the darkness of my room.

As I saw them leave, I caught how tall and large that they were— the only reason that I hadn’t heard them in the darkness sooner was because I was too deaf to my own surroundings, and they were wearing a light layering of clothing.

In spite of their light layering of clothing, I couldn’t make out if they were a man or a woman. If It was a woman, they carried many manly features— a bulky figure, a pounding of their feet whenever they took a step, and a great strength. Though, if they were a man, they seemed rather agile— especially for their body type.

I was inclined to believe that it was a man, but they moved away far too fast for me to thoroughly determine every possibility. One thing that I knew for near certain, however, ids that this person was not Detective Crusoe. They were too slow— too short in their responses for them to be nearly as effective as they could’ve been. If it was Crusoe who I’d pitted battle with, I would’ve been knocked to the floor before I could’ve even dived out to grab him. Moreover, he wasn’t the kind of person who would’ve left himself cornered, or exposed himself through heavy breathing. This clumsy approach simply wasn’t his style.

“You’re not escaping to anywhere,” I called out, as I watched the person run to my front door— another sign that this couldn’t have been Crusoe, since Crusoe tended to take far more unconventional escape routes. “I’ll stop you next time you come here— and you’ll have no ability to prevent me from doing so. You might think that you have the upper hand, and that you’re even smarter and faster than I am. But, I’m onto you. And, you’re not going to be able to play this game with me for much longer.”

As I shouted these out, and struggled to pull myself back up from the floor, they left my house— not even bothering to lock my door. They didn’t even bother to keep listening to my idle threats— they didn’t even care about my anger They knew that they’d done their job, and that’s all that seemed to matter to them.
That’s all that seemed to matter to either of us. I knew that they’d won. That’s why all I had left to use against them were words.

“There’s only so long that you can keep yourself hidden from me,” I said, still calling out to them. I knew that they couldn’t hear me— but then, I was speaking more to my own self confidence in my abilities, than anything else. My words had been spoken out of my ego— I’d known this since the beginning of my speech. “People can’t crawl behind masks forever. Not even if they’re incredibly good at it.”

It wasn’t until these words were finished, and I realized that they’d changed nothing, that I truly began to grasp the weight of reality— that I was alone in the room, and that there was nobody to hear me. Nobody to sympathize with me. It was simply me— alone— bearing my struggles on my own. It was all in me that everything had to confide. I had to deal with pulling myself up from the ground, despite only having one good arm— despite having only one good ear. Despite having only one good heart, which was thumping in my chest with a forcefully, stinging agony. It was an agony that I had to slowly digest as I pulled myself up from the ground.
“Too much stress…” I said to myself in annoyance. “If only there was a way to eradicate it all… If only there was a way to know everything…”
Then, after another huff of breath.
“I’m definitely not telling Lieutenant Jackson about this one— I can’t be made a fool two nights in a row.”
The rain puttered downward, as heavily as it usually did. I listened as it turned the wheels of my car into squealing pigs.
How can my wheels squeal in delight, in weather like this…? I wondered.

The answer of which still eludes me. However, that was probably the least of elusive answers, which were on my mind. The grogginess of dawn had managed to get its grip on my sinuses and ears, making my entire face feel as if it were swelling and expanding from an oncoming sickness. MY face wasn’t the only thing that was swelling. In my scuffle from the night before, my broken arm had puffed up like an ever-expanding cloud. It was burning and sweating terribly, making my feel as if my entire body was trapped within it. The cast had been tormenting me for quite some time, but I’d only begun to notice how bad it was today— my limits were being pushed upon, and this was clearly their way of retaliation.

I’d begun to feel like I’d become far slower in everything that I did— not only in my thoughts, which seemed to constantly be struggling to catch up with everybody else’s but also in my day-to-day activities. There wasn’t a single thing I did where I didn’t find myself in an agonizing regret of how much time that I was wasting and squandering— and, just how much the clock was really stacking itself against me. I was trying my hardest to beat this invisible opponent of slipping time— a fading hourglass— but it was just becoming too overbearing for me to truly keep up with.

There’d been another robbery the night before— as I was busy, sleeping in my house, the rest of the police force was making sure that everything was being done with a pure efficiency. To a large extent, I had a regret when I thought on this. Unlike many on the police force, I didn’t have a family— I could afford going to work late at night. Though, I continued to go with the constant excuse that I had far too much to investigate during the daytime, and I was starting to see how much I was missing. To a large degree. I was losing touch with the city in my attempts to avoid doing the hard, dirty work.

I pulled up into Miss Prestel’s familiar neighborhood, with all of its grandly decorated mansions and houses. I started to see just how many of them weren’t as beautiful as they should’ve been, and just how much Chicago had made sure to beat them down— turn them back into the grungy gray of the city slush, from which it came out of. And, as humanizing and important as these musings might’ve been for me, I stopped thinking on them when a group of officers started crowding around my police car, and began shouting at me. To comply, I hopped out of my leaping car and said, “Lieutenant Jackson sent me here. He said that he wanted me to inspect the premises, and see if the crime scene is similar to the one that occurred on Prestel Manor, last month.”
One of the officers, who’d been blocking my path, immediately stepped out of the way.
“Sorry sir, I didn’t realize,” he said. We’ve been trying to block all of the people trying to come in here for their family members, that we didn’t realize…”

I’d been rushed over to the crime-scene when I first woke up in the morning, to a ringing telephone. Lieutenant Jackson had only informed me that my presence on the crime-scene was urgent, and that he didn’t want me to allow myself to be caught up in distractions. He said that I was needed and that, if I didn’t go over there as soon as possible, he feared that the wrong assessments of the situation might be made.

Remembering how late that I’d come to Miss Prestel’s home, I complied. However, it wasn’t until now that I realized what a mistake I’d made in rushing over, immediately. I could already see that I had a very thin and fragile understanding of what had happened, and all of my lines of communication with Lieutenant Jackson were completely cut off.
“What o you mean by, families,” I asked, with a confused reluctance. I didn’t want them to know that I was clueless. Though, at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t allow myself to remain clueless.
I watched the officer’s face, which was previously subservient, morph into that of skepticism.
“Lieutenant Jackson didn’t tell you?” he said, trying his best to subtly block my path as I walked over the caution tape, and nearer to the house.
“No, he didn’t say a word,” I said. “he only told me that I needed to be here as soon as possible— he acted as if it was urgent, and gave few explanations. Why do you ask?”

“Because, that doesn’t sound like something Lieutenant Jackson would do…” he said, cautiously. “You must admit that I have every right to be skeptical here. What happened last night— even if you’re unaware of it— was extremely devastating. If you’re a rookie officer, looking to make a name of yourself, then I suggest that you turn back.”

I grinned, as I looked at him. He was clearly in his early twenties, and yet he was calling me a rookie. I struggled to keep myself from laughing as I pulled out my badge, and revealed that I was a Sergeant.
“Sergeant Kyler?” he said, cracking a wry smile. “Sorry— I didn’t realize. Please— let me tell you what happened.”

At this point, he was now practically tripping over himself to make up for setting us off on the wrong foot. And, to my own satisfaction, and partial regret, I actually enjoyed being tripped over. I hadn’t met somebody who looked upon me in respect for a long time, and it was refreshing to see this rookie act as if I were some sort of legend, who had seen a lot of things– it was as if the mere mention of my name had immediately alerted him that I was in the wrong.

“I’m sorry— I don’t know how I could’ve made that mistake,” he said with an over-eagerness, as he led me down the house’s walkway. “You’re the same man who worked with Detective Crusoe, on over a dozen cases.”
“Yes,” I said.

I was preoccupied with studying the house. Like most mansions on the street, it had an older tinge to it— it was bright, and clearly painted over, to make it look as if it were newer and richer.  However, I could see right through it. By its awkward posture, clearly caused by settling, it falling shingles, and its look of overall tiredness, I knew that the place was merely adopting the look of a grand and regal appearance. It was actually just as ruined and dilapidated as any other building that had been born in Chicago. It was no different from the rest— it wasn’t impervious to the depression that we’d all fallen in. Whilst Prestel Manor was one of those houses that could sell the lie, and make it work, this house merely looked filthy in trying to do so.
