I couldn’t help but feel disgusted and distrustful just by looking at it. Even under its paint, I could see the true hints of molding darkness poking out.
“That’s amazing!” the officer continued. “MY name is Paul Blake, by the way. And, I’m a great fan of your work, let me just say. It’s a big disappointment that Crusoe turned out to be a—.”
“I don’t like to talk about it,” I said, cutting him off.
“Yes, well— it’s a shame… but, at least it will be able to help you in this case.”
“What case? Stop beating around the bush, and spit out what you know.”
Paul’s face immediately went red.

“Sorry sir— yes sir. I was just getting to that. This is— umm— another crime committed by Crusoe, clearly. The witnesses say that they saw a man in a trench coat, and fedora, breaking into the house, and then throwing a smoke bomb in there. Three people went missing…”
“How many witnesses were there?”
“Thirty, this time around,” Officer Blake said. “This time, it’s undeniable that Crusoe did it. We’re no longer relying on the eye account of one old lady…”
I grimaced, but told Officer Blake to go on.

“They were all having a party last night— that’s why there are families trying to go here, this morning. Some people are only just beginning to find out what happened. Anyway, this was a dinner party, meant to hold first class citizens— I’m sure you get the gist. A bunch of pompous rich snobs, flaunting the little bit of cash that’s left in this city. Anyhow, they say that Crusoe crashed their party, and the party host was abducted during this crashing, along with three other people that were next to him… The party host also being the owner of this house…”
“Their names?” I asked, starting to get annoyed.
“The host was Mr. Rufous Donald. I’m sure that you’ve heard of him— he’s a close friend of Miss. Prestel, and a great influencer of the wealthy in here?”
“Yes— of course I heard of him,” I said, partially condescendingly. However, I no longer cared how angry I sounded. These questions were becoming borderline offensive to my knowledge base.
“Yes— yes, of course,” Paul said, with a reddened face. “Sorry— you’ve probably had a greater experience in this city than even I have…”

“Not probably— I have,” I said, mere inches away from shaking my head in disgust. Clearly this person had no experience in their field, and had a far bigger ego than was good for them Though, I decided against letting him hear those words come from out of my mouth.

He’ll learn when reality hits him— when he hits a case that he has to do on his own, and realizes just how little he really knows about this town… I thought to myself. The greatest mistake is to assume that you can’t make it…

“Yes, well…” Paul said, still unaware of his arrogance. “I have seen a lot in this field. But, I’m sure that this is unimportant to the conversation at hand. I want to look at this case and house, objectively, and untainted by our current conversation. So, maybe we should stop talking about our experiences.”

“WE definitely should,” I said, allow a scowl to form on my face. “Now please— begin practicing what you preach, and tell me what you think happened at this house— could there be a possibility that this wasn’t Crusoe? What have you observed about what happened? Did you find any evidence that suggests what tools might’ve been used to accomplish this act? I could go on with the questions… But, I’m sure that somebody with the amount of experience that you possess can already guess where I’m going with this.

“Yes, of course,” he said with a chuckle. “I know exactly what you mean. Well, we’ve studied the premises. The room where Mr. Donald was kidnapped clearly smells of sulfur, and we’ve even been able to catch some sediment of a sort of gunpowder, in each corner of the room. However, I sadly haven’t been able to find any images of Crusoe, taken by camera or such— I wish that more people carried them around, but that’s expecting far too much out of people— and, from what we can tell, the smoke bombs would’ve eliminated the witness’s ability to actually discernably tell who did this. It may very well be that the claims of Crusoe having a hand in this are completely unfounded, and baseless…”
“They are baseless,” I said, with a grunt. “There’s nothing that indicates this was done by him, from what you’ve told me…”
“Yes well,” he said, gesturing to the door of the house. “I’m sure that you can make a better determination if shown the interior of the house, rather than relying on my testimonial evidence, yes?”
“Yes, of course…”
“Also, one other thing— look for smoke bombs. I don’t know where they might be, but we need to find them…”
“Smoke bombs… Right…” I said. “And, these smoke bombs— you don’t have any idea for where they might be, do you?”

“Of course not,” Paul said. “That’s why you’re here. Speaking of which, do you actually think Crusoe is the one who is guilty of doing all of this. I heard that you weren’t so convinced, but, II personally think that those claims are complete lies. After all— we all know that you are one of the top deductive experts within Chicago. Of course you wouldn’t deny such blatant evidence as we’ve been able to find and exploit…”
“Just open the door to the house,” I growled, getting more impatient than ever before.
I’m getting a lot shorter with people than I used to, I thought to myself. Then again, people have started to neglect keeping conversations short— maybe that’s part of the problem.
The door opened rapidly, with Officer Paul quickly sensing and responding to my apparent annoyance.
“I’m really sorry about that,” he said, instantly. “It’s not often that you get to speak with a legend… I’m simply expressing my over-eagerness to talk with you.
I kept my scowl on my face, making sure to not allow a seem of repentance for my short behavior to slip through.

“Yes, well,” I said, getting a good look around the entrance of the manor, “I’ve been to a lot of robbed mansions in my day— it seems to happen a lot more to me, than with anybody else.  Anyway, this is my second mansion in weeks, and I’m getting rather board of this trend… Maybe it’s just me? It’s probably just me…. Nonetheless, I don’t have time for constant chatter going on in the background, while I’m trying to do my job. You can either act like a fan, who doesn’t know when to stop gushing, or you can act like a trained professional on the field. You can’t do both, and if you decide to do the former, then I’ll have to ask you to leave…”

Paul looked angry, this time around. It seemed to me that his claims of being a fan of me had been far from legitimate. Rather, they’d merely been attempts to flatter me. In fact, as I reflected closer, I began to suspect that it hadn’t even been to flatter me— rather, he’d only been trying to edge up onto my good side, so that he could steal all of my findings. I was able to tell just by his increasingly desperate look, that he allowed to come onto his face when I said that I wanted him to leave.
“Aren’t you being rather harsh?” he said, still standing by the entrance— trying to remain attached to me, like a leech.
“I just have to pull him out, with tweezers,” I muttered to myself.

Then, I turned, and said, “Aren’t, you being the one who’s incredibly unreasonable. I’m in the midst of an incredibly dens case, and you don’t appear to have the gall or the willpower to stop yourself, and leave my sight. I’d be shocked if I saw you leave right now, and shut your mouth. If there’s anything that I’ve learned about rookies, in all of my years on the force, is that only half of you are willing to stick around… And, out of that half, only a quarter are worth keeping around. Now, please leave me be— at least for a moment, if you honestly don’t have the self-control to leave me be for any longer stretch of time than that. I’m in the middle of observing this scene, and I’d prefer to do so in quiet.”
I think that I must’ve infuriated him at this. However, even as I continued to investigate the crime scene, I realized that it was better for him to be infuriated than I.
This isn’t a daycare, I found myself thinking.

As far as the entrance hall was concerned, it was like most entrance halls of manors— expansive, expensive, and extraordinarily excessive. There were five chandeliers hanging from the ceiling, all of them jeweled with diamonds. They were no doubt fake diamonds. However, this knowledge didn’t kill the splendorous stupor that I was put into when looking at them. The walls were, surprisingly, devoid of any paintings. It seemed that the owner had opted to keep the room classier, decking it with flowers and candles that gave off perfumes— perfumes that gave off an overabundant stink, which would’ve compelled nearly anybody walking by to plug their nose with a clothespin.

The walls weren’t painted nearly as flamboyantly a I might’ve expected, either. In comparison to Miss Prestel’s house, which treated bright paints and pricy decor as if they were the cheapest thing on the market, they instead kept the walls painted in a thick black paint— a rather odd sight, considering all of the options that the owner must’ve had available to himself.
The floor also wasn’t carpeted. Instead, it was a smooth tile, which was so slick that I thought it might’ve been washed just before I walked into the hall.

The architecture was a mixture of gothic and Greco-Roman design, having delicate stone carvings, pillars, and arcs all throughout it. Each one of these stone designs lacks that black coating that the walls had, making the walls clash even more so.

“Just the entrance, and I’m already beginning to feel overloaded with information…” I said, trying my best to make amends with Officer Paul. “It’s funny— of all their money, you’d think that they’d use it to make more rooms around their entrance hall.”
As I said this, I gestured down the entrance hall— it was about five yards down before it actually led to a room.

“All that time, and you have no new observations to make?” Paul asked. “Also, the reason that there are no doors is because Mr. Donald likes to have only one exit for his guests to take— that way, they’re more likely to talk to each other, on their way out. He’s the kind of person who’s all for charisma… Did you know that he’s already campaigning for a new political seat?”

I scowled with annoyance— I despised just about everything concerning Mr. Donald. He was a rich man with a poor sense of community, and morals. Despite all of his wealth, he tended to use it to further himself, rather than furthering the community. Whilst he saw himself as the sort of person who had the ability to bolster the community, he tended to be self-indulgent— all of the answers in his purpose that he came up with was usually utilizing his abundance of cash to build himself up. His thoughts were more focused on solving his own problems, even when he claimed that he was a philanthropist.  He never helped charity, despite claiming himself to be charitable.

“Yes… I’ve heard,” I said, still in a wrenching clenching of teeth, which was fed out of anger. “just guide me into the ballroom, like I already told you to do. Your job isn’t to question me, but to question your surroundings. The longer that you focus on the primitive trivialities of socialization, the deeper that you fall into the well of unanswered questions. I know this, because I’ve tried solving cases in the reverse approach. Speaking from experience, I know just how many follies the mistake in non-critical thinking can birth. I’m unwilling to entertain it, and you should be too.”

I’m prone to vehement ramblings, when I feel that things aren’t going my way— I suppose that it’s a major flaw of mine. It’s possibly the biggest flaw out of my gargantuan quantity of flaws. However, I can’t quite help it. When I see something that I can’t control, I’m compelled to find a way to control it in every way that I possibly can. This is clearly a massive mistake, on my part—but then, what am I to do to avoid such errors? I’m afraid that I’m not any sort of uberman. I can’t be expected to do everything with a brilliant and impenetrable perfection and accuracy. Such is to expect the impossible from a man who is limited by what is possible.

My anger came out of just how disgusting, and shocking, the character of Mr. Donald really was. In spite of being a soft, pasty man, with no moral fiber to him at all, I was in the position where I needed to help him. Moreover, I needed to help him in political affairs. I hated the man, and his plans for the city. Yet, if I didn’t help him them, by extension, it would be for me to accept some of his policies— after all, if I didn’t work on this case to help him, then he wouldn’t even be able to enact any of his plans in the first place.

Such is the duty of an officer, I thought to myself. It doesn’t matter if you care for the victim or not. You’re compelled to help them, no matter the circumstance, because they’re innocent. And, it’s your job to protect and serve the innocent, even if you know, deep down, that not all of the innocent are quite as innocent as they might seem.

I still couldn’t accept my own thoughts. Even in my attempts to be progressive, and think about my job and duties in a non-discriminatory way, I couldn’t help but look at everything in a way that was full of a hateful anger. This man was on his way to mass-manipulate the public, and I what to save him— protect him in his attempts to use his money to incite power. To gain a position that he had no reason to take or steal, especially in light of the fact that there were far more worthy people of political seats that didn’t have their pockets completely full.  My head was moving in an impossibly fast cyclone, completely confused and full of misdirection. I didn’t know quite where II wanted to take myself. All that I knew was that I wanted to take myself somewhere, and completely rid myself of this man— this duty— and the fact that I had to help this man, despite my convictions being to the contrary of such.

There was something else that angered me. Even in the fact that my head was incredibly distracted, and that I was trying to pull myself out of my flurry of fury, I had something that my mind would not leave alone— something that it focused on with an unmerciful attention. It— or, more accurately, I—couldn’t fathom how such a man was capable of pumping himself up in such a way, or how anybody was capable of taking the person seriously. To me, such was nearly insane, considering that everything he did was proof against his legitimacy.
How could people become so tricked. I just didn’t make sense to me.

The pathway to the ballroom was an odd one. It lasted about only two minutes, according to my watch. However, according to my eyes, and my feeling of entrapment and claustrophobia, I couldn’t help but feel as if it had taken an hour. I know that I’m exaggerating when I say this— however, there’s no true way to describe just how much time slows down when you start to feel weary, and the world around you appears to be slowing down. I know that I might sound wrong when I say this, but I don’t really care about that. It’s simply how I am, and the mistakes of my cogitative bias. Nothing can really help that.

I wish it could… I thought to myself. My deductive abilities would become so much easier, in that way. I wasn’t wrong. To this day, I wish that it was possible for one to achieve a superhuman ability to solve mysteries. Maybe it’s just me, but I think that super intelligence is the only way that enormous problems can truly be solved. I’m not even sure if once can imagine how effective one might be if they were stripped of all intuition and bias, being left to go based upon only the raw facts of situations. It would probably make reasoning and thinking expand far beyond the limitations that we currently face in my field of expertise.

However, I digress— as I find myself doing a lot in my narration. What I intend to say is that the hall was a terrible place to walk through, despite the intention for it to be more unifying. It seems to me— while I could be totally wrong in this— that the attempt at bringing people closer only resulted in a stupid and inferior structure, which made one wish to be farther apart from other people than ever.

I shouldn’t be surprised in this. Like I said prior— Mr. Donald was a man who waved around false promises and lies, as if it were a flag of his extreme pride. He contradicted whatever he professed to be his core values, because his true core was mere contradiction. It’s these sort of folk who always have something to hide. So, they hide their darkest secrets within their most beautiful lies, hoping that nobody will notice just how many terrible things exist within those lies.

The ballroom was so wide, and expansive, that I forced myself out of my state of enraged instinct. Perhaps it was the love of answers, and the seeking out to destroy questions, that I finally was able to snap myself out of my adrenaline induced focus on an inclination toward incredible hatred, and visceral anger.

The ballroom had so much money put into it that it could even convince a hateful person, such as myself, to feel a sort of love towards this man that was obviously corrupt. He had a rarified and dignified sense of architecture and culture, to be sure. While I’d seen in Miss Prestel’s house to be a completely ignorant and ugly waste of money, there was something to the gothic but enlightened sculpting that had taken place in Mr. Donald’s house— something that made me look at, at least is house, in quite a different way. I actually felt a sort of reverence.
“I might not like the man who built this place,” I said to Paul. “but, that’s not going to stop me from liking the place that he built.”

In comparison to the claustrophobic, stuffy, and uncomfortably bright entrance hall, the ball room appeared to be some brilliant sort of heaven— I’d never actually seen something before, in my entire existence, that truly compared to the room. It was full of some of the most beautiful things that I’ve ever laid eyes on. And, that’s not just to be flamboyantly exaggerative, or provocative to the mind’s sensibilities towards beauty and light— I’m actually being very earnest in my descriptions, and feel deeply about the descriptions that I’m providing.

The entire floor, as well as pillars spread throughout the room, appeared to be made of an exquisite marble— almost appearing to shine like pearls. There was also grand furniture, such as richly decorated chairs, wide and expansive stone tables stretching across the floor, as well as large lamps hanging from the ceiling above. Once again, it looked to me that Mr. Donald had decided to avoid using paintings as a decoration. However, as I began to closely inspect the place, I saw just how much gorgeous precision had really been put into tit, in spite of the lack of paintings. In fact, it began to seem to me that the lack of paintings actually ended up instituting a far more gorgeous and insightful design than anything else that Mr. Donald could’ve built. The closer and longer that I looked at everything, the more that I happened to see in everything. There were gorgeous stone carvings on the wall, hearkening back to ancient Greek statures that I’d seen in museums, as well as old photograph’s that I’d seen of Michelangelo’s work. There are few words that I could use to describe the place. It held the very essence of intelligence, and grandiosity— I felt the wells of Aristotle’s mind utterly filling the place, giving it a splendor that was near impossible to come by, under mundane circumstances. Yet, I still had a way of looking at it all, and not feeling entirely lost, or incredibly small. It had an artificial sense to it, as well. Despite all of the work that had clearly been put into the room, it was all clearly mimicry. While I was confounded at how Mr. Donald could’ve amassed the wealth required to craft such architecture, I still had the ability within myself to scoff at it— it was impressive, but it wasn’t so humbling that I was forced to remove myself of self-pride and dignity.

There was only one thing in the entire room that really caught my eye, and made me feel the same punitive grasp on reality, such as that the old Michelangelo sculptures might’ve been able to give me— it came from a grand fountain, placed in the center of the room.

The word grand is probably a grandly overused term, similar to how beauty is. When describing a fountain, there are so many more unique and original ways to describe it— such as a sputtering window into the ways of the waters, which puts the mind into such a trance that it becomes the water itself— that it becomes a part of the slickness, and the tranquil patterns that the fountain provides. Its water is so clear, that it can no longer be called water— such is made all too clear, when the water pours over the stone, in a way that makes everything glimmer in a dance of silver. The water is not water— it’s liquid crystal.

Though, I’ve found that the word grand still suits the fountain far more. I’m sure that I’m mistaken as I say this, and that I’ll probably even find myself as subject of regret long after I’m done saying this. However, when did I ever halt in my speech, simply because I knew that I’d go on to regret it? The place was grand. My words still stand.

Somehow, I made myself start staring at the ground— I looked and searched, with all of the extreme focus that my eyes allowed me, to stare a t the ground. I thoroughly searched for any kind of proof or evidence that might’ve allowed me a way back in time.

Thinking back on this, with an increasing inspection of my ability to ignore the great things that hung around me, I’ve started to recognize just what drives me— the very thing that allows me to sole mysteries, and pay distractions no notice. The seeking out of clues, and evidence, can allow somebody to both travel back in time, and travel forward into the future. Based on evidence, things can be judged. Things, which might not be able to be understood otherwise, can come in complete clarity. That’s the unique grandness of what I do— the grandness that can even allow me to ignore the grandness of everything going on around me. I might not be the most intelligent of all people, and some of the things that I do can be utterly ridiculous. Although, there’s one thing that I now know I can never apologize in— and that is in being able to look at the world around me, and scrutinize it to the point where I’ve eliminated all possibilities of lies, and now can only dissect the truth from out of it. The mind is something that must be tamed, in order for it to tame the untamable world around it. This was probably the greatest lesson that Crusoe ever taught me.

I kept my eyes locked on the floor. There was dust, in certain areas, which tainted the pearly glow of the floor. Like Officer Paul had said, from these I was able to assess that smoke-bombs had certainly been used, as well as where the smoke-bombs had been placed. However, similar to when Detective Crusoe had fought me with the police, the samples were once again unidentifiable. The chemical composition appeared to being lacking of any unique qualities. In fact, the lacking of unique qualities was probably its only unique quality.

“I honestly can’t see anything special here,” I said to Paul, judging between whether or not I should tell him what I found. Finally, I admitted, “But, these smoke-bomb dust remnants suggest that Detective Crusoe was here. A few weeks ago, the entire police force was caught in a fight between Detective Crusoe. We pretty much had him pinned down, and there were virtually no ways in which he could escape— he’d practically been arrested. Though, he managed to set off a smoke-bomb, and utterly evade our grasp. It left behind a similar composition to this. While the forensics department has yet to identify the comical substances that Crusoe has been using, I can firmly state that this chemical residue is a result of Crusoe being here. That, or somebody who has managed to steal Crusoe’s attributes…”
Officer Paul laughed.

“I’m glad that you were able to figure out that Crusoe is behind this,” he said, in an almost apologetic way— he clearly regretted laughing at me. “but, do you honestly think that there’s somebody out there who’s capable of copying everything about Crusoe, and trying to frame him? For one thing, that simply doesn’t make any sense— if this really is a fake Crusoe, they’re putting themselves at risk of getting caught in the act, and arrested. If that were to happen, then they’d utterly get rid of any need for us to search out Crusoe— they’d single-handedly put us off Crusoe’s back. But, if they do succeed, there’s still the fact that nobody would have any reason to get rid of Crusoe… After all— if he’s being framed, that would mean he still hasn’t been active for years… Therefore, the person will have wasted their time. Besides— what reason do you even have to think that this was an act of trying to frame Crusoe? If you really think about it, it makes no sense, in the slightest… It’s all a friendly, childish delusion… You’re just living in the past. It’s time that you stop, and accept the evidence for what it is.”
I shook my head, in disappointment.

“Haven’t you heard about the clothes of Crusoe, which happened to be found at Job’s house… Clearly, there’s a lot more to this that’s going on than there seems to be. You might think me to be crazy for believing this. Heck, you’re probably even right. But, when I look at everything that’s going on, I can’t help but feel that we have a lot more questions than we have answers. And, I can’t help but feel like that’s simply not right… Yes— I’d prefer to believe that Crusoe is innocent. But, I have good reason to believe that he is. Haven’t you heard that I’m working on a new case, trying to prove Crusoe’s innocence. If there’s anybody that might know anything about whether or not Crusoe is good, it’s me.”

Officer Paul looked as if he were on the verge of laughing again— he seemed to have a very low opinion of me, form what I was beginning to sense from out of him, and he clearly didn’t take any of the words coming out of my mouth with any sort of seriousness.

“I heard that you case is how you nearly got a concussion, and broke your arm… Sergeant, with all due respect, you don’t know what you’re talking about. I agree that there are strange things going on. But, let’s be honest— a man who’s willing to resist the police simply isn’t an innocent man, no matter how one tries to spin it. I can’t conceive how Crusoe can logically be innocent… No matter what, he’s a criminal, whether or not he’s guilty of these crime sprees.”

At this point, I couldn’t deny the facts. AS much as I despised Officer Paul, he had a sort of shrewd and cold truth about his words— while he was arrogant, he certainly had no softness towards the arrogance of others. Rather, the was somebody who had a love of being brutally honest.

“In all my years working with Crusoe, one thing that I never noticed about him was that he was a criminal,” I said. “He was a good man, looking to change the corruptness within society Does that necessarily make him a good person? Obviously not… obviously, I was misinformed and delusional in a few areas, concerning Crusoe. But, I just don’t know…  After all, that he helped me with, I don’t feel quite right inn turning him in as repayment…”

“Fine then,” Officer Paul said. “Repay Crusoe in any way that you like. I just want you to make sure that you know what you’re doing when you attempt this. After all—m as nice of a person as Crusoe might seem to have been to you, he was still a man— he still deserves to have to face the justice system, and give up his anonymity— he needs to be held responsible for his actions. And, you can’t twist the truth to suit your wishes and beliefs for it to be otherwise.”

I scowled— not so much at Officer Paul, but at myself. In a way, I was even scowling at my past scowling. Officer Paul had been right in a lot more ways than I was willing to give credit— probably more ways than I’m still giving credit. Whilst I might’ve liked to look at Paul as a rookie, he had a lot more experience and wisdom than I’d ever allowed myself to experience

“you’re right,” I said. “I am quite biased in the favor of Detective Crusoe. And, that’s clearly one of my greatest flaws—if not, my greatest flaw. It’s just, with all of his contributions to solving crimes, and my own skills, I can’t help but feel indebted to him… I can’t help but deny the possibility of him being the vile traitor that he seems to be painted out to be. Clearly I’m wrong in thinking this. Clearly the evidence goes against me. But, you must understand— there’s a part of me that doesn’t care about any of the purported evidence, or the fact that it might be wrong on every front. There’s a part of me that cares only about the friendship I made— however hollow that friendship might’ve been. If I were to be honest, I’d have to admit this— I don’t have many people that I can call my ally. I avoid this for the very reason that I don’t have to defend complete criminals. And yet, it seems to me that this has backfired in practically every way. It’s near impossible for me to do away with Crusoe, without me feeling as if I’m doing away with something incredibly integral to myself. In a sense, I’ve tied myself to a terrible poison— ‘m needing of a separation from it, but that doesn’t stop me from feeling incredibly linked with it…”
Officer Paul didn’t give a response for quite a while. Instead, he looked around the ballroom one last time, to see if there was anything that he missed.
“It’s quite strange that there doesn’t seem to be any available escapes, that were easy to take…” I heard him mutter.
Finally, he allowed his voice to reach full volume as he gave me his answer.

“I don’t care if he was you friend,” he said. “I don’t care how he might’ve made you feel, or how he honed your skills. At this point, the entire police force recognizes him as a menace— even you do, somewhere inside that logical mind of yours. The problem here is, you’re not seeing Crusoe as the real beast that he is— a cruel, unforgiving, unjust person, he never stops to think about the consequences to his actions. I like what Crusoe did, in his great tenure, just as much as the next person. Corrupt of a character that he might’ve been, he really did know what he was doing— he was a mind that was truly hard to match. However, this doesn’t stop the fact that his legend has been largely tainted throughout time. This doesn’t prevent the truth that he’s pulling you down. In your worship of Crusoe’s fine skills, and his great efforts and achievements, you’re letting your own skills and achievements whither to dust. I respect you, Sergeant Kyler— at least, I respect all of your work. Though, I must admit, you’re not the sort of person that I thought of when I was training for office. When I read the newspaper articles about you, I gained the perspective that you were a man of great integrity, who possessed a mind of even a greater capacity and size than that. Now that I’ve seen you face to face, and studied your practices, I now realize that you were either lucky all those years, or you finally lost all of the skills that made you so unique from the rest of the force. I have yet to see you do anything that makes me feel awe, or a reverence toward you. This is all because you don’t actually have anything to you that’s worth respecting… My past, childlike admiration was just that— childlike admiration. Similar to how you have no reason to have any faith in the character of Crusoe, I have no reason to have any faith into the character of you…”
After that, he stalked off, towards the narrow exit out of the manor.

“We already have all of the eye-witness accounts, and answers that we need,” he said after me. “We have a few mysteries that we still have yet to be answered in this room, but, as far as I can tell, you’re no closer to solving them than we are— in fact you’re farther off. Until you have the answers, I’d like you to get off your high horse and learn some humility. Clearly, you’re not the great detective mind that you might like to see yourself as… There are more questions than you can ever answer, Kyler. And, if you ever wish to get them, you’re going to have to learn to work with people outside of your fantasies with an untrustworthy and anonymous Private Investigator. Don’t let yourself stoop any lower than you have to. Personally, I think that you’ve already let Crusoe destroy the once great and admirable character that you had… When was the last time that anything you did actually mattered?”

With that, he was gone. As wordy and obtuse as his monologue to me might’ve been, I knew that there was a lot more truth to it than my ego wanted to allow. In fact, I now recognized that a lot of my misgivings towards Officer Paul hadn’t been from Officer Paul at all— instead, most of them had to do with my own jealousy, and insecurities. As I peered throughout the room, for anything that might’ve brought me remotely close to some answers, all that I saw was how truly blind I was. There were no answers that I could find that others weren’t capable of finding— I’d only let myself think that there were such answers.

I kneeled down, and studied the dusted ground one last time. Upon my second viewing, there looked to be a trail of fingerprints on the ground. AT first I was quizzical of it, but I then rationalized that one of the investigators must’ve forgotten to take their gloves off, and contaminated the crime scene by doing so.
“And, this is why I hate working in large groups…” I said to myself. “If only I could’ve been here earlier.”

Those last words ran off my tongue with a far greater sincerity than I initially expected them to come with. I did deeply wish for there to be a better way for me to take care of the growing questions— I wanted to know what the crime scene first looked like, when it was fresh and untainted. I suddenly had an overflowing well of regret toward the fact that I had no way of telling what happened, and that I’d wasted my time sleeping.

I shouldn’t have had to have been woken up by lieutenant Jackson… I thought to myself. I should’ve already been here. I should’ve been the first person here at the crime scene, making sure that everything was as it should be. I should’ve been the one to look at everything for as it was- to gain all of the eye-witness testimonies, all of the missed knowledge, and all of the facts that I needed. That way, I wouldn’t have been so caught up in my personal biases. I would’ve had to face the facts, and only the facts— there would’ve been no way for me to distance myself from the evidence, or laugh everything off. It would’ve appeared self-evident— things would’ve appeared intrinsically true.
“I guess that I’ll have to resort to reading everybody else’s scribbled journals for eye-witness testimony,” I said to myself. “Because, this scene isn’t talking.”

I pinched a bit of the powder from off the reflective marble, and placed it into a plastic bag of mine, before putting the evidence in my pocket. After that, I gave one last look a t the room around me. A great point had been made from Paul— it looked to me that the entire place lacked all of the required evidence to judge anything off of. And, there was no clear escape route for somebody that might’ve ambushed the party. It was a strange sight to look at, the more that I thought about it. Using all of my common sense, and rationality, there was no way to explain how the kidnapper could’ve come to the center of the room, and snatched up the host and a few other guests, without ultimately being caught for what he was doing. None of it added up. To me, it all seemed to almost be a fairytale that somebody had spawned. Even with the smoke, it was all very hard for me to conceive.

“I’m not in the business of what seems conceivable,” I found myself saying under my breath. “As much as I’d want it to be like that, the business that I’m in is a far dirtier one— a business of facts. From what little evidence I have, this is all that I’m able to believe.”

I found this work as a magic spell upon me. After saying this, I immediately felt alleviated. It was all very true— without any evidence pointing to the contrary, however unlikely these events might’ve seemed, it was the only thing that I could rationally believe in.

“The odds might be against me having eaten a bagel for breakfast this morning,” I said to myself. “The odds might’ve been against me getting out of bed, due to a ringing telephone. The odds might’ve been against my conversation with Paul— or anything that I’ve gone through today. Though, that’s the thing about odds. They’re always stacked against everything. Ultimately, I can’t look at the odds, but at what happened. And, I’m going to have to agree upon what happened, whether I like it or not.”

With this, I left the room, and the rest of the crime scene. After everything that I’d witnessed, I no longer felt as if I had a place in the case. Even with all of my expertise, I now was beginning to see just how problematic my observations really were. I was probably among the most biased people on the case. And, this had led me to make observations that were utterly false.
“I can’t let myself do that again, “I found myself saying as I stepped into my squad car. “I’m going to find the answers— and, I’m not going to let them become altered by what I want them to be…”

Three days had passed since last at Mr. Donald’s mansion— three days of toil and strenuous thought, over something that I was becoming increasingly aware to be an utter waste… There was no way to save the people that had been kidnapped, from what I could tell, on my own.

According to the eye-witness accounts— which probably took me an hour to read, due to the terrible handwriting— there was no possible way that the culprit could’ve escaped. Nothing added up. Apparently, Detective Crusoe— or, a party dressed up as him— had grabbed Mr. Donald, after jumping down upon the ballroom from the ceiling. Already, this didn’t make sense to me— From what I’d seen in the room, it was impossible for one to get in without having been invited, or having been let in without any attention. Everybody in the ballroom had gotten there upon invitation.

Moreover, after this happened, they grabbed two of the guests, and urged for Mr. Donald to come, so that they might release the guest. From what I was able to gather, Crusoe had placed his arm around the guests’ necks, and threatened to choke them. Mr. Donald appeared to be a true hero in this situation, too— having told all of his guests to stand back, and walked up to Crusoe to comply.

If this already made no sense, and sounded like complete fiction, it only started to become more far-fetched, and ridiculous. Once Mr. Donald came over to Crusoe, Crusoe supposedly found a way to cuff Mr. Donald to his arm, so that Mr. Donald couldn’t escape. In this way, Crusoe never had to let go of either of the guests. One might think that Crusoe, or any person in such a situation, might’ve had a decidedly hard time doing this, seeing that Crusoe had no free arms. However, the account said otherwise.
At this point, the accounts said that a few people tried running towards Crusoe. But, this was when the smoke bombs went off, and the four individuals utterly disappeared from sight.

At this point, I was almost certain that the accounts had been faked— it was the only way that I was able to make any sense out of what I was reading. Although, I was forced to believe that it was real, despite all of these facts pointing to the contrary. I didn’t want to believe it, but it was the only thing that I could believe, lest I would be forced to submit to my own individual fantasies.

One thing that surprised me about the accounts was that there were seldom any inconsistencies between them, Normally, this would seem to be good thing, but I couldn’t help but be largely skeptical. Most of the time, there would be several difference between each account, due to the flaws of memory. Though, I rarely even found a discrepancy between the color of Crusoe’s clothes.

None of it was adding up for me, and I was even more surprised when I found that my police department didn’t seem to care. While they were busy trying to find the answer to who might’ve kidnapped Mr. Donald, they didn’t seem too receptive to the concept that nobody might’ve kidnapped Mr. Donald. Not that I entirely blame them. If I were in the same position, I would’ve been compelled to do the very same thing. After all of my experience in the field, I’d learned just how easy it was to make a mistake, and fall in to trivial wanderings. Nobody likes to be proven wrong, and so, most try to stick with what they have and try to prove themselves right— even if the source they have is completely wrong, and it will only end up making them ignorant in the long-run.

Meanwhile, I didn’t really have the time to keep searching for more clues and evidence that might’ve supported my case. What I found was that, the date of Eddy Mulligan’s funeral was looming over me, and I felt the weight of his death taking a greater threshold over my life and thoughts. Normally, his death didn’t quite bother me— nor did funerals. I remember one time when a police colleague of mine died— he was a good man, if a little arrogant. I had a hard time shedding a single tear for him. Don’t mistake me— I was deeply upset at the funeral, and I even felt somewhat bad that I wasn’t crying. It’s simply that, I have a hard time expressing my emotions, especially in extreme circumstances. I’ve found that I tend to keep everything inside of myself. In fact, that may very well be why I have such a hard time interacting with other people, and the very reason that I’m so good at what I do.

Nevertheless, Eddy Mulligan had proven to be a n exception. While I never knew Eddy as a man very well, I knew him before manhood— and, the very fact that he was gone pushed me to the point where I felt as if I’d disservice him in a very great way— I was the only person in his life who had the ability to know him very well, before death, and I’d squandered it. It was this thought that I still couldn’t get over. And, the fact that I was coming closer to the day where I’d have to face it was really making me struggle amidst my daily affairs.

Another thing that incredibly stunted me was the fact that I knew Amelia Mulligan would be coming soon, and that I’d have to keep her company. Not only did I fear that this would be an awkward discourse, but it would also distract me from the thing that mattered most to me at the moment— making sure that the mystery was solved.

These encumbering fears had really put me in a place of complete loss. I’d felt this several times within the past month— the urge to just give it all up, and seek a different occupation or position. However, this time I felt it more than ever. And, I was more aware of it than ever, as well. I knew that, if I followed how I felt, I would be pushed further from where I needed to go— and I felt as if I were closer to my answers, and my success, than I’d been in quite a while. It was this sort of thinking that pushed me over the edge, and led me to believe that I might’ve been wasting a good deal of my time— that, in spite of my beliefs to the contrary, I’d become quite obsolete. Even in all of my ponderings, and my wish for answers, I was beginning to see just how unoriginal that my thoughts really were. There wasn’t much that distinguished my abilities from the rest of the pack of the police. In fact, and argument could’ve been made that I was becoming far slower, and less skilled than I should’ve been. And argument could’ve been made that I was already being surpassed— that my right to hold my high position was on the verge of necessary termination.

There were a lot of thoughts penetrating my mind, and I couldn’t help but fall susceptible to all of these inquisitions. In truth, I had no defense against them. They all made incredibly strong points, and I had incredibly weak refutations to them. In my mind, there was no way that I could get out of my mounding questions. As usual, I felt as if the questions had grown greater than me— that I was losing to them, and that they’d gained a high ground. Some people might laugh at me for having thoughts such as these— when I really think about it, I have no reason to gain all of the worries and fears that I have about the world. The world seems kind enough, to me. I’ve never been threatened by it to the point where I could no longer overcome it— where I could no longer push forward. It was too demanding against me, even if it was just a figment of my imagination.

That’s probably the greatest folly in this world— to think that an imagination has no hold over reality. It’s probably the greatest opposite. Without imagination, the world would be a place without any human invention, or human thought. Without imagination, reality would be something that is impossible to conceive. It might be thought that, life is a way for us to experience the universe. But, in the same sense, it’s also the only way for the universe to experience itself. It’s that very thought which I find to be both very dark and very bright at the same time. Because, without life, nothing can be understood— it’s simply there, without explanation.
“Maybe I’m just confused because I don’t know what to do…” I sound myself saying to myself.

I wasn’t entirely wrong, either. I didn’t know what to do, and this did confuse me… A times, I felt like I was supposed to do one thing— but, at the next moment, I felt as if I were supposed to do another. It was an odd thing, which left me feeling lost— and, even slightly alone. In a way, the fact that the whole world around me seemed to be turned against me was causing me to feel so many contradictions about the world around me. I didn’t know what to think. In fact, there was a degree to myself that didn’t want to think. The truth was, I’d been beaten down by the surrounding situations. Despite being taught to be a great officer, I found that I was doing away with everything that I’d been trained to do— and, this had led me to the point where I was questioning whether or not I should be doing what I was trained to do.

I’d talked to Lieutenant Jackson about the facts that Id found, and how hard everything was beginning to feel to me— I neglected to inform him about the fact that my house was vandalized again. He, of course, refused to sympathize with me. There are only so many times when you can get your competitor to see the same way that you do— I’d been lucky when he was willing to talk to me a few nights prior.

When sitting at my desk, in my tiny apartment, I found myself penning a letter out to Detective Crusoe. I knew that I was crazy for doing so, and that I had no reason to think that the letter would work. Moreover, I found that there was no reason for me to think that Crusoe would even bother reading my letter. If our past history with each other had proven anything to me, it should’ve proven that Crusoe was no longer a friend, but an enemy that should’ve been avoided. However, one of my greatest weaknesses is easily the fact that I think Crusoe can still be my ally, even after all that we’ve gone through. So, when I penned him the letter, none of that mattered to me, I was transported back to the days when Crusoe was a new figure in the city, and we were brand-new allies— when I had everything to gain, and the city was still a place that looked upon me in optimism— a place that I, in turn, looked upon in optimism.
Things have gotten so much harder without your help, Crusoe… I don’t know what I’m doing, or the answers to any of my questions…

I know that, after my attempt to arrest you, this is probably the last thing that I should be asking you about. I have far too many transgressions dealt against you, and you similarly have too many transgressions stacked against me. At this point, we’re on opposite sides. To think that we could be allies is probably one of the greatest mistakes that anybody could make.

Though, I’ve decided that I want to make that mistake… Crusoe, I need your brain on my side again. You see, even with all of the crimes that you’re being accused of, I have the feeling that you’re innocent. The only person that can prove that is you. Despite me having proven myself to be somebody who’s incredibly untrustworthy, I ask you to forgive me— to put the things that I’ve done aside, so that we might be able to move forward— and make a big difference.

I probably sound insane to you. In fact, you probably don’t care a bit about this note that I’m writing to you. Knowing you, all that you’re interested in are the specifics of the case at hand— that is, if you’re still loyal, and you’re not guilty of committing the crime that the case at hand consists of.

Whatever the truth is here, I just want to tell you that I don’t want you to change from the person that I once knew… I don’t want our past partnership to erode away. I’m being too sentimental here, and none of my words actually matter. But, I’ve found that writing letters is the only way that I can really use my voice, without feeling an immense guilt afterward… I know that I’m stupid in thinking that I can actually change anything, or get through to you. But, the illusion that I can is something that I’m simply not going to abandon. It’s one of those things that I’m going to hold close to myself, with my entire life.

Thanks for being a friend that was there to help me, back when there was nobody else… Everything has changed now, and I’m certain that you don’t care about my problems like you used to. It’s not as if I ever cared so much about yours, especially due to your anonymity. Though, I still appreciate what a great person that you were, and still are. You’re the champion of mysteries— stay that way. And, don’t forget to try helping me on this case, by meeting me at my apartment— I’m sure that you’ll be able to find me. I just hope that you find this, before anybody else does…
Sincerely,
Sergeant Kyler

I took my pen off the paper, and looked down at the note in pride. It was overlong, filled with frustrating dialogue, and run-on sentences… Yet, it was mine. And, I couldn’t help but feel a sort of self-satisfaction and gratification when looking at it. It was a piece that couldn’t be matched by any other pieces. It was the sort of thing that I knew nobody else would be able to compete with, because it was mine. I was the only one who was going to be able to get through Crusoe’s thick skull— and, I was determined to do anything, in order to accomplish that, even if it meant me having to give up all of my other efforts…

It was about an hour of listening to the radio, and musing about the events going on around me, before I went to the lamppost. I had a cloud of stress still over my head. There were so many things that I had to keep up on, and I felt as if I would constantly be at work— that there was no real room for rest in my life, even though I deeply wanted to take hold of it. However, this was something that I eventually was able to put aside. Because, when I looked at the lamppost, I saw the same old mysteries of life facing me— I saw myself, fifteen years ago, putting the same note-paper on the lamppost, and being able to figure things out with Crusoe’s aid. It was clear to me that I wouldn’t be able to solve all the answers… But, I ignored this, preferring to look on the bright side. The fact that I still had a shot at making thing s right. Even in the city’s vast complexity, I’d built myself a bubble in which everything was just so. I was on the verge of returning to that. Even though I had to deal with the passing of Eddy Mulligan, I realized that I was also observing the birth of something just as great, and monumental. Iw as observing the resurrection of a dying partnership.
I walked back to my apartment, not even bothering to go into the police station. It was late at night, to be sure— though, that didn’t disturb me. Everything seemed as it should’ve.

Back in my apartment, I felt a bundle of mixed feelings rush throughout myself. I began to realize, with an aching severity, that I wasn’t going to be able to know if Crusoe was on my side, or not. Even after I gained his favor, he’d always be a mixed bag— I’d always have to wonder if he was truly fighting for me, or if he was vying for some other agenda— he’d certainly proved himself a traitor long in the past— it was the very reason that I constantly felt at odds with myself, even to this day.

“But, I can’t constantly throw myself into my useless ponderings…” I said. “I always was taking a risk with Crusoe. Even on the day that I ‘d first met him, he was always a strange case— a mystery. I could never quite understand him, or calculate what he was about to do next. This was always part of his grand appeal to me. While I know that I can’t fully trust him, I also know that’s part of who he is— and, I’m going to have to take him seriously if I ever hope to make any sort of impact.”

For some reason, I found that these words convinced me, even in the face of the fact that they were the definition of unconvincing. Within myself, I felt entirely lost, and helpless concerning Crusoe— he might’ve been a monster, and yet, I also knew that he might’ve turned out to be a hero. It all depended upon the choices that he would make— and, I sadly knew that his choices were not anything that I could put my faith into.

It’s a funny thing— when you don’t know what you’re supposed to put your faith into, and when the very thin that seems to be where you should put your faith is untrustworthy, what are you supposed to do? Kneel down to your primitive superstitions, and simply go for what feels right on the spur of the moment… Something tells me that there must be a better answer…

Inside, I feel as if all of my efforts are going to waste, and that nothing I can do will ever really amount to anything. I’ve been around for nearly half of my allotted lifespan— maybe more, maybe less.

This stings, with the pain that might be felt amongst a swarm of a thousand bees. I know that most of my pains are in my head, and that a lot of my problems could be caulted over if I just looked at them straight on— if I faced them with a vigilance.

Though, I hate looking at the ugliness of my problems. They never make any sense, and they typically come back around to bite me. I know that I’m being dishonest with myself whenever I think that I can eventually get out of my eternity of questions. Som, I don’t know wjhy I’m beginning to find it to be so hard. I just can’t figure out how my head keeps spinning, and yet, my heart feels as if its trapped in the past—  I want to make everything like the past again. I wish that I didn’t have to leep trying, and fighting, to make things feel a lot more at peace, and normal… Soometimes, I think that the whole world is aimed against me, and I ‘’m the only thing standing between ultimate annihilation. I know that I’m delsuusional, petty, and even arrogant to think this way. But, I’ve found a sort of charm in believing that I can make a difference… And, I don’t want to have to let go of it…
“These problems… They’re just mounting too high…” I found myself whispering to myself…” I don’t know if I can combat them any longer. To be honest, I feel like they’re all beginning to combat me…”

I was inches from laying my head into my desk, and letting all of my problems swallow me wole— submitting my entire self to forces that were beyond me. Though, by some act of miraculous magic, I was able to keep myself from doing so— my mind seemed to be being conducted by a will that was beyond my superstitious thoughts, and fears. It was something beyond the strangling connections of human frailties, and the sentimentality of growing age. The hoarding of the past, which was steadily turning the space within my mind into a stuffy closet that had hardly any room….

“I just don’t have any more answers…” I said. “But, that doesn’t mean that the world doesn’t. Just because I can no longer solve my own problems, it doesn’t mean that my problems can’t be solved. And so, I don’t care what becomes of my choice— my decisions. Humanity has managed to last this long, amongst all of the fears and terrors that are rampant in society. Eventually, it will be able to deal without me and, it probably is already beginning to… My problems are but something small, in the grand scheme of everything. I’m simply going to have to become open to that possibility, even if it’s something that I hate to think on...”

After this, I finally left my lucid visions and running thoughts of growing irrelevance. It wasn’t as if it had been eradicated. I’ve learned that nothing can truly be eradicated– all energy must go somewhere, whether one likes it or not. Though, this doesn’t change the true facts of everything— the cold hard truths, which nobody likes to face. And, that is this— everybody is going to have to face cold hard truths. And, those cold hard truths will never go anywhere. The sadly, help make up the entire world that we live within. To try to rid the world of them would be like trying to rid a contaminated house of pests. No exterminator can truly make the house clean of all the issues that might reside within it. It’s simply too optimistic, and too much of a fairy tale to believe otherwise.

My eyes turned from my desk, and to another paper of mine— a list of notes that I’d taken after my conversation with Jonah, a couple of days ago. I’m embarrassed in saying this— but, I hadn’t followed any of his advice in fear that it all might’ve been a lie. I look back at this in a degree of shame now, but back then it really seemed like a legitimate worry.

Opening up my phone book, I started looking through the list of people that I’d neglected to talk to. All of them concerned the masked robber that had been going into people’s houses— the same one that was associated with dozens of crimes.
The same one that was associated with what was going on with Crusoe.

I shook my head in shame at the thought that I might’ve been a contributing factor in the robbery that occurred at Mr. Donald’s house, by not bothering to go and check out Jonah’s advice sooner. Though, I was ready now— and, I was no longer afraid of what might be awaiting me.

I would think that all of my efforts wouldn’t have gone to waste— that, everything would start falling into place after putting an extreme amount of determination and willpower into it. Though, it appears to be quite the opposite. I’ve been told throughout my life that willpower is the greatest tool towards getting anything done. I now start to think that isn’t true. Instead, willpower is the greatest tool towards exhausting oneself, and reaching a breaking point.
I’d assigned myself an appointment with Margaret Rosemary, but I was already beginning to taste the spice of stress— the idea that my toil would not be one that bore any fruit.

My car was screeching down the sleet-paved streets, and into the sludgy underbelly of the city. The night prior, when sitting at my desk, I’d called up Jonah at last minute. Like the unwise genius that I am, I asked him for the phone number to Margaret Rosemary— something that I should’ve done a while back, but neglected to under the weight of procrastination and internal weights that I had yet to wrangle.

He eventually provided it to me, and I came to see just how uncontradictorily oxymoronic the entire situation had been— I’d gotten what I wanted, but far later than I should’ve gotten it. And, yet, I still felt as if everything was just as it should’ve been— as if everything were in its proper place.
I suppose that might be the strangest thing about me— I’m able to see the bright side in things that don’t have bright sides. I’m able to see things in ways that aren’t meant to be seen by anyone.

Does that make me absurd, or irrational? Most likely. Though, that’s also what makes my mind so keen for the work of investigation. I’m able to study the parts of areas that nobody else dares to look upon. It might be unimpressive, and even annoying at times— though, I’m now beginning to see just how necessary of a thing that it really is for me to be doing.

My car turned a left down the street and I found myself driving through an ever entangling web of building shadows. They started to sprawl over every aspect of my car, and I found myself having to keep my eyes roving everywhere. I was starting to see just how terrible my eyes really were— weak betrayers that ran at the sight of any darkness.

I felt the shadows clutch me, and threaten to throttle me into the abysses that were encircling me with an ever thinning distance from me. They were the alleyways, and from out of them I could hear the darkest parts of the city’s belly belch and groan. It threatened to breathe a fire down my back, and throw me into a tail-spin. Thankfully, I was far too crafty to fall into its clasp. My mental fortitude is one that doesn’t faze so easily.
Rather, I repeated the phrases that I’d heard in nursery rhymes as a child, to pacify my urges to run and hide truly the instinct that everybody else in my situation would’ve listened to.

Of course, my bravery and courage didn’t last long. I’m afraid that, in spit of all of my genius, I have far more weaknesses than I’m able to acknowledge. I found that the street overcame my senses, and my car slowed to a crawl. Eventually, I had to leave my car and walk out into the streets.

I felt a sort of bare nakedness as I did so. Within that car, there was a bit of removal, and distance from everything that was going on. Once back out in the street, I was forced to confront the fact that everything was out of control, and that I had no hand in anything that was going on. It seemed to me that every building looked down upon me, and attempted to rapture me should for itself. I felt it carve deeper into me, leaving me with only the base layers of my consciousness— the primal fears and surges of anger, which was the only way left for me to respond in.

In a sense, while everything appeared turned against me, I felt as if there was nothing that I could do. I looked at the buildings, but I didn’t know that I was looking at them. Instead, I was looking at g=figures draped in a darkness that I couldn’t quite understand. Instead, I was listening to the whisperings from the pits of hell. The groaning, not of building’s aging, but of my own soul coming under threat.

Within the darkness, any of my fears might’ve come true. Without the car’s headlights to guide me amongst the blackened street, and without the lampposts to give me any sort of guiding heat, I was aware that everything and anything could’ve occurred amongst the darkness. Wherein, my mind decided to accept every possibility as going on. It constructed my nightmares, and made them into something solid.

Anybody else, if they were to have stood next to me, would’ve told me to snap out of my slipping grip on the truth— they would’ve told me that what I feared was something that wasn’t there to fear in the first place. However, I now know that this is a grave mistake. What we find in our dreams, or inside of the spinning terrors of our brains, are just as real as the ground beneath our feet— or the skull that encloses the brain which dreams. For, dreams are a gateway into the circus that goes on around us. In exploring our dreams, we explore the worst— and, in exploring the worst, we confront the worst parts of ourselves.

I squinted so that I could read the address on every building that I passed. I was once again in a downtown area, but it was far more abandoned and destitute than even Jonah’s place. In the air, I could smell the debris of death, and abandonment. It was perhaps the only sense that I could really trust— and, it was one that made me feel more fearful than any other.

Oddly, with it being the only sense that I could understand, it was also the only sense that gave me a sort of courage or hope. I felt that, in understanding what I was smelling, I might soon be able to understand everything else that was going on around me. I’d be able to get rid of the torridness was haunting me.

The water drained into my eyes, and I found myself spluttering to get a hold of it. I could tell that I’d started to walk too closely toward the buildings. The rain was splashing down onto me with the force that might be found in a bb gun, and I instantly knew that I’d taken steps too close to the edge of safety. I had grazed slimming thread of my mortality, and I could feel it start to screech, like a guitar string that had been tightened too much. I was standing under the roof of the house that I needed to go into—right in the targeting position of their overflowing gutters. My misery in having done so was like a raw cut.

Feet dragged against the gravel as they climbed up a case of stairs. Knuckles crunched softly, as they smacked themselves against the wood of a rotting door. There was a mushy bristling, sounding like a parade of soggy sponges, caused by a pair of drenched clothes.

My pair of drenched clothes. My crunching knuckles. My feet. Yet, not mine at all— I wouldn’t have had the courage to have knocked on the door on my own. It was something else inside of me— my instinctual duty— that had ordered me to do so.

The door opened with the sound of a wailing cat. There was a tearing at my ankles, and I realized that there really had been a screeching cat. However, I couldn’t look down or kick the cat away, even as my muscles tensed and told me to. Instead, I was forced to stare into the eyes of a man, who was far more disturbing to look at than the cat probably would’ve been.

He had a ratty look to him— crooked teeth, untended whiskers, beady eyes, mussy hair, and skin that was tough and matted. As I looked at him, I wished that I couldn’t look at him. In that instance, I wished that I was blind as I had been before the door had opened.

That was possibly the only good thing that had come out of the door opening— while I had to stare and feel all of this ugliness, at least “I knew that this ugliness was the truth— not some conjuring that my head had built for me.
“What are you doing here?” the voice croaked, staring at my police uniform.
I could’ve sworn that I heard the sound of a gun being loaded as he said this, and I realized that I’d made a mistake in coming.

I suddenly wished that I had only come in plainclothes. It would’ve made things so much easier for me. In fact, I was beginning to sense that going around dressed up as an officer was perhaps my greatest weakness. It seemed that, in everything I did, there was somebody who looked upon my uniform in disgust. I couldn’t blame anybody who did. I would’ve done the same exact thing, Should I have been placed in the same situation. There was something to coming to houses dressed as a cop, in an area like this. Everybody looked at us as if we were the villains. Many places were robbed, and many people were arrested. Those who remained in this area had come to associate the police with the many friends that they’d lost. When I came to their door, dressed as I was, I represented that very thing to them— I represented all that they feared and resented. I was a monster.
“I am here,” I said, “to speak with Miss Margaret Rosemary. Is she here?”
“You’re here,” the man said, preparing to spit at me. “Why not, eh?”
He had a look of terror in his eyes, in spite of his fury. I could see that he was just as weak as I felt inside— maybe even more so.
“I only want to ask a few questions.”
“You’ve already asked, them…”
He stopped, to read the nametag on my suit.
“Sergeant Kyler,” he said, uttering my name with a strong sense of revulsion.

I grasped my collar with my finger. Even though I was drenched, I couldn’t help but feel incredibly hot on the doorstep. I was getting the feeling that my visit wasn’t going to work out in the slightest.

“I know that you’re planning to arrest me,” the man said, under his breath, Then, with a booming yell, “Just do what you’re going to do already! Cuff me! I don’t need to wait any longer! If you’re going to do what you’re going to do, then there’s no reason in making me wait for it! I’m not playing gmames1 I’m not interested in playing cat and mouse!”

“Neither am I,” I said. “You’re taking things into far higher proportions than they’re actually in. I’m not planning to hurt you in any way— I’m only here to speak with Miss Rosemary. Are you going to answer me, or not? That’s all I need to know, and once I know, our conversation will be over.”

I looked down at him, and watched him twitch in the struggle between giving his answer. I felt incredibly fearful when I looked at him. I didn’t know what to expect out of him. For all I knew, he was preparing to strike at me I would be helpless, if he chose to do so. Though, I also saw that he was just as afraid as I. This was probably the single thing that kept me standing there, at his doorstep. In spite of all the strangeness that was taking place.

“Fine!” he yelled. “She lives here on this floor, in the back room. But, if you do anything to hurt or trick any of us, then you’ll have made a big mistake. We’re not playing games here, with you officers. If you want to take us down, then you’ll have to do better than decide to come here all on your own.”
He made sure to give several quick glances at my arms— particularly my broken one—0 in order to drive his point in.

I suddenly realized that I’d walked into far more than I’d bargained to. If this was just a sample of the sort of people that I’d be dealing with, then the conversations would be a lot more straining than I possibly could’ve anticipated.

As the man stepped out of the way— still not bothering to give me his name, and with me not bothering to ask for it— I was tempted to ask for guidance. I didn’t know the building very well, and I had a feeling that I was going to get lost. The back room wasn’t a very specific instruction. However, a quick look back to him reminded me why I wasn’t going to dare to ask him. He had the fiery anger of a thousand suns within his eyes. The very idea of daring to keep trying to speak with him was one that put me into a daze— the beginning of the conversation had been terrible enough, and I was in no mood to go through the conversation a second time.

As I walked through the stuffy hall, I saw that there were two back rooms— one to the left, and one to the right. I had to assume that the man had been referring to the left back room, as that room appeared more abandoned and unused. But, I was honestly clueless.

There were only six rooms on this floor, but it felt like they were probably all half the size of what they’d been intended to be. Everything was so condensed that I hardly even felt as if I were actually walking through a single floor. Instead, it was like a sad excuse for a maze.

Everything was crumbling too. This wasn’t at all new to me. In fact, I pretty much expected all of this. The entire city seemed to have caught the virus of age, and there didn’t appear to be any avoiding it. Though, this floor took the cake. There wasn’t a single space that wasn’t covered in some kind od stain, mold, or hunk of missing plaster. It appeared to entirely lack any sort of maintenance. It even smelled terrible. Usually, buildings in the downtown area smelled bad— but this building was something different entirely. It was as if I was walking within a rotting tree.

My knuckles rapped against another door, and I found myself feeling the same terror that I had felt the first time that I’d knocked on the door— there was no telling what kind of person would come out of the room. However, just by judging everything else that was going one, I was starting to suspect that it wouldn’t be a person who would be very amiable.
“Who is it?” I heard the person on the other side of the door yell.

I instantly knew that it was Margaret Rosemary. However, I also instantly knew that she was not interested in my visit. The apparent annoyance coming from out of her throat spoke this, and much more to me.
“It’s Sergeant Kyler, of the CPD,” I said, in response.
I caught the woman’s eye staring through her peephole, before the door finally snapped with the sound of its locks being opened.

The door steadily swung open, in the same way that the original door had. Except, this time, I didn’t have to fear another cat jumping out at me. In fact, I was no longer caught amongst the concern of having to deal with rats either.

“What do you want?” she said, in the same way that the apartment building owner had. Thankfully, it took just one glance at her for me to tell that I wasn’t quite dealing with the same threat. Instead of having a desperate, ratty look to her, she appeared to be very clean— at least, when compared to everything else around her.

She was a fairly young woman, looking to be in her mid to late twenties. Though, she looked as if she’d seen a lot— her face was worn and tired, and her clothes had the same coarse look to them. Her hair was probably the only thing that looked to be abhorrent of the grimy nature that the rest of the building held. However, her hair was a jet black, so it was probably fairly easy for her to have been able to hide any dirt that might’ve been in it.
“Are you Miss Margaret Rosemary?”
“At the moment, I wish that I could say no.”
Her face was scrunched into a non-receptive scowl. I’d clearly pushed her to the edge, and she wasn’t entertaining my stay. Although, I wasn’t keen on entertaining her anger either, so I continued.
“Can I come in? I have a few questions for you, concerning a strange series of capers… I’d prefer to speak with you in private on these matters, since this is strict police business.”
“I’d prefer for you to not speak to me at all… It’s nearing night, and I was preparing to go to sleep.”
“I’m afraid that I can’t satisfy those wishes— you can wait for sleep. Right now, I have a few questions that I need to ask you…”
“Yes, I think that I’ve already figured that out… Since you want to so much, come in. But, you’re not going to be satisfied…”
I stepped into her doorway, only to be greeted by a massive stink of perfume. My eyes started to water, and I had to force myself to keep them under control.

“So…” she said, pulling up two cheap lawn chairs, and taking a seat in one. “What do you need to know so badly? I you think that I’m the one who’s been doing all of those capers, then I’ m afraid that you’ll be thoroughly disappointed. I’m no mastermind, I’m afraid… I f I was, then you probably would’ve never gotten to find me.”
“I’ve caught plenty of convicts ma’am. If you were one, I don’t think that I would’ve had that hard of a time… But, I don’t suspect you of anything at the moment, anyway.”

“I’d believe you, if it wasn’t for the fact that you police rarely ever get anything done. Though, let’s entertain the idea that you’re presenting to me for the moment… Why are you coming to me at all?”

“I need to know your story…” I said. “Eye-witness testimony might be terrible, but I’m in a cloud of eye-witness testimonies right now If that’s all that I can get, then I’m gladly taking it. I need to know what you know about the robberies that are going on, because you’re the next person that my sources have informed me of...”
“What sources?”

“I’d prefer to not expose them,” I said, taking a glance at her ceiling. The light above me was flickering, distracting me from talking. Cleary, it was a bad lightbulb that needed to be replaced— just like a lot of things in the apartment.
The place around me was so poorly built and occupied that it was almost hilarious.
“Now, enough with your questions,” I continued, trying to take the reins of the conversation. I think that we’ve chatted in circles long enough. You need to start giving me answers.”

“If you have the right to your questions, you should at least have the courtesy to give me the right to mine,” she said, rolling her eyes. “but., if you insist for me to give you answers, then fine. About a year ago, my house was robbed. I went inside to found the place completely ransacked… I didn’t know who did it, so I started running out my door to tell the apartment manager. But, some black figure knocked me to the floor before I could. I couldn’t get a good look at them and they left. That was it— that’s all I have to say. The robbery began and ended— it really isn’t that big of a deal. I can’t see why you’re so interested in something so trivial.”

I knew that she was lying. Jonah had told me that there was a lot more to the story than his own. I just needed to give her the right motivation to give me her story. Amongst the rain and the sleet of downtown, I knew that anybody was willing to do anything, should thwey be provided with enoughgh positive reinforcement.
“What occurred before the robbery took place? Any important events? Anything of note that you can think of?”
She scowled again.
“Who sent you here?” she asked. “and, why aren’t you leaving. I gave you the answer to your main question, didn’t I?”

I looked into her eyes, and returned the scowl. I wasn’t in the mood to play games, any more than the front-entrance manager had been. I could feel her willingness to give me the truth steadily grow. I knew that, if I pushed long and hard enough, I’d be able to get my much-needed answers from out of her.

“There are a lot of questions that I have. You should know that I can’t leave until I have all of the information that I need. Now, answer my question. What happened before the robbery, that might’ve caused it?”

Miss Rosemary looked down to the floor for a while, without giving a clear answer. I heard her mumble a few things, but I knew that she wasn’t speaking anything worthwhile. Rather, she was weighing her possibilities.
I’ll never be able to understand this part of interrogation. And, afterwards, I’m never fully able to tell if the person is ever telling the truth or not.
“You didn’t answer my question either,” she said. “Who sent you here?”

“Jonah,” I said.  Felt my tongue sting as I said this…I knew that I’d betrayed Jonah’s trust, to degree. Though, I also knew that I’d had no other choice. “He told me his own story, and then told me that you’d have some answers. Though, I also saw your name somewhere else— it was written in graffiti, at an abandoned hospital wall. Those are two times that I’ve seen your name.”

I felt my breath heavy after having said this— an adrenaline rush, as well as a jolt of shock. I now partially understood the reluctance of everybody, in the interrogation position. The revealing of the truth didn’t feel as a very pleasant thing to do.
“Now, I’ve given you your answers…” I said, still groping for breath. “It’s your turn to give me yours… What happened before the robbery?”

I watched as Miss Rosemary’s face crunched up, and her eyes started to water. There was something that had changed in her, after I told her about her name on the hospital wall. It seemed to me that she knew something, which not even I had suspected.

“Fine!” she said. “Similar to Jonah’s story— if he told you his entire story— my house was robbed after a series of robberies occurring in a friend of mine’s house— my brother’s house, to be specific. He too, like Jonah’s friend, was in strange dealings. And, after his house had been vandalized and stolen from enough times, he disappeared… We held a funeral for him, and everything.
