The whole family was there, to mourn for him. He was way too young— younger than me, at about he ag twenty when he passed. I thought that he was truly gone, as well as everything that I’d known him for…

“My brother was a great man; from what I could tell. Very unsuccessful, and poor, but still a great man. He provided for our family when he needed to, he held a steady job— even if it paid him very little— and he seemed to deeply care about the whole family. There was never a day when I worried about him. Although, something shifted when was at the funeral… I realized that there were a lot more dimensions to him than I knew. A lot of his friends came to his funeral, and most of them were people that I’d never even met.”

She paused, to reposition herself in her chair. I saw that there was sweat on her forehead, and her lips had started to quiver. My question had had a far greater effect than I’d ever thought it would have.

“I’m probably getting into details that are too personal,” she said. “But, you asked… Anyway, after my brother’s funeral ceremony, my house was robbed. The dark figure was in my room, writing on everything, and making a mess of my stuff. The whole place was a complete mess, and I feared that the figure would take me away. I never actually went to tell anybody, nor did I say anything. Part of me thought that I was dreaming, and part of me thought that I was looking at my brother’s ghost. For some reason, even though the figure saw me, it didn’t leave either. It was as if it recognized that I wasn’t willing to alert anybody of its presence. Somewhere inside of it, it saw that I thought it to be harmless. It saw that I wasn’t any sort of threat. It was a supernatural being like no other, to be sure.

“Eventually, it finally left, making the terrible whirring sound that might come from an old motor. I had been reduced to a statue, but I forced myself to move. I found that the robber, whoever it was, had only vandalized the things that were sentimental to me. A lot of the items that traced back to my childhood were gone. Eventually, I had to wonder if the robber had known me. however, it hadn’t bothered to touch everything— just a few things. A few things, and my wall.

“on the wall, it wrote a message to me, warning me that my brother was still alive— warning me that, if I tried going to look for him, it would return— and, I wouldn’t make it out alive. Finally, the message scribed on the wall told me that I would have to start sending it money, and that I could tell nobody about what was going on— or else, it would find out, and it would return to spite me… I had this wall cleaned, and the manager never told anybody about it… But, it’s still engrained in my memory.”
She stopped again. But, this time it looked like there wasn’t a way for me to get her to talk again.
“This wasn’t’t the last time the shadowy robber came— is it?” I said, giving her a look of concern.

“No,” he said, her voice giving off an air of relcuctance. “Not even close.. The shadow robber followed through on its warning. It came back for the money, a week later. I remember all of my bones feeling llike gelatin, and my eyes not being able to move focus. The shadow actually spoke to me, this time around. And, it was one of the most terrifying things that I’ve ever heard in my life…”
“What did it say to you?” I ssked, in conern.

“It said many things,” she said. “It was always saying many things, from this part onward. IT toold me not to ask any questions about my brother— that I should only be worrying  about myself from now on. The only thing tha tit was willing to tell me about my brother was that my brother was a cowardly, treacherous man. The shaodow also told me to give all my money away to it— this was something that I, regretfully, easily obliged to. The shadow was just  so angry— overbearing too. I even tried to fight it at one point. But, it was as if it were oprepared for every sudden movement from me— as if it could reas my mind, and stop me from doing things before I was even willing to do them…”
I shivered myself. I knew exafctly what Margaret was talkling about. I knew it all too well.

One of my greatest problems with detective cases had always been the fact that I had a hard time relating with my clients. I don’t know why— but, throughout all of the interrogations, I could never really feel their pain— never really worry when they were worrying. It was probably always an effect of my stone heart, and a strong sense of removal. However, today, I realized just how close I was to everything that was going on— the fact that I was only mere steps away from habving become the very same thing that this woman was. I suddenly realized that I was no different from her. In learning so, I also realized that my only hope was listening to her.
“It sounds all too similar to the cases that I’m currently working on,” I said. “I definitely think that this is relevant to the topic at hand. How long did this keep on happening?”

I regretted asking this question. I started to regret asking all of my questions. Because, as she answered them, I would steadily begin to know the severity of the criminal that I was dealing with. And, I would steadily begin to see just how much clout they really had, without even my slightest awareness.

There was something else that haunted me. All of the people that were victims of this haunting vandalizer seemed to be people who had lost good friends. My thoughts instantly went out to — the only man who seemed to fit the description for me. It was a startling and unsettling notion, but I was starting to be forced to recognize that he probably wasn’t the great person that I’d wanted him to be.

“I would hope it doesn’t sound too similar…” she said. “I wouldn’t want anybody else to be going through the same exact things that I went through. There are other people who have gone through things that sound akin to what I’ve gone through. But, none of them quite match my extreme.

“To be honest, this has been going on nonstop, twice every month. I can never know when it’s coming each month. One time, it came twice within two days. I’ve told a few people about it… But, never within this room… I’m afraid that he’s always listening. I’m afraid that, somehow, someway, the shadow will eventually find out that I’ve spoken about it— I’m afraid that it will eventually find a way to make me repay, if I do.”

“You don’t have to worry…”  I said. “I’m here to protect you from that happening. That’s the whole reason that you’re talking to me— so that we can finally get rid of this thing, and take them— or it— to prison.”

“Yes— well, I didn’t tell you the full truth… I actually have told somebody about what was going on, in this very room. However, that’s when I learned just how big of a threat that I was dealing with. When I escorted them out the hallway, and then returned to my room, I found a knife stuck in the place where I was sitting. There was a draft in the room as well. When I looked up, I saw the shadowy figure standing within the light of my window. And then, it left without a word.

“The only thing that I can say I was glad about, concerning the visit, was that the monster never dared speak to me. That was probably the only gift that I received. Because as much as I wished for it to talk at times, its words were only threats. Moreover, his voice was like the sound of iron being welded.”

I looked at the window after she said this, with a wariness. I swore that I could’ve seen something stalking through there, beyond its greasy screen. However, I also had to pass it off as a dream, because it disappeared as soon as I began to look after it.
“You honestly think that the only reason this shadow is after you is because it wants revenge over your brother’s actions?’ I asked.
“That’s the only reason that I can come up with…” she said.
We sat there for a moment, with me pondering about the ramifications about all of this— about just how much it had shifted what I was thinking about everything.
“I know that it’s been a while, so I don’t really expect accuracy. But, describe the shadowy man in the best and most accurate terms that you can.”

There was a pause when she didn’t say anything, and all that I heard was a sniffling. I felt a sudden sympathy for the poor girl. But, then Miss Margaret offered me a tissue, and I realized that the sniffling was my own.

“Yes, I suppose that I might as well give you as much information, however inaccurate it might be,” Margaret said. “Well, from what I can remember, the figure wasn’t particularly lightweight, or heavy. It seemed to balance somewhere in between. However, something that I did happen to notice was how unusually tall that it was. This was how I was able to see it, despite its efforts to hide itself in the shadows as much as it could. I never did get a good look at its face— but, I always smelled a sort of perfume whenever I was close to it. In fact, it was the perfume of a woman. I’m not sure if they were trying to mask their scent, if they were in fact a woman, or if here’s some other explanation. But, as far as I can tell, nothing of it can really be understood. It’s all just garbled information that I’ve managed to retrieve from the corners of my memories. Who knows— amongst all of my nightmares concerning it, some of my details might be slurred. I know that you might expect me to know more, but this person is simply too hard to measure. In fact, sometimes I wonder whether or not it could be different people each time, with all of them stalking me with the same information. It’s these sort of questions that keep me up at night.”

For a minute. I didn’t’ have any answers for her. I just scribbled down all of her descriptions, and hoped that I might be able to make something out of it. Although, the more that I thought upon it, the more that I realized it wasn’t something that I could rely upon at all. It began to appear to me that there was in fact multiple shadowy caper culprits. That, or there was a lapse in memory concerning all of the victims— including myself. There were so many varying descriptions— a short, heavy, womanly figure, a tall, normal weight, womanly figure a lightweight, tall, manly figure, and a short, heavy, manly figure. Though, none of this actually brought me any closer to a conclusion. Instead, it just made me wonder if there were any conclusion that I could draw at all.
Finally, I closed my notebook after reading, and re-reading everything that I’d put down. There was so much information. Yet, none of it seemed to be lining up.

I checked my watch, and saw that it was a quarter to seven. Then, I took a glance out the window— storm clouds hadn’t done the daylight any justice, and had made it look as if nighttime had already started its reign.

“At least it isn’t as late as I thought it was…” I muttered to myself. Then, with a louder voice, “Miss Rosemary, all of this is fine and good information. However, I now need you to show me where in the room that you’ve seen this shadow y figure. I need to know as much as I can in as short of time that I can— I have a tight schedule tonight that I really need to keep.”
Miss Rosemary didn’t seem too eager to comply, and squirmed in her seat before she got up— probably due to the fact that she was annoyed by my rushed manner.

“There was one spot where the intruder consistency like to hang around— it was my window. I’m not sure why, but they constantly found a comfort being there, often seeming to elicit the spirit that they felt the window was a sure escape for them. At other times, it would hang around my front door.”

She paused, and turned to gesture to the ceiling over the door. “Whoever it was, they must’ve been crazy. They’d crouch upon the thin ledge above my door, and a thin lightbulb in the ceiling, above my head. That way, if I ever tried to attack them, they’d have the ability to jump over me and leave. This month, I actually tried doing so with my broom, and ended up knocking them off balance. They landed on the floor with a hard thump, before finally deciding to leave.”
She then walked over to her desk.

“They’ve also hung around this area, whoever they were, sorting through my personal files and papers. This is probably why I despise them the most, and I feel that they really need to go. Now that they’ve gone through a lot of my personal belongings, I feel that the only logical course of action to take is to completely remove them from the equation.”
I nodded, in a placid agreement.

“Yes— this is all very terrible,” I said, studying all of the locations for anything that might’ve serviced my investigations. I found a strip of brown cloth near the window sill, a smattering of blood and dust remains on the carpet in front of Miss Rosemary’s door, and a few grubby fingerprints on Miss Rosemary’s desk. I figured that they were all from Miss Rosemary, and that the criminal had probably taken measures to wear gloves at all times, but I went to the trouble of collecting as many samples as I could anyway.

“Well, that should be good enough for now,” I said, taking one quick glance over her room. “I should probably stay to search the premises longer, but I really don’t have the time tonight. If there ever happens to be another one of these occurrences, make sure to tell me. Oh and also…”
I pulled a slip of paper, with my address on it, and gave it to her.
“Make sure to send me a letter if you have anything else you want to tell me about.”
Miss Rosemary nodded.
“Yes— Yes, I will…” she said. “But, what will I do, if you can’t find me— if something terrible happens to you?”
I grimaced, but knew that I’d had to answer her anyway.

“If that happens, then be prepared for the worst,” I said. “There’s only so much that I can promise—m only so much that I can do. However, I’m going to need you to be able to do this for me. You’re going to have to inspect the premises yourself, as well— tell me if you see anything in here that isn’t yours, and also send me a note containing the list of all the things that this man destroyed. I would love to stay here and jot down as many notes about it as I can. But, I really have to go.”

She frowned— although she’d been angered by my sudden visit to this place, she was now instead angered by my sudden decision to leave. “There’s no need to try leaving. WE still have plenty of time on our hands! Don’t go! What’s with the rush?”
I shook my head.
“I’ve spent too much time here already,” I said.

And, with that, I opened her flimsy door and left. I noticed her face as I left the room— a really sad sight to be, for certain. Though, I also noticed the flimsiness of the door— how easy it would’ve been for a very skilled individual to pick the knob’s lock, and break into the room. It was in focusing on this that I was able to ignore her, and leave for my studies. In fact, without this to guide me, and give me a sort of drive, I might’ve stayed. Thankfully, I didn’t.

As I hopped into my car, there was one other thing that consoled me as I left— one other bit of motivation I had, which gave me a sort of confidence— the fact that the entire place had smelled horrible.
“I just had to leave that place,” I chuckled to myself. “There was no other choice. If I’d stayed there any longer, I might’ve started smelling like the stuff.”

I later found that this joke wasn’t nearly as funny as my mind made it out to be. But, it seems to me that the mind loves making things out to be a lot funnier than they actually are, in the toughest moments of life. Leaving Miss Rosemary was something that I’d done in extreme reluctance. There was so much that I still had to talk to her about, and I could already feel the rocks of regret pounding down my back. It was probably going to be set back, due to my decision.
Though, I also knew that I was making another decision– one of which might’ve been able to be paid off thoroughly.

“I need to go meet,” I said to myself. And, I can’t afford to miss it. Not only that, but Detective Crusoe is coming to my house tonight as well— I’ve had plenty of experience with double dates in my time. Perhaps the greatest mistake concerning them is making the rookie decision to skip them over…
I pulled up to my apartment, and ran up to it, thirty minutes behind the designated time. My decision to go exploring downtown had been one that easily set me off.

Technically, I was actually an hour and a half behind my actual schedule. I’d planned to get dressed into my nicest outfits, and to clean up my house in the preparation of the coming guests. Yet, all of that time had slipped through my fingers now… In attempting to make a time for myself, I’d only begun to feel far worse about everything. I was so far behind, that I knew I’d have a hard time getting everything accomplished. It was all going to become a horrid mess, of which I would end up regretting, if I didn’t keep up rushing.

So without bothering to take my notes or anything out of the squad car, without bothering to park the squad car in the police station, I went to my house— nothing mattered to me anymore, except making sure that I was there on time, so that my two guests wouldn’t be coming to an empty house. I knew that I was going to be walking upon a thin rope as it was.
It was a daze on my way up into my apartment. By the time I’d shoved myself onto the other side of my apartment door, I could hardly remember any of the rushing that had led up to it.

I wiped the sweat off of my brow, and then placed my police jacket onto a coat rack next to my door. After that, I strolled up to my chair with a sense of ease and relief. In all of my rushing, I’d finally reached my goal. There was something satisfactory about that thought— the realization that all of your work has paid off, and that you’ll finally begin receiving the rewards for it.

I hit the floor, and I suddenly felt pricks of shock and surprise rip into my forearms, back, and chest. MY eyes scanned for what had happened, and then they met Crusoe— he’d been the one who knocked me to the floor.You would’ve been able to prepare for something like that, years ago,” Crusoe said. It was clearly Crusoe, no doubt in my mind.
“Yes, well you wouldn’t have exposed your voice so quickly, years ago. In fact, you would’ve made an attack that would be much harder to evade…”
“I suppose that we’ve both gotten old then…” Crusoe said. “Not that it matters. I have the upper hand here.”
“Come on,” I said, struggling to fight him off of me. “You know that I’m no threat, and I know that you’re no threat. Why don’t you get off of me, and start acting civilized?”
Crusoe laughed. His laugh had a loud, and haunting element to it— a sort of echo within it that made me feel deeply disconcerted.

“In all of our years of knowing each other, you should know that I’m not the type that’s civilized,” he said. “I don’t know what’s funnier. The fact that you didn’t acknowledge that, or the fact that you act is if I’m the sort who obliges to people’s pleas for me to stop. The very fact that I returned from my grave proves that I’m not limited by your foul wishes to put me under.”

He chuckled again, before getting off of me— clearly acting as if his words were said in light jest, and not meant to be taken seriously. Though, I couldn’t help but swallow every word that came out of his mouth. I don’t know— something didn’t feel quite right around him. And, the one phrase that particularly set me into a spiral of questions was him saying, “I returned from the grave.” I don’t know… I knew that he didn’t seem to be taking himself too seriously, but there was always a mystical element amongst Crusoe. And, I was no longer so certain that I was a man who was against the arts of mysticism— not after all of the strange things that I was constantly seeing, and everything that was going on around me.
“Yes,” I said. “I do remember the plunge you took— we all thought that you must’ve been dead afterwards.”
“I don’t know, “Crusoe said.

He’d stopped holding me down at this point, and was now standing in the shadows, far from where my eyes could see. I’m not sure what had changed his mind, but I’d clearly appealed to some sort of latent better nature from within him.
“Though, I don’t know how you’ve survived your growing heart condition, either….” He said.
I stood up, and brushed myself of, before hissing, “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“Yes you do,” Crusoe said. He’d now returned to his usual calculated self, and the very thought that he was capable of laughing seemed impossible. Though, it was perhaps better that way— his laugh was not one that I’d prefer to remember. “You’ve done quite a few strenuous exercises in the past month, and I’m sure that your ticker is starting to tick down to its last tick. You’ve been tumbling through too many mountains of stress. I have no doubt that this was why you gave up on all of your pursuits…”

“No…” I said. “I gave up on detective work for a little while because it wasn’t suiting me. You see, you don’t understand. There are too many encumbering cases… It’s all mounding on top of me, and there was a span when I thought that rest would be preferable to this. Of course, there was something that drew me back. In spite of the stress of the job, I realized that—.”

“There you go again— the stress of the job. I should’ve known that it was coming to you. Unlike I, you haven’t learned how to forget about all of the cares of other people in this business. You think for others too much, and are constantly focused on solving all of the other cases— never realizing that you’re sticking yourself into a trap. Your heart, mind, and body can’t take all of it.

“The irregular heartbeats, the constant sweating you have, the strain in your ability to move fast, your distaste for terror— all of it, and more, has added up to what I perceive to be your heart starting to fail. Tell me that I’m wrong. In fact, I’d love to hear that I’m wrong. It’s been quite a long time. But, I know that I’m right… and, you know it too.”

I didn’t want to hear any more of it. Even now, my chest thumped horribly, and I was aware of just how correct he was. My doctor was consistently warning me about my heart at every time I met with him— telling me to keep the stress down, to take things easy, and not to let my urges to run this stressful environment win. But, there was something within myself that wasn’t willing to listen to the doctor. I didn’t want to have to listen to Crusoe either.

“Bravo, you figured out the mystery, just like all the rest,” I said, with my eyes darting around the room so as to avoid Crusoe’s gaze. “You know, I always look to you to solve problems for me, and give me your results. But something that I hate about you is just how effective you are. One of these days, you need to figure out how to only give me the answers to the mysteries that I want to hear the answers to– I’d prefer not to know the mysteries within myself, as appealing as that may sound at first glance.

“Now, to the answers to the mystery that I actually brought you here for… You see, I’ve been dealing with a series of capers. A lot of people think that you’re guilty of them, but I’d prefer to think otherwise. However, I still need some answers from you— everything that you know. WE got off on the wrong foot, sure. But, I no longer think that it’s you who’s doing all of—.”
I stopped, mid-monologue. Off to the side of Crusoe’s shadow, I saw another shadow— the shadow of the burglar that I’d been dealing with so often.
“Crusoe, behind you!” I shouted.
Crusoe turned, and the other shadowy burglar turned with him.
“No… It’s not possible…” I heard Crusoe whisper, with shock.
The other shadowy burglar said nothing. Rather, it just stared, with the piercing glare that might come from a stalking wolf, or a preying owl.
“What’s wrong now?” I finally said to the shadow, after Crusoe and the shadow had stared for a while. “I thought that you were satisfied with your work— that you were done with me!”

There was a part of me that was deeply terrified. Not because the shadow was in my house, or that Crusoe even seemed scared. It was the fact that this shadow was looking at me, with a sort of knowing. It was as if it were trying to tell me that it knew what I had done with Miss Rosemary— and that it was waiting to strike.

I might not have had any basis for these thoughts, but this didn’t stop the continuous waves of terror from finding a way to crash upon the shores of my mind, and make me feel chronically helpless— forever entrenched in a loss.

I know you,” Crusoe said. “I’ve been chasing after you for months on end. What do you want now? After all this time, why have you finally decided to show up in front of me. You certainly have gone to a lot of trouble to ensure that I wasn’t here!”

That was one thing that did ease me. Despite the discomfort in the scenario, and that this shadow refused to talk, there was still the fact that the shadow and Crusoe were in the same room— the overwhelming fact that they were two spate entities. I no longer had to be concerned about whether or not Crusoe was guilty of the shadow’s crimes.
I only had to worry about whether or not he’d still be perceived as such.

“When are you going to talk?” Crusoe shouted, stalking away from the shadow in a sort of regretful disappointment and distress. “You can’t keep trying to hold yourself over me. I’m just as informed in the matters of mysteries, and stealth, as you are. You might think yourself to be the superior mind in this room, and that you can hide forever… But, you can’t.”

Something odd that I noticed was that, as Crusoe backed away, the shadow started to back away as well. The only thing I could presume was that the shadow was just as afraid of Crusoe as Crusoe was of the shadow.
“Don’t worry,” I said, “I know how to take care of this guy… He isn’t a threat.”
I started charging towards the shadow, but I watched it dive away from me, prematurely— and, at the same time, Crusoe dived away from his spot, and into me, knocking me back onto the ground.

“I’m sorry about that,” Crusoe said. But, this being is incredibly dangerous. I’ve encountered it on multiple occasions, and it’s not one that you want to mess with. In fact, it will kill you if you give it the means to. I know that your arm is broken, and that me knocking you to the floor has probably lengthened it’s healing period. But, I need to do this on my own…”
There was a sudden laugh from the shadow, as Crusoe stood back up, and I crawled further away from it.

“I’m here for him,” the shadow said. “Sergeant Kyler has been digging his nose into places that are far too disgusting and vile of evidence against me— against me, and my enterprise. I can’t let him get by, without hearing my warning.”
I looked upon the shadow with a disturbing feeling of hatred— it was at such levels that I’d thought myself incapable of expressing, or feeling.

“You’re not going to stop me from continuing to explore what’s going on in this city,” I said. “I don’t care how many threats you throw around. The truth of the matter is, the longer that I leave you alone, the bigger influence that you’ll have. You expect me to let you continue to garner your influence, and take the city as your own? As long as I have the power to do so, I’m going to make sure that you fall. You already hurt Eddy Mulligan— I’m not letting you hurt anybody else that I know, without trying my best to put an end to your antics.”
“An awful lot of words, all used to little effect…” the shadow said, pacing back and forth.

The voice was probably just as disabling as the shadow’s presence. It was tinted with a sort of melancholy shade, which made me feel the most depressive periods in my life return to the labyrinth of my thoughts. It also had a mixture of a manly and womanly voice– it was incredibly neutral, with it being on the brink between discernment. The neutrality was one that was used to a harmfully alarming effect. I could no longer feel any assurance as I listened to it. In a way, being able to hear the voice had only scared me further. I’d used to have thought that its voice was its one weakness— that, when I heard it, the shadow’s humanity would be entirely exposed. But, instead, it only showed me just how much the shadow really had a hold of. It was this grip over everything that deeply jolted me.
“Crusoe, now!” I said.
Crusoe never came out, even with my beckoning. Wherever he was, he’d made sure to keep himself from out of my sight.
The shadow clucked its tongue in disappointment.

“Crusoe can’t hurt me. Nothing can hurt me. In this city, everything is a toy for me to play with. Everything is a ball of yarn, of which I can push around to my own wants and desires. There’s nothing here that’s sacred, or that’s capable of saving you. You see, even in everything that you’ve explored, you’ve gained virtually nothing.
“I’ve already shown you, once before, that you have no chance at besting me. Your arm will be a constant reminder. Do you wish for me to implant another reminder?”
“If it means that you spend another second to try besting me, rather than my city, then yes. I’ll take anything over my city becoming your stead.”

“It’s not a city, Kyler. Not in my eyes. This place is but a chunk of land, designated as a city… You might have the concept that there’s something about it that stretches beyond such... but, nothing that you can say will convince me otherwise….”

“Well, it is far more that what you act that it is…,” I said, desperately searching for some kind of point that I could make to put him in his place. “I’s way deeper than you might like to believe it to be, because the city is more than just a designated plot of land. IT’s the people that live within the city that makes the city into what it is. And, I’m not going to have you take that away from them. You can’t just come in here, and take the people’s rights away— terrorize them, without ever having to pay the consequences.”

The shadow laughed, again— it had become an obscene and absurd thing, in my eyes. If there was anything that took me out of my surroundings, it was the laugh of somebody who laughed at something that they weren’t supposed to laugh at— for the laugh to come from something that never laughs. It has always left me with an unnatural amount of squeamishness, which I’ve never been able to rid myself of dealing with.
“You can’t win this,” I continued. “You can’t run away from your ultimate vindication. You’re going to have to pay, eventually… In some form, or another.”

“The world is ambivalent to your code of ethics, Kyler…” the shadow said. I began to wonder where Crusoe was, amidst all of this. Deep down within myself, I was worried that he’d run away. Though, I still felt as if I could hear him, at some points during my conversation— he must’ve simply been lurking outside of my range of vision, looking for the perfect moment to act. “You act as if this city is the people‘s city.. But, is it really? All of the banks own the people, and all of the businesses own the people. Most of the people are wandering on the streets, and some of them have left to find work elsewhere. This entire city is a wreck, and you know it— we all know it. You better be prepared for the reality that, nothing is as ideal as you’d like to paint it out to be. The entire world is moving passed your mentality to see things in cherry-tinted lenses. You might want to believe that there’s a great hope for your city. But then, on what basis do you believe this...?

“This might be an odd proposition for me to make, but how would you like it if I called you the terrorizer? IO wouldn’t be lying if I did, you know. You are a hypocrite, to the nth degree, whether or not you wish to admit to such… I’ve watched and studied you in many ways, and you rarely ever act in ways that you should, as an officer. You infringe on other people’s rights all the time, especially in your attempt to solve this case. You’re intruding upon others, in the name of upholding the law. But, all that you’re upholding is your own ego.

“You can stand atop your pedestal all that you want, and declare that you know better than I... but, the fact of the matter is, you’re absolutely clueless, even in your search for clues. I pity you. And, no matter how many near-endless speeches I recite to you, I know that you’ll always remain ignorant to this truth. After all— you don’t care about the people, or how you might affect the…  I mean— you do, but I know that you don’t… all that you really care about is getting the job done, regardless of the people that might be involved in accomplishing such a grand mission…”

“I shook my head, and prepared to speak against him, so that I might be able to correct him in his flawed thinking— but, I was interrupted when Crusoe jumped out from the dark, and crashed into the shadow y figure— surprisingly, when he did, I watched his hands clasp the shadowy burglar’s hands, in a perfect symmetry.
“You’re not going to keep this up any longer,” Crusoe said, with a growl. “As long as you’re under my watch, you’re going to be submitting to the laws of Chicago.”
The shadowy figure let out another laugh.

“How are you supposed to enforce the law upon somebody who you don’t even know the identity of? Surely you’re not so immature as to assume enforcing the law is as simple as pinning me to the ground, and using violent words and actions to strike fear into my heart?”
“While I might not be capable of enforcing the Chicago City laws, yes— that is my brand of law enforcement. If you don’t appreciate fear-mongering, maybe you should try to stop using it on others.”

As they said all of this, their arms remained locked, and my eyes remained locked upon them. I was entranced by them. It was watching a flock of birds fly south for the winter. The symmetry and organization, amidst the randomized madness, was something that I almost couldn’t wrap my mind around.
It looked as if they could’ve gone on for hours— but, they were interrupted from their heated arguing by the ringing of my doorbell.
“Who is that?” I heard Crusoe say with a grunt, as he still struggled to hold his own amidst the dark corner of my room.
“It’s Amelia Mulligan,” I said. “She’s the sister of Eddy Mulligan. I invited her to come and visit today…”
I heard Detective Crusoe moan in frustration— but, his moan was now far quieter, with him keeping in mind the new presence. And, the shadowy figure had quieted as well.
“It’s about time that the volume in here thinned down,” I said, waltzing to my door.

I found myself suddenly feeling lightened by the fact that they’d calmed down. It reminded me that, even in their grotesque and great amounts of influence, they were still human. They couldn’t act against such forces of nature as a friend dropping by, no matter how much they seemed to want to.

I opened my door, with an eccentric grin, after making sure that all of the lights in my house were turned off, save the ones in the kitchen. I knew that, no matter how long Amelia stayed at my house, the shadow would be watching, and Crusoe would be battling with the shadow. And so, I didn’t want them exposed— I knew that I needed to spare my guest.

As my door opened, I was greeted by the face of Amelia. She no longer looked anything like I’d once remembered her to be— granted, I didn’t remember her very well. Just like it had to me, age had stripped some amount of youth from her. Not only that, but the lighthearted joy was also gone. I could see in her face that she was incredibly weary, just like I was, and looking for a way to escape it all. She looked trapped inside herself, and as if she were looking for an escape route out.
“SO, I see that this is your house,” Amelia said, putting on a big smile. Then, she outstretched a hand. “If you haven’t figured it out already, I’m Amelia, by the way.”

She let out a laugh, and I did the same. There was a lasting awkwardness afterwards, but I was quickly able to do away with it by saying in response, “Yes, well that’s a shame… Because, I’m afraid that I’m not Mr. Kyler, if you haven’t already figured it out yet.”

I then stepped to the side, and let her walk in. I still held a pernicious fear that she’d be able to see Crusoe and the burglar hiding in the shadows— watching us, with a cold, hard gaze. Btu, thankfully, she never said a word— and so, I was never put into the position where I had to say a word either.

“I suppose that it’s been long enough,” Amelia said, with a wry chuckle. “It wouldn’t be wrong for you to stop calling yourself a completely different person, after all these years. After all, you’re extremely changed from those days— all of your ambitions gone. As well as most of the color in your hair.”

I would’ve frowned if it hadn’t been an old friend that I was talking to. While it had been so many years, and while I’d hardly ever known her, there was a strange sense that I was still able to catch up with her, in spite of all of this.
“Hmm…” I said. “Awfully brave words for somebody who doesn’t even know how to tell the difference between me and.”

Amelia laughed— there was so much laughing, but I wasn’t willing to let it stop. It was very infectious, in an almost cyclical way. One would bring it into being, and then it would become something overwhelmingly influential. I would want it to return the moment that it started to go away. So, even as it was odd and strange for me to be experiencing so much of it, I knew that there was a quality to the conversation that I wasn’t willing to let fall apart.
“Yes, well…” Amelia said. “Sometimes, you need to say things that nobody else will say. Isn’t that the sort of logic that you came up with, when you decided to become an officer?”

“It was a lot more than that,” I said. “At least— it’s become a lot more than that. It’s no longer just about doing the job that nobody else will… I can see that there are plenty of people at this time who would easily trade my job over their current position. Instead, it’s about making this city and the world a better place…”
“Hmm…” Amelia said, studying my apartment. “After twenty years, it seems like making the city, ‘a better place’, doesn’t pay very well.”

Then, she looked at the back of the room, where Crusoe was— there was a long moment where she stopped to stare, as if she’d seen something. However, just as quickly as she was willing to do this, she turned away. It seemed that she didn’t really care— all of my worries about her having seen the shadowy figure was but in my head. “It also has bad lights?” she asked. “Or, are you just one of those cheapskates who can’t keep a light on without feeling that you’re wasting money?”
I smiled, nervously.

“You, and all of the hard questions,” I said, fingering my wrist. “To be honest, I don’t know. Maybe a mixture of both? I just don’t like it here, in the light. It can get so lonely— you know? I’ve always thought that it was easier to pretend that there was something there, in the darkness, than it was for me to stare into the emptiness, exposed by the light.”
I then stopped to pause, and reflect.
“That, and I’m a slob who doesn’t like to have to look at his own messes,” I said. “Trust me— if those lights worked, you’d see a whole mess hidden in there.”
Amelia grinned.
“Well, I guess that I won’t bother with it then.”

She then walked into my kitchen area— a very sparse area, furnished with only a gas-oven and a countertop. It was a big joke, considering all of the restaurants in town. For a moment, I even considered asking her to go to one. I knew that it would’ve been far easier than trying to skate by on the little space that I had, hoping that she wouldn’t come across my visitors.
“It’s pretty quaint,” she said. “For the city, anyway. What have you been doing all these years, that left you like this?”
“Like what,” I said, gesturing to the room around me. “This place is a dream… Are you honestly going to act as if I’m not living the dream...?”
I couldn’t help but find myself holding back a laughing, even as I put on this show. Clearly, my place was a wreck. Even as I spoke, I watched plaster crack, and start to hang from the ceiling.”
“Yes…” Amelia said, still unimpressed— and, returning my sarcasm. “I am suggesting that. Now, how could such a successful officer as you end up in a dump like this?”
I grinned.
“Dump is a strong word… I agree that this place is a mess. But, there is a rustic charm to it, and even you can’t deny it.”
“The whole building will be leveled within twenty years— I can bet on that. Anyway, since you don’t seem willing to talk, I might as well update you on how things are going on in my life.”
“I always thought that it was the courteous thing to wait until somebody asked you, first…” I said.
“Yes…” she said. “Well, when you start to catch on that the other person isn’t going to do the courteous thing, then it’s often time to take matters into your own hands, I’m afraid…”
There was nothing that I could say to that in response, no matter how much I racked my wit.
“You win; I guess…” I said, waving the flag of surrender. “I might as well have the courtesy of doing that.”
“I’m sure that you could do a lot more, if you tried. But, I guess that I’ll be satisfied with that.”

She looked around my decrepit apartment once again, and found my kitchen table. Hastily, she stole a seat there, and beckoned me to join her. I felt tempted to deny her of this— I could feel Crusoe calling out to me, telling me that I had to figure out a way to make her leave. But, I was simply unwilling to… Not only was there the problem with the fact that Amelia was already here, and that I couldn’t afford to have bad blood with her while she was grieving over her brother’s loss. There was something more— a selfish motive. I felt that, no matter how much Crusoe might’ve wished it to be otherwise, I was tired of fighting. I couldn’t stand the thought of having to withstand another one of Crusoe’s insane brawls, without having my head spinning back upon the floor.
“Sorry Crusoe…” I found myself whispering, with a regret that I hadn’t thought would be there.

“So,” I said, clearing my throat so as to make sure Crusoe could hear my decision of loyalties loud and clear— I’d chosen Amelia’s company over his. “How much has really happened in the span since we last met?”

“Considering that we hardly knew each other, in the past, quite more than you might think… I moved out of Chicago, as I’m sure that you already know. I went out of the city in order to find a quieter life, that wasn’t so overrun by the stress that was within the city. My brother, of course, never did see the reasoning in their logic— he claimed that it was stupid of me to go out of the city, and that the city was where all of the wealth was at… I tried my best to give him all of my arguments for why I was leaving— lower population density, which offered better job security. There was also the potential to make close friends easier, since you’d be around people a lot more in the quainter parts of town. There would be a better closeness to nature. And, of course, there would no longer be the constant sound of car engines roving all over the place.

“While all of this had been enough to convince me that leaving the city was a good idea, he never was so convinced… I guess he needed more proof that it was really as good as it was made out to be. Not only that, but he was comfortable in the business that he was making...”
Amelia suddenly paused.

“This might be a very personal discussion, towards somebody that I hardly know,” Amelia said. “But then, I need to tell somebody about this... I don’t know, but I just don’t feel like I can keep everything inside anymore… Not after his death…”
I leaned back in my chair, with an ease.
“Yes, well… I speak to complete strangers all the time, and get all sorts of personal stories out of them. Trust me— none of this is news to me, in spite of the fact that it really should be.”

I would’ve hoped that my words would’ve gotten across with the same ease that I had spoken them with— but, there were several bangs and crashes resounding from the area where I’d left Crusoe and the shadowy robber.
“I knew that I shouldn’t have left them there, alone…” I growled to myself.

However, I was angrier at the situation, than anything else. Everything seemed to be in a perfect arrangement, with I and Amelia suddenly starting to bond over something that both of us had been bursting to let go of— and now, that moment was being stripped away.
I found myself having to restrain a scowl— I was unwilling to let myself become exposed.
“What was that?” Amelia said.

“Oh, just another example of how cheap this place is…” I said, in response. However, the response was probably just as cheap as I was making my apartment out to be. “The maintenance here just isn’t as good as it used to be— there are all sorts of things that are constantly falling over. That’s why I left that section in the dark— it’s honestly too much of an eye-sore for company…”

Amelia looked skeptical, but stopped further questioning— even as the bangs continued. Having the grace of a bird landing into its nest, a sort of bonding trust had come between them. In a way, to outmoded all other things that dared bring my words into question.

“Yes…” Amelia said, looking like she was now no longer to finish her past conversation. Instead, her eyes started to wander, clearly looking for ways to change the subject. “My old house isn’t the nicest of abodes. Back in my small town, down in one of the southernmost parts of Ohio, my home is one of the humbler kinds. I’m sure you remember the sort of houses that I used to say I wanted to live in, when I was younger— the sort of house with nice hard, wooden floors, and a sturdy build— the sort of house that was built by the hands of a select group, who gave care into building it, rather than a contracted cluster of workers who only were looking to build a big enough square.

“I guess you can say that I got that house… It isn’t the castle that I might’ve wanted it to be, and it definitely isn’t perfect. But, you know— it has a sort of quiet charm to it. It’s open about itself, giving off a quaint personality. And, in a time when everything feels so questionable, it’s nice for me to sometimes feel as if there’s something that’s non-objectionable…”

I placed my hands behind my back, to stretch and let myself breathe. I could still here the sound of Crusoe and the Shadowy burglar fighting— however, it steadily disappeared, after the sound of breaking glass— drifting out of my apartment, and into the streets below. While I could tell that Amelia was concerned, all that I could feel was the complete baptizing of relief, coating over my entire body.

“Yes,” I said. “It is nice to know when everything is as it should be— when there are no more mysteries, or secrets to hide…” I said. Then, with a reddening face, “To be frank, I don’t actually remember much of what you told me when we were younger. I typically ignored you, in favor of Eddy Mulligan. You were always a sort of baggage– the person you’d always ignore.”
“Ha,” Amelia said, half-heartedly. “Well, that’s comforting… all those visits, and you hardly even remember me?”

“It was over thirty years ago,” I said, tasting the sting of age on my tongue as I said it. “It hate to have to acknowledge that… But then, I hate to have to acknowledge how much of an arrogant fool I was back then too. There’s a part of me— perhaps a part of all of us— who prefer to renounce our failings, in favor of shifting the burden onto the grip of age.”
I smirked, but Amelia didn’t return it— she clearly wasn’t enamored by my sense of humor. Perhaps being an officer had detached me a bit from what others found to be funny

“I suppose you’re right...” said Amelia. “It’s really strange for me to think that, something so important to me, might be so irrelevant to you. As time goes on, we think that the words that we’ve said, and that the thoughts that have passed through our minds, are all thoughts and words that ware unique and innate to us. But, there’s nothing quite as unique to them as we might like to make ourselves believe… Do you understand where I’m coming from?

“I probably talk too much when concerning topics of memory— especially due to how touchy I’ve been on my memory, lately… But, there’s simply a sort of majestic art to being able to look back into your thoughts, and recall all of the things that you once found important— watching the clock strike down to midnight, right before new years’ day… The first time you ride your bike… The first day that you step out of the house. All of these moments are so monumental to me. And yet— it’s such a thought to think that none of it might matter at all.”

I scrunched my face in confusion for a moment. I had a hard time grasping how Amelia might’ve been able to turn the conversation from something as harmless as her house, to the concept of how are memories make us who we are— and that who we are aren’t necessarily as connected to the rest of the world, as we might like ourselves to be.

Though, then I realized that Amelia’s words weren’t her words at all. Rather, she was instead speaking out of a clearly latent grief— a depression that she was probably unwilling to reference, up until this point.

“Yeah, I suppose that I can see where you’re coming from,” I said, trying to measure my words correctly, so that they might not have a sting to them. “But— it’s not so desperate of a situation that you’re making it out to be. Life is but a relative exercise— stuck in between the confines of what we can observe. While this might not be the most comforting thought, it’s the truth…”

I paused again. I felt my mouth come into itself, with my dry-chapped lips, rubbing against each other— with my skin chafing against the cheap fabric of my clothes. I felt my hair stand on end, as I felt the fear of messing everything up, and saying the wrong thing. And— I felt my heart thump rapidly, out of a sort of empathy.
Yet, even in these extreme sensations, I was the only one who was experiencing it.

“You know, Amelia… That clock, on New Years’ Day, was clocking down at a different rate from every other clock. No matter how slight the difference, every clock runs differently. The experiences that we have— all the observations that we make— might be stuck with us, and forever removed from everybody else. But, then we still have the ability to connect with one another. We still have the ability to spread our ideas around. And, as long as we’re able to have our own unique observations, that should be something that we find a joy within. Because, we won’t be able to observe forever. And, the observations we make are one in billions— there will never be another one quite like ours, and nobody else is going to experience it for us. Therefore, we need to make the most of the memories that we do have, and share them for as long as we have…

“I’m sure that you’re upset at Eddy’s passing…. I have too. As a man who bases his life upon the observation of facts, and the enforcing of human-designed stipulations, I often find myself trapped in a box… I think that everything matters about the facts that we find, and the things that we understand. But, the things that we don’t understand are just as important too…

“I know that your sadness might be borne out of Eddy’s passing. But, there’s one thing that I find cheers me up, in the face of it all. Whatever Eddy gave to me, I still have— and, what he gave to me will influence the way that I live my life, however slight this influence may be. In a way, Eddy changed everybody in Chicago— because, even the slightest of changes is still a change. And, wherever Eddy might be now, it doesn’t sanction any need to be upset. Something that I’ve found is that, in spite of our wish to be upset about somebody’s passing, we should be happy about the life that they left— the people that they were. Because, that’s all that can ever really matter to us. We might not understand what happens after Eddy’s death— maybe nothing, and maybe an eternity of something else. We never know, nor can we ever hope to know…”
I stopped, and then thought back to Crusoe— choosing Amelia and Eddy over focusing on him, and the oversized pursuits that my career was compelling me to follow.

“Well, maybe we can hope to know… That’s perhaps the greatest beauty in this. Despite the fact that we can never know, we’re still provided of something better, in the face of not knowing— a constant state of hoping to know. In this way, we can always have something to hope for, even within what might appear to be the end. Because, the end of something can always be the beginning of something else. Despite the fact that Eddy is gone doesn’t mean that he’s gone… In fact, his passing might be the brink of turning us to see something new.”
I thought that I saw a tear in Amelia— but, she quickly rolled her eyes.
“Are you done yet?” she asked.

I looked out the window, trying to grin in the face of the weight in everything I said. Amelia might’ve seen everything in a lighter way— and, I knew that I should’ve been able to, too. But, for some reason, I just couldn’t. Even after everything I said, happiness still escaped me. I felt the need to keep looking onward— looking for the answers that I could never seem to find. For some reason, the feeling of joy was one that was constantly hiding its face.
“Yes… I’m done…” I said, hoping that my fraudulent smile was convincing enough.

“It was a beautiful speech,” Amelia said with a yawn. “But, I didn’t come here for speeches, Kyler. Instead of constantly hearing your head, one of these days I want to hear your heart. Anyway, this was a nice talk. I hope to come back soon— there are a lot of things that I wanted to discuss about the funeral, tonight— but, I really need to get to bed.”

She stood up, and began to walk towards the door out of my apartment. For a little while, I found myself harnessing a sort of regret for having tarnished the opportunity to make a reconnection with her. She was an old friend of mine— even if it was more on an acquaintance level. I found myself jolted when I started to realize that I’d been the entire reason that she’d decided to leave. It was in my dark speech, and in my attacks towards the sinking jaws of depression, that I’d driven her away. It was all of my doing. And, the more that I thought of this, the m ore that I regretted having not spoken her in the way that I used to be able to speak— the old casualness of conversation that I’d long abandoned, and was still heavily thirsting after….

The odor clicked shut, but I couldn’t hear it. Not even as I locked my door could I hear the sound of me locking my door. Instead, I heard the sound of my apartment’s emptiness— the fact that, despite all of the guests that I’d invited for the night, I was truly and utterly alone. Somehow, I’d managed to utterly wipe away every chance that I had at socialization. I’d completely bashed every opportunity out the door.

“Why…” I said to myself— partially to break the silence that was encroaching upon my spirit. As I said it, it wasn’t even quite a question— nor was it a statement. AS I thought about why I’d even bothered saying the word, I didn’t know the answer— other than the fact that I wanted to hear my own choice, as all other voices dissipated.

Perhaps the greatest fear of anybody is being truly and utterly isolated— being forgotten, and left in the dust. The complete abandonment by society— by your own mind’s wishes and dreams. Whenever such happens, one must face the facts of life— the fact that, in the end, this will be how it will feel. It will be the utter loneliness. It will be the rottenness in having been forgotten. As your body joins the countless other bodies in the grave, one wonders if they’ll become indistinguishable from them. This grim question that harbors the mind in the visage of the reaper. Though, this question isn’t anywhere near the worst. The worst part is, you’ll eventually have to acknowledge that it isn’t a question it all. The question is in fact the answer to itself.
“Why?” I asked. “I was so happy…. Nothing felt like anything could go wrong. I was doing everything right. And yet— I feel like I did something so wrong… I just can’t explain what’s going on.”

This was an ever greater phenomenon of upsetting facts— I didn’t know what was going on, or quite understand. OI was choosing between two sides of myself— the nature of cordiality and conversation, which I had begun to abandon, and the nature of calculation— of rock solid thinking. Both were threatening to swallow me whole. The real trick was figuring out which I wanted to be swallowed by.

“AS much as I want Eddy’s death to be one that’s great, and monumental— a death that m makes me feel driven to live a life like him… I actually feel that Eddy was not the man that I should be looking up to… The more that I think about him the more that I realize just how corrupt of a person that he might’ve been He was likely a friend of the shadowy burglar, having gotten himself into the darkest parts of the criminal element…”

I stopped myself, before I could let my words get out the ultimate statement that they were bordering upon. Instead, I only let myself think them— the words were too disgusting to me for myself to let my tongue enunciate them.

After all the years that Eddy lived, I thought. And even after the4 friendships that he made… I’m starting to think that nothing he did in life was anything of great effect. He was not necessarily a good man. And, his death very well might’ve been more benefit to society than harm… What if, in my death, the world will see things the same way? What if it all continues on without me? What if nothing I do will ever really matter, in the grand scheme of things? The more that I look out into the distance, and weigh the scope of everything, it’s not nearly as promising of a scheme as I once thought it to be. In fact, all that I see before me is a devastating mess that appears to b e a near impossible clean-up. I become more and more aware that the word. And my fate after it fades from my eyes, isn’t as grand as I’d like it to be…. And, if this is so, does any of my thoughts towards the world really matter? Somehow, I’m starting to think that it doesn’t…

I managed to stop myself from continuing down my path of nihilism. I tried to tell myself that it had only been birthed out of the terrible direction of the conversation between myself and Amelia Mulligan. This, of course, was but a thin cloth that I pulled over the eyes of my mind— it wasn’t convincing, in the slightest. It was all birthed from the reminder of Eddy Mulligan’s death. But, then, it was also the very thing that I need to convince myself to get out of this train of thought. And, for that, I still greatly appreciate it for what it did.

“Hey, Crusoe,” I shouted, looking around the room of my apartment. You still in here? I know that it might look like I blew you off in favor of Amelia— but I promise that it’s not what it looks like. It was all just a big flub on my part. I thought that you would be able to handle the shadowy burglar on your own.”
If Crusoe was in the room, he revealed that he wasn’t interested in talking to me anymore. I had exhausted our relationship trust, once again.
“Well then…” I said to myself. “Clearly, I need to schedule these things a lot better…. And here I was, thinking that this would be a simple and peaceful night. “

I turned my light back on in the house, and was forced to confront the mess that was hiding in the darkness. It looked that I hadn’t lied to Amelia about the mess quite as much as I’d thought I did. The entire space was covered in broken glass, strewn about clothes, my bed sheets all torn up, and other various possessions that had been either damaged or thrown onto the ground as if they were nothing more than bits of dust, covering the span of a beach-front.
“Crusoe definitely still has his fighting spirit… I said, sarcastically.

On the ground, I also found a few blood stains, and bits of hair— the brawly between the two figures had been far more vicious than I had even suspected, and I began to wonder how it was that they never shouted, or even let out so much as a grunt, during my entire time with Amelia.
“Clearly, these two, are far more skilled than me…” I found myself saying.

There was one bit of the artifacts left from the fight that confused me, though. There were bits of mirror glass all over the floor— utterly busted. But, when I looked over to where my mirror was, I found that it was undamaged, and without blemish. Somehow, they’d broken a mirror like object— I just couldn’t figure out what it was.
“Oh well… I guess that I’ll be stuck wondering until I need it,” I said to myself. “No use worrying now.”

There were one things that still concerned me, outside the mess of this room. The shadowy burglar had been capable of doing all of this. And yet, I wasn’t quite sure about what else it might be able to do. Uncomfortably, I realized that a being as capable as this one could do just about anything, undetected— and, to devastating effects.

Immediately, my thoughts turned back to Margaret Rosemary, whom had been terrorized by this figure in the past. From what I can tell, the figure knew that she talked, And, my trust was starting to slip in this figure’s seeming restraint. If there was anything that I’d learned about it tonight, it was that there were few things that it actually expressed as being sacred to it. If there was something in its way, it seemed that it would be all too willing to rid itself of it.

It was all too engrossing, and the fears too frequent for me to focus on it too much, But, as I tried to go to sleep for the night, I realized something dark, that I’d since been trying to avoid. If Margret Rosemary met any sort of harm because of my visit, it would all be weighing on me.
Not only that, but Eddy’s death was also weighing upon me. The burglar had a vendetta towards the friends of his victims… I was within that category. Without Crusoe’s help, I was hopeless.
“Yes…” I said, trying my best to use these thoughts as a comfort. “I just need Crusoe’s help. And then, everything will be made clear.”
The map of crimes was so shifty and confusing that I was beginning to wonder if I’d ever hit an end. Another robbery had occurred as I was sleeping, and this time it had hit the house of the Mayor.
“As if I didn’t already have enough on my plate,” I found myself grumbling as I sat at my desk in my department office.

This time around, Jackson had decided to omit me from the investigation. HE said that my findings hadn’t been of any use last time around, and that I needed to stay where I was needed most— at the department, studying my current cases.
In the meantime, I’d given Jackson some of the testimonies that I’d gained, as well as inform him that I would need to take a day off within a week, because of Eddy Mulligan’s upcoming funeral.

Jackson seemed receptive enough. He still had his slyly obnoxious sarcasm, and his passive-aggressive remarks to give out— I swear that his pale skin only turns to a ghastlier shade of white as he talks to me— but, he had the kindness to give me the day off, and actually congratulate me on my findings. I’m not sure how sincere either of these acts were, but I couldn’t help but gain a sense of comradery as he did so.

In spite of his kindness, I still wasn’t willing to give his orders the time of day. Though I was hard at work trying to unweave my entanglement of facts in my office, I felt that I needed to go to the crime-scene— even if Jackson’s every word had decided to go against it.

In the meantime, however, I was stuck philosophizing over what all of my evidence meant… After the night before, I now knew that Crusoe and the shadowy burglar were different people. Not only that, but I was starting to suspect that the burglar was a group of several people, all of whom had a similar goal of screwing with people’s minds, and bringing a sense of judgement upon people.

I despised this thought, but there was one other thing that I’d noticed, in my studies. Eddy Mulligan was poised to having been a criminal– something that I deeply rejected. Not only that, but Crusoe still wasn’t the clean-cut man that I might’ve liked him to be. From just about everything that I could tell, he was fighting the burglar just like me. However, for him to have discovered the burglar, I think that he should’ve had to do something against the burglar— to have dealt in things that he wasn’t meant to deal in.
For the most part, though, my questions all still remained. I was only a bit closer to a few answers— but, there wasn’t anything of use that I truly knew for certain.
“Oh…” I said to myself, with a bit of a forlorn tone to my voice. “If only things could be made clearer… If only it wasn’t a consistent question.

I wanted to laugh, cry, smile, or frown… But, I couldn’t get myself to express any of my emotions. In a way, the burglar had measured everything in order to make sure that I was emotionally inert, throughout it all. This was probably their greatest talent— being able to make my emotions fall away, while simultaneously making me feel more pain than I’d ever felt before.
“They can torture me and give me joy at the same time… I guess that I should give them credit for something,” I thought to myself.

Oddly, I wasn’t entirely disoriented by all of this, like I should’ve been. I had a way to wipe all of my fears and concerns away, as if they were all trivial matters— matters of which there was no importance. I felt my goals steadily turn back to figuring out the answers to the map that was building around me.

“Maybe the differing accounts of the shadow aren’t really so different as I might like them to be,” I suddenly thought to myself. “Perhaps the differing accounts are spawned from something far darker, and more nefarious, instead… The falsehoods of memory. After all, eye-witness accounts are never what they seem to be. I need a picture— some sort of way to monitor what’s going on with this shadow…”

After saying all of this, I made sure to stop talking, and look around the room. Then, I switched from my audible voice to my simple thoughts. I realize that the shadow might be watching me from anywhere, and that there was no real way for me to tell whether I was being watched or not. I had to retreat to the recesses of my brain in order to ensure that the thoughts that my brain was creating weren’t infiltrated by any outside influences.

I couldn’t help but feel the driving nail of the thoughts outside of me… They were far too effective for me to ignore. I saw that, the only way to ensure that I knew more about the shadow would be to full gain some solid evidence— evidence of which couldn’t be denied.

I already have some of my own observations, I thought to myself. If this criminal is actually anything like he seems to be from my memory, then he— or they, for that matter— must have a relatively light body, and a thin build. That’s the only way that they’d be able to run so fast, hide so well, and jump from place to place, unnoticed… In fact, even from my memory I can recall the shadow seeming to have a thinner build than that of Crusoe.

But then, it will also need to have a very high height in order to make up for this lightness. They’ve knocked my down on multiple occasions, and even broken my arm. Something that I begin to see abut this is that it usually does so through knocking me to the ground. The only way that they could do such a thing, while still being lightweight, is by having a tall build that gives them a bigger leverage in combat. After all— I’ve rarely ever had a moment where I’ve been bested by them in direct combat. In fact, it seems to me that the only way they’ve beaten me is through a form of misdirection—making me think that they were in places that they weren’t. Their way of overcoming me isn’t through any sort of brute strength, but a brutish strategy instead…
It was at this point when I felt myself beginning to reach several different crossroads.

The one issue with it all is that Crusoe seemed to have a struggle battling them, with it having lasted nearly five minutes… I saw them, and it didn’t seem like they would let up. Even during my conversation with Amelia, there seemed to be a persistent battel for quite a while. If this figure truly didn’t have any sort of strength, then they surely wouldn’t have been able to outmatch Crusoe.
My mind suddenly stopped when I came to a shocking possibility.

Or, maybe Crusoe isn’t quite as skilled as I’d like to think he is—n perhaps the years have worn him down a lot more than I’d like to believe… This is an uncomfortable notion… but then, there’s rarely a time when I come across a notion concerning these things that are particularly pleasing to hear…

I was only conjecturing though. I knew that I wouldn’t be able to formulate a clear picture of what was going on with the shadow, or Crusoe, until I had some clear documentation of them. It was at this point that I began strategizing a few ideas. I realized that Margaret Rosemary was about to become a prime target, if she hadn’t already— I still needed to check to make sure that she hadn’t been made into the shadow’s newest victim, in the middle of the night. If so, then the shadow would be back soon…. I just needed to build a way for it all to be captured, and studied— I would have to give her some sort of camera, so that the shadow could be caught on film. It was the only way that any of this would begin to unravel.

“That’s perhaps the single-greatest thing that I’ve learned in all of my years as an officer…” I told myself. “The only way that you can ever dissect the mystery out of something is by removing its ability to be a mystery altogether— by dissecting it from the world of the supernatural, and placing it back into the world of the natural.”

I then opened my notebook, and looked back to all of the names that I’d written down. There were two other people that I needed to track. I felt tempted to go back to Jonah’s shop, and ask about them— but then, I knew that I wouldn’t get the answers that I needed.
“Research…” I told myself. “The grimy coals of research are the only things that I can use to light up this steam engine...”

I spun around in my chair, and turned to my phonebook— perhaps the most important object of my investigations. In all of my career, it was probably the only tool that hadn’t failed me. all of the names within it were so perfectly updated and kept together, that I knew I wouldn’t be failed.
“I just have to hope that the ink isn’t runny,” I said. “That, and I have to hope that there aren’t too many people of the same name.”

Thunder crashed overtop of me, and forced me to listen as it pelted raindrops at the roof of my car. I hadn’t done anything to antagonize the weather, but the thunder didn’t seem to care. It rained down on me, sending down fleet after fleet of depressing sleet— making me want to shove my face into the concrete. I felt as its languid liquids lingered on my brow— in a way, it made me feel one with the waters, and the dashing of lightning that raged on. Though, this was of no comfort to me– rather, it only showed me my frailty, in comparison with everything else that surrounded me. The thunder shouted, with the force that a furious Coney Island magician wouldn’t have even been able to conjure…

Each time that my tires splashed a wave of slush onto the sidewalk, the thunder roared again. In a way, I almost felt as if it was warning it. It steadily became louder and louder— so tremulous that my entire body, as well as the floor of my car, quaked amidst its tremulous power I’d never quite felt a storm like this— somehow, even in the office of my police department where I was exposed to open windows, this storm had found a way to creep up on me. Without me even noticing, it had overtaken the city— it had overtaken me.

In a sense, this was no shock to me— an ironic statement, considering that lightning is perhaps the most shocking thing I know. In everything that I’d been experiencing, I was exposed to far too much of this sort of thing— the seemingly idle threat creeping up, and subsequently conquering. At this point, it came as no surprise to me. In fact, I’d been expecting it— I was always expecting to be thrown off guard

Something that I must admit, however, is that the sensation of being thrown off guard was steadily becoming more exhausting. It was like the task of trying to drive a car for hours. While it’s not all that strenuous a task, and while one usually knows where they’re going, there’s still a point where all senses of navigation and tact start to cease. Even when somebody knows that things will eventually get brighter, and that they’ll soon find themselves on the other side, it’s still a struggle.

This might help explain something else that was going on inside of me. This storm had elicited a new sense from within me. At this point, I’d grown sick of driving to crime scenes. It’s funny to think this, but it’s too true.

There are only so many times that you can sit upon the leather seat of the squad car, shove a rusty key into the car’s ignition, and drive off onto the dark asphalt road, before it all begins to become a worn tedium.
I’ll reiterate this though: there’s still a funny aspect to me feeling this way.

When I first got in the squad car, and rode to a crime scene, I can’t deny that I had a thrill flying through my gut. Granted, it was a reserved thrill— it had the solemnity that you might find within a priest to it, since it was still a crime that I was dealing with. But then, the childish thrill and excitement was still there, and I’m afraid that I simply can’t deny it. I think that I even once remember saying to myself that the joy in my job would never go away— that the great feelings I felt when helping people would never be something that I’d give up, or throw aside.

That’s where I was wrong. There’s only so long that you can go in life before you begin to feel tired of it— tired, and worn. I eventually discovered that the greatness in the career of enforcing the law didn’t have the glamor that I might’ve initially thought that it did. The movies tricked me, really good… Man, do I hate the movies.

It’s a rare time when you’re overloaded with crimes. And when you are overloaded with them, it’s never something that gives you a sense of satisfaction. Instead, you feel like you’re being stretched too thin. After all— even a single crime can be a matter with extreme extraneous weight to it. It requires so much effort, and attention to solve. It’s usually by a fluke that you’re able to solve it, and find the guilty party, and it typically requires multiple crimes, in order to fully formulate a pattern. But then, with multiple crimes, your problems are also just as compounded as they are simplified. There are far too many things to take note of, and far too little a number of things that are actually easy to understand. This partially comes as a relief to me at times— the fact that I have an excuse when things don’t go as planned. But then, most of the general public doesn’t see it this way… Us officers are far too slow to find the answers to crimes, and they oftentimes go completely unsolved. When they don’t, we’re lambasted, and considered to be shoddy at what we do. A part of me wonders if we actually are…

Either way, even if we do happen to get things right, there’s still a part of me that always wonders if we really did. There’s always the chance that we screwed up, and got the wrong guy. That was probably one of the greatest things about having Crusoe on our side. I was able to have a hero— a sort of idol— that I could look up to, and place all of the weight upon. I was able to look at him, and saw somebody that I could never be. In this way, I never had to worry about the things that I probably should’ve been worrying about— all the things that were unsolved steadily became solved. It didn’t matter that they might’ve been solved in the wrong fashion, or that there was little chance that Crusoe was trustworthy. I’d made him into a hero, and I had regained the thrill that I’d once had.

This is probably the greatest mess in building heroes— they tend to fail you, and you tend to fail to meet their standards. It’s a vicious cycle, because one thinks that they need a hero in order to give them a sort of security. The most terrifying thing to all of us though is that, perhaps we’re wrong about our heroes. Perhaps we don’t really need them, as much as we’d like to believe…

Something else that I’d been wondering was even more disturbing… I’d become a police officer for two reasons. I thought that it would help people, and I thought that it was who I was supposed to be. I wanted to be what society had taught me was the right thing to do— what society taught me that I should become.

Though, as society began to bear down on us officers, and criticize us to a higher extremity, I couldn’t help but begin to wonder if everything I did was but a result of what society dictated— if everything I did was but a fluke, at the will of culture’s whim.
It was a disturbing thought. It was a thought that I would have to ignore, for the sake of my own sanity.
“You again?” Officer Paul said. He was standing by, to guard the crime scene. It was just my luck too— it looked like the area was swamped with police.
“Yep,” I said, displaying my badge. “Lieutenant’s orders.”
“Funny…” said Paul, skeptically. “I spoke with the Lieutenant just this morning— informed him of your contribution to the last crime scene. He said that you wouldn’t be needed.”

I looked around the house’s yard— all of its thick shrubbery, its stone walkways, its rather humble house at the center, and its brick walls— to make sure that the Lieutenant wasn’t anywhere to be found.

“You know, he told me about that just this morning,” I said, with a passive chuckle. I was trying to act nonchalant, but I could tell that Officer Paul wasn’t convinced. “He— he umm… He said that he’d changed his mind, and that he needed me on the scene after all. I guess he decided to usurp his own commands.”
“Hmm,” said Paul. “Usurp his own commands? Are you sure that it’s not you who’s trying to usurp his commands?”
Realizing that Paul had a grudge against me, I was forced to recognize that this conversation wasn’t going to get anywhere.
This is what you get for treating people like dirt, I thought to myself.

“No,” I said, plainly. “I don’t know why you’re automatically assuming the worst, but trust me— this is the Lieutenant’s orders that I’m following here. DO you honestly want to have to speak with him about this?”
“I do actually,” Paul said, stepping aside. “I do.”

Ignoring Paul’s ominous words, I strode up the house’s garden. This time around, I’d made sure to inform myself of the crime before walking onto the scene, so that I wouldn’t look so suspicious, and ignorant— I had a hunch that Paul would be shadowing me throughout my entire investigation.

From what I’d been able to gather, this house was a vacation spot for one of the richest man in town— Gregory Humphrey. Mr. Humphrey was a rather prudent ma, with a terrible case for vacation houses. Not only was this property landlocked, but it was also caught in the thick of a rat-infested section of town. The closest thing to this house being beachfront property was the fact that it was positioned in front of a series of large sewer holes.

Despite all of this, the property itself was rather enviable. It had a humble design, and a yard that would make even the best of landscaper’s drool.
