All of the grass, shrubbery, and trees, were properly manicured. All of them were formed into the shapes of very rich and exaggerative figures. It was humorous to think about, and even more humorous to see, but the yard’s shrubs were ultimately a vegetated version of Grecian statues. It was hard to be able to absorb it all, amidst the downpour of rain. But, it was still all there, in full display.

I opened the door to the house, after making it over a bit of caution tape— something that I was now realizing that there was an abundance of. The inside of the house was a lot less intriguing than the outside had been. It was probably the most standard of homes that I’d seen— not to say that it wasn’t a vast improvement over my own disposition. The halls weren’t well-garnered, with them instead being painted with simple drywall. The floor was carpeted, instead of tiled. And, the ceiling was filled with the most basic of lamps.
Not a very worthy place to rob, I thought.
However, I then remembered the testimony that I’d read.

The night prior, Mr. Humphrey had been kidnapped, sharing the same fate that Mr. Donald and his guests had endured. While there didn’t seem to be any missing possessions, and while nobody knew the exact circumstances of the crime, we at least knew the night that they had occurred upon— last night, between ten o clock, when the butler and maids were taken off duty, and after four o clock, at around the time that the butler and maids returned. They reported, and the investigations showed, that the bedroom had been completely ransacked.
I walked into the bedroom.

The bed, around king-sized, was overturned. All of the sheets were torn up, and destroyed. A picture frame, on the opposite wall, had been knocked down. The corner opposite to the bed had a hole busted into it. And, a light had been ripped straight out of the ceiling.

What I found, however, was that the room had a look of being framed. Everything about it simply appeared as if it had been falsified. The bed was overturned, but it was also a king-sized bed— much too big to have been overturned in the accidents of a fight. The sheets were torn up, but without having any apparent reason to be so— there was clearly no reason for a knife having been used. If the kidnapper had actually slashed all of the bedsheets with a knife, it would’ve only slowed them down… The busted hole in the corner had no reason of being there. The picture, knocked from the opposite wall, was too far away from any of the other messes for it to make any sense— if it had been knocked down in a fight, then why was the bed knocked down on an entirely different side of the room. The torn lamp held this same illegitimacy. I could tell that, if anybody had actually tried to take the light down from the ceiling, they would’ve had to have been crazy. If they’d knocked down the light because they didn’t want their victim to be able to see, that would’ve been counterintuitive— they would’ve lost their own vision as well. If they’d knocked it down in a fight, one would have to wonder how exaggeratedly tall the kidnapper was. Any other explanation was just as unreasonable as the next.

Except, of course, that the crime scene wasn’t a crime scene at all. For some reason, the place was had been faked. I wasn’t sure why, or how— it had clearly fooled the other officers. But, there was one thing that I did know— it was definitely fake.
“Maybe the evidence was faked by the cleaning staff,” I wrote down in my notebook. “And, maybe this evidence is a McGuffin that the kidnapper placed here, so that we wouldn’t find the truth.”
Both didn’t make any sense… But then, it was all that I could make out of it.

Out of everything in the room that was a waste, there was one thing that I did happen to find interesting— on the floor, there was a monkey. A glass monkey, about the size of my hand, to be exact. When I looked at it, my mind immediately backtracked to all of the monkeys that Miss Prestel had kept, as well as the picture that I’d seen of a man in an alleyway, holding a monkey— right over a sewer grate.

I put the glass monkey into my pocket. I didn’t know quite what to make of it, or if I should’ve made anything out of it at all— but, I knew that if I was going to get anywhere, it would have to be with the monkey. Nothing else in the room was useful, in the slightest.
“Hey there,” Paul said.
I turned around, and saw his smug face looking me into the eye. He was more annoying than Lieutenant Jackson— and Lieutenant Jackson was the biggest pain that I’d ever met.
“What have you got there?” Paul continued.
“I don’t know what you’re talking about.”
I made sure to shove the monkey statue deeper into my coat pocket, so as to make sure that Paul would have no way to confiscate it from me without looking like a pick-pocket.”
“I saw you grab something from the crime-scene,” Paul said. “What was it?”
“You must’ve missed the part where I dropped it on the ground, I said. “It was my wallet— no need to stick your nose into everything.”
I started speed-walking towards the door out of the house, and Paul made sure to speed-walk after me.
“It was a pretty weirdly shaped wallet, then,” he said.
“Oh, agreed. But, I don’t know if the shape of my wallet is really this interesting to be wasting our time on.”
Paul nodded his head.
“I’d much rather talk about the item that you stole.”
“Me too,” I said. “but then, I’d prefer not to talk about nonexistent objects.”

Paul jumped in front of me, and looked me straight in the face. I could see every inch of his face crease with a fury— he knew that I’d bested him. But then, he also knew that I wasn’t telling the truth.

“You’re going to get caught, at some point, Sergeant,” Officer Paul said. “And, I can’t wait until your arrogance is exposed. I used to admire you… but, you’re clearly just as void of values as any other criminal that we arrest.”

“No,” I told Officer Paul, pushing him aside. “I’m just as arrogant as you, or any other officer. Maybe that’s worse— but, if you’re going to start claiming things about me, you might as well get it right.”

With those words, Paul walked off on his own. It seemed to me that he didn’t actually care about the truth of what he was saying— whether or not I was guilty, or whether or not he was right. Instead, it seemed to me that he’d only chosen to slam me in every way that he possibly could. His wisdom that I’d once thought all officers possessed, was instead proven to be a ruthless drivel— a spray of something so unpleasant that all of society should’ve concentrated their efforts into the disposal of it.
“If only others could see exactly what I see,” I said. “Things would be so much easier— not just on me, but on everybody around me.”

I felt my blood pressure begin to reach higher heights, and my body grow ever wearier about what was going on around me. However, I eventually was able to stand myself back up from off the wall that I was leaning upon, and place my mind back into the things that were actually of importance.
“Time to do some real investigation work…” I said to myself. “Clearly the other people put on the job aren’t qualified. And to think that Lieutenant Jackson put them on the job, over me.”

I laughed to myself as I said this, but I was as serious as could be. It was very shocking to think that Lieutenant Jackson had opted not to put me on this case, only due to the mere angry complaints of a few detectives. I’d never thought Lieutenant Jackson to be the sort of person who would cave in, and give up his ground, over such measly attempts as that. But then, Lieutenant Jackson was always a person of surprising. I don’t know how he hid them all, in that gaunt build of his— but, wherever it was hidden, it was hidden well.

“How do you do, Sergeant?” an officer asked me, as I walked out the front door of the house, and into the yard. “I saw that Officer Paul stormed out of there, really angrily. I think that you might’ve pressed a few of his buttons. I know that it might be easy to take offense oat him, for how he acted, but trust me– he’s just a hotheaded rookie, hoping to wipe out all of the competition. He’ll come around, and see you in the right light, at some point…”
“I sure hope so,” I said.

I was studying the yard— making sure that there were no clues of what might’ve actually happened the night before. I was gaining the sense that, whoever the criminal had been, they were playing us police as fools— trying to make sure that every element of the environment suited our needs.

“No need to hope, sir… It will definitely happen. I’m actually sort of apprenticing the man… He’ll get around to learning the true nature of our work, and just how hard it is. HE still thinks that he’s one of those gods amongst officers— he thinks that he’s capable of solving any crime, at any time.”

“Yes, well I advise you to snap him awake as soon as you can… He’s been butting into my investigations, and causing me to have to juggle two problems at once. I shouldn’t need to be dodging him, whilst trying to solve a mystery… Do you know what I mean?”

“Completely, sir. I entirely understand. You know, I found myself saying the same thing just the other day to him— that he should be focusing on the crime scene, rather than the people at the crime scene. After all— the clues will stay where they are, as long as you search for them first. He seems to have a sort of grudge against you. He isn’t impressed by your seeming dependence on Crusoe, or the fact that you came across as rude to him.”
“I come across as rude to everybody,” I said. “Speaking of which, I think that I’m onto something.”
I was staring into the garden– And I found that there was a trail of broken plants, torn shrubbery, and knocked over pots— all leading to the street.
“You looking at that trail in the yard?” the officer asked, following my gaze.
“Yes… Why do you ask?”

“Eh… We never found anything there. The evidence actually points to the criminal having escaped through the back, rather than through the front. This trail was probably caused by these storms that we’ve been having.”
He then held his hand out, and let it fill with a pool of rain.
“See? This place hasn’t gotten a break all night… It isn’t a wonder that there’s a bit of the shrubbery all messed up. Not to mention, some of this was probably caused by us officers.”

“I’m still going to check,” I said. “but yeah— I need to check everything, with an open mind. I know that there must be secrets kept amongst this wood that I’m just not finding… We’re going to catch this criminal, no matter what. So, I don’t really care what we find. I’m going to make sure that I look everywhere, so that there’s nothing that we missed. It’s the only way that we can safely find an answer to our problems….”

“I suppose so...” the officer said. “but, I’d advise that you slow down there. There’s no reason to take things to such a high extreme. Everything will be solved soon enough. It always is. No need to go on a rant about it…”
“Not everything,” I said, “Not everything.”

I kept walking into the shrubbery, before I began to see the faint hints of footprints in them— at least, they looked like they were footprints. However, pools of water, and the vagaries caused by what appeared to have been running led me to a place where there didn’t seem to be any answers. Instead, I was only looking upon a field of conjecture, in which everything that I looked upon was a big, unanswered question.
“If only things were clearer…” I thought.
At this point, the officer had already stalked off. I think that I heard him muttering something under his breath, akin to, “Paul was right.”

Normally, I might’ve corrected him, and tired pursuing further conversation. But, I was too deeply engrossed in everything that was going on around me to let myself slip up into the temptations of everything that was going on around me. Not even a looming sense of regret scared me off.

The trail eventually led into the street— and this was where it ultimately ended. At that point, it seemed that all hopes of more proof was gone. I couldn’t find anything— not a footprint, not a single article of clothing— not even the slightest indication. I was at a complete loss of clues, and I almost felt as if I were being mocked. In spite of being able to find the clues, all of them were hidden from me by the rain. In a way, nature had found a way to pull the wool over my eyes— to make me look as if I were nothing more than a bloated joke.

Though, there was one thing that gave me a sense of hope and alleviation. I looked ahead of me, and into the street— I cast my eyes into the same direction as where the trail would’ve led, should it had continued. In this way, I was able to see that it went directly towards one of the sewage holes— the criminal, whoever they’d been, was using the sewage lines as a means of escape. At first, I couldn’t believe it. Not only did it seem too good to be true, but it also seemed too unreasonable to be true. Throughout all of my career, I’d never stumbled upon something like this so easily.

“Not that I should be surprised…” I thought to myself. “After setting up the McGuffin for us officers, it probably would’ve been all too easy to get into a rush, get lazy, and then go to an escape in which nobody would expect you to go. Thankfully, there were still people out there who look at every single detail. And, that’s where they must’ve gone wrong.”

I was tempted to go down the sewage shaft myself, and to inform the other officers about what I’d found. Though, I then immediately remembered how easy it might be for me to be wrong entirely. And, I if was wrong, then I would’ve exposed myself, and given myself away to everybody— Lieutenant Jackson would probably get into a fury with me, over having broken his orders for no reason at all. And then, of course, there was also the risk of coming up with something, but never coming back up— my mind trailed back to the monkey statue that was in my pocket. This person clearly had a web of people, and, if not, they definitely knew their way about the own. They’d already broken into some of the greatest houses in town, and were showing no sign of stopping. They hadn’t even bothered to give a ransom threat. They were just taking things, and leaving— they didn’t care about the police, or anybody else.

They were a force that was independent of all other past conventions. They weren’t held down by what people might’ve thought would constrain them. It was in this moment that I realized I was still in a battle that was far harder to get through than I’d initially thought it to be— the answers to my questions might’ve been simple ones, but they were also answers that held a great risk to them.

In gaining knowledge— in gaining the truth— I’d learned just how hard that everything really was. I might’ve gained something, But, at the same time, I also suffered loss. I would’ve liked to believe that the gains and losses were equal and mutual to each other, but I couldn’t help but feel that they were swallowing each other whole.
“So, what do you think about all of the strange robberies occurring at these rich birds’ houses?” the officer asked me, as he walked to his squad car, and prepared to leave.

“The robberies?” I repeated. “They’re some sort of caper— I know that they are. They’re simply occurring anywhere and everywhere… they’re akin to the plague. And, as we all know, all plagues have causes. We just need to figure out what’s going on, and who’s behind it all… Nobody just kidnaps rich folks for no reason. There has to be some sort of ploy to it all…”
“We could just be dealing with a pure psychotic,” the officer said. I listened as he turned the engine on his car, signaling that he was ready to drive off.
“I’d prefer to assume that the people behind these crimes are totally sane. The assumptions of insanity should always come after the fact, when all other explanations are gone.”
“I’d say that we’re pretty close to that point… Wouldn’t you?”
With that, a wave of city sludge sprayed into the air, and the car drove off. I watched as its chrome rear-end faded off down the rain-slicked street, and out of sight.
“Yes…” I answered, reluctantly. “Yes I would….”

Today, I found that I was in a rush to make sure that everything was accomplished. Now that it was the day before Eddy Mulligan’s funeral, I found that everything a had gained a new sense of urgency. I felt that there was nothing that I could do but make sure that everything was covered, so that I would be able to make sure that he was alive. By tomorrow morning, everybody would become accepting of the fact that Eddy Mulligan was dead— even myself would end up adhering to it, on the basis that there seemed to be no chance that he could still be alive. Though, I instantly saw the danger of this thinking, and just how poisonous it would soon become, if not exposed as soon as possible. Above all else, I planned on making sure that I had done all of my research, and that I’d sought everything out.

I was already planning on heading to Mr. Donald’s house— after the revelation that I’d just had, I was getting a new sense of understanding about what was going on. Everything was starting to fall into place, and I was starting to see the importance in making sure that I had sought every possibility out, Though, I was also beginning to see the importance in making sure that I informed everybody of the truth. And so, I was trying to make sure that I had taken care of something that away long overdue. While Mr. Donald’s house, and what I was suspecting about it, was important, it was the next location on my map. I found that there was another stop that was just as important— if not, more so.

After having gone to the crime scene, I stopped back at my house and started to do some digging. I phoned Jonah, to see if he had an y new information, and then went to my police department colleagues for a few more answers. I was able to scrounge up enough information to determine the rough location of where both Bill Clyde and Jack Crowley were. It turned out that they were both companions. They also got around. Jonah was able to figure out who they were through some of the note-cards that he’d printed— a few of them had been directed towards Bill Clyde and Jack Crowley, as birthday cards.

By using the names that he offered me, I was able to talk to my police department and get some answers out of them, too— they gave me the criminal records of the purchasers of the birthday cards, as well as their phone-numbers and address. After that, I caught Jack Crowley’s address, and I was on my way to his house.

Jack Crowley was another one of those people who lived in the grime of downtown— something that I was becoming more conscious of by the day. I t seemed that whatever was going on, t it was intrinsically linked to the poverty stricken areas. It almost seemed to be inherent to these places, which is something that I tend to avoid giving to things. But, it’s true. I don’t think that there was a single place I could look without seeing any sort of ark and distant foreboding sense of a lack of wealth. It was like this series of crimes clang too it, and thrived off of it.

Either way, whether or not my interpretation of things was correct. I found myself driving into an arena of grayish buildings, which looked no more appealing than anything else that they’d recently used. It was hard for me to be able to tell what was going on entirely, but it looked to me like most of the buildings had been ravaged, and were completely neglected. There were broken windows in many of them, and they all seemed to symbolize a lack of wealth and disrepair. The very sight of them brought a cold, harsh terror to my heart, and I wondered if I’d be able to escape the place without becoming subject to tits cruel inventions.
“Well, I guess that I shouldn’t have come here…” I said to myself, as I looked at it all.

I’d seen some of the worst parts of this area, and some of the best parts of the city— I understood the clash in tones pretty well. But, I hadn’t seen anything quite this devastatingly bad for a while This was like a sort of punch in the gut for me. I hadn’t thought, even in my wildest dreams, that something could reach these levels of destruction.

There were bricks that had fallen from the buildings laid out in the streets, and articles of clothing, furniture, and other such things all throughout. It wasn’t something that I could easily look at and discern a judgement based off of it. But, it was definitely something that made me rethink all of my past work, and caused me to wonder if what I was doing was the right thing to be doing. All of the sudden, nothing seemed to be quite so black and white as I’d liked it to be. Instead, there were two decisions that I’d come upon— exposing the damage of this place to everybody that I knew, or leaving it be for the sake of my investigation.
I chose the latter, but not without feeling regret seed itself in my gut.

It all happened as I was in a daze, but I found myself standing face to face with Jack Crowley— a sniveling sort of man, who seemed perfect to punch at first glance. He was very tall and imposing, but was so soft that he didn’t look like his threats had any merit to them. His eyes sneered and glowered as he looked down at me— but, it wasn’t anything that was done deservedly. All that I’d done was knock on his door, and asked to come in.

His eyes were the sort that weren’t hard to miss— both of them were surrounded in thick purple rings, making them look like large bullseyes. He also had a very heavy look to him, and a weathered visage. Though, these both did him a disservice, instead of making him appear more intimidating.
“What do you want?” he asked, with a voice just as crooked as his posture.

“To stop hearing that question,” I muttered. Thankfully, Mr. Crowley was hard of hearing. “I’m here on police matters— I wanted to know your relation with some crime sprees that I’ve been sifting through.”

Jack Crowley opened his mouth, but appeared too slow to come out with a response. Instead, he just took a glance at my arm. Seeing that he was distracted, I took a glance into the room that he was blocking me from— it was full of furniture as old as the building was, and it was also just as much of a mess.

“Just a few simple questions,” I explained. “There have been a few disappearances of people lately, and I’ve found that they’re all seemingly connected to similar past events… I just wanted to make sure that you didn’t have any similar things going on. I wouldn’t want you to end up falling victim to such a crime spree.”

“I don’t think that I have anything to worry about,” Mr. Crowley said, grinning. As he did so, he exposed his teeth— all of which were yellowed, and clearly not maintained. “I’m the sort of person who is very good at taking care of themselves— I don’t need any help from you in order to tell whether or not I’m in danger.”

“That’s fine…” I said. I was already beginning to tell why I’d been avoiding this for so long. Unlike Margaret Rosemary, I’d had no idea what I’d be getting into. And, clearly this person was the sort that was stubborn.
“It better be! Now get out!”
AS he said this, he fell into a coughing fit. I looked at his face— it was extremely pale, and it looked like he’d been battling something extremely harsh.
“You don’t look too good…” I said, with a caution in my voice.  “Are you sure that you’re alright?”
“If you keep asking questions, you won’t look alright either.”

All I did was look back at him, and stare into his face. I thought that I could see something tin him that looked familiar— but, I didn’t know how I thought this, or what that feeling was exactly coming from. All that I knew was that he smelt of a mildew that made my stomach lurch in disgust.

“Well, I’m sure that it must be hard for you to come up with some sort of explanation frog what your sickness is for,” I said. “It’s the middle of summer, you know. You must not think that I’m o stupid as to be unsuspecting about what’s wrong with you.”

I had completely shifted my tone from that of my placid questioning. Though, I could tell that that this was a large mistake just by the look in the man’s eye. He was both angered and unimpressed. Clearly, my wishes to figure out the answers had gotten in the way of coming across as appealing. He was now looking more and more like he was preparing to hit me. The best that I could do was back up, and prepare to block any attack that he might lay down upon me. I had no other real defense. In fact, even if I had I’m sure that it wouldn’t have made a difference— I could tell, just by looking at his arms and body, that he was the sort of person who liked to fight and throw his weight around. I could already feel my heart pounding in my chest, and my breath beginning to quicken.

“Well, don’t you have any answers?” I asked, trying to sound as innocent as possible. He clearly wasn’t impressed with my display. He glowered at me. The best that I could do was try to replicate the look that he gave me, and give him the same exact sneer in return.
“Don’t pretend that you’re the only one around here who has any idea of what is going on,” he said to me. “You might want some answers…. But I’m not giving any to you.”

I looked around for something that I could leverage to get him to talk. I soon found that there was nothing. There could never be anything that I could use to my advantage around this man, as it was. He was the sort of person who didn’t care about using reason, and was only interested in pronouncing his threats to everybody.
“Are you trying to terrify somebody, again?”
I looked back up to Jack Crowley’s face, to see if the words had come from him. It was somebody else.
Jack Crowley’s face turned red, and he reluctantly turned around.
“WE have a cop on our doorstep,” he yelled.
Those words muted whoever had been back there, talking behind him. After that, I didn’t hear much more out of them.

“Come on now, it isn’t like I bite,” OI said. “I was just wondering— do you two know anything about this shadow that has been parading through the streets, and making everybody involved with it disappear?”
Jack Crowley tensed, and I watched as his face turned harder than rock.
“Where did you get any information on that?” he asked. “And, why are you talking to me? I don’t know anything about it… You have no reason to believe that I know anything about it.”
“I have my ways,” I said, “and I know that you, and your friend, are direct targets of it. I just need to know exactly what’s going on, and it will all be over with.”

“Please. We all know exactly what you have planned. You’re just trying to dig up information… And, when you don’t get that information, you’re going to threaten me and my friend here. But, we don’t know anything about what you’re talking about. Even if we did, it wouldn’t be of any use to you.”

“I’m not leaving until I get my answers,” I said, firmly. “I just don’t have the time to get any of this done… Not the way that it’s going, right now. I have a lot to do today, and not a lot of time to play hopscotch with you two. If you want to be safe, and protected, then just tell me what you know. I promise you— I’m on a mission to make sure that everybody in my city becomes safe and protected. My sole goal is to make sure that these crimes are no longer a problem.
“WE don’t have anything to give you!” Jack Crowley said again.
Seeing as I wasn’t getting through to him, and that I wouldn’t be able to get through to him, I instead yelled out to his friend.
“Hey! Bill Clyde! I need to talk to you!”

There was the sound of something crashing and clattering on the floor, in the distance. A fit of coughing and sneezing broke out. Then, nothing. All that remained was an echo reverberating in my ears. And then, it stopped. Not even he was going to give me and answer.
“Maybe they really don’t have anything to say…” I wondered.

I found this doubtful— especially when I considered the place that they were lying in, and how the crimes seemed to correlate with the rich and the poor— not that there was much in between, these days, However, they refused to give me what I wanted. And so, I ended up abandoning it all, entirely, and simply walking out of their apartment building. I felt defeated and humiliated for leaving the place, especially after all of the interrogation that I’d tried to conduct— it had been my duty to ensure that I got the answers that I needed. Though, that rain dumped down onto my head, with such a constant influx that I felt there was no real break it would provide me. Eventually, I overcame the raindrops, by stepping into my car and driving off. The muggy weather wasn’t enough to mug me, even as I felt as if I’d been subject to a complete failure.
There was still so much for me to do. I realized that nothing could stop me from moving forward, if I simply kept up the pace.

My knuckles clicked against the cold, hard wood of Mr. Donald’s door. The nature that surrounded me chirped with a chipper spirit, and the storms had finally decided to subside. However, I could tell that it was all just playing me for a fool. I could tell that, beyond this faux appearance of peace, nature was steadily winding up a pitch of reality towards me— it planned on hitting me hard in the head, and knocking me to the ground. IT was just waiting for the right moment— it was always waiting for the right moment.
“Who is it?” I heard a voice croak, form inside the house. It was clearly Mr. Donald’s butlers.
What one of these robbed mansions don’t have a butler running the show? I wondered.
“It’s Sergeant Kyler, of the Chicago Police Department,” I said. I’m here to investigate the premises for something that I believe the overlooked, during our first investigation.”

“Sergeant Kyler?” the butler repeated, now looking me straight in the eye from the other side of the peephole. I could see him trembling just by the look of me— clearly I didn’t give off the most comforting of presences.

“Yes,” I said. “As I’ve told people that I’ve come to investigate many times over, you have nothing to worry about— I simply plan on inspecting what you have here, and then leaving, IT’s going to be as simple a matter as that…”
“Nothing more?” the butler said.
“Hopefully.”

Seeing that this promise was good enough for him, the butler opened the door for me. With that, I gave him a hello, and then briskly walked down the hall to the place where the marble ballroom was— the very place where I’d found all of the fingerprints.
“How long did it take you to install the plumbing for this place?” I asked the Butler, as I scanned the floor, and then took a quick glimpse at the fountain.

“About three years, in its entirety,” said the butler. “We did it in spurts, as Mr. Donald saw it fit. First, he inserted all of the basic plumbing— that took about four months. After that, he inserted all of his exorbitant additions… I always cautioned him against this, but he apparently never cared about how much money he spent of the place. Beauty was the only aesthetic that Mr. Donald ever wanted in this house.”
“I see…” I said. “how did you go about taking apart the plumbing, and redoing it?”

“We had to get rid of the basement, and turn it into an entirely new space from plumbing line to go down,” the butler said— he was a lot less willing to have actual conversation than Miss Prestel’s Butler, Eustace, had ever been.
“And, why is that? Wouldn’t you have designed all of the plumbing line in the same way, in order to keep continuity?”

“You would think that— especially about somebody as rich as Mr. Donald. But, you see, he decided that he wanted to go a cheaper route— he was always about spending money where he felt it was worth spending, and investing money where he felt it was worth investing. This was a rather frugal and imbalanced philosophy, often causing him to waste money where it need not have been wasted, and to save money, when it need not be saved. Either way, this resulted in him having a plumbing line built down into the basement, and into the rest of the plumbing lines. The basement is now used exclusively for plumbing lines…”
“And, do you ever go down there?” I asked.

“No sir,” said the butler. Not after all of the money want poof. I don’t feel too comfortable going around such a dangerous area when I don’t even have a job security anymore. I prefer to have plumbers go down there, and maintenance it every so often…”

“I see…” I said, “Well, this was all very useful of information, sir. I thank you for you giving me your time. I’m just going to be here a little while longer, and see something for a minute— was every room in your house checked during the investigation?”
“Of course!” said the butler. “Except the basement… We— we umm, closed the entrance to that room up, with bricks. It’s locked off, only for when there’s an issue with the plumbing…”
I bent down to the ground, and crawled to the tile where I’d noted the fingerprints, which had matched Mr. Donald’s fingerprints, having stopped.
“Is the other entrance to the basement under this tile?” I asked, meticulously wording my words, so that the butler would have no way around them.
“Yes…” he said. “But, I don’t know why that should be of any importance to you. Like I said before, it’s just where all of the pipes go. Surely you don’t think that—.”
“Whoever kidnapped Mr. Donald, they were insane enough to force him to go down here…”
I pulled a crowbar out, which I’d been hiding in my sleeve, and then jammed it into the crack of the loose marble tile.
“Are you suggesting that—.”
“I’m not suggesting anything… all that I know is that somebody knew about this plumbing, running under the house— somebody knew about every detail. And, somebody trapped Mr. Donald down here.”
“It wasn’t me, Sir… Whatever you find down there, it wasn’t me. I promise, I had nothing to do with this!”

“That’s fine,” I said, heaving heavily as I tried to lift up the tile with all of my might. “But, the evidence definitely puts you in an awkward place… Why were you so keen on making sure that this plumbing section was closed off?”

“It was closed off over a year ago! It was done for no more a reason than that it was an eye-sore— and, it was done upon Mr. Donald’s request! I promise— there was no devious intent behind any of this!”
“That’s something that I’ve begun to notice a lot lately… The intentions of things tend not to be the meaning of things…”

The tile was eventually pried off, and I found myself staring into the deep blackness of the plumbing basement. Despite it having such a mundane and everyday title, and air about it, I couldn’t help but see it as something far more supernatural, and beyond the realm of understanding. When I looked down into it, I couldn’t help but feel as if I didn’t understand. Everything became a big question mark, and I became a bearer of these many questions. In this weight, I felt the blackness begin to pull me in. In a sense, I wanted it to pull me in. I wanted to become one with it, and feel it all encase me— feel all the questions become so numerous that I could no longer feel them anymore. Sadly, this wish of mine was not one that came to fruition. As instantly as I’d wished it to be, I had to recognize that it wasn’t going to come out. I was too afraid to dive into the darkness. My terror was something that I felt I simply wouldn’t be able to face. I’d need light to guide me through. There was something within myself, inherent to my nature— something tied down by the need to know.

I suppose that those are the two opposing dichotomies that lead to human development— then need to know, and not knowing. Whichever you focus on can determine which one you choose to follow— follow the spirit of exploration, or the spirit of terror.
Against all reason, I chose exploration. But then— I couldn’t tell if this was the right choice.

I dove down anyway, grabbing onto the vague shape of a pipe that my eyes had caught. With that, I allowed myself to slide further, and further down, taking heed to give a look and consideration to everything. I was unwilling to let myself fall into the trap of ignorance.

I turned on my flashlight, once near the bottom. As I did, I found that the basement was far less glory-filled than the ballroom above. In fact, it was almost like going into an entirely different world. It was full of a dirty brown sewage, which I could hear dripping from the pipes. And, as I splashed down into the water, I found that I was standing upon flooded concrete.

I opened my mouth to make a sarcastic remark about it all, but then stopped to listen to the water. At each drip, it signaled and reminded of all the soupy mess that it had caused— it reminded me of just how dark this cavern really was, and just how hard it would be to make it back up— to make it back up with the knowledge that I needed would be an even harder feat to pull off.
“I see that you’re enjoying yourself down there…” the butler said, after I groaned in disgust of my surroundings.

“Yes,” I said, in disgust. “I’m enjoying myself very much…. Please— whenever you find something that pleases you, from up there, just ask of it— I’ll make sure to bring up a bit of this sewage waste for you…”

“I might be the rarest of the butlers in this town,” he said. “I’m not as constrained by what some might see as required of a figure such as myself…. But, I don’t care for the nastiness down there, I’m afraid. I’d far prefer for the world down there to remain desperate from the world up here.”

I started waving my flashlight upon the rusted tubes of the underground sewer, and the broken bits of plaster that were flaking off into the water, and away from the structure of the building. While the mansion above this basement looked too beautiful to imagine, its underbelly was one that was too disgusting to behold. The house was falling apart from the bottom up, despite appearing to be otherwise.
“Yes…” I said, “After seeing all of this, I’m sure that you do…”

“I’m serious though…” said the butler, with a shift in tone. “Whatever you find down there, I don’t want you to bring it up here… I just can’t bear the thought of having to face the horrid mess of my master… If you find his body down there dead or alive— make sure not to let me see him. I only want him to be viewed as he properly should be— in his normal dress, if he’s alive, or at a funeral, should the worst of fates have come upon him…”
“And if I don’t find him...?”
“We both know that you’ll find him… We’re dealing with a madman here… I’d prefer for us both to acknowledge that, in a proper form.”

“Will do,” I said, motioning for him to step back. I can’t tell if he was able to see me from down where I was, or not— it was a far drop, into a black abyss— but, it certainly looked like he could see me, because he stepped back. “Things are probably going to get grotesque… And, if they do, you’ll probably not want to see it.”

I didn’t actually know what to expect myself. However, I had the dread upon me that the butler had. AS I looked upon every corner of the basement, I knew that I was steadily nearing where Mr. Donald might’ve been. Every inch that I covered was another inch closer to him.
I was drawing upon him, whether I liked it or not… and, I knew that I wasn’t going to like it, and so I drew even closer.
I might as well get this all over with as soon as I possibly can, I thought to myself. The dirty deed needs to be done away with, so that it won’t trouble me anymore.
These thoughts pretty much worked, to keep me going forward. But, they didn’t rid me of my terror. Nothing could rid me of my terror.

Within the murkiness that encased me, I felt as if my entire soul were trapped— everywhere that my eyes could perceive seemed to be encompassed by a blackness, and I too felt encompassed by that blackness. The claustrophobia seemed to choke my breath, and make me feel as if the entire world around me had turned to a vapor— one with the smothering proportions that might be found within an oven. There was nothing that I could do to escape the feeling of it. Everywhere in sight was a smoke to me. I couldn’t think of a way to get out— I couldn’t think of any sort of escape. I was trapped. But then— the light above me was the single solace that I was able to take hold of. I t was the only thing that could give me any sort of peace of mind…. But, I still couldn’t help but feel distraught. I knew that, in this tunnel. There was a dead man. I could smell it. It was crawling all over my skin. It made my eyes burn, and water…. I felt as my cheeks began to have hot coals rolling over top of them…

My stomach felt as though it were both nauseous and sick at the same time. There was nowhere that I could look and feel a sort of solace Everything around me had suddenly gained a threatening gleam to it.

I knew that I was nearing the cornered where the suspect was— if he were anywhere at all. I could feel his presence beating into my skull. My muscles tensed, and I listened to them crack under the strain that my body was coming under. There was nowhere that I could look and find any sort of peace of mind. Any thoughts of rest were now gone, and replaced with depraved thoughts of how I would get out of this place, with my mind inn tact. So far, I couldn’t conceive such a possibility— the scars of this mission were already beginning to form upon my mind.
“I think that I’ll be heading back up soon,” I called up to the butler. “Prepare the rope. I haven’t found anything down here, and I think that staying will prove to be useless!”
I heard the structure around me wail— then, I listened as the Butler mimicked the wail.
“Yes, sir,” he said, feebly.
“I never did bother to catch your name…”
“it’s Mr. Dom,” he said, with his voice having turned to a wiry rumble— one that my ears could hardly perceive.
“That’s—.” I began to say. Though, something had stopped me.
Doom.

My foot slipped in the water, and I felt as a thousand pins were jammed into my legs and arms. All of the nerves in my body were now unruly and unorganized, making me feel them everywhere at once. My face was suddenly drenched in the sludge— its filth went up into my nostrils, and I felt my entire body become partially frozen by it. Its nastiness clouded over me, making me feel like but a phantom of who I really was— making me feel like I’d been overtaken by a phantom.

As my throat filled with the unclean sludge, and as my mind began to struggle to retain its level, I began to fear that I was never going to gain any sort of ground— as if everything that I did would be futile, and that the water would prove itself to be the victor.
I wasn’t wrong in the former thought.

I ripped myself out of the water, as if I were a dolphin ripping from out of the ocean. My arms groped, to find a sturdy holding to stand myself up with. Nothing in sight gave me any place, because there was nothing in sight— my flashlight had been submerged, and all that I could see was a faint glow.

My feet finally stood up, but they didn’t feel like they were standing up anymore. I could’ve had my legs severed off of my body, and not have noticed. In the water, where the faint glow was, I saw the face of a man— but, it wasn’t the sort of face that I’d been expecting to see. Instead, it was a face that I’d been afraid to see— the face of the man that I’d deeply wanted to find. But, I now realized that it was also the face of the man that I hadn’t wanted to find.
My mind was so undecided and conflicted, that it was just enough to distract me from the disgust that was forming in my throat.

Under the water was Mr. Donald, in a tight tuxedo. In fact, amongst the water, it almost looked like he wasn’t in a tuxedo at all— instead, he appeared to be wrapped in an oily foil. His entire face was so pale— and dead. I knew that this man was long gone, just by the emptiness that was in his eyes— the way in which his arms floated amongst the glow of my flashlight, and the way in which his head bobbed. His head looked almost as if It were nodding in agreement with something. His unnaturally peaceable face only completed this image
That act of nodding how I truly knew that he was a dead man. The moment that somebody agrees with something that’s working against them is the moment when they’ve utterly died.
“At least I know that he went out happy…” I said to myself, uneasily.

I reluctantly placed my hand into the slimy water and grabbed my flashlight. Steadily, the glow dissipated from Mr. Donald’s body, until it was as if he was no longer there anymore— as if he were gone again.

“Mr. Dom, I think it’s time that you let me out of here,” I said. “I finally found Mr. Donald— I know that you said that you wanted him alive. However, I sadly won’t be able to give you that message of hope...”

I didn’t receive an answer. Rather, all that I heard in return was a muteness. Something was amiss, and I couldn’t even quite tell what was going on— suddenly, I felt entirely alone. And that, beyond anything else, was probably my greatest fear with being under Mr. Donald’s house.
“Is anybody out there!?” I shouted. “Please don’t tell me that you’re gone, Mr. Dom! I need you over here, and quick! I can’t stay trapped down here forever.”

Strangely, I didn’t get an answer the second time that I cried out, either. Nor did I get an answer the next time that I called out for an answer— or the time after that. In fact, I never got an answer. I listened as my voice pinged across the dank and murky walls of the underground cavern, steadily making the water feel like a desperate chain that had made itself around me. It didn’t matter how much my voice went out. It only made me feel words. My body steadily felt as if it were becoming weaker and weaker, with even my mind wishing to fall subservient to the forces that were at work. In fact, I felt like my entire mission had become desperate. There was nobody who could help me because nobody was there.
“Mr. Dom. This isn’t a game!” I finally burst out, as loud as I could.

I’d been telling at the top of my lungs, up to this point. But, this time, I felt as if there were somebody there to hear me. I’m not sure what it was, but the air around me shifted— I could practically smell the shift of atmosphere. Nothing was quite the same afterward.

There was the sound of somebody above me. I know that there was. My ears aren’t the best, having been dulled by years of mileage. But, I know that I could hear the breath of somebody far above me. It was undeniably there. There’s nothing that can convince me otherwise. My senses were so acute and aware of it, that I was shocked that the person never made a peep. There wasn’t a word that rolled off their tongue. Rather, they just stood there. Breathing.

In fact, all the way down where I was, I almost felt as if their breath was upon me, brushing up against my rough skin. In a jolt of fear, my eyes turned down to make sure that the breathing wasn’t coming from Mr. Donald’s corpse— an irrational fear that quickly proved to be false, but one that was pervasive all the same,

Eventually, the breaths stopped being so loud and prominent, and I heard them become distinct. They were replaced by the sound of something scraping against the ground— tearing at my ears, and clawing at the strength of my chest.  My pulse started to climb up into my mind, making me feel as if I were about to burst. Even the room around me started to fade from sight, in my fever of stress— it was all dissipating, and fading away. There was nothing. Nothing, but black.

I struggled to shake myself awake, form out of my feeling of paralysis, and I looked above myself to where the noise had been coming from. To my dismay, I found that the hole in the ceiling that I’d entered through had been entirely sealed up. I was stuck under the rood, in this mess of pipes, without anywhere to go— the only person with me was the corpse of Mr. Donald.
Suddenly, I wished that Mr. Donald had been a ghost, as much as the idea terrified me.

Trying my best to accommodate to the circumstances, I controlled my breathing, and pulled out my flashlight. After flicking the light on, the underground maze of pipes looked to be just as revolting as they had been as they had looked when I had first come down. And, the ceiling above was no different from how it had been. However, as my eyes peered about, and as my wears tried to accommodate to everything that was around me, I found that there was nothing that I could do to adjust to it all. Rather, I felt like I was staring at one enormous question mark, and I was attempting to erase it. But, the question mark was in permanent ink. There was no answer to the question mark either.
There could never be an answer. I didn’t even know the question that preceded it.

My light whirled all about the wide expanse, trying to find some sort of way t climb up, to where the escape tile was— some way to break out. But, there was nothing. Any hint of a ladder upwards had been tucked away from my view. For a detective, I found that I was having a hard time getting any sort of clue. The entire place was about as barren as one of the downtown Chicago streets would’ve been.

Even as I looked up, to where my hole in the ceiling had been, I couldn’t figure out what tile that I’d come in from. The entire ceiling was hard to decipher, with wooden beams keeping it utterly indistinguishable. I came to a point where I realized that, if there had been any hope for me to get out through the ceiling, it was long gone. Whoever had kidnapped me, they’d made sure to leave me in a position where I had no option. That is— no option, except to surrender to my distasteful fate
There was no use pretending, either— I knew full well who had done this.

“I was so gullible. I knew that I never should’ve trusted Mr. Dom…” I said to myself. “You never trust a butler. That’s probably the first rule to these sort s of investigations… Wow— I really have been getting slow at this…”
“Then, I looked back up to the ceiling, with a scowl upon my face.

“Somebody!” I shouted. “Let me out of here! You’re not going to get your way, no matter how much that I know you want to! This isn’t the sort of way that you can win! This time around, you’re going to see the light, and pay! I’m on your tail!”

My shouts were frivolous, and I was certain that both of us knew it. It was too hard for me to ignore— all of the truth was staring me too hard in the face to ignore. I was placed in a position of which I had no other option but to get myself out of with it. The problem was, I didn’t have a strong wit, and the idea of having to rely on it was a troubling one— one that I knew I had little chance of overcoming.

I began to turn my flashlight about, and search deeply for a place of escape. It seemed that they were all placed far beyond me, and out of my reach— no doubt to make sure that I’d fail, and give up. It seemed at everything had been plotted out so that I would be trapped in here, no matter what. While I wasn’t certain that Mer. Dom had been the cause of this all, I had the feeling that he was. There was something inside of myself that was undeniably attracted to the fact that he was. The truth of the matter was that I needed to know who was behind all of this— I needed to feel as if I had the answer to it all. No, the thought of him being behind it was one of comfort, so I didn’t bother to stop myself from thinking it. All of my rationality went out of the window is this idle moment, so that I could pool all of my focus onto the menial worries at hand.

My knees and legs carefully crawled across the sewage waste floor, making sure to avoid all potential dangers. There was nothing under here that was sacred, or safe of disaster. However, at the same time, I also knew that there was nothing here that I could bring myself to be wary of. It seemed that, in the thought of watching out for danger, I allowed myself to become subject to the fears that danger wrought. And, it became to be that everywhere harbored danger, and that I had no possible way to avoid it. While I knew that this was blatantly untrue, and that I’d allowed myself to be tricked, I couldn’t help but still believe in it all. There was something far too terrifying about the arena of sludge that kept all of my plotting and deep-thinking from entering my mind.  Instead, I was just being run by a frivolous drive to escape before my time was out. I had a terrible feeling that the whole house might fall from above me— that the entire place was just one big trap, preparing to jump upon me like a venomous viper.

Eventually, I found that I’d scoured every inch of the room, and that there was no space that had revealed itself to me. It began to seem to me that I’d become a sort of mouse, running around in a cage of emptiness. There didn’t seem to be any area in which I could get out of the maze, though. I was constantly looking for the cheese, placed at the center, but it evaded my grasp. I was beginning to see that it was nowhere in which I’d be able to find it. I’d left myself in a positon where I wouldn’t be able to find it. The entire place was a trap.

These thoughts kept running through my head, as if it were a rusted merry-go-round from at a carnival. I couldn’t quite turn them away, no matter how tempted that I was to do so. It seemed to me that it had a nasty way of ways turning about, and exposing the ugly bits, every time that I thought it had finally turned into something ridable again. There wasn’t an angle from which I could look upon, and feel any sort of peace of mind. It was all blockaded from me— the solace that I was searching for had slipped from my grasp. Instead, all that I had to cling to were a few remaining straws of sanity. That, and brick.
Bricks where everywhere. Mortar was everywhere. Pipes were everywhere. There seemed to be no exit— no entrance. It was all designed so that I’d be lost, and confused.

“Where is the door out of this place!?” I shouted, listening as my voice, once again, reverberated through the room. Though, this time, I listened to it as it even made the pipes in the room rattle, with a sort of terror. It was as if even they were afraid of the situation that had benighted them— even they felt discomfort from the fact that there was nothing apparent, in which they could’ve made an escape. It had all made sure to conceal itself from them, so that all hope steadily was leaked away. In fact, I started to feel that there was no hope at all— that all time had run out, and that I was stuck to be there forever.

I began to remember all of the progressions that I’d made in my case— all of the questions that I’d had, and how few that I’d gotten answered. I began to see that I was on the trail of getting things figured out, and understood, but I’d just barely gotten myself stuck in a place where there was no such answer. I’d brought myself to the den of the culprit, obliviously. And, I was going to have to pay.
“Where is the door,” I found myself whispering. “I know that it’s supposed to be here… It was supposedly blocked off, and placed somewhere… It has to be here!”

I listened as my whisper glided across the room, and over the water, leaving a solitary ripple upon it. There was something about this solitary ripple— the ways that its rings steadily spread and grew, despite the small impact that had changed them. It reminded me of Eddy Mulligan— both of the Mulligans, in fact. He’d changed the entire course of my mystery— give me a sort of motivation. Though, there was something else to the ripple that I saw. It was going to bound across the whole room, and effect everything, even if such an effect wasn’t noticed. It was going to be like a sort of echo of its own, making sure to change things.

This was when I had an idea. With a revolting splash, I dug my hand into the water beneath me, making my best efforts to ensure that my hand went as deep to the ground as t could. I picked up a rock from out of the water, and stood myself back up. After this, I subsequently threw the rock at every portion of the wall that I could. There was a clink, a splash, and another clink, followed d by another splash. Over and over again, the cycle went with me making sure to listen for an echo on every portion of the wall.
I needed a ripple— I needed a way to tell if I was having an effect.
I needed to figure out what portion of the wall was connected to the outside.

For most of these throws, I directed the rock upwards, so that it made an echo in the upper floors— I was trying to make sure that, whatever I discovered, it was in the right place. Finding a hollow section on my current floor wasn’t going to get me anywhere, and I was certain that everybody knew it.

It was a long and arduous task of throwing the rock into the air, without so much as a ray of hope to motivate me to keep going forward. To a strong degree, I felt that I was simply wasting my time, and that nothing was going to come out of my efforts. It certainly looked that way, and it only felt even worse. Though, I eventually gained the clink that I was searching for— when it hit the brick, the different sound was one that filled me with a sort of satisfaction that I still can’t quite replicate in words. It was so grand, and pleasing that I think I’m never going to be able to describe just quite how I felt.

The way that the rock struck against the brick rumbled in such a way, that it couldn’t have neem compared to the dozens of other clinks from the rocks. I knew that my mind was exaggerating the experience, to fit its own needs. But then, that still didn’t change the fact of just how satisfying it really was.
Nothing will change how I feel right now, even if it’s the most dissatisfying thing that happens to me, I thought to myself.

Though, I was primitively wrong. There was one thing that could’ve taken me from my spot of mental leisure— the realization that there was no way to climb up to the spot the I was looking at. I was trapped under the tiles, hopelessly left to look on my escape— but never have any chance of reaching it. It was probably one of the crueler forms of irony, if it hadn’t been for the fact that I knew that there was a way out, beyond where my eyes could see— I had this single ray of hope that I just couldn’t seem to squelch, no matter how much I was tempted to do so. I knew that my way out was just up ahead of me— I just needed to exert everything that was within me, in order to ensure that I reached it.
My eyes turned to the pi pes, and I quickly realized how I was going to accomplish this. It was so simple— but it was also so brash and bold, that I knew it was near unconceivable— near unachievable.
It was the exact sort of thing that I was looking for.

I threw the stone at the brick wall several times, before turning to climb the pipes. I felt my slimy hands slip, and begin to slacken in their grip, and I tried to scale its height. Even my shoes threatened to fly off of my feet, and into the water. Thankfully, I managed to control myself, and bring my body upward. I was going to reach the top— I had something in my spirit, telling me to do so. Nothing— not the darkness, not the sickness that I felt broiling in my gut, not my headache that I‘d gained from the sight of Mr. Donald, and not even my own fears, could ever have taken me down from there.

When my grip finally fastened around the pipe that I’d been looking for, I still didn’t bother patting myself of the back. Rather, I struggled to unscrew all of the large bolts that had been wrenched into there. I quickly found that this idea was nowhere near as easy as I’d hoped for it to be— my hands became cut up by it, and I found that my arms were weak. My heartrate was suffering too, with me falling into a tumult and finding that my heart was threatening to send me tumbling back into the sewage water below. Oddly enough, this wasn’t strong enough to halt me— not even this managed to hoodwink me into a sense of fear. Instead, I continued on my goal, striking my hands harder and harder on the bolts. My palm swelled with blisters, and my eyes swelled with the wrenching of pain— and wrenching— but my own will broke past it. There was something unseen to me that I couldn’t quite detect. A part of me wanted to call it a miracle. Though, another part of me wanted to call it the fruits of brute force.

As the bolts creaked and screeched at the act of e pulling them away, I almost felt as if they were screeching at me— into me.  I felt as if a part of them had leapt into my soul, and that they were beginning to overtake a part of me. Of course this was wrong, and unfounded. But, I couldn’t help but feel as if this was the entire truth, and that there was nothing else going on around me. In fact, I’d argue that the bolts had brought the worst parts of myself to light, and that they’d made me into a me frightened state than I ever would’ve been otherwise.

Either way, it didn’t matter. I aptly made sure to start pulling the pipe from it place, attempting to knock it toward the sewer sludge below. Of course, my plan wasn’t anything close to having the pip knocked into the water. Instead, I had a far more in depth plan. My arms had griped around the entire pipe, and prepared to knock the pipe no the wall across from me. I could already see all of the crumbling elements of the bricks, within the wall across— it would just take a bit of brute force, and I’d have it all under control.

Granted, it wasn’t just a bit of brute force that was necessary. Rather, there was quite a lot that I’d need to utilize. I could already feel my body revving up for the physical beat down that was about to succumb it, and the amount of force that it was going to have to lay down. It wouldn’t be enough. It would never be enough. As much as I wanted it to, nothing could be enough to do what needed to get done. In truth, everything that I’d planned was doomed to failure, and I was doomed to go down with it. I had no chance at making it thorough. I could already feel the water beginning to spurt out of the pipe, with a pressure that I’d never felt before. It was only going to get worse, and I feared that I was not going to have a way of stopping it from flooding the whole place— not that I’d ever had a way of doing so.
The water went into my eyes, and I felt as it burned me— there were chunks of dirt and algae stuck within the pipes, and they rocketed into my face in both a distasteful and painful mixture.

“This is why I never will understand plumber…” I said to myself. “I don’t know how else I’m going to get out of this place, if I can’t get past all of this disgust. I just don’t know if this will be easy, or if I’ll struggle the whole way through.”

My answers came for me. I found that the water started to cease spraying at me, and everything began to clear up. In fact, there was a sense of elation and peace of mind that I began to sense— none of my concerns held the same barring on me that they originally had.

I pulled off the remaining bolts with the same strain that I had with the other ones. While their rusted edges still chomped into my palms, and left my hands running with red tears, I was still able onto overlook it all. Instead, my sights were upon the wall, and that alone. The spray of toilet water, the fears of wound infections, and even the wound s itself, disappeared. I’d felt the mixture of despair, followed by hope, several times within these sewers. But, none of it had quite matched this time. This time, I knew that I was safe— that I was doing things right. And, I was no longer feeling any of the previous concerns that I’d been suffering from.

The brick wall made a loud cracking sound the first time that I wacked at it. The second time, I watched as a chunk of brick plunked into the water, leaving behind a splash of liquid. Another time after that passed by, and there was a substantial dent— but, I was already beginning to get the feeling that the metal pipe wasn’t going to get me as far as I’d hoped. It was about the size of my forearm, and heavy as thirty pounds— but, as I wacked it into the wall, all of these forces were multiplied, and I becoming increasingly aware of just how weak and helpless that I was. Despite all of my best wishes, I knew that I wouldn’t be able to get what I wanted out of all this. In fact, I was gaining the feeling that things were going to steadily avalanche, until I had no way out– until all of my hope was gone, and my chances at renewal were made minimal.

I watched as the whole steadily enlarge, and felt as the spray of water was thrust upon me in increasingly rapid rates. In fact, it became so much so that I started to fear I’d have no hope at breaking it at all. Thankfully, it steadily became more apparent that none of this would matter— rather, I knew that it would all eventually fall apart, and come to an end. My willpower was just too strong. At least— that’s what I’d convinced myself of. The truth within this belief, however, was probably one that was more up to debate.

It came to the point where I’d broken onto the other side, and I could see the light and hope that lay beyond me. There was nothing that I could deny now— I knew for a fact that I was where I needed to be, and that there was nothing that could stand against me. In fact, I felt so confident that all other fears and worries started to appear as small as fleas in the face of me. They were barely worth acknowledgement!

I wanted to convinced myself of this, at east. Though, I then remembered how much effort it had taken for me to break this portion of the wall pen, and just how much harder it would be to breakout a substantial portion— I started to remember just how much I was going to be susceptible to failure on so many fronts, that I wouldn’t even be able to concede to them all. All it would take is the slip of the foot into water. And then, I’d need to find a safe way to get across and over the water, or else become subject to my own issues. And, of course, there was also the fact that my issues were far too numerous. They were all too abundant, that I wasn’t even sure if I’d be able to get all of it down. I was going to have to figure out a way to make sure that Mr. Donald was brought from the crime scene. And, I’d still have to make some last minute inspections— but then., I was getting the feeling that such last minute inspections were going to be too far out of reach. I could practically hear the call of my demise off in the distance. If I were to deny it, I knew that I would deny Mr. Donald too. But then— if I were to accept it, I had the feeling that it would be the need of the road for me.

There were so many other problems that I was being confronted with, but this one seemed to take precedence over the rest.
