Fletcher shrugged. Coincidences didn’t happen. Linda must’ve seen that he was a “successful coding freelancer” on his profile’s bio and been compelled to email him.
It was all the explanation he could come up with. It would have to do.
Clearing his throat, Fletcher read through the email. Linda wanted a website to advertise a “weed garden”, apparently.
She was only willing to pay him his minimum rate. She wanted the website done impossibly fast, too.
Fletcher glanced back at the image of Linda. His chest burned.

He clicked away and scrolled through his email. He’d think about it. He needed to give his mind some time to process it all. Linda was asking for a lot of effort — especially since web-designing was only supposed to be a side-business. The toy shop wasn’t going to run itself.
The computer screen flared as he went back through the stretch of complaints and requests. Fletcher’s eyes passed back over Harry’s email. Maybe he should reply to him — try reconnecting.
Fletcher shuddered. His fingers clacked hard against his keyboard.
“Sounds good,” he wrote. “Will just need a payment sent to my account, and we’ll be clear.”
He typed in Linda’s email address. The send button gave a chirp as it was pressed.
A grin formed on Fletcher’s face. He’d build the website. It’d be the best goddamn website in his entire career. Maybe he could get more from out of this Linda. Maybe he could get out of this place.
The world could still make sense. It just needed a nudge.

With a yawn, he shut off his computer screen, and trudged downstairs. The steps creaked. Fletcher’s hand clenched the railing as he took care to skip the broken step — it had left him with splinters the day before.
“Good morning everybody!” Fletcher said.
The stacks of toys gave him withering glares.
“What? You guys are so quiet today… You all wake up on the wrong side of the bed or something?”
He chuckled.
“Just because all of Dexburg has decided to go nuts, it doesn’t mean that you guys have to.”
His eyes shot to his “Wally Walrus” watch. It was 11:00. How had that happened? The toys must have noticed — that must’ve been why they were so ornery.

Fletcher stiffened his legs, making a tour of the shop. On each shelf, toys posed with warm smiles and shiny price tags. Fletcher brushed his fingers over their soft paint, and smooth etchings. There was a pixie-like quality to them. They glittered under the lamps, which swayed above in a swirl of dust.

Calm settled over Fletcher as he neared his checkout counter. The shop might not have been home, but it was an oasis. The elements were in total balance; in a designated position. They had to be. There was no affording any kind of error.

Fletcher popped open his drawers and counted out the money. The bills rustled, sliding between his fingers. The hairs along Fletcher’s arm rustled with them. All the numbers fit. The shop looked as it was supposed to. Inventory was accounted for. Nevertheless, a twinge of discomfort ate at Fletcher’s mind.
There was a ding as the drawer slid back into the register.
Porcelain shattered. Fletcher turned to see his cup of pens broken on the ground.
Great. The place hadn’t even opened yet, and objects were already staging mutiny.
“I’m just a bit jittery. That’s all,” he told himself. “We’ll be fine, guys! The show will go on, as usual! No worries!”

He went to get the broom from the corner. It should have been right by the oil baron. To Fletcher’s pleasure, he went over to the corner and found his broom. Displeasure came next. His breath left his lungs.
The broom was in the corner, but it wasn’t where it was supposed to be. It wasn’t by the oil baron. The oil baron was a no show.
Fletcher blinked. The space where the oil baron should have been was filled with a fresh patch of dust.

Fletcher ran his hand through his hair. The baron had been there just the day before, smiling at him from under a twisty mustache. The baron’s prim hands were held nicely behind its back, with a large bag of money. His suit had been cleanly pressed and tightened.
He’d seemed so pleasant, and happy to be here. What reason would he have had to leave?
Perhaps it didn’t matter that the baron was absent. Maybe Fletcher could go on without it.

Fletcher’s eyes went misty; he couldn’t. The baron was a critical part of the “Gingham Toys” industrial era collection. The baron had to be worth at least a few hundred dollars. Fletcher’s mind raced back to the garage sale that he’d attended, just a few years back; to the haggling that he had to undergo, with the Baron’s owner. A feeling of pride had swelled in Fletcher’s chest when he’d finally talked the owner down to twenty dollars. It was a feeling that was rare to come by, and precious when it did.
Fletcher’s loss in revenue may have been small. However, the baron himself was irreplaceable.

Though, who would have bothered taking it? It wasn’t as if many people in town were collectors. Besides, anybody who would’ve bothered taking the baron likely would’ve taken the rest of the industrial collection. Wouldn’t they?
Fletcher’s face contorted. There was only one person that it could’ve been.
“President Marigold, are you sure you don’t want to press the nuclear button?”
I look at the button. It’s real shiny. Big, clean, and red. The skull and bones on it throws me off a bit, though.
“Ma’am?”
It’s my military advisor. He really wants me to press it, doesn’t he? Pressing it would be damn fun, too. I’m called the “press-i-dent” for a reason. I press, and I’ll make a dent.
Is it the right time to make a dent though? I’m not sure.
“People are going insane out there. We need to establish dominance, over these foreign powers! Blowing them up is our best option right now.”
Pretty compelling case.
“We should probably talk over this, over lunch,” I say. “The chaos theorem says I don’t need to press it until midnight, a few days from now. Besides, I’m famished. How about you?”
Chapter 2:

Bits of wrappers and discarded coffee cups rolled past Fletcher. A hamster followed the pack, in a plastic ball. It made a defiant squeak as it did and rammed into Fletcher’s shin. Fletcher punted the hamster away and moved past the wave of trash. It wasn’t as if any owner was going to claim the rogue hamster. Nobody ever took responsibility in this town.
A wooden sign gave a slight creak in the wind. It held the peeling pink words, “Carol’s Flower Shop”. Despite having lost its luster, the sign remained as bold in Fletcher’s mind as ever.
His fist pounded against the shop’s glass door.
“Open up!” he cried. “I know that you’re in there!”
A woman with pruned lips strode up to the glass. The glass creaked.
“Doesn’t the sign say, ‘We Are Open. Welcome’?” asked Carol.
“Yeah, I can read,” Fletcher said. He rolled his eyes, though his voice now wavered.
“Well that’s good. And here I was, worried I hadn’t turned it over.”
She walked back through the shop and took a seat behind her counter.
A scowl formed on Fletcher’s brow. Carol was as smug as ever, twirling a packet of seeds along the surface of her counter. Meanwhile, he was just left to watch, behind a locked door.
“Let me in!” he shouted again.
He took a step back and shook his head. He didn’t want to escalate things, but he had to. He charged.
“Let me i—!”
The door swung forward. Fletcher hurtled toward the floor of the flower shop, only just catching his balance on a counter covered in potted plants.

Fletcher’s arm jerked outward, awkwardly. A thud resounded as flowerpot hit the floor and disintegrated to dust. Fletcher didn’t flinch. He was decent at catching his own balance, but catching Carol’s stupidly unbalanced pots was impossible.
“You figured out how to open the door, I see,” Carol said, with a grin. “Anyway, how is your day going?”
“I swear that the door had been locked,” Fletcher muttered.

“Jammed, probably. Nothing to fret over.” Her eyes wandered along the ceiling. She forced a smile. “What’s your gag of the day? Are my lights ‘too loud’? You still want me to pay to have the door removed? You think the scent of my flowers are making your customers loopy?”
“You kidnapped the oil baron!” Fletcher said. “I know it was you. Your fingerprints are all over it?”
Carol feigned a look of shock. Nonetheless, Fletcher caught the twinge of uncertainty in her eyes. There was malice lurking there. There had to be.
Her nose crinkled. “I kidnapped who?”
“The oil baron. He was one of the tin toys I had, sitting on my display shelves. Don’t pretend that you never saw it!”
“I’m afraid I am unaware of who that is.”
“I’d bet you’ve been stealing all of my toys. It’s the only way you can keep a business like this afloat.”

She stood from her chair and between two walls of sunflowers. Sunlight spilled from her new sunroof, setting her aglow. She was clearly proud she’d put the sunroof in place. However, Fletcher couldn’t help but seethe. She still hadn’t bothered removing the hazardous door between their shops.

“Normally your prank complaints are very funny, Fletcher,” said Carol. “I like to think that we can come around and become fine neighbors. But this prank is a bit far, don’t you think? I haven’t even left the shop over the past few days. How on earth could I have stolen any of your toys?”
“You don’t understand! This oil baron is going to cost me hundreds of dollars in potential revenue. You need to return it.”
“And I would. But I would never be so cruel as to take it from you.”
“But…”
“My lord!”
The room trembled. Carol fell back and leaned on her counter. She placed two fingers over her wrist and pinched her eyes.
“Another earthquake…” Fletcher mumbled, once the trembling had stopped.
They’d been more common over the past few days.
“Could you be a dear and get the broom to clean up that mess you made?” Carol said.
She gave a feeble gesture to her left, but Fletcher already knew where to go.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “But I just can’t take any more of these pranks of yours. I know that your business must be struggling. And, you’re right in thinking my business is struggling to stay afloat too. Melinda Clover and her stupid new greenhouse… Can you believe she’s been giving out free pumpkin seeds? The nerve!”
Fletcher gave her a blank look.
Carol plowed forward. “However, in these troubled times? We just need to work to keep our heads above water.”
The dustpan shook as Fletcher swept the shards of pottery into them.
“I still hate your shop. The flowers have me sneezing awake every night…”
Carol laughed. “Enough, you know you like it here.”
Annoyed, Fletcher said, “…But maybe you have a point. You weren’t there yesterday. And, the oil baron was still there yesterday…”
“See?”

“You’re not off the hook. Have you noticed the oil baron anywhere? Or, seen any suspicious persons, in this area? Because, if you have, I have a right to know. Otherwise, you’re still inadvertently stealing the oil baron away from me.”
Carol shook her head. “I haven’t seen anything of the sort. I’ve been preoccupied with the reveal that came out.”
“Oh, the chaos equation, or whatever? I would’ve hoped people would be over that by now.”
“Chaos theorem. You haven’t taken it yet?”
“Why would I? It’s just a bunch of quackery.”
“Well, I assure you. This thing — it’s not going away.”
Fletcher plucked one of the leaves off a plant and began tearing it apart in his hand. Green pigment rubbed off on his skin, staining it.
“Please don’t touch that,” Carol said.
“This plant is so ugly. Honestly, I thought it was a weed. It probably looks better without the leaf, honestly.”
“It’s a rare cicada. Keep pulling its leaves off like that, and you’ll kill it.”
“That won’t happen. If it wants to live, it’ll live.”
Carol attempted to maintain her composure. Fletcher kept his scowl waiting for her to break.
“Anyway, the chaos theorem is definitely something that you should care about. Scientists warn that it’s dangerous to be uninformed.”
“I’m not uninformed. I just don’t care.”
Fletcher sneezed. The stench of flowers in the room was obtrusive, and his head was starting to spin. He wiped his nose and went toward the exit.

Carol gave a pitying look. “I took the chaos theorem. It’s so enlightening! It’ll tell you everything about your life; past, future, and present. You’re honestly telling me that you’re not even the slightest bit curious about what’s in the chaos theorem?”
“What I’m curious about is something that you can’t answer me. Do you know where the oil baron is?”
“I have no idea.”

“Well, he didn’t just disappear! The only time I’ve ever seen that was when my uncle did a magic trick of eating one whole.” Fletcher paused, to cough. Something itchy had caught in his throat. “If you can’t tell me where it is, I’m going to talk to the cops about all this!”
Carol’s face went dark, and she lowered her head. There was a something there. “I’m sorry, but I have no idea—.”
“Good day, then!”

Fletcher went and slammed the door. He couldn’t get Carol’s dejected face out of his head. It left his heart stewing with guilt. However, what was he to do? She was clearly withholding information. Even if she wasn’t, something needed to be done.

So odd, that Fletcher is. Every time he comes here, he distracts me from watering my plants. He always seems upset about something. If only he hadn’t spent all that time with that strange Margaret, maybe he’d be happier.

I could board up that door in the top levels, like he’s always asking me about. But, it gives him a reason to come here, and have some fun. He seems so lonely. He probably needs people like me as friends, to keep his head on his shoulders. Lord knows things aren’t easy right now.
Fletcher needs to take that chaos theorem test.
If only Timothy was still around; for Fletcher’s sake, at least. He was such a great uncle, and he knew how to run that business too. Nothing got by him.
Have I watered my plants yet? I must have. See, now I can’t remember. If only I could remember what the chaos theorem said that I did.
Chapter 3:
“You want me to send out my entire police squad out, as a search party… All over a lost toy?”
Officer Mayhew’s lips curled. He sped his gum chewing to try holding back a laugh.

“That’s what I just said, yes,” said Fletcher. “I give this department my tax money, I respect the law as an abiding citizen… I, at the very least, expect justice to be served when injustice falls upon me.”
Officer Mayhew nodded.
“And you’re sure that you didn’t just… I don’t know, misplace it? It’s just, we have a lot on our plate right now, what with the looting, rioting, murdering… drug trafficking.”
He gave Fletcher a look. Fletcher squirmed in his seat.
“Don’t get me wrong,” said Officer Mayhew. “I’m on your side with this. It’s just… We don’t have enough time.”

He gestured to the grandfather clock sitting behind his desk. The pendulum swung heavily. Fletcher noted the intricacies in the grandfather clock’s design. It was a beautiful work of craftsmanship, completely out of place amid the rest of officer’s office. There were no other decorations, beige smearing all but one of the walls. Moreover, the one wall that wasn’t beige wasn’t a “wall” at all; it was a flimsy divider. Fletcher strained to tune out the chatter from the neighboring office.
“If you can form a search party for my oil baron, I might be able to give you a reward for your trouble,” Fletcher said, managing a wink.
“Much as I’d love that? Once again, there’s just not enough—.”
“I have more than enough money. How much do you need? Two hundred? Five? I can go up to a full thousand, if need be. No need to play hardball with me.”
Rolling his gum over his tongue, Officer Mayhew shook his head. “If you haven’t noticed, Dexburg is kind of in shambles. Take the pickpocket, for example… Still at large.”
Fletcher snorted. “The pickpocket? Please. Who cares?”

Officer Mayhew raised himself in his chair. “Well, just this morning we had a guy throwing himself from Dexburg Bridge, a guy defecating in the streets, a guy slashing tires, a guy quitting his job… And that was just one guy. Our hands are full.”
Fletcher snorted. “You’re feeding into the hysteria. If you just ignore everything going on in the news, it’ll be fine. It’s all just a bunch of bogus pseudoscience anyway.”
Officer Mayhew raised an eyebrow. “You’re really calling the chaos theorem pseudoscience?”
“What would you call it?”

“Uh, anti-pseudoscience. The scientists who constructed the algorithm have one of the most powerful supercomputers on earth — and, they have the lives of everybody in a basket. Every detail of your life, my life, the life of a grasshopper crossing the freeway… It’s there, typed out, listed, and postmarked.”
“Yeah, sure,” said Fletcher.
A brush of air came from Officer Mayhew’s papers, while he skimmed through them. He acted as if it were somehow the more important thing to do.

“If you don’t want my advice, you don’t want my advice,” Officer Mayhew said. “I can have your rear hauled right out of my office any time I want. Just because you’re Timothy’s boy doesn’t mean I don’t remember your record!”

Fletcher called his bluff. “Look, I’ve heard a lot of different things about the chaos theorem on the tv and the radio. There’s no way that it’s more important than my missing figurine. For all the talk, nobody can tell me one lick about how it works. Nobody has even said what the damn thing is. Isn’t that odd, officer? Doesn’t that smell a little fishy to you?”
“I can’t tell you…”
Fletcher smirked. “Exactly.”
“No, I mean, I really can’t tell you. You clearly haven’t done your due diligence and gone to the local ‘theorem booth’, have you?”
“Seeing as this is all a bunch of bolognas, I can’t say I was all that inclined.”
Officer Mayhew throttled back in his chair, and tucked his chin in. Raising a firm finger, he cleared his throat.
“Mr. Fletcher, cool it. You’re skating on some mighty fine ice, right now”
“Cooled.”
“Good. Because, it seems you need a bit of educating.”

Officer Mayhew’s lips tightened as he wadded his old gum into its wrapper and popped a new piece in his mouth. He ran a finger along his mustache. Despite Mayhew’s mustache being well-trimmed, it was covered in crumbs. A grimace formed on Fletcher’s face.

Rolling his wad of gum in his hand, Officer Mayhew assumed an assertive tone. “Okay. So. The chaos theorem might tell you your life’s story before you even lived it. But, if you told somebody how your life’s story would end before it ended, your entire life story would change. Right? The chaos theorem only works if nobody shares the chaos theorem.”
“That’s what my neighbor, Carol, was telling me the other day… Not buying it. If all it takes to break the theorem is somebody talking, the theorem’s logic probably broke a long time ago.”

“Not true. The chaos theorem accounts for that. Nobody can corrupt the chaos theorem, unless the chaos theorem planned for it. And, if somebody does corrupt it? They’ll be punished by the law. The government has made sure of it.”
Fletcher struggled to keep from going cross-eyed as he tried tracking the logic.
He gave up when his head began to ache. “Yeah? What kind of punishment?”
“I’m not sure… It’s never happened. Maybe they give you a hefty fine? Or they blow your head off? One of those two.”
“Mayhew, you’re the law. You should know this.”

Outwardly, Fletcher chuckled. Inwardly though, he hoped to god the punishment wasn’t a fine. There was no way that he’d be able to afford it. His toy shop was barely making ends meet. It had come to the point where he needed to ask Jim Harrigan for another loan — and Harrigan was already hounding him for loan payments.
“President Marigold hasn’t said. Fines or executions,” said Mayhew, with a shrug. “That’s all I know.”

Blinking, Fletcher said, “Everything you’re saying sounds fine and good. But I didn’t come here just to get lectured about the latest fad. I want one thing from you, Mayhew: to find my toy. The pickpocket doesn’t matter, nor whatever other off the rails headline is going around. If you guys can’t find my toy, this entire department doesn’t have priorities straight.”
Heavy breaths flowed through Fletcher’s lungs. His echoes pinged off the walls. The yammering from next door quieted, and Officer Mayhew’s chewing stopped. Fletcher smiled.
Tearing a slip of paper from his notebook, Officer Mayhew scribbled something down.
The tip of his pencil snapped. Mayhew shoved the pencil in his sharpener and cranked the handle. He gave Fletcher a glare, then returned to the sharpening.
“What are you putting down in the report?” Fletcher asked. “If you need it, my address is—.”
“It’s not a report.” The pencil tip snapped again. “It’s my grocery list.”
“That’s ridiculous. Why didn’t you make your grocery list at the crack of dawn, like a normal person?”

“Because, the chaos theorem told me you’d be coming here, and I wanted an excuse for you to leave. So, yes. Leave. Get out of my office. You clearly don’t care about this crazy crisis. I bet you don’t even care about the crazy price of my grocer’s tomatoes!”
“That’s because it’s all gone crazy is over nothing. You might as well tell me that the sun is made of cheese.”

His face burning bright red, Officer Mayhew leaned toward Fletcher. He was so close that Fletcher could count the hairs on Officer Mayhew’s mustache, and feel the warmth of his breath. Mayhew had numerous jagged teeth. The only silver lining was that Officer Mayhew’s breath smelled minty fresh.

“I guess… I guess the joke is on you!” Officer Mayhew said. The back of Fletcher’s chair in tow, he marched toward the door. “Last week, one of my buddies told me that the sun is probably actually made of cheese! According to science, no less.”
Officer Mayhew dumped Fletcher out of the chair and tried pushing him out the door. Fletcher managed to prop the door open with his arm.
“Oh yeah? What kind of cheese?”
“Cheddar.”
“Cheddar?”
“Cheddar.”
“Good to know. I’ll remember that when I make my own search party and do a better job at policing than you cheddar-eaters!”
Officer Mayhew made a grunt and pushed Fletcher’s arm out.
“Goodbye!” Officer Mayhew said.
The door clanged shut.. . .
Fletcher was a squirrely one, to be sure. I don’t quite know why he couldn’t just take my no for a… A no?
I don’t know.
Hopefully he’s not on that stuff that’s being shopped around. God knows it’ll only destroy him. Here’s hoping he takes the theorem, and lets it set him straight.

Why does the lieutenant always set me up with the nutjobs? He’s going around, busting crime lords and rioters. Meanwhile I’m over here trying to figure out where this jackass lost his bag of jacks, or marbles, or whatever.
I’m a serious cop. People should take me seriously.
Great. My phone is ringing again. The password won’t unlock — stupid touchscreen.
After all this, I better not be about to talk to another nut.
Chapter 4:
A glib poster of Mayor Haddock stared out into space. The words, “Vote for Haddock!” were emblazoned below. The poster flinched as another poster was placed overtop, and a staple was shot into it.
Fletcher took a step back and smiled. He read the new poster to himself.
“Wanted: Missing Oil Baron. A nice box of staples will be rewarded to the finder.”

The letters were emblazoned in bright red, overtop a blurry picture of the oil baron. The picture was overblown, and nigh impossible to make out. However, whoever had stolen the oil baron would recognize exactly what was in the picture. They’d return the oil baron, no doubt.
Who could pass up a reward?
“Great work!” Carol said, poking her head from out of her flower shop. “You’re really making some progress now!”

Down the street were dozens of posters, taped, stapled, hot glued, and twist-tied into place. If the posters had been about anything other than the baron, Fletcher would’ve thought them garish. However, there was a charm to them. With the posters hanging among trash and an overcast sky, their bright colors gave a jolt of life.
Fletcher crossed his arms and faced Carol straight on. “Is that right?”
She gave her hands a light clap. “Of course. They look just lovely. I couldn’t be happier to see you finally getting a handle on things. I’ll definitely keep an eye out for that oil baron.”

Her pleasant mood was utterly artificial. It had to be. Deep down, she must’ve been broiling mad. Nevertheless, Carol whipped out a small camera, snapped a photo of one of the posters, and headed back for her shop.
Fletcher fumbled for words when Carol gave a polite, “Have a nice day.”
Carol pushed her shop door open. She was yanked away by someone.
“Come on Carol! Are you going to let this clown get away?”

Marvin Whisk gripped Carol by the forearm and dragged her toward Fletcher. His suit strained to stay seamed at the legs and waist. On his hairline, straggling strands of hair flayed about. His eyes flared, then flitted.

“I and Carol are sick of your antics!” Marvin said. “You come out here on a perfectly nice Friday, and ruin business by shoving your store’s adverts all over the street! You also took down Mayor Haddock’s posters! And without consent, no less. Do you really think we’re going to let you steal focus that easily? Think again, buster!”

Fletcher chuckled. Marvin was quite the practical joker, always putting on an act of fury. It was playful banter though. Despite Marvin’s jokes of them being rivals, there was no beating Marvin’s store, or the prices it had on antiques.
“Yeah, you know me,” Fletcher said, laughing along. “Always trying to destroy rival businesses.”
He winked. Marvin didn’t break character, his facial contortions still winding up.
“Finally, you admit it!” Marvin really was good at keeping his character.
“Admit what?”

“Oh ho, don’t you get me started,” Marvin said, wagging his finger, “Just last week, you painted your name on my shop wall. And let’s not forget the time that you put a mountain of oatmeal packets in front of my window. You — you’re just trying to mess with my head. Make me feel like I’m insane! Don’t you agree, Carol?”
Carol’s face turtled inward. She pulled her arm from Marvin’s grip. “I don’t really want any part of your little fit, Marvin. Fletcher seems like he just—.”
“Carol, that’s very rich. But, it’s time to stop messing around, and just admit the truth to this dolt!”
Carol scowled. Of course she was scowling — was there ever a time when she didn’t seem angry?
“Dolt? I don’t think there’s any need to throw insults. This isn’t a trial, Marvin. Fletcher’s attempts to build up his business are ingenious, if eccentric.”
There Carol went again, being facetious. Fletcher readjusted his collar and tried ignoring her.
“Let’s get out of here, Marvin,” Fletcher said, clearing his throat. “Carol might be starting to take your jokes seriously. Besides, I could use your help setting more of these posters up.”
Marvin spluttered. “Excuse me? Are you calling me a joke now? Carol, can you believe this guy?”
Marvin leaned inward and put his hands on Fletcher’s shoulders.
“Listen here,” Marvin said.

He was probably about to give some insightful advice; that’s what Marvin was always doing. Yet, the conversation was cut short by a tremor. The buildings trembled. Posters fluttered throughout the street. Fletcher jumped from his spot as a chunk of brick hurtled toward the ground.
“That was quite the thing to listen to,” Fletcher said, with a chuckle.
Marvin rubbed the back of his neck and kicked away some broken brick. “Damn earthquakes… I swear, they never stop coming.”
“Obviously,” Carol said. “It’s earthquake season here. If you hate it, wear a hard hat. Wait… Speaking of hard hats.”
Whistling wafted through the air. A man entered the street, flipping a hard hat as he went.
“We finally have a customer here!” Marvin said. “Welcome to Purview Street!”
Carol pulled a grass pot and shovel from her windowsill, then tore toward the man. Marvin pulled an antique knife from his pocket and followed.
Fletcher yanked a yo-yo from his pocket. Yo-yos were his worst sellers, so he always kept one on him to get rid of the inventory.
The unsuspecting man let out a yelp. He hadn’t taken kindly to the sight of three people rushing toward him. Especially three people who were armed with a shovel, a knife, and a yo-yo.
“Please, I want no trouble!” he said, turning to break into a sprint.
Marvin managed to run ahead of him and block his path. “Wait! Would you be interested in purchasing anything? Or, maybe looking in one of our stores? Want to see this unique, antique knife of mine?”
“I have the best pot of grass you’ll ever find!” Carol said, practically planting the man’s face in her pot. “It’s ten times better than what Melinda Clover will give you!”
Fletcher twiddled his thumbs. Perhaps they were coming on too strong.
The man adjusted his hard hat, pulling the brim over his eyes. “Salespeople? I don’t want any of that either!”
Perhaps “perhaps” was an understatement.
The man shoved off from the circle, and speed walked toward the street corner.
“Please, give us a second of your time,” Carol said.
“I’m not interested in buying anything. The chaos theorem said that I’m not. And even if I was interested, I still wouldn’t be, because the chaos theorem said.”
Marvin rubbed his eyes. “Sorry… You don’t want to buy because the chaos theorem told you not to, or is the chaos theorem controlling you to not buy? Either way, I don’t buy it.”
“Look, I just came down here to get to the post office. But seeing that you guys are insane, and there are all of these papers everywhere—!”
Marvin raised his hands in surrender. “All right, all right, we’ll lay off.”
Carol and Marvin walked away, but the man stayed put. He peeled off a poster taped to the ground.
“Wait,” he whispered, “what even is this?”
“It’s a wanted poster,” Fletcher said. “One of my toys was kidnapped.”
“Kidnapped, you say?” the man’s face went grave. “From your shop?”
Fletcher nodded.
“I think I might’ve seen a kidnapping like that, actually… Yes. Remember that day, when the pogo stick parade was going around?”
“That was just yesterday,” Fletcher said.
“Well… I thought it was on Thursday.”
Fletcher paused. “You’re right, now that I think about it. It was definitely Thursday.”
“Anyway, I came down here to get out of the crowds, and to get to the post office. I saw some guy walk out of your store. He was carrying a toy. I think it might’ve looked just like that.”
“You really think that? Exactly like this?”
“It definitely might’ve. Maybe.”
“Maybe is almost the same as exactly. Probably.” Fletcher rested his hand on his chin. “The timeline tracks. What did the man look like?”
“You don’t want to know.”
“I kind of do. That’s why I asked.”
A slight quiver went through the ground. Fletcher grasped a lamppost and brought his gaze to the sky. There was no telling when another quake might strike.
The man looked over his shoulder. “Hopefully we’re safe here. Nothing has been the same, lately; so much crime. He was a big man. Very buff. Dressed in all purple. That’s how I remember it, anyway.”
Fletcher’s eyes widened. It all was becoming clear.
Fletcher forced a wide smile. “Goodbye.”
“Hey! Since I helped you out, do I get the free staples?”
Fletcher slammed the door to his toy shop.
I’m not insane. Who called me that? Whoever did, they’re the insane ones. Just because we need money and customers on this street, suddenly we’re crazy for trying to get some?
That’s crazy talk. It really is.
It’s all Fletcher’s fault. Him, and his stupid antics. Even with Carol on my side, it’s just not enough to undo the damage that he’s causing to our business.

Well… Most of his damage is his fault. There’s also the damage caused by that chaos theorem. I can’t believe so many people have taken it. Ever since it came out, everybody has been acting so strange. Granted, everybody is always acting strange. The world is run by idiots, no matter how much idiots say otherwise.

In any case, I need to fix whatever is going on. This can’t continue. I have to figure out what Fletcher is planning and put a stop to it. He might think that his business is going to dethrone mine, but I know better.
Chapter 5:

Papers and binders fluttered off the desk and crashed to the floor. The room swayed back and forth, while Fletcher and the floorboards groaned from vertigo. He needed some sort of stimulation — a high, to reassure him he was doing what was right.
As he broke into a clammy sweat, Fletcher observed the cold hue his desk lamp gave off. It lit up the walls, exposing cracks and rot.
At least Fletcher’s life wasn’t the only thing doing rotten.
Time was of the essence. He was just on the verge to solving this case. He couldn’t let the oil baron escape him.

His fingers clacked along his keyboard as he scoured profiles of “notable townspeople”, from Dexburg’s website. There were perks to being known for designing websites, even if it was a tedious job. Fast as the biographies scrolled by, he remained vigilant for the profile of a certain townsperson.
His hands clapped together. “Jackpot!”
A flow of adrenaline rushed through him, expelling his vertigo. He’d stumbled across the picture of a balding man in a jumpsuit: Logan Gerri.

A few weeks back, Fletcher had sold all of Gerri’s action figures at a discount, to pay for a new water heater. Gerri must’ve stolen the toy oil baron as revenge. It fit perfectly. Logan Gerri matched the look that had been described, and he had all the motivation in the world. The question was, how was Fletcher to confront Gerri about it?

Logan Gerri had been a famous wrestler, better known as, “the Mop”. In his prime he’d been one of the biggest jobbers on TV. He’d starred in several cleaner commercials and had his own movie — even if the studio never wound up releasing it.
All of this and more was detailed in Logan Gerri’s biography. Though, the detail that caught Fletcher’s eye was an address at the bottom; the address to Logan Gerri’s house.
Fletcher glanced at his Wally Walrus watch and closed out the town website. Time had gotten away from him. He could figure out how to confront Gerri later.

Fletcher rubbed sweat off his palms and onto his pants. He could practically see Uncle Timothy’s disappointed face, glowering at him. Uncle Timothy wouldn’t have allowed him to rest, until the oil baron was found. Though, the day was half over and Fletcher hadn’t made any headway with his clients’ requests.
He opened a new file and pasted blocks of code for a bare bones website. Nothing bad could come of getting a head start on Linda’s request.

Hours whizzed by, and Fletcher’s eyes went bloodshot. A frenzy overtook him. The end of the day neared the end of night, and Fletcher’s hands kept hacking away at the keyboard. Yet, his website was still something barely out of the 90s. Worse, his eyes were begging for sleep; his mind wanted to dream about the 90s, not relive it.
The website was good enough for a demo though. Fletcher smiled to himself. It was a true feat to have made this much progress in such short time.

Opening his email, he saw Linda still hadn’t responded to his request for payment. Nevertheless, he pasted in the code for his website, typed in Linda’s email, and hit send. She’d have to be impressed.
For about a minute after the email had been sent, Fletcher stared at the computer.
He hit refresh, and there was a ding. Fletcher’s heart fluttered. Linda must’ve been waiting for him.
Fletcher blinked. Then, he saw the contents of the new email.

“Fletcher. We need to talk. You can’t keep living in your toy store forever. Me and John Thatcher are meeting tomorrow at the other end of town. We’ll be at Chef Bernardo’s Diner. Coffee!  10:00 AM, sharp. Be there. If you don’t show, we’re busting down the door to your store.”
It was signed “Harry Doswell”.
Fletcher’s chest sunk. No response from Linda.
As for coffee? Fletcher hated coffee. There was no way this was going to go well.
The cup singed Fletcher’s lips.
“Woah, slow down on that caffeine there,” said John. “Jumping from one drug to another, huh?”
Fletcher pushed it aside. John was right; coffee was laced with too much caffeine.
“Easily the hottest coffee around,” said Fletcher. “Nothing beats Chef Bernardo’s. Still not sure it’s worth the price though.”
He made a laugh. Nobody laughed with him.
The coffee jostled. Fletcher’s hands trembled. He rubbed the deep bags under his eyes. He should’ve gotten more sleep before coming.
“I just got a promotion at my new job,” Harry said. “I’m the official assistant accountant of accountant accounts. It’s a very good job. Solid salary. Okay office. It’s nice.”

Fletcher nodded but was overwhelmed by the feedback surrounding him. Dozens of people were about. Seats creaked. Cups clinked. Lips slurped, then smacked. The cashiers spun in place, pouring the same coffee into different cups and giving the same smiles to different people. Smells, sights, and sounds smothered the senses. Fletcher brought his eyes to the ceiling and counted the amount of fluorescent lights.
Weren’t people always saying how diners were quiet? People certainly kept quiet on how loud they could be.
“That’s good.” Jack beamed. “I’ve been considering switching jobs myself. Of course, the chaos theorem never said anything about me quitting my job. So, I’ll probably wait until it does.”
Harry laughed. “I’d definitely do that. At least, that’s what the chaos theorem predicts I’d do.”

Fletcher brought his coffee back to his mouth, taking small sips. He needed the drink to last him the entire chat. With all the talk about predicting the future, he could already tell this trip was going to be a doozy.
“I have a duck for a boss right now, technically,” said Jack. “I’d do anything to change jobs — if the theorem said I could, of course — so I totally get what you mean.”
Harry nodded. “I totally get what you mean, too. I mean, mallards are dullards.”
Fletcher’s head throbbed and a fog clouded over his perception. Its haze left his eyes as stones. His body went motionless.
“What’s with you?” Jack said, turning to Fletcher.
Fletcher gave a slow look at Harry, then Jack. In a monotone, he said, “With me? Nothing is with me.”
“What I mean is... Well, what’s going on?”
They just kept going on and on. Fletcher popped a sugar cube in his mouth, hoping it might somehow clear his head.
“We’ve had quite the time without you,” said Harry, putting his hand on Fletcher’s shoulder. “You been doing the same?”
Pulling himself from his daze, Fletcher shook his head. “I am… Uh, well… Business is less than it’s been, but still more than before. It’s more than before you guys last saw me, that is.”
“You still trying to sell those pants puppets?”
“I was, but they didn’t do too well. Nobody was keen on having their pant zippers be used as a puppet mouth, apparently.”
“Dang. I was so sure those would be top sellers.”

Another sip of the coffee went into Fletcher’s mouth, and down his throat. It was liquid fire, but drinking the fire was better than talking about how much higher sales could be. A bit of the coffee entered his windpipe, and he coughed.

“It’s fine,” Fletcher said, working through the cough. “I’m doing a lot of things online. My website business is really taking off. I’ve done a few other software projects as well. I mean, it could be worse. I’m doing better than the fortune telling business.”
He grasped for a laugh that never came. The haze became heavier, tugging on his eyelids. His cough gained strength.
“Happy for you,” said John. “You know, if you really wanted some money, the chaos theorem might be able to give you a few tips… Or, have you already taken it?”
Fletcher caught his breath. “I di—.”
“You didn’t,” said John. “I already knew that, from the chaos theorem. I only asked you because the chaos theorem said I should.”

Fletcher gave a sympathetic look. “Understandable. In any case, I have a plan to get some money. I’m going to ask the bank for a loan. There’s also this toy that I’m looking for… If I find it and sell it, I stand to make quite a lot.”
“Good luck,” said Harry. “The banks are cranks, right now. Jim Harrigan especially. Pretty sure that their head banker also recently shot himself.”
“That’s horrible.”
“Yes, I think those were the bankers last words. See, he’d been trying to see what a bullet would taste like. It was so terrible, he died. Poor son of a gun.”
“In any case, I’m close to finding the toy. I know who must’ve stolen it: Logan Gerri. Now I just need to —.”
John spit out his coffee. “The Mop?” He stooped over to lap his coffee back up.
Harry leaned in, with his arms crossed. “You think Logan Gerri went into Timothy’s Toy Shop and stole one of your toys?”

Fletcher shrugged. “Sounds pretty normal to me. Just last week, a tax collector came in and stole some of my toy money. Or, was it real money that he stole? Whatever. I suppose there isn’t much of a difference.”
“Even if he stole it, there’s no way you’re getting it back from him. Trust me, I know him. The guy is a superstar!”
“You know him? From where?”
“He — he’s been coming down to Kent Burgess’ coal factory.” Harry’s voice slowed, and his face filled with caution. “You know, the one right on the river?”
“Oh, nice. I thought you meant the one by the park on Mt. Bancroft.”
“Nope. The other one. Anyway, I went there to count their doorknobs — for accounting purposes. Logan apparently has a brand deal with them. He also loves to complain.”
“God, I hate it when people do that.”
Fletcher’s head flooded with relief. Perhaps he wouldn’t have to go to Logan Gerri’s house. He just needed to catch him at the factory. There was a clear direction now; a path to victory.
“Yes, well…” Harry continued. “I suggest you leave him alone. Don’t you have better things to do with your time? New friends, a girlfriend…”
The wings were snipped from Fletcher’s spine, and he plummeted back to Earth. “I haven’t been with anybody for quite some time. Besides, you guys know me — I only really have you two.”
“You haven’t been with anybody since Margaret?” John said, laughing. “It’s been a year. Get over it.”
“How — how is Margaret?”
“She never wants to see you again,” Harry said. “She’s very happy now. She also installed a new security system.”
He smiled, as though to rub it in.
“It’s great to hear that she’s proactive about protecting herself.” Fletcher stopped to take in a deep breath. “Of course, I think I might have somebody else.”
“Who?”
Fletcher’s thoughts trailed back to Linda. “Somebody. Or, nobody. I don’t know. Maybe nobody.”

Harry put his arm over Fletcher’s shoulder. “Look… If you want certainty in your life? Fletcher, there’s a clear answer staring you in the face. You just need to…” Harry paused to make a gesture. “You know.”
“I’m not going to see a shrink. I heard that Dr. Ford makes his clients build castles out of macaroni, as a personality test. I have a deep fear of macaroni.”
John rolled his eyes. “I don’t think Harry is talking about a shrink, man.”

“The chaos theorem,” said Harry, “it opens up the whole world for you. It really gives a sense of perspective. Ever since I took the chaos theorem, my whole life has begun anew. I’m not the same guy. I stopped wearing socks with sandals, I’ve been cleaning my glasses more often, and my allergies aren’t as bad. And, John over here? He just bought a new car.”
“I bought an old car, but it’s newer than my old car, so I guess you could call it a new car.”
“Better than a new car that looks old, that’s all I know.”
Harry took a swig of his coffee and looked Fletcher into the eye. “Look, can you just do me a favor? Go down to the post office and take the chaos theorem screening.”

Fletcher shook his head. “I do that, and it’s all over. I don’t want to know what I’m going to do tomorrow, fellas. My life is under my command — not anybody else’s. Out of the universe’s constant absurdity, that’s the only thing that has ever made life worth living.”
Fletcher’s shoulder stiffened as Harry’s hand clasped around it. Fletcher studied the bristles of stubble on Harry’s chin. The stale smell of coffee breath was strong.
“Bud, you’re going to need to take that chaos theorem,” he said. “Trust me, there’s stuff in it that you’re going to need to see.”

A shadow passed over Harry’s face, and his eyes darted about. John scratched an itch on the back of his neck. He didn’t stop. John kept scratching, with his gaze on the ceiling and his face aimed at Fletcher. John and Harry looked like a couple of apes.
Who gave a crap what some test had to say? Since when did a group of scientists know what it was like to have a life? It was all bunk.
“’ll think about things,” Fletcher said. “Nice catching up.”
Hoisting himself up, he gave Harry and John a handshake.

“Yeah, think about that chaos theorem thing,” said Harry. “Oh hey, there’s this new movie out. Gorillas vs. Monkeys. I think it’s about a bunch of people talking in a boardroom, real bored, for two hours… And then there’s ten minutes of gorillas and monkeys fighting. It sounds great. We should see it sometime.”
The door gave a click, before being drowned out by the whir of coffee machines.
“Sounds perfect,” said Fletcher. “I can’t wait to find the perfect time.”
“Stay out of trouble,” said John. “Don’t chase that Gerri lead — you don’t know where it’ll lead — and get on that chaos theorem!”
Glib. Glamorous. That’s how their friendship was.
It was also a fib.
Fletcher doesn’t seem to be doing any better. Even Jack agrees, and he’s not all there half the time.

Seeing Dr. Ford might not actually be a bad idea. He never has been the same since the shop had to downsize, and Carol bought out half the shop space. You’d think a guy would get over these things, over time.

Then again, he still seems bitter toward me for my success. How is it my fault that Margaret chose me over him? It’s fate. If he took the theorem, he would see that. None of us have any control. It’s all just random chance, guiding us in a logical way.
He’ll see though. He’ll have to see the light.
Chapter 6:

The streets ran with milk and honey. Namely, because a honey truck had crashed into a milk truck, in the middle of the street. Two truck drivers stood outside the trucks, decidedly not truck driving. Rather, they measured the distance between their trucks, the intersection, the size of the holes in their trucks, and the volumes that their voices could reach in a shouting match. Finally, they took turns measuring the lengths of their beards.
All the while, people crowded around the golden goo, lapping it up. A man dressed in a fine business suit entered with a belly flop. He rolled around, turning tarter than a candied apple.
Cautiously, Fletcher stepped out of the bus.
“Hey! Are you going to pay me?” the bus driver cried.
“I’ll pay you later,” Fletcher mumbled. However, his thoughts were squarely on his surroundings.
“Destiny,” a woman cried, grabbing large scoops. “The theorem… It said this was destined to happen today.”
“I’m rolling in gold,” a man said, the saccharine sludge dribbling down his chin. “Fate would have it that I have all of this. This experience… It is experience!”

Fletcher tugged at his shoe, but it wouldn’t budge. The sludge had swallowed it. Brilliant. His toy shop was only a block away, but the entire street was blocked off by this crash. Fletcher pulled his foot from out of his shoe and limped away.
He probed the crowd, staring into their faces. Avarice brimmed their pupils and their faces were swollen. They were a bloated mass of bugs. A blister.
“Join in!” they crooned. “And enjoy!”
“End joy,” Fletcher shouted. “Wake up.”

Fletcher checked his Wally Walrus watch. It was already a quarter to noon — fifteen minutes past the time he’d usually sit down to eat toasted dinosaur waffles. He needed those waffles. Yet, here were all these people, waffling around, clogging up his schedule. He needed the waffles, by god!
As he passed the scene of the crash, a rogue chef ran through the street with a rolling pin, and an apron tied to his back as a cape.
“I’ve found a new purpose!” he yelped. “Chef Bernardo, eat your heart out!”
He proceeded to chase a stray cat, which had innocently been chasing down a mouse. The man didn’t stop until his foot landed in a mouse trap.
“Just as I had planned,” he moaned, struggling against the trap.

Fletcher broke into a stilted jog, praying to avert the attention of those around him. However, the further he went, the further calamity went with him. A ceiling fan shot out of a window, nearly slicing Fletcher’s head off. A man came from an alley, riding a saddled dog. A flock of ducks raided a fruit stand, while the fruit stand’s owner ran into the road.
“The theorem says I’m finally about to get three months off!” the fruit stand owner announced, before being run over by the man with the saddled dog.
Strangely, the pandemonium faded to nothing when Fletcher turned the corner to Purview Street. The street was empty, save for an old man doddering in the center.
“Flies all are skies, in my disguised eyes,” the old man murmured, his eyes frenzied.
Keeping his head down, Fletcher fumbled with the lock to his toy shop. The door clanged shut behind him.

Wild; that’s what it was outside. Why had he even bothered going out? There was a hex over Dexburg. Though, there always had been a hex, hadn’t there? Decay ate away at the outer edges of every building, reducing them to must and dust. The town was in constant battle with the elements. Time and wind would win, in time.

The mouse cursor roved the screen as Fletcher’s computer booted up. Fletcher soaked in the screen’s soft glow, then navigated to his email. A fresh swath of complaints rolled by the screen — ten of them alone were from some angry fortune teller. Nonetheless, Fletcher’s eyes latched onto a lone email. “Thank you,” was its subject line.
Fingers trembling, Fletcher skipped to the end of the email.
“Love Linda,” Fletcher whispered.
He forced himself to track back to the start.

“Thank you for the website demo,” the email read. Gratitude; how gratifying. That almost never happened. “I just adore it. There’s nothing wrong. It just amazes me how someone could find the time to do it all and do it so well. Just one problem: I only feel safe sending checks through the mail right now, due to all the chaos. But I’ll need some extra money for shipping. I’ll make sure to pay you back. Write me back, so I know if you got this. Love, love, love it.”

Fletcher fell back in his chair and ran his hand through his greasy hair. When had he last showered? It didn’t matter. Nothing else mattered. His heart was beating a million times a minute. His head was abuzz. He couldn’t have just read what he thought he had. Yet, the words were there, staring him in the face.
He’d barely put any effort into the website demo. It’d been slapped it together, while he was half asleep. Despite this, Linda was the most satisfied customer he’d ever gotten.
He needed to rush out cruddy websites more often.
His eyes ran back over every line, analyzing and speculating on them. Was there more than met the eye? Some deeper subtext beneath the surface? There certainly were teases, but nothing concrete.
Linda had begged him to write back. Surely that didn’t mean nothing. Unless it did… If that were the case, everything would have to mean nothing.
Fletcher scoffed. Everything meaning nothing and nothing meaning everything — that would be something.

“Dear Linda,” he wrote. He pecked the keys individually, to avoid typos. Even so, he rewrote the first two words two too many times. “Thank you for the thank you message. I saw it. I appreciate having you as a customer. The check system should work. I will an address or routing number though, to send it to you.”

A salamander running across a touchscreen could’ve written something better. Fletcher watched one do as much at the zoo, just the other day. Rubbing his scalp, he hit delete. He attempted a rewrite, only revive his original message.
In methodical precision, he studied the structure of each sentence. Was it good enough? Could more be done?
He planted his face into the keyboard. There was a ding.
“Message sent,” the screen read.
His message had gone out, along with some gibberish written by his face.
Excellent. He had one shot at sending the message, and he’d blown it. There was no deleting it. Could he send in a revised message, maybe? Fletcher feverishly typed one out, only to stop.
Whatever. Who cared, anyway?
The screen let off another ding.
Linda had sent a reply. Fletcher was nearly sent into a coma. He took a moment to recollect himself.

“Ha, glad to hear it,” the message read. “I was confused about your website’s text box prompt. Is there any way that you could show me how to work it? Also, I don’t think giving my address will work. Maybe you could leave the check at a certain location, and I’ll pick it up? Where do you live? You seem close to me. You’re the best!”

She wanted to know where he lived. You seem close to me. Fletcher grinned. It was like a dream. “There are several ways to handle the text box. Though, I’d need to know a little more about you to figure out the best way for you to fill it.”
His fingers then clacked out his address. Fletcher’s face burned red as the message went out.
There was another ding; another message to read.
“Thanks for the address. I’ll write more about where to bring the check, later. Anyway you could give me an example for the text box, for your amazing website? Love ya.”
Creating an example should have been easy enough. The text box was but a matter of inserting text. It would be piece of cake.
Fletcher’s tongue rolled in his mouth as he searched for the right response. His mind was blank. What would he put in the sample bio? Something fake? Something real? Something in between?
Was he going insane? What kind of person flirted over email? Surely half of the emotional weight behind the conversation was all in his head.
His fingers managed a, “Sounds great. It might take me a little while to cook something up for you, though…”
The message went out. Fletcher’s eyes stayed on the screen, pleading for it to ding one more time. He needed one more shot of pleasure. However, the screen was indifferent to his plight.
Linda must’ve been put off. Or, maybe she was busy. She was busy.

Wally Walrus was frowning; half the day was gone. He checked the blank spot on his shelf; the oil baron was still gone. Why had Fletcher let himself get distracted from what was important? He still hadn’t even talked to Logan Gerri yet; there was much headway to be made.
Fletcher straightened his collar and went to his closet for his hat.
“Are you bumming LSD back there, or are you just that excited to be back on my crappy bus?”
Fletcher fidgeted in his seat as the bus ran over another pothole. Somebody needed to repave the roads. Out the window, a group of construction workers were using shovels to put dents in the asphalt.
“So that’s how potholes are made,” Fletcher murmured.
He clicked his pen and fumbled it in his hand. The bus stopped at an intersection, pushing Fletcher against his seat. His leg jittered.
“I’ll take it that you’re on LSD,” the bus driver snorted.

The bus driver hit the gas, not bothering to stop again for a “bear crossing” sign. It was a useless sign. There never had been any bears in Dexburg, so far as Fletcher could recall. Though, that was strange in its own way. What did bears have against being on the street?

Fletcher glanced out the window. Bears weren’t the only ones that didn’t want to be out. The streets were barren and building lots were abandoned. Somehow, the emptiness left him hopelessly claustrophobic. He didn’t want to bring his eyes back inside of the bus, though. The bus’s occupancy was no better.
“Are you just going to keep keeping your mouth shut, like a dumbass?” the bus driver asked.
At least the bus driver was a reassuring presence.
“I have a rule on this bus, you know. The passenger is supposed to talk to the driver, and the driver is supposed to ignore them. You’re breaking protocol, buddy.”

The bus driver pointed upward, to a sign embossed in the roof. Sure enough, it held those exact words. How Fletcher rode on this bus for years and never noticed, he couldn’t say. Then again, there were more distractions before the chaos theorem had struck; back when people still rode the bus.
“Where the hell are you going, anyway?” the driver asked. “I’m obligated to keep going down this route, but I’m going to be honest: I’m not all that keen on stopping.”
“We’re not stopping here. You can stop at Otto’s Grove.”
The driver whistled.
“You have a stop over there, and you’re riding on my bus, money bags?”
“About that… I forgot my bus token. I’ll have to pay you back later.”
“You better be joking, or I’m kicking you off.”
Fletcher’s leg wobbled again.
“I guess you’ll have to find out,” Fletcher said with a chuckle.

“I already know, bud. You don’t think I read the chaos theorem? It said a funny looking dude would get on my bus, ride to Otto’s Grove, and stiff me. I already know how this entire interaction is supposed to end.”

The bus’s motor shirked into a turn, slamming Fletcher into the window. Head aching, and stomach knotting, he gripped the back of the seat in front of him. His fingers ran along the leathery, as he strained for a renewed sense of normality.
“You knew I wasn’t going to pay you, and you still let me on?” Fletcher asked.
“I don’t know that you’re not going to pay me. You know that you’re not going to pay me, and I know that you know it. Or, so it says, in the theorem.”
“But, if you wanted to make money, you could just break the theorem’s prediction and kick me off. You just said you would kick me off, a moment ago.”
The bus swerved, and the bus driver grunted as he attempted to course correct.
“I know I said I’d kick you if you didn’t pay…” the bus driver said. “And, I know I said I know you won’t…”
He grunted again, then rolled down his window to spit.

“But, I don’t know that you won’t pay. Not really,” he continued. “All I know for sure is that I won’t kick you off my bus, even if I said I would, because the theorem says I can’t. Even if I did kick you? It couldn’t actually be me who did it, because the theorem says I didn’t. That is, unless the theorem said I still did it, to spite what it initially said. In that case, though? I only didn’t not do it because I couldn’t. It all has to do with that theorem, Fletcher. You can’t break the theorem. The theorem breaks you. It makes sense, if you really think about it.”

The bus slowed to a crawl as tattered structures fell away, and the surroundings became more vibrant. They’d entered Otto’s Grove. Fletcher counted the expansive houses that rolled past, to help distract from the throbbing in his head.
“I’m sorry,” Fletcher moaned, “but I’m lost. Did the equation tell you exactly what you were going to do today, or did it not?”
“It didn’t not,” the bus driver said, confidently.
“How much did it tell you? Can you tell me how this is all going to end?”
“How much of what? How all of what is going to end?”
“This drive. How much do you know about this drive?”

“Everything, and nothing. That’s what the theorem said. And more. Though, I can’t tell you more, because that’s only the theorem’s knowledge to give. I can’t talk about what the theorem says, unless the theorem says I do. Then, I do talk about it. It’s all very touchy.”
The bus screeched to a halt, in the middle of a roundabout.
“Well, that’s our stop,” the bus driver said, scratching at the scruff on his chin. The door swooshed open. “Time for you to get off my crappy bus, and not pay me.”
Fletcher was leaving when he rammed into the door. It’d suddenly shut.
Turning around, Fletcher gave the bus driver a look. The bus driver only stared back, with a flash of mischief through his eyes.
“What’s the big idea?” Fletcher said, with a huff. “Open the door.”
The bus driver’s face was unrelenting.
Fletcher leaned over the bus driver’s shoulder and pressed the door’s button.
“Sorry, but… Theorem.” The driver shrugged his shoulders.
Fletcher flipped a finger and walked out.
“Good luck with Logan Gerri!” the bus driver shouted.

The bus growled away. Fletcher was left in a daze, searching for Logan Gerri’s house. A rock formed in his stomach. He hadn’t ever mentioned to the bus driver that he’d been looking for Logan Gerri’s house.
Had he? Had he not? Had he not, not?
That guy smells terrible. He could really use a wash. He could also use some cash, while he’s at it. Hopefully he’s going to get himself an actual job.
Who am I kidding? There are no more jobs in this freaking town. It’s all going to crud. This old bus is about all this town has left, far as I’m concerned.
Can’t wait until Kent Burgess tries getting his grubby hands on my boss’s bus… That’ll be a day.
Chapter 7:

It was gorgeous. Built of a stained glass, the window had elaborate rainbow patterns crisscrossed at its edges. At its center was an image of Jesus, riding a motorcycle. Or, was it just a man that looked like Jesus?

Fletcher threw a rock through the cyclist’s head before he could decide. The glass buckling and shattering, Fletcher dove through. Flakes of glass clung to his hair and clothes. When he landed on the floor, more pieces bit into his skin.
“I hope he has insurance,” he muttered to himself.

He used a coffee table to pull himself back to his feet. Another shatter resounded, as he knocked a pot from the table. Guilt rising in his stomach, he tried sweeping the shards under the coffee table. Though, he knocked into a large vase as he did.
“Just a vase he said.”
However, a series of vases lined the hall. The one knocked vase turned to a series of knocked vases, and a domino of crashes resounded.  The regret in Fletcher’s gut morphed to a feeling of panic.

The room throttled back and forth. Fletcher tightened his grip to the coffee table, only to have it slide toward him. Another earthquake? If it were an earthquake, staying inside would be dumber than what he’d already done.
He looked back out the window but was greeted by a mass of dark clouds. A blast of thunder unfurled from them.

Wonderful; there was the choice between a death storm, and a death trap. Fletcher went with the death trap, running from the window and further down the hall. Fletcher took note of how well-adorned the walls were. They held pieces that looked as though they belonged in a museum.
Traveling further into the belly of the Mop’s mansion, he found smears of graffiti, confetti, and whipped cream. The floor was coated in a layer of trash; it was too much to be from the earthquake.
There’d either been a raging party, or a raging riot. Fletcher wasn’t sure he wanted to know which.

Gingerly, Fletcher turned a corner into a dining hall. Piles of food were strewn across a long table, and all over the floor. A television warbled in the corner. At the sight of it, Fletcher began scanning for the oil baron. Gerri was one of those people who were stupid enough to put their television in the same place they ate. Surely, he’d put the stolen toy in the same place. It was simply how logic worked.
“What the hell are you doing here?”
Fletcher took a step backward when a quake knocked him from his feet. The back of his head made a hard smack with the linoleum floor.
There was a laugh. “What a smack! Wow! I’d see Dr. Ford about that.”
Fletcher’s mind immediately went to horror stories he’d heard about Dr. Ford. One of the wealthiest neighborhoods in town, and Fletcher was still being recommended the town’s pond scum.
“No dancing around it,” Fletcher groaned, his head fuzzy. “We’re all in the same boat.”
“Wait… Are you one of those tap dancers hired to come here? Or, are you a break dancer? Wait, don’t tell me: you’re a hybrid!”
Woozily, Fletcher looked up. A man stood over him, his body rippling with tight muscles. Despite his muscles’ intensity, his face was loose and jovial.
It could’ve only been one person.
“Logan Gerri,” Fletcher moaned.
The earthquake had calmed to a murmur. Fletcher rolled on his stomach and attempted a push up. Weak though it was, Fletcher felt a surge of pride when he stood to face Logan.
Looking into Logan’s face, Fletcher realized that he met eye level. Logan was hardly an intimidating figure at all. Logan wouldn’t even meet Fletcher’s eyes, letting his gaze roam about.
“Logan Gerri,” Fletcher repeated, bringing authority into his voice, “I know that you’ve stolen my toy — the oil baron — and I demand to have it back.”
Logan’s eyes focused back to Fletcher, and he gave a bemused glare. He scratched his head, then his crotch.
“Sorry man, but I’m a bit lost,” he said, raising his finger. “Are you… You think that I’m Logan Gerri?”
Fletcher’s lips went to rubber. “You — you’re not?”
“Nah, man. I’m just some stripper that he hired for his party last night. Tell the truth, I’m not sure I’m still supposed to be in here.”

There was another smack of skull against linoleum. Only this time, it had been from an airborne linoleum tile, that flew right at the stripper’s head. The stripper launched from his spot, landing in a pile of pies.
“Who are you, guy?” another man shouted.
Fletcher looked over. “Please tell me that you’re Logan Gerri…”

Yet, as Fletcher said the words, he realized he regretted it. The man stood half a foot taller than him and bore arms that challenged the size of Fletcher’s torso. While the man packed a wide girth, the power in his gait more than compensated for it.
“Maybe I’m Logan Gerri, maybe I’m not,” the man said, gnashing his teeth beneath a thick beard. “Now if you don’t tell me who you are, you’re going to wish that I didn’t punch just like Logan Gerri.”
“I — I’m the maid!” Fletcher said, raising his hands and taking a step back, “I was just telling that guy over there to leave, actually. He, uh… He broke one of your windows. I saw him do it.”
Logan stood over Fletcher, dissecting him. Fletcher withered under Logan’s shadow.

“Thanks, but I can handle rowdy intruders myself,” Logan said, scooping a chicken leg from off the floor, and taking a bite. “Go clean up that glass mess and get out of my house. That, or you’ll end up like that guy over there.”
Drooling on the ground, the stripper gave a wheeze.
“Doesn’t he need medical attention?” Fletcher asked. “I think he might be dying.”
“Who cares? I can’t kill anyone… I’m a celebrity.”
“What?”
“Haven’t you heard? A celebrity being charged with a murder is illegal. I’m fine, guy. Now, get.”
Logan gave a handwave toward the hall, which Fletcher heeded. That is, until his ears pricked at the sound of the television.

“Nation in peril,” a news reporter monotoned, “The president is taking action to keep peace among the country’s citizens, as foreign nuclear threats loom on the horizon. Can we maintain our power, as our populous goes haywire?”
President Marigold came on the television. Her hair was in her face, and her pantsuit was rumpled. Nonetheless, she put on a look of pride.

“We are a smart nation,” she said. “Not dumb dumbs. China? Russia? France? North Dakota? They’re a bunch of little dumb dumbs. Geese. Chickens. I say, bring on the geese chickens! Who cares about the threats? Let’s stop their disease and show ‘em who’s boss!”
The words struck a chord with Fletcher. President Marigold had a point, didn’t she? Everything was going to shit. Who cared? What was the point in avoiding reality?
“Actually, Mop, there’s something I need to talk to you about,” Fletcher said.
Logan’s chicken fell to the ground at hearing the name, “Mop”. Puffing his chest, Fletcher strode toward Logan.
Logan’s brow arched, and he clenched his fists. The room rumbled with the distant echo of thunder.
“I know you stole my oil baron toy,” Fletcher said. “You couldn’t stand the thought that I had a piece of memorabilia that had become more valuable than your own… So you had to take it.”
Logan’s face twisted. He drew closer, letting his gravity overtake Fletcher’s. His muscles inflating and veins popping, a wheeze escaped his lips. Then, an outright laugh.
“Fine,” he said. “You got me. I have no idea where you’re taking this, but you have my attention.”
Fletcher remained firm. “Give up the toy.”
“Wait… You’re not joking?”
“There’s nothing funny about losing a toy… Thief.”
Logan found another chicken leg and took a bite. “That’s funny, Mr. Maid. Let me make something clear: I don’t give two craps about you, or any of my other help.”
“Here’s the thing… I was lying earlier. I’m not the help.”
“What? But you’re dressed just like them.”

Fletcher took a moment to study his weathered t-shirt and jeans. Maybe it was time to consider a wardrobe change. “I broke into your house and came here to threaten you. Because, I know you’re a thief.”
Logan gave Fletcher a light punch in the arm. “Greatest party trick ever. Guts. That’s what you have. Can’t say I wouldn’t have done the same, under the circumstances…”
“You’re telling me you have no idea where the oil baron toy is?”
“No? Why would I—?”

“You’re angry I stopped selling your stuff. You make 80% of your revenue through ‘the Mop’ toy sales, Logan — all of which are produced within this town. And, your demand behind the camera is on the decline. Your sales are on the decline. I wouldn’t be surprised if you’re relying more on the toy industry than myself.”

“I’m the richest man in town,” Logan’s voice gave a bit of a quiver. A chair wailed along the floor, as it was dragged under his legs. “My party last night was the craziest thing ever! I don’t give two shits about you, or your toys…”
“I know you’re in the middle of a criminal conspiracy,” Fletcher said. He tapped his chest. “I know it. Do you want to be remembered as the guy who always lied?”
Logan’s eyes went wild. Glassy, too.

“I am not! Who told you that?” he shouted, face going red. Then, a flip switched. His breaths steadied. “I’ll admit, last night was kind of weird… A few crackpots, maybe. They might’ve brought in some girls, and one of them might’ve stolen my wallet… I don’t know. Did you know there’s a rumor going around that we have a pickpocket in town? Anyway, it was just a normal party. I should invite you to the next one, actually.”
“You had crackpots in your house, huh? The police wouldn’t be too happy to hear that… Of course, they might not hear anything at all, if you just tell me where the oil baron is.”
Logan’s eyes softened, considering Fletcher’s ultimatum.
“Look guy, I have no clue,” he said. “Now, please… You’ve made some good points about certain things. But, how are you sure you didn’t just lose the toy? Just leave me alone.”

Despite Logan’s words, his body betrayed immense insecurity. His hand clutched the center of his chest. His eyes shifted side to side, digging for a way out. Some excuse. Some explanation, to get Fletcher away. Why had he seemed so imposing? He was practically a sheep.
“I didn’t just lose it!” Fletcher roared. “Now, I know you Logan. I know you’re falling from grace. So, give me the info. That’s all I need.”
Logan took Fletcher’s arm in an iron grip. Bone groaned beneath Fletcher’s skin. Fletcher tried yanking his arm away, but Logan merely reeled him in.
“You think I care about my image?” Logan said. “Look at me. Look at this room. Do I have any images of myself hanging on the walls? No.”
Logan wiped his nose on his sleeve. His sights went to the food on the floor. Logan had been right: there was nothing of him in the room.  A gluttony of food defined it.

“I’m trying to be a bit more honest,” Logan said, bringing his voice down. “The chaos equation showed me I’m going to die from a heart attack, and soon. I figure, maybe if I’m a bit calmer… Maybe if I do a bit more good… People will remember the Mop as the hardened badass he always wanted to be.”
The sentiment cut to the core. Earnestness coated Logan’s speech. He was vulnerable. Alone. Perhaps everybody was.

“I don’t know, sounds like you’re fucked to me,” Fletcher said. “But, when you put it that way, you start to make sense. Granted, I preferred when you didn’t make sense, because you making sense doesn’t help me.”

Logan leaned back and looked at the ceiling. Light rested on Logan’s face, sprinkling a dash of youth back onto it. Fletcher remembered the old way Logan appeared; the young way. He’d show up on stage and hold all the power. Suddenly, Fletcher realized that there was nothing he wouldn’t give to have that back. To have the feeling he had when he was a kid, and great men were still great.

“Alright, alright, I think I came up with something…” Logan said. “There’s this toy manufacturer in town, alright? Kent Burgess? Really rich guy? I’m you’ve heard of him, at some point… We’ve worked together on a ton of my products.”
“What does he look like?” Fletcher said, injecting a hint of skepticism into his voice.

“Like any rich douche. Expensive suits, overdone haircuts, nice watch... Overcompensates. He’s been trying to impress this girl he met. He was here at my party with her. Looked untrustworthy to me. But, that’s beside the point: I could see him being interested in stealing the toy of yours. He was telling me how he wanted a toy of himself… Didn’t you say your toy was an industrialist, or something?”
Fletcher rolled his eyes. As if Logan had actually forgotten. “Oil baron.”
“Perfect.” Logan rubbed the back of his neck and gave Fletcher with a lost gaze. “I guess you can leave my house now, right?”
There was a delay as Fletcher processed. “Oh, yeah, sure. Definitely!”
Fletcher said this, but only moved a few inches toward the hall. There was something wrong with Logan. A weight around him.
“Okay, I can’t leave you like this,” Fletcher said. “What’s going on with you? You look half dead.”
Logan’s lungs eked air faster than a popped tire.

“I have two intruders in my house, for one. And, I guess it doesn’t hurt that I’m still feeling the sting of mortality… You just never expect these things, you know? No matter what I do, it’s not going to matter. My die is set. My fate is sealed.”
Giving a sympathetic look, Fletcher said, “Yeah… I guess that’s why I’ve been avoiding the chaos theorem. I don’t want to know how this all goes down. I want control.”

Logan’s chicken leg thudded onto the table. It was chewed bone dry. “You don’t have control, whether you want it or not. Your path is as set as mine, and you’re licked as anybody. The only difference is, you don’t know what the rest of us know… And, you’ve chosen to not know. Of course, you can always change your choice.”
“How much do you know?”
“Enough to know that you wouldn’t need to interrogate anyone, if you just took the theorem.”
A dryness overpowered Fletcher’s throat, splitting his voice. “Well, thanks for all the info.”
Sweat formed on Fletcher’s face. His heart hammered along his ribs. He broke into a brisk stride, toward the busted window. Rain and thunder plundered the air, but he didn’t care. He needed out.
“Promise me that you won’t say anything about crackheads being at my house,” Logan called after him. “And, have good luck on your search!”
Fletcher forced a laugh. “I won’t!”
Such a weird little guy. Shrimp. Annoying voice. What was I thinking, letting him in like that? I should’ve just thrown a tile at his head. It worked on the other guy.

I guess it doesn’t matter though, because he’s going to the factory, and then he’ll be shown who’s boss. Still, I can’t afford to have him catch on to what’s going on. Plus, if he runs into that pickpocket who’s been going around first… That’s just going to wind up being embarrassing. Will probably undo everything.
Then again, what if he is the pickpocket? What if his toy was never stolen, and that’s just a front? Maybe I’ve just been being oblivious, this entire time? That’s always a possibility.
Everything is always a possibility.
I’ll need to call the gang. Tell them somebody will be sniffing around. If they can off this guy at the factory, everything will be fine.
Well, except for me… That theorem is a downer. I need to make sure I’m not screwed, like this guy thinks.
Who am I kidding? What does this guy know? He broke into my house. Hell, I could press charges.
That’s it! I can call the drug dealers and call the cops. With both groups after him, there’s no way that he gets out of this.
Thank god he’ll be dead soon.
Chapter 8:
“Hats off to Haddock! Vote to reelect!”
A swift kick punched a hole in the glib sign, knocking it over.

Fletcher was sick of Mayor Haddock’s eyes staring him down. Mayor Haddock was everywhere, moving in full force to get back in office. He was also the only person campaigning to get back in office. He’d made sure of that.
If only there were people in public office who gave a damn about anything that was going on. Yet then, that would suggest there was anything in the world to give a damn about in the first place.

Dexburg River thrashed and burbled. The factory loomed overhead, coughing plumes of smoke in regular intervals. There was a reassuring air about it. Fletcher was reminded of when he’d first seen the factory. Uncle Timothy brought him there and shown him around. It seemed so grand, back then.

Fletcher rolled up his shirt sleeves and fanned himself with his arm. Jogging all the way from Logan’s house had seemed much smarter thirty minutes ago. In hindsight, it just left him with a sweaty behind.
Fletcher pounded at the steel doors. The doors were brash and heavy, with Fletcher’s poundings a meek echo against them.
A visor flap opened in the left door. Fletcher scrambled over.
“Is that the ice cream man again?” a woman asked, her voice firm.
“Yes,” said Fletcher.
“Then, go away. We never ordered any. Sorry, but it must’ve been a prank caller.”
The visor started sliding shut. Pain shot through Fletcher’s hand as he shoved it between the crack.
“Wait,” he said, repressing a whimper. “I’m not the ice cream man. I swear.”
The visor pushed harder.
“Are you the sandwich man again?” the woman asked. “Because, we don’t want sandwiches either!”
“No… No sandwiches. The only sandwich here is the one you’re making between my fingers.” He paused, to gasp, “And the door.”
The visor slid open, and blood rushed back to Fletcher’s hand. He smiled in relief, until his nerves went off with fresh alarms.
“Then, what are you here for?” the woman said, her eyes bulging beneath horn-rimmed glasses.

“Something of mine was stolen,” Fletcher said. He measured his words with caution, making sure that he didn’t put the woman off. “A very valuable item to me. And, I intend to get it back. I’ve gone to a few places about it and was told to go here. I need to see Kent Burgess.”

Fletcher’s gut brewed with regret at having not said more. Yet, his batting average on getting attention for the toy oil baron was at an all-time low. Keeping things vague was the only way of being taken seriously.
The woman’s eyes darted, and her voice came out in frantic fire. “Nothing out of the ordinary going on in here. No. Nothing out of the ordinary at all. Just business as usual.”
Her gaze lingered to the left of Fletcher. Fletcher followed it and noticed the empty parking lot, bordered by the filthy river. Only a few cars dotted it.
“For a busy day, it sure is empty here,” Fletcher said.
“All of our workers… They have the day off. Most of them, anyway. Nonetheless, we still are very busy.”
“So am I. I’m not stopping until you show me around the factory and let me talk to Kent Burgess. If I just have a conversation, I’m sure we could work something out.”
The woman let out a huff. Her eyes went firm and flickered.
“You’re willing to look around the entire factory for this thing?” she asked.
“That’s what I want, yes.”
“Great. Come on in. Now.”
A minute passed as a series of locks were unlatched, and knobs turned.
A clang resounded behind Fletcher. Fletcher bobbed his head about but saw nothing.
“Did you hear something?” Fletcher asked. The woman didn’t respond. “Hey, is anybody out there?”

The door creaked open, and the woman stood there. She seemed about middle-aged, but it might’ve been her demeanor.
