She kept her arms rigid at her sides, she wore a well-pressed pantsuit, and her hair was done up in bobby-pins. Her glasses were pressed so close to her face that they must’ve been screwed in.
Fletcher followed her as she trotted back into the factory. Though, he gave a furtive look behind, to make sure he didn’t have a follower of his own.

“Sorry if it’s a bit empty in here. I’m going to be forthright, for once: all our workers ditched. The president made some grand announcement about how America shouldn’t have to work for terrible wages, and they just followed along. Unemployment doesn’t pay great wages either… But nobody seems to care.”

Crass machinations rested along the walls, grinding and murmuring. They were coated in rust, with some parts at the point of being nubs. Some machines were practically held together by glue and shoestring. One machine was hooked up to a series of hairdryers.
Fletcher was shocked. He had no memory of Uncle Timothy showing him any of this. Yet, Uncle Timothy had a knack for only showing shiny exteriors.

“Some of them said they were willing to settle for payment in trading cards,” the woman went on. “Admittedly, that actually would be cheaper than what we were paying. But, can you imagine how juvenile that would make our corporation appear? We can’t be paying people in trading cards! The board simply wouldn’t have it.”
Fletcher nodded. “I don’t seem to see my… Possession anywhere, nor any sign of it. And where’s Burgess?”
“And here is the main processing center,” the woman said, making a turn into another row of machines, and ignoring Fletcher. “My name is Debby, by the way. Debby Crowner.”
She thrust her hand out for a handshake but kept her back to Fletcher. Fletcher stumbled after the hand, before giving up.

“I imagine that you could work in the chemicals section,” she went on. “It’s an excellent place to work. Most people get a retirement package after only five years. We have them working with some chemicals that are slightly toxic… But, they’re neither here nor there.”
“Wait, I — I’m not looking for a job. I thought you were leading me to—.”

“Kent Burgess?” she said, adjusting her glasses. “Yes, of course. We’re getting there. Of course, I’m just showing you the ropes of this place, in case you are to get interested in working here. It truly is a great job opportunity. What do you work in now? I smell a sanitation man.”
“I have a shop and do some software on the side.”
“Software? Sounds hard. This job is pretty easy. Just saying.”
She spun in a circle to flip on a few machines, before resuming her pace. “We’re the greatest button manufacturer in the world for a reason,” she said. “We run a tight ship.”

“What are you still even doing here?” Fletcher asked, agitation mixing into his voice. “This whole place should be shut down. And, the president has a solid point… Work is boring. Not working is at least a different kind of boring.”

“Burgess is paying me in gold bars,” she said, with a laugh. “Well, only half gold… Kind of. Not really, but still actually, all the same, with a certain point of view, from Mt. Everest, when it’s cloudy...”

She went on mumbling under her breath, before opening a couple of flap doors in front of her. Fletcher went after her, natural light from the factory dissipating, and he felt as though he were crawling into a dungeon. Yet, he had come this far. Abandoning his search was not an option, no matter how tempting.
“How do you go about making bars that are half gold?” Fletcher asked.
“Quite simple, really. The outside of the bars is a golden foil. The inside is chocolate. And, inside that, is a sort of golden caramel filling.”
“So… He’s paying you in candy bars.”
“Gold… Don’t get things twisted.”
“I think that’s already been done for me.”
“Speaking of jobs, what do you think makes you a good worker?”
She’d pulled out a notepad and pen and was already scribbling information down. Before Fletcher realized, she’d pulled up a couple of chairs and made a makeshift table out of an oversized tire.
“Jobs?” Fletcher asked. “Come on… Debbie, was it?”
She nodded.
“I don’t want a job here,” Fletcher said. “I just want to—.”
“See the man in charge. I know. He’ll be here soon, I’m sure. But, I figure that we might as well make friendly conversation while we’re waiting.”
Her pen scurried furiously across the paper.
“So, how would you contribute to this department?”
“I’d clean up this mess, for one thing,” Fletcher muttered.
A machine came to a grinding halt as something crashed into it. The grinding then turned to a stinging buzz.
“Dear god, what is that?” Fletcher moaned pressing his hands to his ears.
He couldn’t see the cause of the crash, but Debby’s face construed in consternation. She was as out of answers as he was.
She pulled a remote from her pocket, and the machine came to a halt.
“Just technical difficulties,” she said, her voice in singsong. Nevertheless, the buzzing sting wasn’t gone.
“I would fix those difficulties too,” Fletcher said. “Revamp this place, while I’m at it. It’s unbelievably depressing in here.”
He pointed up to the ceiling, where flimsy lamps trembled.
“Look at those things. There are no windows here, but there are those things? They could fall on somebody’s head during the daily Dexburg earthquake.”
Debby pursed her lips.

“Oh, I’m sure it will be fine. Earthquakes… We’re not due to have an earthquake in a little while, I don’t think. Don’t think about it. That’s what we give our workers ballcaps for. If the lightbulbs fall on their heads, they’ll only suffer from light trauma.”
“Light trauma, or light trauma?”
“Our workers’ contracts are only supposed to lay out the parameters, not define them. That’s a question for our lawyers.”

She clapped her hands together, making Fletcher jump. Only barely, of course. There was nothing for Fletcher to be terrified of. A serpent’s cunning wriggled from beneath Debby, but to a certain point. Surely most of it was in his head.
“Moving on,” she said, “What do you plan on doing in the coming weeks, to stave off the existential crisis created by the chaos theorem.”
“I’m not taking it.”
“Cop out if I’ve ever heard one. Most people just get a massage, or skinny dip in the local pool…”
“You yourself linked it with the existential. The thing about the hard parts of existence: it’s easier to pretend they’re not part of existence at all.”

“Only for you. The chaos theorem tells me that everything has a divine meaning. Life is systematized and organized in its insanity. Don’t you get it? I knew that this interview was going to transpire and every word that would be uttered, before it ever was. It’s so wonderful. It’s liberating, to know it all.”
“Isn’t the whole purpose of this interview to learn things about me? Figure out if I’m the right fit?”
“We’re way past that point. The point of this interview is to avoid the point.”
“When you put it that way, it does start to sound not so bad…”
“Alright, excellent. I think that clears things up. Now, all I’ll need is your social security number and your credit card number, and you should be good to stop this conversation.”
“Don’t you need my name?”
“Don’t worry honey, we’ll cross that burning bridge if and whe… never we get to it. Now, info, please.”
Fletcher went to draw his wallet from his pocket.
“Mrs. Crowner, there you are!” a voice erupted. “We’ve been looking for you, all over a place, and under another. Maybe.”
“Definitely maybe,” said another voice. It was one that seemed strikingly familiar.
“I’ve been looking for you, too,” said Debby.
“Wonderful! I was not expecting to see you here!” went the first voice
“Technically, you can’t see me hear, Mr. Burgess.” Debby chuckled.
“Too true, too true. As they say, see no evil, hear no evil…”
“… Especially when nearly evil.”
The man revealed himself, stepping from behind a boiler.
“You’re too funny, Mrs. Crowner.”

He readjusted the cuffs to his dark suit and slicked his hair back. The corners of his lips and eyes were slightly wrinkled, harboring signs of his advanced years. Yet, past his spray tan and strong scent of cologne, it was possible to see him as a man in his 30s.
“Speaking of funny, look at this fellow,” Burgess said. “Who’s he?”
Fletcher stood up and offered his hand to Burgess. “I’m Stuart Fletcher,” he said. “But you can just call me Fletcher. I’m here to talk to you about —.”
John stepped from behind the boiler.
“Hey, Fletcher!” John cried.
Finally, Kent Burgess and Johnny Adams-Apple is here. Such a wonderful boss, that Mr. Burgess. It’s amazing that somebody could be so amazing — wealthy, rich, worth a fortune, and good-looking.
I wouldn’t work anywhere else if I was paid to. Come to think of it, I’ve been offered a few other jobs… And they do pay better. But this job is better. No doubt. My contract mandates it.

This weird fellow seems to have potential. I hope that he sees what Kent Burgess is offering him, and accepts. Nobody has full control in this town — everything in here is purely random, and unpredictable. Burgess has constantly reminded me of that. Nonetheless, if anybody has close to it? Its him.
From the small businesses to the big, everybody goes through Burgess. This coal plant powers the city, and it produces a lot too.
I really hope that he manages to get his foot in Mayor Haddock’s coming administration, before the chaos theorem beats us all. That’ll be a game-changer.
Chapter 9:
Fletcher’s hand dropped back to his side.
“Hey,” he said, mouth gawping at John. “What are you doing here?”
“I was just checking the place out. Same as you, I’m sure.”
“He’s begging for a job,” Burgess said, bluntly.
Fletcher shot John a look. “A job? But John has a…”

“Forget what I told you,” John said, cutting him off. “After buying my car, I was fired. They thought that my car was too expensive. It made their entire place look cheap, in comparison. It was a fair enough reason to fire me, I guess…”
“I guess,” said Fletcher. “Everything in this world is so depraved, isn’t it?”
“Sometimes I wish that I could just tear it all apart, bit by bit,” John said, with a grin. “Leave it all mottled and mortified.

Fletcher gave a grim look back. The world was a cesspool, in dire need of insurrection. John’s outlook only worked as further proof. People toiled day in and day out, and the fruits of their labor forming as pains and boils on their body. Work weathered people to fine granite, sapping minerals from muscle and strength from cerebrum.
“It’s terrible, because I didn’t think it was coming…” John continued. He went waxen. “They called me in, then called me out, and that was about it.”
“You didn’t know it was coming?” Fletcher repeated.

“I didn’t think it was coming. Don’t misunderstand, I knew it was coming. The chaos theorem told me as much. Though, I didn’t want to believe it. Then again, maybe I did. Is life better with a job, or without? We are all slaves to our own careers, aren’t we? We live for them. They burn us in return.”

“Harsh way of putting it my boy.” Burgess gave John a hearty slap on the back. He turned to Debby. “I was just telling him how he’s going to have a place in our new nuclear reactor. The theorem says everything is going to go nuclear, real soon here: John’s job will be the hottest thing.”
“That’s hilarious,” Debby said, stepping toward Burgess and leaning in. “I just scored a job of my own: Filcher over here is going to be our new chemicals tester.”
“I didn’t sign up to that!” Fletcher said, raising his hand.
“And President Marigold didn’t sign up for the presidency…” Burgess said, with a laugh.

“Actually, she didn’t,” said Debby. “Don’t you recall? Her name was picked out of a hat, after the original president, the vice president, the speaker, and the whole of Congress were impeached for pinching parakeets.”
“Odd… Must’ve missed that.”
“It all happened during the season finale of Creeks. Bad reality show. Easy to miss an episode.”

“I wish they’d picked the name of anybody else out of that hat,” John said. “She’s going to kill us all, with her plans to make frenemies with every nation on Earth. Her weapons of mass destruction are aimed at the poles right now. We’re all going to die.”
Burgess raised himself to full height, then jutted his jaw.
“Don’t question the president. Her name was picked out of that hat for a reason. Disrespecting her is a crime.”
Fletcher found himself nodding along. Although Burgess hadn’t known how the president had been chosen until a few moments ago, he had a point.
“Well, her name wasn’t actually picked out of that hat…” Debby said. “It was the name of some plumber, but the guy who chosen to read the names was dyslexic.”
Fletcher’s head kept bobbling. Everybody had points for every side when it came to politics. Except him — he was always on the fence. It was the perfect defense.

“Still, a good deal better than paying to have Haddock get reelected,” Burgess said, with a scoff. “I tried buying some priest for this election instead, but he was too expensive. Haddock was cheapest. But golly — picking people out of hats is much more efficient.”
Debby smiled. “No matter who’s running, they’re all going to get us killed.”
They all burst out laughing, but Fletcher had no clue as to what they were laughing at.
“Except for me,” said Burgess. “I own the bridge out of this town. Control the toll, you’re on a roll, as they say.”
Debby forced another chuckle. “And me too, right?”
Burgess blinked. “Of course, of course. I take care of all my people. Yes.”
Fletcher looked between them, struggling to figure them out. Dexburg may have been a hellhole, but to leave? Practically heresy.
“So, am I going to get my job?” John asked.
“You can only steal your job,” said Burgess. “That’s how the successful politicians do it, after all. Don’t you agree, Fletcher?”
“Actually,” Fletcher said, clearing his throat. “I prefer to stay out when politics are discussed.”
“Politics are always disgust! That’s the fun of it!”
Burgess slapped his knee, and the factory’s machines jittered with his delight. Fletcher maintained a stolid posture.
“A valuable possession was recently stolen from me. That’s why I’m here. I intend to get it back.”
“Something valuable is always being stolen from us, or by us,” Burgess said, forcing a yawn. “You need to be a great deal more specific.”
“It was very valuable.”
Burgess licked his hand, then slicked his hair back. “Very, you say? That changes things very much…”
“In my defense, I didn’t realize it was quite that valuable all this time,” Debby said. “He never said a word about that.”
Burgess strode toward Fletcher, drawing his face in. Fletcher counted Burgess’ pores and observed the way his feathers for hair bobbed in the air.
“Can you tell me more about this valuable?” Burgess asked.
“It was a prized possession, with high value. I asked Logan Gerri about it, and he said that you guys might be keeping the stolen item here. Trying to observe it, for manufacturing and whatnot.”

“That does sound like me,” Burgess said, with a nod. “And you said it was stolen? Yes. Thievery is the game in this town. Why, my own lover… I do believe that she stole quite a few of my valuables just recently. I’ve been trying to get ahold of her, but she won’t answer. And apparently, there’s a big time pickpocket going around as well!”
Debby Crowner kicked at a sputtering machine and muttered something under her breath.
“So, can you tell me where it might be?” Fletcher asked.

“Well, seeing as you’ve told me nothing about it…” said Burgess, circling Fletcher. “I definitely know where it is. It’s funny how that works, actually… Have you ever noticed how it’s always so much easier to know things about things, when it’s about something that you know nothing about?”
John butted in. “That’s how I got my medical degree. Which is how I got my job as an accountant.”
Fletcher’s head buzzed with curiosity. “So where is it?”

Burgess gave a smug smirk and puffed his chest. “I own everything in this town. Should be in my pocket.” He checked his pockets, then came up emptyhanded. “Nothing in there. Of course, it could also be in my office. Or it could be with my girlfriend, since she stole everything. Or perhaps it’s nowhere in particular at all?”
“It was a toy,” Fletcher finally burst out, “a toy oil baron. You haven’t seen one anywhere?”
Burgess and Debby’s cheeks inflated, wheezes squeaking through.
“A toy?” Burgess said, his teeth flashing mockingly.
Fletcher nodded, sternly. “I’m with Timothy’s Toys. This is a class A priority for us.”
Burgess’ ears perked. “Yes, yes,” Burgess said, catching his breath from suppressed laughter. “You worked for Timothy, eh? Good businessman. Smart. Dead, too.”
He scanned Fletcher, eyes picking him apart limb by limb. There was almost a flicker of disappointment.
“I guess it — it might be at a storage facility,” Burgess continued. “That’s where I’d look. It might also be anywhere else that I said. I’m not sure.”
“That’s not fair! You need to tell me! You know! Didn’t you take the theorem?”
Burgess shrugged. “I actually don’t know. The chaos theorem never told me where your toy was. It only told me that it wouldn’t tell me.”
“But that doesn’t make any sense…”

Burgess gave Fletcher a pat on the back and walked him toward the exit. “Sure it does. You tell me something, I tell you something, and the chaos equation tells me nothing — well, except for everything. It’s just… Having everything isn’t everything, you know? You never know.”
Fletcher’s mind bent inward and backward, wringing through the twisty logic. Was there even logic to him?
The factory’s entrance swung open, and Fletcher was shunted out by Burgess’ knee.
“Great meeting you, chum,” Burgess said. “But, I’d prefer not to get too chummy with somebody who won’t make me money. Good luck with your toy.”

“So unfortunate,” Debby said, walking to Burgess’ side and stroking his shoulder. “I was certain that this one would become a new employee. Of course, the theorem said otherwise, and it never falters…”
The doors groaned inward, and Fletcher flailed between them. Burgess attempted to shunt Fletcher back out, but Fletcher persisted.
“Come on,” Fletcher said. He reached for John.
“Sorry,” John said, with a shrug, “but, they promised me a free fire extinguisher. Do you know how much that’s going to be worth?”
Was there something predicted by the chaos theorem that John knew? Or, was John merely being insane? Fletcher didn’t get his answer. Somebody knocked him toward the ground.
I can’t wait until Haddock’s dumb butt is finally reelected. There are so many changes I need to make to my empire, and so little time. The clock is getting shorter every minute.

Perhaps I should look into this toy the Filcher fellow was talking about and see if I don’t already have it. Maybe it really is valuable. If so, cashing in on it might be smart. If not, I better get it.
Dexburg is my town. I own it. I have the control — not any politician, or crime gang, or radical rebels.
If only that Filcher fellow could’ve seen how much I have. He would’ve been shocked, I’m sure. But there’s so much to do still, to make sure my legacy is in place in time.
Mayor Haddock has that dumb party, and then there’s Miss Clover… Maybe I can have Debby run some errands. She owes me one, after being zero help with that girl who stole all my stolen stuff.
Then again, everybody in this town owes me one. It’s my town.
Chapter 10:

Upon hitting the pavement, darkness hovered over Fletcher’s vision. Light warped and blurred. The rushing of the river, the rustle of trees, and the chirping of birds all slurred together. In the back of Fletcher’s head, there was a pounding. A hammering. It became closer and louder.
Burgess’ voice came in a warble. “What’s the big idea? Freaking morons…”
The factory door clanged shut.
Somebody stepped on Fletcher’s back, then his wrist, before running off.
Feebly, Fletcher stood and regathered his senses. The sky cleared, and a breeze brushed along his skin. Sunshine danced along the bus stop, at the bottom of the factory’s steps.

Burgess had been a bust of a trip. However, a storage facility was a better lead than no lead at all. At least, going there was what he was leaning toward. What if it was a waste? Perhaps no lead wouldn’t be so bad, either.
He went down the steps. Either way, things were looking up and down. That was nothing to feel down about.

Fletcher was knocked back to the ground and went rolling. Despite the steps being marble, they were rough against his skin. His throat choked, his arm was poked, and one of his ribs nearly broke. His elbow received a blow to the funny bone, which was decidedly unfunny.
He reached the bottom, a dull ache permeating his ligaments. Though, amid the calamity came a sense of calm. That, or he was in shock.
Maybe calm and shock were one in the same.
“Terribly sorry about all that! That’s not what I meant to happen at all! Are you okay?”
Somebody hoisted Fletcher up from the armpits, before spinning him around to look him in the face. A dull film coated Fletcher’s sight, leaving things just a swath of color.
Fletcher gave a moan as reply.
“Great,” the person said. “With that out of the way… I finally caught you! You’re exposed!”
Their voice was proud and defiant. There was no mistaking it.
“Marvin?” Fletcher muttered.
“That’s Mr. Whisk to you,” he said. He gave Fletcher a kick to the shin. “I see what you’ve been doing. Don’t pretend that I don’t.”
Fletcher’s vision cleared up, revealing a raw fear in Marvin. He must’ve been worried from Fletcher’s fall.
“Ha,” Fletcher said, with a chuckle. “That’s rich. Anyway, thanks for saving me after I fell down those steps. I’m glad you were there.”
Marvin’s eyes flashed. “Oh, I’ve been there more than you know. I’ve been watching you, Fletcher. Following you, as you’ve gone around town. You’ve been to pretty seedy places recently, haven’t you?”
“Yeah, I guess.” Fletcher rubbed his wounds, then gave a wince. “I’m glad to hear that you’ve been looking out for me. Most of my other friends… They think I’ve gone crazy.”
“I know what you want, Fletcher.”
“You found the oil baron?”

“No!” Marvin said. He seemed almost angry, which didn’t quite make sense. Surely Marvin had come with friendly intentions, hadn’t he? “I found something worse, though — your deepest secrets. You’re planning on stealing Purview Street out from under us, aren’t you? Making deals with big businessmen, to make your business into some massive corporate entity? I wouldn’t be surprised if you’re trying to replicate the flower shop and my antique shop too, in some grand conspiracy!”
Just another prank, of course. The lengths that Marvin would go to make a yarn were hilarious.

“Oh Marvin,” Fletcher said, with a snort. “That’s just hilarious. Anyway, thanks again for coming out here. I’m going to be headed to Kent Burgess’ storage facility soon. If you want to come with me—.”
A gunshot went off.
“Everybody get down!” a man shouted.
“Yeah,” said a woman.
The man and woman stepped from behind a dumpster, and cocked guns toward Marvin and Fletcher.
“We were told that there’d be a real reedy guy here, who we need to take in,” the man said.

He and the woman were dressed in grungy jackets and jeans, which looked as though they’d been scrummaged from the dumpster they’d come out from. Their faces were far more pleasant — namely because they were covered by a pair of black ski-masks.
“Which one of you two is going to turn yourselves in as the guy we’re looking for?” the woman said.
Marvin and Fletcher shared a look. Their breathing went heavy and fell in sync. Fletcher’s chest swelled. He knew exactly what to do.
“We’re both the guy you’re looking for,” said Fletcher.

He raised his hands and walked toward them. Perhaps there should’ve been more terror in him — at least a twinge of anxiety. However, he was still high on adrenaline and slightly dazed from his fall. He tensed his muscles defiantly, expecting to be joined by Marvin at any moment.
Marvin scrambled away as fast as he could. “I’m sorry,” he whimpered. “Not me. Don’t kill me. It’s him, I swear! Please don’t kill me!”
Fletcher listened as Marvin’s steps became quieter. Marvin had disappeared within a matter of seconds.
“Have to admit, the other guy seemed a lot reedier than you are,” the man said, shoving the barrel of his gun against Fletcher’s stomach.
Fletcher’s upper lip curled. “He’s one of the bravest people I know.”
The woman snorted. “The people you know must be some of the weakest goddamn people on Earth.”
The man pinned Fletcher’s arms behind his back and kicked his foot into Fletcher’s heels.
“Giddup,” the man said. “You might not be the guy, but you’re going to have to do. Don’t make us regret it.”
The woman tittered, walking ahead. A car chirped off the side of the rode.
“You can hold him down, and I’ll drive,” she said.
“What?!” The man kicked Fletcher in the heels again. His voice hushed. “Sorry — didn’t mean to kick you that time.”
The woman was already hopping into the driver’s side. “Yep. 360 horsepower, all to myself!”
“But I want to drive. The boss named me getaway driver. You’re just muscle.”
“I thought we agreed that the boss is half brain-dead…”
“What’s the point in being given the boss’s car, if I can’t even fucking drive it?”
“Fine… You can sit on him while you’re driving, and I’ll… I’ll keep lookout. Better?”
Fletcher’s mouth went dry. “Wait, where are we going? And who is he going to sit on?”

The man gave Fletcher a punch to the gut, and omitted any apology. “You better be looking behind us this time, instead of in the goddamn mirror,” the man said to the woman. “And for the love of god, shoot anybody tailing us if you have to. If not, I’m going to have to blow your brains out.”
“Not until I blow your brains out first…”
“Honey, not in front of the hostage.”
Fletcher’s face was pressed into the side door of their car. It was anticlimactic for a mob boss’ car; a shaggy Chevrolet, which had clearly seen better days.
“Alright, so are you going to blindfold him, or am I going to have to do it?” the man asked.

The woman rolled her eyes and put a hand on her chin. “Let’s see… Who was the one who figured out where this shmuck was going to be, again? I think I’ve already done more than my fair portion of the job.”
Following a disgruntled grunt, a thick rag was pulled out of the man’s pocket.
“Please, you haven’t done shit…” he said.
“Well, shit — shit is more than what you’ve done.”
“Please, tell me what the big idea is,” said Fletcher, attempting to assert confidence into his voice.

The man added pressure on Fletcher’s body and shoved the rag in Fletcher’s face. Fletcher’s arms flailed at the air, desperately trying to stave off suffocation. Nevertheless, the man came closer. The rough hairs of his stubble grinded against Fletcher’s skin, and his breath reeked of liquor.
“This is a hostage takeover, dumbass” the woman said, before giving a swift kick to Fletcher’s groin.
“Look here, Bonnie and Clyde,” Fletcher groaned. “I’m going to press charges. You’ll hear from my lawyers!”
“They’ll have to be pretty damn good lawyers to find you where we’re going to put you.”
There was a swift whoosh as a door opened. Fletcher was lifted, before being shoved into a tight space –the car’s trunk. He attempted to fight but relented when his back gave him a twinge of warning.

Just his luck that his back threatened giving out while he was being kidnapped. It couldn’t have waited a few more moments? It was one thing if the universe was going to treat him like garbage. Though, his own body betraying him for the universal pile-on? That was a slap to the face.
“You need to at least tell me where we’re going!” Fletcher said.
Fletcher smacked into a wall. The feeling was real. Welty.
The door shut. Fletcher searched for ways to open it, but there were no handles. He could barely move. Barely breathe.
The stench of stale beer bottles and wadded fast food wrappers waded in Fletcher’s nostrils.
“Let me out! Let me out!”
Something banged at the walls. Gunshots went off. There were chuckles.
Moments later, an engine revved on, then wailed like something undead. Fletcher rattled against the walls of his prison.
Panic set in. This might’ve been the end. He might never hear from Linda again. He might never save the oil baron.
He could only hope that Marvin was out there, trying to save him.
Good riddance. I knew that Fletcher was up to no good. Trying to destroy my antiques business… It figures that he was in on some sort of sketchy drug trades or something, with those weirdos.
It’s a shame that he got shoved in the back of a car’s trunk though. That’s not a way to do business. Hopefully he isn’t shot.
Is it bad that I feel bad? He tried stealing business from my shop, the moron. Honestly, who does that? And the gall that he dared to laugh, too… Who does he think he is?
Still. Watching him go in that truck didn’t feel good.
Oh great, the cops are finally here. And, would you look at that… He’s carrying a picture of Fletcher. Perfect.
Time to tell him everything that I know.
Chapter 11:
“He’s still in a daze right now, but we need to get him tied up fast. I don’t think it’ll last much longer.”

Fletcher shook his head. A dull throbbing sat in the back of it, tugging at the roots of his hair. He must’ve hit his head while being driven from the factory. He rubbed the site. It was swollen. Tender. He should’ve been able to remember how he hit it. Yet, everything had been a blur. A big, black blur.
It still was.
Wait — what was he just thinking about?
“Come on, Clair! We take a hostage, and you don’t even think to pack a bit of rope!”
“‘Come on Jack,’ more like it. Didn’t you say you’d take care of the packing?”
“Yeah. I didn’t mean rope though! Who the hell has time to pack rope when they’re busy planning a getaway?”
“Well, sorry. It’s not like I was trying to secure use of the boss’ car, or anything.”
Everything was bleak. Blank. Fletcher went to rip off his blindfold, before deciding against it.
“Maybe we should just screw this interrogation garbage,” Jack said. “It’s pretty easy to dump a body in Drudge’s Cemetery. Just tell the boss we did what we could.”
Fletcher shuddered. He didn’t want to see what was going on around him. He didn’t need to. No matter what it looked like, it was going to be harsh.
“Fuck, he’s up!” Clair said.
“Wait, what? How much of that do you think he heard?”
Fletcher was grabbed by the legs, and somebody groped through his pockets.
“Quick,” Clair said, “we have to find something to tie him up with.”
Jack gave a snort. There was a metallic groan, as something was dragged along the floor.
“You honestly think you’re going to find shit that’ll help us, inside his pockets?”
Clair let off a series of epithets, before giving a whoop. “Knew it! I knew it!”
Fletcher’s arms were forced behind his back.

Resistance crossed his mind. Though, when had resistance ever produced anything of value? People resist things, only to encounter more things to resist against. Resistance goes on evermore. It’s an ongoing gust; a force that’s unrelenting. That is, until one hits a wall and can resist no longer.
Perhaps resisting against resistance was more intelligent. What point is there in wailing at winds that carry no care?
A tight chord wrapped around Fletcher’s wrists. Then, his ankles.
“Good luck getting out of that,” Clair said, with a triumphant snort. “Jack, you can put the chair down. We need to sit him in it.”
“Sit him in a seat? What are we, charity? The guy can lay as a sack, thanks.”
Despite Jack’s words, Fletcher was heaved up, and set back down. A metal chair crudely dug against his back.

He rubbed his wrists against the rope. Only, it wasn’t rope he’d been tied with. He recognized the material immediately — it was string from the yo-yo he’d kept on himself. Of all the things the captors could’ve used to keep him captive, they chose his own yo-yo’s string.
Suppressing a grin, Fletcher attempted to break the string. Yet, it tightened against his skin, leaving abrasions.
“Yeah, that’s right,” said Jack. He snickered. “You won’t be getting out of that.”
Nausea swung through Fletcher’s gut as his chair was tilted back.

“Here’s how this is going to go down,” Jack said. “You’re going to spill everything you know. Everything you’re planning. And after, we’ll turn you loose. It’ll be like this never happened. Even Steven.”
“I’d cooperate, but I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Fletcher said.
The air went muggy. Cloudiness surrounded Fletcher’s mind, and the nausea in his gut got worse.
“The Mop’s house,” Clair said. “Ring any bells?”
Fletcher shook his head.
“Guess he isn’t lying… From what the Mop tells us, you sure as shit didn’t ring any doorbells. Just busted into his house, like nobody’s business.”
“Wasn’t me who broke the Mop’s window. That was actually some other guy. Promise.”
“So you were there!” Jack said.
He let go of Fletcher’s chair, letting the legs fall back into place.
“I didn’t say I was there. It wasn’t me, I swear.”
“You knew about the window!”
Fletcher’s mind raced, searching for an out.
“How do you know? I never said anything about windows. Maybe you were hearing things. Maybe you guys are both idiots at interrogation and have the wrong guy.”
Jack sputtered. “No. I swear to god, you said window! At least… At least, I think you mentioned a window. Clair?”
“He did kind of say it under his breath, all mutter-like” said Clair. “I wasn’t paying close enough attention.”
“See,” said Fletcher. “I’m innocent.”
“We have info on everybody, and everything in here!” Jack said. “There’s no corner that you’re going to be able to hide or crawl behind. Okay?”
Fletcher shrugged.
“Who the hell are you?” Jack demanded. “Undercover cop? Rival gang? We need to know! Clair, did he have any info on him?”
“Name is Stuart Fletcher,” she said. “He has a ton of discount cards for various supermarkets, under that name. Name rings a bell. Not much else though. Not even a driver’s license.”
“I can drive!” Fletcher blurted.

He hadn’t thought they’d bother to steal his wallet. Moreover, he hadn’t felt it leave his pocket when Clair was searching. He shifted in his chair, attempting to feel for what items might be left in his pocket. Yet, everything was gone. His phone, his wallet, his expired tickets to a puppet show… Everything.
“Wait… Stuart Fletcher?” Jack said, with a laugh.
“You guys are going to let me out, or I’m calling the police!” Fletcher shouted.

“Yeah, even if I gave you a phone, you might not want to do that,” said Jack. “Don’t know if you’ve been following the police intercoms, but they’re after you buddy. The Mop didn’t just call us, apparently — he also called them.”
Fletcher’s eyes bulged. He was more vulnerable than he realized.

“Look, you don’t need to keep things a secret,” said Jack. “This can be so simple. You just need to tell us exactly what’s going on. We already know most of what goes on in this town. It’s all a joke, really. What’s the point in pretending that it’s otherwise?”

“Yeah, we do drug deals with everybody in this town,” said Clair. “Especially after all the earthquakes and chaos theorems that have gone down; more business than ever. This entire town is going to the madhouse. Which… I can’t complain. No reason to not tell us anything, now. We have your name, and we can check your info in our books.”
Fletcher considered making something up — anything — when Jack gripped him around the throat.
“We don’t have time to be toyed around with,” he hissed. “Cough the info up.”
Did Jack already know that Fletcher was hunting for the oil baron? Perhaps he’d even stolen it? It was difficult to tell.
A ringing telephone echoed from behind the walls. It was joined by the ringing of another telephone. Then, several others.
“Great — it’s the midday rush,” said Clair.
“I thought you told the boss to make sure that all the boys were here to pick up the calls,” Jack said, grinding his teeth.
“I thought you were going to do that.”
“Dammit Clair! This was supposed to be simple: mine the guy, whack him, then go fishing with the town’s businesspeople. None of this bullshit…”
Jack’s voice had grown more distant. A door squeaked open, letting the ringing of telephones spill into the room at full force.
“They’re all ringing,” said Jack. “Clair, I don’t know what we do…”
“You never know anything. Here’s what we’re going to do: we’re going to process these calls, and the bastard here isn’t going to do anything stupid.”
She leaned into Fletcher’s ear. “Isn’t that right?”
Fletcher pursed his lips. He was thirsty. Exhausted. However, if he said a word, the hoarseness of his voice would be made known.
Silence was the sole solution.  Yet, wasn’t it always?
“We double promise that we won’t kill you, if you don’t try to escape,” Jack said.
Clair made a smooch, then followed Jack’s footsteps. Had she blown a kiss? The door shut before Fletcher could tell.
The loneliness of the room dawned on Fletcher. Nobody was watching.

He rubbed his wrists against the metal backing of his chair, taking care to put pressure along the sharp edges the most. One of the strands gave a sharp snap. The whole string unraveled, flopping to the ground.
He smirked. It was a great thing that his toys were built so cheaply.

He rubbed his scalp in relief after pulling his mask off. His fingers reaching the corners of his eyes, he felt deep indentations left by the taut cloth. Even for a couple of thugs, there should’ve at least been the courtesy to make the blindfold a bit looser.
The room was part of some sort of warehouse. For a split-second, Fletcher desperately hoped it was the same warehouse Burgess had told him to go to. Though, he knew it couldn’t.
Burgess’ warehouse would’ve been ten times filthier, judging by the conditions his factory had been in. It would’ve been filled with an inexplicable amount of spray tan, as well.
The only escape was the door Clair and Jack had gone through. The only items in the room were his chair, and a table that held his wallet, his phone, his tickets, and a jumble of books. Useless.
He blinked. All useless, except for his phone — and the tickets. Though, mostly his phone.

The phone screen flickered on in Fletcher’s hand. Its warmth sent a surge of reassurance. Flashes of blues and reds scrolled by before Fletcher finally accessed his contacts. He needed help, from anybody. He went to call Harry Doswell, when he pulled his finger from the call button and scrolled away.

He couldn’t call Harry — it would’ve been weird, especially after their last conversation. John? Same problem. Marvin Whisk was always changing his number, and rarely ever answered in the first place — he didn’t seem like a phone person. Carol? She might pick up, but he hated her guts. Margaret?
His heart sank. She’d changed her number a dozen times over. Besides, a call with her would’ve gone worse than a call with Carol.

The police would’ve been an obvious solution. Yet, risking arrest by the cops was only slightly less unsavory than staying in the warehouse. Besides: Fletcher suddenly realized he had no idea where he was, nor how long he’d been missing. For all he knew, he’d been taken over Dexburg Bridge, and was outside of Dexburg.
“Think Fletcher, think,” he said, whamming himself in the head with the tip of his phone.
His phone slipped from his grip, landing on one of the books.
“Contacts of all Dexburg Businesses” it read.
Still useless. Though, Fletcher then glanced at the book next to it: “contacts of buyers.”

While Fletcher didn’t know where this warehouse was, there was a solid chance one of the buyers would know. He went to open the book, but his hand snapped back to the book of Dexburg businesses. His heart hummed. Before he realized what he was doing, he skimmed the book for a business run under the name of “Linda”.
There were dozens of examples. Yet, which one was the right Linda? Were any of them? Did Linda really live in Dexburg?
Frustration brimming, he scoured all names listed under “Wilkins”. He finally landed on Margaret Wilkins. She was an advertising agent. Interesting.
Shakily, he punched in the number, saving it to his phone. However, he couldn’t bring himself to call it. He stood staring, guiltily.

“Fletcher, you pathetic idiot,” he said. He tossed the book aside and rummaged through the “contacts of buyers” book. “You could’ve picked anybody to try to call, and you pick the number that’ll be no use to you whatsoever.”
The ringing phones on the other side of the wall were simmering down. He needed to find the name of somebody else. Anybody.
Private vet? No. Personal trainer? Too risky. High priest?
Sounded good. The chances were slim that a high priest would try to kill him, right?
“Dan Carvel,” Fletcher whispered, punching the number into his phone.
The phone spat out static as it sent a call through. A strained voice answered.
“Praises be to god, good life, and my barber! This is High Priest Carvel speaking,” a man answered.
Fletcher coughed, his eyes darting around the room. He hadn’t planned far ahead enough for this.
“Hello?” Fletcher said. “You still there?”
“Yes. Who the heaven is this?”
Stalling wasn’t going to last him long.
“I’m… I’m the substitute for today.”
“Oh, hallelujah. I was worried why my drug-dealer sounded so different…”
Fletcher’s hands were sweaty. His eyes darted about. “Good. Now, uh — have you been experiencing any headaches in your stomach?”
“Any what?”
“It’s a deadly symptom that’s going around, with the drugs we’ve been selling you…”
“You need to be more specific, beloved,” Priest Carvel said. “Is it with the marijuana, the LSD, or the heroin?”
“Yes, that one.”
“Which one?”
“Both. All. You know, whatever.”
A wrenching gag came out of the phone. “Oh, Jehovah… Dear lordy. I knew I shouldn’t have been dumping it all in my smoothies like that…”
“You’ve been drinking it in your smoothies?”
Priest Carvel laughed. “No, no. Drinking the smoothie would be ridiculous. I’ve been injecting the smoothie into my veins. Works better that way.”

Fletcher grimaced but pressed on. “Well, if you have those symptoms I listed, there’s a good chance that you’ll die in a week… We need to have you over at our… At our warehouse, to be checked up. Hopefully we’ll find nothing, but—.”
“Die? I can’t die! I haven’t even gone to Spud-World yet! My, oh my mighty… Dying?”
“Cool it, high priest. You just need to get over here, and everything will be cleared up.”
There was a surge of static, followed by crazed crashing and shouting. Finally, the line cut off.
Perfect. There was no way of telling if he’d lost the priest or not. Fletcher redialed the number.
“Hello, oh child of the heavenly,” the priest answered, serenely.
“Yeah, what was all of that?”
“My cat,” said Priest Carvel. “He gets antsy when—.”
Fletcher jumped when a door burst open. Its knob went flying as it swung into the wall.
“Oh shit!” said Jack. “Shit!”
“I told you that he might escape,” said Clair. “Now, look at him. He really might escape!”
Jack ran toward Fletcher, a bullish rage channeling through him. “I thought I told you to stay put!”
“Sorry, have to go,” Fletcher said.
Priest Carvel broke into a fearful ramble. Fletcher shoved his phone in his pocket, then ran around the table.
“It’s too late,” said Fletcher, “the F.B.I is coming for you guys. You’re better off just giving up now.”
Those had been the wrong words. The moment Fletcher said “F.B.I”, Jack flipped the table into Fletcher. Fletcher hit the ground, the table pinning him down. Books went airborne, then pelted his head.
“The effing F.B.I?” Jack said, standing over Fletcher’s head. He loaded his gun, before resting it on Fletcher’s scalp.
“Yes — the Flaccid Botox… Interns,” said Fletcher.
“Don’t bullshit me,” said Jack. “If you’re F.B.I, you better let me know right now, because I’m not playing around.”
Clair pulled a hairbrush out of her pocket and raked it across Fletcher’s skin. He winced, its bristles ripping into his skin.
“I was just bluffing...” he said. “Just bluffing!”
Jack pulled his gun away, but Clair’s brush persisted, digging ever deeper.

“My apologies,” Jack said, putting on a falsetto voice. “I try to keep myself calm. But, you know, with the president’s plans for our town, and Mayor Haddock doing everything he can to prepare for this... It’s kind of hard to trust anyone. Can’t take any risks.”
“Wait, what’s this about the president’s plans?” Fletcher asked, his voice cracking. “Sorry, I took the theorem. It’s just, I forgot.”
“Mayor Haddock will abandon the town, for a brand-new box of paperclips and a bottle of gin,” said Clair. “We’re in the end times. Not sure how you could forget, but —.”
Jack clamped his hand over Clair’s mouth. “You weren’t supposed to tell him that, you nitwit!” he hissed. “I don’t think he’s taken the theorem yet.”
Clair slapped herself in the forehead. “Great, just great... Classic Clair!”

Jack wasn’t satisfied and kicked the metal chair across the room. “No, not just great! We completely botched the chaos theorem up! We exposed a part of it to somebody who hasn’t read it yet! Do you know what’s going to happen to us?”
“No... Knowing is what the chaos theorem is for. I don’t remember everything it says. Hell, maybe we were supposed to reveal a part of the theorem to this dope. Ever think of that?”
“I would’ve remembered something important though, I think! What if our entire fate is going to change now? We might be completely screwed!”

While Jack paced around the room, barreling through his tirade, Fletcher slowly heaved the table off himself. Once free, he shimmied his way toward the open door. It was a longshot, but if he could get out while they were distracted, maybe it was less of a longshot than he anticipated.
“Oh no you don’t!”
Jack gripped Fletcher by the collar and drew him in.

“You know, honestly, I don’t think what you guys told me is all that impressive,” said Fletcher. “I’ve already seen plenty of signs of decay in this town. What with the mysterious pickpocket, the quakes, the insane hordes, and whatnot. I expected that we were headed toward uncertain doom.”
At Fletcher’s last words, Jack appeared to relax.
“Yes...” Then, his face switched to jealousy. “The pickpockets are part of the doom, you think?”
“Maybe. I’m not sure. Why? Do you know them?”
Jack switched again, his emotions now an enigma. “Stupid, ambitious upstart in the gang world. They’re not quite what they make themselves seem to be.”
Clair snickered, before flicking a knife out from under her sleeve. It gave a harsh glare under the room’s light.

“I’m getting the vibe that this guy is pretty useless to us,” said Clair. “Doesn’t matter who he called— F.B.I or not — there’s no way he knows where we are. I’m thinking that we can make a nice wig out of his hair and just put his body in the river.”
Fletcher held back a grin. He’d been putting more conditioner in his hair, hoping people would take notice. Clearly, it was paying off.
“We can’t do that!” Jack said. “I was dead set on burying him in the cemetery.”
Clair and Jack shared a cackle. Clair’s knife homed in, and Fletcher shrunk back. He’d seen what knives could do to pumpkins — and, he wasn’t keen on being made into a decoration for Halloween.
“I was thinking maybe we could go out for brunch, or something,” Fletcher said. “I mean, we don’t have to do this, right? We’re all locked up in the same crazy world, if you really think about it.”
“We can’t afford to have outliers,” said Jack, his arm tightening around Fletcher’s neck. Clair nodded in agreement, swinging her knife back and forth. “The chaos theorem demands it.”
Fletcher sputtered, fighting for even the smallest breath of air. “How’s that working out? You guys like being criminals?”
“Better than being the hostage.”

“It’s awful,” Clair said, reluctantly, “but, who are we to judge what we are? Clearly, this is what we were meant to be. This is our part in the universe. And, as amoral as it might be, it’s real damn fun. Why not accept it? Why not let the ride take us where it’s going?”
The squeal of rubber on pavement tore through the room.
“Clair, did you leave one of the phones on?” Jack asked.
“I thought I ended all our calls. But you had me rush in here so quick that I’m not sure.”
“Great! I think I can hear one of our customers squealing at us.”
“You sure that was a customer? I thought it was an avalanche?”
“Sounds plausible enough, but honestly… Other than a customer, what else could it be?”
“Well, I said avalanche…”
“Shut it!”
There was the jiggle of a latch, followed by the low grinding of a door being opened. Clair and Jack’s eyes went to the telephone room.
“Open sesame! Praises be to almighty!”
It was the high priest, Dan Carvel. Against all odds, he’d made it.
“That parking lot is terrifying,” Priest Carvel’s voice echoed through the room of telephones. “Nearly crashed into somebody’s truck, peeling in here.”
Jack turned to Clair, his face flushed with incense.
“Did you forget to lock the front door?” he hissed.
“You were the one who was supposed to lock the front door, remember?”
“What? I was carrying this lug the whole time! How was I supposed to lock it?”
“You came in last.”
“I distinctly remember that it was you who—.”
Priest Carvel’s voice thundered, washing over their bickering. “Hello, is anybody there? I’m not going to wait forever.”
His steps paused, and then he said, “Come on, beloved followers. There’s nothing to fear. Well, except for a lack of disinfectant… Do they ever clean this place?”
His words stamped pain into Jack’s face.
“Crud, I think he brought other people with him!” said Jack. “What does he think he’s doing here?”

Mussing her hair, Clair brought herself to her full height. Then, she sauntered toward the telephone room. “Not sure what he has for plans,” she said, adding a lilt to her voice. “But I plan on… Getting some.”
Before she reached the door, Priest Carvel poked his head through.
“Why, hello there,” Priest Carvel said. “Peace be upon you holy ones. In the name of our great saint, Chef Bernardo.”
Jack scoffed. “Chef Bernardo. You mean, the guy in those stupid butter commercials?”
“Stupidly divine butter commercials,” Priest Carvel said, asserting himself. He glanced over his shoulder. “Come on in, lads.”
Behind Priest Carvel entered four people, all dressed in white suits. They too carried a sort of otherworldly presence — their strides were in complete lockstep, and white masks obscured their faces.
Priest Carvel moved and flaunted his massive robe. It was a woven tapestry of several colors. Reflections of deep blues and reds were sent along the walls, giving off pure splendor.
“So, I guess we can get started,” said Priest Carvel, clapping his hands together.

Priest Carvel beamed at the sight of Jack and Clair. However, his face was markedly less impressive than his attire, with there being a tired air to him. Deep bags surrounded his eyes, and wrinkles lined his face.
Jack and Clair looked at Priest Carvel as though he were a creature from another planet. Fletcher smiled inwardly — they had no idea what was going on. They’d know soon.

“I don’t have any clue what you’re talking about,” said Jack. “Don’t get me wrong, you’re welcome to be in here. You’re one of our biggest buyers… But, maybe I was drunk or something when I last talked to you? Because, I don’t remember hearing anything about you coming over today.”
Priest Carvel’s face twisted.
“You just gave me an emergency phone call,” he said. “You told me that I might have a deadly disease, due to all of the drugs I’ve been purchasing? You said that you wanted to test me for it?”
“You probably do have a deadly disease,” said Clair, “but, trust me: we don’t know how to test for it, nor do we care.”
“Excuse me? There’s a chance that I might be dying, and you don’t care?”

“She didn’t mean it that way,” Jack said, with a forced chuckle. “Obviously we care if you die. We need money somehow. It’s just, if you die… It’s not like you’re going to be on our minds, or our conscience, or anything. You’ll kind of just be a blip on the radar, like everybody else in the world who dies. Insignificant. You know?”
Priest Carvel took a step back, aghast. “I’m one of the holy… The holy, besotted ones. Besides, I checked with my horoscope: I am not going to die. You dare lie to me?”
Jack fumbled his gun in his hands, his eyes wild and desperate. “Aren’t horoscopes useless?”
“Oh, great, now we have a liar and a skeptic in our midst.”
“No, no, it’s not like that. It’s just, with access to the chaos theorem, do you really need a horoscope?”
“Sorry, your words make too much sense. Thus, they sound like blather to me.”
Fletcher could no longer stand to sit idly by, watching the scene unfold.
“They want to kill you!” he said.
He ran around the room, waving his arms. People tended to listen more when somebody acted irrationally.

Panting, Fletcher continued, “They captured me, and tried beating me to submission. They’re going to do the same thing to you, I swear! Unless you want to be skinned, and have your marrow harvested to make new drugs, help me get out of here!”
Priest Carvel’s expressions morphed between fury, confusion, and gratitude. At a loss, he put his hand over his patchy beard and stared at the floor.
“I always wanted the honor of being immortalized as a pill,” he said. “Though, this marathon sprinter does have a compelling argument…”
Jack tried to take aim at Fletcher. Spit foamed from his mouth, and his arm trembled. Fletcher attempted to shield his face, fulling anticipating a blast. Though, it never came.
“Don’t — don’t listen to him,” Jack said. “He’s full of shit. The man doesn’t… I bet he cheats on crossword puzzles. He’s that dishonest! You can’t trust him!”
Fletcher gave Jack another look. There was a dash of uncertainty on Jack. The situation’s intensity had divorced him from the ability to act.
Clair strode up to Priest Carvel and put a hand on his shoulder.
“Can’t we all just take a step back, and calm down?” she said, her voice a mix of the roughness of sandpaper, and the smoothness of an object freshly sanded.
Priest Carvel gave a whistle. He gave a wave. His four followers broke from their stony poses, and tackled Jack to the ground.
“We’re long past getting along,” Priest Carvel said, pushing Clair away. “There’s no forgiveness for how this has gone down. I will be informing the police. You two are eternally damned.”
Grunts and screams erupted, as Priest Carvel’s followers dragged Jack to the corner. Priest Carvel grappled Fletcher’s shoulder.
“Let’s get out of here,” Priest Carvel said.
“You don’t want to leave without me, do you?” asked Clair.
“What about your accomplice?” said Priest Carvel. “I’ve fed him to my boys. Don’t you care about him?”
Clair shrugged. “I can leave him. He’ll be fine.”
“A minute ago, you two wanted to kill me… How much are you willing to give me in tithe?”
Clair rummaged through her pockets. “How’s ten cents sound?”
Priest Carvel spat at the ground. “Are you for real? Ten cents? I only accept money in increments of thousand-dollar bills.”
He whistled again and gestured at his followers. “Come on, my only begotten children. We must make our exit, with haste.”
The followers dropped Jack, leaving him to moan in vain. “You guys aren’t going to get away with this,” Jack said. “I will make sure that you pay.”
“Wait,” Fletcher said. He ran to the books, bundling them in his arms. There was no telling when they’d come in handy.

Priest Carvel gripped Fletcher firm around the arm and sped through the telephone room. The room was a quagmire, wires crisscrossing along the floors and walls. While many of the phones were kept on tables, most of them lay on the ground.
Priest Carvel eyed Fletcher’s books. “I just saved your life and told you that we need to be on the run. I beseech you — why are you still clinging to your worldly belongings?”
“I think there might be traces of cocaine inside the book,” Fletcher lied.
He took a whiff of the pages for added effect. He coughed. There might’ve been traces, after all.
Priest Carvel gave an approving nod. His four followers banked around Fletcher, giving full protection. Despite their faces being completely covered, Fletcher felt an instant comradery with them.
Perhaps calling Priest Carvel hadn’t been such a bad idea, after all.
Things are only getting worse and worse.

“Officer Mayhew” this, “Officer Mayhew that.” God, can’t people just give me a break? I didn’t sign up to become an officer to be badgered by a bunch of petty complaints. If I’d wanted that I would’ve just gone into daycare, like I’d originally planned.
A daycare career really wouldn’t have been so bad. Playing patty-cake must beat these patronizing patrols, right?

I’m worn out. That stupid priest called us, telling us that some drug operation was going on at this warehouse. Yet, lo and behold, there’s nothing. Driving to this abandoned warehouse was a wild goose chase.

If anybody had been here, they’re long gone. I don’t even think anybody ever was here. But, Officer Springs tells me that there were druggies, and they booked it. I’m not convinced. They would’ve had to drag their drugs to a car real quick, then gun it.
I’m more inclined to say this was all a waste. Priest Carvel is a loon, after all.
Wait — is that white powder on the table over there? Sure looks like it… I guess I’m obligated to test it, like a good cop.
Yes, it tastes just like cocaine. Huh. Guess Springs was right, for once. This place was probably full of drugs.
Wonder if there are more test samples around here. It’d be great if there are.
Great. Now Springs is chewing me out. Give me a break — if I want to get a little pick me up on the job, is that so bad?
Wait, there’s a yo-yo at Springs’ feet — one of those real cheap ones. Didn’t Fletcher own a toy shop, or something?
Yeah — stinks of Fletcher, all right. He was here. There were drugs here, too.

First the Logan Gerri complaints, then the Marvin Whisk complaints, and now the Priest Carvel complaints… I don’t want to believe it, but Fletcher’s doing something shady. Probably secretly a drug dealer — it lines up with his past. Hell, maybe that toy he told me he was looking for has some of the good stuff stashed in it.
It’s the only explanation for all his behavior.
He won’t be hiding for long. We’re on his trail. We’re going to catch him. This town is finally going to take me seriously.
“Springs,” I say. “Looks like we’ll be making a trip to old Dan Carvel. I’ve got some questions for him.”
Chapter 12:
Priest Carvel leaned back, a smirk resting on his face. He and Fletcher were seated in the back of a black van, while Priest Carvel’s followers drove.
Fletcher hunched into the corner and scrolled through his phone. He’d gotten a message from Linda. His gut lurched.

“I’ve figured out a safe place to bring the money,” the email read. “There’s a dark alley on Grain Avenue, right near Jim Harrigan’s bank. Bring the money there and hide it under the dumpster. We won’t have time to meet, so don’t try. Thank you, Timothy. Love, Linda”
She didn’t want them to meet? Worse, she thought his name was Timothy?
This was a joke. She had to have known his name wasn’t Timothy. This was just a joke. Right?
Stuart clenched his jaw and turned off his phone. He was idiotic for not scrubbing Uncle Timothy’s name from his company.

“Boy, we showed them,” Priest Carvel said. “Of course, I’m not in favor of revenge or anything of that sort. Forgiveness is important, and all that jazz. But yeah — I pray to our lord that those crooks get struck by bowling balls, hollow be his name.”
They were approaching the vehicle’s top speed, and the van gave tired groans and whines. Going queasy, Fletcher held his hands to his stomach. Nonetheless, Priest Carvel was nonplussed.
Fletcher cleared his throat.
“I think it’s ‘hallow’,” Fletcher mumbled.
“Hallo to you too,” Priest Carvel said, with a laugh. “Ah, it’s amazing that things have worked out in the way they have, isn’t it? I would’ve died if you weren’t here.”

Fetcher wanted to share Priest Carvel’s vigor. Yet, the message from Linda was crushing. Worse, virtually no progress had been made on the oil baron.  Yes — the oil baron was the bigger problem on his mind.
Fletcher’s thoughts trailed back to his computer — if he could get access to that, and use the info from his stolen books, maybe he could conduct some actual research.
That, and he could restart his chat with Linda. His heart fluttered.

“Speaking of me not being here,” Fletcher said. “I was wondering if you could take me back to my place? There are some things that I need to settle. I’m looking for a lost toy — it’s very valuable, and it was stolen. However —.”

“Lost toy? Of course, of course,” said Priest Carvel. “Happens to me all the time. But, before you can do that, I need you come to my gathering hall to see my religious ceremony. Give it the lookover. I think you’d be a great fit…”
Fletcher squirmed. “Thanks, but I’m really not into religions. I just need to get back home. My address is —.”
“Also, there’s this fraud that I need you to look out for,” Priest Carvel said, unphased. “If you can help me squelch him out, I might be able to give you a tip on where your toy may be.”
“You know where it is?”
“Men of the spirit never give their secrets,” Priest Carvel said, with a wink.

Fletcher checked his watch. There was still plenty of daylight in the day. Besides, there was an intrigue to Priest Carvel. Perhaps he didn’t know exactly where the oil baron was, but he knew something. In any case, he didn’t seem keen on taxying Fletcher anywhere.
Priest Carvel lifted a cigarette and shoved it toward Fletcher’s face. “Here — want one?”
Fletcher shook his head. “I don’t take stimulants. I prefer to see the world as objectively as possible. I don’t want anything impeding my observation of it.”

“Sounds like a waste of time, to me,” said Priest Carvel, shoving the cigarette in his mouth. “We must be the enlightened ones — we must match reality, with spirituality. To keep order, we must become loose; be willing to take risk. Isn’t that right, dearest followers?”
His followers all nodded.
“Praises be to the father, and the gifts given from the highest,” they chanted in unison.

“In agreement,” Priest Carvel said. He kicked his legs back and took a deep huff. His eyes fluttered, then closed. “The chosen one says we’re on the right track to peace — to stopping Armageddon. We just need to get rid of the fakers.”
He sighed and took another huff. “The meaning of life is within our grasp.”
“You’re looking for the meaning of life?” Fletcher asked. “I was hoping you’d already have it, seeing as you’re a priest and all…”

Priest Carvel coughed up a cloud of smoke. “You’d think that,” he said, between gasps, “but, the chaos theorem threw me for a spin. If everything is predetermined, then nothing I do was ever predetermined by me.”

Priest Carvel paused. His eyes were heavy. “We’re all just going by the whims of our electrolytes. I can’t believe that. So then, what is there to believe? I have many beliefs. That’s what my religion is founded on. One of my beliefs is that the chaos theorem is wrong, and that we can prove it. Of course, the theorem predicted that I would choose to do that…”
He tossed his cigarette out the window and lit another one.
“Course, there’s the faker, sowing doubt among my followers… We need to find him and end him.”
Running over a pothole, the van swayed. Fletcher shuddered.
“Has the theorem been wrong about anything, yet?” Fletcher asked.
“Yeah.”
“And what’s that?”
“I’ll die of choking in a day, while eating a rare steak. I never eat steak rare. And according to the Holy Purple Document of Purloin, I’ll never die. Ludicrous, really…”
“Purple document of wha— something a day away is not something in the past, though.”

Priest Carvel gave a sly look. “It isn’t if it’s a day backwards, instead of ahead. And, if I’m thinking in terms of the day ahead, when I mean to think of the day backwards, am I not thinking backwards? Therefore, doesn’t the universe go backwards, to center around my mind? In this way, the things ahead become the things before, before one’s mind’s eye.”
They drove through a wooded area, under the sweet shade of trees. Green tinted sunlight dripped from the leaves to the windows, giving off warmth. Priest Carvel swooned, at ease.
Fletcher coughed as the stench of cigarettes grew. “That’s not how it works.”
“It is, according to Thor! I’ll be fine. The deities have told me so. Do you really think a theorem made by man can outdo the divine?”
“It’s a fine line… The world works, and then it doesn’t. Doesn’t it? Maybe you’re not wrong, but I’m unsure.”
“Get sure.” Priest Carvel slapped Fletcher in the back. “Believe. In the words of General… Muster? Custard? Whatever: faith is the liquor of victors.”
Fletcher tightened his seatbelt. “I would believe, but I’m confused as to what you believe in. I mean — Thor is your God?”
Priest Carvel gave a hearty laugh. “No. Don’t be insane. I don’t believe in any gods.”
He gave Fletcher a prolonged stare. Priest Carvel looked as though he were undressing him with his eyes.

“Of course, I also do,” Priest Carvel said, kicking a leg back. “I’m a tiny god, for example. So are you — though, probably quite a bit tinier than I. Then, there are higher gods. Examples are the president, movie stars, and popstars. Finally, there are+ the prime gods: Buddha, Krishna, Mohammad, Jehovah, Christ… Christ, there are a lot.”
“So, are you pantheistic then?”
Priest Carvel’s face flushed red, and he clenched his fists. “No,” he said, voice trembling. “What? Do I look like a pancake to you?”
Fletcher shook his head.
“I asked you a question!” Priest Carvel boomed, his tenor echoing along the van’s walls. “Do I? Yes or no?”
“I’m sorry,” Fletcher said, fumbling his hands, “I said pantheistic, not pancake. I was just confused about your religion, is all.”
Priest Carvel gave a stiff nod. “I see.” His eyebrows remained raised, dubiously.

Priest Carvel continued. “The mythology is all very complex and involved. It was gifted to me from on high, by some lady. You’ll learn soon enough. Just don’t get sucked in by the doubters. Remember: your job is to find them and squash them. Me and my followers will all be gathering at the gathering place of the holies, very soon. Isn’t that right?”
The followers broke into another chant. “Holiest of holies, leader from above, will take us to a place built from his love.”
Priest Carvel rubbed his hands together in satisfaction.
“I’ve done a lot of talking about myself,” he said. “But I haven’t asked anything about you. Where do you stand in all of this?”
“Just an impartial observer,” said Fletcher. He measured his words, with it occurring to him that ears were everywhere. “Just been going around town, looking for something.”
“Meaning? I know the feeling.”
Fletcher smirked. “Me? Meaning? No, not that at all. I’ve just been looking for that toy I lost. Remember? Very simple expedition, really.”
“Ah yes. Well, just find the faker, and I’ll make it easier for you…”
He gave a relaxed sigh and looked to his hands. He looked back up.
“But, why do you need a toy so bad? Shouldn’t the pleasures of the soul be enough to placate you?”
“It’s just for my business. I need it for that. It’s kind of the prize attraction.”
“Your business doing well?”
Fletcher’s mind went back to his pile of bills from the bank. He shrugged. “I’d prefer not to say. Don’t want to seem like I’m bragging.”
“Oh, of course. We can just talk your personal life. Where do you come from? What’s your background?”
“I’ve been living in Dexburg all my life,” Fletcher said, simply. “Nice town.”
“Funny, I’ve never seen you around. Who did you live with?”

A photo reel of Fletcher’s life whipped through his head. He’d grown up in a toy shop — any kid’s dream. Though, it was always cold. Timothy had problems with the heat in the winter. As he got older, Fletcher became his apprentice and constantly tried to be enough, only to watch him die.
It was too much. Fletcher closed his eyes. “Look, I don’t have time to get into all of it… My upbringing is — a long story.”
“Have any friends? Lovers?”
A twinge of annoyance passed through Fletcher as his thoughts went back to Margaret and Linda, but he simply gave another shrug.
“Maybe.”

Priest Carvel’s smile went smug and deprecating. “We tiny gods — we encounter many a maybe in life. Yet, lovers are never a maybe, my brother. If there’s somebody you care about, you should get on that.”
Fletcher nodded, a choke forming in his throat. He punched himself in the chest.
“Sorry… Lot of phlegm,” he said. “Haven’t been taking my vitamins. Uh — also, there’s something I should probably do. Sorry to interrupt, but it’ll just be a moment.”
Fletcher turned on his phone.
“Whatever you need,” said Priest Carvel. “You shouldn’t wait. Life wasn’t designed for people to wait to do things that they want. I can wait for you.”
Hands shaky, Fletcher went into his email and typed out a message to Linda.

“Are you sure we can’t rendezvous in that alley? I don’t feel comfortable doing this if we can’t. Hell: I can even give you the website for free if you like. I just want to see you. My name is Stuart Fletcher, by the way. Trust me: my life gets way more interesting from there if you just meet me halfway.”

The moment Fletcher sent it, he looked up with a surge of pride. Yet, it flickered out quickly as it came. There was no telling how Linda would respond, or if she would respond at all. Offering a website in exchange for meeting up — was that weird? He’d never asked it of his customers before.
He desperately craved a connection of any kind. Chases and scrambles for it defined his life, and all for nothing. Nobody cared. It was high time that something changed.
Fletcher hit send. Priest Carvel gave a sniff. He’d been looking over Fletcher’s shoulder.

“You’re done? Great. Now, can you believe how divinely shaped toasters are these days?” Priest Carvel droned. “Did you see the old woman who made toast with a marking that was shaped like the Christ’s mustache? If I didn’t know any better, I’d say the toaster companies are getting closer to heaven than most of us believers.”
Fletcher raised a finger. “Totally agree,” he said, only barely processing Priest Carvel’s words, “but, I’m going to need you to keep quiet for just one more second.”
Scrolling through the numbers in his phone, Fletcher began to sweat. He wiped his forehead with his sleeve. He hovered over Margaret’s number.
Calling her wasn’t going to be smart. Though, he needed to do it.
The call rang once. That was all it needed for her to pick up.
“Hello, who’s this?”
Fletcher’s heart skipped a beat. He attempted to clear his throat, only for it to become stuffier. His skin went blotchy.
“Hi,” he said.
Static. Fletcher redirected his ears to the thrum of his van.
“You changed your number,” Margaret finally hissed. “Who gave you my number?”

“I just want to talk, for old time’s sake,” Fletcher said. “It’s been so long… And everything is so crazy these days. What do you think about everything that’s going on? And… Where do you think we stand?”
There was a groan. “We don’t stand,” she said, “not after what you did. I’m not letting you back in, Stuart. It doesn’t matter what you say.”
At hearing this, a newfound frustration lapped at Fletcher.
“Oh yeah?” Fletcher said. “Well, you’re going to talk to me. I’ll make sure of it. I’m not going to let you keep shutting me out. We need each other.”
He hadn’t meant it. At least, the rational part of his brain told him that. Yet, there was no denying that the words had been said. They couldn’t be put back.
“I put a restraining order on you for a reason. Even Harry agreed with it. If you try seeing me, you’ll only see consequences. Never call this number again!”
The phone call went dead.
Fletcher’s cheeks burned. His mind swam; swelled. It couldn’t be over just like that. Could it? All those feelings that he’d felt for Margaret, tossed to the wayside? Had it ever been real?
Priest Carvel put a hand on Fletcher’s shoulder and gave a tight squeeze. Fletcher pushed back, fighting a light mist forming over his eyes.
“This is going be a lot to bear,” said Priest Carvel. “I can’t even imagine what this is about to take of you... But, I need you to be honest: do you think that I look like a pancake?”
Is regret supposed to be something that you feel regret over? Is regret even something you should feel in the first place?
“Did it seem like Stuart Fletcher was in cahoots with these shooters?” the cops asked me.
I was still cowering outside Kent Burgess’ factory when the cops showed up. Fletcher and the shooters were long gone.
For some reason, I told the cops yes. And when I said that, they looked as though I’d given them the answer they were looking for. Yet, I couldn’t help but feel I’d given the wrong answer.
I should’ve never called or talked to those cops.
My father always said, “Marvin: regret is only something you feel when you’re in the wrong.”
Good to know. But what if there’s a situation where it might be wrong to be feel you’re in the wrong? Is your regret still valid? Is there any way to tell?

I’ve been chasing down Fletcher. Yet, if somebody asked me why, I wouldn’t be able to say. I don’t trust the police — especially after everything I had to tell them about Fletcher, when they interrogated me. I think they might be attempting to arrest him. Yet, Fletcher was captured by some gang. He seemed innocent.

Well, maybe he’s not completely innocent… I’m sure that the guy is guilty of something. Still, the police have the wrong idea. I need to make sure that he’s safe, right? Am I not obligated to, now that the police mistakenly think he’s a criminal?

It’s funny. Fletcher and I are sworn enemies. He probably hates me more than I hate him. He is constantly working to undermine me. I’m still praying he doesn’t destroy me. Yet, I feel so much guilt over being so antagonistic toward him.
Maybe there’s a chance at mending the broken ties — at making something out of all this chaos. It’s not a certainty, but it’s a possibility.
“Officer Mayhew here. We’re headed to Dan Carvel’s to gather more intel on this case,” the police intercom in my truck says, through a cloud of static.
Dan Carvel’s. I think I know where that is…
I need to set my record straight with these officers about Fletcher. Then I need to find Fletcher, and have him make things right with the cops.
Finally, I must stop Fletcher from ruining my business.
Hopefully it all works out.
Chapter 13:
The gate was mottled with thorny vines and patches of rust. Gargoyles ogled from fenceposts, their eyes piercing. They seemed to suck out the soul of their observer.
Fletcher clutched his books tight to his chest. He’d been secure inside the van. Now, the van squealed as it sped away.

Fletcher flicked his eyes away and strained to look past the gate. All he could make out was a dilapidated shack, sitting on a steep hill. Priest Carvel’s gathering hall must’ve been just beyond, hidden from view.
Fletcher shuddered. He’d have to scale the entire hill. If anything were to go awry, a quiet escape. wouldn’t be much of an option.

“Remember,” Priest Carvel said, turning to look back at his followers, and then to Fletcher, “follow me, and do exactly as I say. Once we’re in there, anybody could be the faker. You need to maintain appearances and keep an eye out for the one causing doubt.”
A guard stood by the gate, with his arms crossed.

“Who art thou, those who stand here?” the guard asked. He was dressed in similar garb to the other followers — white masks, and a pure white cloak. Though, underneath it were thick layers of padding and armor.
“I’m Priest Dan Carvel,” Priest Carvel said, puffing up his chest. He then gestured to Fletcher and the rest of the crew. “These are, obviously, some of my followers.”
The guard squinted at Fletcher. He nodded, then cleared his throat. “Yes, well… What is the name of the religion, for which I guard so diligently?”

Priest Carvel spat out his cigarette and scratched his beard. His feet kicked at the dirt. He paced in a small circle. “Damn, you got me at a bad time, chief. I’m really keyed into the spirit world right now. Thus, it’s difficult to remember.”
“How many feet lie upon the head of the beheaded headsman?”
Priest Carvel’s face was blank. “Sorry, doesn’t ring a bell…”
“Password. If you want in, you must have the password.”
“Yeah, well maybe I don’t have the password, bigshot! Now, are you going to let me in, or not?”
“I’m sorry, oh holy one. But, there’s no way to confirm if you truly are the holy, unless you have the—.”
Priest Carvel pushed the guard aside and flipped a key in the air.
“I have the key,” Priest Carvel said, with a scoff. “I’m pretty sure that I’m the real deal, okay? Do you want me to pay the property bills this week, or not?”
With a firm nod, the guard stepped aside. Priest Carvel pushed his key into the gate’s padlock, struggling with it. Despite his begging, the lock simply wouldn’t open.
The guard came over. Ignoring the lock, he pushed the gate open.
“I locked the padlock, but I may have forgotten to loop it through both the gates,” the guard said, sheepishly. “But hey: at least I remembered to lock the padlock.”
Priest Carvel clapped his hands, before walking through the gate. “Brilliant. You must do that more often! Can you imagine how much time pretending that this gate is locked will save me?”
Patches of overgrown grass collapsed underfoot, followed by strips of freshly cut grass. The entire hillside was this way. Whoever had cut the lawn did an incredibly shoddy job.
“Priest Carvel — you do remember everybody in your great hall, right?” Fletcher asked, with a whisper. “Because, if there’s anybody new, or anything that’s changed recently… That might help.”
Priest Carvel laughed. “Of course! Of course!”
Yet Priest Carvel offered nothing more and sped away. Fletcher scrambled after him, only to have Priest Carvel move faster.
“How long do you think finding the faker will take?” Fletcher asked. “And, is there any sort of hint you can give me about the toy?”
“It won’t be long, but it’ll be long enough to not be short,” Priest Carvel said, nodding.
“You’ll make sure to drive me back home after all this, right?”
“No doubt.”
The followers mimicked Priest Carvel, chanting on repeat, “no doubt.” Fletcher mumbled along with them, only hoping he wasn’t making a mistake.
“We’ll have you in and out of here in a jiffy,” Priest Carvel continued, “Just get a feel for my religion, and a feel for the person who is most suspicious. That’s all.”
“And what religion is that, exactly?”
Priest Carvel’s followers laughed, then repeated Fletcher’s words in a mocking monotone.

They approached the shack of a house, prompting another increase in pace from Priest Carvel. From this view, Fletcher could see the entire grove with clarity; he saw no sign of a bigger house anywhere.
“I know, I know — this temple is somewhat intimidating,” Priest Carvel said, giving the shack a proud grin. “Truly, there hasn’t been a monastery cathedral built like this in over a century.”
Priest Carvel creeped up the rotting porch steps and opened the door.
“I don’t think there’s ever been one built quite like this, at all,” Fletcher muttered.
Bits of wood fell from the porch canopy, followed by peeling paint. Fletcher skipped over a broken floorboard.
“It must’ve been quite something to buy this property,” said Fletcher. “I imagine the real estate agent was in shock.”
He waited for a response from Priest Carvel. It never came. Cautiously, Fletcher stepped after him, into the dark entrance into the house.
A festering wave of sweaty hands swept him up. He jostled between dozens of bodies and struggled to keep his focus intact. The faker had to be somewhere. If he found them, he could be on his way.
“Greetings, oh enlightened ones!” Priest Carvel shouted, above the crowd. “Today is a very special day. It’s the day that I make the day a day to forget!”
