The crowd broke into cheers and roars. All the while, Fletcher’s body bopped around. Priest Carvel was nowhere to be seen, amid the peeling plaster and dancing bodies.
Everybody was dressed in familiar white cloaks and held similar composure. They carried their heads high and kept their movements stiff. Constricted.

“I may or may not have forgotten the exact details to the religion that we’re serving,” Priest Carvel went on, “but no matter! So long as we set our sights to the holiest of holies, there will be no stopping us! We are not a force to be defied! We are a force to be deified!”
The crowd repeated after him. “We are not to be defied. We’re to be deified!”
As Fletcher chanted along, he jumbled the placing of deified and defied. He caught others around him doing the same. Nonetheless, palpable pride swelled throughout them and the building.

Fletcher made his way through the room and entered a larger room. Or rather, it was multiple rooms merged into one. To each side of Fletcher, there were gashes in the floor. The walls to three neighboring rooms had been torn down, creating a mega-room.
In the corner of the room, Priest Carvel pumped himself to mega proportions. He stood on a rickety table, holding a microphone and paper in hand.

“We’re getting closer to the divine lightbulb, brothers and sisters!” he cried. “Our lives are intermingling into one, crafting a greater inner-reality for the outside! I beseech you all: I’ve been making strides out in the field. Today alone, I’ve gathered a new follower.”
His eyes swung to Fletcher, and his arm stretched in Fletcher’s direction.
“Mr. Fletcher is the greatest hinderer I have ever met!” he said. “He hindered the blindingly bright forces today when they tried ensnaring me. Fletcher, come on up here!”
Fletcher had no desire to join the Priest Carvel and be made a spectacle. However, upon Priest Carvel’s request, the crowd pushed Fletcher toward the table.
“Don’t be worried,” one of the followers whispered into Fletcher’s ear. “Priest Carvel might require holy fear, but he’s not to be wholly feared.”
“I wish I had the honor to stand next to him, upon the great table,” someone yelled.
Fletcher wished he could be wishing that.
He scanned the crowd. How many people were in the house? Did finding the right person to call a “faker” even matter? It wasn’t as though Priest Carvel would be able to tell the difference.
The table trembled as Fletcher stood upon it. He listened as bits of wood splintered and buckled. It had a weaker design than the tables he’d kept at his toy store.
“Tell them what we did today!” Priest Carvel said, slapping Fletcher on the back. He flaunted his robe and flashed his teeth.
“Well, you did a whole lot of drugs,” Fletcher said.

“Spiritual enhancers,” Priest Carvel corrected, a tinge of annoyance in his voice. “Only for the most enlightened of the tiny gods to consume. And, I say unto you all: I met a revelation today. I learned why squid are called squid.”
“Is it because that’s what they’re called?” Fletcher asked, trying to play along.

“No. Everything must happen for a reason. They’re called squid, because octopus are called octopus. Thus, squids can’t be quads. Nor can they be cods. It’s like how gods must be gods, rather than us sods… Squids must be squids.”

Fletcher was lost among the incoherence. His arms sagged, his books becoming heavy. Yet, as he tried studying the audience, he was bestowed with awe. Priest Carvel carried an assurance in his voice that made everything fall into place.
“Praise be to the logic of the holy one!” went the entire crowd.
One of the followers came up to the table, holding an infant over his head.
“Please, have my baby!” he said. “You alone are worthy!”
Priest Carvel laughed. “Thank you, but I’d much rather have money.”
“No, please! Take my baby! I haven’t slept for a month!”
The crowd folded back in on the follower, in a clamor of singing and swooning. Fletcher felt the urge to hide among them. An itching in the back of his mind left him uneasy.
“The squid is the squid!” Priest Carvel repeated. “It’s inevitable!”
“Of course, not everything is inevitable,” Fletcher said, despite himself. “You’ve acknowledged that — the chaos theorem is wrong. It’s the main tenet of your religion, right?”

Priest Carvel cleared his throat. He gave Fletcher an uncertain look. “Yes. Of course. But, a squid is still a squid because it was meant to be a squid. It wouldn’t be named so, if it wasn’t supposed to be.”

“But what if it wasn’t supposed to be? What if I named a squid a quad, and everybody else in the world called it that too? Then, my choice will have changed the world’s word for squid. We can defy intrinsic meaning, because we define intrinsic meaning.”
Priest Carvel clicked his tongue. “It would still have been inevitable if you called a squid a quad, I imagine. You were meant to call it that, even if you weren’t.”
“But if I wasn’t meant to call a squid a quad, how can I be?”
“Because… You just can. You know what I mean.”
“Do I? Do we? Is what you’re saying coherent, or does my mind just ascribe coherence to it because it can tell you’re saying something — when you’re actually saying nothing?”

The crowd broke into an unintelligible babble of agreement and disagreement. Fletcher attempted to keep eyes on the doubters when the crowd’s eyes turned on him. People were scrutinizing him. Upon catching Fletcher’s moment of insecurity, Priest Carvel puffed his chest again.
“I will continue considering the philosophy of the squid,” Priest Carvel said, voice booming. “Perhaps Fletcher has a point.”
“What if Fletcher is the chosen one?” one of the members of the crowd cried.
“Who said that?” Priest Carvel snapped.
Fletcher studied for the person who’d spoken. It was impossible to tell.
Priest Carvel laughed. “Now, now… I’m not sure who the chosen one is. But surely, members of the purloin lovers…”
“Purloin Believers!” one of the members cried.
Priest Carvel raised his voice, “Surely I seem to be the chosen one.”
One of the members of the crowd laughed.
“Great joke, Priest Carvel,” he said. “But, we all know that you’re merely the mouthpiece for the chosen one, imbued by the great gods with your wisdom. You said so yourself.”
Perhaps this crowd member was the faker? Though, he was dressed in identical garb to everyone else —keeping track of him would be difficult.
Priest Carvel shrugged. “That was just what the great gods told me to say. I always thought you all thought there was a chance that I was the chosen one…”
Several jeers erupted from the crowd.
“You didn’t even know the sanction key of the jelly snatchers,” said one.
“And, you utterly forgot about the exception rule of Peru,” said another.

At this point, there were too many doubters to count. Priest Carvel’s face boiled. Gingerly, Fletcher backed into the corner. Priest Carvel was about to explode. Yet, perhaps he deserved it. Perhaps Priest Carvel’s problem of doubt wasn’t a “faker”, but himself.
A sinking fell through Fletcher’s gut. He needed some way of finding a faker — it was his one ticket forward. Would it be so wrong to choose a random person, after Priest Carvel’s charade was over?
“Alright, alright, maybe I don’t have the best memory,” Priest Carvel said. “Anyway, can we all agree that this session was incredibly enlightening? I imbued you all with a grand revelation!”
Murmurs washed over the room. Priest Carvel grabbed Fletcher from behind and walked him off the table. Fletcher fumbled with his books, caught in sudden shock.
“Just let me do the talking,” Priest Carvel hissed in Fletcher’s ear.
Priest Carvel moved to the room’s center, murdering an attempt at a moonwalk.
“In any case, I’m sure you can all be pleased in my discovery of Mr. Fletcher!” Priest Carvel cried. “Isn’t he just the most adorable thing you guys have laid eyes on?”
He gave Fletcher an aggressive shake, then a pat on the back.

“Fletcher, please, tell us a bit more about yourself,” Priest Carvel said. He made a great, terrible laugh. “Go into what you were telling me on the ride here — how your business is going great, and you have such an interesting past.”
“I was actually really interested in hearing more about your take on squids,” Fletcher said.

Priest Carvel gave a 20-watt smile and shook his head. Envy lining his eyes, he whipped his robe around flamboyantly. He wanted to be in control, no doubt. Though, little could be controlled in this room.
Fletcher coughed. An upsweep of dust filled the air; people clustered around him, rattling the room. All eyes were on him.

“I’m just a guy who’s lived here all my life,” Fletcher said. “I was raised by my uncle, and I’ve been running his business for some time. It’s going okay, I guess. I don’t let fears of failure or anything get in my way.”
“You don’t let fears get in your way?” one of the followers said, shocked. “But Priest Carvel always says that fear is the only way of making one’s way… He loves fear.”
“It’s true,” Priest Carvel said, proudly. “It’s what sets us apart from posers. Never anything like a nice pinch of fear, to get people to do things you want.”

Fletcher nodded. “I guess I have to agree with that… I wouldn’t get out of my bed in the morning, if I wasn’t terrified of what would happen if I didn’t. Hell, I probably would’ve taken the chaos theorem if it weren’t for the fact that I wasn’t terrified.”
The room went deathly quiet. Priest Carvel’s face went slightly rosy.
“Yeah,” he said, sheepishly, “Fletcher is one of the few people who hasn’t read the chaos theorem yet…”
“You don’t follow the chaos theorem? You’ve defied it?” said a man.
“What are those books in your hands?” a woman asked, grabbing at them.
“Just something I found, while I was captured…” Fletcher said, pulling them behind his back.
“He found holy books, while being captured!” she cried. “And he’s defied the chaos theorem! He must be the chosen one!”
Several people grabbed Fletcher by his jacket, pulling him in multiple directions.

“I went to a theorem booth and have been stuck following the chaos theorem for weeks,” somebody said, “no matter how hard I try, I can’t seem to break it. It told me that I would quit my job at Kent Burgess’ factory, become convinced that I’m a telepath, and join a cult. I can read your mind — I know you think I’m lying — but, honest to god, that’s exactly what has happened.”
“You’re luckier than my pops!” one follower retorted. “He was told that he would commit suicide, after going to Dr. Ford’s hospital for being insanely sane. Get this? He did.”

The room flared with more disagreements and comparisons. Priest Carvel attempted to quell the frenzy, only for people to begin clearing a spot for Fletcher. They placed a plush chair for him, its arms ornamented with a staff and a glass.
“Take the cup of Venus’ saliva,” they began to chant. “Take the cup of Venus’ saliva.”
“No, let’s not!” shouted Priest Carvel. “That’s only for sacred ceremonies! Please everybody, stop! Listen to me!”

Fletcher was manhandled into the chair, with the staff placed in his hands and the glass brought toward his lips. He considered struggling, but what was the point? He went with the flow, as Priest Carvel had said. He was just a mini god, being fiddled with at the whims of larger gods.
“Fine, fine!” Priest Carvel said, snatching the glass. “Let’s test his mettle. I doubt he’ll have the courage to truly drink this drink.”
He gave Fletcher a wink. Though, his lip twitched nervously until Fletcher gave a wink back.

“Whoever drinks of the glass will have full control of the Purloined Believers, and all their knowledge,” Priest Carvel rambled, as if he were reading from a script. “Though, those who are unworthy will instantly die. Dearest Mr. Fletcher, will you partake?”
Fletcher’s instinct was to say no. He could just end it here and now. However, a seed of doubt was in his mind.

Full control was a lot — there were countless people here. Doubtless, some of them would know what to do about the lost oil baron. Some might even know who Linda was. They were all at his fingertips, just waiting to be directed.
“Does it taste good?” Fletcher asked.
“Of course. It’s the saliva of gods. How could it not? But — but it’s poison.”
“That’s all I need to hear.”

Fletcher’s head swam with the possibilities. These people could be used for anything. There was even always the outside possibility that they could be used to mend his relationship with Margaret. Maybe — just maybe.
He downed the drink.
“Wait, you can’t drink that!” Priest Carvel said, voice going shrill. “That’s the holy drink. Only those who are chosen can partake of it!”
He leaned into Fletcher’s ear. “That was my smoothie, man. I was saving that.”

Fletcher gave a solemn nod. Then, mimicking the commanding inflections of Priest Carvel’s voice, he declared, “Only the chosen one, you say? Well, it’s a great thing that I am he! I could tell, just this morning, that everything today was going to be grand. You’ve shown me the light!”
Priest Carvel flushed red with rage. He wasn’t going to forgive this. Nonetheless, the redness faded quick as it came.

“Yes — yes, I’ve shown you the light,” said Priest Carvel. “Please remember that, ladies and gentlemen. It’s through my holy water that he was redeemed. Praises be to Allah, Jehovah, Jesus, Buddha, Zeus, Krishna… And me.”
The crowd paid no attention to Priest Carvel. Fletcher outstretched his arms, tossing his books into the crowd. People groped at him and bowed at his feet.
“I have a grand plan to bring restoration to the universe,” said Fletcher, his eyes dancing. “There are two things that I need: a toy, and the name of a certain woman.”
“A toy and a certain woman,” shouted the crowd.
“Will that save us from the certain doom?” one asked.
“What doom?” Fletcher asked. “Oh, yes… Yes, the doomsday prophecy of the chaos theorem will be undone!”
The crowd erupted.
“Does anybody know a mysterious woman named Linda, who’s building a website?” Fletcher asked.
The uproar died out, being replaced by an uncomfortable silence.

Fletcher fought back a rush of embarrassment. “It — it’s alright,” he said, raising his hands. “Have you guys seen any sign of a stolen toy? A toy oil baron, in particular? Or, are there anybody suspicious persons who might’ve stolen one? I promise — it’ll answer the divine.”
Priest Carvel shoved through the crowd and grabbed Fletcher by his jacket collar. “How on Earth will that answer the divine?” he shouted. “Are you pulling our legs?”

“No, no, I know exactly what he’s talking about!” one of the followers said, with a whoop. “The other day, I was in the healing bath for a headache… I met this odd woman, who struck me as a hoarder. She just did. And, she told me she was working for some man. She wanted to know about any valuables in the area…”
“What type of valuables?” Fletcher said, eyebrows raised.
“Anything: money, antiques, trinkets. I told her I didn’t know.”
“What did she look like?”
“Tall, slim… She had dark hair. Her face was kind of square.”

Margaret matched that description perfectly. However, she never had any relationships with strange men, so far as Fletcher could recall. Besides, was she really the kind of person who would steal? It didn’t sound like her.
“That sounds exactly like a woman that I met,” said someone. “I thought she might’ve been that pickpocket who’s been going around. At least, that’s the tingle I’m feeling in my spirit-head.”

There were a series of nods. Fletcher snatched his books back from a follower and pushed his way through the crowd. Everything was falling into place — the shunning by Margaret, the strange targeting of his favorite toy, Margaret’s evasiveness. The thief had to have been her. Why hadn’t he thought her a suspect sooner?
Nearing the exit, he and put on a smile. “Thank you for your help, purloined believers. I’ll make sure to find this person and complete my quest!”
He pumped a fist in the air, prompting a round of cheers.
“No you won’t,” said Priest Carvel, grabbing Fletcher’s sleeve. “This ‘pickpocket’ woman sounds skeevy. You can’t talk to her. It defies the code of —.”
“Well, he will,” somebody interrupted.
Fletcher looked up and beamed. Filtering through the crowd was a man with a molting head of hair.
“Marvin!” Fletcher said.
“It’s Mr. Whisk, and you’re coming with me,” Marvin said, gripping Fletcher’s other sleeve. “If none of you guys knew, the police are after this man. I need to sort that out.”
Fletcher’s eyes widened. The cops were after him. He’d completely forgotten.
“Thank you!” Fletcher said. “I knew you’d help me prove my innocence. How’d you find me?”
Marvin Whisk scoffed. “I was actually trying to get to the police.”
Marvin looked away — he was likely directing his disgust at the cult. Fletcher completely sympathized.
“He’s a sacred follower in the Purloin Believers,” Priest Carvel said to Marvin. “You’re not taking him anywhere.”
“He’s the chosen one,” the crowd chanted. “The chosen one. The chosen one.”

Marvin Whisk laughed. “The chosen one? Please, Fletcher couldn’t tell you the difference between a Bible and a door stop. Hell, I think he uses his Bible as a door stop. Plus, the cops are after him because they think he’s a drug dealer. Did I mention he’s one of the most aggravating people that I know? He’s no chosen one, that’s for sure.”
Fletcher smiled — Marvin’s plan was genius. They’d get out of here with ease, now that everybody thought he was a fraud.
Yet, the crowd wasn’t taking it as easy as Fletcher had hoped. Ruptures of anger rose through countless eyes. There were rounds of grumbling and muttering.
Somebody elbowed Fletcher, then snatched the books out of his arms.
“I’ve purloined this faker’s holy books,” they shouted. “We no longer need this fraudulent chosen one any longer.”

Priest Carvel puffed his chest, confidence surging. “Yes!” he said. “Let’s tear this faker apart, limb from limb. He’s sown doubt among us, dear faithful ones. We must show him what it truly means to be chosen.”

Priest Carvel grappled Fletcher, yanking him toward himself. Fletcher attempted to fight back, before giving in. His hands fumbled at Priest Carvel’s body, before finally reaching into his pockets. He grabbed at a knife. He winced as the blade sliced his palm, and he put it back. He found a wallet.
That could be useful.

The crowd charged on Fletcher as he pocketed the wallet, and caressed his damaged hand. They clawed at his skin and shoved him in multiple directions. The only thing moving him forward was Marvin’s steady hand.
“I’m going to die, I’m going to die, I’m going to die,” Marvin said, his voice reduced to wheezy breaths.
Fletcher glanced at his wounded palm and felt the same way.

“Maybe that’ll be a good thing,” said Fletcher, gritting his teeth against the pain. “Right about now, I want death more than anything else. At least they have some nice cushions to rest on, up in heaven. Or, so I’m told.”
As Marvin pulled Fletcher further through the crowd, the fighting dissipated.
“These followers don’t have any idea what’s going on,” said Fletcher. “If we hurry, we can get out of here.”
“Does anybody in this town have any idea what’s going on?” asked Marvin, eyes frantic. “In any case, what do you think I’m doing?”
They ran out of the house, knocking a few people over as they went.
“I think that old lady just hit the dirt,” Marvin said, with a choke.
“She’ll be fine,” said Fletcher. “Pretty sure that these people have special healing abilities.”

Marvin led Fletcher toward his dilapidated truck. Fletcher buckled himself in the crusty passenger seat, and wrapped his wounded hand with a pile of napkins. Marvin fought to bring the engine to life.
“Come on!” Marvin shouted.
Priest Carvel let out a shriek from his shack, running toward them. His cult was behind him, following at full throttle.
“You can’t just yell at a stalling engine, during a chase,” said Fletcher. “You need to punch it. It’s more dramatic.”
Fletcher gave the dashboard a heavy pound, knocking the radio box out of its place.
“What did you just do to my car?” Marvin cried.
Yet, his voice was drowned out by the roar of the engine.

Fletcher leaned back and put his hands over his head. Rocks crunched underneath, the tires accelerating away. After they’d been driving for about a minute, there were distant echoes of other cars revving. Yet, they were so far away. There was no chance of them being caught.
“Thanks Marvin,” Fletcher said. “If it weren’t for you, I’d be dead meat.”
“You still are,” Marvin said. His voice cracked. “I need to turn you in. I — the police think you’re in a gang. You need to set things right with them.”
“Turn me in? That makes no sense…”
“Neither is what you’re planning.”
“You think I have a plan? Please. I’m the antithesis of a planner.”
“You must be planning something, because it feels like you are. According to the police, you’re breaking the law… Thus, I have to turn you in.”
Fletcher nodded. He had a twinge of understanding for Marvin’s position. Marvin was just doing what made sense to him.
“Have you read the chaos equation?” Fletcher asked, his mind spinning.
The car swerved, and Marvin stammered. “Well, no. I know I’m supposed to, according to Mayor Haddock… But I’m not into the idea of being told exactly what I’m going to do before I do it.”
“Don’t you like following orders though?” Fletcher asked.
“Only when there’s no order. Once there’s a set order to everything, what’s the point in trying to have order? The order is already in place, whether you like it or not.”
“Is it? What if the order of things is for you to break order? And, what if you’re breaking that?”
Marvin gave Fletcher a look. “What do you—?”

“There’s always the possibility that you’re not supposed to drive me to the police, because even if you’re supposed to drive me to the police, you’ll be doing what you’re not supposed to do. You get me?”
“That doesn’t—.”
“You want to let me go, don’t you? We’re friends, right?”
“We’re not—.”

“You can just stop this car, step out, and let me drive off. Nobody could blame you. You wouldn’t have been able to help it — you were only doing what you were always supposed to do, because it’s what you were always going to do. The chaos theorem can’t be defied, nor controlled. So, why not just do this?”
Marvin gulped. The brakes slammed and the vehicle grinded to a halt. He popped the driver’s door and stepped out.
“I have no idea what I’m doing,” Marvin moaned.
“It’s fine,” Fletcher said, scooting to the driver’s seat and taking the wheel. He gave Marvin a wink. “Thank you.”
Marvin cradled his head in his hands, rubbing profusely. “I hate you.”
“Heh. Ever the sarcastic one, eh?”
The driver’s door swung shut, and the gas pedal pressed to the floor. Fletcher was off.
“Hit it, Mayhew!” Springs shouts at me.
Priest Carvel and a brigade of his followers are making their way through a forest, just outside his property. It’s as though he’d known we were coming.
Of course, with the chaos theorem, I suppose he did. I knew that this chase was going to happen, myself. Still, I wasn’t prepared for it to actually happen.
“This car is already going as fast as it can go!” I say to Springs.
“Good god man, we’re losing them! Next time, we take my squad car, instead of yours. This thing is a piece of crap.”
I can’t disagree with him one bit. My one chance at a serious car chase, and I’m blowing it.
Screw this job.
I hate Jack. Such a jackass. Makes us drive all the way out here, to get this loser. Why can’t we just lie to the boss, and say that this Fletcher guy offed himself before we could do anything?
“I swear, this entire place is empty,” I tell Jack, as he ruffles through the shack. “Dan Carvel knew we were coming and ditched.”
“He’s playing hide-and-seek, I swear.”
Jack doesn’t want to believe me, for whatever reason. Whatever. He can keep waltzing around this empty house for all I care. It’s not like the police are on our ass, or anything.
We’re so screwed.
Wait — there are some deep tire tracks leading into the forest. Just noticed them. Those fresh? They must be.
There are only two explanations for them. Either the postman got horribly lost from his route, or Dan Carvel took a secret trail in the forest.
Kind of having a tough time deciding. Either way, I tell Jack. He takes notice, and now we’re back in the truck. We’re driving off, into the forest.
We’re going to catch up with this Carvel guy. Hopefully we’ll find Stuart Fletcher too.
Nobody pulls one over on us and gets away with it.
Chapter 14:

Fletcher attempted parallel parking between a meaty pickup truck and a bug. He was cutting it close when he hit park and cut off the engine. He pulled his foot off the brake. The car jolted forward. There was a slight crack; the front bumper swung into the backend of the pickup truck. One of the taillights were knocked out.
It was fine. It’d be fine. Nobody looked at the taillights of other cars anyway. He looked around — weren’t any stop signs anywhere, either. Just a sign saying, “bus stop”.
He gave a sigh of relief. How was he to know when to stop his car, when the only stop signs around applied to buses?
Fletcher glanced through his phone. There were no new messages from Linda. Had she seen his email yet? Maybe she was busy.
He kept scrolling. More complaints from customers. A message from the bank.
From the bank? That was new. He crossed his fingers, hoping it was a loan approval.
“Warning: if you don’t pay your loans back by the end of tomorrow, we’re going to seize your teeny tiny little toy store away,” the email read. “Get fucked. Sincerely, Jim Harrigan”
Fletcher quivered. This email had been on the horizon, but he hadn’t expected it to come so soon.
He shook his head. It’d be fine. If he found the oil baron, he could probably sell it and make enough money.
He slipped Priest Carvel’s wallet from his pocket. There were no credit cards of any kind. He unzipped it, spilling a wad of dollar bills.
He counted them out. There were ten in total. Not bad. It would help.
He slammed his head into the car horn. Like hell it would help.
Stumbling out of Marvin’s car, he fixed his eyes toward the apartment complex across the street. Margaret’s complex.
Talking to her would be the cure to his woes. She probably had the oil baron. She had money too — maybe she’d be willing to give him a loan. Everything was going to click into place.
“Give me your bathing shorts!”
Fletcher stumbled back, being shoved into a vehicle. An alarm went off, piercing his ears.
Fletcher stared into the face of a woman with a crazed face. A broken plastic spoon was in her hand. She reeled it behind her head.
“Hey, lay off, I’m injured,” Fletcher said, raising his wounded hand. “Besides, I left my bathing shorts in my dishwasher, back at the toy shop.”
The woman gave a cry and her hand thrust forward. Fletcher’s shoulder was stabbed with the edge of her plastic spoon.
“What — what was that for?” Fletcher said, clutching the gash along his shoulder.
“I need a collection of bathing suit trunks,” the woman said. “The chaos theorem has deemed it so.”
Fletcher slid from under her and ran into the street. To his left, a stampede of people charged toward him.
“You can’t escape it,” the woman with the spoon shouted. “I tried. I used to be normal too. In the end, the calamity of reality always win out!”
Biting as the words were, Fletcher wasn’t convinced of the reality of calamity. At least, that’s what he told himself. As the crowd of people barreled on him, he reconsidered his position.
His legs pumped, speeding across the street. He slid between two cars, then rushed toward the complex. The door was just ahead.
There was a splat. A raw chicken breast hit the pavement. Several more pelted at Fletcher.
“Food fight!” somebody cried.
“What in god’s name —?” Fletcher said.

A gruff man shot from behind a car, and shoulder checked Fletcher. Fletcher teetered back and struggled to keep his balance. His foot slipped on a raw chicken breast, before he caught a sturdy hand on the brick wall.
“My wallet!” Fletcher cried.
It wasn’t his wallet, but Priest Carvel’s. Nevertheless, Fletcher scrambled toward it. Upon picking it up, he was given a swift kick to the gut.
“You going to buy my poultry, or not?” the gruff man asked.
“Please,” Fletcher said, his legs turning to sticks of butter. “I don’t want your paltry poultry. It’s on the ground, for god’s sake. I will now be on my way.”
“It tastes better after it’s been marinated by the ground, I swear. I need some money. Please!”
Shock jolted through Fletcher. He gave the man a second look and squinted. The man was John. Fletcher had been shoulder checked by one of his closest friends.
Fletcher’s horror switched to pride when he realized how great of a football player John could’ve made.
John jumped toward Fletcher, and pride switched back to horror.
“Wait, wait,” Fletcher said. “John, it’s me. What are you doing? You’ve gone nuts, John.”
John stepped back and looked on his hands. He gave them a sniff. “You’re right… I really should’ve put on gloves, before throwing raw meat around.”
“You should’ve let me put on some gloves before throwing me around, as well,” Fletcher said. “We’re friends, John. And, I thought you were getting a job!”
John’s voice broke into a shrill laugh.

“I was never getting a job,” he said. “Kent Burgess is a tightwad. Besides, the theorem says everything was always going here. I was doomed to wind up in the gutter, from the get. It was just getting there that I was getting hung up on.”
“This isn’t right. John, you’re one of the smartest people I know.”
John winced at the words. Fletcher couldn’t help but wince in return.

“I just want some money, so that I can feel alive again,” John said. He barred his teeth. “Give me some money. Be happy that your fate isn’t mine — that you can handle the chaos equation, without going insane.”

Hands trembling, Fletcher unzipped Priest Carvel’s wallet and tossed the money to the wind. While John bounded after the cash, Fletcher tried the door to the apartment complex. Annoyingly, the doorknob was busted — but, the door was also unlocked.
He didn’t bother turning his head, to see what had become of John. He couldn’t bring himself to look.

While he scaled the stairway, a paradox lapped at him. The more that people suffered under the chaos theorem, the more he wanted to take it. It wasn’t fair that he could enjoy blissful ignorance, was it? Though, he also couldn’t bring himself to go to a theorem booth. If what everybody said was true, it would be an action that couldn’t be reversed. It wasn’t worth it.
In any case, perhaps the chaos theorem had deemed that Fletcher never take it. In which case, maybe Fletcher was safe from the theorem controlling his life. Maybe.
He knocked on the door to room number 12. His racing thoughts melted away. It was just him and Margaret now. Just how it was supposed to be.
“Who in god’s name is out there?” an old woman crooned, bringing her eye to the peephole. Fletcher jumped.
“Just looking for Margaret Wilkins,” he said, stuttering. “This is room 12, right?”
“No, this is room 13! And if you knock on this door again, I’m going to yank you in this room, bash you with my rotary telephone, string you up by its wire, drag you toward the window…”

Fletcher’s skin went blotchy. He caught the faded etchings of a “13” on the door, rather than a “12”. The number “3” had chipped away a bit. Yet, when Fletcher looked at the neighboring rooms — 10, 14, 16, and onward — room 13 should’ve been room 12, even if it wasn’t.
He turned around, ignoring old woman’s rants. Whether in the right place or not, door 12 had been behind him. It was nestled just between room numbers 11 and 15
He gave another knock and bit his lip. He could only hope his knocks would be heard over the women’s shouting.
“… And then the bones will be ground up to put in my gelatin...” the old woman went on.
“Who is it?” Margaret asked.
There was no doubting it was Margaret. Dozens of memories streamed through Fletcher, at the mere sound of her voice.
“Is this room 12?” Fletcher asked.
Margaret let out a shout of epithets, joining in with the old lady from across the hall. The hallway devolved into a chaotic cacophony
“I thought I told you to stay away from me!” Margaret shrieked. “I’m calling the cops if you don’t get away from my door!”
“I’m bleeding,” Fletcher said. Suddenly, he was glad he’d been stabbed in the neck. “I’m injured, and I’m bleeding. I need help, and I thought room 12 might be able to help me.”

“Well, this isn’t room 12,” Margaret said bitterly. “Seriously, it isn’t — when the landlord decided to put engravings on our doors, he labeled them backwards. He didn’t even bother trying to fix it, so the address stuck. But, I technically should be room 13.”
Fletcher laughed. “Just my luck.”

Margaret made slight chuckle back. It died quickly as it came. “I need you to get away from my door,” she said. “I don’t care why you came here. Nothing is going to change. We’re through, and I never want to see you again.”
Fletcher’s eyes burned. They’d been through so much together. And she was just going to cast him aside, just like that.
“I need a bandage,” Fletcher said. “All you have to do is open the door a crack and push a bandage out. Then, I’ll be on my way. I promise.”
Margaret didn’t give a response. Yet, Fletcher listened as she pattered to the kitchen. There was the shuttering of cabinets and drawers.
One of Margaret’s green eyes peeked out of the peephole. The door clicked as the top lock unlocked.
Another click. The door cracked open slightly, and the bandage tumbled out. Just as she went to shut it, Fletcher shoved his hand in the gap, propping the door open.
“Ow —my fingers,” he said. “God, I think you broke one of my fingers.”
Blood had already been pouring through his palm. The fresh pain in his fingers only made the bleeding worse.
“Get your hand out of my door,” Margaret said.
“It hurts so much.”
The door loosened, and the pain lessened. Margaret stepped out, her face stolid. However, Fletcher caught a flicker of a smile pass over her face. Possibly.
“Come in, and let me look at that,” she said. “Then, I don’t want to see you again. I’m serious.”

Fletcher scooped up the bandage and entered the apartment, caressing his wounded hand. To each side of him was a coat rack and a hat rack. Keeping his jacket on, he looked for a place to put his shoes. He left them under the coat rack.
Margaret’s brow arched.
“Sorry, I just don’t want to dirty your carpet,” Fletcher said, gesturing at a crusty floor. “Those new, by the way? Because, they look brand new.”
“I’ve had them for about a year,” said Margaret. “Bought them in a half off sale — half pay for twice what it’s worth. Not like you’d know anything about that…”
“I don’t know anything about a lot of things,” Fletcher said, unabashedly. “I think it’s part of what makes me so successful. Ignorance is bliss, right?”
“Last I checked, you weren’t successful at anything.”

Margaret pulled out a first-aid kit and brought over a chair. Fletcher sat in it, letting his shoulder be dabbed by a disinfectant wipe. A stinging ran through his nerves, which crisscrossed over themselves.
“I was successful at getting in here, wasn’t I?”

Margaret smiled. She scoffed. “I know you, Stuart. You didn’t just come here because you miss me. And, I’m not just fixing you up because I care about you. Deep down, we both want something: namely, to go insane. I’m just crazy enough to admit it, and somehow still go along with it.”
Fletcher swallowed as the bandage coiled taut around his wound.

“Okay, fine… I need a loan, for one thing,” Fletcher said. “Your parents still have money, right? Because, I’m about to go out of business. Been thinking about becoming an ice cream man, but somehow that doesn’t appeal to me.”
Margaret wrapped another bandage around Fletcher’s hand in hard, rigid movements.
“I don’t rely on others for money anymore,” Margaret said. “I’ve grown up, Fletcher.”
Fletcher blinked. “I need help with a loan. That’s all I’m asking for. What, did the chaos theorem tell you that you can’t help me, or something?”
“Not sure what you’re talking about.” She stood and reclipped the first-aid kit. “But I think it’s time for you to get out. This was a bad idea. I wasn’t prepared for this.”
She tipped the chair, dumping Fletcher out.
“Get your shoes on, and leave,” she said.
The apartment’s walls seemed to bend inward, turning on him. He took note of the various pictures Margaret had — all of them were her together with Harry. They made him feel alone. Left behind.
“You can’t make me leave,” Fletcher said.
Margaret pulled out her phone. “Oh yes I can.”
“There’s so much I need to ask you about,” Fletcher said. “The oil baron, for one — did you steal the oil baron?”
Margaret shook her head, lips furling in disgust.
“I know that you stole it!” Fletcher went on. “You had to have. All of the evidence points towards it being you.”
“You need to get out,” Margaret said. Her face was harsh. “I thought you’d finally gone clean, but clearly you still need help.”
“Please, are you honestly telling me that all the stuff I saw from those drug dealers was bunk?”
Margaret’s jaw slacked. “You’re working with drug dealers now?”
“You knew that the toy oil baron would be extremely valuable to me, and you stole him.”
“I haven’t been within ten miles of your ugly toy shop in over a year.”
Fletcher ignored the horror on her face and surged ahead. “Well, tell me that I’m crazy about this then: you’ve been ghosting me, as a woman named ‘Linda’, online. It all lines up. You’re Linda.”

Margaret raised a finger and tilted her head into her phone. “Hello? Yes, officer? Stuart Fletcher has broken into my apartment and refuses to leave. Yes, he’s the man I have a restraining order against. Yes. Yes.”
She shot Fletcher a look of pure venom and put down the phone.
“It’s over, Fletcher,” Margaret said. “You can walk out of here on your own, and never talk to me again. Or, we can have the police walk you out of here. Your choice.”
Fletcher shook his head. “I’m sorry — I must’ve been mistaken about all those accusations I made,” he said. “Really, I had no idea that this conversation was going to get so toxic.”
“There’s always a conversation, Fletcher. It always goes south. And, I always have to sit back and pretend that everything is alright. Not anymore.”

“You don’t understand, Margaret. The entire city is after me, right now. The police, a gang, a cult… They all want to kill me. See, I’m one of the few people in town that hasn’t taken in the chaos theorem. It makes them out to get me.”
Margaret had moved to her kitchen and was ruffling through her drawers. She put the first aid kit back.

“You need some serious help,” she said, with a choke. “If you came here for opioids, I don’t have anymore. I can’t take care of you. You have to get out of here before this escalates into something we regret.”
Fletcher’s eyes misted over.
“I’m sorry that I blamed you,” Fletcher said. “I really am. It all seemed to fit. But, I can’t go on without you. I need you in my life. Margaret, we’re meant for each other.”
Margaret shook her head. Her face was hot and puffy. Her posture was rumpled. With trembling arms, she took a step forward.
“No,” she said. “No, no, no. No going back.”

“Remember our second date? When we went to that picnic?” Fletcher laughed. “I brought banana and peanut butter sandwiches, instead of turkey sandwiches. Had to have been one of the biggest fails of the day. We had so much fun.”
Crinkles of disgust mapped Margaret’s nose. “The type of sandwich wasn’t the problem. The bread was moldy, and you still tried to make me eat it.”
“I don’t remember that. In any case, new experiences are what life is made of. Remember that time when we went to the museum, and I tried touching the —.”
“I don’t remember, and don’t want to. It never worked, and it never will. There’s a reason why we were only together for four months.”
“It didn’t feel like four months… They must’ve been the longest four months of my life,” Fletcher said, grinning.
Margaret shook her head. “Yeah, they were the longest four months of my life too.”
Fletcher took another look around the room and noted the large number of posters for Mayor Haddock. Margaret had always been quite politically active. Though, never to this extent.
Perhaps her advertising agency was paying off after all.

“’Don’t vote for the guy who doesn’t even like honey, honey…’” Fletcher monotoned, reading one of the flyers sitting on Margaret’s coffee table. “’Vote for the guy who cares.’ Have to say, that’s almost convincing. Who wrote that?”

“Haddock came up with it himself,” Margaret said, proudly. She skimmed cabinets in her kitchen, before pulling out a stack of flyers. Mayor Haddock’s face was emblazoned on them all, his teeth white as bone. Bare bones as the slogans were, something about him bore down on Fletcher.
Fletcher snorted and kicked his legs up. “If you wanted to get me out of this apartment, I think you’re finally starting to succeed. That guy is pathetic.”

Margaret’s face furled in disgust, clearly affronted. “Mayor Haddock is among the few people still fighting for change in this town. He’s already drafting a plan to figure out the problems with President Marigold, the Chinese and the Russians… He’s going to erase drugs completely. And Kent Burgess — he’s going to give him tax incentives to completely expand. He can probably save our country.”
She held up a coffee mug that had Mayor Haddock mugging on it.
“Come on, Stuart,” she said, “tell me that he doesn’t look impressive. He’s going to plaster these all over his fundraiser. It’s today.”
“Looks like he’s had a silver spoon in his mouth since birth, in his mansion off 123 Rich-boy Avenue,” Fletcher sneered. “You like him, don’t you?”
“It’s in Otto’s Grove, and I’ll have you know: me and Harry are happy together. I happen to be running Mayor Haddock’s advertising campaign for him.”
Fletcher’s eyes went fierce. That was the first confirmation she and Harry were an item.
“Oh, that explains everything,” Fletcher said. “And I’m sure that he’s not hiding every corrupt thing from you, right? He has no ulterior motives, and is so much better than me?”
“It’s not,” Margaret stuttered. She couldn’t tell if Fletcher had been talking about Harry or Haddock. Fletcher couldn’t either. Her eyes betrayed a bit of distrust. “It’s not like that.”
“You sure?”
Margaret shifted her stance, her gaze dodgy.

“Haddock has been courting a lot of crazy people…” Margaret said. “Potential donors, I guess. There’s this one guy who drives me up the wall. An eccentric collector. I swear he’s a kleptomaniac. People even say he’s a crook, just trying to gain political sway. But I mean, that’s what you have to —.”
The room froze in time.
“Kleptomaniac?” Fletcher asked. “Sounds like somebody I’m looking for. Tell me more about him.”
Margaret covered her hand over her mouth and hung her head. “I shouldn’t have told you any of this. This was all a huge mistake.”
“What? Is there something personal about this person?”
She looked up, eyes flaring. “You shouldn’t even be here!”
Fletcher smirked. “Where did you say Haddock lived again? Otto’s Grove?”
“No!” Margaret said. “You leave him alone! Go on your crazy antics someplace else! He has nothing to do with you!”
Sirens wailed. They were distant, but sliced Fletcher to the heart.
“I have a fundraiser to get to. I guess this is it between us?” Fletcher asked. He clenched his hand into a fist, fighting off a quivering.
He had his answers. Margaret never cared from the start, and it was time to move on.
“We never should’ve been a thing to begin with!” Margaret shouted.
“No, we shouldn’t have.”
Fletcher’s head throbbed. He took the prompt, shutting the door behind him.
“High Priest, almighty. Are you sure that we’re going to the right place?”

I shake my head, before bobbing it up and down. How on Earth am I supposed to know if we’re going to the right place? I mean — I know it’s the place that the chaos theorem said we were supposed to be at. But then, the chaos theorem isn’t supposed to be right, is it? At this point, it’s hard to say.
Either way, my methods are foolproof.
I skim through one of the books we’ve stolen from Fletcher.

“Fletcher must’ve circled that women’s address in that book for a reason,” I say, as I reach the page of a Margaret Wilkins. “Plus, I heard him talking to her on the phone. He’s with her, with god as my witness. There’s no way I’m wrong.”
Also, I took a good load of spiritual enlightenment before this trip. That always helps.
“Do you want another injection of the spirit?” my lackey asks, again.
“Yeah,” I say. “Praises be. It always helps.”
Chapter 15:
The sirens rang in Fletcher’s ears, before cutting off entirely. The police had arrived
“Where do I go?” he muttered to himself.

If he went to the roof, he could hop from building to building. Frogs could jump far enough to do that, right? Surely, he was at least as strong as a frog. Of course, maybe he could just take the elevator down. The police couldn’t possibly recognize him.
“Looks like I’m going down,” he finally said.
“Damn right,” the old woman cried, from behind her door. “Get the hell out of my apartment complex you moron, before I tear you a new larynx!”
“Will do, ma’am,” Fletcher said.
His fingers pushed frantically against the elevator button. Though, no matter how hard he pressed, the elevator didn’t move any faster. It were as though it was taunting him.
The door gave a ding.
“Finally!” Fletcher said, with a whoop.
He stepped into the elevator, only to accidentally bump into one of the passengers.
“Sorry about that,” Fletcher said, giving the passengers half a look, and pressing “Floor 1” on the elevator.
He gave the passengers a second look. The passenger he’d bumped into was a burly police officer, who’d been standing among two others.
“It’s alright, we were just leaving,” one of the officers said, pulling a pair of dark shades to his face. The other officers did the same, as if in sync. Fletcher squinted — it was Officer Mayhew.
The other officers stepped out, and the doors began to shut. Mayhew used his foot to prop the door open, just before they closed.
“Say,” he said, clearing his throat. “You wouldn’t happen to have seen this gentleman mucking about, would you?”
He held a picture of Fletcher, from only a few months prior. He was slightly happier, and healthier looking. It was from long before the chaos theorem had taken its toll.
“Don’t recognize that man at all,” said Fletcher.
Officer Mayhew looked at Fletcher, then back at the photo. He pulled his sunglasses off to give them a rub, then placed them back on his face. He whistled.

“Yeah, guess I shouldn’t be too surprised,” Officer Mayhew said. “Master criminals like this — they’re great at hiding in plain sight. I swear, we need to put electric shock collars on all criminals. It’d solve all our problems in a jiffy.”
Officer Mayhew tipped his police cap, and the elevator door shut.
Fletcher ran to the street, through a fresh hive of people. They were as frenzied and crazed as John had been. Yet, they were also oblivious to Fletcher, moving like zombies.
“Crud,” Fletcher said.
Marvin’s truck and the truck it’d crashed into were gone. They must’ve been towed away.
This day was getting better and better. Losing the truck, losing his girlfriend, being chased down by everybody in town. He kicked at a signpost. Nothing was working.
There was a ding from his phone. Fletcher looked down. He gushed with a fresh pride.
It was Linda. She’d emailed back.
“Anything for you,” she said. “Make sure to bring it there, as soon as possible. I’ll do anything you need.”

Fletcher’s eyes bulged, and he lingered on the last words. They were the antithesis to everything Margaret had been. Despite the tundra of people he’d just walked out through, his chest felt light. Warm.

“Going to be honest,” he typed. His tongue hung in the corner of his mouth. Hopefully all the right intentions would come across. “I’m doing real bad, right now. I need somebody to talk to. It also might be a bit before I can go to the alley. Also, I might not be able to bring you the money when we do meet. You’re the best!”
He hit send. Maybe him and Margaret were over. Yet, he still had a chance with somebody. At least, there was a chance he had a chance.
He turned around and jumped.
A dozen of the townspeople had been standing over his shoulder, watching what he wrote.
“Dear god, what are you guys doing?” he said. “Can’t you leave a guy in peace?”
“We can’t, because the theorem says,” one said.
“The theorem says that this many of you are supposed to be here, for no reason?”
They nodded. “We’re meant to go on the bus, to nowhere.”
“I have no idea what you guys are—.”
Fletcher smirked. Just down the street was the Dexburg bus. He could see the bus driver’s face through the window — his expression of absolute apathy could be recognized from anywhere.
Tire’s screeched. A large black van careened to a stop behind Fletcher.
“Stop!” Priest Carvel cried. “You aren’t going to get away, Mr. Fletcher! The lord of bananas deems it so!”
He had his head hanging out the van’s passenger window. His van was first in a caravan of several vans, all of which were part of Priest Carvel’s cult.
“Sorry old man, but he’s ours!”
A gunshot went off. Jack and Clair barreled beside the caravan, in their shaggy pickup truck.
“Fletcher!” Marvin wheezed from far in the distance. He was atop a dinky bike, sweat pouring down his face. “Where the hell is my truck?”
Fletcher’s head spun. This wasn’t supposed to be happening all at once. It were as though fate itself had forced his pursuers all to unite in this one spot.

The bus banked to a halt, and the door sighed open. A stream of people bumbled in. Fletcher pushed his way forward but was jostled by a mess of shoulders and elbows. The door to the bus shuddered, threatening to shut.
“Wait! Wait for me!” Fletcher said. He tried catching the bus driver’s eye, but the driver’s eyes were half-closed.
Fletcher glanced back. The priest, the thugs, and Marvin were almost on him. Grimacing, he stretched out his bandaged hand, shoving it between the door. It was already bandaged — what would it hurt?
Fletcher cried out. The door cried with him, its gears grinding. God, it hurt!
“Looks like you have nowhere to run,” Clair said. She’d jumped out of the truck and was reloading her gun. “That is, unless you want to run to me. That’s somewhere you have left, I guess.”
Officer Mayhew stumbled into her, knocking her over. His mustache was wild. “Stop in the name of… The name of god?”
Fletcher banged on the bus door, striving to ignore the pain coursing through him.

“Hey guys, do I need to read him his Miranda Rights before I arrest him?” Officer Mayhew asked, his voice suddenly unsteady. He readjusted his belt. “Or, can I just remain silent? Because, I kind of have trouble remembering them…”

Officer Mayhew was rendered mute as an earthquake erupted, putting him off balance. Gargoyles tumbled from one of the buildings, falling into cars below. Both Jack and Marvin ran back, rubble falling in their path.
“Oh my god!” Officer Mayhew cried, as a gargoyle fell into his crap cop car. “My baby!”
He went after it, when a stampede of Priest Carvel’s cult members trampled over him.

“Behold, my holy army!” Priest Carvel said, leading the forefront. The earthquake was still in full force, causing bits of brick and dust to fall into his path street. “God himself is fighting on our side.”
The bus door shuttered back open. Fletcher scrambled in, only barely getting a glimpse of Priest Carvel tripping over his robe.
“Gun it to Otto’s Grove, stat! I need to see Haddock!”
The bus door closed back up, with Fletcher still climbing the steps.
The bus driver gave Fletcher a glare.
“I have a route to take, and we’re at full capacity,” he said. “These people need me to take them to the toll bridge, and out of this town.”
Fletcher looked down the bus, to see every seat crammed full. He looked back out the bus door. The earthquake had stopped, but his pursuers were still clamoring to get in.
“Look I’ll pay you…” Fletcher rummaged through his pockets, only to come up empty. Priest Carvel’s wallet only had a few stray coins.
For a split-second, he considered bringing up the chaos theorem to convince the bus driver. Though, the bus driver’s scowl told him that he’d be unwilling to put up with nonsense.
“I’ll scrape all the gum from the bottom of your seats,” Fletcher said. “You know me. I drive your bus all the time.”
The bus driver shrugged his shoulders. “Whatever. Steal yourself a seat… It’s not as though things haven’t already gone off course today.”

The bus pulled out from its spot and turned the corner. Clusters of people jumped in its path, attempting to bring it to a stop. The bus driver didn’t bother, picking up speed and chuckling as people had to dive away.

The bus trembled. Had they run somebody over. It was probably another earthquake. Besides, the people in this town weren’t worth worrying about anyway. Fletcher squatted on the bus steps. His eyes glazed over as the bus made its way through town. They passed numerous decaying shops, and dejected people. Dexburg had gotten old, since Fletcher was born. When did that happen?
Fletcher’s phone rumbled in his pocket. His heart skipped a beat. Linda? No, it couldn’t be. It wasn’t possible. He pulled his phone out of his pocket — it was Harry. What could he possibly want?
Reluctantly, Fletcher answered it.
“Where the hell are you?” Harry yelled. “Margaret just called me! What’s going on? Didn’t I tell you to stay out of trouble?”
Fletcher considered pulling the phone away and hanging up entirely.
“I’m just doing what I told you I’d do,” Fletcher said, reluctantly. “Is that so wrong?”

“Fletcher, this isn’t about what you told me you’d do. This is about what you should do.  Give this up. Go take the chaos theorem, like the rest of us. Become sane again. The world doesn’t revolve around you, Fletcher…”
“Have you seen what happened to John?” Fletcher asked.
“He’s just hit a rough patch. I’m telling you — you can keep your head about you. Just do what I say and abandon all this. Life can still go back to normal.”
Fletcher shook his head. “I’m sorry. You’ve deluded yourself. I can’t listen to any more of this.”
He hung up the phone and went through his emails. Linda had responded.
“If we can’t talk in the alley, maybe we should just talk now. How’s life?”
Fletcher couldn’t help himself. He poured it all out in email —his thoughts on the chaos theorem, his failing business…
He thought about bringing up the toy chase. His friendship struggles. Margaret. His uncle.
Though, a twinge shot through him. That would be like pulling off a bandage.
Certain parts of the past were best left private. Nevertheless, it was reassuring to know there was somebody out there, who felt just like him.
“I’m telling you Jack, I heard him say something about Mayor Haddock and Otto’s Grove,” I say.
He doesn’t want to listen to me. Classic Jack. Though, I can already see the priest and the police listened. They’re heading to their vehicles, to go catch this Fletcher guy.
“Well, it’s not as though I remember anything from the chaos theorem,” Jack says, face contorted. “Do we catch him? Do we not? It’s tough to say.”
“We could go check on the chaos theorem again,” I suggest.
I think it makes perfect sense. Though, Jack only seems more infuriated.
“I don’t want to go back. If we go back and listen to the theorem, we suddenly become part of the theorem. And, we can’t become part of the theorem, because we want to be in the theorem — not of it.”
My mind twists, attempting to wriggle its way through Jack’s logic. However, the task is unforgiving.
“Hallelujah! In the equation, but not of it! You can say that again!” shouts the Priest.
I give Jack a glare. “We’re going to Otto’s Grove, just to make sure.”
My phone rumbles in my pocket. I pull it out and show it to Jack. It’s Logan.
“I’m going to tell the boss what’s going on,” I say. “Now, do you want me to tell him that you don’t want to go to Otto’s Grove?”
Jack gives me a sheepish look.
“I’ll go, so long as I get to kill somebody before the end of today,” he says. “I bought myself a new knife. You better have a reason for me to use it.”
Chapter 16:
The bus door creaked open. Fletcher tumbled out, hoping to get ahead of the other passengers. They knocked him on the head and clamored past him. He was left curled on the ground, gasping for breath.
“Good luck, moneybags,” the bus driver said. He spat. “Next time, I expect more than scraping gum off my seats. You owe me cash, and a pedicure while you’re at it.”
The bus drove away, leaving Fletcher to pray that the bus driver wouldn’t cash in on his pedicure request.
An explosion went off. Fletcher gave a jump, then looked to the sky. The dimmest of fireworks were exploding in the air.
“That was the big one,” somebody said. “Wasn’t it impressive?”
Who was the genius who decided to launch fireworks in the daytime?

He looked to both sides of himself. All down the street were gated driveways, undoubtedly leading to oversized houses on hilltops. A large line of people had formed in front of a specific house. What were they gathered for?

Although he searched for the answer, Fletcher’s eyes become lost among the river between two hills. It sparkled a crystal green, and the spire of Kent Burgess’ smokestack gleamed along the edge of it.
Somebody stepped on Fletcher’s heel, nearly knocking him over. They snickered. “See, I told you he was a wax figure!”
Their buddy snickered with them. “I’m still not so sure…”
Fletcher limped to the front of the line, before running into a heavyset man dressed in black. Fletcher was given a shove back and colliding into a brick wall
“Is this Mayor Haddock’s place?”  Fletcher asked, attempting assertiveness.
Ahead of the guard was yet another line, winding down the block.
“Excuse me,” Fletcher said, cutting between the guard and the line.
“You’re excused,” the bodyguard said. “Now, back of the line.”
“But I — I’m important, see.”
“That’s what they all say. Last person I talked to said he was some internet celebrity, for cooking dinners or something… Doesn’t mean I’ll let you in.”
The bodyguard glowered over Fletcher. Fletcher counted the veins and muscles pulsating beneath the guard’s skin.
“What if I was the sole arbiter of God’s great word?” Fletcher said, suddenly.
Having no idea what had taken over him, he pulled Priest Carvel’s wallet from his pocket and shoved it toward the bodyguard’s face.
“I’m the highest of high priests, in all of town,” Fletcher continued. “Surely I’m on the list.”
The bodyguard looked at his list. He looked at Fletcher’s fake ID card.
“You’re right,” he said, with a grunt. “I guess you can head on in.”
The gates shuttered open, and Fletcher slipped through. Immediately, a crowd of people groped at his coattails, straining to force themselves through.
“Don’t worry, you guys will make it eventually,” Fletcher said, despite not believing his words.
“No we won’t,” they said. “The chaos theorem deems it so.”
The chaos theorem couldn’t be wrong about everything.

He strode past various socialites, who clinked glasses and laughed amongst each other. He frowned inwardly. There were so many of them up here, living high on the horse. They were utterly cut off from the suffering throughout town.
It was wrong —he should’ve been living up here with these people.
Such an idiot.

He walked by a group setting fireworks into the air. Fire flared in their faces as the rockets went off — some of them even caught bits of their clothing on fire. Nonetheless, every time the fireworks went off they clapped.
“It’ll be fine,” one of the people consoled a woman, as she tried putting her enflamed dress out. “Just enjoy the show. Fire burns people every day, and I’ve never once been harmed by it.”
Fletcher studied the faces, looking for the glib face of Mayor Haddock. He had to be around here somewhere.
“Looking for someone?”

A reedy looking man tapped Fletcher on the shoulder. The man was done up in a tight suit, and drew his glasses close to his face. Overall, he seemed composed. Though, he had the odd quirk of a bowtie cinched overtop a regular tie.
Perhaps he hadn’t looked in the mirror?
“I just need to talk with Mayor Haddock,” Fletcher said. “You know where he might be?”
The man laughed.
“Yes, of course,” he said. He outstretched his hand. “I’m Mr. Pardus, by the way. I’m the historian at a prestigious college, here in Dexburg.”
“I’m — I’m Priest Carvel,” Fletcher said. “Of a great religion. Also, I didn’t realize we had a college here in Dexburg. That is, aside from Dexburg Community College.”
“We don’t,”
“Oh. Ha, of course. Sorry.”
He went to give Mr. Pardus a handshake when Mr. Pardus snatched his hand away and pulled it down the side of his head.
“You have to be fast, or you’ll be stuck in the past,” Mr. Pardus said, with a wink.
Fletcher began to laugh, only for Mr. Pardus cut him off.
“So, you said that you need to talk to Mayor Haddock? I can walk you to him — he’s just inside, getting prepared for this big bash.”
Mr. Pardus became a peacock, weaving between waiters and guests. He sprung up the steps to Mayor Haddock’s mansion, giving Fletcher only the briefest glance back.
Fletcher ran after him, hoping his heart wouldn’t fly out of his throat.
“What do you need to talk to Haddock about, anyway?” Mr. Pardus asked.

He made a curt smile and gave Fletcher a lookover. He popped the doors to Mayor Haddock’s mansion. Fletcher rubbed his bandaged hand, suddenly aware of how shabby his clothes were. Maybe he could steal something from somebody in the bathroom.
“Well?” Mr. Pardus said, with a snap.
They rushed down a maple hued gallery, with portraits of various rock musicians along the walls. Fletcher strained to recognize any of them.
“Oh — well, there’s something I’m looking for,” Fletcher said.
“Isn’t there always something?” Mr. Pardus asked, chuckling to himself. “Hell, I was looking for you only a few minutes ago.”
Fletcher was going to ask why but stopped to dodge a waiter who came running at him.
“The chaos theorem,” Mr. Pardus said, as if that explained anything.
What was the chaos theorem supposed to be, that it could answer any problem, and create every problem at the same time?

“I’m looking for a valuable possession of mine,” Fletcher continued. “I’m led to believe that it was stolen by a pickpocket who’s been going around town. And, apparently Mayor Haddock knows somebody that sounded like a pickpocket to me.”

Mr. Pardus nodded, dragging Fletcher through a bedroom. His straw legs jumped atop the plush bed and paced around, before finally settling down. “I might just know a thing or two about that. Maybe more. Yes — isn’t it just wonderful how our leadership is so intimately involved with the criminal element? Sometimes, it’s hard to discern the difference. And letting that pickpocket around… Bleh.”
“You — you know the pickpocket too?”
“I know enough to know that he’s real bad news, yeah. Or she… That part is real inconsistent, depending on who you talk to.”
“That actually lines up with—.”
“Save it for the Mayor.”

There was a thick smell of aftershave about the room. Running water echoed behind the walls. Light poured from underneath what must’ve been a bathroom door. His muscles tensing, Fletcher searched for a place to sit. Though, nothing looked comfortable.
Mr. Pardus lounged further back in the bed, staring at the ceiling fan.
“Mayor Haddock should be just in there, by the way,” he said, “probably hanging in his hot tub. He’ll be out soon, I’m sure. Just have to wait it out.”
“And you’re sure that we’re fine in his bedroom? Couldn’t we wait out in the hall?”
“Please, people come in and out of his room all the time! This is practically the city’s room. We’re fine!”
“What if he comes out undressed, and isn’t expecting us?”
Mr. Pardus gave a knowing smile. “I’m sure he’d love that. Be a climactic topper, to his day.”
For all the confidence that Mr. Pardus asserted, his words didn’t seem true.
“So, might as well burn some time,” said Mr. Pardus. “After reading the theorem, I’ve wondered: how is it, doing what you do?”

Fletcher sighed. “I mean, being a toy shop owner sucks. I have to do a ton of web development on the side. I would just abandon it, but there’s this whole thing with my uncle’s legacy… It tugs on me real hard.”
Mr. Pardus smirked. “You operate a toy shop, develop websites, and are a priest?”
The words were a sledgehammer to Fletcher’s gut. He moved from his place, knocking a set of Russian nesting dolls to the ground. He bent down, fumbling the pieces in his hands.
“Of course,” Fletcher said. “My holy connection to the spirit world keeps me constantly awake. I need something to do with that time. Besides —I need money.”
“A man of faith, needing money? Funny.”
“Yes, well… Learning to live with contradictions is part of the faith, I believe. At least, I think…”
Mr. Pardus’ face switched from smug to sympathetic. He readjusted his tie. Then, his bowtie. “No, I get it. Completely. I’m a walking contradiction myself.”
“Yeah, the bowtie and the tie…”
“Beg my pardon!” Mr. Pardus gave a huff. “What’s wrong with having a tie and a bow tie together? You have something against the bi-tie?”
“No, no. It’s just—.”
“No matter. My true contradiction is that I’m a historian who… Well, I hate history. Past history, that is. Though, I love new history.”
Fletcher had very nearly finished putting the nesting dolls back together, when they fell back to the ground.
“What?” Fletcher said, with annoyance.
“New history? You’ve never heard of it? All of the old history is clearly baloney… Bottled up by stodgy historians, to make us feel confined to a single sense of place.”
“I’m not sure I follow…”

“Did you know that the Americans never betrayed the British, for example? No, no. They loved the British, and they loved taxes. They loved them so much, in fact, that the British practically gifted them freedom.”
“Hmm… Yes, I do think I remember hearing that.”

Mr. Pardus jumped on the bed, l limbs wild. “No you didn’t! Nobody has heard it before! It’s new history. I just made it. See, history changes based upon the history of the present and the future. It moves, to fit with where our head space is now. I understand that my theory makes causality a casualty… But, in truth, causality was always a myth. The chaos theorem proves it!”
“So, you’re telling me George Crum didn’t invent the potato chip? Some other guy did?”
“Crummy, but yes. We must let the chips fall how they may.”
“And Napoleon never lost at the battle of Waterloo?”

“Of course. Why, Napoleon was never born in the first place! Look, my fellow historians already agree that Edison didn’t really invent the lightbulb… And Columbus didn’t truly discover America. We’ve been being lied to about the little things since birth. Sucking it from our binkies, without a blink. How much of a stretch is it to assume that it’s all been lies? That history is constantly changing, without our knowledge?”
Fletcher shook his head and listened for the running water of Mayor Haddock’s bathroom. Hopefully he’d be out soon. “I guess it’s a way of taking things.”

“It’s the only way. The chaos theorem proves that the entire future is mapped out and set in stone. Thus, what does the past matter really? It has no tangible bearing on anything. Unless we can touch and observe the past, it didn’t exist. Not really.”
“That’s not true, though. Yesterday… After starting my morning, I brushed my teeth. That can’t change.”

“Only because you believe it can’t. If you believe you had brushed your hair instead, even if you didn’t, who’s to say you didn’t? The truth is, you did, even if you didn’t, because that’s what your brain says you did.”
Fletcher’s brain said Mr. Pardus’ reasoning was utterly off. Though, he had no way of articulating why.
“History is what we make of it,” Mr. Pardus said, ruffling the bedsheets, “nothing more. Don’t make more out of it than you have to.”

The repaired nesting doll was carefully placed on Mayor Haddock’s mantelpiece. Flecks of dust whirled about, falling atop the doll. Was it in the right spot? Fletcher rolled his eyes — what did it matter? As if the Mayor would notice.
The doorknob to the bathroom turned, and the door swung open. There was a scream. Fletcher jumped, then burrowed under Mayor Haddock’s covers.
“Get the hell out of my room!”
Peeking out from under the sheets, Fletcher watched a candlestick hurtle toward him. He tried going back under, only for the candlestick to smack him in the face.
“No, it’s fine!” Mr. Pardus said. “It’s just me, and one other guy.”
Fletcher pulled himself from out of under the sheets and stared at Mayor Haddock. His dingy mop of hair was done up in curlers, and a bathrobe did a shoddy job of obscuring his flabby body.
This was the guy who Fletcher thought was a threat of stealing Margaret from him?
Mayor Haddock’s eyes were locked on Mr. Pardus. His lips spread into a smile.
“Oh, hey Mr. Pardus,” he said. “You gave me such a scare!”
“Sorry about that. I figured you’d be expecting me.”
“Yeah, but not like this,” Mayor Haddock said. “Anyway, how’s your latest history paper coming along?”

“Oh, just great,” Mr. Pardus said. He lounged languidly. “You might’ve loved what the last one did in furthering the cause of ‘new history’. But, this one? Everybody in town is going to devour, and finally get it.”
“Good,” Mayor Haddock said. “’New history’ will definitely be key to winning me this election.”
He chuckled and gave Mr. Pardus a pat on the back. He then rummaged through his drawers, moving through piles of socks.
“So, who’s the slobby looking hobo over there?”

It occurred to Fletcher that he couldn’t tell Mayor Haddock he was Priest Carvel. Mayor Haddock knew Priest Carvel well enough to put on the top of his guest list, he would automatically recognize Fletcher as a poser.
Mr. Pardus glanced over, as though Fletcher were no more than a pest on the wall. “He’s just priest—.”
“I’m — I’m Marvin Whisk,” Fletcher said, drowning Mr. Pardus out.
“That’s odd, I don’t remember inviting a Marvin Whisk,” Mayor Haddock began, drowning out Mr. Pardus’ attempts at protestation. “Have we met—?"
Fletcher lifted the candlestick, and smacked Mr. Pardus in the head. Mr. Pardus rolled back, unconscious.
Mayor Haddock’s socks dropped to the floor, followed by his jaw. “What was that for?”
Mr. Pardus’ slumped head looked at Fletcher serenely, as if taunting him to come up with an explanation. Fletcher gulped.
“This is a demonstration of why you shouldn’t throw candlesticks at people,” Fletcher said. “As you can see, they can be dangerous.”
“You knocked out one of the most important people in my campaign,” Mayor Haddock said. He looked up, and blinked. “Who am I kidding? He should be easy to replace. You want a job on my campaign?”
Mayor Haddock leaned on his bed and pulled his socks on. He shimmied into his pants.
“That’d be great, really,” said Fletcher. “But, I’m here to get a few questions answered, first.”

Mayor Haddock snorted. “Don’t tell me that you’re one of those petty journalists. For the last time: the deal with the President, me, the Chinese, and the Russians is underway. Our city will be fine.”
“No, it has nothing to do with that,” Fletcher said. “I’m no journalist. I’m actually trying to… Run for senator. In another town. The town just over, actually.”

Mayor Haddock gave a look of reverence. “A senator, eh? So that’s why I invited you. Good.” He sighed in relief. “Great. Glad I don’t have to keep lying to you. Because, yeah… Dexburg is totally screwed.”
The words prowled around the room. Fletcher squirmed back in the bed, hoping to avoid their full bite.

“Don’t worry,” Fletcher said, more to himself than Mayor Haddock. “A screwed city sounds like just another day with you in office, to me.” Fletcher paused and gave a firm nod. “Anyway, there’s this pickpocket who’s been going around town. That’s what I really need to talk to you about. See, he stole something of mine, and I need to get ahold of him.”
“Pickpocket?” Mayor Haddock nodded. “Ah, yes… That guy.”
“So, you know him! Can you tell me anything about him?” Fletcher asked.
Mayor Haddock pulled down his shirt and tightened his belt around the waist.
“Not his name,” Mayor Haddock said. “He really doesn’t want to let that get out. He hasn’t even told me his name before.”
“What about what he looks like?”

“Well, he’s always wearing a mask… I’m fine with it. Money is money, no matter how you get it. But yeah, I have no idea what he looks like. He could be a Russian, for all I know. Boy, would the journalists love that!”
He let out a laugh, buttoning the jacket to his suit. He pulled a pack of powder from his breast pocket.
“Ah, that hits the spot,” he said, breathing some of the powder through his nose.
“Is that what I think —.”
“Yes. Pure cocaine. Dr. Ford is the best source for the good stuff — and I always make sure that I spend on the best stuff. Want to try some?”
Fletcher watched on in horror, as the Mayor breathed copious amounts of the cocaine. He rolled back onto his bed, in a fit of laughter.
“We need to stay on task,” said Fletcher. “If you can’t tell me anything about him, how have you been contacting him?”
“We meet at some place… Oh, it slips my mind now. I’m sure it’ll come to me, eventually.”
Mayor Haddock snorted more, his pupils dilating to bowling balls.
“Stop taking that stuff and listen to me!”
“No can do, buttercup. I’m in the grasp of euphoria, right now.”
“I thought that you had a hard stance on drugs and crime,” Fletcher said, incredulously. “How can you even afford drugs, with your big campaign going on?”

“All of that war on drugs stuff is just a load of bull. Dr. Ford’s hospital is the main supplier. You haven’t figured that out, by now? I have the cops bust all the criminals who buy from him, and then I rake in the goodies. It’s a win-win. Plus, most drug dealers actually love me for buying from them. I think I’m one of their biggest buyers.”
“Biggest?”
“Campaign money, baby. It stretches real far. Especially since all I need to do is put up a few cheap billboards with snappy slogans, to get everybody’s attention.”
“So, this pickpocket… You’re spending most of the money that he gives you on drugs?”

The euphoria on Mayor Haddock’s face melted away. He sat up with a glare. “What else am I supposed to do with it? Nobody in this town has any clue what they want out of life. Life is a massive game. A charade.”
The Mayor was going into a trance. Fletcher was losing him.
“Sort of like, the pickpocket,” Fletcher said, quickly. “Speaking of the pickpocket, where—?”
“No, not sort of like the pickpocket,” Mayor Haddock slurred. “More like running a town. Which you should know about, right?”
“Of course,” said Fletcher. “Well, honestly… I’m just faking the senator thing. It’s a complete sham that I told you about.”
For once, he was telling the truth. Yet, Mayor Haddock remained unperturbed.

“Exactly!” Mayor Haddock punched a fist in the air. “Nobody in power wants to do anything. We all know we’re hopelessly stupid, and that our people are hopelessly stupid. The chaos theorem only confirms that everything is going to fall apart real soon here. So, what’s even the point in putting in any effort?”

He stood and tore one of his posters from the wall. The poster was carefully airbrushed and angled, to give Haddock the perfect appearance. Though, Haddock himself somehow managed to look more impressive than his image. He gave it a kiss.

“Look at these things,” Mayor Haddock said. “This is all it takes to win, these days. The chaos theorem was perhaps the best thing that ever happened to me — in everyone’s complacency, they realized that they couldn’t do any better than me. All of America realized.”
“And this theorem doesn’t bother you at all?”
“Bother me? All that it’s told me is that the whole world is going to fall in my lap. Why on Earth would I fight against the chaos theorem?”
Fletcher shook his head, while rereading the poster. “’A vote for me is a vote for my victory’. Can you get any more generic than that?”
“It’s what people want — the same old thing, in the same old package that it’s always been in. Nobody dares to create anymore. To risk. What’s the point?”
“My girlfriend, Margaret Wilkins...” Fletcher began, despite himself. “Do you know anything about her?”
Mayor Haddock shook his head. “Fun woman. Bit odd though. She’s constantly giving me advice on this whole America vs. China-Russia thing… Doesn’t realize how futile it is.”
“What thing? People are constantly talking about some thing…”

“Russia and China don’t have the chaos theorem, but want it badly,” said Mayor Haddock. “That, or they want us to disable our nuclear weapons. And, American leaders — they all know that this is going to escalate into a massive war. The chaos theorem says as much.”
Fletcher tightened his lips. Was that the fate of the town John and Clair had been afraid to reveal to him? If so, it didn’t seem quite so dire as they’d made it out to be.
“Like I’ve said, I’m negotiating,” said Mayor Haddock. “It’ll be fine.”
“Of course.”
Fletcher’s head was spiraling off course, though. How much did finding the oil baron matter, in the current state of things? Was anything he was trying to do rational?
Mayor Haddock took another snort of the cocaine, before walking toward the door.
“Well, I guess it’s about to be showtime,” he said. “You coming, senator?”
“Yes, yes,” Fletcher said. “I just need to know one thing: where has the pickpocket been at, whenever you’ve spoken with him?”
Mayor Haddock beamed. “Why, in an alley by the bank of Dexburg, naturally. Such wonderful people by that bank, by the way. One of the bankers — Jim Harrigan — is an absolute gem.”
Jim Harrigan — Fletcher’s face burned at the mention of his name.
A woman in a tweed suit stepped into the room. Her hair was frizzed, and her glasses sat slightly lopsided on her face.
Debby Crowner.
“Who’s the new guy?” she asked. “Haddock, you’re not trying to put somebody in indentured servitude again are you?”
Mayor Haddock shook his head. “Please, that was a phase. Butlers are in right now, anyway.”
“An improvement, I guess.” Despite her words, she still sounded disappointed.
Fletcher cowered, waiting for Debby Crowner to recognize him. However, the moment never came.

Mayor Haddock puffed himself up, hooked Fletcher’s arm into his, and waltzed into the hall. “Indeed,” he said. “Let’s go out to enjoy to food and fireworks. I think we had some pizzas brought in from Chef Bernardo’s. It’s going to be the highlight of this entire event!”
Fletcher squinted. Mayor Haddock had some of the biggest socialites in town over, and Chef Bernardo’s was his choice?
“The speech will be the highlight too, right?” Debby Crowner asked. “Also, you are going to go with my speech, instead of Margaret Wilkin’s speech. Kent Burgess is paying you good money. Right?”
“Of course, Downer, of course,” Mayor Haddock said.
“Crowner.”
“Right. I have the speech right on me. I don’t promise to do something and then not follow through.”
Fletcher hadn’t noticed any papers while sitting in Mayor Haddock’s room. He squinted his eyes, studying Mayor Haddock’s face. If Haddock had been lying, he was too good to give anything away.

Perhaps it didn’t matter. Laughs banked around Fletcher, removing weights from his feet. His heart pumped with a new life. The hallway gave off a glow, flowering clusters of people into bouquets. Haddock had a calming sway over the space.
Yet, Mayor Haddock’s talk about the pickpocket and the bank kept pressing against Fletcher. Fletcher needed to leave, and fast. He couldn’t let himself fall under Mayor Haddock’s easygoing charm.
Mayor Haddock stepped outside, following Crowner. They managed to slip behind a stage at the edge of the yard, avoiding any eyes.
