“Alright, who is he, really?” Crowner finally said with annoyance, once fully backstage. “I swear I’ve seen him somewhere, and I don’t like his face.”

“Some guy I found,” said Mayor Haddock, his eyes sparkling. “He’s apparently a senator, or something. My main guy was knocked out, so I figure he’s a good replacement. At least, it seemed that way. I’m high.”
He chuckled, while Crowner shot a concerned glance.
Fletcher scanned for some sort of escape. He couldn’t let himself be thrown on a stage again. Not after Priest Carvel. Not with Crowner dissecting him.
He needed to get out of this weather, too. The sun gave a marmalade light. It was too nice, and it gnawed at him.
He tunneled back to years past — to his youth, in the ritzy toy shop. Crunching numbers for Uncle Timothy. Making sales. Keeping on a smile, while the sun lazed its way through the window.
So many hours, working on someone else’s dime. So little recognition.

“He was knocked unconscious?” Crowner said, with a hiss. “I told you Haddock — getting yourself high with those drugs is one thing. But, if you knock up another guy in your bedroom like this, you’re going to get caught. People always get caught.”

“Not according to the chaos theorem,” Mayor Haddock said, stepping out from behind the stage and into the crowd. “It always seems guilty people get caught. But, it’s only because we only hear about the guilty ones.”

His face suddenly was covered in pricks of sweat. Gait swaying, he was a gust of wind away from matching a falling tree. Fletcher sped next to him and nudged him deeper into the crowd. The further from the stage he got, the better.
“Get back over here,” Crowner said. “We’re going to do this speech, and we’re going to do this right.”
“I think I can wing it,” Mayor Haddock said, with a twitchy wink.

He leaned into Fletcher’s ear. “She’s nuts,” he said. His voice came in a thin rasp. Though, it was loud enough for anybody to hear. “She thinks we should try keeping order, even when all of the order is already mapped out for us. I just try entertaining her, because it’s funny seeing her struggle.”
People crowded around Mayor Haddock, their faces lit up and their mouths filled with praise.
Mayor Haddock raised his hands, gesturing for everyone to simmer down. He gave a loud sniffle.
“I — I have a speech prepared,” he said. “And, by prepared, I mean that the universe prepared it. I’m utterly unprepared. Which, of course, is something I always prepare for. Just look at this town!”
Mayor Haddock laughed, and everybody laughed with him.
Fletcher attempted to run off, but was yanked back in. Why was it that insane leaders had such an affinity for him?
“I really have to go,” Fletcher said. “To the bank.”
“You can’t go yet, and you can take that to the bank,” Mayor Haddock said.

Mayor Haddock looked back to the crowd. “So many poor suckers out here, who still haven’t realized how things operate. Whales eat the little fishies, not the reverse. I feel slightly bad for the earthquakes. But, hey: federal loans help, and I can’t help that.”
Cheers resounded, but Fletcher struggled to follow along.

“Loans always help, actually,” Mayor Haddock said. “This is why I’ll be instating the future loser tax. If the chaos theorem deems that you’ll be a loser in your future? You must report it to me, so you can get taxed heavily and help our economy out. No point in investing in somebody who’ll suck us dry, am I right?”
A few people dipped from the crowd, uncomfortable. The rest of the crowd took deep swills of their expensive drinks and tittered from under their elaborate masks.

“I know I may not have the best past,” said Mayor Haddock, slumping his posture in false guilt. He quickly raised himself back up, and gestured at Fletcher. “However! A genius in our town cooked up a brilliant new theory, which will be of help to all of us. According to him, the past doesn’t exist. It’s just a figment of our imagination, which can be changed to our will. Only the present and the future are concrete. We are all entirely new people every moment, because nothing we did before has any effect on what’s happening right now.”
The crowd burst into applause.
“I didn’t devise it,” Fletcher said, feigning an abashed grin. “That historian did.”
Mayor Haddock shook his head. “No, no. See, you are the historian, because I said so. That’s your new history, now.”

He turned to the crowd. “See, everybody? Anything can be changed, in a heartbeat. That’s the heart of my campaign: we’re going to remake the facts, to match our internal reality! We’re going to change history!”
Everybody cheered.
“With so much new history, how can we be sure what new history is the truth?” Fletcher asked.

“Whichever new history we all believe in, of course.” Mayor Haddock shook his head, patronizingly. “That’s the thing about truth: it’s not about what’s real or not. What’s real tends to be real fake. No. I believe the truth is this: the thing that defines ‘truth’ is what everybody chooses to believe. It’s whatever the people deem trustworthy.”
Mayor Haddock gave Fletcher a slap on the back and leapt into the crowd. His hands gripped the hands of others in tight handshakes, and he pulled a crisp smile around his face.

“Say it with me,” Mayor Haddock said. “I didn’t embezzle money from the government. I didn’t send our economy into an economic spiral. I didn’t punch that old man in the nuts, at the town parade. I’m the greatest mayor that Dexburg has ever had. And, it’s all thanks to Marvin Whisk!”
The crowd promptly repeated Mayor Haddock’s words — which didn’t sound quite right coming out of their mouths. Nonetheless, they pressed on.
That is, all but one.
Logan Gerri pushed a few people aside, making his way to the front of the crowd. His suit was partially unbuttoned, exposing his bare, oiled chest to the sunlight.
“That man is not Marvin Whisk!” he said, pointing a meaty finger. His brow furrowed and his mustache bobbed with it.
The crowd gasped. Another burly man had made his way through the crowd — it was a bodyguard.
“Hey, what’s the big idea?” said Mayor Haddock.
“That man is not Priest Carvel, like he pretends to be,” the bodyguard said, catching his breath. He gave Mayor Haddock a look. “The real Priest Carvel is at the gate, and he’s furious.”
Mayor Haddock raised his hands putting himself within the triangle of Fletcher, Logan, and the bodyguard.
“Alright, hold up guys,” he said.
He attempted a deepthroated laugh, but it came out as a cough. He punched himself in the chest, to clear his throat.

“This man is obviously not Priest Carvel,” Mayor Haddock continued, his eyes going watery. Fletcher couldn’t tell if it was from the betrayal, a coughing fit, or the cocaine. Probably from the cocaine betraying him with a coughing fit. “Trust me, I would’ve recognized Marvin as a fraud, if he’d ever tried to claim that. And, what’s this about Marvin not being Marvin?”
Logan prepared to explain when Fletcher was dragged by the bodyguard. The bodyguard shoved his hand in one of Fletcher’s pockets and pulled out Priest Carvel’s wallet.
“What’s this?” the bodyguard said, voice heavy. He pointed at the name on the card. “It says Priest Carvel, right on it!”
Mayor Haddock glared at Fletcher. “Why did you have Priest Carvel’s wallet, Marvin?”
“I already told you, he’s not Marvin!” Logan said.
Logan tore Fletcher from the bodyguard’s grip and held him up by the collar.
“His name is Stuart Fletcher!” Logan was practically feral. “The punk broke into my house, just the other day!”
Mayor Haddock went enraged.

“Stuart Fletcher?” he said. His voice dropped all sense of glib, showman inflections. “You — you’re the guy that the pickpocket won’t stop yammering on about? It can’t be. He’s been chasing you everywhere. You’re a very wanted man!”
It was Fletcher’s turn to be in shock. The pickpocket who’d stolen his oil baron was now after him? Things were far more dangerous than they seemed.
“Get him out of here,” said Mayor Haddock, to the bodyguard. “Make sure that he the cops get to him. I don’t want him anywhere near me.”
Fletcher’s head spun as a top, desperately looking for a way out.
“I’m not Stuart Fletcher though,” Fletcher said, even as his arms were being forced behind his back. “I — I only used to be Stuart Fletcher. Now, I’m somebody else entirely.”
“Is this guy for real?” Logan said, taking a fighting stance.
“It’s my new history. A different truth than the one I had before.”
“That’s a load of bull,” Mayor Haddock, gauging the crowd to make sure he still had their support. “You can’t just create new history out of thin air. People around you have to believe it, too.”
“I believe it stronger than the rest of you combined, though,” said Fletcher. “I have to… Or else, I’ll wind up in jail. I’ll be no different from any thug… Or, drug dealer.”
His eyes bored through Mayor Haddock’s head. Mayor Haddock scratched the back of his nec, uncomfortably.
“He’s right,” Mayor Haddock said. “He couldn’t possibly be Stuart Fletcher, because Stuart Fletcher is no longer part of new history.”
Logan shifted his fighting stance toward Mayor Haddock. “Are you for real?”
Yet, Fletcher had already broken from the bodyguard’s hold, and was sprinting for the gates.
He had enough of Mayor Haddock’s group of loons, for one day. Dealing with Priest Carvel had already been terrible. Though, seeing insanity in a place of such power was only more demoralizing.
“Prepare to taste the fires of hell, anti-chosen-one!” Priest Carvel said.
The locks to the gate lay shattered on the concrete. Priest Carvel held a large axe in his hand.
“Stop!” Priest Carvel said, as Fletcher came closer. Priest Carvel’s cult flanked around him, hoods drawn tight.
Fletcher picked up his pace. Barreling through them was likely the only way to go.

“No, seriously, stop,” said Priest Carvel said. “I have a ton of axe puns that I need to try out… ‘I need to axe you a question’. ‘I have an axe to grind with you’. ‘I think it’s finally time that you get the axe’. ‘Today, the axes’ powers will claim victory!’ Wait… That last one is actually quite terrible.”
Fletcher slipped around Priest Carvel, causing Carvel to trip on his robe. Priest Carvel hit the ground and gave a grunt. “You’re going to regret that!” he shouted. “Boys, take him out!”
Fletcher was making his way through the swarm of cult members when Marvin let out a shout.
“Marvin?” Fletcher cried.
Marvin was tied in the fetal position, at Priest Carvel’s feet.
“Every religion needs its sacrificial lamb,” said Priest Carvel, his face solemn. He slapped the hilt of his axe against his palm. “Any takers?”
Fletcher’s instincts yearned to escape through the gate. His heart concurred. Marvin didn’t matter that much, right?
Nonetheless, Fletcher found himself clambering toward Priest Carvel. He grappled Priest Carvel around the legs, taking him to the ground.
“Dear Krishna,” Priest Carvel winced, “I think you crushed my tushy, Fletcher. I really shouldn’t have done that heroin, before playing hero…”
Snatching Priest Carvel’s axe from the ground, Fletcher cut Marvin’s constraints..
“Don’t kill me, don’t kill me!” Marvin moaned. “You already have taken enough away from me.”
The rope fell away. Fletcher dropped the axe. “It’s alright, you’re safe,” Fletcher said. “Now get out of here.”

Marvin stumbled to his feet and ran toward the crowd of socialites. He gave a glance back before fully disappeared among them. In his eyes was a heavy gratitude. It was a new look on Marvin. Weary lines on his face faded, if for a moment.
“Give it up,” Priest Carvel said, grabbing Fletcher around the neck. Fletcher’s grip tightened around the axe.
The rest of the cult crowded around Fletcher. Accompanying the cult were a few bodyguards, attempting to maintain the peace. Yet, to no avail.
“Can’t give it up. I need the axe for… For cutting my hair.” Fletcher choked.
It was the best he had.
“Let go of him!” Mayor Haddock shouted. “This house is my jurisdiction!”
Fletcher tried to turn, but blood drained from his head. Breaths came in shallow. Perception was a shadow of itself.

“This universe is my jurisdiction!” shouted Priest Carvel. “It terrifies you, doesn’t it Mayor? Despite all your political power, the world doesn’t spin on its axis anymore. Me and my radicals… We’re the new rulers. I’m going to make this guy into burrito meat, and you must remain helpless to the inevitability of it.”
Sirens blared, followed by the familiar rumble of Jack and Clair’s truck. Priest Carvel’s grip around Fletcher’s neck loosened.
“The cops are back!” Priest Carvel shouted to his cult. “How are they always tailing us? Everybody, run!”
He dropped Fletcher altogether. Blood rushing back to Fletcher’s head, Fletcher made out a blurry image of Priest Carvel trampling over the guests and Mayor Haddock.

Fletcher scratched his chin; the cops were likely just down the block. Despite this, he grabbed the axe and stumbled into the street. Fletcher looked to the sky, and saw the sun hitting noontime. Would this day ever come to an end?
One of Priest Carvel’s vans gave a thrum. Fletcher walked up to it and thrust the door open.
“Get out!” Fletcher said. “The holy one demands it!”
A cult member trembled in their seat, his eyes glued to the tip of Fletcher’s axe. Fletcher jumped forward, prompting a flinch from the cult member. They scurried out.

Fletcher hopped into the van and slammed the door. His hand cranked the windows down, and he gave a wretch. The van stank of liquor and incense. Shifting the car into drive and hitting the pedal, he took a gulp of fresh air. With it, he got a good look at the police and the drug-dealers’ truck, as they sped past him.
His muscles froze. Though, the cars kept moving, oblivious to him. He let out a laugh.
He needed to head to the bank, and he’d be home free.
“He never said where he was going. All I know is that we talked about a banker… Jim Harrigan. Doubt the idiot even knew where the bank is though.”
“Well, he was smart enough to escape from us three times,” I say.

I look around to see if anybody is watching. Sure enough, there’s a couple just behind us. They’re looking at me like I’m the dumbest man alive. I look over to Mayor Haddock; his expression is no more forgiving.
“Wait, wait… You’ve let him escape from you three times? And, you’re just now telling me this?”
Mayor Haddock is pissed. I mean, I don’t blame him. Me and my officers haven’t done the best job, even if it was the damn best we could do.
“We initially didn’t view him as a priority,” I say, knowing full well that this is a lie. “Besides, you should’ve called us. You’re lucky we followed that cult.”
“Who also escaped!”
The Mayor gestures to his yard, which is ravaged.
So that’s why everybody was fleeing the premises when we arrived...
“Can’t we just focus on busting drug dealers and whatnot?” I say. “Honestly, we have no idea where he’s at, at this point.”

Mayor Haddock shakes his head. “No can do. I’ve already let you bust all the best ones. Besides, this town is about to be taken to task, by the U.S government. I’m going to need all the drugs I can get.”
I want to believe that he’s joking. Though, at this point, I’m pretty sure he’s just an airhead.
“Just think hard,” says Mayor Haddock. “If you were an utterly corrupt individual, where is the first place would you go?”
Screw Mayor Haddock, and screw this chase. Me and Officer Springs should go to Chef Bernardo’s, to get some doughnuts.
Chapter 17:
The van had been parked in front of the bank for fifteen minutes. Yet, Fletcher didn’t flinch. His focus was on his email.

“That sounds rough. Thankfully, I have something that might cheer you up. I have that toy you’ve been looking for — the oil baron. Just tell me where you’re at, and we can make some better memories. Linda.”
Fletcher wanted the easygoing peace he usually had, when reading Linda’s emails. He wanted to be able to tell her that he was near the bank; that he could see her. However, something was amiss.
Fletcher had never written a thing about the toy oil baron to Linda. How on earth did she know about it?
He did the only thing he could consider rational, on the spur of the moment. He typed in a response.
“How do you know about the oil baron?”
The moment he’d sent it, he knew he’d committed a stroke of genius
The moment after, he knew he was a hair away from having a stroke.

Completely stupid. That’s what he’d been. He had a chance to interrogate Linda, and mine information from her. Instead, he’d utterly compromised his suspicions. She would know he thought something was up. There would be no way for him to parse out if her following responses were honest or not.
Yet, for Linda to already know a bit about him, was she ever honest?
He put his head in his hands, letting himself sweat it out. He just needed to breathe and think.
His thoughts whipped him around in several directions.

The pickpocket was chasing him down. That much was certain. Yet, why was it that he was being chased down? To his knowledge, he hadn’t done anything. Yet, here was the pickpocket, with his stolen oil baron toy, trying to find him.
Now, Linda knew where the oil baron toy was. Did she know the pickpocket? Was she the pickpocket?
Was she real?
No, she had to be real. It wouldn’t make any sense if she wasn’t. That would be too much. Even for him.

Still, the perturbing thought sat at the edge of Fletcher’s mind. With it came another one: the only people who should’ve known that he was looking for the toy oil baron were the people who were chasing him. Officer Mayhew, Marvin Whisk, Priest Carvel, and the drug dealers… That is, them and his friends. Was it possible that any of them were somehow also the pickpocket?

He told himself that he was being delusional. There couldn’t possibly be a conspiracy against him. Yet then, there was already a crowd of people who hated his guts, wasn’t there? How much of a stretch was it that one of them was toying with him?
Nonetheless, maybe Linda’s unfounded knowledge was innocent coincidence. Maybe — just maybe.
His phone squawked at him. He looked at the number. Harry, naturally. Why did he have to call at the most inopportune of times?
“Hello?” Fletcher said, furling his lips.
“I just got a call from Margaret,” Harry said, in rushed breaths. “You were at her apartment again, weren’t you?”
“It was a new apartment this time, Harry... Nothing ‘again’ about it.”
“Cut the bullshit! You weren’t supposed to be at her place!”
“Wasn’t I though? According to the chaos theorem...”

“Enough with that. You knew what you were supposed to do, and you didn’t do it. The restraining orders — they were put against you for a reason. Fletcher, you can be better than this. You can do better than her and move on.”
“I have moved on,” Fletcher said.
His mind whipped to an image of himself on his bathroom floor, surrounded by pills. He was languishing on the tile, waiting for the pills to kick in. He didn’t want to feel cold anymore. Just numb.
He shook his head. So dumb. Mints were so much better than pills.
Watching as people walked out from the bank, Fletcher caught the eyes of a few. Their strides were slow, and their faces heavy. He’d have to go in that bank, soon.

“You clearly haven’t. Fletcher, she has the cops after you. You probably are going to get arrested. Do you realize how much trouble that you’re in? Don’t get me wrong, I’m going to help you if I can... But, after what happened with John, I don’t want to see another one of my friends go insane. Do you get me?”
Fletcher rolled his tongue around in his mouth, marinating it in Harry’s words.
“Yes... And, why is it that John is insane, Harry?”

“I see what you’re doing,” Harry said, chuckling derisively. “Look, it had nothing to do with the theorem. John couldn’t handle reality. The theorem would’ve worked on him if he’d just been the person that could handle. But, he couldn’t.”
“And, what if I can’t handle the inevitability of my own life? What if I’m another John?”

“What if you’re another me? My life is going just fine, despite all the absurdity that’s all around me. I know where everything is going to wind up... Rather than winding me up, this gives me a sense of peace. Can’t you be that kind of person?”

“That kind of person isn’t a kind person though, are they?” Fletcher asked, dodging Harry’s inquiries. “You only called me because you want me to be just like you — to let the chaos theorem become me. Tell me this, Harry: if the chaos theorem hadn’t told you to call me, would you have? Would you have even cared?”
“Of course I care, Fletcher! Deep down, I’m a good person! You know that!”
“Do I? Do you do what you’re supposed to do, because you genuinely want to do what you’re supposed to do? Or, do you do it merely because you’re supposed to do it?”
The other end of the line went static. Then, Harry opened his mouth again. Fletcher could tell from Harry’s lips smacking as he did it. “Is there a difference?”
“I like to think that there is,” Fletcher said, “to the people who make a difference.”

Fletcher slammed the phone down, his blood boiling. Perhaps he’d been too harsh on Harry — but then, Harry didn’t really care did he? He couldn’t have. Harry had never been help during the worst of Fletcher’s addiction. Yet, once Margaret came in the picture, Harry was suddenly a white knight.
Harry’s call was all just self-oriented ego, and nothing more.
Fletcher stepped out of his car, smiling to himself. It was time to take care of the thing that mattered to him.
“Woe to those who enter here!”
A man was curled up into a ball, in front of the bank’s revolving door. Fletcher stepped over and pushed through the door.
“You go in, and something else comes out!” he said. “I saw in the newspaper that the bankers were having a ball, in there. I think what I saw was a fall — the world’s greatest typo.”

Spinning through the revolving door, Fletcher watched light warp and filter through the windows. The bank’s interior gave off a balmy glow. When he stepped into it, he was met by a cold rush of air; heavy air-conditioning. Fletcher looked to the dozens of desks covering the floor space. He looked up to the second level, littered with more desks. At any moment, he expected bankers to suddenly appear at them, talking with clients. Yet, no bankers came. The place was a wasteland.
He walked up to the bank teller’s desk, near the entrance.
“Hi, I’d like to speak about a loan,” he said. “Specifically, with Jim Harrigan.”
“Name?” the teller said, in mild annoyance.
“Stuart Fletcher. Now, could you hurry on up?”
The bank teller wiped a plume of sweat from his forehead and typed into his computer with the pace of a scurrying rat.
“I’m not sure you’d actually like to speak with Harrigan, at just this moment,” the bank teller said, in a hushed breath. “If I were you, I’d...”
The bank teller craned their neck toward the door. Fletcher’s own neck and shoulder muscles tightened. Perhaps leaving would be best. There were other things to do, right?
Fletcher shook his head. Harrigan was the only good lead that he had.
“Come on,” Fletcher said. He glanced at the bank teller’s nametag. “Don Key, is it? Just cool it, okay?”
“My name is not Don,” the bank teller said, their face now reddening. “I’m just borrowing my coworker’s clothes. My real name is Noah Nam.”
“No name?”
“No... Noah Nam, not no name, you no name.”
Fletcher blinked blankly.
The bank teller huffed. “Whatever, I’m done...”
Fletcher shrugged. “Whatever, Don. Anyway, what’s the worst that could happen?” Fletcher gave the bank teller a pat on the back. “I get turned down for a loan?”
The bank teller grinned. “That, or thrown into the river...”
A door behind the bank teller burst open.
“Harrigan, here again! Sorry for the wait! I was just filing a couple of people’s bankruptcies.”
Harrigan’s hair shone chrome, and he smelled of fresh tires. He leaned over the desk with a Cheshire grin, gripped Fletcher’s forearm, and gave a firm shake.
“So, you in here to talk about a loan?” Harrigan asked.
A thick minty smell wafted from his mouth. His hands wove through the bank teller’s drawers, nimble as threading with thimble. He lifted a file the size of a brick.
“There we go,” he said. He swung from behind the desk, and slapped Fletcher on the back. “Follow me. Hey, you feel cold. You cold?”
Fletcher rubbed his arm, to find an outbreak of goosebumps. Rumbles of the ceiling fan rolled over his head.
“Now that you mention it,” Fletcher said, “it is pretty cold in here.”
“Don’t worry. We’ll take care of you, here. I’ll have you in a spiffy hot seat in a jiffy.”

Harrigan slowed his pace to sync with Fletcher’s. The syncing gave a moment’s reassurance. Harrigan was left under the control of Fletcher’s every step. However, when Harrigan’s steps sped, and Fletcher inexplicably found himself speeding with him, he questioned who was truly in control.

Harrigan banked at a couple of plush chairs, near a coffee table. A coffee, labeled ‘Jim’ was already on the table — almost as though Harrigan had predicted this meeting. Yet, with the chaos theorem, hadn’t he been able to?
“Heated seats,” Harrigan said, practically pushing Fletcher into it. “Some of the best we could find, too.”

He turned the dial on the side of his seat. His eyes flitted to the window at the side of him. The employee parking lot was just outside it, glittering with freshly paved asphalt, and brand new sportscars. Harrigan swiftly brought the shutters down.
Fletcher attempted to comfortably situate himself, only to go stiffer.

“And why don’t I sit right with ya?’” Harrigan said, already letting himself stretch into the chair. Easing into a comfortable position, his file thudded onto the coffee table. “Ah. It’s warm. Maybe too much, I should warn!”

Fletcher nodded primly, while his hand groped toward the dial. The heat was putting his butt on fire. Yet, could lower it, without drawing ire? He needed to stay on Harrigan’s good side, if he ever hoped to draw info of the pickpocket from him.
“So, let’s just dig into this,” Harrigan said. He wagged his head, and his tongue panted out.
Whisks whipped from the file, as Harrigan thumbed through them.
“It looks like you’ve taken a lot of loans in the past year, here,” Harrigan said. “Of course, plenty of successful businesses do that, so no worries there...”
“Plenty of successful business,” repeated Fletcher. “Yes. I’m doing that.”
“Seems to come so natural to you. Just lie back, and let things do their thing.”
The pages stopped turning. Harrigan drank them in, and muttered something beneath his breath.
“Of course,” Harrigan said, looking up to Fletcher with a saccharine grin. “Still shocking to hear, considering how business has been doing lately.”
“Definitely. Speaking of which, how are businesses doing around here?”
Fletcher had thought it was a good leading question, toward the pickpocket. Though, Harrigan simply set the file aside, and took a long drink of his coffee.

“It’s the lopsided circle cycle,” he said. “The economy goes through a surge of profits, only to fall off it. Don’t have to be a prophet, to predict it... Still, this whole new chaos theorem thing hasn’t helped matters. You should’ve seen how many bankers that committed suicide the other day, when the stock market crashed. To die for!”
Fletcher laughed. “Would’ve loved to see that.”
Harrigan’s face went to stone. Great — stupid Fletcher. What had he been thinking?

“Of course, because it’s so tragic,” Fletcher said, backtracking. “Seeing death helps it feel all the more real. It’s so hard to know that all of them dove to the end, upon seeing their fate. So enlivening to know we didn’t.”

“It’s fine,” said Harrigan. He let out a bursting laugh, then cut it off. “You know the old joke... What’s a good banker? A dead banker. Anyway, you know your fate? Have to say, that’s surprising. You don’t seem like the type of guy who would know.”
Fletcher nodded proudly. “Yes, I’m not into seeing my fate myself. Been avoiding it.”

“Smart enough, I suppose,” said the banker. “Me? I’ve found it beneficial to know where everything is going. I knew I was destined to win, so preparing myself for the upcoming slumps and successes in life only made sense. Gives me an edge over the poor suckers who have no control.”
Fletcher smiled. “Yeah. I can see that.”
“Can you?”
“I just said that—.”

“Alright, it’s time that I cut the bullshit.” Harrigan slammed a fist on the table. “You clearly never read the chaos theorem, like you claim to have. But, you really should’ve. All this? I’m putting an end to it.”
He took a sip of his coffee, studying Fletcher’s face all the while. His eyes held the twinkle of anticipation. Though, rather than giving a reaction, Fletcher sat dumbfounded.
“I’m not sure what you’re talking about,” Fletcher said. “Honestly, I’ve been going through so much rigmarole lately… Am I missing something?”
“You’re not getting a loan,” Harrigan said. “From all the numbers here? It’s safe to say your business is dead. Done. Kaput.”
“It’s not dead until it’s dead.”
Fletcher clenched a fist. Anger was rising in him now. Harrigan leaned back and rested his hands on his stomach. He’d been preparing for this, hadn’t he?

“That’s what they all say,” said Harrigan. He looked around and gestured at the door to the bank. Several people entered. “Take those guys, for example. I bet they think the world is smiling kindly at them. It’s not. They’re dead. The world doesn’t care about any of us. We’re chess pieces on a board, moving in a discorded game that will never hit checkmate.”
“I never was one to participate in chess,” said Fletcher.

“We don’t have a choice. Nonsense is brewing. Everything is about to come to a head… And, if you don’t suck up everything you can, when you can? Everything that’s yours? You’re going to go down the tubes, with nothing to your name.”
Harrigan’s coffee cup crumpled under the tight squeeze of his hand.

“I’m going to have to repossess your business,” Harrigan said, his voice steel. “You’re probably going to have to declare bankruptcy, to account for all the loans you have weighing you down. You should’ve paid more attention to the payments. The numbers. You would’ve seen this coming.”

The words cut to the bone. Being turned down for a loan was predictable. Yet, being told that the business was failing? That it was going to be repossessed? His finances hadn’t been brought to that dire of straits, had they?
There had to be a way to change the course of things. It wasn’t inevitable unless something said it was. Who was Harrigan to say what was possible, and what wasn’t?

However, Fletcher could already feel Harrigan’s attention shifting to new clients pouring through the doors. Harrigan’s pose was easy, and his breaths uniform. He knew. He probably knew every step of this interaction. Fletcher suddenly felt inferior, in his shabby hoody, disheveled hair, and torn jeans.
Much as Fletcher didn’t want to believe the chaos theorem, it’d gifted Harrigan the upper hand.
Why hadn’t he just gone and taken the chaos theorem himself? Perhaps if he’d been the type of person who would’ve read the theorem sooner, he would’ve had a better fate.

A moan fled Fletcher’s lips. “I’ve lived in that toy shop for years,” Fletcher said. “It was my uncle’s shop. He raised me there. It’s how I learned everything I know about business… About life… It wasn’t the best, but it’s mine now.”

His eyes burned. Flashes of anguish and mildew memories flitted by. The bank flushed with fresh murmurs and faces, but Fletcher barely noted them. All focus was on keeping his flushed face from spilling tears.
“Sorry,” Harrigan said, bluntly. He held his crushed coffee cup in the air. “Don! Hey Don, I need more coffee!”

The bank teller came stumbling through a swath of people. They were all crazed, sobbing about death and destiny. Despite their anguish, they held a zombified air about them. Much of them were peering at Fletcher, as though he were some exotic exhibit.
Couldn’t the quiet of the bank have stayed quiet? Why did insanity coalesce wherever he went?
“Your coffee sir,” the bank teller said, setting a new cup on the table and taking the crushed one.
Harrigan nodded up at the bank teller serenely. He didn’t touch the cup. “If you’d just consulted us sooner, you might’ve been put on a debt plan that could save you from all this.”
“Maybe I didn’t want to consult you. Maybe I thought I could handle it, because I always have!”

“The world sometimes moves us into doing things we thought we’d never do,” Harrigan said. His hands folded into a pyramid. “Though, if it’s any consolation, I’m a genius financier. I can get you through all of this muck, so that you can at least get back on your feet from this.”
Fletcher wanted to get back on his feet more than ever. Namely, to leave his seat and run out of the bank. Yet, with all the people clustered around, no clear escape was afforded.
“I think I’ll be fine having you suck me dry, without paying a fee for you to do it.”
Harrigan laughed.

“Yes, well… I suppose it does look real bad for you, doesn’t it?” He smiled. “Of course, for me it was an amazing turn of events. All my comrades were so focused on stocks, and investments… Stocks are such a sad thing to put stock in though, when everybody can now know what everything is really worth — nothing. Me? I bet on people losing all their money. I wound up winning out with that.”
Harrigan’s face filled with glee.
Fletcher shook his head. “Is there any way you could cut me a break? Help me with this?”
“No, no. Why would I? Too much money in this.”
“All you can focus on is money, isn’t it?”
“It’s the closest thing we have to a value system, in this society.”
“Value? And what is the value of value? See what your value does for you years from now, when justice finally comes knocking…”
Harrigan’s eyes hooded over. He snorted.
“Justice? Me? You really need to read that theorem. I’m going to become untouchable.”
Fletcher turned down the dial of his seat. The heat was too much, with the crowd of people making the room ever stodgier and stuffier.
“Do you want a private room?” Harrigan asked, his eyes dissecting Fletcher.
This time, Fletcher took the turn to smile. “No. I actually have a plan for how to dig myself out of this.”
“Do you now?”
“Yes… I just need a bit of help from you. There’s this person I’ve been looking for, see…”

Harrigan’s head bobbed, invitingly. The questions concerning the pickpocket and the oil baron seemed futile, at this juncture. The business was doomed, after all. Still, Fletcher told himself that pursuing it was better than giving in.
“There’s a pickpocket going around, apparently,” Fletcher continued, “and they have something of mine, that is extraordinarily valuable.”
“Something that can pull you out of debt?”
“Possibly, but that’s irrelevant. I was told that you know who they are? Mayor Haddock told me.”
Harrigan’s jaw dropped. He groomed his hair. “You’ve spoken with Mayor Haddock? About me?”
“Just about. More the pickpocket, though. What do you know about them?”
Harrigan cleared his throat and took a sip of his coffee. There was a bit of sweat on his brow.

“Now, I don’t know much,” Harrigan said. “I’ve only handled the money transfers between him and the mayor. Honestly, I’ve tried to keep my name out of most of these things, and Haddock’s too. The real person who’s been signing their name to all these transactions, and who introduced me to the pickpocket? Mr. Glenn Clover.”
“Already sounds like a great guy…”
“He’s been the middleman to my position of middleman. You can never have too many middles. Besides, this guy deserves it. We used to be friends, but he’s a bit of a pathetic prick.”
Fletcher gave a blank stare.
“Surprised to see you’ve never met him, Fletcher. I know he only ever hangs around with his wife, these days… Never leaves her side. Still, you didn’t even know he’s Mrs. Clover’s wife?”
“Never heard of her, either.”

“If only you’d heard her,” Harrigan said, bringing his hand to his heart. “She was an amazing singer, in her heyday. She toured across country. You should’ve seen her perform! These days though, she’s a major conservationist. Runs a greenhouse.”
Harrigan pulled a pen and pad from his breast-pocket. After a bit of scribbling, he handed a note over to Fletcher.
There was Mrs. Clover’s full name — Melinda Clover — and her address. Harrigan’s phone number and business information was tucked at the bottom, as well.
Fletcher took a second glance at the name — Melinda. It was like Linda, wasn’t it? It had to have been a coincidence. Yet, coincidences had been anything but coincidental, lately.
Fletcher looked up, to see Harrigan giving him a diamond stare.

“Hopefully that helps,” Harrigan said. “Specifically, my business information. I wouldn’t mess with the pickpocket myself. Going to be honest: I heard him say he was looking for you. That he had some grudge to settle. He didn’t say it nicely. Heard he recently killed a guy just for their fruit cup. And now he’s looking for you…”
Fletcher’s head buzzed. There was no doubting it anymore — whatever was going on between him and the pickpocket was personal. Yet, worse was that the pickpocket knew who he was. He wanted him dead.
Suddenly, Fletcher wished he was dead.
“He’s a fruitcake, with a lot of money,” Harrigan said, finishing his thought. “Not a good combo, from personal experience.”
Fletcher glanced at Harrigan’s gold watch. It was already an hour past noon.
“Not a good combo from my experience either,” Fletcher said. “Anyway, I really have to be going. Somewhere to be.”
He stood up and outstretched his hand. Harrigan squeezed it, as though it were one of his coffee cups.
“Pleasure doing business with you,” Fletcher said.
“No, the pleasure is all mine,” said Harrigan. “I look forward to seeing you here again.”
“I look forward to…” Fletcher began, before dropping it entirely.
If he were back in this bank, that would mean the end. He wasn’t ready for that. Shoes dragging on the marble floor, Fletcher shuffled away. People filtered past him, eyes crazed and distant.
“Alright, what the hell is going on in here?” Harrigan cried. “What’s with all the people?”
“The stock market just crashed,” the bank teller squeaked, from somewhere deep in the crowd. “People want their money.”
“To hell with the people! Get them out of here!”

Fletcher ducked as a chair hurled over his head. There were crashes and bangs as the bank was turned over for everything it was worth. All around him, people were gnashing at the teeth, begging for money.
One man grabbed Fletcher by the shoulders and throttled him.
“I was recently diagnosed with middle age,” the man said, eyes red with tears. “I need money, now! It’s a crisis, I’m telling you! A crisis!”
There was a slap as Fletcher smacked the man in the face and ducked back into the crowd. He felt invisible among them, and utterly naked, all at the same time.
“Doomsday clock is nigh,” somebody monotoned. “And our mayor just sits there, high.”
Fletcher reached for the revolving door. It poured out a fresh cluster of people, when Fletcher hit the glass.
“I’m getting the hell out of here,” Harrigan said.
His business suit was torn at the seams, and his hair was lopsided. His skin flushed orange under its fake tan, and rush of fear.
“Coming in today was a mistake,” Harrigan continued, slipping through the door. “Big mistake…”
The ceiling buckled from a man swinging on the chandelier, overhead. The air was raining papers and desks, tossed from the floor above. The people had come for a remedy. They’d settled for disrepair.

Despair filling his veins, Fletcher plowed through the revolving door and back into the street. He glanced at the note in his hand and laughed. It was completely smudged, and he could barely make out the address. Though, he was one step closer to his goal.
That much couldn’t be overstated.
Now, how long was the bus going to take?
“Tell us where Fletcher is, donkey!”
“That’s not my name!”
Likely story. Real likely. I think about telling the reedy bank teller that. But, then, who gives a flying fuck about what he knows about what I think?
No. I have to keep pushing. Gunning for him.
I shove my gun further against his nuts.
“Talk!”
“I — I can’t disclose info on our clients.”
Shit, I think he’s getting hard. This is getting hard. I look over to Clair, but she’s clearly no help. Just twiddling her cheap cigarette and ogling at Logan Gerri. Typical.
Why’d I even lug that rat with us?
“We overheard the mayor telling the cops that Fletcher would be here,” Clair said, putting out her cigarette on the bank teller’s forehead.
Maybe she does care. Maybe.
“Alright, alright!” the bank teller squeaks. “I’ll talk. I’ll talk. I saw him talking with Jim Harrigan. I think he said—.”
Then, Logan Gerri gives the bank teller a heavy punch to the head.
“He told you to fucking spill, cretin!” Logan Gerri shouts.
His veins are pulsing, and his muscles are raised. The bank teller’s head, though? It’s slumped to the table.
Logan Gerri just knocked him out cold.
“Wow, you pack some punch,” Clair swoons.
I shoot a glare in Clair’s direction, and shove Logan in the chest with the butt of my gun.
“He was our only lead!” I say.
Logan rubs the back of his thick neck. “I think he said something about Jimmy Hendricks.”
“Jim Harrigan,” I say. “I’ll look in our files, for his number. Then, I’m going to dump you on the side of the road, you dumbass.”
I’ve never met a man quite like myself. I used to take pride in that fact. Though, this Fletcher… What if he’s holier than me?

I ransacked the mayor’s entire party and found no sign of him in there. Somehow, he managed to slip away, and steal one of our vans. Worse yet, he seems to have stolen my keys — I’m now trapped in a cramped van, without any way of getting back into our house.
Am I now the fool, who I used to take my followers for? Am I just as much a follower of Fletcher, as my believers are of me? It seems so, from how much I’m chasing him.
I have no idea where I’m looking anymore. Perhaps spraying myself with more holy water will help do the trick. Still, something tells me I’ll just be tricking myself.

Fletcher continuously refreshed his phone. At any moment, Linda could send him another message to contact him. It was inevitable. Though, the message still hadn’t come yet. It were as if she was ignoring him.
She’d taken some time responding to him earlier, throughout the day. Though, this was new. This was several hours.
The bus groaned, careening to a halt.
“Alright, there you are,” the bus driver said. “Hopefully for the last ride of the day…”
“Trust me, I expect plenty more bus rides where that came from,” Fletcher said, walking toward the exit.
The bus driver rubbed his scruffy face. “You’re already due to scrub this entire bus clean, Fletcher. How much more do you plan on offering me? Because, I’m nearing where I won’t keep biting.
Fletcher shrugged. “I’ll find something.”
“You better, because I’m sick of this crap.”
The door swung shut, and the bus sped away. Fletcher moved tiredly forward. The greenhouse was just in front of him. Yet, he felt hopelessly behind.
He couldn’t disagree with the bus driver. He’d gotten sick of this crap too. He couldn’t let himself give up — but he sure as hell wanted to.

Peering into the greenhouse, he saw stalks of sunflowers craning for the sky. They obscured the rest of the greenhouse, and Fletcher began wondering the sunflowers’ functionality. There was no way that the sunflowers could be sold, was there?
He knocked on the glass and listened to the hollow ringing sound it created. He tried the handle, but it wouldn’t budge.
A woman came from behind the sunflowers and sped down the cobbled walkway.
Her hair was done up in a lopsided bun, with bobby pins. She wore a plain, loose t-shirt and baggy jeans, and held a sunhat at her side.
She smiled, showing her teeth. She frowned when Fletcher tried to return it. The door jiggled a few times, before finally coming open.
“Hi, this is the Clover Greenhouse,” she said.
“Don’t see many clovers.”
She gave a tight smile. “Yes, heard that one before. Anyway, I’m Melinda Clover. You are?”
“Stuart Fletcher.”
Fletcher cautiously stepped inside. An overpowering aroma swooped him up, and he held back tears from his eyes.
“Beautiful place,” said Fletcher, still only making out the sunflowers.
Bad as the flower shop had been, this was somehow leagues worse.
“I wanted to come see your husband, actually,” Fletcher said. “Glenn Clover?”
Melinda looked dumbfounded, before switching to a gleam.
“Oh yes, of course! Glenn!”
She smiled to herself.
“I love Glenn,” she said. “He should be here any minute, actually. Me and my gal pals are just having a bit of a fling back here. Yes, I’m sure he’s coming.”
There was a dreamy way in which she said it. Her eyes brimmed with her coffee pupils, and her voice spilled out as silk.
“Glad he’s coming, rather than not,” Fletcher said. “Because, if he wasn’t, I’d be… I’d be mad. Mildly, of course.”
“Of course,” Melinda said, with a curt nod.
Fletcher studied her face — the creases from her faded smile. The supine curves of her neck and chin. She matched his vision of Linda. Though then, visions always fell short of reality.
“Why are you here?” Melinda asked.

“Isn’t that the million-dollar question?” Fletcher said, beaming. “To be ground into ash in a few decades, maybe? I used to think I was here to find why I was here. Though, now that we all have a way of finding it, I find my old meaning meaningless.”
“Very funny,” she said, “but I meant why are you looking for Mr. Clover.”
“To get answers about a person who stole something from me,” Fletcher said.
Melinda took a step back, letting the sunflowers brush against her back. The sunlight made her skin glisten, but it’d pruned prudishly, toward Fletcher.
“I can assure you he hasn’t stolen anything. My husband is a wonderful man. He never harmed a single soul.”

Fletcher shook his head. “No, that’s not what I meant at all. I’m sure he is. It’s just, somebody — a banker, Jim Harrigan — told me that Mr. Clover was the guy I was looking for. Said he was buddies with a real shady pickpocket. Are you familiar with that?”
Melinda’s face broadened purely into smile.
“Did you say Jim Harrigan?”
It was the first time her voice sounded genuinely interested.
“Yeah. Yes. Bit of a prick, though.”
“My husband was friends with a ton of harmful individuals,” said Melinda. “If Jim Harrigan told you that, he wasn’t wrong.”
“Was friends?”
“Was, is, will be… No difference. We’re splitting hairs now, Mr. Fletcher.”

She put an arm around Fletcher and pulled him deeper into the greenhouse. Passing the sunflowers, Fletcher saw overgrowths of weedy plants, and vines. There was no vegetation though. At least, not any he could make out.
“Would you like to join me and my friends in our little game, while we wait for — uh — Mr. Clover?” Melinda asked.

Fletcher shrugged, continuing to look around the greenhouse. They approached a shed at the greenhouse’s center. It was a fresh yellow, the wood and nails sitting firm. The air it exuded was entirely wrong, amid the weedy ground.
“Did you already harvest all your plants, for the season?” Fletcher asked.

“What plants? Power plants?” Melinda snickered to herself. More of a snorting squeal, than anything. “No, I don’t do much gardening in this greenhouse. The sunflowers up front are plenty, to make people think we grow food in here.”
“Then how do you make money? Harrigan told me that you sell fresh produce.”
They were already turning around the shed. Fletcher could see a burbling fountain, and a group of people clustered around it.

Melinda’s expression went sharp. “I do sell fresh produce, though. Of course I do. It’s simply that I buy it from the supermarket, at a very low rate. Then, I sell it back to them as “organic” produce, at a very high rate.”
“Sounds scummy.”
“Money is money — don’t care how it sounds. Isn’t that what we’re all here for?”

A woman gave a whoop, holding a deck of cards in the air. She was dressed in frumpy clothes, and her jewelry dangled loosely. She was unabashed, oblivious to herself. Fletcher walked up to the table and snatched himself a seat. He kept his head down. He very suddenly felt out of place. He knew none of these people. None of them knew him.
He didn’t belong.
“You took the last seat?” Melinda said, with a laugh.
Fletcher looked up, to see the four other chairs occupied by people who were hidden behind their cards. “Sorry, I thought you’d already have an extra one out for Mr. Clover.”
A woman stood from her seat and gestured toward Melinda. Fletcher squinted — it was the same woman from Mayor Haddock’s fundraising party. He stiffened. Lydia, was it?
“You can have mine,” she said. “I can go get us more chairs.”

If she’d recognized Fletcher, she didn’t show it. She scurried off to the shed, before Melinda could even manage a “thank you”. Holding her grin, Melinda took up the man’s deck of cards and took his seat. She then shuffled the stack of cards at the center of the table and began handing a deck to Fletcher.
“Why hello, Fletcher.”
Fletcher snapped his head up from his makeshift deck.
“Don’t tell me you’ve already forgotten about me.”
It was Debby Crowner. She was in the chair just across from him. She readjusted her glasses and gave a lopsided smile. On her face, traces of scowls came out more prominently.
“What are you doing here?” Fletcher asked.
“Just got off my shift, and decided to play cards with one of my best friends of course!” she winked at Melinda, and Melinda winked back. “You’re still considering the job at the factory, right?”
“Considering is the operative word,” Fletcher said, cautiously.
“You should take it!” said the other woman at the table. “I work at the coal refinement plant, just a couple blocks at the factory. Very rewarding work, if I do say so myself.”

A man pulled his cards down from his face. “I work on the trash barge. It’s also like factory work — you’d think it’d be intense, but it’s real fun. Trust me, nothing beats the thrill of trying to find places in the river where you can dump people’s trash, without anybody catching you.”
Fletcher glanced at Melinda, hoping for help. She merely nodded her head receptively.
“Yes, they have a point,” she said. “Very fine work, they all do.”
Fletcher fought to keep his jaw from dropping. Why weren’t Melinda’s conservationist tendencies affected by the words around her.
“I’m Anna Gingras,” the woman said.
“Larry Puck,” the other man said. “Your name?”
Fletcher cleared his throat. “Stuart Fletcher.”
“And what brings you here?” pressed Larry, voice gruff.
“He’s a friend of Jim Harrigan’s!” Melinda said, proudly.
“Harrigan?” Anna said with a squeal. “Oh, I can’t believe it. He’s so dreamy, isn’t he?”
Fletcher nodded softly. “He’s definitely like something out of a dream… I’m not really his friend, though. More like a client.”
Melinda gave Fletcher a playful nudge with her elbow. “Please… Harrigan doesn’t just help anybody, for no reason. There must’ve been something that got him to melt.”
She winked. Suddenly, Harrigan made mounds more sense. He loved Melinda. Melinda? She must’ve still loved him. Yet, what about Mr. Clover? Didn’t she care about him?

“Damn right he doesn’t care about helping anybody,” Larry said. He raised his hands in the air, letting a card slip out. “He ran my brother over last week, while he was crossing the street. Gave him a coupon to the local barber shop. He told my brother he would have never run him over, if his head had just been shiny enough.”
He broke out into a wheezing laugh. “Good thing is: I hate my brother’s guts.”
Anna laughed with him. “I hate your brother too.”
Melinda nodded. “Same.”
Debby gave an icy stare to Larry, before breaking. “I hate your brother, and you.”
“Right back at you.”
“I hate you all,” said Fletcher, with a wide grin.
The table went dead silent. Fletcher went to give Larry a playful jab, but Larry shifted to the side.
Fletcher glanced at the pile of cards at the center of the table.
“So, what game are we playing?” he asked.
“Nothing, until Lydia gets her ass back out here,” Larry said.
He rolled up the sleeves to his shirt. It was a plaid material that looked so thin it could slice an atom.
“I’m coming!” Lydia said. There was crash. “I’ll be out there in just a minute.”
Fletcher’s foot tapped against his will. He felt his skin go flush.
“Speaking of people, Mr. Clover will be here real soon,” Fletcher said. “Right?
Anna let out a long breath of air. “Oh yeah. Right… You were friends with that tight-ass.”
“Never met him, actually.”
Debby clucked her tongue. “So you were online friends? Even worse…”

The shed door sputtered open, with Lydia heaving the chair behind herself. It was a cushioned armchair, complete with elaborate engravings on its legs and backing. The legs thudded as they were set by the table.
Fletcher hid behind his cards as Lydia sat down. Though, she was wincing as she did, clearly distracted.
“We can finally start Go Fish, with you back in!” Melinda said, with a clap.
“Think I threw my back out,” moaned Lydia. “Seriously, you didn’t have any lighter chairs than that?”
“I don’t know, but it’s pretty messed up that you didn’t say anything while you carried the chair out,” said Larry. “Honestly — you couldn’t be bothered to ask me to ask you if you needed help?”
“Sorry, didn’t think of that,” Lydia said, adjusting herself in the chair.
Fletcher tried breathing easy. He couldn’t let Lydia think he was guilty of anything. How much longer would it be until Mr. Clover finally showed his face?
“No chair for Mr. Clover?” he blurted, despite himself.
“If he can crawl out of his hole, he can come get one himself,” said Lydia.
The whole table laughed.
“Got any tens?” asked Melinda.
The table gave a resounding round of “no”. Fletcher looked at his cards and gave a “no” of his own.
“Hey, do I know you?” Lydia asked. Her face contorted as she looked him over.
Fletcher gave yet another “no”, followed by a “go fish”.
“Odd,” she said. “You look so familiar.”
“I knew him already!” said Debby, her glasses bobbing over her nose. “He’s going to get a job at my factory!”
“I never said that,” Fletcher said.
“Factory worker, huh?” said Lydia. “You like working through the soot, and shit?”
“Anybody got any nines?” Fletcher asked. He tugged on the collar to his shirt, peeling it from his drenched skin.
As the table went up in another round of “no”, Melinda leaned in Fletcher and Lydia’s direction.
“Go fish,” she said. Her eyes were inexplicably on Lydia. “He’s friends with Jim Harrigan too. And, he apparently likes toy oil barons.”
Lydia nodded, then gave Fletcher a thumbs up.
“Glad to hear that we’re all in the same boat, here!” she said.

Fletcher pulled a card from the center of the table. He thought up ways to perhaps steer the conversation back toward Mr. Clover. Yet, the more he tried thinking them up, the more at a loss he found himself.
The entire group was grating at his mind. They all seemed privy to something, and he was desperately flailing behind them.
“Alright, I’m confused here,” he finally said.
“We’re all confused in this world, aren’t we?” Larry said. “I can’t even tell if I put my shoes on the right feet this morning.”
Fletcher gave a glare. God — was he that annoying when he pulled the same sort of line on Melinda?

“No, I mean — I don’t get why Melinda is friends with all you people,” he said. “No offense intended, but you guys should all be scum of the earth to her. You make money by finding clever ways of muddying up the environment!”
“No offense taken,” said Debby. “In fact, thank you for recognizing the brilliance of our work.”
Melinda’s smile went thin as she set her cards down.

“Let’s not pretend that none of us are responsible for environmental damage,” she said. “Just the act being alive slowly kills the world. It’s only nature. As a conservationist, isn’t nature what I’m supposed to conserve?”
“Damn straight,” said Larry. “All this fuss about conserving trees… But never any talk about conserving the people who don’t want trees!”
The table had gone around to Fletcher’s turn. He inevitably took another card from the deck — he had no matches.
Thus far, the entire table had no matches. Logically, it didn’t line up. Though, his brain cautioned him against speaking up.
“You’re a conservationist, but you support pollution?” Fletcher said, raising an eyebrow.

“I’m a classical conservationist, Mr. Fletcher,” she said, giving a snide glare. “It’s no surprise you don’t understand. Though, it’s why I’m friends with all these people. They need the support of a gal like me, to have the public on their sides.”

Anna snorted. “It’s so true. She sent out a report to the community that my coal factory was ten times better for the environment, emissions-wise, than solar energy. I’m not quite sure how she pulled it off, but… She did. Quite the feat!”
Melinda blushed, and finally set down two matches.
“It’s all simple arithmetic, really,” she said. “Just add a few numbers together and say that they’re related to pollution. I’m surprised more statisticians don’t use it.”
“And I thought that my client, Mayor Haddock, was the next Weinstein!” said Lydia.
Fletcher cleared his throat. “Don’t you mean Einstein?”
Lydia rolled her eyes. “As if I don’t know the difference.”

The entire table turned toward Fletcher, as though awaiting a standoff. Sunlight baked through the greenhouse’s glass, burning Fletcher’s skin. Not that he needed the sun’s help. His skin burned two times hotter than the sun, all on its own.
“How’s the campaign with Haddock going, anyway?” asked Melinda.
Tension ratcheted up. It was in the air, carried on the faintest scent of sweat and terror. Fletcher’s gut clenched.

“Oh, just dandy,” said Lydia. Her eyes remained on Fletcher. “Mayor Haddock’s conservationist stance has saved him quite a lot of voters, like you predicted. Everybody is for his reverse recycling stance.”
“Reverse recycling stance?” Fletcher asked, innocently.
“You haven’t heard? He’s having one of our factories produce a ton of bicycles, which can cycle in reverse.”
“My factory,” Debby said, waving her cards.
“Then, he’s going to have us smelt them all back into metal blocks, at a coal factory.”
Anna gave a grin. “Mine.”
“Finally, we’re going to toss the metal blocks into the river.”
Larry straightened up with pride. “My specialty.”

“The plan is perfect and involves everybody. See, we all know bicycles are better for the environment than cars. Plus, building bikes and trashing them is a quick way to drive business. I couldn’t come up with something more genius if I tried!”
“I definitely wouldn’t try,” said Fletcher. “You guys sound smart. But, the plan sounds so dumb, it has to fail.”
“That’s where you’d be wrong.”

Nimbly, Lydia plucked a card out of Fletcher’s deck, and added it to her own. Fletcher thought to point it out, but Lydia’s eyes burrowed into him. She was peering into his soul. Had she finally recognized him?
“The dumber a plan is?” Lydia continued, setting a freshly matched pair down. “The more likely that people are to buy into it.”
The table went up in murmuring agreement.
“Besides, it’s destined to work anyway,” said Melinda. “The chaos theorem predicted it.”

“We didn’t need the theorem to predict it. Everybody saw this working, especially that one weird guy,” said Lydia, with a laugh. “You remember me telling you about him, right? He’s really into polluting the environment. Good distraction, or whatever. He’s planning on going all out with the marketing, and everything.”
Fletcher’s breath escaped his throat.
“What one guy?” he snapped.
“You ever hear about that pickpocket?” Lydia said.
“He definitely heard about him,” Melinda said, putting a hand on Lydia’s wrist. “Why, apparently the pickpocket wants to kill him. Isn’t that just sublime?”
“She’s right!” Fletcher shouted. “My life is on the line! Who is he?”
“Hell do I know… Mr. Clover knew though, didn’t he?”
Lydia looked over to Melinda, who gave another nod.
“When will Mr. Clover get here, then?” Fletcher asked.
The table went quiet.
“Got any tens?” Larry asked.
The table went into another series of “no”.

Precious time was being wasted. Fletcher squirmed in his seat and looked toward the exit. The weeds and plants around it seemed to crane toward the handle, as though they too desperately wished to escape. That, or they wished to bar anybody else from escaping.
“Do you know where Mr. Clover—,” Fletcher began.

“So,” Larry said, cutting him off. Larry readjusted his overalls and stared at Lydia’s trim suit. “Is there anything the chaos theorem predicted for Haddock’s inevitable win that we donors might want to watch out for? Don’t want my money going to waste.”
“Well, the nuclear strike is all but official,” said Lydia. “In fact, time has caught up with the theorem. The president announced the planned strike about an hour ago.”
Larry shrugged. “I’ve stuck my head in the microwave a few times. A little radiation never hurt anybody.”
Nuclear strike? Fletcher’s heart turned inside out. He wanted to wriggle out of his skin. He had to get out of here. Out of this town.
“I saw that,” said Melinda. “Quite crazy. Still, it’s hard to believe that it’s launching tonight. I heard it’ll hit by midnight.”
“I know what I’ll be doing until then,” said Anna. She mimed a wine bottle and made a few glugs.
“Wait, wait, wait!” Fletcher said, his voice coming out in a wheeze. “We’re going to be hit by a nuclear strike?”

“Yeah, apparently it’s the most affordable option,” said Lydia. “See, Dexburg is constantly hit by earthquakes. We’re on track to have one that’s going to level the whole city. Every time that happens? Federal must step in and shell out cash for us to rebuild. They figured out it’d just be more affordable to nuke us all and be done with it.”
“It only makes sense,” said Larry. “I mean, it’s hard to blame them for being efficient.”
“They’ll probably just pin it all on the Russians, anyway,” said Lydia. “Say that they’d been attacking Dexburg with earthquakes, and forced their hand. They’ll use it as an excuse for war… “
“The lousy Russians deserve it, for being Russian,” Debby said, with a firm nod. “Never met a Russian that I liked. That’s what I always say.”
“Agreed,” said Melinda. “Hell, I’ve never even met a Russian.”
Nausea filling his gut, Fletcher shook his head. “This entire town is about to be blown to smithereens, and we’re just going to sit here? We’ll do nothing to stop it?”

Lydia chortled, and readjusted her business suit. “Look at the people around you. Look at yourself. You working class folk… Doing nothing is the only thing that you can do. Guys like Mayor Haddock are the ones in control, and even they know that there’s no controlling this.”
“If we don’t get out of here, we’re all probably going to die.”

“We’re all definitely going to die, at some point. My doctor told me everyone is born with a preset amount of heartbeats. Running around in a frenzy will only speed up our heartrate — bring our deaths to us faster. Enjoying the flames as they come down upon us is the true order of life.”
Anna looked up from her cards, eyes welling. “That’s beautiful. Are you going to make that into a speech for Mayor Haddock?”
Lydia gave an abashed shrug of the shoulders. “Maybe. If I combined this, with his new ‘new history’ slogan, he might just win in a landslide.”

For Fletcher, death wasn’t good enough. He needed to get out of this town. Perhaps if he collected all his possessions, and hauled them away, he’d have a surefire means of rebuilding. Though, without the oil baron, and all its value, would he really be able to get back on his feet?
He couldn’t leave this town. At least, not without the last parts of his questionings answered.

“As much as I adore Mayor Haddock and his policies, I’m probably going to want to leave this town,” said Fletcher. “I need my life. More importantly, I need this valuable item that was stolen from me… It’s the only way I can get back on my feet.”
The entire table looked at Fletcher with blank faces.
“I’m here waiting for Mr. Clover, remember?” Fletcher said, putting on a smile. “I — you guys haven’t already forgotten, have you? I want to meet the pickpocket?”
Melinda blinked. “Mr. who?”
“Mr. Clover? Your husband? You said that he’d be here, soon!”
Melinda gave a slow shake of her head. “That’s right… Uh, Mr. Clover died the other day. Yes, the pickpocket killed him. Something about him getting too close. I’m sure you know how that is.”
Fletcher didn’t know. His body went completely numb.
“He was a moron,” said Debby.
Melinda nodded. “True. He always was leaving the toilet seat up… And, whenever he made eggs, he’d burn the things to charcoal.”
“Aren’t they hosting a funeral for him this evening?” asked Lydia.
“Probably. Think his family sent me an invite. The burial is at Drudge’s Cemetery. I sure as hell am not going, though.”

All this time, he’d been waiting for a dead man? A man who was killed by the very man he was searching for? Nonetheless, his mind was stirring up all the pieces that he did know. Clearly this pickpocket was somebody he was already familiar with. They had political goals at the forefront of their motives. They were in support of pollution. Moreover, they were capable of murder.
He tried narrowing the suspects, as he considered who it could be. Marvin? Carvel? Jack? Logan Gerri? Officer Mayhew? Haddock himself?
Lydia was staring at Fletcher, her forehead raised.
“What did you say you were looking for, again?”
“Sorry, I’m still shocked that this Mr. Clover guy is dead,” Fletcher said, wiping a bead of sweat away.
Melinda played with her hair. “Yeah well… In case Jim Harrigan asks anything about me, I’m definitely single.”
“He didn’t answer my question,” Lydia said. “What did you say you were looking for?”
“A toy oil baron,” said Fletcher. “The town pickpocket stole it from me.”
Lydia nodded. “I thought you looked familiar… You’re that guy from the Mayor’s fundraiser, right? Marvin Whisk?”
Fletcher shook his head. “Me? No. My name is definitely Stuart Fletcher.”
Lydia pulled up her phone. “You sure about that? Because, the Mayor is on his way. He’s been looking for you. I called him, little while ago.”
Fletcher’s face flushed red.
“You can’t be serious,” he said. “I haven’t done anything. Honest to god.”

Yet, he was already stepping away from the table, and moving toward the door. He suddenly noticed all the thorns on the plants that covered it. All this time, he’d been caught in a trap. He hadn’t even known it.
“I really have to get going, now that I think about it,” said Fletcher. “If Mr. Clover isn’t here, that leaves my leads dead… I have other places to be.”
Larry laughed. “You can’t just drop your cards like that. The Mayor is looking for you! I mean, Christ, I wish I were you!”
Fletcher bit his lip. He wished he could only be so naïve as Larry.
“It was nice having you,” said Melinda.

As Fletcher made a brisk stride through the grass, he was gripped around the forearm. “I can’t have you leave,” said Lydia. “Come on — finish the game with us. Who knows? Maybe you’ll have a good draw.”
Fletcher attempted to yank his arm away, but her grip was too firm. There’d be no breaking away without breaking an arm, would there?

Glass shattered from above. Shimmering shards sprinkled in Fletcher’s hair. He glanced up, then clenched his eyes shut. A portion of the ceiling had fallen away. Somebody in a ski mask had fallen with it.
Shrieks and shouts resounded from the card table. There was a thud. Fletcher reopened his eyes, to see Lydia fleeing the scene, and somebody in a ski mask flailing on the ground.
“That hurt…” they wheezed, “Hurt much more than I expected.”

It was difficult to determine the voice. They were dressed in all black, and their head was covered by a ski-mask. It had to be the pickpocket. Fletcher stood dumbfounded, while the rest of the card party ran around him. He didn’t want to leave his only chance of retrieving his oil baron and discovering the identity of this pickpocket at the door.
He snatched up a gun from the ground — it must’ve fallen from the pickpocket’s hands. He trembled, gripping it, and stepped back. He wasn’t all that keen on dying, either.
He made a swift kick to the pickpocket’s side.
He grunted. It was most definitely a he — there was no mistaking that.

Fletcher made a few more kicks, then ran for the exit. Yet, the pickpocket gripped him by the shoelace, bringing him to the ground. There was a blast as Fletcher accidentally pulled the gun’s trigger. The gun went flying from his hands.
His head throbbed after hitting the grass and taking in a mouthful of dirt. Even as he spit it out, the dirt maintained a muddy mixture with the saliva.
“Get over here, you fuck,” the pickpocket wretched, crawling toward Fletcher on his elbows.
Fletcher struggled to get back to his feet, only for the pickpocket to clasp a deft hand around the ankle. He gave a swift kick back, hoping to remove the grip. To no avail.

“Just — just come with me,” the pickpocket wheezed. Blood burbled from his exposed skin, where shards of glass had cut it. “This has been far too much trouble, at this point. We can keep this simple. I — I have that stupid toy you want. It’s at my place. Promise.”
“Taking promises from a pickpocket? Better than promises from my banker, I guess…”
“So long as you follow me, and cut me a fair deal, we can get out of this. Even as pi.”
“Wrong idiom, idiot.”

Fletcher managed to land a kick to the pickpocket’s head. Back on his feet, he ran for the exit. After bounding a few strides, it occurred to him that he should’ve grabbed the gun. At this same instant, gunshots rippled through the air. Fletcher ducked and went for the door.
It was too late to try confronting the pickpocket. In any case, Fletcher felt that the pickpocket wasn’t one to be talked with. He glanced back. No — too risky. He could die.
A bit of his jeans snagged on a plant, ripping. He tore forward, until he’d barreled through the door.
His eyes widened, and he skidded to a halt. Harry was right ahead of him. Harry gripped Fletcher around the shoulders, straightening his balance.
“Woah, woah, woah!” Harry said. “Where are you going, slick?”
Fletcher shook his head, flabbergasted.
“Where did you come from?”
“I heard you on the police intercoms,” said Harry. “Apparently, the cops are on their way. Plus… It always helps that I saw us meeting here in the chaos theorem. It was inevitable.”
Fletcher nodded. It was an acceptable enough answer.
“Look, I don’t have much time to talk,” said Fletcher. “I’m glad you’re here. But, did you bring your truck with you?”
Harry clicked the fob to his key, causing a truck behind him to beep.
“Of course I brought my truck,” he said. “But, if you’re coming with me, we’re going to need to talk.”
A gunshot went off.
“I’ll talk about whatever you want,” Fletcher said. “Just start the truck.”
I always knew that greenhouses are supposed to make people feel green. However, I feel a whole lot greener than I think I should.
The entire place has been reduced to shards of glass. The greenhouse’s metal frame has been preserved, at least. Maybe it could make a nice jungle gym, still? Yeah, I’d pay to have that.
“And how are you doing, Marvin?”
It’s Officer Haynam. He’s doodling a flimsy sketch of the crime scene on his notepad. It looks more like a lopsided pizza, than anything. Though, he’s clearly trying. At least there’s that.

The police are putting yellow tape around the whole scene. Priest Carvel and his cult are being pushed back. It looks like Logan Gerri and a couple of his buddies are being blocked off too. For whatever reason though, Officer Haynam still hasn’t made me leave.
“Did you see anything suspicious when coming through here?” he asks. He takes a bite of his doughnut, and brushes a couple of crumbs off his upper lip — classy.
“I never saw anything,” I say. “I just was walking by here, when the entire place went up in gunshots. A ton of people were screaming and running away… It was a madhouse.”
Officer Haynam gave a grunt.
“I could imagine. I can imagine a lot of things, actually.”
I give Haynam a look. He’s looking at me.
“Like what?” I say.
“Maybe you rode in here on a dragon. You know those awesome looking ones, from the videogames?”
He looks to his fellow officers for support, who give firm nods.

“But, something tells me that you didn’t come in on an awesome dragon,” said Officer Haynam. “Something tells me that you didn’t. Something that you didn’t just walk by here, either. You’re friends with Fletcher.”
“Not true! I hate that man’s guts!”
Officer Haynam grabs me by the arm. “Oh well. You’re coming with us, and you’re going to talk.
I guess I’m in his custody now. Just brilliant.
Even when he’s not around, Fletcher is screwing me over.
“You’re going to explain what’s going on,” Harry said. “Like, right now. No games.”
Fletcher rubbed the back of his wrist.
“I’m just looking for my lost oil baron toy, okay?” he said. “It’s a very valuable item. This guy stole it from me. And, I want it back. For some reason though, this whole town is against it.”
Harry glared at Fletcher. “You’re telling me that you risked your entire fucking life to get back a toy, just now?”
“It matters a lot,” Fletcher said, with a shrug.
The truck rattled, as it picked up speed. They were climbing up a steep hill, into the heart of the city. Slouching office buildings flew past, and quivering signs waved them by.
“Why, though?” Harry asked.

Fletcher’s memories flashed by him again. He pinched his eyes shut and attempted to wipe them away. Though, they flailed at the gates of his consciousness, doing everything to break their way through.

“It — there’s no why,” said Fletcher, “What, is what you should be looking for. There are a lot of what answers. What I was doing, what I knew, what I had… All things that were around, when I had the oil baron. It has memory attached to it. Value. I have to have it back.”

Fletcher’s eyelids fluttered going heavy. He strained to keep them open, suddenly wishing he had pliers or toothpicks to pry them open with. He was in a room. A dim room, with a label maker. He was sticking prices on toys — searching for a window outside of the room. All the while, his uncle looked over his shoulder, piping mad. Perhaps a little drunk.
“Stop letting them stick to you like a spider, stupid bug boy,” he roared.
His Uncle was always a dumb drunk.
“It can’t possibly mean that much to you,” said Harry.
He’d put on a face as though he were only joking. Yet, beneath the brim of his brow was concern.
“It does, because it does,” said Fletcher. “Things don’t have any meaning, aside from what we ascribe to them.”

The truck swerved around a bend, before entering a parking lot. Harry slowed his speed — they’d entered the Elementary school parking lot. If it hadn’t been for the fact that Fletcher had grown up in this school, he would’ve hardly recognized it. It was utterly abandoned, save for a couple of school buses and a rusting car parked near a dumpster.
“You don’t mean that,” said Harry. “I can tell you’ve been in a rough patch… I — it doesn’t matter. But, like it or not, some things have inherent meaning.”
He tried putting a hand on Fletcher’s shoulder, but Fletcher leaned away.
“Gee, jumpy, huh?” Harry said.
“It’s been a long day.”

Harry rolled his eyes. “Okay, look: maybe nothing means anything unless you give it meaning… I’ll give you that. Though, if you’re dead? You can’t give anything meaning to begin with. Thus, isn’t life the most meaningful state of being? Thus, doesn’t life, at the very least, have meaning?”
The truck sputtered to a stop, when Harry turned the key out of the ignition. All the while, Fletcher’s mind turned, weighing the question.
“Can water be wet?” Fletcher asked.
Harry shrugged. “Course it can. Fire can be hot, right?”

“Yes. But, fire can’t be caught on fire. Life is a conduit, through which we’re given meaning… But it can’t be meaningful. The very fact that life gives meaning makes it so life can’t have inherent meaning of its own.”
Harry sat for a moment, dumbstruck. He leaned back and looked toward the ceiling of the car. Biting his lip, he gave Fletcher a glance.
He winked. “Ice can be dry though, can’t it? Therefore, water must be wet. Seems you have another think coming, buddy.”
“Dry ice, wet water, room temperature slush… I don’t even care anymore.”

Harry flipped his keys in the air. “See, that’s why I actually followed you to the greenhouse Fletcher. See, I know that you’ve been considering suicide. I know that you want to give up. But, you just can’t, okay?”
Fletcher raised an eyebrow. “What are you talking about? I feel more alive than I ever have. This whole toy chase — it gives me a sense of purpose. Isn’t that good?”
“You have half the town on your tail, at this point. We’ve talked about this.”
“Why do you care so much? You haven’t talked to me in weeks, and suddenly I’m the most important person in the world to you?”

Harry’s eyes went downcast, and his voice soft. “Margaret and I have been talking. And, I really think you could benefit from taking the chaos theorem. Seriously, it could clear so much shit up for you.”
Fletcher’s face went hot. His muscles stiffened. His voice came out as ice.
“You’ve been talking to Margaret?” Fletcher asked.

Harry shook his head. “I’ve been — I’ve been dating Margaret. For quite some time, actually. It’s been going great.  However, you… You can’t keep coming to her apartment like that. I know you’re a good guy, Fletcher. But, you need to find a life.”
The sun was drooping behind the school. Yet, obscured as it was, its rays pierced Fletcher’s eyes. Its heat left Fletcher’s skin a hot wax.
“You promised me that you wouldn’t date her,” Fletcher said.
“A wise man once said, things happen. Penguins start flying, the President goes loony, our town falls into ruin… It’s just life. You live it and move on.”
“Who?”
“Me.”
“Sounds more like a wise guy than a wise man, to me.”
The truck stewed for a bit, as the sun and their body heat steadily turned it to an oven.
“This school is actually the hub for chaos theorem tests,” said Harry.
“I figured.”
“It’s set up just like any election booth. Go in there, and you can finally have your entire life plotted out for you.”
Fletcher laughed. “I hate elections. A game of pick your poison.”

“Look… I know that you haven’t been getting anywhere with your toy oil baron search. It’s going to run you ragged man. If you just take this thing, you’ll have all your answers. The past can be left in the past. Hell, you can create a new past. You can finally enjoy your future.”
“You want me to completely give up on searching for something, and read the equation?”

“You’ll know how everything is meant to be. Imagine a life where you don’t have to worry about whether you’re doing the wrong thing — where what you choose, whatever you choose, was the choice you were going to choose no matter what. You can finally have that, Fletcher. All the answers you could ever want. And, it’s right inside that building. In that booth.”

Harry gave Fletcher a smile. It was the odd smile that could melt icecaps, yet completely freeze someone in their place. Unlatching the door, Harry stepped into the sunlight. His skin was a light bronze, and his hair swung with the wind. The summer had been good to him.
Fletcher realized how tight his seatbelt was against his chest. The car’s air was stuffy. Suffocating, even. He unlatched his seatbelt and opened his door.
“You going to step out, or not?” Harry asked.

Harry was right. It was a terrible thing, really. Though, the logic couldn’t be denied. Life was a futile endeavor. If the chaos theorem existed, there must have been a set plan to everything. There was no point in continuing to try avoiding it, was there?
