He stepped out of the car and followed Harry toward the school. Somehow, the parking lot was emptier than it’d been when they’d entered. It was just a slab of drab concrete. The finer details of the scenery filtered through Fletcher, in a aloof osmosis.

The metal doors to the school yawned open. A guard stood in the way. He patted down Fletcher’s pants, before guiding him through another security check. Trembles shot through Fletcher’s body. Everywhere he looked, there were security guards. The school building wasn’t in the best of shape either, with bits of eroded brick scattered along the linoleum.
Fletcher read the messages scrawled along the walls.
“The universe can suck it.”
“I broke my pointer, to make a point.”
He shook his head. This was what needed to be done.
Harry broke into a sprint as they reached the end of the main hall and neared the doors to the school gym. Bursting through the door, he let out a hoot.
“You’re finally going to do it!” Harry said.
Fletcher entered the gym. A small line wrapped around the outer wall, as people worked their way toward the theorem booths. Fletcher took his place in the back of the line.

The gym was notably cheerier than the rest of the school had been. The lights gave off a reassuring glow. A sheen hung over the floor. A janitor must’ve recently buffed it. Indeed, it felt as if the entire gym had been recently tightened up, in preparation for his arrival. Had it? Much as Fletcher told himself this question was irrational, he gave it more thought than he wanted.
It wouldn’t stop coming back at him. Perhaps the universe was arranging itself in his favor. It wanted this.
It was like Harry had said, wasn’t it? It didn’t matter what he chose, because it was what he chose.
“You’re doing the right thing,” Harry whispered into Fletcher’s ear. “Just look at how I turned out. You can have what I have. Maybe more.”
Harry slipped away, behind the crowd. Fletcher looked for him among the bleachers. His eyes flitted to the door. However, Harry was nowhere to be seen.
He’d probably just gone to the bathroom. He certainly couldn’t have made it far.

The line crept forward. Giggles gushed from the end of it. A lady handed out the tickets to each booth, a smile plastered to her face. Her face said she loved her job. Fletcher could’ve believed it. Yet, did anybody love something, truly?
Things of no note droned by, until it was nearly Fletcher’s turn. John’s voice burst from the front of the line.
“Please!” John intoned. “I want to forget! I want a refund! Please, take it back!”

John was a shriveled ball. His jacket was wadded over his shoulders, caked with mud. Ruddy clumps were on his hands and face. Had he been bleeding? In any case, he’d been battered. Alongside the muck were clusters of scrapes and bruises.

Yet, the crowd held no sympathy for John. Rather, their eyes were distant, holding disgust. Worse, Fletcher found himself going the distance with them. John had lost every shred of his humanity. A viscous foam seeped from his mouth. His eyes were fiercely bloodshot. Patches of his hair were mangled, and others were torn out entirely.
A day could change a person. Nonetheless, the change Fletcher saw was beyond any he could comprehend.
“We don’t give refunds here,” the lady said, despite John’s pleas. “Once you’ve learned your destiny, there is no denying it. No defying it. It remains stuck to you, and you with it.”
A chill ran down Fletcher’s spine. What he found in the chaos theorem — whatever he found — was something that couldn’t be changed. Could he truly be prepared for it?
“But you must!” John shrieked. “I can’t live like this! This isn’t me!”
The lady’s smile deepened, keeping with her air of patient accommodation.
“It must be you,” she said. “Who else could you be?”

John growled, then leapt toward her. He was given a swift kick to the head, by a member of the crowd. Several guards rushed toward him, but John was already being picked apart by the crowd. The guards gave a few bats with their batons, breaking the crowd apart. They lifted John from the ground, and dragged him from the room.

There wasn’t much left of John to be dragged. His mouth had burst, upon losing several teeth. He flailed at the air, but one of his arms moved against its joints. Indeed, it seemed the crowd had broken it.
Ghastly black marks were left on the gym’s basketball court, from the heels to John’s shoes.
The gym echoed with a muffled cry, as John disappeared through the doors.
Ahead of Fletcher, one of the people snickered to themselves.
“Good riddance,” they said. “Inferiors… Why can’t we just keep them all in ditches, like a civilized civilization?”
Fletcher’s mouth went dry. John had been an inferior. That was why his life had frayed. Yes, it all made sense now. Only inferiors fell to pieces from the theorem.
Concern welled as the man was handed a ticket and directed toward a booth. It was nearly Fletcher’s turn. Yet, his uncertainty was higher than ever.
John may have been an inferior. Though, wasn’t there just as much chance that Fletcher, too, was an inferior?

Granted, there was just as much chance that he was doomed to become insane either way. Turning out as John was something to be feared, but surely he wasn’t a destined failure like John. Was he? No — he was meant for success. The theorem would attest to this.
It would have to.

“You get what you deserve out of life, not what you want,” said Uncle Timothy. “You must remember that. It’ll keep your head on straight. You can either be a failure or be a success. Take your pick, then pick at it.”
Uncle Timothy’s face was bloodshot, and bloated. He’d been out drinking.

There was a shatter as Uncle Timothy bumbled into a table. He let out a howl — he’d just broken a ceramic pizza maker into eighty pieces. Fletcher stared at the pizza maker’s face. The jaw and its smiling mouth were decimated. All that remained of the face’s lower half was its mustache — a black gape.
“Look at what you did, you moron!” Uncle Timothy cried, both to himself and at Fletcher.
He gripped Fletcher by the shoulders, shaking him as though he were a ragdoll.
“Look what you did!”
“How’s your day going sir?”
Fletcher blinked, holding back the mist rising over his eyes.
“Sir?”
Fletcher read the nametag on the woman’s chest — Petunia.
“Peculiar name,” Fletcher said.
“Excuse me?” Petunia said.
A ticket hung slackly from the edge of her fingers, bearing Fletcher’s name and booth number.
Fletcher cleared his throat. “Your name is peculiar. See, I hate petunias. I’m allergic to them. Quite a funny coincidence, really.”
Petunia nodded stiffly.
“You have booth number 13,” she said. “Also, another funny coincidence: I happen to be allergic to coincidences.”
Her skin stretched in a smile that might’ve covered a mile, if mapped.

Sapped of all energy, Fletcher stumbled his way toward his booth. He drew back the curtain. It clung to the skin, with an annoying static. The interior of the booth was dimly lit, save for a single screen. It shone as a pale moon would, dull and barren in all its luminosity.
Harry had been right. The past could be left in the past.
Fletcher tapped the screen and entered his name. His address. He was about to press the enter button. He truly was.
However, he had no clue as to how to go about it. What should’ve been the last thought in his head, before he took that last step?  Should he just press it without another thought? Could he?

Life would never be the same again. Indeed, it would lose all spontaneity. It would be entirely the same as whatever flow of information this machine spat out. No matter how much he may wind up wishing to damn it, there would be no damn that could stop it.
His finger hovered. Wavered.
He placed it back in his pocket. That was when his phone buzzed.
It was his email. His heart gave a flutter. Linda had emailed him.

“I’m sorry that I’ve been so evasive,” the email read. “I thought I could talk to you — tell you the truth about what’s going on. But, I don’t know how much I can trust. I don’t have too much time. The truth is, I don’t know who you are, or where you are. I’ll have to cut off our ties, before things get worse.”
There was an image attached to it. Fletcher clicked on it, downloading it.

It was the grainy image of an eye. It was a light hazel, with a hint of green. Long, delicate lashes led from the lids. The skin was soft. Blur from the camera probably helped. Yet, the eye held an undeniable grace. Fletcher had spent many a day obsessing over the eyes of older toys — polishing them, and refining them — though, this eye had an inherently Euclidian texture about it. It exceeded what any craftsman could replicate.
It was just an eye. That, he couldn’t deny. However, it was proof that this person was tangible. Real.
“You can tell me anything that’s going on,” Fletcher said. “I’m at the school right now. I’m about to leave. I will find you. I’ll help you. I love you.”
He sent it. When he did, his head was a flurry of second thoughts. Though, he knew sending the message was the right step.
He stepped out of the booth and sprinted toward the exit.
“Sir!” Petunia shouted. “Sir, you’re not to abandon your booth until you’ve completed the process! You haven’t finished, sir!”
There were heavy footfalls from the guards chasing after him. Fletcher looked behind — their faces were damp with concern and rage.

Fletcher lightly pushed open the doors, sliding between the crack. The door slammed behind him, and he considered taking action to lock it. Though, the guards were bound to break through before he could manage that, weren’t they?
He kept running.
“Fletcher?” Harry said. “What’s the rush? You finally get the theorem?”
“I have somewhere I have to be,” Fletcher panted.
He had no idea where to go. Yet, it couldn’t be here. Anywhere but here.
Harry blocked Fletcher’s path.
“Woah, woah, woah,” he said. “Slow down there. You can’t just chicken out now. You’re nothing like a chicken —more a pigeon, than anything. Seriously, how bad can what’s in the theorem really be.”
“It could be the end of me,” said Fletcher. “Pigeon though I may be, I can’t be pigeon-holed.”

He gave Harry a shove and tried to make his way through the door. Though, the sheer look of dejection gave Fletcher pause. Clean-cut as Harry’s face was, a part of him appeared broken by Fletcher. Betrayed.
Fletcher slipped his hand into Harry’s pocket, and pulled out his keys. The metal winked at him, with the gleam of fading sunlight.
The sun would be gone, soon enough.
“I know a part of your journey,” Harry said, “at least, the parts that intersect with mine.”

Fletcher could hear the guards making their way down the hall. Heart pounding, he barreled through the door and into the parking lot. The gravel was aggressive on his feet, and his chest pooled with sweat. A slight breeze carried him. Harry’s voice tried drawing him back.
“Fletcher, you have a good future, predicted by the chaos theorem!” Harry said.
His voice was shallow, and full of desperate pants. Though, the words rattled inside Fletcher’s skull.
“Then why don’t you tell me it?” Fletcher said. He’d turned around, running backwards. “Why don’t you just spare me the trouble, and give all this information to me? Huh?”

“I overrule the rules. Harry. I can control every step of the way — right down to the number of seconds I spend washing my hands, or the number of times I shave my knuckles.”
Harry’s face furled in disgust. “You shave your knuckles?”
“Not the point! You think that life can be labeled, and stuffed in a file? It can’t. I’m in control of my own destiny.”

“Turkeys think they’re in control of their own destiny on thanksgiving,” Harry shouted. “That doesn’t mean squat though, when thanksgiving rolls around. Our births aren’t in our hands. Neither are our deaths. Why do we have the hubris to think we have control of what comes in between?”
“There’s always that one turkey who our president pardons, though. What if I’m that?”
“Our president is a mistake. Look — just come back! What are you going to do? Where are you going to go?”

The school was already several yards away, and Harry a small speck in it. Two guards burst out and ran past him. Fletcher looked over his shoulder and hit the unlock button on the keys. Cherry red and cheery, Harry’s car gave a beep.

Harry’s small figure desperately fumbled at his pants pockets. It must’ve only just been dawning on him as to what happened to his keys. He was reminiscent to one of the windup soldiers that Fletcher had dusted on his shelves, all these years. He was stiff. Though, his movements were quick. Frantic.
“Fletcher get back here!” Harry shouted. “That’s my truck! Fletcher, you can’t have my truck!”
Fletcher snorted to himself. As if any of this was something he had a say in, anymore.
“We order you to stop!” one of the guards said, mimicking Harry’s tone. “You must complete the theorem!”
“Nice to see you that you dodos finally caught up to me,” Fletcher said, beneath the roar of Harry’s engine. “I’m amazed it took so long, though. The place isn’t a maze…”
Foot hitting the gas, the truck petered out of its spot. The guards and Harry fell further away, even as their voices went louder. Shriller.
Fletcher’s phone beeped aggressively. It was undoubtedly Harry — he must’ve been desperate to get him to stop. Though, then, why would he stop? There was nothing here. No hope. No life. No friends.
Just raw calculation. The place was dead inside.

It reminded him too much of his uncle. It all had held a glossy, childish texture to it. However, at its belly, there was no escape. The wonder drew itself in, until it smothered — and one was left wondering why they ever felt such wonder in the first place.
Fletcher smiled to himself. He’d escaped though. He’d proven himself. It was a great thing he was a good pickpocket.

He only had one step left to truly proving himself, didn’t he? Finishing out his search for Linda, and the oil baron — showing up the pickpocket — it was the sole goal. Now, if only he were equally as good at finding the real pickpocket’s whereabouts as he was at being a pickpocket…

That said, he did only need to find the whereabouts. Fighting the pickpocket was out of the question. He needed to avoid another confrontation, as best he could. The pickpocket would pay, no doubt. Though, it couldn’t be done through fisticuffs.
Fletcher’s only lead was dead, though. Trying to find the whereabouts was a fool’s errand.
“Fool’s errands are my kind of errands,” Fletcher muttered to himself.

He bit his lip. His only lead was Mr. Clover. He was literally dead. Deader than a politician at a charity fundraiser. For Christ’s sake, today was Mr. Clover’s funeral. It could be Fletcher, next. Did he really want this?
Yes… It could be him next. At the funeral.
Wasn’t Mr. Clover supposed to have family at the funeral and burial?
Harry’s truck skidded to a halt. Fletcher turned it around.
He needed to get to the burial, before his lead was buried once and for all.
“You moron,” Jack says, tires squealing as he turns the corner.
I sway into the wall of the car and grip the handle to keep balance.
I can’t tell if he’s talking to me, or himself.
He pulls the gun from his pocket and aims it at my head.
“Hey, what’s the big idea?” I say.
“The cops were here right when we got here,” Jack says. “You squealed to the cops. You must’ve.”
I laugh to myself. I could take this guy with ease. I’ve chewed up and spit out guys half his size. Somebody twice the size of them should barely be harder, right?
Still, a part of myself feels slightly intimidated.
Slightly.

“Look, I didn’t think that they’d be here anymore than you did,” I say. “Sure, I might’ve thought about calling the cops once or twice. But, do you think I would have myself implicated with you scumbags, if I could help it? I’d be arrested too, dumbass!”
Nodding stiffly, Jack relieves the gun from my head and slides it back into his pocket.
“At least this guy is dead though, right?” Clair says, looking through the car’s window. “I mean, there’s no way he survived all of that, right?”
She gestures at the decimated greenhouse. I’m inclined to agree with her. However, Jack merely shakes his head dejectedly.
“Saw him get away in a truck, with some buddy of his,” says John. “Couldn’t get the plates though. Couldn’t have us chase him either, with the cops arriving — needed to keep a low profile.”
“So, I guess we’re fucked again then?” Clair asks.
Jack nods, morosely.
Much as Jack likes to call me the king of morons? He’s definitely the king of the kings of morons.
Kings have kings, right?
Crud, now I feel like king isn’t even a word…

Chapped grass crunched beneath Fletcher’s feet. Clouds obscured the sky, reducing it to gray. He looked over his shoulder to see if anybody was following him. A crow squawked, from its perch on the iron fencing. A gash was mapped down its face. Fletcher winced at what could’ve caused it.

Another series of iron gates swung open, engraved faces upon their spires scowling down at Fletcher. One of the faces was that of a sphinx. Another was of a man who looked so ancient, he might as well have been a sphinx.

Fletcher took note of the tombstones he passed, upon entering through the gates. Weeds strangled them, leaving cracks and fissures throughout the rock. Some tombstones were reduced to disparate chunks of rock, undoubtedly caused by the many earthquakes throughout the decades. Of these unfortunate tombstones, only metal plaques left to hold them together. Yet, even the plaques of some were decaying to rust and grime.

Fletcher paused by a tombstone with a small statue placed atop it. It was reminiscent to a Greek sculpture, featuring a man in a relaxed contrapposto. The muscles along its body rippled and flowed. Its face, made of stone though it was, had a soft texture. A delicate design and craftsmanship had been put into every bit of its structure. It was all going to waste, in a place where nobody would remember to view it.

Though, perhaps art that went unnoticed was art in the truest sense of the word. The toy shop was like this, wasn’t it? People no longer cared for those who worked hard to produce a bit of joy in the world. Quick fix businesses like Mrs. Clover’s and Kent Burgess’ — those were all that anybody cared about.

There was a rustle. Fletcher turned, hoping to find some sign of people around him. Yet, there was none. Just the shuffling of dead leaves in the breeze. Either Mr. Clover’s burial had already occurred, or it was still yet to occur.
Then again, there was a third possibility — the burial was currently occurring, and absolutely nobody had bothered to show up.

Fletcher made his way toward the cyclone of dead leaves. There was a tree near the end of the graveyard. A craggy magnolia, magnificently insignificant in its placement. Its branches were sturdy and told stories of bountiful leaves. Though, they were currently scant sticks.

Fletcher picked a yellowed leaf from the ground, revealing a bald patch of dust beneath. Beautiful as the tree might’ve once been, it was killing the grass surrounding it. Perhaps chopping it down entirely would be a solution.

A root tripped Fletcher up. They’d weaved their way between the dozens of tombstones surrounding it, as if straining to grasp something just beyond its reach. If chopped and uprooted, the tree would leave a massive hole in its wake. What could go in its place?

Shudders ran through Fletcher’s body as he drew closer to the tree. Specifically, to the gravestone centering in front of it. Much as he desired to avoid it, it was something that needed to be faced head on.
“Timothy Fletcher,” the tombstone read. “Dexburg’s toy-shop owner of fairytales.”

Fletcher swallowed, eyes brimming with tears. He collapsed in front of the tombstone and ran his hand along its surface. The familiar overgrowths covered it, and cracks were all throughout. However, so far as Fletcher could tell, it was impenetrable. The words inscribed upon it would never disappear.
Uncle Timothy had always been such a towering figure throughout town. He was truly impossible to live up to.

The day Uncle Timothy had been buried was a balmy one. In fact, it was one of the hottest days of that summer. Nonetheless, Uncle Timothy had put it in his will that he’d prefer his funeral be within a month of his death. Dozens of people from throughout town were dressed within their best dark suits, sweating their guts out.
Even from beyond the grave, Uncle Timothy knew how to make everybody miserable while maintaining the veneer of a pure soul.
Indeed, among the dozens were some of the most influential people in town. Wealthy business owners, socialites, officers — even Mayor Haddock had been there.
Mayor Haddock had always been mayor, hadn’t he?
Fletcher was much younger, then. He’d felt it then, too. People looked down on him, but more in a pitying sympathy than the disgust he now knew.
His role was to replace Uncle Tim as the toy shop owner — to keep the place running smoothly as it ever had. Yet, was he truly up to the task?
The legacy Uncle Tim left behind was broad and suggested nobody could. Fletcher wasn’t enough. He could never be enough.
However, perhaps none of it had happened that way. Perhaps he was just misremembering. The past was flux, and utterly subject to change, wasn’t it?

That’s certainly how everybody acted toward Uncle Tim’s past. His darker nature was lost from memory. Everybody remembered when he’d helped some old lady cross the sidewalk, or when he’d muttered some inspiring speech to his garbage man. Yet, the times when he’d dropped his twinkie, and then slapped Fletcher across the face? Or when his shouts from a stubbed toe turned to tearing up rooms, and throwing furniture into the street?
Those remained forgotten. They’d never happened at all.

Perhaps it was just as well. Uncle Tim had always told him this was how it would be, in the end. He’d been obsessed with horoscopes. Specifically, of the astrological variety. The day, hour, and months where he was born, burped, and bred all had some sort of significance. He had some sort of significance — all the good he’d done would outweigh the bad. The bad was necessary to outdo the good, even.
Hell, bad was good. A constant flow of good was bad.
That’s what had always been wrong with Fletcher. He’d been too good. Too much of a pushover.

“You never push enough toys!” Uncle Tim seethed. “You let yourself get ignored by everybody around you. Nobody will remember you! You don’t even polish or dust the toys well enough. You could at least use a little spit, to give them a little sheen, you little shit! How will you ever get rid of them if you don’t take care of them? Don’t build them up?”

Uncle Tim had always been right. Even when he was wrong, he was right, as he’d so often say. Fletcher was meant to take over and make the toy shop into something big — something greater than it’d ever been. Yet, he always fell flat.

Meanwhile Uncle Tim, wrapped in all his sorcery and mysticism, constantly proved his superiority. His life flowed with a general ease. People loved Uncle Tim. He was the town favorite. The golden boy.

He knew how to make people happy through his toys — many of which he designed himself. Even middle-aged men would play with them, in an unbridled glee. Fletcher didn’t know how to design like Uncle Tim, much as he tried. These days, he only ever sold toys from manufacturers, or old toys that Uncle Tim had built all those years ago. The toys Fletcher made were always just short of perfect. A craggy joint in the elbow here, a bit of asymmetry in the face there — the uncertainty had no end.
He’d once built a toy toy-builder, hoping it would solve his problems. Beyond all rationality, there was a desire for it to build the toys in Fletcher’s stead.
Fletcher wound up bashing the thing into a million pieces. Its hair was slightly off.

Every day, Fletcher steadily became older. The toy shop was approaching entropic decay at an ever-increasing rate. Though, the figure of Uncle Tim loomed larger than ever. He’d prophesied Fletcher’s failure. Now that failure was here? Fletcher wasn’t ready for it.
Tears spilled from Fletcher’s eyes. He licked them from his lips and cheeks after they’d rolled down. They’d tasted salty.
Perhaps Fletcher could go for a burger.
He cried again. Burgers had been Uncle Tim’s nineteenth favorite food.
Somebody placed a hand around Fletcher’s shoulder.
“Sir, are you okay?”

An older man dressed in a jet-black shirt and frayed jeans stood behind him. His face was weathered at the edges, but much of it was obscured by a white beard. Much as Fletcher wanted to observe the old man’s eyes they were hidden behind the tint of sunglasses. Most of the man was obscured, in fact. The sleeves to his shirt rode over his wrists, and his hat kept the rest of his scalp from view.
“Excuse me?” Fletcher managed, catching his sopping breath.
“Sorry, I’m the groundskeeper here,” the man said. “Groundskeeper Greg, I like to call myself. Though, you can just call me groundskeeper.”
Fletcher gave a blank stare, while trying to recollect himself. Though, the groundskeeper merely took it as invitation to keep going.

“I know that the flora around here isn’t much to scoff at. But trust me: I have one of the most dangerous jobs in the world. As groundskeeper, I have to keep these dead people in the ground. Can’t have them becoming zombies on us, after all.”
He pulled his arm away. It had held a sturdier than Fletcher would’ve expected, coming from somebody the groundskeeper’s age.

“Pardon my talking a lot,” the groundskeeper continued, with a wheeze. “It’s just, talking to these tombstones is so dull, compared to a real person. And seeing somebody crying in this place… Well, it’s a rare sight.”
Fletcher looked around. “This is a graveyard.”

“Yes, well… Crying is still rare. Most of the time, people seem rather happy to be rid of their loved ones. I once had a guy stage a dance-off during a burial here, on their brother’s grave. Quite the feat, I must admit.”
The wind began to howl. Perhaps it was laughing, in its own way. Fletcher gave a slight snort, to appease it if nothing else.
“I only wish I could’ve escaped the stages of grief, like he did,” said Fletcher.
“Well, technically he made quite the stage out of his grief… But yeah, I get what you mean. Anyway, what’s bringing you down?”
Fletcher gave a glare. “Isn’t it clear? I’m mourning a dead loved one.”
The groundskeeper stroked his beard and shook his head. “Yeah, still not buying it. Never seen a person in this place cry, myself.”
Fletcher glared at the groundskeeper. “Not even once?”

The groundskeeper shrugged, and pulled down the brim of his sunglasses. “Well, I do have a lazy eye,” he said, pointing at his left eye that hung slackly. “Makes things a bit rough, every so often. And, of course, I sleep through half the day… Or more. Same goes for nights. Being a groundskeeper is hard work, don’t you know?”
“Hard work, hardly work… Hardly a difference,” said Fletcher. “You can either die from boring holes in the soles of your feet, or die from boredom. In any case, you die.”
Light glared off the edges of the smoother tombstones. The wind picked up, wailing at the magnolia tree. Its branches creaked at each gust, cautioning against breakage.
“Nobody just comes here for the dead though,” the groundskeeper said, walking away.
Inexplicably, Fletcher followed. There was no point in letting himself be crushed by a falling tree. Being crushed by a nonsensical centaur was vastly more sensible.

“I used to be a farmer, myself,” the groundskeeper continued. “I grew bamboo. If you can believe it, a lot of people are loving that stuff right now. Putting it in their salads — think they call it the panda diet.”
“Ah, yes. Caused quite the pandemonium when it came out.”

“Don’t you know it. The people in this town love the taste of cyanide that the bamboo contains. It really does help bring out the flavor in everything. But… My crops were crap. The ground here is cursed, I swear. Plus, as it turns out, I accidentally seeded weeds instead of bamboo in my fields.”
“This going somewhere? Because, I’m really needing to get back to mourning, before it becomes morning.”

“Well, I was smoking a blunt one day… And, my grand-nephew bluntly told me that my green thumb was gnarled as all shit, and I had one foot in the grave. I figured that I may as well put both of my feet in the grave, right?”

The groundskeeper walked to a ring of tombstones, near the outskirts of the graveyard. Surrounding it was a barren patch of dirt, pimpled with weeds and bits of grass. Unlike the graves from the front, these ones were decades old. The names inscribed on them belonged to family lines that Fletcher found wholly foreign.
“I gave shooting myself a thought,” said the groundskeeper, voice cracking. “Then, I decided to come here. Now, shooting myself is all I can ever think about.”
Fletcher’s eyes burned at the sight of him. He went to put an arm on the groundskeeper’s shoulder, only for the groundskeeper to burst into a fit of hysterics.
“Why are you laughing?” Fletcher said.
“Nobody cries, in this graveyard,” said the groundskeeper, simply. “You can’t spell ‘funeral’ without ‘fun’!”
“Yeah, but you can’t spell ‘grave’ without ‘grave’ either…”
The groundskeeper snorted, then stroked his beard a bit.
“Huh,” he said. “I never thought of that. You do have a point, don’t you?”
“I have a lot of points… My biggest one is that there is no point. To anything.”

“Glad you pointed that out,” said the groundskeeper. “But, see... I’ve found quite a lot of points to being, being here. The closer that I’ve gotten to all these dead bodies, the more I’ve realized how beautiful it all is. Closeness to death — it’s a remarkable thing. There’s a sort of elegance to it. Everything is situated in its place. Organized. It stays exactly where it belongs. It never aspires for anything greater, because nothing is everything that anything needs.”
There was a throbbing in the side of Fletcher’s head. He’d been out too long today — he could feel the stressors steadily wearing at him.
“My Uncle always believed in greatness, though,” Fletcher said. “I’d say that it worked out pretty well for him. He has some nice real estate here.”

The old man scoffed. “The real estate in this grave is all alike. Whether you die filthy rich or die dirt poor, you still wind up buried in the filthy dirt. There is no prejudice here. No hierarchy. That’s the true reason why people fear death so much. When one truly confronts the core of death, they must come to terms that nonexistence isn’t the true horror of life. Rather, the true horror of life is existing — of pretending that making order out of chaos was ever possible.”
He sat on a tombstone and began to stretch out his limbs. Picking a wilted rose from the ground, he gave it a whiff. The tip of the stalk entered his mouth. His lips smacked as he chewed.

“Back to your uncle — I don’t reckon any man was ever meant to be great,” the groundskeeper said. He chewed deeper. “What the hell did a guy like Leonardo Da Vinci ever to help with my electric bill? Huh? Bet he was too busy kissing his ugly-ass paintings.”
Fletcher pondered on those words. Da Vinci had been a bit of a loser, hadn’t he? Locking himself in a cave, working on stencils for no purpose? For no person, other than himself?
He could’ve become the greatest bagel maker. The greatest house builder. There were countless people who’d kill for a bagel, or a house. Especially a house shaped like a bagel.
Though, Da Vinci was revered, nonetheless. What logic was there to it? For what reason did the universe grant him such fame?

A desperation railed at Fletcher’s throat, begging him to speak his mind. However, his tongue kept tame. The groundskeeper had the demeanor of a scrappy old dog about him. Perhaps befriending him would work — however, caution was imperative.

The tombstones glowered at Fletcher, their elaborate designs taunting him. An etching of a mermaid sprawled from the end of one tombstone. Fletcher followed its curves and edges, which gushed with the life of oceans. Yet, as he reached the mermaid’s head, it became more ghastly. Gashes had been put in its once seemly face.

The statuette was near the center of the circle of graves. No doubt, the sculptor had once thought it significant enough to hold this place. Yet, clearly its beauty had dulled. Clever as the painter had thought himself, he must’ve been a dullard.

“In subtraction with my disbelief in greatness, I don’t believe a great many things.” The groundskeeper spat the chewed head of his rose to the ground. “It’s probably because I don’t know a whole lot at all, honestly. You might call me stupid. Thankfully, stupid is the best thing any person can be. Stupid people are the happiest people you’ll ever meet. You’ll never find a sad stupid person.”

Chunks of dirt fell from the mermaid’s slackened jaw, as the wind picked up. Flecks of rain fell from the sky, stinging Fletcher’s skin as they landed. Parts of the ground were already muddying up with eddies of water.
He swiped a few droplets of rain from his face. He needed a jacket, or an umbrella. Anything to keep him out of this rain.
“Never find one? I think you’re talking to one,” said Fletcher. “I’m here. But, I’m not happy. And, I don’t know what I’m doing.”

“You’ve come to the center of the town,” said the groundskeeper. “I’d say that only the smartest people in town come here. The rest of the town might have a pristine sheen about it… But, in here? In here is where the truth about this town comes out. Death and decay is the true destiny of this place.”
“You can say that a million times, but that doesn’t make it profound.”
“I’d like to know why you find yourself here. Really, truly.”

Fletcher scratched the back of his neck, measuring the words he was about to say. “Besides mourning my uncle’s grave? I was planning on hijacking the grave of a complete stranger. I heard there was supposed to be a burial for a man who goes by the name of ‘Mr. Clover’.”

The groundskeeper dug a heel into the dirt and gave another stretch over the tombstone. “Ah yes… Mr. Clover,” he said. “Funny… For somebody so insistent on that being why they came here, it sure took you a while to ask me about him.”

The collar of Fletcher’s shirt tightened around his neck, his skin going clammy. Why hadn’t he bothered asking about Mr. Clover? He’d practically forgotten about him the moment he’d entered this graveyard. Was it just the melancholy of it all? Or, did the groundskeeper have a pint?
Did he come here for Uncle Timothy, more than anybody else?

“Mr. Clover had his burial earlier today,” said the groundskeeper. “You just missed him. Of course, only two people showed up to his funeral. They spent most of the time checking their phones, and discussing what they should do with the rest of their evening. And, even then, they left after about ten minutes, when they saw to it that he was tossed in his hole.”
“They didn’t even care?”
“If you want to put it that way. They cared a whole lot more than most of the people who come here. Besides, if you care so much, why were you late to his death?”
“I didn’t need him… I just needed to talk to his family about something… I needed information, for something I’m doing.”

“Yes, I suppose that holds true for most of the dead, doesn’t it? They were utterly useless to people in life and are only useful in death to get something out of. I’ve never seen a person die, and not have vultures surround them. Well, okay… I’ve seen a few people with just gophers. Trust me though: gophers are far worse than vultures.”
“Yes, well… If it were up to me, nobody would die.”

“You can’t know life without death. Something must always die, for another thing to live. Maybe I just noticed because working at this graveyard is what puts food on my plate… But, the food on everybody’s plate is something once living.”
“Pretty sure that there was no life in the processed twinkie I ate with breakfast…”
“Twinkie or not, you can’t have being in the absence of not being. It’s just like you can’t know peace without war. Or, happiness without sadness. Comfort without pain.”
“Maybe a world without life would be better. At least there would be no death. You yourself said it: the horrors we endure vastly exceed whatever anybody deals with in the grave.”
“Aye. I can’t fight there.”
Droplets of rain clouded Wally Walrus’s hands, and Fletcher had to squint to make them out. It was already four. There were eight hours left until midnight — and he had made no headway.

“I should just turn in, for the day,” said Fletcher. “I heard that this town will become a blast zone, at midnight. Might as well be able to enjoy the show. Beats running around town for something I have no hope at getting...”

Fletcher turned, moving toward the entrance of the graveyard. Hopefully Harry’s car would have enough fuel in it to get him back to the toy shop. Of course, getting it back to Harry would be another thing entirely. That, and there was the unfortunate fact that the cops would be after him.
Whatever. He’d deal with it when he came to it.
“Wait,” said the groundskeeper. “Could you at least tell me what you needed Mr. Clover was for? Who knows: maybe I could help you.”
Fletcher gave the groundskeeper a derisive shake of the head. “If there’s anything I’ve learned today, it’s that nobody can help.”
He was going to add to that thought, when his phone buzzed.
Linda. Again. What were the chances?
Clouds whirled in the sky, like milk against a heavy brew of coffee. Milk in coffee always made Fletcher feel sick. The clouds weren’t much of an improvement.
Fate was toying with him, as though he were one of Uncle Timothy’s old puppets. It had to have been.

“I absolutely adore you, Fletcher,” the message from Linda read. “But, I still can’t talk. Maybe soon. I need some information from you: where exactly are you? Where are you going for the next few hours? And, if you’re planning on getting out of town: where are your savings, and how much do you have in them? I need to know these things, so that I can maybe give you back the oil baron and get out of this town with you.”
There was the slightest flush of reassurance as Fletcher read the last sentence. However, nothing at quite right.

It didn’t sound like Linda at all — the usual, “Love, Linda” that punctuated the emails was absent. Moreover, Linda had called him “Fletcher”. She never called him Fletcher. Linda only ever addressed him as Stuart.
“I think that my girlfriend just got kidnapped,” Fletcher said, hardly believing the words a they escaped his mouth.
Though, escaped they did, echoing against the gravestones. Did he really think of her in that way, after only a day of communications?
He was getting desperate, wasn’t he?

“Well, isn’t that just dandy?” said the groundskeeper. He gestured toward the exit, trying to shoo Fletcher away. “Go call the police and get her then. Otherwise, she might wind up in here. Good luck, and what have you.”
Fletcher ambled awkwardly, directed by the groundskeeper’s nudges. He bit his lip.
“Thanks,” he said. “But, here’s the thing: I’m kind of being chased by the cops right now.”
The groundskeeper stopped in his place, his mouth agape.
“Motherfucker,” he muttered. “Why is it that all of the convicts decide to come here?”
Fletcher raised his hands, innocently. “Look, technically I haven’t done anything wrong, okay? I swear. I just have a ton of bad luck, is all.”

The groundskeeper’s lips puckered, before giving a capitulating smile. “Alright then,” he said. “You want to find your girlfriend, and you can’t call the cops. Sounds like you and your girlfriend are screwed.”
“Technically, what I really want is a toy,” Fletcher said. “The girlfriend is more of the side thing. I can do with or without.”
“Glad to hear you have your priorities straight. Either way though, you aren’t going to wind up with what you want out of this. I say cut your losses and get your ass out of dodge.”
Waves of nausea rose in Fletcher’s gut. He clutched his stomach, brushed the sweat blooming on his forehead.

“I don’t think that I’m ready to leave just yet,” Fletcher said. “I — I haven’t even seriously thought about leaving town, until now. There are still so many things that I have to finish. My Uncle — he would’ve never given up if things became desperate. He would’ve found a way.”
“You taken the chaos theorem for answers about life yet?”
“No.”
“Thank god then. You’re not a complete idiot.”
“You haven’t taken the chaos theorem either?”

“That shit is toxic. Besides, look at me! I live in the middle of nowhere. Course I’m not doing what the rest of the town is doing.” The groundskeeper placed a reassuring hand on Fletcher’s shoulder.  “Alright, so… Time to problem solve. Say your Uncle needs to find something. He has no idea where it is, and no sort of direction.  Everybody in town is after his blood, too. What the hell would your uncle do?”

Fletcher racked his mind. This was the exact sort of situation that Uncle Timothy would’ve never found himself in. He always had everything under control. Discomfort, fear, uncertainty — they couldn’t have been a thought in his head. Those sorts of things were defects that only Fletcher himself dealt with.

Nonetheless, there’d been a few times when Uncle Timothy sought advice and direction on his affairs. Those were rare moments. Those moments hardly were a blip, even. However, he would go to people. Namely, his horoscopes. The superstitious. Fortune tellers.

Fletcher cleared his throat. “My Uncle was a mystic,” said Fletcher. “Much of a mistake as he called me, it was never all him — my astrological sign was inherently unlucky. My Uncle? All the luck in the world was on his side. He didn’t go to the mystics for answers often… But, he was never disappointed when he did.”
The groundskeeper’s face broke into an expression of utter disillusionment.

“This infallible uncle of yours believed in freaking fortune tellers?” he said. “Goddamn… And I thought that you and I were freaks. But, hey: if that’s what your uncle would do about this, who am I to shit on his memory?”
“You really think I should be talking to fortune tellers to solve my problems?”

“Buddy, you’re fucked as fucked gets. You should be talking to every existential loon in town.” He rummaged around in his pocket, before finally pulling out a wad of paper. He shoved it into Fletcher’s hand. “Here’s the card of fortune teller Judy Malcolm. She comes here all the time, dumping her business cards on me… I hope for the best of fortunes for you. And, by the end of tonight, you better pray your soul is on its way to heaven rather than hell.”
Fletcher had been ready to burst into a flood of thanking — until the groundskeeper’s final words.
“You believe in heaven and hell?” Fletcher said
“Course I do,” the groundskeeper said. “Half the people in this town are destined for eternal bliss. The other half is destined to writhe in eternal torment, having their souls sucked dry.”
“Can’t say I could see one enjoying eternal bliss in heaven, knowing there were people enduring hell…”
“That’s sure as hell the case for those who know too much. Thankfully, I never said that either of us were going to heaven…”
His eyes bore through Fletcher’s head. Fletcher gave a shaky salute and ran for the graveyard’s exit.
The fortune teller would be his last desperate attempt. He’d just about had enough of insane people, for one day. He just needed to get his stupid toy, and his online girlfriend, and get out of here.
“Looks like he created utter havoc on this place,” Officer Mand says.
I took another bite of my doughnut. I have the sinking feeling that I won’t have time for another doughnut break today.
I look over to Marvin. He’s acting the squirrely cretin, as usual.
“You knew about this, didn’t you?” I say, a chunk of doughnut flying from my mouth.
I wipe my face, then give him a death glare. He’ll crack at some point. I know it.

“As far as I knew, Fletcher was staying as far away from the chaos theorem booths as possible,” Marvin says. “I had no idea that coming over to one as something that he had in him. Why he’d come here, and then leave, makes no sense to me.”
I’m about to grab him by the collar, when a man taps me on the shoulder. I turn around, my face flushed. I should’ve just taken a sick day today. I don’t get paid enough for this.

“He’s telling the truth,” the man says. “I’m Harry — one of Fletcher’s friends. It’s true what this guy is saying. Fletcher would’ve never normally come here. I convinced him to try getting him tested for the chaos theorem… And he ducked out.”
It’s a friendly looking guy. Sharp dresser, nice face. How on Earth he became a friend of Fletcher’s I don’t know.
“How many friends does this guy have?” I ask, putting on my nice face.
My fellow officers are just keeping their traps shut. They’re reminding me exactly why I want to quit this job.
“I’m not his friend, for the last time!” Marvin says. “I’m just his neighbor, okay?”
“It’s true,” says Harry. “I have no idea who that guy is.”
“I couldn’t tell you what the guy has planned if I wanted to,” Marvin continued. “Guy steals my car, and then just goes freely throughout town…”
These idiots aren’t getting me anywhere. “What for?”
“Can’t say,” Marvin says. His eyes are dancing everywhere and tell another story.
“He stole your car too?” Harry says, with a laugh. “That’s funny — he just stole mine, too. He must just have a thing for cars.”
Okay. There’s some stuff that I can work with.
“Wait, wait, wait. Can you tell me what type of car you have?”
I’m a genius investigator. Momma would be proud.
Fletcher tapped his knee uncomfortably, with the tip of a pen. Cop sirens had been everywhere, when he was pulling into the front of the shop. Clearly they were on high alert for him.

Half the town was probably trying to evacuate, or breaking into frenzied mobs — and the cops were looking for him, of all people. Much as Fletcher tried keeping his nerves under control, he couldn’t help but find it difficult.

Taking in a deep breath, he broke into a fit of coughs. He wiped his nose with his sleeve, and made his breaths go shallow. There was a pungent stench of incense in the air. Fletcher struggled to keep himself from feeling incensed.

The entire atmosphere left Fletcher feeling as though the world were rotating backward. A pink disco ball hung from a ceiling fan, lighting up the room. The room was garnished with thin purple curtains, which itched as they brushed against Fletcher’s skin. He tried making himself comfortable in the waiting chair, but the plush cushions attempted to swallow him whole at every adjustment.

He wafted the clipboard in his face. Despite the ceiling fan above him, the room was an oven. If he’d been told it’d been hours since somebody had checked on the temperature, he wouldn’t have doubted it. Indeed, when he’d pulled the clipboard from the wall to fill out the appointment form, nobody came out to greet him. It’d been as though he were all alone.
Still, he could here whispers on the other side of one of the larger curtains. The slightest hint of music wafted out as well. Somebody was there — they were just ignoring him.
He cleared his throat and clicked his pen again.
“Anybody there?” he asked.

He hated the idea of breaking the silence. The mood of the room was a delicate porcelain dish, and his voice a hammer. Though, then, there wasn’t going to be anything gleaned from the porcelain dish until it was smashed to bits.
“Coming.”
A woman poked her head out from behind the curtain, then laughed. “And who are you supposed to be?”
“I was directed here with one of these.” Fletcher paused for effect, then pulled out the crumpled card the groundskeeper had given him. “I’m looking for a Judy Malcolm.”
The woman lit up, her smile encompassing her entire face.
“Great news, she just got back from an intense session in the ninth inning dimension,” she said, with a giggle. “How do I know this? Because I’m her! I am: Miss Mystic Malcolm!”

A puff of smoke ejected from one of her baggy sleeves. Malcolm’s face went elastic, in anticipation of Fletcher’s reaction. Fletcher remained nonplussed, staring at the billows of smoke as they dissipated.

Even by fortune teller standards, Judy was anticlimactic. She wore a tunic, which only reached halfway down her calves. From its numerous stains and frays, must’ve been circulated through five thrift stores before getting to her. Countless beaded items adorned her, from head to toe — a bead tiara, a beaded necklace, several beaded bracelets, and beaded anklets. Beneath her beaded anklets? She wore cheap flip flops, which had been worn to the bone.
“Yeah,” Fletcher said, letting his words roll in his mouth, “I’m just going to call you Malcolm, thanks.”
Malcolm shuffled, readjusting the scant decorations in the waiting room. Namely, a dying flower pot in the corner.
“Sorry, I had no idea that you were sitting there,” she said. “If I had known, I would’ve come out much sooner.”

Already, Fletcher knew this was going to be one hell of a trip. “You’re a fortune teller though, aren’t you? You could’ve just been able to tell that I was going to come in, with your predictive powers or whatever… Right?”

Malcolm had already pulled her curtain back to the main room and was readjusting the scenery. The main room had two more of the plush chairs set up, which surrounded a coffee table with a candle. Malcolm pulled a bottle of perfume from her pocket and spurted it into the air. Then, she picked a coffee cup up from the table, and tossed it into a wastebasket beneath the coffee table.
“I was busy, with another customer,” she said curtly. “That’s why I couldn’t —why I couldn’t help you, clearly. All logical, cosmologically.”
She took one of the seats. Fletcher hovered behind the other one.
“Funny, I didn’t see anybody leave,” said Fletcher.
“They turned invisible, as they were exiting. That’s another one of my powers.”
Fletcher studied her face for any signs of sarcasm. There were none.

Malcolm closed her eye and pressed her fingers to her forehead. Silence fermented in the air. It was silent as the dead. Tension rose, like yeast in bread. Fletcher’s attention redirected to the walls, in the hope of finding a conversation starter. Though, the walls were barren. They had a popcorn paint job, mixing different shades of white. Though, even this was obscured by the room’s dim lighting.
For all the fortune teller’s emphasis on open spirituality, much of her room was left hidden.

“I’m desperately trying to make a connection with you,” she said, half muttering. “Though, something is blocking me out… I sense a skepticism. You must hand over an offering, in order to reconnect with the spirits.”
Her eyes took on an ethereal paleness and turned to saucers. She reached over the chairs and made a grope at the pocket to Fletcher’s pants.
“So, you need cash?” Fletcher said.
Malcolm’s face went back to pedestrian, and she shrugged. “Just a small payment. Say twenty bucks, or so.”
Fletcher fumbled through his wallet. All his cards were maxed out, and he was fresh out of cash.
“Are you sure that you’re worth twenty bucks? What’s your track record?”

“My predictions are renowned,” Malcolm said, an air of pride in her voice. “I once gave a prediction that helped the police find the location of buried treasure. In another instance, I helped Chef Bernardo
Fletcher gulped. “Alright. Sounds like I’m dealing with somebody way above my pay grade.”

“Yes, it does. Of course, in the case of the buried treasure, the police were actually looking for a missing body… And, in the case of the chef, the secret ingredient was simply more salt… But, hey: I still predicted something immense, didn’t I?”
“That’s more like it,” said Fletcher. “Would you take a coffee shop gift card?”
He slipped a card out of his wallet, and waved it in Malcolm’s face.
“How much is on it?” Malcolm asked, twirling a strand of her dark hair.
Fletcher shrugged. “I don’t know. Probably about fifteen bucks, or so?”
Malcolm snatched it from his hand.
“So, what brings you here?” she asked, crossing her legs.

“I always thought going to medical school to become a doctor was as vanilla as it gets. Suddenly, you have me getting second thoughts.

“Being a cosmetic surgeon is a great prospect.” Malcolm took a deep inhale of her cigarette. “You can get great pay, for one of the most superficial things out there. Fletcher stood from his chair and walked toward the door.
“So, is that everything?” the fortune teller asked. “Or, do you have more questions?”

Malcolm nodded. “No. I probably will soon. A fortune teller that doesn’t fully know their own future — it sounds so wrong, doesn’t it? The problem is, I’m worried that the theorem is better at predicting life than I ever could be.”
“Maybe people can’t be predicted, unless they’re predictable enough to try being predicted,” said Fletcher.
The door opened, letting the flood of car engines and murmuring voices flood in.
“What was the other question?” Malcolm said.
“You stick your dog in a box, your cat in a box, but leave your goldfish in its bowl… Which one do you feel has the worst view on things?”
Malcolm took a few moments to let her thoughts bake, then shrugged. “Probably the cat,” she said. “I hate cats. If I put a cat in a box, it’d probably be because I’d killed it.”
“Perfect answer.”
The universe is an oyster, and I’m the fish that eats the oyster to get the pearls.

Fletcher clenched up as an ambulance roared by him, and out of the parking lot. The sirens left an aching throb in his ears. Though, the stress it left wheeling through his mind was worse than anything from the sound itself.
Sirens were still all throughout the city, just behind him wherever he went. At any moment, the cops might show up to take him in. That would be the end of it all.
Thankfully, the cops had proven to be slow. That, or he’d proven to be lucky.
It had to be the former. Wherever he went, luck never followed.

Fletcher weaved between the fancy sportscars and convertibles littering the parking lot. His eyes honed in on the door to the hospital. It wasn’t like that of the regular hospital — cold, and clinical. It was painted with soft flower designs and built of bright red brick. The sign was made of gold engravings, which shone boldly in the sunlight.
There were ads in the windows, of cheery people with grins plastered to their faces.

Fletcher stepped into the waiting room. The linoleum shone as a pale moon, and the chairs yawned, yearning for somebody to sit in them. A woman’s tinny voice filtered from out of a television set, in the corner.

“He’s nothing, okay?” said Dr. Ford. “I tried convincing the pickpocket to get surgery when he came here, like I do for everyone… He wouldn’t take it. Then, he decided to take all of my drugs. He forced my hand. It’s not my fault, really.”
“Funny, I heard that you’ve been doling out opioids to a lot of people,” said Fletcher.
“It’s a decent business, sure. I’ve been making more money off them, than I have on my surgeries. But, that’s neither here nor there, okay?”

Fletcher peeled his hands from the sheets and observed them — they’d gone sheet white. He rolled his tongue between his cheeks and slipped from his place on the stretcher. He towered over Dr. Ford and glowered at him.
“Hey, what’s the big idea?” Dr. Ford snapped. “You’re the patient, and I’m the doctor here. Get back on the stretcher.”
“I think I’ve been patient enough,” said Fletcher. “I know that you’ve been trading your opioids for other drugs, Dr. Ford. Behind all your beautiful makeup is the face of a druggie, isn’t it?”
Dr. Ford flipped his hair abashedly, before making doe eyes at Fletcher.
“This ‘makeup’ is all natural, bud,” said Dr. Ford. “What makes you think that I do drugs?”
Fletcher showed off his palms. “This is cocaine,” Fletcher said. “Besides, I have it on good authority that somebody has a hit out on your life, tonight.”
Dr. Ford snorted incredulously. Then, he pinched a bit of the powder from Fletcher’s hands and snorted that too.

Dr. Ford kept an easy smile. It was soft. The lamplight of the office had his skin shining as porcelain. Fletcher could hardly make out a blemish. Yet, the words coming through his teeth left Fletcher’s stomach queasy with disgust.
Dr. Ford’s desk was stacked with papers that spoke to his intelligence. His acuity of mind. Though, beneath it all, he was a dullard and high as a kite.

“You’ve made countless dollars, all by taking advantage of people who knew no better,” Fletcher said, seething. “You make money off those who feel ugly, and unloved. You make money off those with addictions that they can’t help. And, all the while, you…”

“I enjoy myself,” said Dr. Ford. “Have you ever wondered how a goat can eat wrappers and cloth, wholesale? And enjoy it? It’s because they freaking enjoy it, okay? That’s how they feel. That’s what they are. And, that can’t be changed.”
He laughed, then pinched more cocaine from Fletcher’s hands. Fletcher pulled his hands back, only to see Dr. Ford pull a packet of cocaine out from his pocket.
“Cat is out of the bag, I suppose,” Dr. Ford said, pouring cocaine into his hands, and snorting it. “Or coke is out of the bag… Whatever.”
He gave a high-pitched laugh and spun in his chair. The wheels groaned and squeaked, but he ignored it in all his laughter.
“So, what are you still doing here?” he finally said, once his chair had careened to a stop.
Fletcher’s ears felt hot. He wanted to cover them, along with the rest of his face. Though, he kept his hands at his sides in fear of spreading the cocaine across his body.
Strong as the part of him that desired to get high was, there was nothing quite so surreal as what was going on around him.
“I need to save you, and my girlfriend, and the toy from the pickpocket,” said Fletcher. “You know stuff about the pickpocket. You need to help me. And we need to get out of here.”

Dr. Ford gave another nonchalant shrug of the shoulder. “Did you know that I wrote my college thesis in a single night, while stoned out of my mind?” Dr. Ford asked. “It was about how nostril hairs are the undiscovered vestigial limb, or something… I knew it was shit, and my professor knew it was shit. I still received my PhD though. You want to know why? Because, nobody cares in this world, and I had parents with money. There are always strings pulling things.”
Fletcher broke, and put his hand in his face. “Dear god, you really are high,” Fletcher said. “And I thought that my awful florist of a neighbor was bad.”

“You haven’t you caught on yet to what I’m saying, have you? Fletcher, the pickpocket has me in their pocket. They have the entire town in their pocket — trafficking drugs around, and whatnot. Tons of people owe them favors. Practically everybody. And, another thing about the pickpocket? It’s not just one person. It’s two people.”
Fletcher’s jaw dropped. “Two? That’s twice as much as I thought.”
“Yes, I’m pretty sure that’s how math works. Also — dear lord — close your mouth. I’m sorry, but you have a massive underbite.”
There was a loud crash. Fletcher’s head darted around, prompting Dr. Ford to put a steady hand on his shoulder.

Dr. Ford gave an annoyed look at Fletcher, before looking away.
“Are you implying that I’m—?” Fletcher began, before stopping himself. “Look, just tell me more about the pickpocket.”
Dr. Ford pursed his lips and brushed off a bit of cocaine dust from his purple tracksuit. “One of them is definitely a dude. The other one though? I’m not so sure…”
Fletcher scrunched an eyebrow.
“What’s that supposed to mean? Tell me what you’re sure about!”

“They operate out of some big empty building in town, naturally,” said Dr. Ford. “Granted, about half the buildings in this town are empty… They also keep themselves very masked, and never show up in masks together. It’s only ever one person. Though—.”
Blood spurted through Dr. Ford’s chest, as a burst shot through the air. He flung from his chair and began flopping on the ground like a live fish in a frying pan.

Fletcher ducked behind what meager cover the stretcher provided, staring at a bullet hole that’d been put through the wall. It was jagged, and pitch black. He watched it as though it were an eye, studying him. Dissecting him. Though, the hole made no movement. It remained.
Fletcher couldn’t help but feel relief in knowing that he remained. Though, then — if the pickpocket was lurking, it was likely he wouldn’t remain much longer.

Wheezing gasps escaped from Dr. Ford’s throat, his chest spasmodically rising and falling. Grabbing him by his limp arm, Fletcher dragged Dr. Ford toward himself. His face was mottled with blood. The erudite smile that had lain there was slain, replaced with one of distress. Rage flooded Dr. Ford’s eyes.
“That has to be the worst acupuncture I’ve ever experienced,” Dr. Ford said, still wheezing.
The door to the office jiggled violently, then finally stopped.

Fletcher used one of his hands to cover the blood pooling in Dr. Ford’s chest, and the other to caress Dr. Ford’s face. The pickpocket’s steps pattered out in the hall. Yet, were they moving closer or further? Fletcher couldn’t tell. If anything, they were pacing in place.

The pickpocket must’ve been bluffing — waiting to see if Dr. Ford was truly on his dying breaths, or if there was still life left in him. It was cowardly. Though, the cowardly thing was always the smarter thing to do, wasn’t it?
Heartrate raising, Fletcher, drew Dr. Ford closer to himself. Whatever the pickpocket’s mindset, Dr. Ford’s strained breaths said that he wouldn’t be breathing for much longer.
“You’re going to get out of here, and you’re going to be fine,” Fletcher whispered into Dr. Ford’s ear. “I’m going to get you to a hospital.”

“Alright, you’re right,” Fletcher said, hurriedly, “You’re going to die, probably. So, just tell me where the pickpocket’s base is.
“I knew it! I’m dying! My mom always told me that I was going to eventually die some day. Why didn’t I believe her?”
“Please. Can you answer my question?”
“My life is flashing before my eyes,” said Dr. Ford. “I spent way too much time doing online shopping… All those crocs. Why did I buy all those horrid crocs?”

Fletcher put his finger over his lips to quiet Dr. Ford down, but it was already too late. His voice was booming off the walls.

Dr. Ford wrenched his head away from Fletcher’s hands and went into a bout of convulsions. It were as though some wicked, writhing thing had entered Dr. Ford and was fighting from within. Once the convulsions had stopped, Dr. Ford’s body relaxed. However, whatever life had been in him was reduced to the slightest tremble.
“Open up!” said the pickpocket banging on the door. “I don’t want to have to bust this door down! If I can, I want this to be as clean as possible! But, you have to work with me!”
Fletcher’s eyes darted about the room, looking for some place to hide. He looked back to Dr. Ford.
“Do you know who the pickpocket is?” Fletcher asked.
“They… They hate your guts,” said Dr. Ford, with a guttural choke.
“So, they’re somebody I know?”
Dr. Ford’s hacking continued, until a fountain of blood sprayed out of his mouth. Fletcher winced as a bit of it splattered onto his own face.
“Do you know who they are?” Fletcher pressed.
“I hit my head once as a child, by running into a stop sign,” said Dr. Ford. “Probably why I wound up so stupid.”
“You’re on your last breaths,” said Fletcher. “If there’s anything you want to tell me, or want to get off your chest, do it now.”

Dr. Ford lifted frail arm and stared into Fletcher’s face. “My surgery rates are 50%... Off,” said Dr. Ford. His lips were blue. His foundation left his skin more waxen looking than ever, as the color waned. “You really need to fix that underbite…”
Dr. Ford shoved himself away from Fletcher, collapsing on the ground. As he did, his eyes went frail. They were just orbs now. His skin was just a flesh covering, over a jumble of bones.
Fletcher looked around — jumble of bones. Of course.
“Alright, that’s it, I’m breaking in there,” said the pickpocket. “Didn’t want to do this, but you forced me!”
Fletcher lifted the tarp to Dr. Ford’s skeleton, covering himself under it. Just as he did, the handle to the office door was shot off, and the door was kicked open.
“Alright, if anybody is in here, you better show yourself now,” the pickpocket roared. “I’m fully ready to kill. If you don’t come out, I’m going to kill you twice as hard.”
Fletcher closed his eyes and held his breath. Perhaps it would make no difference, but he’d heard stories of escape artists who’d succeeded by holding their breath.
The pickpocket shuffled around a bit, the sound of their movements stiff and jerky. There was a click as the pickpocket reloaded his gun. Several gunshots went off.

Fletcher flinched, and nearly lost his balance. He gripped tightly to the back of the skeleton as it swayed back, praying that it wouldn’t collapse. The human skeleton was meant to be a resilient thing, wasn’t it?

True as that may have been, his bones ached while pressed tightly against the skeleton’s anatomy. The plastic bones were jagged and jabbed into the flesh. Couldn’t the manufacturer have produced a friendlier model of the human body?
A cruel laugh came from the pickpocket. Swallowing, Fletcher opened an eye, and peered through a slit in the covering cloth.
The pickpocket hunched over Dr. Ford’s dead body, nudging him in the buttocks with the butt of his gun.
“You really the only one in here?” said the pickpocket. “Or, your corpse, anyway? For the record, not what I wanted. Ah well. At least I get this…”

He pulled the packet of cocaine from Dr. Ford’s pockets. Then, he pulled out Dr. Ford’s wallet. The pickpocket’s head bobbed around, to make sure he wasn’t being watched. Relief flooded Fletcher upon the pickpocket not looking in his direction.
“You poor son of a bitch…” said the pickpocket, head hanging. “Did you really think that you could slip one by me? In your own office, of all places?”

Fletcher considered tiptoeing out of the tarp and running down the hall. The mouth of the door hung open, practically begging for him to leave. Though, Fletcher’s gut told him otherwise. A predatory alertness remained in the pickpocket’s muscles.
“I’m talking to you!” the pickpocket shouted. “I know that you’re in here, Fletcher! I saw the extra car in the parking lot! There are only so many places that you can hide!”
Sweat poured down Fletcher’s face. The pickpocket knew, and Fletcher was clueless on how to escape.
The pickpocket’s rear in the air and nose to the ground, like some deformed bloodhound, the pickpocket shoved his head under the stretcher.

Fletcher blinked. His golden opportunity, for escape, and it’d practically fallen into his lap. He slipped from beneath the tarp and tiptoed out the door. All the while, the pickpocket’s head remained stuck beneath the stretcher.

His calves tensed, preparing to break into a sprint. Though, just before he did, he paused to blow the skeleton a kiss. It’d saved his life, after all. Furthermore, being pressed against it had been oddly intimate. He rubbed a tender bruise that the skeleton had left behind.
“I’m a master tracker!” the pickpocket shouted. “Trust me: in the boy scouts, I gained countless merit badges! You don’t know who you’re messing with!”
His voice could barely be heard beneath a series of bangs. The foreboding message struck a chord with Fletcher nonetheless.
There were certain organizations that simply had a knack for producing deadly trackers. The marines. The green berets. The CIA. Yet, the boy scouts? One was practically dead meat.

He sprinted down the hallway. If the pickpocket had heard him running, there hadn’t been a way to tell. No gunshots followed him. Yet, as he hopped in Harry’s car and hit the gas, the heavy weight of being watched donned on him.
The pickpocket knew where he was going. He had to have, didn’t he?

It was purely going to be a matter of outdoing him. Whoever got to Chef Bernardo’s first would have the girl of his wildest imagination — only really existing in his imagination, come to think of it — and the toy oil baron for keeps. Worse yet, he wasn’t quite sure where Chef Bernardo’s was from here. Fletcher’s brow furrowed, and he pushed the gas down harder.
Fletcher looked down to his phone. No new messages had come in from Linda. It was odd —she’d always seemed to text him after his heady confrontations. Had she finally been silenced?
Wheeling in a circle around a block of crusty buildings, he plugged in the address for Chef Bernardo’s. All the while, his fears stewed.
There were two of these pickpockets. At least, that was what Dr. Ford had claimed. There was a chance that the pickpockets already had him beaten to Chef Bernardo’s.

Who was the second pickpocket, anyway? Dr. Ford had suggested a man, and maybe a woman? Though, then, he could have just been referring somebody who was a very effeminate man. Who, out of everybody he’d met, could’ve fit the bill?
The truck picked up speed, but Fletcher tried keeping to the back roads. There was still a solid chance that the cops were after him. Mayor Haddock likely had the entire city on high alert.
Fletcher blinked. Mayor Haddock.

As his car squealed and swerved along the road, he ran through the possibilities. The banker and his teller seemed to fit, but the teller wasn’t quite a woman. There was Jack and Clair, but they’d been clear that the pickpocket was their competition. Priest Carvel had always seemed like more of a solo person, despite his massive following. Officer Haynam and Officer Thatcher seemed close enough, but too incompetent to do something so sinister.
He shuddered — Marvin and Carol were possibilities. As were Harry and Margaret. Though, they were too close. They were his best friends. It couldn’t have been them, could it have?
No, it had to be Haddock. Haddock and Lydia. Haddock was a clear influencer, who commanded immense fear over the entire town. Furthermore, he had a close relationship with Chef Bernardo.

No, it had to be Haddock. Haddock and Lydia. Haddock was a clear influencer, who commanded immense fear over the entire town. Furthermore, he had a close relationship with Chef Bernardo. He’d had Chef Bernardo’s food catered at his ceremony, hadn’t he? Furthermore, he had a strange fixation towards Fletcher. He’d known Fletcher’s uncle and had a hatred for how Fletcher was moving about town.

It all seemed to fit perfectly. All he needed now was to prepare himself for running into Mayor Haddock, once he reached Chef Bernardo’s. That, and hope Mayor Haddock wasn’t spry enough to make him die.
He was going to be completely alone in this.
Fletcher blinked. He didn’t have to be completely alone though, did he?

He yanked his phone out of his pocket. His eyes roved over his list of contacts. He couldn’t call Harry — there was no trusting him at this point, even if he was driving around in his stolen car. John? He was also completely out of the question.
He saw Marvin’s name. He dialed it.
At this point, while he may not have been much, Marvin was the closest thing that he had to a confidant.
“Paxton,” Marvin said, after a pregnant wait.
“No, it’s Fletcher,” Fletcher shouted, swerving through the narrow roads. He’d accidentally turned into the other lane, prompting a series of honks from nearby drivers.
“Yeah, I know it’s you,” Marvin said with a hiss. “I can’t really talk right now, though — the police have me in their custody.”
“They what?” Fletcher said, incredulously. “I thought that you were going to get off scot-free. Don’t you have a ton of exciting antiques you’re supposed to be selling?”

“I was going to do a giant sale today, too,” Marvin said, “Finally was going to get rid of some of the garage I had in storage, for good prices. But, yeah… Now I’m stuck trying to catch a massive criminal.”

“I’m going to need your help, though,” said Fletcher. “See, I’m going to Chef Bernardo’s. Apparently, there’s a giant drug stash in that place. The thing is though, I think the town pickpocket is on my tail… Everywhere I go, he somehow knows to be there.”
“You want me to follow you? To Chef Bernardo’s?”
“Yeah. Is there any way you can escape, and help me out?”
Marvin snickered. “Just your luck. I’m being driven there right now. I guess the cops got a tip that a certain Fletcher was going to be there.”
Fletcher became nauseous, and his head swam. “A tip? How? I guess it doesn’t matter… Can you help me, and stall the cops for me? I just need to get in and out of there.”

“Look, you’re asking for a lot,” said Marvin. “I’m in police custody right now, and you want to know whose fault it is? I don’t care about you. Nobody does. There’s a reason why the entire town seems to see you as a nuisance. All you care about is what you want, everything else be damned.”
There were warbled voices from off the phone. Marvin’s own voice became distant, for a moment.
“I’m just talking to my grandmother,” Marvin hastily explained. His voice then became close again.
“Marvin, we’re friends,” said Fletcher. “Deep down, you know that. I know that. Why else have you stuck your neck out for me, all those times?”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” said Marvin. “Things are falling into place exactly how they’re meant to be: we’re business competitors. That automatically makes us sworn enemies. We never had a real relationship. You just thought that we did.”

“Star basketball players are good at exposing government corruption?”
“When they’re not taking steroids, I’m pretty sure…”
“If we were really so close as you say we are, why are we talking on a phone?” asked Marvin. “Why aren’t we talking face to face?”
The phone suddenly went dead. Fletcher’s eyes stung.

All this time, Marvin had seemed one of the few people who truly understood him. Yet, it’d all just been an illusion. His uncle had been right. He’d always been right. Fletcher was a terrible craftsman. He couldn’t make toys for anything. He couldn’t make money. And, he sure as hell couldn’t make friends.
In the end, the only person who cared about how anything turned out was himself.
Chef Bernardo’s was only about a mile away. Yet, Fletcher was beginning to wonder if it wouldn’t be better to just invest in a bunker and spend the rest of his life in it.
“Damn, that sounded harsh,” says Officer Haynam.
“What, is your grandmother the spawn of Satan?” Harry asks, with a chuckle.
If only they knew. I mean, Fletcher is close enough to the spawn of Satan, isn’t he? That’s what the town is convinced of, by this point. That’s what I thought of him this morning, as well.
Still, as we drive by the dilapidated buildings, and make our way toward Chef Bernardo’s on main street, I feel self-doubt.

Self-doubt is a rare thing, to me. Usually, I feel so certain. However, Fletcher has been making some valid points, hasn’t he? Perhaps life really isn’t meant to be calculated, and written out on a piece of paper. Perhaps randomness is the true answer.
“Do you really think we’re going to catch him, this time?” I ask.
Officer Haynam laughs to himself. “At this point, the entire town is listening to these intercoms. Everybody is going to be there. Fletcher is dead meat, whether he knows it or not.”
“And what are we going to do when he’s caught?”
Officer Haynam paused for a moment, and stroked his chin. “After all that effort, and deliberation? I’m going to get drunk as hell.”
“Amen,” says Harry.
Isn’t Harry supposed to be Fletcher’s friend. I mean, sure — Fletcher stole his car. Though, why is he acting like his prayers have been answered?
Either way, I feel like maybe I should start making some prayers of my own.
“Shit,” said Fletcher.

His truck teetered to the side of the rode, behind a moving truck. The parking lot of Chef Bernardo’s was just out of view, hidden behind the truck — though, Fletcher found himself wishing that the parking lot hadn’t been there at all.
Despite the anxiety rising within him, he had to move. Just off in the distance was an ice cream truck, playing the latest pop music.

He jumped out of the truck, in lock-step with the ice cream truck’s beat. As he did, he nearly ran into a couple of movers who were heaving a sofa through the sidewalk. Fletcher stood patient as he could manage, tapping his foot all the while. I was about a minute until the mover’s had finally rested the sofa on the truck. For a man without a minute to lose, this came as immensely aggravating. Though, Fletcher simply jogged past — their slowness it wasn’t worth complaining to them about.
“Hey, hey, hey, what’s the big idea!?” one of the movers shouted.
He bumped into Fletcher, biceps rippling from taking the weight of the sofa again.
Stepping back, Fletcher watched as they pulled the sofa from the moving truck and moved it back toward the apartment building.
“What are you doing?” Fletcher hissed.
He darted his head around, making sure nobody was behind him. At any moment, somebody might jump out and attack. It was simply a matter of time.

“We’re movers,” said the other mover, with a surly look. Even his tattoo of a cartoonish monkey seemed peeved. “Only, too many people are trying to move out of town, today.
