Fletcher was dumbfounded.
“You’re getting paid for that?” Fletcher asked. “I know that most jobs accomplish effectively nothing, but I still thought that movers had to be effective…”
“If we’re moving stuff, our company pays us,” said one of the movers. “That’s how it works, I think. Nobody said things had to make sense. We’re following the chaos theorem!”
The other mover laughed. As he did, the couch slipped out of his hands, and hit his foot. He kept at laughing, nonetheless.
“Yes, we’re following the chaos theorem,” he howled. “From here on out, things are only going to get crazier!”

Fletcher pushed by them, before they could pick the couch back up. Curious as the movers were, he couldn’t keep talking with them. An air of unease hovered about them. Besides, the ice cream truck had gotten twice as loud in the time he’d been sitting behind them. They were merely a distraction from the true problem at hand. Deep down, he was too afraid to face what was ahead of him.

Gusts picked up, tousling Fletcher’s hair. Clouds swirled in the air, carrying the same disorder as static on a TV screen. Shadows hovered over the day, with a few rays of the sun just barely eking out light from over the tops of buildings. The Wally Walrus watch on Fletcher’s wrist said that it was 7:00.
Night was right around the corner. Only five minutes remained, until apocalypse.
Fletcher’s head peeked over the roofs of cars. The ice cream truck was just off in the distance, pulling from over the hilly street. Perhaps he could wait for the truck and get some ice cream.

However, Chef Bernardo’s was just across the street. It was a one-story diner nestled between two grubby office buildings. Its neon sign blinked in the dim light. Most of the letters in “Bernardo” had been knocked out, with just the letters “B”, “A” and “D” remaining. Fletcher’s eyes normally would’ve lingered on those letters.
Though, no night in Dexburg was ever normal.

The main entrance to Chef Bernardo’s was blocked off by a cluster of squad cars. In front of the entrance stood Officer Haynam with a few of his fellow officers. Harry and Marvin were there too. Worse, in the parking lot there was a whole lot of Priest Carvel’s cult. Strangely, Mayor Haddock and Lydia appeared to be standing with Priest Carvel, helping to give orders. Fletcher squinted — were Jack, Clair, and Logan, all standing by the parking lot entrance? The bank teller and the banker appeared to be there too. It had to have been them. All of them.
Brilliant. It was simply brilliant. All these people had arrived, all at once. It was a lion’s den. The clock was ticking, and he was being tested on how long it would take to enter.

He sighed and ran his hand through his hair. Mayor Haddock must’ve planned for this to go this way. At least, it seemed it was him, wasn’t it? At this point, it was impossible to tell. Too many people had their hats in the ring.

Sweat poured down his face. He clenched his fists and stood up from behind the cars. Upon looking across, he came to the realization that there was no way he’d make it without being detected. Yet then — the very fact that he had no chance emboldened him.
If he failed, at least it would be because there was no other outcome in the cards.
His legs carried him across the street, and he ducked behind the squad cars. Everybody had to have seen him. He could already hear the frenzied shouts of officers.
“I swear, he just disappeared,” Officer Haynam shouted. “You guys all saw him, didn’t you? That was definitely him, right?”

Fletcher gave the quickest of glances from behind the car. Everybody was following Marvin, as he led them away from Fletcher. As Marvin did, he looked over his shoulder and met Fletcher’s eyes.
It was for no more than a split-second. Nevertheless, a warmth flooded Fletcher’s chest.
Barreling from behind the squad cars, he made it through the door to the restaurant.
Fletcher took in a big whiff of the greasy air. The place was a dump.

Half the tables were cluttered. Vague traces of soda and gum stained the walls and floor. In the corner was a group of guys huddled around the flat-screen, watching a game of baseball. They flung fries and shouts into the air, all while taking shots.
Dump as it may have been, it was Dexburg’s dump.

Ahead of Fletcher was the overlong line to the counter. He walked toward it, trying to make out the cruddy blackboard hung over them all. Over the years, Fletcher had come to believe that the blackboard held the menu items — though it was impossible to truly tell.
It probably didn’t matter. Chef Bernardo would serve out anything anyone asked for anyway. At least, he’d serve out the burnt attempts.
“Hey there.”
An officer had been standing on the other side of the door, watching him. Fletcher swallowed. It was Officer Baker.
Of course, they’d made sure to have an officer keeping guard. How could he have been so stupid as to let his guard down?
“You going to say hello, or what?” Officer Baker asked, her eyes piercing through Fletcher.
“Hi,” Fletcher said, sheepishly.
Officer Baker didn’t seem to recognize him. Or, she didn’t care if she did.
Officer Baker gave a firm nod and took a large bite out of a charred burrito she had in her hands.
“Aren’t you going to pat me down and check me and stuff?” Fletcher asked.
He was orbiting around Officer Baker now, and toward the line. It was surprisingly crowded, considering the blockade Officer Haynam had outside the building.
“I’m off the clock,” Officer Baker said. She gave a burp. “This is my lunch break.”

Fletcher gave a sigh of relief, and wiped a plume of sweat from his forehead.
“Thank god,” he said. “And you’re the only one here?”
“What does it look like?”
“I thought that you’d have ton of officers in here too.”
“Too?” Officer Baker asked, incredulously. “I thought I was the only one here.”
“There’s a blockade of officers, just outside this building.”

Officer Baker snorted. “Huh. Had no idea. We’re nowhere near coordinated enough to talk to each other about these things. Hell, it’ll probably be fifteen more minutes before they even bother to look in this building.”
Fletcher’s muscles tensed. Yes — they could look in the building and find him at any moment.
He made a weak chuckle at Officer Baker’s comments and rushed himself into the line.

Immediately, questions arose as to what his plan was supposed to do. It was all so nebulous — clearly there was a secret bunker in the restaurant, somewhere. But then, where? How was he supposed to convince the staff to even let him into the kitchen?

Despite the line’s length, it seemed to fly by. People were ordering their burgers, bowls of shrimp, pastas, soups, and subs without second thoughts. What was Chef Bernardo’s supposed to be, anyway? It didn’t matter. The line dwindled to nothing, and  Fletcher remained stressed over what he was to do. Why couldn’t the line ever stay slow when he needed it to?
Once the line had reached the last customer in front of him, Fletcher finally reached a brilliant conclusion.
He’d just wing it.
Air bleated into Fletcher’s face, from supersized ceiling fans fixed on the counter. Did everything have to be supersized here? They made for sizable hurdles.

A hefty customer standing ahead of him let out an extended groan. Fletcher considered bypassing him, to jump over the counter and into the kitchen. Though, then — the man was probably large enough to knock him over.
“How many calories are in the salad, compared to the milkshake?” the man asked, popping a piece of mint in his mouth, mid-sentence.

The word “milkshake” came out as a pudding of spittle. Fletcher wiped a bit of the spittle from his face, once it had arced back from the fans. At least the spittle smelled alright. However, Fletcher couldn’t help but wish breath mints could be made for a person’s entire body. Sweat had eked through the man’s shirt, leaving him smelling like a week old mud puddle.
“Just buy the milkshake, man,” said the cashier, standing behind the counter. “We all know that you want the shake.”
It was a reedy looking teenager. His face was broken out in acne, and his voice was in just as much of a wreck. A smirk stretched across Fletcher’s face. Getting through him would be a piece of cake.

“Maybe I don’t want the shake, though,” said the man. “See, the chaos theorem said I’d drop dead from a heart attack in two weeks. And, it said that I should start eating healthy right about now. So, I’m trying to stay healthy. Do you have any low fat milkshakes? Or, maybe, could you pour a little bit of milkshake on my salad instead of dressing? Hell, are salads really that much better than milkshakes?”
“You only have two weeks left,” said the cashier, “you can blow it all while standing in line, or you can buy some food. Take your pick.”
The entrance door chimed. Fletcher glanced behind, to see Priest Carvel entering with Mayor Haddock at his side. A breathless Marvin entered in after him.
Fletcher whipped back toward the counter and hung his head low. Hopefully they hadn’t seen him. If they had, maybe they didn’t recognize him.
“Give me the biggest salad that you have, and the smallest milkshake,” the man said. “Or the smallest salad, and the biggest milkshake. Surprise me.”
“Your total will be ten dollars, or thirty dollars,” said the cashier. “We’ll surprise you.”

He printed off a ticket and handed it to the man. Relieved to finally have the man out of the way, Fletcher stepped toward the counter. Though, even then, the man was still attempting to talk to the cashier.

“I’m so confused,” he said. “I know everything that I’m supposed to be doing, but I can’t do it. Instead, I’ve been doing the things that I have to be doing, according to the theorem — but, they’re also the things that I shouldn’t be doing.”

A flicker of sympathy dashed across Fletcher’s lips. Though, he locked his gaze with the cashier. The irrationality of reality affected everyone. There was no point in focusing on the impact it had on one person.
“And, what do you want?” the cashier asked.
Fletcher shrugged and attempted to make out the shaky menu above him. “Still deciding,” he said.

The cashier gave a groan. “The chaos theorem lays out a person’s entire order for them. Most of the time, it’s the same thing you always were going to get, anyway. And you still can’t figure out what you’re going to eat?”
Fletcher thought about explaining that he hadn’t taken the chaos theorem yet, when he heard footsteps approaching him from behind.
“I want some pigeon eye, myself,” Priest Carvel said, in an undertone Fletcher could only just make out. “I heard it helps strengthen one’s third eye.”
Priest Carvel must’ve been talking with Mayor Haddock. They must’ve been distracted. Though, they also must’ve been hungry, and he was in their way.
“Well, actually,” Fletcher said, weighing his words, “I came here to see if you had any job applications available.”
Jealousy flashed through the cashier’s face, followed by annoyance. The cashier stroked the scant hairs growing on his chin.

“In this economy, we’re not exactly providing jobs,” said the cashier. “If you haven’t heard on the news yet, the president finally sent out an air force jet to our town. They’ll be here in an hour, and hover in the sky until midnight. This whole place is going to blow.”
“Maybe if I just chatted with the chef…”
“This whole place blows!”

The cashier was laughing to himself now, while the fans quivered. They almost seemed to be trying to make laughs of their own. Yet, tension coiled in Fletcher’s chest as a spring. He leaned toward the cashier.
“Let me in, so that I can talk to Chef Bernardo,” Fletcher said, his voice a razor. “We need to talk.”
“You can talk to the chef after you order your food,” said the cashier.
Fletcher smirked. “Technically, according to the chaos equation, I’ve already ordered my food.”
“You have, have you? How do I know you’re not tricking me?” the cashier asked.
“The chaos equation doesn’t allow you to be tricked, does it? Everything is clean cut. I can’t trick you.”
“What if the chaos equation says that I have to be tricked, then?”

Fletcher stopped short. It should’ve been easy enough to answer. However, could somebody still be tricked if they were told exactly how they were going to be tricked? Probably not, since they’d be prepared. Yet, if somebody thought they were prepared enough to not be tricked, would that then make it easier to trick them? Would it not matter?
“That’s a trick question. That, or a tricky question.”
Fletcher lunged toward the counter.
“Come on already,” whined Priest Carvel. “I want to order my—.”

Fletcher landed on the other side of the counter in Priest Carvel’s mid-sentence. Yet, graceful could hardly describe the landing. His stomach and chest had broken the fall, with the two fans crashing atop Fletcher.
“Not… Fun,” Fletcher moaned.
He wobbled to his feet.
“Not… A fan?” the cashier moaned from beneath him.
Fletcher’s eyes bulged. Even after all that, the cashier remained conscious. Fletcher lifted one of the fans from the ground, and dropped it on the cashier’s head.
“That too,” said Fletcher. He then raised his voice. “Just keep calm, everybody. You’re all just observing a shift switch. It’s a new protocol. Store policy.”
He ran from the counter, and down a narrow passage that led into the kitchen.
“See, I told you,” he could hear Mayor Haddock saying.
“Didn’t he sound like Fletcher, though?” asked Priest Carvel.
Fletcher was already in the kitchen before he could hear the response. His gut told him that they knew. They’d be after him.
He just had to get through the kitchen fast enough.
“Is Chef Bernardo in here?” Fletcher asked.

Each counter was a galaxy unto itself, filled with clusters of food particles and dirtied dishes. Yet, only two people were in the kitchen. There was a teen, hunched over a sink with a mountain of dishes. Then, there was a reedy man dressed in a torn t-shirt and jeans. Rather than an apron, he had a ragged towel tied around his waist. Rather than a chef’s hat, he wore a backwards ballcap.
“Who in the hell are you?” the man asked, glaring at Fletcher.
Fletcher instantly knew it had to be Chef Bernardo.
“I was expecting you to look different,” said Fletcher. “You must be Chef Bernardo. And I — I’m new.”
“I’m not Chef Bernardo,” the man said, with a snicker. “That’s my stage name. My real name is Bernard. Or, Bernie. Who hired you, because I never approved a new hire? Was it Dave?”
“I’m here about the secret stash,” said Fletcher.
Bernie nodded his head, then winked. “Okay. So, not a new hire then. Got it. Thing is: you’re shit out of luck.”
“Trust me, I know I have terrible luck...” Fletcher said, rolling his eyes.
“No, I mean — look, the stash is gone,” said Bernie.

His pupils dilated and his eyes went wide. Fletcher squinted and gave him a closer look. The dry skin, the sallow bags beneath his eyes, the bloodshot veins crosswording across his eyes — Bernie was high. He had to be.
The kitchen’s aroma of burning charcoal swirled around Fletcher. Suddenly, it all made sense.
“You used up all of those drugs?” Fletcher said, in shock.
Bernie shook his head and chuckled. “No. The guy who owns all the stuff — the pickpocket — he came back here not ten minutes ago and stuffed all his stuff in the back of an ice cream truck.”
“Just like that?”
“Just like that.”
“And, there’s no trick to it? You’re not going to make me weed through a million riddles, or listen to a speech, or anything?”

“Look dude, the dude is on his way out of here,” said Bernie. He’d turned to his stove now and was flipping a couple of hockey pucks for pancakes. “You can try to catch him, or keep talking to me. Meantime? I have a mean meal to make.”
Just beneath the sizzle of the food, there was the faintest melody of “row-row-row your boat”. It was becoming ever fainter. It was unmistakably there, nonetheless.
“You’re the most reasonable person I’ve talked to, today,” said Fletcher. “Thanks for the food.”
Bernard nodded, with an empty smile burned to his face. Then, his face flashed with concern.
“Wait, what food?”
Fletcher grabbed a burrito off a plate and plowed back out the kitchen. He’d gone practically all day without eating, and he realized how starving he really felt.
“Also, I accidentally knocked your server unconscious,” Fletcher shouted over his shoulder.
He was already bounding back over the counter, as Bernard’s shrill cries echoed through the kitchen. Immediately, he was met by a swarm of disgruntled customers.
“Where’s our food?”
“We want our money back!”
“They just announced an air strike! I deserve my last burger!”
“Do you accept personal bank notes, in the form of note paper?”

Their eyes were rabid, and their faces construed into something from out of a zoo. Despite their folksy clothes, and the fact they were people Fletcher had seen a million times before, he hardly recognized anyone.
“Everybody, everybody, calm down!”
It was Marvin’s voice. He was somewhere in the crowd, somewhere.
“I’m the new chef, for the day,” he continued. “If you wish to put in any complaints, all you have to do is talk with me.”

The crowd turned from Fletcher and centered somewhere near the restaurant jukebox. There were crashes and shouts, as the situation steadily devolved. Though, Marvin’s voice remained above it all, confident and strong.
“Get out of here, Fletcher,” Marvin said. “I’ll hold them off.”
Fletcher gave a genuine smile — one of the few he’d made all day. Hell — he hardly ever smiled. Though, people hardly ever did anything for him, either.
Did people never do anything for him because he never smiled, or did he never smile because people never did anything for him? Quite the question.

Then he squinted, looking for the officer, Priest Carvel, and the Mayor. Presumably, they were in the crowd somewhere. However, he couldn’t make them out. Perhaps they’d already escaped, for the ice cream truck.
He took a large bite of his burrito and hurtled out the door.
“Howdy,” Officer Haynam said.

He’d been standing stiff as a pole, beside the restaurant’s door. His eyes had gone dull, and his face expressionless. Fletcher tipped his burrito toward Officer Haynam, before jumping over the hood of his car.
“Wait, stop!” Officer Haynam shouted. “If you’re Fletcher, I need you to stop!”
“History has changed!” Fletcher said, through a mouthful of food. “I’m Marvin Whisk!”

The streetlights cast a milky sheen to the street, blinding out the budding starlight from above. Glaring sunrays had all but disappeared, leaving the day for the night. Upon pressing the button to his keys, Fletcher watched Harry’s truck blink into the darkness.
Fletcher smirked and gave a last look to the withering sunlight on the horizon. It was one of the few places where day and night met.
The lights of the ice cream truck were just beneath the setting sun, winking at him. Fletcher pulled open the door to Harry’s car, and hopped in.
“Guys, he’s not inside the restaurant,” Officer Haynam yelled, from behind him. “He’s out here! We can’t let him make fools of us again, damn it!”

Fletcher hit the gas to his car, speeding down the road. His tires squealed behind him, pulling up a plume of smoke. Though, Fletcher kept his pedal to the floorboards. He couldn’t let the ice cream truck get away.
Whoever was in there, they had his oil baron. They might’ve even had Linda. He couldn’t let them escape.

The truck made a turn at Elmer Street. Fletcher’s truck careened sideways as he pulled it into the sharp turn. Already, the road had become narrower, and the buildings were covered with bits of graffiti. He plunged forward, nonetheless.
His head throttled. He’d just been hit in the rear by Officer Haynam. Fletcher took a glance in the mirror — Officer Baker was with him too.

Fletcher took one last bite of his burrito, and tossed it out the window. Following this, Officer Baker jumped out of the car, after it. She was on all fours upon reaching the burrito, and scooping it in her mouth. Officer Haynam’s came to a prompt halt, and craned his neck out of the window.
He shouted something at Officer Baker. Though, the words were lost to the air. Officer Haynam’s head was already becoming miniscule when Fletcher turned another corner after the ice cream truck.

The road was cragged now, covered in a patchwork of potholes and mismatched gravel. Swerving and whining, the truck went around as many of the potholes as Fletcher could make it. However, he finally gave in upon running over three potholes in a row. There was no avoiding them.

The street was covered in bits of trash and shards of glass. Apartment complexes banked either side of the road, built of a bright red brick. They were newer structures, having been built within the past five years. However, they were also cheaper — the residents had betrayed them to the elements.

Indeed, the ice cream truck picked up speed, clearly to get out as fast as possible. Already, there were people chasing after the truck, their eyes enraged and ravenous. An alley cat jumped in front of the ice cream truck, but, the ice cream truck simply barreled over it. A heart-piercing yowl resounded as the cat was creamed.
“No! Snowball!” one of the residents to the buildings bawled.

Fletcher’s headlights gleamed off the boxy rear of the ice cream truck. The apartment buildings leaned inward, glowering over the pursuit. Fletcher’s friend’s truck’s engine sputtered. An explosion shot from its tailpipe, threatening to do it in. All the while, the ice cream truck remained at a steady speed, showing no sign of struggle. Its stereo let off the calming song of “wheels on the bus”.
Fletcher wheezed. Nothing was going to stop the ice cream truck. He was going to lose it.
A glass bottle went flying, before landing in the street.
“You cheated!” somebody shouted.
“You can’t cheat at spin the bottle!” shouted another.

Fletcher swallowed. Flashes of his adolescence returned with a fury — the rejection he’d faced by so many peers. His Uncle’s claims of his incompetence. He’d never managed to land a kiss, without being laughed or yelled at straight afterward.

The ice cream truck spun out of control. Fletcher’s own truck squealed, as Fletcher hit the breaks. He nearly hit the dash, but already jumped out of his car as the fatal implications of his halt began to hit him.
“Stop in the name of me,” Fletcher said.

The ice cream truck had crashed into a street light on the side of the road. Sparks spat from overhead. The backdoor of the truck hung open, a sugary sludge spilling out of it. The back tires were flattened — they must’ve been shredded by the bits of broken glass.
Fletcher smiled to himself and looked behind. There was no sign of the cops, still. It was better that the ice cream truck went down, than himself.
Fletcher waded through the vomit of ice cream and hopped into the back of the truck, just as people clustered about the spill and lapped up the ice cream.
People had a way of reveling in the devastation of others, didn’t they?
“Alright, I’ve had enough of these games,” Fletcher shouted, upon entering the ice cream truck.

The interior of the truck was surprisingly bright, almost to a blinding level. He kept his head down, kicking away the toppled buckets beneath him. He pulled up his pants, to keeping them out of the river of ice cream.

Nearly all the ice cream had been knocked from out of the coolers, and off the shelves. Yet, there were still sacks atop the shelves. Specifically, sacks of powder. Sacks with needles. Sacks with pills.

Countless drugs surrounded him. An indescribable urge suddenly overtook Fletcher to snatch one of the sacks, for his own use. Surely nobody would notice. Hell, he probably wouldn’t even notice. How could anybody verify if he took drugs or not.
He shook his head. He had a person to sack. People may have been worse than drugs — but, at least they weren’t drugs.
“Did you hear me?” Fletcher said, speeding up his face toward the front of the truck. “The cops are almost here. You’re not going to have time to get back up and running, to escape. This is over.”
There was a moan.
“I can still teleport away, can’t I?” they said. “Or, maybe I can pretend that I was framed? Yes, that’s it! I was framed.”

The front of the truck looked worse than the inside of Fletcher’s closet. The passenger’s seat had been torn loose, the windscreen was shattered, and both airbags hung limply. A man sat in the driver’s seat, arms outstretched and quivering.
“Please, don’t do anything to me,” he whimpered.

He was a pale dumpy man. He was dressed in all white, even if his apron was smeared with chocolate and strawberry ice cream. If the truck’s interior had been a bit dimmer, and Fletcher a bit more dim-witted, he may have mistaken the man for one of the polar bears that covered so many ice cream labels.
“Oh don’t worry, I can’t just do anything,” Fletcher said, with a smirk. “According to the chaos theorem, there’s only one thing I can do. Now, where is the toy oil baron? Where is Linda?”
Fletcher lifted a soggy ice cream cone, and reeled it behind his head. “Come on, tell me,” said Fletcher. “There are only a few more hours left in today. You better not waste them.”
The man gulped. “I think I might know what you’re talking about,” he said. “The pickpocket said something about you wanting something…”
“We all want something out of life! Is that a crime?”
“Maybe? The cops are after you too, right?”
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
The man scrambled back in his seat, into the fetal position.
“Just don’t hurt me, okay? We’re in the same boat, with the cops after us.”

A twinge of sympathy formed in Fletcher’s chest. The ice cream man’s face had gone pale, his lips quivered, and the hairs on his arm stood on end. It was chilly in the ice cream truck, but it was clear that fear had the stronger sway.

“I just wanted to sell some ice cream to some depressed suckers, today,” the man whimpered. “Is that really so wrong? It’s not my fault that the pickpocket stormed my truck, and shoved a ton of drugs in it…”
“So, the pickpocket just dumped all of this on you, despite you having no relation to them?” Fletcher asked, his voice harsh.

It took all his restraint not to roll his eyes. The ice cream man could’ve resisted the pickpocket, couldn’t he have? Or, at the very least, cried for help? Why didn’t anybody ever cry for help, in times of desperation? Why did the ice cream man simply let this all happen to him?

The ice cream man let out a long wheezing laugh. “Yes, well… It is hilarious, isn’t it? The pickpocket thought that, if you were busy chasing me, you’d get caught by the cops. Plus, you wouldn’t be able to go chasing them.”
“That’s pathetic. That doesn’t make any sense!”

“They told me they were a champ at playing tag, when they were a kid. According to them, now it’s just a game of figuring out who’s it.” The man paused, to let his eyes dart around the truck. He wiped away a dribble of blood rolling down his face. “Also,” he said, “the pickpocket told me he wanted to get out of this dump. He was going to the toll booth to leave town, apparently.”

Fletcher snorted. Of course — the pickpocket must’ve known that he was chronically afraid of leaving town. Indeed, doing so would be a betrayal of his family legacy. There’d never been somebody in his family who’d ever stepped foot out of town.
Yet, he had an obligation to his toy. To Linda.
“You’re never going to catch them, by the way,” said the ice cream man. “It’s inevitable. They told me. You might as well give in, now.”
Sirens wailed from the distance. Head pounding, Fletcher bounded from the front of the truck and toward the back. He grabbed a glob of ice cream from the ground and shoved it in his mouth.
“Hey, that ice cream is expensive!” the ice cream man said, a quiver in his voice. “I’m going to need you to pay for that!”
“Why pay for something that’s already ruined?” Fletcher asked. He spat the ice cream out, and kicked another glob into the air with his foot.
“I’m going to salvage it! I’m going to stick it back in the buckets!” the ice cream man said, voice going shrill.

The music went shrill with him, as the lamppost came loose and crashed on the roof of the truck. Fletcher hopped into the Harry’s truck, and hit the gas. He checked his mirrors — Officer Haynam was just behind him. He looked ahead, and his brow furrowed. The mayor’s limousine had stretched across the road, blocking the exit.
Mayor Haddock stood atop a man’s back, shouting into the distance. Fletcher couldn’t make out what he was saying, but it sounded furious.
He turned a sharp left, down a back alley, before emerging on another street. Haddock probably should’ve invested in more limousines.
Hopefully this nightmare was all almost over. How much worse could the day become, really?

The pickpockets couldn’t have been Marvin. It couldn’t have been the Mayor and Lydia, either. And, it couldn’t have been the police. At least, if anything that the ice cream man had said was to be believed. After all, the pickpockets were supposed to have been heading toward the toll booth. They couldn’t have been busy chasing Fletcher, during all that time.
Albeit, trusting in ice cream men had never served Fletcher well in the past. They always managed to get something wrong.

While the ice cream man had said the pickpockets would be by the toll booth, they weren’t anywhere to be seen. Harry’s truck puttered down a chapped stretch of road, lit only by its headlights and the sparse glow of the toll-booth’s sign. Surrounding the tollbooth were bulrushes and a thick metal gate. Behind it was a bridge, which led over Dexburg River and into the world outside.
Fletcher shuddered. Harry’s truck shuddered with him. The entire world seemed to shudder.
Only as he crawled towards the toll both did the shuddering stop. Had there just been a minor earthquake? Fletcher couldn’t tell.
A thin metal rod lowered from the toll booth, between him and the bridge. Fletcher rolled down his window and looked to the toll booth operator.
It was an older woman, with fraying hair and spotty teeth. A cigarette hung from her mouth, and her eyes hung to the ground.
“It’ll be eighteen bucks,” she said. She took a deep whiff of her cigarette, then looked Fletcher dead in the eye.
Fletcher ruffled through his pockets, his face heating up. He had no money. It were as though the toll booth operator knew he had no money, too.
“I — I forgot my cash,” Fletcher said, with an awkward chuckle.
“We can just charge it to your plates,” the woman said, tiredly. “You’ll be sent the bill, or whatever.”
Fletcher gulped. His plates might’ve been on a wanted list already, since he’d stolen it from Harry. He couldn’t afford to be traced.
“It — it’s fine,” Fletcher said.
His foot tensed, preparing to jump from the brake to the gas. He could probably ram through the blockade, if need be. Or, at least he could try.
“Did anybody shady come through here, recently?” Fletcher asked. “I’m just asking because… Well, I’m chasing someone shady.”
“Sounds like you’re chasing yourself,” said the operator.
Her face creased rigid, like the spine of a weathered, leather-bound book. She peered at Fletcher, as though she were analyzing him. Looking into his very soul.
“I think you have a bit of spinach in between your teeth,” she said.
Fletcher wiped his mouth. “Must’ve been the burrito,” he said sheepishly. “But, look, I’m definitely not chasing myself. If I was chasing myself, I’d know it.”
He looked in the mirror. His eyes were black marbles, in the dim light. He hardly recognized the person staring back out at him. If he really was chasing himself, would he be able to tell?

“The people in our dreams are ourselves,” Fletcher’s Uncle once told him, vigor in his voice. Fletcher had just woken up from terrors, and hallucinations of people burglarizing the toy shop. Even as his heart hammered at his chest, he thought he could still hear the burglars down in the shop. “So too goes for our nightmares. The things we’re most afraid of are within…”
“If you aren’t chasing your own tail, then who are you tailing?” the operator asked.
She inspected her yellowed nails, then snickered. “Anyhow, I’m not going to let you in, unless you have cash.”
“I don’t quite know who I’m chasing!” Fletcher said. “That’s the thing! They have my online girlfriend captured, along with one of my valuables… That’s all I know!”
“You have an online girlfriend?” the operator said, with a snort. “What an accomplishment. Bet you worked real hard to reel her in…”

“Actually, she just contacted me out of the blue,” said Fletcher. “She wanted me to help build a website, for her — I’m a pretty tech savvy guy — and we’ve taken a liking to each other ever since. Totally beats my ex-girlfriend. It’s like she knows me, inside and out!”
Harry’s truck sputtered as it sat, as if it were groaning at Fletcher. The operator gave a reflexive roll of her eyes.
“How long have you known this cat?” she said. “A week? A month? Because, she smells more like a catfish, to me...”
“A day,” Fletcher said.
“A day?”
“Love at first type is a thing. I read about it in an article once. I think I’m going to marry her.”

The operator burst out, nearly falling back in her chair. A paralyzed horse would’ve had a more appealing face than her, with her incessant braying and snorting. Yet, her laughs had a way of getting beneath Fletcher’s skin. She had a point, didn’t she?
“I married my husband after getting extremely hungover in the back of his band’s tour truck,” she said. “But, even for me, it took me three days… And, I saw his face, damn it!”
Fletcher’s face flushed red. It was true — all of it, so true. His relationship was built on the flimsiest of explanations.

He’d never drawn Linda in. Rather, she’d drawn in him, tricking him into a false sense of security. The way she pretended she cared, the way she shared things about herself, the way she called Fletcher by “Stuart”… It’d all seemed so perfect. Too perfect. Could she have ever been real at all?
The eye from the picture she’d sent railed at his mind. It’d been so familiar, and so distant, all the same. A photo that he’d seen before? It was something out of a sculpture or oil painting.
Fletcher shifted his truck into park.

“I’m going to have to ask you to pay, or get fined. That, or turn around,” said the operator. “Honestly, it’s all the same to me. I just want to get back to watching my reality TV, on my tiny screen.”
She gestured to her phone.
“Can’t,” Fletcher mumbled.
“Can’t what?”
“Can’t be,” said Fletcher. “But it must be.”
“Sounds like nonsense.”
“Who ever said that reality had to make sense, though?”
Margaret. It’d been Margaret, all along.

The dark eye from the photo matched hers, perfectly. And, the use of the name “Stuart”, instead of Fletcher? Nobody else, outside of Margaret, had ever called Fletcher that. Furthermore, Linda had known an uncanny amount about Fletcher, as if she’d researched him. It only made sense that she was somebody close.

“My ex-girlfriend,” said Fletcher, “I think she’s been posing as my online girlfriend. Everything that’s been going on around me — it’s all been a plot, between her and my best friend, Harry! It all fits! All the pieces fit!”
Fletcher broke into a hysterical laugh.
“That’s just beautiful,” said the operator, scrolling through her phone. “You’ve been made a punk by your ex-girlfriend. A tale for the ages.”
“You believe me, don’t you?”

The operator looked up from her phone, and gave a shrug. “Look, man, I have no idea what the hell is going on in this town anymore. Figure it out, and get out of my booth before the crazies all get here.”
“What are you talking about?”

The operator nudged her head to the right. Fletcher whipped his head around, to see a caravan of headlights floating toward him. It had to be a chain of at least a hundred cars, all streaming down the road.
“Thank you so much for the help,” said Fletcher.
He put the truck in reverse, preparing to turn back around on the road.

Margaret’s apartment. That was where everything was going to go down. Her connections with the mayor, her contacting of the police, her assortment of odd collected items — she was the pickpocket. If she wasn’t it could’ve been nobody else.
“Yep, just don’t bring your ugly face here again,” said the operator. “I could’ve finally figured out which Marlboro sister is pregnant, if it weren’t for you.”
Fletcher had no idea what she was talking about. He didn’t care.
He let out a whoop as his car rushed by the endless rows of cars, all headed out of Dexburg.
“What are you doing, you moron?” A man said, craning his head out of his car window. “the entire town is going to be reduced to ash!”
“Sounds like a party to me!” Fletcher said.
He turned on his phone, shooting a text to Margaret.
“I’m going back to your place,” it read. “We need to talk. For real, this time.”
There was no response. Though, Fletcher didn’t need one.

Fletcher was struck by a sledgehammer. All this time, he’d hated Carol’s guts — and, she’d been so simple-minded. He’d been thinking so many steps ahead, that he hadn’t realized he should’ve been looking a million steps behind.

Carol was just sitting on the sidelines, waiting for this all the end. She didn’t care who she talked to, or how anything went down. Meanwhile, he’d been beating himself, struggling and striving for some brass ring that had never even mattered.

Fletcher cleared a bit of mucous from his throat, and pulled his hood further down his face. Clarity bordered on his mind — he could almost taste it. Yet, there were still things to do. Outside the shop, the mob was mopping the streets. Literally.
“Keep mopping, men! We’ll find him buried under all this street gunk at some point!”
None of it was going to go away. Not until he was done, and maybe not even then.

Fletcher shook his head of the crowd, then looked Carol in the eyes. “Ending the day, by watching everything end, sounds like the perfect way to go,” said Fletcher. “But... I still have a few things from today that I need to take care of, before I can enter tomorrow.”
“I’ve been wondering where you’ve been all day,” said Carol. “I was starting to miss all your wild antics.”
Fletcher gave a nervous chuckle. Those had never been antics. However, Carol didn’t need to know that.
“I have to save somebody,” Fletcher said. “Or, at least, I have to know who they are. I can’t spend the rest of the day without knowing.”
“That new poem you’re working on…” Carol said, “it just sounds plain beautiful. Also, what does it mean?”
Fletcher merely gave a supplicating nod. Some things would never change between him and Carol.
“Look, I just need your help,” Fletcher said. “You know the door between my shop and yours? I need you to unlock it, so that I can go and get something from in there.”
“Is it the toy oil baron?” Carol said. “Did you finally find where it was?”
He thought back to his uncle. What he would’ve thought about the toy being lost. Would he have been disappointed? Would he have been understanding?
There was no way of knowing. Though, perhaps that was for the best. Perhaps it was finally time to move on.
“No. Don’t plan on finding it. I have other obligations to keep, though.”
Carol rummaged through her pockets, then pulled out her keys.
“Well, there you go,” she said. “Not a problem at all! Good luck!”

Fletcher tossed the keys in his hand, and ogled at them. They’d been freely given. They were remarkably light, compared to Harry’s stolen keys. Granted, that just could’ve been because Harry’s keys had the giant flashlight on them.

Eyes watering from his allergies, Fletcher made his way up through the creaking steps at the back of Carol’s shop, and up into the rafters. She’d never bothered getting her second floor finished, always insisting that it would “block the plants too far from the sun.” Nonetheless, the door between her shop and Fletcher’s hung in mid-air, behind a center rafter.

His balance swung from side to side as he made his way across. He’d never been one to shy away from heights — though, that didn’t stop his stomach from ramming into his throat as he looked down. Directly beneath him was an oversized flower bed, to break his fall.
Out of everything, it just had to be a flower bed?

The key didn’t want to budge at first, when he shoved it in the door. The beam beneath him groaned, begging to snap. He looked behind, to see it bowing in the center. He jiggled the key and throttled the door. Just as it opened, the rafters gave a snap. Fletcher jumped, landing on the floor of his bedroom.

The rafter still held together, but only by the thinnest splinters of wood. He kicked the door shut — he didn’t want to watch the beam collapse. Upon the door closing, Fletcher was met by a lopsided silence. Far below him were the muffled cries of the crowd, who were no doubt still searching for him. Though, they were distant. He could also hear the steadiness of his breathing. He could hear the rhythmic gusts of the air vent above him.
The crowd would have little chance of finding him, if he was fast. He just had to get to his safe open, get the cash, then get out.
He pulled his chair from out of his computer desk, then pulled out his lunchbox. He undid the latches, then pulled out an oversized book.
Fletcher smirked. It wasn’t really a book, though. He flipped open the cover, to reveal a lock. He put in his passcode.
“Come on guys, let’s just head back down! Have some fun, party… There’s no way that Fletcher is in here, so why waste our time looking for him?”
It was Marvin. From the volume of his voice, he was just outside the door. From the pitch of his voice? Things were dire.

Nonetheless, Fletcher flushed with a sort of renewed confidence. Marvin was out there, helping him out. Though he had every reason to abandon him, he’d never given up. Maybe there were countless other people among the mob, too, bent on helping him. Who knew?
“Let us by! Let us by!” the mob shouted. “We all want to kill Fletcher!”
Maybe he’d been giving the people too much credit. He began stuffing the wads of cash in his sweatshirt pockets, sweat pouring down his face. He just needed to get in, then get out.
“I’m telling you, he’s not in there,” Marvin said, voice cracking. “What, do you guys think that I’d lie to you?”
Marvin was answered by a series of jeers. The top lock to the door was undone.
Fletcher bit his lip, then kicked his safe away. Three thousand dollars were sitting in his pockets, now. Now? He just needed to head out.
He gave a reluctant glance at the door to Carol’s shop. He gave another to
“The chaos theorem says he’s in there. And, we have to chase him. There’s nothing that will stop us!”
The door burst open, Marvin spilling through. He held the handle of an antique gun, with several barrels sprouting from its end. He shut the door, then redid its lock.
“We need to move, and fast,” said Marvin, face flushed purple.
“First thing first, what the hell is that thing?” Fletcher asked, pointing at the gun.
“Duck’s foot pistol,” said Marvin. “Doesn’t work, and I might accidentally shoot myself if it did. But, hey: it was Greg Dexburg’s favorite gun.”
“How’d you get in here?” Fletcher asked.
“The entire wall to your bottom floor has been blown open,” Marvin said. “What, you didn’t see?”
“I’m talking about this room. The door was locked.”
Just as Fletcher said this, the door to his room buckled.
“Oh, I have the keys to all the doors in your place,” said Marvin. “I paid a locksmith to come in here and build them for me.”
Fletcher gave Marvin a blank stare. Marvin gave a shrug.
“Look, we have to get you out of here, and fast,” Marvin said. He gestured toward the door into Carol’s shop, but Fletcher shook his head.
“The rafters broke,” Fletcher said. “I’m not doing that unless I want to fall into a bed of flowers.”
Marvin moaned, and tugged the skin on his face.
“I don’t know what made you act like such an idiot to come here, but… There’s a chance you won’t be coming back out.”
Fletcher strode up to the window and started shunting it open.
“You’re not going to jump out the window!” Marvin said.
He leapt at Fletcher, knocking him into his closet door.
“You’ve gone too far to just give up your life now!” Marvin said.
Fletcher sputtered, trying to catch his breath.
“There’s a giant street lamp by the window!” Fletcher said. “I can just grab onto that, and then slide my way—.”

The door to Fletcher’s bedroom went flying before wedging right between Fletcher’s bed and the wall. Dozens of people came streaming in, but Fletcher and Marvin were just blocked from view. Marvin slid open Fletcher’s closet, and slipped in. Fletcher followed, then shut the door.
“Maybe I could still make it,” Fletcher whispered.
Marvin shook his head, then moaned. “No, they’ll see you. All it’ll take is somebody jumping after you, and you’ll be egg on the sidewalk.”
“I saw a few people cooking eggs on the sidewalk. Doesn’t actually look half bad.”
While Fletcher had felt he was sweating before, he was practically melting now. With Marvin’s body pressed against his, and the crashes from people tearing up his room, stress was at a fever pitch.
Fletcher tried readjusting himself in the closet to make more room for himself, only to bump into Dave — his oversized dummy. Fletcher was suddenly beginning to seriously regret his toy collection.
“Give me your sweatshirt,” Marvin hissed.
“What?”
Marvin unzipped his own jacket and began putting it on the dummy.
“Just give me the jacket,” Marvin repeated. “They’re looking for me, and they’re looking for you. We only have one option to get rid of them: giving them both.”

Fletcher’s arms trembled as he unzipped his jacket, then gave it to Marvin. He wanted to choke as he watched Marvin zip the jacket up, then pull the hood over his face. He was about to make the greatest sacrifice he could — and he didn’t even seem to care.
“Don’t tell me you’re thinking what I think you’re thinking,” said Fletcher.
“Wouldn’t think of it,” said Marvin. “Still going to tell you what I’m thinking, though.”
“You’re going to feed yourself to the mob?”

Marvin shrugged. “Kind of. I’ll toss out the dummy, to make them think it’s my body. Then, I’ll run out there, dressed as you. Once they’re gone, and after me? You can make your escape. Like cake, right?”
Fletcher furled his lip.
“I hate cake.”
“Even better.”
Fletcher began rifling through his rack of jackets, looking for one that might give him easy camouflage once he was back in the street.
“You sure about this?” Fletcher asked.
Marvin shook his head. It was impossible to make out the look on his face, from the darkness of the closet. Though, from the heaviness of his breathing, the fear was still palpable.
“One thing I have to tell you,” said Marvin. “I hated you, for the longest time. I really did.”
Fletcher’s jaw dropped.
“You? Really? Could’ve sworn we were pals.”
“Maybe we are, maybe we aren’t… But, after this?” Marvin chuckled. “God… I don’t know why I’m doing this. But, you’re going to owe me big time, if this works.”
“On every level, there’s no way this should work,” Fletcher said.
However, Marvin didn’t hear. He’d already opened the closet door and tossed out the dummy’s body.
“Oh god!” a man shrieked. It was the voice of the banker — had to be. “Fletcher killed him! He’s going to kill us! Holy hell, why didn’t I lock him down to declare bankruptcy when I had the chance…”
Marvin stepped out. Fletcher watched the scene unfold from between the slits of his closet.
“It’s him!” the banker cried. “I’d recognize that face anywhere! We can’t let him escape — the chaos theorem says we will, and we can’t let it be right!”

Marvin bopped the banker in the head, then scrambled for the doorway. People grappled at his coat and attempted to whack him with oversized fly swatters. Yet, Marvin managed to slip through all the same.
“You want me?” Marvin said, making his voice lower and gruffer. “You’ve been chasing me all day. May as well chase me, one last time.”
The banker bumbled around the room, bumping between members of the mob. Most of them seemed equally clueless. He rammed into Logan, whose beefy frame seemed equally lost.
“I’m going to find him, and then I’m going to squash him like a grape,” Logan said, while people streamed past him.
“I think he turned invisible!” the banker said, voice shrill again. “Everybody, keep an eye out, or he might poke it out!”

The room had nearly dissipated, when the two headstrong leaders finally realized they were being abandoned. Logan gave a sniff, as though some part of him had picked up Fletcher’s scent and could tell that he lingered.
“Don’t leave me!” Logan cried, stumbling out the door. “I’m still relevant!”
The banker stepped past Logan, somehow managing to push his beefy body aside.

Once they were finally gone, Fletcher stepped out of his closet and rushed for the window. He readjusted his new jacked — a brown blazer. He’d only just pulled it out of his uncle’s chest a couple days ago, to try it on. He hadn’t thought it fit him, then. Though, now here he was, full circle, wearing it for his escape.
He peeked at his phone again. Mt. Bancroft. Whatever he did from hereon out, that would be the endgame.
He opened the window. It crackled and shuddered as he pushed it up — Fletcher almost worried it’d tear from the wall entirely.

Marvin streaked across the street. The cloud of people had already congregated to meet him, voices raised in fury. Their chants were impossible to decipher, though Fletcher could make out one thing from them: sheer terror.
Beneath the anger, they were afraid of the end. Of the inevitable. Despite everybody in the crowd knowing what was going to happen? They couldn’t live with it. They didn’t want to live with it.

Fletcher looked to the flagpole, hanging just outside his window. Nobody would notice him as he made his way down. It would be completely safe. Still, his gut rocked back and forth, with the uncertainty of it all.
Perhaps the rest of the world knew where it was headed. Yet, he had no clue. Which was more terrifying.
“I think I left my toenail clippers in here,” a man said, bumbling in. Despite himself, Fletcher gave a glance behind — it was the ice cream man, from a mere hour before.
“Wait, how the hell are you here when you’re down there?” the ice cream man croaked.
Fletcher dove out the window, and toward the flagpole. As he did, the ice cream man hurled a pillow at him.
“Take that!” the man said.

The pole was rough against Fletcher’s hands and groin. It took every ounce of willpower to hang on. That, and the fact that the ice cream man brandished his 16-ounce ice cream scoop mere feet above him.
“Come up here and face me, like a man!” the ice cream man cried.
Fletcher made a graceful landing on the sidewalk. Then, he nearly toppled over as the feeling came rushing back to his groin.
“Oh god,” Fletcher moaned.
Just across the street sat Harry’s truck. Though, the tires had been slashed, and the windows smashed. Marvin stood atop the truck, doing his best to hold back the mob.
Somebody tugged Fletcher on the sleeve.
“Are you an angel?” a woman asked.
Fletcher shook his head. “If I am, then the whole world must be on the verge of ending.”\
The woman moaned. “I knew it! The world is ending!”
“Says who?” asked some goon, from the crowd, dressed in white. It must’ve been another one of Priest Carvel’s followers.
“Wait, look at that! It’s Fletcher! A second Fletcher! That loser, who claimed to be our savior!”
“A second Fletcher?” said another. It was a man dressed in a construction uniform. Yet, they wore the badge of the cultists as well.
Fletcher rolled his eyes, and searched for a way out. Great. There were already more converts of Priest Carvel. How long would it be before people figured out that the goon was a loon?
“It’s the second coming of Fletcher!” declared the first man. “Get him!”
“What was that, my loyal slaves?”
Priest Carvel poked his ruddy head from beneath a throng of supporters.
“Why, paint me purple, and then bleach me white! It’s Fletcher!”
Fletcher shook his head, and took a few steps back. Though, he only found himself backing into more people.
“It’s not me,” Fletcher said. “I just happen to be somebody who uncannily looks like Fletcher.”
He went to gesture toward Marvin. However, he’d already been knocked from the top of the car, and dragged into his antique shop. Fletcher winced at the sounds of shrieks, and shattering glass.
“You just so happen to look like him, huh?”
Fletcher was given a light jab in the back, from behind. It was one of the guards from the school. Had they really bothered to follow him, all the way here?
A woman, foaming at the mouth, stepped out of the crowd. “I tried killing him, earlier today! And, he wouldn’t let me!”
Fletcher trembled at the sight of her, attempting to break her way through. Yet, she was only replaced by somebody more terrifying.
Indeed, the tycoon and his employee pulled her away, the tycoon standing tall and proud.
“I offered this vagrant a fine job,” he said, undulating his voice. “A damn good job too, I may add, producing gunk up our river. And, what did he do with my gracious offer? Zip.”

An old man’s voice wriggled through the crowd. “Darn right. He’s a screwy one,” he said, voice cracking as he did. It was the groundskeeper, from the graveyard. He kept balance on his cane, but still had nearly withered to the ground. “You should’ve heard some of the stuff he told me. Absolutely sickening!”
“I should’ve known this man would be trouble. His past dictates such!” cawed the historian.
“I foretold this would occur as well,” cried the fortune teller. “

Everybody Fletcher had seen that day was there. The drug dealers, Logan, Mayor Haddock, Priest Carvel, the socialites, John, the police… It was an unending stream of faces, all of whom were steaming. Fletcher bit his tongue, to keep from screaming. The crowd towered over him, faces twisted in contempt.
Some of them held hints of remorse — sympathy. The ones who’d tried helping him. Though, even then, it was the contempt that defined them all.
There were only a few people who weren’t there. His Uncle… Dear god what would he think of this?
Poor Marvin, too. He was trapped in his shop, being torn apart — and, all for nothing.
Though, at least Harry wasn’t here to see this. Or Margaret. They’d only rub in the wound further. They always had been warning him that things might come to something like this, weren’t they?
“Fletcher?”

The crowd suffocated Fletcher, their bodies thrashing against his. Holes were torn through Fletcher’s jacket. Then his shirt. His pants. Teeth and nails gnashed at his skin. Nevertheless, Fletcher managed to turn around.
Margaret’s face hovered within the crowd. Her expression was an enigma. There was delight in his plight, no doubt. Though, also pity. Even shame.
Fletcher looked away when Harry’s face showed up next to Margaret’s. Fletcher’s own shame was overpowering.
Linda, and the toy — he was just chasing a dream, wasn’t he. All of these relationships were all that mattered here, at the end.
“I warned you Fletcher,” Harry said. “I didn’t want it to come to this. But, it had to, I guess. And, I warned you.”

The fury of the crowd intensified, with them increasing the boldness of their attacks. Yet, Fletcher could hardly feel it. It all meant nothing, didn’t it? All that Fletcher could truly feel was a dumb, dull ache at the bottom of his gut, and in the back of his head.
It was the same pain, in two places at once. It shouldn’t have been possible. However, the most impossible of things were always what seemed most real, weren’t they?

“Stuart Fletcher!” Mayor Haddock said. His voice was a gunshot in the dark. The entire crowd stepped aside, allowing Mayor Haddock to stand in his full might. He should’ve been a terrifying sight of might, that is. His suit was perfectly trim along his body, accentuating his thick arms and legs. His watched shimmered, as though it were a token of past exploits. Yet, looking him in the eyes, Fletcher could only see the softness there.
Days gone by, swamped in decadence. That’s all Mayor Haddock had ever known. That’s all that life ever had to offer him.
The man was a farce. Perhaps the entire crowd was.
“Tonight is the night that you end,” Mayor Haddock continued. “The chaos theorem has deemed it such.”
A meek voice peeped up from the crowd. “Sir,” said, “doesn’t the chaos theorem dictate that we don’t dictate what it says, unless it says?”
Mayor Haddock gave a smug smile. “I’m the Mayor though, see,” he said. “And, this is my town. That overrules the theorem.”
He laughed.

“See, we’ve all been doing such a great job about keeping quiet toward you,” Mayor Haddock continued. “We couldn’t let you know how the theorem says it all ends… But, yeah: you’re doomed to be sent to your death, by us. And, in turn, we’re doomed to be killed by you.”
Fletcher glanced at Mayor Haddock’s watch. The minute and hour hand synced on the eleventh tick mark.
Mayor Haddock laughed again, his face almost maniacal.
“It’s absurd, really,” he said. “This whole town… All so absurd! It’s all destined to revolve around one man? And, you’re our demise? We’re yours? It shouldn’t work like that.”
He gave a sniffle, then raised himself up.

“I mean, it’s almost something out of a fever dream. I suppose that that’s how towns are meant to be… But then, that one man who everything revolves around? It was always supposed to be one of us!” He turned and gestured to Logan, the banker, and finally Priest Carvel. Finally, to himself. “Somebody like me!”
The crowd broke into a series of cheers. Fletcher’s stomach went inside out. He couldn’t listen to them — they were tearing him apart. Moreover, awareness of the bus bordered on the edge of his mind.
It was scheduled to come through here, at any moment. It always did, didn’t it? It was inevitable that it would again.
“I just want my fate to end,” cried the historian. “I’ve had enough of all this new history!”
“Give me a piece of him!” Logan shouted above the crowd. “Just a piece!”
He made his way through the crowd, knocking people over like a bowling ball through bowling pins.

Jack shouted something at Logan. Clair too. Logan remained enraged as ever, his eyes targeting only Fletcher. Yet, Fletcher could only hear the roar of the bus’s engine. It was near, now. The back of the crowd was already thinning out, making way for it.
Fletcher smirked. The bus driver had made it on time, after all. Admittedly, not as had probably been planned. Though, then, did anything ever go according to plan?
People screamed as the bus tore through, forcing them to dive aside. Even Logan dove away, albeit reluctantly. Yet, Fletcher ran toward the bus, waving his arms.
“Hey! Wait! I need your help!”
He banged on the side of the bus until its door slid open. Fletcher knocked away a couple of townspeople who tried to make their way through.
“Shut it!” Fletcher said.
Yet, the door had already been shut.
“Back I see…” the bus driver said, in a drawl.
Fletcher glanced out the window, at all the pandemonium. People bumbled into one another searching for him. The town was clueless as to where he’d gone.
“Tonight is insane,” Fletcher said, his breaths short and shallow.
“Every night is insane,” said the bus driver. “You should’ve seen the pack of geese that waddled onto my bus, the other night. Geese! All migrating south, on my bus. Idiots, right?”
Fletcher gave a supplicating smile.
“Ah, yes, definitely,” he said, nodding.
The bus driver smiled back.
“You’re not going to pay me tonight, are you?” he said.
The bus driver kept his bus in a crawl, as people streamed by in all their confusion. How long would it be before they figured out where Fletcher had gone?
“I never pay you,” Fletcher said, with a chuckle. “I figured we had an agreement about that, by now.”
The bus driver nodded. “It’s a nice setup. But, you want me to give up my bus to you too, tonight. Don’t you?”

Fletcher’s eyes bulged. He hadn’t thought to ask that. However, the bus driver was right. The bus was moving at such a slow pace. Moreover, the townspeople weren’t going to be slow to figure out where Fletcher was. Not if he didn’t move quicker.
“Yes, now that you mention it,” Fletcher said. “Where I’m going… Maybe I don’t want anybody else to be. How did you predict I was going to ask that?”

The bus driver shrugged. “I want to ditch the bus, tonight,” he said. “I heard a few things on the radio. Apparently the world is ending tonight? I don’t know. But, it sounds as good a time as any for me to finally go get myself a suntan.”
He stroked his beard and took a sip of his coffee. Standing from his seat, he smiled at Fletcher.
“Well, go on,” the bus driver said, nudging his head toward the seat.

He then ran for the escape at the back. Fletcher’s mouth was stuffed with cotton. He searched for the right words — the right actions to take. However, the bus driver was already leaping out the back of the bus. Fletcher pulled himself into the driver’s seat, and hit the pedal.

A unique pride welled in Fletcher’s chest. He’d stolen several cars that day. All of them were pretty good. Yet, nothing felt so right as driving the bus. Everybody got out of the way for him. Some people ran alongside the bus, in a desperate attempt to get him to stop, and let them aboard.
Laughing, Fletcher picked up his speed. His laughs were broken by an overdrawn beep. Fletcher looked in the mirror — a purple minivan was tailing him. Fletcher squinted. The driver was Logan.
Logan was hunched over, hands clutching a plush, pink steering wheel. Unnatural as the sight was, Logan looked oddly comfortable.

Fletcher turned the corner and gave a last look to Purview Street. His toy shop was being torn apart by the seams, people were having dance offs atop his broken toys, the sign was being made into a swing, and a fog of hysteria entrenched it all.
His home was gone. He finally was saying goodbye. Yet, it felt right.

He pressed his pedal further to the floorboard. However this car chase with Logan ended, and however everything turned out on the top of Mt. Bancroft? Everything was going to go exactly how it should.
That was the only way anything could ever go.
This is a real crappy golf course. It is a golf course, isn’t it? That’s why there are so many golf clubs, right?
“Get out of my antique shop.”
Some twerp is shouting at everybody. He has a golf club of his own. Doesn’t really look like he knows how to use it, though.

Oh, whatever. Who cares. This place is kind of cute, I guess. That is, if we hadn’t broken the doorway and window, searching for that Fletcher fellow. Maybe I should buy it? Nothing is stopping me, after getting all that inheritance from Mr. Clover. Yes, if I bought this place on the spot, that would surely impress tons of people. Wouldn’t it? Living to impress others is my fate, after all.
And, would you look at that? A man has just come walking in, carrying bundles of money. Looks like I have somebody new to impress!
“Jim Harrigan? Is that you?”
Dear god. Some woman is ogling my money. It’s the Clover lady. Doesn’t she already have enough money? Can’t I just steal some money in peace?

Here I was, thinking that this place would be in shambles due to that Fletcher fellow. But, it looks like everybody is thinking as sharp as ever. Still, maybe I have a chance at getting their money, yet.
Ah, money. The greatest green thing on god’s green earth.
“I’m just carrying some money I found,” I say. “If nobody is able to claim it, I do believe it’s mine.”
Of course, everybody in this room is going to claim it. But then, everybody in this room probably owes me money, too. Bunch of suckers, this town is…
“Wait, I think that’s Fletcher’s money!” a man says.
It’s that sickly Marvin fellow. He’s rifling through the pockets of his jacket right now, his oversized hands grabbing at thick clumps of cash. It appears I have a new victim.
“Marvin Whisk, is that you?” I say. I flash a smile, and Marvin manages one back.
God, unloading the fact that he’s two thousand in debt is going to be delicious.
“Don’t you owe me money?” I say. “If so, I do believe I should be keeping all of this…”
A man slaps me in the back. I turn around — it’s Kent Burgess.
Ah, hell.
“Hello,” he says. “I do believe that your bank owes my company quite a bit of money.”
Ha! Jim Harrigan, finally being done in by Kent Burgess.
That’s what he gets, for calling me Don Key!
Poor guy. Doesn’t know what hit him.
My chaos theorem told me that business was going to be booming tonight. I guess it wasn’t wrong.
“Thank you very much,” I say filtering through the money that I’ve snatched from his hand.
The banker’s face is ruddy from rage. He really does look like a petulant five year old in some ways. Perhaps that’s why he’s such a miser.
I should’ve never given his stupid bank cash. That he was going to hoard it all from my company was all but inevitable.

“No!” cries the man in the corner. He shoves what little cash remains in his jacket deeper into his pockets. He’s such a pitiful looking fellow. His hair is wilting from his head, and his skin is bursting with burst blood vessels.
“You don’t understand,” he continues. “Fletcher needed that money, to save somebody from a ransom. But, he stuck it all in my jacket. Fletcher has the wrong jacket!”
I ignore him while I recount my money, then give the banker a firm handshake. I couldn’t care less about what this dweeb has to say.
“Much appreciated,” I smirk. “I do believe that this should be plenty to cover me. Looks like I can go ahead and hit the road!”
This trip hasn’t been a bust, after all. I’m making my way toward the busted door of the antique shop, when somebody jumps in front and lets out a bellow.
“Nobody is headed anywhere,” I say. I show off my badge, and it shimmers in the pale light of the room.
If only it would shine a little brighter. I keep telling Mayor Haddock that he needs to make room for badge polish in the police budget, but he just doesn’t listen.
Honestly, “police polish” practically sells itself. Why won’t he listen?
“And why should I listen to you?” Kent Burgess says, staring me dead in the eye.
Dear lord, this guy is intimidating. No wonder we haven’t busted him for all of the drugs he’s supposed to be stockpiling.

“I just received word that there was a terrible traffic accident on the main road,” I say. “An entire bus flipped over, and exploded. It apparently got hit by some purple minivan? I don’t know, but we have to close all of the roads.”
The Marvin dude looks like he’s just been hit by a bus himself.
“Fletcher was in that bus,” he says. “Do you think he survived! I need to get to him, to help him save somebody being held under ransom.”
Sounds exhausting to me. Honestly, why do all the wackos come to me? Can’t this town have a single day where an officer like me doesn’t have to deal with anything?

“He’s dead. According to experts, nobody could’ve survived that crash,” I say. I’m talking out my ass. I have no clue what the crash looks like, but I’m probably right. “Plus, if there was a ransom involved, you should’ve come to me.”
“But I am coming to you!”
“Tough luck, buttercup. Little late for that. Ransoms and briberies aren’t things that can just be handled lightly.”
Readjusting my badge to reassert my dominance, I feel a wad of cash pressed against my chest.
“Can you let me out of here, chief?”
It’s Kent Burgess again. Tilting my mouth into his ear, I whisper, “you can just take the squad car.”
I hand him the keys. He should be fine. If he knows how to run a business, he should know how to run a car.
Looks like Officer Haynam just gave him the squad car. Ha. Rich. Pretty sure that rich boy has never been driven anywhere, without a chauffeur.
Why is he going to be promoted to Sherriff over me, again?
“Hey, you’re just letting him go?” a woman shouts, beneath a web of jewelry. “I knew you’d be biased toward him. That’s how it always goes!”
Great. Finally somebody is calling him out.
I take a big bite of my taco. This is going to be fun.
“Hey, I’m treating everybody equally here!” says Officer Haynam. “Fletcher is the root cause of all this chaos, okay? If we can all just calm down, we can get thing back in order.”
“Order will never come,” I say. “The spirits have foretold as such. As a close confidant of Fletcher’s, I know his spirit will be haunting you all for the rest of eternity.”
I have no clue what I’m saying. I’m pretty sure I was ticked off with Fletcher, no more than a few minutes ago. Wasn’t I? See, now I’m not even sure about that.
Though, there are a ton of people in this room, which means a ton of potential customers.

“Everybody who ever harmed Fletcher will soon face consequences,” I continue. “This whole town must prepare for reckoning! The rich can squander the weak no longer. People like Mayor Haddock and Kent Burgess need to pay for their crimes against the average person!”

The crowd nods their heads agreeably. I must be making some sort of impression. Maybe Fletcher was right — maybe the feeling that fate is set in stone truly is something that everybody is searching to avoid.
I’m going to continue my spiel — this is the perfect opportunity to try selling some healing crystals. Though, I’m pushed aside.

“Burgess truly is one of the greatest men in town,” I shout. “Everybody should know that. He pays people a decent wage, even if it’s slightly below minimum. And, for at all, our town produces great things. Like steering wheels! How could any car have direction without steering wheels?”
I hope that I’m swaying the crowd. Though, they don’t seem so convinced in what I’m saying. It doesn’t make any sense. People should be enthralled.

If only Kent Burgess were here to defend himself. When you spent hours waxing a man’s shoes, singing praise into his ears, and making sure that his company doesn’t go down the tubes, you learn a lot about them. Kent is a man for the ages.
“Besides, people like Mayor Haddock would never be where they are without guys like Kent Burgess paying them to do what they do!” I say.
More mutterings emerge from the crowd. Odd… Shouldn’t that have only instilled more faith in the people.
“Don’t you all want jobs?” I say. “We can give everybody jobs. We have tons of jobs open! We always have jobs open!”
An old man totters toward me, and stares me in the face. His dentures begins to slip out of his mouth, before he shoves them back in.
“I’ve lived most of my life in this town,” I moan. “And, I’ve never seen a Burgess do anything good for us. Nor a Haddock, for that matter.”
A wheeze builds in my throat. A cough pumps through my lungs. I lean against the wall and try catching my breath. Why does everything have to be so tiring these days?

All these young people are staring me in the face. They look at me like I’m some apparition. Maybe they’re not wrong. In part, I wonder where they all came from. Though, part of me wonders where I’ve come from.
“Sure, maybe Fletcher is a nutcase,” I say. “But, nutcases and crime are all over this town. A racket is being made of it, and nothing is being done.”
Memory is so hazy. I think I know who I am. Yet, all I am is what I remember. And, there’s so much about me that I don’t remember.
So much about me that I used to be, that I’m not anymore.

“We need to stop funding these greedy moneybags! We need to follow Fletcher’s example!” I raise my cane in the air, and people give cheers. “We need to start investing more money in building graveyards, instead of big, ugly factories!”
There are moans, and disgusted glances. Funny, I thought that’d go over better. Doesn’t the chaos theorem say the city is supposed to explode in an hour?
“Please,” a woman says, rolling her eyes. “And I thought Debby Crowner was a Debby Downer…”
“Ladies and gentlemen, perhaps Kent Burgess isn’t here to support himself,” I say. “But, Mayor Haddock and his team are.”
Mayor Haddock shoots me a supportive glance — probably the first I’ve seen from him this entire campaign. He mouths something.
“Go on, Libya.”
Still hasn’t remembered my name yet, has he?

“I know for a fact that Mayor Haddock cares about each and every individual in this town,” I say. “Do we have a drug problem? A crime problem? Perhaps. But Fletcher clearly just died. We’re in the clear now, and it’s all thanks to Mayor Haddock and his police force.”
I clap my hands, and a round of applause begins. Despite my self, a smile spreads across my face. I always knew these simpletons would eat
“Sure, maybe the rich are rich,” I continue. “But, we need rich people in society! Without them, where would all the money be?”
Killer closer. Plain killer!
“Pain killer! The doctor said it was pain killer but it was drugs!”
The butterfly looks at me like I just swallowed a bottle full of jars. Why is the butterfly looking at me like that?
Is it too buttery? That must be it. I need to put it in the toaster, to fix that.
“Does anybody know where Fletcher’s toaster is?” I say. “He saved the world, by the way. Greatest man ever.”
That should be enough to help out. I start building spit in my mouth. If I build up enough, it’ll almost be like I created a spit smoothie.

“There’s a big conspiracy,” I say, through my spit. “The chaos theorem said we were all going to come here, and be blown to bits. It’s because of him, and this whole town. They want us to be stupid sloths. Or, was it cloths?”
Marvin grabs me by the shoulders and pulls me from all the talking, dancing sporks. He hisses at me. He has a snaky tongue.
Where’d he buy that?
“You’re not helping,” he says. “Just stay quiet, okay?”
The chaos theorem told me he’d say that. It told me all of this would happen. So, why does it feel so unreal?
I’m a little paperclip, holding together some origami.
I always knew that Fletcher and his friends were decent, upstanding people. It was simply in the way that they carried themselves, around my plants. Such a positive energy about them.
Oh, I hope this all pans out well.
“Anybody want any ice cream? Anybody?”
Nobody seems interested. That’s definitely new. I’ve spent countless years in this town, selling people cruddy ice cream, and nobody has ever said no.
Too many noises are going on around me. Things were much simpler, back in my bus.
Shame that Fletcher blew the thing up. Bigger shame that it might be the Mayor’s fault somehow.
Shame that the town is blowing up, too.
Ah well. Doing nothing still counts for something, doesn’t it?
Did somebody say that this whole town is about to explode?
I have a pot roast in the oven, and it won’t be done cooking for three hours, at least. Why didn’t Freddy warn me?
Great, the boss is shooting me a dirty look.
Can’t he just drop the Chef Bernardo act for one goddamn second? The mayor might’ve caused Fletcher to die, and he just wants to ignore that.
You know what, I don’t care anymore. I lift a chair, and hurl it at the mayor’s head. Screw this. Screw it all!
“Bring back Fletcher!” I shout. “Bring back Fletcher!”
Somebody just hurled a chair at Mayor Haddock’s head. Looked like one of Priest Carvel’s crackpot supporters. The mayor should really be getting out of here. Why do people always listen to the loons?
I suppose it’s time that I give Lydia a layup
I clear my throat. “People of this fine town, take a piece of advice from me, a historian. Everything that we know about our history is completely bunk!”
The people become only more agitated. A natural response, really. Hopefully they keep this up — it shows that they’re comprehending.

“If the future is infinitely definite, then the past must be finitely indefinite,” I continue. “Everything that we’re talking abut tonight? It’s all just a wash! We need to go with the flow, and look to our brave leader for guidance.”
Not even Abraham Lincoln could’ve given so fine a speech.
Granted, I’m pretty sure Abraham Lincoln was bad at giving speeches. Hell, Abraham Lincoln might’ve never existed at all. He was probably just invented as a way to sell Lincoln Logs.

So odd how my town tosses between me, and fights over me. Perhaps the chaos theorem has them getting tired of my lies. Yet, don’t they realize that I’ve been their mayor for two decades? Don’t they realize that, no matter what anything says, they’re destined to fall for me?

It’s simply how the system is designed. It’s all so intricately built so that it comes in my favor. I don’t blame them for wanting something different. But, god… Can’t they figure out that they don’t have a choice.
“Don’t eat into the hysteria, everybody,” I say. “Are there claims that I’ve been killing my opponents to shut them up? That I’m ignoring our town’s problems? Maybe…”

I readjust my suit, and give a moment to stare several people in the eye. Staring people in the eye always helps them listen to whatever you say, for whatever reason. I should probably tell my cops that — maybe they can get more false confessions from interrogations, that way.
“But, let’s just ignore that for a moment. I’m about to take our town into the stratosphere. Indeed, the president of the United States, herself, already has a package sent our way!”
My words ring throughout the room. Yet, nobody is surrounding me. They’re all surrounding Priest Carvel. Why? Why him?
I spin in a circle, letting my robes majestically flutter through the air. People are enthralled.

“Lots of words are going around,” I say. “So many words. Why do we all give so much meaning to such trivial a thing as words, though? It’s so complicated. Why can’t we just run on the spiritual plane?”
Yes, everybody is walking toward me, waiting to hear what I have to say.

“Fletcher was a man obsessed with upsetting order,” I say. “I saw him as the coming of the savior. And, staying in line with his message? We need to overthrow society! We need to wake up, become aware of our surroundings, and make this town anew! We need to remake it into the image of holiness!”
The crowd loves me. Some of them are kissing the back of my neck. My feet. Others are desperate to kiss the back of the neck and feet of those who are kissing me.

They all adore me. It’s righteous! Holy! In the face of all the chaos theorem’s predictions, Fletcher wasn’t my undoing after all. No —I have the last laugh, in the end. I get to use his name, for my own means!
“Anybody want to go out to eat?” I cry out.
I have the sudden inexplicable urge to eat some rare steak. It’ll probably be amazing.

I look over to Jack. He’s on the verge of bursting out laughing at all these pathetic people. Especially Marvin — that guy is just sitting in the middle of the room, watching the crowd flock back and forth between each other, sending insults and lies.
He could probably end it, if he wanted. He knows enough. Yet, he’s just too simpering to do so.
“You think we should lay it on them?” I say to Jack.
Yet, he’s already walking into the fray.

So many people have been fooled. They’re everywhere. Half of them are my customers, too. I’d like to think that my customers would be smarter than this — buying into a conman’s desperate last-ditch effort at relevance. Though, I live in a town of antiques. I’m standing in an antique shop. Why did I ever have such high of expectations?

“You’ve all been hoodwinked,” I shout. “I more or less know what happened to Fletcher. Maybe he’s dead. Maybe he’s alive. In any case, I know what’s important: he wasn’t some god for you people to go holding up.”
I snicker. Should I tell them it all? I guess. Might as well.

“Fletcher used to be a drug addict,” I continue. “And, me and Clair… Well, we worked for Logan Gerri, the town drug dealer. He had us keep files of everybody in town who ever bought from us. As it happens, Logan’s been needing to pay off cops, to keep them off his scent… And, he was desperate for cash. So? Me and Clair began collecting money from people who owed us, as ‘the pickpocket’. We also began catfishing people from our files, with a fake email profile.”
