Marvin is staring at me, jaw-dropped. He’s shocked, isn’t he? Poor guy.

“This is where it gets rich: Fletcher was the only one who responded to our catfish scheme. Apparently he was just that desperate for a date. Even funnier? At the same exact time, Fletcher was sniffing around town for some stupid toy of his. And, me and Clair?”
I break out laughing. It’s too much. Really. I’ve held it in for too long, too.

“We thought that Fletcher was some guy who was trying to bust us, at first. We tried offing him, not realizing he was the same ‘Stuart Fletcher’ from the emails, running the toy shop. That is, until we did… Ever since, we’ve been sending him on a wild goose chase, to nudge him back to us — so that we could get whatever money he had left. Nobody else in town seemed to be biting, today.”
Marvin stares at me, wide-eyed. He doesn’t want to believe, I can tell. Nobody around him does, either. Though, all the pieces are falling into place.
“You mean you guys didn’t steal the toy?” Marvin asked. “And the girl he’s trying to save… She wasn’t real?”

I snort, and orbit around him. I move my orbit further out into the crowd. “No,” I say. “Still have no idea what’s going on with that thing. Logan never got the money from Fletcher after chasing him, either. But, it’s all good. The chaos theorem predicted all of this. In the end, we still got what we wanted.”
“What do you mean?” asks Marvin.
I shrug. Then, I slip deep into the crowd.
I can see the horror on the faces of the Mayor, Officer Haynam, Priest Carvel, and so many others. They know I’m the pickpocket. They hate me for it.
Yet, I’ve moved too fast for them.
I’ll be gone before their shock ever has the chance to wear off.
I feel my jacket pockets. Empty.
Stupid Marvin! Why didn’t I hide the money?
I look over the crowd, in the hopes of catching where the pickpockets went. Yet, they’re gone. They have the money, and they’re never coming back. They’re just going to get away with it, aren’t they?
Fletcher was right.
My pocket vibrates. I look at my phone.
“Meet me on Mt. Bancroft.”
Oh my, god. He’s alive.
“He’s alive!” I shout. I run out the door.
Kent Burgess is sitting in the squad car, fumbling with the keys. I yank him out, and hop in.
“Sorry!” I say. “But, I have a friend to catch.”
My heart flutters. The engine thrums noisily at the night.
Time in this town is short. I’m not ready.
Though, at least I have somewhere to be.
So sad, to see him like that. At the start of today, Marvin couldn’t care less about Fletcher. Now, look at him — chasing a dream.
He’ll never be coming back. This vacuum of a town is just going to swallow him whole, for all he’s worth.
I put my arm around Margaret’s shoulder, and pull her close to me.
“Come on,” I say. “Let’s get out of Dexburg.”
The crowd is dissipating now. The hysteria has decayed. It’s finally being realized that Fletcher’s goals were just as shallow as their own.
He was never a good person. Selfishness was his primary motivator. That, and whatever felt good in the moment. If only more people could realize this about him.
In the end, none of anything he ever did is going to matter. Me and Harry — we’re going to be fine. Even when this town is in a heap, it’ll be alright.
Though, for Fletcher? For the man who always thought he was right? I only hope he learns, before he burns.

Marvin let out a heave as he reached the summit of Mt. Bancroft. He’d had to abandon his car a mile back, once the road had hit a dead end. Though, the amount of sweat he’d produced could’ve filled a river of three miles, at least. He fanned his face and unbuttoned the top few buttons of his shirt. Of all the places Fletcher chose for them to meet, it had to be here?
It was just like him. He’d always known how to push his buttons, hadn’t he?
Fletcher sat on the edge of a cleft, clutching a clump of grass.
“I’m here,” Marvin said. He waved his phone. “You texted me to come here?”
Fletcher tore some of the grass from the ground and inspected it.
“I lost the money,” said Marvin. He choked. “I lost it, Fletcher. The pickpockets took it. It’s gone.”
Fletcher shrugged. “I figured that they’d take it. It’s kind of what pickpockets do.”
“Everybody thought that you were dead!” said Marvin. “They thought that you’d been killed, in that car wreck!”
A breeze swept through, and Fletcher let it carry the blades of grass away. They fluttered down the height of the mountain. Marvin took in a deep breath, as he was struck by the magnitude.

“I thought I was dead myself for a bit, until I realized I wasn’t,” said Fletcher. “Logan Gerri definitely threw me for a loop. I managed to crawl out of the wreckage though. Logan was so disoriented after the crash that I think he had a heart attack. He never saw me leave for the mountain.”

Fletcher’s mouth hung open, as though he were about to add more. However, he was interrupted as the ground trembled. Fletcher’s eyes went to the sky, and Marvin’s followed. A streak of light had split through the darkness of the night. For once, they were no longer hearing an earthquake. They were hearing a missile; apocalypse.
“So, the pickpockets told me what happened,” said Marvin. “They were apparently part of a drug operation. And—.”

“Yeah, yeah, I get it,” said Fletcher. “I think I understand the gist of what happened. I was played. Yes — I was so desperate to feel something greater, that I didn’t want to believe it. I guess it was inevitable, really.”

Fletcher stared out over the cliff, to the town of Dexburg. It seemed so small from the summit. All the lights, which had once been so blinding, barely outshone the stars. The river, the factory, all the little shops — it was so small. He practically could’ve fit it all on one of his train tables, back in the toy shop.
“After all of this, there’s just one question that I have,” said Marvin. “Did you ever wind up finding the oil baron?”

A wry smirk formed on Fletcher’s face. He put his hand into his coat pocket and pulled out the infamous doll. Fletcher had been right to obsess over it. It was practically in mint condition. Marvin ogled at the amount of artistry that had been put into painting its stern little face — it practically took on a life of its own. Furthermore, the way that the cloth of the oil baron’s suit fit so nicely was priceless.
“I did wind up—.” Fletcher paused, reeling his arm back.
Marvin gave a shout and leapt to stop Fletcher. Though, it was too late. The oil baron shot over the mountain, hurtling toward the city.
“—finding it,” Fletcher finished.
The oil baron shrunk into the distance, before finally being swallowed by the town.
“You spent all day trying to find it… And you just tossed it?” Marvin said, dumbfounded.
“It was apparently in my other coat pocket, this whole time,” said Fletcher. “This entire chase? It’d been for nothing.”
He laughed, putting a hand on Marvin’s shoulder.
“It’s gone now,” said Marvin.
“So it is. We’ll be gone soon too, buddy. This whole dump will be gone, soon.”
“We don’t know that,” said Marvin. “We haven’t seen the chaos theorem.”

Fletcher gave a grim smile and looked to the missile. “I thought about going to take the chaos theorem again. I really did. But some things can’t change. Some things are doomed to happen, no matter what…”
Fletcher glanced at his cheap, plastic watch. “According to this, it was midnight two minutes ago.” He snickered.  “We should already be gone. Maybe this old toy watch is fast, though.”
Marvin picked up his phone. “I guess I can check what the time actually is,” he said.
“No,” shouted Fletcher. He then lowered his voice. “I’d rather not know. I’d rather…”
Marvin nodded. “Who needs to know exactly what’s going to happen?”
Marvin tossed his phone over the side of the mountain. Would it land in the same place as the oil baron? Would it land far away? Would there ever be a way to know?
“Exactly,” said Fletcher. “Who needs to know?”
They looked to the sky again. The missile was dipping toward the river, preparing to contact with Kent Burgess’ coal factory.
“So, I guess it’s over now,” said Marvin.
Fletcher nodded. “I guess so.”
“After this, do you want to come over to my antique shop and help me get things organized?” asked Marvin.
“Sure,” Fletcher said. “And then, an early breakfast after. I’ve been wondering what I’ll have for breakfast tomorrow.”
The world went up in a brilliant blaze of light.

title: The Cog and the Machine (In Progress)
paragraphs: Chapter 1: Late Nights at Work
The Cog
Some people look at me and think I'm an idiot who got extremely lucky. Like, absurdly lucky.
Others look at me and think I'm some kind of genius. Maybe a genius from some other planet.
Some look at me and hardly give a second thought. Sucks to suck.
Whatever I am, I better at least be me.
Maybe we're all right about the nature of me.
Maybe none are.
My name is Cog. The Cog. That's the name I'm most known by, anyway. It's the name I chose for myself. It's my hero name.
The name on my birth certificate is George Jetson. Nah, I'm just screwing around. Please don't sue!
Did I mention how dumb it is that I have a certification for being born? Like... It's pretty obvious people. Whatever, that's Earth for you. Not as clever as it thinks it is.

"Fuck you Fletcher, you little cocksucker weasel!" somebody wheezes. They lift my co-worker's desk chair and toss it at me. I try to leverage my instincts and dodge it, but it's too fast. The chair hits my gut and I hit the ground.

The office ceiling is above me, a smear of beige. The lights were already dimmed when I entered, but I swear the room is getting hazier. Also, that was the voice of one of the office managers: Bobbin Locke. I can already see his crazed eyes meeting mine, moments from now – a déjà vu of a moment yet to come. He better be ready to pop-and-lock.
George Fletcher is my actual name, by the way. For real. And, I have precognition. I can see snippets of the future. For real, real.
My head rings. It's warning me. Out of instinct, I roll to the left. A printer crashes where I had been laying. Close call.
I snort blood out my nose and try to catch my breath. I've already had all the snot kicked out of me, and my bones ache. I'm straining to keep awake.
“That’s Cog the cocksucker to you!” I manage.
"Aren't you up past your bedtime?" Bobbin bellows.

Gonna be honest: Bobbin shouldn't be here at this time either. The reason we're fighting is that I caught him after he broke into the office building, while I was doing a scouting mission. But I can only manage a gurgle when I try to call him out.

He drags me up from the ground, one of his hands clasped around my throat. His face is now pressed up to mine. His form is sloppy, I can still breathe through my windpipe. His breath rushes up my nostrils. It reeks of garlic.
I land a few punches against his chest, but he's already knocked away most of my strength. Plus, he's wearing bulletproof gear. Off-brand, clearly: he looks like some kind of tactical scuba diver.

He dangles my mask and goggles in front of me. He tore them off my face during a struggle when I first entered the building. I wasn't expecting anybody to be by the back entrance and he managed to catch me off guard. We've only been fighting for a few minutes, and it's clear he works out.
My eyes are burning. My vision is blurring. My mask and goggles look like a fuzzy streak of black and blue. Bobbin rubs them across my face.
"I can't believe you're the Cog," Bobbin says. "Never would've thought that was in you, Fletcher."

I try to punch him again. His grip around my throat tightens, and I choke. His breath wafts into my face again. Stupid Bobbin, and all the garlic pills he takes. I don't care about how much lab work he approves: his stink should've gotten him fired instantly.
"Gee," I sputter. I struggle to catch my breath. "Gee Bobbin, your routine is really paying off," I manage.
"Is this supposed to be some kind of joke?" Bobbin snarls.
"Yes."

Little does Bobbin know, there's a trick in my back-pocket. Literally. Bobbin was quick enough to disconnect my Fluxion-Drive from its cable to the power pack and knock it out of my hands, back when I first entered the office. But I have a spare.
I kick Bobbin in the shin. He yelps. I then wrest my neck out of Bobin's grip and unlatch my extra Fluxion-Drive from the back of my utility belt.
My hand grips its contours as naturally as it might grip a computer mouse. My thumb finds the rubber activation button I installed. It gives a crisp click as I press down.

I designed the Fluxion-Drive to work with my hand like a glove. It hums, whirring to life. Each beat moves with my heartbeat. It's an extension of me. I can already see it now: electricity bursting out its rounded tip, and into Bobbin's face.
There's a loud buzz, and a blue arc jumps through the air. The spark lands in Bobbin's eye, just as I saw in my mind's eye.
Bobbin screams. His hair stands on end.

I'm pretty sure Bobbin will be fine when we're done. At least, I think. Regardless, it's nice to watch him squirm. While the Fluxion-Drive is high-voltage, it's designed to stun. The arcs for the Fluxion-Drive run on a solid-state Tesla coil of my own design.

While I'm on the subject of the Fluxion-Drive, it has a few other party tricks I invented. Even though blood is still running out my nose, I give a smirk. I'm about to switch the Fluxion-Drive from spark mode to force mode.
I hear a fizzle. My heart skips a beat. My eyes flit from Bobbin to the Fluxion-Drive.
The wire bundles from near the tip have come loose: a solder joint sheared. Copper wire hangs loosely in the air. The rubber around the wiring glistens like a melted candle.
Crud. I didn't see this coming. Did I mention that pre-cognition has its limits?

I start running through my list of screw ups. I should've used higher-gauge wiring when making repairs yesterday. I could've made a stronger joint. I should've stress-tested my repair, instead of assuming it'd be fine.
The wiring must have gotten caught on something while Bobbin was tossing me like a chew toy.

I start scanning the room for where my communicator went. I see it in the far corner of the office with the LED blinking red. Bobbin must've knocked it away when I first entered. Thankfully, the communicator only blinks when the distress signal has been hit.

The Machine should check in at any moment. And yet, I haven't heard his voice give confirmation through the communicator. Maybe I missed the Machine's confirmation, due to the chaos. Hopefully I missed it.

I start wailing at Bobbin as best I can. He's still trying to reorient himself. He grunts as my steel-toe shoes give some damage. I unlatch my baston sticks and start using those as well. However, without my tech, I'm at a grave disadvantage.
Bobbin gives a greasy smile. The muscles in his neck flex. Then, his biceps. His hair might still be a statically charged ball of fuzz, but he is clearly regaining himself.
He grabs the tip of one of my baston sticks as I go to hit him with it.
"Nice baton," he says, plucking it from my hand.
"It's a baston," I correct, kicking him.
Christ. I sound lame.

I should be watching internet videos right now. This was supposed to just be a quick check-in – in and out. I was just supposed to be making sure nobody was stealing microchips in the night, not fighting to the death.
Where's the Machine?
The Machine
I'm falling from the sky. Also, I'm fighting a dragon.
I blink twice, just to make sure I'm not dreaming.
Yep: I'm falling from the sky while fighting a dragon.
Welcome to my world.
The air starts to warm up. I tuck my head into my chest and a burst of fire shoots just above. It smells like my barbecue.

I pull my knees up to my head. My muscles and my suit are stiff. The steel mechanisms of my power-fists pinch against my joints. I grit my teeth and make it work. The wind and sky spin around me while I hurtle through it as a cannonball.
I create a thud when I slam into the dragon's scaly flesh. It responds in a terrible roar. I manage to dig my feet into its sides, and my hands grip around some of its scales.
I raise my right hand and grip the lever to its respective power-fist. It's time to let her rip.
"Take that!" I grunt. "And you should take a breath mint while you're at it!"

There's a screeching of metal, then a thrum, as the pistons to my power-fist put themselves to work. The power ripples through the dragon's flesh as an intense vibration. Some of the vibrations recoil up through my arm and into the mountings on my shoulder. I probably should've oiled the mechanisms over the weekend.
It's alright. I can take it. I'm the most durable man alive.
I'm the Machine.

I breathe in deep, taking in the aroma of fresh biofuel. My power-fists run on a small engine mounted to my back, and the engine is singing. The dragon is writhing through the air, teetering between buildings in the city scape.

I wince as it hurtles toward the spires of the Cantor Bank. A jolt shoots through me, and I wrench the root of one of the dragon's wings. The dragon rolls to the left, the course of its flight now along the centerline of main street.
"You're gonna need to rob a bank some other day," I say. I punctuate my command with a heavy blow.

The beast responds with a whimper. It has taken me on a ride all through town, but it's starting to wear out. Its wings are pulsing at a frantic rate. It breathes heavily, but no fire comes with it. Though, before it gives its dying breaths, I have a particular destination for it in mind.

My eyes are on Everman Technologies. It's a towering steel brick, with the logo "ET" emblazoned across several stories. It's my pride and joy. It is straight ahead, and the sun is setting just above it.

I have a meeting there at 7:00. With a quick glance at the watch, I see it's two minutes from now. No worries: it should be a straight shot to the top floor, if I can just keep this stupid dragon in the sky for a little bit longer.
The dragon's snakish eyes droop. It's panting. I clamber up its spine. Once I'm near its head, I pop it in the maw.
"Stay awake," I say.
It suddenly occurs to me that I can't fly. And, if the beast dies in the air, I'm not going to have a soft landing.
Far below me a large crowd of people is gathering around. They're cheering for the spectacle. Some of them are even holding banners. I'm not sure how to feel.

It's funny: back when I was a technician, I had all kinds of people treat me as though I wasn't human. I've spent most of my life trying to get that to change, and some might say I'm the most successful man in New Vinci as a result. Yet, I'm not so sure how successful I've been. People still treat me as though I'm not human.
My phone vibrates in my pocket. I let it vibrate. A shrill voice then comes in on my earpiece.
"Hugo, where are you?"
I put the earpiece between my fingers and crush it like a grape. The board chairman is going to need to wait a minute.

The dragon is losing altitude. I yank its head back. The wind quells as the dragon tilts its wings and gains a bit of altitude. The top office to Everman Technologies looks like it's only 10 seconds away, if this dragon can just keep its head up.
No, 3 seconds.
I rock back, and a swarm of glass buzzes by my face.

I can't open my eyes, even if I'd like to see the reaction on my board's faces. The instinct to shut my eyes is too strong. There's a bunch of crashing smashing and thrashing. The dragon gives a broken roar, launching me off its back. By some miracle I land on some soft carpet.
The shattering of glass quells. I brush the bits off my clothes, struggle to my feet, and allow myself to open my eyes.

The window to my boardroom is gone, exposing the mouth of the city. The dragon hangs over the edge. Its purple scales have lost their color from a cloud of debris, and its movements are frail. It gives me a defeated look. It falls off the edge and is swallowed by New Vinci.
I stumble toward the window and look down. The dragon has left a crater in the street. Thankfully, nobody was nearby. Still, I wince. The cleaning crew is going to have a rough time tomorrow.
"Woah, woah, woah," somebody says. There is a quiver in their voice, likely brought on from my entrance. Nevertheless, they sound a little too glib. "Well, hello there."
"Hugo Everman, the man of the hour!" another voice says.

I turn around while coughing up some dust. Ned Escorgier, the board chairman, stands to my left. He straightens himself. His lips are twitching, but he manages to look up at me with a smug smile. The lenses to his glasses glint like small moons.
Boris Reade is to my right.
With a hearty laugh, I outstretch my hand and give Reade a firm handshake. He's a large shareholder and a great golfing buddy.
"Hey Reade, how are ya?" I say.
He wipes dust from his stubble and sweeps some of his hair back into place. "Doing good Everman, doing good. That was some entrance, I almost wet myself! By the way, you gonna RSVP?"
"For what?"
"I need to know if you'll make it to the golf tournament this weekend."
I nod my head and start walking toward the boardroom table. "Of course."

My seat at the head of the table is still there. Debris somehow just missed it. I look down the table and see that there are about 20 members gathered here tonight. It's my entire board. Also, while my seat is fine, my board is covered in debris.
My board's eyes are wide. Some are gazing out the window, still in shock from my entrance. However, most have already moved on. They are looking between me and Escorgier.
The air from the open window blows at my back. My shadow flanks behind me, trying to reverse the current of the air.
I take my seat. Reade takes his seat. Escorgier stays standing.
It occurs to me that I'm still wearing my super suit. The apparatus to my power-fist was mangled upon crashing into the room, and it scratches the table's mahogany.
"Have you been having fun saving the world?" Escorgier asks, with a cold timbre.
My communicator suddenly buzzes. It's Cog. Dear God, Cog. Why now?
I clear my throat.
"The Cog is calling me," I say. "I'm really sorry, but I'm going to need to take this call."
Escorgier doesn't move for a moment. His mouth thins into a mere line. "I see."
Reade gives a chortle. "Your twerp sidekick?"

"I had him doing a scouting mission regarding some quantum chips," I blurt. It is the only excuse I have. Thankfully, it's also true. "He needs me to take over for him. It's related to the business. I promise."
"That's nice," says Escorgier. "However, tonight's meeting about the quantum chip supply chain and Byrd Enterprise's impact on our market share is much more key to the business."
A hush falls over the room at the mention of Byrd Enterprises.
"Wouldn't you say?" asks Escorgier.
A fire rises through me. "You should be talking to Opal about all this, honestly. She's Chief Technical Officer. I'm sure she can sort this out, this is below my pay grade."
I get up from my chair and head toward the door. Escorgier' voice follows me.

"Yes, we've talked to Opal. If our costs keep skyrocketing like this, you'll no longer have a pay grade. I and the board have been talking a lot: we need to take another look at commercializing our biotech division."
Commercializing Everman Biotech? Never.
"You should really think twice before walking out that door."
Screw Escorgier and the stiff board. I have somewhere to be.
However, as I get closer to the door, I feel the weight of Escorgier' words drawing me back in. How much does Cog need me, really?
The Cog
I need the Machine to get here bad. Like, on a scale of 1-10, I'd say this is a 70.

Not going to lie, this Bobbin guy has me creamed. My lungs and tendons are screaming. I crawl along the floor, wondering why I haven't lost consciousness yet. I try peering into the future for fate to give me an out. And yet, it's drawing a blank.
Screw fate. There's gotta be a way.
I stop at the corner of the office and try hiding under a standing desk. Bobbin can almost certainly see me, but it's worth a shot. Maybe he's got bad eyesight.
"Get over here you little freak."
Nevermind, that sounds like 20-20 vision right there.
Bobbin bends over and tries grabbing me by shoe. I struggle and knock against the desk. A lamp falls to the ground behind me, and I grab it. Not a great weapon, but better than nothing.
I give another kick at Bobbin's hand. He staggers back.
"Give it up Fletcher," Bobbin says. "We can end this the easy way, or the hard way."

I give a gurgle of defiance. The lamp I'm holding is plugged into an electrical outlet behind me. Bobbin is at his full height in front of the standing desk. I lunge toward his feet and wrap the lamp wire between his ankles.
Bobbin gives a grunt and starts bending down to respond.
"Get over here you piece of shh– "
I yank the wire back. His feet slip. His forehead slams into the edge of the standing desk.
He crumples in front of me.
I drop my lamp. "Lights out."
Dang, I'm going to need to write that one down.
A minute passes. There are no more noises, save some shallow breathing from Bobbin. I'm pretty sure Bobbin is unconscious and that he came alone, but I just need to make sure.

Moving slowly, I grab Bobbin's wrist. His wrist is limp, but he still has a pulse, which is good. I always need to check that when people go unconscious. Next, I go to his pockets. As it happens, they're loaded. I scatter a clump of his stuff across the floor – quantum chips, quantum sensors, slips of paper. There's also a notepad. I start ruffling through the pages.
"I'm sorry Bobbin, but I'm reading your diary. I just gotta know if you have a crush on me too."
Bobbin gives a snort, and then nothing. He sent a shiver up my spine for a moment there.
As the pages flip by, I see there is an assortment of names and addresses. Also, some random notes scattered about, like "check manhole". Gross.

A lot of the addresses seem to be warehouses that are related to Byrd Enterprises and Everman Technologies. There are also some addresses that I don't recognize, usually on streets that I wish I didn't recognize. Finally, a lot of references are made to a "Mr. V", a "Mr. G", and a "Mr. T". I think I recognize that last name, at least. Mr. T would explain where Bobbin has been getting his workout tips from.

In terms of the electronics on the floor, there are some chips that I don't recognize which have the Everman logo on them. Others are from Byrd Enterprises. They look to be state-of-the-art voltage sensors. They remind me of electromyography for muscle sensors that I've worked with, as well as some sensors for brain computer interfaces. But the closer I look, there seems to be multiple purposes. These chips are much finer and more precise in their circuitry than anything that I've messed with before. I feel like I might break them just by looking at them.

I pull my phone out of my pocket and take some pictures. I also start jotting down some notes of my findings. This is the third time in the past week that an attempt was made to steal chips from Everman Technologies, and I never would've expected an attempt would happen in my own office lab. Let alone by somebody as high up in the pecking order as Bobbin. What's up with the big push?

I'm also still shocked that there are chips this advanced coming out. Did these come out of this lab? If so, how come I've never seen anything like them before? Part of me wants to take these chips back to my apartment to study them. However, there might be trackers still embedded in them, so it's better safe than sorry.

I feel a yawn coming on. It's been a long evening. I limp around the room and start collecting some of my things. I slip my mask back on and readjust the helmet's fin to be in-line with the center of my head. I reactivate my goggles.

These pictures and notes should be good enough to show the Machine tomorrow. Once I have all my stuff, I'll call the cops about the break-in on the office phone, and then head to my apartment. There are a few cat videos which are calling my name.
There's a creak, which jolts me back awake. It's from the exit. It better not be another knob.
"Hey Cog, how you doing buddy?"

The door has swung wide open, but it's still barely enough to make room for the Machine's massive frame. The dim light in the room bounces off his suit, which glows citrus orange. I know the Machine has dabbled in some bio-hacking, but it still strains the imagination how much of a giant he is.
New York has the "Big Apple" to its namesake. New Vinci has the "Big Tangerine", and he looks like a million bucks.
"I was just heading out," I say. My voice is hoarser than I'd like it to be. Hopefully he doesn't notice. "I kicked ass though. You should've been there to see it."
I look up. The Machine has jogged across the room and is somehow already in front of me. How does he do that?

"You aren't supposed to be fighting people bud, we talked about this!" the Machine says. He starts patting me down and looking me over. His eyes dart like a hawk's and he clenches his jaw. "Christ Cog. Your face. You look like you need to go to the hospital."
I shrug. "I'm fine. I promise. I've been through worse before."

"This mission was supposed to be remote! Your anonymous tip said you only needed to look through files tonight," the Machine says. His voice is gruff. "If you thought there was somebody stealing stuff from your lab, you should've told me."

I had been half-honest with the Machine. It's true that I received an anonymous tip on a forum the other night, where I was chatting with some online sleuths. I was told that I should do some ethical hacking on this lab's files to check for discrepancies in inventory. I didn't lie to the Machine about this.

However, the anonymous tip also said that there might be a break-in tonight, to steal some more chips. In my defense, I didn't have any reason to think it was a sure thing. I thought there was maybe a 20% chance at most, probably.
I think about telling the Machine this. But he's already rummaging through the room to assess damage. He's not going to buy the excuse.
"You make great gadgets Cog," the Machine says.
I nod my head and smirk. "I know."
The Machine wipes off a few desks and chairs, then straightens them.

"But you need to get your head on straight," he continues. "We can't be a duo if you're just going to lie to me. Your job is to work on tech and handle data. Occasionally, I'm okay with you scouting out a few things. But, let me repeat, you are not supposed to be fighting people. That's not your job. It's not. It's my job."
I've heard him rant a bunch of times before. It's been a little while since I've heard him go off, to be fair. Still, nothing new. I just saved the freaking day, and he doesn't even care.
"You understand where I'm coming from?" the Machine asks.
"Sure, yeah."
The Machine is standing on the other side of the room now, looking at Bobbin. The room has been cleaned up from the scuffle. It's quiet.
"He's a big one," the Machine says. "You really nailed a big one here."
I chuckle.
"Seriously," the Machine continues. "Holy hell. How?"
"A magician never tells his secrets."
"That's some sleeping spell you've put on him, that's all I gotta say."
The Machine is rummaging through some of the quantum chips now. His brow furrows, and he strokes his stubble.
"He's got my state-of the-art solid-state," he says. "How'd he get access to these? I didn't even get to see one of these until a week ago."
He puts them into the pockets of his jumper-pants. He rubs his eyes. I didn't notice until now, but the Machine looks sort of worn out.
"I know that I told you we aren't supposed to take stuff from crime scenes, but I'm making an exception tonight," the Machine says. "I can't afford to have any of this tech leak right now."

He unlatches a pair of handcuffs from a panel in the side of his body-armor. He clamps them around Bobbin's wrists. Finally, the Machine places his palm on the large white "M" logo emblazoned on his chest until it emits a flash of light and a crisp beep.
"Alright, I think that the police should've gotten my signal," the Machine says. "They'll probably be here in the next ten minutes. You want to wait until they come?"
I rest my palm on my forehead. Tonight has kicked the crud out of me. At the same time though...
"I'll talk things over with them," says the Machine. "I think I have a rough timeline of when everything took place."
I grimace. My butt is really sore.
I nod.
"Yeah, I think I should be good to head to bed for the night," I say. "I'm exhausted. Also, no hospital. I've had more than enough drama for one night."
The Machine takes a moment to look me over. Then, he chuckles and gives me a firm pat on the back.
"Alright then!" the Machine says. "To the Machine-Machine!"
He pumps a fist in the air and then charges for the door. Do I seriously need to run after him? I'm not entirely feeling it tonight.
Then again, the Machine-Machine is hard to top.

A cool breeze from the night air wafts by my face. New Vinci is abuzz with the hums of airships overhead. I glance at them as they swim through a sea of stars. I adjust my goggles to enhance my view. I can make out some nebula, in all their colors. Though, I can't keep my eyes on them for long.

The Machine-Machine is parked on the side of the street. It's a silver wedge, glinting in the starlight. It chirps at the Machine as he pops open one of its winged doors and hops in. The Machine-Machine's windows are one-way silver mirrors, so I can't see the Machine's face. But I know that he's grinning ear-to-ear.

I've reached the car and my fingers brush along the fin on its back. Tracing my way to the car's siding, I reacquaint myself with each groove and contour. The siding features iron gills which inhale the night air. The purr from a pair of jet engine lungs runs through me while the car opens its passenger door. I hop in and settle into a leather seat.

The doors lock shut, and the car goes dark. There's a flash. A holographic display envelops the void in front of me. I start reading some of the system metrics. They're off the charts, and there are caution symbols littering every corner. I look to my left to see the Machine's signature smile.
I can already feel my arms going numb while I clip in my seatbelt.
"Machine... What did you do?"

The Machine gives a loud laugh. "Hoo boy! I made a few tweaks to this baby, and you're in for a ride that's gonna feel like launching from a rocket... From inside another rocket! You're gonna feel so awake, you're gonna wonder whether you've always been half-sleeping!"
I start to protest, but my tongue suddenly jumps to the roof of my mouth. My teeth clench together. I try to move, but I'm glued to my seat.
We're flying. We're on the road, but we're flying.

I'm not sure what level of g-forces this thing is putting out, but it's a lot. Too much. Well, almost. The city streams past as a flow of neon. My eyes strain to stay in my skull and try to find something solid, but it's futile. All is fluid.
The Machine's jovial laugh fills the car. Alongside his laugh are the vocalizations of the jet-engine. The jet-engine is singing falsetto, while the wheels and the road play the instruments.
I let out a laugh of my own. This is insane. There's no way this is legal. Then again, this is New Vinci.

The jet-engines shift to a low whir. The tires squeal, and I jolt forward. The Machine jolts forward too, and I watch as his arms bend the steering wheel and dashboard out of place. As the car reaches a stop, its suspension sloshes back and forth, shifting with the immense weight of the Machine.

Finally, the car reaches equilibrium. I can still hear recoiling from the suspension and the holographic display is flipping through an array of error messages. But I'm too disoriented to question anything. My apartment is just outside the window: a brick hole in the wall, 68 ½.
"Well, that settles it," the Machine says, "I need a safer seatbelt."
I nod, still in a daze. "Uh-huh."
I shake my head, to try to wake myself up a bit. "That was definitely insane."
"I know right?" the Machine says.
Smiling, I open the door. I head toward my apartment. Maybe one of my neighbors will see me enter with my suit on, but I'm honestly too tired to care.
"Have a good night Cog!"
"You too!" I say. "Always great working with you!"
The Machine gives a firm nod.
"Also, Cog!" the Machine says, his voice gruff.
I look back. "Yeah?"
"Don't take any of this too seriously," he says. He gestures at his costume and smiles. "Relax. Have fun."
He drives off.
Being a hero is one of the most exhilarating things ever. It's also one of the most exhausting. It's time for me to doze off.
Chapter 2: Project Mismanagement
The Machine
"In due time... All in due time..."
I grunt. I sigh.
I steadily push a needle into my bicep. Part of me always feels guilty when I do this. It feels like I'm taking steroids or something. Am I cheating in some way?
"You say that a lot," Opal Winslow says, tapping her foot. "Look Hugo: you might be able to borrow time for now, but eventually the loan will need to be paid back."
I groan. The orange liquid has gone in, and I pull the needle out. For once, the tip doesn't snap off while sliding through my skin. Nice: I get a break from something breaking.
Much as the needles feel like cheating, the truth is that the city needs me. There's no other choice.

I drop the needle on my iron, office desk. Then, I lean back in my chair and look around my office. There are blocky windows above me, letting in the sunshine. My walls have no windows. It's pure stainless steel. My floor is mahogany.
It hasn't occurred to me for a while but I'm still not sure why I insisted on mahogany for the flooring. It is soft wood and can barely handle all the steel furnishings that my office holds.
"I can handle it," I say. "I've got thick skin."
Opal brushes some of the hair out of her face. It's a frizz-ball. She looks like she just rolled out of bed, after having a balloon rubbed on her head. I guess it's part of her charm.
"That line might work for the commercials," Opal says, "but the banks aren't so easily swayed. You know you're not a walking commercial, right?"
I shrug. "Everything we do here is commercial."
Opal looks down at her feet. "When was the last time you did something outside of work?"

"I never have time, you know that," I say, with a forced smile. "After twenty years, this place is part of me. Work family is my only family, y'know? You might be CTO, but Everman Technologies is my brainchild. Also, I owe everything to it. I'm in too deep."
"That's a lie. You don't have to do all of this. Some things matter more than ego."
I roll my eyes. "Yeah, yeah, you've said that before..."
"I'm just saying. At a certain point, you need to ask yourself: are you more man or machine, Everman?"
Opal's eyes flit to the needle on my desk. She pats me on the back and takes it.
"You like the new needle, by the way?"
"Sure."

Opal adjusts her glasses. "The needles are titanium tipped. If you're not going to let me administer the injection, I at least needed to do what I could to keep the needles from breaking. The stuff is harder than your skin."
"You think I'm as hard as titanium?" I wink.
"Haha... So I hear... Anyway, the biotech division has really been working wonders."
I nod. "I still am not sure that it's doing enough. It enhances my biology, which is great. But, the more I use this mRNA stuff, the less I feel like me."

"Hugo: I don't know what it's going to take for you to let us go public with this, but you need to start thinking straight. The stuff works. It works better than anything else in industry, and you're using it at a level that none of us would've dreamed of a couple years back."
She has a point. I had been wearing down a few years back. When I started taking the mRNA treatment, it gave me a new way to do superhero stuff. The treatment has only enhanced me from there. But...
"The mission isn't done yet," I say. "The stuff is good. I feel privileged to use it in the way that I have. But, with each batch, we still haven't achieved the main goal: curing cancer."
"What kind of excuse is that?"

"This treatment is supposed to be used to cure people. Not enhance them. If I take it to market, it'll be a complete reversal of my ethics. I've seen the legislation the board and my lawyers have cooked up, and I won't stand for it! Changing genetic makeup... People can't just treat it like a makeup product!"
There's an anger churning in my chest. I try to keep myself cool and take deep breaths. Due to the stress, I have to take deep breaths more often these days.

"Everman Technologies is hemorrhaging cash!" Opal says. "Look... Last week, when you said you wanted to donate billions of dollars from your ET stock to charity, I helped you. I told you it was a bad idea, and it was, but I helped you. And now your options are limited. Millionaires don't have the same leverage as billionaires."
"Billion, million, zillion... It's all zeroes Opal. I'm still the same old me."
I only partly believe this. My movement of money was processed this weekend. ET stock already hasn't been doing great and watching ET stock crash harder than it ever has this morning has been rough.
Opal huffs. "The supply chain is not your friend right now, and neither is your board!"
I shrug. "This mRNA stuff is a company tax write-off. Plus, the company gets good press with me as one of the guinea pigs. It's more than paying for itself. Again, I refuse to compromise my ethics."

"No, you don't get it. This isn't about tax write-offs or charity drives anymore, this is about lifting your stock before it falls through the floor. Also, ethics?! Are you for real!? You're enhanced beyond the entire known animal kingdom, and you're not sharing this with anybody else! Just listen to yourself! Think of how many lives you could improve, and you're just sitting on it!"

"Look, I had to do this. My machines can do a lot of the heavy lifting against space monsters, crime lords, and all. But I was nearly beat out of commission a few years ago. And think about how many people I've saved since then. The world has benefitted greatly from me using this stuff, even if I take a risk by taking it. And... I don't know if the world can handle the burden of this technology forced upon it. They didn't ask for this. I take it because I was in the right place at the right time. I'll stop and destroy it when my job is done."
"When is your job ever done?"
"The biotech is the exact reason I sold my stock. This stuff was supposed to cure cancer, not make people superhuman!"
Opal catches my eyes and gives me her classic death-stare. I'm not sure why though. Was it something I said?
"Hugo!" I know that voice too well.
Peter, one of my head engineers, is standing in the doorway with an electronic. His bald head shines with a film of sweat and I can see his eyes bulging even beneath his glasses. Great, what now?
"Pete, I'm kind of in the middle of a meeting right now," I say. "Also, how'd you get in here?"
"Clearance," Peter says itching his beard. "Technically, we were supposed to be in a meeting an hour ago. This was set last week. Did you not see the message?"
I did see the message. But also, I forgot. I probably shouldn't tell him that.
He drops the electronic onto my desk.
"We saw the magic smoke come up again," Peter says.

I inspect the electronic and turn it over. It's one of the motor controllers for our latest robots. Some of the enamel appears to have melted off the inductors, as well as from the copper leads going into the controller.
"Odd. This motor controller looks like it should work," I say.
"It does," says Peter. "That's one of the ones that survived. The other robots let off the magic smoke while in flight, then crashed and burned."
I raise an eyebrow. "I thought you told me you fixed that problem? Didn't you guys add some more heat-sinks to these boards?"
"We did, here's version 1.2," says Peter. He drops another electronic onto the desk.
I look it over. The enamel is completely fine.
"It's clean," I say, with a nod. "So, what's the bad news?"
"The motor controllers saw damage when we didn't add the heat sinks. But: even with the heat sinks, the robots seem to be exploding."
I look the first board over. Then, the second one.
"Peter, did you guys change anything since version 1.0?" I ask.
"What do you mean?" says Peter.
"I don't remember you coming to me about version 1.0. Which means... Version 1.0 worked, correct?"
Peter looks at his feet. "Yes."
"So, what did you guys change?"
"Not much. Mainly software," Peter says.
I shoot a glare. He's lying, I can tell.

Peter clears his throat. "We added the new quantum chips to help with predictive control. However that shouldn't have done anything. We cycle-tested them a ton and also tested the behavior in a virtual machine, before putting them in the bots."
I nod again. I give a smug grin. "It's the quantum chips," I say.
"That doesn't make any sense!" says Peter. "In all the robots that crashed and exploded, the motor controllers that we managed to salvage are completely burned up."
I place a hand on Peter's shoulder. "Peter: think."

"Look man, our team has been thinking," Peter says. "I understand our deadline is this month, and that you gave us top priority for a reason. We thought about the quantum chips, there's nothing wrong with them. We've also been working around the clock 24/7, and we're certain that something is going wrong with the motor controllers."
I adjust the boards on the table so that they are neatly side-by-side. "Opal, come here. Take a look at this."
Opal reluctantly walks over. She's been sitting in a corner of the room, watching while on mute. I'm still having trouble figuring out whether she's ticked at me, or just has a tick.
"Hugo, you know I know nothing about this," she says.
"You don't need to know anything," I say. "You can know less than that, and still sort this out, I swear."
I can smell the sweat beading down Peter's forehead. His face is red. I glance at Opal, and she rolls her eyes at me. Why isn't anybody impressed? Whatever, they will be.

"One of the robots has a board that melted a little bit, due to overheating. Also: we know that the robot using this slightly melted board worked," I say. I point to its board. "Also, we know that, even if we add heat sinks, some robots still won't work. Finally, we also know that we recently added a new quantum logic board to help with predictive control, which might be messing with things."
"Hugo, what are we doing here?" Opal says. "You're not an expert on this, listen to what Peter has to say."
Peter's hands flail at the air. "Yes, listen! Every time that the bots crashed, the motor controllers were burned up!"

It's my turn to roll my eyes. "If the robot exploded, it doesn't count. The controllers are probably burning up after the explosion. Do you guys have the motor controllers situated close to the battery pack?"
Peter squints at me. Then, at the boards. He picks the slightly damaged board up, and then looks at me.
"The robot that was using this board was working," he says. He squints deeper. "You have a point. We need to take a closer look at what might be going wrong with the new chips."
I fold my arms and give a chuckle. "Happy to help. All in a day's work!"
There's a warmth in my chest, but Peter still seems cold. "You have any idea what could be wrong with our quantum chips?" he asks. "Because, that's still a pretty big issue."
I rub my temples. "With everything going wrong these days, it almost feels like corporate sabotage."
"That doesn't make any sense, let alone sort this out," says Peter.
Gah, why doesn't anybody want to listen to me? I pause for a moment, pretending to think really hard. "I got nothing. I guess that's what I pay you for."
"It would've been nice if you'd taken any of my meetings over the past week," Peter says. "We could've sorted it out."
"I've been busy with a million other problems," I say.

"Not as busy as you're going to be today," says Peter. He shuffles to the door. As he opens the door, the chattering of a crowd spills into my office. Another person walks in. It's Susan. She's holding a giant hunk of metal.
She drops the hunk of metal on my floor. Not the floor! I'm about to yell, but she interrupts.
"Some line out there," Susan says.

A line? I walk toward my office door and look down the hall. Normally, my hall is a series of rectangular steel arches, linked together through glass paneling. However, today there's a mass of people clogging it up.
"Why is there a line?" I ask.
"Respectfully sir, you restructured the company's org chart so that all senior managers have to report through you," Opal says.
"I did not!" I protest.
Opal pulls her phone out of her pocket, then shoves it in my face. I read an email. As it happens, I stated that all senior managers are my direct reports... Apparently. Whod've thunk?
Also, I sent the email last night at 1AM.
Damn it.

"I was drinking with Boris last night, after a golf match," I say. I try making my voice deeper, to seem more commanding. Oldest trick in the book, but I'm not sure if it's working this time. "You guys weren't supposed to take anything I sent at those hours seriously."
Opal brushes some dust off her coat and forces a smile.
"Trust me," she says, looking me in the eye. She pauses. "Nobody is taking anything you say seriously."
She walks out of the office and disappears into the mass of people.
I'm totally screwed.
The Cog
"Well, well, well... Hello there!"
My head jolts up from my workbench. Crud! I can feel my heart racing. I'm not sure what's happening, but my sixth sense tells me that I need to act fast.
My hand reaches to my pocket for where my Fluxion-Drive is. But, when I go to grab it, it's not there.
Double crud.
"What's wrong with your face?"
Found it. It was in the back pocket. My finger is just about to trigger the Fluxion-Drive when I stop myself. I get a snippet of a potential future.
"Zapped Lin," I murmur. I shake my head out of my daze. "Err, slapped, sorry. I was slapped in the face pretty good during martial arts practice."

I look over, and Lindy Earhart is standing next to my workbench. Her emerald eyes go downward and are obscured by a sweeping of blond hair. There's a tinge of red on her cheeks, which are flecked with freckles. She's fiddling with the soldering iron.
"Hey, I was using that," I say.
"I've been sitting here for ten minutes," Lin says. "You haven't moved a muscle."
"I'm sore," I say, gesturing back to my face. "Can you blame me?"
Lin squints at my face for a moment. "You okay?"
I just nod. "Yep, yep. Was rough, but a fun weekend. Just finishing up some stuff from last Friday. How about you?"
"I'm fine," Lin says. She gives a quick smile, then becomes stern. "Also, Dr. Skully: he mentioned you're behind on your test data. That true?"

I shrug. "He's having me design circuits for him too. Also, there are all these company meetings, training modules, and seminars... Also, I need to fabricate components for another one of his dumb robots. Only so much time in a workday."
"You don't like Hand-E?" Lin asks.
I feel my face going red. Not sure why. I blow a raspberry and start shuffling around the workbench. My printed circuit boards are supposed to be here. And yet, an irksome premonition comes over me.
I'm pretty sure that I left the PCBs at my desk.
"Err, gotta go," I say. I whirl from my spinning chair and toward the door of the lab. I notice a few jumper wires that attached to my hoodie during my impromptu nap, and I start brushing them off.
"Forgot your PCB at your desk again?" Lin asks.
The exit is just ahead. I nod without looking back.
"You're not going to find it without me," Lin says.
I look back. Lin holds one of my PCBs in the air.
"Sweet," I say, "you're awesome."
I run over and try to grab at it. She pulls it away.
"Hey, give it!" I shout. I hear my voice crack. Great.
I laugh. She laughs back. We're now standing in the middle of the lab staring each other in the eyes. I wait for her to flinch – to give me some kind of opening.
"Make a move," she says, dangling the PCB near my face.
I grab at it again, but she's already running away.
This is absurd. Absolutely absurd. And yet, I find myself chasing after her, running in circles by my workbench.
Finally, the PCB slips from her hand. Or maybe she drops it on purpose. I'm not sure.
I stoop to pick it up. Grabbing one of my cloths, I start cleaning the dust off the board.
"How has your week been, by the way?" I ask.
"Pretty good," says Lin. "I submitted my latest report. Dr. Skully had a bunch of notes. Half as many as last time though. I'm calling that a win."
I nod. "This for the new control scheme?"
She nods back. "I showed it to Ethan, and he wasn't able to tell the difference between teleoperation mode and autonomous mode. It's that good now!"
I raise an eyebrow. "You didn't show me?"
Lin shrugs. "I thought you were busy."
My eyes dart.
"It's fine," she says. "I have a lot of work outside of work too."
I need to change the subject. "You didn't even show Bobbin?" I give a chuckle. Pretty convincing, I must say. "Gonna be honest: pretty sure he'd be hurt if he knew you didn't show him."
Lin grins. "Yeah, where is Bobbin anyway? I heard he got arrested!"
"Yeah! I heard he was doing cocaine in the bathroom."
"Um... I did not hear that."
"Trust me, I know Bobbin. If he's not on cocaine, it must be something a lot stronger."
Lin gives an awkward smile. "I'll take your word for it."
She looks at me again. Her eyes scan the bruises on my face.
"I heard the Machine and his sidekick Cog were here the other night as well," she says. "The Machine and Cog – here. Crazy, right?"
"Yep. Definitely crazy."

I put my hands in my pockets, and try shoving the Fluxion-Drive deeper in. I double check the power switch and whether the cable to the power pack is disconnected, to make sure it's turned off. Suddenly, there's a loud buzz.
The alarm.
I check my phone. I and Lin are about to miss our meeting with Dr. Skully.
"We better get a move on," I say, "Dr. Skully is going to tear his hair out again if we're not there."
Lin is already halfway out the door.
"Also: last time I was late, I swear that he left spit on my EMG sensors," I say, calling after her.

We start jogging through the lab, toward the conference room. If Dr. Skully saw us, he'd probably be squawking about how we need to be walking. That said, knowing Dr. Skully, he's probably been in the conference room setting up for the past half hour.

We're in the lab's invention center, and it's quite the wonderland. At the very least, it beats the damp offices that are kept floors and floors below. Sunlight spills in from an expansive sunroof overhead. Around me is an open eggshell white floor. Various glass lab benches are scattered about, with tools, papers, and electronic devices mounded atop.
Some of the devices in the invention center are next generation technologies: cutting lasers, electrical generators, robots... Also, more robots.
Other devices are entirely novel and do things that I couldn't describe if I tried.
Did I mention robots?

Some of the top talent works here and each lab member is assigned a variety of different projects. The guiding philosophy is cross-pollination between research groups. Everybody can see what everybody else is working on. Ideas from a small project are easily able to jump to large projects.
"Hey George!" somebody calls after me. I think it was Jack.
There's a flash, and I blink. Definitely an array of high-powered LEDs. Definitely Jack.
"Turn that down, will ya," I say after him.
"Turn down the speed, and I will," he says back.

I can't slow down. I've already lost Lin. Gotta rush through this. I dodge and weave between various scientists and engineers as they move about the lab. I catch a few glares, and I swear that somebody wheels a giant Van De Graaff generator right into my path just to screw with me. I close my eyes to get a clear picture of what I want.
I lurch out of the way of a person hauling a large glass cathode ray tube, managing to narrowly avoid knocking into them. Pre-cognition, working at full ignition.
"Watch it!"

I've already found my way through another wall of people. The conference center is just ahead. It's a glass cube with walls that extend to the ceiling and entrances to different rooms at each corner. I go to the corner entrance on my left.

Trying to slow myself down, I hear my shoes squeal against the ground and feel my legs clench. My body bumps against the entrance. It's fine, the door's silicone layers dampen the impact. I squint to try to see into the meeting room. It's blurry in there, but I don't think anybody noticed.
I place my thumb on a pad to the left. There's a chirp and the door is swallowed into the floor. As I step into the room, there's a whoosh of the door flying back into place.
"Efficiency and productivity is key to our future in this lab!" Dr. Skully says, in a commanding tenor.

I shudder, then start shuffling to a back corner of the room. Dr. Skully is still droning on, so I don't think he noticed me. The holo-pyramid at the front of the room features a display with a bunch of charts. The word "efficiency" is highlighted at the top of the display in bold comic-sans. Blech.
I have no clue what the graphs mean, and I somehow doubt that anybody in the room does. My eyes look for Lin, but I can't find her.
Settling down into my chair I take in deep breaths and check the clock. 10:01. Only 1 minute late this time. Not too shabby.
"Hey, George," Ethan says, whispering into my ear. "You were supposed to be here at 9 to help set up. What happened?"
Ok, 1 hour late. My face feels hot. It completely slipped my mind.
"It's fine," Ethan says. "I got Lin to help me carry in the bot. Also, what happened to your face?"
My arms swing in a half-hearted karate chop.
"MMA man," I say. "MMA."
Ethan snorts. "You'd think you'd be getting the hang of it at this point."
"It's fine. My sparring partners gotta leave their mark on me one way or another, right?"
"Right..."
Ethan straightens up, his eyes now to the front. Dr. Skully is really getting into his lecture.

"There are a few things I've been seeing in this lab which I am not happy with," Dr. Skully says, waving his laser pointer around like a wand. "First off: too many people aren't turning the machines off. Somebody left the vacuum pumps on for the particle accelerator, for example."
He shoots a glare somewhere into the audience. Not at me, thankfully. I lost accelerator access awhile ago.

"Leaving the equipment on for extended periods can lead to a total shutdown of the accelerator," Dr. Skully continues. "We run expensive experiments in the accelerator. Losing the accelerator for an hour costs Everman Technologies a million dollars. So, unless you want job cuts, cut the power and... Double. Check."
He slaps his pointer into his palm for emphasis.
I hold back a smirk. His wordplay with "cut" is smooth. I need to keep a mental note of that.
Dr. Skully swipes his hand, and the holo-pyramid moves to the next slide. 3D models of shelves throughout the lab appear.

Dr. Skully clears his throat. "In terms of inventory, some of the technicians have also noticed issues there. Key resources and equipment keep disappearing, without any account of it. While it's fine to use things as needed: usage of lab inventory needs to be submitted as a request in the virtual catalog. We can't have people stealing from the lab."

I shift in my seat. Rarely ever do I submit requests for the inventory I use. To be honest, I've only ever been vaguely familiar with the virtual catalog, and have never used it. I look around the room to gauge the mood. Some people are scratching their heads. Others are unphased. Many have their brows furrowed in concern.
My stomach is churning.
"These slight errors ultimately cost the lab a lot," Dr. Skully says. "So, I'm going to play everybody a quick video here to give a sense of what I'm talking about."

Dr. Skully swipes his hand again and a video begins playing. The holo-pyramid has automatically mapped the video to 3D space, so the people in the video almost look like they're here. However, they are dressed in clothes that look like they're from the 90s. Their equipment looks even older than that.
"Yo Francis," somebody in the video says. "You're wasting the rubber gloves. Also, the alcohol wipes. It doesn't fly with me."
I yawn. A cost-cutting video. The characters go through the motions, and I keep thinking of my bed. It doesn't help that I didn't get to finish my nap at my workbench. My eyelids strain to stay open.
Ethan bumps into me. His body is stiff, and his eyes are wide.
"You nervous?" I whisper to him.

He forces a shrug where his shoulders barely lift. Classic Ethan. He gets nervous easily. He really cares about doing a good job and receiving good scores on his reports. The annoying thing is that he pretty much always nails it.
Maybe it's not fully annoying. The fact that Ethan is my friend probably helps my job reviews out, by association. Dr. Skully isn't exactly the biggest fan of my work.
"Who directed this thing?" Ethan asks. He squints, then readjusts his glasses.
"Kubrick," I say. I cross my arms and give a firm nod.
Ethan chuckles, then sweeps a mix of sweat and hair out of his face.
The video on the holo-pyramid ends, with a long line of credits. I attempt to get a count of the producers, but quickly lose track.

Dr. Skully makes an attempt at fielding questions from the audience. However, everybody is speechless. A pause hangs in the room for a few seconds longer than it should. I've never understood why Dr. Skully thinks people will have questions.
"Ok then, I guess we can move on," says Dr. Skully.
He quickly swipes through some slides with metrics and bullet points. There must've been another lecture that he had prepared – probably passed down from corporate. I guess he isn't into it today.
Ethan bumps into me again. He's shivering. It's not cold here though. In fact, this glass greenhouse traps a lot of heat.
"Alright, spotlight time," Dr. Skully says. "Every few months, our research groups manage to put out work that is quite the breakthrough. Lin Earheart and Ethan Ackers, come on up here."

Dr. Skully gives a rare grin which spreads into the scar on the left side of his face. Somehow, when I look at Dr. Skully smiling, I feel awkward. How is it that Lin and Ethan made so much progress together without me knowing?
Ethan stands up and gives a nervous wave to the crowd. I know I should give him a word of encouragement, but suddenly I'm feeling nervous too. There's no sign of Lin, and I didn't ever see her enter.
Where is Lin?
The Machine
"Everybody, calm down and quiet down!" I yell.

A turbulent rumble of voices settles to a murmur. The mass of people become still. Taking a deep breath, I try to reset myself. The hands of my mechanical watch are only a few hours through Monday and it already feels like this has been a long week.

I'm looking down from a balcony in the hall. My balcony is spherical mesh of stainless steel and doubles as a Faraday cage. There's also a sphere of noise cancellers surrounding the cage. The cage connects to a gigantic dumbwaiter in my office, which I use to come here and decompress from a long day interfacing with technology. Today though, the struggle is not so much technology as it is people. The people below remind me of the random static on an old TV.

I close my eyes for a moment, then reopen them. I try to count all the faces that I know. As my eyes make it down the hall, I stop myself. I know most of them. I even know their families. This company has been my labor of love for the past two decades, and I can't help but feel the love right now.
That said: it's time for some tough love. They're going to hate me for what I have to say. Oh well. I want to be remembered positively, but I can't let being remembered make me forget who I am.
"We are looking at the most intense period in our company's history," I say. "Our corporate board of directors is trying to take control of us. They want to take control of our company."
Gotta keep my head held high. Gotta project confidence.

"Productivity and efficiency is going to be key, going forward! We have major deliverables coming up in terms of the intersection between quantum computing and robotics applications. Due to geopolitics, a lot of the board is disappointed in our decision to keep going this direction. But, screw the board. If any of the board is listening right now: sorry to disappoint, but we are about to nail our upcoming unveil!"
I let out a hurrah. The room hurrahs with me. I clear my throat. Only a little bit until the hurrahs turn into haranguing.

"It's true that we are facing critical issues in supply chain and production infrastructure. It's also true that previous prototypes have lagged behind some of our competition, like Byrd Enterprises. And yes, it's true that the board has had me overleveraged for the past year. But I promise: while many think this tech is a scam, it works. This is why I sold my entire stake in Everman Enterprises this weekend. I'm in the process of transferring these funds and my Everman Biotech contracts to some nonprofit organizations that I helped start. I believe this is the only way I can ensure this technology is used to fulfill the vision our team shares."
I smile as I look around me. Regardless of how things go, this is an incredible group of people.

"While there are lots of rumors right now, I won't be leaving ET for competing companies. Firstly: my contract won't allow me to leave for another company, unless the board fires me," I laugh. About half of the team laughs with me. The other half has eyes like saucers. "Also, I will be dedicating more time than ever to direct sub-teams in the company. This is why you are all now reporting directly to me. I gotta keep a tight leash."
My chest feels tight. The room is starting to shift around. It's time for me to say the hard thing.

"I know that a lot of people have a lot of their savings tied up in ET stock. A lot of people are also wondering about job security. To those people: you're just going to need to be patient. Like I said: this is an intense time, and it might be like this for a while. But, even if ET goes bankrupt, I promise we'll get through this. If you're a person who does good work, your work is safe with me. And if you're not... Brace yourself."
My voice echoes through the hall. It sounds angry. It sounds harsh. I can smell the discontent in the air.
It had to be said. This feels right.
A few burbles of questions rise to my cage. I don't answer them and stare into space. The chain reaction has begun. Questions continue to bubble up, until the air in the room is sloshing with voices.

I turn around and enter my dumbwaiter. I was only half awake this weekend and haven't been getting enough sleep. If my decisions are bad, that's my excuse. This all feels like a dream. A deep truth is this: there's never enough time to do it all.
I hit a red button on my dumbwaiter. I don't want to go back to my office. I want to go to the machine shop. Anywhere is better than here.
I open my phone and am hit by another wave of questions and reports. So many things are behind or going wrong. We haven't even purchased the new jet engines yet. What is that about?
Squinting, I turn down the brightness on my phone. It's too bright.

Navigating through a wall of apps, I go ahead and activate my machine intelligence, Aardvark. Having studied it closely for the past year, it has only been getting better. It is effectively an extension of me and is trained on everything I've ever written or interacted with at the office. It's even trained on things that I do outside the office. It should be able to handle this deluge of emails and will send me back anything that seems urgent. Today is going to be a real test of how good it can do.

Glancing at some charts, it looks like it has already been able to gauge performance on various people and projects. I select the filter button. Hopefully I can start cleaning up some of the projects which are not getting us anywhere.

Aardvark is one of the reasons why I think I might be able to manage all these people in the company. I wouldn't have been able to do this until the past few weeks. Thankfully, I'm getting it just as I need it. Managing this large team is going to be rough, but Aardvark's raw compute and reasoning is there. Successful management is merely a matter of whether I can keep my executive functioning up and running.

The dumbwaiter vibrates and shifts around me. On instinct, I place my hand on the wall to stabilize myself, only to feel the dumbwaiter rock about. My hand puts a dent in the wall. The dumbwaiter crashes into the ground and grinds to a halt. Great. It took my team a week to install this thing, and now it needs to be replaced.
I let out a huff, then feel a rush of air hit my face. The dumbwaiter door has opened. I exit the dumbwaiter to enter the machine shop.

There is a groan from high overhead. I look up to see the cables of the dumbwaiter tangled with the cables that suspend an old rocket of mine: the Ricochet. I used the Ricochet to travel around New Vinci, once upon a time.
I give a second look at the tangled cables. Shoot. A proper chute might be needed for the dumbwaiter after all.

I give a firm pat on the hood of the Machine-Machine as I walk past her. I have yet to fix the damage made to the cabin the other night, but the polished exterior glints as bright as ever in the cool glow of my machine shop.
At the back are my machinists, Rudy and Julian. Half the time, they're great. The other half of the time, they're slackers. I'm not sure which I'm going to get today.
"How do you do Everman?" Rudy says. He turns from his workbench and gives a wave. Julian is right by him, working on the drill press.
The welding equipment is in the back corner, untouched from when I saw it last. Nobody has used it today.
"Doing good, you guys making progress?" I ask. "I need the suit and power-fists working at 100% by this Friday, for when I make the announcement."

"We aren't focused on the suit right now," says Rudy. "We actually have been needing to manufacture some replacement parts for the bots upstairs. Apparently, they've been having a ton of issues and are quickly working through their fleet. We're not going to have a lot of time to repair your suit."
Rudy grabs a greasy rag from his bench and wipes his forehead with it.
He puts the rag back. I furrow my brow.

"We have 3 production facilities in this building, and this machine shop is only for prototype projects," I say. "That's what I pay you for. Also, I booked you guys for this whole week. Why are you guys taking orders from upper floors?"

"Production lines are shut down for maintenance," says Rudy. He stoops over his bench and doesn't look at me. "Several of them were breaking down, and apparently maintenance has been put off due to the layoffs from a month back. We're needing to outsource repairs, and this shop is the only thing the building has got."
I put my hand on my forehead as my temples begin to throb. There's just too much coming at me, and I can hardly keep track of it all. It all feels as though some outside force is working against me.
"I know this might sound crazy, but it's starting to feel like sabotage! Somebody wants this whole place to fall apart!" I say, raising my voice. "Why wasn't I told about this?"
"We might support your tech, but we ain't tech support," says Julian. "All I know is that we were told these robots are high priority."

Rudy clears his throat. "We've been working massive overtime trying to get these parts working. Been sleeping here, and not getting much sleep either. We'll get to your stuff when we get to it. But, honestly: we need more people."
Glancing around the machine shop, I can see piles of robotic limbs and panels. Rudy and Julian look like they've been busy. But something doesn't sit right with me.

"We need quality work I say," holding up one of the robotic limbs. The aluminum is scarred and has a few screw holes that look more like tears in the metal. "We can't present our fleet with parts that look like this."

The drill press squeals to a halt. Julian knocks some scrap metal to the floor, then throws his hands up. He walks toward me, his wild hair flaring behind him. His eyes have bags under them and are bloodshot.
"Jesus, what do you want from us?" Julian says. "We're putting in everything we've got over here! We're not your slaves!"
Rudy is still working away at some metal at his workbench. So far as I can tell, he's just trying to look busy. I'll deal with him later.
I rest my hand on Julian's shoulder.

"I need my tech to work if this presentation has any shot at working," I say. "Also, I need it to work to protect the city. I don't care what anybody else tells you guys, that's the priority right now."
Julian shakes his head. "You have backup tech, and the repairs you're asking for are going to take days! We're already two days behind on the production line. There's no way that we can do both!"

"I just feel like Cog could do both," I say, holding up the shoddy robotic limb. "I don't know if you've seen the gadgets he can build for me, but they're pretty damn good. Almost as good as the stuff I get from you guys."
Julian snorts.
"Ok then, go get Cog," Julian says, his voice sharp. "Grab him and bring him here! Let's see how well he handles needing to fit ten schedules at once!"
Julian snatches the robotic arm from me.
"This is from the scrap pile by the way," he says.
"Scrap?" I ask.
"That's where we had it!"
Julian tosses the robotic arm back into the pile that I had grabbed it from.
I raise my hands to show surrender. But, Julian recoils at the sight of my arms raising. It's only when he sees that my palms are open that he relaxes a bit.
"I'm sorry," I say. "You're right. This is a lot. You guys have a lot. Keep up the good work."
Julian takes a deep breath. He shrinks back and nods. He returns to his drill press without a word. Any hint of obstinance has subsided. There's a submissive blank expression on his face.
Did I intimidate him? Or, is he just too tired to argue? Hard to say. Regardless, there's not enough time to focus on feelings right now.

I go to a back corner of the room where my steel wardrobe is kept. Undoing a latch and swinging open the doors of the wardrobe, I smile. My suits might not be in peak condition, but at least they are still intact.

There are a few rips in the chainmail of my main suit, from the battle with the dragon. The orange paint has dulled and some of the torso's armored shell is cracked. Finally, some of the augmentation mechanisms are worn down.

I could spend time trying to repair it. However, some electronics integrated into the suit are a bit beyond me. I don't want to run the risk of breaking them. My machinists double as electronics repairmen, which makes them uniquely suited for the job.
Too much is on my plate right now, as it is. The proto suit isn't that bad, is it?

The proto suit is to the left. Its architecture is obsolete. The mechanisms are passive and hydraulic powered, rather than using a mix of combustion power and battery power. Only the power fists are combustion powered by the proto suit. Also, the outer shell is a duller orange, interlacing with a black, diamond grid.
A grimace forms on my face. This presentation needs to be clockwork, and the suit's tech is a bit behind the times – even for me.
"You'll have to do," I mutter, pulling the suit from its rack. My hands brush along the shoulder-pads, removing some dust. Giving it a closer look, it might be worth giving a test drive.

I unlatch my communicator from a buckle on the back of my pants. Hopefully there's somebody who needs saving, a calamity, or some sort of villain to fight. As I swipe through the map of New Vinci, I feel a rush of adrenaline. There must be some problem.
My eyes catch a few red blips in a few locations. But, these lights are just indicating traffic stops.
Nothing is wrong. The rush fades.

My phone vibrates. Rolling my eyes, I open the phone and start scrolling. There's an ever-growing list of concerns and issues to take note of. My day is already booked with meetings that I don't remember ever setting.

There's a particular message that catches my eye: an interview offer for tonight. It's a dinner in Neon Square, during the city's tech showcase. It'll be the same night that Byrd Enterprises plans to hold its major showcase.
I smirk.
I sling my suit over my shoulder and head toward the stairs.
"I have an interview coming up that I need to start preparing for," I say. "Be sure to put the dumbwaiter into your schedule, we gotta get that fixed."
My machinists don't look up.
"Have a good one gentlemen," I say.
"Yes sir," says Rudy.
Julian doesn't say a word. I must've defeated him.
Energy brimming in my chest, I begin what should be a long jog up the stairs.
The Cog
"Beep boop," somebody says. “Hi.”
I jump in my seat, then look behind me.
It's Lin. How does she always sneak up like that? How does she always get me? I swear, it's like she just magically appears sometimes.

She's now walking toward the front of the room. Ethan is already there, messing with a tarp kept over a lumpy object. Must be his robot. They start pulling the tarp off the robot together and I squirm in my seat.
"Lin and Ethan, explain what you two have here," says Dr. Skully.

Ethan is holding his laptop up to his face and starts fiddling with his keyboard. He looks to the side, then removes the tarp. He gives a whoop like a matador and slings the tarp over his shoulder. Beneath the tarp is a pearl-white robotic arm which covers an entire table: Hand-E.
I've worked with Hand-E a few times before. Though, there's a buzz in my head. There's something different from Hand-E this time. Much different.
Ethan glances at the crowd, then his eyes return to his computer.
"We've developed an algorithm which allows a robot to mimic human movement," says Ethan.
Lin nods. "Me and Ethan started working together on this project a month back. Ethan showed me some good nonlinear machine learning approaches."
Ethan suggested to approach things nonlinearly? Pfft. Nonstarter for me. Still, I force a smile.
Lin walks toward Dr. Skully and smiles at him. I grin bigger. Is she looking at me out of the corner of her eye?

She trades a coffee cup Dr. Skully is holding for a handshake, then places the coffee cup on the table. Ethan's fingers whir as he types something out on his computer. The robotic arm moves and picks the coffee cup up.
Lin outstretches her hand. The fingers of the robot nimbly rotate the cup, until its handle is facing Lin's hand. The cup then is placed in Lin's hand. The motion is seamless and graceful. Brilliant.
Lin takes the cup, gives a thank you, and goes to drink.
Dr. Skully protests. "Hey, that's a fresh cup."
He takes the coffee cup from Lin. Coffee splatters over the cup and onto Dr. Skully's jacket. Dr. Skully frowns, then chuckles.
"Well, would you look at that?" he says. "I guess the robot knows how to hold a coffee cup better than I do."
The room laughs. I laugh along.
"Lin and Ethan, care to explain what we just saw here?" asks Dr. Skully.
"What you just saw was entirely autonomous," says Ethan.

Lin nods in agreement. "Yep. Hand-E uses a smart-camera to respond to hand gestures. It makes decisions all on its own. The latest control scheme is also able to mimic human motion. Holding coffee is not its only trick, by the way."
Lin makes a gesture to Ethan. Ethan picks the tarp from over his shoulder and hands it off to Hand-E. Hand-E grabs the tarp and begins folding it on the table.
