A hush falls over the room. My folding isn't quite as good as Hand-E's, if I'm being real. Hand-E finishes folding and places a square block of tarp to the side. It waves to the audience, before going dormant.

Lin hits a button on the table and the holo-pyramid lights up again. A video starts playing on the screen, with clips of Hand-E's various exploits. Then, the video starts going into the specifics of Hand-E's functions and overall control scheme. Lin and Ethan speak throughout the video to help explain things, and crisp graphics come up to assist their descriptions. Occasionally, the video pauses and Ethan or Lin will clarify something that the video shows.

The video ends. It was great. Thus far, this has been a far better presentation than anything I've ever put together. I rest my hand on my chin, trying to form a contemplative look – it's a move that the Machine often does when talking to people.
Dr. Skully nods. "Yes. Excellent work. You two have done a truly brilliant job."
My contemplation deepens and I nod along. Yes, yes. Truly brilliant. Nonlinear. Why yes, I was just thinking of trying that myself.
Dr. Skully doesn't seem to notice me and goes on. "To do such a great job, it must've really taken you two a lot of dedication, communication, and collaboration. Would that be correct?"
Lin and Ethan nod.
"Can you give some examples?" Dr. Skully asks.

Ethan gives an eager yes, and then starts elaborating on the amount of hours they spent on some technical glitches. Lin offers supporting examples. All the while, Dr. Skully asks clarifying questions to help smooth out their accounts.

It sounds interesting, but I'm having a hard time keeping focused. My mind is wandering to my apartment. I still need to finish repairs on the Fluxion-Drive, and it has also been awhile since I checked the ethical hacking forum for new leads.

My attention returns to the meeting when Lin borrows Ethan's laptop from him. She laughs as she moves the robot around, before handing the laptop back to Ethan. It really is surreal. The arm is just like a human, albeit smaller. How far can they take it?
"Once again, good work. Everybody, give these two a quick round of applause!" says Dr. Skully.
However, I and the room have already started applauding before Dr. Skully finishes his sentence.

Dr. Skully gives a wry smirk and begins to cover some remaining topics. There's a quick overview of some timelines, deliverables, and reports. Dr. Skully brings things to a sharp close and the room starts filing out. Lin and Ethan are cleaning the table off, but Dr. Skully swats at them. He mutters something and they head for the door.
I make my way toward the front of the room.
"Great work guys!" I say with a wave.

Lin and Ethan smile and wave back. They leave. At the front of the room, Dr. Skully is shuffling some papers from behind a podium. The robot is still at the table. I guess it's being left for maintenance to take care of.
"Hi Dr. Skully," I say.
Dr. Skully doesn't look up and keeps shuffling. I wait for a moment, and Dr. Skully finishes his shuffling. He places his papers in a briefcase and starts moving toward the door.
"Hey: Dr. Skully," I say again, raising my voice.
Dr. Skully stops and turns, looking me in the face.
My eyes dart.
"I was wondering if you got my emails?" I say, breaking the silence.
"What about?" says Dr. Skully.
"I sent in a first draft report of my work from the past month. Was wondering what you thought about it?"
Dr. Skully strokes his beard, which is a flurry of salt and pepper.
"Yes George, I read it. It was short and to the point. Going to be honest though: I don't feel like it goes into the depth that it needs. Did you read that list I sent you a few weeks ago?"
I don't want to answer that question. The list had many strange requests that were tough to find clear answers for.
"I sent you several other documents," I say. "They should have what you asked for."
"Hmm... I reread them just this morning. Speaking for myself: some of the modifications I suggested have been keeping me up at night. There are definitely some tough problems that you were handed."
Dr. Skully clears his throat.

"You don't need to do that entire workload you were sent, by the way," says Dr. Skully. "There are other people in the lab that you can have the work be assigned to. Occasionally, we each get a chance at a role in leadership. That could be you."
Dr. Skully gives a wink.
My heart flutters. I shake my head. "No, that's fine. I'll double-check your emails and see how my deliverables line up. I'll be sure to ask questions if anything doesn't make sense."
"Are you sure? Your plate seems like it's pretty full."
I force a smile and give a strong nod. Dr. Skully nods back, but he doesn't look convinced.
He makes a sudden heel-turn and goes back to the podium. "Almost forgot."
He hits a button on the podium, and the holo-pyramid resets. It begins playing default images of Everman Technologies and icons from throughout New Vinci.
The phrase, "be a hero" shows up on the pyramid. A carousel of images spins beneath the text. Most of the people featured have a background in service: firefighters, police officers, and soldiers.

As the carousel reaches its end though, the Vitruvian of Byrd Enterprises shows up: the world's richest man, smartest man, and the greatest hero in the world. His eyes are fierce, and his jaw is clenched. He's standing in his hall of paintings, his trademarked tuxedo buttoned up and his red cape flowing behind him.
Following this there's Sir Bertrand Polka, New Vinci's founder. He has a wizened and knowing look. His beard goes past his chest. He's sitting on a balcony, overlooking New Vinci's skyline.
Finally, the Machine comes up. He's wearing his latest power suit and standing with the board of directors for Everman Technologies. He has a big smile on his face.
These images play on the carousel every day. However, today, a rush flows through me.

"Slightly unrelated to work," says Dr. Skully, "a holiday weekend is coming up. I saw in the system that you haven't taken any vacation days this past year. You should consider using this opportunity to take a vacation."
I give a nod, but my eyes are still on the carousel. For some reason, I'm having trouble taking my eyes off it.
Will I ever be enough?

"Hey, are you okay?" says Dr. Skully. "Remember, we all need help sometimes. I probably am not supposed to say this, and maybe I'm just seeing things... But you haven't been quite the same since that accelerator accident."
The accident...
Oh God. No! Why did he –?
My mind beams back.

The air of cooling fans blows behind me. The chamber is dark and musty. I'm underneath the accelerator beam, using my screwdriver to fiddle with superconducting wire. I glance through shielded glass for the beam, hoping my safety goggles will pick something up. Nothing. I then take my screwdriver and start tuning one of the voltage regulators.
The screwdriver heats up. My hand jolts back and the screwdriver bursts into shards. There's a sonic boom. The shielded glass shatters overhead.
Light drenches me. I'm inside of a star.

My mind has returned me here a million times before. For better or worse, it acts as the nexus of my consciousness. Most have no memory of when they were born. I do. I am born in this accelerator blast. Anything that indicates otherwise is just illusory.
This time though, there's a strange vibration. The light begins to drain away, and Dr. Skully stands off in the distance. Odd. Hand-E is there too. Hand-E reaches out.
Hand-E grabs Dr. Skully by the throat.
"No!" I shout.
There's another flash.
I've been beamed back to the lab. Dr. Skully is fine and looks at me with intense concern. He must think I'm insane.
Good. That means I still have a few seconds.
Hand-E whips toward his neck, but I've already lunged toward the table. The table topples over just as Hand-E's fingertips grace Dr. Skully's neck. Hand-E hits the floor, snapping in half.
Dr. Skully breathes heavily. Sweat beads on his forehead. He straightens the collar to his jacket and wipes the sweat away.
"You could've just unplugged it," he says, managing a smirk.
I realize that I'm also breathing heavily. I struggle to catch my breath, then shoot him a glare.
He doesn't seem to notice and crouches down.
Gingerly, he grabs Hand-E's snapped limbs. Hand-E has powered down, any sign of life now drained from it. Dr. Skully flips it around to look into the camera. He scowls, then looks up at me.
“What was that?” he says, more to himself than to me.
“Maybe it was a glitch?” I say.
I’m not convinced. Dr. Skully doesn’t seem convinced either.
"Could’ve been,” Dr. Skully says. “But, with all the chaos going on in this place, also might’ve been some kind of breach. I’ll need to get in touch with our IT people.”
I nod. I can’t disagree with Dr. Skully. That said, the idea of Everman Technologies being hacked feels unthinkable. Who would even do such a thing?
Dr. Skully takes a deep breath, then turns to look at me. “Thanks, by the way.”
"No problem, Skully."
"Doctor."
"Right...”
He's looking me over, studying me. He tries to catch my eye – I feel him get a glimpse at my soul.
Damn. I think he likes me more than Lin right now.
Chapter 3: The Interview
The Machine

The reporter, Amanda Taft, is already by the VIP lounge’s entrance for Neon Square. She’s wearing a blue jacket and a bright green dress. Her foot gives short taps along the floor to match her short expression. Her eyes lock onto me with a squint.
We’ve conversed many times, and she’s always terse.
“10 minutes early this time,” I say, pointing at my watch. I flash a smile as her face is caught in a glare from the metallic orange of my suit.
“Finally learn the early bird gets the worm?” she asks, shielding her eyes. She adjusts a microphone clipped to her jacket.
“Sure,” I say with a shrug. “Speaking of birds, is Culver Byrd here?” I start scanning the VIP room for signs of him, only to find a few maintenance workers cleaning the room up.
“He left a few hours ago,” says Amanda.
“So, he was here...”
“Yes, for the Byrd Enterprises summer showcase. You know... The tech showcase of the year. What, you somehow didn’t hear?”
She has a point. Each summer, Byrd uses Neon Square to put on some elaborate, overdone wank.
I give a sheepish wink.
Amanda turns away. She walks through the entrance as it automatically slides open for her. A soft glow washes through, highlighting her hair with a brilliant white hue.
“Hugo?” Amanda asks.
I clear my throat.
“I heard about it, but I figured he’d be back for reruns or whatever,” I say, trying to explain myself.
Amanda gives a snort, and I begin adjusting the sleeves to my suit. “Is there a chance I’ll get a second chance to see it?”
“It’s over man,” Amanda says. “Maybe try catching his show next year or something.”
I give a chuckle. “That’s fine, our dinner should make up for that I guess.”
Her back becomes stiff and she speeds ahead without addressing me.

I look around the showcase hall. The floor, walls, and ceiling are white marble brushstrokes, which converge to a point far in the distance. Along the walls are various installations of neon origami, woven in and out of the marble. It’s like being on the inside of a giant sculpture by some 25th century Michelangelo. My only gripe would be the glass displays from the tech showcase, which obscure some of the neon installations.
I wave at some people crowded around a display for a new laundry folder, giving the classic grin I put on for photoshoots. I also pump my muscles a bit, to heighten the effect.
Taft might refuse to address me, but I refuse to be ignored. She has missed the whole point of an interview, after all: to make sure that the movers and shakers like me are heard.

Neon Square showcases are usually dominated by the whirs and beeps of state-of-the-art electronics, shown off by various tech companies throughout New Vinci. Right now though, it’s dominated by chatters and calls from a crowd of people. The crowd might be here to see the tech showcase, but now all eyes are on me. I give a grin as a group comes toward me. They hold out pamphlets from Byrd’s latest Neon Square showcase and begin begging for my autograph.
“I love the suit!” a young boy says, his eyes wide with wonder. “Going retro again?”
I laugh and nod.

The boy gives his showcase pamphlet at me. I unclip a laser pen that I have hooked to my utility belt and turn it on to lightly etch my signature onto his pamphlet. I also laser a mustache into Culver Byrd’s stupidly perfect face.
“Can you say the phrase?” the boy asks.
“Imagine it, machine it!” I say.
The crowd erupts with cheers, and I start signing a few more autographs as they’re pushed toward me.
“Imagine it, machine it! Imagine it, machine it!” the crowd begins to chant in unison.

I finish signing an autograph and begin jumping with each chant. I pump my fists into the air. In the corner of my eye, Taft is swallowed by the crowd. With a laugh, I steady myself and move through the crowd.
“Alright, settle down everybody,” I command through my jovial laugh. “I have an appointment tonight.”

The crowd parts as I push my way through, allowing me to move back to Taft. There are some dejected faces from people who had been holding out for an autograph. That said, nobody is going to tell me no.

I find Taft near a corner of the hall, studying a display kept behind glass. The display features a large metal cage with several robotic arms shooting out of it. The arms are spidery, with sharp edges and thin components.

A scientist wearing a silver jumpsuit stands in front of the display, with one of his hands resting on his chin. The logo “B.E.” for Byrd Enterprises runs along his chest. I try to read off his nametag, but it’s written in a phony cursive font which is impossible to decipher.
He’s talking about something to do with joints, which I can barely make out. I’m willing to bet Taft can barely make it out either, despite the gracious smile she’s putting on.
“I thought you were supposed to be talking to me,” I say, towering over the pair.
Taft and the scientist continue to talk.
“Uh, hello?” I say. I raise my voice, hoping they’ll somehow get the message.
Taft looks at me with a raised eyebrow. “I’m in the middle of something.”
“Yeah, an interview with me.”
“I thought you were busy with a publicity stunt,” she says with a smirk.
“Looks like you are too,” I say, gesturing at the godawful apparatus in front of us. “Like, let’s be real: that device is garbage, nobody is ever going to use that thing.”
The scientist gives a grunt of protest. “It’s for excavation,” he says. “It’s one of the most advanced excavation devices in the world.”
Taft nods in agreement. “Byrd Enterprises has put out quite the showcase this year and warrants some of my time.”

I give the device a second look. Despite Taft and the scientist projecting an aura of confidence, there is something to the excavator’s needle-thin linkages and the dominance of its operator cage which puts me off. Is a person expected to sit in the cage all day, operating this thing?
“Whatever, I get the feeling nobody will be talking about it by tomorrow,” I say. “Especially now that I’m here.”

I turn and say hi to a group of people across the hall. Despite the hall being dominated by Byrd Enterprises and some partner companies, most people are interested in the small display that Everman Technologies installed this week. It’s a little helper bot, which levitates along metal surfaces.

I never put much energy into the Everman Technologies displays since I prefer for Everman Technologies to hold an in-house showcase each summer. There’s usually no point in competing with Culver Byrd and Byrd Enterprises. So, admittedly: maybe some people are only interested in the Everman Technologies display because I’m here. However, I get the feeling that my display is a nice appetizer for the announcement I have coming up at the end of this week.
I hear Taft say thank you to the scientist before she comes to my side.
“That was super rude,” Taft says.
“I know right, why did you abandon me like that?” I retort.

Taft gives a huff and starts walking toward a corridor near the end of the hall. As I follow her, we pass by several more electronics displays and an empty soundstage. Groups of people are mostly looking at their phones and taking free merchandise that Byrd Enterprises has set out – cheap pens and portable charging devices. Those who aren’t are watching me and Taft, with their mouths agape and their eyes starstruck.

We make a turn and move toward the end of a corridor. We arrive at an armored door that features a hand scanner. Taft holds her hand out in front of it, and the door opens. Suddenly, we find ourselves on the top floor of the restaurant Chez Neon, with a balcony overlooking a mass of people below.

The restaurant is blanketed by a pulsating white glow, produced from neon tubes laced through the ceiling above. Electronic music plays along with the pulses of the neon lights. The flooring is an interactive screen, which sends out digital ripples of cool blues and greens as I walk along it. There are about a dozen tables on the VIP level, which hover over metal plates and seat various business leaders that I’ve brushed shoulders with over the years. One of the tables hosts a mayor New Vinci had a few years back. I watch a robotic waiter take his order and then move to another table.
Over the balcony is a carousel of benches and tables. A couple jumps over the balcony and onto the tables. The setup is wildly risky, but that’s how we do it in New Vinci.

Taft walks me to our table, which already has a bowl of bread and waters set out for us. We take our seats opposite each other. I try resting my hands on the table, but quickly have to pull them away. Eddy currents from the magnetic levitation has made the table extremely hot. An egg could be cooked on it.
Taft rests her microphone next to her silverware and grabs some bread. I brush some specks of dust off my armor as I wait for her to finish it.
“You sure are quiet,” I say.
“And you’re clearly not quiet enough,” says Taft, her mouth still full with some bread.
“What, am I supposed to just keep my mouth shut all the time or something?” I ask. “If I see something, I say something. It’s the hero way.”
Taft swallows and smirks. Her face flushes, her lips turning red as blood.

“Your stock has completely collapsed,” she says. “Word on the street is that your board wants you gone. Your charm might be able to keep you afloat with the average person, but a lot of the industry hates your guts right now.”
“You really need to bring that up?” I ask.
“You accepted this interview, and you really expect me not to? Honestly, any other person in your shoes would’ve chosen to stay low profile.”
“Not my style. Everman Technologies has one of the biggest announcements in its history set for the end of this week. I can’t stop for bad press.”
Taft pulls a pad and pencil from her purse and laughs. “What do you think this is, exactly?”
I furrow my brow and speak through clenched teeth. “Everman Technologies is in a tight spot right now. From the bottom of my heart: I need something to go right.”
Taft scribbles something down on her pad. “Fair enough.”
She fiddles with her bracelet and then looks me in the eye.
“You and I have a checkered history,” she says, leaning forward with her cleavage in full view.
I can’t argue with her there. I’ve seen a lot of Taft in my past. A lot more.
“I’m very familiar with your exploits,” Taft continues, “and lack thereof. But, I’m going to try putting that aside and spend tonight focusing on you, Hugo Everman. What makes Hugo tick?”
I smirk back and place my hand on my chin. “I want to change the world for the better. Ultimately, that’s why I became the Machine.”
Taft looks me in the eye again. It’s as though she’s looking for something, but also unsure whether she’s already found it. “You see yourself as an every man, Everman?”

“Yeah, definitely. I started from the bottom. Did technician work for a lot of different contractors. Then, I worked my way up. Started my own business with a lot of talented people, about 20 years back. And, here I am today.”
“You say you’re an every man. And yet, you’re a billionaire...”
“Millionaire as of Monday,” I say with a chuckle. “Keep up.”
“Ah yes, thank you for the reminder. You’re super smart, superhuman, and all-around super-duper. Deep.”
Taft makes another note on her pad.
“The saving the day thing...” she says. “That is motivated by...?”
“Saving the world has been a dream of mine since I was a kid.”
“The whole world? Ah, of course, very relatable...”

I feel my face becoming hot. “I was pushed hard when growing up. And I was always worried about being a disappointment. Also, the world disappointed me a few times. I’ve always been good at fixing things and I wondered, what if I could fix it?”
“You say you were pushed hard. How exactly?”
“Growing up was tough. We’re talking about the world pre-cyberwars, mind you. Let’s just say that space monsters aren’t the first way the universe has landed some hits on me.”
Taft lifts her microphone from the table and hits the record button.
“I’ve seen you fighting various villains on the news,” she says. “What’s your favorite battle?”

I look at my hands. “Oh man, there are more than I can count. Lobster Mobster was classic. I also had a great time fighting Professor Hurricane. That guy nearly took out all of New Vinci with his sonically induced tsunami!”
“I remember that. Bad hair day.”

“And then there were the Squid People. Remember them? They nearly took over the planet. Thankfully though, their evolutionary cycle—,” I have to stop myself, to burst into a laugh, “was — was a thousand times faster than ours – so they devolved back into squid as they took over city hall!”
I howl.
Taft rolls her eyes and clicks her pen.
“I thought the time that you saved me from Mega-Frog was pretty nice myself,” she says. “But then, if your goal is to save the world, why focus so much on New Vinci?”
“Because it’s my world. It’s a hub where artists and artisans work alongside each other,” I say. “It’s a place where science and philosophy actively intermingle. It’s singular.”
“Nice. Any inspirations?”

“Sir Bertrand Polka,” I say, pumping my fist in the air. “The Global Federation was founded in the aftermath of the World Cyberwar, and people needed a new vision for the future. Polka built New Vinci with the desire of a rebirth. I think ‘revival’ was his specific word choice.”
“I recall him saying he was after the hope of utopia.”

“You know it. Anyway, I started my company here back when the city was being built and like to think my success is due in large part to his success. Just look around us, and the world he helped create!”
Taft takes a quick glance around, then goes back to her pad.

“Some people might say that billionaires like you and Sir Bertrand Polka have only obtained their wealth by exploiting the workforce for cheap labor,” says Taft. “All at the behest of shareholders. What say you to that?”
Wow, she’s doing a poor job of pulling her punches. It suddenly occurs to me how hot and stuffy my suit is.

“I and Polka are prime examples of people who aren’t doing it for the profit,” I say. “Polka has always been a big proponent of workers’ rights. Early in my career, I spent a lot of time busting executives for poor working conditions in manufacturing facilities. Even tied a few of those executives up with some mob bosses. You should know that.”

“That was an iconic picture,” says Taft. Her eyes light up for a moment, then go dark. “Lately though... Hasn’t your company been a bit of a mess? There have been numerous reports of manufacturing facilities breaking down at Everman Technologies.”
I scratch an itch around my neck. Despite all my efforts to keep Everman Technologies running smoothly, I’m not able to refute her. It seems like everything is going wrong these days.

“Taft, just look at this city,” I say, making a broad gesture to the room. “A whole city as a public works project? People thought that Polka was crazy! And me... A stooge for shareholders? Come on! This past week clearly speaks for itself.”
Taft bites her lip and gives a begrudging nod.

“The cancer research you’re doing,” she says, “quite admirable. That said: nothing has been brought to the public. This includes any sort of research data. You’ve also taken a cavalier approach to testing, with yourself very publicly acting as a guinea pig.”
I shrug.
“That’s the cost of doing science!” I say.

“Are we all just supposed to buy that this is an ethical way to be running a business?” Taft asks, raising her voice. “You’re artificially enhancing your biology, and there is nothing keeping you in check.”
“Not business, nonprofit,” I say. “I very deliberately am keeping Everman Biotech a nonprofit endeavor. Therefore, I don’t need to do things the normal way.”
“All your money has recently gone into your nonprofits. You say that you’re just a millionaire now, but many are wondering whether you’re trying to liquidate your billions for other means.”
It’s always infuriating to hear somebody suggest that I have some sort of ulterior motive. Can’t anybody just believe that I am who I say I am?
It’s my turn to raise my voice. “This is a battle of morals, okay? Money is no object to me. I know what it’s like to have no money. I know what it’s like to have all the money.”

“But you do have billions being funneled into your nonprofits,” Taft presses. “And, they’re mostly supporting your personal hero stunts, as of right now. If your true goal is curing cancer, what does a cure for cancer even mean for somebody like you?”
My mind flits to Polka. He hasn’t been doing too great these past few years and has been stuck in the ICU for months. My eyes go misty, and I shake my head to snap myself out of it.
“I’m saving the city, I’m saving the world,” I insist. “I don’t want to go any deeper into it than that.”
Taft gives a frown but nods again.
“On that note: Culver Byrd, savior of Earth,” Taft says, savoring the words as they roll off her tongue.
My lip curls, and I hold back a snarl.
“Some would say he’s your main competitor,” she says.
“He’s my teammate,” I say. “The Vitruvian and I worked on a few different hero teams over the years, as co-leaders. Our companies have also worked together many times.”
Taft gives a thin smile. “He is the greatest hero in the world though. He’s saved the world several times at this point, at scales far beyond just New Vinci. Surely there’s some friction there.”
“No,” I say quickly.
“None? Okay. Even with his background? You started out as a technician at a small engineering contractor.”
Taft pulls a pamphlet from the event from her purse and pauses.

“Looking here, it says Byrd was a... Quant, was it?” Taft says, her eyes moving down the pamphlet. “Went to some top schools. Was employed at some large investment banking firms. Made a good deal of money at the start of his career. And, would you look at that? He’s spent much of his resources supporting research, charities, and volunteer projects. Have you ever felt as though you’ve been living in his shadow?”
I rub the back of my neck. It’s been feeling sort of tense, and I’m especially noticing it right now.

I glance at Byrd’s photo from off Taft’s pamphlet. Byrd has a massive smile on his face. His teeth are showing, including his oversized canines. His red cape flows behind him, and his tuxedo has a popped collar that helps his face stand out from the background.
The photo is cast in a marmalade glow, making Byrd look like a Greek god.
“It’s like you said: by any count, Byrd is the savior of the Earth,” I say. “I mean, how can you compete with that?”

I’m about to add something snide, but there’s a sudden blast. Taft gives a yelp and jumps from her chair. When I look up, I can’t help but jump back too. I try regaining myself and stand to my full height.

Adrenaline rushes through my veins. There is a green blob of gelatin floating in the air. Rings of a green energy pulse beneath it, allowing it to hover. A slimy appendage branches from its side, holding out a ray gun. There’s crackling from fissures that form within the gelatin, which slowly develop into a puppet-like mouth and bubbly eyes.
“I am a Murph-Zplat, from the planet Oozle!” the goopy alien gurgles. “Prepare yourself!”
The restaurant erupts in screams, and some begin jumping for the carousel. Taft pulls her hair back, pushes her chair out of the way, and holds out her microphone.
“You sound like the sort of alien who wants to destroy the Earth,” she says. “Care to comment?”

Bits of goo fall from beneath the alien and splat onto the ground. I can make out something like a brain or a ball of energy held at the center of the alien’s gelatin head. However, it’s hard to say what it is for sure.
I jump on top of the table and jut my chin in the alien’s direction. “That’s a lot of goop you goof!” I cry.
It’s not my best one-liner, but hopefully it gives something for Taft to put on a headline.

The alien aims its ray-gun at me. “Millennia ago my people sent me across the galaxy, to guard your sector of space. Recently, my alarms were triggered,” the alien says. “I have dilated my time to align with yours. There are signatures of technological anomalies in this sector of space, which threatens the stability of this planet’s development!”
I raise an eyebrow. Should I try punching this thing?
There’s another sudden blast, and the alien bursts into a puddle of goo.
“Well, that was fast,” I say with a chuckle.
I look over to Taft, to find she’s already looking at me. Her eyes are wide with horror.
“Behind you!” she shouts.
I feel something grab me from behind, then knock me to the ground.
The Cog

I’ve always believed that if I worked hard enough and did enough people would love me. If I ever failed at a project, it was just because I needed to be smarter. That, or more efficient. To feel love, I had to become a better person.
I had to be the better person.
It’s what the Machine would do.
I’m starting to think that maybe I was wrong.

I’m riding on a magnetically levitating train. I don’t feel like I’m levitating though. I feel like a lump and slouch deeper into my seat. Out the window, New Vinci flies by. Running parallel but in the opposite direction there’s another train, contained in a glass tube. Cars ride on a road paved above the tube. It’s not the best system, but it works. I listen to rumbles from a road of cars above my own train, even if I can’t see it.

New Vinci is a vast network, covered in spiring structures. Some of the architecture is gothic, featuring gargoyles, brick, and stained glass. Other structures seem to come from centuries into the future, formed of ceramic glass and synthetic marble. Systems of tubes and wires interlace the buildings. Some buildings double as pillars for trains and bridges. This tapestry is a bit unruly, but there’s comfort to it. The architecture is allowed to be whatever it needs to be, wherever it needs to be.
The train gives a whir as it begins to decelerate. I lurch forward in my seat and grip a handlebar above my head. The doors to the train whoosh open.

I enter Euclid Street and weave through a bustle of people. There are also service robots mixed in, which only serve to slow everybody down. Making my way down the street, I glance at various neon signs and peer through windows. Most of the signs mark restaurants and shops. They’re empty.
Business usually doesn’t come alive until late at night, when I’m either hard at work or fast asleep.

The ground below is made up of metal gratings. They’re covered in graffiti, which is a surreal mixture of primary colors and abstract shapes. I pass a rainbow lion that looks like it was sent through a kaleidoscope. The city often claims that it wants to clean up the graffiti, but it never does. I don’t ever want the city to clean up the graffiti either – art is part of the city’s spirit.

Above me, there are successive layers of city. The sky is a deep blue fabric, covered in patches made of metal gratings and concrete. Looking back down, the layering of city structures doesn’t stop. I squint to glance through the grating. I forget how far down the true ground-level of the city is, but I know it’s far.
I shudder, and then return my gaze to my immediate surroundings. Eyeing my apartment just ahead,
I adjust my backpack and check my pockets for my keys. I give a sigh of relief to find that my keys are still there. They usually are, but I always need to check.
As I place my key in the door lock, I give a jump. There’s a flash of my roommate, Jack, jumping at me to try to scare me. I roll my eyes, and then unlock the door.
“Boo!”
Jack jumps in front of me, blocking the walkway.
“Hi Jack, nice to see you too,” I say. I give a yawn.

I take off my backpack and place it on the table by the doorway. There’s Jack’s skeleton in the corner, giving me the death stare. I roll my shoulders and stretch my arms: home sweet home. I feel freer already.
“Man, you’re impossible to scare,” says Jack, opening the walkway and scratching his head.
He has his band shirt on and is holding one of the needles he uses to give himself tattoos.
“Some people just inherently aren’t scary,” I say, with a wry smile.
I go to the kitchen and start shuffling through the cabinets. My head is a buzzy fog, and I’m starving.
“How have things been going, by the way?” Jack asks. “You got any new gizmos or whatever that you wanna talk about?”
I shove a protein bar into my mouth and give a shrug.
“Mrmff...” I say.
Jack nods, pretending to look spellbound. I keep chewing through my protein bar and force a smile.
I already know what’s coming – no need for pre-cognition on this one, either.
“By the way,” says Jack.
Here it comes.
“My band...” he continues.
Yep.
“We need to practice for a venue we’re appearing at this weekend. We were wondering if you’d be cool with us practicing here tonight.”
Nope.
“Sure, why not?” I say. I don’t know why I always say yes when I really mean no, but I do.

Jack gives me a thumbs up and runs toward the back of the apartment where his room is at. Before I can pick a fruit out from the fridge, Jack is back with his guitar. He starts thrumming the guitar strings. It’s too late for me to go back on my word now – the countdown has started. The band will be here soon.

Jack’s band is called The Transnationals. It’s a mixture of foreign exchange students and trans students. Jack is trans, and his band’s music is not exactly subtle about it. But then, I guess that’s part of what makes it work.
Going to be honest: sometimes Jack being trans makes me feel uncomfortable. He’s tolerable enough though, which is better than I can say for a lot of past roommates.
Jack watches me as I toss wrappers into the trash bin and grab my bag from by the door. He plays a note slightly out of tune and waves to grab my attention.
“Hey, spaceman, you wanna join in and listen tonight?” Jack asks.
I shake my head but give a smile.
“No, I’ve got other things right now that are on my mind.”
Jack gives a huff. “You never want to hang out. We’re roommates man. What’s so great in your room, up on the moon?”
There’s a lump in my gut. In a lot of ways, Jack is right. However, I really am busy tonight.
“Maybe we should grab a bite to eat or something sometime,” I say.
Jack nods, but his eyes are now focused on his guitar. He resumes strumming to no tune in particular.

My mind flashes back to all the times I’ve spent regaling Jack with technical knowledge and lists of trivia. Rarely do I stop to ask him about his passions. I hold back a frown, then shuffle to my room.
Jack is an okay roommate. I might be a bad roommate.
As I unlock my bedroom door, something brushes against my leg. There’s a gentle purr. Looking down, I find my cat PB. He’s a small fluffy white ball with some brown sugared in for extra flavor.
I kneel down. “Hi there little guy,” I say. I pet the streak of brown fur along his back and can’t help but smile. There’s a warm kind of feeling PB always gives me, which is hard to explain.
“You hungry?” I ask.
PB purrs deeper, as if to say yes. I pull myself up and finish unlocking my door.

I’m greeted by strings of old Christmas lights braided around the room. I feel like it gives the room character, even if it took forever to put them up. My desk and my bed are at the back of the room. To my right, there’s a collection of various robots and gadgets I’ve toyed with over the years. My favorite robot, Bit-Bot, is among them. He’s a helper bot who can waddle around and perform assistive tasks. Normally I’d be tinkering with him, but I got home late tonight. I had to stay overtime in the lab, to get the Fluxion-Drive fixed. Truly a test of patience.
Speaking of patience, PB has taken a seat next to his food and water bowls, near the foot of my bed.
I grab a jug of water and bag of cat food from my desk and begin filling the bowls up.
“Here you go sweetheart,” I coo. I give him a few pets as he begins to dig in. He seems content.

I grab my laptop from my bag and head toward my bed when I hear the chatters of several voices and the slamming of a door. With a smirk, I activate my phone’s sound recorder and place it near my door.
The band has begun to play. The air rumbles with the clamor of drums and guitars going in and out of harmony.
“Tonight... Is the... Night!” somebody cries out in a hoarse voice.

It’s going to be a long night of this. But at least it’ll be funny to play some of it back tomorrow. I hop in my bed and begin scrolling through my laptop. I’m on the ethical hacking forum again, checking for updates. The silhouette of an owl stares at me, as an icon in the corner. Underneath it are the letters “E.H.” for ethical hacking.
Going to be honest: the content is often eh. But every once in awhile, I can find some useful information on here.

My eyes widen as I see a new chat show up in my feed. I click on the chat and am hit by an onslaught of dire information. There are several accounts reporting on accidents that have occurred throughout the city over the past few hours. Multiple office break-ins and car jackings. I glance at my communicator, which is poking out of my backpack. How come I haven’t seen anything about any of this on my communicator feeds?
As I scroll further, it looks like a lot of the issues were benign and already handled by the police.
Still, the muscles in my neck have become tense.
I scroll back to the top, and my chat icon blinks a bright green as I begin typing. Though, I’m only halfway through my sentence when the chat updates with a new message.
“Potential attack at Neon Square,” the message says, listed under the pseudonym ratcatcher.
“What kind?” I quickly type back, under the pseudonym of monkey-wrench.
The chat stalls for a minute. A bead of cold sweat forms on my forehead. The hard thumping of Jack’s band outside my room is overwhelmed by the thumping of my heartbeat.
The chat suddenly overflows with replies. I struggle to make sense of it all.
“Can confirm,” an account called Turtle-Dove says. “More attacks throughout quantum chip supply chains.”

I give a sigh of relief seeing a familiar account. I have interacted with Turtle-Dove many times, and I trust her. She always has great tips, too. I think she works in my lab, based on past information she’s managed to give. But, I’ve never been able to confirm this. Regardless, she’s extremely familiar with the R&D going on throughout New Vinci.
I ask her if she has more info, and she leaves me a frowny emoji. Dang – her replies are usually spunkier.
“That’s it?” I write. “You’re just going to leave me hanging like that?”
“That’s all I know,” she says. “Going to be honest, I’m just as confused as you right now!”
I’m about to send a crying laughing emoji when our chain is bombarded.
“This is an especially unusual guy,” ratcatcher writes. “He wants to make a scene according to my sources. Send a message to the executives who will be there for the tech summits tonight.”
I stroke my chin. Neon Square has a lot of high-profile people, and they’ve been holding a lot of tech summits recently. However, this usually comes with tight security.
“Have any authorities been alerted?” Turtle Dove writes.
There’s a pause. Then, a “yes”.
Ratcatcher drops a .zip file into the chat.
“They are armed with some bootleg electronic gear, but this software package should have everything you need to override their stuff. You just need a device with good Bluetooth connection.”

I feel my heart race as I prepare to download it, but something feels off. I glance at my laptop battery: 10%. My laptop battery drains faster than the drain on a sink – there’s no way it’ll make it before I get to Neon Square.
I check my phone: 5%.
My mind jumps to my cubicle on my office floor. I’ve left my chargers at work.
My fingers race along my keyboard.
“Battery low.”
It’s not the cleanest of excuses, but it’ll have to do.
“What? You have no other way to connect?!” ratcatcher writes. “This is life or death!”
He sounds more ticked than usual.
“I generally don’t do field work, especially when it’s dangerous,” says Turtle-Dove.
“I love when it’s dangerous,” I write, “but I need more than what you’re giving me.”
“Fine,” says ratcatcher. “Close range is also a weakness. There should be an off switch installed in the back of the attacker’s neck. Try getting as close as you can, and then disable him.”
Sounds legit.
“Also, tell nobody. Contact nobody. We need this done as securely and safely as possible, as fast as possible. I’ve already shared the same info with the authorities.”
I roll my eyes – sketchy as hell – but still write a “thanks”.
“Are you sure we shouldn’t contact anyone?” Turtle-Dove asks. “You’re not making any sense.”
I click to like her comment.

Suddenly, a stream of text pervades my screen. Dozens of accounts I’ve never seen before are spewing random nonsense. I turn off auto-refresh and blink a few times to regain my composure. I manage to filter for comments by ratcatcher, amid the barrage of noise.
“Crud,” says ratcatcher. “We’ve been hacked.”
I close my browser and shut my laptop.
Man, I didn’t even get to tell Turtle-Dove goodbye. Whatever, I’m sure she knows how I care.
I hop off my bed and grab for my communicator. I need to tell the Machine. I’m not sure what to think right now, and he always knows how to help.
A green dot is lit up on the communicator’s map display. It’s located at Neon Square. The Machine is already there.
Huh. Does he already know about the attack? Yes, of course. Of course he does. He must already be on it.
But then... Why didn’t he contact me?
I scowl and clench my fists. He needs me... He must need me. That, or he totally has no clue. I drop my communicator, without sending my message. Better safe than sorry.

My fluxion-drives are on the floor. They’re poking out of my bag, which doubles as a power pack. The fluxion-drives are a couple of bowling-pin shaped devices, with rubber grips and silver tips. I place them on my desk and start turning their dials from “inert” to “thrust force” mode. They give a swoon and glow a cool lavender at their rounded tips. I begin bumping and banging about my room, struggling to get my super-suit on. My boots are a pain in the neck, and barely budge as I yank them up my leg. Probably should’ve gotten bigger shoes to fill.

PB gives a mew as he watches. There’s a thud as I go back into a wall, before finally getting the zipper to my shirt loose. There’s a click from the zipper reaching my collar, and PB resumes lapping water from his water bowl.
I snatch my fluxion-drives from my desk and unlatch the lock to my apartment window. I give a few firm shoves and pull it open. A chilly breeze welcomes me to the city’s nightscape.

I press down on the rubber triggers to my fluxion-drives and feel them push against me. While I’ve operated them a million times, the thrust against my body still feels surreal. The force reminds me of the push and pull that can be felt by two polar magnets.

My feet are lifted slightly, so that only my toes are touching the ground. My curtains and the breeze are pushed out into the city air. I glance out the window. Why does my apartment need to be so high?
“Make sure to keep a close eye on things for me,” I say to PB.
Swallowing a lump in my throat, I shift my stance and ready myself. I jump.
To the stars.
The Machine
I roll over on the floor and look behind. There is a pale creature looming over me. I squint.

It almost looks like a man, but not quite. His forearms have been replaced with plasma blasters, and metallic talons are placed along the rim of the barrels. There is a visor where his eyes should be, grafted tightly to his face. A tube runs from out from the top of his head and appears to feed behind him. Another set of tubes seem run from the blasters and to behind.

The man is wearing a plain white t-shirt that is so tattered I can make out his ribcage from beneath. His arms and neck are awfully thin. The man opens its mouth to say something, but only drool comes out. I raise myself to a crouch and stagger back a bit. I don’t have my power-fists with me, and this guy looks a lot more decked out than the usual villain I face.
I’m missing the goop alien quite a bit.
“Hey there, I’m the Machine,” I say, raising my hands to signal peace. “I’m the protector of New Vinci. You interested in talking this out?”

The man’s jaw moves again, only for more drool to form. Lights flash along the visor on his face, and his head swivels a bit to scan the surroundings. His face then locks back onto me. The blasters crackle and it spits sparks from the barrel. Looking down the barrel, I see a fiery red glow.
I stand back up and look back to Taft.
“Call the police,” I say. “This man needs help.”

I’m not able to make out her response. The room turns to a bright red as a plasma blast that contains molten metal gets me in the shoulder. I blink several times to recover my vision, while skidding back a few feet. My knees groan. The skin along my shoulder and chest burns as the heat radiates through my suit. I glance down to see a small dent has been left in the chest armor.

My eyes jump to the levitating tables. I leap toward one and tilt it to create a makeshift shield. As a second blast reaches me, a dent forms in the table. However, I feel the heat from the blast quickly radiate away.
“You just ruined a perfect alien dinner invasion!” somebody says in a sarcastic tone.
That can only be one person: Cog.

Pulses of sound vibrate through the air. I watch as the cyborg man staggers back from an unseen force. Cog descends down from somewhere in the ceiling, his arms flailing like a rag doll. He uses his fluxion-drives to slow his descent. There’s a click as Cog flips a switch. The glow from the fluxion-drives changes from a slight purple to a greenish-blue glow. It reminds me of the aurora from the northern lights.
Cog laughs, then takes aim toward the cyborg. He starts blasting.

Cog’s blasts mostly miss, and Cog only narrowly dodges a few of the cyborg’s plasma blasts. A pulse from a fluxion-drive manages to hit the cyborg’s head. Cables flop about, and the cyborg’s metal joints screech. Lights in the cyborg’s visor flash randomly, and its legs begin to buckle.
The cyborg manages another blast of plasma, and Cog finally scampers toward me.
“I’m fine if you just want to play look out,” says Cog. “But –.”
“Look out!” I shout.

Cog ducks and a burst of plasma hurtles over his head. He scuttles along the floor, then huddles with me behind the shield of the table. The cyborg lets out a roar as he begins to regain his strength.
“Nice timing,” I say, giving Cog a playful punch in the arm.
Cog winces from beneath his mask and gives a weak smile. “It was mostly the pre-cognition,” he says. “Also, my head is very hazy right now. I’m sensing a lot of unknowns with this guy.”
“Good to know,” I say. I clear my throat. “How’d you know to come here?”
“Pre-cognition,” Cog says with a wink.
“Haha, very funny,” I say, rolling my eyes.
I pause to grab a dinner plate from off the ground.
“But seriously, how’d you know?” I continue.
I quickly look from behind the table and then toss the dinner plate into the Cyborg’s gut. The Cyborg staggers back, randomly sending blasts of energy into the air.
“Nice!” Cog says, jumping up and down.
Cog really needs a new suit. He’s wearing blue sweatpants and a frayed jacket, which are sky blue.
His logo is the letter “C”, cut out from a profile for half a gear.
His mask could also use some work. His goggles are clearly glued together from spare parts, and the large purple fin coming running out the top of his mask sticks out like a sore thumb.
Yet, I can’t help but smirk.
“You didn’t answer my question,” I say.
“It was the forum I use,” Cog says. “I got an anonymous tip. They said there’d be an attack here.
Also, I was told the attacker is weakest at close range.”
“I’ve been at close range, and felt the blast from that thing,” I say. “I’m pretty sure that’s false info.”
Cog gives a nervous chuckle. “Yeah, I’m not sure. My source was pretty sketchy.”
“Why didn’t you tell me?”

There’s another blast putting a dent in the table and forcing pushing it back. I manage enough force to keep the table in its place, but my muscles groan and my feet slide along the tile floor. Cog pokes his head from the side of the table, sends a pulse from his fluxion-drive. There’s a screech from the cyborg going on the fritz again.
“I thought there was no need,” says Cog.
“Why?” I repeat.
“I thought you already knew and were handling it without me.”
“I definitely would’ve preferred to handle this without you,” I say, in a stern tone.
Cog lowers his head, gives a sniff, and then a nod. He starts fiddling with the dials on his fluxion-drives.
I feel a sinking in my gut. Maybe I’m being too harsh. However, the people I fight are very dangerous, and Cog should know that by now. He just can’t keep shutting me out like this.
“I think I know its weakness,” says Cog.
I ignore him and pretend to scan the floor.
“You’re right, by the way,” Cog continues. “You’re going to need to handle him.”
I take a deep breath to calm myself. Cog pulls his power-pack off his back, then pushes it and his cabled fluxion-drives toward me.
“Take it,” Cog says, looking at me. I wish I could see his eyes from beneath his goggles, but I know he’s stressed from his urgent tone.

Begrudgingly, I pick the power-pack and fluxion-drives off the ground. Putting the power-pack on, I have to admit that the pearl white casing Cog recently added to the fluxion-drives are quite nice. That said, there’s a slight crack along the siding of one of the casings, and the devices are extremely small in my hands. The power-pack is also tight around my shoulders. I grip the rubber handles to the fluxion-drives and hover my thumb over the rubber trigger button. I can’t help but worry I might break it.
“I tuned their frequencies to maximize the electromagnetic pulse. You just need to get close to him and press the button,” Cog says. “I’ll keep lookout.”
“Lookout eh?” I say with a chuckle.

“There’s some kind of brain computer interface at the back of the cyborg’s neck,” Cog says, his voice stiff. “I tested sending a few electromagnetic pulses at it, and this seems to put the cyborg on the fritz. I think if you can get close to him with a good pulse, you should be able to shut him down.”
“Sounds good,” I say, tightening my grip around the fluxion-drives.
I glance from the side of the table. I have a good opening – the cyborg is shifting its attention to another table.

I charge toward the cyborg. I was hoping to be subtle, but I can hear my boots stomping against the ground. The cyborg turns and starts blasting at me. I manage to dodge a couple of the blasts, but one of the blasts gets me in the chest. It nearly knocks me over, but I manage to land on my feet. My chest burns, my chest plate is left with a large dent in it, and molten metal drips down, but I push through.

I drop the fluxion-drive in my right hand to my side, letting it hang from its cable to the power-pack. With my right hand now free, I then grip the cyborg by its left arm and try holding it back. The motors at the cyborg’s joints screech, and fight against me. I aim my left arm toward the cyborg’s head and prepare to press the trigger to the fluxion-drive.
A jolt of pain rips through my left arm as the cyborg’s talons clamp around my wrist. My fingers are jammed and work against me. With a grunt, I force them down and press the trigger.
“Sorry pal!” I say as the fluxion-drive lights the air with rapid bursts of energy.
The cyborg is twitching, and I can feel its grip weaken. Gotta give it to Cog, the fluxion-drive works like a charm.
There’s a thud at my back.
“Sorry!” Cog says sheepishly.
I glance behind. Cog tried tossing the table at the cyborg and hit me instead.
I give a scowl. Why can’t Cog see that I’m busy here?

There’s the snapping of linkages as the cyborg digs deeper into my flesh. I let out a yelp, force my arm closer to the cyborg’s head, and send more pulses from the fluxion-drive. The talons on the cyborg’s arm snap back and I watch the lights in the cyborg’s faceplate go out. Its legs buckle and I let go of its arm. There’s a clang and a snort as it collapses to the ground.

The cyborg’s skin is extremely pale and clammy, and drool oozes from their mouth. The metal interfaces have jagged welds, and the cyborg’s skin has numerous scars near where the interfaces link to the body.
What sort of person would do this to somebody?
“So, was it awesome or was it awesome?” Cog asks.

Cog comes toward me for a high five. Begrudgingly, I raise my arm and give him one. There is still blood on my arm from where the cyborg bit me, but I can deal with it later. This night has been too crazy to let my guard down.
“You should’ve warned me,” I say, showing Cog the bitemarks in my arm as I bring it down. “If I had known there would be an attack, I could’ve gotten more prepared.”
“Sorry,” Cog says, before scurrying to scoop the power-pack off my back.

I go to hand him the fluxion-drive I’ve been using. “Also, you should’ve waited before tossing that table. The table was a good shield, and the cyborg’s firepower was too strong for you to be messing around like that.”
Cog gives a huff and brushes some dust off himself.
“Okay, okay, I get it,” Cog says while putting the power-pack back on and snapping his fluxion-drives to the belt. “Was just trying to help.”
I can’t see his eyes from beneath his goggles, but he’s gritting his teeth. His movements are tense.
“Other than that, good work,” I say, with a smile.
I give Cog a pat on the back. Nevertheless, he remains tense.
“The Machine and pre-cog!” Amanda Taft says, walking toward us.
“It’s the Cog,” says Cog. “Pre-cog is just my powerset.”
“Duly noted,” Taft says. She aims her microphone toward me. “How are you holding up? That fight looked pretty rough.”
I nod and laugh. “I’ve seen a lot of evil in my day, but this was something else.”
“That wearable tech is pretty nasty,” says Taft with a quick nod. “Just to confirm, Everman Biotech hasn’t been working on anything like this, have they?”
“Absolutely not!” I say, raising my voice. “We work on robotics, we work on biotech, and we occasionally – emphasis on occasionally – offer consulting for the military. But we don’t make cyborgs.”
“But you acknowledge that this was very advanced technology.”
“The only two places I’ve ever seen tech like this are from Byrd Enterprises and some of the companies that Polka has invested in over the years.”
I pause to glance at the gash on my left arm. Blood is still oozing out, and the cut runs deep.
“But that was years and years ago,” I say, placing my hand over the wound. “I couldn’t imagine this coming from Everman Technologies. I’ve never seen cybernetics this high tech. Never.”
Taft nods. “So, how did you –?”
Cog chuckles and interrupts.
“Me,” he says. “I’m the one who saved the day!”
He gestures down to the fluxion-drives at his belt.
“I tuned the frequency to send an electromagnetic pulse through the cyborg’s brain computer interface,” says Cog.
Taft shifts her focus to Cog, aiming the microphone toward him now.
“Fancy gizmos you got there,” she says. “Did you –?”
“Yes, I designed them myself!” says Cog.
“Maybe wait for me to finish my question.”
“Sorry, it’s my pre-cognition kicking in,” says Cog.
Taft laughs. I feel my face burning and clear my throat. Taft is supposed to be talking to me.
“How did you two meet by the way?” Taft asks.
“Dating website,” says Cog. “In case you’re interested, I’m a great dinner date.”
“Right...”
I tap my foot on the ground.

“I met Cog at a talent program dinner, hosted through Everman Technologies,” I say. “He showed up there by chance, during an attack by some supervillain. I think it was... Captain Flapjack? Anyway, impressive showing, and we’ve been working together ever since.”
“See?” Cog says, outstretching his arms. “Dinner date.”
Taft gives an awkward smile and shakes her head. She then scribbles something down on her pad.
“Well, I think I have everything that I need here,” Taft says.
I cross my arms and give a wink. “I think we just about have thing settled here too.”
I press a button on my wrist, and it gives a clean chirp.
“The police should be on their way,” I continue. I glance at Cog. “You want to help me sort this out with them, and then get a ride back home?”
Cog smiles and gives a thumbs up.

Taft’s heels click against the ground as she starts walking away. She pauses to turn her head and look at me. “Machine and Cog is a cute name by the way. I always liked puns. You guys seem like you work well together.”
My face goes red. I think Cog’s does too.
Cute? But I’m the most durable man alive!
“You ever need anything, just give me a call,” I say.
Cog elbows me.
“Okay, okay, give us a call,” I say, with a chuckle.
Taft laughs, then disappears down a corridor.
“She was nice,” says Cog.
I look down to the cyborg. Much as I hate to admit it, I was lucky to have Cog show up tonight.
“Yep,” I say. “Hopefully the rest of the night can be so kind.”
A shiver goes down my spine, and goosebumps form along my arms. Only Byrd or Polka have the technology capable of building a cyborg like this.
That, or there’s something going on in my company that I don’t know about.
I’m not one to be easily spooked. But something about all of this just doesn’t sit right.
Chapter 4: Dinner With Coworkers
The Cog

My eyes burn and my goggles blur. The air is damp but warm. I smile. My fluxion-drives give a steady beat against my palms. I just got off from a long day at work, but I’m humming with delight. I’m flying on the inside of a cloud.
I glance at the clock in the top-left corner of my goggles. It’s only a quarter past five. I’ll make it back in time for Lin and Ethan. The flux from my hands can outpace the hands of time.
I laugh as I think back to the smile on Lin’s face from yesterday. I give a deep breath. Focusing my mind, I watch the seconds turn to molasses and my precognition beams me to memory.
I’m in my cubicle, on the bottom floor of Everman Technologies. A stack of papers has piled up on my desk this week, and I don’t want to look up right now.
“You called me over?” Lin asks.
My thumb flips through my papers as I try to conjure some paper-thin excuse.
“George?” says Lin.
I clear my throat and force myself to address Lin in the eye. Some invisible force tries to draw my gaze away, like a magnet. I forge ahead anyway.
I can’t take the easy way out this time.
“Yeah, I was wondering if you and Ethan would be interested in having a dinner at my apartment,” I say.
Lin smiles. There’s no other smile quite like hers.
“I’ve already talked to Ethan, and he’s up for it if you are,” I continue.
I can already see that she’s going to say yes.
Yes!

Yesterday’s memory fades, and I’m beamed back into the sky, among the clouds and gliding on a flow of force toward my apartment. I stretch my arms toward the edges of the cloudy mist. I imagine that my arms are cans of paint spray, and that this mist sprays forth from them.
When I was a kid, I wanted to touch the clouds. For some reason, I believed they were more like pillows than mist. So much for that myth.
I’ve always had an issue where my imagination will get away. Life will often get away, too. Somehow, Lin and Ethan haven’t caught on yet.
Suddenly, I hear a strange noise. It’s a buzz. It sounds like drone propellors. My ears are ringing. “Hrrgh!” a voice grunts. I feel a punch against my shoulder.
Definitely not a pillow.
I struggle against successive blows to my back from some unseen attacker, before directing my fluxion-drives to hurtle away. I choke on the stench of exhaust.
“Wow you’re exhausting!” I exclaim. “I don’t know who the heck you are or how you found me, but I’ve got better things to do! You’re gonna make me miss my dinner date!”
Okay, I shouldn’t get too excited – maybe it’s not exactly dinner date. Lin and Ethan probably would say it’s more of a coworker get-together.
Whatever, I get the feeling my attacker won’t care about the difference.

My thumbs pulse the trigger to my fluxion-drives. I try to aim blasts of force in the direction of my attacker, but I also need to stabilize myself. My fluxion-drives pound frantically, and my heart pounds with them.
As I steadily regain control, I use my elbow to rub mist off my goggles and tilt my neck upward to make my attacker out. He’s directly overhead. Also, he’s a freaky drone-man hybrid.

His eyes are covered by a dark helmet that features a visor and two ducted fans protrude from his back. Plumes of fumes spill from an engine mounted between the ducted fans. His arms are ensnared in a network of metallic linkages and jerk at the air aimlessly.

I wince as the fans generate a boom. My hair flies into my face and my body is tugged by a vortex of air. As the propellors draw closer toward me, I use my fluxion-drives to redirect myself out of the path of the vortex.
Gah! Why couldn’t my attacker have been some kind of balloon-man hybrid instead?

The muscles in my arms groan as I restabilize myself again and take another look at the propellors.  A jolt of revelation shoots through me – I’ll need to get closer to them if I have any hope of taking him out.
The clouds have begun to part, as if to confirm my revelation. Below me is the scattered house of cards that I call my city. Above is a smear of Klein blue sky.

I lunge toward the guy, use my thumbs to turn a dial on my fluxion-drives from force-mode to spark mode, and send bursts of electricity toward his face. The drone-man spins as a corkscrew, and I ran into the side of one of his ducted fans.

My thumbs desperately turn the dials to my fluxion-drives back from spark to force. My body shakes and my head throbs. I can’t let myself look down. The fluxion-drives and some nerve are the only things keeping me in the air.

I quickly attach the fluxion-drive from my right hand to a latch at the center of my belt buckle, then flip a switch to set it for automatic hover. Thrust directs downward, along my center-of-mass. If this fluxion-drive does its job well, I should stay stable while the fluxion-drive in my left hand does the real work.
My teeth chatter from gutted nerves and gusts of air, but I have to keep it together if I want get to my get-together.

With my right hand now free, I use it to grip the rim of the ducted fan. Gingerly, I bring my left arm and its fluxion-drive into the mouth of the ducted fan. As I aim for the center, the propellors rattle with a rage that shakes me to my core. My stomach churns. Sweat beads down my forehead.
I press down on the trigger.

There’s a blast and my head goes fuzzy. Carbon-fiber shrapnel tears through the air. A crack forms in my goggles as bits of shrapnel get me in the face. My muscles spasm and pangs shoot through me. Time seems to slow. My muscles freeze. I can’t move. In fact, nothing is moving – time has frozen with me.
Crud. Precognition? Not now! I can’t be doing this now! Yo, universe: I feel like I might die right here, right now.
My heart skips a beat, taking me back in time and to another memory.
I’m at a party of some kind. The music is raging. People are dancing. There’s a band on stage, and they’re singing loud and proud. Too loud, actually.
I’m in a back corner of the party, drinking from a paper cup that’s basically empty. There’s a banner above me: “Welcome Back, Interns!”
I remember this party. It happened about two years ago. I didn’t know anybody and was super out of place. Was feeling spacey. Too afraid to talk or interact.
I walk toward the exit. There are hushed voices, and I’m sure lots of people can see me leaving, but I don’t care.
There’s a flash as I’m sent away from the memory.
I’m now in the office cafeteria.
Wait… What? What happened to the sky?
I look down to find I’m carrying a water cooler full of Kool-Aid to a table. I suddenly realize that it’s really freaking heavy. I try to get a handle of myself and press ahead.
I feel the edge of the cooler slip from my fingers. I feel the color drain from my face. Oh no – I remember now – it’s too heavy.
“Hey, you need any help with that?” I hear Ethan ask, coming up from behind.
Nice gesture, but he’s too late. I gesticulate, fighting gravity. Gravity wins. The cooler crashes on the ground and the Kool-Aid gushes out.
Uncle!
Wow, I’m so uncool.
“It’s alright,” Ethan says, giving me a pat on the back. “Don’t worry, I’ll help you clean it up.” I nod my head in a daze, while Ethan runs to go get napkins.
I feel dizzy. There’s another flash, and I’m beamed once more.
“Twice,” I say.
“He’s asked you twice?” says Lin.
I scratch my head. We’re on the office floor again.
“Three times, maybe?” I say.
I’m holding a can of tuna. My palms are sweaty. My hands are shaky.
I remember this. It was about a year ago, back when I first met Lin.
“It’s whatever, I’ll get to it when I get to it.”
I can’t remember what it was that I had to get to. Something for Dr. Skully, no doubt.
I try to laugh when my finger slips on the edge of my tuna can. I feel a twinge as the can gives a slight cut to the tip of my finger and a burble of blood form.
It’s just a small cut. A minor inconvenience, really. Yet, my skin gets cold and clammy. The room is hazy.
“You alright?” Lin asks, with a concerned look in her eyes.
“Yes, I’m alright,” I manage, even as my anxiety mounts.
My chest feels tight.

I don’t think she’s noticed the cut, but she’s noticed the look on my face. I can’t let her see me. “On the subject of being late: I just realized, I have an online meeting that I’m running late for,” I say. I make my way toward my cubicle.
“Alright,” Lin says. “I’m always here to talk if you need me.”
I’m already in my cubicle shuffling through papers as she says this. My heart flutters. I close my eyes.
“Thanks,” I say.
I’m back in the sky, caught in a total death spiral.
My knuckles are white, holding onto the edge of the ducted fan as best I can. My limbs are splayed, and my torso makes a thud as it flops against the ducted fan’s walls.

“Grah!” the drone-man bellows, his voice an equal mix of digitized and zombified. The air bellows with him. We’re flipping end-over-end now, and I can taste stomach acid. I squint to try and make out the city below. I think I can see Euclid Street from here.
I press the trigger down on my fluxion-drive and try aiming my descent toward my apartment building.
“Yeehaw!” I cry. “Let’s ride on home!”

I cough from the fumes given off by the drone-pack. Its engine Is sputtering, straining to stay alive.  My fluxion-drives aren’t doing so great either. Excess waste heat burns from the fluxion-drive in my left hand, as well as the fluxion-drive near my groin. I’m tempted to adjust the fluxion-drive attached to my belt but stop myself.
No time for navel gazing.
My body slams into the drone frame again as our trajectory shifts closer to Euclid Street. I feel my body go numb. My mind is starting to fade again. I’m tunneling away.
No! Not again! This never happens this often!
My mind is thrown into a carousel of memories. Failed projects. Verbal diarrhea. Missed opportunities. Mess ups. They’re all charged with a flurry of regret.
I need to stop. I need to forget. I can’t waste my time here!
I’m slung back into the sky, and I’m once again clinging to the back of the drone-man. Somehow I’ve managed to not lose control.
I vomit up a bit of stomach acid.
Okay, maybe I have been losing control just a little bit.
My street is only a few hundred feet below now. The drone-man is writhing and growling, striving to break free. Unfortunately for him, you can only do so much against gravity.
We pass by some rooftops and then zip through the street. My muscles and joints scream at me as I force us into a tight turn, into an alleyway.
My foresight is already forming an image: the vision of a graceful entry into my apartment. The drone-man kicks me in the shin.
“Screw you!” I shout.
Our path is diverted, and we’re headed for a dumpster. My pre-cognition now says this is about to be a literal dumpster fire.

I use my fluxion-drives to blast out the drone man’s other propellor, then use the fluxion-drive’s thrust to push myself off the drone-man and decelerate. Nevertheless, the dumpster insists upon itself.
I clench my teeth. I crash into a pile of trash.
“Years of university, just to become a garbage man,” I say.
By some stroke of luck, the drone-man crashes next to the dumpster, into a pile of sewage. Well, maybe not so lucky for the drone-man. But then, who cares about him anyway?
I switch a dial on my goggles to get a read on the drone-man’s vitals. His respiration is still in good condition, even if he’s unconscious.
Looks like, against all odds, we both made it out alive. I can’t help but smile. Maybe I care about him a little bit.
Then again… He nearly killed me.

My smile is replaced by a rush of agitation. As I study the machinery attached to the drone-man, something is askew. Bits of metal interlace through his skin, and a truss is built along the drone man’s spine. Impressive as the technology may be, the sight of flesh meshed with metal is depressing.
How did this guy find me, anyway?
I probably should call the Machine. Or maybe the cops. I’m kind of machined out after some of the friction we’ve been having. That dude never gives me enough credit.
My hand hovers between the pouch for my communicator and the pouch for my phone. Which to choose?
My phone buzzes. Must be a message. I grab it.
“We’re headed over now.”
The message is from Ethan in our group chat, sent a few seconds ago.
“ETA, 10 minutes.”
10 minutes?
My eyes go wide.
“There’s no way I’ll be able to microwave everything in time!” I say, shifting around on my throne of garbage.
The drone-man gives a zombified snort. My fists tighten.
“You weren’t invited to the dinner, to be clear,” I say.
Should I delay the dinner? I quickly scroll through the group chat to find that I’ve been bombarded with texts from Lin and Ethan for the past half hour.
At this point, they can probably see that I’ve seen their messages. Also, maybe they can tell that there is a delay.
What should I say?
9-1-1. Maybe I should call 9-1-1 first. I can take care of dinner after.
I go to dial the number when my communicator buzzes. I pull it from my pouch and take a look at the message.
Oddly, it’s not from the Machine. My communicator took in a signal from an address I’ve never seen before.
“Cog, you ok?” the message reads.
“Who is this?” I write back.
“Turtle-Dove,” the message reads.
I wipe some sweat off my brow and send a thumbs up.
“I saw you flying around town on some cyborg, all over social media,” Turtle-Dove continues. “He’s neutralized,” I write. “Also, how’d you get my communicator line?”

“You have a distinct vibe, you know? Distinct frequencies,” Turtle-Dove says. “Usually I wouldn’t pry, but I had to get into contact with you somehow after the forum got hacked. Had to do some hacking of my own.”
My eyes twitch and my ears itch. While it’s nice to hear from Turtle-Dove again, is it really that easy to track me down?
I glimpse at the drone-man. I can’t help but wonder if he found me through my communicator signal, the same way Turtle-Dove did. Am I and the Machine being targeted?
I send a “:/”.
“I work with a guy who is an idiot-savant at getting info,” Turtle-Dove explains. “He went by Ratcatcher on our forum. He has a lot of other pseudonyms too. Generally, goes by Nimrod.”
I laugh.
“Nimrod?” I write. “That was Nimrod!? The legend himself?’
“The one and only. ;)”
I send a thumbs up.

“Speaking of which,” Turtle-Dove writes, “he wants any information he can get off these cyborgs you’ve been fighting. They should have brain-computer interface chips on them. Can you get access to those? Pics, or it didn’t happen.”
My eyes dart to the back of the drone man’s neck. There’s a steel panel linked onto him. The brain computer interface must be hidden somewhere under there.
“Might be an hour or so,” I write. “But I can definitely get that sent to you.”
“No problem, I can wait for you. I have other plans tonight to keep me busy.” My chest feels lighter. Then I see the time listed on my communicator.
Only five minutes until Lin and Ethan arrive for dinner. Not even enough time to reschedule.
I pull myself out of the heap of trash, then jump from the dumpster and onto the alleyway pavement. I look up to my bedroom window, several stories into the air. Then, to the drone-man.
“Guess you get to crash at my place after all,” I say.
His jaw is slack and he breathes with a drowsy snore.

I latch my fluxion-drives to each side of my belt and hug the drone-man from underneath the armpits. The engine and ducted fans to make this awkward, but I manage to squeeze between.  Activating my fluxion-drives, I steadily hover into the air. The weight of the drone-man is immense, but what must be done must be done.
“I hope you know you’re a serious flight risk!” I shout as we make our way up to my window.
The window is slightly cracked open, and I use my foot to push it open all the way. Biting my lip, I shift my weight to angle my hover. Some way, somehow, we need to fit through this window.

We descend. I bump my elbow on the edge of the window frame and feel my arm go numb with pins and needles. One of my shoes is pulled off and falls to the alley below. The screech of metal on wood skewers my eardrums.
We land in a lump on my apartment floor.
“That was tight,” I say, steadying myself to my feet.
I don’t have much time to soak it in. A doorbell goes off.
“Just a minute!” I shout, scrambling to my window. I lock it closed, then start pulling off my clothes.
Off with the shoe, then the goggles. I take off my power-pack and super hoodie too. Oh, and the mask – I have to take off the mask.
I toss it all into a clump on top of the drone-man. Switching into new t-shirt and sweatpants, I head for the hall. I make sure to lock my door shut as I do.
“Mew,” PB says, chasing after me as I run down the hall.
“Did you hear that noise? What was that noise?” Jack says, popping his head out his bedroom door. “Band practice,” I say, still running.
Jack rolls his eyes. “Haha, fair enough… Also, what’s the rush?”
Ignoring him, I beeline to the front door. I start undoing the locks.
“Oh, right,” Jack says, “your work dinner.”
He gives a yawn and closes his door.
I chuckle. Despite the turmoil of tonight, my mind begins flipping through a scrapbook of memories out of anticipation. Games, good meals, jokes told, stories shared…
I open the door.
“Well, hello there!” I exclaim.
I brush some debris from out of my hair. It suddenly occurs to me that I might smell like garbage.
Lin and Ethan beam at me with wide smiles. Lin is wearing a dress. Ethan is dressed similarly to me, in t-shirt and sweatpants. They’re also both already holding Tupperware, with containers of food.
Funny – I didn’t tell them they needed to bring anything. But I guess I should’ve assumed they would.
“Hi, how are you doing?” Ethan says, stepping into the apartment. “You have something good cooking?”
“Uh…” I say, rubbing my eyes.
“Hi!” Lin waves at me while following Ethan.
I wave back and shut the door behind her.
“Gonna be honest, I still have to get dinner going,” I say. “Gotta put it in the microwave.”
“What? You put something off?” Ethan says in a sarcastic tone of voice.
Lin shoots him a glare and Ethan gives a chuckle.
“Don’t worry, we figured you might get distracted with all your… stuff,” says Ethan, putting on a stiff smile.
I give him a thumbs up and he relaxes.
“Awesome, you guys can go ahead and set it on the table,” I say, pointing to a plastic foldup table, complete with a set of foldup chairs.
I jog into the kitchen and snatch a bag of cat food from the counter to fill up one of PB’s food bowls.  PB gives a chirp and runs up to his bowl.
As he reaches his bowl, I’m already in the fridge getting out a box of chicken. I pop open the microwave and set it to two minutes.
I’m a whiz.

“Is that lil’ PB?” Lin asks, coming into the kitchen. She stoops down and starts petting him. “He’s been feeling a little shy lately,” I say. “But I’m sure he’s happy to see you.” “Oh, I’m sure,” Lin says, giving PB scratches behind the ear.
PB rolls onto his belly.

I roll on into the dining area and grab a remote from the edge of the dining table. I stop myself for a moment. Lin and Ethan have already taken the lids off their food containers, revealing bread and pasta.
I flip on the TV that’s in the corner, before heel-turning back toward the kitchen. I skid to a halt as I nearly bump into Ethan. He’s crouched on the ground, sifting through his backpack.
“Sorry,” I say.
“No, it’s fine,” Ethan says, pulling a pack of paper plates out. Lin is standing behind him, already holding a box of plastic silverware.
I give a sigh of relief.
“How’d you know to bring silverware?” I say. “I was gonna need to wash some dishes.”
“We’re psychic,” Lin says.
I raise an eyebrow, until Lin gives a playful laugh.
I try to laugh back, when the timer goes off. I jog into the kitchen and pop open the microwave.  Steam wafts into my face.
I can hear Lin and Ethan taking their seats at the table, but my mind is tugging at me. The steam reminds me of the jet exhaust – the battle in the clouds.
I shake my head, and head for the dining area with the chicken.
“What’s with the old TV, by the way?” Ethan asks as I set the chicken on the table. “Not into the new?”
“Too chicken,” I say.
Lin laughs. Ethan rolls his eyes.
My face goes tingly. I’m pretty sure there’s nobody else but Lin who’d laugh at that joke.

I take my seat across from Ethan and Lin and start filling up my plate. Suddenly, I feel claustrophobic. This room is so small. How should I hold my fork again? Also, should I have taken a seat next to Lin?
I turn my head to look at the TV behind me. Everman Technology’s rocket launch and tech showcase should come on tonight, but right now it’s just some ads for toothpaste.
Come to think of it, did I brush this morning?
I brush away some hair from in front of my eyes and turn back to Lin. I make eye contact and grin.
“Those vintage TV sets are actually gems,” I say. “Particle accelerators are built into them. They shoot beams of electrons. Did you guys know that?”
Lin shakes her head.
Ethan shrugs. “Yeah, I think I took one of them apart as a project in high school. Pretty neat, I guess.”
Lin nods, then looks down to start cutting her chicken into smaller pieces.

“It’s actually dangerous to stare too close at the screen,” I say. “It gives off mild amounts of x-rays and stuff. True story: it’s one of the reasons people weren’t supposed to stare at their screens for too long.”
“Definitely sounds like somebody has been on screens for too long,” says Lin with a playful smirk.
