Ethan chuckles. “So, like… If I sit in front of the TV for too long, my eyes will just melt or something?”
“If amped up enough, who knows what it can do,” I say, with a laugh. “Eye melt, mind melt… Who knows. We’ll need to mind meld on that one. I think it’s got potential.”
Ethan gives a slow nod. Am I crazy? Am I being an asshole? Do I sound like a crazy asshole?
“I was being sarcastic, just to be clear,” I say.

While it’s true that the accelerator in my little TV isn’t much, I’m still mystified by particle accelerators. My accident with the large particle accelerator at Everman Technologies remains seared in my mind. Should’ve never had the harebrained idea to stick my head in there.
Ethan grabs some chicken from near me and begins removing the bone with surgical precision. “How have your projects been going in the lab?” I ask.
“Pretty well,” Lin says. “Surprised we haven’t seen a lot of you lately. I’m sure you’d love what we’ve worked on. All state-of-the-art stuff.”
“I’m not much for art,” I say. “Plus, I’ve been super busy lately.”
“With what?” asks Ethan. “Whenever I see you, you look like you just woke up from a nap.”
Lin nods and gives a raised eyebrow.
“Hey, not all of us can work on the glamorous stuff,” I say. “Trust me, I –.”
I stop myself when I hear a loud clang. My chest falls.
“What was that?” Lin asks in a hushed tone.
I drop my silverware and cock my ear toward the hall.
Half a minute passes. Nothing.
“Probably just squirrels,” I lie. “They have a nest outside my window.”
“A nest of squirrels?” Lin says with a chuckle.
“Must be flying squirrels,” Ethan says, cracking a smile. “They’re closely related to birds, right?” Before I can defend myself, a swell of music blares from the TV.
“The Everman Showcase!” I say, raising my fork into the air to change the subject. Lin looks unimpressed.
“I think they’re testing chips and launching a new rocket tonight,” I explain.
“We’ve seen it all over the work newsletters already,” says Ethan. “To be honest, I don’t want to think about work, especially when there’s only a 50% chance of things working.”
The TV has an awesome overhead shot of the Machine striding to a stage near a rocket launch pad. I sigh.
“No fun,” I say, switching the channel to a nickelodeon.
“The Vitruvian announced something way better for next week,” says Lin, with a warm smile. “I heard he’s hosting a ball at the National Art Museum. Will be displaying artwork and giving a speech.”
I clear my throat and pour myself a glass of water.
“Oh? Art? I love art,” I say.
Ethan snorts.
“I love art,” Lin says, leaning toward me.
My face is hot. She’s hot. Her eyes seem enchanted. I feel my own eyes get reeled in.
This room feels like it shrunk yet again. Did that drone-man happen to have a shrink ray with him?
“They just announced it,” Ethan says. “Tickets go on sale tomorrow.”
“Damn,” I say. “I’ll be keeping an eye on that then. Gives me something to go to.”
“At the rate Everman Technologies is going, definitely need something to look forward to,” says Ethan.
For some reason though, I’m having trouble paying attention to him. I can’t take my eyes off Lin. “I’ll get those tickets,” I say.
There’s a violent crash, which shakes the whole apartment. PB skitters from somewhere in the kitchen and hides under the table.
“Okay, seriously, what was that?” Lin asks, her voice severe.
“One second,” I say, standing from my chair.
There’s a quiver in my voice but I try my best to walk casually down the hall.
“You sure you don’t need help with anything?” Ethan asks, standing halfway up from the table.  “That was pretty loud.”
I shake my head and continue down the hall.
“No, I actually have a surprise to show you,” I say. “You guys can watch the cartoons or whatever, it’ll just be a second.”
Lin and Ethan’s sharp whispers between each other echo after me as I enter my room. I quickly shut my door.
“Okay, I need a plan,” I mutter to myself, while staring at the giant cyborg in the middle of my room.

He’s still in a lump, but he’s moved a few feet from where I had him. My piles of clothes have been flung about, and my desk has been knocked over. I run to my closet and pull out loose electrical wire. I begin untangling it as I run back to the drone man and grab his wrists.

I start trying to tie the wire around his wrists when he jerks at me. I jump back and watch as he writhes around the floor, causing the room to shake. He doesn’t seem fully awake, and the various electronics along his body spit electric sparks.
My dresser topples over, falling onto the drone man. He goes still. Maybe I can stall from here. A brilliant idea flickers into my head.
“Jack!” I shout. “Jack! Why does this have to be so freaking loud, Jack!?”
I finish cinching the drone man’s wrists, then leap to my door. I open it, and Jack is already there, staring me in the eye. His eyes are bleary and his hair is frizzy.
“Ok, what the fuck is going on?” Jack asks, with a hiss. “I’m trying to sleep over here, and it sounds like you’ve summoned a demon.”
I swallow.
“What’s your price?” I say.
Jack squints.
“Excuse me?”
I draw my face close to his.
“Suppose I ask you to help me hide a dead body,” I say, my voice hushed and rushed. “And, since you’re my roommate, you decide to help out. Out of the goodness of your heart.”
Jack scoffs. “Goodness…”
“What’s your price?”
Jack’s face contorts. “I can’t be bothered, let alone bought.”
“50 bucks.”
“Fuck it, “Jack says, studying me. “I’m in.”
Jack pushes past me, making his way into my room.
“Holy –!” Jack exclaims, before I put my hand over his mouth.
“I need you to make sure he doesn’t move while I see my guests out,” I say.
Jack’s jaw is slack, and his eyes are in a daze.
“You weren’t – you didn’t,” Jack stammers. “Is he actually dead?”
“Doubt it,” I say, putting my hand on Jack’s shoulder. “I need him dead silent though, for these next few minutes.”
Jack shakes his head as I head for my guests.
“50 bucks,” I say. “It’ll only be a few minutes.”
“Double it, “Jack says, eyes still in a stupor.
“Done.”

As I leave my room, I find Lin and Ethan, looking toward the front door of my apartment and whispering to themselves. Their plates of food are nearly finished – clearly my detour took more time than I had hoped.
“Sorry, there’s a big mess I need to fix,” I say.
“Yeah?” Ethan says, raising an eyebrow. “That was definitely loud.”
“I was worried we needed to call the police or something,” Lin says.
My mind freezes as I search for the right thing to say.
“Do we need to call the police?” Lin says in a rushed tone. Her eyes dart between me and Ethan. I shake my head and raise my palms in the air.
“Slow down, calm down, it’s fine,” I say.
“Then what was that?” Lin asks, pointing at me. “It shook the whole place!”
My eyes go to the ceiling.
“A robot,” I say. “Jack’s band… My roommate… They commissioned a robot that can give a nice beat. And it’s gone on the fritz.”
“You’re taking commissions now?” Ethan asks. “You once told me you’d never turn your hobby into a business.”
“Always time to start. You guys always thought I had business potential, right?” I search for sympathy in their faces, but I’m getting none.
Ethan doesn’t take my bait to change the subject and persists. “Also, I thought Jack hated robots.”
There’s another crash from my room, followed by a shout of “Fuck!” that can only be Jack.
“Jack loves robots,” I lie.
Lin’s face twists. “Do you have some other guest here tonight?”
I scratch an itch on the side of my neck. “No, not at all. Totally just you guys! I only really know you guys.”
“It’s just, you took awhile to open the door and everything,” Lin presses onward. “Also, I’ve seen you talking with other guys and gals at work. We’re not the only people you know, don’t lie.”
I look at my hands, still grimy from my battle with the cyborg. “You know me: I’m not good with people, even if I pretend to be. There’s nothing fishy going on here, I promise.”
“I mean, he’s got a point,” Ethan says, backing me up. “Dude barely talks to anybody.”
Lin gives a reluctant nod. “I mean, that was some raucous. But yeah, I guess I can agree Ethan… George, you’re a total recluse. When I first met you, I thought you were a mute.”
“Thank you!” I say with a grin. “Also, mute beats mutant, am I right?”

She rests her hand on her chin, then squints her eyes quizzically. “So then… Uh… Guess I’ll drop it. Anyway, have you seen the various news reports lately? All those crazy tech crime attacks and stuff? You ever messed around with any of that?”
Wah! She can’t know my sacred secret! It’ll erect too many issues!
Waving my hands in the air, I sputter. “No, that’s ridiculous. Commit crime, fight crime… I’m… I could never! I’m no hero! I’d never do anything that insane!”
“What made you think I thought you were a crimefighter, George?” Lin chagrins. “That’s a big leap. I was just trying to change the subject to news stories.”
I clear my throat. “Right, of course.”
There’s a boom, throttling the entire room again. Sweat beads on my forehead.
“You sure you have no idea what that noise is?” Lin says, her hands gripping the edge of the table.
Ethan is equally tense, his hair standing up with goosebumps.
My body is shaky. Thoughts intercross and cognate, all with negative connotation. Are we safe? Is everything going to fall apart? Will they hate me?
In terms of a backup plan if things get any worse over these next few minutes, I have none – I need to get my friends out of here.
“Maybe we need to cut this dinner short?” I say, my voice breaking into a high pitch.
“Okay, if that’s what you want, I think we can leave now,” says Lin, her eyes downcast.
Ethan and Lin stand from the table then head for my front door, putting their coats on as they do. I want to stop them—I want to take my words back— but, my body feels as though it’s caught in amber.
She grabs Ethan’s forearm, and my foresight sees her disappearing with him into the night.
“Wait,” I say, finally forcing myself from my seat as Lin opens the front door.
She looks back at me.
“Yeah?”
“You still interested in going to the art gallery next week?”
Lin gives an expression that is half frown, half smile. “We’ll see.”
“Thanks for having us!” says Ethan, now standing on the other side of the door. A pit falls in my stomach.
“Yeah, thanks,” says Lin, following after Ethan.
“Thanks for coming!” I say through a forced smile.
My hands are trembling, but I can’t tell if it’s anxiety or anger. Why couldn’t this night have just gone smoothly?
“Really sorry about this, I promise I will make it up to you guys,” I say. “It’s always a lot of fun hanging out.”
Ethan nods. “Yep, we had fun, no worries.”
Lin nods with him.
“All the best,” Ethan continues, “hope everything works out!”
Lin makes a heart with her hands. “Stay safe! Have a nice night!”
“You too!” I say.
I lock everything up once they’re gone.
I try so hard, and it often doesn’t work out. This is the sort of stuff that always gets me out of sorts.
“Okay, you’re good,” I say to Jack, as I reenter my room.
“You underpaid me, this thing is insane,” Jack says, giving a smirk.
He’s sitting on top of the dresser and drone man sandwich with his legs crossed. He stands from his seat, then outstretches his hand.
I outstretch mine and give him a handshake. Oddly, he lets his arm go to a limp noodle. “I wasn’t going for a handshake,” Jack says. “Cash. I want my cash.”
“Later,” I say, still shaking his hand.
“As for the police?” Jack asks.
“Again: later,” I insist.
“Okay.”
We break off the shake.
“Just know, this will come with a lot of interest,” he says, walking around me for the hall. “Whatever, tell me what else is new.”
I pause.
“He’s not one of mine, by the way,” I say, gesturing to the drone man. “Also, don’t breathe a word.”
Jack laughs, then pats me on the back.
“You’re a mad lad,” he says, before leaving to his room.
It’s now just me and the drone man. I would’ve preferred to end the night with somebody else in my room, but I guess beggars can’t be choosers.

I snatch a screwdriver from the scattered mess on my floor, then move to the back of the drone man’s neck. With some effort, I manage to pry off the metal plate attached to his neck, revealing a web of chips and circuitry beneath.
I grab my communicator and use it to snap a picture. I send it to Turtle-Dove.
“Here you go,” I write. “No clue what’s going on in this picture. Things feel totally overwhelming and all over the place.”
Turtle-Dove sends me an instant thumbs up.
“Everman,” she writes. “Analysis still needs to be done, but this tech is clearly coming out of Everman Technologies. Seems to be their new stuff, too.”
My face goes hot. I bite my lip. Something is very wrong, and I need to let the Machine know as soon as possible.
“But how?” I write. “All of this stuff should be under tight wraps.”
“Clearly somebody high up, but no clue who,” writes Turtle-Dove. “Still a lot up in the air.”
There’s a pause, then another message.

“Also, we need to rendezvous at the art gallery next week. More secure. Also: all signs point to there being an exchange of chips of some kind during that event. There might be a chance to sniff out who the source of this is.”
I grin. Poorly as this night with Lin went, at least something is going right.
“I’ll be there,” I write.
“You better. ;)”
Chapter 5: Product Launch
The Machine

I slam my foot on the accelerator and yank my yoke to the left. My tires squeal with delight, and its vibrations rush from the dash through my body. The Machine-Machine is the best car in the world, probably. I'm definitely the best driver.
My car gives a sputter as I shift gears, and my body shifts forward. The slack on my seatbelt turns taut.
Okay, maybe there are some people that are better drivers than me.
I press harder down on the accelerator and the Machine-Machine gives a low rumble. Look, I never promised anyone I was humble.
I'm driving on an open concrete plane. A tarmac. I grin. I give a whoop. I love living in the fast lane.

Things have been rough on me lately. The company is a mess. I feel like I've lost control of it. Also, the cyborg attack during my interview with Taft was extremely disconcerting. I recently sent components from some of them for my machinists to analyze, and I'm worried about what they might find. Ditto for Cog – I know he's on the hunt, and I just hope he stays safe.

I see the world and I wonder whether we've made a wrong turn. Maybe I'm the wrong guy to try being a leader. This ride helps to renew my soul, somehow. It's dumb fun, and that's exactly what I need right now.

Just ahead is my rocket stage, secured atop its launchpad. A crowd of people is gathered around a smaller announcement stage for my product showcase, set in front of the launch pad. Beams of sunlight bounce from the tip of the rocket. It's covered in pearl white tiles for heat shielding, making it look reminiscent to an obelisk.
It's also a bit phallic, but what can you do?
I make a tight turn of my wheel and listen to screeching as the path of my car arcs toward the back of the announcement stage.
I slam my brakes and prepare to shift into park, as I crash through a stack of crates.
"Park! Park!" I bark to myself, slamming my brakes harder.
There's another crash as I close my eyes. I manage to shift into park and my car engine settles to a soft purr.
That was trash.
Oh well, at least the audience didn't see. All they saw was my entrance through the back of the announcement stage, when I was moving like a bullet. I'm sure it looked awesome.
I reopen my eyes. I've crashed into the back of a forklift. I squint – it looks like nobody was inside. Good.
I hop out of the Machine-Machine and check its front bumper. I wince. The hood and front bumper are totally mashed in.
"Incredible," I mutter to myself. "Bulletproof car, and I still manage to damage it."
"Holy cow," I hear my head engineer Peter exclaim.
I force myself to look away from my wreck.
"This is nothing," I say with a scoff.
"You alright?" Peter asks, scrunching his brow.
He's standing in the stairwell, holding a clipboard.
"Just a little burnout," I say with a chuckle. "All the best racers gotta go through it at some point."
Peter's lip quivers as he takes another glance at the wreck behind me. He returns to his clipboard.
"The board is here," Peter says.
I roll my eyes. "I know."
"So is Sir Polka," Peter continues.
He swallows. I swallow with him.
"I thought Sir Polka was still in the hospital," I say.
Peter shakes his head.
"Apparently not. You prepared your speech, right?"
I nod. "Sent it over to the teleprompter guys."
"You practiced it, right?" Peter persists.
I snort. "I had my AI write it. I'll ace it."
Peter's face goes tight and he clenches the sides of his clipboard.
"You can't just CliffsNotes your way through a product announcement, Hugo! Do you realize you're on a cliff's edge with the board? They want you gone!"
I look at my watch.
"I could probably use a vacation," I say, forcing a yawn. "How those bots, by the way? You fix the capacitors in the quantum chip."
"Our problem wasn't capacitors," Peter says.
"The inductors then?"
Peter coughs into his sleeve, then glares at me. His forehead features a dew of sweat.
"The bots are working now, and that's all that matters. Okay?" Peter says, with a tremble in his voice. "The team had to scramble like mad, and work around the clock... But, hey, we made it."
"Awesome! See, you guys just needed a push."
Peter pushes his glasses up the bridge of his nose.
"I've seen a ton of CEO types like you over the years," Peter says in a mumble.
I give a smug smirk. "Oh please, you've never seen anybody like me."

"Look: you might think you're master of the universe. But I just want to make something clear to you... You're not an engineer." Peter pauses to gesture at my car. "You need to learn to stay in your lane."
I wince. That really hits like a gut punch. I glance at his clipboard.

"Why are you using paper?" I say, grasping for a comeback. "So outmoded, Peter. Use a tablet, much more advanced. Having info delivered to me on paper signifies poor workmanship, and it gives me the willies."
Peter nods and drops his clipboard to the floor.
"You see the new article that came out about you, from Amanda Taft?"
I shake my head. Peter pulls his smartphone out of his pocket.
"It's not a tablet, but here you go," Peter says, showing his phone screen to me.
The article has a photo of me in my super suit. Only, it was taken on my bad side. The headline reads, Hugo's Hubris: Turning a Titan to the Titanic.
My face heats up. I want to punch something.
I clear my throat. "That bi—."
"By the way," Peter says. "The last company I worked at went completely under. The reason? Their CEO turned management into a living hell."
I'm about to snap back, when I see Opal coming down the stairway. Peter gives a wave.
"Best of luck," he says.
He's gone.
I flip through my phone screen and get to the article by Taft. As I read through, a rage inside of me acquires more and more pressure.
"You in a wreck again?" Opal asks.
"Blech," I mutter.
My car wreck is the last thing I want to talk about.
"Opal, have you seen this new article?" I grumble hoarsely. "It's ridiculous! Completely twisting my words!"
Opal walks up to me, nodding in sync with her steps. She looks me up and down.
"You look great, nice outfit," Opal says. "Is that cashmere?"
Opal points at the orange sweater I'm wearing.
I grin. This day has been pretty crappy so far, but at least something is going right.
"Yeah, glad you noticed," I say. "I like its effect. There's a certain gravity to cashmere, don't you think?"
Opal rolls her eyes and begins flipping through her phone.

"You might be aiming for utopia, but the difference between dystopia and utopia is oh so slight," she says. "Taft wasn't trying to slight you. She's making an important point, if you read through her article."
"Article? More like artifice," I say, holding back a growl.
"Ooh, artifice. Interesting term," Opal says sarcastically, while giving a half-hearted nod. "Nice and short."
I throw my hands up. "Honestly, I'm burning the candle at both ends here, and I feel like nobody realizes how hard I have it!"
Opal taps her phone screen, then glares at me. "That's real rich," she says, placing emphasis on the words real rich.
Is she poking at my wealth again? Before I can retort, my phone buzzes. I open a new email from Opal.
"List of updates from my biotech division." Opal says. "Also, some talking points you might want to hit."
I chuckle.
"Thanks, you're a lifesaver."
Opal nods. "Not sure how much I can keep sending these lists for you. Managing things has gotten insane, ever since you cut our headcount."
I snort. "It's fine, you guys are fine. You'll tough it out."
Opal shakes her head. "By the way, is Everman Technologies still hosting bring-your-kid-to-work day? Or is that getting cut from the budget too? It isn't on the calendar anymore."
I cough. I clear my throat.
"Yeah, yeah, yeah," I say, scrolling through my phone. "We'll sort it out."

I give a quick gaze into Opal's eyes and notice how dark the bags under her eyes are. The truth is, I don't want to think about the fact that Opal has kids. I suddenly feel a bit of a headache. Opal is doing a ton, but she does it well and we also work well together. My team and I get way less done when she's not around.

People always get mad when I say this, but: I need everybody focused on their work family just as much as their biological family. It's the only way I see Everman Technologies getting through this rough patch. Does that make me a bad person?
"You need to consider working with a proper assistant," Opal says. "I have a whole division to run, and these meetings we have are really cutting on my time."
I shrug, trying to roll with the punches. To be honest though, something sinks in my chest. I'm starting to feel like this day just won't let up.
"An assistant? You're thinking too old school. I got AI and robots for that," I say. "This is Everman Technologies, I don't ever need an assist. Just a good roboticist."
"Publicist?" Opal persists.
I rub my temples. "You're gonna give me a cyst..."
Opal shakes her head. "Much as you hate hiring internal assistants and publicists, you might run into some today. And I don't want you to go blaming me when you do, because I didn't do the hiring."
I raise an eyebrow.

Opal continues unperturbed, "A public relations team for the biotech division is here. They're near the VIP row, up front. I was talking with them a few minutes ago. They're looking forward to meeting you, and they want to do a photoshoot for the results from our latest trials."
My eyes go wide.
"Since when did we hire a public relations team?" I ask. "This is all out of wack."

Opal clears her throat. "Speaking of things being out of wack," she says, her face red. "There's one last thing I need to talk to you about, before I split. We've gotten some blood results back from the trial runs. Some of your vitals seem kind of odd. The medical team is suggesting that you get checked out."
I shake my head to dismiss it. "I don't have time for this. How bad?"
Maybe I should be more afraid. Maybe I'm just in shock. But, after being hit from all sides, it sort of feels like nothing can faze me at this point.
"Hopefully it's nothing," Opal says. "But they need to give you a checkup to know for sure. They're worried it's your heart."
"What about the other trial batches coming out of our division? I thought we've been doing incredibly good? Like, stupidly good?"
Opal forces a smile. "We have. Overwhelmingly positive results. Treatments have been ongoing for a year, and the results were very positive. Most patients see full remission."

Opal pauses, to let the weight of the results hang in the air. She then continues, "But, those trial runs are to help treat cancer. Your super treatments are different. We're usually not using treatments to try enhancing people. It's like you said to me the other day: our biotech isn't supposed to make people superhuman."
I rest my hand on my chin, still struggling to soak it in.
"See, nothing to worry about," I say, more to myself than to Opal.

"I'm sorry," says Opal, staring at her feet. "I don't like being the bearer of bad news. But you can't use money and tech to solve all your problems. Things should probably be fine for you, but only if you change how you're doing things and soon."
Before I can say anything in return, a thrum booms through the air.
"Get ready to rumble!" an announcer cries.

A vibration runs from my feet and through my bones as an electronic remix of heavy metal and rock albums begins to play. That's my cue. I only have a few minutes until I'm supposed to enter the stage.
"The nonprofit public relations team – who they got for me to meet?" I ask.
"It's a group from some of our first cancer trials, using our latest treatments," Opal says.

"Thanks. I just want to let you know, you and your team are miracle workers," I say with a smirk. "I'm sorry about earlier. I know that this is a good cause. And I can afford to be fashionably late to the stage."
Opal smiles back but her smile is stiff. She seems a bit aloof.
I turn to leave, then turn back around.
"Where they at again?" I ask.
Opal rolls her eyes. "VIP row, in front of the stage. You can't miss it."
I give a wink.
"I wouldn't for the world. Thanks again Opal. Also: We'll get this organization tightened up. Promise!"
I give Opal a wave, then break into a jog. I move through a passage beneath the stage, then enter the front of the stage near the VIP seating area.
Much as I hate to admit it, Opal has a point. If things don't change for me, and fast, everything that I've built might go away. But then, do I even have the time to change?
Bam! There's a flash before my eyes.
I flash a smile in return, posing for the cameras.
"Imagine it!" I bellow.
"Machine it!" I hear the crowd roar.
My eyes peer out to a large sea of people, all clapping and cheering. I put up my palm, signaling for the crowd and the audio to simmer down. They follow my whim, and the air quells.
"Hugo Everman, over here!"

I turn to see a photographer standing near a VIP row. There's a group of people wearing Everman Biotech t-shirts. There's also some lady with a clipboard – god, so many clipboards today. She grabs the photographer by the arm and drags him toward me. I walk toward them.
"Hi, I'm Susan Lang," the lady says. "I'm a public relations assistant."
I give a fake grin. "Wonderful," I say, speaking through my teeth. "While I generally don't work with PR –."
"P.S., I hate BS," Lang says, giving a broad gesture to the crowd behind her. "This is about the miracle work going on here."

She gives a new gesture to the row of people wearing Everman Biotech shirts. She signals for them to come forward, and the row of people come one-by-one. There is a silver fox of an older man wearing a brown suit and spectacles.
"That's Ed Kettle, a librarian and schoolteacher," Lang says. "Also, a major blood donor and community volunteer. He's a real hero in his community."
I force a smile but feel a bit uneasy. Ed definitely sounds like a real hero. But then, what does that make me and all my work?

He's followed by a much younger man, wearing a black t-shirt and sweatpants. His muscles bulge from beneath his clothes, and he looks like an athlete. Finally, there's a girl of about ten, wearing a pink t-shirt and jeans.
"After that, we have Cole Gander," Lang continues. "He's a paramedic currently going through med school. He also is a triathlete in his spare time."
I quickly recalibrate myself and shake Ed's hand before going to shake Cole's.
"Finally, this is Lucy Birk. She's in 4th grade and spends a lot of time on her school's soccer team and newspaper," Land says, still reading from her clipboard.
I give Lucy's hand a firm shake.
"Nice to meet you all," I say.
I then side-eye the PR lady.
"A bit awkward to be following a script here, but –."
I chuckle to try to release any tension.
Lang gives a thin smile.
"Sorry, just trying to bring you up to speed, I agree that this whole thing feels very rushed," she says. Her eyes dart toward the crowd. She steps back, then raises a finger into the air.
"One other thing I was supposed to tell you. These three are all cancer survivors. Also, they were all patients of the latest Everman Biotech treatments. Full and speedy recovery."
I blink. I feel as though I've gone from zero to sixty back to zero again, in the span of a few seconds.
"That's incredible," I say, my voice going soft.
I watch as Lang's eyes go from steely to warm.
I turn back to the group of people.
"Super great to meet you all, once again," I say. "This really is just amazing! Thanks so much for coming!"
Mr. Kettle adjusts his spectacles.
"No, thank you," he says. "We could really use better – uh – billionaires like you around. Just imagine where we'd be without your support."

I swallow. To be honest, I hadn't even been interested in cancer research until Polka began to have issues. Also, the way that Kettle says "billionaire" almost makes the word sound like a personal failing. I sigh. What is this money even worth if everybody hates you for it?
"You really are a lifesaver Mr. Everman," says Gander. "Without the medicine you invented, I wasn't able to do a third of what I can do now."

I swallow. There it is again – my guilt. The truth is, I don't know the first thing about this treatment other than that it worked. All I did was dump my billions into it. But then, what if that's money I'm not even supposed to have? My subordinates have been getting more and more obstinate lately, and likely for good reason.
I glance at Lucy. Her short frame is sort of hiding behind Cole. She's probably the only one here who is more uncomfortable than me. Maybe I intimidate her. Kids get like that around me sometimes.
"How have things been going for you? Liking school?" I say trying to keep my voice from getting too high, but also loud enough to be heard over the crowd. "Don't be shy."
She smiles. "Are you a doctor?" she asks.
My face goes hot.
"No," I say.
She looks at her feet. I look at mine.
"I'm more of a mascot, really," I say.
The photographer whistles and we all turn around.
"Everybody get ready to say cheese," the photographer says from behind his camera.
We all shuffle around. I waddle in front of Lucy, with a few playful stomps. She snorts.
"Wait, you go in front," I say, with a dopey grunt.
Lucy laughs, to be joined by Cole and Kettle. Finally, I laugh too.
There are flashes of the camera as it snaps its photos. I try my best to freeze our moment in time, for the camera to capture. Nevertheless, something in me feels a bit uneasy.

Helping with cancer cures might be another exploit to add to my list, but what if this is all just exploitative? Has any of the tech I've worked on ever come close to the positive impact of this treatment?
The cameraman gives a thumbs up and steps aside. I turn back to Lucy.
"What's your favorite subject in school?" I ask her.
She lights up. "Art."
"What kind of art are they having you do?"
Lucy begins regaling me with the various clays, pastels, and paints she's been able to experiment with. I try to ask insightful questions. She obliges with insightful answers.
Cole and Mr. Kettle begin to join in with their own life's passions, when Susan Lang juts in.
"Just a moment," Susan says. "Sorry to interrupt, but we just have to have you all take another picture with Sir Bertrand Polka!"
I look over and can't help but feel my eyes fall. Polka's frail and emaciated body is being wheeled on a wheelchair. His eyes are sunken and glassy.
"Isn't he still undergoing treatments?" I whisper to Lang. "I'm not sure if he should be here around all these people, let alone doing press."
Lang shrugs. "He and his estate insisted. He's an eccentric billionaire. Kind of hard for people to tell a billionaire no. I'm sure you know that firsthand."
I nod and give a slight frown. It's extremely hard to see Polka like this. For all my life, he's been a huge motivating force.
I feel somebody suddenly run into me, and I step to the side.
"Hugo! Hugo!"
It's one of my machinists, Rudy.
"I'm kind of in the middle of something right now," I say with a raised voice.
"This can't wait," says Rudy. "We think that Everman Technologies has been hacked."
My face contorts. The world seems to spin off its axis. He just confirmed one of my worst fears at one of the worst times.
"How?" I say in a hushed tone. I step away from the charity group as he tries to drag me to the side.
"You know the cyborg you just had sent to our machine shop for analysis?" he asks.
I give a grunt in the affirmative and bite my lip.
“I thought we had the cyborg sent to the biotech med bay?” I say. “He’s fine right?”

It was extremely hard to convince the police to even work with us on that setup. But then, the Everman Biotech med bay is one of the best, and we need to get to the bottom of what's going on with this cyborg problem.
Rudy nods his head dismissively. “Yeah, yeah, yeah. Last I heard he’s recovering. Anyway: I was referring to the cyborg components you sent us.”
"Well, what’s the issue?" I say.
Rudy seems to freeze.
"The components are all Everman Technologies," Rudy says, his voice cracking a bit. "All of them. I don't know how, but they are."
It's my turn to freeze. But Rudy keeps going.
"I'm also not sure about this robotics and rocketry demonstration we're about to do. I'm worried there's some sort of bad actor who has a backdoor to your stuff."
I shake my head.

"No, this was probably just the black market – uh – misappropriating our company's technology," I say, trying to pull a rationalization from thin air. "Everman Technologies is extremely secure, and we must go on today to improve public relations. All practice sessions were good, Peter already confirmed that to me."
"You're not taking this seriously enough!" Peter shouts, his voice hoarse.
I hear Mrs. Lang scoff from behind me. She's followed by a series of haggard coughs from Sir Polka.

"I don't have time for this," I retort. "I was in the middle of helping my nonprofit division. Charity. I couldn't care less whether these robots work right now, I was in the middle of something very important. I won't be able to get the moment back."
"Ok, that's enough," Mrs. Lang says, grabbing me by the forearm and pulling me away from Rudy. "I knew you'd be a handful, based on everything everyone had told me. But this is –."
"We'll talk more later," I say, glancing back at Rudy. "Sorry for the outburst."
Rudy gives a look of derision. My eyes dart to the crowd, then to patients. They all look uneasy. Impatient.
My eyes go to my watch. Crud – I'm ten minutes over from when I was supposed to start.
"We gotta get you on that stage," Mrs. Lang says.
"But, all of this time," I mutter. "I'm never gonna get it back."
Lang seems to ignore me. She gives a whistle and music begins to play. The crowd is abuzz once again.
I turn to Polka and the group of patients.
"Sorry everybody, I'm sorry," I say in a hoarse voice. "I've gotta do this presentation. I'll try setting another gathering to make it up for you guys."
The words fall flat for me. Oddly, the group seems less disappointed than me, and I can see their attention being carried away by the wild crowd and showmanship on display.
In the corner of my eye, there's the flashing of a jumbotron. No doubt it bears my name. Everything here is for me – everything for Everman. So, why do I feel so cornered?

"It's fine, you guys and Polka have a dinner scheduled for the middle of next week," says Mrs. Lang. "Also, we could try meeting again after the presentation. I figured we might run out of time, it's fine."
I smile. A dinner – yes. A winning idea.
The entire group nods, including Polka. Or, maybe he's nodding off to sleep.
Before I can sort it out, Lang is nudging me toward the stage.
"Go! Go!' she hisses.
"I'm going," I say.

I break into a jog toward the stage. I take deep breaths. Inhale. Exhale. My chest feels tight, as though it's coiled in a knot, and I wish there was more time to take everything in. But there's just not.
"Hugo Everman!" an electronic voice roars as I make my way up the stage steps. "Built like an Evergreen! The Big Tangerine! Hugo, a hero like no one has seen! The Machine!"

Upbeat drumbeats from the speakers overhead begin to swell. I puff my chest and raise my gaze toward the crowd. I then give a wave, followed by a pumping of my muscles. There's a flaring of light from the screens behind me. The air fills with screams of delight. A throng of my fans jump to the tempo of the music.
All eyes of the crowd are united in a look of wonderment, with the stagecraft having put them into a kind of a trance.

In the past, I was terrified of the stage. Even today, I've found myself looking for ways to put it off. Nevertheless: these days, it's all the same song and dance. I absorb the atmosphere and attempt to assume the identity of the hero they think me to be.
My arm gives a quick swipe, prompting the music and lightshow to fade into the background. My gaze shifts to my teleprompter, situated inline with the center of the crowd.
"Welcome everybody!" I say, my voice washing over the wave of people through the loudspeakers. "Sorry for being late, hopefully it's not out of fashion!"
I chuckle, then gesture to the Everman Biotech group I was just with.

"I want to give a quick shoutout to Everman Biotech," I say. "They're truly doing amazing things with cancer research, and it warms the heart. Everybody, please give these people a round of applause, they're – they're the true heroes!"

It's hard for these words to come from my lips. It really is. I want these people to see me as the true hero. But then, there's something about acknowledging the work of my biotech branch which just feels right.
Thankfully, I don't think the crowd catches any of this. They quickly erupt into applause. I let them go on like this for about a minute, before they finally begin to settle down.
"You guys are awesome! I can already tell this is going to be a great crowd and a great presentation!" I say with another chuckle. "Now, time to get into the true meat of this thing!"
I look back to my teleprompter. Time to start reading – hopefully I didn't just jinx myself.
"You all may have heard Byrd and his companies making a lot of noise. Annoys me! You guys?"
The crowd roars.
"That's right, make a noise!"
The crowd roars even louder. I wait again for them to settle down. It always helps build energy.

"Today, Everman Technologies is about to blow the roof off! We've been testing new robotics, which will be smart enough to be butlers, using our latest quantum chips. They'll be able to do anything, from your lawn to your laundry!"

I jut my pointer finger into the air, giving signal for a flurry of Everman Technologies' latest robots to fly overhead. They're silvery humanoids, retrofitted with powerful ornithopter wings. They're metallic daimons, worth more than diamonds.

The crowd ogles. Wingspans for these bots are a sight to behold, with each bot having a wingspan of 30 meters. There's another shift in the crowd as the formation of the robots takes on various shapes, resembling flower petals and hexagons.
"That's not all," I say, as a video begins playing on the large screen behind me. Humanoid robots are shown serving people in their homes, yards, and workplaces.

I turn to gesture at the massive rocket looming behind me, then return my eyes to the prompter. The warnings from Rudy just moments ago still itch at me. But, in defiance of Rudy's fears, the robots seem to be working like clockwork. I guess the test sessions were safe after all. They better stay that way.
I give a sigh to quell my nerves and hope nobody notices.
"Our collective future is in space, among the stars. I'm sure all of us are sick of this planet's tech illiteracy getting in the way of progress, am I right?"

Images of Dyson Spheres and people living in manmade space stations populate the screen behind me. The crowd whoops, but not as loudly this time. Odd – it often seems like people are not as enthused about the utopian visions as I am. I'll never understand why.
"This is why we are retrofitting our rockets with our latest quantum circuits, such that they can navigate to asteroids more easily. We should be able to do this within three years."
I blink. Three? Why did my AI, Aardvark, put that there? Whatever, I'll just roll with it.
"Furthermore: with our latest mining robots we might be able to mine these asteroids for rare resources. This can be used to help prevent resource scarcity on Earth!"
The crowd bursts with applause.

"Back when I was an electrical technician – an ET," I pause to gesture at the ET logo for Everman Technologies emblazoned on the screen, "I never thought I'd come this far. And now look. If you'll indulge my monologue for a moment: my guiding star has always been a world beyond material. Plato's realm of forms. And, with technology like this, we might be looking at a utopia where we can transcend our current system of materialism. No longer will we need labor, toil, or suffering. We might all be able to inhabit the space of ideas."

The audience was able to follow me for a little while, but they don't seem as enthused with my words on materialism. I rub my eyes. Maybe trying to sell the robotic cherubs above me as a product isn't helping my case.
I catch a glare from my board, who are seated in the front row. Escorgier in particular looks ticked. Even Polka doesn't seem impressed.
That said, maybe Polka is just tired. Heck, maybe that's my problem too.
Clearing my throat, I continue.

"Rich or poor, I think we can all agree that materialism is the chief problem in society that we share," I say, pretending to look out at the crowd as I begin to read the teleprompter verbatim. No room for slipups right now.
Even though I'm on a wide-open stage, I feel claustrophobic. My board is now signaling that I need to change topics.
"Sorry if this speech seems canned. I've been testing with a new machine intelligence, Aardvark," I laugh, forcing myself to break from the teleprompter.
I only manage to receive some weak chortles from the audience in return.
Suddenly, I hear a groaning. I glance behind me. Was that from the rocket? There seems to be steam coming from beneath its launchpad.
No, that can't be steam. That doesn't make sense. Probably just fog. I must be seeing a mirage.
"But, seriously," I continue. "An Age of Aquarius is upon us. We all need to start thinking about –."
"Machine!" Rudy says, cutting me off. He's somehow made his way onto the stage.
"Not now," I hiss. "These people clearly don't understand how our technology works, and I need to show them where we're at."
"The rocket is about to launch!" Rudy shouts.
The crowd falls silent as a mixture of dismay and disappointment falls over them. They don't seem happy with me. Maybe I should've been more careful with my words. More careful with planning.
I'm the strongest man alive, but I feel so weak.
" The quantum circuits have gone completely haywire!" Rudy shouts, waving his arms. "We gotta do something! We gotta stop this!"
I snap out of my daze and look out to the crowd.
"Everybody, evacuate!" I shout. "I need to catch a rocket!"
The crowd breaks into a frenzy and starts filtering away from the stage. The board is engulfed in utter fury, and Polka looks to be in shock. I break into a sprint, bounding off the stage.
"Hey, wait!" Rudy calls after me. "What are you doing?"
To be honest, I'm not sure myself. But there's no time to look back. Just run. Can only run.

My arms and legs pump back and forth as pistons as I move across the tarmac. My breaths go in and out with the rapid rhythm of an engine exhaust. After about a minute, I make it to the ladder for the rocket platform. The rungs bend under my strength as I climb, but I press onward and upward.
I'm on the metal platform. I pause for a split-second to take in the scale. It's a long stretch of metal to the rocket stage – about 500 feet, straight ahead.
Can't stop. I'm running again. The platform grating clangs beneath my feet. I'm running so hard.
Hard. This is hard.
My lungs burn. My eyes too. I've never run this fast before. But then, I've never had to chase down a rocket before.

My gaze locks in on the rocket. It's my target. It's my prey. Maybe if I pick up enough momentum I can knock it over or something. Maybe I can punch it into submission. There must be something I can do. There has to be.
I'm the Machine.
Tired. So tired. My body is straining, strength waning. I haven't felt this taxed in ages, and the rocket stage groans ever louder.
"Everman," I say to myself, through rapid breaths. "This is crazy."
Deep down, I know the truth: I can't stop a rocket. Not even with all my might.
All warning alarms on the platform are blaring. I can see off in the distance that the crowd has all but fled the scene.
The rocket engines flare. It's only about a hundred feet away. Maybe I can still get it somehow. Maybe there's a way.
My foot snags on something. Can't tell what. I stumble and collapse onto the metal platform. I want to pull myself back up, but I can't. I'm out of fuel.
The platform roars with an immense power.
There's an explosion.
I breathe in. I breathe out. Again and again. I can't bring myself to look up. I don't need to. I can already feel debris crashing down around me.
Today needed to go well. I needed this event to boost the company. Boost my people. Boost myself.
And yet... It's too late. I couldn't save it.
Teardrops hit the platform. I'm bawling. Broken down to the bone.
I don't need to cry. I don't. I'm the toughest. I'm the strongest. That's my superpower.
I am!
Still – I'm bawling. I feel weak.
My communicator buzzes. I force myself to stop crying and read it.
It's from Cog.

"We need to talk," says Cog's message. "I think somebody has infiltrated Everman Technologies, based on some new findings surrounding the cyborg problem. Just got attacked by another cyborg. Also: whoever is instigating this, they're planning an attack on the Vitruvian's ball next. We need to plan."
I send a thumbs up.
Suddenly, there's another buzz. It's the Vitruvian. Odd – he almost never messages me these days.
"Sorry I couldn't make it to your rocket launch party you had today," the message reads. "Sounded like it was a blowout."
I clench my jaw. My fist tightens around the communicator until the screen nearly breaks.
The Vitruvian couldn't be behind this, could he?
I take a deep breath. Regardless of the cause, one thing is clear: whoever did this is due for some major payback.
Chapter 6: Work Culture
The Cog
“It is I! The one you’ve all been waiting for!” the Vitruvian says, standing behind a pulpit.
As I make my way toward the middle of a crowd of people I take in a deep breath, then smile at Lin. We’ve arrived about ten minutes late. As it happens, we’re also right on time.

“We as a collective are standing on the edge of reality’s final horizon,” the Vitruvian continues, his voice like the roar of a lion. “It is about to be a new age! We must push the collective’s conscious reason to its limit! We must decide what we will become! And, in so doing, we must be cautious!”
Lin brushes her arm by mine. My face goes red, even though there’s nothing to be embarrassed about. In a crowd like this, I don’t think anybody notices.

The crowd is crammed into a room which is to double as a dance floor and dining area. We’re packed together tight. As for how the organizers plan to pull off everything they have planned in such a small space, I have no clue.

“Finding oneself is so hard. What are we? Why are we? What should we become?” The Vitruvian pauses, letting a hush fall over the crowd. “The actor of fundamental substance is one of understanding. In my view: the deepest reason of existence is reason itself!”

The crowd is enraptured by the Vitruvian’s sermon. The stage he stands on is a sheet of white marble, placed at the front of the room. The Vitruvian is dressed in a pure white suit to match. He also is wearing a pure black cape, which is of much darker material than anything I’ve seen before. It swallows all light, letting nothing escape. Above him hangs a sweeping holographic display, and behind him looms a statue. This statue is of a large boulder, held on the precipice of a steep slope. Finally, to the Vitruvian’s side is an object hidden under a tarp.

“The monsters we face are deep, dark, and eternal,” the Vitruvian continues. He causes his cape to wave with a subtle twirl of his torso. “They’re good at morphing. Hiding. But they’re always there. We’ve collectively been sleeping on this. They will never go away. They will continue to eat at us if we do not learn to destroy them.”

All the advertisements claim the Vitruvian is about to unveil a masterpiece tonight, and I believe them. While this is the first time I’ve seen the Vitruvian in person, it’s undeniable how otherworldly he really is. His complexion is porcelain. His person is defined by soft and delicate features.  A deep, dark brown sits at the center of his eyes, and his hair is equally dark. It’s gelled into two steeples, which sit on each side of his head.

When I’ve seen pictures of him on TV or in photos, I never thought they were entirely authentic. I figured they must’ve been edited or airbrushed somehow. I no longer believe that. The whole room is caught under some unknown spell that he cast and seems to bend to his whim.

The holographic display begins to play footage from over the island of New Vinci. The ocean is presented as a churning dark froth, and our island is just a speck of light amid it. The Vitruvian strides toward the tarped object beside him, taking slow and measured steps. The room gives oohs and ahs, including Lin.

The hall we’re standing in is for the Foucault Art Gallery. Grand Corinthian pillars hold up the ceiling, which is covered in paintings of the stars in the heavens that rival the Sistine Chapel. Stained glass windows stretch from the floor to the edges of the ceiling, as if to try touching heaven. Yet, everybody’s attention is down here, on the Vitruvian’s tarp.

“Mankind effectively has all the powers of the gods,” the Vitruvian says. He speaks in a soft voice, but my ears ring from the speakers being set to the maximum possible volume. “And yet… We still must die. Why? In light of our struggles, today I will reveal to you all my latest masterpiece. The source of catharsis. The source of salvation!”
The Vitruvian unveils the tarp.
“I give you… The Overman!”

The crowd breaks out in cheers and applause. I join in. To be honest though, the piece is sort of ugly. It features the figure of a man with his arms and legs outstretched into the shape of an X, and it’s painted in blood red. The man’s figure is warped out of proportion, to perfectly fit into a set box inscribed within a circle.

“I have achieved in the Overman what the great Leonardo failed to, with his sketches of the Vitruvian man!” the Vitruvian cries. “I have attained the perfect man! A man who is both circle and square!”
The room is ablaze with whooping and flash photography. The Vitruvian outstretches his arms, mimicking the X-shape of the man in his painting and soaking in all the praise.
“Some may decry my art as artificial,” the Vitruvian says. “To them, I say this: for humanity, the artificial is only natural.”

There’s a fresh round of praise doused on the Vitruvian. I scratch my head. Personally, I don’t see what the hype is about. The linework and colors are aggressive and clash. The cheering is just getting annoying.
“Is he trolling us?” I say with a snort.
“It definitely looks like a troll,” Lin says with a laugh, then a smile.
I squint to look at the picture again, then laugh with her. She has a point. The figure in the picture has a squashed troll figure. Impressively impish.

I shift uncomfortably in our spot. Did my laugh sound too weird? We’re mashed in between a bunch of people and are very close to each other. I want to impress Lin so much, and I can feel the connection building between us. She’s so soft. Gentle. Also, there’s a spice to her that’s hard to place.

But my mind is also in a bunch of places right now. At some point tonight, I’m supposed to rendezvous with the Machine and Turtle-Dove. What will I do then? Ultimately, saving the day is my sacred duty. Tonight though, I kind of just want it to be me and Lin.
I glance at Lin. While the Vitruvian has been covering my dead air, I can tell she thinks it’s weird how spacy I’m being.
I rub my temples.
“What’s wrong?” asks Lin.
“Sorry,” I say. “My head gets yanked in a million different places. Especially in crowds like this. I disassociate. I feel a lot like a ghost in the machine lately. You know the feeling?”
Lin bites her lip and nods. Her eyes are wide. I can’t quite tell if she thinks I’m insane, or if there’s something she wants to tell me.
She looks at her feet.

“Yeah,” she says, her voice soft. “Sometimes I feel that way too. When I get stuck and go into a dark place, I try talking to my friends. ‘Oh Lin,’ they say. ‘It’s all just part of growing up. It’s all in your head.’ I guess it sort of helps, but…”

She gazes into my eyes. They’re sparkling, but there’s also a darkness there. They remind me of the surface of a frozen lake. I draw the memory from a blizzardy night when Jack Frost and Father Christmas were going at it.
I’ve never seen Lin look more beautiful than tonight. I’ve never seen her look so sad.
“Hey, do you want to see something cool?” I say, trying to change the subject.
I crouch down to pull Bit-Bot out of my backpack. I cup him between my hands as I switch him on. He leaps from my hands and I watch as he begins to waddle across the floor.
Lin scrunches her nose.
“Uh, are you sure that thing is safe in this crowd?” she says.
“I guess we’ll find out,” I say with a snicker.
The crowd around us erupts with a few yelps and groans as people have to step over my little robot.
“Bit-Bot has cameras and LIDAR. He’ll be fine.”
I whip out my phone to show Lin the map and footage Bit-Bot has of the area.
“Maybe he’ll find something cool,” I say. “Might also make for a good guide.”

In the back of my mind, I also know that Bit-Bot needs to be on the lookout for any possible threats tonight. Something weird is going to happen – my precognition has been buzzing at me all night. I need to be ready.
Lin grins.
“You need a guide my guy?” she says.
She grabs me by the hand and we’re dashing away from the crowd, down into the hall.
“We’re gonna miss the rest of the talk!” I exclaim, while trying to make sure I don’t trip over myself. “He was just about to do Q&A!”
Lin laughs.
“You really want to sit around for that old bird?”

We move further and deeper through the art gallery until the sound of the crowd has all but drowned out. We’re walking side by side. I’m trying to catch my breath. So is she. Despite her having taken my breath away, somewhere inside of myself is oddly at rest.

These are still waters. Friendly waters. My head starts searching for the right thing to say, to try wading in. I wait a moment, but nothing good comes to my recognition. Stupid precognition! Honestly: if there was ever a time I needed it to bail me out, it’s now.
“How you liking life so far?” Lin asks, her eyes scanning the paintings in the exhibit.

The pieces around us are mostly abstract. This section is focused on warmly colored lobes, configured in circular patterns. I can barely make out what any of it is supposed to be. Total enigma. But, I can tell that Lin is into them.
“Good,” I say.
“Only good? Wow!” she says, feigning excitement.
I laugh and shake my head.

“Okay, I’ve been a little stressed lately,” I say. “Dr. Skully wants me to start assigning tasks for one of my design projects. They’re going to other people in the group. But, I’m just not sure, you know? I don’t like meetings.”
Lin gives an awkward smile.
“I thought you did a good job with the documentation you sent the other week,” she says. “Was a big help.”
I nod with my eyes on the linoleum floor tiles.
“I just know how to do basic corrections and fixes,” I say. “Useful I guess, but not all that important. Also: I don’t want to be stuck leading projects. I’d hate that.”
Lin laughs. “What do you want?”
The question hits hard, even in the face of the hard hits I’ve taken this past week. I look at Lin. I look back to the floor. She has a point. What do I want in life?
“It’s been going better,” I say, trying to sound positive. “Just need to take more initiative, I guess. Anyway, how about you? I thought your presentation the other day was awesome!”
Lin shakes her head.
“Oh, don’t even get me started,” she says, giving another laugh. It’s weaker this time.
“What do you mean?” I say, scratching my head. “Everything coming from your side of the group is amazing. Honest. I’ve never come close to doing anything as good.”
Lin’s face contorts, going from awkward to annoyed.
“I don’t want to talk about work,” she says.
“I thought everything was going well for you though,” I say.
She nods.
“I don’t want to talk about work, okay?” she repeats.
She turns away to study one of the art pieces. It’s a green blob which looks like it’s being swallowed by a larger white blob.
“So, you like art right?” I say.
Lin nods, still studying the piece intensely.
“What do you think of the art here?” I persist.
“A lot of it is really good,” she says. “A lot of it isn’t. Regardless: lots of pieces to consider, even in a single piece.”
“What’s your favorite?” I ask.
“Maybe this one,” she says. “Still deciding. I really like the abstract, though. Always a fun puzzle, and rarely is there a wrong answer.”
I nod. “It’s a green egg,” I say, pointing at the blob.
Lin snorts.
“Green eggs and ham,” I continue.
Lin squints then puckers her lips, as if she just ate something really sour.
“Definitely a ham in there,” she says.
I chuckle.
“You like to work on abstract art as a hobby?” I ask.
Lin nods.
“What type of designs have you worked on?” I continue.
Lin gives a sly smirk. “I can’t just describe it,” she says. “It’s abstract.”
“You can try.”
Lin shakes her head. “Can you describe the way that warmth feels? Can you describe the color purple?”
My face twists. Quite the puzzle.
“I, uh… I can give it a wavelength,” I say. I pause. “Can you show me?”
Lin grins and her eyes go to the floor, shading her eyes with her lashes. She pulls out her phone.
“Finally, you’re on my wavelength,” she says.
She holds her phone out to me, using her thumb to flip through various pictures of paintings she’s made. I come closer to her as she does this.
“These are really good. I really like that one!” I say, stopping her on a picture with a spray of rainbow.
The rainbow twists in and out of itself. Lin’s eyes light up.
“I really like that one too,” she says. “Took me a whole weekend to put it together.”
“It definitely looks like a lot of passion went into it,” I say, nodding. “Reminds me of rainbow skittles.”
This time, Lin forgets to laugh at my dumb joke. Dang it.
Lin closes her phone, now beaming, then looks at me. “What about you? Any interesting hobbies?”
I give a sheepish grin.
“Uh… tech?”
“Yes, of course. Beep boop bop. George needs a battery.”
I laugh. “I also like to do MMA.”
Lin smirks. “Still technically battery.”
She takes a quick glance at one of the bruises on my arm but says nothing.
“So, MMA,” she says, “tell me more.”

I begin giving her details of the various awesome practice sessions I’ve had during my weekends, as we make our way from the hall of abstract paintings and into a hall of illusions. An applause echoes softly from somewhere, barely audible over the sound of our steps.
“The Q&A session must’ve ended,” I say. “I guess the dinner should be starting soon.”
Lin runs down the hall, clearly distracted.
“Hey, look at this,” she says. “Trippy.”
It’s a set of mirrors within mirrors, which are configured in such a way as to almost move in and out of one another. I rub my eyes, beginning to feel like I’m going cross-eyed.
“Ooh, look over here!” Lin says, her attention now on an entirely different piece.
I force myself out of my mesmerized daze and follow Lin. She’s studying a painting that features spirals within spirals.
“I’m starting to get a headache,” I groan, rubbing my eyes even harder.
She reminds me too much of my mom.
“Oh my God, look at this art that Byrd made,” Lin says, having jumped to yet another painting.
I instantly burst into laughter.
It’s a rip-off of the old lady and young lady illusion. Only, it’s constructed from very shaky and scattershot linework.
“For all of Byrd’s supposed genius, definitely a bit stiff,” I say, inspecting the painting closer.

There are a few addendums to the painting, such as a chimera and a bird-man hybrid. Most of the painting is in harsh reds and blacks. These contrasts only serve to detract from the main illusion on display though.
“The Vitruvian was always one of my biggest heroes growing up,” I say. “But, I guess the myth really was just a myth after all. And, it’s not even the painting: his speech was a farse too.”
Lin shrugs and gives me a playful pat on the back.
“Hey, you know what they say,” she says, “never meet your heroes.”
Somebody clears their throat from behind us. A sudden jolt moves through me and I feel blood drain from my face. My precognition beams me a vision of who it is, but I can hardly believe it.
I shift. I turn. It’s the Vitruvian, flashing his thousand watt smile.
How did he just appear? Did he hear us speaking about him?
“Why, hello there,” says the Vitruvian, with a fine baritone to his voice.
“Hi,” I say sheepishly.
“Hi,” Lin says after me, feigning a playful wave.
This guy is setting off all my alarms. Lin’s body goes stiff, and I can tell she feels just as awkward as me.
“Have you enjoyed the illusion I created?” the Vitruvian asks.
I give a slow nod. The Vitruvian clears his throat again and tilts his head to the ceiling. What could be up there? I’m guessing ceiling fan.

“I call it the Cogito,” the Vitruvian says, now resting his right hand on his chin. His fingers nimbly rap along his cheekbones, as though he were trying to play them as an instrument. “In reference, of course, to the phrase ‘cogito ergo sum’. I think. Therefore… I am!”
I give a thin smile. He gives one in return.
“You paint this all yourself?” Lin asks.
The Vitruvian gives a firm nod.
“That this is my handiwork, let there be no doubt,” the Vitruvian says, now moving toward Lin. “I love my craft. Here are the real mysteries: what is my motive, and how do all the pieces connect?”
He then grabs Lin by the hand and grins so wide that his large canine teeth are showing.
“Oh, where are my manners?” the Vitruvian says.
He plants a kiss on the back of Lin’s hand, and Lin lets him. She’s blushing. Why is she blushing!?
“I must have you know, I am a gentleman of the first order,” the Vitruvian says, with an odd rumble in the back of his throat. “I am a gentleman to end all gentlemen.”
He seems to put on a fake British accent. Or is it a speech impediment? There’s a sudden chiming of a clock, from some far-off place.
“Ah, time to feast!” the Vitruvian says, letting go of Lin’s hand.
He turns away, his cape swooshing behind him. I swear I hear Lin give a swoon. But, when I look over to her, her face is blank. Maybe I’m just hearing things.
“Good timing too!” he continues. “I’ve worked up an appetite.”
The Vitruvian disappears into a dark hall. It’s just me and Lin again.
“What was that?” I say.
The echoes of my voice sound more forceful than I expect.
“Uh, no clue,” Lin says with a laugh.
The Machine

I’m standing in the back corner of a lavish dining area. People are everywhere and keep trying to take pictures of me. At any other point in my career, I’d oblige my adoring fans. Today though, I can’t take my eyes off my phone. All the chatting, cheering, and chorusing is secondary to the stress coursing through me.
“It’ll all be fine,” I mutter to myself for what is probably the hundredth time this week.

I scroll past yet another photo of my rocket explosion. It’s been nonstop coverage these past few days. Constant dogging and logging of my mistakes. I scroll past an article entitled Everman Tech or Everman Blech.
“That’s not even clever,” I growl to myself.

My one reprieve is knowing that all this coverage has taken attention from Byrd’s big week. I’ll never let him make me feel weak! Everybody remains entranced by me and the dozen plates I’m spinning, even if they all seem to be spinning out of control.

I sigh. To be fair to Byrd, maybe I’m being too harsh. Too hypercompetitive. We’re good buddies at times, and this whole art gallery showing is his big day. But then, he has always been so hard to trust.

My eyes laser in on another article entitled Doped Blackmarket Brainchips: Digital Drug Addiction? and a churning forms in my gut. I’ve been seeing more articles like this lately. Especially over the past day. So far, a widespread issue with blackmarket brainchips only seems to be a rumor. But, from anonymous tips I’ve been receiving from police, it might be more than that.

Moreover, the cyborg issue has only gotten worse, and I’m worried it’s all connected somehow. Cog and my staff have encountered new issues and confirmed that blackmarket brainchips are using Everman Technology designs.
How though? Where am I being hijacked? What am I doing wrong?
There’s a round of cheers and applause as Byrd walks through the crowd, on the other side of the dining area. My muscles tighten and my eyes narrow.
To calm myself, I check my communicator for any messages from Cog. According to his anonymous tip, some sort of threat could happen any time tonight. We need to be ready.

Nothing from him, oddly. Then again, maybe I should just try to enjoy the night. Police have already been alerted. Byrd always runs a tight ship and puts on a good show. I think Cog even said he’ll be hanging out with one of his friends for tonight’s dance.
I smirk to myself. Dancing with a friend, eh?
With everything going on, everybody deserves a good time.
“Everman, there you are!” somebody says, chuckling like they’re God’s perfect chucklehead. “I’ve been looking all over for you!”
My face contorts. Unmistakably Escorgier. Reluctantly, I turn to find him with a greedy gleam in his eyes. Despite being my board chairman, he constantly looks like he needs a chair thrown his way.
“What’s wrong, cat got your tongue?” Escorgier asks, giving a playful punch at my armor.

He immediately winces and pulls his little fist away, cradling it in his other hand. Tough as he may want to play things, he’s about a foot shorter than me. And I’m the Machine, for crying out loud. Who does he think he is, trying to mess with me?

“Sorry, just checking for any messages from my sidekick,” I say. Escorgier rolls his eyes, but I continue. “News is nuts too – I just gotta stay on top of things. I’m really worried the company has been hijacked. All sorts of weird reports and incidents involving our quantum chips and brain computer interfaces. To be honest, I’m also worried about tonight.”
Escorgier clucks his tongue. “We’re at a party right now, why talk business?”
I want to slump my shoulders but I force myself to stand tall.
“I’m worried that my technology is being put on the blackmarket to hurt people,” I say.
“My?” Escorgier snorts. “My, my, my… You sold most of your stake, friendo.”
I bite my tongue. He acts as if I haven’t had that emphasized to me by my friends and lawyers a million times this week.
“Anyway,” says Escorgier, leading me into the center of the dining area, “the Vitruvian wants to have dinner with us.”

Escorgier takes a seat at a table. My eyes go wide – the Vitruvian almost never wants to meet these days. Nevertheless, I find myself standing in front of a seat I don’t remember reserving, which has my name on it.
“Hey Hugo,” Boris says from a seat on the other side of the table. He shifts about, then scratches his bush of a beard.
Boris? What is he doing here?
I go to say hi, but Boris is already chugging down a beer. He gives a resounding burp, and I take my seat. I feel the seat is straining beneath my massive frame, but it’ll have to do.
“You planning anything for boating season?” Boris asks.
I shake my head and start filling my plate with some of the bread and vegetables left out as appetizers.
“I’ve been boat shopping,” Boris continues. He gives an enormous belch, and I can smell halitosis all the way across from him. “I want a huge boat. Like a… Like a yacht, ya know?”
Boris spreads his arms way out, nearly knocking his glass over. He swiftly grabs at it, then takes another swig.
“You seen Denny’s yacht?” Boris says.
I don’t think I have. I don’t even know who Denny is.
“It’s huge, like a giant floating football,” he says. He pauses. “Uh… Stadium. Yeah.”
Boris elbows Escorgier, nearly knocking him from his seat, then gives a broad gesture in my general direction.
I remember nights with Boris as being less of a bore. Then again, I’m generally drunk when I’m with him. Tonight, I’m not in the mood to drink.
“We could all play golf on it!” Boris slams a fist on the table, and Escorgier nearly tips over again. “I’m tellin’ ya, my farm and my fam have been doing doggone good this year! I’m gettin’ a boat!”
I wince.

“The stock is crashing though, Boris, and you’re currently our biggest shareholder,” I say. “This really isn’t the best time to be buying boats. We’ve got a company to keep afloat. We can’t risk having your stake at stake.”
Boris gives me a funny look. Then it flickers away, and he gives another belch.
“Yeehaw!” Boris shouts, before grabbing more bread. “Eating good, eating good!”
I’m about to press harder on Boris when Escorgier interrupts, his fingers intermeshing into a sausage web.
“You sure you don’t want to start reconsidering your own assets?” Escorgier asks. “The ground is shifting beneath our feet as we speak. And, what way can you hope to profit from a nonprofit?”
I clench my jaw firmly.
“It profits the soul,” I say.
Escorgier gives a hoarse, “Wha?” then whinnies like a horse.
“Tax breaks? It’s the tax breaks, right?” Escorgier says, rubbing tears from his eyes.
I say nothing.
“Clever man, Everman,” Escorgier continues. “That said, if you really want some fun funneling funds, I have a few –.”
“It’s not about the number of zeroes,” I say. “The biotech division needs to be run ethically. It can’t be made commercial. If we do that, I don’t know if I could live with myself.”
Escorgier gives a wide smile. Too wide. He licks his chops, then takes a chomp into a carrot.

“With our quantum chip breakthroughs, we also have something very rare,” I continue. “If luck permits, I want to expand the nonprofit into serving the community. I feel like the wealth disparity is getting worse. We need better equality, ecology, technology, sociology… Shelters. That sort of thing. It’s what Polka would do!”
Escorgier’s eyes go dark as the few hairs from his combover manage to blot them out.
“Shelters are for dogs,” Escorgier sneers. “And Polka? He’s half-dead.”
Escorgier is about to take another bite of his carrot, then stops. I’m staring him down.

I could punt this runt into the Sun, easy. So easy. My muscles are begging me to give it a whirl. It’d just take a moment to show this Escorgier jerk who’s boss – to make him lick my balls. He can tell too. My fury is radiating through the air. If the world was just a little less civilized, all of these lies would’ve had Escorgier torn asunder.

“Anybody want to go to the strip club when this is over?” Boris says, leaning back in his chair while picking his nose. “I’m sick of waiting for this Vivian guy. Name a place, and we’ll go. I’m a VIP pretty much everywhere, thanks to pops.”
I raise an eyebrow, while trying to force myself to cool down. Boris starts a new chorus of burps.
“Row, row, row your boat, gently down the stream,” Boris says in burp, “merrily, merrily, merrily, merrily. Life is but a dream!”
He’s about to start again when the divine finally intervenes.
“It is I, the Vitruvian!”
At the very least, it’s somebody who thinks they’re the divine. And, to be fair to the Vitruvian: there’s only one man quite like him.

I stand from my chair to meet the Vitruvian, looming over him. As usual, the Vitruvian feels the need to subtly stand on his toes, to get an extra half an inch of height. He attempts to stare into my soul with that charcoal gaze of his.
I grip his hand. He grips mine tight. I grip his tighter, until I hear his knuckles crack a bit. His gaze withers and the smile fades.
“Hey Qbert,” I say with a chuckle.
Boris roars with laughter from behind me. “Ha! He called him Qbert!”
The Vitruvian rolls his eyes. “Cute, right on cue. I’ve told you before: only call me by Byrd.”
He mutters under his breath.
“Don’t sulk Culver, it’s uncool,” I say, still chuckling.
The Vitruvian brushes away from me with a huff.
“Come on Viddy, I’m only playing around,” I say.
“I know,” the Vitruvian says, in a voice barely audible.
Escorgier rises to greet the Vitruvian.
“Great Vitruvian!” Escorgier says, raising his hands in the air like a brainless automaton. “The man with the photograph memory!”
The Vitruvian takes his seat, ignoring Escorgier’s advance. I also retake mine.
“Camera memory. Video memory,” the Vitruvian says in a steely voice. “Don’t ever call it photographic memory. Get. It. Right.”
Escorgier sinks back into his seat.
“So,” Escorgier says, rubbing his hands together gingerly. “Let’s talk business.”
As he says this, a robotic waiter places plates of noodles at each of our spots at the table. It also places down a bowl of condiments and mustard seeds.
“We’ll all have water, waiter,” the Vitruvian says, holding out his glass.
The robot is an egg shaped rover, and a robotic arm retracts out from its center. A nozzle at its end-effector sprays into our glasses until they’re full.
“Excellent,” the Vitruvian says.
I try to sort out whether he’s making an egg pun as he tries to discretely wipe specks of water from his face.

The Byrd Enterprises waiter could clearly use some work. It is only serving one meal tonight, and its articulation is jerky. The stuff Everman Technologies works on is clearly better. But I know I can’t say anything, or else Byrd will flip his lid.

“Vitruvian,” Escorgier says with a squeak, not even touching his noodles. “I – I was wondering whether you wanted to start talking business. As you know, Everman Technologies has been struggling with its nuclear reactor business, biotech business, electronics business…”
Escorgier pauses and looks at me. “What exactly is our specialty again?”
“Everything,” I say.
“Everything, Everman?”
I give a stiff nod. I’m not liking the attitude from Escorgier or where this is going.
“Ah yes, thanks for the reminder,” Escorgier says, looking smug. “Anyway, a little birdy told me that Byrd Enterprises has been doing really well lately.”
Escorgier glances at Boris and jerks his head in an awkward gesture. Boris gives a gag, having been caught while shoving a waterfall of noodles down his throat.
“Yes, mmrff,” Boris finally manages, struggling to talk through a noodle-and-hair hybrid of a beard. “You rolling in cash amiright? Packing a lot of dough Qbert?”
Escorgier glares at Boris, then clasps his hands as though he’s about to pray.
“Please excuse him,” Escorgier says.
Boris slurps his noodles up, then burps again.
“Yeah, excuse me,” says Boris.
Escorgier’s face goes white.
“Look sir,” Escorgier says, “we were thinking we could—.”
“Everyone quiet,” the Vitruvian snaps, putting his head in his hands. A hush falls over the table. “Everman. I only want to talk to Everman.”

The Vitruvian then looks at me as though I’m the most important thing in existence. Flattering. But then, I didn’t like what I was hearing from Escorgier. I hold back a frown. Escorgier and the board aren’t trying to strike deals behind my back, are they?
“What did you think of the unveil?” the Vitruvian asks.
I look across the room to the ugly red blotch of a painting the Vitruvian showed off. I look back to the Vitruvian.
“It’s alright,” I say. “Name is a bit on the nose though, don’t you think?”

The Vitruvian snickers. “You don’t like me calling my work the Overman, Everman?” He gives a smile that has a spice of spite to it. “I thought about calling it the Übermensch, but I’m too nice to completely steal Nietzsche’s niche.”

We glare at each other for a moment. Then, we burst out laughing. Our laughs grow ever louder, filling the dining room. I stop as we risk overpowering all other sounds, and I’ve made my standing clear.
“Phew… Man… Hugo… man!” the Vitruvian says, regathering himself as we come down from the high. “I didn’t realize until now how much I missed this intermingling of ours.”
I nod. “We do make a solid pair. Me, being the greatest hero in New Vinci. And you, being the greatest hero in the world. These days I’ve got Cog, but…”
The Vitruvian almost seems to sneer at that. But, maybe it’s just a veneer.
“We do share quite the history, don’t we?” the Vitruvian says.

I give a chuckle, then take in a fresh breath of air. “Remember back when they were still building this place? This was all just forest, mountain, and ocean. I still go to the nature preserves to remind myself of how far we’ve come. Granted, I also love to reconnect with mother nature and all that.”
“The artificial bedrock developed by Polka was definitely an underrated miracle,” the Vitruvian says, looking off in the distance wistfully. “None of this would be anything without that.”
The Vitruvian takes a sip of his water. He drinks slowly. Cautiously.

“On the subject of none of this being anything…” he says. The hairs stand up on the back of my neck as he glares at me. “That day when the hydrogen bomb was about to be launched on the capital, all of this… All these grand dreams of utopia that we talk about… It all nearly went up in smoke, didn’t it?”
I clear my throat, and my suit begins to feel suffocating.
“I get it,” I say, “you saved the world from the H-bomber. You don’t have to rub it in.”
“You should’ve been there,” the Vitruvian says, with a shadowy smirk.
“Look, how was I supposed to know to take that threat seriously? The public was told that all nuclear capabilities had been disposed of, when the Global Federation was formed.”

The Vitruvian scowls. “The entire world, and everything we’ve struggled for, was going to be turned to ash! All it was going to take was the press of a button by some mad man! And you were a no show!”
I’m starting to feel dizzy. I expected this night to be tough, but I wasn’t prepared for this.
“I was in the middle of a bunch of other things,” I say. “Honest. I didn’t realize. Besides: you’re the world’s greatest hero now, full-stop.”
I think I see the Vitruvian’s eyes go blotchy. Are those tears? He wipes his face with a napkin before I can discern for sure.
“You’ll never know how hard that day was,” the Vitruvian says. “And I’ll never let you. The things I was forced to do…”
“Look, we need to move forward. It was a mistake. Stop talking about the past, okay? We’re futurists, after all.”
The Vitruvian smiles again. “Yes. My camera memory has made me into a great futurist. I can forgive. But, keep in mind: I can never forget.”
His eyes go darker still as he picks up his knife and turns it near his face.
“We might’ve stopped the H-bomber and Armageddon,” he says. “But, the price was Esther the Athenian… Esther the Aetherial…”
It’s my turn to fight back tears. Why did he have to bring this up? And why here? Why now? Why not some other place, some other time?
“I’m sorry about what happened to the Athenian, I really am,” I say. “If you want to finally talk about it, I’m here.”
The Vitruvian bites his lip and shakes his head.
