“The Athenian was definitely an amazing soul,” I say. “The smartest of us too, for sure. I still spend nights wondering what happened. What went wrong?”
“I loved her,” whispers the Vitruvian. “That was my first mistake. And so, she left us. She’s now some other place.”
I can’t help but raise an eyebrow at this. What exactly is that supposed to mean? The way he says things, I often feel like he’s saying several things at once.
“Really though, what happened?” I press further.
“You should’ve been there.” The Vitruvian looks at Boris, then Escorgier. “Even if I thought you had the guts to know, I know that they wouldn’t.”
A silence falls over the table.
“Anybody want to talk about my plan for a golfing yacht?” Boris pipes up. “Yahtzee!”
Everybody stays quiet, but Boris somehow still laughs.
“Haha, get it?” Boris says, waving his hands in the air. “Yahtzee? Yacht? Ya?”
“Nobody gets it,” the Vitruvian says, his eyes downcast.

“It beats what he’s planning on spending his money on,” says Boris, pointing at me. “Other day he was telling me he wants to waste a bunch of cash on shelters made of food. Like, woof. Can you believe that?”
“I was talking about food shelters,” I explain.
“Exactly,” says Boris. “Now, I ain’t no instruction worker, but I’ve heard the tale about the three piggies, okay? A food shelter ain’t gonna work Hugo!”
The Vitruvian shoots me a desperate look.
“How’d he get his money again?” the Vitruvian asks.
“We’re all very savvy investors here,” Escorgier cuts in, “and I agree that Hugo’s moves have been dicey lately.”
“It’s what has to be done,” I grunt. “Wealth inequality is at an all-time high right now. Also, I believe poverty is getting worse, even if it’s subtle.”
The Vitruvian snorts. Escorgier copies him.
Boris burps.
“This is the most prosperous time in history,” says the Vitruvian. “Suffering is a choice at this point.”
I furrow my brow. “Look, I’m just saying, we could be doing better.”
“And I’m saying we don’t need to. I, at the very least, am content with keeping my charitable contributions as is.”
“I’m going to buy a new golf club,” Boris butts in.
I sigh, relenting to the attempt by Boris to change the subject. I can smell in the air that the Vitruvian is readying for a verbal strike, and I don’t want to deal with him.
“Okay,” I say. “Like, a golf club golf club? Or, like a club club?”
Boris pauses, his face twisting in confusion and consternation.
“Both,” he says.
“How’s Cog, by the way?” the Vitruvian says, his eyes laser-focused on me. “How much you pay him?”
I shift in my seat. It’s extra wobbly right now. “He’s a volunteer. I thought about making him my ward, but that’s just weird am I right?”
I’m hoping Boris will laugh at the attempt for a joke, but he’s dead silent. I guess he’s finally had too much to drink.
“And yet–,” the Vitruvian begins.

I cut him off. “Cog is great. That’s why I gave him his cool sidekick name.” The Vitruvian gives a groan but I plow ahead. “The name Cog is his cognomen, if you will. This might sound funny but, way back when, I thought that you and I could’ve been a Machine and Cog. That would’ve been fun, right Viddy?”
The Vitruvian shudders, clearly put off by the very notion.
“Viddy and the Orange,” he says. “I wanted us to be Viddy and the Orange.”
It’s my turn to give a groan. I’ve told Viddy a million times: I’m known as the Big Tangerine, not an orange. What kind of fruitcake calls themselves an orange?
“Long story short, Cog is a solid adapter,” I continue. “Can we get back to talking about golf clubs?”

“Let’s stay on the subject actually,” the Vitruvian says, resting his elbows on the table. “This Cog guy really strikes me as something special. Did Everman Technologies build that gadget I see him swinging around?”
The Vitruvian’s face develops a tinge of something beastly. Angry. Fierce.

“The fluxion-drive? No,” I say hesitantly. “Like I said, he’s a big help. I’d rather have him out of the spotlight, though. He’s young, you know? Also, Viddy: this isn’t your business, our discussion should focus on other things.”

The Vitruvian nods slowly and starts playing with his silverware. “I’ve been diving deep into philosophy again. The Philosopher’s Stone. You mention the being upset by world’s problems… I think it could be the solution.”
Oh great. This again. Whenever the Vitruvian starts talking about the Philosopher’s Stone, he almost never shuts up.
“Viddy, we’ve been through this, over and over again,” I say, “even if it’s somehow real, who cares? Let’s keep it light.”
“I’ve tried everything,” the Vitruvian rasps. “I’ve even tried squaring the circle, ad infinitum. I’ve tried new ways to unveil the secret, but to no avail.”
The Vitruvian’s eyes are wild now. Veracious.

“All my life I’ve chased the chaste lifestyle,” he mutters. “I’ve chased the dream of the perfect sphere. Yet, even with my camera memory, it remains a chimera! Oh, the ein Stein! The one Stone! The Philosopher’s Stone! Why do you evade me!?”
The Vitruvian is standing in his chair, shaking his hand in the air. His hand has taken the shape of a claw. Who is he yelling at? Does he even know?
“Viddy,” I say softly, “are you okay?”
The Vitruvian sits back down, acting as though nothing has happened.
“Please pass the mustard seeds,” he says.
Escorgier passes them, brimming with devious delight. Does Escorgier not notice? Does he not care? Does nobody care about what just happened?
“I told you to keep it light,” I say in a low voice, nearly at a loss for words.
The Vitruvian is sprinkling mustard seeds into his food.
“Everybody is so obsessed with the light,” he says. “Its wavelength, its intensity, its speed…”

His eyes seem to go pitch black and their reflection pervades the edges of his cup. “So limiting… Has anybody ever stopped and considered the speed of dark? The speed of shadow? It’s infinite. If I were to cast my shadow upon the moon, there’s no limit to how fast it could move.”
Okay, he’s officially nuts. I clear my throat.
“Have you been seeing a therapist?” I say.
The Vitruvian shakes his head.
“It might help,” I continue.
The Vitruvian shrugs.
“I just feel like I see you diving into these dark spirals sometimes,” I say. “You can think positive, you know?”
“I try,” says the Vitruvian. “But this world… It’s draining me.”
“Oh, come on Viddy. You’re like ten years younger than me. You’re not allowed to complain yet.”
“Fifteen years.”
“Ah, ok. No need to rub it in.”
The Vitruvian gives a weak laugh, then raises his glass to his lips. Somehow it slips and hits the floor.
“Oh great,” mumbles the Vitruvian. “Another mistake.”
“It’s fine,” I say. “They’ll clean it up, and mistakes happen even to the best of us.”
I pass him my glass. “Here, drink from this.”
The Vitruvian grimaces. “Germs,” he says.

I laugh and take back my glass. “You know, I get existential myself sometimes. I guess I don’t want people to just remember me for a bunch of commercials and magazine covers. I want something more. I sort of want to be remembered as that philosopher king thing I read about.”
The Vitruvian gives a slight frown, staring off into space.
“Viddy?”
“It’s nothing.”

“Look: I know you like to organize and tabulate everything. But sometimes you must live and forget the past. I like to think everything has a reason, but we don’t always need to know the reason. In many ways, our ignorance is our privilege.”
The Vitruvian grins. “You don’t like reason? Odd… Ah. A Kantian, are you?”
I return the grin.
“With how advanced everything is getting, I really think we need to emphasize our ideas and ethics. We’re looking at a world beyond the material.”
“But aren’t you called the Machine for a reason? Isn’t the material all there is?”
“I’ll always have the better stuff than you Viddy,” I say, holding my smirk, “and I promise you, it’s not about the stuff.”
The Vitruvian winces. “But without stuff, what is there, hmm?”
I groan. I scowl. “Look: you keep this up, and I’ll flip the table. I’m dead serious.”
The Vitruvian seems unphased by my iron ire. He places his hands in a steeple beneath his chin and raps his fingers together.
“I used to be annoyed by your posturing as king, leaving me to just be prince,” he says in a hush. “These days though, I’ve come to terms with being the prince.”
Escorgier and Boris keep their heads down, wanting no part in this. At this point, even I am ready to throw in the towel. Holding a conversation with the Vitruvian is borderline impossible.
I am about to stand from my chair when I’m interrupted by the blare of the speakers within the dining room. The room fills with a techno bastardization of Mozart.
“Ooh! The dance is starting,” the Vitruvian says clapping his hands together.
He then glares at me. As I’ve already had to do with him many times tonight, I dish back what he’s dishing out. I also clench my jaw for extra measure.
“Let’s dance Kant,” the Vitruvian says, jumping from his seat at the table.
At least, I think he uses the word Kant. However, it almost sounds like he says something else.

I’m about to snap at the Vitruvian, but the Vitruvian has already begun a broken attempt at breakdancing. His limbs flail, and he gesticulates back and forth at the waist. As he spins about his cape flaps wildly, like an injured bird wing. He points a finger into the air. It isn’t his middle finger, is it? He moves too fast for me to make it out.
The Vitruvian pulls another spin and makes a strange face. I can’t tell if he’s trying to mimic the sly snout of a fox, or if he’s had a hernia.
“Suit,” I say. “Unfurl my cape. I’ve got a dance off.”

There’s a whir as the motors to my suit unroll my cape through a slot in my suit’s backplate. It slides through the slot as smooth as the window to a car. I give  a quick smirk at the glorious streak of red cloth, then stand from my seat. My cape whooshes in a flow behind me as I stomp onto the dance floor with my signature Machine shuffle.
“You might think you have all the moves,” I say to the Vitruvian, dancing toward him, “but I still have a few moves of my own.”
Chapter 7: Getting the Ball Rolling
The Cog
Her hands are on my shoulders and mine on hers. We waltz at the center of the dining area as crappy music plays.

I’ll probably never know why dance music usually sucks so bad. To drown it out, I’m forced to focus deeper on what’s right in front of me. Lin’s face is a painting. I pause to study the fine linework. I realize she doesn’t have much makeup, and somehow she becomes more than fine. I’m drawn to her. I want to kiss her.
But then, how would it feel? How would it go? Would we fuse or fizzle?
The room’s speakers fiddle a the air, the pitch climbing higher. As it begins to pierce our eardrums, I crane my neck toward hers and bring her close. I need to hold onto this moment.
The music begins to settle and Lin unveils her eyes from beneath her eyelids. I’m swimming in a deep sea of blue. There’s a whole other world in there.
“Do you like it?” she asks.
Her voice is sweet, but also a bit high. I guess she needs to overcome the music.
“I really, really like it,” I say. “Tonight is great.”
Our waltz stiffens up a bit and she tilts her head slightly out of my eyeline. The deep sea of her eyes is out of sight.
“What do you actually think about all of this?” she says.
I glimpse at her dress. It is a clean violet streak, glowing such that its outlines meld with the air and floor. My eyes go wide, and I return to her face. She has put on a smile.
“What do you mean?” I say.
“All of this. What does it mean to you?”
I shrug. “Not anything in particular. What about you?”
She gives a sly smile. “Not to put on airs, but I think it’s all air.”
I laugh. She laughs back. Her laugh is insane, and I laugh harder.
“I guess it’s how we choose to define it,” I say. “That’s the vibe I get, anyway. Life is only special if some parts of it are uniquely yours.”
There it is. Those eyes again. It’s a magnetic pull, nigh irresistible.
Maybe I need to get out more.

“I always wondered what it would be like to have somebody feel the world as I feel it,” she says, “or see the world as I see it. Ever been caught in a rainshower and thought how weird it is that each drop that falls was destined to only fall for you?”
I hold back a laugh and watch Lin’s face go red.
“Sorry,” she says. “I just thought—.”
“No – no, I totally get it,” I sputter. “You have no idea how alone I am. I wonder if that’s why each of us are here: to do something that nobody else is able to do.”
Lid’s face fades from red into pink.
“To make links,” I continue, leaning closer as our eyes lock. “To see something in a way nobody else can see it.”
Lin somehow is able to bat me away with her eyelashes. Her eyes go to the side, toward a long picture of the Vitruvian hung on the wall. I snort.

“I’ve always wanted the power to read minds,” she says. “I’ve always thought the little islands of consciousness the universe puts up are so weird. I want to understand what’s underneath. But then… Does that ruin the mystique?”
She stares at me with a wild, catlike gaze.
“If you could have any superpower, what would it be?” she asks as the music picks up pace.
My ears burn. Gotta tread carefully here. I need to keep my Cog thing discrete as possible.
“No idea,” I say.
“Oh really?” Lin says with a wink. Why is she winking? “No power that comes to mind?”
“Uh – super speed,” I spit out.
Lin giggles. “Why that? What would you have to run away from? Or run away to?”
I blow a raspberry.
“Brain fart, I guess,” I say. “Maybe pizza delivery?”
“Pizza?”
“Beats – uh – beats the excuse for the food they have here,” I snicker.
She snickers back.
“You know what?” I say. “We should both get super speed. We should run away together.”
Her eyes go wide. “But where?”
“Anywhere,” I say. I take my hands off her shoulders for a moment and outstretch my arms. “We could see the whole world. Do anything. Be anything.”
“But what would we be?” Lin asks in a hushed tone. “Come to think, do we even know what we are?”
“I’m George Fletcher,” I say, giving a mischevious smirk. “Most fetching man in the galaxy. And you…?”
“All these identities we put on,” Lin says, “all these titles and words… If it were up to me, I’d take on a new name every day, and do whatever served that day’s flight of fancy.”
I snort. “Oh god…”
“You’d learn how to keep up, don’t worry,” she says, tightening her grip on my shoulders. “You’d have super speed, remember?”
I nod. “If it were up to me, I’d spend my life creating things,” I say. “Preferably with other people.”
Lin’s eyes study my face. “We’d figure something out. I like creating too.”
“Would it be you and me? Or, would it be you, me, and the many versions of you and me?”
“Like I said: it’s gonna depend on the day.”

Something bonds together, through these words of ours. How it happens, I can’t say. An energy teases at my mind. My precognition gives me a taste of something from off on a distant horizon. It’s both beautiful and horrible. It’s also a part of me now. I’ve found some kind of nexus, and I can’t imagine it feeling any other way.

So, we dance. We weave in and out of a river of people, synchronizing with the music from above. Sometimes I step on her toes. Sometimes she steps on mine. We’re not great dancers. But then, if we were, this place would feel less like play.
Off in the corner of my eyes, I see the Vitruvian strutting the dance floor like a peacock. The Machine shuffles him around, doing the robot with high intensity.
I smirk.
“What is that?” Lin says.
“Some things defy explanation.”
We lean close again.
“I’m really sorry about the other night,” I say. “It – it was just the wrong time, wrong place.”
Lin shrugs. “It was fine. Ethan was able to keep me company.” She pauses. “What was all that racket about, anyway?”
“I told you: some animals decided to make themselves a nest.”
“You’re lying,” she says, giving me a nudge. “You had way too much noise going on for that to have been a nest.”
I scoff and feign annoyance.
“Maybe I’ll need to take you back there some time and prove it,” I say.
She throws her hair back.
“Maybe you will.”
My phone chirps. I force myself to stop, stumbling into Lin.
“Sorry,” I murmur, opening up my phone

There’s an alert being given off by Bit-Bot. Some weird signal noise is being detected from the other side of the room. I swallow. The signal’s signature matches what the Machine’s people managed to map to the other cyborgs.
I check my feed – it looks like the warning message should’ve just been sent out to the Machine and Turtle-Dove as well. I find myself floating away from Lin as a current of other dancers flow by.
“I – I have to,” I stammer.
“No, it’s fine.”
I look up tot see that Lin is already scroling through her own phone, with an annoyed expression on her face.
“Something came up. Personal matters,” I say. “It – it’s not personal.”

My precognition is starting to flare up. It’s ablaze with scattered images. Screaming people. The looming figure of a cyborg. Chairs and tables flinging everywhere. The visuals are noisy, but they’re unmistakably there.
Lin repels further away. If only I could tell her what I know. If only she could see what I see. But then, she’d just think I’m nuts. And, even if she didn’t, would she ever feel safe near me again?
“I have to go,” Lin chokes.
Her eyes are misty and I watch her fade into the crowd like a fine mist.
“Lin, wait!” I say, wading through.
Gah! Where is she? I wasn’t done explaining!
Must’ve just missed her.

My heart is pounding and my precognition’s signal is getting stronger. But, I can’t help but feel I should fight it. Ignore it. Saving the day might sound important. However, maybe I also need to start thinking in terms of saving my relationship.
There’s another chirp from my phone. Turtle-Dove has been messaging me.
“I’m at the back of the ballroom, near Bit-Bot,” the message reads.
She sends another message. “Cog! This might get bad, and time isn’t going to stop for you! Where are you?”
I send a wink emoji, then begin to scan the ballroom for where the bathrooms are. I really need to find a way to change. Also, I need to pee.
Err… Okay, bathrooms at back corner. I readjust my backpack and move toward it.
Time to go incognito mode. Time to go in Cog-neato mode.
Ugh. I need to work on my catchphrase.
The Machine
“You look gorgeous tonight,” the Vitruvian says, slightly shielding his face with his wrist.
My face contorts. Is he trying to insult me in some way?
“Thanks,” I manage.
“No need. I was referring to myself.”
Of course he was. The Vitruvian swipes his wrist watch past my face, showing off its mirrored surface.
I grunt.

We’re dancing underneath a large chandelier as he flashes a Chesire grin. Sweat beads down my face. We’re moving at too fast of a pace. I’m a better dancer than the Vitruvian, to be clear. He’s just trying to push me around too much, that’s all. I push back.
“How is Everman Technologies pulling everything off?” the Vitruvian asks as I pull him toward the center of the room.
The crowd’s attention is on us and they can sense our tension. People crane their necks and stop in midstep to catch our every misstep.
“Luck and pluck,” I say. “Looks like it pays dividends in innovation.”
The Vitruvian clucks his tongue. “Don’t get ahead of yourself. Byrd Enterprises is close on your tail.”
I move ahead of the Vitruvian, forcing him off his rhythm. “Our quantum chips have leapfrogged yours. It’s going to take you years to catch up, I bet.”
“How do you figure your figures are doing?” the Vitruvian presses.
I readjust my collar.
“With quantum tech? Really good,” I lie. “Hard work pays off. You know me: I’m the perfect mix of a Hugh Everett and a Howard Hughes.”
Byrd brings his face closer to mine, his hair feathering and visage weathering.
“Byrd Enterprises won’t acquire, just wanted to inquire,” the Vitruvian says in what I can only imagine is a lie of his own. “Your chips might be key for compact brain computer interfaces and AI—.”
“Aye.”
The Vitruvian eyes my neck. “But I have my ways of getting what I need.”
The Vitruvian’s eyes flit from my neck to my face.
“What is your secret anyway?”

“Design,” I say with a gesture to my armor. “Above all, my companies push on the merits of design. The grand design is the whole reason we’re here, after all. Each of us are gears, in service to the universal clockwork.”

The Vitruvian smuckers his lips and snatches a glass of wine from off a table. Bubbles burble over the glass’s rim, due to the turbulence the Vitruvian introduced into the glass. The Vitruvian slurps the wine up before any of it can spill onto his clothes.
“I always thought your secret to innovation was high energy,” says the Vitruvian, handing me his glass. I’m not sure why, but I oblige. “That particle smasher you have is just smashing.”

“I guess the government is into it,” I say with a shrug. “Personally, I’m not even sure why the powers that be are interested in high energy. But hey: my company built it for cheap, and it’s a nice paycheck.”
The Vitruvian’s pupils turn to small pinpoints, and he nearly stumbles into one of his own robots as we walk by.
“And – and that nuclear reactor of yours, at the city center,” he stutters, “how are you managing that?”
“I always wanted to get a reaction out of people,” I chortle. “As it turns out, it’s much easier than it seems. I poke a little bit, and they do the rest.”
I hand the glass over to the Vitruvian’s robot, which just barely manages to get a grip. The Vitruvian’s nostrils flare as I do this.
“It’s all too much,” the Vitruvian says. “There’s no way you can possibly have control over it all. And the biotech, on top of that?”
“That’s exactly the point,” I grunt. “You can’t have control over it all. Nobody can. Trust me, I worry too sometimes…”
My mind jumps back to the warnings Opal gave me about the biotech treatments I’ve been trying. Also, the resource troubles my various divisions are facing. My body is so doggone tired these days.
It really is too much, isn’t it?

“But time marches on,” I insist. “Much as I don’t like to work like a machine – to be the man – this universe is all one great machine, isn’t it? A giant clock? It’s my role to courageously weather storms as they come. It’s my duty to handle my problems as best as I can. As for the true engine of things, that’s out of my hands.”
“Kafkaesque,” the Vitruvian coughs.
“Bless ya. Need a tissue?” I retort.
“Kafka. Esque.”
“I don’t speak French.”

The Vitruvian throws his head back and gives a squeal of delight. “The system is becoming an overbearing beauracracy. Haven’t you been paying attention? Surely a man as powerful as you has noticed where this is all headed. You’re the Machine, after all.”
My stomach churns. “I’ll admit that there’s a bit too much inequality. But, technology always fixes that.”

The Vitruvian rattles his head. “Cattle. Technology always makes better cattle for us, the elite. Honestly, stop and think for yourself for a second: bioengineering, brain computer interfaces, machine cognition… Put it together. Get it together!”
“We’re about to achieve a new stratum of consciousness – uh – together,” I say, gritting my teeth. My hands clench around the Vitruvian’s shoulders, but he seems unfazed.

“No,” he says. “Stop lying to yourself. All these sacrifices us technologists are making? It will result in gods and monsters. Man? Emancipated from existence. There will be nothing left for man to do that the transcendent won’t be able to with a snap of their fingers.”
“But what about creativity? Passion? Soul? These technologies are going to be capable of making life easier and giving people more ways to express. To explore.”
I stop and begin gesturing at individuals dancing by us, as the temperature between us rises.
“Idiots!” the Vitruvian cries. “We’re surrounded by idiots in this culture, don’t you realize? And, the system is ultimately designed to irradicate them in the end!”

He chuckles. The people around chuckle along, nervously. Some even pause to pat the Vitruvian on the back. I’m strangely both disgusted and flattered. It’s nice to know that the Vitruvian thinks I’m worthy of him. But then: what of everybody else? Why isn’t anybody angered by his words?
I blink. It hits me.
While the Vitruvian might insist we’re all idiots, all of us listening to him want to believe that we are somehow his exception. I feel my blood pressure rise.
“Don’t delude yourself, you are part of the problem,” the Vitruvian sneers. “You are the system. You are the Machine.”
I shake my head and scowl. “We can fight it. We can change it. If we had more equality – better opportunities – things would change. Humanity would rise above.”
The Vitruvian stops and whips out his phone. It’s tough to tell whether he’s shaken by my defiance, or just annoyed.

“This is the final era where a human can hope to surpass an AI,” the Vitruvian mutters. “Your juggling act is admirable Hugo Everman, I’ll admit. One of a kind. Alas: you are the last universalist. It’s not to last.”
“Alright, that’s it!” I snap.
I’m about to lift him up and throw him over my shoulder. If he wants to just rag on people, maybe it’s time to ragdoll him.

The Vitruvian shrinks back with an odd gleam in his eye. The room suddenly erupts with screams and an intense screech. I turn around and find a cyborg moving through the corwd. His torso is hooked into a makeshift chassis and a large ball-shaped roller has replaced his lower body.

I wince. Similar to cyborgs I’ve seen recently, his body is destitute and drained of energy. His eyes are glazed over and aimless, as though an invisible wall has been placed between him and the world around him.

A bunch of metal foil has been sloppily taped over his head, and I can make out the blinking red light of the characteristic brain chips for these cyborgs. Shock shoots through me. There’s a key detail to this cyborg that’s different from others I’ve seen: massive Everman Technologies logos are emblazoned across his body.
“One of yours?” the Vitruvian asks, with a tone of surprise that’s phonier than his lip fillers.
I glare at him. He must have something to do with this. But why? How could he?
“We’re in this together,” I growl.
The Vitruvian snickers and pulls a taser from his pocket. He wields it in the direction of the cyborg. “Don’t I know it?”
The Cog
The air is cloudy. Chaotic. Try as I might to mediate a sense of order from out of it, things are ultimately out of my control.

I readjust my goggles and start scanning the room for potential threats. Thus far, all I can discern is wild concern in the eyes of the crowd. They stream toward the exits in concert, toppling anything and everything in their path.
I’m hopinh to find a sign of this Turtle-Dove character. I’ve never met her in person before, so I hope she’s nice. At the very least, I want to find the Machine. Yet, they’re nowhere to be seen.

There’s a quack, like from a duck, which I manage to make out from all the ruckus. I look at my feet to find Bit-Bot bumping up at them. He glances up at me with his chunky, digital pupils. As he gives another quack, I scoop him up.
“You do a good job scouting things out for me?” I say as I unzip my backpack.
Bit-Bot’s flippers for feet give excited little kicks, as if to answer in the affirmative.
“Cool robot you go tthere,” a woman says.

She’s standing to my side, wearing a jumpsuit that’s colored red and white. The upper half of her face is obscured by a bandana mask, but I can make out her eyes from beneath. They gleam like sapphires. Her hair bunches out from beneath the mask – a fine gold. Her features and her eyes are extremely distinct and familiar.
Just going to put it out there: she looks like Lin. Am I going crazy?
“Yeah, he’s a lot of help,” I say, putting Bit-Bot back in my pack. “Also, learning new things all the time. You Turtle-Dove?”
She nods, then gestures at the bird logo across her chest. “You Cog?”
“The one and only!” I say with a laugh.
Yeah. She totally sounds like Lin. Maybe she’s a clone? She laughs back, a little longer than me. What’s so funny?
A fresh stream of screaming people run by. The center of the room opens up to my view. There’s a cyborg shooting bursts of flames and molten metal. I tremble, but force myself to stand tall.
“What’s the plan?” I say.
Turtle-Dove’s jaw hangs open. “Wha?” she manages.
“This Nimrod guy… You said he had a way to help, am I right?”
Turtle-Dove shakes her head out of a daze.

“Oh, right.” She taps a band hooked into the bandana across her head. “Nimrod wants to transmit signals at this cyborg thing and see if he can hack into it. The last few cyborgs had electronics which were too damaged for proper analysis.”
I yawn. “Yeah, yeah, yeah. How long does that mean we need to hold this guy off for?”
Turtle-Dove’s face twists in concentration as she taps at her headband and earpiece in her ear.
“What type of transmitter is that anyway?” I say, focusing my goggles in and drawing closer.
“Nimrod’s junk,” she mutters. I give a funny look, and she groans. “No, I didn’t mean it that way…”
She pauses, then puts a hand up. “Okay, Nimrod says he needs at least five minutes. Also, we need to get closer in for better signal strength.”
Turtle-Dove clicks the heels to her big red boots together and a pair of skates pop out from the bottom.
“Keep up,” she says with a wink.
There’s a motorized whir and the skates send her faster than Hermes.
“Hey!” I say, chasing after her.
I unclip my fluxion-drives from my belt and pulse their triggers. There is a crackle, then a buzz as I’m sent through the air like a dart. I’m flying.
Drawing nearer to the rogue cyborg, I notice how it has logos for Everman Technologies plastered all over it. Great.
The Machine’s face is heavy, and his frame is in a slump. He’s totally ticked. Oddly, the Vitruvian is right beside him, and has somehow managed to put all signs of frustration aside.
“What’s up everybody?” I say, falling into a smooth landing as I turn down my fluxion-drives.

Okay, I stumble a bit. But, it’s fine. The Vitruvian and the Machine are both preoccupued by driving the cyborg back, anyway. The Machine is pumping his power fists, and the Vitruvian brandishes his signature taser. It might not be their finest hour, but pretty cool to see them together like this.
“I’m Cog, by the way,” I say, standing behind the Vitruvian. Turtle-Dove glides to my side. “Oh, and this is Turtle-Dove!”
Turtle-Dove gives a little wave, and I can’t help but smile. The Vitruvian turns to face us and gives a slight smile of his own, before returning to face the cyborg.
“I’m a huge fan, by the way,” I say, “one hero to another.”
“Who wouldn’t be?” the Vitruvian says, with a slight laugh.
The Machine turns to me now.
“Cog! Thank God you’re here!” he shouts. “This cyborg thing is a complete mess. You think you can do that EMP thing again?”
I shake my head, prompting a look of defeat from the Machine. Odd. Generally he is not so easily distraught. These cyborgs are really doing a number on him.
“Calm down,” I say, “We have a different plan.”
“I’m going to try hacking in with a transmitter,” Turtle-Dove adds, “Ideally, we shut this cyborg down without breaking anything.”
“Huh? What?” the Vitruvian grunts, as a he dodges a blast of flame from the cyborg.
“It’s already in process,” Turtle-Dove says, her face frozen in focus. “I’m in communication with another teammate. I just need you guys to hold him in place. Keep anybody from getting hurt.”

The Vitruvian furls his lip. “Well, in that case…” He unclips an electronic brick from his belt, and begins fiddling with it. “I have a transmitter of my own. Completely slipped my mind! I can totally help hack this thing.”
The Machine shoots the Vitruvian a look of incredulity, which is immediately diverted by a shot of plasma. No clue what’s up between them. Probably better to ignore it right now.
The Vitruvian whistles at me.
“Hey, you!”
“I’m the Cog, not a dog,” I say, trying my best to sound upbeat. “You can call be by my name.”
The Vitruvian gives a sly grin. “Kay, you and Everman hold off the cyborg. I’ll help Mrs. Dove with the hacking. Got it?”
Turtle-Dove’s head is down and the Machine is sweating bullets.
“Ok,” I say, turning the dial to my fluxion-drives and running to the Machine’s side. “Let’s get a rhythm going.”

As I say this, I also turn a dial on the music circuits for my fluxion-droves. It begins filling the air with an electrified remix of my favorite dance songs. I dance to its beat, sending out sprays of electricity to help drive the cyborg back. The Machine works with me, helping to direct the crowd toward exits and also trying to keep the cyborg back. We each take great care to steer clear of the flames and plasma blasts.
My head buxxes. An image tears through my mind of a metallic boulder, tumbling down a slope. It hurtles into a crowd of people.
I shake my head out of the hazy vision and start running toward the statue of the boulder held at the center of the ballroom.
“Where are you going?” the Machine calls out.
“Precognition,” I call back. “Just trust me!”
“Ok,” the Machine grunts, as his armor is grazed by a plume of fire. “But hurry! Don’t get too cocky Cog!”
I whoop, making my way up the slope. “Wouldn’t dream of it!”
As usual, the Machine is second guessing me. Why can’t he ever just trust me? We could get so much more done if we just worked as straight up partners.

As I near the top of the slope, I notice how a weld at the base of the boulder is shearing and partially melted. Molten plasma drips along its surface, courtesty of the cyborg. The boulder groans and shifts from its place. My precognition is sending off all the alarms.

On instinct, I link the two butt ends of my fluxion-drives into one another. Their force emitters face in equal and opposite directions. Looking at the size of this boulder, I’m going to need it that way. I point one end of the linked emitters toward the boulder, and keep the other end pointed away from me. Hopefully the fluxion-drives don’t crumple in on themselves under the loads of force I’m about to have them emit.
“Machine!” I shout, as the weld begins to give out.

I don’t have time to check if he heard. The boulder has broken away from its weld and is rolling toward me. Immediately, I pulse the force to my fluxion-drives, cranking up their power. The boulder picks up momentum at first, then steadily slows. Cautiously, I use my fluxion-drives to bring the boulder back to the top of the slope. I take care to keep a safe distance.
“Look out!” the Machine cries.
A blast of plasma hits the boulder, and some of the plasma ricochets toward me. I slip and fall to the surface of the slope. My fluxion-drives give a whine, then sputter.
I scramble back to my feet. The boulder is rolling back down from the top of the slope, and my fluxion-drives are misbehaving. Their music has gone out.
“Come on, you sissy force,” I mutter, smacking the sides of my fluxion-drives.

The percussive maintenance fails to awaken them, and the boulder is tumbling toward me at full speed. I sprint down the slope and find that the Machine is stanidng at the bottom, his arms at the ready.
“Move!” the Machine shouts.

I dive from the slope and back onto the ground. Somehow, I manage to land on my feet and I keep on running. I have no clue whether the Machine will have the strength to hold this boulder, but I can see the cyborg coming up from behind his back.
I pulse my fluxion-drives toward the cyborg, but nothing comes out. They’re officially fried.
“Crud!” I exclaim.
AS I say this, the boulder rams into the Machine and he manages to lift it above his head.
“At last!” I hear the Vitruvian announce, and the cyborg crumples behind the Machine at the last moment.
Turtle-Dove and the Vitruvian must’ve finally hacked into the cyborg’s chip. Luck. Pure luck.
I give a triumphant yelp, and I hear Turtle-Dove give one after me. The crowd of people who remain in the ballroom break out into cheering too.
“Machine! Machine!” they chant.

Some of them are taking selfies and recording video as they do this. As for the Machine, his face is beet red and covered in sweat. The veins in his neck and forearms bulge. His hands keep an uneasy grip in the grooves of the metal boulder.
He smiles, taking in the mix of pain and praise like a champ. It’s as though as he holds the boulder he also holds the weight of the entire world on his shoulders.
“Anybody able to help?” the Machine bellows, between grunts.

I desperately want to pitch in. However, all my best tricks are broken. I glance at my baston sticks, still latched to my belt – useless, as usual. Maybe I should start carrying an extra pair of fluxion-drives instead.
The Vitruvian gives a whistle, managing to overpower the cheering people. He pauses, then whistles again.
“Where are my robots?” he groans. “Why aren’t they acknowledging me?”s

As he says this, a robotic bed rolls to the Machine’s side. The Vitruvian gives a cry of delight and the robotic bed sprouts forked arms, like from a forklift. They tilt up toward the Machine, and the Machine slowly lowers the boulder onto them. The robotic arms take grip of the boulder, settling it at the center of the bed.
“Ugh, finally,” the Machine heaves.
He rests his hands on his knees, collecting himself with deep breaths.
“Give me a long enough lever, Everman, and I can move the world!” the Vitruvian shouts, striding up to the Machine.

The Virtruvian gives the Machine a firm pat on the back. The crowd bursts into another round of cheering for the Machine and I join in with them. Oddly, a flash of envy crosses the Vitruvian’s face. Even odder: I feel envious of the Machine too.
“Alright, settle down everybody,” the Vitruvian snaps.
“Yeah, it was a team effort,” the Machine declares, regaining his height. “Everybody deserves the credit.”
The Machine looks at me and Turtle-Dove. Somehow, Turtle-Dove is standing right next to me – where’d she come from, and why is she standing so close? My eyes go wide for a second.

“Seriously, thanks guys,” the Machine says. He looks over to the cyborg, which still has the Everman Technologies logo clearly emblazoned all over it. “This would’ve been a hot mess without your intervention.”
“It’s fine,” the Vitruvian mumbles.
My gaze jumps between the cyborg, Turtle-Dove, and the Vitruvian.
“How – how’d you guys,” I stutter.
“It was cake,” says the Vitruvian. “I was stressed for a minute there, but we eventually hacked in easy peasy.”
Turtle-Dove doesn’t say a word. She’s just studying her hands for some reason. The Vitruvian leans toward me, appearing to leer.
“Interesting gizmo there,” the Vitruvian says, eyeing my fluxion-drives. “Novel capabilities, truly. Life saver, I’m jealous. What did you study to build that?”
“Mechatronics engineering, mechanical engineering,” I say, gripping my fluxion-drives close to my chest. “i.e., M.E.”

“Hmm, interesting,” the Vitruvian says, grabbing at my fluxion-drives. I let him hold it. “I went into philosophy myself. Philosophy of logic. That said: spending some days studying M.E. is always a fun exercise.”
The Vitruvian shoots the Machine a quizzical look, then returns to the fluxion-drives. He toys with the dials.
“It’s fried right now,” I explain. “Be careful, I’m not sure what broke.”

The Vitruvian nods as though he heard, but I can’t help but feel uneasy. He unclips the fluxion-drives from their cabling to my power-pack, then turns the fluxion-drives over in his hands. He’s studying them at every angle.
“So, this thing can shoot electricity… And force. Seriously, how could this possibly work?” the Vitruvian grumbles. “Radiation pressure? Some sort of ion propulsion?”
My hands tingle. I need to grab my fluxion-drives back, but I keep my lips sealed. Turtle-Dove is becoming noticeably distant, drifting away from our group.
“Can you – can you grab things with this too? Tweeze things?” the Vitruvian persists.
My muscles twinge. I’m repulsed, but I relent with a nod.
“It’s sort of finicky, but it can grab stuff if the force pulses are properly directed,” I say with a quiver in my voice. “It’s much better at pushing things forward.”
The Vitruvian licks his lips. “But… But the energies to do that… They’re insane. You’d need to know how to turn matter directly to energy!”
The Vitruvian shoots another look at the Machine. “You sure that your companies don’t have any other breakthroughs you’re not letting me in on?”
The Machine gives a nervous chuckle and shakes his head. “It’s all Cog. Anyway, shouldn’t we stay focused on this cyborg issue?”
The Vitruvian scowls at me. “There’s no way he built this by himself.”

“The Machine is right,” Turtle-Dove cuts in. “If we’re not going to focus on resolving the problem at hand, what are we doing here? A lot of people could’ve been seriously hurt by that cyborg, and we still have a bunch to sort out.”
The Vitruvian yawns, then gives that unhinged laugh of his. “We can settle that in a split. That tech is bland. Seen a million things like it. This though…”
Turtle-Dove rolls her eyes before rolling off with a huff on her electric skates.
“Wait!” I shout after her.

I force a growl and snatch my fluxion-drives from the Vitruvian. As I do, he gives a ferocious glare. He looks like he wants to devour me. Fortunately, the Machine yanks the Vitruvian back at the shoulders.
“Go catch up with her,” the Machine says. “Good work tonight. The Vitruvian and I can take care of everything else.”
“You too, Machine,” I beam, before running across the ballroom.
For all the wonkiness between me and the Machine lately, I’m gonna be real: it’s great to hear him give some credit for once. Maybe the guy runs on something more than engine oil after all.

I think I hear the Vitruvian give something of a whine, but I’m already sprinting through the hall and toward the exits. Turtle-Dove is not far off, but something deep inside me says that I’ll lose her if I don’t act quick.
“Hey, don’t leave me!” I call after her.

I’ve bursted through the exit and I’m making my way up a stairwell. The steps creak beneath my feet. Old brick crumbles off the walls, following after my upward stumble. I’m huffing and puffing. I can just barely make her out. She’s far above.
“You know, for a turtle you’re pretty fast,” I cry, my voice echoing through the musty stairwell.
“It’s Turtle-Dove, love,” she echos back.
I fake a scoff, then fight a cough, Awful. Running up stairs is just awful. To only add to the annoyance, my fluxion-drives still won’t turn on no matter how much I fiddle with them. Gah!

Turtle-Dove’s silhouette disappears through a door onto the roof. Somehow I manage to slip through just as it’s closing. A storm god is raging at the air, exerting its reign with a slurry of rain. The flow from the heavens gushes at me.

My goggles cloud with speckles of water and the hairs on my arm stand up. There’s a distinct scent of high voltage in the air. My precognition jolts me with the image of electricity. A massive spark is on the horizon.

I’m beamed back to the present, and the sky is torn through with two lightning bolts that could only be from Zeus. They cross into eachother and crackle like fireworks. For reasons that are unexplainable, the bell of a clocktower strikes with them. The light is brilliant. The light is blinding.
“You shouldn’t be out here, Og,” Turtle-Dove teases.
“Ugh, Cog,” I correct.
How come so many people don’t get that right?
“Then what’s with all the ogling?” she says. She gives a grunt. “Just want to make sure you’re aware: I can see you oggle behind those goggles of yours.”
I look over to find her hooking herself into a psychotic apparatus. It’s a massive robotic ornithopeter, with a wingspan that stretches several car lengths.
“How’d you fit that onto the roof?” I shout over the rain.
“The same way you fit that head of yours through the door.”
She finishes strapping into the ornithopter and the silver wings beat against a silver evening sky.
“Where are you going?” I say.
“Gotta meet up with Nimrod,” she replies, her eyes now focused on the sky.
My eyes burn. “Then take me with you!”
She shakes her head. “Too dangerous. Also, whatever you do: don’t trust that Vitruvian guy. In fact, be careful around everybody. Whatever this is that we’re dealing with, it has deep roots.”
I groan. “But I trust you!”
“I don’t want you to get hurt. You don’t know how deep this goes. You don’t know how lonely it is.”
“I’m a reckless recluse. I can take it.”
The wings are beating harder now, as Turtle-Dove hovers into the air.

“You don’t understand!” I shriek. “I feel empty and isolated so often! The people I meet – they’re just repeats of other people. They’re walking mimics. They’re mirrors! Mirrors of my thoughts, and the thoughts of others!”
“We’re all mirroring, some way or another,” Turtle-Dove says, raising higher still. “And, oftentimes things in life don’t turn out as fair as we want them. Mirror, mirror…”
A mix of rain and tears streams down my face. A mix of rain and mascara seems to run beneath the edges of Turtle-Dove’s mask, but it’s hard to say for sure.

“I often feel like a lone candle, burning in a dark room!” I shout, raising my voice above the ornithopter’s thrum. “Others I interact with are just other dead candles that I used my flame to reignite. But you? You’re different! You’re my twin flame!”

Turtle-Dove shakes her head. “Oh Cog, you’re wrong. You need to be careful. Whatever you think is between us? There’ll always be so much more to your life than that. The ideal is only ever ideation. Ideals are made to fade.”
There is a crack of thunder, and Turtle-Dove is carried away on a gust of air.
“I’m sorry,” she says, flying further away. “I have to leave you!”
She flutters into the arms of the storm. She starts as a gray streak on the sky, looking like a mix of rain and mascara. Then, she disappears.
“I’m sorry,” I whisper to myself, spittling rain from my mouth as I do. “I have to love you.”
Chapter 8: Parks and Recreation
The Cog
Why is it that, on a work day, the clock always feels clogged?
Cog. I just want to become Cog again.

The keyboard goes click clack as the office clock goes tick. But, something about me just isn’t keyed in. I rub the side of my forehead where the old wound from the particle accelerator accident is. The accident still haunts me. How could I have been so careless and scatter brained?
The wound is scarred over, but still tingles sometimes. Today it’s a bit hot.

When I received the wound, the doctors thought I’d never be quite normal again. They said that there was trauma inflicted upon my prefrontal cortex. At least, that’s the bit I still remember. My memory and precognition are pretty hazy from that time.
My face was all swollen. I could barely talk for awhile.
Thankfully, I recovered.
At the time, there also weren’t many people to talk too. I was mostly alone in that hospital bed. Friends and family are really busy people.
Nothing has been quite the same since then. But, I recovered. I recovered. I moved forward. That’s what matters at the end of the day.
I’m better now, for better or worse.

I yawn as I skim over the documentation on my computer screen. Looks like we’re upgrading some vacuum pumps and related components. Whoever drafted this was careless – quite a few typos and misspellings.
Whatever. A “va cum pump” is close enough to a vacuum pump I guess.

Suddenly my cranium transmits me to an old mission with the Machine. The wind beats against me. I’m gripping two large vacuum-powered suction cups, which sucks brick. They link along the length of my forearms. I move my left forearm upward, having its vacuum pump suckle a glass window. It is the window of a skyscraper.
Two more vacuum pumps are strapped to my shins.
“Great work Cog, keep it up!” cheers the Machine.

I look down and feel queasy. The Machine is standing on the side of the building, gripping a tether that feeds through the vacuum pump on my back. I gulp. Below him is a raging gulf of city. A deep basin of business.
The tether feeds above me, grappling the roof of the skyscraper. But, I’m not sure I trust it.
“Are you sure about this?” I whine. “I want to go back inside!”
The Machine shakes his head and stomps on the flass window beneath his feet.
“The Window-Dresser is hiding here somwhere!” he declares. “He must be addressed with justice!”
My mind tunnels me back to my office chair and I try to catch my breath. Up until that adventure from about a year ago, I’d always wanted to climb a building. Never again!

I lean back and draft an email to one of the office managers with my corrected documentation for the vacuum systems. A few design ideas are listed with them. Maybe they’ll listen and really make some changes!
Probably not.

As I do, I let my precgonition slip back to another adventure with the Machine. My seat turns to a hard plastic and rattles violently. The Machine is to my left, throttling a jammed stearing yoke. Air rushes by with high intensity over the wings of the Machine’s biplane. It’s painted a bright orange, which is slightly  chipped and rusted at the edges.

The Machine likes to call his plane “The Flying Machine”. Bit dumb, but not my place to butt in. I’m in charge of steering a turret below the plane, which sprays a dense ttrail of mist into the air. It’s bug spray. Also: the air is filled with a field of giant mosquitoes. The Machine probably should’ve mentioned that on the job application.
We dive just as a couple of mosquitoes are about to mash into the wing.
We’re totally gonna die!
“Focus on your controls, you’re supposed to be spraying these things!” the Machine grunts, unjamming his yoke.
I know my eyes should be on the controls of the sprayer, but I can’t take my focuse off the Machine and his yoke. The Machine shoots me a grin.
“I’ll show you hwo to fly some other time,” he says, before returning to his steering. “Now, get back to the spraying or I’ll send you down into the belly’s ball turret!”
My stomach cramps. Ugh – not the claustrophobic ball turret! I swallow. My veins are pounding. A behemoth mosquito screams as I spray it in the face. Why mosquitoes? Why?!
I shield my eyes, then reopen. I’m standing in a boxing ring now. Another memory from the old memory box.
“Introducing,” an announcer bellows, “The Machine vs. the Log!”
“It’s Cog,” I whimper to myself.

The Machine is across from me, polishing his gloves with spit and vigor. This is not just a normal boxing ring. The boxing platform hovers in space, purplish lava and stardust surrounding us. Overhead is a twisty being. It appears to be some kind of crystal liquid. Various images and environments burble along its surface – restaurants, farmlands, yards. There are even other planets beyond Earth that are mixed in. My head aches.
“Don’t worry Cog,” the Machine says. “We just need to play the Dreamweaver’s game and he’ll free us from his web.”
I bite my lip and tighten the straps to my gloves. I don’t believe a word.
“Just one KO and we’re okay,” the Machine isnsists.
Dreamweaver is a funny fellow, but can also be the worst. Just the worst.
I already know he’s lying. If we carry out this fight it’s gonna suck, my precognition knows it.
“Go! Entertain me!” Dreamweaver gurgles. “Just one KO!”
Blech, I don’t want to deal with this.
“Knock yourself out,” I mutter.

I muster my precognition to blast my consciousness to a different memory, and my body falls toward the floor of the boxing ring. As my body falls I feel Dreamweaver relent, freeing me and the Machine from his landscape. The Machine will need to resuscitate me once Dreamweaver has finished sending us back to New Vinci.
But, that was then. This is now. As my body sits in the office, my memory is tunneling me into the future.
I’m relieved to for my precognition to tunnel me into an icy tundra. I sit in an igloo, my fingers being threatened with frostbite.
Okay: I’m semi-relieved.

In front of me is a warm fire. The carcass of a giant ice slug hangs over along a spike, its yellow guts oozing into the fire. The Machine sits next to the fire, rotating the slug like rotisserie chicken. The guts slosh around, but the Machine rotates the slug fast enough so that most of the guts aren’t lost to the fire.
“You gonna finish that?” the Machine says through a frosty beard.

I shiver and my teeth chatter.  I and the Machine have been chasing an Abominable Snowman for a week, and no luck. I glance at the platter near my feet. It’s filled with the yellowish glop from the slug.
“Uh…” I groan.
“Well, if you’re not going to finish…” the Machine begins.
As he says the word finish, the air goes static and I fuzz back into my boring old office chair.
“Well, you finished with it or what?” I hear Ethan say.
Crud. Ethan – I totally forgot!
“I sent you the code the other night,” I say, spinning in my chair before finally facing Ethan. “You didn’t get it?”
Ethan’s eyes glaze over but he gives half a smile. “That was crud code. You gotta commit!”
“Yeesh,” I grumble. “It took me several hours to write that thing, and I do not want to look at it again. It did the job, didn’t hit?’
Ethan scratches his head. “The movements of the motor are still jaffed. I thought you knew of a smoother control scheme.”
I sigh and close my eyes. “Sometimes things are just going to be jagged. I’ll send you some of the forums I was using for the motor. Hopefully you can make it better, but it took me forever.”
Ethan bites his lip, gives a reluctant nod, then takes a look at my computer screen.
“Hmm… You got a minute?” Ethan asks.
I laugh. “I’m kinda busy procrastinating, but sure.”
The clock says 5 minutes until 4:00. The day is basically over anyway. I stand from my chair and Ethan is already walking down the hall.
“Dr. Skully is out of town and he needs me to go pick up a package for him,” Ethan says, hitting the up button for an elevator at the end of the hall.
His hand goes to his pocket and he slips a silver passcard between his fingers. He swipes his hair out of his face. I catch the name “Dr. Skully” on the passcard as he does this.
“Get out of town!” I say, ogling at the passcard. “Is that—?”
I’m interruped by the ding of the elevator as its doors whoosh open.
Ethan enters. “Yep. Dr. Skully gave me his office card.”
My eyes are still fixed on the passcard. “He did, did he?”
We stare at each other for a moment as my mouth goes agape. We burst out laughing.
“We’ve got only a few minutes before the mailroom closes,” Ethan says, collecting himself.
I step into the elevator just as the doors slide slyly into place. We both know exactly what needs to be done.
“How’ve things been going by the way?” Ethan says, going to button 74 on the elevator’s control pad.
The elevator responds with a tweet, then yeets us up. I settle into a lean on the armrest to Ethan’s left.
“Alright,” I say, casting my gaze to the roof of the elevator. “I’m liking life.”
In many ways, I’m being real with him. Life is steady enough. However, it gets harder for me to stay in the moment. Exiting the existential and just existing has never been my strong suit.

“You’ve definitely been a big help these past few weeks,” says Ethan, the gleam of the elevator lights obscuring his eyes from behind his glasses. “The way you talk, the way you present… You’re present again. It’s nice.”

His eyes go to a TV screen in the top corner of the elevator. It’s playing footage of the fight I and the Machine had at the National Art Museum. Quite the showpiece. That said, the news anchors on the screen don’t seem to appreciate it. All that they want to hit on is that the cyborg we were fighting came from Everman Technologies.
“Are we to believe this is a responsible use of our tax dollars?” a newscaster warbles
I shudder.
“This is definitely the end of the world,” their co-anchor snickers.
“Thanks Ethan,” I manage, taking my focus off the TV.
“No problem!” Ethan puts his hands in his pockets and gives a whistle. “Still a bit sloppy workmanship. But whatever you’re doing seems to be working.”

My eyes go to the floor. “Sorry that I can still be all over the place,” I sigh. “Been cutting back on stuff like social media. Gets me stuck in my head and all neurotic. I’m glad I’m not the only one noticing a difference.”
I pause and give him a pat on the back.
“Anyway,” I continue, “you give me something to shoot for. You’re always nailing it and have a great attitude about it.”

Ethan nods then gives me a grin. “I do pride myself on quality work,” he says. He gives another quick whistle. “Granted, sometimes I feel like it’s a bit much. I like to think I’m working for a good company, but there’s all this pressure I sometimes feel. And I don’t feel like Dr. Skully understands.”
Ethan glances at the newscast, then back to me.
“I know that feeling,” I laugh. “Feels like I’m always in a pressure cooker to perform somehow.”
Ethan snorts. “Bud, you might be doing a lot better. But, come on now. You got things way easy. Pretty sure half your work this week came from me asking for a favor!”
“Still needed my help though,” I wink.
Ethan shrugs. “Fair. Just don’t get too high and mighty about it. I get worried about that with you – you are too quite sometimes.”
I laugh weakly.
Ethan shoots another look at the TV screen. “Just look at what’s happening with the all-powerful Everman. I don’t like the news, but they have a point. Nobody can do it alone.”
I stay quiet, twiddling my thumbs.
“Sorry, I know I should be more focused on boosting you up,” Ethan says. “Speaking of boosts: this elevator is taking forever.”
His hand moves toward a fiery orange button on the control pad.
“Oh no!” I exclaim.
“Oh yes!”

He hits the button and I’m floored. Literally. I fall on my butt as the elevator blasts sky high. The floor presses hard against me. Ethan clings to the armrests on the elevator wall. He is in a daze, his soul swept up in the thrill. I feel my soul pulled up along with his.
The elevator jerks to a halt. My stomach somersaults. The floor number listed on our elevator is 137.
“We overshot!” I cry.
“OSHA should… Oh shi—!”belts Ethan.
The elevator falls downward.
It’s falling faster than falling!
My body floats into the air, then slams into the ceiling. Pain twanging my veins, I push off the wall and swim through the air. I’m stimming. Ethan’s eyes are skimming the walls for a way out.

Gravity reenters the elevator as gracefully as it left, and I get a faceful of carpet. I look up to find we’re at floor 74. There’s a ding from the doors and they swing open, signifying the end of the ride.
“Never again,” I groan, stretching my muscles into place as I limp through the exit.
Ethan musters the will to pry his hands off the elevator handle and follows me out. “Elevator from hell,” he says with a shudder.
The elevator doors shutter closed. We make our way to the mailroom. Nobody is around, so Ethan just grabs Dr. Skully’s pacakage and signs Dr. Skully’s name on a formsheet.
“Forgery,” I mutter.
“Fortune favors the bold,” Ethan flushes with a fluorish of the pen.
Ethan begins filling out the form’s other entries and I chuckle. Checking my phone, I look for any new messages from Turtle-Dove. Annoyingly, none. Lin isn’t responsive either.
I frown. The only updates come from my social media streams, such as the Byrd app. Each one yields reams of negativity and fear towards the Machine. Towards the Cog – me.

I swallow. The toughest thing is that they have a point. I keep capitulating to the capitalist Machine, as the Cog… And, I keep getting disappointed. Much as I try to cooperate, it’s all clearly coopted.
“Come on George!” Ethan snorts, already halfway down the hall.
Dang – he finished that form fast! I run after him to catch up.
“How have things been going with Lin?” Ethan asks, his eyes following my phone as I put it in my pocket.

My chest falls. “Good,” I say. “We had a dance the other night. I might’ve already told you. I could’ve done a better job near the end of the night – I’m not good at goodbyes. But, we had a good time.”
Ethan nods along, occasionally pausing to check the names on office doors while we progress further into the hall.
“I know Lin said she had a good time with you the other night too,” I say, side-eyeing him. “Apparently this was after that dinner we all had together.”
Ethan shrugs and bits his lip. “Was alright. She was really upset after you had us leave, to be honest. You really hurt her feelings.”
I look at my feet. “Sorry.”
“No, it’s fine,” Ethan says, putting a hand up. “Just be more – uh—cognizant is all.”
Ethan gives an “Aha” as we reach Dr. Skully’s door, and he swipes the passcard across. The door pops open and I give a low whistle at the scene.
“Well, wouldn’t you know it?” I say, drinking in Dr. Skully’s office, “Mr. Physicist has lots of physical possessions after all.”
Ethan smirks then sets the podsized package on Dr. Skully’s glass pond of a desk. It’s only then that I notice a label on the package: Byrd Enterprises.
I shudder. Odd. But then, maybe it’s nothing? Byrd Enterprises sells a lot of useful tech, maybe it’s just a standard purchases.
“I haven’t been here myself either,” Ethan says, his eyes running along one of the bookshelves.
I rush to Dr. Skully’s whiteboard.
Scanning it, it’s a bit dry – some basic diagrams and equations. I snatch a dry erase marker up and draw a sloppy stick-figure, riding a racecar backward.
“Hey, you’re not supposed to mess with that!” Ethan protests.
He tries to growl, but it sounds like he’s holding back a howl.
I slot a permanent marker from my pocket and into a holder lipping the bottom of the whiteboard. I keep drawing in dry erase, my heart racing.
“It’s fine, we can just blame the janitor,” I say.
I scrawl the phrase “Yours truly, Janitor” next to my artpiece.
“Trust me,” I insist, “he’ll never think this was you.”
Ethan transitions from nearly rubbing my drawing away to rubbing his chin. “Good point.”

He snatches the marker from me and begins crafting caveman scrawls of his own. I move to Dr. Skully’s desk and litter it with a couple of paper airplanes formed of sticky notes. I also hang some pens to a lamp of his, using a mix of paperclips and rubber bands.
“Okay, we done here?” I ask Ethan, coming up behind.
“You gotta tell me what you think,” Ethan winks, stepping away from the whiteboard.
My face twists. Then, I chortle. It’s a picture of a giant brick, with a caricature of Dr. Skully’s face placed at its center.
“One more thing,” I say, taking the marker back.
I start to form a handlebar mustache right under Dr. Skully’s nose.
“Uh, what are you two doing?” a voice pipes up.
Ethan and I jump, then turn. Ethan rushes toward the door, and on instinct I follow after.
I blink. Lin. It’s Lin!
“How’d you—?” I begin with a grin.
“I came to pick up a package,” Lin explains, hugging a manilla envelope close to her chest. Her eyes go wide, her head peering deeper through the door. “Poor Dr. Skully! This office looks awful!”
She gives a giggle as Ethan drags me through the door and locks it shut.
“You saw nothing!” Ethan hisses deeply.
“That was definitely… Something,” Lin says with a raised eyebrow, as Ethan’s hands wave in the air. “You sure you want to leave things on such a low note?”
“Keep it on the down low,” I cut in.
“No clue what you two are on about,” Ethan adds. “And, on that note: George and I are leaving to—uh— the mountains for an evening hike. Want to join?”
“What?” I utter.
What is he talking about? We never agreeed to that.
“The hiking trails by Mount Brashly,” Ethan says.
I wince thinking about all the hobbies and responsibilities on my docket for the night.
“I’m not sure I have the time,” I grumble.
Ethan returns my grumble with a groan. “You said you’d come!”
Ethan jabs me with his elbow before I can jabber any more. Lin gives a smile.
I take Ethan’s hit. Also, his hint.
“Yeah, sure,” Lin says, checking her phone. “We taking the 4:15?”
Ethan is already sprinting down the hall toward our building’s highrise high-speed rail station.
“Better jump to it!” Ethan cries. “4:15! Let’s go for it team!”

Somehow we manage to whip through the gates and onto the train just as 4:15 is withering away. In my signature style, I hop aboard as the doors are closing. Magic! It’s as though time itself aligned for us.
Can time do that?
“We made it!” Ethan whoops.
We all share a laugh.

It’s basically open space on this train, so we take seats in one of the front rows. My seat feels cushy as I settle in. Nevertheless, I clench my body tight. My seat suddenly turns to rock and the train rockets forward. After about a minute, it achieves a steady speed.

I let the tension in my body subside and I look to my side. My friends are both at rest. Out the window, te city rushes by. It’s somewhow a blend of fairytale dreams and the stone cold rigidit of an unyielding black box. Stacks of blocky skyscrapers traipse between bubbly glass palaces. Many tracks run in parallel toward the center of the city, converging near the Everman Technologies nuclear reactor. The reactor pumps steam into the air, forming a milky swirl.
Byrd Enterprise’s building is also right by the nuclear reactor, a thin spiral aspiring for the mist. Though, it pales in comparison to the reactor, looking almost like its twisted shadow.
“Which trail are we taking?” Lin asks, poking her head into my view.
I’m still focused on the cityscape and try to get my head around her. As the city’s misty swirls eddy, sun rays stream through as rainbows.
“What say you, Edison?” says Ethan.
I shrug. “All fine by me. They’re all headed toward the same destination, more or less.”
Ethan groans. “Definitely not all the same. Some trails force you to ut in more effort – to be more active. Others, we can be more casual about things.”
“I don’t have all day,” Lin says with a twirl of her hair. “We should keep things casual.”
I nod. Ethan nods. The train seems to nod as it runs over some kind of speed bump.
“Wherever we go, it better not be Marshland Trail,” Ethan says. “I’m already swamped at work. Don’t need to be swamped outside of work too!”
Lin crinkles her nose, then crumples up a bage from a notepad in her lap. She scribbles something down.
“I’m pining after Pinecone Trail myself,” says Lin.
Ethan rolls his eyes. “Put a pin in that Lin. Last time I tried getting getting through it felt like it took forever. Hours. Also, so much of it is closed off now.”
Lin is still blockking the window, even as I try to see around her. I’m being a jerk – I know I’m being a jerk. But then, I’m so anxious.
I relent and look to the notepad on her lap.
“Right, a short trail,” Lin says with a quick stroke of her pencil. “Let’s try Black Swan trail.”
Ethan gives a half frown, then a “hmm…”, followed by a “mmm-hmmm.”

Like that, it is settled. We are going to Black Swan trail. What we still are sorting out though is what Lin is drawing a picture of. It’s cloudy. Hazy. All a silvery pastel from what I can tell, outlined with some blacks and grays.
Ethan pulls a pen from his shirt pocket and draws a crude square at the edge of Lin’s paper.
“Hey!” Lin says, giving Ethan a playful shove. I’m suddenly regretting having taken the edge seat.
“Hey,” Ethan says back. He eyes Lin’s hazy sketch. “If you could have a dream life, what would it look like?”
My face goes hot. What is he doing? These are the sorts of questions I’m supposed to be asking!
Lin grimaces, then shrugs. “I’m up for just about whatever life that’ll allow me to quit Everman Technologies,” she musters with a slight laugh.
I shift in my seat. Maybe Everman isn’t doing the best right now, but it’s still a great company.
“Have you thought about just using universal basic income?” I pipe up.
Lin snorts. “Come on, we all know that’s a joke. It’s a fast track to living with parents. And we all know how that goes.”
I shift again. “I mean, maybe moving back in with my parents wouldn’t be half bad. Would it? With the state of things, it’s a backup.”
Ethan and Lin both burst out laughing. I force myself to join in.

Stress in my muscles pique as the train shifts and we’re all thrust forward. Taking a peek out the window, it’s as though we’ve passed on to another world. The purple grandeur of mountain terrain surrounds our train. It’s clothed in lush greenery and jeweled with ponds and streams.

Miles behind us is the sprawl of New Vinci, looking like something from a child’s trainset. The air here is somehow both tighter and lighter. The train’s inertia finally goes inert. Its doors swoosh open, and Ethan rushes toward them.

I want to chase after, but something brings me in toward Lin. She’s still scribbling furiously at her pad. Her tongue is focused out the side of her mouth. I want to tell her we need to move before the door closes.

I take her pencil from her. I sketch a picture of two stick figures, standing atop a triangle. I give the triangle a smily face. She laughs, taking the pencil back and rushing after Ethan. I race after the door just as it’s closing, for the third time this day. Somehow, I know I’ll make it, and I do.
Some things are better left unsaid.
“What were you drawing a picture of anyway?” I ask, coming into the outside.
“Guess,” says Lin.
“Molten metal?” I say, squinting.
Lin huffs.
“Uh,” I say, “bottom of the ocean? Sorry, I’m scraping bottom of the barrel.”
We’re firmly along the trail, traintracks far back. Ethan takes measured steps toward the spot in the trail where several paths converge with one another.
Lin’s fingers ride along the lines of her inked figure. She winks.
“It’s the rainbow, like we saw on the ride here,” she explains.
I cock my head to the side. “You going to add color to that?”
We’re crunching through Black Swan trail, along its steady incline.
“Of course,” Lin says, putting the pad in her pack. “Something to know about me: it’s never finished until it’s finished.”
“I actually prefer a black and white drawing,” I say, itching my arms.

Mosquitoes nip at me and cicadas chip at the air. Ethan gives a playful roar as he fills the air with bug spray. Lin swats one of the bugs away from my arm and I can’t help but smile – she’s too sweet.

She looks at her pack, then back to me. “I like black and white too, George. But, only seeing the world in black and white is blinding. You can try swapping it for grayscale… But, grayscale is so bland. The world is so much more. It’s color! It’s rainbows on top of rainbows! And, rainbows never end.”
Ethan stops in his tracks, coughing through the bug spray. “Holy cow! You practice that?”
Lin laughs, her face going pink. “I have a lot on my mind.”
I try to hold her hand. She lets me hold it for a moment, before pulling away.
“So gorgeous today,” I say, breathing in the atmosphere.
It mostly smells of pinetrees and flowers that are in bloom. There’s still a hint of bug spray, which bugs me but whatever. Worth it.
As Lin’s face goes red, I bolt up the mountain trail. “I wonder how long it could take to run to the top!” I cry. “Maybe we could calculate it… Using the angle of the trees and stuff.”
I huff and puff, picking up my speed.
“Hey, wait up!” Ethan says.
“Yeah,” says Lin.
I shake my head. “There’s so much to see. We gotta get as close as we can to the mountain top.”
I slow my pace as Ethan grumbles behind me.
“We’re not doing a competition today,” Ethan says. “We’re just here to enjoy, you know?”
I stop and turn to see Lin nodding.
“Life isn’t a race,” she says.
“Yes it is!” I announce, clapping my hands together.
Lin gives me a disappointed look but says nothing. Dang, I really thought that’d go over better. I jog back toward her and Ethan, keeping with their pace as we scale the mountainside.

I gotta admit: sometimes I come off as an arrogant prick. In these important moments of exploration, I get tempted to act like I’m all important. As we stroll the mountainside, water winding by, I get the sense my friends care about something deeper than that: connection.
Why is the concept of connection so hard to connect with me?

We trod further into the wild, whiling the time away. There’s a tranquility in our trek that I rarely feel. I’m the sort of person who likes to go on long walks alone. Although I appreciate the peace within loneliness, it’s nothing compared to acting as a piece of the greater whole.

Ethan stops and stoops, pulling a baggy of snack bars from his bag. We’ve reached Black Swan pond. It stretches a few hundred feet in front of us, with a waterfall rushing down at the other side of it. The sun is beginning to set, casting the lake in a marmalade glow.
“We made it to our stop,” Ethan announces as we sit at the pond’s edge. He lays the baggy of snack bars onto the grass. “Snack break! I always like to come prepared.”
“Awesome, we got here quick,” says Lin, taking one of Ethan’s bars.

I take one too, but my gaze is still focused on the other side of the pond. Idyllic as it may be, there’s a blemish. A crowd of people are gathered. There also is what looks to be an intrusive machine penetrating the Earth and kicking dust into the air.

Swans are nearby, coated with white feathers that are regal and plush. They crane their swooping necks toward the crowd and excavator, then flap their wings uncomfortably. As another screech resounds, they fly off.
A little animal comes up to us from somewhere in the grass. It looks like a mix between a ferret and a beaver. I swoon. Lin swoons with me.
“So cute,” Lin says.
“I know right?” I nod. “What is that?”
I toss a nut from my snack bar toward the animal. The small animal comes close and sniffs at it.
“A marmot,” Ethan says.
“Aww,” I say. The marmot nibbles the nut away and I come closer to it. Lin giggles as I do.
“Careful,” Ethan says. “They’re cute, but they’ll bite your finger off if you don’t set your boundaries with it.”
I drop the nut with a grunt and my hand shrinks back. The marmot takes the nut. It then runs off as another mechanistic shriek echos from the other side of the pond.
I take a bite into my snack bar and look at Lin. She’s back at her notepad, making a sketch of our surroundings.
“You want to try drawing something again?” Lin asks.
I give a shrug, then scrawl another stick figure. This time, it’s riding a unicycle. I scowl, then spend another minute trying to flesh it out. Eek! It just won’t come out right.
Lin draws her own. Oc course, it’s a million times better.
“Come on, you can do better than that,” she snickers.
“Eh, I’m more daft than deft at drafting,” I say. “I’m more of a tech guy than an arts guy.”

I’m sort of lying. I can definitely draw better, if I just put in some more time. I make sketches for design work, occasionally. But, I’m not the most comfortable with it. Why try? What if I put in my best effort and it’s still not very good?
Deep down, I know my skill at art is no match for Lin’s.
“Art can be technical and the technical can be art,” says Lin, her pen moving off the edge of her page and etching slightly into the dirt. “Don’t put yourself in a box.”
Grr. Why does this girl always have to be so right?
“Okay, what is that?” Ethan says, between bites of his snack bar.

He points toward the crowd and an excavator that are across the pond. The scene has been doing plenty to call attention to itself. The drilling of the machine overpowers the burbling of the waterfall.

I squint. The excavator machine has many arms, needle-like and jerky in their motion. They toss rocks and debris into the air. The crowd appears to have breached a barricade, in a cascade of shouting and sign waving.
Just horrid. Why couldn’t everybody have just stayed home, instead of disturbing peace and progress? Totally backwards behavior.
“Looks like some kind of protest,” says Lin.
Ethan opens his phone and snaps a picture. “Surreal. I do hiking here a lot, and I haven’t seen anything about this on the news or social media!”
Lin nods. “Same! Just checked my Byrd app, and nothing. It looks pretty crazy over there too.”
I scoff and toss a rock into the lake. “Just ignore them. They want to make a scene? Let ‘em. Worst comes to worst, we can go somewhere quieter.”
Lin’s jaw drops and she glares at me. “Excuse me?”
Did I say the wrong thing? I shrug, then rub my eyes.
“They’re just working the land over there,” I say, feeling more and more like I hit a landmine. “I don’t see what all the commotion is about.”
Ethan throws his hands up, then shakes his head. “Okay. Yikes!”
Lin grimaces. “They’re just exercising their right to protest!”
I can feel the heat of her rage radiating from where I’m siting. I scooch toward Ethan, but he seems equally annoyed.
“I mean—but, like—it’s a disruption,” I say.
The excavator’s creaks and groans carry from across the pond. The crowd might just break it!
“It’s their freedom to express themselves,” Lin says.
“Freedom of speech,” Ethan adds, readjusting his glasses.
I swallow and put my head in my hands in submission.
“Sorry,” I say, looking back up to Lin. The look on her face says she’s readying for another pitch.
“Do you want to be stuck in a world where you can never just blurt out what you really feel?” Lin says, her tone sharp and final.

Man: this crush is really starting to crush my ego. I can’t say that she’s wrong. But then, as the superhero crimefighter Cog, I’m also familiar with how unruly protests can get. What about submission to the arbiter of law? To the police? I can’t help but feel that the police are usually in the right. Right?
I wince and Lin stands from her spot in the grass. She’s walking away.
“Wait, where are you going?” I say, faking a laugh.
Lin says nothing. Something in me burns and wants to shout. I’m angry. Why am I so angry?
I’m interrupted as a giant rock crashes into our side of the pond, showering us all with a splash of water.
“What was that?” Ethan splutters. “Was that rain?”
Above us, a maelstrom of more rocks come our way.
I glare at the machine across the pond. Some sort of switch within me flips. Those rocks could’ve hurt us—killed us, even. It’s not the protestors who are the disruption. It’s the machine!
I gulp. I’m going to need to do something. I’m going to need to become Cog. Wiping my thoughts for a clear mind, my precognition kicks in and all worldlines warp around me.
“George,” Ethan and Lin say in uneasy synchronicity, running toward me.
I dive out of the way just as a boulder is about to make me go extinct. Ugh, why not somebody else?!
Part of me just wants to play it cool as George Fletcher and hope divine intervention will stop the rogue excavator. But then, I’m sure the dinos also thought divine intervention would save them.
I need some kind of excuse. Some kind of out.
“Crap!” I shout. “I—I just crapped myself!”
“You what?” Ethan spits out.
I flap my hands wildly and start sprinting. Screaming. I scream like hell. I’m screaming better than the ultimate scream queen, I’d bet.
“George, we have to stay together!” Lin screams after me.
Too late babe. I have a date with destiny! I’m already many yards away, deep into an overgrowth of pinetrees. I yank off my shirt and pants, unveling my sweaty supersuit beneath.

I slap on my mask and goggles, pulling them from my pockets. Unzipping my backpack, I grab at my fluxion-drives. I zap them awake, then zip into the air. Branches smack me in the face as I burst from the trees.

My friends are far below and seem to be taking the trail toward the protestors. Odd.  Anyway, I use my goggles to focus in on the excavator and the ugly drill it’s using. If I hook my fluxion-drives into its side, maybe I can emit enough force to tip it over.

I sigh. The excavator is so obviously an invasion of nature. Lin and Ethan were right. I was dead wrong. For some reason, there’s this part of me that likes to ignore problems. I pretend to myself that, if I imagine the world as different than it is, maybe the problems will exit existence. Nevertheless, the universe has its way of forcing my hand.

As I draw nearer to the excavator, I flit my eyes to flip through a social media stream on the Byrd app. So far, no reports on this excavator or this protest. Instead, my goggles bombard me with hitpieces on the Machine and Cog.
