I gulp, sweat rushing down my face. I refocus on the excavator, and I land at its side with a clang. A throng of shouting people surround me as I grip ladder rungs in the excavator’s side. The excavator thrashes back. I magnetize the butt ends of my fluxion-drives into its metal paneling.

The fluxion-drive emitters purr while I turn their dials. I get a glance of a Byrd Enterprises logo on the excavator’s side and grin. Nice to not have this technological atrocity be the fault of Everman Technologies for a change!
“Go back where you came from, super cop!” a protestor yells.

My fluxion-drives are warming up to full throttle. The excavator’s many arms act to resist the force. It’s a battle of which will buckle first:  the excavator’s robotic joints, or my fluxion-drives. As the excavator’s weight shifts against me, my attention shifts to the protestors.
“I’m no cop, I’m Cog! I’m here to help!” I cry.
“That’s cap!” I hear a different protestor bellow.
Several of their fellows join in. There’s a sinking in my gut. Maybe you can’t please all of the people all of the time. But, I’ve definitely figured out how to displease all of the people.

Waste heat from my fluxion-drives thrusts out their exhaust. Nevertheless, the excavator doesn’t seem to budge. My fluxion-drives crackle with energetic pulses, but the excavator bears its frame against them.
My fingers burn a bit, and I swivel my head to face the crowd. They seem to be cooling down a bit, even though my situation is heating up.
I take a moment to read the signs the protestors wave, and the protestors move toward the excavator.
Among them is a sign that reads “Worker’s Rights”.
“No Taxation Without Representation!”
“Tax Billionaires Their Fair Share!”
Each sign is painted with painstaking detail, vibrant and bold. It’s a gut punch. Despite all the villains I’ve stood up to, what do I really stand for when compared to these people?
The excavator pitches back as several of the burlier protesters pitch in. My fluxion-drives are also picking up steam, even though they’re hot as a stovetop.
Suddenly, the digital feed on my goggles is hit by waves of static noise. The excavator’s motorized limbs start to stall at the same instant.
“Well, hello there,” a voice warbles through my mask’s headset. “This is Nimrod: master hacker.”
“What the heck?!” I cry.
The robotic limbs to the excavator give out, and I feel myself yanked forward by its immense inertia. The protestors all fall behind.

“I’ve taken control of the excavator,” Nimrod continues in a nasally undertone. His face flickers across the screen – a man with a bushy beard and an unruly mane of hair, huddled behind a desk in a dark corner of a room.
“Now, I’m going to need you to do just as I say,” Nimrod whinnies. “Each move you make is critcally important.”
His words of advice come too late. With the excavator’s motorized resistance gone, the fluxion-drives are carrying me and the excavator into an upward arc.

The excavator is several tons of metal, and I’m a flap of flesh hanging to its side. There’s a coarse screaming from the excavator operator as we hurtle higher into the sky. I catch his eye – he’s clinging to his seat with the anxiety of a cat after being doused with water.
“What was that?” Nimrod yelps.
From the fuzzy video feed I’m getting, Nimrod looks like something of a mole man. Definitely an underwhelming unveil. Why do the best programmers always gotta be some neckbeard? Why not a gigachad?
“Sorta in fight or flight mode right now,” I manage.
Nimrod’s feed becomes a rage of static. “Tell me what’s going on! None of the gyroscope data I’m getting from you makes any sense! This is all over the place!”
“I—I’m in the sky!” I sputter. “I’m flying! Come on, you’re a master hacker and you aren’t checking my goggle cameras?”
Nimrod’s footage spritzes out, but his heavy breathing is still audible through my headset.
“Crud nuggets!” he cries.
“Crud nuggets?” I repeat.
“Scratch that—double crud nuggets!” he repeats, voice rising. I don’t think he heard me. “Is there some kind of feedback issue? You were supposed to hold tight and listen to my instructions!”
Sweat rolls down my face in a torrent and my body feels all tore up. I and the excavator are soaring and I’m not sure there’s a way out.
“Look man, I have no clue who you even are!” I shout. “You think you can just hack crap out of nowhere and everybody can somehow keep track?”
There’s a bunch of crashing and smashing over Nimrod’s audio feed. “Gah, my knee!”
Is this guy for real?
“I thought Turtle-Dove told you about me!” Nimrod moans. “We also interacted a bunch of times on those ethical hacking message boards!”
I give a groan of my own. He thinks the message board will massage this?
“Look,” Nimrod continues, “I know phreaking your goggles and this freaky robot probably isn’t the best first impression. But, desperate times call for desperate measures!”

I need this guy to just shut up. I’m shooting ever upward, still with no plan out. On the side of my goggles, I’ve also regained access to my social media feed. However, its negative headlines are getting to me. Now more than ever I need to find a way to tune it out.
“Ok, finally!” Nimrod exclaims. “I got camera access!”
“Uh-huh,” I bleat, air beating at my face.
The fluxion-drives are threatening to melt.
“Damn!” Nimrod says with intensity. “Yep, you’re high in the sky alright!”
My social media feed somehow grips my with a greater intensity. So many griping headlines. So many are directed at Everman Technologies and me.
Why me?
Why?!

“Ok Cog,” Nimrod says, his voice finally cooling down from its erratic flurry. “I need you to tell me if there’s anywhere or any way for you to land that excavator safely. You have to get down from up there, Cog.”
I breathe in. I breathe out. In the corner of my headset blares the headline “We’re Not Cogs in a Machine!”
The headline is oh so right. Yet, what am I?
“Cog?!” says Nimrod.
My breaths are rapid now. Unsteady. I’m pretty sure that the excavator operator is frozen in shock. I am too, my eyes primarily focused on the corner of my headset.
“I’m sorry,” I wheeze.

“Come on Cog! You gotta fix your mindset Cog!” Nimrod screams in a squeaky screed. “Your camera is showing me a lake just below you! I’m gonna need you to do everything you can to maneuver the excavator into the lake and get out of this safely! You got that?”
I swallow. My mouth is so dry. My eyes are too. Precognition has utterly blanked out. My hands are baked.
“Come on Cog!” Nimrod jabbers. “You gotta pull out of this spiral!”
My augmented reality feed undulates as Nimrod communicates, its social media images searing my mind.
“I can’t,” I whimper. “Too much negative feedback. Too heavy.”
“Cog!” Nimrod shrieks. “Stop it!”
“Stopping it… Nimrod, you’re asking for the impossible.”
“Cog, cut out the noise! Cut it out! Grow a set of balls!”

The words are a slap to the face. A slap I need. I snap back to reality. My mind flickers with the flickering of my augmented reality display, and I’m reminded of the ball joints in the base of my fluxion-drives. Of course!
I hit the buttons near their base, unlocking the ball joint mechanism. Slowly, I steer the flux of the emitters, changing the course of their path down toward the lake.

How I manage to do maneuver so smoothly, I’m not sure. Somehow, I intuitively know how to move. An energy vibrates through me and guides me. It feels like my precognition at work, but it could be something more. Hard to say.
“Eureka!” I resound, my body rolling forward with the body of the excavator.
“Yeah!” Nimrod joins in. “Whatever you just said! More of that!”
With the excavator hurtling toward the lake, I demagnetize my fluxion-drives from the excavator and push off.
“You’re doing it!” Nimrod says. “You’re doing it!”

I clip the fluxion-drives to my belt and take flight. As I do, the operator to the excavator jumps out, screaming his head off. Darting toward him, I manage to hug him in the gut. We whoosh over the face of the lake. The excavator crashes into the water behind. Approaching the shore and its protestors, we’re doused in a splash of water.
The operator slips from my grip.
“Screw you, Cod!” the operator squeals, falling into the water.
Oh my god—I just saved his life. Why can’t he at least say my name right?

I manage to slow my momentum from the fluxion-drives and pull myself into a hover just over the face of the water. The sole of my feet and the lake slightly kiss, sending out fierce ripples as they do.
I wave to the crowd, hovering over the ripples. The crowd raves, and Nimrod joins in over my headset.
I’m practically walking on water. The operator? He’s crawling toward shore, his bright white Byrd Enterprises suit all matted and muted. His hair hangs in his face, making him look like a wet dog.
Ha!
Ah!
My fluxion-drives spit spurts of random energy, then short out. I plunge into the waves.

I guess walking on water ain’t for me. At any rate, I’m in the shallow. The water only reaches my chest. Unfortunately, I can already tell that my fluxion-drives are completely drowned out. Probably should waterproof them soon.
“That was incredible,” Nimrod says as I clamber toward shore.
I try closing out all the apps and crap on my AR headset, but I can already tell that shutting out Nimrod will be a chore.
“Thanks,” I gurgle, splatters of water running down my face. “Now, can you please explain what’s going on here? How’d you get access to my stuff?”
The Byrd Enterprises operator is slinking into the forest as the crowd forms around me. Nimrod gives a grumble.
“Look kid,” he whines, “I had to do what I had to do. Byrd Enterprises monitoring is all over the place. I’ve been keeping tabs of my own on things – specifically, on you. But also, Everman.”
“You what?” I shout.
The crowd doesn’t seem to notice, ogling all agog.
“Cog!” they chant.
Finally – they know my name. Took them long enough.
“I saw you’d need help, and so I stepped in,” says Nimrod. “Shouldn’t happen again.”
My headset flickers.
“Anyway,” Nimrod continues, voice fading, “that’s quite the crowd. Seems like you have your hands full. I’ll hop off.”
“Wait, wait, wait!” I say. “Thank you! Also… Still, screw you. Also, double also: you need to tell me what you and Turtle-Dove are up to! You need to keep me in the loop!”
There’s a low growl from Nimrod. “Look: you know what I know, and you’ll go loopy. If we need you, we’ll call you. Hopefully soon. Until then: live life.”
I snort. “What’s that supposed to mean?”
The flickering on my headset stops. The static in my earpiece goes away. Nimrod is gone.
Brilliant! For a master hacker, dude seems like a total hack. Also, what does he mean that Byrd Enterprises has eyes everywhere?
Whatever. I push through the crowd, which is still electric with cheers and shouts. I gotta get out of here and go someplace quiet. Today has been too much.
“Cog, wait!” a gal’s voice cries after me as I turn away from the crowd.
I smile. I know that voice all too well. It’s my gal: Lin.
“And what can I do for you, stranger?” I say, folding myself back into the crowd and drawing close to her.
She’s sparkling. Ethan is at her side, and he waves too. His jaw is also agape, clearly in awe.
“Thank you so much!” Lin says. “What you just did there was a big help! Can you take a picture with me?”
Still smiling, shake my head. I can’t let Lin find out my secret identity!
“You can’t just leave! You need to at least get a picture with everybody!” Lin insists, her arm brushing against mine.
“I don’t – I don’t deserve it,” I stutter.
“Deserve what?” she snaps back, pulling her phone from her pocket.
I shrug and rub my shoulder, trying to ignore my slightly burnt fingers and burning face.

“I screw up a lot,” I say, clearing my throat. “I get self-conscious. Does that make sense? I’m trying to become more self-aware about it, but… Sometimes I can’t. Much as I try, maybe I’m too selfish.”
Lin is locked at my side, her phone screen’s camera facing toward us. I feel oddly comfortable. Granted, I look ridiculous in my wet costume, but what can you do?
“Yeesh, lots of negative self-talk over here,” Lin says.
I bite my lip. “I need to be real with you.”
“Smile!” Lin says, pretending not to hear. She pauses, then looks me in the goggles. “What you’re talking about isn’t real. It’s all in your head. You’re amazing!”
I clear my throat again. Getting choked up over here.
“I’m not sure,” I persist. “Have you seen what they say on social media and the news?”

Lin shakes her head, her hair flowing with the motions. “What does the news know?” she says with a rush. “Look, I won’t be coy Cog: you’re amazing to me. You matter to me. You’ve been tricked into thinking you need to beat yourself down. But, you’d see through it all, if only you could see yourself the way I see you.”
She laughs with a sweet cadence. I laugh with her. She honestly seems more into me as Cog than George Fletcher. Is it weird that some part of me feels jealous of myself?
“Okay, we’re smiling for real this time,” she says.
She snaps a photo of us two. Behind us is the entire crowd. Ethan too. It’s a moment. A wonderful moment.
“That was awesome!” Ethan says, catching my gaze.
I give a nod and laugh again. “Thanks man!”
Ethan shoots me a thumbs up and I look back to Turtle-Dove—err—Lin.
Screw it, she’s totally Turtle-Dove. At least, I’m pretty sure. Mostly. Maybe I’m wrong?
“Say,” I say to Lin, cracking my best smile, “you have a sister? Or, maybe a cousin or something?”
Lin twists her face.
“Uh, what did you just say?” she snipes.
Woof. Ok, I’ve really done it now.
“Cringe, sorry,” I wince. “It’s just, you look so… Eh, never mind!”
I run away from the crowd.
“Captain Cringe, up and out!” I shout, moving toward the forest.
My fluxion-drives are totally busted for the millionth time, so I better just book it.
“Where are you going?” Lin calls after me.
“It’s the call of the wild!” I whoop. “Until next time!”
I give my best wolf howl and make my way through the trees. To peace.
It was a long journey here. It’ll be a long journey back. But: all in all, I consider today with Ethan and Lin a win.
Uh… Screw Nimrod though. Like, seriously.
Chapter 9: Performance Review
The Vitruvian
Am I a cosmic joke? Some sort of comic relief to the universal web?
This fear of mine ebbs and flows. From logic, it follows that my concerns are just meaningless coincidence. In that, there is grand wisdom: all is meaningless. Yes.
Nevertheless… This vexes me. In the grand opera of existence, there’s an internal insistence that even the meaningless has a role to play.
Of course, I might be wrong. Ugh.
I’m sitting in my ice bath in the middle of my conference center. Is it confrontational? Yes. Would I have it any other way? No.

I shift through the stacks of ice uneasily, then begin typing away on my laptop. My muscles feal weak. Inferior. Sometimes I wonder why I torture myself with this ice bath treatment so badly. Then I remember: I deserve it. I need it.

My computer screen has a split in how it’s displaying itself. On one half are all of my business apps. Email, news feeds, corporate data, the works. On the other half is a videogame I’m playing: Super Strat. It’s a strategy game where I play against an advanced AI, vying for dominance of the world’s resources.
Right now, I’m using my most advanced AI: Maniac IV. All possible futures must be weighed and predicted, to have any chance against it. Right now, I’m winning.
“Hi sir,” Izzy says, resting her elbows on the side of my ice tub.
Clasped in her dainty hands is her clamshell of a purse. Why she doesn’t come to me with materials related to the organization? I have no clue.
Glancing at the heroic visage of Caesar in the corner of my screen, I jut my chin into the air and take in courageous breaths.
I am the alpha. The emperor.
The king.
“Glad you came, darling dear,” I say to Izzy, clicking through options on my game. I adore my game. She is nearing climax, and my heartrate climbs with delight.
Despite MANIAC being a master at implementing game theory to resolve problems, its knack for Nash equilibriums is no match for my button mashing.
“Are the doors locked?” I ask, my voice tight.
“Yes,” Izzy says, still trying to look me in the eyes.
I squint into my screen. MANIAC just took three of my cities in a single turn.
How?
I scrunch my face. I want to throw this awful trash at the wall. This doesn’t compute. It simply doesn’t.
“So, what do you want to talk about?” Izzy persists.
Wow, just wow. Can’t this chick tell that I’m extremely busy over here?
“Izzy,” I hiss, my voice thin, “do you think that the Author hates me?”
Izzy contorts her snout inward. She smacks her lips, which are doused in sparkly lip gloss.
“Uh, what?” Izzy titters.
Gah. Obnoxious. Obtuse!
“Obviously, the Author,” I repeat, my voice turning to a brash brass. “The Creator. The Designer. I think he hates me. He must! It’s the only explanation for my plight…”
Izzy gives a mousy sneeze, then bats her eyelashes at me.
“Ok pooky,” she says, “don’t get all poopy on me.”
She waves her purse in my face, bopping me in the nose.
“François De Boodle uses snake leather,” she says. “Do you really think a designer who uses snake leather would have hate in his heart?”
“Yes.”
Izzy itches her butt. I inch away.
Hopeless. She’s hopeless. Nobody understands my genius!
“Oh, come on Mr. Ice Cold!” Izzy says, grinning at me. “You’re the one who called me all the way over here!”
“Mr. Ice beats always pretending to be Mr. Nice,” I snarl.
Izzy whines. “You’re not making any sense!”
I blink. My gaming screen blanks out.
“Game Over!” it reads.
A replay begins – MANIAC nuked half my remaining cities, then took my capital.
It’s no fair.
IT’S NO FAIR!
I stand from my ice bath and lift my laptop above my head. There’s still ice up my Vitruvian themed underpants, but I don’t care. I’m going to toss this damn thing across the room! I—
“Culver! Culvie-pie! My lovey-dovey!” Izzy cries, groping at my wrists. “Not another one!”
I relent with a groan, setting my laptop on the bath’s edge and settling back in. There are still ice cubes riding up my crotch, but I’m just going to need to learn how to deal with it.
“MANIAC cheated!” I announce. “That move set… Positively impossible!”
Izzy bites her nails. “Maybe you just did a really good job training him,” Izzy says, her eyeshadow glimmering as she shimmies close to me. “How is he?”
“Her. It’s a her.”
I smell Izzy’s body odor. She has a rank stink that outranks most, mixed in with a flagrant helping of some fruity fragrance.
I force myself to give a tight smile.
“Do you know what MANIAC stands for?” I say through my teeth.
Izzy shakes her head. Ah, what a simpering simp.
“I thought so,” I mutter. “It’s the Mathematical Analyzer Numerical Integrator and Automatic Computer!” I beam. “Can you repeat that?”
Izzy squeals. “Ooh! There’s math in there?”
I nod, and Izzy laughs.
She flaps her hands like little wings. “You know me and math! You lost me there. I’m so bad at it!”
Oh Izzy, you perfect ditz. Couldn’t even get a word in?
“I thought so,” I say with a huff, leaning back in my ice bath. “Anyway, this baby– she’s top of the line. No other can compare.”
Izzy chews some of her hair while twirling the end of it. Her emerald eyes pierce mine.
“Wow,” she says. “Doesn’t that mean she’s way smarter than you?”
Izzy bats her eyelashes again. My face twists into a scowl.
“Also,” she says, holding her tongue to the roof of her mouth, “I thought Everman had a better computer pooter to play with? Doesn’t he?”
I elbow her purse into my ice bath.
“Hey!” she says, splashing after it.
Whatever. She needs a bath bad anyway.
My computer screen breaches my focus. There’s a garish gambit of videos and reports spamming through.
“Byrd Enterprises destroys ozone and violates zoning laws,” the reporter Amanda Taft grumbles into her microphone.
Great. Just great.
I lean into my screen and scroll through more images. More info. How can this be? My Byrd app is supposed to have the tightest regulations.
“Whargh!” Izzy screams, diving into my ice bath face first. “Brain freeze! My brain is frozen!”
Ugh. Is it ever not?
“Will you please get ahold of yourself?” I say, stepping from my tub with my laptop. “Act like a professional! Honestly…”
I can finally brush the irritating ice cubes from out of my underpants and try ignoring the goosebumps forming along my skin as I adjust to my new climate.

There’s footage of protestors and Cog destroying my latest excavation robot. The video quality is blurry and stilted, and the audio is overpowered by obtrusive protestors. Nevertheless, it’s clear that Cog used those weird gadgets of his to take my tech out.
He broke it! He broke my stuff! Mine!
My fingers go tight and knuckles white about the edges of my laptop.

“This makes no sense!” I shout. “Izzy, this is the last straw! You’re responsible for social regulation! You should be ensuring that info on the Byrd app is closely monitored and regulated. How could you let this get through?”
Izzy pokes her head out of the tub and makes duck lips. “Quack!” she says.
Incompetence. Utter incompetence.
“Enough,” I persist. “You want to know why we’re having this meeting? Get over here!”
I look over and Izzy is still splashing through the ice bath. “Gah! Get– come take a look at this, will you?”
She’ll figure out how to get over here eventually.
In the meantime: how could Hugo let that Cog kid go out wearing those cruddy pajamas? Awful design, just awful.

I let the footage loop. No matter how many times I play the video back, somehow Cog lifts my robot and dumps it into a lake. His motions are inexplicable. His tumble with my robot is utterly unstable, and a slight shift at any moment could’ve put him under.
It’s too coordinated. Too perfect. It defies logic. It’s as though it’s all prearranged.
I pause at the part of the video where he hovers over the swamp.
“How?” I whisper, studying his handheld thrusters. “I let it loop over and over again, but nothing yields.”
For those devices to defy gravity must break physics. They must be using a propellant. Yet, I’m compelled to somehow fully explain it. The way that air warps around the thrusters looks off.
Is it a new reaction? A new element? And, what is it emitting exactly? I must know. I need that tech, whatever it is.
“He’s cute,” Izzy says, looking over my shoulder.
I moan and close out the tab, diving back into the overflow of outrage being posted about Byrd Enterprises.
“You see all this?” I say, keeping a steely monotone. “This much negativity isn’t supposed to be getting through. How are these accounts not all banned?”
Izzy rolls her eyes. “It’s fine. Isn’t this supposed to go to tech support or something?”

I rove my head around the empty midsummer conference room. The carpet has been torn up, leaving exposed linoleum in its wake. The walls have also been laid bare. Usually it’s more crowded this time of year, but all this remodeling I’ve been doing is really taking a toll. Suddenly, I miss the days when this was all just a startup, and I was working in a dinky research lab.
I grumble. “Lots of talent is in flux right now: we’re poaching people, people are poaching us. I need you to sharpen your approach!”
Stepping back, Izzy examines her nails. “Got it. Duly noted.”

“We’re at a critical juncture right now,” I say, opening up my metadata feeds. “Also, some of the people criticizing our company are from within Byrd Enterprises. One of them was our chief scientists, using a sock puppet account!”
Izzy snickers.
“Don’t worry, I had MANIAC fire them all,” I say, lacing my fingers together. “I’m not afraid to keep going either.”
“You what?” Izzy says, hand over mouth.

“I’m surprised you’re surprised,” I say with a smirk. “You know how time sensitive this all is. We need the edge—the competitive advantage. Much as I’ve had myself and MANIAC game theorize all possible paths, there’s still no room for error.”
“But you’re already Earth’s savior– smartest man alive. Do you really need to be so rash? So rushed?”
I stroke my chin. “Would it make you feel any better if I told you that the chief scientist whistleblower is dead?”
Izzy stumbles back, nearly falling into the icy bath all over again. Oh Izzy: you haven’t yet figured out life is a meat grinder, have you?

I burst out laughing with a deep mirth. Ah, so refreshing. It’s been too long since I’ve been able to laugh like that. I hit a button on my laptop, turning on my playlist of the finest German expressionist music. Bach blares out my speakers, whisking my ears to another realm, sweet and fine.
“Big Byrd!” Izzy balks, ruffling her hair. “We talked about this! You can’t just do that!”
I lick my lips, then turn up the volume to my laptop. “It’s fine. The police report determined that he died due to unrelated causes, okay? Forget about it.”
Izzy’s eyes are blotchy. Great. Now I feel bad. I have to try and pretend that I don’t notice.

“Let’s make sure that we’re focused on the real enemy here: Everman,” I say, my voice rising with the swell of my music. “All of our AI resources and media apparatuses should be focused on taking him down. I refuse to let anybody else try controlling my story—controlling my narrative. You get that?”
I catch Izzy in the reflection of my computer screen, and she’s nodding submissively.
Perfection.

“You—you have a lot of Everman’s Tech now, don’t you?” Izzy says with a pout and a quiver in her voice. “And—and, with the meeting you have scheduled for today, I’d say you already have him on the ropes!”
Oh yes, our meeting! I chuckle. I’m looking forward to that.

I give a slow nod. “Yes, very true. But, bear in mind: I owe much of my luck to great corporate spies. Now, imagine a world where Everman has great spies too. Imagine what that might mean if he knew all my secrets.”
I struggle to hold back a shudder. Izzy shudders for me.

“And his tech—I’ve tested it on all manner of cyborgs,” I continue. “But there’s only so much that reverse engineering can get me.  I can’t let there be a single crack in my operations. I need as much monitoring and regulation as possible.”
My laptop somehow slips from my hands and hits the floor. I tremble.
“As much. As. Possible,” I repeat, icy water and venom dripping from my lips.
“Really, why compare yourself with Hugo Everman anyway?” says Izzy, pitching up her voice.

I wrinkle my nose. “I’ve put in more time and effort than anybody! He’s a tabloid void who sucks up all the oxygen. All my life, I’ve been on this quest for fame and fortune… And the people, they never notice. They never care. They just give all their adulation to him! He does not know the first thing about anything, by the way.”
Izzy shrugs. “Everybody craps. Just because somebody has a successful story doesn’t mean anything. That guy has plenty of issues, I’m sure.”
“Thank you!” I cry. “Screw Hugo and his huge ego!”

“Also,” Izzy says, scrolling through her phone, “Hugo Everman apparently left a message recently. He congratulated you on the ball you held and your recent product launches. Said he enjoyed reconnecting. He also said he’s got your number, but you wouldn’t answer.”
I put my head in my hands and grit my teeth.
“He said he’s ‘got my number’, eh?” I whisper. “No… No, no, no.”
I kick at my laptop.
Izzy howls. What is wrong with her?
“He was just trying to be nice,” Izzy says. “I really think he cares. Here, I can play it for you if you want.”
I shake my head. “No need. I’m telling you, he’s onto me. First it was the protestors… Then, his lame sidekick… And now this? It’s a counterattack, I can smell it.”

There’s a heavy sinking in my gut. My mind begins flipping through all the things I’ve been doing recently– all the mistakes. My stomach aches. If people knew what I really am, would I be able to live with myself?
My face flushes. Izzy simply puts her hands on her hips. Good old Izzy – always able to bring me back down to Earth.

“Come on, Culver,” Izzy says, flipping her hair. “You know Hugo: he’s like a golden retriever. Loyal to the end, always looking for another squirrel to chase, kinda oblivious… You should know better than anybody. There’s no way this guy has any clue. It’s coincidence.”
I take a deep breath. She’s right. Hugo has no clue. He’s the mental equivalent of a blunt object.
I’m fine.
“Also, I really think you’re picking on the wrong guy,” she continues. “He’s so nice to people and everything. Life of the party. I know he’s got competitive tech, but…”

“This is personal, and having a bunch of sycophants means nothing,” I mutter in rapid-fire, as Bach soars to new heights through my cracked speakers. “The fact that Everman is a man of people says everything you need to know about people. Everybody wants to act like this beige soulless world is the fault of visionaries like me. But, the truth is that people like beige. They like bland. This world is the product of the people, and the people have no imagination. They take the most lazy-minded approach to things! They take shortcuts! Always on the path of least resistance… It’s practically a law of nature.”
Izzy is inspecting her nails and gives a yawn. “Come on: you know you weren’t raised to talk like this.”

“I wasn’t raised!” I say, my voice rising up. “The Byrd family—it’s just day after day of being bored. The Byrds are all soulless feudalists! Unbearable! When you have everything—all the technology, entertainment, clothing, and material comforts—you have nothing. You know this.”
My words are shooting out ever faster and may soon hit escape velocity. Maybe too fast?
Good.
Izzy unplugs her ears once she realizes I’ve stopped.
“I mean… Uncle Brad ain’t bad,” Izzy whispers.
“Screw Brad!” I shout.
My music cuts out. I take a moment to cool myself down, then pick up my laptop to get the music going again. It truly is medicine for the soul.
“Do you think Napoleon would care about people’s feelings? What about Caesar?” I announce. “I learned too late in life that society needs its slaughterhouses to make the bacon, awful as they may be.”

Izzy does a curtsy with her hands behind her back. “Understood your highness.” The music hits fever pitch as she does this. “On that note: your meeting with the Machine is in an hour. You want to take the private jets to his landing pad?”
I wipe a bit of snot dribbling out my nose – screw all these allergies. I flash a grin. “Fun as that sounds, it’s only a block away. And it’s so much fuel…”
Izzy saunters up to me. She snatches my laptop away, then scampers toward the door to the conference center.
“Come on, you know you want it,” she teases. “It beats bus. Or subway. Or… I guess blimp?”
I burst out laughing. “Good point. Honestly, what is up with this city’s culture and its transport system? Completely all over the place.”
I rub my temples as I follow after Izzy. “But, uh…  Only the small jet. I can’t afford to do anything more expensive right now, especially with this massive company purchase that’s coming up.”
Izzy’s lips curl into a wide smile and she closes my laptop. “Big jet, big Byrd. Big. Jet.”
Her tongue coils around each syllable. My body tingles.
“Ok,” I say, pumping my fists and thrusting my hips. “You got me. Big jet it is. The biggest jet I have. Everman will be blown away!”
I suddenly stop, remembering I’m only in my underwear. “I will need a bathrobe though…”
“No worries, already on it,” Izzy says, slipping out the door. “We should be good. Thank you Cuthcake!”
I nod cautiously, closing the door to my conference room and taking care that nobody sees me.
“Yes,” I say. “And thank you, sister.”
The Machine
Up. Down. Up. Down.
Up and down she goes. Hnngh!
Ok, that’s 60 reps. Good. But, gotta keep going. Go! Gotta represent!
I wipe sweat off my brow. Good God! Hnngh!
“Impressive,” says Opal.
I give a sigh and relieve myself of the dumb dumbbell I’ve been fighting, resting it in its slots on the bench press. I let my arms fall at my sides as the cool wash of accomplishment flows over me.
“Wow!” exclaims my doctor who comes to me from Opal’s side. “A thousand pounds! That thing is a monster!”

It’s Dr. Livingston, my company’s dedicated MD – medical doctor. Also, he’s a bit of a mad doctor, as is the case with some of my best people. His eyes always have dark bags under them, which match his equally dark hair and grimy doctor’s coat.
He goes to yank the electrodes from my body. I brush him away, rolling off my back and onto my feet.
“Great to hear,” I announce. “I’m built like a tardigrade.”
I’m a bit surprised, since I haven’t taken treatment since the rocket explosion. Ugh… Rough.
Pulling my bottle from my pants, I attempt to cool my panting between gulps of icy drink.
“What are we looking at?” I say with a gurgle, my face now dripping in equal parts sweat and tap water.
“Your metabolic rates are great,” Dr. Livingston states, still looking somewhat stunned. “Same goes for the rest of your vitals.”
He pauses to do a double take at a sheet of paper he’s holding, before turning to view a table at the back corner of the room. He gives some mutters as he ruffles through them.
“Well?” I say, raising my voice.
Opal’s arm brushes against mine. She jerks back and brushes hair from out of her eyes.
I grin. “Boundaries.”
Despite the tightrope I walk, trying to keep things professional with Opal, I’m glad to have her by my side right now.
“Sorry,” she says with a huff. Bits of sweat are beading down her face. I struggle to place why – the air conditioning in this room is on full blast.
Admittedly, I’m pouring sweat since I just finished a giant workout. But outside of that, what is there to sweat?
We’re all in my building’s state-of-the-art recreation and health center. Floor to ceiling is decked out with AI enhanced workout equipment and amenities. Also, HVAC. Gotta love it!
“Hey, space cowboy, mission control needs an update,” I say, clearing my throat. “What’s going on over there?”
Dr. Livingston bobs his head and shuffles his paper into a neat stack, before staggering over. Poor Livingston– the man could clearly use a nap.
“On a positive note, your heartrate and blood pressure seem to be normal,” he says, licking his thumb before thumbing through his things again.
I raise an eyebrow. “Seems to?”
He leans on the bench press. “It’s a drastic improvement from what I was looking at earlier this week, I’ll say that much.”
The cool blue lighting seems to flicker along the linoleum floor and eggshell walls. I bit my tongue. Is this good or bad? Is he readying up for a negative note to go with this positive note?
“Let me say this much,” he says, “you’re looking better than lots of the athletes and astronauts I’ve worked with. If you stick with what you’re doing, you should be okay Armstrong.”

I give a half frown. It’s nice to hear him liken me to one of the astronauts. They’ve been heroes of mine since I was a kid. Nevertheless, something doesn’t quite sit right. I sigh and fix my posture.
“Give it to me straight, doc,” I say, fanning my shirt.
I feel wrong inside all the time and I never quite know why. It’s like some bolt or joint within me wasn’t screwed on quite right. My creator may have– just maybe— screwed up.
I look over to Opal, then to Livingston. They’re so quiet. Gah!
Say something to me! I’m the Machine!
I – I’m…
I’m human too!
Doesn’t anybody understand? Why is there so much resistance to getting what I want? Why does my body fight and wear on me when I’m trying to get where I’m going?
Whenever I move toward something, my motions get all stiff. Jerky. I need things to loose and I often lose. And my emotions. Ugh! They boil me up, from inside out.
My face goes tight.
“Why am I never enough?” I mutter.
Do I even matter?
My body itches from all my sweat and I can smell my own body odor. So aggravating – I need to just get this over with and get in the shower.
Opal checks her smart watch and awkwardly shuffles over a few feet, the knots in her hair springing as she does. Dr. Livingston is still scanning the page and scrunches his nose.
Crud. What’s the hold up? Why they holding off on me?
“Well?” I grumble.
“You stopped taking that gene therapy for performance enhancement, yes?” Dr. Livingston says, nose still in notes.
I nod. “Yeah. Earlier this week, when I noticed I was feeling weak and out of sorts, sort of.”
Dr. Livingston gives a sniff, then wipes his nose with his sleeve.
“Great. Keep that up. You might not want to hear this, but this data conclusively confirms negative side effects. You can’t keep taking that stuff.”

I stiffen. “We need some sort of compromise on this! Those enhancements – it’s about something bigger than just me. Progress on key medical issues is being accelerated. Also, they’ll help massively with space-mining initiatives for astronauts, protecting them against cosmic rays. Think about the future among the stars! You’re asking me to leave it on the table. It’s our future!”

Dr. Livingston sniffles and preens his hair. “I believe you that the treatment is important. I’m sure biomedical advancements will get us to this future you talk about. But, for the present moment, I strongly advise you stop the treatment.”
I rest my hand on my forehead and take deep breaths.

“You just don’t get it, do you? The world needs heroes. It needs protectors. Without this treatment, I’ll have to stop. I won’t be able to save the day if it ever comes down to the wire. I just… I just know it.”
Opal walks in front of me and gazes into my eyes. Her skin is flushed and her mouth twitches all flustered.
“This doesn’t always have to be about you, Hugo,” she says. “There are plenty of capable people and systems in place, keeping things safe. You don’t need to put yourself out.”

I rub my forehead some more, my mind going back to old footage of space heroes and astronauts I saw as a kid. Traveling to the stars and worlds of the heavens always felt so right to me. It can be here, if I just play hero a little bit longer. The celestial kingdom will be humanity’s with the right technology and science.
I side-eye Dr. Livingston, then look back to Opal.
“Everything in this world changes so fast. And, I need to be able to save things,” I say.
Opal gives a lopsided smile. “We can’t save forever. We have to savor what we have while we have it.”

I shake my head and look to the pale blue lights in the ceiling. “All my life, I’ve been fighting to be like one of those heroes from stuff I saw as a kid. You know, like the astronauts. Space men. Our future is up there, you know. I always feel like something keeps getting in my way. I can’t give up. That’s the only reason I’ve come so far. That said, maybe I’m missing something. Hard for me to say.”
Opal shifts her weight to one side, as though thrown off balance.

“I’m always wondering how to be more of a hero in daily life myself, haha,” she says, before pausing to give another soft laugh. “But, an enhancer isn’t the answer. No amount of strength can move heaven and Earth, but a single voice can.”
A rash tingles through my body and my face feels warm. Something shifts in my soul. Nevertheless, a strong part of me still feels agitated – off-kilter.
“I strive. I fly. I believe… And, success is out of reach! Ugh! No matter what I do to help, it’s never the right thing. I’m always falling short. It never ends!”
Opal makes a broad gesture with her arms. “Air hug, Hugo. Also, don’t keep saying that. You’re more than enough! Life isn’t meant to be Neverland, Everman.”

I give a snort, then make an air hug gesture back. I still feel a bit off and miffed, but she has a point. Maybe the reason things keep spiraling out of my control is that this control was never meant to be mine to begin with.
“Just sleep on it is all I’m saying,” says Dr. Livingston. “I’m sure you’ll come to the right choice.”
I shrug. “I wouldn’t bet on that, Doc.”

“I mean, it’d certainly help clear up your ethics questions, right?” Dr. Livingston states, scribbling something that appears as a smudgy riddle to me. “Useful technology, but you need to be careful with how it’s deployed and wielded.”
I force a smile. “True.”

This is all a bit depressing. But then, what else is new? I tried convincing myself that, if not me to use it, then somebody worse gets it first. Maybe I was shortsighted. All the heroics and triumphs I’ve been chasing are artificial. Something within me has gotta give. Deep down, I know the truth that nobody else is willing to say.
Opal checks her watch again, then clucks her tongue. “We about done here?” she asks. “I have a quick errand to run, and then Hugo and I have a business meeting with the board.”
Dr. Livingston gives a thumbs up. “Yeah, yeah, yeah. By the way, did you want to see how the guest patients are holding up?”
I blink as I feel a sudden weight settle on my chest. I wipe the sweat from my brow. “Of course.”
I let Opal and Dr. Livingston ahead of me, toward the exit. “Thanks, by the way,” I say as the automatic doors swoosh open.
“No problem,” says Opal.
Dr. Livingston says nothing, his motions distracted and impatient as ever.

We make our way into a ward where there are patients laying in stretchers. We’re separated by walls of brick and glass, but I somehow am still able to feel twangs of pain reach me from where they’re sleeping.
There are three of them. They’re the cyborgs that I’ve fought with over the past week. However, most of the haphazard weaponized limbs have been replaced with proper biomedical prosthetics.
“Those are new to me,” I say, my eyes still scanning the scene.
Dr. Livingston gives a slight grin. “Yeah, we had them sent in from top medical centers.”
“That Everman Technologies?” I ask. “I don’t recognize it.”
“No,” Opal and Livingston say in unison.
“And… I’m footing the bill?” I chuckle.
“Yes,” says Livingston. “That’s what you—.”
“Sorry, just messing around,” I say, taking a deep breath as my chest goes rigid. “Cover every cost, don’t worry. I know I really need to work on my Hugo humor.”
“Hugo humor?” Opal says, scrunching her face.
“It’s patented, don’t steal it,” I say, drawing closer to the windows.
I want use to all break into laughter, to relieve the tension. I want the darkness in the air to somehow goa way. Instead, it stays lying among us, unflinchingly.
“They okay?” My voice has a quiver in it, and my face is nearly pressed up against the glass.

There are various wires and tables deeding into the patients, and a long array of biometrics line the walls. The patients are withered and frail, almost devoid of muscle tone. A slight reassurance is that they’re breathing more steadily than last time I saw them. The color is also returning to their complexions.

One of them seems to open their eyes from under gauze and gaze at me. I think they give a smile. Eh, could be in my head. Still, they’re all positively glowing relative to their condition when they got here. I lose my tough guy guise and smile back at them.
“You are going to be able to cover these healthcare costs, right?” Opal says with a nudging gesture of her shoulders. “The shareholders got wind of this, and they are refusing to pay.”
I grimace. Oh, they’ll pay. One day, some way, they will pay.
“For the time being, the charity should be able to cover it,” I say with a forced shrug. “You can have fun funneling funds. I’ll try talking to them when I get the chance.”
Yeesh, that wooden board. Not looking forward to the meeting I’ve got scheduled 15 minutes from now.
“You might also want to consider upping security and lawyering up,” says Dr. Livingston. “The police have a warrant out for their arrest. You might be looking at a little litigation.”
My face contorts in disgust. “Utterly unwarranted. Also, you know I don’t like lawyers. Justice should be self-evident.”
Dr. Livingston gives a soft guffaw. “You should know all too well that law can easily be bent. The justice system is only as just as the money justifies.”
“Fine, we’ll get it sorted,” I say. “Money is no object. These people aren’t going in a prison.”
Money, money, money… Man, he ain’t making my day easy.
I peer into the window again at the victims. They have the laminar flow of youth running down their skin. Can’t be much older than Cog.
“This isn’t right,” I say, my voice cold. “This isn’t fair. And it was my company’s tech. My tech. My fault. I refuse to let these people take the fall.”
Dr. Livingston gives me a warm smile, then pats me on the back. “It’ll be alright. We’ll get there.”
He better be telling the truth. I turn away from the window, my vision blotching.
How could my tech have gotten hijacked like this? How could this happen?
“I think it’s time,” Opal says. “We gotta go to other meetings. Keep your spirits up Dr. Livingston, and good work.”
“You too,” Livingston chirps.
I follow Opal out of the health center and into the hall, lumbering with the energy of a zombie. My head is still in that patient ward, but good old Opal is a master at bringing about peace.

“You ready for this meeting?” Opal asks. “I’m going to try my best to help, but I’ve got a ton of other things on my plate. I heard they want to pivot on some things after the mishap at the Byrd showcase.”
I bite my lip. “I’ll do my best, but can’t make any promises. Last thing I want on my mind right now.”
Opal laughs with a wide smile. With everything I’ve screwed up, it’s nice to see her be herself again.
“I’m dead serious,” I say, keeping just a hint of sarcasm. “I’ve got all this robot rocket stuff to deal with. And the charity… I don’t have time for another chairman battle.”
“You check your stocks?” Opal asks.
I grimace. “I can’t look at that stuff these days, things are way too insane.”
“Stock just jumped up 10%,” Opal says. “Maybe the product announcements and public appearances you’ve made are finally paying off? Hopefully that keeps your spirits up.”
She turns the phone back toward herself, studying the data in disbelief of herself.
“Ok, I really have to stop,” she says. “Other things to run to, see you soon. Good luck!”

Opal whips out her phone, displaying a graph with a whole lot of green. There’s a slights pat on the back and then she’s off, jogging down the hall to who knows where. Business—why must you come with so much busyness?

I take measured breaths and make my way toward the main meeting room, my mind bouncing between various initiatives and pressures I’m gonna get hit with. I’m barely ready, and I’m still shocked  my stock is not in the red this morning.
I chuckle to myself. Wall Street suckers. Whatever, I guess I’ll take it. Uneasy as I am, maybe my heroic efforts are finally paying off.
Reaching the door to the meeting room, I pause and begin to breathe. In and out. I just need to clear my mind. Time begins to cool and peace washes over me. All will work out.
“Stop right there bitch,” somebody caws.
My face puckers in on itself. Stopping in my tracks, I look about my marble hall.
“That’s right, you big bitch!” they repeat.

Something slimy gets me in the forehead, then splats on the ground. I turn around. There’s a man stuffed in a banana suit, which is a size too small. His yellow tights have holes in them and the suit is colored a dull beige. Wilkins. The tip of the banana suit slumps to the side, and stains dot its seams. His face barely fits through the hole in his costume, and he wears a yellow bandanna over his forehead that is cinched too tight.

“It’s the Banana Bandit baby!” Wilkins cries, bandying his phone about in one hand and his oversized banana cannon in another. “Your greatest nemesis! It is time for the battle of the century: a bad, bad banana vs. the big tangerine!”
I groan, then roll my eyes while rolling up the sleeves to my orange shirt. Wilkins and I go way back. But, our relationship is totally not what he makes it out to be.
“How’d you get past security?” I grunt, wiping some of the banana gunk off my face.
Wilkins doesn’t seem to hear me. He’s twerking in the middle of the hall, making sultry kissy faces through his five o’ clock shadow.
“Na-na-na-na-na,” he sings to his phone, waving it around. “This banana is feeling real fame hungry today, subscribers! I’m down bad! Bad banana bad!”
Well, okay then. Looks like this has been is still trying to go viral?
He gives a tragic attempt at moonwalking on his banana peels for shoes. “I’m over the moon, Everman!” he declares, just as I go to snatch his phone away.
Wilkins staggers. “Hey, you can’t just jag stuff from the next Mick Jagger like that!”
I turn his phone off, then scoff. “Excuse me? Last I checked, I thought I had a restraining order on you!”
“Wilkins laughs. “It’s going through the court of – uh – appeals!”
There’s another splat at my head of banana peel, shot from the banana cannon.
“And that!” I shout, pointing at his cannon. “The banana cannon! I thought we banned it!”
“Well, I am a bandit,” he says in sing-song. “Also, it’s called the unappealer!”
“Onion peeler?” I snort.
“Unappealer!” Wilkins whines, stomping a slimy foot. He pauses to cock his big floppy head. “Banana cannon… BC… It made me sound like I have a big ol’ complex!”
My mouth gapes a bit as my eyes run over his big banana suit. “Well, I hate to break it to you, but…”
Bah! I’m hit with another banana before I can finish. Why does he keep doing that?
“Time for me to peel out!” Wilkins says, sliding down the hall. He shoots bananas wildly into the air, blotting doorways and lamplights alike.
I jog after the joyrider. I need to get that cannon!
“That’s right you monkey, come get the banana!” he says with a giggle.
I’m just about to get at him when I slip on one of his banana peels.
Yow! I hurtle onto my back. My legs manage to kick at the Banana Bandit, toppling him over.
“Ungh!” he guffs, falling on top of me. “Can I—can I have my phone back?”
My eyes burn and narrow to thin slits.
“Get. Off. Me,” I say, my voice stiff and rigid.
“Make me!” the Banana Bandit says with a wink.
Holding the phone away, I clench my jaw. “I’ll have you know, I’m a black belt in ninjitsu!”
Banana Bandit’s gangly arms outstretch for the phone. “Come on, you wouldn’t bruise a perfectly good banana would you?”
“Uh… Perfectly good?”
“Fruit punch!”
The Banana Bandit gets me in the wrist. A successful block! Much as I’m getting sick of this coconut’s puns, I can’t complain if he wants to announce all his punches before he makes them.
He grumbles, catching my smirk. “You think you’re a master fighter, eh? I can fight you blindfolded!”
He pulls his bandanna down over his eyes and begins wailing at me, feigning a powerful roar. I feint. He fights back. I counter.
I give a whoop of laughter, and he rejoins. We’re really at it now. Two men, wrestling to the end!
Bam! Blam! Pow!
Yahoo!
“You’re stupid!” Banana Bandit howls as I pin his elbows in a bind.
“No, you!” I snap back.
“Yo mama!” he grunts.
He kicks me in the groin.
Oh. Oh no. Not the balls!
Owweee!
Oh, the heavens… Heavens why?!
I fart. I groan. I moan. A stargate portal seems to open up in the corner of my vision. Waves of pain. Unngh!
“What in the world are you doing?” the voice of Escorgier booms.

My ears pound and I groan, barely gathering myself to my feet. I and the Banana Bandit are still close to the meeting room’s entrance, but a gaggle of shadowy figures have gathered around. I blink, clearing my vision of sweat, spit, and adrenaline. I gag.

It’s the business brigade – a bunch of animals wrapped up in tight business suits, a harsh clash of black and white. Also, Peter and Opal—chief engineer and chief technology officer, side by side. I give a limp wave, then readjust my sleeves.
“Supervillain,” I mutter with a weak laugh, pointing at the Banana Bandit. “You know—the usual.”
Something in my chest sinks as I read the faces of those around me. Pure disappointment is upon them. Even the Banana Bandit ain’t buying my excuse.
“You couldn’t have just called security?” Escorgier asks, shoving his hands in his pockets and giving a droll grin.
Total troll, this guy. The toll of dealing with him—it’s too much.
“You know what?” I say, my voice soft. “He’s fine. He can stay, he’s my guest today.”

I hold back a snicker as I unlatch the meeting room door an unleash a rabble of grumbles from the group. Banana Bandit gives a whoop. I can feel the fury burning off Escorgier at the notion, and I’m loving it.
Here comes everybody! Each board member waddles beneath my smelly armpit as I keep the door propped open for them. Escorgier gives a glare, and I just try to pretend I don’t see him.
Gotta give myself props: earlier this month, I would’ve blown my top. At this point though, I can only accept whatever happens.
Peter and Opal take uneasy steps as they enter last. I try to give a comforting nod. It’s the best I got. All I can do is try to speak softly, and carry a big stick.
“Where’s Boris?” I ask, scanning the room.

Silence greets me as I make my way to my seat at the far end of the table. Behind me is a taped up window, still broken from my battle with a dragon a week or so back. Escorgier grabs a seat at the opposite end. Banana Bandit is right by him but somehow Escorgier doesn’t seem to care. Something in his eyes crackles with a cracked delight.
“Where’s Boris?” I repeat.
Escorgier shrugs. “He’s out, as of today.”
Peter and Opal are seated near me, wound up like compressed springs. Peter opens his mouth to say something, then sucks in his cheeks.
I glance at my initials etched on a plaque that distinguishes my seat: H.C.E.
Escorgier is still staring at me, clutching his mechanical pen. Ech. He’s giving off bad chi—a bad energy. He’s gonna make me justify everything, from my latest tech to my very existence, isn’t he?
“Machine, egos are going to clash today,” Escorgier decrees with a scree. “Let’s eschew the pleasantries: we’re starting an executive search.”
I feel as though I’ve just been hit by a truck.
“Excuse me?’ I say, my voice icy. “Are you questioning my authority?”
“I’m surprised you take issue with this!” Escorgier neighs. “Don’t guys like you like the hero questing, questioning thing?”

His mouth twitches. “Anyway, the search is on. I know—I’m being a tough man. But, this is how all things are. Start, then stop. Is, then isn’t You’ve had a nice run Hugo, but we’re thinking it’s time you go.”
I lean back in my chair and kick my feet up onto the table.
“I’m sticking around,” I say. “Maybe this has been a rough quarterly cycle, but it is still just part of a cycle. Things come back around.”

There’s a snapping of the handle on Escorgier’s pen, from him picking at it too intensely. “That’s the problem, Everman: you let problems and things go on for forever. Your insistence on continuing your way… Always forging ahead, despite requests to slow it down. You keep foregoing and forgetting that all is tentative. You’ve rode out your peak and your tenure must end.”
“I don’t have to stand for this,” I snipe back, holding my palm in the air. “The company has quintupled over the past five years.”
Escorgier laughs. “That’s the trouble isn’t it? For a man who wants to stick around, you’re not putting much stock in your own stock, are you?”
Escorgier pounds a button on the table, blasting a hologram of charts and metrics into the glass pyramid at the center of the table.
“You can’t force me out,” I say, my voice breezing as wind. “Between I and Boris, there should be a majority stake. While I and Boris have our differences, he’d never…”
I swallow. Even as I say this, I already sense I’ve made a mistake. Deep down, I know the truth.
Escorgier gives a Cheshire grin. He’s about to make me pay. But then—if my blunder of words forces the truth out of him, it might be worth the price.
“Weren’t you listening? Boris is out,” Escorgier says with a hum. “He sold. Everman Technologies has absorbed his stake.”
Holy crap Boris! You moron!

“We’ve been riding high,” Escorgier says, adjusting his chair to ascend with his condescension. “But, your role as this heroic Hugo figure—go figure—is played out. Sales on your merch are down. The Machine franchise is trending as white bread and inauthentic. People see the Machine as a manufactured persona, and your attempts to branch out as a desperate attempt to escape typecasting.”

Escorgier scrolls through a bunch of social media impressions, sneering as he does. Much of the board joins along. My veins flare up with fire. I close my eyes to regulate myself. His angle of attack is difficult to deflect.
When did saviors start serving mankind through subscription services?

My mind winds back to when I was young, biking around rural Lanesville. Back then, I always thought it was Lamesville, but those winding dirt roads and ephemeral forests always had a place for me. Every day there was something new to discover.

I’ve spent much of my adult life trying to discover myself through money and performance. But, it’s all a front, and it’s time to explore the frontier beyond it. What does it mean to be Everman? Am I an overman or an everyman?
I was once entranced by tales of rags to riches. But maybe my rags were never the problem. Maybe the problem was the riches.
I chuckle. Rich, isn’t it?

“I mean, this was inevitable: your strength comes from rehearsals and exercises,” Escorgier says, grinning madly as he digs the proverbial knife in deeper. “When you couple in the annoying sidekick, the string of public controversies, and your corrupt transfer of wealth into the nonprofit… You’ve jumped the shark. The brand damage is simply irrevocable.”
I shift in my seat. My friends shift with me. He might say I’ve jumped the shark, but I feel I’ve jumped into the shark tank.

“My sidekick needs a mentor,” I state firmly. “And, the nonprofit—it’s a matter of principle. Biotech is a public service. The true measure of wealth isn’t how much can hoarded, but how much can be given away.”
“So I’ve heard,” Escorgier lisps. “Look, Cork…”
“Cog.”

“Gah—Okay? You should’ve gotten a super pet or something instead, this kid is really messing with the brand synergy.” Escorgier chortles. “As for the rest of your prattle: you need to look at your business catalogue like cattle. Your flagrant misuse of company resources and security protocols will not stand!”

Escorgier might talk a big game, but I can’t help lasering in on the 10% uptick featured on the holographic stock ticker. I rise from my chair. My palms plant solidly on the table surface and I hold my arms in a truss.
I have one power move left.

“The cyborg and chip leak mishaps are a massive mistake, I agree,” I say, the words flowing low and heavy. “And yes, our spending outstrips our revenue. I’m struggling to keep it together, I won’t lie. I don’t know how this all slipped through the crack, and I’m sorry.”
I give a sigh of relief. My friends and some of the board seem on board. Escorgier isn’t buying it, but what does he know?
I clear my throat. “Mistakes happen though. Also, you need to spend money to make money. I have a vision of where everything is going. There’s a pathway to onward and upward, you have my word.”

Ungrounding my right hand from the tabletop, I gesture at the stock. “Even the public seems to believe in where we’re headed. The stock jumped 10% today! That simply doesn’t happen unless things are going well.”
Escorgier gives a snicker, and my face goes hot. What is he laughing about?
Escorgier takes a chomp at his pen. “You’re not in on the loop. The big movers and shakers are.”
A lump forms in my throat. It has become too dry to even swallow. “What’s that supposed to mean?”
“We’re not just performing an executive search!” Escorgier bellows. “You’re being ejected from the board, and we’re looking to perform a new merger. Wall Street clearly got the memo before you did.”
He squints at the uptick in the graph, then gives another snicker. My head spins. What was the wrong turn I took to get here?
“What is this, a Banana Republic?!” the Banana Bandit shouts into Escorgier’s ear, bouncing from his chair.
Woof. I almost forgot he was even in here.
Escorgier rolls his eyes, then hits a button in his chair.
“Somebody get this fool out of here,” Escorgier says into his armrest.

“You tech oligarchs can’t just get rid of me,” Wilkins says, dashing to the corner of the room. “Somebody needs to keep things regulated! Keep things regular! Also, if you get any closer, I can shoot antimatter out my banana butt!”
A couple of security guards emerge through the entrance doors and grab at Wilkins.
“Hey!” I say as they carry him off.
My voice is utterly drowned out under the tumult of Wilkin’s protests.
“This stuff should be handled by vote! By a process among the people! Among all!” Wilkins presses.
The security guards drag him into the hall.

“You might think more robots and AI will increase freedom, but innovation is not always this way!” Wilkins whimpers, his voice nearly echo. “The invention of the cotton gin initially increased slavery! Increased bondage! What do you think the next great revolution will do?”
Escorgier closes the door.
“Seriously,” Escorgier says with a hum, before retaking his seat. “This is the sort of thing I’m talking about. Why let that nutter in here?”
I can’t take my eyes off the door.
Aww man... Poor Banana Bandit.
I scratch the top of my head. “He’s mostly harmless. Mostly… Besides: he has a point. Sometimes the wisest among us are those we deem fools.”
My eyelids hold a new weight, and I let them hood my vision with a hint of darkness. “You better make sure he’s safe.”
This comes more as a declaration to myself than anyone else. Escorgier and the board don’t seem to hear me, their eyes glued to the data flipping through the holographic display.
“I’m sure you must be on the edge of your seat as to who we’re performing the merger with,” says Escorgier. “The board has decided it’ll be Byrd Enterprises. Surprise!”
The holographic display flickers, opening up to a video call. The back of a chair emerges, held in steady high definition. The familiar backside of a head covered in jet-black hair pokes overtop.
“Everman,” Culver Byrd grumbles through the conference room’s loudspeakers, my name rolling off his tongue.
His voice is inescapable, coming at me in pressurized surround sound.
“Ever. Man,” Byrd repeats, rolling my name in another direction as though it were a hard candy. “Ever… Everman.”
The chair spins with a creak. It’s him, unmistakably.
It’s so over.
“Why, hello Hugo!” declares Byrd. “What a coincidence! I was just talking about you! Almost didn’t see you there!”
I just gotta let this pass. This’ll blow over.
Escorgier is beaming, and his eyes brim with avarice. “Yay! It’s the big Byrd brain! You finally made it!”
Byrd gives a hiss and the camera flickers. “Don’t call me Byrd brain!”
Escorgier readjusts his collar and bobs his head. “Of course, of course. On that note: we were just talking about the Machine hero, mascot, branding thing. Did you want to look at all that?”
“No,” Byrd says with a swipe of the hand. “I want to take a tour of your latest tech prototypes. Who cares about the stupid action figure brand?”
Escorgier gives a sniffle, then gestures at Opal and Peter. “Yes, yes. Our best techies are here, no worries.”
Byrd juts his chin in the air, proud and foreboding.
“First order of business though, I need to set some boundaries,” Byrd says, before giving a whistle. “Time to begin an inquisition on this acquisition.”

A woman enters the meeting room holding a towering stack of papers. She’s wearing a snowy fur dress, which drags behind her and spits sparkles with her every step. On her head is a bunny ear head band. The papers land on the table with a thud and Escorgier passes them around.
“This is my sister, Izzy,” Byrd says with a smile. “The Velveteen.”
“Hey y’all!” the Velveteen says with a jump. “I’m his sis!”
“You didn’t want to do this in person, Viddy?” I say as a stack of papers comes my way.
Byrd shudders, then shakes his head. “No, in person break ups are so awkward!” He laughs. “Also, germs. I don’t want to get stuck dealing with a bug. Viddy is partial to video, what can I say?”

As I skim the paper, electric shocks run through my body. While much of the document is gibberish legalese, one thing is certain: my company is out of my hands, and all the pieces are already in place.
“Uh, who is Mr. T, Mr. G, and Mr. V?” Peter says, reading off the title of the document.
“Mr. T and Mr. G are my two layers, Mr. Teller and Mr. Gallagher,” says Byrd. “They get things done and do a lot of heavy lifting on my behalf.”
Peter scratches his head. “Err, why list them that way? Also, Mr. V?”

“Mr. V is me, the Vitruvian, of course! I needed the contents of this report to be kept confidential. It’s a stylistic thing, okay? I’m sorry if these names are a big distraction, but I have too many other things to get to right now!”
The Velveteen nods. “Boss is right. You guys have no style!”

My mind runs back to notes and evidence given to me by Cog, surrounding chip robberies at Everman Technologies facilities. Some of these nicknames and abbreviations have come up before, as clues. I now realize that Byrd has been after me and my company resources for far longer than I’ve given him credit for.
“Why are you doing this?” I say, my voice streaming as molasses. “You realize that, deep down, you and I are the same… Right? Don’t you?”

“We couldn’t be more different,” Byrd says, leaning back in his chair. “I am one of the fiercest thought leaders in the world. I will stop at nothing to ensure my impact on history is storied and exceptional. You? You’re a dropout. You want a system of handouts. You’re not built for this high-paced atmosphere, and you know it. You promote the average median, mediocre person instead of people like me, and pretend like it’s some virtue! You need to get over yourself and stop posturing as my equal! Everman, we will never be equal! We will never be even, man!”
I hang my head, letting my shadow cast across the table. This is so unlike him. I always have seen him as a friend, even if a rival.

“Byrd, please,” I say with a slight choke. “Have empathy. Think about everything we’ve done together. Consider your morals. Morality – it’s the highest modality of reality. The rest is just window dressing.”
Byrd groans. “Give it a rest. Your company is all but mine. It’s all there in the black and white. Our corporation creations, Byrd and Everman, are to merge into the same entity. It’s fate!”
Byrd pauses, then scowls as though annoyed with himself.

“But then…” he says, “maybe you’re right. Maybe that’s all there is. Wrong and right. Black and white. Of course, maybe there’s also a twist on this. It’s so constricting to always be in the right. You ever think about that, Mr. Righteous? There might just be a dark side to light! Maybe I’m allowed to be wrong!”
I wince and wipe the hair out of my face. “Between good and bad, bad is a bad look Byrd. It’s risky business. You can’t just run around stepping on everybody. It’ll catch up to you eventually.”
Byrd bows his own head. Parroting me? Parodying me? I’m not sure.

“It’s just business,” he says. “I’ve measured the business risks. I need your tech, and this is what I must do. If this risk makes me a reckless and evil man in your eyes, Everman, oh well. It’s the price I’m willing to pay.”
Escorgier and the board are all squirming and murmuring among themselves. I’m sensing some buyer’s remorse over here.
“You tell him, hot stuff!” the Velveteen says while skipping around the board room. “My bad boy!”
Gross. Isn’t she his sister?

“Insist,” the Vitruvian says, with a wide grin. “Err—you always insist upon yourself. It’s your greatest sin. Hugo always needs to be the hero… To be the bigger person… To be the better man… Somebody else always needs to be the bad guy! It’s sickening Everman, it’s sickening! Your days of playing king are over!”
The Vitruvian stands from his chair, his cape flaring behind him, harsh and terrible. Most of the light is blacked out from the video camera, leaving the hologram of a smoky figure.

“There’s an asymmetry tucked away at the base of existence,” the Vitruvian growls. “You see it in the stars. In the atom. In the heart of all things… Imbalance. Such is the nature of chirality. Such is the nature of time. Spin… There’s no other way to spin it.”
The hologram is looming ever larger. Inexplicably, a cloud passes by the sun through the window and the room dims.
“Did you know there’s a highest possible temperature in the observable universe?” the Vitruvian inquires.
I refuse to answer. I have nothing left to say to him.

“There’s also a lowest possible temperature,” the Vitruvian continues. “Between the two, when you look out to the sky, you see the universe is so much colder than it is hot. All but absolute zero. Cold… Oh so cold. This is the true nature of things, which we so often try to hide away from ourselves. Do you have an answer to that?”
I can’t let myself take his bait. He has a point, but so do I.
Byrd pulls back from the camera and settles into his chair. His form has returned to that of a mere man, dressed in a trim black and white business suit.
I smirk. His cape completely contradicts with his put-together performance. But, who am I to judge?

“One more thing,” the Vitruvian says, resting his hand on his chin. “The Machine brand goes to us. Your likes, your likeness, your frame, your fame… We now reserve all rights! You’re now property of Everman Technologies, Machine!”
I suck in my cheeks and clamp down with my teeth.
He deserves to be chewed out so bad. He needs to be chewed up, then spit out!
Okay, I need to get ahold of myself.
I’m starting to understand why Viddy insisted on a video call.

“Here’s the best part…” The Vitruvian sways toward the camera, then away again. “The stuff that’s in your blood? Those experimental bio-enhancers? You need to stop taking them. Come on, you gotta have a response to that! We’ll effectively own your body. Ha!”
I give a soft laugh. Didn’t want to stop taking the enhancements, despite the advice of Opal and my doctors. Though, the universe is really forcing my hand.

The Vitruvian only laughs louder in response. “And that brings me to your tech people: Opal and Peter. I want to start with learning more about the biotech treatments from Opal, then work my way to Peter on your applied research prototypes.”
I finally raise my head, then my voice. “The biotech division is squarely within the domain of my nonprofit. You can’t do that, it’s illegal.”

The Vitruvian’s laugh turns to a wolfish howl. “Illegal? Everman, this is the law we’re talking about. Anything can be made legal with the right lawyers in place. We’ve already discovered a zillion ways you’re in violation of your contracts, which renders all stock agreements with you null and void!”
I lift my chair into the air, then toss it at the holographic pyramid. The schema bursts into a million pieces.
I walk toward the exit without another word. The entire room is frozen in shock. They get the message.

“I have defeated you Hugo!” the Vitruvian’s voice warbles through the room’s speakers as a phantom. It catches me off guard – for a second there, I thought it could be a voice in my own head. “I have vanquished you! Do you hear me!? You are about to go down as the greatest failure the world has ever known! It’s over man!”
“Never man,” I say. I stop at the exit. “Maybe it’s true. Maybe none of this is working. Maybe I’ll fail at making my dreams a reality. But, to try for a dream is one of life’s greatest privileges.”

I walk out the door and slam it shut. My veins throb and my muscles tremble as I make my way down the hall. The walls seem to wallow with me as I walk by, the paneling dry and cracked. My fingernails run along the paint, scraping some of it up.
Several of the paintings that hang to the walls are tilted a bit off center, and the glass is smudged with fingerprints.
I furl my lip at what somebody has done to a painting called the Wick Rota– a tunnel painted out of cubes, embedded within a translucent sphere.
I give a weak chuckle. Maybe I don’t like things being slightly askew, but it actually adds a new dimension to this picture. Much more dynamic, somehow.
That said, who’s putting their grubby hands all over my stuff?
There’s a squealing of rubber. It’s at the end of the hall – a man, vacuum sealed into a Byrd Enterprises uniform. He’s carrying some sort of device. A robot?
Is that my tech? Is this place being infiltrated?
The man disappears behind the corner. Sprinting to the end of the hall, I call after him. “Wait! Stop!”
Turning the corner, I watch the man slip through the entrance to the company’s delivery bay. The door took his biometrics without a moment’s hesitation.
I stumble a bit as I slow myself and skid into the bay window. My nostrils flare and my ears get hot.

The delivery bay is flooded with vans and trucks, all labeled Byrd Enterprises. People skitter about, carrying a mixture of Byrd and Everman hardware. It’s hard to watch. Clearly, I’ve been slow on the uptake. If my company was infiltrated, the time to sort it out must be long gone.
“Fuck!” I cry out, kicking at the wall.
My foot leaves a dent. I stub my toes as I do this.
I don’t give a fuck anymore.
“FUCK! FUCK! FUCCCCK!!”
I’m panting. Seething. Writhing. My fists curl in on themselves with such force that they start to stall out. My body locks up.
“Hugo?” a soft voice comes to my ear.
I turn, pulling my face from the glass.
It’s Opal. Opal, and a kid. Why is there a kid here?
Opal wraps her arms around the kid. Fuck. It’s her kid. It’s bring your kid to work day, isn’t it?
“Sorry about that, stubbed my toe,” I say, my body sputtering toward them.

It’s at least partly true. That said, my chest wells with guilt. I can’t take my eyes off the boy. He had to see my ugly side—hear me blow a gasket. Old memories from when I was a kid scratch at the back of my mind.

There were so many authorities and father figures who I held up on a pedestal. All were flawed. As I travel deeper into the boy’s eyes, something in there is shattered. I’ve joined the pantheon of failed men and ideals. My anger got the better of me.
I’m the bad guy, aren’t I? This whole Machine thing… Trying to live up to some timeless image of a man that the world could never give me… It was all a farce, wasn’t it?
“Go to the waiting room honey, I need to talk to the Machine,” Opal says to her son, patting him on the head.
He takes his mother’s phone out of her jacket pouch, then skips off with a sort of glee.
I activate my signature smile. Maybe I’m being too hard on myself. Maybe my outburst hadn’t been so bad after all?
“How’d you get here so fast?” I ask, “The meeting over already?”
Opal puckers her lips, then brushes her willowy hair to the side. “They’re still going I bet, but I couldn’t stand it in there. I quit on the spot.”
She pauses to blink. Her lip quivers, then she places a hand on my shoulder. A warmth fills my cheeks.
“How you doing Hugo?” she says, peering into my eyes. “I’ve never seen you look so afraid of things.”

I grimace. “No. Not afraid. I’m not afraid of anything.” I stop myself and give a dejected look. “What I’m afraid of, if it is possible for me to be afraid… It’s not a thing. It… The physical, it’ll always ebb and flow.  However, what lives deep within an imagination? What hides within the consciousness of others? What hides within myself…? I’ll admit, sometimes that scares me.”
Opal’s face sharpens and floods with a ruddy ferocity. “Don’t ever let them talk to you that way again. You hear me? You don’t have to listen to that bullshit. Next time, just leave.”
She pulls her hand back. I offer a crooked smile.

“It’s fine. Sometimes I gotta take the L and let all this stuff sort itself out. None of this would’ve happened if I hadn’t let it,” I say, giving a shrug. “Day after day, I insist on my way or the highway… I refuse to bend. I opened up the doorway for all of this.”

I bite my lip. “Also, my body needs a break. I need it all to slow down. Byrd has me pegged. I want to solve all the world’s problems, but it’s too much for me. I tell myself I’m essential, but what I do will only ever be a drop in the bucket. I’m like an old piece of tech, Opal. Maybe it’s finally time for me to go on a shelf.”
Opal looks to the side, then back to me as a twinkle forms at the center of her pupils. “You love it though. You love this place.”

I itch my nose, then nod. “I do love this. We’re a merry band of wild Muppets! But… There’s always going to be this part of me that thinks being a leader is trying to be a one-man-band. I forget to care about others. I need to hit the brakes. I need to find that part of me that cares again.”
Opal opens her mouth, then zips it shut. She zips her eyes shut with it, and slows her breaths. When she reopens her eyes, her face is telling me goodbye.

“Hugo, I have to go. My son has soccer practice to get to,” she says. “Take care. For what it’s worth: you’ve left a mark on me. Or, maybe a scar… At any rate, I care. I hope you can find a way to care again too.”
She walks off. It’s just me now. Me and my thoughts.
I can be just the biggest downer, can’t I?
Eesh – my toe still hurts like crazy.

My feet stutter over to another window in the hall, overlooking the city skyline. There’s nothing quite like it. My eyes dance about the sprawling grandeur of architecture, drinking in the light that runs down them. Shadowy as my mind’s eye might be at the moment, it’s good to see that the world I’ve helped build still stands strong and proud.
I gotta leave this place soon and head back home. I’m hungry and I’m tired. But, for the time being, I just want to be right here. I want to stay standing in the glory of this view.
I need to hang onto the moment. I must. It’s the only thing I’m certain I know how to do
Chapter 10: Open Workspaces
The Cog
Bobbin Locke is back. Him and the garlic breath. Blech.
How he was let out of jail or brought back, I have no clue. Being real, I’d love to try kicking his butt again. But then, this is an office, not the real world.
“You sure that you put it in, right?” Ethan asks Bobbin.
Bobbin bobs his stupid head, as a bit of drool dribbles out the side of his mouth. Must still be recovering from our battle a week back, when he tried raiding the office in the night.
It seems that he has amnesia, because he has yet to acknowledge that I’m Cog or that we fought. There’s a grapelike welt dwelling on his forehead, purple and puerile.
“I only know how to do things the right way,” Bobbin says, rolling back his broad shoulders to pat Hand-E on the tip of its lil’ head. “You know me! I’m Mr. Straight-and-narrow.”
Yeesh. What a load of crock.
Bobbin winks at Lin, then lumbers closer to her. Lin readjusts her turtleneck. Oh brother…
“You sure we should even be installing these chips?” Lin asks, shuffling away from Bobbin, then back toward him a bit so as to not piss him off.
Bobbin stomps a foot. His face is beat red, swollen with what I assume is high confidence and high cholesterol.
He gives a wheeze, then a woof. Oof. I know he’s supposed to be feigning laughter, but I thought he was about to drop dead for a second there.
Bobbin is the one man who could put fun in funeral.
“Of course, losers!” he bellows. “Dr. Skully handed me this package himself! All defective Everman chips in the robotics division are to be replaced with Byrd chips!”
Ethan wipes sweat out of his face, then sputters. “I– I thought Byrd’s tech was incompatible with our stuff. Also, this is the research division. Are—are you sure we want this linked to Byrd’s data?”

Bobbin smacks himself in the forehead. “Byrd is the best in the world. You guys just don’t get it. Byrd provides a zillion features, widgets, and user interfaces for a chip, all in one package. Everman chips… He’s got none of that!”
Bobbin’s stomach gives a bad gurgle at the word chips.
“Don’t they experience lots of dysfunction?” Lin says, now edging Bobbin.
Bobbin scratches his chin. He scratches his groin. “Err… Eck… I tell ya, dysfunction is a touchy subject.”
