“I just don’t feel comfortable doing all this without Dr. Skully’s explicit approval, this seems rushed,” says Ethan, rubbing the back of his neck. “Can’t be safe or reliable.”
Ethan shuffles in place, body swaying side-to-side.
Bobbin blows a raspberry, then smiles to himself as though it were the master stroke of a silver tongue.
“Why, this is the most safe and reliable setup of all time!” he announces, giving Hand-E another violent pat on the head. “Byrd is… Uh… Lion!”
Hand-E gives a sudden whip, whacking Bobbin in the forehead. Instinctively, Bobbin blows another raspberry before he falls backward with a hellish scream.
Landing on the table, Bobbin causes the table to fold.
I rub my eyes. I had a hard time sleeping last night, and I wonder whether I’m still dreaming.
“How the who’ll did me?!” Bobbin splutters incoherently as he staggers to his feet.
Bobbin is now more red and swollen than a tomato.
Ethan, Lin, and I huddle closer together, unsure of what will happen next. My precognition is buzzing.

A roving robot zooms from the side of the room and toward Bobbin. Bobbin is left to run away, screaming ever louder. His pace is stilted, but he manages to stay ahead of the robot as they move in circles about the center of the room.
“Could’ve sworn he was the picture of health before being sent to prison, only a week ago,” Lin says.
“Prison does that. It’s a rough place, trust me,” Ethan says.
I raise an eyebrow. “How would you know?”
Ethan gives a half-frown. “The internet… Let’s just say there are some mysteries in life I wish I could unlearn the answers to.”
Bobbin’s screaming hits a fever pitch, his arms flailing spectacularly, before he finally breaks out into the hall. The roving robot barely manages to slip through the door after him.
“On that note, Bobbin is walking internet meme,” says Ethan. “So many forced revelations he’d share in restrooms that I’d love to forget.”
There’s another scream from Bobbin that leaks into the room, as though he somehow agrees. Then, nothing.
Sweet, maybe he’s finally dead.
Eh… With my luck, probably not.
“When I took this job, I really thought I was looking at a stable paycheck,” says Lin.
I snicker. “Nobody is stable in the adult world, let’s not kid ourselves.”
My precognition blares, and I shift my body to face the back door.
“Dr. Skully is about to enter in a few secs, just a head’s up,” I announce, before winking at Lin.
She scowls, bemused. This switches to bewilderment, her mouth going agape when Dr. Skully’s footsteps resound and he opens the door, like clockwork.
Even Ethan stares, clearly impressed.
I hold back a laugh. Maybe I shouldn’t be using my powers as a party trick. But then, a guy has to have fun with things at some point, right?

Dr. Skully’s brown blazer is marred by grease stains and crumbs. His face is crumpled, holding the weight of a martyr. Catching the strange looks on our faces, he pulls his glasses off his own face. An attempt is made to clean the smudges off them with a mixture of his breath and the cloth of his breast pocket.
I’m not sure whether he succeeds, but he has managed to clear the air of any suspicions of magic Lin and Ethan were feeling toward me. All focus shifts on Dr. Skully.
“What was that noise? Everybody okay?” Dr. Skully utters, his eyes aflutter.
“Bobbin. Bobbin is back,” says Ethan.
Dr. Skully mutters something about boobs under his breath.
Err– maybe he’s calling Bobbin a boob?
The muscles in Dr. Skully’s neck go tense as he cleans some of the scraps Bobbin’s “repair” left on the table with Hand-E. Dr. Skully tosses these debris in a wastebasket.
“You sound enthused,” remarks Lin as she joins in to help.
I stay back. I have a reputation as a useless wallflower, and I’d rather not give Dr. Skully any sense of the contrary.
“You not a fan of Bobbin?” Ethan pitches in.
Dr. Skully simply shakes his head and gives another grumble.

“He nearly broke a few of the robots with his recent mods,” Ethan continues, brownnosing to the max. “Violated the hardware safety protocols we have in place. Did you authorize those? Also, did you let Bobbin back in?”
Dr. Skully uses a hand to flatten out rumples in his pants, while using the other to try cornering Hand-E. I force myself to jump in, gingerly nudging Hand-E alongside Dr. Skully.
“Seriously, you normally keep such a tight ship,” Ethan presses harder. “This guys was ruining the lab’s resources. How could this happen?”
Dr. Skully finally steps away from the table. He glares at the ceiling before offering each of us a warm smile.

“I’ll say this much,” he rumbles, “throughout my professional career, I’ve convinced myself that there’s no such thing as a stupid person. Everybody in life is merely at a different stage of knowledge, with infinite potential for learning. Bobbin Locke though? He just might be truly stupid person.”
Wowie. Really not pulling any punches for the Bobbin roast session, are you Dr. Skully?
Ethan’s eyes well with sadness. “Then why would you approve of these awful chip replacements?”

Dr. Skully readjusts his glasses. “It’s not up to me,” he says. He pauses to itch his beard. “Byrd Enterprises just took control of the company, as of today. There’ve been rumors about this shakeup for awhile from the higher ups, but now it’s official. Can’t say I’m happy about it. Hopefully things work out, but we’ll see. This corporate politics stuff has always been too complicated for me.”
We all shuffle about as a chill passes over us.
“Don’t worry, things will sort themselves out,” says Dr. Skully. “I’m sure I’ll find a place for you wherever I wind up next, if worst comes to worst.”
“Thanks!” Ethan says with a thumbs up.
My guy is way too excited for Dr. Skully’s approval.

“On a lighter note, any good updates you guys have for me?” asks Dr. Skully. “I have a packed schedule today, but should have enough time to help guide where you might need it over these next few minutes.”
“Good. Things have been going good,” Ethan blurts.
Dr. Skully raises an eyebrow. “That’s surprising. I mean, I’m glad to hear it. But, I know the organization has been a mess recently…”
“It is what it is,” I say, patting Ethan on the back. “I’ve been helping out with some software patches and stuff, where I can. Not perfect, but… It works.”
Dr. Skully smiles through the bushy beard of his. Buddy could really cut it down a bit.
“Glad to hear you guys all found a way to work together and help each other out,” he asays. “You never know how these connections might serve you down the line.”
We’re all so close together in this moment. The air is electric. And I should know— I’ve accidentally shocked myself more times than I can count.
I give my friends a grin. They grin back. Somehow, in some small way, a part of each of ourselves is being shared when we’re in this place.

Nevertheless, I can’t shake the feeling that this is all impermanent. How much about my friends will I ever really know? How much have I bothered to try knowing? How many friends from my past have stuck around?
Not many. Not much.
And that brings me to Lin…
It’s so hard to stop my feelings for her. But then, am I doing right by her? Am I to learn that relationships at work can never work?
Probably.
Probably definitely.
Cunning as I like to think myself as, there sure is a lot about life I’m always struggling to make sense of.
Dr. Skully seems to have picked up on my angst and flanks around us.

“This is all somewhat my fault,” he says. “Somewhat. I should’ve been more transparent with the team about what I thought was going to happen. Lots of programs are being reshuffled or scrapped entirely, in the name of artificial intelligence. This merger is pretty ruthless too.”

Lin and Ethan rejoin with annoyed grumbles. I attempt to add grumbles of my own, but my mind beams back to conversations I’ve had with Hugo. He’s seemed so off lately. Worn out. The pieces are all coming together. I feel bad for not noticing sooner.
“What happened to Everman?” I say with a wince.
Ethan and Lin are groaning now. Suddenly I’m the suck up, eh?
“Seriously, nobody cares,” says Lin.

Dr. Skully gives one of his signature huffs. “Agreed. Greed… Pure greed at the top. Everman is a funny character, I’ll give him that. But also, total nutjob. If you had to deal with half the insanity I’ve had to deal with, you’d now that he had to go.”
Ugh. If only I could let Dr. Skully in on my time as Cog.

Dr. Skully catches the downcast look on my face, then pauses to stroke his beard. “The ejection is a bit of a paradox though. This place will probably collapse faster without him than with him, I’ll give him that. Not sure what the business strategy is.”
I feel like a kid again, being told Santa isn’t real. Of course, this was all just a sham. How is it that I was the last to catch on?
To placate myself, I check my phone. As I do, I find a message that has been waiting for me over the past few hours from the man himself: the Machine.
“Meet me at your apartment in an hour,” it reads. “We need to talk.”
A fire brims in my chest. Maybe the myth is still kicking after all?
“Well, I gotta go,” I say. “Dentist appointment this afternoon. Forgot to tell you guys.”

I scuttle out the door Bobbin took. My exit is likely just as disruptive as Bobbin’s was as well. That said, I don’t care. I can’t let myself feel guilty. I’m not going to bother pretending to be happy about work when it’s simply not working. Life is too short for that.

Making my way down the hall, I feel my throat go dry. My chest sinks. I think back to all the wild stuff that’s been happening. Could I be doing more to keep a handle on things? What if my standoffish nature is putting everybody out? I like to be self-defined, but how expensive is this for others?
My mind burns, running through all the possibilities. It feels like it’s on fire.
I stop at a water fountain and dunk my head in. I drink. I drink and I drink, until water fills my stomach and the awful dryness goes away.
I lift my head and make my way down the hall. It’s okay. None of these problems were of my choosing. I’m just a cog. I can relax.
A bit of burning remains at the back of my mind, but I feel better now. I’ve cooled myself somehow, through the water and the fountain.
I put my hand through the fingerprint scanner of the building exit, then head out of the Everman Technologies office building. I’m out of the manilla mindscape, escaping into a vanilla sky.

Above me, the sun is razzling from a venue of clear blue and through the web of city. My eyes sizzle in delight. All clouds are on vacation. The air is as free as my spirit. New Vinci has no room for clouds in this vicinity now.
A siren calls out as I make my way toward the maglev station, but somehow I feel at rest. My spirit feels whole.
“Hello,” Lin calls out by the train stop, with a wave.
“What are you doing here?” I say, trying to stay nonchalant as I stride to her side.
Lin shrugs. “Also got a dentist appointment.”
I smirk. “Right.”
“Just a coincidence,” Lin adds. “Don’t get any ideas.”
I scratch the back of my neck. Sure would be nice if my precognition could tell me if this gal likes me or not. Would save me a lot of hassle
Honestly, I’m a busy guy. Also, low-confidence. Also, also… Love has yet to have worked out for me. Screw it, I should still say something.
“I’m nothing if not ideas,” II say, filling the dead silence between us. “Also, I don’t believe in coincidences.”
“Oh?”
Lin’s hands are in her pockets, and her eyes are coldly trained on the train tracks.
“That said, I’m sorta nuts,” I continue. “Just want to make that clear.”
Lin bites her lip. “Figured. Figures.”
Grr. Should I ask this girl out again? Is that what she wants?
Is that what I want?
I’m often flipping polarity on this question. I’d love a relationship. I’d love to no longer be lonely. But, do I really have enough time to give? Enough heart?
Plenty of other guys out there would be better for Lin, I’m sure. Surely she deserves the best?
“Do you want to go somewhere to eat together, some time?” I blurt.
Blurgh. Didn’t think that through at all.
“This weekend,” I clarify.
Lin gives it a second, then a weak smile. “Camping trip, can’t do it. Maybe some other time. Also we’d need to bring Ethan along!”
I grimace, then check the time. Wow, this is awkward. Was really expecting my natural charisma to do me a solid for once.
“What train you taking?” I ask. “Mine arrives in about a minute.”
Lin twirls her hair. “Mine arrives in 15 minutes.”

My face goes hot. Lin turns her head, nestling her chin into her shoulder. She’s being a bit of a poser, but cool at the same time. “I thought about taking the same train you are taking. But then I realized I had a better option based on where I’m going.”
I brush some hair out of my face, then try pulling off her shoulder move. I’m guessing it’s not as cute as when she does it, but it gets a crick out of my neck.
She doesn’t laugh. I totally expected her to laugh! Even my precognition is telling me that something is off.
Man – I miss some of that magic we had when we first met. Me and my big head really ruined it.
“I’m surprised there’s no rain today,” Lin remarks. “Was really hoping for a rainy train ride.”
She pauses, then looks at me. I look at her. We look away.
“I love a good rainy day,” she continues. “What about you? Do you like rainy days?”
I shrug. “I like sunny days myself. There’s nothing quite like looking up and seeing a sea of clear blue.”
Lin snorts. “I don’t like when there are no clouds. Not much dimensionality. Just a bit weird, you know?”

I brush my hair to the side. There’s only one blemish in the clear sky, hiding in the margins: the moon. It’s decided to show up today, and rests there as a pearl. Or, maybe I should look at it like a neighboring planet, which likes to stay close for some mysterious reason. Is it lonely?
Fuck.
I use my hand to squeeze my cheeks together and rub out some of the funk I’m feeling.
“Lin… I love a blue sky, actually. Especially as things get dark. When you can finally see all the stars, you realize the dimensionality is insane.”
My train pulls into the station. It’s time for me to go. Yet, as I head toward the doors and Lin stays standing at the train stop, I can’t help but feel like I’ve forgotten something important.
I check my pockets. Odd— everything is there.
“Bye!” says Lin with a wave.
“Bye!” I wave back.
I probably should say more. Share more of what’s within me. But the doors close, and our moment is over.
Why must my attempts to play Casanova go supernova?
The Vitruvian
My ears are still ringing from Everman’s shattering of the holographic display. I turn the volume down on my earpiece and struggle to pick up the pieces from the outburst.

“I was really expecting him to put up a bigger fight,” I announce. “I mean… It was like he was barely paying me any attention. Surely he realized how special my visit was? Doesn’t he usually have more fight in him? More fire?”
“I mean, you did fire him,” Izzy blurts, wiggling the bunny ears to her headband as she does.
“I’m sure he’ll be fine,” I grumble. “Hugo Everman always finds a way. He’s annoying like that.”
“Hugo Everman? Blasé,” Izzy continues. “What kind of name is that? Honestly, everything about the Machine is so clunky.”
I laugh the boincy, boisterous laugh I always do when Izzy makes a joke at Hugo’s expense. But, for once, something feels hollow.
Hugo gave up too easily. No fun.

My eyes water a bit as I stare deep into the abyss of my laptop’s screen. It feeds me finicky footage of Hugo’s meeting room. It’s a mess of shattered glass, and all the businessmen have moved their chairs away from the meeting table by a foot or two.
“He seemed pretty ticked,” Escorgier lisps through the warped audio systems.
I pick at my fingernails.
“It’s fine,” I say. “I’m just glad that I streamed from my jet instead of visiting in person. I mean, when he threw that chair… Could you imagine if I had been in the room?”
I give a weak chuckle as I rise from my chair. “Thankfully there is no possible way he can get me from in here!”
There’s a thud. The top of my head rings with pain, and I tuck myself back into my seat. I scowl at the low jet plane ceiling above me as I rub my fresh welt.
“Fergher—fuggin!” I shout.
Fuck Everman! Fuck him! Fuck, fuck, fuck!
“Are you okay?” Escorgier gasps.
“I’m fine,” I manage with a moan.
The pain is already subsiding, but I might as well milk it. “I bumped my head, but I’ll make it through.”
I’d forgotten that they can’t even see me, since Hugo broke the projector. The posturing and subsequent bruising I just did was all for nothing.
Ah well…
“You poor baby,” Izzy cries through the speakers.
I snicker. “All is well.”

I drape my cape across my chest and over my face as a blanket. My brain-in-a-jar, Carl, jostles on the desk in front of me. I pull Carl off the table and cradle him close to my chest. My chin rubs against the jar’s glass rim, cuddling him.
“Bwa-bwa,” I whisper, my cuddles intensifying and the pain fading away.
Carl jostles and sloshes in protest. Oh well. He’ll get used to it.
“What did you say?” Escorgier gurgles through my earpiece.
Ah great, they heard me.
“Sorry, bit of turbulence,” I pronounce. “I need the tech support guy to give me the rundown on all the tech that Everman has been cooking up!”
Everman’s employee readjusts his baseball cap and gives a snarl in Escorgier’s direction.
Wonderful… Hugo hires people who are just as ill-tempered as him. When will he finally wake up and realize that robots are a million times better?
“I’m chief engineer, not tech support,” the man says with a laugh. “Also, my name is Peter. Nice to meet you!”
Oh wow, he can talk too! Well, isn’t that just gravy?
“There’s no difference between engineering and IT, let’s be real,” I snicker. “It’s all the same to me!”
“Excuse me?” Peter protests. “I am aware of your reputation as a bullheaded businessman. But I like to think my contributions to innovation demand more respect than what you are giving me.”
Ugh. I hate people so much! Exhausting! Honestly, nobody cares who this Peter guy is. He speaks in total monotone, despite his dude bro demeanor.
He’s a charisma vacuum. Whatever happened to shoving guys like him in a corner to sort screws or whatever?
“I hear you, I’m in your corner,” I chuckle. “That established, you are extraordinarily lucky to be speaking with somebody as important as me, let’s not get things twisted.”
Escorgier groans. “Byrd, don’t be a boor.”
I snuffle some of the snot dribbling down my nose. Is that dissent I sense from Escorgier? Clearly it’s time to start putting people in their place!

“Just telling it how it is,” I say, as I flip Carl around in my lap. Such an adorable pet to snoodle with, I must admit. “We are talking corporate jobs here. The cubicle rules the land and that’s how it’s meant to be. The people love it! They like their prison! Hugo running around as hero in some orange jumpsuit only reinforces this. Such an awful example he’s setting… For real, when did people suddenly get it in their heads that these jobs are supposed to be important or something? Why does everything suddenly need mission or meaning to it?”
My audio feed is dead silent, save for static.
Good. Maybe they’re finally scared straight.
“What have you got against Hugo?” Peter finally pipes up, flipping his ballcap around.
I snort. “Those claims of my jealousy or rivalry with Hugo in the medium of media are just part of the propaganda machine. Greatly exaggerated. Our real relationship is actually friendly!”
Peter rubs his chin. “But you just booted him from the company!”
Brilliant observation. Just brilliant. Honestly, these tech people can be quite slow, despite the whiz-bang gadgetry.
I smile. I suppose I’m smiling more to myself than to anybody else, seeing as they can’t see me.
“Dr. Opal Winslow just left,” I say. “She quit and followed Hugo right out that door. Tell me now Peter: why didn’t you? Answer me that and I’ll be able to answer your question with no problem.”
Peter stands from his chair. “Touché.”
He shuffles a bit, but stays in place.
Hopefully this means I’ve earned his loyalty. Or, maybe he’s just married to the company. Who knows?
“I’ll help you, but only because I still believe in a lot of what we’re doing here,” Peter grumbles. “I won’t stand to see all the hard work done by good people go to waste.”
I lean back in my chair and form my hands into a steeple, my fingers rapping against each other.
Sucker! Such a sucker.
Lifting Carl into the air with one hand, I guffaw softly.
Doesn’t he realize how futile and illusory this whole thing is?
To be or not to be… That is the question. Oh Carl, do you know the answer?
I shake the jar, letting the brain bounce around with that question. It’s a tough cookie, no doubt.
“I want to know a bit more about the quantum computing division,” I say with a smacking of my lips. “How does that feed into your AI?”
He’s squirming. Oh well. I love a little smack talk.
Peter claps his hands together like he’s some trained seal. Wonderful.
“We managed to achieve quantum advantage by applying quantum computing to our machine learning models,” Peter states.
One thing I love Hugo for is that when the hero looks like him, people will fall over themselves to follow his whim. He receives unchecked power toward his goals without any questions.
Such gullibility to deify a man… Can’t believe that this was once me.
People never take me seriously in my grand personal narratives and missions, no matter how much I invest in making them work.
“Oh?” I say. “Playing devil’s advocate: my impression was always that quantum computing is nifty, but an unworkable waste of time.”

Peter gives a slight laugh. “Everman’s bullishness definitely lost business revenue,” says Peter. “Not sure if we’ll ever see a return on investment. The computations are good at functions involving optimization though.”
“So it is just huckster hustling?” I say, adding a rattle to my prattle.
I refuse to be played a fool.

“I mean, clever… Err… Classic computing architecture can definitely replicate the data scaling from quantum, most of the time,” Peter says, his voice shaky. “Getting the quantum circuitry to work was also borderline impossible. Our lasers still require certain superconductors to be cooled with helium to nearly absolute zero, and maintaining entangled states is a juggling act. Nevertheless, yes: we’ve noticed some nice improvements in the general performance of our AI. For all chemical and material simulations we do, we’re also experiencing a massive edge. It also helps with building hyper-realistic world models – we notice that our AI isn’t acting as parrot as much.”
Peter flashes some performance charts onto the screen.
Ok… Bingo. While my AI algorithms are better than Everman’s, this clearly is the AI hardware breakthrough I’ve been looking for.
It’s all coming together now.
“Excellent, excellent,” I say. “Pairing that with your research in brain chips and biotech, I suspect you have some interesting ideas rolling around the lab to blab about.”
Peter scratches the back of his neck. “We’re really not supposed to talk about those divisions too much. They predominately exist with philanthropic aims in mind.”

“My AI agent prompts me to use the same double-speak around tech,” I state. “It’s okay. My main focus for the rest of this meeting is the high energy division. Specifically: nuclear, your accelerator programs, and the compact fusion reactor program.”
Peter leans back in his chair, spinning side-to-side.
“Alright,” he says. “What do you want to know?”

“How?” I say. Snot is streaming down my lip and I wipe it with my sleeve. “Byrd Enterprises has tried to compactify fusion so many times… Also, I thought Everman gave up on fusion for fission decades ago, and insists on building out fission infrastructure. Thus, the big fission reactor at the center of our city.”

Peter laughs. “Oh, it was rough. See, we wanted to get compact nuclear devices for the space-mining program. Basically: we can use nuclear thermal processes— compact fusion in this case— to superheat hydrogen, which is a massive boost in propulsion tech. Good for powering the next generation of robotics too. We started with trying out fission reactors, or fission-fusion hybrids… But, the shielding required was just too heavy and complicated to keep compact. We needed lots of lead, which is a very dense metal.”
I stroke my chin. “All adds up so far. Yes. Fission leads to lead, a dead-end for compactness. Continue…”
Peter spins his chair all the way around and fiddles with a pen, a grin on his face. I grin with him— this hardware talk is the stuff of life.

“Fusion was the only way to go. Hugo had always secretly wanted to building working fusion anyway, due to the existing risks with fission reactors,” Peter continues. “Specifically, we needed aneutronic fusion since we want to minimize shielding for gamma and neutron radiation. More specifically: deuterium and helium-3 fusion, because it gives the best energy yields. As it happens, we were already mining for lots of helium-3 to use in our superconductors.”
“Superconductors to help with magnetic fields to sustain the fusion?” I surmise.

“Sort of. In general, the company is using superconductors for the laser accelerators, to generate entangled states for quantum computation. These entangled states are sort of like intermeshing cogs – if you turn one at random, the other one turns in kind. This only works if we’re using something like helium-3 to achieve ultra cold temperatures. And, if we can also use the helium-3 we acquire as an energy source, it kills two birds with one stone.”

I wince. The conglomeration of technical resources and initiatives makes so much sense. These problems of fusion and quantum computing connect up quite nicely. But, the expenses and technical hurdles to solve these problems—it had always seemed insurmountable.
“You still haven’t answered my question on how you compactified fusion,” I say, with a firm thunk of my tongue.

“Hold that thought, we’re getting there,” says Peter. “We’ve built prototypes using inertial confinement fusion— laser-driven fusion—since experiments historically give the best gains in energy. I expect you’ve seen those specs.”
Ah, I know so much more than Peter can hope to suspect.
“Yes,” I say with a laugh.
My spy Bobbin Locke has snitched on all kinds of prototype specs kept under lock and key.

“Anyway,” says Peter, “we looked into lasers and decided to use our existing laser technology for radiation pressure and plasma wakefield accelerators. They’re much more efficient than standard laser tech, and we’ve already been using them to help the superconducting entanglement in our quantum computers out. These lasers can hold immense pressures required for high temperature superconductors—albeit, the lasers themselves still require ultracold superconductors to maintain efficiency. Anyway, we can maintain entangled states in electrons, and also at the scale of nuclear spin. We essentially have a hybrid approach to entanglement being utilized in our quantum computers, thanks to these lasers…”
I rub my forehead. This guy is all over the place, and it’s seriously giving me a headache. “Okay… Laser beams?”

Peter hangs his pen in the side of his mouth. “Yessir. We bundle a bunch of fiber-optic lasers into a coherent laser beam, to hit insane power outputs. Like, petawatts and beyond. They give pressures that are used to drive accelerators which can hit super high voltages! We’re talking energy gradients on scale of teraelectronvolts. We can do this in distances that are on the order of a meter or less. To put it in perspective: teraelectronvolt energies can normally only be hit via one of our kilometer long accelerators.”
This guy is intensely excited, but he seriously needs to get to the point. I’m picking at my nails again. Ugh… Why do I keep doing that?
“What’s the point?” I mutter.
“Efficiency!” exclaims Peter.
I roll my eyes. For all this talk, it certainly doesn’t seem to me that efficiency is top of mind.
“Does the reactor work or not?” I say.
“Works, we had several good prototypes,” says Peter.
Escorgier and the rest of the board are ogling at him. It seems even they didn’t know.
Peter’s pen is quivering like a lone branch in the wind. “Extreme materials like superconductors and a bit finnicky, but all promising. You should see the lab sometime.”
I give the snot running down my face another wipe. All these little germs are just awful.
I replay the conversation in my head and loop back to the section involving the particle accelerator.
“Such extreme energies on the laser accelerators, even for fusion or quantum computing,” I say. “What does Everman think he’ll find, a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow?”
Peter itches his neck more fiercely than at the start of our conversation. I must be getting to him.

“The emphasis on high energies is more for the theoretical stuff,” he says. “You want to talk physics? Dr. Skully is great for that. That said: to my understanding, we’re trying to hit energy scales that allow for gravity wave emission. Warp tech. Everman wants to build a warp drive. He keeps a tight lid on our propulsion research though, so who knows how true that is. Officially, they only research superheated hydrogen propulsion.”
Warp tech… He’s building warp tech!?
That must be how the Machine’s elfish sidekick is doing it!
“The Machine’s selfish hoarding of knowledge cannot stand,” I declare.
Peter stands from his chair.

“Honestly, you’re super rude,” he says. “Hugo always said you were cranky, but he generally gave a good impression of you. This is something else. While Hugo might be the reason we’re always on the verge of going under, he put his heart and soul into this place. Why dog on him so much?!”

“I used to be a forgiving person, but not anymore,” I say, pursing my lips as I do. “It only leads to coming in behind. Fact is this: nobody becomes a multibillionaire without cheating a bit. He has screwed my companies out of contracts more times than I can count. Everman might try to rewrite history with charity and such, but I’m not so easily swayed. Much as he pretends to be like everybody else, always forgetting and making mistakes… It’s an act. There’s much more to him than meets the eye.”
“You don’t have to be so ruthless though,” says Peter, inching away from his spot at the table.”

“When you go into work, do you have much choice? How about this parable… When you throw a rock, does it have a choice on its parabolic trajectory?” I smirk. “Or does it do what it must do…? What it is forced to do? This question is rhetorical, but to be clear: one does what one must do.”

“You still have a choice though,” says Peter. “We’re all more dynamic than a simple trajectory, most of the time. The arrow of entropy generates randomness and whatnot. Certain decisions are between only you and the universe, up until you make them. Surely you feel guilty, don’t you? Don’t you feel bad about how you treated Everman? And, on the subject of trajectories… Haven’t you considered the karmic trajectory that you’re on?”
I burst into snickers. It’s a sea of laughter that I’m sure will confuse and that not even I can fully understand.

“I’m aware of karma,” I say, sharpening my words. “But… Life is more dynamic than a simple trajectory, as you yourself brought up. Even if it wasn’t… I’m willing to pay my karmic price. I want what I want, and I can take the pain. Why should I feel bad for those who are too weak to take the same pain that I can take? Must I diminish myself into some slave to a moral law that can only ever balance to zero? Sheer meaninglessness…”
“But the hatred toward Hugo… I mean, I hate him sometimes too, but come on! We all love Hugo, let’s be real here! Who hurt you?”
I shake my head and babble to myself for a moment.
Finally I manage, “Everman is an egotistical brat, man. A butt! He thinks he’s the Brahman or the Atman or something. It’s narcissism of religious proportions with him!”
Peter smiles into the camera. I feel as though he can see through me, but that’s obviously impossible. “And what are you?” he says.

I clear my throat. “I see this castle in the sky as a casino. A structure built upon chance. A deck of cards. And the deck is stacked against those who play by the rules. As for me? I’m the wild card. The joker card. The trump card. I will always win, because I can change reality to do whatever I want. Ha! On that subject: I have everything I want.”
I shut off the video. Screw that guy, honestly. Utterly unable to take responsibility in his own hands. What a whiny loser, with a capital L.
I’ve lived through all this talk of sympathy… Where’s the sympathy for the devil? Daredevils aren’t always pure evil, for example. People are averse to inverting their first impressions of things.

I open my Byrd’s Eye view app on my laptop and watch the city move. How gorgeous! So many people to peep in on. All following precise schedules, as they should. There’s a message from my spy, Bobbin Locke. The old Everman chips have apparently been replaced with Byrd chips throughout the robotics facility.
I send him a smiley face.
I grab my jar Carl and shake it around again. Do you finally have the answer to my riddle? To be or not to be?
It seems to whisper to me.
“I am the God of doubt,” I hear it say. “Doubt me.”
I scrunch my face and shake it again.
“I am the God of hate. Hate me!”
Chapter 11: Double Dealing
The Cog
I love Lin. She should be mine! My gal! The gall of her to tell me no…
But then, no means no, you know? Maybe I make more of our loveship than I must.
I cloak my chin behind a steeple I make with my hands.
Yes… Yes… Ah.
All goes nil eventually. I gotta get used to it.
All is sound, each of us a musical verse in the swan song of the universe.

The bullet train belts a nightmarish caw. I rock at the back of the train car, with the intense desire to kiss burning within me. Also, my loins burn with the desire to piss. Like, I need to pee super duper bad. Super duper ooper.
I really shouldn’t have drank so much water at the office without going to the bathroom. Ugh.
In selling myself to Lin, I’d forgotten to take care of myself.
My phone gives a sudden buzz in my pocket, making me want to go pee even more. Ouch. Eek.
Maybe in cellphone it’s Lin? Maybe she had a change of heart?
I answer the mysterious call, as every true hero must.

“Hi there,” a maple voice lilts into my ear. “This is the Polaris District Hospital. We’re calling to ask about some overdue hospital bills in the amount of $300. Is this George Fletcher? We’re about to move into collections or wage garnishment.”
Crud. Could’ve sworn I paid it all off. This is bad!
“My bank account is empty,” I whine, before hanging up.
I smile to myself and kick my feet up to the back of the chair in front of me. Suckers! Bet they weren’t expecting that!
Err… Why couldn’t it have been Lin Earheart there to talk my ear off? Why a hospital?
I gaze out the window of the train, staring into the busy city.
I still need to pee. Getting harder and harder to hold it in.
Maybe I should practice to be a monk. Would that work? I think so. The world needs its monks. If not that, maybe I could become a monkey.
Curious… Monkey or monk? Which is the better fate?
More than anything these days, I feel like I’m trapped in the rat race.
Cog? More like Cog the cockblocked. Cog the cuck.
Uck…
Part of me wants to use my powers to peer into the future and see what I and Lin can be. Maybe we go on walks together… Share ideas… Hold hands…
Maybe I get married with her.
Maybe I get her pregnant.
Maybe I can make her want to be with me by using my precognition... Peer into all possible futures?
I take a pregnant pause.
I can’t use my power for that. I can’t perturb a possible future with somebody else without their consent. Much as I’d like to manifest such a future, it’d be wrong.
Unless she was into it…
Hmm…
Oh, why isn’t she?
Whatever. I know how it feels to be caught in a system that forces one to merge with it and sustain it, against one’s will. I live it every day.
Capitalism: capitulation is its greatest asset. Capital punishment is doled out to any significant threat to it.
I open the Byrd App on my phone and begin looking at pictures of Lin. I scroll through all the places she’s been and people she’s met. I drink up her lemonade face. It’s art. It’s tart.
Now I really need to pee.
Hard… So hard.
Why do I do this to myself?
I shut my phone off.
It’s easy to feel guilty, but it’s okay. I’ll figure some other way to spend my time. I and the Machine have cool stuff to do tonight, I’m sure. He wouldn’t tell me otherwise.
Everything happens for a reason, even if it often feels like the reason is pure chaos. While life is full of uncertainty, there’s an infinity of possibility that comes with the journey of life.

We all come from the same babbling, bubbling, burbling source and inevitably return to it. A person can only judge themselves on the now, on some level. Thus, empathy should be had for past and future self. While guilt and anger toward the past self and toward a potential future serves a role, these projections often get in the way of the present. It weighs things down. Only the present version of oneself is presently here.
Much of my life I’ve been afraid of my own shadow. But that’s a funny thing isn’t it, to be afraid of one’s own shadow?
While my alter ego has created a lot of trouble for me in life, I wouldn’t trade it for the world.
Well… Okay, maybe I’d trade it if it meant saving the world, since it’s the role and whatnot.
Relief comes to me with these thoughts. I feel warm inside. Peace. I don’t even feel the need to pee anymore.
My pants are warm.
Great… My pants are warm. I’ve peed myself!
Yuck. I set my bag into my lap.
At least it’s number one. Going number two would be so much more painful, haha.
I seriously should’ve taken more time at work to take care of myself. One needs to take care of oneself to truly be able to take care of others.
Hopefully nobody notices. Thankfully, I’m almost home.
The train screeches to a halt. I jog out the exit, into the hustle and bustle. Bestial honks and shouts follow after me as I make my way across an intersection.
“Hey, I’m driving here!” somebody bellows as attack from a yellow taxi.
I’ve walked right into terrifying traffic. Terrific, just terrific.
I may have overstepped my bounds, bounding out into the street as I did. Oh well—bound to happen.

My chest sinks a bit while I weave through a crowd on the sidewalk to my apartment. Despite many smiling and having a happy time, too many individuals hold apathy and sadness behind their eyes. Why oh why must we while our days away in this way?
When I moved to the big city from my family’s rented suburbia home, I expected the city to somehow be cheerier. Does jeering count as a form of cheering? The city might be jeerier, I’ll give it that.
Making my way up the steps of my apartment, I check my phone to find that the Machine will be here soon.

I pat the wet patch from whiz near my groin. A change of pants is in order. The apartment whizzes by me and I’m in my room. My entrance is marked with a moan from me stubbing my toe on one of my baston sticks. Bastard.
Off with the soggy pants and on with the sweats to my Cog costume, no sweat. I am now the Cog! Next, I speed into the bathroom to relieve myself. It’s all a blur, but whatever.

Finally, to the kitchen for an energy drink—another way to relieve myself. I crack open the can and take a big swig. Maybe I shouldn’t be drinking this stuff, but I don’t care. I love the feeling it gives me. It’s a way for me to relive comfort. Even if it might be bad, it helps me feel less alone. I become more whole in this hellhole I call an apartment.
Besides: is a robotics guy getting his energy from something that tastes like battery acid really that surprising?
I rock my head back, gulping down the last drop.
Ok, cool. I’m back online, and I’ve not got a second to lose. I sprint back out the apartment and wait for the Machine to show up.
He needs me at the ready.
Any time now.
I sit at the steps to my apartment. I wait.
My mind wanders.

Sometimes I wonder whether I’m being sucked into a black hole. Maybe I’m already at the center of one. But then, maybe that’s not such a bad thing. I watch the world move by and realize that even at the center of a black hole vibrancy and life can be had.
Still, I feel lonely. Does the universe ever feel lonely too?
Maybe the Cog is more like one of the cockroaches crawling by. They seem to want the crumbs from my suit. Such nasty creatures. I hate them.
Part of me is always afraid of the end, when I pass off into the universe…. Does it just end?
Gah. Where is the Machine?
I scroll through my phone, reading through the black and white text of the messages. Will I receive a new one?

Regardless, there is something comforting to this scrawl of words—squiggly black letters, defining meaning against the uniform white backdrop. The black and the white… The 1 and the 0… Such a succinct way to convey meaning, isn’t it?

There’s a roar like thunder from off in the distance. New Vini traffic pulls to the side of the road, making way for what can only be the Machine-Machine as it’s hitting mach-1. No other car can match.
It blasts in and a sonic boom shoots through the street. It’s moving with such violence that sounds in the air Doppler shift from red to violet.

Of course, if somebody else was moving at the speed of the Machine-Machine, they’d exist in a reference frame where the sound isn’t Doppler shifted at all. It’s only to most of us standing on the street that sound has been Doppler shifted. Funny how something seemingly objective as sound is relative. Reality is democratic.

It halts with an awful snort. Plumes of fumes roll out its jet engines as it pulls into the side of the road. I curdle my face—the Machine-Machine is all dingy and dented. Its silver has faded to gray. It’s cloudy. The front nose is all cracked up, like a broken Dorito. For one of the fastest cars on Earth, I’d expect the thing to be in better shape.

The door hatch pops open, and the Machine comes tumbling out. His olive complexion is grimier than usual, and dark circles hang below his eyes. I catch his gaze and find a blackness in there. Pure black. Ack: guy looks like he could use some rest.
Guess the stuff in the press has taken a toll on his rep. RIP.

Several people on the street stop and ogle. Oddly, most don’t. He begins singing some tune in that low hum of his, the lyrics mysterious. The Machine-Machine gives a friendly chirp as the Machine zips her up with a soft press on his wrist pad.
His steps are more calculated than usual. Jagged. Still, he sings. Is he trying to sooth himself of something? I thought the Machine didn’t feel pain.
“Pretty sure that’s not where you’re supposed to park,” I mumble. I’m in a bad mood, and I’m not even going to try pretending otherwise.
“Crap,” says the Machine. He gives a look back, then keeps going. “Whatever. Already had my car towed two times this week. Plus, I’ve got smart assist on, it can move if need be.”
I readjust the straps to my backpack. “Even you aren’t invulnerable, eh?”
I guffaw. The Machine gives me a look, but says nothing.
“What business are you here for, anyway?” I say as the Machine makes his way up the apartment steps.
The stairway rattles in his presence. Not sure if it’s awe or annoyance.
“Serious stuff,” the Machine says. “I’d prefer to talk in your apartment, but it’s all very serious.”
I search for a reply when a cry resounds.
“Stop right there,” somebody announces.
An officer? The voice is squeaky and I look over.
“It is I, the Banana Bandit!” says a man in a moldy banana costume.
His face looks moldy too. No clue what skin care routine he’s doing to manage that, but it’s definitely something to behold.
The trunk to the Machine-Machine is busted open, and this Banana Bandit guy is standing inside it.
“How’d that guy stowaway in my car?” the Machine says, staring with his mouth agape.
“Guerilla warfare! Come get me, you gorillas!” the Banana Bandit decrees.
“Oh please,” I mutter.
“What’s the matter?” the Banana Bandit says, breaking into dance. “You don’t want to deal with a Banana Bonanza? Is that what it is?”
The Machine groans, his head in his hands. “Cog, do you want to take him?”
“I think we should let him decide,” I say with a smirk, pulling my fluxion-drives out of my pack.
“I don’t know, I’m pretty banana split on this!” the Banana Bandit declares. “Also, your name is Cog? Come on!”
“Yes, I am the Cog,” I chuckle. “Don’t gawk! It only seems lame at first, it’ll grow on you!”

Pulsing my fluxion-drives, I manage to tweeze the Banana-Bandit between their blasts of momentum. Despite me being in a stairwell and several yards away from him, my fluxion-drives are able to get a good grip on him and hover him into the air.
“Ow!” he screams.
Not sure why. Pretty sure it shouldn’t hurt.
I send him flying into a tree.
“Yow!” the Banana-Bandit says, as he gets caught on a branch through his underpants.
He begins to mew.
“Meow! Help, I’m a cat stuck in a tree!” he cries. “Come on Everman! You know you want to save your pussy!”
The Machine groans. I groan with him.
“That was underwhelming,” I say. “You seriously need to start filtering some of these guys out!”
Hugo rubs the back of his neck and is staring at my fluxion-drives.
“I will be,” he says. “Also, I thought you did a solid job. Could’ve scooped him a little quicker, but no notes really.”
I give a thumbs up and head into my apartment. “I’m fine man, I’m adept at adapting. You can come in, my roommate knows what’s up.”
The Machine manufactures a classic beam on his face and follows in, but something still seems off with him. He can’t take his eyes off my fluxion-drives.
Odd. My fluxion-drives are sexy, don’t get me wrong, but the fella’s eyes should be elsewhere.
I’m used to seeing more of a gleam in his eyes and a high-reaching gaze. To be so morose is out-of-character for him.

I take a seat in the coffee table at the center of the living room, my back facing the hall to my bedroom. The Machine shudders at the skeleton in the corner of the room, then takes a seat across from me.
“It’s ok, just a decoration, no need to be on edge,” I say, shifting in my seat.
The power pack and tubing to my fluxion-drives are somewhat bulky, making it tough to sit right. Ah well— hopefully this meeting is short.
Strangely, the Machine lets the air linger for longer than he ever does. The dominant sounds come from my cat P.B. and Bit-Bot as they roam around the carpet, chasing one another.

“Thanks for letting me come over,” says the Machine. “I’m sure you’ve already heard, but I’ve sort of lost board control. The company will be merging with Byrd Enterprises and I don’t feel secure holding meetings over there right now. We take in too much data at that building.”
“Oh?” I say with a snort. “I thought all that data was only being used to train your amazing AI, amiright?”
The Machine stiffens. I chortle.
“Just busting your balls,” I say. “Don’t take me too seriously.”
The Machine chortles back. “Wouldn’t dream of it.”
Great. Of course he thinks that, deep down. All this work we’ve done, and it makes no difference. Same as ever.
I glance at P.B and Bit-Bot, my beautiful spawn. Bit-Bot’s motions are still stilted in some ways, but I’m delighted to watch him move. The Machine watches with me and rubs his shoulder.
“It’s been pretty rough on me lately,” the Machine says. “Will have a lot to talk about in my therapy sessions, that’s for sure.”
I raise an eyebrow. Is he for real?
Everything about our interactions always is fake. Scripted. From the crypt.

“It’s the real deal,” Hugo says, as if in answer to my questioning. “Sorta like me. That said: been using some of my mental health AI too, and that works quite nicely. MENT-AI. You should try it, it’s great.”
Why can’t this guy just be himself?
“Uno memento,” I say. “First: you gotta tell me why you’re here.”
There’s a shrug, and he leans back in his chair. “Well, I’m here, aren’t I?”
The Machine always seems to be in a million other places, but I nod anyway.

His eyes gravitate to my fluxion-drives. “In all seriousness,” he says with a slight grumble, “you probably shouldn’t have that device. This has been a long time coming… Look: I spoke with my lawyer, and he strongly suggested that I take any and all tech I may have ‘borrowed’ over the years and return it to the company. Your fluxion-drives? Top of the list.”
I clutch my fluxion-drives close to my chest.

“Absolutely not,” I say. “They’re mine. I’ve designed for them. I guide them. I take care of them. And… They do what I say! When I press their buttons, they respond nicely and right on command. They don’t try to stir up emotional drama and baggage!”

The Machine pickles. “What’s gotten into you? Be real for a second here: you’re using stolen technology! I know for a fact that you must be the guy who stole advanced prototypes from the R&D lab a few months back. You seriously shouldn’t be talking that way, it’s more than just your property. Other personalities went into that, I’m sure of it.”

“I definitely designed the Tesla coils in this thing!” I shout. I usually don’t let loose, but he’s seriously backing me into a corner here. “Also, you’re one to talk! Billions in cash are being funneled to the top. On the daily things are always going wrong, and people like me at ground zero are just supposed to pretend like it’s normal. Inflation forever spiraling upward… Falling deeper and deeper into debt… You want to talk about theft? That’s theft!”
The Machine gives a weak wheeze and rocks in his seat. “Sir Bertrand Polka studied philosophy quite deeply and is a philosopher king of sorts…”
“No kings!” I cry, wagging my fluxion-drives at him.
I’m about ready to fling him around like I did the Banana-Bandit.

“Now, now, don’t get all out of sorts,” the Machine says, flashing a poster grin. He raises his hands in a look of surrender. “Look, things are always going to be wrong on some level. And New Vinci is a city that’s perpetually under construction, just like Polka wanted. All is always changing and in flux. With any luck, it gets better with time.”
The lush flow of the rainbow city tickles the corner of my eye, from through my dirty apartment window.

I flush and latch the fluxion-drives back onto my belt. “Everything has been going to crap. You’ve bungled control over your own company. And, you are the system—the Machine—basically. In the past, you claimed to fight against all kinds of social injustices by corporations, even though most media reports saw you as a villain. You don’t get to play corporate pirate and then tell me I can’t play Robin Hood! You gotta let me have this. It’s better to give than to receive, y’know?”
My mind bounces between all the different security protocols I had to crawl through to get this prototype.

Ever since, it has been day after day of saving people to stave off my fears of being caught… Of having to give this gadget up… After all of my experiences, I can’t bring myself to give my gadgets up. The fluxion-drives are something else. They’re my baby.

“That’s just a phrase people who want something from me say,” the Machine finally says, breaking our silence. “Sorry, but I gotta say it. I feel like everybody only wants to be near me due to my wealth and fame, and you’re no different.”

Magma pours through my pores. All my life I’ve been met by holier-than-thou cliques that refuse to have me as a member. The fluxion-drives drove some of that away for me somehow. They accept me. They might just be objects, but they know me.
“Come on,” the Machine persists. “You’re my right-hand man! I wouldn’t ask this of you if I didn’t need it!”
“Please! The Vitruvian was your right-hand man and look at what happened to him!”
“Fair enough. Gotta admit, our falling out was a bigger surprise than this. He was more talented than you. Perfectionist. I enjoyed using him to put my stamp on things.”
How dare he! Where is the filter? Does he have Tourette syndrome?

“Wow,” I say. “Everybody was right about you. You’re just a selfish opportunist, with a PR team to clean up from the fact you’re propping up a broken system! And it’s betraying you! Maybe my greatest invention is just stolen intellectual property, but guess what: you weren’t using it for anything better! Fair game! Furthermore: you don’t pay me anything for being your stupid sidekick Cog, and I’m performing as Cog via a secret identity! It’s all volunteer work!”
The Machine rubs the bags under his eyes. “I thought you love being Cog.”
I glare. He leers.
Ok, fuck this guy.

“You don’t do that much, it’s just a symbolic thing, we agreed on that,” the Machine growls. “The company didn’t even want me to have a sidekick due to branding disputes. Plus, you didn’t ask for money or help. If you don’t ask, you don’t receive. Do you really think money will fix everything?”
“Yes.”
“Well, I thought your actual job is fulfilling and pays you enough, amiright?”

“New Vinci isn’t cheap,” I say, keeping my voice firm. “And prices keep skyrocketing. Your AI race makes my electricity bills a bitch. Add in hospital bills, student loans… I’m okay, but this is a rigged game and you know it.”

“Hey now: I’m a busy guy. I don’t have time to make sure everything is going fine if nothing is said. The company already has enough hell for me to focus on. Plus, I figured you’d rather find out your own way most of the time, and I don’t want to overstep. You really just want handouts? Finally, at this present moment, money is tied up in a total legal mess… As I’m sure I’ve made clear when coming here.”
I clench my jaw. “I don’t believe you. You only know façade.”
His smile fades. “You’re right. Even if you asked me, I probably wouldn’t give it to you. Something tells me you’re gonna be a pretty successful guy in your own right… Just a hunch.”
I throw my hands in the air. “Dude, I could use some money. If the ship is going down, I might as well get something out of it over here.”

“I refuse to be treated like I’m a walking wallet. I’m just a guy,” he says. “My whole person is just a put-on. A myth. But it’s fun to tussle when the scenario calls for it, and punching the occasional monster is also cool. Gotta admit.”
My head is burning now. “And what if I’m one of those monsters to you? Am I somehow supposed to pretend that’s still fun?”
The firing of my precognition makes something abundantly clear: this conversation is going to hurt.
I can already see the flash of him from the future, walking out my door. He doesn’t have my fluxion-drives, but I sense our partnership is over.
“Stop believing in me,” he says, or at least something like it. The vision is fuzzy, but it’s there.
I’m whooped back to the present where the Machine is grumbling.
“Imagine fighting your whole life to get people to love you in a society that constantly wants to put you down…” the Machine says, his voice soft and his eyes losing some glimmer.

“I’m already there,” I snip. “I’m invisible to the point it’s basically another superpower. It’s like I don’t exist. And when I’m not invisible, things get hard for me in an entirely different way… It’s like this all the time, and there’s no way you feel like I do. You’ve got all the stuff you could possibly want.”

A clammy palm of the Machine’s runs along a wrinkle on his forehead. “Fair enough. I’m pretty convinced at this point that I made a mistake in how I defined success, because I can promise you I’ve never found any solace in money.”
There’s a buzz. The Machine checks his phone, then groans.

“At any rate,” he says, shoving the phone back in his pocket, “these days everybody hates me or ignores me, and it seems like the sandcastle I made is about to be washed away. It’s a tough spot I’m in. You ever heard how the bigger they are the harder they fall? I don’t know how I’ll keep steady if I wind back up where I started. I’ve been breathing the air at the top of the world for awhile now.”
I reach across the table and offer the Machine a pat on the shoulder, even though all the gadgets I’m wearing make this awkward for me.

“So long as some part of you is planted down here on Earth, you’ll stay on top of the world in my eyes,” I say. “All us humans are always living on the top of the world, aren’t we? I’ve been having trouble finding its bottom, that’s for sure. Uh… But, if I find its butt, I’ll let you know.”
I chuckle.
“You don’t get it, people love you,” the Machine says.

I shake my head. “No they don’t. Online they hate and argue. And at work…. People are great, and I care about them too, but relationships are tough. Work is equally tough… It’s menial and repetitive tasks. Often not as creative as I’d hoped it’d be. The ethics also get me. All these resources Everman Technologies extracts can ruin the ecosystem, biodiversity, communities… Labor conditions are often poor… Unions to protect workers are suppressed and nigh nonexistent… Let’s circle back to the subject of people hating you: maybe that’s why. Maybe all your grand promises aren’t quite bearing fruit.”

The Machine sighs. “Most jobs are boring, you’ll be okay. Find other interests. As for everything else you mention… I’ll back off. Keep the fluxion-drives. Just… I’m kinda concerned about how you go about things and how you think of things. Take time to go outside and meet other people. Live life.”

His eyes track my Bit-Bot again. “Okay, look: in terms of the resources, I agree a better system is required. But in the meantime, somebody has to be steering the ship. There are all sorts of things I need to fix and get done. If I could go back and rewire it all, I would. It’s kinda funny: the Vitruvian has put me in the role of his nemesis, and I’ve always been sold as either a villainous or heroic figure… But, fighting with him is the last thing I want to be doing right now. We used to be partners, you know?”
“You and me both,” I say, forcing a smile. “All this techno cybercrime stuff is too much for me…”
I study his face. It’s weathered and depressed, like the skin of an old shoe. I never thought I’d see him this way.
Deep down, some part of me sympathizes. I could never relate to his kind of intensity, but I can see how it must suck to be him in some strange way.
“That little robot is pretty neat,” the Machine observes, resting his hand on his chin.

I nod. “Yeah. Silicon based life at its finest! Took forever to get him to walk good. I have it configured with an accelerometer and a gyroscope. Neat fact: I initially was only working from a matrix that tracked 3 dimensions in space to model its motion. 4 if you count time. I eventually lumped in the mathematics of quaternions to my program, to account for rotations… Adds a bunch of extra dimensions to keep track of, but… Uh… These degrees of freedom really made the robot’s motion click!”
I look to my fluxion-drives and wink at them. They’re still my favorite invention, even if Bit-Bot is hot stuff.

“You ever think about trying to build some kind of product using your robotics skills?” the Machine asks. “Definitely seems like you might be able to generate value for people, especially if you work with others on it. I’ve always wanted a robot butler myself!”
My face twists. I thought he’d be more impressed with Bit-Bot.
“I only create out of the joy of creating,” I say. “My stuff isn’t for sale. I don’t want to waste my time building something that might fail or get swallowed up by vulture capitalists.”
The Machine shrugs. “You never know if you never try, just saying. If you don’t put yourself out there, you’ll eventually put yourself out.”
“Phrases. Just phrases.”
The Machine shifts, clearly irritated.

“What about using your precognition to just game the stock market or win the lottery or something? Because, I feel like that’d clear up a lot of your excuses, and you can finally stop begging me for money.”
Wow, now I’m irritated.
“Excuse me?” I say.
The Machine laughs. “I mean, it’d be a pretty clean solution.”

I groan. “That’s not how it works. Stuff like that… Too much randomness. Too much noise. My precognition is like trying to see the world without my glasses or contacts in. Everything in the future is pretty blurry, but I can sense out certain details. Also, it’s not always right.”
“Just saying, the lotto is a lotta money…”
“I’m not wasting my powers on the lottery!”
The Machine serves up that mythic mirth of his. He calms himself down to scan me over with his gaze.
“But, like, the logic of your powers… I’m not convinced.”

“It usually takes effort for me to access, but I swear it’s legit! It’s like a sonic boom or soundwaves,” I say. “It’s sorta like how you can see an object break the sound barrier off in the distance, before you hear the sonic boom’s sound. Or, or… Ripples on the water! I can tell where the ripples are going to go and how the end of their propagation will look before it happens. Something completely unexpected can always disturb or perturb the signals I get, but… So long as the environment flows laminarly rather than turbulently, I have a good feel on what’s going to happen.”
“Not buying it.”

“Sometimes reality gives you saddle points. Unstable equilibriums. Take a spinning top, for example: the centrifugal forces are equal in all directions. As it loses momentum, in which direction will it fall? The slightest of nudges from the environment can drastically change the outcome. The system of motion becomes a black box, and you’re generally forced to use probability to sort out how something like that is going to move.”

“So you’re telling me you’re a fortune teller? Don’t get me wrong, you’ve had some incredible predictions that’ve really gotten us out of a bind before! But, like… Is this the blind leading the blind?”

“I mean, predictive technologies have existed for a long time! Ever had an email sentence finished for you by an AI or played with a 20 questions gizmo? With sufficient input from the environment, predictions can be made by anything!”
The Machine scratches his head. “Yeah, that’s normal though. I can predict how the moon will move, but that doesn’t mean I know what my coworker will get for breakfast.”
“Sure, but… Apart from entropy, time works the same way backwards as forwards. Think Newton.”
“I think not!”
“No kidding…”
“Hey!”

“Anyway, everything is one big circuit of energy. And with retrocausality, entanglement, closed timelike curves… There are all sorts of ways that cause and effect might intermix that we normally don’t think about.”
“So quantum woo and buzzwords you have no expertise in? That’s your justification?”
It’s my turn to scratch my head.
“Yes.”
“So long as you’re honest about it,” says the Machine, petting P.B as P.B’s furry body ruffles against his leg.
P.B purrs sweetly as the Machine gets him behind the ear.
Traitor.

“So, the fluxion-drive,” the Machine says, pulling a cat treat from the table and feeding it to P.B, “that had to have come out of our top-secret facilities. How’d you manage to steal it without getting caught?”
“Precognition.”
“Right…”
“It covers for a lot.”

“I’ve noticed. Anyway, I’m convinced I’m looking at the most expensive propulsion hardware that Everman Technologies has produced. But, I’m not sure which propulsion method the prototype you stole is using. What is the fluxion-drive running on?”
I twirl the fluxion-drive between my fingers. “Newtonian fluxions: geometry made fluent and fluid. Aka, calculus. It runs on calculus.”

The Machine does a spit take. “Come on Anatoli Bugorski, stop pulling my leg. Don’t be an anal pissant. What’s it emitting? Do you know, eh? We explored superheated hydrogen for an ion drive, effectively… And a few other designs like that… I wanted something better than a standard Oxygen and Hydrogen rocket for the Machine-Machine. And, to be frank, after all that investment I wasn’t sure that it worked.”
He purses his lips.

I scrunch my face. “Maybe the fluxions are a flux of ions. Or, maybe it’s a flux of something else, like spacetime itself. Or maybe it’s a mix of both, to optimize energy expenditure. Wouldn’t you know?”

“I know it’s running on our compact fusion reactor. At least, I think…” The Machine bites his lip and his eyes light up with that greedy look of his. “That said, I think one of my guys were also talking about quark fusion or something. We were trying to mimic the internal conditions of neutron stars. Squirrely whirly stuff, but: it started to seem like we were close to a genuine gravity laser.”
“Glaser,” I say. “Not to glaze you, but yeah: I’ve seen interesting speculative stuff on it.”

The Machine nods in agreement. “Yeah. Top guys were working on compact accelerators and compact inertial fusion devices. Super advanced materials were involved. Also: very expensive! Investors pulled the plug on the development and muzzled any ability for me to help shepherd it. Had to stop all contact with those research groups to appease the board. I knew they had some interesting data coming through, but I wasn’t able to see how it went.”

“Higgs scale?” I say, leaning back in my chair. “String theory, right? Were you guys counting on extra dimensions to compactify micro black holes at the Higgs scale? You try to emit gravitational energy that way?”
The Machine gives me a blank look.
“I’ve had a lot of long conversations with Dr. Skully near your collider,” I explain.

Rolling his eyes, the Machine shoos P.B away. “There are lots of different models involving the possibility of gravitational energy at that scale. A Higgs portal that hooks into dark matter is usually what guys like Dr. Skully talk about these days, right? Weakly interacting massive particles and strongly interacting massive particles are candidates… Never ceases to amaze me that it’s usually all about the WIMPs and SIMPs.”
He sticks his tongue out, as if to tease me. Or maybe he’s making fun of himself. Not entirely sure.
“I’m not going to pretend to understand all the different models for quantum gravity,” he continues. “But yes, the one you mentioned is among them.”

I cackle. “Dang, if only one of them was correct… You’d need a collider as big as the galaxy if micro black holes are only at the Planck scale, correct? Planck scale is a billion, billion times more energy than Higgs scale? Dr. Skully definitely suggested micro black holes need to compactify somewhere near the Higgs scale, otherwise odds go way down for building the glaser in compact form. Oh well…”

Hugo’s eyes skate the surface of the table. “Yep. Was really hoping they almost had it, but wasn’t sure. Going to be honest, data was spotty. Seems impossible by vanilla laws of physics… If it actually can’t work, I want it to be the case that we live in a simulated reality where it can. Of course, with crazy stuff like dragons and fortune telling, the odds of us being in a simulated world are better than not.”
I snort. “Nah.”

The Machine snatches the fluxion-drive from my hand and puts his thumb in the path of its beam. The flow warps his thumb out of proportion. He pulls it away from the beam and it snaps back into shape.

“Okay, so this is warp tech 100%,” he says with a foxy grin, before handing it back to me. He slicks his hair. “You sure you don’t want to turn this in? This tech could lead to all kinds of breakthroughs and new technologies. Faster than light travel, teleportation maybe… Who knows what else?”

I scoff. “Absolutely not. I know for a fact how stuff is misapplied, and your company is a complete mess. Also, it’s too powerful to be in the hands of a corporation. Just look at what humanity did after the invention of the atom bomb!”
“Look, I’m trying, okay? Do you know how hard it is to be altruistic when there’s this much wealth and power involved, rather than act on greed? It feels impossible!”

I offer a weak frown. “Society says that we are all trapped within debt. The sins of one generation must be paid in sacrifice of the next. I’m done with it. Despite my knowledge and skills, the world wants to shut me up! It wants to hold me down! It’s man vs. machine! The economic machine! All mediating mechanisms are a joke! Where’s regulation? Where’s taxation? Democracy? Why do you have your own personal monopoly? Why do you have a billion times more in personal wealth and value than the rest of us?”

The Machine heaves. “Look, I agree change is inevitable when it comes to the economic system. I feel like I can’t win! Investors are eating me alive for giving away too much money. You’re angry at me for not giving away enough. The system reinforces bad behavior it seems.”

“You’re not getting it. The rich are rewarded for hoarding and penalized for exercising their wealth. It’s the reverse for the poor. Why do we keep sleeping through this aggressive workaholic culture as though it’s some dream? It’s a broken nightmare and I’m done trying to save it!”

“Exactly, exactly… I totally get you. Time is money, time is power, and it should feel egalitarian rather than like tar. I’m going to let you in on a little secret: I’m actually trying to crack this problem. Lots of my wealth is going into a decentralized and distributed chain of logic blocks – a blockchain. E-currency! It’s resistant to hoarding and it’s more fluid dynamical than standard currency. More mechanics for regulation, taxation, and reinforcement of teamwork. This economy also is simulated on quantum computers.”
“Yeah, that just sounds like the stock market with extra steps.”

“I’m thinking it might be a useful basis for a digital democracy as well. Rather than representative democracy, everybody can vote on issues through a secure blockchain. Everybody has an equal say. Teamwork makes the dream work!”

“You talk a big game about teamwork, but I’ve never gotten the sense we’re equal partners! I’m a person, and you always treat me like an object! You can’t keep trying to solve human problems with more tech!”
“Look, Everman Technologies owns your device. My advice: think twice.”
“Everman Technologies is not a person, even if the law says otherwise. I own these fluxion-drives, period.”
I probably sound like I’m on my man-period. Oh well.
My fingers stroke the soft rubber buttons budding from my fluxion-drives. I’m never giving them away.

“Okay, you got me,” says the Machine. “I try to see both sides of every issue and then make firm decisions, in order to get things done within groups of people… And, maybe this means that I compromise my moral compass when I shouldn’t. But, we’re innovators. Inventors. Technologists. We work hard. We fail. We make no excuses for ourselves. We solve the world’s greatest problems. And, in doing that, we inadvertently create the next set of the world’s greatest problems. It sucks, but it comes with the job. And, I wouldn’t have it any other way.”
“This technology is going to kill us all, isn’t it?”
“You catastrophize too much. It’s going to be fine, trust me.”
I give my fluxion-drive a slight kiss. I pretend to chew down on a loose wire, but I know what I’m doing. “You’re not getting my babe. This is my masterwork. My Jack Pollock.”
The Machine clears his throat. “Incorrect. Jackson Pollock. It’s Jackson.”
My face contorts. “Uh, no. It’s Jack.”
“Jackson,” the Machine insists.
“Checking my precognition… Hmm… Damn—you’re right!”
We share a chuckle.
“Y’know, I really love this little apartment,” the Machine says. “Reminds me of my small little room: pure white box. It’s good for sensory deprivation.”
I shrug. “You have that because you can afford it. As for me: I’d be happier with a bigger place, but this works for now. It saves me lots of money.”
The Machine crosses his arms. “Happiness is a choice, just as it is a function of what you have.”
I cross my eyes. “I’m not so sure of that, based on what I’ve seen in this world.”
“Ok then. If you’re having trouble balancing life and being my sidekick, just stop being my sidekick. You don’t need to sacrifice everything that you are to help me out. We’re good.”
My eyes twinge. This is a slap in the face. But then, I saw it coming.
“I want to stay your partner. I don’t want this to end on a bad note. Isn’t sacrifice the basis of our myths? One person to sacrifice themselves for all of mankind?”

“Yes, but people feel free to choose self-sacrifice. If it feels forced, then it’s not really a self-sacrifice is it? Besides, it’s a myth… A noble lie. Wonderful to taste its order, but it only serves to keep people in line like sheep. That’s the extent of its purpose.”
I’ve been stabbed in the back many times in life, so I’m numb to this. Still, I don’t think the scar he’s leaving will ever truly go away.
I outstretch my hand to Hugo. We shake. My body shakes along, out of anxiety.
“I guess that’s it then,” I say. “Goodbye to our partnership.”
“Apprentice becomes the master, reluctant as I am to admit it,” says the Machine. “You’re a cogent gentleman Cog.”
I offer a sheepish blush.
“By the way, you should look into dating and social apps if you’re struggling finding friends,” says the Machine.

I shake my head. “Been burned too many times. Never get any matches. Besides: it always asks for more money. I prefer meeting a girl in person and looking into her eyes. The colors… I like blue and green. Is it weird that, when looking back on my life, I feel like I’ve only ever had a crush on one girl? I’ve met a lot of different girls but… It often feels like I keep falling for the same one, somehow.”
The Machine nods. “Been awhile since I’ve felt love myself, but it’s always nice when it comes along. I’d give the apps another try my guy.”
Geez, this dude just never gets it.

“I don’t want an algorithm to profit off of how I love… How I live… It’s an inversion of my values. I’d rather monetize my death than have this society monetize my life. Give me liberty or give me death!”
The Machine stands from his chair, clearly disturbed. Strange, considering his strength.

“I’m sorry,” he says, walking toward the door. “This was all a front. A fiction. A meticulously constructed fiction, but fiction nonetheless. I was hoping you would’ve figured that out by now. I’ve always hoped that, if people believed in me, maybe they’d learn to believe in themselves. And… Maybe I’d learn to believe in myself. This is why I never say the Machine is faux outright. But yeah, that’s what it is.”
He opens the door, standing halfway between the inside and the outside.
“One more thing,” he says. “If believing in me means you stop believing in yourself? Stop believing in me. Like, yeah… Just stop.”
The door slams shut.
I’m not sure how to feel.

Maybe I’m just bitter and jealous. That probably plays a slight role in all of this. I love creating and inventing things. But, in my quest for legitimacy, I often fall short. I’ve never been the best at keeping track of numbers and analysis, much as it pains me to admit. I love tool building, but I can become a tool when I start comparing myself to others.
I don’t want others to trust me because I don’t entirely trust what is within myself.

The Vitruvian is one of the worst people I’ve ever met, I think. To be honest, the Machine also ranks up there at this point. But, giving the devil its due: I share in a lot of their worst attributes. Is that wrong?
I guess it makes it easier to forgive them, so there’s that.
Sometimes this world feels unsalvageable. Will it work itself out in the end?

A quote from Newton bounces through my mind. “Like a watchmaker, God was forced to intervene in the universe and tinker with the mechanism from time to time, to ensure that it continued operating in good working order.”
Beautiful sentiment. I get the sense of an infinite being and the infinities beyond it.
But then, in terms of God… Humanity tried making God in its own image. Humanity failed. I guess it’s still fun to develop an imaginary space though, where the concept somehow works.
I’m often meditating on the end. Should I end things? I shouldn’t, right?
There’s a soft click and pitter patter behind me. I turn to find Jack standing in the hall. He waltzes up to a coffee table where his plant Perry is.
“What was all that commotion?” Jack asks.
I give a huff and readjust my goggles. I refuse to say a word.
“You water the plant?” Jack presses, wiggling one of Perry’s leaves a bit.
“I don’t care about your stupid plant,” I say.
Jack adjusts his hoodie and scowls at me. “You can’t talk to me that way, okay? If you have a problem, you better say it.”
“This city sucks,” I say. “Leave me alone.”
Jack goes into the kitchen to refill a pitcher of water, then comes back looking pretty bitchy.
Great, now I’ve really done it…

“You always need to play victim and act like you’re being persecuted,” he says. “But maybe the problem is often yourself. You ever think of that? Nobody should be expected to roll out the red carpet for you if you can’t even advocate for yourself.”
“Sorry,” I say. “It’s just… The Machine. We had a rough go of it. He fired me as his sidekick.”

“Ignore him, you’re better than that,” says Jack while watering his plant. “Don’t waste your life getting hung up on people living lives in an entirely different stratosphere from your own. Learn to be happy just being you!”
Perry bristles, enjoying its drink.
“We should do something fun together,” says Jack. “Play board games. Have dinner. Roommate stuff.”
“Too busy,” I grumble. “Got a headache.”

Jack’s hands are in his pockets. “You keep isolating yourself from friends and refusing to be happy. That’s not a sacrifice. That’s selfish. People care about you man, but we can’t help If you refuse to connect.”
I check my phone to see if there are any messages from Lin. Still zippo. Great!
I really have a headache now!
I toss my phone at the floor and I watch the screen crack. Why do I do this to myself?
“What was that?!” cries Jack.
“Percussive maintenance,” I declare. “You obviously wouldn’t get it…”

Jack picks up the phone and carefully sets it on the table. “You need to cool it, I’m worried about you. I get that you want others to know you’re smart, but do you need to act like you know oh so much more than everybody else? The internet and stuff makes all this information you try to lord over people just a click away.”
I click away at my fluxion-drives, hovering into the air. Electronic music pulses out their ends in a flow of force. The room buzzes and quakes. I cross my legs and I’m spun up into the air.
I’ve reached my ceiling.
I’m angry at Lin. I’m angry at the Machine. I’m angry at society.
Society man. Like dude, bro, society. We live in a society bro.
But, it’s my fault isn’t it? All these unrealistic expectations for people, which are so obviously delusion. I observe clear concern on the faces of Bit-Bot, P.B, and Jack.
“I’ll leave you to it, butthead Buddha,” says Jack. “Let me know when you want to talk.”
He walks away while the walls and room warp in and out with a syrupy symphony.
I’ll clear things up with that phony later. For now, precognition carries me in and out of time. I am the storm, and I am the rainbows that come after. I float on air as a feather.
It is the privilege of all life to defy gravity in its own way.
Ugh… Maybe I’m the phony. Stark examples abound.
I’m only young once, and I’m always worrying whether I’m running out of time to get it right.
Why does it feel like everyone abandoned me? Why has Everman abandoned me?
It really does seem that my quest for gnosis has hurt more than it has helped.
Another quote I revere comes to my mind. This time, it is from Einstein: “Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world.”

My music blares to ever raising heights. My space gets increasingly spacious. Infinity intensifies, and I am part of it. Time is space. All is space, flowing at uniform pace.
