I sit there for a few minutes, me and my cat, decompressing. Processing. Sincerity seeps through my pores. Only once PB’s purrs turn to snores do I pause.
In the corner of my room is the “Machine” hero stuff. I get up. I toss the stuff in the trash bin. All of it.
Screw the Machine. Some hero…
Material things only ever distract from how we all are one, anyway.
I stare out my window. A street lamp is flickering in and out. 1 and 0. An open loop. A sign? What does it mean? Morse code?
Gah—I don’t any know more about Morse code than its name.
All this time play-acting as the Machine’s psyched ward, but maybe I belong in the psych ward.
I swallow. I go to my phone. I text my mom and dad group chat.
Hollow gesture, maybe. Truth is, they have reason to hate me as much as anybody. But, my safest connection.
“Love you. Been having a rough time, trying to figure things out. Thanks for always being there.”
Somehow, I get a response almost instantly—a true superpower. “I love you too. Now, go back to sleep.”
Mom.
Dad simply gives a like.
I grin. Sometimes in life, I wish I can easily erase or take back the past. Moments like this make me glad I can’t.
Life was never normal. There’s no normal to run back to. But I can find a new abnormal to make peace with, always.

title: The Outer
paragraphs: By: Christian Mueth
Dear [insert editor],
Enclosed you will find a sample for my manuscript, The Outer.
Thank you for giving the time to read this. I hope you enjoy it.
Sincerely,
What would happen if somebody who had everything lost it all?
The Outer Snyopsis:

Centuries into the future, civilization is pushed in the confines of several mile high buildings that are peppered across the earth. National governments have been compressed into one unit: The Tower Federation. During the turn of the millennium, a man named “Michael,” is elected as their new representative. Though, everything shifts when he’s exiled from the Federation, and thrown into the world outside the buildings... The Outer.
About the Author:

Christian Mueth (born May 4th, 2000) has already self-published a fantasy novel called, “The Secret of Blackneck”. He’s also written numerous short stories, many of which are featured on his website, “CEMueth.Com”. “The Outer” is a science fiction novel, and the second novel by Christian Mueth.
Sample:
Chapter 1

A man bit his lip and wiped his hand across his sweaty brow. He had prominent cheekbones and crinkles between his eyes formed from a habit of smiling. Because of them, the look of exasperation appeared foreign on his face.

He let out a strained breath and started pacing in wide circles around the room he stood in. However, it was more deserving of the title room than most rooms are. The reason for this was that the space was utterly empty, save the man, a steel door and a single chair— the chair being anchored at the room’s center with thick screws. It had more room than most rooms could ever wish to have. It wasn’t decorated— besides the stainless white paint that was smoothed across every inch and the glowing light-fixture built into the ceiling. “The Serenity Center” is what this room was known as and there were at least two hundred on every floor.

Although nobody could’ve been able to tell that this room was designed for serenity from the man’s demeanor. He had his head buried in his hands and his back slumped toward the ground like a wilting flower. He was a very tall man, at the height of about six feet. However, he slouched so much that one would’ve thought he was a foot shorter.

The white paint in the room was in stark contrast to this man. He was dressed all in black. He was colored charcoal from his metal shoes— which had been neatly tightened with magnetic straps— to his crisply tailored suit and neatly combed hair. The only thing he wore that wasn’t this color was his expression. It was flushed in a thick crimson.
A low rap erupted from the door.
“Hey, Michael! You in there?” another man’s voice said. “The award ceremony is about to start. Unless you want to be sacked, it’s about time that you start moving!”
A blank face appeared on the fretful man— Michael.
Who’s talking to me? Michael thought. Are they even talking to me, or are they referring to somebody else?

There were a million other Michaels in the building— it wouldn’t come as a surprise to Michael if there was even one in a neighboring Serenity Center. There were only a few names that were used throughout the towering city, due to people choosing names on the basis of popularity. So, distinguishing between identities became a tricky task.
Michael let out a short laugh and the jubilance made his face look natural again.

Of course he’s referring to me, he thought, recognizing the familiar voice of his friend— Peter. Why am I overthinking everything? Any other day, the term “stress” wouldn’t even be a thought in my head.

This soothing knowledge was all it took to shoot Michael upright. Standing up so straight that he looked as if he were a breathing pole, he ran his hand through his hair and tried smoothing it out, despite it already being brushed. As he strutted over to the door, he flashed a winning smile and swiped his hand across a touch-screen to unlock it. Though it almost looked like he’d unlocked it by using his smile. With his newly calm posture, he felt his mind clear and the world around him shrink. It was as if his troubles had been compressed to the size of an ants and he was sprouting above them all.

While the door slid open to reveal Peter, the empty room around Michael, which had once appeared intimidating and overbearing, seemed mundane and commonplace. The sight of Peter, with his casual rumpled clothes, ruddy face and matted forest of auburn hair, was comforting. The two had been friends for most of their lives— thirty years to be exact. Seeing Peter reassured Michael that tonight was going to be fine.
I’ve been planning for this day to be one of the most monumental days of my life. I’m not going to let a small dose of fear tarnish years of planning. I can’t spend today worrying over nothing.
“What were you doing in there? Don’t tell me you’re having stage fright on tonight of all nights!” Peter said, chuckling as he slapped a hand against Michael’s back.
“No, I was just using the white walls to compare my teeth with,” Michael said with a grin that shielded any doubt from consuming him. “See! Perfectly clean!”
“Well they better be! If tonight goes well, that smile of yours is going to be lighting up every screen on the planet as we enter the next year!”

“Every screen on the planet”— those words punched Michael hard in the face. He’d been aware of how great of an impact the ceremony would make— but every screen on the planet? As much as he’d dwelt on the subject, he’d never thought of it that way.

The end of the year would mark the beginning of the 31st century and the greatest ceremony known to the world was taking place. It was the choosing of the Model Human of the Year— a yearly title that was bestowed to the person with the greatest occupation, ethics, charm and— most of all— efficiency. After a year of campaigning, Michael had been lucky enough to be chosen as one of the candidates. His success now depended upon the average voter. Michael rarely liked to focus on it, but the event was extremely delicate. A single, common voter might have the power to alter his future— for better or worse. Though he refused to believe that he was so powerless.

Michael was determined to earn the title and his stubbornness wouldn’t leave the outcome to chance. This is why he’d sided with Peter. Peter claimed that he knew people who would bring Michael the victory.
In spite of the peace that should have been brought by that, Michael thought that he felt his stomach churn.
Even if I win, it will have been earned through swindling.

The momentary guilt he felt fled when he remembered that he couldn’t afford to lose. From the time of his birth, he’d watched faces of the winners appear on screens every year, proudly showing off the bright badges and awards they were gifted. The hunger to taste the essence of their glory consumed him beyond all measure.
“Hello? Are you still there?” Peter asked, waving his hand in front of Michael’s face.

Michael snapped his head up from the ground and awoke from his daze. Adjusting to his surroundings again, he saw that he was already approaching the back door to the stage— and a massive hive of thousands of people.
How had everything happened so quickly? he wondered, flustered.
Michael’s hands began to quake neurotically and they pulled themselves into his pockets.

“This is probably going to sound ridiculous— I completely forgot that we were talking! I was just— just thinking about the scores on my game!” Michael said, grinning like a clown as he slipped a thin band of goggles out of his pocket and started adjusting it onto his head.

These devices were commonly known as smart-goggles. The lenses in them doubled as screens, allowing people to play on it. It was an addictive pastime that Michael, along with many others, often immersed himself in. Playing videogames helped Michael forget about his mounting troubles— it placed him in a world where he had easy control. He felt the twitching pangs that covered his body slowly come to a halt.

“Hey, not until after the ceremony!” Peter snapped, tearing the goggles off of Michael’s face and shoving them in his pocket. After seeing Michael give him a look just short of horror, his face softened. “Sorry Mike for being so intrusive… I don’t know what came over me… It just annoys me when you put that thing on!”

An unpleasant silence leeched onto the pair for a moment. Michael stared at the backstage door, unmoving. He tightened his body to the point that it was just as still as the room around it. The goggles gave him a sense of relief in times of stress. They put him in a world where nothing could hurt or disturb him. Peter had just taken that away.

“Well, you wouldn’t have wanted it on anyway, considering that you’re just about to meet the crowd!” Peter said with a nervous laugh, as he shuffled around gruff men wheeling podiums and stands out the door and onto the stage. “You don’t want to anger them! After all, some of these candidates end up getting thrown out into the… Outer...”
His voice lowered into a coarse whisper.

The Outer was the world that lay outside of the shell created by enormous scrapers, which society now dwelt in— each scraper contained a stuffy mass of around fifty million people. The world relied on these structures— which were usually built three miles into the sky— to supply safety from the nauseating smog-filled atmosphere that lay outside it. To be thrown into the Outer meant you’d failed the Tower Federation somehow. The Tower Federation— also known simply as the Federation— was the ruling government that held all of the towers together.

Unlike the majority of the population, Michael favored the government. Perhaps this was because he was among the hierarchy— but he always felt that the Federation’s decisions were just and that they had strong reasoning to them.

Even though Peter was among the hierarchy, he held an opposite view and saw the Federation as cruel. As much as he wanted to, Michael couldn’t deny Peter’s claim— whether it be for disturbing the peace, or becoming obsolete and a waste of precious oxygen, people would find themselves spiraling down a near bottomless chute and landing in a trash heap somewhere in the deadly world below. There, it was said that people had to rely on your own wits to survive— that is, only if they managed to survive the drop. Despite the miniscule chance, Michael was of the belief that survival was simpler than most made it out to be.

However, as much as Michael tried, he couldn’t ignore the travesties that were caking around him. There were only a few skyscrapers peppered across the Earth— thirteen to be exact. There had once been dozens more, but the resources on Earth were dwindling and the success rate of the towering colonies were to blame. The Federation had become more eager than ever to cast people out, due to the fact that it was becoming harder to support the needs of the masses. The prevailing logic was that if the Federation couldn’t support the obsolete people, then it was doubtful that the harsh environment surrounding these towers would be able to do any better.

While Michael’s views were ignorant, there was still reason behind them. The tower Michael and Peter lived in was the powerhouse behind them all— often known as the “Hub”. The reason for it being the ultimate power over all of the other towers was because it held most of the Earth’s remaining resources and it was run by the Federation’s Board of Initiators. Because of this, poverty was a rarity among the Hub’s population. Whenever it did crop up, it was treated as a fluke or an act of chance.

Although even Michael recognized that Peter’s view had the stronger base. Despite the Hub’s advantages, it was still losing the necessary resources to keep running. Like every other tower, it was willing to remove any baggage produced by dysfunctional members. Peter’s father had suffered this fate. He’d been tossed in a riot when Peter was still a five-year-old child.

“Michael…” Peter said, holding back the emotion aroused by such a topic. “You have to promise me that, if you win, you’ll do all that you can to keep people from needlessly being thrown into the Outer… I can’t… I can’t bear the thought that others have had to deal with what I did and sometimes worse. You’ll have such an influence if you win— you need to use it wisely.”

Michael didn’t respond. He remained as adamant as a mule. He knew that Peter meant well, but Michael felt bare inside. He felt that Peter was putting too much weight on his shoulders and that Peter used no grace while doing it.
“And now, it’s time to welcome our candidates onto the stage!” a cerebral voice echoed through the door opposite to the apparent strain behind it.
“I have to go,” Michael grumbled.
“You’re acting out like a child! You know that, right?” said Peter, with a scornful glint in his eye.

Michael ignored him. Swiping the door open, Michael was nearly drowned by a fountain of flashes and cheers. Immediately, his face lit up with a vibrant grin that stretched from his high cheekbones to the corners of his eyes.

“Hear that?” Michael asked smugly. “Does that sound like they’re cheering for a child to you? If you really think that I should take advantage of my influence, then why haven’t you taken advantage of the influence that you claim to have?”

Peter opened his mouth angrily, though, before he could utter a word, Michael bounded on the stage, to his podium. Waving to the crowd, he gave a hearty handshake to the announcer and then cracked a few jokes that ruptured the audience in laughter.
Michael’s glee was but a facade. Peter could detect a bitterness hidden behind it.

Every so often, Michael’s eyes would flick to the door at the side of the stage from which he’d entered. While he couldn’t see Peter, Michael knew that he was there. Peter’s spiteful gaze was too potent for Michael to be unable to sense. So Michael made sure that he gave a few spiteful glances to the door in return.

Peter couldn’t take his eyes off the sight of Michael even as people pushed past him. He was looking at the image of the friend, whom he’d known nearly all of his life, swelling in a self-righteous pride—he was clearly enjoying his success without Peter’s help. The two had worked together for years, with Peter always supporting him. As Michael gave his welcome speech, however, there wasn’t even a mention of Peter’s name. Clenching his fists into a tight ball, Peter stormed away
Chapter 2

On the stage, Michael instantly forgot all of his fears. The weights seemed to have instantly rolled away before he’d even taken his first step outside the backstage door. He was like a new man in the midst of the masses and the people were easily swayed by his charm. They seemed to hang onto every movement he made, as if he were a rare spectacle and marvelous to behold. Whether he was playfully interrupting the other candidates to make a few jests or mocking the announcer's contorted expressions, the crowd gladly devoured it all.
However, the energy he carried steadily simmered as the ceremony drew closer to the voting. There were six other competitors, all who seemed deserving enough to win.
Will my performance be enough to convince the crowd to pick me? Michael asked himself.
After his fight with Peter, he could only hope.

As the last candidate gave his speech, everyone on the stage gave Michael a quick scowl— clearly, they weren’t pleased with his interruptions. Although he wasn’t able to worry about them now. The announcer was already stealing center stage and adjusting his microphone.

The man was a stubby old fellow, so it took him a minute to bring the microphone down to his level. This gave Michael a much-needed moment to think. Michael saw that his fate rested in the announcement the old man gave after the votes were cast. Michael instantly regretted belittling him.

Clearing his throat with a sickly gurgle, the stubby man began to speak. “And now, we reach the portion of the event where you vote for who you wish to win this year’s title of “Model Human of the Year." All of these candidates have earned their right to stand among you today, whether it be for exercising exceptional productivity, or simply keeping you… Entertained…”
He glared at Michael.

For a moment, Michael was highly offended— he’d worked countless hours advertising for a company that sold a spray which supposedly made people, “like you better”— at least those were the lines he was taught to recite.

While it might not be the highest of positions, I’ve offered an important contribution to society that’s beyond simple entertainment. After all, I’m good enough at my job to charm dozens of people into buying the product. That achievement can’t be replicated by a simple robot.

The announcer’s glare didn’t last long. With a quick jerk, which left his curled red wig bobbing in the air like a loose spring, the announcer returned to face the audience. “With each of the candidates having offered their position, which one which one will you choose? Beginning now, you have until a quarter to eleven to submit your vote. That should give you about ten minutes! That’s plenty of time to think and choose— as long as there aren’t any interruptions…” he gave another look towards Michael. Michael flashed an innocent wave in return.

The announcer grumbled but returned to his monologue. Struggling to bring cheer back into his voice, he said, “You can all start pulling out your smart-goggles and linking them with our voting server. If you need any assistance, we have our tech-governors that you can call on.”

The announcer then swiftly removed himself from the microphone and retreated to the backstage— swiftly when compared with most people his age, anyhow— while a flock of machines, hovering on propellers, descended from compartments in the ceiling. Several people launched red lasers out of an inch-wide instrument in their goggles and the robots— tech-governors— responded to the signal by spiraling towards the lasers. With their blades whizzing like a hummingbird’s wings, they carefully descended upon those who needed their aid. The whole audience went abuzz with excited chattering and laughing as they voted for their favorite candidate.
Michael bit his lip in apprehension. His concern fought against the flurry of a joyous cacophony.

What if they don’t choose me? I’ll never have another chance at this title again—not without feeling undeserving of it, anyway. How could I ever consider myself a good model for the masses if I’m unable to gain their favor?

These thoughts contradicted Michael’s initial plan to have Peter help him cheat. Michael’s fight with Peter that had quelled his confidence. Declaring independence from Peter might have meant declaring independence from Peter’s plan. It was then that Michael felt truly alone. If he failed, it would all be because of his own mistake. He knew that if the failure found a way to come upon him, he’d never be able to reconcile with himself.
As a friendly face waved at him through the crowd, he reverted to his normal demeanor— cool, collected and bearing a cheery grin.
I can’t hope to win if I’m not even willing to cater to people who will vote for me.
“I would be voting for myself right now,” he said, gesturing to the crowd in a mock speech, “But my goggles were nabbed by something that was reminiscent of a wild monkey!”
The announcer poked his head out of the backstage door, giving a wrinkled scowl at Michael. A few people chortled as they held back laughs. Michael wasn’t among them.
“There goes my right to speak with the audience,” Michael muttered, fumbling with his hands.
At this point, he was furious that his goggles had been taken.
What am I supposed to do without them?

He felt a dull headache fall onto his head with the crushing force of an anvil. Clammy beads of sweat slid down his brow. The last portion of the ten minutes seemed to drag by like molasses, leaving him in a fit of twitching that he struggled to control. He hated it when he was left without his smart goggles— it always left him feeling hollow and exposed. He couldn’t have felt more humiliated and inferior if his clothes were stripped from him.

There was something about the goggle’s metallic rims—the smooth indents etched into its sides to account for its many compartments— its dark screens that lit up in an opulent blue once activated. As he stared at a pair of goggles that his opponent was using, they almost seemed to call out to him, asking him to place them over his eyes and let their cold metal smolder the blazing concerns that licked at his mind.
Michael shook his head— he was letting his hands twitch uncontrollably once again.

“When are you going to get a grip?” he could already hear the voice of his father saying in reprimand. Michael’s temptation had always distracted him from his studies when he was younger and made him lose his focus on the straining nights when he’d needed to direct all of his attention to schoolwork. Everyone around him always complained about the addiction, whether it was his peers, his animatronic teacher or his parents. He couldn’t seem to help it. And when he did look for help with the issue, he’d found that everybody who could’ve helped was too busy immersing themselves in their own smart-goggles.
As he’d advanced in years, he’d accepted the problems— most of the people he knew dealt with them. It was seen as “just a part of life.”

Although he now found the problems it had caused him were too tough to ignore. They had put him in a position where he couldn’t afford to fail but he wasn’t able to succeed. The goggles had distracted him from his studies to the point that the career-system gave him the job of a salesman only three years prior. While it was normal for people to start their jobs at the age of thirty and to get minor positions, Michael’s parents had always been part of the hierarchy. Gaining a job was the sign of adulthood and there was nothing more disgraceful than for children of the hierarchy to stoop to the level of the lower class. Thus, after he was chosen for such menial work so late in his life, his parents had never let him live the deficit down.

He knew that tonight was his chance to prove his worth to society— a chance to prove that he was a capable individual that deserved the luxuries and leisure he’d grown up with. Somewhere out in the crowd, his parents were watching him with a steady gaze— it was his duty to make them proud.
The backstage door swung open with a sudden whir of gears and the announcer hobbled out, his rubber shoes letting out a stiff squeak against the platinum floor.
Please tell us that the voting session has come to an end! Michael thought, wincing in anticipation.
He couldn’t stand the idea of sitting in the chair any longer. He found the experience more agonizing than being starved.

Taking center stage with a graceful sweep, the old man lightly patted his fiery red wig to ensure that it was adjusted correctly. His lips stretching like an elastic band, he opened his mouth to let his voice boom throughout the room. “I’m pleased to announce that the voting session has drawn to a close! The winner is mi—”
He was interrupted when Michael shot out of his chair, his arms pumping into the air. “YES! I won!” Then, turning to the other candidates he said, “Against all odds I crushed you all!”
All of the candidates appeared both puzzled and annoyed. A couple of them were even whispering to themselves.

The announcer’s eyes squinted in disgust. “And this is a shining example of exactly what we wish you not to do, prestigious viewers in the crowd,” the old man said, letting Michael’s face turn redder than a cherry. “Please take notes. Now as I was saying… The winner is minutes away from being announced.”
The announcer hung on the letter "i" in the word minute, to make an extra dig at Michael’s mistake.

Michael had been doing his best to smile at the announcer all this time, but he couldn’t help but return the scowls that had been dished to him. Michael was sure that the announcer had purposely pronounced the word minute in such a way that would ensure a blunder.

“So, we ask that you are all able to remain patient and calm as our drones calculate the votes,” the announcer continued, clearly proud that he’d coaxed aggression out of Michael. “Within five minutes we should have our model human of the year! So get excited! We’ll try our hardest to get our results in— we apologize for the wait.” The old man once again left the podium and returned to the backstage.
Five minutes?
Angrily, Michael slid back into his chair.
I’ve had just about enough with tonight! How can anybody be expected to wait this long without the soothing comfort of their devices?
He didn’t let his anger seep through again, masking it with a smile as he waved cheerfully to the crowd.
Surprisingly, Michael found that the minutes slipped by with an ease— at least until the unnaturally beady eyes and contrasting wide grin of the announcer returned to center stage.

“We’ve finally come to a vote,” he said with a burble, his brow furrowing in discomfort. Michael caught that the announcer was in distress. “The winner of this year’s award— while I found it highly improbable— is in fact…” the man suddenly stopped and every muscle in Michael’s neck strained as he awaited the answer to the question he’d been pondering all night. Finally, the announcer cleared his throat and continued, with artificial mirth, “The winner is Michael Burrow! For his excellent performance in this year’s booming field of advertising, prime genetics, prime looks, high intelligence and, most of all, his outstanding charisma. Effective immediately, he’ll receive the grandest of our estates and will be put into a higher position of influence in the Federation.” As upbeat as the announcer tried to sound, his disdain bled through. “Congratulations Michael, you have won the crowd over!” Then, bending down to Michael’s ear, he whispered in a coarse tone, “If you botch this up, I’ll see to it that you’re relieved of your position. Furthermore, you’ll discuss the limits of this new authority in a private meeting with the Board of Initiators— don’t begin thinking that this position grants unending power, like so many others have…”
Michael’s eyes widened in disbelief.
Ecstatically, he thought, I’ve been chosen! I’ve won the award!

He would have shouted those thoughts aloud too, if it hadn’t been for the mistake he’d made when yelling earlier. There was also the inescapable doubt over whether he really won, or if he was merely trapped in a lucid dream.
It wouldn’t have been the first time, Michael thought. I remember one instance where I played on my goggles all day and confused it with real life…
Yet, when he caught the looks of despair on his competitor’s faces, it was all the proof that he needed.

All the apprehension eased from his limbs and he stood up, outstretching his arms, to embrace his victory. The only time he turned from this pose was to relish the image of his face— it was plastered every jumbotron in the auditorium. His many smiles were like candles, lighting up the entire room.
Once the clock hits midnight, this image will be planted on every screen in the Federation.
A fervent pride welled in Michael’s chest.

“Standing here tonight,” said Michael, stealing the neon microphone from the announcer in a movement that was quicker than the flick of a laser, “I realize how much hard work really pays off when you put in effort! I couldn’t have made it here without the help of… Well, myself!” he let out a quick laugh and continued, “But really… If it hadn’t been for your votes, I couldn’t have been chosen. It humbles me to know how much I’m admired!”
The crowd cheered wildly and began flooding the borders of the stage in a wild stampede. The only thing holding them back was a thin band of tech-governors.

“Why are you restraining them?” Michael asked the announcer, displaying exaggerated gestures for the crowd as if he were in a play. He was enjoying the attention more than he enjoyed using his goggles. “As the Model Human of the Year, I make the choices here… And I wish for the people to have free reign over the stage.”
The announcer stammered. He was helpless for the first time that night. Even his wig had lost its springy energy.
“Don’t resist me. This is a shining example of what not to do, prestigious viewers in the crowd,” Michael smirked as he watched the announcer squirm in an indignant scowl.
The crowd jeered and hissed, some of them managing to make their way onto the steps in an attempt to reach the announcer. Finally, the bewigged man relented.

“Fine, you can have your way!” he chuckled, raising his arms in surrender, “You can enjoy your big celebration with minimal monitoring from the tech-governors. Although, once it’s finished, you’re expected to report backstage for additional instruction and direction concerning your new situation. Don’t come any later than one a.m.”
Flicking his wrist, the announcer spouted out a few commands that made the tech-governors retreat to compartments in the ceiling.
Michael marveled at the sight. He’d never seen the robots forced into sleep-mode so abruptly before. He tried remembering the words the announcer had used.
Maybe they will be useful in the future.

“Don’t think about trying that yourself,” the announcer said. He walked briskly toward the backstage door, catching Michael’s eye as the crowd scrambled up the stage. “The access code has already been changed. So, don’t bother trying to misuse it.” He then disappeared behind the backstage door.

While those words came as a blow, Michael knew that he didn’t have time to focus on the access code. In an instant he was swept up in the vibrant screams and chants of the audience and everything else was forgotten.
“Michael! Michael!” they sang in a harmonious chorus.

He could remember, with distinct detail, enduring waves in one of his videogames. The crowd was no different. Michael went through a cycle of being smothered by the crowd’s enthralling roar and then being thrown back into the air with a powerful rush.
When the cycle finally ended, he was carried by the crowd’s firm grasp. All around, eyes peered in a strange amazement.
They make me feel like I’m something magnificent to behold, Michael thought. Not that this isn’t the case.
He’d earned his place above the rest. He was confident in that. However, he still found the way he was looked at to be strangely unnerving. It left him with an untamable feeling of discomfort.

After a while reveling in the crowd’s enfold, he was set down onto the ground, where a massive circle of people began to surround him. His eyes went blind and his went ears numb with the endless flashes of cameras and questions.
“Could you explain your road to success to us?” asked one sharply dressed lady.
“Would you like to sign a business contract with my company?” asked one man wearing an oil-smeared jacket and his hair slicked back.
“Could I have a clump of your hair?” goggled a young fan.
As much as he tried to address each person, all the words sent him spiraling and he soon found himself lost in a sea of confusion—until a voice harbored him to shore.
“Michael!” Peter cried through the thick mass of people. Michael could sense that he was strained and tired.
“Peter? Where are you?” he responded, trying to keep his anger penned. He didn’t want to make a scene in public.
As Michael weaved his way toward the voice, a hand shot out of the dense wall of people, followed by the rest of Peter’s body.
“Michael, this is really important! Something horrible is going on!”
Purple in the face, Peter was doubled over on his knees, heaving heavily in an attempt to catch his breath.
“Did you lose my smart-goggles?” Michael joked, cracking a smile.
“No, they’re right here,” said Peter, pointing to his pocket. “But that’s not important right now! There are people who are—”

“I doubt there’s anything more pressing than me getting my goggles back,” Michael laughed, holding out his hand. He ushered a nodding agreement from the crowd around him and then quickly slipped his hand into Peter’s pocket. Michael held back a sigh of relief when his hand clasped around his goggles.
“Boy did I miss you…” Michael whispered, running his fingers along the smooth metal.
“Michael, people’s lives are in jeopardy! They—”

“Can wait,” Michael finished, grinning toward the crowd. “Right now I want to take a selfie. I’ll only be able to have this crew with me once!” He then pressed a button on each side of the goggles, prompting the lenses to fold into each other. As he stretched his arm out in front of him, the screen on the lens transformed into a camera. “Everybody say— Fleas!!”

With a quick movement, Peter smacked the goggles out of Michael’s hand and onto the floor. “Get out of your head! We have bigger issues! A mob is tossing innocent candidates into the Outer! There’s only a little bit of time left, but I think you can still save them if you hurry!”

Michael heard a shrill scream break out in the distance. Peter was right— time was running short. Then he looked around himself. He found that the crowd had been reduced to expressions of shock and disgust. His goggles had been reduced to a sparking pile of glass shards and scrap metal.
Peter might have been my friend— but he’s crossed a boundary.
“I’m not going,” Michael said sternly, “If you think that you can just storm through here and interrupt our fun, you’re mistaken!”
“I’m sorry…” said Peter, his eyes turning blotchy, “But these people… They’re going to die! Help me help them... Please!”

“I’m—I’m sure that they’re getting what they deserved,” said Michael coldly, “If they aren’t strong enough to fight for their own lives— to make their own way out— then what role do they have in the Federation? If they’re taking a trip to the Outer, then I’m sure that they earned it. Let’s not extend the ordeal… Now leave me alone and let me enjoy the rest of my night without interruptions.”
“But we can’t just… After all we’ve done for each other, you’re just going to leave me— leave them? I thought we had an agreement— a plan!”

“That was before I realized that I didn’t need you. You were just using me— holding me back. All it took was a slight disagreement and you tried robbing me of my property,” said Michael. Peter looked like he’d been slapped in the face— no physical fight could have hurt him more than this. “Look around me! I have more help than I could ever ask for. Any agreement we had is dead. Now, get out.”

Peter shook his head, shooting Michael a look of pure hatred. Then, Peter trudged through the web of people and toward the victims that awaited his help. Michael didn’t take his eyes off Peter until the tip of Peter’s head disappeared.
Chapter 3

The world entered midnight and Michael paraded proudly with his easygoing gaze fixed jovially on his new throng of fans. Although, hard as Michael might have found it to believe, there was a set of eyes that stared out into the masses with an opposite emotion— fury. They belonged to a girl at the age of thirteen. Her name was Sarah. Like two small wooden saucers, her almond brown eyes gazed at the image of this man on a screen. Leaving a splash of luminescent light across her face, the screen burned a potent message into Sarah’s mind— the New Year had come.

As she kept her focus fixed on the screen, she remained as unmoving and stiff as a door. Even the long brown hair that rolled down her back didn’t waver. Her face wore a straight expression that matched the rest of her tense body.

Despite her wish to be otherwise, she was far from the ceremony— both in mind and body. In contrast to the grandeur of the festival, she lay covered under her dingy sheets in an otherwise bare, slouching mattress. The mattress had an odd bowlike shape and a yellowing color. On some sleepless nights, Sarah would drowsily confuse it with an oversized banana.

The rest of the room was only more depressing. In blatant disrepair, the walls and ceiling were caked in a grimy layer of filth. There was a faint remnant of what the walls had once been— a flowery shade of pink— but grime had overrun it. They were chipped and cracked, the peeled layers making it so thin that it would’ve only taken the severing of a small sliver to be able to see through to the other side of it. Contained within the wall’s sad confines was a square of empty space. That is, it was empty aside from the bed the girl lay in, a small dresser that suffered the same fate as the walls and the screen the girl was staring at.

Despite the appearance of seclusion, she wasn’t alone in the room. In front of her was a woman— while Sarah had a hard time calling the creature that— perched on an iron stool. Although Sarah’s dismal situation was depressing, she would’ve been better off alone than with the raven of a companion seated at the end of her bed. Even the floorboards trembled as their hate’s power flowed into the room.

Having a high stature, the ravenous woman glowered down at Sarah. They stared at one another, both of their faces overflowing with malice for the other. Their locked gaze was a twisted version of one shared between two lovers. The woman’s stony expression was mirrored so deeply by Sarah that it became hard to distinguish the two of them. It was as if there were an invisible funhouse mirror between the two and they were merely warped reflections of the other.

The lady to whom Sarah owed much spite was known as Mrs. Giber. In Sarah’s eyes, everything about the woman screamed fatal. It was almost impossible not to wince when staring at her hideous snaggletooth grin and her deformed knobby nose. It was the nose that especially unnerved Sarah. Its shadow always curved crookedly into the stony glint made by Mrs. Giber’s penetrating eyes. Those eyes had a testing squint to them. For Mrs. Giber to prove her superiority, they almost seemed to taunt Sarah. Sarah would’ve pinched the eyes fully shut too, if it hadn’t been for Mrs. Giber already having a wretched pinched figure. It looked like it was made of a barbed wire that would pierce Sarah’s skin, if she were unfortunate enough to brush up against it. Mrs. Giber’s hair wasn’t any more appealing to look at, propped up by pins and needles into a wobbly bun that resembled a mound of rock and mud.

“Sarah Screw,” she said in a sickly sweet voice, “Your behavior has become extremely concerning to us. We didn’t want to keep you in our Serenity Center as long as we have, but you’ve given us no choice.”

Sarah didn’t offer a response. However, Mrs. Giber only grew more imposing at the sight of this, showing off her yellow teeth. Sarah wasn’t sure If the teeth were trying to taunt her, or if they were innocently greeting their brethren— Sarah’s yellow bed.
Her question was answered when Mrs. Giber opened her mouth wider to reveal her malignant tongue. “Would you like to tell me why we’ve kept you in here so long? Or do you need a reminder?”
Unwavering, Sarah sneered.

Mrs. Giber appeared oblivious and plodded forward, with pleasure filling the corners of her mouth. “In the past few months, you’ve broken every rule that we uphold. You might think us to be fools, but we know how hard it is to forget the Code of Morals we recite each morning.

“I’ve told you multiple times, but you still won’t respect my words. You will not be allowed to participate with the rest of the orphanage when you act out like this. We’ll be willing to bring you back into our happy little community, only when you start to show that you’ve had a change of heart. Is it really this hard to apologize for your blatant disrespect and wrongdoing?”

While Sarah was guilty of disrespect, she’d never resorted to wrongdoing. Though blame was often placed upon her, rarely did she have anything to do with the constant troublemaking that ensued throughout the orphanage. This is why Sarah had to restrain herself from another outburst.

“Why can’t you take example from our new Model Human of the Year?” Mrs. Giber asked, making a quick gesture toward the screen thin screen suspended from the ceiling. “Surely you remember that breaking the Code of Morals is how your parents were thrown into the Outer?”

Sarah let her face contort into a knot. Exactly a year ago her parents disappeared and nobody was sure what had become of them. There was a time when the Federation claimed that they’d found them. Since Sarah had never been given the chance to see them, she questioned the legitimacy of these claims.

Her parents had supposedly been interrogated by the Federation. Afterwards, the Federation claimed that her parents were guilty of crimes of, “severe enormity.” This all eventually led to her parents being thrown into the Outer— an event that nobody but the Board of Initiators witnessed. When questioned for details, all they’d disclose was that her parents’ crimes were too ghastly to speak of. Sarah had a hard time believing this— she knew that her parents weren’t bad people. There must’ve been more to their disappearance than what was supplied.

Being reminded of her parents was a constant sting to Sarah. She felt that when people mentioned them, it was only to jibe at her. However, no matter how much people deprecated the memory of Sarah’s parents, there was more to their disappearance than anybody would admit— she was certain of it. Her one comfort was a confidence that they were still in the Outer, finding a way to survive. Of their many traits, which she remembered with affection, resourcefulness was the most prominent.
Perhaps it was this specific draw of the Outer that gave leeway to Sarah’s constant disobedience.
If my parents are in the Outer, Sarah thought, then why should I care if the Federation threatens to place me in the same wilderness?

“Sarah?” Mrs. Giber frowned after watching the girl’s lips purse and her muscles clench. Sarah’s gaze had moved to the screen and hadn’t wavered since. “I— I’m sorry that I reminded you of your— Look, I know that today marks a year from the day that your parents were… Never mind, there’s no reason to focus on the past... The point is, you don’t have to share the same fate as so many others. I’m here to help you. We hate to see people corrupted by tragedy so young. You have much potential to offer the Federation…”
Sarah finally burst. “I don’t need to conform to the rules of you monsters!” she screamed. “You think that you can just come and— and tell me what to do!?”
“Yes, that’s exactly what I think. I have the laws of the Federation to back me on that presumption.”
“I’m done with your fake smiles and calm tones! My parents were thrown into the Outer! You want to know why I’m so angry? It’s because of people like you!”

Mrs. Giber paused for a moment. “Sarah, just look at yourself. You’re a mess. We’re not monsters sweetie, but as for those that break rules, for the sake of their own anger? They’re true monsters. We— I— don’t want to see you turn into one. I know you think that your experience is different from everybody else’s, but remember eight out of ten children lose at least parent to the Outer. Do you think that your behavior is helping anybody else who is grieving over loss?”
Sarah’s face was red and her hands were balled into a fist.
What does this lady know about loss!? Sarah thought. She’s one of the most respected caretakers in the orphanage!
With a shriek, she leaped at Mrs. Giber. At that moment, any sense of sanity had been replaced by a venomous drive. All that mattered to her now was venting her aggression.

Mrs. Giber dived out of the way, tumbling onto the filthy floor. With a groan of disgust, she let out a shrill screech of her own. “Tech-governor! I need a tech-governor! Orphan One-One-Three-Nine is out of control!” After running towards the door, she turned towards Sarah, who had the scowl of a hungry lion on her face. “Because of this new outbreak of yours, you’re going to have to pay the consequences by staying in this room for much longer. Enjoy the emptiness... I hope you’ll find satisfaction in the path you’ve chosen.”

As Mrs. Giber left the room with her stool hanging against her side, Sarah thought that she could hear the lady snickering to herself. A tech-governor entered in sequence, but Sarah couldn’t help but smile. While she had led Mrs. Giber to believe otherwise, there was something else in her room besides the bed, the dresser and the large screen.

When the tech-governor had entered the room to monitor Sarah’s behavior, it droned on in an endless ramble about the Federation— but it only took moments before it was lying motionless on the floor like a rock. Sarah had found a way to deactivate it through a hidden switch lodged inside one of its arms.

Sarah climbed out of under her covers and onto the floor. The shag carpet, crusty and brittle, made a dull crack under her weight. She’d grown used to the sound, but she now feared that it would somehow reawaken the sleeping bot.
She brought her hand under the bed, outstretching it as if it were an iron pole. Smiling when she gripped what she was looking for, she peeked her head under and pulled the object towards herself.

The object that came out of under the bed was a small cube, about the size of a shoebox. She set the box in the center of the floor. Despite it being empty, the floor provided little space for the cube. However, that thought was put to rest quicker than the tech-governor had been when she bent down and started feeling around the cube.
“There has to be an opening her somewhere!” she whispered to herself.

She’d never seen a box like this anywhere else. On its sides was a glistening, ghostly white light that burned her eyes and on its edges was a flowing neon green glow that shifted shades the more she viewed it. At one moment the neon glow was such a light green that it almost looked yellow and at the next, it was such a dark green that it was almost black. The corners of the box were the most intriguing of all, because each one was cut so that there was a triangular slant. Here, the pale light from the sides and the green light from the edges slurred. They formed into a spiraling yellow design that pulsated and moved with Sarah’s heartbeat.

Sarah opened her dresser and studied a note that had come with the box. In spite of the hundreds of times that she’d read it, she inspected it once more to see if there were any clues as to how she would get it open. As she did, her mind cycled through the history of the box. It had arrived just a week ago and the events surrounding its arrival remained both strange and mysterious to her.

After waking from a nightmare one night, she found herself unable to fall back asleep. As on most nights that she had a nightmare, her mind played tricks on her by making a fragment of a noise sound as loud as a clap of thunder. Despite this, she actually caught something creeping in the night that was more than a tired hallucination. At hearing the crunch of something walking across her carpet, she screamed. She watched a blinding flash spark in front of her, followed by an earsplitting bang and crash. She stumbled around, trying to see who or what it was, but the spark of light had happened so suddenly that it left her momentarily blinded. When she regained her eyesight, the box was on her bedside, along with a note. The very note that she now held.
On it were written these words: Tell nobody of this package. Don’t open it until the New Year.
She had her fingers run down it and her hands feel into the rough grooves made by the inky stroke of a—
Aren’t they called pens? Sarah asked herself.

The note wasn’t signed in her name, but that didn’t make a difference in Sarah’s eyes. When she looked at it, she saw it as hers. There was an internal connection that she’d developed with it. The note could have come from anybody— maybe even somebody who was looking out for her.

She savored the mildew smell the paper gave off and the strangely comforting crumple it made whenever she moved it in her hands. Notes were rare treasures to come by and were usually kept behind glass display cases and in expansive storage vaults of the Federation’s museums.
Still, the paper wasn’t what held most prominence to her. It was the message that captivated her imagination. Her mind ricocheted from dozens of questions.

Why can it only be opened after the New Year? Why was it sent to me? What if the box was sent by my parents? she wondered, retreading questions that relentlessly plowed through her mind throughout the day. I need to know what’s inside.
Once she collided with the blunt force of reality, she landed in another thought that she couldn’t let go of.
Am I actually meant to have the box? If I hadn’t let out a scream in the middle of the night, things could’ve played out much differently.
Whether she was meant to have it or not, the box was stuck with her— that fact couldn’t be denied. There had to have been a reason behind it and she was determined to find out what.

“I’m not going to give up trying to open it until daylight!” she declared with a determined grin. At these words, she forgot the meeting with Mrs. Giber. All that mattered now was gaining hold over the contents of the box.
After half an hour of grunting, shoving and pulling, she finally relented with a defeated look.
Raising her hands in defeat, Sarah said, “I’m done.”

She angrily gave the box a firm kick and stormed towards her bed. However, before she made it to her banana of a mattress, Sarah heard a quiet swooshing sound rush past her ears. With a quick jerk, she turned to find the box open, with its loose lid revealing a small sphere inside.
What is that? she wondered. Scooping up the ball, she rolled it around in her hands. From its smooth metallic surface and cold feel against her skin, she could tell that it was metal— but what kind?
The material appeared strikingly familiar, though foreign at the same time.
“Is that all that was in the box?” she asked herself.

She bent down to check again, but found it completely empty. It made her wonder why it had been packaged in such a large and secure box. She couldn’t see how the small metal ball could be that important.
Sarah turned back to the sphere and started fiddling with it again. She tried pressing her fingers harder along the sides of the ball, to look for a button— when it suddenly shifted shape.
Sarah’s almond eyes grew so wide that they nearly rolled out of her head and onto the floor. She knew exactly what this material was.
“Mutometallum,” she whispered.
Chapter 4
“Are you ready yet?” a lumbering man asked gruffly. He was stuffed in a stiff leather suit and his face was concealed by a heavy metal helmet and a pair of smart-goggles.
Because it was late into the night, the hall that he stood in was dimly lit. His voice echoed until it melted away into the hall’s darkness and its simulated sound of chirping crickets.
Michael nodded his head in response.

His reception party— which was a blast— had ended hours ago. Since then, he’d been thrust into an ordeal so exhausting that he was now resting to catch his breath. The many chaperones he’d gone through, who explained the new changes that would be taking place, dragged him around as if he were an animal on a leash. He was still trying to catch up with everything that was going on and his gnawing need for sleep wasn’t helping matters. His tiredness could be observed from the thick circles around his eyes, all the way down to the heavy pounding that surrounded his footsteps.

He was near the end of his tour, facing the door to his new estate— “The Model’s Manor.” It was built into a slick curved shape and the entrance was a thing of architectural prowess. Atop it was a twisted arch, made of a pearly metal. Its design had a simplistic beauty to it— one that provoked jealousy toward all who viewed it. Everybody in the Federation craved an apartment as luxurious as this one. If Michael hadn’t been struggling to stay awake, this new estate would’ve dominated his thoughts.

“Good,” the man said, giving a thick nod in return for Michael’s. He swiped his hand over the door’s scanner, prompting it to open with a smooth swoosh. “As with all doors, the touch-pad will respond to fingerprints of all the citizens in the Federation— but this one has been programmed to activate exclusively for fingerprints of the Board of Initiators. Thankfully, we’ve already linked yours into the database, so you shouldn’t have any problems.”

When they entered the room, it sparked with a sudden fluorescent light. Michael smiled as he looked from wall to wall and found them covered in screens that displayed brilliant designs. Some of the designs were abstract, while others appeared to pop out into space, tempting Michael to grasp out and touch them. Measuring twenty feet in height, these screens stretched from the floor to the ceiling. They were placed everywhere, so that there was one at every turn. It all left Michael awestruck. The sight planted him there in a mesmerized state.
“This is all mine?” he asked, breaking free of the trance and taking a cushy seat in the center of the room. “I couldn’t ask for more!”
“This isn’t all— it also has the most up-to-date model of our tech-governors. It will serve as a guide to you from now on and we expect you to begin training with it tomorrow.”
A hole opened in the ceiling and a robot descended.
Michael was left speechless. It was all becoming too overwhelming.
“Here’s a replacement pair of goggles for your last ones, by the way,” the man said with a grunt, tossing it into Michael’s hands. “Our bots detected your friend breaking your last one.”
Michael stroked the goggles meticulously, each brush against the metal giving him a rush of relief. He’d been fretting over whether he’d be able to sleep without them.

“You’re welcome,” the man said snidely as he walked out the door. “Oh and there’s one other thing I need to make you aware of, before I leave you alone for the night. The walls in this building are constructed out of a rare synthetic material— mutometallum. Or— as you might know it by— ‘trans-metal.’”

“What!? I thought that was just a rumor! How could you possibly have gathered the funds to build a whole house out of it!?” Michael waited for an answer, but received nothing in response. “So… Does this mean that I can reprogram the structure of my home to my liking? I have total control over it now?”

“No!” the man chastised, arching his eyebrows— one of the few things on his body that weren’t covered. He started to look almost wary of Michael’s presence. “What makes you think that you can have free reign over something like that?! You should feel lucky that you’re even allowed to live here! Mutometallum is highly expensive to use and almost impossible to program— the very pinnacle of both multiferroic technologies and molecular nanotechnologies. Not to mention, it’s a dangerous weapon that people like you shouldn’t even know about.”
“But, suppose that I dented a wall, or lost my goggles under them…” Michael said, in a bumbling attempt to be sly. “Where would the controls be during such emergencies?”

“They wouldn’t be there. And, if you were only going to use it to fix dents, then there’s good reason for that! This is why we keep the controls in a secure building of the Federation— not that you would understand the controls, even if you had access to them.”
Under the man’s harsh reprimands, Michael felt like a worthless animal. His eyes turned to his pocket where his goggles were kept and he struggled to keep from putting them on his face.
“Hello? You still there!?” the man barked.
Michael snapped himself back into the present. “Sorry— I’m just tired is all. Thanks for the tour and everything— but I need to head to bed…”

Without looking up, Michael gave a pitiful excuse of a wave goodbye. He didn’t move from his spot until the door had shut and the room quieted. Suddenly, the urge to sleep took him like a heavy gust of wind.
“What an exhausting night,” he yawned, stumbling toward his bedroom while he played a game on his goggles. For the first time that night, he felt a steady sense of rest and contentment.
After he settled under his sheets and shut off his goggles, memories of his outburst with Peter came flooding back.
Was what I did to the other candidates wrong?
He shuddered at the thought that he might have been the cause of their deaths.
No, of course not! I had nothing to do with what happened to them!

He couldn’t push the horrid visions away— people screaming as they were led to the chute that marked the final barrier between the Federation and the Outer. Their stomach’s lurching as they fell down an endless hole, looking like lifeless dolls. Though, unlike a doll, Michael knew that at the end of their fall would be a slow and painful death.
What would have happened if I’d lost and was put in their place instead?
He winced. Sitting up and pulling off his sheets in a cold sweat, he called his tech-governor over.
Maybe talking to it will comfort me.
The warm beat of the robot’s blades entered his room. “What might I help you with?” the robot’s mechanical voice sputtered.
Michael phrased a question in hopes of a soothing answer.

“When I hear about the Outer and the terrifying things surrounding it, the world seems so frail and dangerous. I can’t help but wonder— what do you think the meaning of everything is—the meaning of the universe?”
The machine sat for a moment. “Buffering… Buffering…” it spouted. “Pulling up results for, meaning of the universe…”
For a short moment, Michael was shocked.
Does it really have the answer?
“Results found,” the robot continued. “Universe, noun. Definition one—the totality of known or supposed objects and phenomena throughout space— the cosmos— macrocosm. Definition two— the whole—.”
“That’s enough,” Michael said, crestfallen. Of course there wasn’t an answer to his question. He felt ridiculous to have even asked.
What am I so upset about? he wondered. After all, I’ve just achieved my life goal! The whole world envies me. They admire my very essence!

Still, as he pulled himself under his covers and let himself lapse into a well-earned drowse, he couldn’t help but feel a sinking weight fall onto his chest. He frantically shoved his pair of goggles into his face and succumbed to the game displayed on the screen. He felt the pain numb with a relative ease and he slipped into a steady slumber.
Chapter 5

Sarah slept soundly under her covers, with the ball of trans-metal tucked between her fingers. At least, it had been a ball. Now it was a messy metallic strand, with a cluster of her fingerprints imbedded into it.

As the hours passed, the metal began to merge with her wrist— coiling around it like a spring. As if it were a living creature, it progressed from there. As Sarah’s breathing increased, the metal moved wildly. Then it started stirring when Sarah stirred. Eventually, it began taking on shadowy, abstract forms. It was as if it were embodying her very dreams.
However, Sarah and the trans-metal weren’t the only things moving in the night.

As she ruffled her covers, languidly trying to find a more comfortable positon to rest in, creeping creaks resounded. After she’d settled back into her dreams, the presence of the creeping thing was compromised by the faint glow that still emanated from Sarah’s box. The glow revealed a thin shadow— the width of a piece of paper— across the wall. Wiry as it was, a stooping figure could be made out of it, crawling along the floor.
From its rigid movements, it was clear that it was preparing for the moment to strike. It prowled swiftly and quietly, without the slightest crunch of the carpet.

Slyly and steadily it neared Sarah with each step it took. It didn’t stop moving. Its shadow melded with the mustard mattress, before clambering over it. The figure’s fingers crawled along Sarah’s metal covered wrist. With a darting dip, it gripped the metal. A moan filled the air as it clawed at the metal’s edge. The shadow’s arm thickened as its grip was lost and was thrust into the air. It had tried to yank the metal from the girl’s arm but it hadn’t budged.
“Great,” it hissed.
With a moan, Sarah opened her eyes. The moment she saw the figure, she let out a yelp. In the dark room, she wasn’t able to make out much but she could tell that it was a tall man.
Sarah’s shout probably would have been loud enough to alert the rest of the orphanage, but he’d placed his hand over her mouth before its sound could spread.
“It’s alright,” he whispered, trying to calm her. “I’m the one who sent you your package.”
“You’re not one of my parents,” Sarah snapped, once he pulled his hand.
He’s undoubtedly a lingerer, she thought.

Her instincts told her to yell again and alert the others of this man’s presence. She needed to fight back. Lingerers were people who were meant to be thrown in the Outer, but managed to escape. Many of them lurked in the lower, abandoned floors of the Hub’s tower that had once housed many resources and homes. They only ever surfaced to steal food and clothes. Sarah pitied most of them, but they were notorious for their nefarious character.
Although, there was something about the man and the box he’d sent that was intriguing. In addition, she felt that her situation couldn’t get much worse than it already was.
“What are you doing in my room?” Sarah asked.

“My name is Johnathan. There’s a lot that I have to tell you— but I can’t do it here. I was sent here by your parents. If you want to keep one of the last memories of your parents, you’ll need to get out of here. Which means you’ll have to follow me.”
Sarah closed her eyes and put her head in her hands. “Are you saying that I have to leave the orphanage… right now!?”
Sarah thought, I’ve been secluded in this room for too long…

“Look kid, you aren’t dreaming and this isn’t time for games. You can read yourself a bedtime story and play ring around the rosy later. I’ll explain everything, best as I can, but you have to trust me. I was sent here on a special—umm— on a special errand to see if you were able to use that— that— that magic piece of metal. Now, people—.”
“I can understand what you’re saying just fine,” Sarah said, cutting him off.
“Kid, I don’t have much time—.”
“My name is Sarah.”

“Whatever… The point is, people are looking for me and that piece of metal. Since you’re so smart, I’m sure you already know all about it… It’s the synthetic element, mutometallum. It shifts to electrical charges.”
“Yes I know— it’s similar to muscle tissue. But, why does it respond to my hands? After all— it’s only supposed to respond to electric charges.”

“Are you going let me talk, or not? I was just getting to that part. You’re special kid— err— Sarah. That thing you have on your arm doesn’t respond to just anybody. And, you can control it with a lot more than your body… It listens to the commands of your brain. We’ve been searching long and hard for somebody who can control it. The reason that we waited so long to test you is because everybody will want to control your ability. The New Year was the ideal day to do it, because the Board of Initiators are busy dealing with their new puppet— the Model Human of the year. Their security will be diverted— and I need it that way, so I can safely take you to my base.”
“Wait— you’re going to take me where?!”
“My base! You want out of here, right? I’m sure that you hate being stuck in here… Well, I’m giving you a way out. Haven’t you ever wanted a chance to go into the Outer?”
“No! Why would I ever— wait— you live in the Outer?!”
“Where else? I can’t live here, that’s for sure! These days, hiding in the Hub and living like a lingerer isn’t an option— unless you want to end up dead.”
“Your base is in the Outer?!”
“Well— the base we’ll be going to isn’t in the Outer. It’s hidden within the Hub.”
“I thought you said that you’d wind up dead if you lived like a lingerer!”
The sound of a distant door screeching open crept into the room— followed by the familiar clicking of heels.
“Mrs. Giber,” Sarah said in a hush.

Johnathan’s face paled. “You need to lower your voice,” he whispered. “There isn’t that much time left for me to explain. You can either come with me, or stay here. But, you better make your choice quick.”
Sarah bit her lip.
“Where is the way out?” she asked, after a brief pause.
Johnathan smirked. “Just follow me.”
After they’d hastily scurried across the room and into a corner, he pointed toward a small opening in the ceiling. “It’s up there,” he told her.
“But that’s the tech-governor shaft! We can’t go in there!” Sarah said.
“We can and we will.”
Johnathan grabbed Sarah by her legs and lifted her up toward the ceiling. Sarah’s fingers grazed the edge of the opening, just barely catching hold of it.
Johnathan whispered up to her, “Good, you’re almost there. Now just pull yourself up.” Then, he scurried back to the center of the room to retrieve the glowing box.
Just as he bent over to scoop it up, there was a loud rap at the door.
“Sarah, are you up?” Mrs. Giber’s voice cooed in an artificial sweetness. “Could you open this door for me, dear? It seems to be locked.”

Sarah’s palms began to sweat. With her grip on the ceiling opening slickening, she felt a sense of hopelessness take anchor. Everything leading up to this point had been the things of dreams, but this current weakness tried to yank her back to reality.

While she wasn’t aware of it, there was a drive within herself that refused to accept this. Wrapping tighter around her arm, the band of metal extended and stretched. It disappeared far into the inky vent, before pulling her up with it. Dark as the vent was, she felt that she was moving into something far brighter than what she was leaving behind.
“I’m up,” she mouthed down to Johnathan, who was now standing just below her.

Johnathan tossed the box up into the air and Sarah barely caught it. Once again, the metal around her wrist assisted her. The act felt strange— the motion had happened out of reflex. It was as if the metal were acting as another limb.

Just as Sarah caught the box, Mrs. Giber used her fingerprints to unlock the door. “I’m using the emergency override now,” she said with a croak, as the door creaked in unison. “I know that you’re in here. If you plan on being relieved of this room, you need to start following orders like a decent human being.”

Johnathan leaped into the air, hardly nearing the opening. Luckily, Sarah had outstretched her arms. He pulled himself up, his hands locked with hers. He couldn’t have afforded to be any later either— as his dangling legs disappeared into the dark shaft, Mrs. Giber entered the room. For a moment, the gnarly-toothed woman was oblivious to what was transpiring. However, when that she heard the click of the shaft’s cover latching back into place, she recognized that something was awry. In spite of her shouts, she was too late— Sarah and Johnathan were far from her reach.

“It’s time for some explanations,” Sarah declared, once the pair had made it far enough from the bedroom— or the prison, as Sarah would have called it. “I have a long list of questions, but I’m going to start off with my first one— why is this trans-metal so important to you?”

“Don’t pretend that you don’t know. It’s the most valuable material out there— especially when you consider capabilities. As the saying goes, ‘it’s rarer than trees are.’ There are people who will pay an arm and a leg for just a gram of it. So, it’s no surprise that there’s a lot of people who are desperate to get their hands on the two pounds of it that I stole— the exact two pounds that you have wrapped around your arm.”
“You stole it?” Sarah scowled, stopping in the middle of the shaft.

“How else would I get it? Not that it’s a grand accomplishment or anything. It’s hardly an impressive steal when you compare it to the amount that we need. Now, here’s the more important question— when did you start caring about rules? Last time I checked, you’re one of the biggest rule-breakers in the orphanage.”
“You know about my history in the orphanage?”

“Nothing is sacred— anything can be found if you search for it. Back at our base in the Outer, we took a peek at your personal record… It isn’t pretty,” said Johnathan, making Sarah’s face go red. “Don’t worry about that, though. The people I work for aren’t looking for pretty— they’re looking for results. You’re a special kid, Sarah.” Johnathan opened a door in the rectangular tunnel they were crawling down. “I have all of the checkpoints throughout these tunnels hacked— I can control them at will through a remote. I know that these tunnels are usually used to store tech-governors and distribute oxygen— but, I’ve found a way to make these ventilation shafts suitable for us as well.” As they continued to crawl down the tunnel, he slipped a flashlight out of his pocket and turned it on. “It’s about time that we had some light down here.”

Sarah could fully read Johnathan’s features now. He had bronze skin and large grey eyes that matched the size of his bulbous nose. A forest of matted black hair covered his forehead from sight. Though, from the faint wrinkles around his eyes and face, he looked to be in his middle to early thirties.
“Don’t you have smart-goggles?” she asked, pointing towards his flashlight. “They’d probably do a better job of guiding you.”

“They don’t let you keep your goggles if you’re sent where I come from,” he said, with a hint of bitterness in his words. “The only pairs that I’ve found are the ones that are dumped in your trash-heap.”
“What trash-heap?”

“There’s a trash-heap all around the base of the Hub… It’s in what you call the Outer and in what I call home. It’s actually funny when you think about it— the only place that I can find valuable things is in your waste…”
“And you still think that the Outer is better than being a lingerer?”

“Definitely. I don’t need those dumb frames. They make you stupid. And this light-stick I found can be pretty useful when you’re trying to prowl around at night without being detected. Tech-governors are programmed to recognize smart-goggles.”
Sarah smirked. She recognized the flashlight as the blinding flare she’d seen on the night Johnathan had left the box in her room.
With the box and its contents in her mind again, she tried steering the conversation back to it.

“So, you’ve explained to me why the trans-metal is valuable to you…. But, what’s so special about being able to control it? And how does it work? Most importantly— how did you know that I would be able to control it?”
Johnathan stopped maneuvering through the shaft and looked Sarah straight in the eye. “Do you have a shortage of questions? Or, is this how it’s going to be for the next week?”
“I’d take your offense seriously if it wasn’t in the form of a question…”

“Touché. You must think you’re so clever. If I didn’t know any better, I’d make you find the answers for yourself because of that attitude. But I do know better. I can’t afford to wait that long, so I’ll just get to the answers."

“We’ve needed somebody like you for years now. Somebody who could control the metal, without having to fight against the vast limitations of computers. This concept originated two centuries ago. There was a mass of people who went through experiments, in an attempt to control trans-metal. This was at the peak of the medical community’s strength, when they were still trying to discover new ways to lengthen lifespans. Trans-metal— or mutometallum— was believed to be their answer. Thousands were tested but only a few dozen people survived. Those who did were merely outliers…

“The plan was to have the outliers pass on their genetics to future generations. They were supposed to use their abilities to change the world. Mutometallum has more potential than you can imagine. Though, the experiments were stripping the world of its resources and action was finally taken against their plans. Those special people dissipated and for a while, they were believed to have died out before the Federation’s formation. Although, that rumor isn’t entirely true, because your mother is a descendent of them— you are as well. With your abilities, you’ll be able to help us overthrow the Federation and undo the doom that they’ve brought upon themselves. They’re going to fall to pieces because of the mistakes they’ve made– you can fix them.”
“I was always told that the Federation’s current state is a result of rioters ruining their resource storages in the lower levels.”

“The Federation is clouded in lies and they aren’t willing to take responsibility for their actions. The Federation’s lack of resources wasn’t caused by riots— it was caused by their negligence.  Even if the Federation says something is true, it doesn’t mean they’re being honest. I’m sure that they told you your parents are still alive, too…”
“Does that mean—are you saying– are you saying my parents are dead?!” she said, choking back tears.

“They suffered a fate that everybody pities… But, they died fighting for the right purpose. They were secretly members of the Rebirth while they lived in the Federation. They knew they were special and that it was their duty to serve the greater good.”
“If that’s true, then why didn’t my parents ever tell me about it?!”

“They never told you about it, because you were too young— it would’ve made it harder to keep their dual-identities a secret if you knew. This proved to be the right discernment, because when the Federation found out about their dual-loyalties, they were exterminated. If your parents had told you, you might have met the same fate as them…”
“Why didn’t you save them?!”

“We couldn’t do anything about it— the distance from the Federation to the Outer is too far and tortuous. But hey— that’s just how things are these days. That’s why we need to strike back against the Federation— it’s all of their fault.”
“Did they kill your parents too?”
“No— I was born in the Outer,” Johnathan said hastily. As he said this, Sarah’s face sunk. Catching his mistake, he grimaced.
To try and lighten the mood, Johnathan tried changing the subject.
“Do you think that they might still be alive?” Sarah asked, once Johnathan’s attempt at a conversation had been reduced to senseless rambling. “Did you actually see them go?”
Johnathan’s face went blank. “I never saw them go. There might be the slightest chance they survived. Although, the Rebirth has declared them terminated.”
Sarah looked distraught.
"Speaking of the Rebirth… Do you want me to tell you more about them?”
Sarah didn’t say a word. The heavy news of her parents’ death hung around her mouth like a padlock. It had sealed a new notion in her mind.
With my parents gone, there isn’t a chance at returning to my old way of life.
In that instance, nothing else mattered to her.

“I’ll take that as a yes,” Johnathan said. “The Rebirth is a resistance force in the Outer that has been against the Federation for years. We were built upon the concept that we could bring a new age of peace and freedom into the world. We live off scraps and struggle to maintain our base— but it’s all for the cause of renewal. We named ourselves after the Renaissance— an event of renewal that took place in the Ice Age, I believe— because that’s what we hope to bring into the Federation.

“I’m one of the Rebirth’s top-ranking members— I’ve helped build them to the level that they are. They might not still be standing if it weren’t for me. That’s why they sent me here to retrieve you and the mutometallum. You have no idea how hard it is to steal a chunk of that stuff…”
“You’re one of their top members and you still needed me to help pull you into the shaft?” Sarah asked, half out of bitterness and half out of jest.
“Any important questions?” Johnathan asked, sourly.
Sarah paused for a moment, before bringing up the question that had been tugging at her mind the strongest. “If you knew that I would be able to use the metal, why didn’t you come to me in person?”

“I didn’t know. Since your father’s genetics didn’t have the special ability I was looking for, it was a coin-toss over whether you’d be able to use it. I had to let you discover the ability on your own.”
Sarah raised an eyebrow in skepticism, causing Johnathan to turn away.

“I knew that you would keep it hidden from the authorities,” Johnathan said, stumbling over a few words, “since you’re smart enough to know that the orphanage would confiscate it if you didn’t. If it didn’t work for you, I was going to take the package back tonight. Most of the orphanage thinks you’re insane so I figured that, at that point, nobody would believe you if you told them about it. Overall, I thought I was taking the least amount of chances in my approach. Up until now, the Rebirth has thought it wasn’t worth risking one of their best men on this mission. Blowing my cover was the last thing I wanted to do.”
Sarah yawned, “You talk too much…”
“That’s what you get, in return for asking so many questions,” Johnathan said. “It sounds like it’s time for me to take you to my base for some sleep.”
He started crawling into the tunnel, moving with the stealth of a cat. Sarah tried following his example.
We can’t risk alerting sleeping tech-governors of our presence.

However, the small space made it hard for her to breathe and her limbs suffered in consequence. They thumped against the metal, creating a vicious cycle. Her thumps were followed by breathless gasps, which were followed by more thumps and more breathless gasps. She’d hoped that breathing would grow easier as she continued, but she eventually felt that the amount of space and oxygen was only shrinking. Occasionally, she’d even hear the whirring of tech-governors, which made the experience exponentially worse. The shaft turned so claustrophobic, that she felt as if she’d been stuffed into a keyhole-sized space.

They didn’t stop until they reached a spot where a small hole— just wide enough for Johnathan to pass through— was carved out into the wall. They crawled through it. The hollow space within was shaped into a humble cube— about twenty-five feet in length and width.
“This is your base?” Sarah said, unimpressed.
“Yep,” grunted Johnathan, pulling up a worn sleeping bag. “Only the finest around!”
Despite herself, Sarah managed a slight laugh and pulled herself into her own sleeping bag. “Such a bright idea… Because, everybody imbeds their safe haven in the base of their enemy…”
“I believe it’s called, ‘hiding in plain sight’.”
