“It’s called, ‘you need a better plan’…” Sarah said, as she closed her eyes and let out another yawn. “The only reason we made it here is because of sheer luck… You don’t realize how hard it is to escape out of under Mrs. Giber’s crooked nose.”

“Don’t get too comfortable. She’s not going to be clueless for too long. And she’s only the least of our worries. Tomorrow, there are going to be scouts all over— and they’ll not only be looking for trans-metal, but they’ll be looking for you as well. The Board of Initiators hate to have disorder, so they’ll make sure to keep you as target number one— and they’ll use their Model Human as a public distraction, like they always do.”
“Ah yes— the Model Human. That’s always a nice thought to have in my head before going to bed for the night. That clown’s grin is terrifying…”

“For the night?! It’s morning now. Also— I won’t be letting you get him out of your head any time soon. We have a two places that we need to loot trans-metal from— and one of them involves the Model Human.”
Sarah groaned and covered her head with her covers. Her mind started to surrender to a deep slumber.
“His grin is still terrifying,” she muttered.
Chapter 6

In the morning, Michael awoke to his tech-governor’s blaring. As if he were a ball of yarn, the robot rolled him out of bed. Bringing his hands to his ears, he had his tech-governor scramble to his closet and began to stuff him into his clothes. While the tech-governor carried him out of his bedroom door, Michael shoved his goggles on and started filtering through it.
“How many people have been talking about me?” Michael asked the goggles, grinning. “Let me guess— they’re in love with my smile!”
“As many people as you have neurons in your brain disagree with your smile…” the computer warbled.
“And, is that a lot, or a little?”
“Whichever answer is most pleasing to hear, I will give you.”
He froze for a moment, realizing that he was sandwiched in between two unfavorable answers— he’d never been placed in one by his goggles before.

“Just show me all of the positive feedback,” he said, grinning again, while his tech-governor brushed his teeth. “And then delete all of the others— I’m an Initiator now, so that shouldn’t be a problem for you.”
The rest of his day continued with the same rapid and automated pace.

After the tech-governor made him swallow his breakfast pill down with a chug of water, he darted out his door for the daily exercise route assigned for him. Given aid by his tech-governor, he completed his daily portion of strength training and mental exercises. At each error the tech-governor would correct him through a slight shock followed by a long-winded monologue. It was in portions of the day like these that Michael felt the urge to use his goggles tug on him the most, but— as usual— he managed to resist it.

However, the rest of the day was a more pleasing procession and was completely apart from his average routine. During his meeting with the Board of Initiators, he enjoyed a satisfying exchange where he was given a new list of duties that replaced his old ones— speaking engagements, parades, picture shoots and commercial filming. He felt his heart throb in shock during some of it. Though, he managed to swallow the feelings up in an ecstatic excitement.

His meeting with the Board of Initiators wasn’t the only enormous change from usual protocol. He was also bombarded by people who were eager to speak with him. For a stretch of several hours, he hardly had a chance to check the time, before being whisked away into another interview. At first the flood of praises was unsettling, but it soon became clear to him what it meant.
This is a small sample of how much I’m adored by others, Michael thought to himself. My role in society has been expanded— I’m now far beyond anybody else.

This brought a sort of aura around him that added an extra boost in each stride. A surge of purpose filled every part of his body, leaving him overflowing. For the past few years, a feeling of inferiority had hung over him like a wolf hangs over its prey. It hunted him through his dreams, chasing Michael away into the safety of his goggles. The feeling had now dissipated. New confidence launched Michael into a series of energized conversations. His goggles began buzzing like a whizzing bee— everybody sent him messages, in the hope of befriending him.

Yet, everybody was a slight exaggeration of Michael’s mind— there were plenty of people who were displeased with his new position. A few of them came out and openly harassed him, calling him a puppet. Thankfully, Michael found support from tech-governors who took care of the rebels. Michael didn’t take the attacks to personally, either— most of these people were lingerers, a class of citizens which Michael looked down upon with extreme loathing.
The feeling was mutual. It was because of Michael’s detest that the lingerers revolted in the first place.

After this strenuous day, Michael earned permission from his tech-governor to visit his parents’ house.  He wanted to go and celebrate his new victory. It had been weeks since he’d last seen his parents in person. He was overwhelmed with pride when he began wondering what their response might be.

While the lights within the building dimmed at the pace of a snail trying to scale a wall, Michael arrived at his parent’s apartment— room two-three-six-nine. There were tens of thousands of higher-class apartments like these on every floor of the Hub’s higher levels. Though, amidst those facts, Michael couldn’t help but feel that this apartment had a specific personality to it.
“Nothing like home!” he exhaled, standing at the doorstep.

The door’s familiar dents— gifted by Michael’s younger counterpart— and its bitter smell of old copper took him back in time, to the days of his youth. Michael had lived in this apartment for his entire childhood and his parents had lived here even longer.

The place was a part of his identity— bound around his heart like a bow. Michael had missed it dearly and regretted ever having to part with it. Although, there was only so much room available in the buildings that encased civilized society, so people– or units, as the tech-governors referred to them— were often assigned to apartments far from their families, in order to account for the limited housing in the dense towers.
Michael swiped his hand across the door’s lock-pad, which consequently let out a low beep.

“Locked again…” he huffed. Normally, doors within the Federation were left open to public— it was considered rude and selfish to isolate others from your home. Although, lately there had been an increase in lingerers and people all over had begun to hide themselves away in their homes.
“I guess I’ll just have to wait until their tech-governor identifies me,” Michael said.
After what felt like eons of standing on the doorstep, he heard a muffled voice yell through the thick copper door and he watched it open to a warmly lit hall.
“Congratulations on your promotion sir,” a tech-governor said.
Michael ignored it.
I’d expected my parents to greet me— not a useless piece of metal.
“Where are my parents?” Michael asked. “I thought that you and my tech-governor arranged dinner.”
“Right this way sir,” it said, turning to guide him down the hall.
As the robot hovered into the dining room, Michael found his parents seated at the table with their goggles strapped on—eating without him.
For a moment, Michael was upset. Although, he smothered these feelings— it was considered inappropriate to lash out your anger towards others.
They probably just forgot that I was visiting, Michael told himself. They wouldn’t have started eating if they’d known I was coming over. I’m too important to dismiss.
Trying his best to make light of the scenario, he took an empty seat at the table. He flashed a mischievous grin and waited to see if anybody would notice him.
They’ll probably be shocked when they see me.

At least, that was what he’d thought, until his parents’ tech-governor came over to serve him his plate—an unruly mixture of fruits and vegetables. As he started to pick at his food, he realized that they couldn’t have possibly forgotten him. Otherwise, they wouldn’t have prepared him a plate. For most people, dinner was the only meal of the day that didn’t consist of pills. Despite this, only the rich could afford authentic vegetation on a daily basis. His parents wouldn’t have spent money on expensive food and then forget about him.
“Hello son,” his mom nodded, with her goggles still strapped on. She didn’t even bother to turn and face him.

Michael’s father did even less to acknowledge his presence. Taking a mouthful of greens, he managed a stifled explanation for the scene. “We figured that, since you were so busy, you wouldn’t mind if we ate without you.”
Michael was confused, but nodded his head in a faux look of understanding.
Are they even going to congratulate me for my success? he wondered angrily.
“So… Anything new?” Michael asked, trying to steer the conversation.
Transfixed to their devices, the pair said nothing.
Michael was about to mutter, “This conversation is hopeless…” but stopped himself.
Michael slipped on his own goggles and played to its lenses’ luminous glow.
If I’m going to spend the evening here, he thought, I might as well get some enjoyment out of it.
His father let out a grunt. “Good job on the award last night by the way. We heard that you won.” He said stiffly.
Michael was appalled.
Heard I won? He thought. They were supposed to have seen me win! They needed to see me, in my full glory!
“You weren’t there?” Michael asked.
“We were busy…” his mother said monotonously, her long black hair swaying as she swerved her head to the game on her goggles.
“Nothing could possibly be more important than me!” Michael scowled. “What were you doing?”

Catching Michael’s defiant tone, his father snapped his head around to Michael and frowned. With his goggles on, he utterly missed eye-contact with his son. Though, this didn’t make the disapproval on his face any less potent. “We could ask you the same thing!”

“Well of course you could, because you didn’t even make an effort to watch me last night! I’ve worked really hard all my life to get to where I am! I spent nearly three decades in your apartment, trying to figure out what I would do with my life— and you don’t even come to watch me and appreciate my extreme efforts?!”

“We didn’t need to watch you! Your face is plastered in the corner of every goggle lens, every TV screen and on every tech-governor! And, besides that, we heard that you made a complete fool of yourself last night by degrading an announcer— in front of a whole crowd! Do you know that’s a crime? I would’ve been embarrassed to make an appearance…”

His mother added, “Not to mention, news has come out that you had a fallout with Peter! I thought you were friends and breaking a friendship is unhealthy and frivolous! Not only that, but it’s a public embarrassment! Peter is such a nice young man— you should be looking up to his example, rather than detonating your relationship over nothing! If I had a son like him, I’d be proud— you should feel lucky that the supercomputer ever matched you two as friends.”

Michael was fuming. “Don’t you even care about what happened last night? I have more friends than I can count now! You should be proud of me! Not to mention, you probably would have made the same mistakes if your friend went ahead and broke your goggles!”
Michael’s dad spat out his food, which fell to his plate in clumps. “That’s ridiculous! Peter would never just—”
“Sir,” their tech-governor interrupted, “Spitting out your dinner is an enormous waste of food and is an action that can be punished severely if continued.”

“Sorry, I saw it in a movie once,” Michael’s father replied, hanging his head sullenly, like a chastised dog. This only lasted for a moment and, once it passed, he instantly resumed his authoritative composure. “Now, as I was saying… Peter would never take your goggles— he’d know that taking them off of somebody is an extensive crime— we need our goggles to focus.”
“Peter’s character is averse to such unruly behavior,” Michael’s mother said, nodding in agreement. “You should stop lying to us and admit how much you failed!!”

“I’m going to report Peter to the authorities!” Michael said. “And then you’ll see! I’m going to make the whole world know that he broke my goggles! And then you’ll realize how wrong you are for getting angry about miniscule things— I’m going to prove that I’m the bigger person, by showing you both just how big I am!”
He didn’t really care about Peter anymore though—he was done with him. His mind was far from his meal or parents at that point.
A glaring question confronted him with a brutal force.
Do my relationships mean anything anymore?
He was the model human of the year now— but he suddenly felt like none of that mattered.

The thought seemed to come out of nowhere and it nearly knocked him out of his seat. Yet, he couldn’t ignore it—it was too strong. He couldn’t think of a time where a relationship of his didn’t prove to be shallow in the end.
They always turn out to be made of pure motives.
His hands began to fidget like a whirring blade and Michael placed his goggles back over his eyes to calm them.
At least my troubles can’t reach me in the shell of my game, he thought coolly.
Smiling, Michael felt something strike his mind.
I have fans by the thousands! What am I thinking? he wondered, Of course I’m not alone.
This severed the bind around his heart, as if it were a bow. With that in mind, he was able to play with his goggles and eat his meal contently, until his tech-governor came and dismissed him.
Chapter 7
“It’s time to wake up,” Johnathan said, shaking Sarah awake.
She moaned and tried stretching to rouse herself. Her whole body felt groggy and sore.
“How long did I sleep?” she asked. It was impossible to tell what time it was in the darkness of the metal room.
“About four hours.” Johnathan said, taking a quick look at a rusted watch he had around his wrist. Then, he waddled over to his backpack for food.
“Only four hours!? No wonder I still feel exhausted!”

“Get used to it princess,” he said chewing on a bar of mush. “I only slept for three…” After rifling through his bag for a minute, he tossed a bar over to Sarah. “Here, try some real food— that should wake you up. We found some remnants from trash heaps and abandoned factories in the Outer. It beats those nasty pills that you guys have to swallow. If you’re still hungry, don’t worry about getting another one. I have three bags full of them— enough to last us two weeks.”

Taking the bar from Johnathan, Sarah said, “Thanks.” It only took one bite for her to gobble the whole bar. Food was becoming a scarcity for the lower classes of the Federation and Sarah was famished.

“You enjoy it, huh? Too bad that just scratches the surface of the quality of food you could be eating. Just another one of my reasons to despise the Federation.” Johnathan leaned back against the wall and let out a deep sigh. “Well, enough with the chit-chat. We have work to do. Once you’re done eating, I’ll need to update you on my plan.”

Once Sarah had finished eating, Johnathan said, “So, the Rebirth needs us to collect as much of this mutometallum stuff as we can get our hands on. If we succeed, we’ll ultimately use the supplies to storm the Federation and unlock a secret algorithm they’ve been hiding from us— it could potentially regenerate the Earth. I know that this is all a lot to take in at one time— but the world’s atmosphere is devastated. The Federation’s process of drawing energy from the stratosphere has been ruined by the Sun’s increasing size.

“The algorithm was supposed to be utilized to save the Earth years ago— that was why the original Federation was founded. They planned to use their power to regenerate the Earth… But, we’ve had many different revolutions within the Tower Federation since then and every new form it takes on gets overrun by greedy dictators.”

“Are you sure that’s all true? I hadn’t even heard that there was more than one form of the Federation. Not to mention, the Federation claims that they live by the same rules they did at their foundation.”

Johnathan’s face turned red as he slapped his thighs and let out a long wheeze. “They feed you guys that garbage!? Even worse— you guys believe it!? I’m not surprised about you, kid— you don’t know any better. But, those who do know better should be aware that a new law is being passed every month. At this point, they’re completely contradicting the first laws they put into place.”
“Well, at least they haven’t gotten rid of them.”
“Sure— but they don’t hold the same weight as they once did. They might as well have been tossed away! This just shows their strategy— to keep the people blind, so they can strike them down easier.”
Sarah’s eyes closed as she soaked the somber truth in. All of her life she’d been being lied to— kept in the dark. What hurt the most was that her own parents had never even told her about this.
They didn’t even leave me a clue, she thought. I really have been living with monsters— and there was nobody to tell me that when I needed to hear it most...
It was in that moment that her heart drove toward a powerful decision. She was determined to give the Federation a taste of what they’d dished out to her.
“So… Where exactly do I fit into the plan?” she asked, gritting her teeth.

“You’ll be in charge of— well, you’ll basically be doing all of the main physical work. You’re going to be the one moving the trans-metal and ultimately breaking us out of this towering dump. Meanwhile, I’ll be giving you your instructions.”
“Sounds good… Now, where are we going to get the trans-metal from?”

Johnathan smiled proudly and rubbed his palms together, “I’ve been waiting for you to ask me that question. That’s where their unintelligent ‘Model Human’ comes in… I managed to gain the information that the house he’s going to be living in— ‘Model Manor’—has walls built of the stuff. Trans-metal is extremely lightweight, so a whole house full of it won’t be as heavy to carry as you might expect…. There’s only going to be around ten tons of it— hardly anything when compared to the hundred and fifty tons it would weigh if built out of any other material…” Johnathan stopped to let Sarah’s mouth gape. “I know… It’s still a ridiculous amount of weight. That’s why we’re going to start you off with baby steps. You’ll need to master controlling the mutometallum first, before you can be trusted to move a ten tons of it. Which is why I’m going to spend the next few weeks training you in stealth and the trans-metal.”
Sarah smiled. “When do we start?”
“Oh, so now you want to get to work. You kids are ridiculous— you’re much harder to train than anybody else…”
“Wait… You’ve trained other kids? How many kids are there in the Outer?”

“I haven’t trained kids to use mutometallum before. But yes, I was once a trainer and there are plenty of kids back at the Rebirth who I’ve trained. Although, I’ve had experience with mutometallum— I worked with your mom, which is why this shouldn’t be too tough.”
“You knew my mom?”

“Yes… Very well, actually. But, we should be focusing on training,” Johnathan said, tossing a container of water to Sarah. “The water might not be that clean and you’re probably not used to it being so filthy. But you’ll need lots of water if you want to strengthen your abilities and this is all I have.”
Sarah nodded her head.

“Now, try your best not to get killed!” Johnathan yelled. A split second later, a giant metal tile was flying at Sarah’s face. With a scream, she winced and closed her eyes. When she reopened them, the metal plate was hovering in front of her face— latched onto a wiry strip of trans-metal that was protruding from Sarah’s wrist. The trans-metal resembled the tubular trunk of an elephant.
“Don’t ever do that again,” Sarah scowled at Johnathan, heaving heavily.
Johnathan simply laughed. “Sorry Sarah, but this is only the first of many times that I’m doing that. You were the one who asked me to train you— this is what you get.”
“As if I had an option…” she said, with a grumble.
“So, did you see how your reflexes kicked in? That shows you’re beginning to strengthen your mind’s link with the metal.”

“It’s kind of hard to see when your eyes are closed. But, I guess that’s what happens when you hurl a giant metal plate toward me! What were you thinking!? Did you want me to have a black eye and a mouth full of missing teeth on my first day!?”
Johnathan chuckled. “Even if you did, it’s called trial and error.”
“Yeah— go ahead and smile about this… After all, you’re the one who has to worry about losing their smile from flying chunks of metal!”

For the next few hours, the two continued on like this, with Johnathan pushing Sarah through seemingly endless rounds of drills. Most were like the first one, being both terrifying and exhilarating. However, as time passed, her adrenaline lowered and her instincts acclimated to Johnathan’s rapid movements.

The training session progressed further and Johnathan’s shock-based exercises were halted in favor of less dangerous ones. Whenever Johnathan called for it, Sarah would make the trans-metal band around her wrist stretch out into simple shapes. When she was struggling, his advice could be disturbingly accurate. From his descriptions, it was almost as if he’d controlled the trans-metal himself.
After years of training my mother, he must’ve become a sort of expert.
It was these calmer exercises that she liked the most. Even so, she also found them to be more strenuous, since it was difficult for her to control the metal.
By afternoon, Sarah was exhausted and surrounded by puddles of sweat and muddy water.

“Yeesh… You sure made a mess!” Johnathan said, handing Sarah a towel. “Now, mop it up…” After watching her in silence, for about five minutes, Johnathan couldn’t stand to keep his mouth shut any longer. “So, did you have fun?” Johnathan asked, gulping down his water.
“It depends… Does your definition of fun have something to do with sweating your guts out?”
“Just like your mother…” Johnathan said under his breath, shaking his head.
“What did you say?”

“Nothing— I was just saying that… We’re going to be doing this training for the next two weeks, until we can head out for our first mission. Every day we’ll alternate our training— tomorrow we’ll head out to train in the field of stealth.”
“Oh joy…”
“Hey, at least you’re a natural. I’ve seen plenty of kids go through my stellar training regimen for the first time and have to give up!”
“Really?”
“Of course! Although, I’ve also seen people go through my stellar training regimen and blow your performance away. So, don’t get too cocky.”
“When I asked, ‘really’, I was referring to your claim of having a stellar training regimen… After seeing how you train firsthand, I think you’re the one who’s acting too cocky.”

“You can keep trying to offend me like that— but, if you really think I’m a bad trainer, then we’re both in a bad place,” Johnathan said, deflecting Sarah’s jibe with ease. As lighthearted as his retort was, it had a tinge of grimness to it. It dashed all life out of their conversation.

Sarah found more sleep that night, but she also found herself to be more restless. She tossed and turned to vicious nightmares about the Federation, their experiments and— worst of all— what they’d done to her parents. She couldn’t be sure if these nightmares were brought from the stress everything, or only from the uncomforting sleep situation she had on the floor. Though, whatever it was from, it left her exhausted when she awoke the next day.
“Rise and shine kid!” Johnathan said, with his booming voice. “The artificial daylight is burning and we need to get moving! Hop to it!”
Johnathan slapped his hands together for extra measure.
“Did anybody ever tell you that you have a loud voice?” Sarah yawned in annoyance.
“Nope, never even crossed my mind!” Johnathan said, his voice sounding loud as a blow horn.

For the rest of the day, the two crawled through the shaft, avoiding tech-governors as they went. Johnathan’s never-ending clamor of words poured out a long list of the rules Sarah had to conform to. This list included no wandering, no dawdling, no stomping and— most of all— no talking.
I wonder how he keeps that last rule… Sarah wondered to herself as Johnathan continued going on.

Once they’d covered the rules, they went exploring. At least, it was exploring in Sarah’s eyes. In spite of Johnathan’s claim that he was new to this portion of the Hub, he moved through the shaft with a clear sense of ease.

For the most part, the journey through the shaft was largely uneventful. Sarah didn’t find anything that sparked her interest— aside from Johnathan’s lack of speech. To Sarah’s relief and bemusement, they managed to utterly avoid the tech-governors. That is, until they neared the end of their journey.

As they were headed back to their base, the floor ahead of them slid open and gave away. Following Johnathan and his rules, Sarah scrambled to avoid tech-governors. Yet, as she and Johnathan hurdled the opening, Sarah saw something on the tech-governor caught her eye— it was an enormous screen with a face on it. For once, it bore the face of somebody other than the Model Human— it was herself. Atop the photo were written these words— “Report to the authorities if found.”

They’re looking hard for me, she thought with amazement. It’s a rare occasion when somebody is prominent enough to appear on a screen in the Federation. They must think I’m a threat of some kind… Do they suspect that I can control the mutometallum?
“Come on kid! We need to get moving!” Johnathan hissed, as he saw Sarah peer down into the opening. “What did I say about no dawdling?”

Sarah nodded her head and followed Johnathan. Even so, nothing— not even the call of Johnathan— could take away the image welded into her foresight. It was the image of being captured by the tech-governors. It was the image of being dragged away, back to the dreaded orphanage. She shivered at the thought.
After yesterday, I’m not going back there, she thought. Not again! No! Never again!

For the next few days, Sarah speedily progressed in her training with Johnathan. Although, it was a struggle. She constantly found herself exhausted, to the point that she could hardly keep herself from toppling over at the end of the day. She struggled to understand why using the metal wrapped around her arm could exhaust her so much, but Johnathan explained it clearly and willingly.

“When you use your mind to control the metal, your brain is spending its energy as it strains to connect with the extension,” he told her while glugging a bottle of water. He did this much to Sarah’s irritation. Sarah sometimes wondered if he drank while talking solely to annoy her— the dingy water didn’t taste good enough to legitimately enjoy. “I know that the concept might seem a bit complicated, but that’s nothing compared to how much more complex it becomes. Your body is not only sapping energy as it makes the connection— it’s also exerting the body’s energy as it transfers it into the metal. Don’t worry though— the connection will strengthen over time. It’s like learning how to walk. Once you start controlling a large enough mass of trans-metal, it begins to sustain itself with minimal energy. Soon, you’ll be able to manipulate over a ton of it!”

The training slogged on and Sarah became stronger and smarter. She became used to waking up sore in the morning. She became used to collapsing into a deep sleep by the end of the day. In fact, the routine became comforting to her once she realized that it gave her clout over her nightmares.
By the end of the week, Sarah was ready to take on a new challenge.
I might be inexperienced— but what does that matter? she thought.

The new confidence growing inside of her, made her feel like she could take on an army. It came to a point where she questioned if she still needed Johnathan’s help. She felt ready to go out on her own.
“Wake up, princess,” Sarah snickered as she roused Johnathan late one night. It was finally the day that she was going out in to the field. The day that she would prove herself.
Johnathan snorted awake. “I sleep a little late for just one night and all of the sudden I’m the slacker…”
“Hey, you said it, not me…” Sarah said, recreating Johnathan’s mischievous smirk.

“Alright kid, I take it back, ok? Gee, you can hold a grudge…” said Johnathan, rolling his eyes. “Now, to the first order of business. Tonight, we’re headed to one of the Federation’s most tight security bases. It basically contains the Federation’s entire supply of mutometallum, as well as the main controls for all of the mutometallum in the Federation—including the metal contained in the Model’s Manor. Don’t worry about having to do too much work. We’re just going to get as much metal as we can and then get out— there’s not as much metal in there as you’d think and this is only a trial. They only store one eighth of their small supply in there. You’d be surprised to know that the Federation’s main supply of Mutometallum is contained in the ‘Model’s Manor’— only one and a quarter tons are kept in their base compared to the ten tons built into the house. The Hub must think that nobody would suspect that they’d store their main supply in an average apartment. Although, I know better”
Sarah shook her head, shocked by the pure magnitude of what she’d be dealing with. “Remind me… how much metal do we plan on taking from the Model’s Manor?”

“About one ton. We need to be able to bring it back to base so we can implement our plan of attack. The metal will give the Rebirth a massive leverage, since we’ll be the only ones who are able to use it.”
Sarah nodded her head and bit her lip.

What is the Rebirth planning to do with this metal? Sarah wondered, teetering between two beliefs. If it’s a weapon in the hands of the Federation, then it will still be a dangerous weapon in the hands of the Rebirth. Although, what am I concerned about? Johnathan has taken me from the orphanage and given me a new purpose—hope. The Rebirth is all he stands for. I’ve probably merely become untrusting of other people in my time in the orphanage.
“Alright… Where is this base at again?” Sarah finally asked.
Chapter 8

Michael stood up from his chair and waved to a crowd of roaring fans. He was being carried by tech-governors down to the center of the Hub, where the main A.I— which controlled all the workings of the Federation— was kept in an enormous dome. As usual, Michael shot his familiar wave and smile to the crowd, setting them in a fervor.

However, this charade fell like a castle of cards when a spectator crawled out of the crowd. It was a man with bruises and burn-marks covering his arms and hands. He was dressed in torn rags, which were made filthy by an oily gunk. His face and hair had suffered the same fate as his rags and a few teeth were missing from his mouth.
“Excuse me,” he warbled, shaking violently as he held out his hand. “Would you be willing to give me some spare points? I don’t need many— just enough to pay for a single meal.”
Michael raised an eyebrow and motioned for his robots to keep moving. His father had taught him how to deal with begging lingerers— it was best to avoid them at all costs.

“If you even merely make eye-contact with one of them, they’ll persist,” he told Michael once, during a hearty dinner. “And if you happen to slip up and give to one, you’ll soon find a mob of lingerers chasing after you. The first chance you have, you’re supposed to report the lingerer. Never, under any circumstance, aid them.”
“Tech-governor,” Michael called out, taking one last look at the beggar. “Are there any spare tech-governors around? We have a lingerer.”

The man shrieked instantly. “No!” he cried. “You— you need to help me! I thought you were a better man than this! You said that your interests were for that of the common people!” He looked into Michael’s eyes in desperation, his eyes bloodshot and wild.
“They are,” Michael declared proudly as a couple of tech-governors arrived and took hold of the lingerer.
The man thrashed about, but he no longer had the vigor within him to go on. He collapsed in defeat.

Michael was lowered down, after giving the order to his tech-governors. With his feet planted on the ground, firmly as a tree, he walked over to the man with confidence in his stride. Glowering over him with an air of superiority, Michael said, “Here’s the thing… You aren’t the ‘common people’. You’re a result of the worst aspects of humanity— a lazy blob that did nothing in its life, besides shoving pills down his throat. You expect me to ‘save you’ although, you were supposed to have saved yourself before you ever reached this point. I’ve met people like you before— people who I’ve even been willing to waste my time on. You’re all the same— obsolete and a waste of space.”
“You don’t understand…” the man moaned.
“Take him away…” Michael said, flicking his wrist. “I have better things to be doing.”
The moment the words left Michael’s lips, his tech-governors came. Using their robotic arms, they tore Michael away from the lingerer and the crowded mass of the city.

He was willing to stop at nothing to head to the main A.I and ask it a question— it was where people were supposed to go when they had a problem that they needed to solve. However, it was very limited because the A.I that the public had access to was programmed to withhold certain answers. Unless you happened to possess a high enough position in the Federation, you couldn’t even go near the Initiator’s version of the A.I— it was said to be hidden away somewhere, behind locked doors within the dome.
Its limitations were why people rarely visited the public A.I center. The other reason was that most of the people who went to the A.I were thrown into the Outer.
No doubt because they were too old and too poor to even get themselves goggles, Michael thought. Uselessness always comes with age and poverty…

Whenever people did visit the enormous A.I center, it was usually to gather for an event. However, Michael was still going to the empty dome. While most of the questions could be answered by asking tech-governors, Michael felt that he had a question that nothing had the answer to. He was willing to tap any resource to find it.

Arriving at the center dome of the Federation, Michael studied his surroundings. It had been a while since he’d last been there. Maybe it was from seldom seeing it, or maybe it was from his bad memory— but, every time he saw the room, it was as if he was seeing it for the first time. He always noticed something different about it.

It was a giant dome, made of a turquoise glass. The whole space was enormous, being miles wide in every direction. The only parts of the dome that weren’t made of glass were the parts that hugged the tower walls. From nearly every angle, he could the sky outside of the Federation and peer into the Outer.

He was accustomed to always viewing hives of activity, bustling about. As he looked into the wasteland, all he saw were mounds of abandoned trash heaps and blackened dust. Just as Michael began to face the gravity of the world behind the glass, a cluster of holographic computers sprouted from behind him and out of the chrome floor. They distracted him with their flashing colors, which changed at each passing moment. There were at least a hundred of them, but most were empty. However, out of all of them, Michael looked for a specific computer.

As he looked, he passed an enormous fountain. A golden statue of a book, full of the Federation’s rules, rotated on its pinnacle. From atop the book, a tower of water shot into the air, landing in fountain with a graceful, musical splash.

Even as he absorbed the beauty of the room, he found that there was no enjoyment that came with it. The eventful confrontation with the beggar had put him in a daze. His mind had trouble accepting that people could end up like that lingerer— rejected and obsolete.
I know that I was doing the right thing… But why did it feel so wrong?
He looked back to the golden book.

I must just be disturbed because of the increased number of lingerers. Their very existence is worrisome… Everybody in the Federation is supposed to receive the same pay and treatment— with the minor exception of political authorities, like myself. If everybody’s job has equal value, then the blame for the growing punishment of the Outer must be coming from an external force… Something corrupt and conniving, hiding behind the stage.

“Maybe the lingerers are sabotaging things, thus creating more of themselves,” Michael hissed. “They’ve been ruining everything from the start… They must have a secret plan. They’re trying to override order in the Federation, because they don’t want to have to work hard. Meanwhile, people like myself have to fight tirelessly, to rid ourselves of them.”

Michael began to worry if the common people were starting to become corrupt. The very thought disgusted him, but logic told him that it was true. Lingerers were everywhere. There wasn’t a single place in the Federation where he could feel assured that he wouldn’t run into one.
There was one thing that relieved Michael. He knew that, at the end of the day, he and the Board of Initiators would still be working late into the night, to protect the people of the Federation.

Michael heaved a sigh of fulfillment and had his tech-governors to lower him to the ground. He waltzed to the grandest looking computer in the room and started to type out his question. It felt strange not to relay his command through voice, but he was still pleased with the sensation. He didn’t want his question to be heard aloud.

His fingers pressed against the soft touchscreen keys, while they let out a pleasing note at each click. Michael knew that, if the keys had known his dour question, their melody would have turned to a curdled clack.
“What is the ultimate goal of the Federation?” Michael mouthed silently, as the words appeared on the sleek, holographic computer monitor.

If Michael had been asked that question by somebody, he would’ve pretended that he knew the answer— in fact, he had done that exact thing the other day, during a conference. However, he hadn’t a clue to what the real answer was.

During his pursuit for the title, “Model Human of the Year”, he’d ignored where everything would be going and whom he’d be serving. After Peter left the scene, he became clueless. He had everything he could ever want at his fingertips— but none of it mattered. There was a nightmare that he couldn’t get rid of— one where he was groping through a labyrinth that had his face plastered upon every wall No matter what he did in the labyrinth, he couldn’t get out. Nothing he did would wipe the vision from his mind. He felt that he needed the answer to what the Federation stood for.
Maybe once I know what they stand for, I’ll be given something to stand for. I might find a solution to all of my problems, he thought. I might be able to sleep calmly again.
The answer that came up left Michael crestfallen.
“No results found,” the computer said, monotonously.
Michael was about to groan in disappointment, but he felt something lightly press against his shoulder and pull him away from his work.
“I see that you’re busy,” said a familiar voice— Peter.
Michael jumped.
“What are you doing here?” Michael asked, jerking his head around.
“I— I followed you here,” Peter said, his voice turning distant. “I saw what you were typing… Very interesting. It’s a shame that they don’t hold the answers.”
“Why would you follow me?! Why do you even care about what I was typing?”

“I don’t know… I’m not even sure why you care about what you were typing. After all— it’s been made very clear that nobody in this building cares about what created the Outer. Why are you so interested in it, all of the sudden?”
“I’m not interested in the world outside! I’m interested in the world inside— that’s all that the question concerned.”

“But not the place that you’re asking it… You could’ve asked that question anywhere you wanted. But, you decided to come here, of all places— the only place where you can view the Outer. I know you Michael— you get obsessed with things and surround yourself with them. You find a place where you push everything else away, so that you can focus on whatever petty thing that you think is important.”
“If you’re still angry about what I did to you, get over it! All I did was take advantage of a great opportunity!”

“You didn’t take advantage of a great opportunity! You took advantage of me, so that you could pursue your own selfish desires! You might think that you outsmarted me— that you proved me wrong, but all you did was show how ignorant you are.”

“Show my ignorance?! You’re the ignorant one! You’ve been chasing an idle dream— to save your father— for years! It’s never going to happen. When I neglected our plans, I was only neglecting your frivolous goals. If your father was so great, he would’ve come back to you by now! If any of the people being thrown in the Outer were worth saving, people would’ve cared enough to lead a revolt! You need to wake up to the reality of things— you need to realize that your dreams can never be achieved. You’re chasing after clouds!”
Peter’s face scrunched into a scowl.

“Maybe chasing after clouds is a mistake… But, what are you supposed to do when the clouds start chasing after you, blotting out any light that you had in your life? You should look around yourself for once. The world isn’t what it’s made out to be. Just take a look out these windows, for once! Does the dark and cloudy world look right to you? How about the floods of lingerers, which permeate the confines of this building? The closed off lower levels? The limitations on energy and oxygen usage? Nothing is as it seems to be, Michael! Clouds are everywhere and you’re never going to see anything clearly until you get above them! As I said before— chasing after those clouds might be a mistake. But guess what? That’s all that some of us will ever have!”

“Go away Peter,” Michael said, putting his face in his hands. “We’ve gone through this battle before. This should’ve ended the night that I was turned Human of the Year. I want you to never speak to me again. You can come back when you’ve taken hold of your all-important clouds— once you’ve passed them and reached Mount Olympus, tell Zeus that I said hello…”
Peter turned and walked away, his anger going with him.
“I will,” Peter said.
Chapter 9

Sarah brushed her long hair from her face, as it blew toward her in a gust. It was dusky and uncomfortable where she sat— she was perched on a thick iron bar, built into a ceiling. Above her was a lofty vent that chilled her body and gave her goosebumps— or, perhaps the goosebumps were from the excitement tingling through her body. Ahead of her, Johnathan was stealthily moving ahead, making sure that his every step was taken with a fluid and precise grace.

After two weeks of training, the pair were finally in the trans-metal warehouse. It had been a long journey from their hovel to the warehouse’s ceiling. From her height, Sarah could see why Johnathan was hesitant in coming— the place was infested with security. Every few minutes, a tech-governor would whiz past her face. The blades were close— so close that she thought she could feel their cold edges brush against her skin. After that, piercing terrors came to her mind at the sight of these mechanical nightmares.
What if I fail the mission? Sarah wondered. Will I ever be able to prove myself worthy of my parent’s cause— the one that they were willing to die for?
As she lamented on this grim potential, she slipped on the iron bar and teetered on the edge. Johnathan turned around to offer her a hand, but she refused.
I don’t need any help.
With a swift swing of her hand, she forced her body back into balance and regained her firm grip.

For the next half hour, they progressed in the same manner, the only difference being Sarah’s whittling patience with the stakeout. To make the dull procession worse, she had no clear direction of where they were going— Johnathan hadn’t given her a map of the area.
“So much for all of that training,” she grumbled to herself.

Johnathan came to a halt. For a moment, she thought that he was angry at what she said. Though, when he swiveled to face her, she saw his look of exaltation. The message translated before Johnathan spoke a word— the wait was over.
“Come on,” Johnathan mouthed, beckoning excitedly.
While she carefully moved towards him, he tossed a length of rope to the ground. Then, he tied the opposite end to the iron bar.
“Alright,” he whispered. “We’re going to head down on this rope to retrieve the trans-metal.”
“We’re going to what?” Sarah asked, so shocked that even the dust jumped from her face in surprise.
I haven’t been trained to climb down rope! Sarah thought. I haven’t even been made aware that this was part of the plan!
“Why didn’t you tell me this?”

Johnathan snickered. “This is the very reason I tend not to give away my plans. When I give out the tough parts, nobody wants to attempt them. But, don’t worry— I’m sure you’ll be fine! If our mission is successful, you won’t even need to use the rope again— you’ll be able to use the trans-metal to get us out of here. Besides— I’ve slid down rope many times and the only thing you have to worry about is looking down… Oh and there’s one other thing you’ll have to worry about— running into tech-governors. If we don’t head down now, they’ll find us and our cover will be blown.”
“Real comforting,” Sarah said, mockingly.
She stared down from her height. Because of the dimness in the room, it seemed like the distance to the ground was unfathomable.
“You expect me to climb all the way down there!?” she asked.
“Yeah… Pretty much. You remind me so much of your father. Unfortunately, this means that I have to do to you what I had to do to him…”
“What are you talki—,” Sarah, began, before her words were cut short by Johnathan, who pushed her off the bar.

She felt herself spiraling down, with her hands fumbling wildly about for something to grip onto. Her stomach sloshed into her throat and her muscles turned tight as a coil. Her every instinct was being put into action in order to prevent herself from plummeting to the ground.
When her fingers managed to wrap around the rough rope, she was relieved.
What a miracle!
After her first hand had gripped onto the rope, she found herself easily able to descend.
What was I so worried about before?

The sturdy feel of it against her hands gave her an assurance that felt worlds away from the trauma of plummeting. Though, even the rope’s sturdiness couldn’t pull the memory out of her head. She felt as if she was reliving it over and over again. Being pushed off the edge— sinking into the inky black—
How could Johnathan have turned on me so easily— without even a second thought?
“Did you enjoy your ride?” Johnathan asked, once Sarah had reached the bottom.

Sarah simply scowled in return. She was standing in a large open expanse, filled with rows of giant metal crates and forklifts. Once Johnathan had reached the bottom himself, he threw a blade into the air, severing as much of the rope as he could. When he stuffed the cut rope into his pocket, the blade clanked in the distance.
“Welcome to the warehouse and all of its dingy glory,” Johnathan said. “There were a few times where I had close calls up on the rope. I was almost caught by the tech-governor. How about you?”
“We’ll have plenty closer calls if we keep gabbing. Where are we supposed to be headed next?”
Johnathan made a mischievous smirk. “Here’s where things get real easy… Try to keep up with me if you can!”

Johnathan started sprinting down the pathway. As Sarah chased after him, she heard the beating of blades and the rush of wind follow after them. For a moment, she thought the wind to be a comforting boost in her stride. Then, she realized the dark truth.
The tech-governors must have detected us.
“Our cover is blown!” exclaimed Johnathan. “We’re just going to have to run for it, kid!”
The two ran relentlessly, with their lungs bursting for oxygen. Despite the air always feeling shallow in the Federation, Sarah now felt that it was lacking more than ever.

“Stop right now, Sarah Screw! You’re property of the orphanage,” the tech-governors spouted in a mechanical chorus, before sounding an alarm. Sarah winced at their every word— they were like knives to her ears.

“We’re almost there! We just have to make it a little further!” Johnathan said. “I remember seeing a disabled tech-governor in your room when we first met— that means you know how to shut them off, right?”
“You can’t sit trapped in a serenity center without learning a trick or two,” Sarah said.
However, she knew that she didn’t have the time to manually turn them all off. If she tried that, she’d run the risk of being captured.
After running for another minute Johnathan halted. “Over here! We’ll make quick work of them!”

Sarah was alleviated when she neared Johnathan, who was  in front of a locked door, with his hand nearing the touch-pad. She lunged toward him and the tech-governors followed her. Though, if they’d been more aware of their surroundings, they might have shrunk back.

Sarah skidded toward Johnathan, just as he started giving out orders. “This is the one chance we have,” he said. “We need to make it count! I’m going to show you a picture of a fingerprint and you’re going to replicate it with your trans-metal— got it? You’re going to use it to activate the keypad and open the door. Meanwhile, I’ll disable the tech-governors. Once we’re in, we’re going to shut the tech-governors out. Got it?”
Sarah nodded.

The moment a tech-governor made the first attack, Johnathan shoved it toward the ground and pried a knife into its head where the switch was. It immediately fell down, lame and lifeless as a stuffed animal.
Despite his victory, he was crestfallen when looked out toward the hall and found more tech-governors than he could have imagined.

“It appears that the Federation cares about you a lot more than I suspected…” Johnathan said, grumbling. “There has to be at least forty tech-governors out there— probably closer to sixty. I’m going to have to show you the picture now, Sarah and hope for the best.”
Quick as a flash of light, he whipped a crumpled wad of paper out of his pocket. Catching Sarah’s inquisitive look he said, “What? You haven’t seen a picture on a piece of paper before?”
Sarah’s face turned red as Johnathan started smoothing out the wrinkled mess.

“Here— try your best to recreate this print by using the metal that’s around your wrist,” he told her. “This picture is stolen from the files of the Board of Initiators. It was pretty tough to get our hands on that, so you better be careful with it!”

Then he left her and faced the throng of tech-governors that were pouring down the warehouse. Their size had already doubled and was starting to triple. Johnathan ran towards them with a brutish force and tried his best to disable as many as he could. Although, the battle had become futile before it even started and Johnathan was like a ball of yarn being tossed about by a kitten.
In the meantime, Sarah struggled to replicate the fingerprint. Her focus was diluted by a pang in her heart. Something about the whole ordeal felt wrong— she’d never stolen before.
The Federation is a destructive force made up of monsters… But, if I break my own moral code to stop them, will I really be making a difference— or will I be making the problem worse?
Then she then reminded herself that she’d already broken her morals many times.
“Are you almost done over there!?” Johnathan grunted as he fell to the floor. “I can’t keep this up much longer!”
Sarah didn’t answer and her forehead was wetted with perspiration.
Why can’t I bring myself to do it?
“Come on kid! Are you going to do this or what?! If you don’t start now, we’re going to be turned into tech-governor meat, like your parents were!”
Sarah flinched— the words pricked her conscious.
What did my parents have to do with anything? Sarah wondered angrily.
“What makes you think that you can just talk about my parents that way!?” Sarah said, dropping the fingerprint image to the floor.

“I’m sorry— I didn’t mean it that way…” said Johnathan, trying his best to juggle his attention between his conversation with Sarah, his war against the growing wall of tech-governors and his wounds. “It’s just— we won’t make it out of here alive if you don’t finish this plan of yours! Think back to the training!”

Sarah was teeming with fury— but she was willing to let that wait. Picking up the picture, she began exerting the wells of her willpower to recreate the fingerprint. Tiring as the task was, it brought a sensation of peace and calm over her. The trans-metal made her feel an assurance that reminded her of her parents. It was like a link to her past— a window to her lost loved ones.
Once the metal had shifted shape accordingly, Sarah brought it up to the fingerprint-pad. In response, the door slid open with a clean whoosh. It was simpler than she had expected.
Everything else around her was far from simple. Johnathan hobbled toward her with his clothes torn and his body in shambles. Not too far behind was a horde of tech-governors swarming toward him.
“Run Sarah!” Johnathan said. “Get the trans-metal! Don’t worry about me until you have it— you can use the trans-metal to save me!”
Sarah didn’t waste any time and retreated into the storage room.

While she stumbled through, she found it to be very stuffy and dim. There were no lamps to be found, so any hope of being able to see was gone. In spite of this, she was still able to vaguely distinguish her environment.  The primary features were walls of metal crates packed along every side.  They were stuffed so high and built so thick that they reached the height of the ceiling.

“How am I supposed to get these open!?” Sarah wondered to herself, as she studied them. Their number was overwhelming. Upon closer study, she was befuddled by how the packages had even been produced— there were no crevices in them, or any sign of an opening. Besides sharing a similar cubed shape, they hardly even resembled the crates in the rest of the warehouse.
She grabbed one, pulling it off the shelf and came to a revelation— they weren’t crates.
They’re blocks of trans-metal!

Sarah recognized the metal by how warm it felt against her hands and by the shock of electricity it gave her. It meshed with her arm and began stemming from there to all of the other blocks of trans-metal. The room morphed into a glob of silver. Once connecting with the blocks started to become strenuous, she rode out of the room, carried on a wave of metal.

The tech-governors were easily swallowed up by her machine. It wasn’t long before the floor, which had been littered with robots, was swept clean by a slivery blanket. The only thing left untouched was a bruised sack that resembled Johnathan. He was spared by a shimmering arm that extended out of the metal.
“Did you plan on taking them all on without me?” Sarah asked Johnathan.
“Yes,” Johnathan said, trying his best to chuckle through his battered jaw. “As you can clearly see, I had them covered. So, I was never too concerned…
“Were there any tech-governors guarding the trans-metal?”
“Not one…” said Sarah. While the words slid out, a perplexing mist came over them.
But, shouldn’t it have been guarded?

Catching Sarah’s look, Johnathan scanned the room. “We better get moving, then. I’ll give the directions out of here. This time, don’t hesitate to take my orders—we’re going to need to trust each other if we want to make it back to our base.”
Johnathan’s finger then shot out toward their first destination. Sarah and her current of metal heeded the command, screeching along the warehouse floor as it went.
“There goes my hope for subtlety…” Johnathan said. “Hopefully you’ve taken enough of the metal. If we plan on escaping the Hub within the next month, we’re going to need as much as we can get.”
A red light flashed and a dreaded whirring returned.
“To the left!” Johnathan shouted, his eyes filling with terror.
The remaining portion of the rope was illuminated in the meager red light that tech-governors gave her.
Hopefully, the trans-metal will keep us safe for long enough to escape.
“Alright kid,” Johnathan said, “I want you to use the trans-metal to throw me toward the remaining piece of rope that I left behind!”
“What!? Are you crazy?! I still need your help! I don’t remember how to get out of here!”
“You’re going to have to trust me!”
Sarah didn’t listen— she couldn’t.

New tech-governors arrived, bordering Sarah’s metal glob. Some of them were already tearing away at it. Sarah exhausted her mental capacity trying to drive them away, but her concentration was running out and a question ate at her mind.
Will I have enough metal to make it to the rope?
Johnathan’s fists clenched as he watched the tech-governors advance. “Sarah, you need to listen to me! We don’t have much time left!”
“I’m not going to throw you that high— I’m not interested in killing you!”
“If you’re not interested in killing me, then you need to do what I say— throw me to the rope!”
Sarah couldn’t bring herself to do it.
I’ve already trusted Johnathan to fend off the tech-governors and he barely survived. How am I supposed to expect him to follow through on his promise now?

It was then that she made her decision. She ignored Johnathan’s pleas and continued trying to plow through the mounds of oncoming tech-governors. At this point, the only thing keeping herself and Johnathan safe was a small island that she’d made with the metal. Under it was a swarm of the malicious robots, clambering atop a heap of broken trans-metal.
As Sarah drew nearer to the rope, her concern of not having enough metal had become more prominent.

She looked over her shoulder to see Johnathan. His usually light spirit had fled and in its place was a nervous ball of fear. Clenching his teeth and scowling in the face of potential defeat, he gave his last order. Pointing up toward the ceiling he said, “Wish yourself luck… You’re going to need it to get up there.”

Sarah’s head throbbed and her body stiffened under the growing intensity. Mustering all the strength she had left in her body, she raised the metal into the air, making a spiraling pillar. She made it link to the rope, to give her a sense of stability while she climbed. In that moment, in the darkness of the warehouse, she was able to forget the troubles of the world around her. The weights peeled off like an old skin.
I feel free as a— what are those winged creatures called again? Ah, yes— birds.
The feeling was brief. Once they’d reached the rafters, Johnathan brought back the anxiousness of the situation.
“Sarah, you need to move the trans-metal. The tech-governors are going to snap it apart!” Johnathan said, leaping from her pillar.

Sarah heard a brittle cracking below her. She felt the ground teeter. Leaping into the air, her limbs spun like the spokes of a wheel. She pulled the trans-metal along with herself as fast as she could. Just as she landed on the ground with a thud, the remaining trans-metal trailed toward her. The amount wasn’t nearly as much as it had been when she started— Johnathan would be disappointed when he found out how much was left.
“Stop lollygagging and get a move on!” Johnathan said, barreling toward the shaft in the ceiling that they’d entered through.

Sarah followed. Soon, she was alongside Johnathan. However, when she saw that his face was twisted into a knot, she wished that she’d stayed behind. This wish was sealed when he banged fruitlessly against the door to the shaft— which was now closed tight. Sarah knew that there was no chance of getting through by brute force— but Johnathan didn’t appear to have the same knowledge. He banged relentlessly for a full minute, before he subsided to the floor. His demeanor shifted and he started to look as hopeless as a rowboat caught under the current of the ocean.
“There’s no escape,” he said.
“I thought that this was our way out!” Sarah said, hurriedly.

“I did… But you wasted too much time— it closed before we were able to make it here. My controller won’t work because the Federation’s computers have put this room on complete lockdown. Now, we only have a minute left before the tech-governors come up here and tear us to shreds.”
“I thought that you had the controls to get the door open!”

“Didn’t you hear!? This room is in complete lockdown— not even a tech-governor could open this door if it was given orders to. If you had let me up here when I told you to, I might have been able to counteract it— we had a window of time. But, it’s too late now…” Johnathan pounded his fists against the door for extra measure.
“What good is sulking going to do!?” Sarah said, with annoyance. “We still have a chance at getting out of here… You have to have some sort of backup plan. You do have one, right?”
“No. How am I supposed to make a backup plan?! There’s only one way to open these doors and it’s gone! If you had just done what you were supposed to—.”
“And how am I expected to do what you say when I have no idea what your plan is!?”
“It’s called ‘faith’. You would think that it would come easy for somebody as young as you... Besides— I can’t give you every aspect of the plan, because you never know who is listening.”
Johnathan’s body slumped further down the iron rafter.
Sarah was unimpressed.
Johnathan shouldn’t just give up so easily. There has to be a way out!
Sarah searched around herself for ideas. It didn’t take long— the solution clicked into place within a second.
The answer is so simple.

The whirring of the tech-governors was everywhere. Not only was it everywhere— it was also gaining volume. In addition, their red light stained the walls. The crowding orbs, from which their light originated, looked like glinting balls of fire. They stung Sarah’s eyes. This sight gave her a fierce message— one that finds a way to infect everybody. Time was running short.

Sarah brought her hand down to the trans-metal and lifted it further toward the ceiling. Her energy was mostly drained from earlier, but she ignored this. Fighting against her senses, she pushed a metallic arm, which she’d formed, up toward the entrance to the shaft. She felt her own arms twitch and groan under the weight and a lump formed in her throat from the mental undertaking. Yet, she continued on.

Above her, cracks formed in the shaft’s door. She then watched as the cracks spread from the door and throughout her own trans-metal pillar. Sarah knew that she depended on the pillar outlasting the door— she neither had the energy to sustain the pillar, nor move it.

Johnathan had caught her plan and was doing his best to help keep the pillar steady. Small as his effort was, she appreciated it. Sarah could hardly keep her balance in the rafters, let alone hold up the giant metal pillar at the same time.
She could feel the last ounces of her strength beginning to deteriorate. The world around her was hazy and her hands were tingling. A steady numbness was taking hold of her.

Underneath her feet, a tech-governor’s whirring blades tried drilling through the rafters. Johnathan left Sarah on her own, doing his best to fight the tech-governors. His energy wasn’t much better than hers and he had a struggle just trying not to fall over as he walked. There wasn’t a chance that he would be a match for a single tech-governor, let alone several dozen.

Finally, the iron door gave away, with its pieces splintering all across the warehouse. Sarah closed her eyes— partly out of concern that the splinters would reach them and partly out of exhaustion. To her right, Johnathan crawled backwards toward the entrance, using his legs to kick tech-governors away from him as he went.

When Sarah reopened her eyes, she found her remaining trans-metal broken into small pieces and scattered across the rafters. Sarah gathered as much trans-metal as she could and used it to pull herself into the shaft.
“Wait for me, kid!” Johnathan shouted, hobbling to the entrance.

Sarah was relieved to hear the calm tone return to his voice. Although, this relief only lasted for a moment. As Sarah extended a bar of trans-metal down for Johnathan to grab hold of, she knew that their night’s battles were only half-over. Within the next two weeks, they’d return to their problems again. Only, success would matter more than ever. They’d be approaching the Model Human.

title: The Return of Blackneck (Unfinished Sequel)
paragraphs: Once upon a time, in a kingdom far, far away… The king of the kingdom has died. His son is the only one left to take his place, but he doesn’t want to be king. Everything is about to topple over into itself— and nothing is going to be able to save it.

It’s officially the first winter of the year 1132— the first snow has come upon us. Though, I wish that I could go back to a winter ago. My father, has died. It’s been three days since the date of his death— December 19th. Some say that it was by chance, and others say that it was a conspiracy to overthrow the throne. There are a group of people who even blame me for his death. They claim that I poisoned him, so that I could become king— so that I could rule the land.
All I’ll say is that I don’t find this kingdom worth ruling without my father being the one who rules it.

One might believe that I’d be overjoyed to be the next in line for the throne— to be the one who will take his father’s place. They’d be wrong. I’m overcome by grief. I haven’t felt quite so alone and desolate in ages. The world around me has become a dark and horrid place. All beauty has been sucked from it. All that remains are the bare bones.

I’m not quite sure why, but I feel as if the world has reared its head and finally revealed how ugly it is. Everybody is looking to me for excuses and explanations about what has happened. There are riots in the streets. There are cries of rebellion down even the halls of my own castle. There are whisperings of the end being nigh…

I don’t know what to think. I don’t even know if I should think— perhaps I should give up the throne to some other worthier heir. I don’t even want the throne. Everybody looks up to me, expecting me to be the answer to all of their problems. Though, I’m not. I never will be. If they’re going to find an answer to their problems, they’ll be finding it somewhere else.

Perhaps the largest reason for me thinking that I can’t solve their problems is because I can’t even solve my own. I’ve been looking for a way to bring my father back from the grave. I’ve come across a rumor that across a lake further down the mountain, there’s a person who has the ability to cure anything. Some call the person a “he”, and others call it a “she.” Sometimes they apparently even shift location to other parts of the mountain. I’ll admit that there aren’t many definite things surrounding these rumors. In fact, there are plenty of people that are calling me inane, and a complete fool for thinking such a thing could help my father. Even a few of my advisors, who have their own personal interests more at heart than my own, claim that such thoughts would only lead to dangerous sorcery, and self-destruction.

Once more, I don’t know what to think of this. If I were to be honest with myself, I don’t know what to think of anything. I’m so lost. Now that my father is gone, everything has transformed into something new and different. I used to have the belief that new things were positive things. However, I’m no longer so confident in that.
I’m willing to do anything to make things back to the way they were. I might be wrong in trying to do this— but I feel that it’s the only way to bring myself to where I need to be.

Sorcery or not, I’m going to seek out a way to restore my father. I won’t rest until I’ve found the answer. I won’t rest until everything is brought back to how it once was— how it should be. If it takes sacrificing a part of myself and my kingdom, then so be it. The most integral part has already been lost to us— the most integral part has been lost to me.

A girl shivered, under a blanket. Her hair, once coal black, had been turned a ghostly white from a thick padding of snow. Her lips were coated a sickly blue, matching her eyes. Not that one would’ve been able to tell that they matched her eyes— her eyelids were frozen shut.

The rest of her face hadn’t fared better from the cold. Her nose, usually pug-shaped, had been morphed by the wintry air to look like an icicle. Her teeth chattered, to the point that she sounded like a rattle. Her ears were the only thing on her body that wasn’t turned white from snow— they’d instead been reddened to the point of them looking like oversized holly berries.
Only the crackling fireplace beside her matched the intensity of her ears.
Still— her reddened ears couldn’t make up for the rest of her. The very sight could bring a chill down somebody’s spine. She couldn’t have looked colder if she’d dived to the bottom of a frozen lake.
“How many times do I have to tell you— stop diving into frozen lakes!” an old man said.

His face was worn and leathery, and all of his hair was but a wisp. Though, age hadn’t worn down all of his features. Some bits— like a pointed nose, a rounded chin, and a thin mouth— remained prominent, hovering over his face like a bee does over a flower that has withered away.
“Just like last time Joshua, it was an accident,” the girl said, managing to open her eyes.
“Susan— you want me to believe that you accidentally walked out onto a frozen lake, for the second time in the past month?”
“It was different this time. I was chasing after a dog that went loose.”
“Why did you veer off so far that you were chasing the dog over there in the first place? If your friends hadn’t warned me about what happened, you could’ve died!”
“Maybe— but it’s not as if there are many other places to go in this village.”
“I’d keep arguing with you— but I’ll let you win. You want to believe that there aren’t many places for you to go? Then, you’re going stay in the house for the rest of the day— no exceptions.”
Susan gave a scowl, and then a smug grin.
“Feeling as cold as I am, I wouldn’t want it any other way.”
Joshua walked away, muttering something about “ungrateful children.”
“And no books,” he added, as the creaking of an opening door resounded. “I’m starting to think that they’re putting a bad influence on you!”
Susan moaned— but she didn’t even attempt combating the punishment. His word was always a final one.

Earlier that day, she’d been exploring the world outside the village. She’d known that it was winter, and she’d known that wolves ran ramped in those parts. However, none of that mattered at the time. It still didn’t matter.

There was something to the world outside the boundaries of the village. It was wild. It was untamed. Despite the dead frigidness of winter, it was full of a life that wasn’t anywhere else. An overturned boulder looked like it could’ve been a castle. A towering tree could’ve been the leg of a giant. The shadows that spread across the sunlit snow, wriggling as the clouds passed by, could’ve had a soul of their own.

Although the mountain that stood in the western horizon capped it all. The sight of that alone, with its rolling purple cliffs, and its white plumage that appeared to be like a dove’s feather, made the trip fully worth it.

Sometimes, Susan whispered to it. It almost seemed to speak to her. She knew, of course, that it couldn’t. Though, whenever the wind whisked into her ears after she’d explained her troubles to it, all of her reasoning was whisked out.

The truth of the matter was, there had been no dog on the lake when she’d fallen in. According everybody else who had been around the lake with her, there hadn’t been anything on the lake. If they hadn’t known her so well, they would’ve said the same thing about the first time she walked onto the lake, as well.

Although, Susan’s eyes didn’t agree with everybody else’s. While theirs saw nothing, Susan’s saw a silhouette. Each time she’d gone there, there’d been some sort of figure standing on the other side. It might’ve just been a trick of the sun, or perhaps just a hallucination derived from the chilling temperatures. Susan had ignored those possibilities each time. When she saw the silhouette outstretch an arm, and seem to beckon for her to come closer, Susan followed.

Each time, she felt a surge of energy— in a sense, as she walked across the thin sheet of ice, she walked across water. Pride filling through her chest, there was a moment when she thought that there was nothing that could stop her stride.
“I was meant to do this… The silhouette— I’m being led to it for a reason,” she thought.

Though, the ice didn’t seem to agree. Each time Susan crossed the lake and thought this, the lake snarled back and cracked underneath her feet. Each time the lake snarled and cracked, Susan looked down, and saw a milky reflection of the sun and the clouds. Each time Susan saw this reflection she felt as if she’d been transported into some other world.
Then, she was transported into another world.

The ice snapped beneath her feet, and she fell into a portal— a portal to a cold, dark and icy place. The world behind was full of muffled screams. Though, they were far away now. Everything was too cold and biting to focus on them— far too cold.

Back in front of the fireplace, Susan stared at a cobweb that had been weaved near there. However, she didn’t see a cobweb. Instead, it combined with the crackling of the fireplace to blur into the image of the cracking, icy lake.

A freeze ripped down into her bones, and she felt as if she might not be able to climb back out of it. She let out a cry for help, but all that left her mouth were bubbles. Her nostrils and ears filled with scalding ice. Her tongue finally tasted the breath of breathlessness. Her eyes caught sight of sightlessness.
All pride that she felt before coming onto the lake had been sucked from her lungs.
Susan shivered, and returned to the warmth of her blanket. The cobweb was once more just a cobweb. The fire was once more a source of warmth, rather than chilling cold.
“Just a bad memory,” she said. “I’ll never go back there again.”
Half of her statement was a lie. She’d be back. An instinct tugged at her, telling her that she needed to go back— that there was no other option. There was no other option.
“What was that silhouette?” she asked herself. “What did it want from me?”

Not being able to stand the unanswered question any longer, she left the fireplace and went throughout the well-treaded house. The wooden floors, once well-sanded and smooth as a pebble from the side of a brook, were now weathered and full of splinters. These days, Susan always took care to wear shoes when walking through it.

It certainly wasn’t the largest house in the village. It had only one floor, and five rooms— two bedrooms, a kitchen, a living area, and a room where Susan’s Joshua kept a large storage of books. Most of these rooms all shared the same splinters, the same wobbly furniture, the same crumbling walls, and the same sloping ceilings— all except one.

Susan’s feet took her to the book storage room— the one place in the house was set apart from the others. It always seemed to be meticulously kept, and cleaned. The room was the house’s closest grasp at perfection. Every floorboard seemed to be meticulously sanded down, every book was meticulously dusted, and every furnishing was amongst the sturdiest in the house.

Susan soon found herself standing in front of its entrance, staring at the glint made on it by some nearby candlelight. Her hand grasped the well-known door handle, and pushed it open. Here, she felt at home. Here, she had her “happy place”— as Joshua would call it.

“The only life worth living is your own,” he would often say. “That’s how you know you’ve found your happy place— when you can go there, and feel like it’s solely your own life that you’re living. Your life— not anybody else’s. It’s when you can go somewhere and feel independent of the troubles of the world.”

Right then, as she walked into the room, with its musty scent of books, nothing else that had happened prior mattered. She forgot what Joshua had said about her not being allowed to read. She forgot about falling into the ice. She forgot about the distant silhouette. All that she could remember were the days that she’d spent reading at Joshua’s side, when she was younger. She wasn’t willing to leave that memory. She didn’t want to be anywhere else. The room was her home, and she felt as if there was nowhere else in the world that was better to be.

“I figured that you’d come in here soon enough,” Joshua said, peering over from out of under one of his books. He was seated in his favorite chair— a bright red one, which came with a cushion. Susan could only think of a few days where she hadn’t seen him sit there, with a book in hand. “But, I’m afraid that you’re going to have to deal with the fact that you’re not allowed in here for the time being.”
Susan then felt the leaden weight of her Joshua’s word come back upon her. He’d rarely ever grounded her— though, Susan also knew that she’d rarely ever done anything to upset or disappoint him.
Susan wanted to shout— she wanted to prove her right to this spot in the house.
“Don’t shout,” she thought to herself. “I can’t let out my anger… I’ve rarely ever clashed with Joshua, and I’m not going to start now.”
“I— I,” she said with a strain.
“I’m going to my room,” she finally said.
She left the library with a feeling of regret.
“Why didn’t I say that I understood, instead of that I was leaving?” she muttered under her breath. “Why didn’t he say anything in return?”
With a swoop of anger, she swung her door fast to shut it— but not before catching it.
“I can’t let my anger get the best of me,” she said to herself.
Though, those words were steadily becoming harder and harder to follow.

It used to be so much easier. We used to talk more. It used to be easier to talk with him. But now— now he’s starting to seem so distant. He rarely ever gets up from his books… He always sits in that chair nowadays… There have been some days when he hasn’t even gotten up to help make dinner. What changed him?

She looked at a chair from in the corner of her room. She and Joshua had once sat there and read together in the evenings— sometimes for an hour. She felt another wave of frustration rip into her mind.
It’s so much harder now… What changed us?

Susan then thought about how her evening ventures into the snow had progressively become longer. Then, she remembered how she’d become more and more distant herself, oftentimes staying in her room from sunrise to sundown.
What changed me?

Her memory trailed to when she was eight years younger, and at the age of six. She’d gone out into the snow to play with Joshua. Although, after wiping a snowball that he’d thrown into her face from her eyes, she noticed that he was gone. She ran around, calling and looking for him for, what seemed then to have been half an hour, and what seemed now to have been five minutes. Then, Joshua jumped up from out of the snow.
Susan gave a squeal of shock, which then turned into delight. They both shared a laugh, as the snow steadily melted off of their faces.
Eight years later again, back under her covers, Susan fell asleep to this happy memory.
