Although, in her sleep it transformed, and shifted. It became like an innocent caterpillar that goes into a cocoon to transform into a hideous moth.

In her dream, Susan was once again looking for her uncle in the snow. Although, this time she truly couldn’t find him. She’d left him. He’d left her. They were forever separated by and endless sheet of white.

It’s been two weeks since I last wrote in my diary. Since then, the kingdom has begun to settle, and I’ve started to be recognized as king. A coronation is already being planned. The people who were once talking about rebellion are now parading through the streets declaring tidings of joy. I’m afraid that I have a hard time listening to them.
All that I feel is a strong sorrow. Maybe I’m falling too far into grief, and maybe I’m being too sentimental. Yet, I think this is wrong. I think this is all wrong.

I complained two weeks ago about my people claiming that I was some monster that needed to be cut down, and that I had murdered my father. I was sickened by their thoughts of rebellion. However, what I’m even more sickened by is that I’m now going to have to replace my father as king— and it feels like it’s happening far too soon. We haven’t even had an official funeral for my father yet, and my coronation is already being talked about.

There’s also the bit of me that believes I can still bring my father back, and that there’s hope for this kingdom to be renewed to its former glory. Some might call me a pessimist for believing that I’m not good enough to lead this kingdom— but I truly think that there’s not a person under the sun who could replace my father.

I’ve already dispatched a man to go on horse and find the supposed healer who can cure anything. I have a feeling that he’ll come back empty-handed, but I’m not without hope. Even if he doesn’t find the healer, I know of other ways to look for them. There are passages about these mountains— craggy places of rock and dirt that have fallen from high cliffs. Some say that these are where the healer makes their home. And, with everything surrounding this mystery healer, I wouldn’t be shocked if that’s the truth. There have been stranger things said about this mountain… Far stranger things.

Although, that’s enough for now. One of my servants just sent me word that a tailor is coming to make me new robes. As I said before, I’m disgusted by the very thought of this coronation. However, if my plan goes well, everybody will understand, and apologize for all of their trespasses against me. Everybody will wish that they had never acted out against the memory of their true king.
All will be made right.

It had only been five days since Susan fell in the lake, but she still found herself coming back to it. There was a drive in her gut that told her she needed to know what the silhouette had been doing there the past two times she saw it. She felt that she couldn’t be satisfied without knowing.

“Why do you constantly take us here?” one of Susan’s friends asked— a boy with bushy hair, a mouth that was bigger than for his own good, and a nose that stuck out like a reed. “Do you like jumping into ice cold water? Do you want to keep making a fool of yourself?”
“I don’t know Tim… Do you like constantly being the shortest one of the group?”
A girl with short hair and a mouth as thin as Tim’s mouth was wide jumped in Susan’s path.
“He has a point. What’s on that lake that keeps bringing you back?
Susan gave a sigh of annoyance.
“I saw something there, alright Isabella?”

The trio were once walking outside the village’s main borders, and into a mostly empty area. Dirt and footprints ceased to be seen as they came onto land that had barely been traveled by people, other than themselves. A smell was in the air— it was fresh, and it was free of the odors that came with animals and people. It had an almost liberating property to it.

“We can’t keep coming out here every day just because you ‘saw something’,” Tim said, with a mocking tone. “There’s only so many times that I can trick my parents into leaving before they start to figure out what I’m actually doing. We’re all supposed to be learning our trades.”
“Go do that then,” Susan said, unwaveringly. “I’m coming out here, whether you guys are following or not.”
“You’re still following after that imaginary talking shadow— aren’t you?” Isabella pried.
“I don’t understand why you both have such a hard time believing me on this— I saw something out there. And, I saw it twice. You can try ignoring me, but I know what I saw was real…”

“I’ve heard people say things like that hundreds of time,” Tim said. “That’s the sort of thing that creates all of the fake legends that swirl around for years— and they all come about over nothing more than a twig, or a fluttering leaf. Whatever you saw out there probably didn’t matter…”
Susan looked at Tim in annoyance.
“You believe me, right?” Susan asked, gesturing to Isabella.

“Susan, these sort of things are just a trick of the eyes. To be frank, this is all being blown out of proportion. Why don’t we leave the lake alone for today? I thought that the whole point of leaving the village borders was to go to places that we haven’t gone before. After going to the same place every day, I start to wonder what the point is.”
Susan folded her arms, and remained standing where she was.
“This is too important,” she said. “If you’re leaving, I’m still going.”
“Fine then,” Tim said, walking off.

Isabella followed, her footsteps breaking through the snow and her ties with Susan’s route. At first, Susan grinned at their exit, thinking that she’d called their bluff. However, as they continued to move further off, her unwavering position suddenly began to shift. Her eyes tracked their distance. Her feet moved restlessly, under the snow.
By the time a minute had elapsed, Susan was racing after them.
Tim turned his head over his shoulder, and caught sight of Susan’s racing feet.
“I knew that she’d break,” he said. It seemed that he’d intended for these words to be kept to himself, but they flew across the plane of snow and tore through everybody’s ears.
“You couldn’t keep your mouth shut if your life depended on it, could you Tim?” Susan asked, with irritation.
“You’re one to talk— you clearly didn’t have the will to go out on you own.”
Tim laughed, despite nobody else sharing his sense of humor.
“I didn’t think that you’d actually leave,” Susan said, holding back a smile and refusing to encourage Tim’s laughter.
“I think that was made clear when you came running after us only after a minute of walking had passed,” Isabella said. “It looked ridiculous.”
It was at this point when their wills snapped, and they all broke into laughter.
“Where are we headed?” Susan finally said, with a tiredly wheezing in an attempt to recover.

“I heard about an interesting place near here,” Isabella said. “It’s around the underside of the mountain— there are giant boulders that remain from an avalanche. From what I’ve gathered, a few animals roam over in that area, and make their homes there. Who knows— we might find a few things while we’re over there. We’ve found several treasures doing this sort of thing before.”

When Isabella said, “treasures,” she was referring to several abandoned trinkets. Most of these were assorted pieces of junk, such as an abandoned glass vial, the remains of a tattered map, pieces of an old tent, and a piece of rope.
“And where did you hear about that— from the old geezer, Jon, who you’re always hanging around?” Tim asked, mockingly.
Isabella’s face went red from embarrassment.
“No, of course not,” she said.
“You’re clearly lying through your teeth.”
“Maybe you’re just too afraid to go near the mountain…”

The pair both stopped, and stared at one another. Even Susan had nothing to add. Majestic as the mountain might’ve seemed, there were terrible stories surrounding it. Most people within the village called it haunted. While such stories were typically only swallowed up by gossips, that particular tale was one that continued to remain prominent. People oftentimes spoke of strange creatures and voices that came from at the mountain’s foot. Some even swore that there wasn’t a single person who’d tried trekking the mountain who’d come back to state otherwise.
“Fine,” Tim said, trying to prove his bravery. “Let’s go. I see the mountain every day, and it has yet to do me any harm. I’m not scared of it.”

These words burned their ears right as they leaped off of his tongue. Something about them left a knot in each of their stomachs. The tall, unchartered mound of rock had always held a benevolent presence. Speaking about it in the passive way that Tim had felt wrong— even disgraceful.
Still, Tim had a way of making his loudmouthed outbursts leave some sort of imprint. Now that he’d spoken, the word was final. Nobody had the callous to back out of it.

“I was told that attempting mountain climbers would plant pine seeds over all of their pathways, so that they would be able to tell which direction they were going in,” Isabella said, as they began walking toward the mountain’s image, which was obscured by a fresh sprinkling of snow. “It could be another tall tale concerning this mountain, but we might as well give it a try.”

Winding like a vine around a tree, the path to the underside of the mountain was an ambiguous and tortuous one, moving amongst steep inclines, cliffs built from erosion, and spires of rocks that seemed to rip out of the ground. Several feet of snow had coated over most of this pathway, making it so that every step they took felt as if it was resisting against the earth itself. It would sometimes cause them to trip, and then fall to the ground. A face covered in snow was an unpleasant predicament all on its own, but the deep snow became an especially pervasive problem when Tim tripped, and started toppling down into the snow and nearer to an eroded cliff like a loose rolling pin.

They managed to stop him from taking a drop off the edge and falling to his undoing, but this didn’t seem to be a strong enough signifier for them to stop their journey. Maybe it was because of their promises to themselves, or maybe it was because of the priggish stubbornness that had led them to start their journey in the first place, but nothing seemed to phase them. There was a point when the hungry howling of a wolf harried through the clouds, with such a strength that they ripped apart and changed shape. There was another when a screeching of an owl swooped overhead, and the very sound of its claws sharpening left a scratch down each of their backs. None of it made a difference. Their will was as hard as the ice was cold.

Their stubbornness didn’t give in until the sun began to lower behind the thick clouds for the evening, and the snow’s brightness began to wane. By that point, the mounds of rock had already come in sight, and their minds had broken from their chains, leaping into a spirit of imagination.
“I told you that this trip would be worth it,” Isabella gloated, as her voice reverberated off the rocks and the sloping sides of the mountain. “And you all thought that I was crazy.”
Tim wasn’t so impressed. He gave a huff, and remained irreverent.
“You’re the one who brought us here on only Jon’s word— what else were we supposed to think?”
Normally, this would’ve led to a verbal brawl between the two, but curiosity managed to shove these habits to the back of their minds.
“Just take a look at the scope of these,” Susan said, standing in front of one of the fallen boulders.

She was so close to it that she could press her hand up against it. However, her eyes weren’t focused on the boulder, which was right in front of her. Instead, she was focused on what she couldn’t see. No matter where she turned her head, the boulder’s breadth— it stretched so wide that she couldn’t see passed it from her position.

From Tim and Isabella’s distant view, the boulder was no smaller. In fact, it seemed larger. Compared to Susan, the boulder was already its own mountain. In the space that it would’ve taken to make a dozen of Susan, only a fourth of the boulder would’ve been made up.

Despite this being a boggling sight, the formation of the multiple boulders took precedence over their size. They were all stacked in a neat pyramid that built its way up to an overhanging mountain cliff.
“How did this get down here? Giants?” Tim asked, in his over-loud voice.

Nobody else was paying attention. Isabella was busy trying to count the number of boulders— she could only make it to thirty, before tripping up and wondering which boulder she’d already counted. Meanwhile, Susan was looking for an entrance into the boulder mounds— though, whenever she found a place where a gap might’ve been, she found it sealed up with mounds of mud and smaller rocks. At first, she thought that it must’ve been crafted by animals. However, upon closer inspection she noticed that some of the mud sealing would have marks that were similar to handprints imbedded in them.
Who would’ve done such a thing?

Walking back to from whence she’d started, with an unsatisfied frown, she planted herself next to Tim. He had his own defeated look, and appeared somewhat daunted by the sight of the mountain. Susan supposed that it might’ve been due to her and Isabella’s mockery of him. However, she caught his neck craning to focus on the mountaintop, and remembered his fear of it.
“I dare you to try climbing one of those boulders,” she whispered, into his ear.

She wasn’t quite sure where these words had come from. At first, she wanted to believe that it was from a part of herself that wanted to coax Tim out of his fear. Though, then she caught Tim’s look of terror at hearing her dare— and Susan felt a swell of pride. She didn’t know where the pride had come from— at least, that’s what she told herself for a moment. However, she soon found that she couldn’t keep the lie up.

As Tim walked up to the boulder, and began struggling against its sides, she found herself chuckling at his plight. A sense of guilt streamed into her stomach at the revelation. Yet, her mind found a way to combat it. It brought back each of Tim’s snarky comments, as well as how he’d been the one who’d incited the series of events that led them to this terrifying mound. It was simply retribution.
Where is this coming from? she wondered, becoming sickened by an internal, frothy mixture of joy and self-disgust.

All of these thoughts lasted but a second. She quickly tucked them away when she realized that it was all amounted from a simple dare. However, as Tim sat at the top of the boulder, giving Susan a smug and angry stare— as his eyes seemed to scowl at her, and ask her why she’d tested his fears, built up from generations of deaths surrounding the mountain— as the boulders groaned and rolled at Isabella’s exclamation of, “Forty-seven! There are forty seven boulders— as Tim slipped down his boulder, and the rest of the boulders slipped with him— Susan realized how powerful the dare had really been. She realized that, even something as seemingly innocent as a game could ignite a series of unfortunate events.

The rocks cracked and rumbled along the ground, making the soft snow, which should’ve deafened their roars, seem nonexistent. Although, Susan’s focus was hardly on them. It was even hardly on Tim, although it should’ve been. It was on the high cliff, where she’d seen Tim’s eyes go round with fear. It was on a silhouette that stood there— beckoning for her to follow it.
It’s only been three days since I’ve last written to this diary— and yet, so much has happened that I can hardly believe that only a few days have passed. I hardly know where to begin.

It can perhaps be argued that it all started off three days ago, when I was first introduced to a new servant. All of my advisors claimed that he was the man that I needed to help me get through my new coronation. Although upon first setting eyes on him I knew that he was going to be trouble.

Nobody quite knew where he’d come from— some of my advisors claimed that he’d traveled from another kingdom, whilst others stated that he’d always been serving in my castle, and he’d merely been overlooked by my sight. There were even a few of my advisors who claimed that he was a good friend of my father’s— however, I made sure to send those advisors outside of my castle.

What I could clearly discern, just by the sight of the man, was that he was a vile and sickly creature. His clothes were an inky black, made of a material that reminded me of molding leaves. His face lacked color, he stank of fish, he had fidgety mannerisms that brought me great displeasure, and he had eyes that never seemed to shut or open. His eyelids were positioned in such a way that it was hard to tell when he was blinking.

I would like to say that his presence gave me a chill down my spine— however, it didn’t even allow me the relief of that. Rather, whenever I was around him I’d feel the room begin to grow hot and stuffy. I felt as if I was being suffocated and that I could hardly breathe.

He seemed just as uncomfortable around me as I did with him. Whenever I looked him in the eye, he would look away. It was if he was harboring some guilt, to the point that he couldn’t bear the sight of me. I half-wondered if we really had met, and he had been friends with my father.

That was the strangest aspect of being around this man. Whenever I was around him, my mind would go foggy and my lips would go numb. I would try to speak, but I found that I couldn’t— I tried to remember why I’d called him into my chambers, but the memory escaped me. In the fogginess of my mind, it seemed that anything and everything was going on at once. I could hardly even remember what the advisor was supposed to look like— it was as if he’d found a way to crawl into my mind and pluck such a memory out.
The advisors name was Lumpkin. Emener Lumpkin. However, he didn’t seem to like when I called him that— he far preferred for me to use the term “advisor.”

The reason for this advisors being placed above all the others is that it was believed Lumpkin would help, “bring me to my senses.” Whispers were flowing down the halls that I’d become a student of sorcery. All of this was complete nonsense— but, I respected their attempts to help prevent it.

What I didn’t respect was the result of their attempts. Lumpkin had nothing that he could offer me, save a few uncomfortable stares, and a sullen spirit. He wasn’t even capable of giving me advice, as my advisors had said he would. Instead, he only gave me incoherent grunts, and a few obvious warnings.

I tried to concede with my advisors wishes, and to allow Lumpkin to continue his efforts— however useless— in trying to help me. In spite of this, I eventually cracked and failed to be able to handle the man. After two days of enduring his nonsense, I spoke with one of my advisors about Lumpkin’s disappointing performance. Then, like all terrible servants, Lumpkin was thrown out of the castle. I made sure to advise all of my guards to keep him away.

Perhaps that’s where I made the mistake. In hindsight, I now see that Lumpkin was no ordinary man. I now understand why he’d acted so odd. I only wish that I’d known that before I threw him out— a realization that’s only come to me earlier today.

My real troubles began this morning, when I was reminded of the horseman that I’d dispatched to search for piles of boulders at the foot of the mountain, where a wizard might’ve been. Although, I was probably reminded in the worst way possible.

My guards had been busy that morning, letting in parades of people who needed to prepare my castle for the coronation. I don’t blame them for their error— they let a horse into the castle, without my permission. Perhaps they thought that there couldn’t have been any harm in doing such a thing— perhaps they were at ease, and comfortable in their own skills. However, perhaps they were also wrong.

The beast came into my castle’s courtyard, and began terrorizing the people in it. I was amongst those in the courtyard, and saw the monster with my own eyes— it was in hysterics. Its eyes were bloodshot, it foamed at the mouth, and, wherever it looked, one would feel as if the animal was judging them. I recognized it as the very horse I’d placed the dispatched rider on.
The very horse that I’d expected to bring me good news was instead giving me threats.
I stared at the creature stonily— but it wasn’t willing to return the gaze. Instead, it charged at me without taking any hesitation.

Should’ve ducked, or dove out of the way. I should’ve done something to protect myself— the soon-to-be king of an entire kingdom. Although, I instead embraced the monster’s raving. I stayed where I was, as if accepting the fate that it had chosen for me. It hasn’t been until now that I’ve realized why I stood there, letting it come at me— it was because I wanted it to. It was because I didn’t want to be king.
Thankfully, one of my knights had chosen a different fate for me. He ran the horse down— and then out of the castle.

Several of my guards followed after him, chasing the horse all the way outside of the castle gates. In fact, they chased the horse all the way down the mountain. I wish that I’d seen it for myself— it must’ve been quite the spectacle. However, even with the close call against my life, my business within my castle courtyards hadn’t ended.

Later this evening, after the chase was long ended, I was informed by one of the guards who’d been part of the chase that the wild horse had died. He told me that it smashed its head up against a boulder, right next to a rotting tree full of rotting leaves.

He told me that the horse left behind a slight dent in the rock simply from its sheer power. One of its teeth were even lodged within it. I don’t doubt that the horse’s imprint will be there far longer than my own life.

Normally, hearing that a horse that attempted to kill me had died wouldn’t have disturbed me. However, as the guard walked off, and a rotting leaf fell from his shoulder, I was reminded of one man— Lumpkin.
I’ve begun to suspect that there was more to him than it once seemed. Despite the horse having died, I have the uncomfortable feeling that my problems are nowhere near ceasing.

After the avalanche, innocent play had suddenly gained a grim membrane. Isabella and Susan managed to pull Tim out of amongst the rocks, but it was clear that things would no longer be the same. Tim was smothered in bruises and dust that the stones had gifted him. When forced to stand up by his friend’s combined heave, it was discovered that he had been rendered limp— every attempt at standing was succeeded by a harsh moan, and a demoralizing thump. A seemingly simple act had broken him.

Isabella and Susan tugged him through the snow and back toward the village. However, seem impossible. Their muscles cried out from exhaustion, and turned more malleable to the influence of Tim’s weight by the minute. A new downpour of snow caked their faces, obscured their sight, and caused a numbness to cut through their skin. Daylight had waned, with only a slight blue tint in the horizon to guide their eyes. However, Tim’s moans didn’t wane with the daylight— rather, the moans grew.
Finally, Susan succumbed to the contagious suffering that was plaguing them all, and stumbled into the snow.
“I can’t go any further,” she said, uttering the words with only half of her facilities in focus.
A simple act had broken all of them.
“Can’t isn’t an option,” Isabella said. “We have to keep going. Tim isn’t going to make it through the night like this.”

Another moan was heard. Except, it didn’t come from any of their mouths— it resounded from the ground beneath them. They were standing on a thin, corroded cliff, and it was beginning to break away from beneath them.

There was no need for another word to be spoken between them. The mere thought of tumbling into an abyss had driven the vigor back into their bones and forced a sense of perseverance. Their feet dragged from the edge of the cliff just as it began falling into itself.

Despite her instinctive act, Susan’s lungs felt smothered and hot, as if they’d been touched with a hot iron. Strain was starting to get the best of strength. However, she didn’t allow that to weigh down her steps. She pulled against it. Her muscles embraced the exhaustion, even with it threatening to steal her very consciousness.

The whinnying horse was heard off in the distance. Fear blasted its way into Susan’s chest. Then, smoke from a torch wafted into their noses. Susan couldn’t see the soft glow of a torch behind the immense sheet of snowfall, but she could sense it. It wasn’t far from her grasp. She knew that it was but a flame. Though, to her, it meant safety.
“Susan? Timothy? Isabella?” a voice cried out.
Susan and the rest responded with the loudest shouts that their frozen mouths could muster. Their voices rang out with a greater synchronization than the tweeting of birds in the morning.

The whinnying of the horse came closer, before being followed by the sight of a black stallion. At least, it seemed black when put up against the snow, and the darkness of the falling night. Several more whinnies followed, and the one horse was joined by several others.

Atop the steeds were their parents, and Joshua. While they all had expressions of relief when first catching sight of their children, they soon devolved into expressions of deep disappointment. The deepest of them was on Joshua’s face. Just by looking at him, Susan felt an extreme guilt well up inside of her.
“What happened to Timothy?” he asked.

For anybody else around Susan, it might’ve been hard to decipher the intention in his lifeless voice, and expression. However, Susan caught on rather quickly— she recognized the fury hidden behind his slight inflections, which gave a message as cold as the weather around them.

Susan had seen Joshua angry before. She wasn’t quite sure from where, but had foggy glimpses of stealing pastries, screaming to the point that her face turned purple, and breaking a delicate object made of glass that had been put in reach of her younger, grubbier fingers. They were all childhood memories— fading things that came and passed, leaving behind the same amount of rippling that a stone does in a river. It wasn’t anywhere near the overbearing splash that this was.

When Joshua was angry, he didn’t shout. He didn’t cry. He didn’t scowl. Not a word would leave his mouth. Instead, he would look at somebody with a blank expression, searching for some sort of explanation for what had angered him. He had a way of conveying his anger through saying and doing nothing at all.

As she looked into his face, searching for the words to appease it, she felt her mind go blank. She had nothing to say. Her tongue suddenly felt like a wad of sandpaper, and her lips felt as though they’d been sealed with glue. It was as if all the eyes on earth had turned to stare at her in disgust. Although, it was only one pair of eyes that were looking at her this way. Joshua’s eyes.
In spite of this, Susan couldn’t help but feel that there was no distinction between the two.
“He fell under an avalanche of rocks,” Isabella explained, continuing to drag Tim toward the horse.
Susan had stopped dragging with her. Under the gaze of Joshua, she couldn’t help but feel frozen.
“And where was this?” Joshua asked, not taking his eyes off of Susan.
For a moment, everything seemed to stand still, and wait for Susan to give an answer. Even the snowflakes had decided to pause from their freefall.

“Under the mountain,” said Tim with a haggard cough. He spit out his words with such a rapidity that Susan nearly thought they’d been trying to run away from him. “Piles of rocks there. Never should’ve gone.”
“What were you doing under the mountain? In this village, we have few rules— but, among those few rules, nobody is supposed to go exploring around the mountain. Too many have gone there to die.”

The words had come from one of the parents, in the form of a thick scolding. However, Susan had tuned them out before they went any further. Their voices faded away in the wind, blowing among things as insignificant as winter’s white powder.
Susan didn’t need to hear anybody else’s words, as it was. The only words that mattered to her were Joshua’s— and his stern gaze, which had yet to yield, were words enough.

Memories swirled out of Susan’s head, and amongst the snow. She watched them as they showed her the dozens of cautioning that Joshua had given her throughout her life about going around the mountain. He’d often said that it was a place riddled with dangers and fatal drops. He’d even informed her about the hauntings that were claimed to have taken place upon it.

Usually, Joshua was against supporting the rumors, and said that all they led to were decaying towns and missed opportunities. However, when it came to the rumors of the mountain, he discussed them with an unwavering solemnity. Most of the time when Susan looked back on those stories he’d told her and assumed that he’d always been pulling her leg. Though, it had never seemed that way— especially since Joshua rarely allowed his mouth to utter anything outside of full truths.
As Susan jumped onto the back of the horse and let Joshua ride her back home, she could hear his unspoken words whistling into her ears.
“Why did you disobey my ruling, Susan?”
She couldn’t answer him. Even if she’d asked this question to herself, she wouldn’t have been able to come up with a true answer. All she had was a sheet of excuses.
Why didn’t I just stay in the village, like I’ve been being told all my life? Why did I think I could keep going out without his permission, and not face the consequences?
A sense of self-disgust crept into the places that had once been proud to be solving new mysteries and trekking places that hadn’t been trekked before.
If I could go back before this had all started, I would’ve done this differently. This would all be different… None of these mistakes would’ve happened.
Though, her sense of hope and potential redemption quickly deteriorated.

They’re hollow words… “If I could go back in time,” is a phrase that everybody uses after making a regretful mistake. No matter how many times I repeat what I did, it would’ve had the same outcome… What I’ve done is something that I’m never going to be able to go back on— and that’s something that I’m going to have to learn to live with…

She sighed as more snow blew into her face and the village, with its steadily glowing torchlights, greeted her back home. It was home, and no matter how many times she abandoned it, she could always rely on it being there to greet her.

After listening to the horse trod over the slushy paths through the town, they finally had to dismount it and give it back to a stable where Joshua had borrowed it from. As they walked back through the maze of old log-houses, passing by old, friendly faces, Susan felt Joshua’s upset spirit drag farther on her soul.
“Do you know how long I looked for you today?” Joshua asked, breaking the silence that he’d maintained for the past hour.
“A lot?” Susan asked, meekly.
She knew that nothing she could say to alter the cloud of dissatisfaction that had settled over Joshua’s face.

“It was about three hours into morning, and you hadn’t come down to help me with my trade by repairing the mayor’s books. I’d been lenient with you for the past few days, so I decided to look for you.  Yet, nobody had seen you all morning. Nobody saw you by noontime, either. It was afternoon by the time I had to borrow a horse from Bert’s overpriced horse stable— I’m going to have to find some way to pay him back— and I had to form a search party with Timothy and Isabella’s parents. I was outside of the village limits for hours, just looking for you. This is the third time in two weeks, Susan. How many times are you going to risk your life until you’re willing to stop? Not only is this becoming costly to our way of living, but it’s also becoming a threat to your safety.”

Susan wanted to speak, but had nothing to say. She simply gave a dejected look down the well-trodden path, and nodded. In the time that Joshua had spoken to her, they’d made it to the slumping entrance of their house. It smelled of mushroom, and a damp mold. Though, all that Susan could smell was the stink of horse emanating off of Joshua’s upset figure.

“I understand your wish to be independent. But you’ve been running from your responsibilities for too long. Independence isn’t a right, Susan… It’s earned. And, if you’re going to keep getting closer to the top of that mountain, then I’m going to have to take your ability to do so. For the next week, you’re grounded from coming out. You’re going to stay in the house with me for most of the time, and help me catch up with the book repairs that you’ve caused me to miss.”
As Joshua opened the door, and let Susan in, Susan knew that she was walking into the end of her free adventures.

The week passed by as dully as a leaf does when a breeze steadily makes it pass by a rock. For the first two days, Susan spent her time sewing book bindings, musing about what their strange covers might mean. Some of them had straightforward titles, such as, “One-Hundred Ways to Cook a Chicken”. Though, others had more mysterious titles, such as, “The Wind’s Will”. Sometimes, she would be compelled to read the pages behind these strange titles, and figure out what was harbored within them. However, whenever she tried to open these covers, she’d feel Joshua pull her hand away.
“These are other people’s books,” he would tell her. “We don’t read them.”

This seemed to be a rule that he’d created for her, more than himself. Susan would sometimes walk into the house’s library at night, to find Joshua sitting at a chair with one of the odd books. Though, since she was blockaded from the library as well, he’d oftentimes just drive her away with a few words.

It came to pass on the third day that Susan had gained some of Joshua’s trust. So, he’d decided to go out to give some of his mended books back to their owners, leaving Susan behind. In the wake of his exit, he’d locked up the library, taken a good portion of the mended books with him, and locked up the rest of the books that needed mending up. That is, he locked up the rest of them, save for a select few that he’d decided to leave for Susan to repair.

On his way out, he gave Susan a hearty goodbye, bid her a good day, and then shut the door with a soft click. Before he’d left, Susan gave him a short hug. In a way, it acted as an unspoken peace offering between the two. It was just a simple act— but, in a way, it was far more than that. It said that, despite the rough events that had wedged between them, it hadn’t been enough to entirely change things. All

the while, Susan waited patiently, searching for the exact moment that he’d leave. Once he had, she began searching the house for where Joshua might’ve hidden the books, and where a key might be to unlock them. She knew that Joshua didn’t have a key, because she’d checked his pockets for one when she’d hugged him, and she knew that the books were hidden in the library, because it was the only place in the house that she was unable to access.

However, that was the main problem— she wasn’t able to access the library. She wished that she knew the secret behind opening it, but the truth of the matter was that she hadn’t been around to see Joshua unlock the library door. All answers to unlocking it were elusive. While she thought that it might’ve been openable by a key, she wasn’t quite sure.

She knew that she had responsibilities to complete— the books that she was assigned to repair were only going to become needier of her hand’s careful touch. However, once at the library’s front door, she found that her questions weren’t any less powerful. She tried everything that she could think of– turning the knob in hopes of it coming loose, attempting to pick it with a nail that she’d loosened from a wobbly floorboard, and even going so far as to kick it. Nothing worked.
Slumping down to the floor, she let herself lapse into deep thought. It seemed that the door was impossible to open.
Then, she remembered something from a story that Joshua would read to her when she was little— it had something about a key being hidden beneath floorboards.

Without hesitation, Susan tore up the floorboard that had been loose. To her shock, a key lay below it, shining like a golden star. She looked at it in wonder, took it up, and then placed it within the doorknob. Unlocking the door, the library’s golden light spilled onto her, and she beheld the countless rows of bookshelves that Joshua had pored over for his entire life. It seemed that the sun had broken out from behind its oversized curtains of clouds and decided to place a bit of itself inside the room. The place glowed with a sensation that she’d never experienced before.

Walking amongst the columns of dust-covered accounts and tales, she searched for any of the oddly titled books. It wasn’t long before her efforts had succeeded, and she discovered one of the books laying atop Joshua’s desk. It read, “An Exploration into Shadows and Shallows”. On first glance, she knew that it had been the book she wanted. Its green and gold cover carried a mistiness to it— the same mistiness that she’d see whenever going outside in the snow. At every angle she looked at it, its faint light bounced into her eyes, making her feel both elated and unworthy at the same time. Her instinct told her to leave the book at its place, and to exit the library as if she’d never been there— there was no reason to do anything that would give her future regret. In spite of this, her impulse told her to seize it, and begin reading it as fast as she could.

She wasn’t quite sure why, but it seemed that her impulse had been winning out far more than her reasoning lately. She found herself ripping the book from the table, relocking the library door, placing the key back under the floorboard, and heading to her room to read. It didn’t matter that there were piles of books calling for her to repair them. It didn’t matter to her that there was a faith that Joshua had invested in her, and she was breaking it. It didn’t matter to her that she was breaking a significant promise to herself— that if she was put into the position where she would betray Joshua again, she wouldn’t take it.

Although, perhaps the concept that she hadn’t cared was a lie that she’d told herself. Because, as she sat in bed to read the words written upon the book’s white pages, all she could see was black. It was the blackness of her treachery. The ink spoke to her. Though, the way was far more twisted and odd than she’d expected it to be. Whenever she saw the word “shadow,” she didn’t see the image of the beckoning silhouette— instead, she saw an image of herself. Whenever she saw the word, “shallows,” all she saw was the shallowness of herself.
She’d believed that she didn’t care about what she was doing— however, it was only because she had to repeat those words to herself, in a ceaseless sequence.

It wasn’t until she saw the book beginning to account the appearances of mysterious shadows throughout the village— shadows that were said to appear on the mountainside, before tragic events— that her guilt began to reside, and her focus shifted to the world inside the pages. The contains of the book were answering a question of hers that went far deeper than whether or not she was being loyal to Joshua. Despite her knowing that the sacrifice was costly, she’d known its cost all along. That’s why she’d been willing to break nearly every rule that Joshua had set in place. The answer to her mystery might’ve been a costly one— but Susan suddenly realized that the cost was easily worth the answer.
I’m tired of having sleepless nights, where slumber escapes me simply due to the restlessness caused by not having the answers. I need to know. I need to understand what’s been going on.

Turning the pages of the book, which smelt of mildew and a crustiness that could’ve only been achieved by years of age, she discovered that the book had originated from within her own village, and only described accounts that were specific to it. She then progressed into parts that explained the rumored origins of the said shadow. There were passages that spoke of the thing being some sort of ghost, or remnant of people long passed. Another account spoke of it having originated from within the mountain, growing in there like a flower grows from the ground. There were others that described the shadow as potentially being a lone hermit, that beckoned village wanderers to follow it into the mountain, where it would take their food and valuables.

There were other rumors over where it was easiest to find. Some sections described the shadow having an affinity for shallow areas of lakes and rivers. Other sections said that the shadow preferred to take base on the foot of the mountain. Still, others said that the shadow had no home, and that it went wherever a wanderer that had been dubbed as its victim did.

What Susan found most interesting were the sections that described ways to rid oneself of appearances of the shadow. There were certain parts that described how to drive the shadow away by reciting certain incantations. Others described how to drive the shadow away with certain types of sticks. Still, others described a way of driving the shadow off with certain remedies.

None of these passages were quite what Susan had wanted, and she soon found herself traveling down an unending spiral of searching for the exact words she needed to find her answers. Though, there weren’t any. No matter how many pages she turned, she couldn’t find a cohesive word for as to why the shadow did what it did. No matter how many places she looked, she couldn’t fund an area that spoke of how the shadow did what it did. No matter how many places she went, she couldn’t find anything decisive for as to how the shadow came to be, and why it would target somebody such as herself.
There must be somewhere where my answers are, she thought, flying through each page, tearing through them in a merciless pace.
They weren’t anywhere. No matter where she went, and no matter how much effort she put in looking for them, it seemed that all answers were nonexistent.
“This book is useless,” she said.

However, she didn’t toss the book to the side, or get up to put it back. She found herself glued to its image, and she couldn’t take her eyes off of it. Inside, Susan felt as if no power on earth could’ve removed her from it. It almost seemed as if there were some sort of enchantment to it that kept her from pulling her eyes away. No matter how much she tried pulling her focus elsewhere, she was compelled to keep turning the pages to look for her answer.  Her fingers received several paper-cuts, and she felt her eyes begin to water due to her restraining them from blinking. Though, she couldn’t help but ignore these urges. There was something inside that needed to know everything.
Too much has already been paid for me to give up now, she thought.

There was a part of her that felt the same eerie feeling when looking at the page that she had whenever looking upon the silhouette. It was a feeling that made her resistant to any of her senses, and all-encompassed by the sight of the element before her eyes. Nothing else had any weight over her. Nothing else held any sort of power. She was completely consumed by the sight.

Suddenly, she came to a part that gave her a sense of clarity— it put her mind to rest, and she instantly felt a part of her strained mind relieved from the extreme pressures that had been boring up against it. It was as if the boulder that had been sitting within here brain had been turned into something as light as a feather.

There are few things that are certain about it— but it’s commonly known that it thrives amongst the land that is the mountain. The shadow is a being that dwells on tricking others, and bringing misery upon those who trespass against it. It seems to be driven by some internal force, which makes it have some sort of omnipotence over anybody who dares explore its domain.

Why is its domain so sacred to it? Why is it so driven to make those who don’t respect it suffer? There are many who believe that it’s because the shadow itself is urged to keep the mountain a mystery. That’s why the shadow remains unknown and ambiguous— because ambiguity is the very thing that it’s constantly driven to defend.

Susan’s eyes inflated, and she suddenly felt a strong sense of satisfaction. The hassling that she’d put her mind, eyes, and hands through were now all worth it. She still didn’t know for sure if the passage that she’d just read was accurate, and she didn’t know what she would do with it. Although, a part of the unrelenting wondering that had been going on inside of her had finally been relieved. Susan had a feeling that the constant betrayals against Joshua’s rulings would finally be able to cease.

Susan continued to study the page, absorbing every letter that had been imprinted upon it. In having satisfied obsession, she now wanted to insure that it didn’t continue. There was a piece of her that recognized that she was allowing herself to delve slightly deeper into a pattern of constant obsessiveness— however, her obsessive aspect ignored this, and continued to read on. She needed to know that it knew everything. She needed to know that there wasn’t a single thing that she’d missed.

Her obsessive studying was suddenly broken when she heard the jiggling of a doorknob. Following this, she heard a phrase that she’d hoped she wouldn’t hear for several more hours— a phrase that brought an unmatched terror into her marrow.
“Susan, I’m home!”
In an instant, she when charging out of her room, making sure to hide the book under her covers.
“Joshua?” she said, letting her voice bounce through the halls. “What brought you here?”
“I finished returning the newly-repaired books. You didn’t think that I’d spend a whole day out there when we have tons of books to repair, did you?”
He was still a room away from the kitchen. So, as he talked, Susan started shoving her unrepaired books into the cabinets, with a pounding heart.
“Don’t be ridiculous… What made you think that I’d believe something as outlandish as that?” she said with a laugh.
“Good. So, how have the repairs been going on those books that I gave you?”
“Very well,” Susan lied, running through the kitchen and to the hall. “I’m pleased with how they’re coming along.”
“That’s great. How many of them have you gotten done?”
It was at this point that Susan felt a burst of nervousness rip through her.
“How many have I gotten done?” she repeated.
Joshua and Susan were standing eye to eye now, in front of the front door. Joshua was busy putting his shoes away, but he didn’t let that stop him from pausing and making eye contact with her.
“Yes,” he said. “What’s with the pause?”
“I— I forgot,” Susan said. “I was so wrapped up in preparing them that I didn’t take time to count them.”

Susan crossed her fingers, and hoped that this lie would somehow get passed Joshua’s wary ears. Strangely, it seemed that they did. Joshua didn’t do so much as raise the usually inquisitive eyebrow. It seemed that his focus had been directed elsewhere. Right as Susan gave her explanation, she watched his eye flick over to the library door– particularly in the vicinity of the piece of wood that Susan had plied from the floor, and grabbed her key from.

“I need to go check on something,” he said, with a slight nervousness. “In the meantime, you can go count the books that you’ve repaired for me. As long as this doesn’t take as long as I think it will, I should be back there in a minute to check on your work.”

Normally, Susan would be distracted by the chaos in what Joshua had just suggested. In telling her to admit to her number of books, she’d either have to continue her lie before it was found out, or let Joshua find it out— her only hope was that Joshua’s “checking” would require a lot less effort than he made it out to be.

Though, Susan wasn’t distracted by it. In fact, she’d put the trivial matter to the back of her mind. She couldn’t help but find herself caught up by Joshua’s abnormal conduct. He’d seemed to be overeager to rid himself of Susan. And, while such and eagerness might’ve been easy to pass off as caused by him not wanting Susan to see how he pulled the key out from under the floorboard, Susan couldn’t help but notice that there was more to his eagerness than just that. There was also a look of slight fear that had leaped across Joshua’s face— a look of fear that she’d never seen him bear before. Once again, there was a chance that it was still unrelated.

Maybe the slightly unnerved gaze might’ve just been caused by him thinking that she’d found the key. Though, Susan couldn’t help but feel that he wouldn’t have reacted so vulnerably to something as mundane and simple as that.

Perhaps he’d had a bad day while out in the village, or perhaps his odd look had only come across his face by mere coincidence. The possibility of him not wanting Susan to see the inside of his library hung in the air as well.

These possibilities, as much as Susan tried to put more weight onto them, were easy for her to neglect and toss aside. None of them came across as likely to her. Something different was glazed over him this time. There was an air of desperation that he carried in his gait.
“Go on,” he said.
It was almost haggard. However, Susan didn’t dare try to test it. Walking back to her stuffed away books, she was forced back into her grave situation of having to decide what she’d tell Joshua.

The decision didn’t take long for her to make. Soon enough, Susan was hastily reweaving the spines of her books, doing a half-baked job at trying to conceal her lies. She knew that Joshua would catch the neglect of her duties the moment that he walked back in the room. However, somewhere deep down inside of her, that was what she wanted. The detached and unfocused gaze that Joshua had held in front of the library door was both sad and uncomfortable to look at. She couldn’t help but wonder what was going on inside of him, and what could’ve made the man, who seemingly feared nothing, have his breath stop short— especially when the thing that seemed to have made his breath stop short was the sight of a loose nail.

She wasn’t left to wonder for too long. After about ten minutes in of pondering and shoving spines back together, Joshua walked in. Susan had been caught off guard by his entrance, and she felt her heart skip a beat. However, Joshua seemed to take no mind to the matter, and walked over to the corner of the room with a relative ignorance. His eyes were still distant, as if peering off at something far away, and his body was still. He stood behind Susan’s chair, and Susan tried following his gaze. However, she found that it took her to nowhere.
There was an unnaturalness to it— the room was only a few feet wide, and yet the purpose behind his melancholy spirit had to be miles.
“I counted the books out,” Susan said, shoving the books into a pile at her side. “I managed to repair seven of them.”

She was still weaving one of the spines of the book together as she said this, waiting for him to interject upon her obvious lies. For a while, he didn’t say a word. It wasn’t until Susan asked, “Did you hear me” that he seemed to snap back awake and become aware of everything.

“Did you say that you only repaired seven books?” he asked, looking at the eight books in front of his eyes— Susan had made sure to miscount them at first, to see if he was paying attention enough to notice. He hadn’t— at least, not until now.
Susan nodded in response.
“And you only managed to get them this repaired?”
Susan nodded again.
Joshua shook his head, flustered.
“Either you’re somehow far more inefficient when I disappear than when I’m here, or you’re lying to me. Which is it? What were you doing when I was gone?”

His own version of fury— the somewhat monotonous ringing of his voice, and the flatness of his expression— had tripled in size. All traces of his past fear and detachment were seemingly nonexistent. He now acted as if they’d never happened.
“I wasn’t doing anything,” Susan lied. “What makes you think that I’m lying to you?”
“Stop playing dumb… Just because I was distracted earlier doesn’t mean I can’t see the obvious now.”
“I repaired some of the books while you were gone. Wasn’t that the agreement?”
Joshua stopped talking for a moment, and even gave something that was close to a grin.
“You figured out how to get in the library, didn’t you?” he asked.

Susan shook her head no, and explained that she had no idea how to get in— but it was no use. She could tell by Joshua’s resolute and firm gaze that he wasn’t interested in hearing what she had to say. He already knew the truth.

“Go to your room and bring me the book you stole,” he said, with his words leaving a rash upon Susan’s mind as if they were sandpaper. His tone wasn’t harsh or abrasive— but, his easy diffusing of her lie had come across just as abrasive as any harsh scolding would’ve.
“I don’t have any books in my room,” Susan said, continuing the lie.

At this point, she wasn’t quite sure why she was still lying. Joshua knew that she’d stolen the book, and he could probably even see through her vast fibs. Though, there was a stubbornness inside of her— an iron will that refused to let Joshua take the book away from her. There was a majesty to the book— a majesty to everything that surrounded it. The very thought of having to let it go entangled the fabric of her mind, as if it had been caught in a spider’s web.

“Give it up Susan,” Joshua said. “Whether or not you hid the book in your room, I know that you hid it somewhere— and I’m going to find it. You might as well admit yourself to be guilty now, rather than later. You’re just making things harder on yourself— the longer that you take to tell me the truth, the longer your eventual punishment will be.”

Terrible as this notion was, Susan stood her ground. Her heart hammered, her eyes fluttered with a nervousness, and she could feel her face go hot from fear. In spite of this all, there was an impeccable will inside of her. Self-destructive as it was, it wasn’t willing to abandon its cause. It had become far too invested into it. Even as it dug itself deeper into potential catastrophe, it remained unwilling to give up.

Joshua left the room without another word. As Susan struggled with her internal stubbornness, and wondered if its decision to remain resolute had been the best plan of action, he’d left the room to put an end to all of the chaos. Although, she hardly noticed that he left. His presence still remained, as a suffocating mist. It strangled Susan, leaving her in a fog of a sickening regret.
Ten minutes managed to remove this regret enough to where Susan followed Joshua in her room, and watched him as he searched for the book
“I told you, I don’t have it,” Susan said, as she watched Joshua look under her bed and covers for it.
“Are you going to stick with that statement, Susan?” Joshua asked, with a raised eyebrow.
“Why don’t you trust me? Yes, I’m sticking with it, because it’s the truth.”
Right after those words had left Susan’s mouth a bitter taste formed on her tongue. Joshua slipped a book from out of under his clothes— and it was all over.

“I can’t believe that you’re willing to keep a complete lie like that going...” Joshua said, walking to the bedroom’s door. “I trust you, Susan. And, when you tell me lies like this, that trust starts to deteriorate. What made you think that it was ok to take this book? More importantly, what made it matter so much to you that you were willing to lie to me for that long?”
Susan didn’t give much more than a shrug as an answer.
“I’m extending your punishment for another week,” Joshua stated plainly. “I told you not to mess with these books, and you didn’t listen.”
“It was just a book!”
Joshua opened his mouth to give a rebuttal, but had to hesitate for a moment. For a moment, it was as if he himself didn’t know the reason behind his actions.
“It’s the principle of it,” he finally said.

Though, Susan wasn’t so sure that this was the truth. Joshua once again had an uneasiness while holding the book. His anger was beyond the book— it had latched onto something else that was hidden from her view.
Her suspicions were proven out when he said, “How much of the book did you read?”

“I didn’t have the chance to read it,” Susan said, continuing her lie. “I was so busy trying to find a way into your library, and then trying to hurriedly fix the books that you were back before I could even try opening it.”

Susan looked at him, trying to appeal to his better nature, but he no longer looked convinced in her words. It was as if something between them had finally broke— the bridge that had allowed them to speak without harboring a sense of distrust, had dissipated.

Joshua left the room to put the book in the library, and Susan watched with a sense of sorrow. Although, she found that she didn’t feel it as much toward Joshua, like she would’ve expected. Instead, her sorrow was directed at the book. As it disappeared out of her room, and down the hall, she knew that her chance of uncovering the silhouette’s secrets went with it.

The next few days overflowed with tedium and tiring effort. Susan was constantly kept busy with cleaning the house, and making up for the books that she’d neglected. However, she soon found that Joshua made sure that she more than made up for what she missed— there was a stretch of three days when she hardly had the time to take a break to eat, let along work. Her conversations with Joshua had also been minimized, to the point that they were near nonexistent. He’d give Susan the minimum of orders, and then left her to clean up after her mess. It was all a very strenuous ordeal, and Susan found by the end of it that she was on the brink of rebelling against orders. Thankfully, this only occurred by the end of it, and no repercussions came out of her impulse.
“You’ve done a great amount of work,” Joshua said, after he’d come out of the library with his own pile of repaired books.
He leaned over to count all of Susan’s books, and gave an approving nod.
“Five dozen in three days,” he said, with a grin. “That’s a new record for you.”
“Still doesn’t beat your record. A hundred and fifteen books in three days— I can’t even imagine.”
Susan swiped her hand across her forehead to exaggerate her exhaustion. Joshua chuckled in response, and then slammed his books onto the table.

“Make that one hundred and seventeen,” he said, with such a self-pride that he might as well have been patting himself on the back. “This pile that I brought in here is only a fraction of the books I repaired…”

Susan gaped at the sight. Joshua had only brought in three books, and they were all big enough for him to express an apparent strain while carrying them in. The thought of there being over a hundred more was beyond daunting.
At this point, she was just waiting for Joshua to say the words that were inevitably coming.

“I’ve given Bert word that I need him to haul all of these books to my customers in his horse drawn carriage. He’s expecting them to be set out on our porch by sundown. Could you help me out and carry some of these books with me?”

Within the course of ten minutes, Joshua had strategized a way to get those words out, and Susan was wheezing as piles of books drained her breath away. Each of the books felt like miniature boulders, and her fingers felt as if they were crushing beneath their weight. Even Joshua, who she’d become accustomed to seeing as having everything under control, appeared to be struggling by their tenth load.
Ten more loads proved them weaker still.

By the time all of the books had been loaded for the carriage to pick up, Susan’s muscles had been reduced to something that was undiscernible from the slushy snow beneath her feet. At that point, making sure that all the books were set out, or that they’d been set out in time no longer mattered. Neither her, nor Joshua, bothered to check. Once they’d placed the last book onto the porch, all that mattered was that it was the last book— and they didn’t care to check and see if there were any others.
Exhaustion had beat them down to the point that the very thought of looking for more was hard to bear.
“I think that we’re going to call it for the night,” Joshua said, with a smirk. “Why don’t we go inside and make ourselves some of that nice warm soup that we’ve left cooking in there all day.”

At the time, nothing sounded better to Susan. Though, once the soup had traveled down her throat and into her stomach, that thought was quickly replaced with the converse. In spite of their hard work, it seemed that their reward was a lukewarm broth that had obtained a somewhat slimy texture. It wasn’t appealing in any way.
“I should’ve checked the fire more throughout the day,” Joshua said. “If I’d done that, we wouldn’t have had to deal with this.”
He managed to get out a laugh in spite of his words’ sullen composure, but the weight of the bad meal and the bad taste in their mouths kept much else from coming out.

There was another reason why things kept quiet— Susan had a question that she wanted to ask. Though, the work of the past few days and the strain that had grown between her and Joshua kept her from asking it.
After the third scoop of her food, and the third attempt of swallowing it down, she finally realized that asking the question would be far easier to focus on than eating her food.
“What do you think about the myths concerning the mountain?” she finally asked, giving her best attempt at being nonchalant.
Joshua saw through all of the holes in her act as instantly as he was able to see holes in the binding of a book. He gave a slight scowl and a squint of an eye to Susan in return.
Finally, he set down his spoon and flatly said, “Nonsense. It’s utter nonsense. What makes you think otherwise?”
“Nothing… It’s just— I couldn’t help but get curious, with all of the rumors that are constantly swirling about.”
Joshua passively spit some of his food back into his bowl, and pushed it aside.

“You’ll find that the reason rumors constantly ‘swirl about’ in the mountain is because a single person is constantly spreading them. The snow is blown about by only one force— the wind. Rumors are only blown about by one force too— gossips. The sooner you get that into your head, the sooner you realize the truth.”

Susan felt a bit of her morale torn away by this statement— but, for some reason, it didn’t tear her apart in the way that it seemed Joshua had been expecting. She remained still. Her thoughts didn’t whither. In fact, they persisted. There was something about the particular rumors that she’d seen— something about how personal they’d become— that she couldn’t quite pass them off as mere rumors.

All it took was a mere glance at Joshua, and she read confusion from upon it. The expression of confusion was slight— as always with Joshua, it was ambiguous and hard to map out. Whenever he felt anything, he seemed to try his best to veil it. Though, the confusion was undeniably there.
“I know that they’re just rumors,” Susan said, “but rumors can’t be wrong all of the time— right?”
“What are you getting at?”

Joshua’s brow raised. It was a very hard movement to catch— just half a centimeter of an adjustment. However, it was undeniably there. Just by viewing it, Susan could tell that he was assessing everything, and allowing no moment of leniency. Nothing got by from under his inspective mind.
Susan had learned from experience that the only way to deflect such inspection was to change the movement of the subject.
“Do you remember those fairytales that you told me when I was little? The ones with dragons, weird quests, and—.”
“Yes, I remember them very clearly.”
For some reason, Joshua’s face had gone red and had bent toward the ground.

“There were so many of them— and they were all very alike,” Susan continued. “I just came to the conclusion that maybe there’s more to them than just fairytales. I know that you think that I might be being nonsensical and ridiculous— and, you’d be right in that. But, do you honestly think that all of those stories were wrong? They all focused on a similar setting, and a similar place… I just find it hard to believe that they’re all completely fake.”

“Just because it’s hard to believe that something isn’t real, it doesn’t mean that it isn’t… The reason that most fairytales are similar is that they derive from one another. Unicorns and Leprechauns are all subject to the confines of the imagination. It may be true that the stories in books all have a link into reality. Though, that link is oftentimes only there because it’s hard to conceive of something that is nonexistent… And so, we infer beings from elements of the nature that surrounds us.”
“Then why are you so terrified of me going onto the mountain, if you think that the mystical rumors surrounding it are nonexistent?”
His question gave Joshua a moments pause.

“The reason that rumors surround the mountain is to scare younger children away,” Joshua finally said. “It was never real, Susan. I hope that’s not what you’ve been looking for during your journeys to the mountain’s foot. If so, you’ll be sorrowfully disappointed in what you find…”

It was now Susan’s turn for her face to go red. She could feel a sinking guild in her chest for having believed in the silhouette— for still having that belief. Despite all evidence to the contrary, she couldn’t deny what she’d sensed and seen at the foot of the mountain.
“What do you know about odd silhouettes near the mountain,” Susan asked.
Joshua fingered the side of his bowl.
“How much of that book did you read?” he asked, with concern filling out the edges of his voice.
“None of it. I already told you that I hadn’t read any of it. What would make you think that—.”
“Stop lying to me. There’s no need to keep hiding… I already know that you wouldn’t have stolen a book without taking the time to try reading some of it.”
“It was only a few pages,” Susan said, giving up some ground.
“How many pages? What were in them? Most importantly— what brought you to look in it?”
Susan knew that she was cornered, and that there was no use trying to fight out of it. Joshua had craftily put her in a position where honesty was the only available option.
“About fifty pages,” she admitted, trying to pull out any guilt.
She watched Joshua’s face flare— at least, in the closest possible way of him flaring— though there was also a sort of fear in his gaze.
“Fifteen pages?” he asked, as if he’d misheard her.
Both Susan and him knew that he hadn’t misheard. Her words had been clear as the snow was white. The real reason that Joshua had acted as if he’d misheard was the true mystery.

“I thought I told you not to read any of those books,” Joshua said, in his placid fury. “The things that were in them— they weren’t for you to read. They weren’t your books. They weren’t your property…”

Once again, Susan quickly caught on that he was distracting from the true reason that he was upset. Joshua couldn’t have cared less about whether or not she’d read the books that she repaired. It was true that she’d been punished for reading the silhouette book. Although, this was mostly due to her prior punishment, and the punishment was already in the past. In addition, Joshua often read the books that needed repair— he wasn’t the sort of person who was particularly susceptible to hypocrisy.

The most telling element that Joshua didn’t mean what he said was how long it had taken for him to say it. If Joshua had been so upset with her having read the book, then it would’ve been the first thing he’d complained about. Though, it seemed to Susan that his complaint had been an afterthought. To her, the real thing he was saying wasn’t that the book wasn’t hers to read, but that he hadn’t wanted her to read it.
But… Why didn’t he want me to read it? Susan wondered.

“I didn’t think that anything bad would come out of reading it… I was curious, and that book happened to focus on a subject matter that I was interested in… The thought that reading it was infringing on another’s property had never crossed my mind.”

“It never crossed your mind when you went out of your way to search for the key to my library? It never crossed your mind, despite all of my forewarnings against it? And also— how did it happen to have subject matter that you were interested in?”
Reluctance dripped in Susan’s every breath— but it didn’t matter. The words that she’d kept locked off from Joshua started coming out of her mouth.

“In my visits to the mountain, I’ve seen a few strange things— odd shadows that seem to be beckoning for me to come closer. I know that sounds ridiculous, just like a lot of other thing that I’ve said today… But, that doesn’t make it feel any less real.”

“That doesn’t make your actions any less unfounded either. How many times have I told you to avoid going under the mountain? How many times have I had to tell you that it’s a dangerous place and that you can’t go there? If you’d just listened to me, then we wouldn’t be having these problems…”
“I was just curious. The last time I went out was the only time that I’ve been that close to the mountain…”

“And look at where curiosity brought you. I know that living in this village isn’t the easiest. And, I’m aware that it’s hard to cope with the claustrophobia of our winters… But that doesn’t justify completely doing away with everything that I told you to do.”
“I’m sorry. It won’t happen again. If I’d known that reading the book mattered that much to you, I wouldn’t have bothered with it.”

At hearing Susan’s words, Joshua suddenly stopped his tirade of scolding and came to a halt. His face reminded Susan of a knot of rope that she’d once made by accident. In a sense, Joshua had become tied up in himself.

Susan held no animosity toward his position— but, she didn’t feel her usual curiosity either. She felt herself in an odd in between of wondering what he was hiding and feeling anger in the fact that he was hiding something from her.
Joshua bent his head deep into the table, before pulling it back up.

“I’m sorry as well,” he said. “There was no need for me to keep hammering in the fact that you shouldn’t have read that book— especially since we’ve already covered that ground almost a week ago. I understand your natural curiosity. I once felt the same as you, when I was younger. It’s partially my fault that you feel such a sensation, since I read you grandiose stories about the mountain when you were younger. Though, you can trust me on this— there’s nothing under or on that mountain that’s worthwhile, and you’ll come back from your search with a sense of regret. If I’m not mistaken, you already have…”

He looked into Susan’s eyes, and Susan looked back into his. It was a moment of staring at each other— perhaps a second or two— though, it was the longest moment that Susan had ever felt. Joshua’s eyes had a scathing quality to them— their very look was all that he needed to express himself. While that often came as a positive, tonight Susan couldn’t imagine how she could’ve ever seen it as such. All that she could feel was his disappointment— his wish for things to have been easier, and different. And, when looking back into his eyes, Susan couldn’t help but feel taken adrift by his infectious look. She too had wanted things to be simpler and easier to judge.
But, it just can’t ever be that way again, Susan thought, wistfully.

The scratching groan of wood against wood erupted as Joshua pushed his chair back and stood up from his place at the table. His eyes finally turned from Susan’s, relieving her of the somewhat unendurable discomfort that she’d been trying to reckon with. Then, Joshua picked up his bowl of mush and began to walk off.
“I should’ve checked the fire more…” he said, placing the bowl into a basin.

His figure eventually disappeared into a dark corridor, and Susan could eventually hear the distinct closing and shutting of the familiar library door. As this happened, a sort of revelation came to Susan’s mind. The unendurable discomfort hadn’t ended after the awkward stare had. Rather, there was a feeling in her that discomfort was only just beginning for her.

Repetition had become something that Susan had repeatedly shown a grudge toward. Though, the consistent onslaught of the next few weeks knocked her into a position where she had to submit to repetition’s power. I seemed that she could no longer escape cycles that were going on around her. For the remainder of her punishment, she found herself stuck repairing books while trying to read them without Joshua catching notice. Afterwards, she’d cook, clean, knit clothes back together, and, if she’d been lucky enough to get all of those jobs done before the day ended, sanding down the splinters on certain wooden furniture.

In a way, the exhaustion she felt was no longer perceived as exhaustion. It had just become a given— something that she no longer saw as an option. At that point, the only point had become getting to the end, and making it to the other side. She could hardly stand the fact that she felt as if she were hardly getting anywhere, and that it was as if every moment that she worked, she was working toward something that appeared purposeless. However, the end goal, and the power of pattern had put her in a place where she no longer resisted it as strongly.

Conversation with Joshua had come at an all-time low, as usual, and there wasn’t much to give her solace, other than her own thoughts and the warming fireplace. However, that too became something that she was compliant with, and all of her rebelliousness had leaked out of her.

As with nearly everything, there was a clear positive that came out of this— Susan had reached a position where the punishment didn’t faze her. She could deal with it without feeling any apparent strain, and her feeling had grown numb. Though, there was a terrifying element to the numbness— she felt as if a part of her soul had been drained in the process of it. The draining was slight and subtle, but it was undeniably there. All of its effects were easy to observe.

She no longer took interest in whether or not the shadow existed, or even whether or not the mountain was dangerous. Her eyes started to see her imagination as a sort of prison, from which she’d been bound. If she hadn’t gone so far as to explore the shadow in the first place, she believed that she wouldn’t have had so many issues with it.

So, the shadow faded, and all dangers subsided. To a degree, this gave her a relief of the strain that had been built between her and Joshua. The one thing that she failed to notice was how the subtraction of her fantasy had made little to no difference. Joshua was still distant, only speaking to give orders.

Although, declaring that there wasn’t a single difference would be a slight exaggeration— the one difference was that Susan had become as bland and lifeless on the inside just as much as the snowy world outside of her had.

Changeless repetition continued, with each one fading into the next, and them seemingly becoming endless. However, the end did come. After a little over a week of all this, with Susan’s spirit somewhat broken and nothing of consequence having taken place, she’d reached the last day of her punishment.

Despite having built up her past series of dull days by telling herself that the last day was coming, once the last day came to pass she no longer felt such an eager excitement. Instead, she felt a remaining bad aftertaste of dry blandness remaining in her mouth, and sucking her back into her normal schedule of the day. It came to be that she treated that day no different from any of the other days, having expected not much more from Joshua than what he’d already been doing with her.
She’d been wrong in thinking this.

After finishing her daily repair of twenty books, Joshua came to her work table. On the usual day, he came with a straight-face and a list of orders. Although, today he came with a sort of smile— and when he opened his mouth to give his order, it wasn’t the kind that Susan had been expecting at al.
“I’m extremely pleased with the way that you’ve worked for the past week,” he said. “And so, I’m having you go out a day early.”
Susan gave a grin— among the few that she’d had in several weeks.

“Don’t think that you’re going to get out of work,” Joshua said, giving his closest thing to a grin in return. “I’m going to have you take my usual place for the day, and have you return some of these books to their owners. I’m sure that you can easily handle it— right?”
Susan nodded— even if she’d had no idea as to how to take the route, she would’ve lied anyway, just so that she could escape the vacuum of a house that she felt trapped in

“Good,” Joshua said. “There aren’t any houses on the outskirts of town this time around, so you shouldn’t have any need to wander too far off— and, if you do happen to have wandered far off, and somebody finds you there, I’m going to make sure that your punishment is extended.”

Joshua tried saying these words in the most threatening way that he could muster— though, Susan easily saw through the act. If truth be told, even the timidest of people wouldn’t have felt threatened by his words, in spite of their content. Whenever Joshua spoke, even with the intention of inciting fear, he had a soft overtone to his voice. He couldn’t have been any less intimidating if he’d been a mewing cat, playing with a ball of yarn.

“Also,” he continued, desperately struggling to pound in the idea that this early taste of freedom wasn’t one to take lightly, “I want you to take the normal route. If you have houses that are more west, go to those first. They’re close to the mountain, and are the most dangerous to be around if the weather suddenly gets bad, so you’ll want to have those pinned down first thing. I know that the houses further west are worse off, and are no means our most important customers— but integrity is something that I strongly condone, and we can’t just—.”

It was at this point that Susan tuned out. Joshua was usually one to keep quiet and say little— though, when he came upon a subject that he felt deeply for, he had the tendency of tumbling into a pit of over-talkativeness and rambling.
“Do you understand?” he finally asked.
Although not hearing most of what he’d said, Susan nodded anyway. Thankfully, she was lucky enough to get Joshua on a good ramble, and he didn’t bother to ask her to reiterate what he’d said.
“Will I be going to Flanders’?” Susan asked, trying to change the subject before it might turn its subject onto her.
“Yes,” Joshua said.

In spite of Joshua’s laborious monologue, this one word was all that Susan really bothered to listen to. She hastily grabbed the pile of books that Joshua had set out for her to return, and left the house.

The reason that she’d been so excited at hearing of Flanders was for his eccentric personality and identity. While on the thinner end of his lifespan, he had a vigor to him. He’d throw enormous gatherings at his house, and make sure that everybody would participate in an excellent romp. His giant-sized sociable presence, and irresistible charisma were a flaky aura that followed him wherever he went.
