It was often said that he could just look at a person and make them feel an extreme sense of joy and fulfillment.

It seemed that every week he had some sort of party going on. There were some claims that Flanders had held a party every week for the past fifty years— and there was no evidence to the contrary concerning that notion. Flanders’ house was built entirely of stone because of the parties— it had used to be entirely made of wood, but people consistently entering and exiting his house had put such a strain upon it that he needed to replace all of the broken wood pieces with stone. At this point, the house was nearly a completely different structure from what it had been when it was first built. Additionally, while they couldn’t be seen from under the snowy coat of winter, hundreds of muddy footprints covered his yard, to the point that it was full of visible holes and ruts.

Some of his parties were so extreme that the night would be flooded with the busy whinnies of loose horses, the smell of smoke from his massive bonfires, and the screams and shouts of parties. There were claims that, during certain parties, the stars would be knocked out of the sky, and try trailing down to join them. Other than a few children, and people who harbored a bit of a grudge, everybody in town had gone to at least one of his parties. Even people outside of the town had gone to his parties. He was the sort of person who everybody liked to be around— the sort of person who liked everybody to be around.

Susan skimmed through the houses that Joshua had sent her through without so much as a second thought. Each stop appeared as a mere obstacle that she could easily surpass. At a few of them, she didn’t even bother to knock and open their doors— she’d leave their books on their damp snowy porch, and then run off to the next house. Nearly all of her energy was oriented towards Flanders that day. Her focus on each task apart from him was fleeting. It was as if every house were just a clover amongst a field of clovers. In spite of it being one among thousands, the only one that held any significance out of them was the four-leaf clover.

As she finished her last house, and made her way down the snow-covered village-trail to Flanders’, she suddenly remembered a person who’d never bothered to attend one of his parties, and who had a grudge towards Flanders— Joshua.

Though Flanders was considered to be the most prominent out of all the individuals in town, and though he seemed to provide work for nearly everybody, Joshua constantly spoke of a bitter taste that the utterance of Flanders name brought to his mouth.

Joshua had often denounced Flanders’ consistent need to make raucous in the town, and make a joke out of people who made a hard earned living. Susan never quite understood Joshua’s grudge, but was aware of his dislike towards Flanders’ ideal of making everything into some sort of joyride. Joshua held the standards of living honestly, and working hard to reach prestige. Flanders was the polar opposite of Joshua in every way in this regard.

Nobody was certain as to how Flanders’ made his money, but there were plenty of suspicions that he made it through dishonest trades, trickery, or even outright thievery. Whenever Susan came across the man, with his magnetic personality, she could hardly believe that these claims could even be possible. She’d once traded a few words with him, and he’d offered some of the best compliments to her that she’d ever heard. While she knew that he was very superficial, she also knew that not everything that came out of his mouth could’ve been a lie— there was too much a soft sweetness to his voice to believe otherwise.
Most people held the same belief as Susan, and any accusation of Flanders being dishonest was always declared to be false. It was the unpopular opinion to think down on him.

Joshua held the unpopular opinion, and constantly pushed his beliefs down onto Susan. Susan had often asked him why this was, but Joshua never gave an answer. He only provided his usual pattern of giving opinions without reason, and directing his thoughts through his straight facial expression, rather than words or body motions. There wasn’t any definite way for her to tell if what Joshua had said had any justification to them or not— he rarely adopted a belief without reason, but she rarely ever got any reason from him either.

All of this buildup had played a major part in why she’d held so much anticipation in her meeting with Flanders. In a way, he held not only a charismatic air about him, but a mythical air as well. Just like the mountain, he held a strange mystery to him— and he posed as a hole in Joshua’s often seemingly impenetrable armor.

Despite their differences, there was one thing that Joshua and Flanders had in common. They both had an extreme infatuation and love towards books. Susan remembered stretches of months when Joshua would cycle through piles of books of Flanders’ that needed repairing. All of the books would typically have enormous gauges put in them, as if Flanders had purposely maimed them. Though the purposeful maiming of the books was apparent, this was one of the few habits of Flanders’ that Joshua cared relatively little about. In fact, he would express a sense of respect toward Flanders’ vast collection, and allow his own presuppositions to dry out.

It was by Flanders that Susan had also been convinced that the man couldn’t have been everything that Joshua claimed he was— Flanders’ taste in books was too varied and intriguing to pass off as such. To her, passing Flanders off as a time-waster was like viewing a cocoon and instantly passing it off as a moth rather than a butterfly. Only careful judgment and the process of time would be able to prove whether it was one way or the other.

With these thoughts in mind, she reached the door of Flanders’ house. The building was just as majestic as she’d remembered it, with it being adorned in a smooth stone that reminded her of the stories of castles she’d often heard. It didn’t have tall spires, a drawbridge, or an enormous scale, but it was far greater than the castle to her.  Unlike the castle, this house was right in front of her eyes.

The house was very simplistic, with it only having the necessities, such as holes for windows, a chimney for an indoor fireplace, and nothing more. Bothering with the trifles in superfluous designs and ornaments wasn’t something that it was willing to waste its time on. Though, it did have a welcoming atmosphere to it— maybe it was the design, the open size, or the knowledge that many had enjoyed the company in this building. Susan didn’t bother wondering— when she saw the house, she saw the image of Flanders that she’d conjured up in her mind. There didn’t seem to be a single flaw about it— save an odd boulder with a massive dent in its side. She knew that, whatever this house held, it could’ve only been greater than what she’d viewed on the outside.

She knocked on the door, using a golden knocker that had been installed onto it. A minute passed, and there wasn’t an answer. So, she grasped the knocker again and prepared to slam it onto the door again. However, this time the door had opened before she could finish the act. Susan found herself stumbling forward. The hand of somebody else caught her before she could clumsily hit the ground. Looking up, she saw a man’s face— the face of Flanders.

He didn’t need to introduce himself, or say a single word when she looked up to him. Words were unneeded in his presence. He had a distinct look to him— wrinkles all around the mouth and eyes, you not a single one crossing his rosy cheeks. His hair had mostly faded out, doubtlessly due to time’s tests. His stature was far less fine-tuned than expected from a man with his social status as well— it seemed that age had slumped him lower than his expected height.

Yet, he still had managed to obtain and maintain a youthful joy and look in his eyes. As Susan looked at him she saw his mouth curve into a smile— and she couldn’t help but smile back. His power of joy was infectious, and he made Susan feel as if she possessed the same charismatic energy that he did. It was akin to looking at a painting. The very sight of one would oftentimes have the power of making one feel as if they themselves could become a painter.

“And what are you here for?” Flanders said, retaining his grin. There was almost an unnaturalness to it, and as he displayed and waved his arms about, Susan experienced an odd mixture of awe and trepidation going on within her.

She’d been so distracted by Flanders’ captivating spirit that she found that she’d refrained from answering his question. Even with his incomparable happiness, she could see Flanders’ face beginning to lose a bit of his magnitude as she kept him waiting.
“I—,” she began, but Flanders interrupted her before she could finish.
All of her books were swiped from her hand, with Flanders giving an uproarious shout of pleasure.
“You must be Joshua’s adopted apprentice,” he said, grabbing Susan’s hand and shaking it about as if her hand had been some sort of tree branch, and he was a young child waving it about.

Susan cringed at hearing his latter words, but found a way to look past them when Flanders’ magnetic abilities pulled her back in. Even in his rude interruptions, and fumbling introductions, he had an unabashed spirit about him. He had a way of not allowing his flaws to let him stumble, and this somehow covered up all of his mistakes and flaws from sight.
“So, how are you today?” he asked with a toothy grin. Then he grabbed Susan by the shoulder and opened his door wide open, to the point that Susan could see the entirety of his entrance hall.
Susan prepared to nod, but was once again trampled by Flanders’ speech.
“Good, yes? That’s good!”

He began leading Susan into his house, with the front porch morphing into the interior of his house. As this happened, Flanders leafed through his newly-repaired books with an unmatchable grin on his face.

“Astounding!” he said. “What excellent craftsmanship. Why, I haven’t seen anybody repair books so well— not even the people outside of this town. I used to think Joshua ridiculous for stuffing himself in the somewhat limiting niche of book repairs. But, now that I look at how well of a job he does, I see just how necessary people like him are! He’s amazing!”
He let out a laugh.
“Actually, I repaired those books,” Susan said, with heat flowing through her chest and up to her head.

In the wintry cold that surrounded her, heat was normally a thing that she gladly welcomed— but, this heat was one of clammy and uncomfortable proportions. She now clearly understood what Joshua meant whenever he said, “A spineless book is a broken book— but, I’ve found that books with good spines are always the stiffest of the bunch… How is it that such a positive thing is also a negative thing?”
Susan realized that Flanders symbolized both the uncomfortable and comfortable in socialization.
Perhaps that’s why his character sometimes has such a polarizing view, Susan thought.
“You repaired these books?!” Flanders said, with his eyes widening in an unnatural sort of wonder.

Susan had never seen a look quite like it on the face of anybody else— it had the wide-eyed innocence of a child, but was clearly influenced by the age of this man. Susan couldn’t help but feel as if Flanders was merely pandering to her, and putting on a show as if he thought her to be a young child— but, Flanders’ natural good-naturedness and hospitability diminished the potency of these feelings.

Susan told him yes, but it was clear to her that this wasn’t the end of their conversation. At hearing her answer, his eyes widened even more. His head turned about side to side, as if looking to see if anybody else was watching. His exaggerated responses had a freshness to them, despite the discomfort that tailed them.
“You have a talent, young ma’am,” he declared, playing with his vocal chords so as to give himself a presence of authority.

Susan grinned. In spite of Joshua having told her that he wanted her back early, she had hoped that Flanders would strike up a conversation. There was an element to him that was both mysterious and enchanting— she’d deeply wanted to explore it, and it seemed that she was finally getting the chance to. It didn’t matter that Joshua had told her otherwise. All that mattered to her was taking the chance, and looking deeper into something new.

In a way, Flanders represented the very same thing that the mountain had to her. Joshua’s secrets. A part of her felt that, if she looked into the things that Joshua forbade her from deep enough, she might find the answers to Joshua’s secrets— the secrets hidden within his odd quietness that she’d come to constantly associate him with.

“Why, I think you’ll eventually eclipse your teacher, Joshua,” he said, recovering from the shock of discovering that Susan had repaired the books. “These books had been torn to shreds during one of my parties— I can hardly believe that you managed to bring them back, as if they’d never been damaged in the first place.”
Then, he placed his hand on Susan’s shoulder.
“It’s unusual for women to run their own businesses— it’s not the way of the land. But I tell you, this is a skill that you can’t allow yourself to lose. You could run an entire business doing this.”

Susan gave a quick thank you— although his comments were done in kindness, she was once again taken aback by them. She felt that his words dug a bit too deep, and they made her feel odd— out of place. While she knew Flanders had good intent, she couldn’t imagine having to rely on repairing books for the rest of her life. She’d only been doing it for six years, and it was already becoming a tiresome and tedious job.
“Say— would you like to have a look around my library. I figure that a book repairer such as yourself might be interested in seeing my varied collection.”
“Yes.”

All it took was that single word, and Flanders led her down a hall, and through their destination’s doorway. To Susan’s surprise, the house’s design was much like her own. In spite of Flanders’ vast wealth, he wasn’t one to embellish it. The house didn’t have the exorbitant size that she’d expected, and the walkways were very simplistic and raw. The walls rarely adorned anything, apart from a few solitary markings, which had no doubt been put there by rowdy guests.

The library was just as unglamorous. It was certainly bigger, better lit, and better maintained than Joshua’s, with not a bit of dust coating the bookshelves. The bookshelves themselves were also very impressive, with them all being built of an expensive wood. Though, overall, Susan found it to be very mundane and uninteresting— especially with the infamous identity of Flanders put into consideration.

“What do you think of it?” Flanders asked, with a proud swoop of his arm. The library was clearly a gem to him— Susan could tell just by the twinkling of his eyes. However, no matter how hard Susan looked upon the library of books, that’s all she was able to see— books.

The primary reason for this was that Susan was so exposed to the sight of many books. While books were a sign of wealth and intelligence, it had become slightly dull to her. In a way, it had become similar to a knife. While a knife might start out sharp and brilliant, it becomes extremely dull as it’s overused over time.
“It’s very impressive,” Susan lied. “How did you get all of them?”
Flanders beamed.

“I was hoping you would ask that question. While my collection might seem rather large, and look as if it would’ve taken me traveling from several corners of the known land around us to garner, it’s actually quite simpler than that. I’m a man of trading, so I’ve gotten a few books from that. And, as a man of parties, I retrieved books from that as well. It was really just a few here, and a few there. It slowly grew in size, until it reached the size of this enormous mound. Really, it was quite a simple thing. I hadn’t put much thought into it until very recently.

“This is also why I’ve constantly employed Joshua to repair these books. I’ve found that, a lot of the time, the books are only given to me because they’re either damaged, or near unrepairable. Surprisingly, your master is a miracle worker. He’s managed to fix things that I thought weren’t savable. I would’ve used half of these books for kindling if it hadn’t been for him. Joshua is worth every coin I put into him— he’s come a long way, and there needs to be more people like him.”

All of reality seemed to pause for Susan at the phrase, “he’s come a long way.” Something in Susan’s mind altered at that moment. It was reminiscent to when one realizes that every mound of snow on the ground is made up of thousands of snowflakes. A new complexity ripped into Susan’s mind— thoughts that she never considered came scrambling in, and she saw hundreds of different details falling into position. All of Joshua’s odd and unexplainable behaviors instantaneously became mundane and explainable.

He’s been hiding something from me, after all, Susan thought, with her eyes and brow squinting in unison. The very notion was so hard to believe that she had to squint her eyes to believe what she was seeing. His complacent facial expression and tone were always concealing something from me.

“I’m really happy to hear that you like our work,” Susan said, trying her best to crawl into the cracks of Flanders’ kindness. “But, what do you mean by ‘he’s come a long way’? Is there something about Joshua that I’m missing here?”
For the first time during her entire visit, she saw Flanders reveal a part of himself that was less than electric. In fact, she could’ve sworn that she saw some sort of dread leak into his eyes.
“No— just a slip of the tongue,” he said, before lapsing into an incoherent mutter, and laughing his statement off.

“Sorry— it was an abrupt change of subject,” Susan said, trying her best to say this without revealing that she’d caught Flanders’ unusual behavior. “It’s just— sometimes I think that there aren’t enough answers in this town. Maybe I’m being unreasonably curious, but the town’s small size makes it hard for me to avoid bringing these uncomfortable questions up.”
Flanders nodded understandably.

“I don’t place any blame onto you,” he said. “I suppose that it’s a tendency for children your age to begin putting things into question. It’s a part of the natural order of things. However, I advise that you don’t go any deeper than you’ve already gone.”

He said these words with an eerie seriousness that Susan hadn’t expected to come out of him. It seemed that all of the lights in the room started flickering and darkening in response to what he’d said.
Although, he then let out a laugh that attempted to erase all of this seriousness.
“Who knows what shenanigans it will bring,” he said, acting as if this tacked-on statement had been part of his initial warning.
Susan wasn’t convinced in the slightest. However, trying to conceal her growing discomfort, she laughed along with him.
Flanders wasn’t convinced in the slightest.
This is becoming a cycle of lies and falsehoods… I came here to get answers, not questions. I never thought that I’d come out of here thinking that Flanders is less forward than Joshua…
“Well, it was nice talking to you,” Susan said, subtly gesturing to the door.
Susan was about to explain herself, but Flanders hastily interjected.
“Don’t go yet— there’s still so much that I need to show you.”
He gave an almost pleading look to her, as if he was desperate to have her company. Then, he gestured to the hundreds of books that were crammed into the shelf behind him.

Suddenly, Susan no longer saw the majesty within Flanders that she’d originally thought to be there. In its place, she saw something that was desperate— conniving even. All of the magical, youthful glow hat had once rested upon Flanders face had been stripped bare. The stripes of age were all that remained.
“It’s just— I don’t know how much time that I have. I don’t want to waste it all here, and go back to a disappointed Joshua.”

If Flanders had heard her, he’d done an amazing job at making it seem as if he hadn’t. His eyes hadn’t diverted from his shelves of books. He filed through all of them, knocking each one down as if they were a domino.
“Didn’t you hear me?” Susan asked, preparing to repeat her words.
Flanders once again ignored her— however, this time he didn’t put any effort into pretending as if he wasn’t.
“Mines of Ether, Bridges of Emerald, The Epic of Bray a Wolf…” Flanders said, listing off the book titles with such a rapidity that it was hard to tell what he was even saying.
“I don’t want to sound rude, but I really have to go,” Susan said.

If it had been anybody else, she would’ve followed through on this statement. Although, Flanders clearly wasn’t interested in her leaving, and Susan knew that Flanders was too valuable of a customer for her to risk offending him. Not only that, but she still had a lingering interest in Flanders that had remained, even in spite of his odd behavior and resistance in giving her clear answers.

“You know, I actually haven’t read half of these books,” Flanders said, carefully articulating each word he spoke, as if they all had an immeasurable weight to them. “It’s really odd, whenever I put a large amount of thought into it. I’ve inserted a vast amount of wealth into this collection— even if I didn’t put that much work into it. But, I can’t help but feel that I’ve done it for nothing. It’s just a lot of wasted space. That is— I thought it was a lot of wasted space until now. I figure that you’re the only person in town who will be willing to take a look at these books, and appreciate them for what they’re really are.”
Susan struggled to keep her face from construing into a confused expression.

“I know that this might seem extremely odd,” said Flanders, “but, after years of hosting parties in this house, I’ve come to realize how lonely the life of an eccentric character, such as myself, really is. It has become straining to keep up the illusion, and even more straining to find somebody who’s willing to appreciate the things that I appreciate.”
Susan had no response to him— his words were so extraordinarily odd and out of nowhere that she didn’t know what to make of them.
“If there’s any book in here that catches your eye, it’s yours,” Flanders finally said, with his mouth lighting up. However, when Susan watched his eyes, she saw how sullen they’d become.

At first, Susan was still confused about Flanders’ behavior. Though, she then saw the advantage to his offer— any book in the library could be hers. While there was no explanation to Flanders’ strangeness, it had been eclipsed by the context of his offer.
“I can take any book from this library?”
“Yes!” Flanders exclaimed, almost too eagerly. He pulled out a few books from a shelf to get his point across.
He was almost too eager in doing this. It was as if he were trying to get rid of them.
“Do you have ‘An Exploration into Shadows and Shallows’?” she asked.

There was no doubt in her mind that the answer was yes. Though, this lack of doubt didn’t change the fact that she felt as if Flanders wasn’t willing to give her the true answer. The book was odder than anything about Flanders— and that was saying a lot. If Flanders had bothered to give any attention to the book, she was certain that it would’ve been the prize jewel of his collection— it wasn’t comparable with anything else that he possessed.
In a way, her very asking of the book’s title was a way for her to test Flanders’ loyalty to his word.

She was right in assuming so. At hearing Susan’s words, Flanders’ face started to look as if it were being pulled in all directions. His gaze of desperation altered into one of reluctance. His very gaze appeared to be full of some sort of stinginess. Whatever connection he had to the book, it had been even Stronger than Susan had expected.

“Where did you hear about that book?” he asked, as quick as his old lips would allow him. He tried playing his words off as if he were confused in what Susan was asking. However, he was a terrible actor, and Susan could clearly tell that he was withholding something from her. And, it seemed that he thought that she was withholding something from him.
I shouldn’t be surprised, Susan thought. Joshua has always told me that the signature nature of liars is that they suspect everybody else to be a liar.
“I heard about the book when Joshua was repairing it for you,” Susan said. “It was one of the more intriguing titles that had passed through our house...”

Flanders nodded, and muttered something inaudibly. Then he said, “It must have been somebody else’s book. It sounds interesting, as you claim it to be... But, it’s not a book that I possess. Why don’t you look for other books?”
Susan said yes, and began searching through his shelves. However, she kept a close eye out for the book that she’d asked Flanders about.

After nearly ten minutes of looking through the clutter of books, she came to an unwanted realization. If Flanders had truly thought the book to be valuable, he wouldn’t have kept it amongst his collection of assorted books.

As Susan dug deeper into his collection, she began to wonder if he had been telling the truth when he said that he didn’t have the book, after all. Settling to the unwanted circumstances, Susan finally grabbed the next best book that caught her eye.
“Whispers of the Mountain’s Wisps…” Susan said, grabbing a book with a superfluous golden binding, and an image of a mountain embellished onto its cover.
“How did that get in there?” Flanders said with a raised voice, ripping the book out of Susan’s hands.

He stumbled backward after doing this, and looked at Susan with an almost feral expression. However, this feral angriness went away as quickly as Flanders had snatched the book out of Susan’s hand. Susan half-wondered if Flanders’ angry glare had been nothing but a conjuring of her imagination, because as soon as she’d seen his angriness it turned into Flanders’ usual happiness.
“Sorry about that,” he said with a chuckle, letting his hand roll over the books leathery texture.
Then, he put the book back into Susan’s hands, with such a delicacy that he might as well have been handing over a feather. It was apparent that he was trying to make up for his rash jumpiness.

“I don’t know if I’ve ever had a visitor that I’ve had to apologize to as much as I have had to apologize to you,” he said laughing again. “This was one of those books that I’d prefer not to give away. It has a sort of sentimentality to it…”
He paused, and his ravenous gaze ran over his face again. It was subtle, but it had undeniably been there.

“But, a promise is a promise, and I told you that you could have any book that you like,” he finished. “Enjoy the book. It’s among the few that I’ve read, and it has very interesting passages concerning the lore about our town mountain. It’s definitely an interesting read.”

Susan thanked him, and then walked down the hall and to his front door. As she opened it, she heard Flanders’ older footsteps pound after her. Turning around, she found that Flanders had followed her to the door. She gave a quizzical look, but merely gave a goodbye— Flanders strangely forgot to give a goodbye in return. It was as if he’d followed her to the door not to give her a goodbye, but the book that she’d brought with her.
There was one thing he did to acknowledge her presence, though— he gave her a glare. Susan didn’t know what to make of it, and left before she could.
This has been one of the strangest visits that I’ve had in a long while, Susan thought to herself. Joshua is going to be furious when he finds out just how long I spent here…
“What have you been doing?” Joshua asked, after Susan had opened the door.

Quickly, Susan tried hiding the book that Flanders had given her up her clothes. Her heart thudded like a boulder does as it rolls down a mountain, and she felt as though she were going to impact the ground— the grounding— any minute now.

“I was just— just really busy with some of your customers today,” Susan explained, throwing her shoes to the side, and scanning for a better place to hide her book. She could already hear Joshua’s footsteps coming down the hallway and felt a terrible dread at the thought that he might come at any moment. Her time was running short.
“That sounds nice… You didn’t bother any of them for too long, did you?”

Joshua’s voice sounded so clear that she could tell it was almost in the same room as her. Beads of sweat and melted snow began to cascade down Susan’s face. Finally, she snatched the coat off of her body, held the book in her left hand, and then draped her coat over the book.
She then leaned onto the wall to her right, trying her hardest to seem natural.
“No… Well, I mean, I guess it depends on your definition of the phrase ‘too long’.”
Joshua laughed— something that he’d only do if he thought somebody had said something hilarious.
“It looks like I’ll have to write up a ton of new apology letters,” he said, entering the same room as Susan. “So, what were you busy talking about? Who did you talk to?”
Feeling sheered of any other choice, she said, “Books, mainly… Flanders was particularly impressed with my repair job.”

As she’d expected, she watched all sense of joy and pleasurableness be wiped off of Joshua’s face, as if it had been a slate, and somebody had rubbed it with an eraser. All that remained was a cold blackness. She was simply waiting for the new meaning to be scribbled onto it.
“You spoke with Flanders?” he asked, clearly trying to pace around his anger.

“Yes… He was pretty nice, actually. I know what you’re complaining about when you say that he’s too much of a partyer. He doesn’t seem to know when to stop talking… But, it never really matters much, because he’s so hospitable, and so good at talking.”
Joshua nodded, with a skeptical look remaining on his face.
“And, you only talked about books?” he asked. “Nothing else came up in the conversation outside of that— correct?”

Once again, Susan was faced with the choice of lying or telling the truth. To her, telling the lie was becoming more tempting by the day, especially when it seemed that lies were a trade that everybody was giving out in this town. However, she also knew the guilt and issues that came with the lie— it chipped off a sense of a much-required honesty. It whittled away trust— not only the trust for herself, but her own trust towards others.
“Yes— that’s all we talked about. That is, other than a few other things concerning his house, and history with his books.”

Joshua nodded again. This time, he didn’t look skeptical. Instead, he was simply unbelieving. Susan knew that he’d caught her lying. Though, Susan also knew that the lie she told was only a few degrees off from the truth— she really had talked to Flanders about only a few subjects, and they really had only concerned his house and his books. The only thing that she’d omitted was the fact that she’d tried steering the conversation elsewhere a few times— but, these attempts at steering the conversation away had always ended in failure.

“Did you know that he hasn’t read most of his books?” Susan asked. “He probably has about a thousand of them— he might have even more. But, he said that he’s hardly touched any of them… He doesn’t even know most of their names.”
Joshua didn’t respond to her comments.

He probably caught onto the fact that I was trying to steer the conversation in a different direction, she thought. Not that I should be surprised— I can never seem to make that work… But, I’m going to have to if I want to avoid this continuous interrogation.
“I don’t know… Maybe it’s just me who thinks that strange,” Susan said. “I just couldn’t imagine not bothering to read hardly any of the books in our personal library…”

“Yes, Flanders is good at ignoring things that are right in front of his face,” Joshua said. “I tend to think that a lot of his ignorance to his books has to do with the fact that he doesn’t really care about them. To him, they’re just another space that can be filled on his shelves, and another pretty object that he can impress people with. It’s just like his parties, and everything he owns…”
Susan was taken aback by Joshua’s continuous attacks on Flanders. She’d never heard Joshua sling around so many insults concerning anybody— not even concerning Flanders.
“Why do you hate Flanders so much?” Susan finally asked, after Joshua began to cool down from his heatedness.
Joshua stopped, and leaned on the same wall Susan was. Then, he looked down at Susan’s coat with an almost knowing smile.
“You’re telling me the truth when you say that you and Flanders’ didn’t discuss anything outside of books?” Joshua asked.
Susan answered yes— her stubbornness had once again caught traction, and closed up her willingness to answer anything but affirmatives.
“Then, you have no reason to know anything outside of that,” Joshua said, walking down the hall. “Why would I be willing to tell you something when Flanders wasn’t…”
Is it just me, Susan wondered, or are front doors making people act very strange today?
Closed doors are making people act very strange today… Including myself.
After the mess that was the invasion of the horse, my guards have turned more overprotective than ever. I haven’t been let outside for weeks.

In a way, this is a positive thing. I no longer fear the mysteriousness that had come with the odd advisor I’d been paired with, and the coronation has been pushed back. This gives me more time to plan, and strategize solutions. However, with this positivity, there’s also an element to everything that drags at me. Nobody will allow me the freedom to venture outside of my palace. And, even if they did, I’ve become aware that my entire kingdom is starting to turn against me. Unsurprisingly, seeing their future king be attacked was quite demoralizing to them all.

Trades have been halted, workers are declaring that they won’t return to work until I’m overthrown, some of my guards are whispering about turning against me, and even the grave of my father, which I can see from the window of my room, has faded into a grungy gray.

My father’s grave is what hurts me the most. I can’t let him down. Despite everything that’s going on, it’s only a slight weight compared to the weight of the earth that encompasses my father’s coffin. I might be at risk for becoming food to the conniving people, but my father— he’s at risk of becoming food to the worms. The longer he stays under, without me finding a solution, the longer I fail him.

I don’t know what to do, nor do I know if I’m doing the right thing. Although I’m glad that the wizardly advisor of mine mysteriously disappeared, I feel that my only chance at resolving my issues will be in finding him again, and asking him questions. I might be insane in thinking this, but, it’s like my father would often tell me— “If you were to look close enough, everybody is a little insane. They all care about something, striving after it with an irrational intensity— and, most of the time, everybody fails to get a grasp of what they strive after. Insanity is merely an illusion. There are times when an illusion is a harmful thing. Though, there are others when illusions are a thing of beauty, and wonder. While both illusions and insanity might be looked upon with bitterness, the truth about them is that they change the way that one responds to the world around them. It’s the response insanity incites that you must be cautious of.”

At the time, I wholly ignored him whenever he said that. It was one of those repetitive speeches that I thought was overly flamboyant and self-congratulatory. Though, I now think that he was more right than I’ll ever be willing to admit.

I haven’t even begun to discuss the other things that have taken place since the horse smashed its face into the rock. Perhaps it’s because I didn’t want to discuss it— it was a rather uncomfortable moment for me.

After my guards had taken care of the horse, and everybody who the horse had injured and damaged, they returned to tell me about everything that had happened— I’ve already written about all of this. Thought what happened afterwards is something that I have yet to write about.
It happened that I found a strange jewel sitting on the floor of my palace. It was left behind in the courtyard, presumably from when everybody left the party.

Normally I wouldn’t care about such a thing. In fact, I initially thought that it was the most trivial action of my day when I picked up the jewel. Though, then I inspected it, and I found discovered something far more disconcerting than I ever could’ve expected.

The jewel was an emerald, which sparkled green when I turned it in the light. It had an unnaturally profound beauty to it— it was like holding a miniature star, a mountain, or an entire ocean, all at once— all in the palm of my hand.

I stared at it for a while— I’m not sure how long it was, but it was long enough for the sky to go from sunset to pitch darkness. However, I didn’t see any of this. All that I saw was the emerald. That, and vivid images that appeared in my mind.

It happened that the vivid images that appeared in my mind gave me glimpses of the mountain— strange fires, and flakes of ice at the same time. Continuing to see the images, I came to a stunning realization that I would’ve preferred to avoid— my wizardly advisor had owned this emerald. And, while it was most certainly a magic gem, I supported the fact that this gem was giving me visions into the mountain’s secret depths. Every tunnel— every cavern— all of them combined into one, to make an unerring map of the mountain. It was a beautiful thing— and I felt as if I needed to spend every second staring at it, and to allow myself no exception. I was glued to it. Its beauty and detail had such undeniable breadth and beauty that I couldn’t help but feel its power intimidate me. It was among one of the most prevalently glorious things that I’d ever experienced.

There was a part of me that suspected that there must’ve been some evil force, or some revolting charm that was controlling the will of this magic gem. I suspected that every second I spent with it might’ve been a second whittled away from the clock of my life. There was even a part of me that held the belief that my discovery of this gem had been preplanned, and that the disappearance of my wizardly advisor had been so that my discovery couldn’t be traced back to him. He might’ve planted this object in order to trick me into following his path, and falling into some sort of wickedly contrived trap of his. Though, I couldn’t help but ignore all of these facts, and pass them off as nothing more than unfounded superstition.

A charm resided atop the gem— it was so powerful and benevolent, that it didn’t matter what costs came with experiencing it, All I knew is that I wanted to hold it in my hand and keep it under my control.

It was after this when I did something that I now look back on and regret. I saw a trail through the mountain, as I held the emerald. It led through numerous mines, and into the heart of the mountain. As I looked upon it, I had a knowing in my heart telling me that I had to chart down the sight.

So, I sent for one of my scribes, and they came to me as I held the emerald. Then, I took their pen, and jotted down everything that I saw. I worked at such an inhuman pace, that even my scribe was shocked by the speed in which my hands moved— he claimed that he himself was incapable of such, and he asked me if something was wrong. I consistently answered with a no, up until I’d finished with the map. It was at that point that I realized what a mistake I’d made— I’d allowed the gem to control my actions. Without hesitation, I smashed the gem to the ground and then walked off.
Though, not before giving my scribe order to place my map in a book. For some reason, I couldn’t bring myself to getting rid of the map.

Little did I know what a mess it would bring. I’m now tempted to follow the map, and to allow it to lead me through the mountain. I’ve gone back around the circle, and returned to the position where I don’t know what to do. I don’t know if there’s anything that I should do.

Susan’s punishment subsided, and so did her overbearing amount of work. While her duty to repair books persisted, their dominance began to whither out. Having taken care of most of Flanders’ latest maimed books, Joshua’s customers had begun to fade out. There was a stretch of days when Joshua didn’t have any business at all.

In this time, Susan returned to her friends. Tim still held a bit of a grudge toward her, and his injuries hadn’t fully healed. There weren’t many more gatherings or exploring either— that had apparently stopped occurring in her absence, due to Tim’s injuries. Though, other than that, everything had returned to normal, and it was as if there hadn’t been a lapse in her appearance at all.

Having all of this return to her, Susan felt a bit off center. It gave her an unnatural feeling to have bounced from days of work to a mere few hours, and there was something strange in not having to answer to Joshua’s stern, cold face anymore. In fact, it wasn’t just strange. It came to the point where she felt upset, and guilty.

She wasn’t sure why, but there was a part of her that felt unworthy of having been made free of Joshua’s labor. A portion of her felt that she was to blame for the lack of Joshua’s work. There was a portion of her that was fully aware of all the things wrong with this notion— the lack of work shouldn’t have had anything to do with her, and was a separate thing entirely. Yet, that didn’t help shake the feeling.

Whenever she entered her home, Joshua was sitting on the rocker chair in the library, staring into empty space. This was unusual, even for Joshua. It seemed that, in spite of his lengthy career that had gone on without any issues, there had been a sudden drop in customers. And, this had resulted in a sudden drop of Joshua’s conversation skills.

Susan tried to distract herself from this as much as she could by staying outside, away from Joshua, as much as she could. Yet, his depressing mood was somewhat infectious, and it came to the point where it began to leak into her daily life and sap her of some of her joy and mental focus. There were some instances when she was even made unable to concentrate due to the overwhelming presence of these feelings.

Her book that she’d gotten from Flanders had also been neglected because of this feeling. It had a mystical quality to it that Susan didn’t want to dare test— especially in the midst of Joshua. She couldn’t help but feel that her meeting with Flanders had effected Joshua in some extremely negative way. Wanting to know why, she looked for any clues that she could find. Though, the only link between Flanders and how the meeting could’ve affected Joshua, was that Flanders had given Susan the book. And, she had a feeling that Joshua suspected her possession of the book.
Finally, after a week of this going on, she brought herself to asking Joshua for the meaning behind his idiosyncratic behavior.

When she found him, he was in the library as usual. The faint, warm light of candle flames dribbled onto the wooden floor, and she watched it create a sort of warm and humid mist that seemed to encase everything. In a sense, it created its own miniature world that separated itself from the bitterness outside of it. Even the scent of mustiness, mixed with wax, was pleasing to smell.

Though, just as the room’s atmosphere was apart from the outside, Joshua’s atmosphere was apart from the room. When Susan looked at him, she saw something gloomy and damp— it reminded her of the rain that came just after a storm’s end, dripping to the ground and steadily muddying everything it touched. Joshua didn’t frown, but he didn’t move either. Everything he did seemed to be an attempt to do as close to nothing as was possible.
“Why aren’t there any books coming in?” Susan asked, trying to indirectly steer the conversation to her will.

Joshua paused, and then stirred in his chair. Susan steadily watched the layers of idleness peel off of him, just like dried dirt steadily falls off of a muddied object. It took a full minute of this before he finally began to give his answer.

“Why aren’t you coming in every day? The answer to both questions is that it’s just not the season for it… There’s too much going on outside right now, and the cozy house behind my closed doors has fallen to the back of everything.”

Susan nodded, trying to act understanding. Though, if she’d been honest, she couldn’t understand a bit of Joshua’s explanation. There was no doubt in her mind that Joshua, as usual, was concealing something from her. She wasn’t sure what— but she did know that, whatever it was, Joshua wasn’t going to give easy answers.
“Is that why you’ve been stuck in the house all this time?” Susan asked.
“I’ve been stuck in this house all this time because I’ve been stuck in the house,” Joshua answered plainly, keeping his answer as vague as he could.
“You know that there’s more reason to it than that.”

“There’s more reason to everything than what it seems, Susan… But, that doesn’t mean that it should matter to you. Even if you knew the reason why I’ve been stuck in here, that wouldn’t give you the answers you want… The only way into a person’s actions is by their thoughts. And, out of everything people have designed, we still haven’t gotten smart enough to where we’re able to perfectly communicate them…”
“Just because I can’t read your thoughts doesn’t mean that you can’t tell me what’s going on.”
“You’re too young to understand… Besides— a person lives more in their thoughts than anything else. Nobody can live somebody else’s life, Susan. Nobody can read somebody else’s thoughts…”
“Life is a lot more than sitting in a chair, though. You’ve been like this for a week.”

“It doesn’t matter,” Joshua said, suddenly. “I’ve come to realize that life is very similar to growing an apple tree. You spend time maintaining it, doing your best to control its health, and trying to make it better than the rest. Though, once it’s done, you see just how little control you really had over it— you see how insignificant it is, once compared to the hundreds of thousands of other trees that pepper the earth…”
Susan watched Joshua begin to relapse back into his state of idleness.
“That’s not true,” she said. “What are you even trying to get at?”
“Just leave me alone, and in peace…” Joshua said. “I’m tired.”
Then he closed his eyes. Susan left, and closed the door.
“I just don’t understand it,” Susan said.
She picked up a rock, and tossed it as far as she could into the direction of the mountain.
“He never talks to me, but then gets upset when I don’t talk to him… But, whenever I talk to him, he gets upset about that too…”

Lifting a dozen more rocks in her two hands, Susan flung them in every direction. They didn’t go as far this time, and the indents that they made in the snow were far less prominent. Though, that didn’t change the fact that Susan’s level of fury was reaching its peak. If she’d been any more vehement, the snow around her would’ve begun to melt.
“I think that you’re probably taking things far too personally,” Isabella said, putting her hand on Susan’s shoulder. Susan pushed it away, and walked deeper through the expanse of snow.

The mountain’s purple peak made its way through a coating of falling snow, and a flat plane, made up of nothing but white, surrounded them. The town was nothing but a speck off in Susan’s peripheral vision, and it seemed as if the entire world had gone away, with all of its bondages and tedious requirements being distant.
“I would just ignore him,” Tim said, rolling a clump of snow into a ball. “It sounds to me like he couldn’t care less if you talked to him or not, so why don’t you give him what he wants?”

“You don’t think that I tried that?” Susan asked, annoyed. “I had to endure his silence for a week. Do you know how hard that can be? It’s like constantly walking by a mess, and refusing to clean it up. Eventually, it just gets bigger and bigger, and it almost feels like it starts to pull at you. It begins to drive you partially insane…”
Tim just shoved his hands in his pockets, and offered a blank face.
“You just don’t understand what it’s like to feel something constantly nag at you. Even without Joshua ever saying a word, it’s as if he never stops.”
Tim let out a wry chuckle.
“Considering that you didn’t stop nagging at me until I would follow you guys here; I think that I know full well what it’s like to have somebody nag at you.”
“He’s just bitter that you had to bring him back here…” Isabella said.
“I wouldn’t even be wasting my time here if my arm wasn’t broken,” Tim retorted bitterly. “Because of this, I’m not able to play any of the games that everybody else is.”

Susan and Isabella ignored his dull jabs. The real reason that he hadn’t ceased to join them was that he was extremely weak, and unable to do things that the other boys were able to. If Susan and Isabella were to have been fully honest, one of the main reasons that they even bothered to keep Tim around was out of a sort of pity for him.

“I just don’t know if I’m doing the right thing or the wrong thing,” Susan said. “ To be honest, I don’t know what I’m doing at all. It’s strange… I feel so angry inside… But, I don’t know what I’m angry at.”
“It’s called growing up,” Tim said.
Strangely, this time his words didn’t come out so harsh.

“You know, I’m not even supposed to be out here with you guys,” he continued, with a strange retreat in his previously angry breaths. “I was ordered not to come out of the village— I’m not allowed to go passed a new amount of restrictions. And yet— you guys were able to convince me otherwise. No— that’s not even it. I was able to convince myself to come out here. In spite of my broken arm, and other injuries, I feel freest when I’m acting as if they’re not there. I get a strange joy out of pretending that my problems and harsh restrictions in reality don’t exist…”

Susan and Isabella were both left dumbstruck, and didn’t have a word to say. For the longest time, the only noise that passed between them was the soft falling of the snow. There was a hypnotizing element to it— though they were all far off from where they were supposed to be, and though they were breaking every rule that had been placed over them, they didn’t feel as if they’d begun hanging over the edge of a cliff and were on the verge of tumbling down. The mountain was far off in the distance, making an imposing glower. The sun in the sky had turned away from them, and the clouds were pulled in front of it so as to hide it from view. Wind ran through their throats and lungs, threatening to continue biting them. Though, the only thing that these bits of nature did to affect them was the fact that it didn’t affect them. All of its threats began to appear menial and in vain. A sense of awe encapsulated everything— the elegant and vibrant colors, the unending complexity, the intricacies, the minute details, and the strange but glowing combination of it all at once had a voice.

It spoke to Susan in the deepest possible way. Everything that had bothered her suddenly turned to flaking bits of dust, and suddenly the immense gravity of nature had gained a foothold. Amongst everything, what she’d once thought to be everything looked like a pebble. Unique as her own little universe was, it was just a snowflake floating upon a pile of snowflakes.
Maybe I won’t be able to find the answers, she thought, but, at least I’ll always have this immense tapestry to comfort me.

“You know what,” Tim finally said, doing his best to toss a stick with his broken arm. “Let’s just forget about this following orders nonsense altogether. Who cares what happens to us out here? It’s a whole lot better than being stuck in the village, constantly wondering what the world outside is like.”

Susan nodded, but didn’t fully agree. While she knew that, in the grand scheme of things, her decision wouldn’t really matter, she couldn’t shake the feeling of something missing that had welled up in her soul. She didn’t just feel an anger. Rather, she now realized that the anger was stemming from something far deeper than what she’d initially thought.
“Let’s not,” Isabella said, trying her best to laugh what Tim had said off. “What good will that do for us, in the long run?”
A brush of wind went by, tickly Susan’s nostrils and ruffling her hair. Then, she turned over and found that a large chunk of snow had found its way onto Isabella’s face.
“I don’t know about you guys, but I think that I’ve spent enough time out here,” she said, with frustration lining every syllable that she uttered. “I’m ready to head home.”

She had a shiver at the end of each word, and her hands were pale and shaky. A thick powder had found a way to douse an entire side of her body. The very sight of her was enough to make somebody feel freezing.
Before Isabella spoke, Susan’s hands had been out in the open, hanging on opposite shoulders, trying to warm herself up. Though, they’d since moved into Susan’s sleeves and coats.
“Are either of you going to help me head back?” Isabella asked, with a slight tremor. “I’m freezing— I want to go home!”
Tim was kneeled over, busy drawing lines in the snow. He didn’t even bother to look up when Isabella spoke.
“You can head home,” Tim said, “but we’re not going back to the village with you— not yet. We’re only just beginning here.”

Isabella looked like she was preparing to walk off, but her feet merely shuffled in the ground. The holes in the snow, which her legs were planted in, grew larger and more prominent. Though, rather than this coming off as intimidating, the lengthening of the hole’s size only seemed to strengthen the stance of Susan and Tim.

“I don’t like this,” Isabella said, with a slight whine. “The only reason I agreed to coming out of the village limits was so that we could talk, and let Susan calm down after her straining past few weeks… But, the whole reason that she had a straining past few weeks was because we came out here. If we start straying too far, we’re going to have a complete repeat of that whole scenario! Don’t you guys remember last time we stayed out here, and strayed too far? It was a complete mess! Besides— I think that we’ve been breaking enough rules lately. Don’t you think that our luck is going to start running out?”
Tim only let out a scoff in response.

“For the first half of this day, I was the one who was bitter and timid about coming out here,” he said,” and now you’re going to turn around and encourage me to be timid and scared again? If there’s anything that I’ve learned from being scared to venture out here, it’s that it doesn’t fruit in anything. I spent most of today afraid, and irritated— and it wasn’t until I stepped outside of that shell that I finally felt fulfilled and at peace with the rest of the world.”
“Spare me of the sugar-coated lies,” Isabella said. “I’m not in the mood to play games with you. I want to go home, curl up next to the fire, and—.”

“And you can do that. Also, last time I checked, weren’t you the one who last pushed me to follow your directions and come out here? Weren’t you the one who acted like going with Susan was a genius idea?”

Susan’s head was pounding— both from the chilling cold, and the heated argument. Expecting Isabella to make a retort, Susan braced her eardrums from another series of shouts. Though the shouts never came.
“What do you have planned?” Isabella asked, to Susan’s shock.
Isabella was still dragging her feet— both literally, and metaphorically— but, surprisingly, it wasn’t as prominent as it had been.
“You’re actually taking us seriously?” Tim said.

Normally, such a question would’ve been followed by Tim’s sarcastic and slightly arrogant laugh. Though, this time he was fully serious— there wasn’t a hint of humor in any of the words that he spoke.

“You’re right, to a degree, I guess,” Isabella continued, reluctantly. “I’ve been kept in my house all winter, and it had gotten hard to stay in line… But, what happens if one of us gets hurt again? Nobody is going to be able to save us, since nobody thinks that we’ll be willing to come back out. If you’re under a pile of rocks again, Tim, how do you expect to be safe?”

Tim was left without anything to say. Susan actually watched a striking expression of fear jump onto him— something that she’d come to know he liked to hide from them. The very thought that going back exploring could be so troublesome was perhaps the most troubling thing that had come out of their entire conversation.
“Then, we’ll have to pull him back out,” Susan answered.

I can’t not keep looking for answers, she found herself thinking at the back of her mind. Joshua might be encouraging me to give up the search— as well as everybody else around me. Though, if there’s anything that I’ve begun to learn, it’s that giving up a search for answers out of fear is just as terrible as not searching for answers at all… I’m never going to be able to find truth unless I can convince them that we’ll be safe the entire way through.

To Susan’s dismay, neither of her friends looked convinced. In fact, the very suggestion that the events of their last mishap might repeat themselves, and that they’d have nothing to change that form happening, was probably the most demoralizing thing that could’ve been said.

“We’re just going to have to try to be careful,” Tim said, more to himself than anybody else. “I know that it might be arrogant and self-important to say this, but I’m going to anyway— we’re too resilient for the forces of nature to stop us from exploring it. My arm might be busted, but then, why should that stop me? Why should that stop any of us? We shouldn’t give up on curiosity just because terror and fear is licking at us…”
If it hadn’t been for the fact that they were frozen solid, Susan would’ve clapped at Tim’s speech.
“So then, let’s make a full circle, and return to Isabella’s original question,” Susan said. “Where are we going?”

“I have it all mapped out,” Tim said. “At least— I have it mapped out in the best possible way that I can… I’m not actually sure how the foot of the mountain’s layout really looks like, but I’ve made a few educated guesses and placed it into the lines that I’ve graphed onto the snow.”

Susan bent down, and took a close look at all of it. Though, she was disappointed to find that none of it was very clear, nor precise. In fact, most of it looked like it had been brushed away by the wind.
“There’s no possible way that we’re going to be able to use that to guide us through the snow,” Susan said.

“I agree,” said Isabella. “It was already hard enough to convince me that exploring the mountain was a good idea…. And now you’re expecting me to take this mess of a map seriously? I’m sorry, but I can only see us getting into serious trouble from this…”
Anger swept onto Tim’s face.
“And what else are we supposed to do? This is the very best that we have to work with…”

“Well, then we’re going to have to find something better,” Isabella put, simply. “I’m sorry, but I just can’t follow this loose of a guide. I feel like it’s just going to end in us being completely lost, wounded, and disjointed… Plus how are we going to be able to bring this map around with us? Most of all, even if we did bring it with us, what would it matter? It’s just a bunch of scratches you put in the snow…”
“Once again, can you do better?”
“I can,” Susan finally announced. She then pulled Flanders’ book from out of under her coat. “Remember how I was telling you about this boo that Flanders gave me? It’s a map of the mountain…”
Isabella and Tim nodded, but still looked utterly confused.
“A map of the mountain?” Isabella repeated. “How would somebody even be able to make something like that if nobody has ever charted the mountain?”
Susan shrugged her shoulders.

“I know just about as well as you,” she said. “All that I know for certain is that Flanders had it on hand, and that he gave it to me… he never went into the specifics of how this book might’ve been written, or even who he got it from. In fact I wouldn’t be surprised if he didn’t know the answer himself.”
Isabella didn’t look so convinced, and she opened her mouth to ask a question. Though, Tim had pushed her aside before she could ask it.
“So, you’re saying that Flanders’ owned this book?” he asked, clearly impressed. “That settles it then! Flanders has the biggest and finest collection of books in the town! We’ll be fine.”
“Well, I actually think that Joshua has a better collection of books,” Susan almost caught herself saying. However, she stopped herself when she realized that she was about to destroy her own case.
“But, Susan just admitted that Flanders doesn’t even know that much about the book,” Isabella said. “WE could be walking into a complete mess!”
“Or, this could be genius,” Tim said. “Think about it— there must be tons of hidden crevices that this map has.”
At saying this, Tim snatched the book from Susan’s arms. It didn’t take long before he was leafing through it with a rapid speed— and a grin came onto his face not long after.
“Just like I thought,” he said. “This is probably the most advanced map that I’ve ever seen.”
“What’s in it?” Susan asked.
“You haven’t even bothered reading it?” Isabella asked, looking more worried than ever.

“Of course not,” Susan said, trying to maintain a sense of confidence. Although, she felt just as wavering as Isabella did. Just by taking a quick glance of the map, she was able to see Tim’s point— it was far more advanced than any other map she’d seen. It was covered in webs of tunnels through the mountain, landmarks, grids, and even graphs. While this should’ve been comforting, it only came across as intimidating. Susan had never dared trek so deep through the mountain as the map described. And, even if she had, she’d never tackled a map so complex as this one. It seemed that even a slight miscalculation, or misreading, in some places, would be capable of sending them down a ravine, into a pit of bats, or under an avalanche.
All of the sudden, I’m starting to lean towards Isabella’s standing, she thought.

Though, she didn’t dare say this. Nothing under the sun would’ve been able to convince her to say that she was wrong. She’d already sided with Tim, and was dead set on figuring out what the silhouette might be— in a way, this was one of her only chances at finding answers to either of these questions. She was unwilling to sacrifice that chance.
“Don’t you see the risks?” Isabella asked, at a final attempt to appeal to their senses.
“Risks are everywhere,” Tim said. “But, I feel like we have the least amount of risks that we could possibly have.”

These words acted as a mark upon them. It didn’t matter what could’ve been said after that— hey could’ve come across the greatest proof in the world that this was a bad idea. Tim’s words were enough to tell them that everything would be alright, in spite of the numerous odds against this.

The wind blew harshly, but their feet carried them against it, in spite of this. There was some sort of drive within their hearts.Susan felt a strange urge to keep going, despite the uncertain and unwanted climate that encased them.
“I think that we’re going to deal with a large storm soon,” Isabella said. “Are you sure that we don’t want to head back?”

She’d been complaining like this for an hour— Susan knew this, because she’d counted the number of times that the wind blew into her face, which measured as about a chunk of snow a minute. Though, there was something potent to Isabella’s words this time around. Susan could swear that she could smell the distasteful circumstances in the air. The climate whipped about her, stinging her nose, and choking her throat.

Susan had become accustomed to these sorts of conditions. It was a rare winter day when she didn’t feel this way. Yet, there was something unique to this particular gust of wind. With its coldness, it also carried a sort of warmness. It didn’t just burn Susan due to its cold, but also due to its immense heat. It was entirely unnatural.

At first, she thought that this was all in her head, and of her own imagination. But, then she looked over to her comrades and found that they had similarly distressed looks on their faces. Whatever this force of nature was, it was licking at all of them. And it seemed that it was unwilling to stop resisting them.

For some reason, none of this stopped them. They didn’t even feel compelled to stop. There was a point where Susan’s feet felt leaden, and she had the urge to give up and lie down in the bed of snow. Though, she had an internal element of herself that entirely refused this proposition. She found herself thinking of it in a taboo, and evil light. It left a bitter taste in her mouth.

I can’t do it, she thought. It’s so odd… When I try doing the right thing, I find myself being resisted against, as if it’s the wrong thing. Though, when I try doing the wrong thing, I find myself thinking that it’s the right thing. I just can’t comprehend how this could be possible. Is there something inherent to us all that forces us to think of the wrong thing in a favorable light? Or, is it merely a chance— a roll of the dice— that makes us think of negative things in such a way as this?

Maybe it’s my inherent love for doing what I know is wrong— going against the grain of what Joshua orders me to do— that Joshua is upset with. Maybe that’s also what has made me upset with Joshua. Perhaps my problems in this world have nothing to do with what’s outside of myself, but what’s inside of myself. Perhaps it all has to do with an instinct.

The real question that I must ask myself is this— should I follow my instinct, or shouldn’t I? I’ve begun to discover that both options have favorable outcomes. And yet— they also have their negatives. It’s like judging between light and darkness. Except, I can’t tell what’s the light, and I can’t tell what’s the darkness…
“Hey Susan, check this out!”
She came out of her trance, and found herself standing at the foot of the mountain, in front of the pond— the very same pond where this had all began.
“Over here!”
It was Tim’s voice that was calling out to her. Only, it didn’t seem like Tim’s voice anymore. It was so distant, and far off. Susan could’ve sworn that it even had an ethereal element to it.

A part of this had to do with the fact that she was standing in the spot where she’d thought something magical to have occurred. Though, she couldn’t help but feel that there was something more to it than just this. When she looked over her place on the pond, and over into the snow covered landscape. She started to feel as if she were far off from any other influences— as if she were entirely apart from everything else, and that she’d been connected to something unique. In this moment, she almost believed that the magic that she’d thought to have experienced might’ve been real.
“What are you doing over there? Get over here! You can’t miss this!”

The voice was coming from Isabella this time. Yet, once again, Susan could hardly tell. The only way that she’d been able to discern this was by judging a slight variation in the vibrations of the air. It had been so subtle, that it could’ve been extremely easy to miss.
There’s a lot of things that I could be missing, Susan suddenly thought. I’ve never felt like this anywhere else, except here on the foot of this pond. However, I don’t know why…

She looked around herself to see if the silhouette would appear out of the darkness— to see if there was something that might help explain the way she felt. However, there was no explanation— nothing to compensate for the strangeness that seemed to encompass her.

Suddenly, she started seeing lucid visions— there wasn’t a silhouette anymore, but something other. There was screaming, and she could hear somebody calling her name. She tried to decipher the rest of what they were saying, but the figures calling out to her remained obscured by the limitations of déjà vu and memory
“What’s taking you so long?”
It was Tim again.

At this point, Susan felt her head begin to throb, and herself crash back into reality. The vision faded, slipping from her mind. By the time it was gone, it felt like a lost dream— yet, she found that it still left a bigger imprint than a dream would.

Back on earth, she found her frozenness disappear, and she was back where she was supposed to be— stuck in the snow, being tempted to walk across the pond again. This time, she walked around the pond, and ran towards her friends.

They were about a hundred yards away— at the very moment she found this out, she realized that she’d been in a trance for far longer than she’d thought. Susan found herself running out of breath as she came near to them.
“Why did you guys just leave me,” she asked once she was next to Tim.
He didn’t answer, and neither did Isabella. They both looked awestruck— nearly as awestruck as she’d been in the presence of the pond.
“Are either of you going to answer me?” she asked.

There was no immediate answer, so she followed their gaze— and that’s when she saw it. Up ahead of them, there was an enormous cave. It was about twice the size of Susan’s own house— but it didn’t look anywhere near as constructed or orderly. In fact, it appeared no different from an enormous gash.

However, Susan still couldn’t see what had gotten them to stop in their tracks. That is, she couldn’t see anything until her eyes went above the cave entrance and to the top of the cave. There was an enormous boulder overhanging it. It was as if it was daring them to try entering the cave— asking them to test their bravery on it. Susan knew that it would be too big of a risk to try entering the cave— and yet, she still found herself feeling as if it might be the right thing to do.
“It’s right here— just like on the map,” Tim said. Though, he almost sounded disappointed. “But— the map didn’t say anything about that enormous rock…”
“Maybe it’s because it’s not a real threat,” Susan said, attempting to rationalize with the notion of going into the cave— it didn’t even work on herself.

“Are you crazy?” Isabella asked, driving Susan’s uncertainty in further. “If we try walking under there, then we’ll get crushed. I think that this is where we should stop. I know that I said this earlier, but I really think that this is true now— we’ve pushed our luck and I don’t think we should push it much further.”

At first, Susan was going to give a hasty retort. Though, then she realized that Isabella was right. There wasn’t really a way that she could see them going inside the cave without risking getting crushed. And, even if they did, there was the risk of them not being able to get back out.
What really convinced her and stopped her line of thinking, though, was when she looked into the darkness of the cave. For a flicker of a second. She could’ve sworn that she saw the silhouette.
“Yeah— let’s go back,” Susan said.
For some reason, her word found a way to be the final one.
Dear journal,

Things have jumped far from what they once were when I first touched the jewel and received the map. While I might’ve thought that my country was in shambles, it hardly compares to the madness that is now at my feet. The kingdom has become riddled with a plague, and there are all sorts of heinous crimes being committed. Our farm-owners are doing no better, with their store-houses now running low on food due to an infestation of bugs and rodents. In the meantime, all of our trades with neighboring kingdoms have ceased, and we’re now mired in a position of no trades or profits.

Ah, prophets— they cause such messes. That strange advisor warned me about might come out of denying him. He warned me that everything would come to a halt if I didn’t take all of his words with utmost respect. Little did I know how much it really mattered— how much that I’d be regretting it in the future.

In my defense, I’ve dealt with my fair share of lying advisors in the past. They usually claim all sorts of things in order to keep their position, but nothing ever comes of it. It’s a rare day when an advisor’s absence will cause mass-hysteria.

I only wish that I could’ve been able to take the advisor’s words far more seriously… My father always did warn me that the way you heed a person’s words can often be a great ruler for how great of a ruler you’ll be.

I can’t say that I wasn’t warned— however, I still never expected something quite like this. If my father were to have been in charge of this kingdom still, he would’ve never allowed such madness. He would’ve made sure to have brought it to a close long before there was a chance of this insanity occurring.

In the insanity, I’ve been looking all over for some sort of prevention to repetitions of the problem at hand. I’ve gone from speaking to every advisor, to asking for help from neighboring kingdoms, to even talking to my father’s grave. The only one that seemed to make a difference was the latter option— but I’m certain that any difference I observed was all in my head. It seems that there’s no clear option to my strange plight.

This was when I came to the decision that the map I had written down would be my solution. I had my scribe sent after it, and then reread the map. It was clearly the answer— I’m not sure why I hadn’t seen it sooner. There were so many passageways throughout the mountain, each one leading to where the wizard’s location was. If it was still in the same position, that is.

That was something that upset me deeply. The way that I’d designed everything was so that it had all cornered me into a spot from which there was no sort of escape. The necklace, which had informed me of the wizard’s location, was now all burned up. I had no way of using it as a guide anymore.

Though, at the same time, the map that I’d written out was the very best thing that I had available. I informed my scribe of this, and he had me a horse prepared within the hour. I was shocked by his speed in doing so, but then I remembered the motivation that ran my castle— anything that might put me in harm’s way seemed favorable to them, since they viewed me as a terrible king. Unlike my father, I’d given them no reason to respect me. In fact, everything had begun falling apart under my rule.
“I can only hope that this mission will change their view of me,” I found myself saying.
I was ill-minded. Nothing can change the will of fate.

I’ll say this much to you— after following the map, I’ve learned in perhaps the hardest way that the mountain is a thing that should not be tested. I once thought that it was an inanimate object that could easily be taken advantage of an explored. I thought that the gold mines going through there were something that we had a right to. Nothing could be further of the truth.

In my journey to the mountain, I’ve been perjured of my pointlessly perfect perception of the passages into the mount. The place is riddled with nasty turns and corners. Just the very thought of it makes me squeamish inside… I truly doubt that you’d be able to make it through there, should you try braving the juntoes journey.

I decided to follow the map through the mountain depths, but that only helped me to a small extent. It soon came to be that my attempts at exploration started to lead me astray, and my body was cut against the rocks and jagged bits of jewels and gold. Something that I can be grateful for is the fact that I had brought a guide with me, so that I could be directed through the narrow straits that the mountain’s innards provided me. But, I was clearly arrogant in thinking that this was all the guidance that I needed.

Whether it be the will of the strange sorcerer or the mountain itself, I don’t know. However, it seemed that the place had a mind of its own. Whenever I felt at peace, it seemed that it would bring out an obstacle to make me feel weak again. Whenever I felt assurance, it made sure to strip me of all those feelings. The only thing that I had remaining in myself was a sense of pride— that was something that could never be taken away from me, no matter how hard the mountain tried.

Throughout my entire life, I’ve become accustomed to dark passageways— castles are fool of tricky, hidden passageways, and hardly lit halls. Though, the mountain made my castle look like child’s play. Every portion of it was slathered in an assorted variety of dangers, and my own mind was sent into a spiral at just the thought of having to be able to avoid them all.

By the end of this first journey through the mountain, I’ve been left with more bruises and injuries than any self-respecting king should ever wish to bear. To a degree, I’ve begun to see myself as the butt of all jokes when it comes to being a king. In nearly every circumstance, I prove myself to be a failure on every level. When I don’t then I watch everything else fall around me and fail me.

It’s a strange thing. In my travel through the mountain, I found that every time things seemed to be getting easier, life would find a way to bar down on me and make things become harder. Whether it be a slight creak of the rocks, a bump into a large stone, or the terrible screeching of bats, I was constantly running into something that left me with my heart pounding terribly in my chest, and my body throbbing from various degrees of pain.

Some might call me a weak man for this, but I’m largely incapable of pursuing the wizard through the mountain. As much as I’d like to tell myself otherwise, I’m weak and frail. This entire day of walking has drained me to the point that I feel as if I’ve endured many degrees of torture. I’m aware that most of this is all inside my head, but that doesn’t change the fact that I constantly feel as if I’m pursuing for a way to escape the pain. My weakness may be entirely conjured— though, even if that’s so, my conjuring has made it so that I have no other option but to endure its effects.

Does that then make me weak-minded, as well as weak in strength? Or, does that make me only weak-minded? Or, am I merely hiding behind my own mountain— a mountain of denial— trying to tell myself that things are other than what they actually are.
I don’t know. I can’t ever know. That’s one thing that I know for sure.

The mind is just like this labyrinth that I journey through— complex, burdensome, and impossible to truly understand. I can go through it for a little while— though, I eventually find myself left exhausted, and utterly drained by doing so. The very concept of braving the depths of the mind is just as hard as trying to brave the depths of the mountain.
That’s something that I never considered– maybe I’m dealing with everything at the same time— the trials of my brain, and my body.

No— not only my body. Also, my spirit. I’ve been driven in a thousand different directions, and it’s not entirely something that I can control. I feel as if something is tugging at me. As if something is— watching me. At first, I thought that it was the ghost of my father. After all— my mind is constantly on him, and I’m certain that he’s waiting for me to relieve him from the grave. However, if it is my father, he’s amazing at keeping quiet. I haven’t heard a word from him. All that I’ve gotten is an uncomfortable feeling that there was a presence of something lurking behind me, watching me as if I were some sort of animal in a pen.
