My only clear explanation to this is that my spirit doesn’t feel entirely right about the journey— that it fears that there’s something wrong in what I’m doing, and so it’s trying to strike terror in my heart– it’s trying to drive me away from my goal.

If this is the case, it doesn’t entirely make sense to me— although, I understand that what I’m doing is dangerous. Even if I manage to raise my father from the dead, the price to all magic is known to be a high one. Even now, with my limited experience with magic, I’ve begun to learn that it has wrought chaos that was once unimaginable to me.

If I continue down this path, I know, without any doubt, that it’s one from which I ‘ll never be able to return. And, if that’s so, will I regret it? I hope not— I hope with all my heart that all goes as planned— that somehow, there’s something beyond the scope of my vision— that there’s a hope for me and my father that I’ve been ignoring. I don’t want to continue pulling through the darkness as if it were a vacuum, and I were the only speck of dust that’s remaining. I no longer want to feel alone– as if there’s nothing else to grip onto, and that I’m trapped— trapped to swim through endlessness, and hope that, somewhere, there’s an end.

To distract myself from all of these overwhelming feelings, I’ve tried relieving my burdens onto my partner. To be honest, I think that he despises me for all of my mournful thoughts. He rarely ever speaks to me— and when he does, it usually concerns rest and food.
In other words, the only time that he ever speaks is so that he can get relief— relief from both me and the journey.

I actually find these circumstances to be overwhelmingly hilarious. Despite me paying him pounds of gold to join me, and to go on a sort of quest, he acts as if he’s being disservice— burdened. And, I almost feel that he is.

This doesn’t really make any sense, however, when one inspects the scenario deep enough. I’ve treated him far better than most masters would be willing to. In fact, I would be surprised if there was anybody in the kingdom that paid such large sums of money that I have. This goes to show me that money and wealth isn’t everything— that what I’m doing probably is right.
After all— if you’re unwilling to do something, then it seems that, no matter how much is paid to you, you will always work begrudgingly. Thus, the reverse must be true— right?

I don’t know… I say that far too often, but it’s probably the only statement that I can say with utter certainty. I’m no philosopher, and everything that I’ve ever known has been handed down to me with ease. The work and sweat of labor is invisible to me. The work and sweat that comes with knowledge is also invisible. I feel that I’m set apart from everybody else— but, it’s in the worst place possible. I;’m too unintelligent to speak with the wise that hover around me. Though, I’m also far too wealthy to ever be able to speak with the poor. I have a language of my own that I speak— and, I begin to see that it’s a language nobody else knows ow to speak. I’m forever wondering how I’m going to be able to relate with everybody… However, this is just a way to keep myself from saying that I am constantly wondering if anybody will ever bother to see if I can communicate with them. Because, I can’t. I don’t have the ability. I don’t have the ability to do anything, know anything, or see anything.
The mountain has taught me all of this. Though, that’s not the strongest thing that it’s taught me. Not at all.
What it’s taught me the most is that, when I yell loud enough, my echoes have more depth than anything that I said. Even the emptiness is more full than me.

I need to find a way out of the emptiness. I go into the shadows, constantly questioning. However, that’s the only way I’ll be able to get answers– that’s the only way I’ll be able to get fresh questions.

Susan’s heart was pounding and her chest was beating. Darkness filled everywhere, and her only direction was the snow and the sound of footsteps bounding after her. They were terrible footsteps, with the gravity of a boulder. She could feel the cold emanating from off of her pursuers— furry beasts with a cry that was like no other.
I need to figure out a way to escape these wolves, she thought.

Though, even as she thought this the spray of snow flung into her face, making her burn and slow down. The snow underneath her feet was no more of a help. While it might’ve been her only sense of direction, it was also a wall between her and freedom from her pursuers. As long as the snow was beneath her feet, she was limited by it. Her speed was unable to grow due to the tiredness that the snow provided her.

Why did I ever try running away, she thought with regret. Though, she didn’t bother trying to answer this question. She didn’t want to. While she knew that she’d placed herself in a mess, there was no way out but by running— and so, she was unwilling to give up on the running until she felt that the act of fleeing had finally lost its point, and that the wolves had subdued her.

In the blackness of night, the things that had led up to the fleeing had become very distant and foggy— it was almost as if it were all but a dream– a flake of snow that would melt as soon as it touched her skin. However, she knew that the goosebumps on her skin didn’t only come from the cold, but also from her extreme internal fear.

She’d finally decided to run away from Joshua after another battle that had been wrought between them. It had turned out that she’d returned home too late, once again, and that Joshua had finally had it with her trying to escape outside of village limits. Susan tried explaining herself to him, but it didn’t matter— he was too upset to hear any of it.

For once, he seemed very angry and hot-headed. Susan had seen Joshua angry many times before— his spurts of disappointment and anger had begun to become more pervasive and reoccurring than usual— however, never like this. His entire face had gone red and he went so far as to yell. Joshua never yelled.

Susan tried explaining herself to him but it came to a point when she realized that he wasn’t open to hearing any of them, and that her efforts were futile. What happened next was entirely random— it came out of a spurt of anger and desperation that she’d never really felt before. Her feet carried her out of the house, and they kept on carrying her. They didn’t stop when she was out of the yard, nor when she was out on the village paths. She didn’t even stop when she had surpassed the border of the village.

Even now, she could hear the voice of Joshua calling after her, beckoning for her to stop. She couldn’t help but feel her stomach line with regret— and yet, she didn’t give into it. She couldn’t she knew that she’d pushed too far, and that there was no other option but to keep running forward, ever expanding her boundaries.

A howl filled the air, warning her of her pursuer’s might. She knew that there was no hope for her to escape their wild chase. There was only surrender. Whether the surrender be willing or involuntary, the wolves didn’t care. Both Susan and the wolves knew just how fragile and soft the human feet and mind really are— there was a limited amount of time that they could run, before it came to a point where they could run no longer.

Time continued to slip by, and Susan’s breath slipped with it. She could now feel the wolves’ breath rippling down her back, and threatening to knock her into the ground. Meanwhile, the ground’s chilling texture threatened to subdue her as well— the cold was becoming too much for her body, and she could already feel herself becoming weak due to the strain.
This is all too stressful, she thought. Why can’t everything just be easy? Why does it all have to be so hard to maneuver through?

There was no answer to her question. All that she got in response was the tearing of the wind through her ears, and more howls. Both of these combined to make her ears endure a pain that she thought largely impossible.

The whole mess of the wolves chasing her had occurred not too long after she’d left the village borders. It seemed that the wolves must have caught her scent and begun chasing after her. Before now, Susan had thought the wolves to be mostly mythic creatures. She’d heard stories of the things that they’d done to other people, and even seen firsthand what they were capable of. However, the howl of the wolves and the howl of the wind had always been largely indistinguishable to her. The beasts had always managed to find a way to make themselves remain discreet and hidden. She used to view this as proof that the wolves were nonexistent— or, at the very least, a non-threat. However, with the wolves chasing her down, she no longer had any way of pushing the threat away. The truth had found a way to lunge itself onto her.

The truth always has a way of doing that. Whether one agrees with it or not, it eventually finds a way to affect everyone— and no matter how hard one runs, they’ll never be able to outrun such truths. Its reign is inevitable.

Susan sped up her run, making her legs break into a sprint. However, her surge of energy only lasted so long. Within moments of speeding up, she found herself feeling more winded than ever. Winter had found a way to wear her down to her most basic elements, covering her with sweat and dirt.  She felt deprived of all chances to escape such feelings of exhaustion, but she didn’t allow herself to let it knock her into the ground. There was a will within her— one that was unwilling to give in. Even the wolves could smell it, and their pursuing legs sped up to accommodate for it. Susan had chosen not to surrender to the will of the wolves, but to take her own path— to run as fast as she could, until exhaustion forced her to stop altogether.
“I’m not going to give in!” she said groaning.

For a moment, she couldn’t quite tell who she was referring to— herself, or the wolves. In a way, it seemed to be both— as well as far more. The situation between herself and Joshua was also something that she directed her words at. As much as she wished to deny it, there was something about the argument that had affected her way of looking at things. She no longer felt confident in her stability. It seemed that the world around her was confirming that feeling, for it had sent the wolves out to attack her, and make her feel weak— to make her feel victim to the forces of the world.

Susan racked her mind for another solution to her problem. She knew that there was no way that she’d be able to outrun the wolves forever. The main reason that she’d even lasted so long as she did was because she’d led the wolves through winding trails of the mountain. If she’d happened to guide them through a more open place where they wouldn’t have been at risk of falling off of a cliff, she was certain that the wolves would’ve overtaken her by now.

Feet pounding heavily, one of her steps finally caused her to slip on a patch of sloshy snow. She nearly fell onto her back, becoming victim to either the cliff or the wolves. Yet, she managed to catch herself before this terrible worst-case scenario managed to play itself out.
Being careful not to allow her feet to slip again, her mind returned to the subject of evading the wolves. It was at this moment that her mind came to a jolting conclusion.
“The cliff… That must be my answer…” she thought.
This was before she realized that she was being run by adrenaline, and that the wolves were far too coordinated to fall into the cliff of their own accord.

I’m just dreaming, she thought. Nobody has been chased by wolves and lived to tell the tale… Or else, I would’ve been convinced of their existence until now. If only I could’ve known about the wolves beforehand… If only I’d been informed of a way to escape their clutches, before everything had spiraled down to this.
She halted her thoughts here, realizing that she didn’t have any time to wallow in self-pity.
I can spend my time in contemplation once I’ve become a feast for the wolves…

Her eyes began looking an all sides of her, carefully studying for any sort of answer to her problem at hand. Her vision was extremely limited, with the night’s darkness making sure to conceal all details from her sight.  However, there were a few things that managed to escape this tidy cloak— sometimes she managed to see a branch that was reflecting the moon’s light. In another instance, she caught a bush in her path, and managed to jump over it.

It was at this instance where Susan was able to knock one of the wolves off the cliff. Whether it had been from poor eyesight or the speed of the chase, the wolf wasn’t able to hurdle the bush in time— thus going into a rocky plummet.

Subsequently, Susan tried replicating this moment of success. She knocked one of the wolves off the cliff by grasping a heavy tree branch, and making it swing backward into one of the wolves. Another time, she kicked at a rock on the side of the winding cliff, causing a landslide. This pattern continued, and she managed to knock away several wolves in this procedure. However, she eventually came to a point where this wouldn’t even work. The thin trail that she was on began to widen, and she soon saw that she was coming into an open plain of snow— one where she would surely be subdued by the will of the wolves.
“Think!” she continued to yell to herself, in a frivolous chant.

If the chant had any effect on the wolves, it certainly wasn’t one that was visible to her. One of them leaped into her air, preparing to claw at her face. With a swift sweep to the side, she managed to avoid this— but, it was only one of the many attacks that she had to face. She found herself having to intercept many other attacks, and weariness heaped onto her with a greater forced than any of the wolves ever could’ve. She was coy with her movements, making sure to stay as far away out of the moonlight as she could— however, this wasn’t something that she was able to keep up for very long either. The wolves began to catch onto her game, exploring the same dark parts that she was hiding within. Without being able to see any of the wolves, she became just as at risk of being attacked as she would’ve if she’d decided to try and run in the moonlight.

Beads of sweat started slipping down her forehead— she knew that her scent was becoming stronger every moment that she sat in the snow. However, she refused to move a muscle. As much as she was terrified, and as close as the wolves were getting to her, she couldn’t help but feel as if she had no other option but to stay. The circle of wolves had become too dense, and her own abilities were far too small.

I know that I told myself that I wouldn’t give in or surrender… but I’m just too tired. I can’t go on. There’s no other option… The wolves had won, and I can’t do anything about it… I’m just going to have to accept things as they are. If I try to avoid this, I’m just going to shorten what little that might remain of my life.
Susan was aware that this view was one of utter pessimism. Although, it seemed that there was no other option but to sit, and let the stink of the wolves’ breath come closer.

There was a sudden crack in the air. She looked up into the sky, and could’ve sworn that she saw a part of it divide into two. There was some sort of figure that flew through the air— it seemed to have the grace of a bird, but the powerful speed of a horse. She listened for it, and found that she could hear a swoosh in the air, and that she could smell an odd scent— it was a mixture of the smell of spring flowers, autumn leaves, summer dandelions, and winter snowfall. It went into her body, filling her with a surge of energy. Then, she looked at the wolves. Their eyes shrunk, and their fur stood on end. Even their breath had been weakened, with her now feeling a chill in the place of where their hot breath had once been.

There was another crack, and Susan watched the snow beneath her tremble. However, she herself felt no effects of the trembling at all. In fact, the small patch of snow that she was standing on seemed largely unaffected, with it appearing to have no blemish whatsoever.

The wolves howled in a whining pain that made them seem far less intimidating than they once had. She could already hear their feet carrying them off, and the snow crunching, with an immense speed. She was shocked that their tails didn’t get forgotten in their extreme haste.

Susan would’ve asked what it was that had caused such a turn of fates, however, she already felt that she knew what had happened— something inside of herself spoked to her, giving her the answers that she’d always known were there.
“Who are you?” she asked.

She could’ve sworn that the mysterious silhouette descended in front of her, because she watched the moon and stars become blocked out by its shadow. However, it didn’t bother speaking to her— it remained quiet, as if it had never heard a word before— as if it was nonexistent.
“You’re willing to save me, but unwilling to speak to me?” she said again, hoping to get some sort of response. None came to her.
Susan kicked a chunk of snow in the direction of where she thought that she saw the silhouette. However, it fell to the ground with a common plunk, as if nothing had occurred at all.
“Can you talk?” she asked.
The question, just like all the others, remained unanswered. However, she didn’t let that get to her.

“You were the one who drove away the wolves. I know that you are… When I first met you, I thought that all you were was trouble. However, now that I’m speaking with you, I’m starting to suspect that you’re far more than just that. Maybe you’re both a help and a hindrance— maybe it’s the act of chasing after you that’s the hindrance. Whatever it is, you’re going to speak to me, whether you like it or not. I know that you can affect far more than you’re letting on. And, I know that I’m not crazy.”

She felt a brush of wind up come up against her skin. It wasn’t quite cold. In fact, it had a sort of heat to it. However, it wasn’t hot either. It was a strange mixture of both. It made her feel different things as well— happiness, sadness. Tiredness, and alertness. Strength and weakness. Sight and blindness.

“I can’t describe it…” Susan said. “But, you’ve suddenly made me feel— feel unfortunately fortunate? Happily upset? Chillingly warm? I can’t tell if you touched me with a breeze, with a breath, or with a strong gust…”

As she expected, she didn’t hear any response. Although, she didn’t need one anymore. There was a sort of charm to feeling alone with the wind— the mixture of being with it, but not being with it, gave her a sort of internal freedom. There was something to the solitude that gave her a sense of liberty that wasn’t elsewhere. The light that was coming out of the darkness was one that she couldn’t quite deny herself of. It all had a contrary majesty to it— a beauty that was self-evident. While she couldn’t view it, all wishes to view it had dissipated from her.

Suddenly, the silhouette rushed passed her. Except, she felt as if it had rushed through her at the same time. In fact, it was an odd mixture of both, just as everything else concerning the silhouette seemed to be. She could’ve sworn that she could feel both the past and the future at the same time of the shadow going through her.

Once it had gone by, she shook her head in amazement. The way that she’d felt was so strange and otherworldly that she felt oddly repaired of something that she hadn’t known to be broken. Her eyes went back to where she thought that the shadow had been and found that the moon and stars were back out, pouring onto the spot of the silhouette. There was a word there, engraved into the snow— remember.
Oh I will, she thought to herself. I will do a lot more than just that…

I used to think that the abyss was the only problem that I’d face— that my thoughts and my journey were the only things that I’d have to think on. Not so. It turns out that we’ve come no closer to the wizard. We’ve passed the fixed location on the map, and found the space to be completely vacant.

However, that’s not to say that the mountain itself is vacant. You’d be wrong to think such incredulous nonsense. The mountain is alive; so how could it be that there’s nothing living inside it? It can’t be. That’s why I’ve starting hearing things as I lay down to go to bed… There are creeping things in the night. Eyes surround me, but my own eyes can never catch them— they’re too adjusted to studying the poor souls that dare to come in here— too prepared to pick us off, just for looking around.

Even my guide, who claims to have been prepared for all sorts of things, appears to be terrified by the surrounding circumstances. He’s told me that there are rumors of creatures that dwell with in here. He told me that he’s known people to come in the mountain, only to never return again. Suddenly, the silence that he’s constantly been sharing with me makes sense. It’s not that he doesn’t like speaking with me— although, that might be a large part of it. It’s that he doesn’t trust the mountain.

“The place has ears…” he said. “It frowns on those who walk through it without any sort of respect or fear. It’s been shown to give its wrath upon those who don’t know its paths, and those who disrespect its fragile ground.”

This sort of talk used to be something that I’d pass of with a laugh, and then distract myself from. I’d always thought such tales to be the work of people who are trying to spread doubt and fear— anarchy. However, the surrounding mountain had proven to me that there was nothing that could be trusted… My father’s death had left me a mess behind. And, as I began to clean it up, I started to see all of the other little messes that he’d never cleaned up himself…
“Maybe my father wasn’t capable of stopping everything, after all,” I said, with a laugh.

“You’re not wrong…” said my guide. “He did very little when it came to improving the small corners of the kingdom. While he might’ve been able to clean up the outside, and make all of the aesthetics look nice and pretty, he’ never dealt with the majority of the problems that dwell beneath his shallow surface. Rather, most of the problems in this kingdom come from your father, and his constant neglect of these parts… If you manage to keep your station as king, without finding yourself killed at the hands of a bloodthirsty traitor first, make sure that you don’t forget about these parts of your kingdom. Or else, they’re never going away. They’ll always be there to haunt, and slink about— steadily poisoning what good remains in your kingdom.”
I listened to him, but my ears didn’t believe the words.
“My father was a good man,” I said. “He wouldn’t have left big messes If he knew that they’d end up becoming bigger trouble later on.”
The guide laughed so hard that I found myself feeling disturbingly uncomfortable.

“You really believe that your father was such a great man, don’t you?” he asked. “Well, what about all of the dragons that he let fly around these parts. They’re always looking for gold, but your father— he never made sure to stop them. In fact, he let them come and take all the gold that they liked. They steadily crawled down under the belly of the mountain, steadily infesting it. And, what about all of the dwarves? He let them become steadily overworked, and underpaid. He never cared about any of us, Henry… I doubt that he ever even cared about you…”

All of these words stung me at the heart. But, I couldn’t help but want more… I needed to know how much of what he was saying was true. There was something inside of me that had driven me to this place— and it wanted to know more. It wanted to understand everything.

“Ha! You believe in dragons?” I said. However, I said so half-heartedly. If I were to have been honest to myself, I would’ve admitted that the entire reason I had laughed at him was because I wanted to test what his answer might be— what his response was. I wanted to test if he was telling the truth.
He looked at me and laughed. It was in that moment when I realized that what he was saying to me held some truth to it— that it wasn’t all lies that he’d simply conjured up.

“You don’t believe in them?” my guide said, incredulously. “Haven’t you payed attention to all of the gold that goes missing every year? How about the burnt streaks down the side of the mountain? Forest fires? The rumbling that comes during storms, clearly being the dragon cries? Proof of them is everywhere and in everything… You’ve simply been denying them…”
For some reason, I found myself feeling more unconvinced than I ‘d felt when he’d started the conversation.
“That can all be attributed to other factors,” I said. “Just because it seems unexplainable, it doesn’t mean that the dragons are guilty. I’ve never seen a dragon once in my life.”

“Don’t hold your breath,” he said, scowling at me. “You haven’t seen much of anything. As far as I can tell, you’ve never even ventured outside of the kingdom’s borders. No— if you truly wish to understand what’s going on, then you’ll have to admit that you don’t understand what’s going on— that the impossibilities very well may be possibilities. Otherwise, the world will go out of its way to prove you wrong…”

“This has taken a morbid turn,” I said, trying to make the conversation become light again “Just because my father neglected many parts of the kingdom, it doesn’t mean that he let invisible dragons come inside of it… Do you realize how ridiculous that sounds?”
“You’re denying the fact that dragons could exist… Do you know how ridiculous that sounds? Have you ever gotten the feeling that something is following us through these caves?”

Reluctantly, I nodded in agreement. Then, I jerked my head around my shoulder and back, for safe measure. I might’ve not have been sucked in by the superstitions, but I still had great fear inside of myself.

“People get it all the time in these caves… Especially people who carry a lot of gold, and disregard the possibilities of creatures living within this place… Dragons are very greedy and selfish creatures, who are always lurking about in search of their first chance to strike. That’s why you constantly have to keep your guard up, and never let yourself fall out of the world of superstition. Or else, the world of superstition will thrust the ugly truths of the world upon you. You’ll be forced no other option… You believe in magic, right? After all, that’s why you plan on raising your father from the dead— an utter impossibility. What makes you think that you’re so invulnerable to outside forces acting upon that potential magic? Why do you think that you’re the only one that’s capable of venturing through these mountains, undetected? There are far stranger things than the wizard, Henry… And, you don’t want to test them…”

I didn’t believe a word that my guide was saying anymore, but I decided to keep the conversation going. Perhaps this was an error on my part, but I was far too interested in what he had to say. He had a view entirely different from my own, and he clearly knew things that I wasn’t aware of.
“How did you happen to gain all of this knowledge?” I asked. “Do you come from somewhere foreign? Or, have you gone through the mountain enough times to learn all of this?”

“Both,” he said, putting the words down rather harshly. “You can’t know as much as I do without going to many places and seeing many things. I’ve gone to many of your neighboring kingdoms, and seen them falling into most of the same problems that your own has… This one though— it has an odd spirit about it. I can’t quite explain it, but I feel as if this place has a life to it that I can’t find anywhere else. Maybe I’ m just a lucid dreamer, who like to believe in nonsense… But I’ll tell you what, if you explore this place deep enough, you’ll be surprised at the things you might find…”

The conversation went on for far longer than that, but I feel that this is where it truly ended— where I felt a note of closure. There’s something in this mountain— something in this entire kingdom— that is extremely deep and mysterious. I’m never going to give up until I’ve found the answer to what that might be. I need to know. And so, I won’ stop until I do know…

As Susan came into the village, she had an uplifted spirit within herself. Though, she soon started to see that something seemed amiss. She couldn’t quite tell what it was, but the people in the streets didn’t smile towards her like she’d come to expect. The lamps on each side of the road had begun to dim, and the snow on the paths had gone from white to a dingy grey. It was as if a dark shadow had come over the town, and painted it into a skewed image of what it once was. A pretty house had been turned into a crude, misshapen, dagger. A post had become an oversized claw. A stone had turned into a hurdle, waiting to trip her.

As somebody who was never afraid of the dark, she was surprised to find herself feeling terrified. It was as if something had come within her, and changed her person entirely— making her think thoughts that were completely foreign to how she actually thought.

Knowing that there was an absence of something, she ran towards the only place where she knew comfort to be— home. Despite having made a scene with Joshua, he was the only person who she’d ever known to be able to console her from these thoughts of terror and fear. There was something to the dark atmosphere that surrounded her— an element that left her with a complete feeling of shock and fear.

The spindly path thinned as she drew herself closer to her house. However, for some reason she felt no closer to it. Grimness had taken ahold of her. Her legs became leaden, and nearly felt as if they’d been paralyzed. Her eyes stung, making her vision smudge like a penned letter in water. Everything began to seem wonky and out of joint.

How she could’ve gone from a feeling of complete tranquility to one of horror, she didn’t know. Though, her mind immediately directed toward the silhouette. Even in the pleasurable encounter with it, there had been something wrong. As she came closer to her doorstep, and found each step she took to be harder than the last, she couldn’t help but feel as if the shadow had something to do with it, making herself and the world around her far darker.

Once her hand grasped the rusted iron knob of the entrance door, she instantly turned it and broke into her house. However, when she opened it, there wasn’t the warm and fuzzy candlelight to greet her. She didn’t hear Joshua’s voice, or watch him come bounding down the hall. The whole place felt like a vacuum, abhorrent of any energy.

It was at this moment that it occurred to Susan what she’d felt so oddly out of breath about, and put on edge by. The closer that she came up to her house, the more that she saw how vacant it was— the more she saw that it lacked the usual, casual light that came seeping out of its windows. Her home had gained an identity to her— a place of coziness. It was when she saw how tired it had become that she realized something was wrong— even if this recognition had been entirely unconscious, she now saw how powerful it had been.
But, If Joshua isn’t here, then where is he?

The answer to this wasn’t one that she needed an answer for— just by thinking it, she knew the apparent fact. Joshua had gone out to search for her. He’d gone out into the snowy wilderness, hoping to find her.

Thoughts have an odd way of flipping people over, as easily as it might be to flip a coin. Once again, Susan felt adrenaline rushing through her blood, and her eyes were dripping with suppressed tears. Hardly thinking, she burst out the front door, and let her feet carry her out to where Joshua might’ve gone. However, there were no footprints left. Snowfall had decided to come down heavily while she was inside the house, and everything had already become obscured.

For a while, she ran back towards the borders of the town. She wasn’t quite sure why, She felt that, if she were just able to find Joshua’s figure lining the horizon of the snowy plain, she might be able to catch up with him and show him that there was ano need to risk his life— that everything could be back to normal again, and that there was no threat of peril. However, it wasn’t long before she realized that there was no chance of Joshua being rescued that way. Just as she reached the border of town, reality crushed her. Even if she were to go where Joshua was, the chances of them being able to return to the village, through the dark, were slim. She’d already seen the worst of the snow, with many of the wolves having chased her. Alongside the blizzard, the only chance of her being able to save Joshua would be by pure miracle.
Her pounding feet stop slapping against the lathering snow, and she found her breath begin to decline from weighty puffs to shallow hyperventilation.
“There’s no way to help him…” she repeated to herself several times, before looking back into the village.
An idea came into her mind— an unintelligent idea, but it was the best idea that was available.

Swiftly squeezing her way through, in between the hundreds of cottages in the village, she consistently directed herself towards one building— a building that was always lit up like a miniature sun, and was about as quiet as a den of wolves.
Flanders’ house.

All it took was a knock— then a quick shove of the door open, and pushing through a large crowd of people. She wasn’t sure how she’d mustered the courage to do such things, but love is a force that can cause people to make even the most blustering of mistakes for some people. Her thoughts weren’t centered on herself, but on Joshua. In that moment, nothing else mattered but him. All other concerns, fears, and worries had been pushed away in order to make sure that what she felt was most important was carried out.

She found Flanders standing at the center of the crowd. When she found him, she saw a dumbfounded look on his face. Clearly, he hadn’t been expecting anybody to burst into his party uninvited. However, when he caught sight of Susan’s face, his tone immediately shifted.
“I’m going to need to take a break and have a chat with her,” he said, temporarily shutting down the party. “Don’t worry— I’ll return to host again very soon. Don’t stop in my absence.”

The room filled with whispers, but, like Susan, none of this mattered to him. All of his cares had shifted to accommodate for the thing that seemed to be troubling Susan. Everything else had suddenly lost all of its precedence.
“What’s wrong?” he asked, pulling Susan away into his library.
“Joshua has gone missing…”

Torches filled the night sky, painting it with a gray smoke. Even the moon was blotted out by their marching lights, and the snow strayed from them, melting in their presence. There were hundreds of them, and, wherever they went, they looked like a streaking fiery worm, wriggling all throughout the tiny village.

There wasn’t a place where searching voices didn’t reach, or a hole where their questioning parades didn’t poke their heads through. There was a single trodden patch of ground that hadn’t been studied— and they were still looking, with a ceaseless diligence.

Susan was among these torch bearers, and was now beginning to follow them into the wilderness. She was shocked out how great of a pack Flanders had mustered. The mass of the village had stretched in to the hundreds, and, with all of them combined, they started to look as populous and organized as an ant colony. It seemed that there were far more people in the village who cared about Joshua than she’d originally thought.

However, she also felt her heart fluttering in the massiveness it all. All around her, there were people. They cared for Joshua, and were willing to go to any extent to help him. They’d all come to Flanders for a party— and what they received was a search mission. To a degree, Susan felt responsible for all of this. If it hadn’t been for her, there wouldn’t have been a search party. Joshua wouldn’t have gone missing. The wolves wouldn’t have been preparing for a chance at a meal.

She didn’t used to understand how guilt could be so crushing. However, she felt this understanding now, more than she’d ever felt in the past. Her stomach became curled into herself, and her entire body became stiff.

There was only one way that she was able to channel her guilt from out of herself, and project it into the world. Flanders was grasping her side, unflinchingly. With his arm locked in hers, she felt a strong sense of freedom and relief— a sense that everything would be alright, no matter how hard things started to become.

“Flanders— do you think that we’ll be able to find Joshua?” Susan asked. Her thoughts were very worried and scrambled—but, she found that the very act of speaking her own mind had released some of the pressure that had been building up inside of her. Her words came off far smoother than she might’ve expected.

“I think that, if there’s a way to find him, we’ll find it…” Flanders said, stirring a confidence up within her. “In all of my days, I haven’t found a single thing that I haven’t been able to obtain. Just look at my house for proof of that. If there’s anybody in this village who won’t give up until they get what they want, it’s me.”

At first, Susan couldn’t see his face— just the shadow that the torch emblazoned upon his face. However, the longer that she looked upon him, the more that his head began to turn in her direction. It was as if her eyes directed her thoughts into his thoughts, and compelled him to lock his own eyes into hers. Finally, his eyes did. They became as clear as the night was dim, and their rounded shapes were lit up like gleaming pearls in the face of the torch. Though, while it might’ve just been because of the cold, and the torch’s red coloring, Susan thought that she saw a reddened embarrassment within Flanders’ face. In fact, she could’ve sworn that she even saw a sort of regret and guilt— a wish that, he too, had done something differently.

More melted snowflakes dripped into their torches, slowly dampening their light and their grip. While most of the search-party saw this as an ill-sign, Susan found it more disturbing than that. At each death of the snowflake, she saw Joshua coming one step closer to his own death. The snowflakes returning to the elements signified how easy it might be for Joshua to return to the elements— for him to return to the elements, and disappear from her, forever.

Herself and Flanders were soaked to the skin, and a rash had formed on Susan’s elbows and shoulders, due to them rubbing against her coarsely frozen cloth. When she looked to Flanders, he appeared no better. His graying hair had begun to blead a black, inky liquid— no doubt caused by him dying his hair. His eyes had lost their piercing ability, being covered in ice, and a blackened ring of tiredness. His limbs appeared to be the most uncomfortable aspect of him, with them moving at the speed of a tortoise, and gluing to chunks of the ground’s snow.

All warmth had been sucked from him— sucked from all of them. The delight that she’d once felt was now replaced with a barren despondency. Hope had become a flower. Though, flowers never sprout in the wintertime. Everybody knows that, by the time winter comes, flowers are but a dream.

“Flanders,” Susan asked, “how did you come to know Joshua? I used to think that you and him that had bad blood between each other. But, all of this— you couldn’t have done that for somebody you don’t know.”

“I do a lot of things for people I don’t know,” Flanders said, mysteriously. His tone immediately changed to something much more mundane. “After all, I gave you my books, before I knew much about you. I still don’t know much about you. I’m a man who doesn’t care who you are, as long as you can have a good time. I’m a man of party— not a man of petty.”

Susan laughed. She wasn’t quite sure why— what Flanders had said wasn’t particularly funny. However, it seemed that the surrounding atmosphere had made his words funny. In the harshness of the cold, anything warm— even if it was cold, and just warm in comparison to the current cold— was enough to make her feel a sense of joy.

“But, you did know Joshua…” she said, reflecting upon the words that she’d remembered Joshua saying. “He knew you, too. He wasn’t very respectful of you— but, I know that you two had once held something between yourselves.”
Flanders stirred uncomfortably.
“Yes,” he said. “But, whether or not we once held a friendship doesn’t determine whether or not I knew who he became. He was good at binding books— but, I didn’t know much more about him than that…”
Susan laughed again.
“I guess he didn’t know much about you, either,” she said. “He never was able to give me a reason for why he didn’t like you…”

“Let’s not use the word was, just yet,” Flanders said, trying to be reassuring. “We might still have a chance at finding Joshua.” Flanders paused to give Susan a pat on the back with his meaty hand. “But yes— Joshua is a very unique man. Sometimes he seems to be a scoundrel, and at others, he seems to be quite amiable. His personality can be very contorted, in this way— there’s never a clear way for me to tell who he really is. Though, I don’t want you to fault the old man for these things. I respect him, despite this. He— he’s very unique. If we find him, you should ask him about some of the adventures that he had when he was younger. I find them to be very— enlightening.”

Susan grinned at the thought of Joshua once being able to go on wild adventures. However, what grabbed her focus more was Flanders’ claim that Joshua was a criminal of sorts. He made sure to say such as a passing statement— however, Susan caught it instantaneously, and recognized a spice of begrudging in it. She tried to pass it off herself, but it wouldn’t go away. There was something that Flanders wasn’t telling her, and she was unsure if she were willing to keep pushing, and find out exactly what it was.
She was only able to distract herself by focusing her mind on another statement of his.
If we find him.

At first, this statement gave her a feeling of levity. Her own heart had begun to feel that there was no chance of finding Joshua. When Flanders said that there was still a chance, her dreams rocketed upwards. Though, there came a point when the torches had lost their brilliance, the stars had faded behind the clouds and smoke, and when their footsteps pounded into the snow slower than they had at the start of the search. It became clear to Susan that the sludge of the procession would only become murkier. Already, the spirit of unitedness that had put the search into action had been transformed into a spirit of desperation.

The words, after we find him, continued to repeat in Susan’s head. She heard them as they came to the spot where she’d been chased by the wolves. She heard them as the entire search-party became infected with moans and yawns. She heard them when her eyelids began to fall into each-other, and sleep tried taking her mind by force. She heard the words crescendo as their feet traveled back to the village, crunching through their premade footsteps.

She now realized why Flanders had worded the phrase, if we find him, in the way that he had. It was because he never was certain that they’d find Joshua in the first place. He’d merely implanted the words to instill a false positivity within her— a positivity that she should’ve known was naught.
He was wrong, Susan thought. In believing that we might find Joshua, I’ve only crashed, and realized that the crash would’ve bene much softer if I could’ve been prepared for it…
Bitterness flooded her. It didn’t leave, even when she was placed under Flanders’ roof, and in Flanders’ guest-bed.
“Joshua is gone for good…” she whispered to herself in a sudden disparity. “And, it was out of my own mistakes…”

There was a long debate that she enacted amongst her thoughts, though it didn’t matter. There was nothing in her head that could convince her of her decisions having been the correct ones. The more that she thought about it, the more that she felt guilty. Even in going out to search for Joshua, she knew that she’ slightly failed him.
Eventually, the circle of guilt pressed her so deep that she could no longer traverse it. Sleep had pulled her from it.
A steaming hot breakfast went down Susan’s throat. She felt as it tried to soothe her, and cast away the internal worries. She didn’t let it.

She was provided with a warm fire, comfortable clothes, full access to Flanders’ library, jewelry, and access to more than enough warm food.  None of it mattered, not even in the slightest. The more that she looked at it all, the more unendurable that the surroundings became. She felt completely lost, and entirely alone. None of the provided possessions came close to replacing Joshua.

Flanders bumbling tried to make up for the absence of Joshua by giving her books to repair, and awkwardly attempting at conversation. The only thing that Susan got out of it was the knowledge that, in spite of all of Flanders’ parties, he was terrible at igniting a conversation.

The hours drained out of her, but they felt like weeks. It was excruciating for her to think that Joshua might be out there, lost, and having risked his life, all for her. This thought had been repeating itself constantly— she’d thought that it would leave after her night’s sleep, but it had found a way to persist and grow bigger than ever. She wanted somebody to share her feelings with, but Flanders was among the last people that she would tell about this. As nice of a man as he seemed to be, he was entirely against Joshua— no matter how much he tried to veil his dislike of Joshua, Susan knew that it was there. It had come to the point where it was laughable whenever Flanders attempted to hide it. If she told her feelings to Flanders, she knew that He’d find a way to push them aside, and blame Joshua for his own absence.
“He should’ve known better than to go out last night,” he said. “He should’ve had the same sense that you did, and come to me to rally a search-party.”

While she knew that he meant well, these were some of the last things she wanted to acknowledge. She wanted to remember Joshua with compassion, not spite. Yet, that was the very thing Flanders was thrusting upon her.
Eventually, Susan couldn’t stand the place anymore, and forced her way outside, so that she could find her friends.

At least, finding her friends is what she told Flanders that she planned to do. However, the further out that she went from Flanders home, the more that she realized she had nothing planned at all. Rather, she was just running about, aimlessly looking for a solace that she couldn’t capture. She didn’t want to talk with anybody at all, yet still wanted to speak her mind to everybody that she could. These contradicting ideals eventually drove her to run back to the border of the town.
“It’s all my fault,” she found herself saying. “It’s all Joshua’s fault. It’s all the wolves fault!”

She kept kicking at the snow, pulling herself closer to the border that had gained an increasing pull on her. At this point, the border of trees that marked the town’s end had entirely lost its fearful nature, and had instead become a friend of sorts, to which that she held a great respect and admiration. While she knew that it could strike fear into other’s hearts, to her it now represented the epitome of freedom.
As she tore through the trees, a thought tore through her head.
“It’s all of the silhouette’s fault!” she screamed, letting her words volley at the sky.

Somehow, these words propelled her further, making her sprint at a pace she hadn’t known herself capable of. Except, the sprint didn’t stop. She found that it kept carrying her, until she was past the barrier, and amongst the cliffs that lead to the mountain’s foot. Not even this stopped her, and she found herself continuing to run forward with the speed of a lion.

The ground beneath her cracked and crunched, threateningly. The sky above rumbled, warning of a storm. None of this mattered. Her feet were carrying her somewhere, and she wasn’t going to let the clouds, or the ground, or any other force of nature halt her.

In her sprint of solitude, she felt a terror that there might be something after her— that the silhouette could be behind her, watching her every move and making her slow down— become steadily exhausted. However, she gave this proposition no leeway, and continued forward. She wasn’t able to look behind herself and check for a pursuer, or else she might risk stopping, and crashing into a hurdle of some sort at her immense speed.

The mountain grew ever closer, and she could feel something rising in her chest. It was as if she had some sort of internal compass, guiding her towards the direction of the mountain— telling her where to go. She even felt as if she knew the mountain, in some strange but deep way. Every element of the environment that surrounded her spoke to her— it had a message to tell, and she listened, steadily learning new things about it. The birds tweeted, make a frigid, chilling noise— no doubt due to the cold around them. The ground was covered in wolf paw prints— but, they only seemed to appear under the coverings of trees, where warmth was hidden.

Despite this, a warm breeze traveled through her hair. Her mind was conflicted by all of this contradiction. However, she remembered how the silhouette had come with warmth, and how it had helped her last time she was in need.

At this point, she became inconclusive in what she thought, as well as how she felt about the scenario. It seemed to her that there was no explanation for what was going on, and that she’d simply have to take everything upon faith.

Once again, she let her feet carry her through the confusing map of randomness, until she found that they would carry her no further. She let her vision, which had become blurred from running, adjust. Then, she looked up, and found the mouth of a cave staring into her— the very same cave that she and her friends had become acquainted with.
My friends, she thought.

The cave was speaking to her, telling her to go inside of it, and explore its deep passageways. Yet, it also offered a foreboding warning— the more that she looked at it, the more that she felt alone. She realized how much safer that she would’ve been with her friends to guide her.
Why did I leave my friends…? Why didn’t I go and get them, like I told Flanders that I would do?

She then gained the worry that Flanders would be out looking for her, and soon find that she was missing. However, she no longer cared. Even with her fears of going inside of the cave alone, she felt like that option provided far more liberty than any other option. In the save, she’d find a freedom that she hadn’t been able to find anywhere else. She didn’t know how she knew this, but her heart had a rigidness within it that told her so. The facts didn’t matter— the strangeness surrounding her didn’t matter.

She pulled out her matchbox, tore a dry branch off of a nearby tree, and then tied a wet rag around the bottom half of the branch as a handle. Finally, she used her matchbox to light the branch, making it into a torch.
Once this task was finished, her map of the mountain’s interior pulled itself out of her pocket, and leap into her hands.
She walked into the tunnel, and let the blackness enclose around her. Fear no longer swayed her. The darkness might as well have been the personification of assurance.

Caves are probably one of the crudest places to explore. They’re full of bats, rats, and all other sorts of creatures. Every turn within them could result in one injuring themselves, or making themselves further lost than they were before. There’s rarely a time when one knows where they’re going in a cave. When they do, it typically means that they’ve hardly scratched the surface of where the cave’s secrets might lie. Safety and assurance is something that caves, and their darkness, abhor.

Susan wasn’t quite certain of what had compelled her to search through the cave. At the beginning, she’d thought it to be a supernatural force guiding her closer to Joshua. Though, the farther that she went into the belly of the cave, the more she realized just how clueless and small that she was compared to the rest of it. All of her assurance had disappeared, and all that remained was an odd sense of uncertainty— uncertainty that she’d previously thought herself immune to.

While she’d once thought that the feeling of something following her was irrational, she now found it to be more compelling of a thought than ever. During every movement that she made, she felt as if there might’ve been something hiding behind the noise of her movement. The darkness started to appear like a cloak that could cover up whomever or whatever might be staring after her. Then, she started to even fear the darkness. It had become entirely probable to her that the silhouette might’ve been watching after her, and making sure that she never stepped out of line— preparing to strike, should she make an action that worked against its will.
A shiver went down her spine, but she ignored it, passing it off as a symptom of the cold.

Joshua always did that, she reminisced. It didn’t matter what he might’ve been experiencing— he always conceded, no matter how formidable the surrounding situations might be, that he was never afraid— and that nothing could make him experience fear.
With him back in her mind, she continued to search— however inconsequential that her search might be.

Her torch remained as luminescent as ever, making sure to light the way wherever she went. It provided but a bubble of clarity— beyond that bubble, she was unable to determine anything. However, it was at least a bubble, and she found it to be more satisfactory than anything else around her.

The caverns proved mostly empty, besides the occasional scurrying rat, screeching bat, and skeleton of dead animals. At one point, she thought that she might’ve heard a wolf’s howl, but eventually passed it off as the mere echo of her footsteps.

Eventually, she came to a corner in the mountain where she was sure that Joshua hadn’t reached. With every other possibility eliminated, she was forced to determine that there was nothing to be found in the cavern—everything that she’d thought was there must’ve been in her head including her hunch.
“It was but a figment of my imagination,” she said, sullenly.

As she traveled back through the cave, she found that she did feel slightly better than she had in Flanders’ house. Even with her immense guilt, something about going into the mountain, and defying what was expected of her, had made her feel as if she’d partially made up for the disappearance of Joshua.
“At least I tried looking for him on my own,” she said. “At least I looked for him when everybody else has given up on him.”

Though, even as she said this, a new burden came onto her. She didn’t notice it, but she gained a new responsibility— a responsibility to keep looking for Joshua, until every possibility had been cleared up. Except, there wouldn’t ever be an elimination of all possibilities. While she could hardly recognize that the thought had linked with her, she knew that the notion would be an endless one— that she’d perpetually be caught in a crusade to find Joshua, even when it seemed that there was no longer a reason to look for him.
“I’m not going to Joshua’s funeral,” she said, as she neared the exit of the cave. “I’m not going to let anything that has happened change me, or how I remember Joshua… Nothing can ever change that.”

At first, she felt as if she were talking to herself, Though, then she recognized that she felt as if she had somebody listening to her, the entire time that she spoke. Even as she left the cave, and felt herself become apart from it, she felt as if she were still being listened to.

“Where are you hiding?” she suddenly shouted out to where she thought the silhouette was. “I know that you’re out there! I know that you saved me, but you didn’t save Joshua! Why is that? Why are you willing to save me, but not him!?”

There was no answer, and, for a while, Susan thought that she was just talking to herself, and that she might’ve been insane. There was a long stretch of time when she waited for the shadow to come out. Finally, she gave up, and walked away.
“You will talk one day…” Susan said. “And, until that day, I’m not going to stop talking to you.”
With that, she left the cave in her wake. This time, she didn’t run.

“What were you thinking?” Flanders asked, trying to stay as calm as possible. “Joshua just became lost out there. You couldn’t have possibly thought that you had a better chance of surviving than him— did you?”
“I didn’t go that far out of the village borders,” Susan said, trying to push the complaints aside. “It’s nto like I went all the way to the mountain or anything.”
Even as Susan said this, Flanders remained fiery and indignant.
“You could’ve died out there— we can’t have tons of people going missing, Susan. It’s too deep in the winter to be risking your life amongst the wolves.”
Susan was compelled to tell Flanders about her own occurrence with the wolves, but stopped herself when she realized that, even if he believed it, it wouldn’t help her case.
“I was just looking for Joshua…” Susan said.

“And, why did Joshua go missing? It was because he was out there looking for you. Nobody can do things out there by themselves Sarah doing things on your own is rarely ever the answer. This village is too small, and the dangers surrounding it are too wide, for you to be trying to traverse places of which you have no understanding.”
At saying this, Flanders’ eyes went down to Susan’s waist where the shape of her book was. Susan knew what he was thinking— he regretted ever giving the book to her.

“I understand that you don’t think I was supposed to go out there,” Susan said. “But I had a hunch. I had some sort of feeling in my gut. You’ve heard the stories surrounding the mountain. Don’t you believe that there might’ve been some force compelling me to go into the mountain. Maybe I was being lead to Joshua.”

“Or, maybe it was all in your head,” Flanders said. Then, he laughed. “Look at me— the voice of the party— now becoming the voice of reason. I don’t mean to put a damper on your feeling of exploration, and wishes to look outside of the box. Though, I want you to think for a moment… Is there any actual proof of there being magic on the mountain? Such is the stuff of legends. Not for a second do I believe that the mountain once hosted dragons, castles, dwarves, and the like. It’s all nonsense, Susan. While most of the villagers might tell you otherwise, I want you to be aware of how unlikely your claims are, and how much you’re risking your life out there.”

Susan took a close look at Flanders, and realized something. He looked hardly different from Joshua at all, and seemed no different either. It was almost as if they were the same person. While Flanders hid behind his partying persona, he was the same quiet, philosophical person that Joshua was— he barely gave a moment for fun in any of his words or notions.
“Are you suggesting that I don’t keep looking for Joshua, even when I feel that I might have a lead?” Susan asked.
“No… I’m just saying that you can’t follow hunches. Trust me, they never lead anywhere. You might think that they have truth to them, but they’re always disappointing.”

Susan’s head hung to the floor, and then looked at the room of Flanders’ which surrounded her. She found it baffling how elegant, and yet how dull it all looked. Even in its cozy warmth, it had a calculated, mechanical design to it, which she felt suck all of the life and thought out of everything. A part of her felt trapped within it— as if the place was the only place in which she could find safety, and that the world outside was far too dangerous to risk exposing herself to.

“I can’t stay in this cove forever,” she said, trying to quell her defiance as much as she could. “You can’t hold me back from what I feel is right. I know that Joshua is out there, waiting for me to come and find him. I’m going to find him, whether you like it or not.”

“That’s fine. But, you at least need to bring a search party with you, so that you can have safety. In fact, we have another search party scheduled for tonight. Like I told you last night— I’m not the kind of person who will give up on something once it seems to be hopeless. I’ll keep looking for Joshua, until I feel that we’ve looked everywhere, and that there’s nowhere else for us to look.

“It’s just— I don’t want you to go with Joshua too. You’re the last remnant of him. Once you go, the last part of him goes… Maybe I’m being belligerent here Susan. I honestly couldn’t tell you if I was, so that probably acts as proof in favor of such. However, I just don’t think that going out on your own, without even informing anybody, is a good idea.”

Susan nodded, but she was nodding off to sleep more than anything else. She no longer cared about what Flanders said. The thought that she’d have to give up chasing after Joshua sounded absurd to her. Out of Flanders’ window, she could see night slowly closing in on the world. As she saw this, she knew that time was running out, and that every moment she spent with Flanders was a moment that was being taken away from the efforts to save Joshua.

“I won’t do it again,” Susan said reluctantly. As she said this, she felt as if the words had been emblazoned onto her, now marking her forever— to go against them would be to go against her own word. Though, she felt entirely willing to go against her own word as well, leaving her entirely confused. She wasn’t sure if she was going to keep her word, or instead turn her word into a lie.
“I need to go see my friends…” she said, this time telling the truth.

Flanders opened his mouth to object, but paused before he said anything. Then, he said, “I’ll come with you, to make sure that you’re going to the right place. I can’t have you going out into the darkness again.”

As he did this, Susan gained the uncomfortable vibe that it would be like this from now on— constant monitoring, and an utter lack of freedom. However, she complied with him, seeing that she had no other option.

The sunset had begun turning to twilight by the time she reached her friends’ house— she’d decided to go to Isabella’s, guessing that Tim would be there as well. He always seemed to be at Isabella’s house, hiding from various chores and responsibilities.

There was something to the winter night in the village… Every time she went out during one, she felt her senses and awareness increase to extreme levels. The crunch of the snow seemed to increase tenfold. She could smell the dirt mix into the dirt, altering it into a filthy mixture. Her pace seemed to pick up as well, with her oftentimes leaving her companions in the dust during their walks in the darkness.
“I’ll come back here for you when I’m ready to start the search party…” Flanders said, patting her on the back and leaving.

He whistled as he walked off, with a newfound joy that he hadn’t had during their walk. Shockingly, Susan found herself crumble inside as she looked at the door to Isabella’s house. At first, she couldn’t tell what it was. Though, she soon realized— she’d never come to her friends with a weight like she now had. Nothing had been all that serious between them, like it was becoming now. She’d never needed them for assurance, and now she did. Although, she had a fear that they might not be enough to satisfy her internal conflicts for her, like she hoped they would.

Despite all of this, the wind was far too cold to endure forever. Eventually, time, and chilliness won out, forcing her frozen fingers to rap against the front door. The door swung open to reveal Isabella’s mother, subsequently followed by Isabella’s father, and a parade of Isabella’s siblings. Somewhere at the end of this parade, she knew there was Isabella and Timothy— she could faintly hear their voices amongst the cloud of greetings. However, the mass of people prohibited her from getting any further than that.

“Quiet down, all of you!” Isabella’s mother shouted above the roar of greetings. Then, much softer, she embarrassedly added, “We just came up from the dinner table. We weren’t expecting you, so we didn’t prepare any food. Though, we do have an extra seat for you, if you’d like to sit down with us.”

Susan, of course, complied, and followed after them into the dining room. Saying no to Isabella’s mother wasn’t an option. She was too sweet of a person to justify saying no to— and, when the idea of saying no did arise, her hidden roughness would always come out to remind one why saying no was such a bad idea. In a sense, Susan saw her as somebody who filled the role of mother that she’d never had.

At the table, hardly any of the meal was left, and everything looked pretty scarce. However, when she took a seat next to timothy and Isabella, she saw just how abundant everything was. The abundance wasn’t within the food, but in the conversation— the connection between them all. It was odd, but she felt that the place had a more joyful element to it than any of Flanders’s parties contained. When she was amongst them, and their conversations, she felt as if she’d been underwater for a long time, and had finally resurfaced to see the light of day. Everything seemed far more peaceful and meaningful. There was a sudden recognition within herself of why Joshua must’ve disliked Flanders so much. It wasn’t because of the type of man he was, but the type of life he led— the life of a person who constantly and consistently pretended to represent happiness, and a type of joy between people, but only embraced a spirit of materialism— a spirit that only focused on the outward, rather than the inward.

Jokes flung in and out of the table, good discussion was had, and great questions were raised. Not once during her entire sitting did she feel uncomfortable or out of place. None of them even made reference to the disappearance of Joshua, or her stay with Flanders. It was almost as if they could read her mind, and that they knew what topics to stay away from.
Eventually, the conversation died down, and she took her friends to Isabella’s room to chat.
“Don’t stay up there for too long,” Isabella’s mother called after them, “I still need you to do the dishes!”
Behind the shut doors of Isabella’s room, the questions immediately started pouring on.
“How did Joshua go missing?”
“What made him think that it was ok to go out in the snow?”
“Did you run away again?”
“How did you get the search party going?”
“What were you thinking the entire time?”
“Are you alright?”
Eventually, Susan followed after Isabella’s mother’s tactic, and used a shout to silence all of the noise.
“I can’t answer these all at once,” she said. “I’m just going to have to tell you everything from the beginning.”

By satisfied the look on her friends’ faces, she could tell that this had been their strategy all along. Susan followed this precedent set by their faces, and told them the entire story of what had happened, only leaving out the part concerning the silhouette.

“I was there when the search party started, as well as Isabella,” Timothy said, proudly. “But I can’t say that we found any sign of Joshua… Not that this means much, since we couldn’t find a sign of you at the time, either.”
He looked out the window, and to the murky shape that the mountain had turned into during nightfall.
“Are you sure that you felt like he was in there?” Isabella asked, skeptically. “I don’t know why… But, it just seems strange.”
Susan didn’t entertain the skepticism for a second.

“Flanders said the same thing to me... I don’t think anybody is going to believe it, except for you guys. That’s why you’re the first people I came to— because I knew that you’d be the only ones to believe it. Here’s the thing— I need somebody to believe it with me. I can’t be alone in this. You guys remember the cave, don’t you? The place was weird! A thousand things could be hiding inside of there! Why couldn’t one of them be Joshua?”

“How are you feeling?” Isabella asked, raising this question for the second time in their conversation.

Timothy scooted back into a corner, and awkwardly said nothing. As Susan spoke, he stared at the ceiling.

Susan didn’t say a word, nor could she think of one to say. She felt as if her friends’ lies had left her with no other option but to sit and think. Outside the window of the room, Susan watched as heavy snowflakes pressed against the window, and the wind threw itself heavily upon it. It seemed that nature had decided to use all of its forces to make the window break apart. Though, the window didn’t break, or waver.

She wanted to go further, and let out more of herself— though, she found that she was only moments away from letting out a cascade of tears. Even her words, which she thought would be therapeutic, had become another hindrance to her.
“None of this is your fault, Susan,” Isabella said, patting her on the back.

Both of their words were half-hearted in Susan’s eyes— they didn’t actually have much to say or offer. Though, for some reason, she felt a change inside of herself after hearing them.

“From what I can tell, being stuck with Flanders is pretty terrible,” Tim continued. “But, at least it isn’t Bart that you’re stuck with. Trust me on this— Bart isn’t the type of person that you’d want to be stuck with.”
