More laughs came out, and the room became a sort of sanctuary, closed off from the troubling winds of the outside. The world had suddenly become smaller, making their world become far bigger.

In this moment of clamorous unison, Susan wondered if she should tell them all about her experience with the silhouette, and the way that it had saved her from the wolves. Though, she eventually went with the reasoning that she’d used when she first told them her story— they wouldn’t believe her, even if she told them. There was nothing that could convince them of such a strange event happening, and she knew it.

Amidst her conversation with her friends, and her newfound reassurance, she found that there was something else that wouldn’t go away. It wasn’t just the guilt— it was also a feeling of abandonment. When the sunset had turned to pitch black, and the pitch black had eventually turned to sunrise, she realized what it was— Flanders had never bothered to come back for her. And, even if he’d intended to come back for her, Joshua had never come back for her either.
The pat on the back that Flanders had left her with now felt more hollow than ever before.
Have you ever tasted sunlight…? No, of course not. How about darkness? Perhaps you haven’t. In fact, I’ll bet that you haven’t. Though, as for myself— I have.

Before you go calling me insane, I must remark that you could very well be right— I’ve been stuck in a cave with my guide, Hemlock, for a week. This might just be a hallucination of mine, or some sleight of the senses… Yet, that doesn’t change the fact that my senses have convinced me of this phenomenon having an incredible significance.

Hemlock and I were traversing through the caves, as one does, whilst I mourned over my father. Rightfully so, Hemlock ignored my whimpering and continued through the caves as if I weren’t even there. Though, this is where things become interesting. Hemlock stopped following the map that I’d written in the book, and instead went off of his own instinct in his anger.

By doing so, he brought us into a cave, which lit up with flames the moment that we walked in. On every wall, there were torches, bursting with an extreme energy. As I stared at them, I felt a part of myself disappear into them. It was as if the torches had the ability to snatch up a bit of my soul.

As this happened, I saw several gargoyles sprout from the ground and ceiling, until they merged together into the shape of a pillar. At first, I thought that all of this lucid imagery was of my own mind’s design. However, then I looked to Hemlock and saw that he was experiencing the same insanity that I was— his eyes looked about as wide as my fist. Not that my fist is much to scoff at…

Anyhow, the room suddenly lit up with all sorts of colors, turning into something that looked similar to a giant rainbow. Then— nothing. The entire room turned black. I felt an enormous scrape tear down my stomach and arms. A girlish scream of terrible proportions sprung into the air. I’m not quite sure who’s It was— it may have been my own, though I find that doubtful.

Whomever the sound was emitted from, I greatly thank and credit them for it. For, at the very moment of their scream, the lights came back on. It was for but a split second, and the lights returned me to the wretched chasm of stretching black, immediately afterwards. Though, in that solitary moment, I saw a being that would make the hearts of even the bravest of people turn to a mush. If only you could’ve seen it— it was a sight that might’ve made your legs turn to dust.

Now that I’ve spent a sufficient time preparing you, I now must inform you of what the thing actually was— it was a sort of wraith, having taken on the form of a massive silhouette. It was the very definition of terrifying, with it appearing to be capable of growing to the size of anything it wished. In the glimpse that I saw of it, I found it to be a very disturbing sight. It had a pulsating, formless figure, and spiky bits flowing all throughout it. In a sense, it was similar to bodies of water such as rivers or streams, except, instead of eventually pouring into some sort of basin, it poured into itself— it was some sort of perpetual motion machine, if one could believe in such a thing.

Having returned to the darkness, I was forced to consider a thought that was extremely disconcerting— the darkness wasn’t a natural one, but a darkness that was being maintained by the silhouette. A far more disturbing thought followed after this one— the darkness, wasn’t just maintained by the silhouette. The darkness was the silhouette.

I felt my whole body begin to weaken at the thought of this, so I began to grope and punch against where I thought the silhouette might’ve been. It was no use, and it perhaps made the situation even worse. As I did this, I felt the air be ripped from my lungs, and my head begin to dizzy. It became clear to me that I’d reached a point where there was little to no options, and I was being forced to be the victim of such. I’m sure that it’s easy to criticize me now, since you’re not part of the situation. Though, for me, in that moment, I felt as if I were entirely stuck, and that nothing I could do would make a difference.

Then, something just short of a miracle happen. There was the sound of a torch lighting, and I could see a slight orb of it amidst the immense darkness. A clang resounded, and then the scent of something burning and becoming charred filled my nostrils. For a moment, I felt trapped again.

Then, I watched the wraith light up right in front of my eyes, into a cold blue flame. As this happened, the room around me came in and out of clarity as well. I couldn’t quite tell if I was supposed to rejoice, or to feel sorry for the poor creature for suffering such a plight. Though, whatever I was supposed to, or not supposed to, feel, I felt it, along with far more. Somehow, the monster had been vanquished— and, such didn’t have to be acquired by magic, or any sort of mystical means. At least, none that I was aware of.
Hemlock’s face shone by the torch, smiling at me. It was one of the very same torches that had been on the wall.
“Thank goodness that you found this!” I said.
He laughed.
“You can thank me for a lot more than that,” he said. “Are you done with your constant complaining yet?”

I, of course, told him no. Though, I knew deep down that I didn’t really mean it. I could never mean such a thing. Somewhere, lodged within me, I had a requirement to find the truth, and cast away the darkness. And, my best approach to that was looking into the darkness, even if it meant for the darkness to consume me.
As we walked from the cave, trying to go our fastest to escape it, Hemlock asked me a question that both discomforted me and gave me something to think on, at the same time.
“Why are you doing any of this?” he asked me. “What’s the point in it all?”

Most people might have the answer for what they’re doing. I’d assume that you do as well. Though, when I really put my thought in, I realized that I didn’t quite know why I was doing any of this. My father was utterly gone; from what I could tell. At the end of the day, there was no way to tell if my journey would be worth it. Despite the love for my father, I began to question if my quest was as rational as I’d initially thought. If it was, then it was certainly becoming harder for me to see it.

Even if magic worked, and was capable of raising my father from the grave, I was starting to see just how untrustworthy it was. The wraith had proven to me that there was no solidity in anything— that, even magic could be dismantled by rather conventional means.

“I have a question for you,” I asked. “Why do you bother with me? You don’t care about the payment, if our words can mean anything… And, you don’t care about the recognition either, since you think that this is all a joke? What drives you?”

“Nothing drives me… Well, maybe I’m too noble in saying that. The money does drive me. The journey drives me. The sense of exploration and seeing the unknown drives me… I believe that I’ve seen every corner of this mountain, but, if today is any proof, there are still things that I haven’t seen. Suddenly, I’m incredibly interested in the concept of raising the dead back to life. I doubt that it’s possible, or even that it’s worthwhile. Yet, I’m willing to see this through, and keep my mind open. Who knows— I might just end up being incredibly surprised with what I might find.”
I smiled, even though I knew that he couldn’t see it in the darkness of the caves.
“Then, that’s my reason too…” I said.

As hollow as my words might’ve sounded, I had put my entire mind and soul into it. I’d suddenly realized how wrong I’d been to think that I could do this to save my father. I needed to keep my mind elsewhere, and my thoughts in a new direction. In a direction towards discovery, and exploration, not senseless wondering, and wishful thinking. I knew, beyond all knowing, that I’d finally figured out what I was supposed to do and where I was supposed to go. I was finally on the right track— and, the right track was not knowing what track you’re taking.
“For the last time… I made a horrible mistake, and I’m sorry.
It was Flanders who was talking. Ever since the night before, Susan hadn’t let up about how he’d abandoned her, and neglected to start the search party. Ever since then, he couldn’t stop apologizing.
“I know that you’re sorry,” Susan said. “I understand why you forgot.”

In actuality, she still couldn’t understand why Flanders could’ve forgotten. Joshua would’ve never been able to forget. He’d always follow through, no matter how tough that might’ve been for him at times.
“I got sidetracked,” Flanders explained, fumblingly, “I was so buy and caught up in what I was doing, that you completely slipped my mind.”

A horse whinnied, and pounded its hooves into the snow. Susan shuddered, but then remembered that she was in the enclosed safety of the carriage car. Not even the snow that flung from the Horse’s rushed movements could affect her.
“Hopefully this can make up for what I did last night,” Flanders said, employing weakness and fragility into his vocal chords.
“It should definitely help me with a few things,” Susan admitted.

Notes of snow played everywhere, turning the air murky, and Susan’s ears red. Susan’s home peeped over a white hilltop, as groggily as a squirrel might peep out of its hole in a tree. In the odd sunlight that struggled from out of the clouds, the windows of the home blackened and whitened, as if it were blinking awake.
“There you are,” Flanders said, stopping the carriage to let Susan into her yard.

Susan jumped into it, and knocked her elbow against a pole. The pain stung her, being multiplied by the brittle weather. Her eyes turned to the pole. In that moment, her pain far exceeded what she even thought it could be. The pole that she’d bumped was the sign for Joshua’s shop— Joshua’s book repairs.

Susan felt her face heat up, but pushed back the emotions that might’ve swayed her. The sign continued to nudge at her. Though, even when she reached the door of her home, she didn’t let it have any effect on her. Her mind had finally traveled elsewhere.

Even inside the house, she didn’t see the house. All that she saw was Joshua. It wasn’t until she was in the library that these visions finally let up. She was searching for a book of hers and Joshua’s that they’d both read together. A specific book, that meant a lot to her. Her fingers thumbed through every single book, before it finally reached a bright read one, with a golden spine. On the cover of it, there was the silhouette of a mountain.
“The Secret of Blackneck,” she said, with a grin.

The book had been one that Joshua had written and read to her as a child— it was one of her favorite fairytales. She wasn’t sure what it was about it, but she always felt as if she were transported to another world whenever she read it.

Her memories flashed back to when she was a little child, lying in her bed as Joshua read the book to her. At the time, she’d thought that there was nothing that could replace it. Of course, she eventually came to know other books, and see this one as something that wasn’t particularly special. Though, there was still something odd to it— a uniqueness that she couldn’t seem to find anywhere else that she looked.
“The uniqueness was never in the book itself,” she said, in the solitude of the room. “It was in the person that I’d read it with.”

While she didn’t feel that it was the proper place to put such a special book, she had to put it in the pouch with her mountain map. As she did so, she couldn’t help but look back at the pouch with the same sentimentality that she’d looked at the book with— Joshua had also given the pouch to her— said that he’d used it on his journeys, and that it was hers now.

When she looked at the library as a whole, she felt like there was something special to all of it. In every single book, she could see Joshua’s mark— something that he’d touched, changed, repaired, or read. It was all a part of him. When Susan looked at the books, she felt as if she could see Joshua reading all of them. It all mattered to her in a way that she’d never thought it would.
“I’m never going to forget any of this…” she said. “Never…”

There was a moment of silence that she offered the library, before finally leaving. She was aware that the practice was ridiculous. However, there was a sacredness to everything in there. Just the mere change of it altered it from how Joshua had left it.
Back outside of the house, Flanders was still waiting in the carriage. He smiled at her cheerily, and looked as if he were ready to do anything.
As Susan sat next to him, he said, “How did it go? Do you feel better now?”
“Yes.”

She must’ve failed at this, because Flanders frowned at her with an upset glare.
Realizing that the book reeked with foul conversation, Susan tried changing the course of the conversation.
“I think that I’m going to Isabella’s house again, tonight,” she said. “I liked it there. I think I prefer sleeping at her house than yours.”
This diversion backfired, and Flanders only looked more provoked than he already had.

“You’re not going to be sleeping under anybody else’s roof until we find out where you’re staying,” Flanders shouted, as a gust of wind started yanking at his hat and clothes. “Isabella’s house is packed full— I highly doubt that they have enough room to consistently keep you there.”
Susan wanted to object, but found there was nothing she could object to. All of Flanders’ points were both valid, and unarguable.
“It worked out last night,” Susan said, trying her best to muster up an excuse.
“And look what came out of last night…”
At this point, it seemed like nothing could convince Flanders, or put him out of his bad mood.

“We were acquaintances and nothing more…” Flanders said. “But, I do care for the man. That’s why I plan on sending out another search party after him, tonight.”

As a child nearing the rebellious stage, I’m sure that you’ve already begun to see that. He might’ve been good in his craft, and a good, kind person at times… but, he could also be a bit misleading…”
Flanders’ mouth closed, before swinging open again.
“That’s all I’ll ever have to say on the subject…”
Susan didn’t bother to test these words.

Nighttime isn’t like most other times of the day. It’s cold— harsh. It’s full of dangers, and hidden things that are willing to jump out at you. It’s only light that can ever combat the night— and, even that is susceptible to perishing in the midst of night.
In spite of this, something that always is capable of keeping night’s powers at bay is the comfort of a home— the walls of civilization that manage to keep all dangers from overcoming it.

Susan slept through these comforts, feeling that there wasn’t much to fear— that is, not much to fear other than the fact that Joshua wasn’t being searched for likle Flanders had told her. Though, there was something beyond that that she couldn’t see. She could only smell it.

Flanders house had a very unbecoming smell to it— due to all of the people that came in and out of it, the house was a soup of smells— both good and bad. However, this smell was one that Susan wouldn’t have expected.
Smoke.

It weakened her lungs, to the point where she felt it choke her and force her to cough. Her eyes, even in their closed position, became watery and puffy. A heat encased her, and she had to pull her blanket off to keep herself from waking up due to the warmth.

Though, this was but a simple fix. It quickly happened that the heat surrounding her and the smell of smoke was too much to keep her mind from waking up. It was a force that she couldn’t shove away. Rather, it was a force that shoved her own will away, and caused her to submit to forces that she would’ve rather been able to ignore.

Her eyes opened, and she ran out of the guest room and down the hall.  Normally, she would’ve shouted about the smoke, so as to alert everybody in case there was a fire. Her own house had nearly caught on fire in a past winter, when Joshua had gotten so tired that he’d forgotten to smother the fireplace. The only reason that the house had been saved was by Susan waking up, and warning Joshua of it.

Although, Susan now was acting upon a curiosity that overrode any of her other desires. It seemed to her that there was no other way to ensure knowledge without making sure she saw the source of the fire herself. She had a feeling that, whatever the fire had been caused by, it had been purposeful. The night before, there hadn’t been fires of any kind. Flanders and her had gotten home late, and his servants had turned off all of the fires for him— those were the orders that they always abided by.

Susan had found it particularly odd that night because Flanders had said that there was something he was busy with— something that he needed to do that night, and that he didn’t have time to put it off until the next day. Yet, in spite of him staying in the downstairs as Susan herself went upstairs, the lights stayed off the entire night. Flanders never had his servants turn them back on.

There was no telling why, but this entire event stuck out strongly in Susan’s mind. There was a unique fire in Flanders eyes— a devious cunning that she’d only ever seen in people who were looking out to cause harm. She knew that this wasn’t Flanders at all. Yet, she couldn’t deny what she’d thought she’d seen. It was too obvious for her to deny.

As she walked down the halls and through the senseless maze of smoke, she was forced to remember what a mess Flanders’ house really was. In every corner, there seemed to be something new that she’d missed— something left to discover, something left to evaluate, and something left to think on. There was almost never any clarity when walking through it, even with its sparse amount of rooms. It was as if, in spite of the house’s small amount of rooms, it had formulated a way to trick people no matter how much they tried to get it down.

Susan felt a slight guilt that she wasn’t telling anybody about what she was looking for, or offering any warning. She knew that, if she were the people around herself in this situation, she would want to be informed immediately, so as to make sure that she was safe. However, her own urges had gotten the better of her internal will.
Downstairs, the smoke became thicker than icy water. Every place she looked, her eyes became filled with a cloudy gray. In this moment, she knew without a doubt that something wasn’t right.

Realizing that there would be no way for her to tell or see what the cause of the flames might’ve been, she started calling out in warning as loud as she could. Then, once she felt that she’d given enough sufficient warning, she began to swim through the smoke— through the smoke, and to the aid of whoever or whatever might’ve been trapped within it.
“Is anybody there?” she asked, as she passed through the ashen covered entrance of the library.

At this point, it didn’t matter to her if anybody was there or not. She knew that, if anybody was there, they were already beyond saving. In front of her eyes, there was a massive flame. It towered over her, making her body tremble in terror. The flames were so blindingly bright that she felt as if she were looking into the sun— that she was only mere feet away from touching it.

She inched closer, looking all over to see if there were any books that she’d be able to spare. Though, she soon saw that there were none. Everything was completely incinerated. Even as her hope began to peak, the fire roared and thrusted her back— ending all chances that she’d once thought to be there.

Seeing that the ceiling was on the verge of collapse, and that the entire library was becoming unstable, she ran from it and towards the exit. While she’d come to the library in a fervor of bravery, she now felt complete terror throughout herself.
“Help me!”

Susan wanted to keep running, and to ignore the voice. Her entire mind was pulling her away from the flames, and the burning room. Although, her heart said otherwise. There was somebody in the room that needed help, and she knew that she couldn’t just leave them there. There was a sense of moral responsibility in her that yanked at her. Like a piece of metal being drawn to a magnet, Susan was drawn to help.

Running into the flame-engulfed room, with a rush of energy, she found herself feeling more bravery than she’d experienced in a long while. All of her thoughts had gone away, and all that she could feel was her pure emotion, compelling her to act.

Once amongst the flames, she quickly found that she wasn’t in as favorable of a position that she had hoped to be. The room had gotten far more burned up in her time away from it, and she could see that she hardly had a chance of escaping the room.

Why did I bring myself in here? She thought. I already knew that I wouldn’t be able to pull myself out of here if I came in. Not only that, but, whoever is in here, they’re probably already out of reach.
The exit of the room groaned, and then collapsed into itself. There was no longer any other option out. Susan was trapped, and she felt as helpless as bread in an oven.

“Where are you?!” she asked, looking for the missing person by using all of her senses and abilities. If they were in the room, they offered no answer— and, they allowed Susan to go deeper and deeper into a feeling of dread— a feeling of confusion.

All of their clothes were covered in water, as well as the bookcase.

For a moment, Susan didn’t recognize the voice. The flames had drowned out most of its unique inflections, and the smoke had whittled down the rest However, when she paid closer attention, she caught exactly who it had been— Flanders. He was stuck amongst the flames, trapped like a lost animal.
“Flanders— how did you get stuck there!?”

There’s no other option. There never was.”

“Flanders, we need to go— now!”

Her eyes swam from ever part of the room, making a careful and calculated assessment of everything around her. Yes— the window. It was in the back corner of the room, back where the burning bookshelves were, but a good distance away from where Flanders had initially been. She could already see the words of escape now, sucking her from her current plight. Everything around her already started to seem like a dream— but an obstacle that had decided to get in the way of her attempt at sanctification from it. The shards of glass on the floor, sparkling and crackling amongst the flames, represented the new hope that had rested within her— in the breaking of her hopelessness, she’d gained shards of hope. As cutting and as risky as it might’ve been for her to accept them, she realized that it was her only chance at escaping everything that was trying to swallow her whole— her only chance at finding a way out of the mess at hand.
“Flanders, we need to find a way to get through that broken window!”
Flanders didn’t say a word, as head become expected out of him in Susan
S mind. Though, he did point to another stick of lumber that was hanging from a nearby ceiling. Susan looked at it, and could already taste the freedom and liberation that might come from using it.

“Some on Flanders!” she said, pulling down the planks of wood handing from the ceiling, with the best of her ability. “If we don’t pull these down, and use them to muffle the flames, then I’m not sure what we’re going to do…”

Rather, she used these thoughts to augment her efforts. In recognizing that her exercises were futile, and that there appeared to be no way out, other than death, she sought a way to avoid such desperation. It was her only option— her only choice. Otherwise, she’d have to burn, willingly.

“This isn’t the time to be focusing on books. I would’ve thought that, by now, you would’ve been the one to recognize that. Think for once, Flanders. Maybe he was stirred by my speech to him, she thought to herself. However, even as she thought this, she recognized how absurd it was. “The rafters,” Flanders continued to repeat.

In fact, she was starting to suspect that it was infectious, because she too felt it within herself. It were as if every thought of theirs had been captivated and detained, and they were now looking for a way to retrieve them— at least, that was how Sarah felt, and how she thought Flanders Felt.

“Flanders… I don’t understand,” Susan said, making sure to repeat herself as well. They’d become subject to circumstance, and were now scooting by on mere chance to make sure that they weren’t utterly destroyed and beaten— to make sure that they survived. “Be clearer… What do you mean by, ‘the rafters’?”

For a moment, all that Flanders could provide was pointing. Though, when he saw that this wasn’t sufficient, he picked up one of the planks, and started banging it at the ceiling. More planks fell down, and he tiredly used those planks to break down more planks from the ceiling. Susan felt terrible fror standing idly as Flanders did this— she felt as if there were more that she should’ve been doing, in order to assist Flanders in his attempts to escape. Flanders provided her no words, no signs, or any other sort of clue that may have made her aware of how she too might’ve been able to offer her own fair share.

Eventually, she caught on to what Flanders was doing— he eventually used his longest plank to knock down the remaining planks in the ceiling— thus, all of the knocked down pieces of wood had provided a trail of rafters in the ceiling, all the way to the window.
“The rafters,” Flanders said again, wheezing. Susan could clearly tell that knocking down all of the remaining planks had taken most of the energy out of him. “We need… We need…”

Susan completely understood at this point, even without the help of Flanders’ words. The rafters offered a way for them to travel to the window, by swinging from each rafter by arm to arm. In that way, they didn’t have to worry about the flames below, or having to rely on a flimsy balancing act on a bridge, in order to make their way out of the house.

Immediately, Susan started stacking the planks of wood on top of each other, forming a sort of ladder for herself to climb up. Flanders Quickly caught on, and started doing the same. Once the ladder had reached a certain height, it started to no longer look like a mundane ladder, but instead a tool of salvation.

“Flanders, we’re both going to need to climb this upward!” Susan said firmly, grasping each wrung that had been made in the odd structuring of the planks. “Don’t waste your energy— pace yourself. We can’t have ourselves falling into the flames.”

Even as she said these words, she felt that they held more meaning to herself than they would’ve to Flanders. As she looked to the window, she saw the fresh air— she saw the clean lighting. She saw a lack of smothering claustrophobia. She badly wanted out there— she wanted to be free of the heat, and to return to a place where she knew that she would feel at rest. In spite of how much she hated the cold, she knew that she’d be greeting it as a friend once she was amongst it again. Although, she also recognized that her eagerness may become her downfall, should she allow her actions to ride upon it.

As she looked into the flames, she felt her face begun to melt into it, and become a part of it. She felt herself tumble deeper into something that she couldn’t quite understand, but felt a great terror for. In this looking into the flames, she saw that she needed to move away from them as quick as she could, or else they’d move into her. However, she also knew that she couldn’t move quickly, and that the flames had stolen all of the swiftness that had once resided within her. In this way, she felt a worry that she might never be made whole again.

Her fingers and knuckles grapes against one of the wooden rafters. They were hot to the touch. Yet, in the midst of all the other flames, they actually felt cool, and almost relieving to hold. Her feet felt the planks wobble beneath her. She knew that they were becoming impatient of her efforts, and were now willing to collapse at any minute. However, Susan denied them of the ability to strike fear into her heart. Instead, she only grasped harder at the rafter, and then had her other hand grasp it as well.

As she did so, she felt a wish to break out into laughter, and to embrace the success that she’d just earned. Though, she also knew that she had to hold it in. In holding the joy in, her grasp weakened, and she had a sickening pit of fear fall into her gut. An odd, unnatural mixture had taken root, and she no longer felt as if she were under control. Rather, her emotions had decided to move around in an unruly manner, acting as out of sorts as a pack of wolves might’ve.
“Just grab at the other rafter,” Flanders said, doing as best as he could to be encouraging, even with his haggard voice.

She now saw everything, even the biggest of barriers, as but a small wall, getting in the way of her attempts at succession.

Realizing that she was now faced with a great risk, she looked behind herself for reassurance— and then found that Flanders was far behind, only just beginning to make his travel upon the rafters. In seeing that she could make it across the rafters, Susan saw that she’d convinced Flanders how he could make it across the rafters— thus, making it across the journey that would save his life.

“You can do it!” Susan said. Though, even as she said this, she watched Flanders’ finger slip. Then, it was his hand. Suddenly, he was only hanging on by one arm, and Susan could clearly see that he had no way of convincing himself how to escape his plight. He’d become far too weak to escape what he’d fallen into.

At this moment, Susan saw as rush of smoke go passed him, she couldn’t determine if it had been her own imagination, or a miraculous phenomenon, but it looked as if the smoke had strengthened Flanders, and lifted him up. Indeed, he even was able to regain his left arms’ grasp onto the rafters.

Susan felt her own arms start to slacken, and her own muscles begin to weaken. Though, as Flanders came closer, none of this had any weight over her anymore. She felt a relief that she realized couldn’t be matched.

And so, Susan added two last words.
“Goodbye Susan…”

Don’t think for a moment that I don’t have anything planned out. Any map that you can devise won’t match the cunning map in my head. Any though that you can have is a thought that I’ve already considered, and devised a way to exploit. I’d love to watch you make me fumble— throw me to the ground. Though, if you can’t do so, then you’ve only proven your own proclamations of my future defeat wrong.”

I prepared to say something in response. I felt dumbfounded by the fact that I’d been left in a position where I could only be speechless. However, then again, I was always terrible with words. And, this voice— even with its speech impediment, it was still incredibly slick in every word that it said, and its articulation of words was still one that I knew I’d never be able to match. I almost felt embarrassed, knowing that I’d have to come up with a way to follow up every word that it had said, and try to formulate a retort. I knew that all of my words would fail me— there was no possible way for me to shoot the voice’s words down, because they were simply too overbearing, and powerful. My mind had been brought to a point where it was so worn down that it could no longer fight with intellect. I truly feel that I’d hid a barrier, and that my tact was no longer any match.
“Well, at least you have a challenge,” I finally said. “After all, you’re speaking to a man of royal heritage, I’m sure that you’ve become very frustrated and stumped tonight, because of that.”

“Ha! You think that you’re a challenge just because your father was royalty? I hope that you were being sarcastic… I’ve waged war with my mouth against nearly all kinds of things, in all manners. II have yet to fall flat in my efforts. I’m not the most intelligent of this world, I’m afraid… there are some that, if confronted with me, would be able to wipe me off the face of the earth with ease. Although, there’s one thing that I do have over them— I’m savvy enough to have made sure that I’ll never need to confront them. I choose my opponents, and my opponents are always ones that I can easily manipulate… I’ve never met a day in which I lived in fear of being beaten by somebody who is inferior to me, because I only ever allow those who are inferior to me to know little of me. An opponent can never harm you if they don’t even know of your existence…

“Your father was nothing ssspecial. I can easily attest to that… From Everything I’ve observed, he was just as much a coward as any other person who sits in a high position. He had no courage to him… he merely led your kingdom as if it were his chattel, never stopping to consider that he might’ve been looking at things the wrong way. Rather than putting his people, and the protection of them, first, he put himself above everybody else. He was a terrible person, to be certain, and I simply can’t see how one could be proud of sharing his lineage…”

“That’s not true!” I now shooed, aghast. The conversation had taken a turn for the worst, and I no longer felt as if I had any hand in anything. I’d clearly been put to a standstill— not that I already hadn’t. It had simply taken me this long to recognize the truth of the situation.

“You don’t have any hold over me!” I continued, making my shouts louder and more prominent than ever. “I know what you’re playing at— you’re trying to make me feel scared, and weak. But, I’m not going to fall for it. I know the truth of the situation. My father was a great man, and you’re only trying to make me lose confidence in him!”
“On the contrary— I’m trying to tell you the truth, and your father was a horrid man. If he were any good, he would’ve made sure to rid the kingdom of me.”

The voice’s sparks for eyes then began to move closer to me, from out of the black. At first, I thought it was just in my head. There was an entrancing element to the fiery orbs, and I was half convinced that the sight of them growing, and propelling toward me, was but an illusion that my mind cooked up, during my distraction. The dragon had certainly put me in a place where I’d begun to doubt myself, and my senses, in nearly every way that I could. However, the eyes became as large as the moon, and I eventually couldn’t reconcile with the idea that it was all in my head. Rather, I had to submit to the obvious, however horrid it might’ve been. The eyes were coming closer to me— and, they were far larger than I ever would’ve liked. So large, that I knew they could’ve only been from that of an enormous beast.

Suddenly, the place where the two constant jets of smoke were pouring out of came into my view— it was two metal holes, atop a crude plane of metal shingles. Though, I soon realized that I was mistaken— the metal shingles were in fact scales— and the holes were nostrils.
The eyes were too close now for me to deny what I was staring at— I was looking into the face of a—
“Dragon!” I shouted.

“I use this line often, but I mean it more sincerely now than ever— you’re far dafter than I initially presumed…” The dragon said, practically biting at me as he spoke his words. “Of course I’m a dragon— wait, my apologies. I’m not a dragon, but an overgrown lizard.”

The dragon’s humor was shrewd, to be sure— not that I could appreciate its humor in its presence. I tried my best to get a clear view of all of it, so that I could fully understand what I was looking at. However, my observations came up blank. I quickly realized that I was wasting my time, and that the dragon had made sure to completely cover itself in an inky darkness, so that I couldn’t clearly make sense of it all.

“Wha— why— how…?” I continued, flabbergasted. I admit that I perhaps came across as too weak and feeble— definitely something that the dragon seemed to despise, and lack respect for. However, this didn’t stop me from continuing on in my shock. In truth, there was no way for me to fully reconcile with what I was seeing, except through shock. It’s only fair to be understandable toward this predicament that I was amidst.
“how? Why?” the dragon asked, in a demeaning tone. “You ask me these questions as if I’m the one to blame for my existence… I never give away the answers to mysteries for free.”
“You revealed what you are— isn’t that an answer to a mystery?” I asked.

The dragon smirked— it was the kind of smile that made me wish I had been eaten by the beast. As its mouth moved, all of its scales cracked and scraped with it— the very act of it smiling made such a raucous that my ears pained to hear it. Though, that didn’t even match the pain that my eyes were in, while looking at it.
“Oh— you already knew that I was a monster,” the dragon declared. “I did nothing, but terrify you by showing that you were more right than you could’ve possibly imagined.”

At this point, I didn’t know how to respond, or think. If I were to be frank, I don’t think that there is a reasonable way that I could’ve responded. I clearly had made a terrible move in making myself out to be royalty, in my conversation with the dragon— it now had a clear and reasonable motivation to eat me— and, there didn’t seem to be any moves that I could make that were wise ones.
“Well, if you’re going to reveal your face to me, you might as well reveal your name,” I said.
Meanwhile, I was actually trying to weasel out as much information that I could— not that I think the dragon hadn’t already caught on.

“Ah yes…” the dragon said. “The old name question… You humans have such a petty, sentimental mentality towards names— don’t you? To be honest, I don’t care for names. They give too much of a label. Everything that I do will now be categorized by my name. If every individual were to be honest with themselves, they would recognize that the practice of names is an absurd one… Every living thing changes far too much throughout its lifespan to be limited by a single title. I would argue that I’m not the same dragon that I was yesterday, let alone the same dragon that I was ten years ago— or, a century ago, for that matter.”
As the dragon said this, I heard its voice become increasingly volatile, and hostile. In fact, it seemed that its very breath had a deadly heat to it.
“Hmm… I appreciate the concept,” I said, “It’s certainly a lot to think on. But, I think it best to give you a name. One that suits you.”
Smoke started filling the air— so much so that my lungs felt as if they were on the verge of collapsing, and my brain began to feel completely deprived of all thought.

“Go on…” The dragon said. Its smile was mostly faded, by there was still a sinister crack in the corner of the monster’s lips— one that allowed me no forgiveness for the being. I knew that the suffering I was experiencing was a suffering that was wrought upon me through a barbaric and childish vengeance– one that, in spite of all the dragon’s years, it hadn’t outgrown.
I guess that, even dragons don’t know how to rid themselves of petty grudges.

“Smoke…” I found myself choking, towards Hemlock. He still hadn’t awoken, throughout the entire conversation. Though, as my thoughts became more and more sluggish, and my consciousness began to fall away with a greater rapidity, I started to see exactly why Hemlock hadn’t awoken.
The smoke had a sleep-inducing element to it.
“Sssmoke…” I heard the dragon say, with a disgusting relish. “I like that name.”
It was the last thing I heard, before finally becoming subject to Smoke’s spell…

The mountain weather tasted nicer than usual. The spray of snow didn’t bite too hard, the winds were mostly tame, the clouds were forgiving towards the sun, and the ground had ceased to threaten collapse, or landslide.

Susan clasped a wet, weathered stick in her hand, occasionally using it to help pull her up the steep mountainside. Of course, there wasn’t actually any reason for her to be clasping the staff in her hand. It was a sort of comfort to her— a thing that she held in her hand for leisure. The stick itself provided no support. It was soggy from being buried under the snow, from which Susan rescued it. It was thin, and rotting, no doubt due to age. It was only the thought of the branch that actually provided her support— the thought that, even if she tripped and fell, the stick might be able to catch her.

“I simply can’t see how this is supposed to work…” Tim said, in a nasally voice. Since the night before, he’d come down with a cold. One might’ve thought that this would’ve driven him away from scaling the mountain with Isabella and Susan. Although, he’d managed to make it into an excuse— he’d been supposed to work with his parents throughout the entire day, but he’d managed to put a bag of pillows under his sheets, and escape the house through that attempted deception.

“And I simply can’t see why you bothered coming out with us, then…” Susan said. “For the last time— I think that there’s something up with the mountain. I’ve seen strange shadows here, had odd experiences, and have the overcoming intuition that Joshua might be here, somewhere… Like I told you before— if you don’t like climbing the mountain,, and you’re queasy with the idea of going ot explore the inside of caves, that’s fine. You can go back home, while we try and figure things out. But, if you want to be of any use to us at all, then sticking here is proabably the best way to go for you. It’s definitely the only thing that makes sense, to me…”
Tim didn’t seem convinced, but quieted himself.

Susan knew that she’d been lucky with getting her friends out of the village on a day with such amiable weather. After all of the bad history between them and the mountain, this seemed to be a stroke of sheer luck— should the weather on the mountain have been bad, Susan had a feeling that she might not have been able to convince her friends to make such a dangerous expedition up into the mountain.

To a degree, she concurred with Tim’s statements. All of them did. At this point, Susan had become close friends with the mountain, and everything had started to feel played out, and repetitive. All reason to go into the mountain, and explore, had lost most of their past weight. After all— she’d gone exploring many times before, and turned up with virtually nothing. If there were any good answers to her constant barrage of questions, she had a strong feeling that they wouldn’t come to her any time soon— and, most certainly not on the mountain, since the mountain had yet to prove itself of anything.

However, the fact that the mountain had failed to prove itself was a double-edged sword. Despite most of them being widely recognized as rumors, and folklore, Susan had the strong inclination towards believing in all of the mysteries surrounding the mountain. The fact that there were so much abounding professions of magic surrounding it had led there to feel as if there were good reason to go up to it, and continue searching— even if nothing happened to turn up, throughout all of her searching.
“I just wish that this cold would end…” Isabella said.
Susan grinned.

“Not me… I love the cold. I know that you might think me crazy for saying that. Though, I’m afraid that it’s true. The cold is something that I love, because it makes warmth feel so much more alleviating. It reminds me just how much the warmth really matters… I know that this might sound ridiculous— but, there’s a sort of beauty to winter, and the snow in the village. I know that our village isn’t much, and that we rarely get anything done inside of it— and, I know that we don’t have much influence. However, I don’t really care. When I look at the village, covered in snow, I see something more than just a village… I see a window into myself, and what the snowy village has forged me into. Similarly, the mountain stands to show me what I wish to become…”

“I wish to become a person who’s warm, and comfortable, rather than a walking icicle… Is that too much to ask?” Time said, sarcastically, as he wiped his runny nose with his sleeve. He quickly began giving off a series of coughs straight afterward.
“The more I think about it, you really should’ve stayed home Tim,” Isabella said. “Not only are you sick— but, if your parents find out that you’re gone from home, they’ll be worried sick…”

“Oh well…” Tim said. “I’m sure that they’ll do well without me, in spite of that. While I don’t want to be out here, covered in snow and battling a potential fever, I don’t want to be at home stuck lying in a bed all day either— and I definitely don’t want to be subject of constant labor while feeling like this.”
Susan smirked.

“Yes, I suppose that I can agree with where you’re coming from,” she said. “Personally, I probably wouldn’t want to be alone in abed all day either, if I was in your position. Still though— just because you’re suffering, it doesn’t mean that we all have to suffer with you...”
“Misery breeds company,” Tim said. “Maybe I came with you guys just so that I wouldn’t be alone like this…”
“Just make sure that you don’t make me catch what you have,” Isabella said, in extreme irritation. “If there’s anything that I hate the most about winter, it’s how easy it is to get sick.”
Susan only nodded in agreement.

“But, I think that we’re beginning to lose focus on what’s important here,” Susan said. “This mountain is something that we can’t take our eyes off of— remember how tricky the place is. It’s not a place that looks kindly upon cordial conversation. Rather, it doesn’t care that we’re conversing. It will attack an unwary traveler, unbiased towards their predisposition. Yes— we can’t take our focus off the mountain.”

Susan’s face tingled in the cold weather. Her feet, which had been riding perilously close to the edge of mountain cliffs, had gone extremely numb. Her hands had too— except, unlike her feet, they desperately looked for a warmth that hid from them. No matter how hard she tried, the cold seemed to overrun every part of her body. However, this wasn’t entirely a bad thing. In fact, Susan felt a sense of ease, and unity with the environment around her, as she walked through the mountain boroughs. Normally, this might make somebody think that she was mad. Yet, Susan could only see the brilliance in everything, despite her pain. In a sense, she could feel Joshua as she felt the cold beat down upon her. She could remember all of the fun that she once had with him in the snow— when she was younger.

Youth has a mystical element to it. While most can’t remember good portions of their youth, there always seems to be bits and pieces that are left behind— things that come into the brain, and mold you— shape you. They make one think of themselves in beautiful ways, as well as see who they were built into who they are. Childhood memories are the stuff that seem to make a person. However insignificant, a memory that stick with somebody always seems to have a word to say on who that personas.

Although, just as often, there are the childhood memories that don’t seem to mean anything— the ones that glue to the back of one’s mind with no particular reason at all. Even if they can be pretty sights, at times, it becomes hard to decipher meaning out of them. Mainly, it’s because there’s seldom any meaning to them to begin with. Memories are odd that way— there’s no real telling which one’s matter, and which ones don’t. Typically, it’s the declaration that a memory doesn’t matter that’s harder to make.

Susan’s memory of playing in the snow fell somewhere in between. She couldn’t remember any great revelation, or lesson taught to her, amidst that snow. She didn’t really remember much of what she was thinking— or even much of how she was feeling. The entire memory was incredibly foggy, and sparse in details. However, there was one element that seemed to surpass all of the limits of bad memory— an unmatchable joy, which she could only see as a true representation of her childhood. A gem that couldn’t quite be matched.

“Susan, it’s been a while since you’ve said anything,” Tim said. “We’re pretty high in the mountain now— and, I’m admittedly getting tired. Do you know where we’re going? Because, if you don’t, then I really need to stop and rest. I feel like my legs can’t carry me any farther…”
Susan turned around to look at Tim. His lips were blue, his ears were a burning red, and the rest of him had been turned frail against the cruel winter winds.
“Why didn’t you tell me?” Susan said, now feeling a mixture of shock and sympathy. “You look terrible. You need to go back home.”

Susan looked above, and saw the clouds— they’d suddenly become black and foreboding, with the dark and brooding atmosphere about them that she might find in a nightmare. She could feel it in her knees— it made her quake, and gain the wish to take flight with the rushing that a jackal might make. Yet, it had also grounded her feet in their place, as if they’d become oversized chunks of ice.

“I did tell you,” Tim said. “I told Isabella too, but she didn’t really care… Didn’t you hear us talking over the past fifteen minutes? Or, have our voices turned to mere wind to you? Honestly— I can’t believe that you didn’t hear me, after all that. It’s this sort of thing that really makes me wonder about you, Susan…”
Susan felt her face become red hot, but tried to keep herself calm and collected.
Did I really miss all of that discussion? She found herself thinking. How can I get so lost in my own thoughts? It just doesn’t make sense…. It didn’t even feel like ten minutes…

AS she looked at her friends, she could see that they hadn’t been kindly to each other either. Just by the look on Isabella’s face, she knew that Isabella had been guilty of berating Tim over his complaints– it was clearly their nature to do so, especially without her own interference. And, Tim’s swelling nose, and puffy eyes told her that he was feeling far sicker than she could’ve possibly suspected. She now felt more self-anger than she’d felt in a long time…
“I’m sorry Tim— we can go back. We just have to beat this storm,” Susan said.

Though, even as she said this, she began to doubt herself. No different from a typical evening on the mountain, the storm was just as formidable and foreboding as usually— and, they’d spent too much time upon the mountain, and trekked way too far, to ahave any hope of avoiding it.

“I don’t know what we’re supposed to do,” Susan suddenly said, as she watched clumps of snow come from up out of the ground, and whirl around her head. She head to duck, and bury her head toward the ground, in order to avoid it all.

“We just need to keep going into the cyclone, back to the village…” Isabella said. “It’s better that, than staying within the storm where we’ll surely beobliterated, and threatened… We’ll be no better here, than we will be down there. We might as well take the risk, and keep going downward. It’s the only way that Tim will be safe.

“Susan knew that this was true— but she couldn’t help but feel incredibly wrong at the prospect. She knew that, if she were to go back down the mountain, she would succumb to her typical story of abandoning her goal, only to try climbing back up the moutntian, and repeating the cycle all over again. Despite her worry for Tim, she felt terrible at the idea of ending and abandoning the vvery thing that she knew was right, and needed. There was something inside of her that simply despised the idea of giving up— giving in— and falling into the same cycle that she’d continuously tried pulling herself out of.

“I can’t do it,” Susan said. “You’re going to have to take Tim down, back to the village, without me. I need to stay in the mountain, and go into the cave that I’ve gained an intuition within. The place seems full of wondrous splendor— I can’t deny the fact that, when I look at the place, I feel alive in a dsort of way. I feel as if I’m coming closer to finding Joshua, and reuniting my family— bringing everything back to how it once was. I just can’t abandon that intuition. It’s rooted to deep within me…”
“Just give it up, Sarah!”
Susan could barely see Isabella, but knew that the words had come from her— there was no mistaking the strained sound in her voice for anybody else…”
“I can’t give it up,” Sarah said, with a choke. “How can you even suggest that?!”

“Joshua isn’t coming back…” Isabella said. “We all know that it’s true— even you do… We all care about Joshua deeply… but, the whole reason that we went on this mountain trek was to see if there was any evidence for what might’ve happened with Flanders— to see if there was anything strange in the area. There isn’t anything strange. This entire place is exactly the same as the hundreds of other times that we’ve gone into this area. And, to be honest, I no longer feel like making this trip is worth it anymore. The more I think on it, the more I realize just how much of a mistake we made in coming there. Tim is hanging on by a thread, and so is your mind. Come on, Susan— wake up to the facts. If there was any way for us to make it out of here, without risking our lives, then we’d come up to the mountain far more often. But, I think that’s why you constantly come up here— because it’s so risky. I think that, in the risk, and in all of the threats of danger, you gain a sort of feeling of mysticism around it— you feel as if everything is larger than life. But, here’s the thing with all of that… Eventually, you have to stop taking risks, and realize that you’re putting your life on the line every time that you come here, and threaten the mountain’s superiority over the village… I don’t like to do this sort of thing Susan. But, I’m telling you right now— you need to give up your fantasy, and face the facts. There’s no way that Joshua is coming back. The sooner you get that into your head, the better— it’s the only way that I’m going to be able to take Timothy back to the village safely…”

The wind began to blow even more furiously, and Susan started to see what a mistake that she’d made. Her guilt became all-encompassing, and her chest throbbed at the mere thought of how delusional she’d allowed herself to be. All of the mysteries on the mountains— all of the beliefs that she’d seen things, felt things, and experienced things– it had all been a hoax of her mind. A fantasy, pumped up to make her believe that she was far greater than she actually was. She now saw just how stupid that thought really was…

Her hair threatened to blow away with the gusts, and her eyes swam about in fear, with them becoming as cold as icicles. All of the mountain weather seemed to have turned against her— in fact, it seemed that all forces of nature had decided to turn against her, and that she was a mere victim, caught amongst a lashing out of its anger.

“I wish… That I’d never come here…” Tim moaned. His voice was mostly drowned out by the ferocious wind, but Susan could still hear it penetrate through. There was something so elegant and provoking to the sound of the storm, and all of the wind. Though, Susan had been reminded just how deadly of a monster it could really be to them.

“Go on,” Susan shouted to them. “Head down to the village. I can’t leave the mountain, but I can’t force you to stay here either. The only way that Tim is going to be safe is if he’s brought back somewhere warm and dry. I don’t even know why I let him come. Go on— save yourselves, and don’t bother coming back for me! I’ll be fine here!” Though, even as she said this, she watched as the storm loomed over her friends. Its wintry mouth began to sweep under their feet, and engulf every bit of their scope of vision. No matter how far Susan’s eyes searched the snow was covering the landscape— it seemed that the storm had smeared across everywhere, and that it was only attempting to gain further ground.

The initial thought that she’d had when traveling up the mountain, when she’d looked upon the weather in deep satisfaction, had been deeply uprooted. She felt as the entire storm began to take away all of her sense of courage, and peace. She was left with a coldness within herself— and, all of the beauty that she’d previously seen within the snow was now replaced with a dark pit, which harbored in her gut with the hollowness of a rotted piece of wood.

Her friends tried tumbling down the mountain, but it was clear that the option was one that would lead them astray. There was no way that they’d be able to make it to the village. Even though most of the storm had clouded her vision, her intuition was still able to see past it— and, she was able to sense that there was no hope beyond the snow. Rather, the snow had smothered all of it.

“Never mind,” Susan said, charging towards where the mountain was. She could see a faint glimpse of where a cave might’ve been— it was but a silhouette, but, as it shone into her eyes, she felt a sense of awe and alleviation. She knew as she looked at it that it would be a place where they’d finally be able to be rescued.
“Guys, the cave is up here.

She pulled out her map-book, to reassure herself. Of course, there was no way to tell where she was amidst the flinging bits of snow— no, she had to base all of her decisions upon intuition. Thankfully, she didn’t waste her time bothering with them. She knew that she didn’t have any. The wind called out to her, barking that all of her time to guess and think was up— she’d have to act, and Susan was doing just that.
“We can’t waste any more time!” she shouted. “The snow is coming closer to us, and if we dawdle, we’ll be swallowed whole!”

She wasn’t able to tell if they could hear her, or if they listened to her advice. She didn’t bother to look, or listen. She couldn’t— everything had been dulled out by the sharpening storm. It had made sure to make all of her senses near impossible for her to measure.

As she neared the cave, she felt the wind pull at her, slowing her down as if she were a piece of metal, and the storm were a magnet. An awful fear whipped up her insides, and she worried what might happen if she wasn’t able to make it into the cave, and if the snow proved itself to be the victor. Eventually, she could no longer let these thoughts have any hold over her mind, and she pushed herself forward with a sort of drive that could only come out of pure motivation— reasoning and logic had been completely removed from her every action. She’d found that it had been too much of a hindrance to her, and that she had too little time to give it any adherence.

Breathing heavily, she saw the opening of the cave come closer to her. It was still curtained behind a transparent but belligerent flood of wind, though she could still see it clear as day— even if the cave had been but a speck in the sight of her eyes, she still would’ve been able to envision it with a crystal-clear clarity. Her mind was so focused on the cave, that her mental image of it was already more than enough to give her full motivation.

She felt as the snow ceased, and a blackness wrapped around her like a comforting cloak. She looked behind herself, to see if her friends were anywhere to be found. Though, when she looked, all that she could find was a furious, ever-changing smear of dark gray, and a faint glimpse of light amidst the whole of it.
“Did you make it? Are you here? How’s Tim doing?”
Her words echoed amidst the darkness, bouncing around as if they were smooth pebbles being skipped across the surface of a pond.
She cringed. The pond had frozen over now. And, no new rocks were tossed at it, in order to break the pond’s shell of ice. No answer.
There would never be an answer, because her friends weren’t there to answer her. They were lost, and she was finally alone— trapped. Stranded. And, her only option was to go deeper into the cave.

She looked deeper into its mouth, and felt all of the dangers that might be held within it threaten her. Her heart pounded with the nervous terror that a squirrel or small bird might at the sight of a approaching human…

Deep into the mountain, she knew that there were secrets beyond what she could conceive. She was sure of it just by the amount of ominous senses that she felt when looking into tit– if the ominous feelings didn’t come from a sort of sorcery, then she was certain that she didn’t know what sorcery was. She badly wanted to seek out this magic, and gain full understanding of it— mastery of it. Though, she also wanted to be able to feel a sense of safety, and security. She didn’t want to have to explore the dangers of the cave alone.
She wanted her friends.

Deep inside of Susan, there was an imbedded fear of the dark— of groping deep into places uncharted, and having to look through it with nothing but her wit to protect and guard her. Such an experience was the sort of thing that made up Susan’s nightmares, and kept her awake when she tried to sleep at night. She wasn’t sure what quite had made her fear the darkness so much— somewhere, in the reserves of her mind, she knew that there was one of those memories. It was the sort of foundational memory, that had built her into the person that she was. However, unlike the needless memory between herself and Joshua, this memory had utterly slipped from her mind. She reached out to grasp it, and to taste its fullness again— but it alluded her grasp.
“It seems that the important memories like to slip away, while the small ones stick around, and take up space…” Susan thought to herself.

She looked back into the cave, and knew these words to be a paramount of truth. Though, she also felt her words echo around her— speak back to her, and almost taunt her. As the words did this, she felt a sort of insecurity within herself— an instability of her mental faculties. The more that she thought on what she’d said, the more that she realized there was a haunting truth in the words.
What was most important to her would always be forgotten…

It was in this moment, when she realized that, if she never found Joshua again, he would be gone from her— forever. Eventually, her memory of him— all that she knew of him— would lapse. And, all that she’d be left with would be a faint skull of the person that he really was.

Susan let out a deep sigh. It barely made a nose, amidst the roaring wind outside, and the words of hers that were still echoing around. Yet, this didn’t make any sort of frustration against her. In fact, this all made Susan feel rather at peace.

In knowing that everything would be alright, and taken care of, she gained a sense of reassurance— even in the face of the coming storm, she felt that everything would work out in the end. She felt the cold grip around her again, and give her the same strange comforts that she still couldn’t quite grasp or understand.
“I know that I shouldn’t feel at peace…” Susan said. “But, I do… Why is it?”

She couldn’t give herself an answer. She knew that she never would. The true answer was, there wasn’t an answer. Her thoughts were unique to herself, just like every storm was unique— just like how every snowflake that fell upon the ground was unique.

There was never anything that was quite identical… Susan suddenly realized that with a sort of glee. Even as she began to forget Joshua, she knew that she herself would eventually change— her reliance upon him would eventually subside, and she would learn to live in a world without him. There was a terrifying— horrifying, in fact— element to this all. Though, she knew that it was the truth. She knew that she would learn to get over the problems that currently seemed all encumbering— and, she suddenly realized that a part of herself was alright with that. She suddenly realized that it was alright for a part of herself to feel alright.

Her eyes shut tightly, and she fell into a sleep that she’d grown all too familiar too. It was an old friend, that she knew nearly every bit about. And yet, as she fell asleep, she found that her sleep was unlike any other sleep that she’d had before.
That was alright.
That was her snowflake.

It was day again— at least, that was what the brightness leaking through the cave, and into her eyes told her. It was still storming horribly outside the cave, and she found that she was laying amongst a thick layer of snow. In fact, it was only the spot that she was sleeping on that wasn’t full of snow– her spot had all melted, and she found that she was lying down in the midst of a massive puddle...
“Well,” she said. “It would’ve been nice if I noticed this while I was sleeping.”

Though, she knew that she’d been partially aware of it in her sleep— even if it wasn’t enough to wake her. Her dreams of swimming within the frozen lake— falling deep under it, after her attempt to chase the silhouette— reminded her that her dreams had been warning her all along. She was simply too stupid of slumber to notice it.

She tried her best to dry herself off on a dry cave wall, at the far back from the blistering blizzard that was taking place outside of the cave. She felt a bit of regret while doing so— she remembered her friends, and how they must’ve been suffering within a similar storm— how she’d left them, and how they might’ve been worried sick for her. Yet, she wasn’t compelled at all to go looking for her friends. In fact, she had a sort of motivation to stay hidden within the caves, where they might constantly wish to look for her— where they would always be too afraid to look. A part of her knew that, if her friends weren’t able to find her, then that would mean there was still hope that Joshua was hidden from sight— that he could be found somewhere that she’d missed. This was, of course, something purely bred from optimism. However, Susan still clung to it with fullest sincerity. Deep inside of herself, she didn’t want to let go of Joshua— even if she knew that, at some point, she’d eventually have to.

For the second time within the cave, she cringed. The cold had been unkind to her, as she was sleeping, unlike what it had promised. At every movement she made, he could feel it brazenly rubbing against her skin, making her feel as if she had burns all over her body. She wanted to take off her clothes, and remove the burns— but, she hadn’t bothered to pack another pair, thinking it to be inconsequential. The truth of the matter was, there was no way for her to remove the discomfort that was beginning to encompass her— she was on her own, and without any chance at solace…

“Well, this has been a fun journey…” she said to herself, opening up a satchel that she’d brought with her. “First I go up to the mountain, and get caught in a storm— then I lose my friends. And, now I’m soaking wet.”
Her throat felt sore as she said this, and she quickly realized that being cold and wet wasn’t her only problem.
“Just my luck… I catch what Tim had… I should’ve known that he shouldn’t have come with us.”

Rather than saying these words with anger, she still had a sense of fear within herself. She was still increasingly concerned that Tim was in danger, amongst the blizzard— completely lost amongst the snow, and clinging dearly to his last breaths of life. These thoughts were ones that Susan couldn’t quite accommodate for. If she were to have been honest with herself, these were some of the greatest fears that she faced within herself— the thought that, in trying to save Joshua, she only led more of her friends astray. Including herself.

There was a splash of water at the back of her neck. Her head turned to stare at the ceiling above herself, and find that there were massive pieces of rock, which were threateningly pointed down at her— all it would’ve taken was a strong quake, or a sort of landslide, for her to have been completely buried under them.

“Let’s hope that none of my friends incite and avalanche…” she said to herself, with a chuckle. Though, her chuckle was utterly sealed in nervousness. Deep down, she knew just how dangerous it really was.

How everything was supposed to be, she didn’t know… She didn’t really know anything, except the danger of her situation. She felt the danger lick at her, and make her ears burn a bright red. It went through her bones, and into her spine, climbing all the way up to her throbbing head. There wasn’t an aspect to her that wasn’t affected by this oncoming sense of danger— a sense that, no matter where she went or what she didn’t. She’d be under the threat of nature, and its propensity toward collapsing in one itself. Susan quickly realized that she was but within a cavity, amongst many cavities within the mountain, and that she was exploring a bit, of many bits. her section of mountain was a small. One.

She shook her head at her massive fear. She recognized that it was unnecessary, and that it wouldn’t get her anywhere. Wherever she looked, danger lurked— and, all that she was capable of doing was the recognition of it. Beyond that, she was at a loss.

Her eyes turned back to her satchel, which was soaked to the core, just like her clothes had been. The contents of it were all but ruined— she’d initially packed dried up fruit, stale bread, and vegetables. But, it had all been turned to a mixture of slime and snow. There was no longer any sense of freshness, or preservatives to it. All of the salt and spice had been completely removed, in favor of a coating of wet sludge.

“Well, this is just great…” Susan said to herself, with a scowl. “I went through hours of labor to get here, only to find that I’m stuck with a complete mess… There’s no food, no water… Nothing that I need!”

She was on the verge of letting her emotions drive her, when she saw something poke out of the top of the bag— it was her matchbox, and her map. Then, a gust of wind blew at her— it was strange, but it pulled her hair in the direction of the tunnel through the caves— the very place that she’d planned to explore.

“The very place that I need to explore…” Susan said to herself. “Why didn’t I think of it sooner. If I’m going to be getting anything done, it’s going to be in the caves. There’s nowhere else for me to go— nothing else for me to do.”

She bent over, and began fiddling with her matchbox. However, the moment that she tried doing so, she found that it was completely soaked, and useless. Whenever she tried striking a match upon it, it would come up dead— not a single flame would light, and she found that she was at a complete loss. There was no way for her to start of fire. The snow had won, and allowed her no other option but to trek into the darkness, unguided by sight. That, or she’d be forced to stay subject to the cold’s harshness. Neither option looked upon her in any sort of sympathy, nor did she look upon the options in sympathy.
Grabbing her map book, and satchel, she decided that she was going to go into the mountain unaided— she would simply have to rely on memory to make it back to her cove.

“It shouldn’t matter,” she thought to herself. “There are probably tons of ways to navigate through this mountain, all of which will probably get me where I need to go. There’s no need for me to worry— I’ll get what I want in no time.”
She, of course, knew that she was lying to herself.

She remembered the book that she’ d read as a kid—  the red book that Joshua had read to her, when she was younger. One of her fondest memories, when she thought about it, were the accounts of the mountain— just how grand and vast it was, despite all of the murkiness that dominated throughout it all. It gave her a sense of awe and wonder, which she now knew was incredibly rare and unique.

“Why is it that it’s always the rare things that I remember?” Susan thought to herself. “Maybe it isn’t what I remember that’s rare, but my memories… The most precious things that stick with me are few. Over time, I tend to toss out what I don’t feel matters— leave it behind, in favor of things that I feel make more sense. It’s time that I begin to see things in a better light, and look at this mountain with a greater appreciation. However, it’s also time that I recognize how experiences aren’t as rare, or unique as I might to think they are– everything that I see will probably be similar to something seen before…”

With those thoughts, she let the darkness of the cave completely swallow her, this time. While she’d only let it taste her before, this time she was willing to take every risk— to see every facet of the mountain, for what it really was. She didn’t want to hide anymore. She didn’t want to wonder. It was finally time for her to explore. And, she knew that the exploration was one that would affect her deep inside, whether or not it had the results that she wanted— there was simply something guiding her from within, that let her know.

I’ve finally spoken with the wizard. Even as I write this down, I can hardly believe it. I might’ve thought that this never would’ve happened. In fact, I till question whether or not this really happened, even though I know that it has.

Normally, I would think that this was all just a dream of mine— I really would. After my strange dream about the dragon, which still bothers me, I couldn’t tell what was true and what was fiction. It really threw me off balance for quite a while. However, I know that this encounter with the wizard is real.

I’m sure that an argument can be made that one can never be certain about anything— that every thought we have is one of uncertainty, and that there’s nothing upon where we can truly base our foundations of life. Though, I still think that it’s true… I know that I’m ridiculous in thinking this. But, I’m actually certain that this thing is real— that I’ve tasted it, and experienced it.

At this point, I’m probably being viewed as if I were mad. And, that view isn’t entirely wrong. I was mad to come here, I was made to think that I could resurrect my father, and I was probably mad to think that a dream about a dragon might’ve been real. Though, none of this is very convincing to me. I still feel completely sane, and nothing within myself has led me to feeling insecure about my situation…

This is probably the point in my diary where I will begin to question myself. AS I write this down, I come nearer to the spots in my narrative that seem too fantastical and extraordinary, even for me to believe that they happened. But, they did. I know that they did, with all of my heart. I can feel it inside of myself— driving me, and pulling me forward. It has given me a sort of confidence. So, I’m not going to distrust myself. I’m going to share my story– and, I’m going to take it seriously.

It was after I woke up my guide, Hemlock, for his turn to take his night-guard post. Normally, he would wake up with quite a fuss, and I’d have to listen him drone on about how good of a dream that he was having— how I shouldn’t have woken him up— before he would ever let me go back to sleep.

Though, tonight he kept me from going back to sleep f a different reason. Every time that I tried closing my eyes, and drawing myself into a deep slumber, he’d shake at my sides, and yell into my ears. Just like anybody else would’ve reacted in such a situation, I started to feel an overwhelming sense of anger. I’d dealt with enough nights of him complaining, and I could hardly bare to hear him go on even more. I’m not sure why, but it deeply annoyed me. I felt as if, even as I tried pulling my own weight, he was unwilling to pull his own. I knew that he was doing his own work during the night watch— and, as far as I could tell, he was doing it without falling asleep, like I was. But, when one is tired, and trying to go to sleep themselves, their judgement begins to fall away— they begin to think things that are completely untrue, and baseless.
“You have to get up!” Hemlock kept saying. “You won’t believe it! Hurry! Get up!”

I thought that he was lying, and trying to get me to take his night watch— so, I tried my best to keep my eyes shut, and pretend that he wasn’t talking to me. Thankfully, I eventually couldn’t do this any longer. Hemlock is a good guide, in that way. Even with all of his complaining, and his consistent lack of encouragement, I feel like he’s willing to go the extra mile to make sure that he’s serving our mission in the best possible way.

I groggily opened my eyes, and looked around the room. It was at this point when I realized exactly why Hemlock had been so pressing and urgent in trying to keep me awake. I immediately felt waves of embarrassment and humiliation wash over me— even a sort of guilt.

In front of us, by some manner of ordinance that still escapes me, there was a golden door, made of a craftsmanship that I have yet to see matched. Off of it radiated a golden light, and a sort of dust— at first, I thought the dust was just dirt. Yet, I began to realize that it was actually something far stranger— they were pure orbs of light, almost like sparks. Except, they didn’t fade. Rather, they floated just like snowflakes. And, in my hand, they melted like snowflakes too. Similar to the warm wind that I’d consistently felt amidst the cold, these were a warm version of snowflakes. Only, these were far harder to believe, or understand, however. A warm snowflake isn’t quite like a warm gust of wind. After all— I’ve experienced warm wind before. These golden flakes were something entirely different, and more outlandish than I could’ve ever possibly hoped to understand.
“Hemlock,” I said, “What is this?”

He of course didn’t have an answer. In fact, he didn’t even have anything to say. Despite him having woken me up, he now appeared to be in a sort of trance. As we both looked up to the door, I felt a surge of a strange power flow into me. I’d felt similar things tin the past. But, there was something quite unique this time around. I felt alleviated of all of my past thoughts. My tiredness had been completely wiped away, along with the rest of my bad feelings. I felt as if I’d been made anew in every possible way. The world around me no longer mattered. All that mattered to me was getting things done— making things that were wrong turn right again. Nothing else really held a stead in my heart. My entire quest had been stamped out, in favor of the urging that came from this door.
“My entire mission…” I thought. “It’s been torn away so easily… all too easily.”

I can’t say that I was wrong. In spite of all the things that I’d done, and all of my efforts, my original mission was completely gone from me.
