I now felt as if I were pressing towards something entirely new and unique, and that nothing I’d planned before mattered anymore… Somewhere deep inside of myself, where the trance couldn’t reach me, I felt upset, and even slightly angered by all of this. I’d lost my goals so easily— all that it had taken was slight temptation, and I’d been able to abandon it with a sort of glee. Not only did this not feel natural, and it came across as slightly wrong. But, it also made me wonder how easy it would be for me to abandon everything else that I’d planned. How could I have any faith in myself if all it took to shake my will was a golden door?

I quickly forgot all of this as I watched the door begin to open. There seemed to be some sort of enchantment upon it, which completely took hold of all the mind’s impulses— even memories— so that all I would do is focus upon it, rather than focus upon anything else.

Along the side of the door, there were thousands of little gears. I listened as locks on the golden door steadily began to open, clicking open with crisp snaps, which reminded me of the days when I was in the palace, listening to the clicking of my people’s feet against the marble floors.

The wider that the door opened, the more that I felt all of this take control over me. And yet, it was also washing away at a rapid pace. Like the tides of an ocean’s waters, it went back and forth, receding only to return again.

A point came where the door was so widely opened that the receding and returning disappeared altogether, and all that I could see was the beauty of the insides of the room streaming into my eyes. I watched as dozens of rays of light came out from within it. I couldn’t even see the inside of the door— all that I could see was a blinding light. Though, the blinding light was all that I really needed. Nothing else cut it, within my mind. All that mattered was that I saw light again. And, in the constant darkness of the cave, that was all that I could’ve wished for.

I’ll no longer have to wonder if I’m dreaming, when dragons lurk… I thought. In fact, I won’t even need to wonder if dragons lurk about. I’m finally at a place where I can hide from all of the threats of the mountain for a little while— a place where I can let all of those fears wash of my back, and merely focus on the things that matter… bringing my father back, and figuring out the mystery of this mountains’ magic.

At this moment, I had no idea that I’d stumbled upon the wizard’s abode, nor did I know that I’d practically finished my journey. In fact, each of these truths weren’t even suspicions in my mind— I’d half given up on the thought of any hope by this point, and was just scooting along so that I could find sort of meaning in the journey— something that I could come back from, and be proud of.

There was something to the door, and everything about it, though— it gave me a sense of levity that I’d never felt before. While I didn’t think that it was from a wizard, or, frankly anything else that I knew about, I had the overpowering sense that it was some sort of grand magic. This single thought pulled me along, in spite of everything telling me not to. The enchantment, while powerful, no longer had a hold. Deep inside of myself, I’d realized that I’d found somewhere where I felt meaning. And, this gave me a deep sense of confidence.

“Let’s go inside,” I finally said to Hemlock. Maybe it had all been my head, but my tongue had been utterly limp until up to this point. Thankfully, by some miracle, I’d managed to overcome this limitation.

I looked over to Hemlock, but he still appeared to be in his daze. In fact, he appeared worse off then  I originally had been. There was something to the entrance that had completely stripped him of all his formerly proud and honorable demeanor. He’d been reduced to a gaping fool.

“Come on now, Hemlock… You can’t just sit there, like a deranged clown. We need to keep going— keep exploring. We’ve finally reached somewhere with light! We can actually explore and see this place, unlike all of the other places that we’ve gone and explored.”

I stood there, and waited for some sort of response out of Hemlock. However, it became clear that he wasn’t going to break out of whatever had taken him over. SO, I grabbed him by the wrist and began pulling him through the door— through he door and into the light.
“Like it or not,” I said, “I’m not going in there without you.”

My eyes were still momentarily blinded, and I could hardly make out my surroundings. It was all far too blurry to comprehend, and I felt as if I was walking into some sort of heaven that I wasn’t supposed to be walking amongst— as if I’d begun to trespass in a place that previously was thought to be impossible to trespass.
Hemlock’s feet stopped dragging, signaling to me that his trance had finally come to an end. Instead, he sped up his pace, took his hand out of my grip, and began to walk in front of me.
“You might have been the one who saved me from a trance,” he said, “But, that doesn’t mean you instantly become the guide.”

With that, I let him take me through the room, and amongst its blurry features I steadily began to recognize that it was made out of extreme amounts of gold, and that it contained hundreds of rich objects— harps, paintings, and extensive piles of diamonds— however, there were still parts that I couldn’t understand. I began walking upon a surface that seemed liquid and solid at the same time. At one step, it would splash, and, at another, it would feel as hard as rock. I looked to see if Hemlock was confused, and listened to see if he too was stepping in the liquid— but, his feet never made a single splash. The splashing liquid floor might as well have all been in my head.

The source of light was also something that alluded me. Everything was so bright that it was a struggle for me to keep my eyes open. Locating where the source of light might’ve been was an even harder task for me to do.
“Hemlock, how can you see so clearly in here?” I asked. “I can hardly make out anything!”

“it’s all in the eyes,” he said. “You need to keep them wide open, and incredibly alert. That’s the only way that you’ll be able to take out anything. However, to be honest, there’s still barely anything that I can understand there. I can only see well enough to guide us through these halls, without crashing us into walls… It looks to me like we’ve stumbled into some sort of Cave palace. What’s odd is that I can’t tell how it’s so large. We walked and stopped to check the other side of the cavern wall, before was slept in front of it and had this door spawned… There shouldn’t be enough room for it to get this big…”

I nodded in agreement. However, it was at this moment that I feared I was walking within a dream, and merely letting everything that I did be controlled by my sleepy head. It very well could’ve been that this was just my mind’s great heaven. Light was something that I deeply wanted. It wouldn’t have surprised me if I discovered that I was just tricking myself into thinking that I’d reached a heaven, when I was really dreaming it all up. Sleep was something that I’d learned to be among the greatest betrayers of reality.
“this sort of thing almost makes me wonder if any of this is actually real, or if it’s all just in my head…” I said.

“I concur…” Hemlock said. “It all appears too good to be true. I can’t help but think the same things as you. However, I know that this couldn’t be from my mind. This place is too vast, and foreign for me to have ever thought this up in my head. Trust me— this simply isn’t the sort of place that I’d waste my time dreaming about, even if I’m desperately wanting of light, wealth, rest, and clarity…”

I’m not quite sure why or how, but Hemlock’s explanation was enough to convince me that everything was but a dream. There really wasn’t any other way that I could explain everything to myself. To me, the only true logical explanation really was the concept that it was all just a dream. But, when /I realized that this wasn’t the sort of thing that I could dream up, the only option left was that it had all been caused by something outside of my understanding— magic.

“Welcome, intruders of the mountain,” a loud voice said, breaking into both of our ears. Suddenly, me and Hemlock knew that we’d been right. And, being right suddenly didn’t have the thrill or satisfaction to it that we might’ve hoped for it to have had. In fact, it was replaced with a sort of feeble embarrassment. In the face of the booming voice, we must’ve appeared weak. And, in our blindness, I also knew that we’d have no way to battle whatever threat that had decided to fall upon us. WE were tuck in a pit in nearly every way that we chose to go. And, I realized that it was all resting ion my terrible choices, and mistakes.

“What is it that has brought you here? You’ve been wandering through these caves for a week, deeply searching for something. And, you’ve only stumbled upon a dragon, and a tavern trap that I’d designed for you both, which you narrowly escaped… I’ve met many people who have come thorough this mountain, and none appear to be deserving of it. However, you do. You’ve avoided every trap that I’ve set up for you, and more. Such takes a cunning that hasn’t been matched by anybody else— a cunning that I’ve constantly been looking for. How have you two done it? What is within you both that has allowed you to accomplish such feats of genius? You should be raving mad by now!”

“I’m of royal blood,” I said. “I’m not weakened by what will weaken most. My luck spreads so far out, that nothing I can do can be done in error. I’m afraid that I’m a genius… It’s a blessing but also a curse. It’s the reason that I’ve been able to survive this torture chamber of a mountain.”

There was a warm chuckle within the voice. In fact, I felt a warm wind blow into my face after Id’ finished talking. There was something comforting to the wind— a homely friendliness that I had yet to find from anywhere else.

“Yes… a royal genius…” the voice said. “I don’t believe that such a thing exists. And, from what I’ve observed, your guide has helped you survive a lot more traps and dangers than you might like to acknowledge. However, there’s a lot more going on in this place than I might like to acknowledge to. It seems to me that you’re no genius. Instead, you’re somebody that feigns it. But, you do feign it convincingly, and I do applaud you for that.”
I felt the heat of embarrassment settle over my face, but tried my best to pretend that it wasn’t there.

“Why don’t you stop talking from a distance, and show yourself?” I asked, trying my best to sound peaceable, and under control. Inside myself, I felt like running out of the room, and back into the darkness of the mountain where I could no longer be judged or tested— back into the kingdom, where all of my problems appeared to be so much easier to solve and tackle.

“I’m already here,” the voice said. “In fact, I’m right in front of you both. You’re just blind to me— no doubt due to the fact that you’ve constantly been stuck groping amongst the darkness for a way out. However, I’ll help you with that problem.”

I heard the snapping of a finger, and then everything became clear. In front of me, I saw the wizard, standing tall— dressed in a flowing white robe, and having a cone-shaped pointed hat upon his head. He also had a flowing beard, and eyes that shone like bright moons. Suddenly, the palace surrounding him also appeared far more beautiful. The floor was actually a mixture of golden tiles, as well as tiles that were actually holes filled with water. There were diamonds melted into pillars, and the floor and walls were all made of a soft gold.
“It’s all so elegant,” I said, looking into the wizard’s wizened face.

I was utterly stunned. I’d been spending day after day, tirelessly searching for this man. And, he was finally in my face, looking upon me. I was looking upon him. There was something to it that was satisfying beyond all measure. It just couldn’t compare to any other feeling that had ever come to me. I felt something that I’d never thought to be possible to feel.
It could only be described as magic. Though, I feel that describing it as such might be doing it an injustice.

“Yes… Elegant…” The wizard said, with a sense of disgust. “Personally, I find that it’s far more evoking of power, than beauty. That’s what I worship more than beauty— knowledge and power. Don’t you see the geometry in everything that I’ve designed? The intelligent architecture? The symmetry? The formulas used to create everything in a precision that cannot be matched? It’s all built in such a way that nothing else can truly compare to it. Don’t you understand that? Or, are you entirely ignorant o wisdom…”
“No, I understand,” I lied.

What I was truly thinking was that I wished that I’d brought one of my mathematicians with me. They would’ve been the only sort of person who would’ve been able to understand the wizard’s eccentricities when it came to his palace.

“Good… Anyhow, Let’s get back to our discussion. While sight is a gift from above, it’s also a trivial and distracting thing…. So, let’s talk about exactly why you’re here. I heard from the talks within the kingdom that you’re planning to revive your father from the dead. I find this mission to sound truly noble, if a bit immature and infantile in design. Do you wish for me to help you?”
“Yes! Yes!” I said, suddenly. “I’ve spent my entire journey looking for you! I received a map, and everything…”

The wizard looked upon me, mysteriously. I looked at him, at the same time, too. Immediately, I recognized the wizard’s eyes. They were the same eyes that had been within my strange advisor, with his horrid emerald. The same advisor who had provided me with a map to the mountain.

What disturbed me most about this was that the wizard wasn’t acknowledging me as if we’d ever met before, nor acting as if he knew me. Instead, he treated me like I was a foreign stranger-as if I were just some wanderer, that had stumbled upon his cave by chance. I didn’t fully understand why or how he could’ve done so, especially after having met me before. When I looked at him, it became obvious who he was— so his attempts at trying to pretend otherwise only came across as creepy, and subtly disturbing.

“Why don’t you just admit that you were my advisor?” I asked him. “Why are you hiding the obvious from me…? I can see it all in your eyes. There’s no reason to keep holding the mystery,” I said. “The mystery is dead now. I can see right through the veil. So, why keep the veil on.
The wizard looked at me, with an anger.

“I’m not quite sure what you’re referring to,” he said. “Though, if I’ve ever met you before, maybe I wouldn’t even know it. I take on many forms, you see. This palace, here, is but one of many abodes that I’ve taken for myself. I spawn wherever I’m needed, and do whatever I need to do. I’m not something g that can be controlled or understood. Not even by myself. So, I’d prefer to not have any blame placed upon me, and instead would like to be given some appreciation for all of the things that I have provided you of— light, a place of protection, and a place of rest. I’m a force of nature, I’m afraid. I can’t be contained, or stopped. And, any attempt to do so will only contain or stop you. So, I’d appreciate it if you gave up your trivial accusations, and shouts of anger, and instead look upon me like the friend that I am…”

“You’re no friend…” I seethed. “You’re not anything. You’re just a lie. You’re just trying to fool me into thinking things that aren’t really true. And, it’s time that you gave it all up, and started looking at the world in a far clearer way. That’s the only way you’re ever going to accomplish anything, I’m afraid.”
He didn’t yell, or scoff at me, like I might’ve expected him to. In fact, he changed his face of superiority, and morphed it into one of sympathy.

“Yes…” he said. “I remember what it’s like to feel human. The frailty and weakness of it— the idea that everything might be a threat, and that there’s no possible way you can understand or overcome anything. There’s a lot to the world that can’t be understood, and even more that can’t be overcome. But, as a human, you feel that you can’t understand or overcome any of it. And, you really can’t… Mortality is the greatest vice, which ultimately stunts you from ever reaching the pinnacle of experience, and understanding. If only there were a way to overcome it… However, at the same time, I also am glad that there isn’t a way for you to overcome it. Because, without it, you wouldn’t be here, talking to me. We would all be in different places. The whole world would be different. The whole world wouldn’t even need magic, or learning, or anything that the world has… That’s the price that comes with understanding. Because, once you begin to understand things, you start to see that you can’t understand anything— and, that there’s no reason in doing anything, because there is nothing to understand…”

There was a morbidity to the wizard’s speech, but he laughed after saying it all the same. It was as if it all was a joke to him, and that he didn’t really care about the effect that his words had.  To a degree, his words didn’t have an effect on me. They felt hollow, and empty— mostly nonsense. Though, there was also a part of the wizard that exposed a humanity. It was a humanity that I couldn’t ignore, and I felt strongly touched by— even amidst the fact that there were few things I could do, or that the wizard was really saying,
“What do you mean when you say that you remember being human?” I asked. “Are you a force of nature, or are you a human like you appear? I don’t understand…”

“I don’t understand either,” the wizard said— or, at least, what appeared to be a wizard. “Maybe there isn’t an answer to your question. I don’t have any clear memories in either direction. Those words must’ve just been a slip of my tongue.”

The wizard’s eyes darted back and forth, in a clear nervousness. However, something else that was clear was that the wizard wasn’t interested in answering any of my questions. Rather, it was far more interested in scolding me for small mistakes, and giving me orders for things that it clearly could’ve done one its own.

“Well, fine then…” I said. “But, I’m sure that you still want to know about the answer to your question— the question about whether or not we need your help, and what we need your help with. So, I’ll answer that question for you— we need your help to raise my father back from the dead. AS I’m sure you know, he recently died. My goal is to resurrect him, and the only way to do that, as far as I’m aware, is by your forms of magic. Can you help me do this, or am I going to be left on my own in this?”

“Oh, I can help you…” the wizard said, “but what you ask for isn’t something that I can actually do. You wish to help the world through my powers, and think that they can solve any problem. But, death is something that I’m incapable of hurdling. I’m afraid that it simply isn’t something that is so easy to hurdle, while it might initially seem to be. Magic has its limits, and death is one of them. Once something is dead, they’ve passed outside the hands of magic. At that point, it will require a magic of dark qualities to fully return them from the grave. And, that’s simply something that I’m not interested in undertaking.”
“Why not?” I asked. “If magic is capable of taking care of life, then what makes it dark magic? Isn’t all magic the same?”

“All magic is the same in the way that it must be done by a wizard, and that it requires a sort of price… But, dark magic requires the price of another human’s life. I’ve been tempted to dive into dark magic before, but it’s just so extreme… It’s not something that I feel that I should be doing.”
I looked into the wizard’s face, with my greatest face of superiority being worn upon my cvisage.
“You are going to use the dark magic, if it means saving my father’s life,” I said. “Don’t you understand just how important he is to me?”
“Yes, but…” the wizard said, with a squeamish awkwardness, “Dark magic requires somebody to die. Surely, as a noble prince, , you wouldn’t bother killing anybody just to revive your father!”
“I will do just that,” I said. “And, I will do much more…”
“But who,” The wizard asked. “If you’re going to do such a wretched thing to somebody, who will be the one to suffer it.”

I felt a strong discomfort at this point, when I realized that I had no real option. I looked over to Hemlock, who looked even more terrified than myself. If it hadn’t been for the fact that he was already too scared of the wizard, I’m sure that he would’ve turned and battled me over my decision. Thankfully though, he was afraid of the wizard, and I did have an upper hand over the situation.
“Me,” I said. “Now, start using your dark magic, or I’ll use it myself.

The wizard didn’t say a word in combat. In fact, it seems to agree with my decision. Personally, I felt slightly disgusted with the idea, myself. But, I also knew that it seemed to be my only option. For that, I was willing to do anything.

Susan was in the deep darkness for who knew how long. Within it, she couldn’t measure time. In fact, she could hardly tell where she was going. In spite of thoroughly searching on the map for where her location might be, she was hopelessly lost, due to the fact that she hadn’t tracked her position outside of the mountain first— the fact that she couldn’t track her position, at risk of death.

She felt a terror try to crawl into her, and as if supernatural forces here moving around her without her awareness. Though, she also knew that searching through the mountain was her only option, and that she wasn’t willing to try any other method. She’d inserted deep thought into everything that was going on around herself, and realized something that she’d long been trying to avoid— there was no way to get herself out of the mountain, without eventually regretting it. There was no way to go through the mountain, without regretting it. In spite of hating her traveling through the mountain, and in spite of the fact that she hated every minute of it, she also knew that it was completely necessary.

She thought back to how easier it might’ve been if she could’ve been able to carry a torch with her, and see all of her surroundings. Thankfully, however, she’d plotted everywhere that she’d gone on a piece of paper in her map. By using the burnt bit of one of her torches, she used the ash to write down an accurate trail of her travels.

There were sounds of moaning and groaning in the mountain wherever she went. In fact, she could hear avalanches occurring from above herself, and storms raging on with a great severity. She was still on the lower portion in the mountain, and in spite of all the distance that she’d made through it, she began to see just how much more distance she’d still need to cover. There were simply too many things for her to think on— too many things, which all held great and dire consequences. So, she didn’t bother pushing herself to go even deeper into the mountain than she already had. Rather, she kept on her steady path.

Though, the avalanches and storms raging above herself continued, and the short line on her map kept taunting her. She started to see just how many hours that she’d spent, and just how much of all of it had gone to waste. She started to realize just how much in danger that she really was— and how hard that it would be for her to get to anywhere, on her own.
Maybe I can’t get anywhere, she thought to herself. Maybe this is going to be a lot harder than it might seem to be.

Then, the roaring from outside of the mountain grew larger still. She had a sudden wish to run off, and return to her initial safe place that she’d come from. However, she had another wish too— a wish that, whatever the noise was, it really was an avalanche. Because, she was starting to recognize that it couldn’t have been an avalanche it all, or a storm, for that matter. It was coming closer to her, the longer that she thought on it. Moreover, she felt her worries steadily grip her harder. She was now so terrified that she didn’t know what to do.

Her eyes danced everywhere that she could, and she moved around in circles with all of the power vested within herself— she didn’t stop looking for the source of the noise until she felt that it couldn’t be found. However, even then she felt unsatisfied. She had no real sight. And, the only thing that she did have— hearing— was telling her that the threat was far too close for her to ignore.

She kept on feeling the need to run, but now knew that she couldn’t run— she no longer had that power within herself nor any power for that matter. She was trapped in her place— lost to the fact that she was so worried when the rumbling sound would strike, and take her by whatever force of nature it acted upon.
“What are you!?” she shouted to it. “If you’re going to attack and threaten me, why don’t you come and face me!”

It was at this moment, when the words slipped off of her tongue, that all of her senses finally left her— she was, at that point, lost to the world and reality. The moment before she’d went, she felt tehe vibrations of the rumbling strongly overtake her. Though, once they were gone, all that hs knew was that she was gone with it. Then, she knew nothing.
“Hello,” a voice said.
Susan looked around in a fright, before she finally reasoned that the voice was in her head.

“I must’ve hit a rock or something, and knocked myself out cold,” she said to herself. “the last thing that I remember is running through this cave, nonstop… After that, nothing… That stupid avalanche. It’s all of its fault.”
She paused to listen to her surroundings, and see if there were any hint of anything— any life. Any direction. Any sign that she was awake, and not caught within a dream.

It was only the latter that she was able to determine. Just by being able to question whether or not she was in a dream instantly wiped her suspicions away. However, there was still the remaining sliver of doubt in everything else.

Susan tried to move from her bed in the ground. It was at this point when she realized that there was far more going on than she’d initially thought. AS she tried pulling her arms up from the ground, and making her feet gain a grip on the ground, she found that she couldn’t move them. No matter how hard she tried, she found that she was stuck on the ground— something was binding her, and keeping her from moving. For a moment, she was worried that she might’ve been paralyzed, in a sleep. But, she was quickly reminded otherwise by the stinging pain that remained in her body, and on her wrists, from her attempts to break free from her bondages.

Fighting against the bondages at full force, she felt it steadily rub against her skin, and burn her. She wished to keep going anyway, but quickly realized that she couldn’t without risking an abundance of gouges in her skin. She knew that she was defeated— that she had nowhere to go.

“Let me out!” Susan finally said, resorting to the conclusion that she had no other choice. As she looked about, from any sign of anybody around her, she realized that she had a blindfold on her face. She hadn’t noticed it at the start, but it was becoming all too clear now— the initial chafing against her ears and forehead, along with the pressure around her eyes, had all come from a blindfold.

There was something else that she noticed. Her clothes felt completely dry, and all of her body no longer felt the terribly sickening chafing that had been a symptom of her wet clothes. There was a warmth around her too. Wherever she was, she was in a far better place from where she once had been. In fact, she felt rather comfortable— if there could’ve been a way for her to remove the bondages around her wrists and ankles, it probably would’ve been an ideal situation.

“Is anybody there?” Susan asked again. “I know that somebody is out there— there’s no use hiding from me! somebody stuck me here, and I’m going to find out who it was— your cowardice won’t get you anywhere!”

Eventually, after continuing on with her shouts for quite a while longer, she finally resolved that she was not making any headway, and that she’d have to change her approach if she could hope to take any effect. So, she kept her ears as open as she could, and studied for the slightest noises. This was all that she had that she could truest— it was all that eventually gave her any information.
At first, she could only hear slight sounds, like whistling of the wind. Though, it steadily became more and more clear, until her ears adjusted so that she was able to hear it all in its fullness.

“There you go again!” she heard a voice whisper, in anger. “You just had to wake up the prisoner! Thankfully, it’s going back to sleep now. But, do you know how hard this is going to be if you go pulling a stunt like that again!?”
“I was just joking…” said another voice, which was a lot softer, and had much more of a shakiness to it. “I thought that our sleeping potion would’ve kept her asleep for a lot longer than it did…”

“Well, we didn’t mix it right. Somebody forgot to mix in the extra reeds. Besides, we didn’t capture her on time either. If we had gotten her an hour later, and waited to set off the boulders— something we should’ve easily been able to do, if you hadn’t been so stupid—then we wouldn’t even be having this conversation, and we would’ve already had the fire burning at its highest temperature by now…”
“I’m sorry again… How many times do I have to tell you?”

“Until we’re eating, and this entire mess is all over with. I’ve had to deal with enough days without food at this point, and I’m not going to go on for another day. I’m sick of having to eat up the scraps of lost, malnourished wolves, who clearly have disease crawling all throughout them… You know, a dwarf like me shouldn’t have to be hunting for food. We should already have plenty of that, and simply have the time to do all that we wish in the mountain— like mining, and crafting... Don’t you remember mining, Romeos?”
“Yes, of course I remember… Stop treating me like I’m stupid. I just don’t know if this is all worth being so angry about.”

“Oh, it is. You’ve also lost us human feasting before, about three years ago… It was to that old coot, Bert— don’t you remember him. You just had to get in a conversation with him, and let him get the upper hand… Do you know how much easier things would’ve been if you’d just ignored him?”
“Yes, I know… You’ve told me that a dozen times before… I honestly don’t want to hear anymore of it.”
“Well, you’re going to have to hear it until you probe that you learned your lesson!”

The voices went on like this— bickering each other and circles, slowly raising the volume of their voices as they did. The longer that they progressed, the more and more they exposed about themselves. Susan was also abole to identify them better, too.
I remember reading something like this in a story once… Susan thought. I just have to find a way to outwit them.

However, no matter how much she thought about a way to escape, she couldn’t ignore the fact that they had her trying to be roasted over a fire— the fact that she had no other way out, except into the fire.

“Well, it appears that there are a lot of things that I could do...” Susan said. “and, most of them would result in me falling into the fire below me. So, how am I supposed to break free with only my mind, and wit?”

She tried running into the direction of where she’d heard the dwarfs bickering amongst each other. There was a part of her that wanted to talk to them. But then, she knew that it would result in nothing. There were simply too many risks.
She scowled to herself.

In every way, I’ve let myself be outwitted. I now have no way out of here… If I’d just been more careful and calculated in my steps through this mountain, I would’ve been able to avoid all of this... but no, I just had to trick myself into going deeper into the mountain without rest. And, now I’m dwarf food.

She felt the sudden terrifying visions of what might happen If she were to have become a victim of the dwarves. She also wondered about Joshua, and how he might’ve been able to evade his way through a wilderness like this. But, she knew that there was nothing that she could actually do for him— not while she was tied up. And so, she elected to ignored her fears in favor of making a difference.

Eventually, after minutes of long, hard thought, she finally came to the part of herm mind’s path of wondering where she recognized there was no other way out, but by speaking. They were, of course, trying to cook her— but, the longer that she went without acting, the more that she’d be cooked— until, the fire became so hot that she’d no longer have a window of acting within anymore.
She also had the other option of attempting to run away. But, even if she managed to escape, she’d have no sense of direction— especially not a sense of direction that matched these two.

She realized that, if she spoke to the dwarves, she might anger them to the point that they put her back to sleep. But, since she was hovering over the fire, she doubted that they’d be able to reach her. Moreover, there was also the hope that her voice would elicit some sort of help to come to her. And, of course, there was always the chance that the dwarves might change their minds, and decide to give her help on their own accord— not that this was something she found to be particularly engrossing of an idea.
“Somebody, help me!” she said, wincing in regret as she did so. She knew that, as she said these words, all of her other options slipped away.

After that, she tried repeating these words as much as she possibly could. She was unwilling to take the risk of having no way out, and becoming the victims of these nasty dwarfs. This was her only way— her only hope at escape now. And, she knew that she’d have to use it up to all of her advantage.

“I told you too tie her mouth in a gag!” one of the dwarfs said— the meaner of the two, from what Susan could tell. “This is what happens when you don’t follow all of the instructions! Now we’re stuck having to talk with our meal again!”
“I’m sorry…” the other dwarf said.
“Well, you say that an awful lot.”
After this their voices stopped. But, Susan didn’t stop her voice. She knew that, the longer she kept going, the longer her chance at life became.
“You’re honestly going to keep shouting at the top of your longs?” she heard on of the dwarfs say. “Please, stop.”

There were sounds of something leaping off the ground, only to fall back down again. Clearly, the dwarf was trying to jump up to her. Most likely to gag, rather than to strike a deal. But, Susan was willing to act on her own strengths and advantages as much as she could.

“Are you supposed to be a frog, or something?” she asked, with a sarcasm. “I wasn’t aware that you were so eager to eat me… but, I honestly don’t think that I’m the sort of thing frogs like you will find appetizing. I heard that you prefer pests— don’t you? I think that would suit you far better than a girl, all tied up. Also, I heard that the wolves were really good this time of year. All you’ll have to do is go outside, and go meet some of them.”
The dwarf growled.
“Romeos, what did I tell you about talking? Now look! The girl knows that we’re dwarfs, and that we’re planning on eating her!”
“I’m sorry sir… I don’t even remember talking about these things!”

“Quiet! Now I’m going to have to figure out what I’m supposed to do with her, and it’s all your fault. She’s too far up from the fire to start cooking anytime soon, and you annoyingly lost the potion that I gave you…”
“It was an accident,” Romeos said.
“Yes, well, you have a lot of those. And now, we’re both paying for it.”
Susan decide to break into the conversation.
“Well, you can at least try helping me out of here, right?”

title: The Secret of Blackneck
paragraphs: Chapter One
The Snowstorm

Not a single inch of land was left untouched by the merciless edge of winter's icy sword in the dismal town of Blackneck. It was a frozen bitter night, the kind of which was so cold that just mere memories of it would send a stinging shiver down your spine on even the hottest day of summer. Whether it be small shivering children huddled around a measly fireplace with chattering teeth, or farm animals struggling in vain to burrow deeper under their frosted hay, the cold left its mark everywhere. Making their faces red and their bodies numb, it conquered them all.

This siege was nothing new to the inhabitants of Blackneck; actually, it was quite far from it! Every year, for over a hundred years, the same bitter cold swept across their town, barring them up in its endless sheets of ice.
“It's a curse!” some of the elders would croak to the children of the town.
“It's the dark king of ice...” the peasants would whisper to each other.
“It's this stinkin' piece of land we're stuck on!” the farmers would shout in rage.

Whatever it was remained a mystery to them... Nevertheless, there was one thing their frantic brains could agree on; it had to be stopped at all costs! Throughout the years the members of the town had made many attempts to survive the cold's wrath. They sent out search missions for, “the King of Ice”, they had tried looking for new land to settle on and they had tried chopping up and storing enough wood for fire. Some had even become so desperate as to simply plead at the cold to go away! Yet, no matter how they approached the problem, their efforts always ended in vain. Nobody returned from the search missions, the wood all rotted, no safe haven was to be found… and as for those that asked for the wind to go away? For them, the situation only became all the bleaker, as they swore that the wind laughed and knocked them off their feet!

The situation of Blackneck was dire, to say the least. What hope did this weak town really have against this ghastly force of nature? The rickety wooden walls that encased them were as meagre as a blade of grass, in the sight of the raging wind! Their homes were falling apart like stacks of cards! And their men? Bah! Only the greatest of fools could have faith in the strength of their feeble frames!

No, only the greatest of knights could have liberated the town, and there was certainly no chance of them ever coming by one. To the misfortune of Blackneck, a knight is hard to come by; you can’t simply breed one in a stable. The grand palaces and kingdoms that knights were raised in were leagues away. Many of the townspeople had strained everything in them to find one, but they only chased after wind…

Yet, what if I told you that the great hero, the knight of Blackneck, could have been a simple boy? Wait, scratch that, maybe not a simple boy… Rather, he’s a miserable sack of bones and rags that dwells, not in a castle, but a shack. And maybe-- maybe he isn’t exactly the noble type… The other day he was caught stealing eggs from the widow’s frozen chicken coop. And I believe, if my memory isn’t failing me, that he stole firewood from the lumber mill the week prior. And he’s certainly not one to look at, with his grubby face and a mess of hair... Why, he really isn’t any sort of knight at all. He’smore of a wretched coward than anything! Yet, what if I told you that he was the one to save this pitiful town from their icy doom?

Of course, one should know better than to put their trust in such a scoundrel. In fact, that was his very name! The townspeople knew little about the boy, save the hole he lived in and the many crimes he’d committed. So, it came to be that they simply called the boy by what he was: a filthy lying scoundrel and nothing more! One should suspect that only a mess could come out of such a character. And they’d be right! This wretch was certainly in no business of being a hero, as it should be. I’d fear for the fate of the townsfolk if it was otherwise! It’s only fitting that his story should begin with a mess, and it does…

It happened upon that cold night, whilst Scoundrel was sleeping soundly in his shack, tucked in a wool blanket he’d stolen the day prior. One might wonder how he could have slept so peacefully within the raging storm, and I believe it was because of the warm milk he stole and drank before bed. He would have continued to sleep too, if it hadn’t been for a loud bang, followed by the crack and snap of splintering wood at his door.
“Come outta yer’ filthy hole ya’ blasted Scoundrel!” a husky voice cried.

Scoundrel snapped awake with a jump. Quickly, clutching his blanket he jerked his head scanning his room. Yet, just as quick as they had opened, his eyes began to shut, seeing nothing besides the mounds of his hoard.
The voice then let out another roar of anger followed by a mighty crash, just before Scoundrel could fall asleep. Finally, Scoundrel heeded the warning, jumping to his feet.
“That’s it, we’ve given ye’ enough time! Boys, it’s time we goes chopping this ‘ere shack down!” the voice pounded, shaking the whole house.

Scoundrel instantly recognized the voice; it was a lumberjack! Those bumbling fools! They’d come to collect the firewood he’d stolen! Scoundrel certainly had issues with people he’d stolen from, but never to this extent. A revolt was the last thing he’d expected.
“Nobody breaks into me house and gets away with it!” Scoundrel whispered to himself with a greedy gleam in his eye, “Me wonders what I could do with a lumberjack’s axe!”

Quickly, Scoundrel snatched up a stick he always carried with him, and charged towards his busted door. However, what he found was much more than his fragile body could take: five tall burly men, armed with axes.

One of the men looked down at him with a smug sneer, “Ye is the one we is always puttin’ up with!? Ha! Ye is just a boy, and a scrawny one at that! Men, let’s teach this ‘ere scoundrel a lesson! Nobody messes with a lumberjack, and we is… we is… we is one!”

With a hefty swing of an arm, the lumberjack knocked Scoundrel off his feet and started tossing him about like a kitten with a ball of yarn. Scoundrel’s mind was scrambling now and his most vicious thoughts were coming into view. He couldn’t just let himself fall to their mercy so easily! Although, his thoughts were swallowed by terror when the other men joined in to trade blows of their own. One of them even went so far as to venture into his house to collect items from his hoard!

Not knowing the folly he was making, with a triumphant laugh, the tallest of the five lumberjacks grabbed Scoundrel around the waist! Scoundrel’s eyes lit up with a fiery spark. With a twist of his neck, he sunk his teeth hard into the forearm of his foe.
“Gah! The ‘ittle beast bit me he did!” the lumberjack yelped, dropping Scoundrel to the floor, “What are ye’ all waitin’ for, toss the ghastly creature out before he escapes!!”
Before Scoundrel could bat an eye, he was snapped up by his feet in the iron grasp of a lumberjack.
“Well, whaddya want us to do with ‘im boss?” the lumberjack said dangling Scoundrel by his feet.

A contorted yellow grin formed on the face of the tallest lumberjack, “Ye’ can throw the sack of bones at the foot of Craggleback Mountain, east of town. And make sure to tie the ‘ittle blighter to a tree so he doesn’t escape, the wolves will appreciate the treat. In the meantime, I is gonna collect the piles of firewood the wretch stole from us; the townsfolk will be needing it.”

Just like that, before you could light a match, the lumberjack heeded their orders. Tying Scoundrel’s wrists and ankles, so he couldn’t escape, two of the burly men ambled swiftly towards the looming shadow of Craggleback Mountain, into the swirling blizzard.
Chapter Two
Into the Mountain

Now, in the town of Blackneck, like any town, there was only a handful of things that could make the people jump out of their skin. Of these few things was Craggleback Mountain… To a weary stranger, knowing nothing of the town, Craggleback Mountain didn’t seem to hold any features that were particularly hostile, in fact, it may even have looked welcoming. Its handsome coat of snow that covered it, its spectacular glow in the sunrise, and the many luscious emerald trees that speckled its surface didn’t exactly scream deadly. However, the folk of Blackneck knew better. The Craggleback Mountain was the very essence of death in the form of mounded rock. Many a traveler went up it, but not once had one ever come down. The few with the wisdom to leave journals behind told this and one thing only: to attempt to conquer its summit is to attempt death. Plagued by an abundance of blizzards, avalanches and monsters of the foulest breed, Craggleback Mountain was a force of nature not to be meddled with. Some even claimed that the dark Ice King himself lived within the heart of it.

So, as one might expect, when the Lumberjacks approached the foot of the mountain, they meant to finish their work as fast as they could. With anxious movements, and heaviness upon their brows, they took caution to avoid all shadows and forms of darkness that lay ahead of them. They couldn’t risk to become lost, not on the foot of Craggleback Mountain! No! Nothing is worse than being lost on Craggleback Mountain!

As the men suffered, huffing and puffing while they carried themselves further up the tower of ice and snow, Scoundrel chuckled to himself, bundled in the unyielding grip of the men’s arms. The ropes coiled around him had been tied tightly, and even now they burned his wrists and his ankles. His face was in an even worse situation, with a gag in its mouth and an oily rag tied around his head like a blindfold. How could this boy laugh in the face of such pain? Well, I’ll tell you now that his laugh certainly wasn’t of the pleasant sort. It was one of the nastiest laughs your ears could hear, and, out of all the struggles the lumberjacks met in that unforgiving cold, his laugh was the worst of it (the gag in Scoundrel’s mouth may or may not have had part in it). As chained as his body was, there was nothing to contain the devious thoughts that spiraled through Scoundrel’s head and even in the midst of the adverse weather around him, he had already plotted his escape.

“Hey John, where is a blasted tree around ‘ere!? We’ve been climbing this wretched rock for hours and ‘aven’t found a bit of green!” cried the shorter of the two, struggling to see past the dense blizzard of snow that encased them.

“I don’t know Bert! ‘Ow should I know!? The snow is everywhere! And it’s not as if our wretched luggage is helping matters!” John, the taller of the two, exclaimed. However, his defeated outlook quickly changed, and, with a jerk of his head, he let out a triumphant shout, “Wait, I think I sees one! Yes, there’s a tree just up ahead! Let’s ‘urry now, we can’t spend any more time than we already ‘ave out ‘ere!”

The lumberjacks started climbing toward their destination and, as they slowly pressed on through the attacking wind, they refused to give any ground. After what felt like an hour of the stinging bite from the frigid wind against their cheeks, they finally tossed Scoundrel to the ground, with a soft thump, infront of the tree.
“It’s finally time boy that ye’ met justice for yer’ crimes!” John snickered, rubbing his palms together, “Come now Bert. Let’s unbound ‘im and tie ‘im to the tree!”

With haste, the two snatched knives out of their pockets. They then proceeded to sever the ropes around Scoundrel. As they began to work though, Scoundrel let out a muffled yell. While they tried ignoring it, Scoundrel only continued on like this, and the lumberjacks finally cracked.
Removing the oily rags and ropes around Scoundrel’s face, Bert spat at him. “What is it that ye want now!?”

Then, an astonishing thing happened in front of them. Scoundrel began to weep! Big fat tears rolled down his cheeks. His skin turned blotchy, his eyes were filled of heaviness and his limbs were quaking in fear. This had been the last thing the lumberjacks had expected! The great Scoundrel of Blackneck, the very thief that had plagued their town for so many years, had been reduced to a puddle of tears. While the two would never admit it, they felt a sort of sympathy for the poor creature.

With a sniffle and a quivering lip, Scoundrel began to speak, “Is-- is this to be me end? All me life I ‘ave pillaged and plundered the homes of those around meself’… and now, in me final hour, the treasures I’ve ‘oarded account me nothing… Yes, it all ‘as abandoned me, and now I’m to die alone at the foot of this raging storm… A cruel fate to be certain…”

“Well—well it serves ye’ right!” Bert said, his voice tremoring. If he could have been forced to explain to somebody why this was, he would have surely said it was simply because of the bitter cold. However, in truth, even if it was only for half a moment in the smallest part of his heart, he actually pitied Scoundrel.

Scoundrel started to sob again, “Ye couldn’t be more right! I’ve backstabbed, hoodwinked, and fooled every livin’ soul I’ve ever met! No not just the livin’! Even the graves of the men that ‘ave passed ‘ave ‘ad no mercy from me greedy hand!”
“A bit late to make a change of heart I’m afraid!” scoffed John through the piercing wind.

“Yes, nothin’ could be truer,” sniffled Scoundrel, as his tears froze in the cold weather, “Yet, to even ‘ave the comfort of knowing somebody was beside me at my deathbed would take a great weight off my soul…”

“You can take comfort from the wolves!” John barked, “We ain’t staying up ‘ere any longer, me footsies are already freezing to the ground! Come on Bert, let’s tie ‘em to the tree, there’s no trusting ‘im!”

But Bert dropped his knife into the snow. “Me thinks that maybe we could set up camp out ‘ere tonight... I know that the lil’ wretch don’t deserve nothin’, but boss never said when we needs to come back…”
“We can’t just sets up camp ‘ere!” John cried indignantly

“Well, maybe we could just chops down part of the tree for a wee fire… and we brought our campin’ gear with us… Think about it John, we doesn’t have much chances makin’ it back in this cold anyhow! It’s already pitch black out ‘ere! I says we just call it a night!”

At this point, John had already tied Scoundrel to the tree. In a rush of force, a powerful gust of a strangely warm wind suddenly hit, leaving John staggering for his balance. He then fell toward the wintry powder below with an ungraceful thump, like a hippo flopping into a pond. Catching a face full of snow, his face began to burn and he felt as though it was frozen to the ground. As he struggled putting himself back on his feet again, his lips turned a sickly color of blue and his teeth started to chatter. He finally relented, “F—ffff-- fine… W-- we can just call it a night. This way we can keep an eye on the ol’ Scoundrel too. I’ll sees to it that the wolves get to ‘im.”

The lumberjacks wasted no time in setting up their camp. Nor would have you or me if we had been put under such circumstances. The lumberjacks couldn’t stand the thought of being in that frigid weather any longer than they had to, it had already begun to take its toll on them (particularly John). With haste they chopped off the top half of Scoundrel’s tree and split it into blocks of firewood. Theirhacking left Scoundrel, who remained tied to the tree all the while, with splinters in his face. Yet they paid no notice to this. The only thought on their minds now was one thing and one thing only: warmth. After an hour’s worth of work, the two lumberjacks had set up their camp and fire. Once they’d settled into their tents, they fell soundly asleep within the bat of an eye.

However, while the two slept peaceful dreams near the warmth of the fire, there was one that was still awake… Scoundrel. Out alone in the howling of the wind he stood tied to half a tree. At least he thought it was the wind, but it could just as easily have been the wolves…

While the grim possibility of this might have made any normal person curl up in horror, Scoundrel’s mind was quite busy with something else. Yes, once again, Scoundrel’s face lit up with a smug smile and he let out a haughty chuckle. Within a mere minute, the boy who had been bound was now free. The icy ropes fell to his feet, and he was relieved of the stiffness the brittle tree against his back.

Now, you may be wondering, how did Scoundrel pull off this miraculous feat!? He had just been bound, tied up, he was even whimpering in fear of his fate! If only you had been told even a few of the tales of this young hooligan Scoundrel, you would have an idea how… He was a devilishly clever creature, with the wits of which no other could match. It happened that he had actually planned the whole ordeal from start to finish, it was all simply been a show. And when Bert had dropped his knife to the ground, Scoundrel snatched the opportunity, stealing it out of the snow. Once he had the knife in his possession, he only had to wait for his chance at freedom.

With himself freed, Scoundrel went on to carry out the rest of his plan. Quietly and nimbly climbing into each tent Scoundrel plundered their goods while they slept. He took their lamps, their food, their maps, their tools… Nothing was missed, and nothing was spared, all of it being tucked away in a satchel he bore. While one would think that the lumberjacks would have been awoken by the presence of Scoundrel, with the raging noise of the wind against their tents, there was nothing that could awake them from their sleep.

After everything of the lumberjacks had been stolen and slung over his back, Scoundrel left the campgrounds in search of a shelter for himself. He started out traveling downwards towards the foot of the mountain in hopes of finding his way back into town of Blackneck that night. Keeping his lantern high above his face to shield himself from the blast of the intense wintry air, he descended the rocky terrain with great caution. A few times he lost his footing and found himself sliding down on his backside (which was only a small punishment for what he had done to the lumberjacks). Yet, after a while, a dour truth dawned over Scoundrel.

Because of his scuffle with the lumberjacks, his presence within the town would never be welcomed again. Scoundrel had dealt with mobs before, but never in the winter, and never in such a desperate time as the town was in now. He would surely be hung, they would stand for him no longer. No, Scoundrel could not return to Blackneck! He would have to find some other shelter, some other safe haven from this cold. He began to rack his brain for ideas, but, even in his clever mind, he found that all of his hopes of survival were futile. There was nowhere in the mountain for him to hide. He had no way to build himself a shelter that could sustain him in the conditions that surrounded him. He was doomed!

As he stood there in the snow fretting over this, a wind rushed past him with a surging force like none he had ever felt before. Its touch was warm, and when he felt it against his skin, he thought that he might have been floating on a cloud. Yet it also had a strength so powerful that it knocked him off his feet and into the cold snow. The contents of his sack began spilling out and were carried away in the current of that strange wind. With a leap from the ground, Scoundrel quickly ran after them, for one of the items was one that he could not afford to lose; this item happened to be his map. The map continued to flutter higher and higher into the wind, and as Scoundrel looked after it he watched it cover nearly the whole tip of the mountain from view. It was at that tip where Scoundrel saw something that made his tracks stop short and his eyes light up in a rapacious glint. It was an enormous block of ice jutting out from the tip of the mountain. Yet, this block of ice was like no other. To Scoundrel it looked to be afortress or a palace. With a tall spire of ice sprouting out from its tip, blankets of snow cloaking it in a majestic glow, and a spiral of ice flowing out of its side, Scoundrel was convinced that it could be nothing but one.

Even after another heavy wind blew through, curtaining the view of the ice fortress with a cloud of snow, the vision of its magnificence remained in Scoundrel’s head. As an infant, long ago, Scoundrel could remember being told grand tales of the ice palace that stood looming high in the radiating glory of the Craggleback Mountain. He’d once heard that the Ice King himself made his home there. These were, of course, simple nursery rhymes he had been told as a young lad. They were nothing but whimsical lies that were merely reserved for the most gullible children. However, Scoundrel couldn’t deny that he once longed with all his heart to walk within its icy halls and to stare with awe at the overwhelming beauty of the treasures that were said to have been piled within them. And now, the very thing that reigned the dreams of his youth stood before him. It had become a reality!

An idea popped into his head that set him into a frenzy of excitement. He would plunder the riches of the ice castle! There was nothing that smelled sweeter to his mind than this! Surely the castle was abandoned, the Ice King was but an old wives tale. And nobody else had ever dared to tread this mountain before, nor would anybody ever dare tread it in ages to come. The castle was for the taking! With all these thoughts combined in his head, a nasty smile spread across his face… He might have lost his place as the king of Blackneck, but now? Now he was going to be king of the mountain! Scoundrel let out a sigh of fulfillment, and ran off to gather the items that remained scattered across the ground. It was a shame that his map was long gone by now, but he had a feeling he wouldn’t be needing it where he was going… Scoundrel was going to climb the mountain.

The journey up the mountain was not an easy one, to say the least. The harder Scoundrel pressed on upwards, the harder he felt the storm oppose him. The night turned to day but Scoundrel still found himself fighting furiously to reach even halfway up the mountain and the storm remained unrelenting.

At times he felt that his mission was hopeless, but he drove those uncertainties away with visions of the magnificent riches that laid waiting for him. Even with his energy draining, those thoughts-- those oh so powerful thoughts!—they’d give him bursts of strength that would fling him further into his trek than before. Nothing could stop Scoundrel, not snow, nor an avalanche, nor even death itself. The greedy will within his eyes was enough to take on anything he encountered. All things that could oppose him already sat under his thumb. His slick mind, his nimble fingers, and his sharp tongue surpassed all; what could even dare stand against it?

So, Scoundrel carried on like this, agilely weaving himself up the mountain. No aching pain in his body, no hunger in his stomach, and no weariness in his bones hindered him. He overcame all the adverse forces of nature before reaching the pinnacle of the mountain. And heDIDreach the top of that mountain, no matter what the people of Blackneck that came after him will say. Some might deny that there’s any truth in this story, while others will only laugh it off as a tall tale. But I tell you now, no matter what any person says, Scoundrel reached and stood before the ice castle, and the events that came before and after this moment stand true.

Yes, after vast amounts of painstaking labor and the use of an iron will like no other, Scoundrel found himself crossing the frozen lake that encased the grand ice palace. It was a tricky task, and he found himself sliding onto his back a few times. Although, he managed to cross the lake without falling through (the frigid weather had ensured it was solid enough to withstand the weight of an elephant) and soon enough, he was standing at the foot of the ice castle in the peak of the mountain. The sight he saw was a glorious wonder, a wonder that no man will ever again, nor had ever before, managed the honor of viewing. Scoundrel was the only living being that had ever managed to reach that point in the mountain, and the only being to ever marvel at the fullness of its splendor.
You might now be wondering, “How is it then that such a castle was built? For, if it was not by the force of a man, nor any other living creature, what force was it done by?”

The answer to the question you seek is one that would be better left unanswered. For, as the answer to all the world’s towering mysteries, it is to be discovered by the labor of the one most deserving of it…

Upon the foot of the castle, shrouded in a mist of mystery and frost, Scoundrel limbs shook, awestruck, as he gazed upon it with reverence. Its beauty was overwhelming. The walls, forming into the shape of a hexagon, were built out of the purest of white snow packed and mounded upon a crystal clear ice glazed over the surface of the lake. The roof of the fortress was a brilliant dome crafted out of a cold blue crystal, and out if its center protruded the unmistakable spire he had viewed what seemed like so long ago. In the light of the sun, radiant rays of light spilled out from every angle of the structure and into the snow, leaving the ground sparkling and glittering like a white rainbow.

Staring at this all, he found himself tripping over the spiraling translucent staircase that led into the wide door of the castle. What a lustrous door it was too! Ornamented in elaborate designs and delicate markings, Scoundrel couldn’t help but muse how anybody could have possibly designed it without shattering the fragile structure.

As he was wondering this, the door suddenly swung wide open revealing a large crystal hall full of mounded treasures. Their sparkling features set the passageway, as well as Scoundrel’s eyes, aglow with an exquisite white light. After making a gradual ingress into the room Scoundrel gazed upon the riches’ majesty and began strategizing how he would spend such an opulent wealth. It was then that he noticed they were unlike the ordinary gold and jewels he had seen traded amongst the villagers in the markets of Blackneck. Scooping a gem up and clutching it tightly against his heart he felt it singe his skin with a chilling cold. The gems were made of ice... Or at least something like it… While the gem was cold, it didn’t melt in his hand like an icicle would have... To make sure it was a true gem, Scoundrel scratched at its flawless surface. To his astonishment, not a blemish was made and his thumb slipped off its smooth surface.
The thief was befuddled now. How was it so cold? It certainly wasn’t the room, the room wasn’t cold at all!
“Wait…” Scoundrel said slowly to himself, “How is it that this room, made of ice, is warm?”

He pondered at this with great unease. It simply wasn’t right. In his distress, the greedy boy found himself grasping the gem he held ever tighter against his chest. He found that this relaxed his worried thoughts and gave him comfort.

Perhaps his senses were just fooling him. The journey to the castle had probably taken a large toll on his body. How foolish of him to think there was anything wrong! He just needed a little food and maybe a nap and he’d be fine to complete the survey of the castle later.

Scoundrel emptied his sack, preparing himself a little food and a sleeping situation. He finished the food rather quickly, gobbling down every morsel. He didn’t stop, except for when he felt a rush of wind and an eerie creak from down the hall. His stomach turned, and he jerked his head down the dark passageways. It had just been his nerves playing tricks on him! There was nothing to be seen, so he returned his meal. Once he’d finished, he curled up on his blanket for a long sleep, with his gem snugly tucked into his chest.
Chapter Three
Scaling the Summit

Scoundrel had slept for a long while when he awoke to an awful noise resounding amongst the imposing walls. His eyes popping wide open, Scoundrel disquieted in the uneasy prospect that the lumberjacks might have found him. However, once he’d listened closer, he realized the sound was nothing like what he’d heard before. It was a howling noise, like a hefty gale and also roared furiously like a great waterfall. Scoundrel didn’t know what to think, but he knew right then that he wasn’t alone. The shock of the noise left him immobile and his joints were as stiff as stone. Then he heard a thunderclap that startled him to the point that he collapsed upon the floor. With apprehension welling up inside himself he tautly clenched his jewel to his chest, and, lifting an axe he had stolen from the lumberjacks out of his sack, he proceeded to search out the sound.

While Scoundrel walked through the castle, he began to fear that perhaps it was occupied after all. What a great mess he had put himself in! He was in such a fright that he swung his axe about like a fool at every turn. His axe smashing into the walls and breaking delicate crystal décor, he created a raucous even louder than the noise he was afraid of. It was when he came to the realization of his foolishness that he finally calmed himself down.
“It’s just the snowstorm that you’re hearing,” he told himself, “A gust of wind never hurt anyone!”
However, soon he’d find out just how right and wrong he was.

He began to realize that, in his search for the sound, he was carrying himself deeper and deeper into the heart of the palace; much deeper than he felt comfortable. He started to regret leaving his packs behind, as he now wondered if he’d ever be able to find his way back. These shadows of doubt passed though, as Scoundrel was confident that nothing as simple as a maze of halls could phase him. He had just conquered a mountain! What worse could this fragile icy framework give him?!

A chilling wind suddenly whistled through the hall in an abrupt wail, and tingling fear paled every inch of his body. With sweaty palms, Scoundrel’s grip on his jewel started to loosen. He clenched his fists to keep his hold; he couldn’t let himself lose it. A belief that the jewel was a sort of good luck charm, something that could keep him safe, had taken anchor in Scoundrel’s mind. While it may have been that his safety wouldn’t have changed much whether he kept the jewel or not (in fact, a free hand might have been more than helpful in his condition), he felt that he couldn’t part with it without losing a part of himself. The feeling of the slick cold stone against his body grown to be one of comfort for him. The rock seemed to give him a sense of direction, and he felt that it was guiding him closer toward the sound. While it was all probably more than a hoax that he had created for himself, it was perhaps his only sense of a companion in the desolate castle.

The feet of Scoundrel reluctantly treaded ever further inward as the rupturing noise grew louder. Feeling the rush of the wind mercilessly surge past his face, he was forced to shut his eyes tightly while a vicious ringing filled his ears. Scoundrel wanted to fall on his knees screaming in pain, but he knew that doing such was an act of cowardice. He slowed into a crawl through a cavernous mouth, leading into an open room. Strangely, the moment he entered he noticed that the raucous stopped with a shocking suddenness.

For a moment, the thief was puzzled, but he shoved away all his concerns to explore his new surroundings. The room was very expansive, having the combined space of maybe twenty of the largest shacks built in Blackneck. Bordering the sparkling crystal pathway that Scoundrel was trudging along, thick walls were built on each side. But up ahead, Scoundrel observed that there was no wall, and he saw a great cliff leading into an abyss. Scoundrel shuddered at the thought of falling into it. Looking up, Scoundrel noticed an enormous dome was hollowed into the ceiling, letting the warm red light of the setting sun dance into the room.
Scoundrel was mesmerized. “Beautiful,” he tried to say, the word almost leaping from his lips. Butjust as he opened his mouth, he was flung to the floor by a ferocious blast of air.

It was during this moment, with the surging whisk returning to reverberate through his soul, when an overpowering voice invaded Scoundrel’s very being. It chilled him to the bone, and he felt it suck the very warmth from his body.
“Fall to the GROUND!” the voice cried, shaking the whole room, “and LOOK upon me, for a KING deserves RESPECT!”

With a force of monstrous strength, Scoundrel felt himself being flattened against the frigid floor. Yet in spite of all the violence, Scoundrel still managed to clutch his gem tightly to his chest. Except now, with his frail body pressed to the floor, he could feel the cold stone digging into his skin. With his eyes bulging wide open, Scoundrel began to behold the being that had overtaken him.

There was a foreboding head taking its form in the center of the room, from a cyclone of ice and snow. Ghastly features covered it; large piercing eyes, and a gaping mouth filled of protruding icicle fangs. Atop this unearthly visage was a crown of ice and snow, with a rigid star-shaped gem placed in the center. But as Scoundrel looked closer upon this gem he realized something; it was not a gem but a man. Yet, to call it a man wouldn’t even begin to describe the fullness of its eerie form.

Instead of having flesh on his body, the figure was covered in a dark icy blue layer that looked as slick as porcelain. It was flawless, besides a strange eerie black stain on his neck that stood out like a wrinkled prune. If you had seen it, you might have said it looked almost like skin. But, it was not skin, Scoundrel was certain of that. It was horrid to look at, yet it still had a strange lure that made it so that Scoundrel struggled to take his eyes from it. What was the story behind this scar? He had to know!

Scoundrel forced himself to shift his focus back to the figure. On it, there was nothing save for two vacant coal black eyes that looked down on Scoundrel, boring holes through his skull. It didn’t even have clothes, unless you would count the chunks of ice lodged into its body, from the blizzard around it.

With his limbs outstretched like a star, he kept his gaze upon Scoundrel with his piercing empty eyes. They never moved, nor flinched. They simply stared down… They almost looked unforgiving, but as Scoundrel was forced to keep contact with them, chilling him to the bone, they showed no emotion. None at all. However, they didn’t exactly lack emotion either. As Scoundrel looked deep into the strange man’s cold barren eyes (and how cold they were) he thought he saw pain, a pain of an eternity in the cold. Yet, Scoundrel watched it seem to pass just as quickly as he noticed it, like dust in the wind. He felt that what he saw could have just as easily been rage, or malice, or nothing at all.

Yes, nothing at all was what he felt he saw the most. He was a both strange and sorry sight, this man of ice. While Scoundrel continued to stare at him and the creature stared back, he felt a part in himself open that he hadn’t felt in ages. He felt a bit of sympathy for this thing that looked as though it couldn’t feel, couldn’t touch. The thought of never being able to feel emotion was a thing beyond what Scoundrel could bear.

Scoundrel quickly buried these thoughts back within himself though, there was too much to worry about. Even now, the blizzard had begun picking up speed and Scoundrel could feel himself being throttled and jolted through the air. Studying the blizzard as rapid as he could, he became aware that the storm was coming out of the very man himself. Out of the ice man’s hands the storm raged wildly, and Scoundrel watched it fill the room.

He couldn’t withhold his curiosity and puzzlement any longer, “Who are you!?” Scoundrel cried in a weak voice, as he was flung about the room in the wind. This wasn’t at all the approach Scoundrel had intended to take, but in the conditions that surrounded him, there was little he could control.

In an instant, Scoundrel found that the wind had stilled, and he was now almost within it. “Who am I?” the wind repeated softly and sharply as it ran through his ears, “I, the great king of legend, that has plagued your town for ages, have revealed myself to you in all my might and glory… and you ask me this… WHO AM I!? I am the great ICE KING! I am the ruler of the storm! I am the great quencher of the heat! I am the mighty emperor of the mountain! ALL forms of ice, snow, cold and wind are subjectto ME!” the wind paused for a moment, “Now it is MY turn to ask the question… who are YOU and by what right do you stand before me!? I have watched you as you climbed my mountain, broke into my halls and stole my treasures, the treasures of the KING!”

At each sentence of the blizzard’s rage, Scoundrel was lifted and thrown to the ground with an awful thwack. He was now quaking in exhaustion. “My name is Sc-- Scoundrel. I have come to your palace by the authority of none but my own. I now humbly beg of your mercy and wish to part ways with your forgiveness.”

“Scoundrel!?” the wind cried with a laugh, “Your name isScoundreland you wish for my MERCY!? I would ask how you came to earn that name of yours, yet I already know… I’ve watched your journey to my fortress, and your treachery against your own people. Where was MERCY when you left the lumberjacks wandering alone in my mountains!? Where was FORGIVENESS?! Perhaps your actions down below were innocent, but now you come and disturbMYriches!? You have earned yourself a punishment beyond death!”
“Wha—What are you going to do!?”

“What will I do!? Your soul is to be frozen for eternity! Your greed has become your doom, oh great Scoundrel! You will be ensnared within the crystal you hold against your chest for ages to come! Prepare to be bound to a curse of endless cold and suffering! It will remain part of you until the world itself meets its end!”
“No! This can’t be my fate! There must be a chance of mercy! I was unaware of your presence within your castle, I swear from the bottom of my heart!”
“Your actions tell me otherwise and the bottom of your empty heart is pitch black! None that live in Blackneck are raised without knowledge of me!”
“But there must be a bit of sympathy within your heart!”

“Ha! That’s the truth of it boy! It has taken me an eternity of the cold to learn that, in this world, there isNOsympathy! Now, it is time that you faced your doom!” With that, a bitter air began to fill the room and Scoundrel felt the crystal he held grow cold and begin to sting at his chest
“There has to be another way!!” Scoundrel screamed shrilly, while a vortex of snow and ice began to encase him.
“Give me ONE reason for mercy!” the wind hissed as it whirled around him, “One reason that you should be spared!”
It was then that Scoundrel’s thoughts returned to eyes of the Ice King, and the empty pain he saw within them. “Love!” Scoundrel burst out.
The wind stilled and the face of the blizzard fell.

“Love?” The voice of the wind said in a strident whisper, “And what is this love...?” The wind sat quiet for a moment, almost as if to try and answer the question itself. “I doubt that you even know! Love is the greatest lie to man! It is the very reason that fools flood the earth. It is the reason people cast themselves into wars, fall into famine, and lose their identity. Why should I spare you for a force as corrosive as love?”

For a moment, Scoundrel was stunned. Yet, suddenly, he began to feel a part in himself hatch open that he’d never felt before. “Love is a truth greater than anything else your cold eyes shall ever see.”

“You babble tales told to infants! The love you speak of exists only in the realm of imagination. On this cold barren earth, there is no place for a bliss as sweet as that, and chasing after such a thing is the very essence of destruction... Where is love in your empty shack in the town you call Blackneck? My winds have passed by it, year after year, always finding it empty, save one soul that lives within it… Your own! Where does your mother lay? Your father? You of all people should know that, in the end, love always leaves you alone in the cold…”
“I have no parents! I am the great Scoundrel, I always have been and I always will be!”
“You may have your townspeople fooled, but such lies don’t hold any power over me. Stop spouting out falsehood and step into the full realization of the truth!”
The wind once again began pressing its full strength down on Scoundrel.
“It is time Scoundrel that you finally submit!” the wind cried, “You shall be thrown into the chamber of your own heart’s greed!”
“No! I can prove to you that love exists!” Scoundrel declared frantically, “I swear, as true as my town stands, I can prove it!”
“Prove it!? PROVE IT!? You grasp at air! How can you prove a lie to be true?!”
“Give me a day, and I’ll return to you with proof! Just one day’s time is all it will take!”

Now, Scoundrel certainly had no proof of love, nor did he intend to find any. In truth, he felt that, with the prospect of being ensnared in a cage of ice for eternity, the hope of even one more day of freedom would lift a great burden off his soul.

“You wish for a day of liberation!? What foolishness this is, you simply are prolonging the inevitable! Why do you expect me to give you the pleasure of one last day of life? What gain shall be made for me by this, once you fail!?”
“You will have… you will have… You will have the satisfaction of being right!”
“Do I look to you as a dog that you should come at me with sticks!? Your offerings are pitiful!”
Scoundrel began to see that the patience of the great beast was running thin. He needed to think quickly.

“Well… You say that you believe you’re king of Blackneck correct? Well, I believe that I’m king of Blackneck! If I fail, all of Blackneck is your dominion to do whatever you wish with. If I succeed, both Blackneck, and my soul, will be free of your captivity!”
“Ha! As if Blackneck and your soul is not already mine for the taking! You crafty coward! You have nothing to support your case!”

“You call me a coward?” Scoundrel said, his mind racing, “Why, the truth is, you are the coward! You do not wish to be proven wrong, fearing that your very way of life will be shattered when you see that love is not a lie!”
The wind hushed for a twinkling.

“Bah! The great Ice King fears nothing! You couldn’t prove me wrong boy, even if you wanted to!” the wind remained still a while longer, until the great face in the blizzard broke into full rage, “Fine, your wish is granted! You will be allowed a pass, to carry out your quest. Although, you shall still remain under my captivity during its duration, and the crystal that you bare across your chest shall bind itself to your heart. There will be no escape from the watchful eye of my winds, and any attempt to do so will result in your immediate termination. If you do happen to succeed in your quest, I shall relieve you of the curse that will gnaw at your heart until the end of the day’s time. If you fail however… You and the town of Blackneck will be thrown under the spell of my ultimate wrath, never to awake from my deadly wintry touch again.”

Scoundrel was in shock! He had managed a chance at freedom! He couldn’t help but begin to feel overjoyed with this new hope that began to take fruit inside him. Yet, all his hopes were quickly dashed when he felt himself begin to be lifted high into the blizzard.
