“Now be gone, and return to me at the setting of the sun tomorrow!” the blizzard cried.

Quaking in the full fury of the wind, Scoundrel then found himself flying through the windows, out of the corridors of the ice castle, and over the frozen lake; until he was flung out into the snow… and a raging avalanche…
Chapter Four
An Unsettling Encounter

He wasn’t sure how long he’d been lying in the heap of stone and snow left behind from the avalanche, but when Scoundrel awoke, he found himself tucked in a toasty blanket. How he came to be there, he didn’t know either, but as for what aroused him, it was the unmistakable sweet song of a flute. Its graceful melody danced in his ears and brought beautiful images of peace and rest to his mind. The delicate tune was a great medicine for his soul. It had been longer than Scoundrel could remember since he had last heard the sound of music, let alone music that he hadn’t stolen and to him, the flute’s voice was priceless. After laying down for a while, absorbing the calm feeling that seemed to wash over him, he began to search his surroundings. The boy’s neck ached as he scanned around, but in spite of the pain, Scoundrel managed to find that he was in a giant tent. The tent he lay in was mostly empty, save himself and the player of the flute; a funny looking man. If you would have only seen him, you’d have chuckled at the sight.

He was dressed in strange garments that looked to be rags, only they were made of a thick velvet that seemed fit for a king. Although, the garments he wore were only the half of it, for his face was an even greater spectacle. It was a unique face to be sure, and, no matter who you are, it was the sort of which you would never forget. The skin on his face was wrinkled and worn almost like the lather sole of a shoe. His features were tired and weary, yet were still strangely full of liveliness and hope. He had a sharp nipped nose and two darting eyes that poked out of his head. Jutting out of his face as a branch from a tree was his chin, which was covered in a thick red beard that nearly fell to his feet. And to say that a beard could nearly touch the feet of a man as tall as this one was is quite the tale. For, this strange flute-player had a towering figure, much taller than that of Scoundrel. Why, he was much larger than any of the men Scoundrel had ever seen in Blackneck. Sitting down even, his head touched the roof of the enormous tent. It was so high that he had to crouch down just to fit.

As Scoundrel continued to study him, he watched as the large eyes fixed in the man’s head began to stare back at him. This gave Scoundrel much unease, but the situation only became stranger. The music slowly started to stop, and the man’s face reddened and turned blotchy. Beginning to search for what was the matter, Scoundrel saw that the man had his hand pressed down over all the holes of the flute. The hermit’s face grew ever ruddier as he started to blow harder into the flute. POP! The flute shot across the tent, nearly hitting Scoundrel’s now irritated face, before landing in a corner.

Scoundrel continued to watch the old fool with an indignant scowl, when the flute-player hopped up and scrambled toward him in a frenzy. Having a worried look on his face, the hermit started rubbing his hands together wildly.

If you could have only seen the man, you would have wished to crawl out of your skin at the sight. His beard wagged around violently, his eyes were ablaze, but his lips somehow managed to remain still as stone the whole time. Any sane man would have been quick to rush out of the tent, yet Scoundrel still remained, partly out of the pain he felt, and partly out of the curiosity that consumed him.

Once the berserk bearded beanpole had finished his deranged ordeal, he then started to smear his hands across Scoundrel’s face. Scoundrel felt the grimy oil that covered the recluse’s palms start to grip his skin. At this point Scoundrel could contain his fear of the crazed man no longer and he pushed him away.
“Hey, what was that there for!?” the man shouted as his beard wagged about, “Don’t ya want to get betta’!?”
“And how is smearing your oily hands against my face supposed to make me better, you old fool!?” Scoundrel said with a huff.

“This ain’t no oil!” the man said, waving his hands in Scoundrel’s face, “It’s a special elixir I brew! It heals many an ailment it does! Now sit down nice and still-like until I’m done puttin’ it on ya!”
“Ailments?” inquired Scoundrel, “What ailments?”

The man’s eyes darted about the room quickly and he started to slow his movements with an apparent caution. “Ya took quite the tumble down the mountain in an avalanche. When I went to the remains of it, I found ye’ buried in a heap of snow, I did. To my surprise, when I took ye into me tent, ye didn’t seem to have that many injuries save a few bruises and scars… and a curious icy mark on yer chest...”

At those last words of the strange man, Scoundrel slapped his hand against his chest to find it colder than the weather that surrounded him. The ice king’s gem… It was still there! Scoundrel had only thought that all the strange events concerning the ice castle high in the mountain might have just been a passing dream, up until now…
The hermit caught the concerned look on Scoundrel’s face.
“Might I ask what ye were doin’ up there, especially with this fierce weather?” he said, raising a bushy red eyebrow.
“I—I was… I was lost…” Scoundrel stammered.
“If ye wish to sputter lies as bad as that, ye may as well not answer. But, what should I know? I’m just an, ‘ol’ fool’, ain’t that right?”
The man then continued rubbing Scoundrel down with his elixir.
“So, who are you anyways?” Scoundrel asked.
“I could ask ye the same thing… yet, I ‘ave the feeling that no matter what your answer might be, it’d be a lie…”

Scoundrel sat quiet for a while pondering on this. Could this strange hermit know who he was? Surely not, that just couldn’t be… They had just met! Yet, as Scoundrel peered into his strange eyes, he couldn’t help but feel that they were more knowing than they seemed.

“If you think me to be such a liar, then why do you still receive me as a guest?” Scoundrel asked, while the man began crawling back to his corner in the tent, “Why did you even bother flinging yourself into the raging blizzard, when you couldn’t have possibly known for certain if there was a person to retrieve from it?”

“Perhaps it was because ye weren’t the only one searching for something on the peak of that mountain,” the man answered mysteriously before sitting back down to pour more of the elixir into his flute.
“How do you know I was searching for something?” Scoundrel asked, but the hermit had already begun playing his instrument.

Scoundrel was transfixed for a while, lamenting on what had happened. The man was, no doubt, a strange and curious soul. However, Scoundrel couldn’t help but feel there was a quality about him that was both kind and welcoming. If you had seen those eyes the man had, you would have felt the warmth and comfort flowing out of them. Even in the devious Scoundrel’s ungratefulness, he still couldn’t muster any ill intent toward him.

However, as kind of a soul this man was, Scoundrel saw that he was costing him too much time. If he had no answers for him, then Scoundrel would just have to leave. Each second Scoundrel wasted lessened the chance of him ever finding his way out of the curse that continued to grow colder on his heart.
Scoundrel plodded toward the bearded man.
“Do you believe in the Ice King?” Scoundrel finally relented.

The hermit smiled through his nest of a beard and set down his flute, “I was hoping ye would ask me that. In this part of the mountain, there’s nothing one can be more certain of. After livin’ on this mountain as long as I ‘ave, there’s no denying it. I ‘ave seen his works many a time. And, if I’m not mistaken, ye bare his mark across yer chest.”
Scoundrel was now in shock, “You’ve met the Ice King!?”

“Met ‘im? Ha! Met ‘im!? I tell ye now, if I met ‘im I wouldn’t be ‘ere today. To make business with the ice king is to make business with death itself! No, I ’ave only observed the beast’s work from afar.”
“Well, what if I told you I made a deal with him?”
The hermit’s face fell.
“Then ye’d ‘ave been a fool,” he said stammering, “I had feared that ye’d done as much with that there mark of yers… What deal did ye make with ‘im boy!? Ye best tell me now before it’s too late!”
“I—I’d rather not say…” Scoundrel said.

“Keeping secrets is a grave mistake, especially in matters concerning something as foreboding as the Ice King,” the hermit warned in a still whisper, “He’s crafty as a snake he is! Has ears and eyes everywhere. Even the wolves answer to his icy call! I’ll help ye the best I can, but I warn ye’, there’s little I can do.”
Scoundrel sat for a moment.
“Do you know anything of his history, or, better yet, somebody who does?”
“Sadly, I only know one who can answer the question you seek, and they isn’t one to talk all that much… If ye could even find them, that is…”
“I’ve climbed this ferocious mountain on my own. What more is there that I couldn’t handle?”

“Ye only stepped foot at the beginning of the Ice King’s domain. Trust me when I say this, the Craggleback Mountain is a place that is anything but easy to conquer and ye ‘ave only scratched the surface of its mysteries. Not to mention, with your injuries, I doubt ye even ‘ave the time for this venture…”
“Where are they? Who are they?” Scoundrel persisted.

“They’re sometimes ‘ere, sometimes there… They ain’t the sort that stays in one place… They ain’t even the sort that stays as one person! I sometimes find ‘em as a widow livin’ in a simple cottage, other times I find a lone lumberjack in a log house, and still, other times I find nothin’ at all… That’s why we sometimes calls ‘em the ‘warm wind’, cuz they’re no more tamable than the wind itself.”
“How on earth am I supposed to find her—or him—or IT!? I can’t just wander around this empty mountain! Time waits for no one!”

Scoundrel was completely thrown out of sorts at the prospect of searching for practically nothing, as would have you or I if we had been told such a thing. With time waning, and little hope to grip onto, an aimless search through the mountain only seemed to drain his chances further. The boy had begun to question the sanity of his host; not that he hadn’t been doing so already.

Yet, even in spite of Scoundrel’s heavy doubts, the man seemed nothing but sure of himself, “Ye are right, time does wait for no one, and the only way you’ll ever find ‘em is by accepting this truth; the key to unlocking the goal to yer journey will be patience beyond all else. Until ye can learn its secret, ye will be searching in vain for quite some time.”
“How is patience supposed to help!?”

“If there is anything I ‘ave learnt in all me years on this lone mountain top, it is this: there are some workings up ‘ere that we can never understand. Accepting that will solve a lot of yer problems.”
The man slipped a bottle of his elixir out of his pocket and cupped it in Scoundrel’s hand.
“I ‘ave the feeling ye might be needing this,” he said, grinning at Scoundrel with a twinkle in his eye, “Now go! Time waits for no one.”
Chapter Six
To Find Some Answers

Scoundrel set off without hesitation, without as much as a goodbye. If you had met Scoundrel, you would have known that he wasn’t the sort to ever take the time to thank others for their deeds (not that having somebody sacrifice their time for him was an average occurrence in the first place)… In fact, he wasn’t the sort to bother himself with the affairs of others at all; he never even attempted to get the hermit’s name!

Flying out of the loose flaps of the tent, he found himself hurling through the pitch black of midnight. If only he had looked back though, he might have seen the old hermit waving him away with a comforting gaze. Perhaps if Scoundrel had, he would have been able to see him mouth to him this one word: patience.
Although, nothing could stop him in his race for his life, not even a warning from a friend. He would not rest until he achieved his goal; until he saved himself!

So, Scoundrel went on like this, running about frivolously, with no distinction as to where he was headed in sight. To make things worse, the rocks piercing into his weary feet, the snow flying into his battered face, and the wind against his tired frame offered a battle that he felt he could no longer fight. Scoundrel began to wonder if the ice king himself might have started to fight against him, but he quickly waved those thoughts away to focus on the task at hand. It had become quite apparent that he wasn’t at all prepared for what he had thrown himself into. Yet, there was no option for retreat. He felt that he was running through the mountain in circles, and he saw no end in sight.

So, moving ever faster, he continued to press on through the wind. He ran with all his might, even as the wind’s force grew ever stronger against him. The cold air blasted against him harder, stinging his lips and numbing his feet, till they felt lifeless as stone. Even in spite of this, Scoundrel refused to give in and pushed on. Scoundrel was not a boy to quit when he had his mind set on something. Though he was a nasty, crafty, devious and malicious soul, of all his adverse traits, his spirit of perseverance was the one that stood pure.

Yet, even the most persistent of hearts must falter at some point. Scoundrel’s chest began to feel as though a needle had punctured it, and it stung with a sharp pain. He pressed his hand against it, in a vain hope to ease his pain, only to find a numbing cold, which left his hand dead as ice, where the beating of his heart should have been. The crystal bound to his chest was getting colder. Whether it was the weather around him, or the curse strengthening, he couldn’t be sure, but there was one thing he had decided upon with a certain confidence: he could go on with his trek no longer. Closing his eyes, he threw himself into the snow and lay there.
You might be thinking to yourself, “How foolish is this wretched boy? What good is casting himself into the snow while, not only his life, but the life of his whole town hangs in uncertainty?”

Well, to you I say this; what else could have he do in such a circumstance? All he had ever known was to look out for himself, and now, in his final hours, he no longer had that ability. He had utterly lost all reason and strength to move on. What was the purpose of letting himself suffer any further? The ice king obviously had him under his thumb. There was little or no chance at all that he’d make it through the day with the ice on his chest slowly numbing his soul.

The wind continued to blow furiously until a gust of wind hit him so hard that the elixir the hermit had given him shot out of his pocket. The elixir! Scoundrel now remembered what the hermit had told him about needing it. While the prospect of it giving Scoundrel the chance to move on was slim, he knew it was his only chance… If he could reach it anyhow. The elixir seemed worlds away at this point, especially with the meagre condition of Scoundrel’s body. Yet, as Scoundrel stared at the elixir, something had begun to stir up inside of him that he had seldom felt. A drive to push forward, not for his own self, but in hopes that the hermit wouldn’t have wasted all his efforts on Scoundrel after all. A hope that maybe, just maybe, the hermit could reap a fruit from his decision to take the old wretch Scoundrel in.

The feeling was a quickly fading one, just a small spark in Scoundrel’s being. It certainly didn’t consume him in any way, it only passed through his mind for a fragment of a second. Scoundrel was farbeyond cowering to such a trickery as a ‘gift’. No, no, the elixir had only reminded him of comfort, of warmth, and how he must save himself from the cold curse of the ice king. As far as the hermit, he had no part in it, nor was it even a shadow of a possibility!

So, that small spark in Scoundrel drove him toward the elixir. One frail limb after another, he dragged himself to the one shining hope he had left. He could see it in his reach, only a few yards away. Now it was only a couple yards. One yard. Two feet! Scoundrel almost had the elixir!
On the spur of the moment, a lusty wind knocked Scoundrel into the air and sent him toppling into the snow.
“NO!” he cried out in despair.

When Scoundrel lifted his now powdered head, he found that his elixir had disappeared with the wind. It was all over... Scoundrel had used all he had left in him. He rolled over to surrender to his fate…
Clink!
“The elixir!” Scoundrel shouted joyously.
He had fallen on top of it when he had been thrown into the air; the thin string that hung from the bottle’s cap had caught onto Scoundrel’s clothing.

Without hesitation, Scoundrel twisted the cap off and took a sip from inside the small bottle. After he had finished and he tied the thread around his neck, he found, to his surprise, his whole body begin to feel rejuvenated. His mind felt clearer, his heart had started to warm, and he felt his limbs renew their strength in full vigor. As he started to lift himself up out of the snow with a new aura of confidence, he saw, out in the distance, the cottage that the hermit had talked about! Its figure was shrouded in the blizzard of ice and snow, but he couldn’t have mistaken it for anything else. How he had found it, he did not know. From what the hermit had described, it only revealed itself for those who knew great patience, but he was sure he hadn’t proven anything of that sort.

Nevertheless, the knowledge that he had nearly reached his goal was too sweet to ignore, and he ran after the cottage with haste. As he surged forward, coming ever closer to it, he began to observe how strange the little house really was. Overlooking a high cliff in the mountain, the small hut looked oddly out of place. Its humble foundations quaked and moaned in the fury of the ice storm. Many icicles that had broken off from the mountain in the wind, punctured into its wooden walls. The slender wisp of smoke, that would normally float out of the chimney, bringing a subtle warmth to the world around it, was torn to shreds in the icy wind. And, in the height of the snow that continued to climb around the cottage, only the roof was left fully visible.

Scoundrel wondered how he would get in. Surely the shutters were iced over to the point that they were hard as stone. And there was no hope getting in through the door with the rising state of the snow…

While the chimney did offer a way in, and while it wasn’t an endeavor he hadn’t done with other houses, Scoundrel was unsure of whether or not it would be perceived as a threat to the person who was said to live within after he fell through it. Yet, Scoundrel saw that there were few ways in, and this would have to be his answer. Approaching the house, he slowly started climbing up the hill of snow leading to the roof. Though the snow was mostly sturdy and packed on tight, Scoundrel nearly fell inside of it a few times when one of his feet would break through a particularly weak area. The prospect of falling into the snow, or slipping off the roof of the house might have been a frightening one to you or me. Yet, Scoundrel had learned to love and find thrill in doing such, for he had done so many times down below in the town of Blackneck. Even though the cottage overlooked a great precipice, Scoundrel felt no fear. Fear was a thing he never left room for in his heart, what purpose did it ever serve? Scoundrel had viewed a lot in his short lifetime, and if he had learned anything, that was his greatest lesson.

Scoundrel had reached the roof taking great caution. All the shingles were glazed with ice, so even the slightest misstep while walking across it could have sent him toppling toward a powdery tomb of snow that awaited him below. Still, even with the fearsome knowledge of his situation, Scoundreldidn’t take the care of wasting his time lingering on it. As a small child, he had learned quickly that lingering on things always ended in despair.

The child paced his strides slow but wide, making sure to keep his feet in the firm grip of the snow, as to prevent himself from slipping. It took a little while, and quite a few close calls but he did make it to the chimney. Hugging it tightly with his two legs, he began gathering the snow that surrounded the chimney, and throwing it down the smoky tunnel. He meant for it to put out the fire down below, as well as to offer himself a bit of a cushion. Once the chimney had finally stopped spitting out smoke, and the sizzling and crackling sound that resounded out from it had ceased, he pulled himself into the chimney. Tightly pressing his hands against each wall of the tunnel, he let himself slide down toward the bottom.
Thump!

Scoundrel managed to land in the remaining pile of ash, kindling, and snow, at the bottom of the chimney, with only a few bruises. After he had rubbed himself off from the sooty mess that covered him, he studied the room around him. He found that the cottage was surprisingly warm despite the adverse weather conditions that surrounded it. The atmosphere of the room he was in appeared just as snug, as it was filled with cozy decorations, and familiar colors that reminded him of the homes down in Blackneck.
“Hello? Is anybody there?” he called out hoping for an answer. His only response was an echo and the pounding of the storm.
Seeing the welcoming setting and that the cottage was empty, he decided to make himself comfortable by finding a seat. He was exhausted after his journey and decided he deserved a rest…
“What are you doing!?” a voice snapped as Scoundrel had just started to doze off on a worn velvet couch in a corner.

Scoundrel jumped with shock, and he found himself staring face to face with an elderly bespectacled woman. Her hair was a dark silver, her face was covered in many wrinkles, and her eyes spoke of years of weariness. She was dressed in a green tattered gown that hung down to her feet and her head was covered in a dark blue bonnet. Gripped tightly in her right hand was an old broomstick, quaking with her bony frame. The height of her hunched body was only slightly above Scoundrel’s, yet, in her presence, he felt as though she towered over him.
“I said; what are you doing?!” she croaked again, her glasses bobbing with her tight jaw.
“I—I came here for—For a story!” Scoundrel said, tripping over his words.
“You put out my fire and break into my cottage for astory!? Do I look like mother goose to you!?”
“No, you don’t understand! An old hermit… He told me to come here! He said he knew you; that you could help me! Aren’t you the ‘warm wind?’”
At this point the old woman was beating the stuttering boy with her broomstick.

At Scoundrel’s words, the old woman finally stopped beating him, “A hermit?” adjusting her glasses back onto her face, she saw the elixir hanging from Scoundrel’s neck. “Did this hermit give you that?” she said, shaking her shriveled bony finger at it.
“Yes! Do you recognize it?”

“Recognize it? Why I taught him how to make it!” She then started to shake her head. “The old fool!” she muttered, “I warned him about going up onto the tip of the mountain! I told him that he wasn’t to give his elixir to anyone!”
“What do you mean by ‘you warned him’? And he wasn’t an old fool by giving me the elixir, I can tell you that right now!”

“But isn’t that what you called him?” the woman said with an all too knowing glam in her eye, “I suppose it’s too late to linger on it now though, what’s done is done… However, I’ll have you know, in that bottle, was the last of the elixir he had. It was the only food he had to sustain himself. Whatever it was he gave it to you for must have been of a great importance.”
“You still haven’t answered my questions!”
“I don’t give answers for free my dear! You’re lucky I haven’t thrown you out of my cottage for your intrusive entrance! What sort of business did you come to me for anyways?”
“In all truth, I’ve gotten into some trouble with the Ice King…”
“The Ice King!? Tell me right now lad, what deal have you made with that snake!?”
“I’m not giving answers for free either.” he said with a smug smile.

The old woman stood straighter and smiled to herself, “Well, then. I suppose you have half the wit I thought you had. If you wish to keep such a thing secret, then do so, but I warn you that it comes at a greater cost than you may think.”
Scoundrel ignored the warning, “I’m digging for history on the Ice King. I need answers.”
The woman raised an eyebrow, “Is this the ‘story’ you seek? If so, his history is a tale I know and remember well. Yet, like all my answers, it will come at a price…”
“What sort of price?”

The woman walked about the room and snatched up a shovel from the corner, “Well, you put out the fire in my chimney, and I’ll soon be in need of replacement firewood,” she shoved the shovel into Scoundrel’s hands, “You’ll be needing this to clear the snow out of the way of my doorway. I won’t be able to leave my house for kindling otherwise.”
Scoundrel was indignant. He came here prepared for a great exchange, and all she wanted was for him to shovel away some snow!?
“But—But…” Scoundrel began in shock, “How am I to even leave your cottage?”
“How did you get in? I suppose that if you wish to enter my house through my chimney, like a complete hooligan, you can exit my house through a chimney.”
“And you expect me to shovel away all that snow?”
“What, is shoveling snow too great a burden for you to carry? You act as though you’ve never held a shovel before!”
Scoundrel’s face grew red. In truth, he hadn’t used a shovel before, as he never had any reason for it. Being raised alone, there was nobody to teach or tell him to do such.

However, embarrassment wasn’t the only reason why his face began to turn red. No. It also was red in rage toward the old lady. He had never been addressed by anybody in the manner she spoke in, and he was certainly never asked to do such chores. He felt as though he was being treated as a mere child! Even if hewasa child, down in Blackneck, the people spoke of him as if he was an unearthly creature, an immortal boy of mischief. While the men would still scoff, Scoundrel could always sense a fear in their eyes when he was in their presence. Why wasn’t such fear in the eyes of this woman?
Yet, he realized that if he truly wished to get anywhere with the old crab, he would have to submit to her needs… at least for a little while.
“Fine,” the boy grumbled, “I suppose I can manage…”
Seeing that there was no use in squabbling with the woman any longer, he went quickly to work. After a bit of an ordeal, he found himself scooting up the sooty chimney on a length of rope.

Up the chimney, down the roof, and towards the spot where the door was buried, he growled and snorted like an ungraceful pig. While his body was focused on getting the job done, Scoundrel’s mind was full of utter resentment. The scalawag was in such a fit of anger that you could have hardly told the difference between him and a raging bull.

This was a dreadfully unhappy situation. The great Scoundrel, the thief of ages, reduced to shoveling snow off an old woman’s doorstep! Why, he’d once gone to the trouble of piling snow in front of doorsteps!

“Perhaps, once my job is done, the vase she is keeping in her corner can be payment for how she’s treated me,” he snarled as he started shoveling the snow away, “I’d just need to figure out a way to distract her…”

And so, he went on like this, grinding his teeth as he flung the snow about. One would have thought that the boy was a lunatic! Wasn’t he though? To be angered by such a thing was outright ridiculous,and yet, to him, it seemed to mean all the world.

After a while, he’d finally settled himself. How he came to calm down, I don’t know, but I suppose that he eventually grew weary of his vexation. The widow would pay in the end anyways, right? There really was no use fretting over such a thing, it wasted his efforts. He’d hardly made a dent into the snow at this point.

Scoundrel continued on in this new approach, and he found that it was done sooner than he’d imagined. Where the ten foot deep pile of snow had once been, a clean walkway from the doorstep and into the snowy mountain was paved. While he had been certain that there was a trick to the old lady’s deal, as of then, it seemed that all was right.
Entering the cottage, after a bit of a scuffle with the frozen door, he found the widow knitting calmly on her rocker.
Not bothering to look up from her work, she asked him, “Is it done?”
“Well what do you suppose?” asked Scoundrel, gesturing to the door.
“I suppose that you need a lesson in some decent manners…”
“Are you ready to satisfy your end of the deal? As you can see, I’ve made my payment.”
“Eh, but that’s just it. While I’m staring at my mess of knitting I canNOTsee what you’ve done. As long as I’m busy troubling myself with these tangled strings, I won’t be able to see anything else.”
“You simply need to look up and give it a rest! There’s time for it later!” said Scoundrel who was frazzled.
“Exactly. Let’s hope that that’s a lesson you’ve learned,” the woman said pointing towards the shovel.
Scoundrel was greatly confused, but he rolled it off reasoning that the woman had merely lost a good deal of her wits in old age, while a rush of warm wind flew over his head.
The woman started towards the door, and, peeping out the small window in it, a wrinkled smile spread across her face.
“Yes, that’s exactly how I wanted it,” she declared, “A job as well done as that must have taken a great deal of patience.”
“I suppose so…”

“So, you wanted the story of the old Ice King, huh boy?” she chuckled, starting back to her rocker, “Come! Come, take a chair and sit. I’m sorry that the room is in a bit of disarray, I wasn’t prepared for company.”
Scoundrel found a seat on an old rickety stool in a corner.
“So, you want his story from the beginning, don’t ya?”
“Yes, as much as I can know.”
“Well, you’re in luck, to be certain. I knew the old boy well. As much of a shock as it may be to you, he was once a normal man, all those years ago.”
“But… In my town of Blackneck, they say he’s been tormenting them for a century! How could you have possibly known him?”
“I don’t answer any questions for free, child,” she said, “You’ve paid for the history of the Ice King, not my own. May I continue the story?”
“I suppose…”

“So, as I was saying… all those years ago; over a century at this point, the Ice King was a normal man, and quite the handsome one too. ‘Handsome Henry’ is what we used to call him… He was a prince in his youth, because, you see, the town of Blackneck wasn’t always the rotting village it is now. It was once a thriving kingdom. Men and women came far and wide to visit it; the ‘City of Gold’.
“The City of Gold?” Scoundrel asked, quite confused.

“You didn’t think that the city was called Blackneck back then, did you? The name of Blackneck came later; it was what we ended up nicknaming it. We started calling it that after the old Ice King truly came into form, because of the black scar he had on his neck! But, back to the story…

“The ‘City of Gold’ was led by the Ice King’s father, until he died that is. The Ice King, or Henry,was a grown man by that point and was grief stricken. He had a close relationship with his father, as most sons do. He had already lost his mother in years prior, so he had become truly alone. I’m sure you know the feeling…
Scoundrel responded with no emotion. How much did she know of his past?

“Anyways, in the event of his father’s death,” the old lady began again, “Henry ascended to the throne. He wasn’t quite sure what he was doing at that point, in spite of his father teaching him the trade. For a while, the city began to fall into chaos. In truth, I believe he had grown lonely, and uncomfortable. Loneliness weakens the mind and heart you know. I think he knew this as well, because not long after taking the seat of the throne, he began sending his scribes to scout the city and neighboring kingdoms for the perfect bride. Not the noblest approach, but it certainly garnered attention. Soon, the whole palace was swarming with women of all kinds, and Henry had his advisors sent out to choose him the perfect ones out of the bunch. They came to him with many pretty girls, some being princesses from distant kingdoms, others being simple peasants, and others being the daughters of the advisors… no surprise there… But Henry found that none of them were right. He felt that none of them truly loved him…”
“Wait! The Ice King believed in love?!”
“He also believed in marrying complete strangers on the spot! He was a young fool back then, and much has changed since… much has changed…”
Scoundrel’s face fell.

“Anyhow, back to the tale at hand. If you wish to continue on interrupting the story like this, I might as well not tell it!” she said, “So, Henry ended up canceling the whole affair, to the dismay of the girls, and his advisors most of all. He resolved that he was going to take a long walk to think about things… Being a king isn’t an easy task, and he felt that he could use the rest. He found that his wandering path took him into the ‘enchanted forest’ (every kingdom seems to have one). Like in all kingdoms, this forest was mostly abandoned, save for the weeds and thorny trees that overtook it. Yet, to the shock of everybody, in this deserted wood, his paths crossed with an astonishing woman. Her name was Lucy, and she was on her way out of the kingdom due to Henry’s cancelation of his event. The two fell in love on the spot, ‘love at first sight’ you might say. There wasn’t ever a more gorgeous couple under the sun, and Lucy proved to be a strong and capable person, able to help Henry bring his kingdom back in order. Yes, if there was ever any doubt that such a thing as love existed to Henry, the bond between these two quickly dashed it. It was as though they were under a spell when they were together, a lovely trance that created an atmosphere pleasant to be beheld by all. In time, the two eventually wed, and the kingdom once again began to flourish under their rule. The world sung songs of their glorious love and the beauties that surrounded their kingdom. If only you had seen it, your eyes would have been dazzled!” the woman sat for a moment with a dreamy gaze in her eyes, and Scoundrel watched as her face seemed to fill with the beauty of those golden days.

“This rule lasted for years,” she continued, “but it seems that all good things must come to an end. Queen Lucy suddenly fell deathly ill. The sickness was one that even the greatest doctors and nurses in Blackneck could not help. The prospect of losing yet another person he loved was too much of a burden to bear for Henry, especially with the fear that he wouldn’t be able to protect the kingdom without her. He sent scribes far and wide for cures. He gathered the help of all his advisors. Yet all his efforts were shattered by the swift blow of vanity.

“In time, Henry concluded that there was only one hope left for his fading wife… In the mighty mountain of Craggleback, there was an old wizard… By some he was called Craggleback, yet none knew if he was called this because of the mountain he lived in, or if the mountain itself was named after the wizard… The one thing that everyone could be sure of though was that he was ancient, and his home and identity was as wild like the winds that blew so strongly in that old mountain…”
Scoundrel began to stir uneasily in his chair. It occurred to him that both the wizard Craggleback and this strange woman were strikingly similar…

“There were few that had ever met this old wizard,” the lady said with a distant look on her face. Had Scoundrel not been seated in the same room with her, he would’ve thought he was looking into a painting of something otherworldly.

She turned her gaze to meet Scoundrel’s for a moment, but then her eyes returned to the window, “Some came to this wizard for help with things beyond human grasp. Most of those that came down, those very few, would say that his works came out of the darkest parts of all creation, and stood as some of the most destructive forces ever seen by man. There were still others, while they were an even smaller portion, who found satisfaction with the works of the wizard… But they never lived long…

“Yet, what was King Henry to do? In his eyes, if he didn’t consult the wizard for help, the whole kingdom would die. His advisors said this wasn’t so, they said his wife’s death would not spell the death of the kingdom. They said Henry was being ridiculous.

“It was a very fragile decision, but, against all warnings, Henry chose to scale the mountain for the wizard. He was aided by nothing but his own sense of direction, for, in the mountain of Craggleback, there were no other guides to follow. How he did it is a mystery to all, but he did eventually find the wizard and his hut. And that is where I will end.”
“Wait, you can’t just end the story there!” Scoundrel cried in disbelief, “I paid for the full history of the Ice King!”

“Yes, but you see, you paid for the history of who the Ice King was. And the Ice King never did leave the house of the wizard, not as the same person anyways… So, it stands to reason that this is the proper place where his history ended… and a new one began…”
“Fine! Then, can you tell me the next history?”
“I don’t give answers for free my dear…”
“Then what price is it at? Please, I’ll give anything!” he pleaded.
The woman started back to her knitting, “I’m afraid there’s nothing left you can—,” she was interrupted when she started hemming away.
“I’m afraid there’s nothing you can give me,” she finished, after her cough started to settle.

Scoundrel was outraged! This was complete injustice! He had paid for this story with hard tedious work; a large portion of his last day! And now she was denying him of his right to hear the rest?! The vase in the corner was starting to look mighty tempting to him…
“But there’s nobody else who I can get answers from! And I need these answers, I only have so much time! Could you at least tell me if there’s any other way for me to get the answers I need?”

The old woman opened her mouth to respond, but then she started hacking away so hard that you might have thought it was the sound of a lumberjack trying to cut down a tree. “I—I don’t give any--,” She managed to wheeze out, before hitting the floor in a fitful cough, until her breaths and movements stopped altogether.
Scoundrel was completely alarmed. He hadn’t expected the old woman to collapse like this. Only moments before she had been ablaze! How was he to get his answers now?

There was something else Scoundrel felt for the old woman; a fear for her life, not his own. It was a tingling sensation, one that drove him to act. He’d never felt this way before… Perhaps it was just the feeling of the frost nipping at his heart, or himself finally recovering from the cold… And perhaps it was just his need of answers… But Scoundrel still felt an overwhelming urge to save this woman.

As Scoundrel frantically searched his head for a way to spare her, his fingers started to grope at the elixir around his neck. Yes, the elixir was the answer! Perhaps that would avert the death of the old woman. Yet, then the ruffian remembered why the old hermit had given him the elixir in the first place; Scoundrel had nearly died on the mountain if it hadn’t been for it. Surely he’d need it later on his journey, and if he gave it to the old woman, it would be gone.

The old woman was certainly a trouble to Scoundrel, and had, by no means, been friendly to him. Not to mention, remembering her last words, he could assume that she’d probably never give him the answers he wanted once revived. Although, Scoundrel remembered the strange look she had on herface that made him feel as if he was looking through a window in time… He couldn’t let that die out. He couldn’t. It was the last surviving bit of Blackneck’s history. And perhaps… perhaps the life of this woman was greater than the importance of his own… What good had ever come by him anyways, the rotten wretched robber of Blackneck?

So, Scoundrel popped the cap of the phial around his neck, and slipped the bottle into the old woman’s mouth. The whole bottle was poured down her throat, not a drop was spared. It took a minute, but the old woman awoke with a gasp. She steadily pulled herself up from the ground and looked around the room with an astonishment. To Scoundrel’s surprise, he found himself smiling.
“Did you save me, boy?” she asked in surprise.
Scoundrel sat for a moment.
“I don’t give answers for free,” he finally said, letting the now empty phial drop to the floor.
“Perhaps you’re half the ‘scoundrel’ people think you are after all…” she said with a gleam in her eye.
“Or perhaps I’m simply a thief that needs something to rob,” he said, “How do you know that I’m called that anyways?”
“I never give any answers for free…”
“Speaking of which, the rest of the history of the Ice King—.”

The old woman interrupted him, “Is a tale I am not going to finish out. If you truly wish for your answers, then seek it. Only those that are willing to pay the price deserve the answer. As for myself, you will be getting no more out of me. You might as well try to get fruit out of a rock.”
“But you don’t understand! The Ice King is—.”

The woman interrupted again, “There are few things that take place on this mountain that I don’t understand. Your story isn’t an exception. Now, you’d better hurry on, time is ticking. The sun will be beginning to rise soon, if I’m not mistaken.”

The old lady was right, precious time was draining. After saying goodbye to the old woman and thanking her for her hospitality, Scoundrel went on his way. He wasn’t quite sure where he was headed, yet that didn’t slow down his pace. Scoundrel thought about going back and asking the old woman for advice, but when he turned his head to where the house should have been, it was gone.

“She wouldn’t have been much help anyways,” grumbled Scoundrel, who was greatly confused. He felt his confusion strangely settle though, when a warm gust of wind pushed him forward as he went from the house.
Chapter Seven
The Rabid Rage

Maybe Scoundrel wasn’t sure of where he was going, yet, if Scoundrel had known that the Ice King had already determined his path, he perhaps would have turned the other way for safety. Yes, lurking in the shadows was the Ice King’s watchful eye; it had been on Scoundrel during the whole journey. It was only a matter of time before it would strike.

As Scoundrel trekked deeper and deeper into the icy mountain, he felt as the chilling sting on his heart pierced him deeper. It was a freezing pain in his chest that delved inward, feeling tougher than thorns as it sucked the tender warmth from his body. He sorrowfully regretted the decision of ever stepping into the ice castle. Why had he not listened?! The warnings in his town had been so clear. Yet, Scoundrel had to admit that he had rarely ever conformed to any rules in his town, he’d always felt that they were for the weak and cowardly. Yet now, it became all too apparent to him that perhaps breaking the rules had ended with the same result.
There was no use sulking now though. No! He had promises to keep. All too important promises. And, for the first time in Scoundrel’s short life, it was a promise that he couldn’t avoid.

As these many thoughts swirled through Scoundrel’s mind, the weather around him seemed to do the same. An ominous wind blew, it was a murky smog that began to put Scoundrel into a daze. The snow around him started to change color from pure white to sooty gray. A howling cry could be heard in the distance, and a rotten musty smell began to surround him.
“The wolves!” he cried sniffing the air.

Indeed, it was the wolves. They were a terror to all in Blackneck, and were known to attack when the weather was at its coldest. Even Scoundrel had been robbed by them before, which was quite the feat. The wolves were monstrous creatures with gnarled black claws, oily fur, small black eyes that popped out of their heads like shining pebbles, and snarling yellow teeth. These wolves traveled in large vicious packs, with even the smallest of the group being as big as a man, and the largest of them being twice that size. They were said to work for the great Ice King himself, and, to anybody smart enough to believe in the legend of the Ice King, there was no denying it.

They seemed to only come once the ice had glazed over all of Blackneck and there was no escape. Scoundrel guessed that they were headed down to the town right now, if the Ice King hadn’t sent them after him. Scoundrel would most definitely have to hide from these scavengers, or else get eaten. With the wolves, there were only two options; either offer them something to eat in order to ward off their wrath, or be eaten yourself. Scoundrel unfortunately had nothing to offer, so he decided upon attempting the third option that rarely worked: hiding.

The noses of the wolves were fierce, like every ability they possessed…to avoid them picking up your scent, you’d have to be very crafty. Sadly, Scoundrel had nothing he could use to weaken their senses. In fact, besides a lone match he had in his pocket, he really had nothing at all. Darting through the snow searching for somewhere to hide, he began to realize he was completely exposed. And, to make things worse, the wolves seemed to be following his trail. He could already smell their dingy scent grow more potent.

After testing all his options, Scoundrel resolved that his only hope was burrowing into the snow. It had grown to be seven feet deep in some places, so, as of then, it seemed to be the smartest option.

However, Scoundrel couldn’t have been more wrong. These wolves were skilled at digging and found great sport in it. Not to mention, only a complete numbskull would bury themselves under such a thick pile of snow. Even if he managed to survive the wolves, he’d still have the next obstacle of insuring that he’d make it out of the pile of snow alive. Scoundrel would’ve been better off running; every inch deeper he dug his hole was another inch closer to the prospect of death.

Once he’d dug a deep enough hole, he rolled himself into it and began piling the snow back on top of himself. The snow was freezing, and the cold burned at his skin, but he sucked in as much breath as he could to keep himself from suffocating, and continued packing it on.

As he sat piled under mounds of snow, the muffled sound of the wolves howling could be heard in the distance. The sound was growing ever louder and Scoundrel started to wish he had been able to smooth out the pile of snow above himself in order to hide his tracks even further.

Thump! Thump! Pounding paws of the wolves started to shake the whole ground. They weren’t the only things pounding; Scoundrel’s clammy heart was throbbing so ferociously that he felt it nearly rip right out of his chest. Clutching the ground tightly, Scoundrel winced as he listened to the sniffing noses of the wolves pass him by. There would be many of them, would he have any hope of escaping their sight? He knew he had his answer when he began to hear scraping claws against the snow; digging above him. The scraping started to grow louder, and louder, and louder still! Every so often it would be halted by the whimpering and harsh growling of the wolves flying into a violent brawl. This never lasted long though, and as one fight started between the wolves, new wolves came in to replace them. Within a mere minute, all the snow above Scoundrel had been diminished to a very thin layer. He could already feel the weight of the sharp jagged wolf claws breaking through the snow. With a heartyhowl a wolf sunk his teeth into Scoundrel’s body, and lifted him out of the snow, flinging him wildly about. However, all the other wolves, who were too eager to have the treasure as their own, began tackling and running each other over for Scoundrel. The angry wolf that gripped Scoundrel started clamping his jaws, and prepared for a battle for his food. He hurled Scoundrel into a tree and began fighting off his fellow wolves one by one.

Scoundrel’s mind started racing, he had not a second to waste. His body was bruised and tattered, but he knew that if he didn’t take this chance now, he’d be made into a meal. Suddenly, a great tree branch fell out of the tree above him and, SMACK! It hit him right in the head.
“Curse these darn wolves!” he moaned rubbing his head.

An idea quickly sparked in his head. Ripping his match out of his pocket, he struck it and lit the branch. He was just in time too, for, just as a wolf came rushing at him, he swung the thick branch into its face.

The poor thing let out a sharp whine and ran off crying in pain with its face afire. The wolf rolled around the snow in an effort to put out the flames, only to have the pain of the icy cold greeting him in trade. This event caught the attention of the rest of the rowdy wolves and they began charging at the lone flame Scoundrel wielded.

The boy hadn’t been sure how long he intended to keep this up, but now, in this instance, he found himself having a surge to go as long as he had a breath. For a moment, he didn’t know where this came from, but then he saw images of the citizens in the town below flashing through his mind... The result of his fight wouldn’t just effect himself, but the lives of all the townspeople in Blackneck. It was a strange thing, he’d been tormenting those townspeople all his life, but now, he found himself fighting against just that.

From then on, when it was learned what had happened that morning, people would go on questioning who the boy was fighting for; himself, or the townspeople. Nobody would ever truly know, but it was said that at that moment, he had a burst of strength to help him fend off those wolves. While he could barely remember all that had happened, the boy would go on to remember a strange warm wind blowing, at that sacred instant.

One by one, the wolves ran off with their faces set aflame by his torch. How Scoundrel could have overcome such odds was a mystery beyond what any could explain, but once Scoundrel had finally conquered the chief of the wolves, the largest of them all, and knocking off a necklace it wore across his neck, every wolf had finally run off in retreat. It might have been in fear of the flickering flame that Scoundrel held, or it might have been that they feared the sun, which had begun rising in the east, but whatever it was, they ran from it as fast as their legs could carry them. Trampling each other, they fled into the mountain, never to be seen again. I personally believe that the ice king went on to punish them for their failure, however, there is no way to tell what truly became of them.

After the wolves had retreated, Scoundrel smoldered his flame in the snow and walked over to observe the necklace the wolf had been wearing. The cold metal gleamed brightly in the rising sun, leaving a stinging glare in Scoundrel’s eye. Looking closer he saw the emblem placed in the center of the chain necklace start to reveal itself; it was what looked to be a golden heart. Yes, it was a heart that hung to the chain!
Scoundrel chuckled, “What a pretty piece of jewelry… a shame that such a nasty looking beast had been wearing it!”

Scoundrel clasped the trinket tightly in his hand and started running his fingers over the designs embroidered to it. They were extremely intricate and delicate. It was so much so, that it looked as if they had been crafted out of mere dust by something as small as a gnat. Faint memories of the emblems he’d seen in the ice castle invoked Scoundrel’s mind, as he marveled at the designs on the jewelry. Actually, as Scoundrel took a closer look at them, they were almost an exact copy!

Scoundrel’s finger then came over a ruby red gem that sat in the center of the heart. Pressing his finger down on it, to test if it was a true stone, the heart suddenly cracked open, splitting in half.
“No!” shouted Scoundrel.
He felt like a dimwit quite quickly after this, as he realized that it was a locket.
“That’s strange…” said Scoundrel inquisitively, “Why would the wolf have a treasure like this?”

He then peered inside. In the left half, there was a portrait of a beautiful woman with a crown placed atop her head. Her face was full of youth, yet her eyes were full of knowing. From her head poured down golden locks of hair that sang sweet songs of prosperity and good health. She smiled at Scoundrel and, even with this being but a picture, it gave him a sense of warmth in the cold. Turning his gaze to the right side, he read an inscription: “To my beloved Lucy, for remembrance that, even apart, our bond shall always remain. Forever yours, Henry.”
Not being well taught in literature, reading this took a bit of a strain for Scoundrel. Yet, once he had read it, he soon realized who this belonged to.
“It’s the ice king’s…” he whispered, under his breath.

The wind started blowing violently, tearing the locket from Scoundrel’s hands. He struggled against its mighty pull and started pulling the chain over his neck. He couldn’t let this go to the wind, it was too precious. After a tenacious battle, Scoundrel secured the locket around his neck. The wind continued blowing harder, but it finally died down when it saw its efforts were vain.

With the wind calmed down, Scoundrel studied the locket some more. As he looked at it he noticed a strange detail. At the bottom of the right side of the heart, there was a small text and symbol. Squinting his eyes, he read these words: Heftyfoot’s Ironworks.

It must have been crafted in an iron mine… Perhaps if he went there he’d find more history on this strange treasure. After all, it wasn’t a normal occurrence to give a wolf such a piece… Gifts are special things, and having one taken from you is a great and sorrowful event. Scoundrel knew this, because he’d stolen many of them, and he’d never seen as distraught a look as the one of somebody he’d stolen from. If there was any act in the world that he knew was conceived as love, it was the giving of a gift. Maybe, just maybe, he’d learn more about how to give proof of love to old Blackneck, the Ice King.

But where was this ironworks at? Scoundrel had an idea. Down below, in the town of Blackneck, there was an old abandoned mine shaft. Seated in the root of the mountain, it had been boarded up and sealed a dozen times over, but nobody was sure of its origin. He’d heard whispers that it used to pour out rivers of gold, that it was filled with riches of many kinds. However, it wasn’t until now that he began considering these rumors true.

The only problem was that he wasn’t able to travel into Blackneck without being hanged… He would have to be careful not to alert any of the villagers in Blackneck of his existence. This, of course, wasn’t going to be too tough of a task for Scoundrel. After all, he’d pillaged many people in their sleep before.
“If this is the path I need to take, so be it…” Scoundrel muttered.
So, into the murky mist of ice of snow, Scoundrel made his descent for Blackneck.
Chapter Eight
Deeper In and Further Down

It took Scoundrel quite a while to reach the bottom of the mountain, and at that point the sun had fully arisen out of the eastern horizon. The further he climbed down the steep mountain slope, the more he began to have doubts about how he would make it back up the mountain in time. If it took him this long to climb down, how on earth would he find the time to climb back up? He finally decided that they were issues he’d have to address later.
“Perhaps the Ice King will take me there in his whirlwind…” he said in an attempt to soothe his worries.

Returning to the task at hand, Scoundrel peered down the slope to see that there was a mass of men at its foot. Gathered by the dozens, they were all armed with pitchforks and knives. Large contorted scowls covered their faces as they stood tall against the current of the wind.
“What are they all doing here!?” Scoundrel thought to himself.

Realization struck him brutally: they were preparing to fend off the wolves. Every year, the wolves came down the mountain in their sleep, before the men could ever prepare for a fight. Yet, this morning, since the wolves had never came the night prior, they were finally ready. The cruelest of ironies was that they had not a wolf to battle, nor would they ever have one… Instead, they had Scoundrel…
“What am I to do now?” the ruffian griped, pacing large circles in the snow.

On Scoundrel’s end, these men served a great problem. After all, they’d be just as willing to kill him as any wolf; the only difference was that the men had Scoundrel outnumbered and outmatched. It was quite the predicament to be in.

Thankfully there were two things Scoundrel had that none of the men did; a remarkable wit and the element of surprise. Yes, dozens of ideas were already whirling around, as for the wind, which was blocking Scoundrel from the men’s view with sheets of snow. Scoundrel wasn’t one to stand idle, and he quickly decided upon what seemed to be the best distraction at the moment: he’d cause an avalanche.

Without hesitation, Scoundrel began howling at the top of his lungs like a wolf, in hopes of striking fear into the men. He stomped at the ground with his foot. He slapped his hands together zealously. He made as much noise as any person could physically muster. Although, it was at this point that his idea ruthlessly turned against him.

The current of the wind shifted and slowed, allowing the men to see Scoundrel fully exposed. To add to this, attempting to cause an avalanche perhaps wasn’t Scoundrel’s brightest idea. After all, he stood at the foot of the mountain where it wasn’t likely that any rocks or boulders would be breaking away. So, to Scoundrel’s dismay, as he stamped about hooting and hollering, the men began charging at him with both angry and puzzled looks. Scoundrel would have been skewered too, if it hadn’t been for a bit of luck. He had been completely unaware of this attack up to this point, with his eyes pinched shut and the wind blocking out the sound of thumping boots. So, when a pitchfork came hurling at him, he might have been brought to the ground then and there. Yet, a warm gust of wind blew the pitchfork to the ground, alerting Scoundrel of the attack. The boy was nimble enough to recognize the situation and snatch up the pitchfork.

This was little use though, and it only slowed Scoundrel down. He soon had the whole hoard of men against him and thrusting the pitchfork at each one of them proved useless. It didn’t help that he himself had become like a piñata for them all.
“Come men, let’s tear him apart limb by limb!” one man sneered.
“Let’s roast ‘em alive!” cried another.
“He stole my breakfast last week! I say we turn ‘em into some in return!” said a third.

The men continued bickering on like this, until they began turning on each other. Soon, instead of only Scoundrel being their piñata, the piñata became every man on the foot of the mountain. While this senseless fighting may seem rather savage, in their defense, cold and famine can bring out the worst in people.

Scoundrel saw his advantage, and tried to escape, but, of course, he was the main target for most of the men. Dodging the fierce barbarians at every inch he advanced, Scoundrel struggled to reach the old mine’s entrance. After being thrown about a few more times though, he began to realize that this effort was useless. One of the few chances of escaping was smoothing out the rough rage that encased him.
Scoundrel cleared his throat, “I am not your enemy!” he shouted over the commotion in a still voice.
“Ha, ye terrorize us countless times over, and now ye say yer not an enemy!?” scoffed one man who was twisted into a human pretzel.
“Agreed, do ye think we are stupid!?” said another man, with his axe caught in his forest of hair.
“I know it may seem hard to believe,” said Scoundrel, “But I’m the one who stopped the wolves from attacking Blackneck last night.”
“Ye mean, yer the one who controls the wolves!?” one shouted, “Everybody, let’s sack ‘em!”
“No, I fought the wolves off one by one, and I’m telling the truth!” said Scoundrel, under a pile of men, “I’ve changed my ways! I don’t want to harm Blackneck anymore!”

Scoundrel’s eyes suddenly went wide, he hadn’t an idea where those words came from. The thought of abandoning his crime in Blackneck hadn’t passed Scoundrel’s mind until now. Of course, one might find that people will say things they don’t mean when they’re fighting for their life.

“Sure…” said one, rolling his two black eyes, “And I’m a fairy! Ye just killed two lumberjacks in the mountain yesterday, didn’t ye? Ye expect us to believe that a wicked wretch like you can suddenly turn all that around!?”
Scoundrel’s face fell, and his eyes became heavy.
“You’re right!” he yelled, “I am just a worthless thief! And you’re all my victims!”

Scoundrel then broke out of the pile of men in a fury (not without pickpocketing a few first though). Running as fast as he could, he ripped the hilt of an abandoned axe off the ground and charged towards the boarded up mine.
“Hey! He has my satchel!” shouted one man racing after him.

Everybody had been put into a sort of daze at the events that had just transpired, so not even one could muster the energy to catch Scoundrel. The boy was like a firework that had just been alit. Even if you could manage to catch it in midair, it would only explode with you.

Once Scoundrel had reached the entrance to the mine, he swung his axe at the boards furiously, until the whole wall gave away. He then dove into the mine without hesitation. A few of the men ran after him, but once they realized what had become of him, they plodded back to the rest of the group with dismal defeated faces.
“That little devil will be back again, no doubt…” moaned one, “He always comes back…”

It was dark in the tunnel. Dark, cold and damp. The very definition of uncomfortable would best describe it. Scoundrel’s skin had been cut up by the rough jagged walls in countless places after only minutes of journeying.

Roughness wasn’t the only problem with the tunnel though. In some places it was much too wide, while in others it was much too small. Scoundrel would sometimes find himself squeezed in between the walls so tight that he’d have to roll over on his side to keep moving forward. In other places, the tunnel would grow so wide that Scoundrel would find himself groping aimlessly in the dark for a way through the cavern.

He had begun to question what sort of person would have been expected to guide themselves through these tunnels. After all, Scoundrel was just a boy, and if squeezing through these mines was a tough task for him, how was somebody nearly twice as large to get through?
“Maybe this is why they closed the old mine down,” Scoundrel said sarcastically as he made his way in deeper.

He had begun to regret not bringing any sort of lantern or light into the tunnels. At this point, the cave had become so dark that he could no longer see. You could have stood right in front of him and he wouldn’t have had the slightest idea anybody was there. In fact, Scoundrel had begun to wonder if just that had begun to happen to him. Every so often he thought he heard the pitter patter of light footsteps across the cavern floor. At one point, he swore he felt the warm touch of another’s breath against his back. Yet, he could never tell for sure… How could he?
“It’s just the echo of your own feet,” he assured himself, “Those idiotic men must have gone to yourhead!”
Yes, more than anything, Scoundrel loathed another encounter with the men.
“I don’t need to deal with any more of their stupidity!” Scoundrel told himself bitterly, “If they think they can make me, the great Scoundrel, pay for my crimes, they are sorrowfully mistaken!”

Even amidst this, Scoundrel was extremely confident that it wasn’t the men’s presence that he was sensing in the dark. While he couldn’t seem to get them out of his head, how was it possible they could have followed him into the mine? On top of the fact that the mine was tough to enter, there was also bound to be countless alternate passageways that could lead the man astray.

Even with this confidence, Scoundrel knew something was awry. At every turn it seemed, he swore that he could see the disapproving nasty look of one of the men staring into his eyes. At one point, he lost his footing in a wide part of the tunnel, and found himself nearly tumbling down into a fathomless abyss. While it might have been nothing but of his own figment of imagination, he thought he felt a firm hand grasp his rags and pull him back onto the hard rock floor of the cave.
“Stop being a fretful child!” Scoundrel told himself, wagging an invisible finger in the air, “Your garments simply snagged onto an old rock!”

Even with that comforting statement, the shakiness in his own voice and the ominous echo that came after it was anything but that. While his silver tongue might have been skilled in convincing others of his lies, he knew that he wasn’t able to lie to himself. Something was wrong, and there was no denying it.

Scoundrel continued on like this in the darkness, moving frivolously towards nowhere. At this point, he hadn’t the slightest sense of direction or motivation. What was he truly looking for? When he’d first decided to come down here, the idea of exploring the mine sounded so simple, so alluring. However, now, he wasn’t even sure what he was doing. How are you expected to find a treasure when you can’t even see? You might as well be a ship that can’t sail.

Ultimately, the whole endeavor seemed to be an utter waste of time. He would have turned back too, if it hadn’t been for the fact that he had no idea of where he’d turn back to. After escaping the arena of men, the rush of success completely wiped away all other concerns. He never gave a thought to plotting his way through the cave!
Truly, Scoundrel had no other options but to wander in the mines with the hope of finding help or a way out.

Unexpectedly, as Scoundrel was walking through the mine, he heard something that made his ears perk up. It was music! Yes, beautiful music! Oh, and what a delightful sound it was to his ears, in trade for empty echoes reverberating off the walls of the cavern. Even if this was all just a hallucination of his, Scoundrel had decided that he’d trade the hope in the dream over a harsh reality of being alone in the darkness.

As sad as this resolve was, Scoundrel set off running through the tunnels in a blur. He might have looked like a mighty fool, running after a shrill sound in a dead empty mine, but he no longer cared. He felt that he had been isolated in the emptiness for hours, and was ready to embrace any kind of company the cave had to offer.

It turned out that his ears were correct, and he soon found himself sprinting towards a dim light. Yet, even with himself being prepared with the fact that whatever company he’d meet in the mine would be strange, he still couldn’t have been ready for what he would meet.

He continued on toward the light, with it growing ever brighter. His feet snagged on the rocks that jutted out of the ground, he tore his clothes trying to break through the thin width of the tunnel, but none of it phased him. His gaze was fixed on his goal, and that alone. When he finally reached the light, he found himself tumbling into a brightly lit room; at least it seemed bright compared to the labyrinth he’d just come out of. It was lit by many candles, hanging from mantles nailed crudely into the walls. In fact, the whole room was crude. Everything in it was either rusted or jagged. Believe it or not, there was even a bed in the corner that looked to be made of rock.

Scoundrel goggled at this visual treat and change in scenery, though, he hadn’t forgotten that his ears were the reason he had been brought here. What had happened to the music? At first Scoundrel didn’t notice the change, in the excitement of finding light, but now, he was extremely curious as to who lived in this strange dwelling. Scoundrel turned his head all about, but he didn’t see anyone…
Whack! Scoundrel felt something hit him hard in the shin.

Looking down, Scoundrel saw a small man with a long white beard that fell to his feet. At least, compared to the man’s height it was long. Truthfully, the man was only half a foot taller than half of Scoundrel’s height. He was quite the sight to be sure, and Scoundrel couldn’t help but laugh (it was a very rude laugh too).

“What are you laughing at!?” yelled the small stout man, making a sour face, “You bust into my mine, trampling through my delicate tunnels, like the rest of your bumbling folk… And then you laugh in my presence?! You should happy that I was kind enough to lead you to my home after watching you wander around for an hour!”

The small man was trying his best to talk down to Scoundrel, and if only he had a chair to stand on that could have been tall enough, he might have been able too. Sadly though, Scoundrel was a tough boy to intimidate, and the tiny man wasn’t making a good impression.
“Sorry,” said Scoundrel wiping the tears from his eyes, “But, you’re not the sort I’d expect to meet in the mine… What is your name anyways?”

“My name is Clenchneck. And what sort of people did you expect to find in this mine? Giants? I’ll tell you right now, there’s a reason us dwarves work in these mines!” the small man said, “By the way, what is the ridiculous ‘human name’ your parents came up for you!?”
“Wait, you’re a dwarf!?” asked Scoundrel
“What does it look like to you? What, do they pretend we don’t exist anymore up in the surface?’ the dwarf rolled his eyes, “Happens in every kingdom! Now, your name…”
“Well, my name is Scoundrel,” the boy began.
“Scoundrel!? I should’ve known not to trust strangers that wander into my mines! Empty your pockets boy, all the jewels in this cave areMINE! That’s why we call this place a ‘mine’ I believe…”
“I swear, I haven’t stolen anything!” said Scoundrel, “I know it sounds bad, but that’s what people call me on the surface.”
“Names like that aren’t just given without being earned,” the dwarf grumbled, “But, suppose that youAREN”Ta thief… What are you doing in these mines, eh?”
“Well, suppose again that I am…” said Scoundrel, “I’ve finally pillaged the wrong person…”
The dwarf raised an eyebrow, “You wouldn’t be suggesting you stole from old Blackneck, would you?”
Scoundrel’s face turned red. Now it was the dwarf’s turn to laugh.
“Ha!” the dwarf chuckled, “Stealing from the Ice King! You’re lucky you’re not a hunk of ice!”
“I’m lucky I’m not a hunk of ice YET…”
“What do you mean?” asked the dwarf curiously, “Are you telling me that you struck a deal with that old buzzard?”
Scoundrel sighed, “I am… I need help with something. I’m looking for history on Blackneck, and I found this locket on the mountain… It’s what led me to you…”
Scoundrel lifted the locket off his neck and began to hand it to the dwarf. As he did, he felt a pang of cold on his heart, but he ignored it.
The dwarf observed the piece of jewelry, while fumbling it around in his fingers.

“Heftyfoot….” Clenchneck whispered, with a twinge of sadness, “This piece of jewelry was forged long ago for the Ice King himself, ages before he ever went mad. We had our best man and chief, Heftyfoot, craft it for him… How did you get your hands on such a precious piece?”
“I found it around the neck of the Chief of the Wolves that terrorize the surface of the mountain.”
The dwarf began to weep, “Such a pity! Such a pity! It’s so sad to see how the world has fallen…”
Scoundrel patted the dwarf soothingly, “I need to know more about the history of the ice king… Could you tell me what happened to him?”
“It’s a long story…” said the dwarf, “A tale that I don’t wish to linger on… Us dwarves don’t even know the whole of the tale, we only know a few of the events that took place….”
The dwarf burst into tears again.
“What happened?” repeated Scoundrel with a concerned gaze.

The dwarf cleared his throat, “Well, if you must know, then I’ll tell you…. You see, us dwarves have special abilities when it comes to mining. So, when the kings of ‘The City of Gold; came into power, us dwarves were employed to mine out the mountain of Craggleback for them. It was a solid trade all in all… we dwarves got a place to sleep for mining out all the gold in the mountain for the kingdom. Many kings passed, but none seemed to appreciate us more than old Blackneck; who was then called King Henry.”
Scoundrel continued listening intently.

“The old King loved our works and was obsessed with obtaining our finest crafts. This pleased us dwarves, especially Heftyfoot, our leader. This was how King Henry eventually acquired this priceless locket. Heftyfoot toiled for days making it into perfection…

“However, suddenly, Queen Lucy, Henry’s wife, became ill. Everything changed. Nobody is quite sure how it happened, but even when the Queen recovered, the kingdom fell apart… The king completely shut himself out from us… After a while of this, Heftyfoot, who could no longer take the pain, died… The whole dwarf hive dissipated… Finally… the unspeakable happened!”
At this point the dwarf broke down into another sob.
“What happened!?” asked Scoundrel.
“It’s too painful. It’s better that you didn’t know anyways…”
“That’s where you’re wrong. I need answers!”
The dwarf looked deep into Scoundrel’s eyes, “You mightwantto know, but do you trulyneedan answer?”
Scoundrel was dumbfounded. He hadn’t expected such a reaction out of the poor creature, it wasn’t like anything he’d seen.
“I need it if I hope to still be alive tomorrow!”

The dwarf frowned, “Then you don’t deserve it. What good has ever come out of the life of the criminal like you…? Only a man with a true sense of sympathy could ever understand the pain that I’ve witnessed… the great treasures I’ve watched fade away… and even then…”
“You don’t understand!” cried Scoundrel.
“I believe it’s quite the opposite,” the dwarf said firmly.
The dwarf then tossed the locket back to Scoundrel, “Keep it. Unlike you, I don’t wish to take something that doesn’t belong to me.”

The dwarf kept his head hung to the ground. It couldn’t have been any clearer to Scoundrel that the small man’s heart was completely shattered. You have never seen such disappointment on a being, such a helpless look. Scoundrel almost pitied the dwarf, but he was also fuming at him. He was getting close to finishing the puzzle, he knew it! He just needed to learn more about what happened, and perhaps there would be the slightest of the chance that he could spare himself… and the rest of those wretched people in Blackneck too…
“Please, I’m begging you!” said Scoundrel, “I need this knowledge!”
“Well you’re not finding it here!” huffed the dwarf, “It’s not as if I know the full story myself!”

The dwarf stopped for a moment, glaring at the ground, when his eyes flared with a flash, in what Scoundrel could have sworn looked to be mischievous. But, once it had disappeared, all that was left visible on the dwarf’s face, was an expression of pure empathy. “But, I suppose that if you truly wish to find the answers you seek, there is one way you can get them… I might hate being intruded upon, but, Idohave sympathy for your predicament… Of course, the person I’m thinking of is not the sort yousteal answers from, rather, they’re the sort that steals answers from you… You might be better off trying to squeeze answers out of old Blackneck himself…”
“Tell me, I’ll do anything at this point! My time runs thin!”

“In the heart of the mountain there’s a dragon… ‘Smoke’ is what we used to call him… The nasty worm hoards all the remaining gold within the mountain, and hasn’t left his nest in centuries. Although, he’s better off that way, for he is missing a wing, and he has quite the grudge against the Ice King I wish I could tell you more, but anything about the history simply breaks me inside… A dwarf’s heart can only bear so much pain. I guess you could say that we’re funny that way… Like the rocks we mine, our hearts are as delicate as the finest stone. If too much a burden is placed upon it, it shatters and the shards splinter everything.”
The dwarf started sniffling again, and pulled a handkerchief out of the sooty overalls it wore. Trudging to a corner, he pulled a candle off the mantelpiece and gave it to Scoundrel.

“Here, I believe you’ll be needing this,” the dwarf said coolly, “Remember, the dragon is a crafty sort, and his eyes spread throughout the whole mountain. He’s bound to hear us even now. You’ll need to be careful navigating through these mines for, just as on the surface of this mountain, it is a great maze in which you must travel with great caution. If you fail to do so, you will surely find yourself circling amongst the rugged rocks aimlessly.”
“Isn’t there a sort of map I can take?” asked Scoundrel.

“Nay… I only have one map in this mountain to guide myself by, and without it, I’m forever lost. You must trek the cave alone without any guidance I’m afraid. I would accompany you, but I’m fear that it’s just much too risky of an endeavor for me to take.” Scoundrel thought he saw the dark flare pass through the dwarf’s eyes once again, but then resolved that it must only have been the light of the candle
Scoundrel was both offended and appalled by this. First the dwarf wouldn’t tell him the tale of Blackneck, and now he was sending him off with no direction?
Nevertheless, he walked over to the old dwarf and patted him on the back.
“Thanks for all the toil you’ve gone to for me,” Scoundrel told him. A quizzical look came across the dwarf’s face, for he couldn’t tell if the boy was sincere or sarcastic.
The boy exited the small cavern and disappeared into the pitch black hole before the dwarf could decide...
Chapter Nine
A Snake’s Salutations

If you thought that Scoundrel would have returned into that darkness so willingly, without aid, you’d be wrong. No, no, Scoundrel had a very clear perception of where he was going. Though his limbs had lost all feeling from the cold, and his eyes could see little, he had no doubt where he was headed.
“How did he do this?” you might be asking yourself

Well, Scoundrel hadn’t forgotten a bit of who he was when he was sitting in that small cave with the dwarf. While the dwarf was making him angrier and angrier, it drove Scoundrel to consult his normal nature; stealing the map. Yes, when Scoundrel went to pat the dwarf on the back to say his final goodbyes, he slipped the map right out of the dwarf’s back pocket.

Normally, Scoundrel might have been worried that the small thing would have overtaken him in the darkness, after all, this was the dwarf’s home. At this point however, even if the dwarf had been smart enough to check his pockets, Scoundrel was long gone. Going after the thief now would be a lost cause.

Scoundrel had already plotted his course through the mines and had a fixed point on his location. Judging by the scale of the map, it seemed that it would take him a while to navigate throughout the vast mines. This could certainly serve a problem in the future, but he could trouble over that later. Right now, he had to keep moving forward towards the dragon…
