As Scoundrel continued walking through the dark cave, echoes matching his every step, he felt the ice on his heart grow colder and colder. By now, the crystal had spread across his whole chest and was now climbing up his neck and down his body. It was a disturbing sensation to be certain. Have you ever placed your hand in a bucket of fresh ice, or dived into newly fallen snow? Do you remember how the cold felt against your skin? The burning desire to rid yourself of its touch upon your skin? This is how Scoundrel felt, only it was much worse: the frigidness almost seemed to be growing on him. Every passing minute, it continued to gnaw away at his being; a constant reminder of how short his time was growing. Scoundrel feared what would happen once the ice reached his limbs. Although, the Ice King had made Scoundrel a deal; he wouldn’t dare interfere with the result of the bargain… Blackneck wouldn’t make it so that Scoundrel was left immobile and unable to carry out his mission, would he?

As much as Scoundrel liked to believe that the Ice King’s deal was a decent one, deep down he knew that it was not. The deal was as unjust as it could get. Even if Scoundreldidmanage to find proof of love, how was he to return to old Blackneck with it? Scoundrel had been putting this eerie thought to the side for quite a while, but now it was all too obvious: it was already midmorning, at the earliest, and he still had yet to come close to finding answers.

Perhaps it was simply because he was looking for answers in the wrong places, after all, what use did the history of the ice king really serve? Scoundrel knew in his mind that it didn’t seem to amount to much, but in his heart he felt something contrary. Maybe if he knew what happened to the ice king he’d be able to convince him that love was real. This decision that he’d made in the hermit’s hut was a longshot, and was almost sure for failure from what Scoundrel could tell. But, at the plan’s core, Scoundrel was trying the only route of which he was good at: stealing. Stealing the Ice King’s history...

Scoundrel lingered on these thoughts until he came across a large cliff in the mine. Out of it came a blast of heat, which was oddly out of place, considering the bitter cold surrounding it. Smelling the air, he began to gag. The air was shrouded in a dense layer of smoke.
“The dragon…” Scoundrel whispered.
The dragon was fathoms down to be sure, and Scoundrel still had a long way to go. But the stench of the monster was already beginning to surround him.

Scoundrel peered down into the empty black hole over the cliff, to see nothing. There was nothing at all but an empty darkness. This struck Scoundrel with surprise; he thought he’d at least see the dim orange light of the dragon’s fire illuminating from far below.
“Maybe it’s just being blocked out by a cloud of smoke I can’t see,” thought Scoundrel.
But, he had the feeling it was a lot more than just smoke. It was his hunch that the dragon was rooted into the mountain much further down than he’d ever imagined.

Scoundrel turned from the cliff and began correcting his path through the belly of the mountain. There was supposed to have been a bridge were the great precipice sat, but it looked that it had completely disappeared.
“It must have collapsed by old age…” Scoundrel reasoned. He wasn’t completely wrong… Yet to say that he was fully right would be a great lie.
Charting his course down a steep decline, his mouth began watering at the thought of all the gold the dragon must have kept in the mountain.

“The old worm hoards all the remaining gold in the mountain,” Scoundrel recalled the dwarf saying. He must have had mounds of it just piled up! However, Scoundrel knew he’d be an utter dimwit toeven lay a breath on it. He recalled with clarity the confrontation with Blackneck and knew with all his being that he wasn’t to mess with another king’s treasure again, even if it was only a dragon that had but one wing.

He began to notice that his candle started to flicker, and a cold chilling wind started to blow as he paced further inward. How the winter winds could have sustained their full strength in the midst of the dragon’s fervent breath was a mystery beyond what Scoundrel could answer. What he did know was that the winds made him feel both terribly alone and unsafe. He could already feel dozens of eyes could be felt boring trough his skull. While this feeling was probably only a product of imagination mixed with fear, at this point, nothing would surprise Scoundrel. After all, he’d been watched by the dwarf earlier without his noticing. How big of a stretch was it to believe that he was being followed again?

Scoundrel quickened his pace and run faster through the tunnel. If it was the dwarf, he didn’t want to be caught by it. While dwarfs might have good eyes in the dark, Scoundrel reasoned that as long as he ran fast enough, he wouldn’t have to worry about the dwarf’s stubby legs overtaking him.
Scoundrel’s plan wasn’t a smart one though, and he soon found himself slamming into a wall.
“Ouch!” moaned Scoundrel, rubbing himself off in pain.

Looking at his map, he didn’t see a wall anywhere. At least, if he was where he was supposed to be… It was quite possible that he’d gone off course, which might explain why he also hadn’t found a bridge.

Scoundrel was starting to sweat, even amidst the bitter cold that surrounded him. How would he be able to find his way through the mine now? It was quite the trouble to overcome, but he knew he’d have to make it through the mine somehow… He’d have to!
As Scoundrel sat rubbing his sores, he began to hear a quiet sharp sound ringing in his ear.
“Tee he he, tee he he,” it hissed.
Scoundrel recognize it as something quite out of place: laughter! Therewassomebody watching him in the darkness!
“Show yourself!” Scoundrel ordered, “What’s so funny?!”
He listened as the laugh hissed a while longer. Scoundrel was about to burst with impatience, when the laughter finally stilled, and an unearthly voice began to speak.

“I just find it funny,” the voice sizzled with such a tone that Scoundrel found his mouth left dry and himself drained of all confidence, “The way you run about through this mine in such a fright! It’s wonderfully entertaining, such a treat! Yes, ssssuch a treat…”

At the word ‘treat’ Scoundrel listened as the voice began smacking its lips and then watched as a pair of gleaming emerald circles appeared in the darkness. They left Scoundrel in a sort of trance and he felt himself nearly fall into a deep sleep.
“Yesss,” the voice hissed, “Ssssleep sssssoundly my ssssavory ssssnack!”

Scoundrel gawked in horror as a tremendous serpent wriggled out of the darkness… It was the dragon! A cloud of smoke that came out of its nostrils concealed most of its features, but Scoundrel still had no doubts.
“How—how--…” Scoundrel tried asking, but his voice faltered. Every breath of the smoke he inhaled only weakened him further.

“How did I find you?” finished the dragon, coiling its thick black neck around Scoundrel, “I could smell your reeking stench from miles away! Do you really think I would let a human that bears the mark of the ice king pass through my caves freely?”
The dragon then puffed another fat cloud of smoke into Scoundrel’s face.

The beast opened its mouth full of fangs and continued, “I’ve been watching you for a while my boy! Or should I say ‘Scoundrel’… Nice name, you must have such an easssy time finding a proper profession for yourself… I mean, you might as well wear a sssign around your chest that sssays ‘arrest me’!”

Scoundrel let out a muffled groan as the dragon tightened itself around Scoundrel’s body. “It won’t be much longer now,” the beast smiled, letting out a spark of fire-breath, “Your bones are very sssstrongyou know, even if you have a wiry frame and no treasure at all… Who feeds you? On another note, your body is dreadfully cold… but, I can sssstill take care of that with my breath I sssssuppose...”
Scoundrel was terrified. Everything had all happened so fast, and he found himself in a struggle to keep consciousness.
“Let me go!” he tried to say. But his body had lost all control, the only thing he still had power over now was his eyes. He could only manage a shrill muffled shriek.
“What was that?” the dragon chuckled, “Oh well, I sssuppose that if you’ll be grumbling about this in my stomach, or outside of it, I might as well have the pleasure of devouring you.”
“No stop!” Scoundrel managed to croak.
To his amazement, the dragon refrained. It looked quite taken back.
“Nobody has ever broken free of my poisonous vapor before,” the dragon lamented quietly, “Nobody…”
“Let… Me… Go!” said Scoundrel.

“Oh alright,” said the dragon with a devious gleam in his eye, spotting the locket around Scoundrel’s neck, “Any friend of the Ice King’s is a friend of mine! Because of your mark you’ll get special treatment… For now…”
Scoundrel knew that he couldn’t trust the old snake. Yet, he also knew that he had to play his charade if he planned on surviving.
“Blast that warthog of a dwarf! He sent me here to die!” Scoundrel thought to himself.
“What’s wrong? Why so quiet?” the Dragon asked, after letting Scoundrel regain his breath, “I know how to lighten your spirit! How about we play a game? All little boys like games, now don’t they?”

Cautiously, Scoundrel nodded his head. He knew quite clearly that this dragon would stop at nothing to kill him in the most devious way. Yet, perhaps he could manipulate this new notion the dragon raised.
“What sort of game?” asked Scoundrel clapping his hands together and putting on a fake smile.
The dragon smiled back too, and his large round eyes lit up in a dark flare. “Well, you have no gold or jewels to give me and your clothes may as well be garbage… hmm… I know! Entertainment!”
This began to fill Scoundrel with unease.

“You sssee, there’s nothing I find more entertaining than the look of pure despair in a creature’s eyes,” the dragon said, quickly clamping its teeth together, “Ssso, I’m going to place a little bet with you… You’re going to confront your greatest fear! If you lose, and fail to do ssso, you’ll be my sssnack! If I lose, I’ll… umm… I’ll ssspare you!”
“No! You’ll tell me the history of the ice king! I’m not wrong in believing that you’re the only one that can tell me his history, correct?
“No, not wrong at all my dear boy! Yess, if that is your true wish, then I’ll give it to you child! If you win that is… Now, what is your greatest fear?”

The dragon began scanning Scoundrel’s eyes, “Hmm… Yes… I sssee… Your heart is like a locked chest young lad! Tightly bound and hidden from sight. So, what I want from you is your true history… Yes… That would bring me sssuch a delight! Oh, great ‘Ssscoundrel’ what sort of feeble person are you under your false mask? I’m not sure, but I’d love to know!”

Scoundrel was stupefied. He’d never expected the snake to ask him such a thing! At first Scoundrel felt like laughing, how hard would it be to tell the old dragon the tale of his past? Surely he wasn’t scared of such a silly thing! But then Scoundrel realized just how much of a chore doing so really would be… He feared telling people of his past, and ultimately avoided it altogether. After all, letting the people of Blackneck believe he was a mischievous imp, or whatever tall tale they came up with, was much better than exposing his story. And now he was to reveal himself to the most intimidating creature he’d met?! It was true that the beast was anything but afraid of Scoundrel, but still… Sacrificing his history would be sacrificing a great deal of his confidence, and his identity! He thrived on his secrecy, the mysterious veil he placed around himself!
“And if I tell you this, you will spare me and tell the history of Blackneck?” inquired Scoundrel carefully mapping out his words.

“I will tell you the story of Blackneck,onlyif you tell me your story full and true,” said the Dragon with a nasty smile, “I can sense a lie from a mile away, so don’t try testing me. I wouldn’t be surprised if you did though, those nasty little fibs cover you from head to toe. Your people are right in calling you ‘Scoundrel’! Yet they’re wrong at the same time… Yes, the name Scoundrel really does fit you, now doesn’t it? A shame that it can’t be your true birth name… No, that name can only befit a person that has earned the title…”
“How do you know so much about me?”

“You should be asking how you know so little about yourself… yes, I sense that evenyouhave yourself fooled by your lies! I know, because I can read your heart… Hearts are funny things you know… They’re like a type of gem. No, theyarea type of gem. I know, because I’ve dwelt in mounds of gems all my life, and I’ve learned how to spot even the tiniest flaw in each one. I do the same with hearts, they are no different in my eyes.”

Scoundrel’s bones quaked. It was true that his body was still recovering from the dragon’s smothering, but his bones throttled and shook for a different reason: pure terror. This ancient reptile seemed to know everything about him! While the demon could spot every chink in Scoundrel’s thin layer of armor, Scoundrel himself could spot none in the monster’s scaly shell. For the first time, he truly felt helpless. There were no other options for himself but surrender, an action Scoundrel loathed.
Scoundrel let out a huff of defeat, “I will submit to the terms of our agreement.”
The dragon grinned. “Good!” he cried flapping his lone wing about, “We shall begin now!”
At the word ‘now’ the dragon shot a burst of fire out of its gaping mouth. Scoundrel watched awestruck, and the dragon laughed looking upon the boy’s timid face.
Stammering, Scoundrel struggled to begin, “So—so… Where would you like the story to start?”

“At the very beginning, when you were at your most fragile state… Your infancy!” the creature said pulling itself behind a curtain of smoke, “I want all of your most vivid memories, from the time of your entry into this accursed world, to the present time we now sit in.”

“Alright then,” said Scoundrel turning his gaze to the ground. He now wished he’d never agreed to the deal proposed by the dragon. Of course, he also knew that there wasn’t much that could be done about it. He’d already made one deal he doubted he’d be able to keep, he wasn’t going to have two.
Chapter Ten
Confessions
In the cold dark damp of that cave, alone with the devilish dragon, Scoundrel reluctantly started leaking his darkest secrets…

“I was born to two loving parents down in the humble town of Blackneck,” Scoundrel began, “Or so I remember. I was very young when they passed away. I do remember this though; I was born with quite a different name from Scoundrel…”
“And by what name were you born with?” asked the dragon meticulously.

“Joshua,” said Scoundrel, “I stopped being called by that name though when my parents disappeared venturing up into the mountain… It was a cold winter that year, and they were headed there forfirewood… they never came back…”
Scoundrel stopped and began staring stone-faced into the cloud of smoke that obscured the cave.

“Ssso very sssad…” the malicious dragon said clicking his iron teeth with his double-edged tongue, “Poor poor boy… I’m dreadfully sssorry to hear that. I wish that I had been there to mend your wounds.”

Scoundrel wanted to keep speaking, but he’d finally faltered.

The greater portion of his life had been spent groveling, hiding, and scheming in the darkness. He had lived, perhaps thrived even, with this way of life… But, it seemed to have proven empty…

They tracked me down to my abandoned shack and they managed to overwhelm me…”

Scoundrel then proceeded to tell the dragon all the events that had taken place since then, leading tothe point in which he reached the dragon. Although he was reluctant, he described his whole journey with great detail. The dragon spurted a cloud of fire within the smog. “Alright then. I’ll begin my turn”

Chapter Eleven
The Story of the Serpent

However, what else could he do?

But it seemed that it wasn’t what I feared either. You see, King Henry had made a deal with the wizard to give up something he’d loved greatly for the cure of his wife, and the king decided upon giving up the horse he rode. Back and forth we thrashed about, fighting more and more violently. Never in my life have I met a creature that was as strong as him, I felt that I was being swung about like a kite. Contrary to my earlier beliefs during the fight, he hadn’t been wrestling me to give me a false hope of survival after all. No, he had beenholding back! “Despite all this, I still found a way to smother my fears, and I sat about in the darkness awaiting Henry’s arrival. It never came though. “The castle ruins are in this mountain?” asked Scoundrel.

“Of course,” hissed the dragon, “How else could I have spied on Henry so easily? As I was saying… The kingdom rejoiced and Henry was exalted even further than ever before. It once again began flourishing, and both Henry and Lucy lived together peacefully ‘happily ever after’… At least, this is what everybody believed. Years passed, and, every so often, Lucy would notice something was amiss. Perhaps it was the undying, yet ever anxious energy, Henry seemed to have, or his constant success on the field of battle… Maybe it was the fact that, while she seemed to age, Henry never did. The wizard collapsed at this spectacle, he wasn’t used to such violence. With a trembling tone, that both thrilled and shriveled my spirit, the wizard finally told him that there was one way that he could preserve Queen Lucy, while it was a decision he would regret for eternity. Chapter Twelve
Meeting the End

Yet, the pure shock of trepidation flooding Scoundrel’s body only grew more overwhelming. For, before the eyes had finally faded into the darkness, Scoundrel heard the dragon utter a few short words that left a biting shiver down Scoundrel’s spine.
“I will have my vengeance boy…” the burning voice crackled, before being smothered by the pitch black of the hole.

Scoundrel’s eyes grew ever wider with fear, as he listened to the dragon’s disdainful laugh echo off the cavern walls. The dragon may have been gone, yet he left a mark ringing in Scoundrel’s ears that preached of his return. He could already feel the burning pain of the dragon’s breath toasting him to a crisp. The crude claws climbing up his throat…

The chilling pain of the ice on Scoundrel’s heart began stinging him all the more when he realized something much worse than the morbid thoughts that already filled his head. The very last memory of the ice king’s wife, one of the most precious and dearest things to Blackneck, had vanished into the possession of a wicked hoarder. A twinge of agony harassed his conscience as images of the frozen Queen flew by. She had been practically dead to the world for over a century, and the same for her lover. Feelings of pity for the emotionless statue that now lived in freezing solitary ate away at Scoundrel’s soul. It was true that Scoundrel’s life was charged an unjust debt from the Ice King. It was true that that the man would be willing to kill the whole town of Blackneck, just so that he could relieve himself of the misery in living. Despite all this, Scoundrel shared an understanding with the devastated soul. The ice king might have had the grandeur of a great palace, fathomless power, and amass of riches that would make a king possessing all the wealth of the earth combined, envious. Yet, Scoundrel knew all too well how deafening the sound of silence truly was… All the riches in the world couldn’t pay for even the voice of one you cherish dearly, calling out to you. Giving away his own past had revealed this all to him… Though the encounter with the dragon might have cost him a great deal of his security, maybe… Just maybe… his eyes had been opened a bit more… If only he could be certain he’d live another day to put his lessons to the test!
Chapter Thirteen
Riddles of the Heart

He’d been wandering through the mines for what felt like a half hour, and Scoundrel still hadn’t managed to recognize where he was, let alone find a way out. Not for the first time that day, he felt the pressing strain of his time limit laden on him. From the darkness of the mines, he couldn’t quite tell what time it was but Scoundrel knew that whatever time he had left was nearly drained. It had to be past noon at this point. It was apparent that he’d have to quicken his pace, but the icy weight on his chest pulled down on him, like an anchor. His body was aching from the toll put on it, he felt he couldn’t put up with the tension much longer.

If only Scoundrel still had his map and candle, but they had been burnt to a crisp by the dragon and were scattered into pieces across the mine’s floor. Not that they would have been much help… Scoundrel had decided that he needed to head for the ruins of Blackneck’s castle in the slim chance of finding the answer he needed to heal the ice king’s wife… Sadly, that landmark was nowhere on the map.

It might have seemed as of then that there was no cure in sight, but Scoundrel’s gut told him otherwise… There had to be an answer… He just wasn’t looking hard enough! There was still a slight hope that the dragon might bring the sacred locket to Scoundrel in another encounter, but he wasn’t going to count on it… It was almost certain that the dragon would stop at nothing to kill him; he’d have little to no chance of escaping another attack, let alone reclaiming the locket. No, he’d just need to find something else.

Still, even with it gone, the secret powers the locket might hold was something Scoundrel couldn’t stop puzzling himself with. He had worn it himself, and it looked to be an ordinary trinket. What made it able to heal the ice king’s wife? It was a strange thing indeed…
After he’d flummoxed himself about this for quite a while, he noticed he’d been scaling a steady incline, and the tunnel had once again started narrowing as it had when he’d first entered the mine.
“This is curious…” Scoundrel thought to himself.

He was right, the incline was severely out of the ordinary. It grew so steep that he found himself relying on the grip of his arms to pull himself forward, rather than his legs. And the steeper the incline, the narrower and narrower the tunnel became, until Scoundrel could barely move his arms and he found them scraping against the cold rocky walls. It was an uncomfortable experience to say the least. He had begun to think that he’d never make it to the top, when he finally found himself crawling out of the tunnel into a wide open expanse. He sprawled across the wide floor, drawing in deep and heavy breaths. Having such space after being in something so small was a much needed change.
When Scoundrel had returned to his wits, the first thing he’d noticed was a blast of light.
“If this is another dwarf house, I’d rather feed myself to the dragon!” Scoundrel grumbled to himselfas he tried to rediscover the balance in his feet.
Looking closer though as his vision started to adjust, he could clearly see that it was remarkably different from anything he’d ever laid eyes on in the past.

Unlike the dwarf’s house, the walls and floors of the room were grandly dressed in polished marble slabs, and in the center was positioned a small pool of water that sparkled as a precious gem. Out of everything in the whole room, it was the enticing pool that stood out. It glowed with an irresistible fluorescent blue light that came from within. During the time Scoundrel locked gaze with it, his eyes full of wonder, he could have sworn that it began calling out to him.
“Come… Come…” the water hummed with a sweet melody.

In a trance, Scoundrel gravitated over to it. Not knowing for certain how it happened, he found himself kneeling down, staring into the heart of the pool. Looking deeper and deeper into it, he thought he saw the elegant face of a person… Or was it a lion…? Perhaps it was a star…? Yes, a bright shining star…

Truly, it was all of these things, or none at all, for the pool moved in a current that was unpredictable, untamable. Still, Scoundrel did not know this, and found himself growing sleepier and sleepier from the calming atmosphere of the room, trying to come to his answer… an answer he’d never reach…

There was something about all of it, the fluorescent pool, the soft humming. It brought a warmth to him that had long been lost, ever since his confrontation with the Ice King. Those troubles were far away now… Much too far to ever reach him now…
“Lean closer… Closer…” the soft voice sang.
Scoundrel perceived himself drifting nearer and nearer to the surface of the pool, never stopping until the tip of his nose had dipped into it.
“Who… Or… What are you?” Scoundrel asked, his voice putting large sleepy ripples into the water’s surface.

“I am the fountain of youth… Like the current of water, I travel from form to form, giving life to things that have yet to be, and giving renewal to those weak in strength. I am the first rain of spring… I am the strength of a weak infant… I am the light that begins each day… And I am your deliverance…”
Scoundrel peered deeper into the pool and he watched as it took on the forms of the things it spoke of. The pool murmured through images as fluently as it did in voice.
“How… What are the chances that I could have stumbled across you?” Scoundrel stuttered, terribly jolted. Coming upon such a treasure was plain ridiculous, unreal!

“If you believe to have stumbled upon me by accident, you are gravely mistaken. I have been watching your journey for quite some time now, and you wouldn’t have crossed paths with me if it hadn’t been for my own divine intervention. Recall the warm wind that has guided your path, kept you from stumbling? The surges of strength you’ve gained in your desperation? It was all of my doing. After studying your ways and your weariness I’ve decided to offer you my full aid. Giving strength to the weary is my calling; it’s my heart’s desire. Your wish, one wish only, is my command.”

One wish… Scoundrel could have any wish? Thousands of the desires and wants of his heart started fluttering through his mind and overwhelming him. He could have anything! He could finally have the freedom from the chains that stung his heart, he had the chance to take a palace of his own! All the riches in the world were now at his beckoning!
“I—I can have any wish? Anything?”

“Yes,” the water trickled, “There are few powers in the world that I cannot overcome. Save those few things, you can have any one thing you desire. This choice is a hard one, one where most struggle to make a decision.”
“Where… Where do I start? WhereshouldI start?”

“The choice is not mine, dear boy, but yours. For, a life depends on choices. All I can tell you is of those who have come before you and what they have chosen: some have wished for herculean strength and others, all the riches of the earth. Some have wished for beauty, and some have wished to beidolized by all. Some have wished for great intelligence, and others have wished for a tongue that could incite influence into the hearts of all. All have been satisfied with my works, up to a point that is, and none have never failed to gain what they had asked for…”
“You have no advice as to what I should choose though?” asked Scoundrel.

“You can only find your answer within yourself, dear child. It is not one that I can grant, but rather, one that you must seek out inside. Who are you truly Scoundrel? That is the question you must ask…”

The water stilled for a moment, and then images of Scoundrel’s own life began flashing through the water. Images of his infancy, his childhood, his raiding of the city… It summarized all he had done, all his works.
“You know who I am?” Scoundrel asked the water with shock.
“I know what you’ve done…” said the water, “Yet, onlyyouknow who you are. I am simply reflecting you.”

Scoundrel groaned. This water wasn’t any help at all! He would have been better off talking to his own echo at this rate. Running his fingers through his hair, he’d thought about all his greatest desires in life, the great achievements he’d made and the failures. He looked back to when he started raiding the town of Blackneck, when he made a name for himself. His mind traced back to the riches he’d stored up in mounds within his shack…
“The wealth you’ve given people… Were they happy with it?” asked Scoundrel.

“They lived in their heaps of gold all the rest of their life, smiling. They were as happy as any creature could be. Never has there been somebody happier with sleeping on a bed of metal and rock than they.”
Scoundrel frowned. It wasn’t at all the answer that he had hoped for, although, he found that he wasn’t at all surprised by it either.
Bringing his hand over his icy heart, another concern came to mind. It had almost frozen into a lump of ice. “Could… Could you take away the curse from me?”
“Yes.”
Scoundrel’s head began to ache. He’d never thought that liberation could come so easily. Yet something inside of him was unsettled by this whole affair. It was all too easy, much too easy…
“And, if you did this, it would come as a free gift?” Scoundrel inquired.
The water didn’t respond, and Scoundrel watched while, for the first time, not a ripple was to be seen within it.

Scoundrel was ready to scream, but he knew better than to do that. There was something about this atmosphere that calmed him; gave him assurance. A wave of peace swept over him, and he felt as though everything was right within the world again, as though the trials that had troubled him throughout the day were just distant dreams… Yes… Just dreams, just fragments of imagination… They were far away now.

The humming that had calmed him earlier returned to seep in his ears and echo around the room. What a sweet melody it was. Yes, oh so sweet! How could anything be wrong in such a beautiful place as this? What had Scoundrel to fear? He would just need to give his wish nice and slowly… He’d be happy again, he’d become one with the soothing atmosphere. He’d be able to live in this beautiful paradise for the rest of his days, drinking of the sparkling water. Yes, he’d just have to give his wish, and all would be well…

Scoundrel opened his mouth to speak, already beginning to let the words, “I wish…” roll off his tongue. He started saying this but when the memories of the ice king, Queen Lucy, and even the citizens of Blackneck came into his mind, he halted. Something in him snapped awake.
“I’ve been being tricked…” Scoundrel thought to himself.

The whole room was a trap. As a child Scoundrel had heard tales like these before: tales of the sirens. They were nasty creatures of the sea, able to break down the wits of even the sharpest person with only the lull of their voice. The greatest sailors would find themselves washed out into the oceanwithout the slightest recollection of how they got there. This was no fountain of youth from what he could tell, but a prison.

Scoundrel lifted pulling his face further away from the water. “I’ve searched myself deeply, and I now realize that I don’t want any of your gifts, save one thing: I wish for you to give me the cure for Queen Lucy. I wish to awake her from the eternal trance.”

The water rippled slowly, and Scoundrel watched as the glowing orb from within it steadily rose out of the water. Ascending inch by inch, water pouring heavily from it, Scoundrel watched as the form of a great statue unveiled itself before him, taking the place of the glowing orb he had seen only moments earlier. It was a sphinx. Made of green limestone. Its eyes were two emeralds that shone down onto Scoundrel. The glowing orb, from what Scoundrel could tell, had turned into this sphinx. He couldn’t explain how he knew, or how it could have happened, but his intuition seemed to give him all the explanation he needed.

When the Sphinx first came into view, Scoundrel was both stunned and surprised; finding himself staggering to keep himself upright. The change had happened so instantaneously that Scoundrel was struggling to comprehend it all.
“I’m afraid a cure for Queen Lucy is the one wish that I cannot grant to you… as it is the only thing my abilities are unable to fathom… however…..I cantellyou what it is able to cure her.”
“What is it then?” asked Scoundrel, eager to get away from the statue as quickly as possible. There was something about the sphinx that made his blood curdle.
“I’m afraid your wish will not be granted just yet. You see, you have only passed the first test, my boy.
I do commend you, as you are the first ever to make it this far.

Neither a single man nor a single woman has ever answered that riddle of mine; the riddle of the heart, correctly. And, not a man nor woman has ever been able to see past my veil through my murky waters. But, solving the riddle of your heart is only the first riddle out of two. I’m dreadfully sorry I have to do this, for few ever pass this stage… But, sadly, I will not allow your wish to be granted until you can answer my other riddle…”
“And what might this riddle be?” Scoundrel persisted with great annoyance. The creature had promised him a wish, but it now seemed to have all been a lie.
This wasn’t the only reason he had been annoyed though. He also used the hint of annoyance in his voice to cloak the true fear he revered towards the creature.

The being was unearthly, and strange. Whenever it spoke, not a bit of it moved, yet the voice came at of it was still clear as can be. It stood still in the midst of the water, staring down upon him with no mercy. What was the creature thinking? How long had it lived within these waters?
“My riddle,” the stony statue began, “Is one that has ignited trouble into many, and has managed to consume lives. It has fooled even some of the wisest of men on the earth…”
“Well then, if it’s only for the wisest of men, I’m more than capable of answering. Get on with it.”

Scoundrel sensed that the sphinx was disapproving of his words. Although, Scoundrel couldn’t be for certain, as it showed no emotion across its limestone face. The same tight-lipped expression mapped across the stony surface, looked that it could be a number of things. At one moment it seemed to be happy, another sad. At one moment it looked to be deep in thought, and at another, it looked as though not a blanker expression could have been manifested on it.
While Scoundrel continued to gawk at this awe-striking spectacle, the thing
started to rattle, staying stiff as ever.
“My riddle for you is this:
First the face of the wolf,
Then the face of a lamb.
This creature has puzzled many a man.
It walks through the masses,
Passing by unseen,
Yet, when it wishes,
It can have the form of a king.
On whomsoever it lands,
Whomsoever is changed,
Into the form of the creature they’re made.
This creature has no rule to what form it can take,
Yet, whatever its form, it is always fake.
Its voice is at times soft,
Yet in others, hard.
It at times measures a foot,
Yet in others, a yard.
My friend, to you, I give this task:
What is this creature? That is all I ask.”
Scoundrel was left astoundingly puzzled by the riddle. What was it supposed to mean…? And more importantly, what would happen if he failed to solve it?
“What if I falter in finding an answer?” Scoundrel asked.

The sphinx growled with the voice of a lion, “You willhaveto give an answer. Only one other option shall be provided. The only way to avoid giving your answer is through death. You will be trapped within this room until you commit to one of these two.”

It was at that point when Scoundrel realized he was trapped inside the room. The way that he had entered through was completely sealed off by a thick slab of marble. Even if he’d been strong enough to lift it, there was no crack or crevice to be seen. The slab might as well have been a part of the rest of the floor and it could have been, while this seemed impossible.

Scoundrel’s breathing quickened, and then stopped altogether when he realized the true desperation of the situation. Considering all the dangers he’d narrowly escaped throughout his life, or even in this day alone, he normally wouldn’t have been concerned. Yet, unlike on a normal day, he didn’t have the whole day to ponder his answer… Let alone the months he’d probably need to discover the answer to this riddle that few men could conquer.

It had all become extremely frustrating, to say the very least, and if Scoundrel had been a bit of dynamite, he would have burst on the spot. He needed focus to come up with the answer, but with everything going on, as well as the extreme time limit he had, he seemed to be at the great disadvantage. Could he truly hurdle all his obstacles, as well as reach his goal? That unsettling question only drove Scoundrel into further frustration, and he began pacing the floor with a greater headache than before. What was strange about all this is that the sphinx seemed pleased with Scoundrel’s loss for words, and lack of peace… almost too pleased. At the same time, what could Scoundrel have expected? Surely this Sphinx only chose the brightest of all the men that walked across the earth for his wretched game, and, even in the most peaceful sanctuary in the world, Scoundrel still was tearing his hair out over the difficult puzzle. The sphinx had all the reason to be proud.
“Could—Could I have a hint?” Scoundrel asked, meekly.
For a moment the sphinx said nothing, but then, with a blinding glow from its emerald eyes, a powerful roar erupted from within it, leaving Scoundrel quaking on the ground.

“Could you speak more coherently? I didn’t catch what you said…” Scoundrel wanted to spout out. Sadly (for his own ego anyways), his confidence had been completely shattered. There was something ominous about the whole affair that left Scoundrel wanting to crawl under a rock and hide.

Why had the sphinx disguised itself as “the fountain of youth” in the first place? What did it have to hide? More importantly, why did it choose to reveal itself now? The only answer that Scoundrel couldcome up with was that the sheer intimidation emanating from the sphinx had made Scoundrel all the more uncomfortable as he tried to answer the riddle… Still, he felt that there was something behind everything that had taken place, more than he had accounted for…

Scoundrel pushed himself into deeper thought. What could the answer to the riddle be? Then he realized: maybe it was closer than he thought! The murkiness of the water… The appearance of the mighty sphinx… They seemed to coincide with the verses of the riddle; “First the face of the wolf, then the face of a lamb.” Still, the conclusion that the sphinx was the creature of the riddle had to be far from the truth. For one thing, as far as Scoundrel knew, the sphinx lacked any ability to change the form ofothercreatures, as the riddle stated. This uncertainty was enough to drive Scoundrel away from choosing that as his answer. He wasn’t willing to settle for anything but a solid solution, especially when he was running the risk of the ultimate failure.

Continuing to strain his mind for the answer, the stress on Scoundrel had grown almost unbearable. With everything going on, it was hard to push all his fears into the back of his head. But, it was once he had finally done this that the answer clicked! It was so simple… It fit so well!
“Might your answer be a mask?” Scoundrel asked the statue.

No different from all its other responses, at first, the sphinx was sluggish to make a sound of any kind. Then, with a sudden motion, the sphinx began to shriek and groan in a high volume. It had appeared this way anyhow but, as Scoundrel examined closer, he realized that the groaning and aching coming from the sphinx was only the sound of it descending back down into the fountain. That is, unless the sphinx really had been groaning, and it was only masking its cries through its return to its watery prison.
Once the sphinx had disappeared into the water, the glowing orb reappeared and once again began to speak, “Congratulations. You’ve passed my final test, to my bafflement. Your wish shall be granted.”
“Not my full wish… What’s the point in being able to wish for anything when you can’t wish for the one thing you want the most?!”
“It is because the very thing you wish for is something even I do not possess the power to wield. You see, the only thing that can cure the Queen of her encasement is the purest form of love.”

Scoundrel almost wanted to burst out laughing. He was fuming! This creature knew nothing about love, and yet he was telling Scoundrel that he needed it! What did this ‘fountain’ know? How could this creature try to give him advice? “Ha! Pure love!? That’s the very thing that has gotten me into this mess, the very thing that eats away at the heart of the ice king! If you are trying to tell me that true love is the answer to my problems, you mistake me for a twit.”
“You don’t believe in true love? You don’t believe in a love that is incorruptible?”

“Well, since you’re the one with the answers to all the riddles, what do you think? In a world that’s full of traitors, death, famine and disease, do you truly thinkanythingcould be incorruptible?Maybelove is something more than just a fleeting emotion, andmaybeit possesses a power beyond the grasp of any mortal creature, but I’ll tell you right now, I have witnessed it cause nothing but grief.”
“Strange… I thought that you were beyond that, that you were hoping to cure the Queen to prove love was real…”
“Isn’t that funny… the very creature who claimed that I knew the riddle of the heart doesn’t even know how to read the heart himself! The only reason I need to cure the Queen is to snap the Ice

King back into sanity! If that doesn’t work, then I have no hope. I can be certain that love has nothing to do with this quest. I think you’ve confused my actions with nobility, and I’m afraid that just isn’t so…”
“I see…” the water rippled.
“Now that we have that cleared up, I’d like you to tell me where I should look for this ‘pure love you speak of’. Where might I find it, what qualities does it possess?”
“My apologies, but if you recall, you can only get one wish.”
“My apologies, but ifyourecall, you only gave me half my wish, if even that. You truly haven’t givenyour fair share yet.”

“You make a just claim. I relent. Let me show you where your answer lies.” The water began swirling around and within it a shape took frame. At first it was merely a shaky shadow that resembled a mountain. But, Scoundrel peeked closer, once again dipping his nose into the water, and he recognized what looked to be a palace.

Something about it was strangely familiar, as though he’d seen it before. “A castle? What an odd hint… Could you, by any chance, be depicting the ruins of the palace King Henry and Queen Lucy had once dwelt in?”
The water showed no response, staying as firm as ever.
“I’d very much like to go there,” Scoundrel continued, “I want you to take me there, or at least show me a way out. I need to reach that castle at once!”

The large slab of marble in the floor began to move. Smiling, Scoundrel walked towards it, staring with wonder at the light emanating from it. He reached the opening in the door, and looked down through it but he saw nothing except the glaring white light.
“Do… Do I go in it?” asked Scoundrel.

He heard no response, save the trickling of the water within the pool. Scoundrel looked into the opening and he felt a strong tremor well up inside himself. What if he didn’t survive? What if the exit was only a walkway into another trap set by the sphinx? Although, looking around the room he was positioned in, he could see that there was no other choice. He could either take the uncertain plunge of leaving the room, or he could remain where he was with the crafty sphinx. As much as Scoundrel loathed the risk he was taking, he knew what he had to do.
Right before he descended into the opening, Scoundrel turned to face the pool and make one final remark.

“Goodbye, whoever you are under that mask of yours,” he said with a grubby smirk spreading across his face. He hadn’t put much thought to it until now, but had the sphinx really been the wizard in disguise?

Scoundrel decided that it didn’t really matter. Either way, the sphinx was trouble, and Scoundrel didn’t wish to remain with him any longer. The thief bounded into the hole, and the last thing he could remember seeing was the color white, all around him. The shade of white was so clean that Scoundrel couldn’t have imagined it ever being more refined. As Scoundrel relished in the warm light, everything turned into a sudden black… And then he felt a vicious chill crawl up his back, when a dense cold
covered him all over…
Chapter Fourteen
Uncovering

Scoundrel hadn’t been sure how long he sat unmoving in the pure cold before he regained consciousness (if he had ever lost it). Scoundrel sat blinking a few times into the dense blackness that sealed him, trying to insure he was still alive. He couldn’t tell for sure. Had the light been so bright that he went blind? Was he in a cage or nightmare? Or was something much worse altogether taking place?

Jolted by terror, Scoundrel flailed limbs around, in the desperate hope that it would give him assurance and, even more desperate, lead to his escape. The freezing temperatures that encased him burned furiously, even more than his own heart.

These anxieties slowed when, giving a sudden kick into the air, he watched a block of light break through the darkness from out of under him. Kicking with his other leg, another burst of light shot through, and Scoundrel found himself peering into a cloudy sky below him. How was this so? Had the whole world turned upside down!?

Scoundrel started to laugh, a muffled laugh that was cut short by a mouthful of snow.Hewas upside down, in a thick pile of snow! After a good deal of scrambling and pumping of his limbs, Scoundrel found himself staring out into the clear outdoors. He was finally free from the nasty mines! With a sigh of relief, the boy sprawled across the ground sucking in deep and heavy breaths. As Scoundrel relished in his freedom, he began to question whether or not the whole encounter with the sphinx had been nothing but a dream. He had, after all, bumped his head quite a few times on his way up through the mines. However, he tried observing his surroundings… Turning around from the climbing mountain slope, he found himself facing a massive pile of ruins. Perhaps the encounter with the sphinx had been real after all! Perhaps it hadn’t been a dream! As Scoundrel lifted himself up and began flattening his wrinkled soggy clothes out, he took in another deep breath of fresh air. It was nothing like that musty old cavern; the flush of renewal was like a refreshing drink after a day of no water. He had gained a new sense of appreciation for the air, one he’d never felt before.
“Look at yourself,” Scoundrel thought, “Rejoicing over a breath of fresh air! Only hours ago you would have thought such a thing insane, ridiculous!”

As much as he wanted to deny it, the experience in the mines had given him a new perspective, it had changed something in him. Perhaps they were only minor changes and maybe they’d only helped him see the miniscule details of life with a crisp set of eyes. Yet, nonetheless, there was no denying that he had been changed, in one way or another; there simply wasn’t.

Sucking in one last fragrant breath, Scoundrel craned his neck as he looked for the sun in the sky. The clouds were very dark and heavy, as if to say it was going to snow again. Scoundrel found it a struggle to catch any glimpse of the sun behind their dreary drapery. However, from what he could tell, it was nearing four o’clock, if it hadn’t passed it already. His time had really become short, and the pain in his chest had grown to be almost unbearable. If he hadn’t known that he was supposed to feel flesh every time he put his hand over his heart, he would have thought he was pressing against a sheet of ice. The pressure was growing stronger and stronger on Scoundrel to find the cure. He couldn’t let his efforts die in vain.
Scoundrel charged towards the ruins of the castle wishing to find the mystery cure; wishing to spare himself of his icy fate. If only he’d known of the shadow that lurked close behind him…

Once Scoundrel drew closer to the ruins, he realized just how spectral and morbid it was. Even in the midst of the winter, unruly clumps of moss and mold managed to thrive atop the fallen rock and plaster. The ruins itself took on an intimidating shape, resembling something like a deformed claw groping its way out of the earth. Though, the fallen spires, and the crumbling base appeared different from each angle he took. It happened so fluidly, that he questioned whether it was some form of magic. Sometimes it appeared to be a claw, yet, in others it appeared to be the foaming mouth of a monster, and at other angles, it almost looked to be a normal castle. Ironically, it was probably the angle in which it looked to be a castle that unsettled Scoundrel the most. It was almost too comforting to see a palace placed in such a wasteland.

What a wasteland the ruins were too! Save the moss and mold, nothing in the ruins was living, nor was anything, not even the moss or mold, clean. The evergreen trees, that must have once thrived there, were now barren and rotting from the inside out. The luscious shrubs and ivy vines had been sucked dry and left into brown shriveled heaps. Even the newly fallen layer of snow was gray and dingy.
“What happened here?” Scoundrel asked himself.

It was true that King Henry and Queen Lucy were the glue that held the kingdom together, but how could their absence have caused such devastation? Surely the dragon hid more secrets from Scoundrel than he let on when he told him his tale. While this angered Scoundrel, he had sensed the dragon mighthave sprinkled lies throughout the story. That’s the nasty thing about liars, only half of what they say is true, and sifting the truth out of what they say is a delicate task.

While Scoundrel walked through the ruins, he tried spawning some ideas of what happened. This started when, half-hidden in the rubble, he found a tapestry of a coat of arms. It was a simple, yet elegant design; a green flag with a bright blue snowflake set in the middle. At least, the snowflake would have been bright, however the flag was covered in a filthy layer of soot. The aging that the flag probably withstood for more than a century wasn’t much help either. Something about the coat of arms disturbed Scoundrel; it was ancient, but it had still managed to survive until now… Why hadn’t it been buried, along with the ruins? The uncomforting feeling that filled him only grew stronger when he lifted the banner out of the rubble to find these three letters stitched into the top of it. “H”, “E”, and “N”. They jumped out at him with a concussive force, nearly knocking him to his feet. It looked that there would have been more letters too, to spell out the name “Henry”, if the rest of the top hadn’t been torn off…
Or had it been torn? Scoundrel observed it even closer and realized that it had been burned in a fire. The only reason the banner survived was the mound of rocks that had smothered it.

Slowly trudging further, Scoundrel found that he hadn’t even scratched the surface of the unsettling artifacts filling the ruins. Strewn about across the rubble, there were more banners, bearing more names. At the center of each one was a symbol; a jewel, a crown and a spear. Similar to Henry’s flag, all the names they bore remained at the top, although, most of them had been partially burned off in a similar fire.

Scoundrel hoped that the scene would grow lighter the further he continued, but he found that the artifacts only grew worse.... Scattered across the ground, Scoundrel found weapons and hollow armor bearing the crests he’d found on the banners. They almost screamed of a devastated past. Not all the armors he found were empty and hollow though… In some, he found the decaying remains of skeletons. Each time he passed one, he wanted to crawl out of his skin and bury himself back into the snow he’d come from. Scoundrel wasn’t usually the sort to be sensitive in the face of such causalities, but there was something about the whole scene that provoked his heart. Something awful had taken place here…
After he’d examined all this, Scoundrel started piecing together what had happened. Once the

King had become absent, there must have been a battle for the throne; the temptation of the jewels had probably been too much to overcome. In their lust, it looked as though the groups of aspiring Kings built up their own armies to fight for control of the castle, until it eventually fell to pieces. The very thought disgusted Scoundrel. How could they have been so greedy in their craving for riches and power that they utterly ignored the destruction it caused? As Scoundrel pondered this, out of the corner of his eye he observed a shining metal helmet, in which he saw his own reflection. It was then that his thoughts stopped short and he suddenly realized that he was hardly any better than those who caused the horrific massacre… How could he really have an opinion on the matter when he was just as bad or worse?

Scoundrel went on to scour the rest of the ruins in the aspiration of finding something uplifting, something that could give him a confidence that his mission wasn’t a completely dire effort. There had to be something that could help him find the cure for Queen Lucy, at least a hint! Scoundrel regretted not asking for a clearer answer from the sphinx, even if there was little chance that it would have ever given him an answer that didn’t come out in the form of a riddle. It was very angering to know how close he was to the cure, to the answer, and still not have a clue as to what he was looking for. Pure love? How was he supposed to find that? The whole endeavor was ridiculous! He would be better off looking for a needle in a haystack. He couldn’t be expected to find his answer under such circumstances, but he sadly had no other choice. The ice continued to gnaw at his heart, and the day was waning faster than ever.

It was at the moment he thought these things when something crossed his attention. It happened thathe took a certain step on the ground where it groaned and a hollow creak could be heard wailing below.
“What was that?” Scoundrel inquired to himself.

He bent down to sweep away the ash and dust that silted the ground, with his hands. As he did such, a small wooden door was uncovered out of the muck. It looked to be painted the same color as the stone that surrounded him, and it almost camouflaged with it too. But, once all the dust and ash had been removed, Scoundrel could clearly see that the paint was peeling off of it, revealing bare wood.
Scoundrel wedged his fingers into the cracks of the door and tried to open it, but to no avail. It was locked shut. Whatever was under there must have been safely hidden.

“It’s probably just an old wine cellar,” Scoundrel reasoned, to keep the excitement that was welling up inside him under control. Yet, he still wasn’t going to run the risk of overlooking even an inch of the ruins. Whether it was a wine cellar or not, he needed to get the door opened.

After making his fingers swell up big as tomatoes in giving another round at the attempt to pry it open, Scoundrel had decided too much time had been wasted, and he’d have to take a different approach. He gave a good deal of thought and noticed once again how ancient the wooden door looked to be. It had to be over a century old, at the very least. If Scoundrel could just kick through it at the center, it might give away… While there was a chance he’d fall right through, diving down into whatever laid below the mysterious door, he knew it was what he had to do. With a powerful thrust, Scoundrel slammed has foot down on the flimsy board, and listened as the wood broke with a crisp snap. The Splinters flew about everywhere, some of them jutting into Scoundrel’s skin. Although, the boy couldn’t care less, for a great mystery was unveiling itself before his eyes. With the wooden plank broken away, he discovered a rickety staircase descending into a dark hole below. Where it went, he didn’t know. There could be anything down the mystifying tunnel! Finding his footing on a wobbly step he plotted his way carefully downwards, making sure to test each board for sturdiness before putting his full weight on it. A few times, the whole step gave away before his foot had even touched the tip of it.

“You’d think that a king would invest some of his wealth in a sturdier design for his castle…” Scoundrel remarked. Although, a sensed that there was an underlying reason as to why the room was constructed so shabbily… Perhaps it was meant to be kept hidden.
Once Scoundrel had reached a point on the staircase where the light from the world above could barely reach, Scoundrel found a timber box hanging from the wall.
“At least they did something right here…” Scoundrel said, using the box to light the torches hung along the wall damp tunnel wall.

In spite of how meagre the tunnel was, it was still a nice and embraced change from the dark and desolate ruins above. Surely it wasn’t the most lavish of places, with its muddy brick structure, and its dank ceiling that leaked water with a steady rhythm. Still, it held a charming personality, with its musty smell of old paper books and wax, along with the warm glow the torches let off. Where was that smell coming from anyways? Scoundrel hadn’t traveled far enough in the tunnel to find anything just yet, and his eyes were still only beginning to adjust with the dim surroundings as he lit the passageway down into the room below. It wasn’t until he’d lit the last torch on the bottom of the staircase that he actually had an idea of where he was…

The room was furnished with bookshelves from wall to wall that were simply crammed full of books of all kinds. Scoundrel, who was quite used to a world without books, or reading in general, was astounded by such a sight. Studying each wall, he tried to read the jammed spines of each beauty.

“On Hunt Red Was To Cock A Chuck In…” Scoundrel read aloud from one, turning his head sideways as he studied the binding. In full honesty, Scoundrel wasn’t very literate, and the title of the book was actually “One-Hundred Ways to Cook a Chicken”. But, if you would have told himself such, I’m sure his face would’ve gone red with an indignant rage, and he undoubtedly would’ve exclaimed that he knew how to read just fine.

There was more to the room than just bookshelves however. It was a fairly small square, but it stillmanaged enough room for a small table, just big enough to seat two. On this small table was a single candle placed on a mantelpiece, and a piece of paper with a wiry scrawl spread across it. It was already hard enough for Scoundrel to read normal letters, so this paper was absolutely unreadable to him. He quickly guessed from the messy signature on it, looking strikingly similar to the word “Henry”, that the paper had been written by the Ice King. Lucy had probably written all the official manuscripts for him…

There were also drawers built within the table. Scoundrel pulled them out, one by one, finding them full of journals. Scoundrel tried reading the titles on them. They all seemed to have a similar signature, resembling the name “Lucy”.

Taking everything in, Scoundrel realized that this must have been a secret place for the king and queen to go for removal from the stress of the world around them. Scoundrel would have liked to have called it a study, but such a term didn’t seem appropriate when he knew that there must have once been vast libraries of books in the castle before it burned to ash. What was so special about this place? Why did it seem that the king and queen had spent so much time in it?

Scoundrel looked about the room; it was so modest compared to everything else he’d seen that day. It didn’t have the opulent decorations and designs along the walls, and it didn’t have the luxurious furnishings that he’d expected from royalty. Yet, it still seemed to have a great worth within it, a personality that surpassed the price of any jewel. Perhaps he only felt this because of all the troubles jewels have caused him that day, yet perhaps he felt this because of a quite different reason… Maybe he was learning that there was more to this world beyond his own personal lusts…

Once he had looked about the room some more, covering every inch, he finally decided to try and read one of Lucy’s books. He knew that it would be a terribly rough undertaking, but it had to be done. The sphinx said he’d find the cure here, and he would go to all extremes to make sure that he had it. So, without hesitation, Scoundrel began leafing through one of Lucy’s journals with the title, “diary” on it…
Chapter Fifteen
The Queen’s Diary

At the start of when Scoundrel began reading the diary, he struggled a good deal, and he only found things that mattered little to him. The first dozen entries were just logs of what Lucy had done that day, along with a few recipes mixed in. While it was dull and tedious, Scoundrel still found wonder in reading a document that had been lost for ages, hidden to the world, and yet he had the privilege to read it. He was reading a diary of somebody that had lived over a century ago!

It helped that Lucy had much better handwriting than Henry too, for if she hadn’t, Scoundrel certainly would have been lost in a maze of words; worse than he was already. Scoundrel steadily gained the rhythm of reading, and started skimming over the logs of some of Lucy’s earlier days to read further in. He passed many pages full of beautiful walks in the moonlight, the improvement of the kingdom, and the many philosophical thoughts Lucy had. As wretched Scoundrel felt at first for turningthe pages recording her life without a second thought, he knew that they didn’t have what he was looking for. He felt something in his frozen heart constantly telling him that he hadn’t reached the point where he needed to yet. He stopped leafing through the pages when he read something that caught his eye; the record of the events that took place during the first encounter with the dragon. She had described the oily beast in perfection, the only difference in her description of the dragon from what Scoundrel had witnessed being his second wing. It seemed that she had been proud of Henry’s valor, and when she spoke of the dragon’s mighty blow to her, as well as the stinging pain she felt thereafter, her confidence in him never wavered.

It wasn’t to say that Lucy didn’t recognize Henry’s failure though. From her words, she made it clear that she noticed the moment when fear started to fill Henry’s eyes. Yet, it was also apparent that she looked at the powers laying beyond what an eye could have seen.

This is what had been written across the last page of this entry: “To most I’m sure it looked as if Henry had failed me and the kingdom. However, there was nothing quite further from the truth. In a burst of confidence, I watched him take action without a second thought. He knew his place, his calling. He went to all costs to protect the kingdom, even if it meant his own life. At the end of the whole ordeal, the only reason he faltered; the only reason that he failed to thwart the creature, was his own fear. In that final pivotal moment, ultimately leading to his defeat and the dragon’s escape, I watched him question himself. I read his face, and he was afraid of failing. This is why I stand firm in the belief that he had never failed me, nor the people he led, but himself.”

Scoundrel read past this entry, and further in. The Queen wrote of her sudden illness, and the terror that had swept over the kingdom. To Scoundrel’s surprise, he found that Lucy herself had no concern of her condition and had only one thing troubling her.

“I’ve seen the weary looks on Henry’s face,” she wrote, “He’s scared that I will not overcome my sickness. Sadly, I wish he knew how much of this is only him fearing for himself... I can sometimes hear him while I’m half asleep, fretting over whether he’ll make a good enough King without my aid… and whether he’ll be able to spare me of the death the nurses are afraid will take me. Yet, what I fear is that he’s losing himself in this fear of losing me.”
On the next page, Scoundrel found another entry, dated a week later.

“Something quite unsettling has set upon our fair kingdom… The doctor says that I will not make it. He says that there’s no cure known for the illness that gnaws at me. Although, this is not at all what makes my heart sink… No, not at all. What happened is that Henry came to me, bringing his face to my ear. He told me that he had a cure… That he knew of a way to restore me. In spite of his soothing voice, something told me from the heavy look he had on his brow that something much darker is taking place. Whether I survive or perish, my greatest concern, above all else, is that Henry will never truly be the man he once was… I fear he is about to meddle with a power far beyond what he knows.”
Scoundrel then read more about the seemingly strange occurrence of Henry healing Lucy. Lucy’s words eerily did not fit with the description of the scene.

“Although the room lit up with smiles and laughs as soon as the color began returning to my face, there was one cheery smile that disheartened me. It was the smile of Henry. As happy as he looked after giving me this mysterious elixir, I could see within the gaze of his empty eyes that something was amiss… When I asked him later in our study where he had gotten the cure, his face went blank. He muttered something unintelligible and went up into his chambers alone for some ‘sleep’.”

How terribly sad… Henry had tried so hard to protect Lucy but it had only led to him completely forgetting about her. Knowing that the tale only became worse, Scoundrel started to moan. The diary went on to chart the following events; the distancing of Henry, the unsettling appearance of his invincibility, the vanquishing of the dragon… Scoundrel sped through most of this, partly because he already knew what had happened and didn’t need to take the time to read it, and partly because he could hardly bear to listen to Lucy’s melancholy thoughts any longer. Something about them tore him apart inside. He didn’t want to admit it, but tears welled up in his eyes.
“Pull yourself together,” Scoundrel told himself, “It’s just a yellowing old book!”

For some reason, as much as he tried to tell himself that, it meant much more to him. He’d never experienced anything quite like this… as he stuttered over the words on the pages, he almost felt as if he were seeing everything in the eyes of Lucy, almost as if he were sharing her very thoughts. Scoundrel had witnessed many strange things that day, but nothing had been more magical to him than this.
Anguish filled Scoundrel all the more when he started nearing the end of the diary, after Henry had left the palace for his final venture to the old wizard in the mountain.

“It vexes me to know what has become of me and Henry… Over the years we have grown further apart, and he no longer is there when I need him by my side. Even when he is with me, he is but a ghost of himself, always staring blankly off into space, and mumbling things that I could never hope to understand. I have asked him many times what is wrong, what consumes him so… But he never responds, almost as if he were just a statue. My heart fills with such a weight for him, although I know that there is little I can do. He has pulled his heart apart from mine, and he has hid himself behind a veil that he does not wish to be exposed through. Now he has left the palace once again, and I listen as murmurings fill the halls of treachery. Henry’s absence has truly done much more to this kingdom than he supposes. I knew that he ultimately would pay an awful price for using what I presume was magic… I just wish it had never come to this… No matter though. Neither distance nor any power under the sun will ever stop me from loving him, my dearest Henry.”

That was it. The very last diary entry. After that, the diary was but a cluster of empty unfilled pages. A sadness consumed Scoundrel as he read and reread those last words… In spite of everything Henry had done, in spite of all his mistakes, she never stopped loving him. In the end, their love had never died…

Once Scoundrel had put the book down, a sudden anger bubbled in himself. A dark truth was unveiling itself... The sphinx had told him that the cure was here! He should have found it by now, but there was nothing in the diary that eventoldhim of a ‘pure love’. Scoundrel ripped out another pile of books from the desk and tore through the pages. There was nothing there! Scoundrel’s muscles clenched and his breaths shortened. Where was the cure!?
“This doesn’t make any sense!” Scoundrel shouted at the top of his lungs.

He pulled at his hair, he pounded the table. There wasn’t going to be enough time to read all the books in the study. He had already spent too much time in the study as it was! There had to be something he missed… There just had to!

He pounded up the stairs out of the study, without another thought. If he was going to find the cure anywhere, it had to be up in the ruins. There had to be something he missed… Yet, he’d checked everything, he’d looked ateverything! He couldn’t have missed it, could he? Dashing through the ruins, his feet thumped and shook the earth, as they rushed over the piles of rubble scattered across the ground. There was nothing, absolutely nothing. Just piles of overturned rock and plaster, rusting armor, and rot. His eyes darted everywhere, he left nothing unseen. How could this be? He was the person who’d outsmarted masses of men and women, even the sphinx itself, and yet he couldn’t find what he was looking for in so simple a place?

Hordes of dismaying thoughts ran through Scoundrel’s head. What if the cure was buried deep under the piles of rubble, deeper than he could see? What if he’d missed the cure amidst the collection of books? What if there was no cure and the sphinx had lied!?

They were all possibilities, and likely ones at that. As much as he tried to reason with them, there was nothing to calm the unruly anxieties down. Scoundrel’s heart burned, both from the ice eating away at it and the stress lumping atop it. He couldn’t fail his mission, he’d put too much effort into it!
“What do I do!?” Scoundrel thought… Or at least he’d meant to only think it, but he found himself screaming it out loud.

He knew that he looked absurd, running about the abandoned ruins in such a fit, but he didn’t care. The sun would be setting soon enough, and he still had no plan as to how he’d attempt returning to itspeak in time.

Scoundrel couldn’t take the tax any longer and collapsed onto the ground. He finally accepted the horrid reality he’d been avoiding; he had been defeated. The battle he was fighting had already ended before it began. All the odds were tipped in favor of the Ice King.

Why had Scoundrel even bothered at attempting to heal Lucy? What good would it have done in the end? Everything about Scoundrel’s mission had all been a hoax that he crafted in his mind; there was never any chance of him finding the cure. Even if he had, what use would it have been to him? By the end of the day, no matter what Scoundrel attempted, nothing under the mountain would be spared, save the dragon. Nothing would change that…

Perhaps the Sphinx had been right, perhaps the curewastrue love. Yet, if Scoundrel had learned anything, it was that there was no true love. In other words, there was no cure. These ruins just represented what the cure was: gone, faded, destroyed, and dwindled down to nothingness. What a sap he had been to think there ever was a real cure… What a sap indeed!
Chapter Sixteen
The Marathon

Scoundrel snapped out of his miserable lamentation and self-pity when a bellowing roar erupted in the air. Jumping to his feet, Scoundrel searched around him. There was nothing to be seen in the thick darkness that was descending upon the earth. If only it wasn’t so dusky…

Scoundrel pricked his ears to accommodate for his lack of clear vision. At first, there was nothing to be heard… Then, all of the sudden, the clatter of something slamming against a mound of rubble, followed by the rubble crashing to the ground, broke out. Yet, when Scoundrel’s eyes flicked to where the scene should have been, there was nothing to be seen besides the murky shadow of night’s fog resting upon the ground. Time must have been running short quicker than he anticipated....
“Who’s out there?” Scoundrel demanded, trying intensely to prevent his alarm from seeping into his words.

There was no response. All too aware that he was being watched, Scoundrel began making his way for the peak of the mountain. He knew that there would be no chance of escaping the sight of whoever had been watching him, but maybe if he could lead them out of the ruins he’d have a clearer picture of his enemy. A twang of regret came over him when he realized he still didn’t have the cure, but he pushed it out of his mind and trudged onward.

With a rush of adrenaline pumping through his veins, Scoundrel began running with all his might. He was almost out of the ruins when he tripped, falling flat onto the ground. He couldn’t quite tell what had tripped him, perhaps rocks, or perhaps his stalker… But whatever it was, it had left him stunned.
“You thought you could escape me? Ha!” a shrill voice cried.
It was the shrewd dragon, Smoke!!
“What do you want from me now?” he asked. It was a weak retort, but the best he could muster.
“Are you sssuch an imbecile that you can’t even remember the conversation we shared only hours ago!?”
“From what I recall, it wasn’t exactly a ‘conversation’…”

“Quiet!” screeched the dragon as it tackled Scoundrel, “I want vengeance! Vengeance!” Its eyes were wild with rage, and its mouth was foaming. Across its body, much of its oily scales had been torn off from the fall in the mines, leaving behind crude patterns of exposed flesh.
“For what?” asked Scoundrel innocently, “You are the one who jumped off the cliff.”
“I’ve had enough of your nasty tongue! You’re lucky you’re still alive. You’re lucky that I’m only wearing your treasure across my neck and not your corpse!”
Scoundrel ignored the threats of the dragon when he noticed Lucy’s locket dangling over his head, around the dragon’s neck. Maybe that’s what the sphinx had meant by, “finding the cure in the ruins”!
“How did you find me here?!” asked Scoundrel, exaggerating a shriek. He was attempting to divert the dragon’s attention.

“How ssstupid do you think I am?! Of course you’d be here, where else? You sssseemed disturbingly interested in this place when I told you about it during my tale, ssso I reasoned that this was the likeliest place you’d escape to, if you were clever enough to find an exit.”
“Oh…”

“I can see that you’re finally running out of your clever retorts. I suppose you must just be awestruck in my genius! It’s a comfort to know that, for once, somebody has managed shut that vile mouth of yours! What a shame it is that you won’t be quiet for much longer. Soon enough, your blood-curdling screams will fill the air. Although, I suppose that won’t be much of an issue when you’re dead!”
“Are you talking to yourself? Because, the only person that has to worry about death is you!” Scoundrel said with a sarcastic tone. Hidden behind his back, his hand fingered a large stone.

“That’s it! I’ve prepared you for your execution long enough!” the dragon bellowed. The truth was, the beast was quite frightened. Scoundrel expressed no panic at all, and while the dragon normally would have liked to believe it was just an act, Scoundrel’s heart had been frozen to a point passed what he could interpret.

The dragon swung its jaw open to let out a blast of fire. What happened next came unexpected. Scoundrel quickly jerked onto his side to throw his stone into the exposed gaping mouth. Its eyes popping wide open, the creature let out a hoarse yowl. It wheezed and gagged, thrashing around on his back, while trying to regurgitate the rock it swallowed.

In the midst of the dragon’s struggle, Scoundrel tore the locket from its neck, slipped out of its massive underside and sped up the mountain. The sun was already setting, but Scoundrel knew that if he could just reach the ice king’s fortress in time, he’d be fine. He was already halfway up… It was a steep climb, but he knew he’d have to make it if he wanted to spare his life-- No, not only his life, but the lives of all those who lived in Blackneck.

It was then that he finally realized how much their lives truly relied on him; his success or failure was pivotal to their survival. It was true that he had never liked the people of Blackneck, that he had caused them much suffering in his life. He really had no business in fretting about their welfare; he was perhaps the last person you would have expected to do such. Yet, this only drove Scoundrel to want to ensure their survival even more; he owed it to them after all he’d done.

While Scoundrel continued sprinting up the incline of the mountain with all his force, the dragon started stumbling after him, gagging as he went. At this point it was quite clear why the beast was nicknamed Smoke. In the midst of the daylight, while he chugged up the mountain, his grungy smog could be seen protruding out of his snout and filled the air around him. It left behind a nasty rotting scent that slowed Scoundrel’s steps and weakened his every movement.

Still, even in the face of this test of will, Scoundrel charged on. He just had to make it to the peak of the mountain at Blackneck’s fortress, and then he’d be free. He’d already conjured a plan to rid himself of the dragon, as long as he could outrun him long enough. Sadly, the truth was Scoundrel’s strength had already begun waning. The sun had nearly set, and Scoundrel’s heart felt as heavy as a boulder. Normally his heart and veins would have been throbbing, yet, the comforting thump in his chest had been replaced by an echo of what had once been. Even with the dragon’s pace slowed down by the rock still jammed in his throat, Smoke had Scoundrel’s speed more than matched. It wouldn’t be long now before the steely claws would overcome Scoundrel and lunge into his back.
“Give it up boy! You little robber, give me my locket back!” the dragon gargled out, “You’re nevergoing to make it, ssso you might as well give it up now!”

Scoundrel rushed forward, ignoring the calls. Maybe he was just a thief, and maybe he was only doing all he’d ever known. Although, for once, this “thievery” felt different… It was satisfying, in a way he’d never felt before. It strengthened his soul. This strength he felt surging through him still wasn’t enough though… No, not nearly enough for the dragon!

Realizing that the monster hade gained considerable ground, Scoundrel started weaving his way in and out of the trees. He knew this would only make his journey up the mountain longer, but it was the one way to slow the dragon down. Sure enough, Scoundrel couldn’t have better in his timing. Right when he decided to take this new maneuver, Scoundrel’s rock came flying out of the dragon’s mouth, followed by a spray of fire.
