The back of Scoundrel’s garments had been toasted to a crisp and a tree had been lit aflame.

Scoundrel ran even faster, dodging the flames of the dragon as best he could. At this point, the dragon had already caught up with him, and there was no hope of outrunning him now. Scoundrel’s only chance was staying alive long enough to reach the Ice King’s fortress, for he had a plan. He was only halfway there now, he just needed to keep going!

Heading for a woody area in the mountain, Scoundrel hoped Smoke would lose him. The shift in direction might have sacrificed a bit of his time, but no matter. He’d still make it to the ice castle before sundown, from what he could tell, there was still a solid fifteen minutes left.
“What are you waiting for snake?!” Scoundrel taunted as he ran into the forest.

The worm let out a mighty roar, and sprayed more of his fervent flame into Scoundrel’s path. Luckily, the boy had just made it through the shelter of the trees before Smoke launched this deadly attack. For a moment, the safety the trees seemed to offer was comforting, yet then the fire started spreading from tree to tree. Thick layers of smoke filled the air until it choked Scoundrel to the point he grew blue in the face. Only to make things worse, as Scoundrel was stumbling through the burning web of trees, the dragon was trampling over them, knocking everything out of his path.

The pursuit had grown brutal now, and Scoundrel feared that he wouldn’t be able to make it out of the woods without becoming a pile of ash. Yet he only had to run a little while longer before he reached the castle. It was only just beyond the overgrowth of pines. He could make it!

A tree fell into his path and then another, but he still ran, hurdling each obstacle. Running with a furious strength, he ignored everything that ailed him, the pain, the hunger, the worry. All that mattered now was making it to the castle in time.

Scoundrel had almost reached the end, when the dragon had finally caught up with Scoundrel’s trail. There was nothing separating the two now. Opening his jaw and craning his steely neck forward, the creature prepared to spray out a burst of fire at Scoundrel. What happened next would put both of them into shock. A burning tree fell right into the dragon’s face, just before a single spark could escape his mouth. With his aim tattered, the fire launched far to the left, missing Scoundrel completely. Scoundrel had never seen anything quite like it. Everything had happened in such little time, but to Scoundrel, it felt as though it took minutes.

Turning his head back from the dragon to face forward, Scoundrel found himself hurtling out of the trees and out towards the ice covered lake that surrounded to the castle. It would only be a moment now, just a few more minutes!
Scoundrel’s thoughts were dashed when he felt the ruthless claws of the dragon thrust him into the air. Smacking against the ground, Scoundrel winced.

“You still try to fight even after you’ve been beaten!” declared the dragon with a sharp hiss, with a single claw poking at Scoundrel’s writhing body. His voice brought a chill down Scoundrel’s battered spine. “Do you not realize who I am!? Do you not realize how easily I’ve conquered the fathers before you!? Ridiculousness!”
Scoundrel crawled forward. The foot of the frozen lake only yards away now.

With another disapproving hiss, the dragon launched itself at Scoundrel’s torn body. Rolling onto thelake, with Scoundrel tucked into his chest, the dragon laughed like no creature had ever laughed before. A toothy smile smeared across his face while the awful sound, like the creaking of rusted metal, escaped his throat. “It was a valiant effort, really. But, I’ve tortured many creatures that far surpass you in wit and skill. I wouldn’t be too upset about this fate though… Dying by my hand is much better than dying by the Ice King’s, to be sure. Be grateful that I’ve decided to spare you of that awfulness.”
Scoundrel gritted his teeth. There had to be a way to escape…

The dragon reared up on his hind legs, preparing to maul through Scoundrel’s chest. There was nothing the child could do now. He winced and prepared for the coming onslaught. That is, until a sharp pang hit his ear. It was the cracking and snapping of ice. Scoundrel opened his eyes and jumped to his feet in spite of the pain he felt. Just as he did this, he watched as the dragon’s body fell through the ice and into the cold water below.
“No!!” the dragon shrieked sinking deeper in the water. Scoundrel could already hear him gurgling and sputtering as he drowned into the lake.

Not wanting to listen to the creature’s screams, Scoundrel fled toward the ice castle. The dragon was gone! He had been finished! A rush of relief filled Scoundrel’s body as he fingered the locket he rescued and returned his gaze to the hole the dragon had fallen through. Relief wasn’t the only thing that rushed through him; a gust of the all too familiar warm wind ran over his skin, and back into the whirling clouds above. Scoundrel grinned.

His unease returned though when he saw the cracks in the ice trailing from the hole the dragon had fallen through, and towards him! He then turned to face the sun; it had nearly set! Only faint glimmers of it remained in the western horizon.

He had to move hastily, he could already hear the splitting and slushing of plates of ice as they separated. The ground under him quivered and quaked at each step he took. Yet, he could already see the steps into the castle just mere yards ahead of him, he just had to hang on a little while longer.

Scoundrel’s senses sharpened as he ran towards his goal. He could see everything now; nothing escaped him and yet, his gaze was only focused on one thing; the doors into the Ice King’s palace. He could sense the thumping of his footsteps, the clammy sweat trickling down his neck, the smell of smoke that remained in the air, and the raw cold air against his tongue. He’d never forget how he felt at that moment. All the thoughts of dread and excitement that filled his head; no, he’dnever forget how it felt.

Running against the wind, and all odds, Scoundrel nearly reached the steps of the ice king’s castle. He could already see the entrance, swung wide open as if to welcome him inside. Scoundrel’s foot reached the first step just before the ground under him shattered and gave away. He’d made it! Scoundrel tore up the steps, as fast as his feet could carry him. The sun was just about to set! Scoundrel could feel the pressure flowing through his veins, the force in every breath. He could feel his very soul scream with anguish in the fear of not making it inside the door in time. It was only feet away now!

With a groan, the ice doors Scoundrel viewed only a day earlier began to shut. Scoundrel leaped over the last step in hopes of making it in between the two doors in time. The whole success of his mission depended upon this one sacred moment! Pinching his eyes shut tight, he couldn’t bear the thought of failing; the whole town would suffer!
Scoundrel hit the ground with a loud thud and watched as the doors slammed shut…
Chapter Seventeen
A Grim Fall
Scoundrel moaned. The feeling he felt was terrible… When he entered the ice castle, his arms flailing all about, he’d slammed his elbow against the door!

That’s right, Scoundrel had made it through, and just in the nick of time. If he had been any later, he would have been moaning for a quite different reason, on the opposite side of the shut doors. Under normal circumstances, Scoundrel would have rejoiced and acted almost comical in the prospect of sparing his life. Although, the moment Scoundrel had entered the castle, a solemn burden came over his whole demeanor. He would need to enter Blackneck’s large cave tucked away within the castle, and, if he had such fortune as to be spared, give his proof that love existed. Doubt filled Scoundrel’s mind as to how the locket could be the purest form of love. He had some ideas, but none of them were firm explanations. Although, both the dragon and the sphinx seemed to indicate that the locket had some sort of power, so it would have to work… It would just have to!

Walking slowly through the halls, Scoundrel felt as if the walls themselves had grown eyes and began using them to bore through his soul. He couldn’t make a single step without suffering a nauseating uncertainty. This same thought continued spinning through his head, he couldn’t push it out no matter how hard he tried: everything relied on his success or failure; he couldn’t afford to do otherwise and the townspeople couldn’t afford it…

As Scoundrel had drew closer to the Ice King’s chambers, the air around him howled at each step he took. Scoundrel knew that he was nearing Old Blackneck and the ice cold feeling flooding his whole body told Scoundrel that his time was nearly up. His very veins felt cold as ice; the blood pulsating through him no longer giving him the comforting warmth he missed dearly, but a chill that made Scoundrel shiver.

His cold veins weren’t the only things that made Scoundrel shiver though. The sharp voice of the Ice King sang through the air, puncturing Scoundrel’s ears, as well as his train of thought. Scoundrel had fully entered into the Ice King’s room; it all seeming to have happened so fast. Scoundrel’s journey through the castle surely had been much longer last time, hadn’t it? Whether it had or hadn’t was no matter now though, for, looking straight down on Scoundrel were the all too familiar eyes of Blackneck. Scoundrel stared into the Ice King’s face, and witnessed a weariness pass over it. He looked so tired and stretched since Scoundrel had last seen him, even though the being’s features were supposed to have stood still as stone. What could have happened to him between the times of only a day? Scoundrel’s thoughts were swept away with the wind of the Ice King’s voice.

“You have returned concerning the business of our deal we struck yesterday, correct?” The Ice King’s voice was as frigid as ever, and the anger that Scoundrel had witnessed within him only the day before had completely dissipated.
“Yes, that’s exactly why I’m here. I’ve done what you asked, and I’ve returned with the proof you asked for.”

“And what proof might this be? For, if I’m not mistaken, I recall claiming that love was but a fantasy, and you did not seem as adamant against that claim as you are now. What has changed within the stretch of only a day?”

“As if you haven’t witnessed my whole journey. You’ve seen the many trials I’ve faced and encountered, and, as of now, I don’t wish recount them. Right now, I’m here to hand you my proof. Look before you Ice King, this is the item that you have desired. The proof lays hanging around my neck.” Scoundrel then lifted the piece from over his head and raised it towards the great whirlwind. Thewind blew wildly, until it ripped the locket right out of Scoundrel’s hands, and threw it into the wall. If the piece hadn’t been crafted by the nimble hands of dwarves, it surely would have broken.

“What a monstrosity!” bellowed the wind, “There is nothing to that locket! It is merely a rusting piece of metal! What a fool you are! There was a reason I gave the worthless trinket to my wolves you know!”

Full of horror, Scoundrel’s mouth gaped wider than mouth of a cave. “No! You must put it to the test before you do such a thing! Did you not read the words written on it? Did you not marvel at its perfect design? Test it on Lucy before you go claiming such things! I swear, there must be something to that locket!”

“What business do you have with Lucy!? What business do you think you have even still standing before me in my castle!? I don’t even know why I bothered giving you the divine right to live one more day and unearth all my secrets! Just because of this alone you should die!” The ice king then slammed Scoundrel into a wall, in the midst of his mighty wind.
“No! Please! I promised you proof, and here it is! Put it to the test, it should heal your wife! I swear to it!”
“Lies!”

Breathing heavily, Scoundrel prevailed, “Just one test! That’s all it will take, and you will be proven wrong! Haven’t you wished with all your heart to restore Queen Lucy? Or has your heart grown so cold that you can no longer live without thinking about how everything effects your own sake…?”

The wind stopped. Scoundrel tried to read the face of Blackneck, but to no avail. He had hoped to see a baffled look come across his face, but instead, he found that it was his own face that was baffled. There was no emotion on that stiff face, no empathy. A deafening echo filled the room, giving Scoundrel a chill.

“One chance,” the stone said rigidly, “One, and that is all.” Scoundrel thought that he might have seen droplets of water slide down the ice king’s cheeks. However, he couldn’t be sure, for as soon as he noticed them, they were gone.

The Ice King lifted his arm, and with the flick of the wrist, the cracking and splitting of ice started to fill the room. The eerie echo still filled remained, but Scoundrel felt that something else was developing. Scoundrel watched as the Ice King’s gaze turned to the ceiling, and Scoundrel did the same. A hole, larger than the doorway into the castle, was breaking through. Snap! Crackle! The ice continued to split, and the hole grew ever larger. A sweet aroma filled the room, more enlightening than the scent of roses on a fresh spring day. A low whistle swam in after it, flying over Scoundrel’s head. A cluster of Goosebumps covered Scoundrel’s body as a rush of warm air hit him in the face. Something magnificent was about to happen.

Sure enough, like the graceful descent of a feather in the air, the frozen figure of Queen Lucy glided out of the opening in the ceiling. Scoundrel stared in wonder. How was she doing such? It was then that Scoundrel realized the winds of the Ice King were carrying her. With a journey as wild as the flight of a butterfly, Lucy came closer and closer to the ground. With a thud, she finally stood between Scoundrel and Blackneck.
“If this does not work on my beloved, you shall forever be under my wrath,” Blackneck declared monotonously.
Scoundrel nodded, with his lips tightly pressed together. If this didn’t work, he didn’t know what he’d do. No, this would have to work!

Blackneck lowered himself, and stood before Scoundrel, his limbs as square as a tin soldier’s. With a gust of wind, he brought his locket into his hand, grasping it tightly. As he lifted his arm and prepared to place the locket back around his wife’s neck, Scoundrel thought he heard Blackneck whisper something, but he couldn’t tell with the wind that surrounded him. Finally, the ice king let the locket drop around Lucy’s neck.
For a moment, nothing happened. The two stood staring at the ice statue without a movement. Then,suddenly, Scoundrel heard a low hum hover past him.
He jumped up and slapped his hands together in joy! It must have been working! Yet, then he caught the look on Blackneck’s face; indifferent.
“What are you doing!?” he snapped, “The humming of my wind is nothing to sneeze at!”
Scoundrel would have blushed if he’d still had warmth in his body. He knew what this meant. “Try reciting the words inscribed upon it! There must be something! It has to work!”

Blackneck turned his head towards the locket and heeded Scoundrel’s orders. Snapping it open he began to read, “To my beloved Lucy for remembrance that, even apart, our bond shall always remain.” His voice remained sharp as the tip of a knife.
Scoundrel stared at Lucy, eagerly hoping for the ice fall off her body; hoping to see her renewed… But nothing happened.

The ice king’s eyes returned to Scoundrel, unblinking. “As I suspected. Nothing under the sun can thaw my wife, not even the sun itself. You have failed to meet your end of the bargain Scoundrel. It’s time for you to be acquainted with the icy chamber you’ll inhabit for the rest of eternity.” A blast of ice shot out of Blackneck’s hands and hit Scoundrel’s chest. Scoundrel crumpled onto the floor in a ball, his lips quivering from the dismaying chill.
How could this be happening? Scoundrel was positive that the locket should have worked… What had gone wrong?!
His vision was already starting to fade, and his whole body felt as if a thousand knives had punctured through it. The cold was too much for him.
Scoundrel labored in forcing his eyes meet Blackneck’s. “Maybe the locket didn’t work. But, I can promise you as long as I have a breath in my body that loveisreal…”

“Ha! Spare yourself of your senseless fighting, we both know the truth. Love is perhaps real, but the ultimate end of it is always destruction! Look upon yourself boy! What happened to your parents!? Where were they when you were left alone in a shack! Where were they when you were driven to steal? They were just another aching weight to add on your heart when you were forced to face the real trials of this world.”

Scoundrel’s face remained as calm as ever, and, even as it grew paler from Blackneck’s icy assault, not an ounce of trepidation had hold over it. “No. It was when I tried to hide them that I felt the pain; when I tried to numb myself of their memory. In truth, the love we shared is probably the only thing that made me bother to come up here. If there was anything that has taught me what love is, it was them. They were a guide of the person I should become.”
Blackneck sprayed another blast of air at Scoundrel, “Pitiful excuses! You of all people know that they have done little for you! Besides, look at where love left me!”

Scoundrel’s body ached, and his jaw was as stiff as ever, but he still pressed on, “I read the diaries of Lucy; her thoughts and her feelings. In the end, she never gave up on you. In the end it was you, and you alone, who caused her doom.”
Blackneck shrieked, and he tossed Blackneck across the room, “I don’t want to hear it! You’re just scum from off the street, a good for nothing Scoundrel! What do you know about love!?”

“I’m not Scoundrel... My name is Joshua. I might not know much, and my word is worth little. Yet, while I’ve refused to admit it, I’ve learned a lot about love in one day. Even if my cold heart never had the chance to feel it, I can still tell you what it is…” a distant look filled Scoundrel’s face as his skin turned pure white. The loss of color was so sudden that you might have thought somebody was smearing a white paintbrush across his face. “It is selfless, slow to anger, and humble. It’s not always found in the finest of jewels, or the great powers of this world… but you’ll find it everywhere in the simplest of things. Maybe the thing isn’t real, and maybe it is but a figment of imagination. Yet, I can tell you this; the thing that allows us to share one heart and mind with one another; and that can bring us into a harmony beyond expression, is more real than anything else in this world. At the end of the day, love is this one thing most of all: selfless. Now, do what you wish with me, sulk in your icy prisonif that’s what you desire. But remember this one thing: you’ll find love if you can muster up the courage to step outside yourself.” Scoundrel’s heavy eyelids quelled and shut once he was finished.

The breath that still was left in Blackneck stopped short. Nobody had spoken to him like that in over a century… Not since Lucy… Lucy! Scoundrel had read her diaries hadn’t he? That must have been his ploy! He must have been reciting lines from Lucy’s diary; he had to have been! There was no other possibility!

“Do you think you can manipulate me!?” the Ice King roared. He shot Scoundrel with a blast of frost one last time, sending him rolling down an abyss in the castle. The fiery fury in Blackneck’s eyes didn’t smolder until he heard the ice of Scoundrel’s frozen body shattering below.

For a moment, the Ice King stood there still as stone. He’d really done it, he’d killed the Scoundrel. Burying his head in his hands, to his surprise, Blackneck found that he almost wanted to mourn. That is, until he calmed himself. He’d done the world a favor. Sparing that destructive creature would have been a monstrosity.
Chapter Eighteen
Removing the Masks

Scoundrel had fulfilled his end of the bargain; he tried to prove love was real. Now it was time for Blackneck to fulfill his end of the bargain and freeze the town below. It was his time to go, he no longer had a place in the world. But, as Blackneck prepared to take to the air, something stopped him from advancing. There was something in the boy’s words… They gnawed at him, made him groan with an agony like no other. It had been years since he had felt remotely anything, this didn’t make any sense.
The Ice King shook the feelings off. They were nothing. The words Scoundrel had spoken were barren as his fortress. They had just been a recital of his wife’s words.

The Ice King pursed his lips and whirled into the wind. He had waited a century too long to conduct this operation. Yet, once again, he was halted. As he hovered into the air, he thought he heard a voice call out to him… It was still, and soft, but firm. As quiet as it had been, it rang in the Ice King’s ears.
“Henry,” it said to him.
Blackneck turned his head to and fro. Who had said that!?
“Henry,” the voice whispered again.
The Ice King’s eyes met the source of the voice: it was the statue of Lucy. Blackneck descended quicker than a sweep of wind, landing in front of the figure.
“Lucy?” said the voice of Henry. It was softer now, calmer. His tone had slowed, and the sharp pang that had once filled it instantly left.

The ice that covered Blackneck started thawing, and looking upon Lucy, he could see that much of hers had melted as well. Around her face, the icy layer grew much clearer and thinner; even now, he could see bits of it fully exposed.
“What… What has healed you?” Blackneck asked staggering. He felt his legs wobble and quake. They could give away at any moment.

Lucy’s eyes shifted to the abyss Scoundrel had fallen through. It had been Scoundrel! His words had reawakened her! A sinking guilt bashed against Blackneck’s chest when he realized what he’d done. He’d rejected the very person that healed his wife, murdered him! Things only grew worse… The cold chilling air around them was freezing the melting layer of ice back onto his wife. Soon enough, she’d be as frozen as ever, lost to him once again.

Knowing that time was fleeting, his gaze met with Lucy’s, “What… What do you want me to do? Ican’t fail you again! I promise, on my life, you will be safe! Just tell me how, and I’ll do it!” Weary breaths filled his speech, he couldn’t take the pain of losing the very thing he loved again, let alone by his own hand.

“Don’t worry about failing me Henry,” Lucy said as the ice began freezing around her. Her voice was urgent, but calm, like the flight of a dove. “But worry about failing your own self. Before trying to avoid failing the heart of another, look within your own. Be true to your own heart… Take off your mask…” At her last word, the ice froze back around her, once again ensnaring her body in the cold.
“No!” cried Henry. He couldn’t bear to see her return into the bondage of the ice. Yet, there was nothing he could do.

An anger started to surge within Blackneck. He was the cause of his wife’s turmoil! He was the cause of the destruction that had been inflicted. It had always been him! For a century he’d tried to avoid facing this bitter truth, but now, he was forced to face it, completely exposed. The struggles he’d endured within himself were by his own cause, his own folly. He’d squandered his life in self-pity, not realizing how fragile it really was.

Blackneck—Henry—couldn’t take the pain anymore. He collapsed into a puddle of tears. All the people he’d loved, and all the things he cherished dearly, had been taken away from him; they’d melted away through his fingers. He could no longer even enjoy the comforting heat of the sun against his back, or the reviving breeze of the spring. In his shell of ice, he could no longer feel anything. It was an aching sore beyond anything he’d ever experienced; it cut him bitterly within the heart. Henry pressed his icy hands around his wife’s body, hoping he’d sense heat, sense something that proved there was still life within her. Although, he found nothing… Not even a steady heartbeat.

“WHY!?” howled Henry, his voice so shrill that the icy walls around him began to crack. His breath began to slow pace as he tried to calm himself, yet a single tear manage to slip out of his eye, and he found his breath uttering the word, “Why?” yet again.

To soothe his vexation, Henry tried remembering what Lucy had said. He even found himself trying to remember what Scoundrel had said. But it was useless, the memories were as isolated from him as everything else in the world.

“Be true to your own heart…” the wind whistled. Henry’s eyes darted back and forth. Who had said that? Were the words only of his imagining? He couldn’t be sure, but there was one thing that he was firm in; those had been the exact words Lucy had said to him.

What did they mean? Henry dearly wished he had the dragon’s ability to read hearts at that moment. He needed to know what might have been inscribed upon his heart, and how he could be, “true” to it. What did it mean to be true to one’s own heart anyways?
Suddenly, Henry remembered what Scoundrel—Joshua-- had told him. He needed to step outside himself…What did that mean? Henry had an idea.

Wiping the tears from his cheeks, he tried about forgetting all the sins he’d done. He tried looking at the world with a new set of eyes. He knew that there was no erasing the past, but he needed to move from it… He couldn’t remained fixed in time, as still as ice, any longer. The time had come for him to move forward.

It was a strain, but, once doing that, the world seemed to light up with a vibrant spark, almost as if he’d been in darkness for ages and had gotten his first glimpse of light. He felt as his weights ebbed from him in this light’s warmth, and the first thing he saw was how dearly Lucy needed help. He’d been buried inside himself for so long that he’d completely lost touch with who he was, along with reality. But now, he was firm in it. He was a leader, and leaders know when to take action; when to make a sacrifice.

Henry no longer feared failure, he’d already done enough of that. It was high time that he made a change, he’d do anything in his power to restore his wife. He’d never be able to make up for the blemishes left behind from the many mistakes he’d made, but it didn’t matter. All that mattered now was helping the person he’d loved the most. Slower than a tree sluggishly sprouting from the ground,Henry pulled himself up. He groaned in the pain, feeling all the ice around him dissolve. The parts of his body that had been numb for so long were beginning to feel again. A new life flowed within him.
In spite of the affliction, Henry smiled, for he knew what this meant. Turning his palms face up, he saw them aglow with a golden flicker, like that of a firefly.
“It’s time,” Henry whispered. “You will be free soon enough Lucy.”
He then aimed his palms to face Lucy…
Scoundrel awoke in a cold damp darkness. His body ached with an unquenchable agony, but that was the least of his worries. Where was he?
“I hope I’m not dead!” he laughed nervously. Although, what if he really was dead? The last thing he could remember was falling, and then the awful shattering of ice.
Scoundrel stood up, in hopes to get a better view.
Crunch!

There must have been ice under his feet... After groping around, Scoundrel’s hands managed to find a wall. He cringed. It was freezing, and when he tried to pull his hands away, they stuck to it like glue. He managed to remove them with only a slight burn, and realized that it must have been made of ice.
"Everything just had to be made of ice today!" Scoundrel declared sarcastically, "Ice people, ice castles... Even my own heart is made of ice!"

His heart! Scoundrel slapped his hand against his chest and was welcomed by the comforting heartbeat he'd known as long as he could remember. There wasn’t the slightest hint of cold! What had happened to all the ice that was on him? Scoundrel paced the floor, hoping to come up with an explanation.
Crunch!

Scoundrel’s eyes went wide with wonder. The ice under his feet… It had come from him! How had this happened? The curse wasn’t supposed to break unless the Ice King relieved him of it… If he found true love… That was it! The magic of the wizard only broke under true love, didn’t it?
“The curse must have relented when I discovered what true love was!” he concluded.

Getting such an explanation was satisfactory for a while, but then a new eerie question came to mind… What had become of the Ice King and Queen Lucy? From what Scoundrel remembered, the Ice King was preparing to freeze the town. How was he to stop the Ice King from causing such destruction if he didn’t even know where he was?! Scoundrel started running through the darkness, feeling against the walls in hopes of finding a way out. He’d have to find a way! The town depended on it.
“Isn’t there a way out of here!?” he shouted.

All of the sudden, a flash of light passed through the pit. Scoundrel could see where he was, clear as day. The space he was jammed in was about as wide as a small room and the walls around him looked to be higher than 100 feet. He’d never be able to find his way out!
Although Scoundrel wasn’t one to quit, especially in such a dire situation. Scoundrel discovered that the wall was flecked in ice chunks protruding out from along its length.

“They look like they could serve as sturdy footholds.” Scoundrel remarked. Although, he was only lying to himself, for nothing could be further from the truth. Many of the chunks looked as though they’d compromise under the weight of a butterfly. “I sure hope this works…”

Step by step, he slowly started scaling the wall. The footholds felt like they would give away at any moment, but Scoundrel ignored his dread. Nothing could hinder his mission; he was determined to make it to the top at all costs and he’d come too far to give in now. The ice cut into his hands, and he felt it tear at his skin each time he tried to pull his hand away. At every step, his feet slipped, and the boy feared he’d fall back onto the ground below. These concerns became stronger the higher he went, but they were muted out of Scoundrel’s mind. All that mattered now was reaching his goal... All that mattered now was the safety of Blackneck.

Ascending the icy wall was a backbreaking effort that would have seemed impossible to surmount byany other spectator. If I had been placed in such a situation, I probably would have never even considered the task. Although, to the town of Blackneck’s benefit, they probably had one of the most determined creatures on the face of the earth fighting for them. Even Scoundrel was unsure how such bravery had been instilled inside him, and I’m certain that question will be asked until the end of time. In my own view, I think that it was not purely bravery that drove Scoundrel, but a strong sense of purpose.

The cracking and splitting of ice overwhelmed his ears at each step he took and sometimes, the ledges would even give away. What filled Scoundrel with pure terror though was that the whole wall itself might fall to pieces. In spite of these ensuing battles raging against his focus, he somehow managed to make it up the wall in a steady crawl. However, his hurdles would only grew more numerous. First an aggressive intonation harassed Scoundrel’s eardrums. It was a deafening noise, like the buzzing of a thousand bees, that left his head throbbing, but this wasn’t even in the forefront of his mind anymore. The ice wall he clung to was melting, and at a rapid rate too. He wasn’t sure how long he’d be able to keep his ground when a crack split down the center of the wall. The whole structure was going to collapse at any moment. Craning his neck upwards to see how far he was from the top, he noticed the golden light illuminating ever brighter above him. What was going on?

That didn’t matter now, what mattered was that Scoundrel was only feet away from the surface, and the wall was on the verge turning to tatters. Just as it fell to pieces, Scoundrel leaped into the air, taking the large gamble that he’d land on safe ground. Too squeamish to witness what was taking place, he listened as the ice broke crisply below him, with his eyes shut tight.

He didn’t reopen them, until he hit the ground with a weighty thud, and he found himself staring eye to eye with Henry. To Scoundrel’s joy, he wasn’t gathering all his power to destroy the meagre town below as he’d dreaded. He could see quite clearly in the man’s face that he was different somehow… He seemed lighter, happier, and stretched across his face, an actual smile! The man’s body seemed to be experiencing its own change as well. It was set aglow with a golden blaze, in place of the bitter dark blue glaze that had covered it before. The ice that had encased him was falling off chunk by melted chunk, and Scoundrel watched each piece fell to the floor with a splash. When Scoundrel viewed the man closer, he realized that he was projecting the glow from his hands to Lucy. It seemed to be doing as he wished too; much of the ice encrusting her had dissipated!

“Joshua! You’re alive!” Henry cried, turning his head from his work, “You have no idea how overjoyed I am to see that you survived! I feared you were murdered by my unjust hand! You changed me ‘Joshua’, in ways you might never understand. I’m no longer the man you met before, but something new entirely. I hope that in years to come you will forgive me for how poorly I mistreated you!” There was no doubting the sincerity and remorse in Henry’s words. Nonetheless, Henry didn’t wait to hear Scoundrel’s response, and eagerly returned his focus to Lucy.
“Does… Does this mean that you’ll spare me?! Does this mean that you’re sparing the town!?” Scoundrel shouted over the roaring noise that Henry was creating.
Henry let out something like a laugh. His smile could have brought warmth into the coldest of days. “Yes! Of course!”

Henry then stopped what he was doing and looked around the room, “You might want to stand at the edge now,” he said pointing to a corner, “The whole place is melting away, I wouldn’t want it to collapse on you!”

Henry was right, the whole structurewasmelting away, as well as Henry himself. Everywhere Scoundrel looked, water was dripping and sloshing, as the room became an oven. Scoundrel laughed, “After what I’ve gone through today, it’s going to take a little bit more than a chunk of ice to kill me!”
Henry nodded solemnly, “Yes… Well, it’s time that I said goodbye now. I’ll be gone from this world for eternity. Yet, do not mourn for me, for, where I go now is a much better place.”
“What!?” Scoundrel shouted over the roaring wind. He could hardly believe his ears; Henry was leaving!

“Goodbye Scoundrel. You are something special. Never forget that… Take care of Blackneck for me.” With that, Henry gave a thick nod, and turned back to Lucy. Releasing more of the golden light from his hands, he spiraled into a breeze, like a leaf in the wind, traveling higher and higher. He brought the figure of Lucy gracefully spinning into the air with him as well, encasing her in a golden light that flooded her very soul. If you had been there to see it, you would have witnessed a dazzling spectacle of golden sparks flying all about as a whirlwind of light lifted itself further into the sky. The roof of the castle broke away in their ascent, with a shower of milky white shards reflecting the luscious moonlight illuminating above. Yes, it was moonlight, for it was late by now, and night had fallen over the mountain.

Covering his eyes and head, Scoundrel tucked into a ball; he’d already had his fair share of splinters for one day. When he reopened them, he found that Henry and Lucy had made their way high into the sky, merging with his view of the full moon, shining in a lactescent glow. As Scoundrel watched with wonder, and brushed the shards off of himself, Henry reopened his locket and began reciting the words inscribed upon it. Yet, it might as well been an entirely different man reading it. His words had a sweet melodious tune to it, like a poem. Scoundrel could tell, although he was far above him, that Henry was putting all his heart into every expression he uttered.

“To my beloved Lucy,” he began, “In remembrance that, even apart, our bond shall always remain.” What remained of the ice upon Lucy’s body immediately broke away, falling away as a golden dust. With Henry’s words finished, Scoundrel witnessed the two stare into each other’s eyes with beaming expressions upon their faces.
“You don’t know how long I’ve waited to see real peace on you again,” said Lucy, “I’m overjoyed to finally see you again as you are, without masks or shackles holding you down.”

“It pains me that I never will. Yet, what I do know is this; it has been much too long. Too long without my heart. Too long without my soul. Above all, it has been too long, much too long without you. But the past is dead, and as this day ends, a new one dawns. It is time that our kingdom was renewed to what it was once known as and we pass to a new adventure… It is time to make this place known as ‘The City of Gold’ once more.”

The most curious of things then took place. Both Lucy and Henry grew so bright that they no looked no longer human but like something quite different; something that was almost unearthly. Their faces illuminated like the moon, perfect and stainless. They still grew more brilliant, becoming as radiant as the stars in the heavens, if not that, more so. A strange ringing flew through the air, and a warm gust of wind blasted past Scoundrel. Suddenly, the two were glowing as vibrant as the sun, and then, there was no distinction between them any longer. It was just a single light, strong but true. It was so blinding, that the light of the moon had been completely drowned out from view. Then, as quick as it had formed, the light burst. Golden chunks scattered across the moonlit palace floor, breaking into a golden dust wherever it hit. It didn’t just effect the ice castle though; staring out the melting window, Scoundrel could clearly see clusters of these chunks streaking across the milky night sky, leaving behind trails of the golden dust behind them wherever they went. The mountain would probably look something like a zebra by sunrise. Nobody in town would ever believe his explanation when he told it to them! However, the dust sat in the back of Scoundrel’s mind, for quite a different thing was puzzling him. What had happened to Lucy and Henry? For a moment, Scoundrel thought that perhaps it had been a tragic accident, but then he remembered Henry’s last words.
“It is time to make this place known as the ‘City of Gold’ once more.”
Perhaps Henry had known what was going to happen… But how had Lucy known? How had Henry gained his strange new abilities? What had become of the locket?

While the rest of them would probably be left unanswered, one of Scoundrel’s many questions was acknowledged sooner than he’d expected… While he was racking his mind to explain what had happened, something came out of the sky and hit Scoundrel hard on the head with a sharp clunk.

“Blast those golden chunks!” he shouted rubbing his sore head. But, when studying the floor aroundhim, he found that he hadn’t been hit by one of the strange balls of golden dust, but a locket… It was Lucy’s locket; it hadn’t been destroyed after all! While Scoundrel knew it wasn’t his locket, there was something about it that calmed Scoundrel, that gave him a sense of connection to the man and woman that had so mysteriously disappeared. He might never see them again, but he could be certain that their memory would never fade as long as he had the locket. As Scoundrel placed the locket around his neck, exhausted from the events of the day, he felt the warm wind return once again. It tugged at the locket, until it lifted from Scoundrel’s hands, and into the air. Scoundrel watched in horror as it was whipped around wildly and lifted out of the roof of the castle. It didn’t stop until it crossed a bright star, one that looked to be almost golden. The moment the locket reached the light of the star, glimmering in its brightness, it fell back down to the floor of the castle. Very curious indeed… Had that star been there earlier, before Henry and Lucy had disappeared? Scoundrel couldn’t be sure; he wasn’t very good with stars. He knew one thing however; he hadn’t noticed this star before, and it stood out above the rest.

No matter, he could save it for the morning. Right now, he was ready for a well-earned sleep. Scoundrel grabbed the locket, and headed to the entrance of the castle for some rest… The events of the day had been exhausting, and he’d need to clear his head. Sleep came easier than he expected.
Chapter Nineteen
Making Amends
Scoundrel awoke on the damp floor of the castle to the sweet morning tune of a robin.

“Don’t they ever rest?” he moaned rubbing his sore body. He ached everywhere, the day prior certainly had been full of its fair share in falls and injuries. His stomach was just as bad, for a gnawing hunger filled it.

In spite of how painful it was, Scoundrel was fortunate beyond all odds that not a single bone in his body was broken. You would have thought that after a day without food or shelter and being knocked around like a rag doll, he’d be nothing but a lifeless sack of flesh and bones. But there was something about him that was tough; he didn’t break easily, and he had most likely fared better than any other person could have hoped.
This amazing revelation struck Scoundrel with a brutal force; against all odds, he had survived the day! He had made it into tomorrow!

“I’m alive!” he shouted, “I’m alive!” He couldn’t help but laugh. It was a laugh like none he’d ever felt in his life, it overtook him. In all of Scoundrel’s days, he’d used his laugh to overcome others, to leave people befuddled beyond all reason, but now, for the first time, it was befuddling him! Not to say that it was exactly an unpleasant experience, rather, it was actually relieving. After living out a day full of stress and trial, there was something about laughing that made it seem so distant, like a fragment of the past.

After a while of this, his laughs started to slow, and he was able to steady his breaths altogether. The room around him had been melting throughout the night, and Scoundrel saw that much of the structure had already given away. He needed to exit quickly. When Scoundrel prepared for the door, his eyes met with the crystals that had brought him into the mess. They still looked as delicate and beautiful as ever, perfect in design. They would be no harm to keep now either, with the Ice King being gone for good.

An idea popped into Scoundrel’s head: he could bring the crystals to Blackneck as a treaty! Maybe it wouldn’t work, but with the locket and all, he had a good chance of convincing the townspeople of theevents that had taken place the day prior; that he had changed his ways.

Quickly, Scoundrel started shoving the jewels into his satchel. This was wonderful! Unfortunately, as he was placing the crystals in the pack, his actions were halted by the sound of ice splitting and breaking away. Scoundrel looked up to see the roof filling with cracks, about to crumble in. He snatched up what he had in his satchel, and ran towards the exit of the castle, skidding across the floor as he went.

Dodging debris that had started falling, he feared that the castle would collapse on top of him before he made his way out. Yet, one way or another, he found himself alive, heaving heavy breaths on the doorstep of the castle, just before it fell to pieces.

“Is this how it’s going to be from now on?” asked Scoundrel sarcastically. He might have made it out of the castle, but all around him, the blocks of the ice that had once covered the lake were broken apart, leaving Scoundrel stuck on an island. Thankfully, it wasn’t long before he discovered that while he had been escaping the collapsing castle, a bulk of it had fallen into the water, leaving behind a somewhat sturdy bridge off the island.

Once he’d made it across the ice bridge, Scoundrel started bounding down the mountain, quick as a flash of light. He didn’t want to waste a moment of daylight. Scoundrel was certain that the townsfolk were already gawking at the golden striped mountain, and he didn’t want to miss the look on their faces when he explained the whole story to them all… That is, if he wasn’t driven away by a mob first…

Although, those thoughts didn’t faze Scoundrel at all. After what he’d been through, nothing seemed threatening to him. Whether or not the townsfolk accepted him mattered much less to him than making it known that he changed his heart. No longer would they have to fear they’d be robbed in their sleep, at least, not by his hand.
As Scoundrel ran down the hill, hooting and hollering happily all the way, he tripped over an odd lump of snow that sent him tumbling down towards the ground.
“Wha—What was that!?” a muffled voice moaned.

It was the voice of Bert, the man he’d been captured by only two days prior! Scoundrel swiftly started digging away at the snow, until he found something that looked like an oversized sausage buried in the wintry powder. After lifting it out and examining it closer, Scoundrel realized that Bert had been all rolled up into his tent after the blizzard.

“Who’s there!? What are ye’ doing! Show yerself now, or else! Me isn’t gonna go warning ya again!” Bert shouted. In truth, Bert was in no position to give out threats, considering the fact that he’d been rolled up in his tent and buried under a pile of snow for nearly two days. However, the man was as stubborn as an ox.

Scoundrel ignored Bert, and went off to search for John. While he knew he should have unraveled Bert from his powdery tent first thing, he wasn’t in the mood to explain himself to the raging buffoon. Instead Scoundrel simply left a pile of crystals beside him in hopes that Bert would break himself free from the tent, being relieved of the bondage of the snow.
“The man is probably delirious after the state he was in anyways. Bert is in no condition to talk with me,” Scoundrel reasoned to himself.

Luckily, it wasn’t long before Scoundrel found another mound of snow lumped on the ground, placed nearly ten yards from Bert. As Scoundrel dug into the pit, he found that John was submerged much further than Bert had been, with the hole being as far as Scoundrel’s waist when it was fully uncovered. Scoundrel managed to pull John out of the ground with only a slight hassle; still, the man felt heavier than a horse! Neglecting to unravel him as well, Scoundrel left another pile of crystals next to John in repayment for what he had done to them. Scoundrel slapped his hands together with a smirk, followed by a jubilant laugh. What a puzzle it would be to the two men once they uncovered themselves from their bondage!

Scoundrel knew he didn’t have much time before Bert and John would escape their coverings, so he headed off for the small town of Blackneck. It was true that the liberation of the two lumberjackswasn’t the most noble of rescues, and that Scoundrel would go on to regret it in later years, but right now, those thoughts were pushed to the back of the scamp’s mind. Scoundrel’s current goal was straight for the town to redeem himself, and nothing would change that.
For those wondering, both Bert and John would eventually go on to free themselves, while it was quite an ordeal. Yet, that is another story.

Down the mountain, Scoundrel’s light feet carried him on, grazing hastily over the golden trails left along a fresh layer of snow. The thought of how the town might be reacting tickled him, and he snickered as he conceived the most nonsensical scenes. Yet nearing the town, his spirit of levity immediately changed to somber.

After a great deal of running, Scoundrel felt a flush of relief as he passed the old crumbling huts that he’d known since birth, and the familiar roads that he’d grown to love so much. The mildew smell of rotting wood in the air, and the soft squish of his feet treading on the muddy dirt path forced a beaming smile. He would have never believed this in days prior, but out of all the things he missed, it had been his town and his townsfolk most of all. A leaden guilt drenched him when he remembered how much he’d mistreated it, but he shoved those thoughts away. Right now, he was on a mission to ask for vindication from that. He would start anew, as hard as he knew it would be. It was apparent he’d probably never be accepted as a true member of the town, but whatever became of him, making this choice felt right. Scoundrel would never be the same again after the day he had gone through… For the first time, that revelation was consoling.

Scoundrel headed for the meeting square that was held in the center of the town. It was a modest space; about as big as a small pond, that was cleared out of the town. There wasn’t much else to it; it was just a big square of mud bordered by a few sorry excuses for buildings.

When Scoundrel arrived, he found a mass of people gaping at the golden-striped mountain. Before he let anyone see him, he dove behind a shabbily built barrel tucked into the corner of a building. He did this partly out of habit, and partly out of anxiety from entering the meeting at a fragile moment. All he had to do was expose himself while they were speaking him, and he’d have a mob running after him. He wasn’t going to come out of behind the barrel until the time was right.
He listened as the people bickered over what the cause of the golden streaks and the halting of the blizzard had been.
“It’s the Ice King!” said one.
“No, it’s the blasted robber!” shouted another, “It’s another one of his pranks!”

“The wolves must’ve done it! I think that they dipped their tales in some mud, and rubbed them up and down the mountain!” a third declared. He wiped his nose with his sleeve once finished, and displayed the nasty yellow smear on it to the rest of the townsfolk as if to prove his absurd claim.

The conversation halted after that third suggestion. This was partly due to its apparent irrationality, but mostly it was because the suggestion helped them recognize that the debate was running in flimsy circles. They wouldn’t find their answer unless they climbed the mountain themselves, but they wouldn’t climb the mountain themselves unless they knew it was safe, and they couldn’t know if it was safe unless they had their answer.

Scoundrel’s brow deepened and his limbs quaked. As reluctant as he was, he could take it no longer; he needed to tell them the truth. Scoundrel arose from behind the barrel and walked over to the center of the square with weighty steps and his head turned to the ground. All the townspeople turned their gaze to him in alarm.
“I have the answer…” he said, raising his arms in surrender. To his shock, the angry faces he’d expected to fill the square didn’t appear, nobody said a word.
Finally, somebody piped up. “And who are you supposed to be? I’ve never seen a boy like you before.” a woman asked quizzically.

Scoundrel’s face turned red. Didn’t anyone recognize him? How could they have already forgotten him?! His wanted posters had covered every building in town at one point, until the blizzard sweptthem away!
“I’m Scoundrel!” he said incredulously.
The scene only grew more stupefying as he watched the crowd stare at him in disbelief

“Scoundrel? That can’t be ye!” a lumberjack shouted, “I saw ‘im… err… ye… only yesterday! Where’s yer’ pale sickly skin, yer colorless vengeful face or yer twisted mischievous grin? Ye don’t even talk like ‘im! Ye ain’t Scoundrel!”
The boy was dumbfounded! Had there really been a noticeable change in himself since the day before?! It was true that he had changed his speech…
“No, I’m Scoundrel! Look, I still have the scars on my arms from the attack yesterday, I still have the tears on my wrists from the ropes that were bound to them!”

The lumberjack nearly fell over and the color drained from his face. “That’s it boy. Ye better pipe out yer story and pipe it fast! Me needs an explanation! This don’t make no sense, no sense at all!”

What had happened? Scoundrel wasn’t sure; perhaps his change had taken place by the fountain, or after he’d fallen from the abyss in the castle. Whatever had taken place, Scoundrel needed to recount all that had transpired.

“It’s best that I began at the very start…” Scoundrel said. He then proceeded to bring the crowd along with him through the journey he had taken through the mountain. Nothing was left out; not even the story he told to the dragon. Most of them listened with skeptical looks, while others, like the lumberjack, soaked it all in, enthralled. Once Scoundrel had completed his tale, he dumped out his jewels from his sack onto the ground, and revealed the locket he had spoken of. At this point, all doubt had faded from the crowd’s eyes, and they looked at Scoundrel with a new admiration.

“As I said, I’ve changed my ways. I no longer will rob you, break into your homes, or vandalize the town. I also no longer desire to go by the name of ‘Scoundrel’, because that isn’t my identity. I now want to go by my true name Joshua. I hope that these gifts will be a symbol for a fresh peace between us and that, in time, I’ll be accepted as one of you. Also, the mine shaft I discovered should be abounding with more jewels and gold than this town can hold. It should be able to replenish our ‘kingdom’ to what it once was.”
At this point, the mayor had stepped out of the crowd with an exuberant grin, preparing to speak with the reformed scoundrel, Joshua.
“We are grateful beyond all measure for your deeds—Joshua is it? Where do you plan to go next from this?”

Joshua laughed. “First, I’d like to return to my shack. It has been a good while since I’ve seen it, and I need a good rest after what I’ve been through. Also, I think it’s time that I returned the items I’ve stolen.”

The mayor’s face turned red, knowing all too well that the shack had been torn down in Joshua’s absence, and the items had been removed. But, he simply nodded his head in signal that Scoundrel was dismissed, and went back to marvel at the new gems, as well as discuss plans concerning the new developments.

Joshua was overjoyed with how well everything had gone. He ran with all his might to his home, singing and dancing all the way. He brought quite the scene, and everybody that viewed him could tell with clarity that he wasn’t the same boy he had been.

None of that mattered to Joshua though. All that mattered was that it felt amazing to finally have all the weights and guilt removed from his heart. Although, it wasn’t long until he was called back by a shrill shout.
“Scoundrel!!! You rotten little beast!! These gems are merely icicles! They’re already melting!!”

In time, after years had passed, the town of Blackneck was restored into its former glory, and once again called ‘The City of Gold’. The dwarves that Joshua claimed to be in the mountain were never found, but the people of Blackneck flourished in their newfound wealth in the mines. The Mayor wasultimately promoted to the role of king, and the castle was rebuilt in its rightful place in the mountain.

As for the star that Joshua had discovered in the sky, once it was found people found, observed that it always stood in its place, being named “Polaris” for always pointing north, a new occurrence which puzzled many. It became a guide for those who were lost on the mountain, and led the way throughout its hilly terrain.

Now, most of you might be wondering about Joshua, and what had become of him. Well, his adapting came gradually to say the least, and he wasn’t always the easiest child to deal with, nor was he ever quite accepted amongst the other children he grew up with. Although, he did end up finding a place in a new family, and, as he grew older and matured, became a respected member of the community. He never did run into another strange adventure with the warm wind under the old Craggleback Mountain. While he claimed that it was only leaving its secrets to be unlocked by another, in all his days, he never did hear another person speak of the strange warm wind he’d experienced so often in that lonely mountain. Some would go on to say that he was a liar and that his tale was made up. Others would say that he’d only dreamt the whole ordeal and it had never happened. Although, no matter what one says, their word isn’t worth a cent. Rather, I know that the story of Blackneck is true, or the “Curse of Blackneck,” as you might put it. Do you want to know how I know such things and why I am so certain that every event on ol’ Craggleback Mountain happened?

It is because Iwasthat nasty old Scoundrel, the raider of Blackneck. I saw the whole thing with my own two eyes. The scars from the journey still reside on my skin, and my memories, they don’t change like those of a dream would. For a dream is only a fading glimpse of a potential reality, but that’s not so with the tale of Blackneck. It was as real as you or me, and the change that it instilled in me was even more so. In all my years, people have tried to deny that such could have happened, they said it was impossible. Although, I tell you now that nothing is impossible, this world is only limited by your own faith and willingness to let your imagination roam free. The time on this earth is too short to submit to ignorance, so never let yourself think otherwise… Don’t let anybodymakeyou think otherwise…
Epilogue

At those last words, “Don’t let anybody make you think otherwise,” the old man closed the dusty yellowing book he had been reading, and straightened himself in his aging rocking chair. He sat in a small dark room, in a cottage, warmed by a cozy fireplace. The fire left behind a warm red glow, almost as if to say that the day was coming to an end. Resting peacefully as he settled into his seat, with his eyes nearly shut, the man exhaled a deep breath. He listened to nothing but the steady beat of his own heart.

His face was worn with age, his hair was silvered and he looked exhausted from what must have been a dragging day. Yet, only across from him sat a little girl, as energetic as ever, staring at him with her bright cheery eyes full of wonder.
“Are you certain that Blackneck and Lucy became a star?” she asked, hopping up and down on her bed.
The old man straightened himself up and heaved himself out of his chair with a creak.

“One can never be too certain…” the old man said softly, tucking the little girl in, “But, if I had to give a definite answer, I’d say yes. Now it’s time that you went to sleep; it’s far too late in the night forlittle girls to be staying up.”
The child frowned but managed to close her eyes anyways as she sunk into her straw mattress, “Do—do you think that I might ever meet the warm wind?” she asked with a sleepy yawn.

“Maybe…” he whispered, “But little girls need their sleep to be wide awake when it does come. Goodnight.” The old man gave a kiss on the little girl’s cheek and left the room, taking care as he shut the door behind him.

Just as the girl was dipping into a deep sleep under her covers, her head filling with visions of worlds far off and adventures to mysterious places, the shutters in the room flapped open, and a warm gust of wind flooded the room…

title: The Seer
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
Chapter 1
The man needed a shower — he had murder smeared all over him.
A click. A flash. A woman appeared in the man's place.

Her face was caked in layers of makeup. Even her dimples appeared to be painted on. A smile managed to find its way from out of under the layers, but it was unnervingly stiff. Despite this, her eyes had an earnestness to them. She was a suspicious character. She was also innocent.
Yet another flash. Another man. His mouth hung open, limply, and his eyes floated off in the distance. A common idiot. Nothing more.

More clicks. More flashes. More people. All of them had a distinct look. Yet, none were undecipherable. A person's face could tell secrets that even the person themselves weren't privy to. All it took was a twitch in a cheek. A flick of the tongue. A dart of the eye.
There was a click, followed by a beep. The holographic screen of faces went to black.
"Only ten minutes!? Alright, that's not fair... You have to give me your secret!"

It was Mrs. Paige, the director of the forensics department. Dice spun around to face her. He could've relaxed his eyes. Instead, he let them narrow and focus in. Mrs. Paige injected an infectious cheeriness into her speech, but it was far too easy to see through the facade.
"What do you mean, 'only' ten minutes?"  Dice asked. His voice was underset by a cold tremor.

"'What do you mean?'" Mrs. Paige said, parroting him with a nervous chuckle. "You went through a quarter of the mugshots from the Monterey District's criminal database, mixed with decoy mugshots from volunteers, and you were somehow able to differentiate them with 76.7% accuracy. And, even though we've been sending the analysis of your performances to our learning algorithms, you're beating them."
"It was only 76.7%..." Dice said. "Explain to me why this is so impressive."
Mrs. Paige crinkled her brow in confusion, before giving a wry smirk. Dice smirked back.
"Alright, you got me!" Dice said, forcing out a laugh.

Mrs. Paige joined in with a laugh far more convincing than his. That is, convincing to everybody in the office except Dice. There was a ringing in his head. She might've been better at laughing, but he saw how the corners of her eyes didn't quite tighten right. He heard the subtly uneven inflections in her laugh.

In mid-laugh, Dice stopped altogether. It struck him how odd a sight the two of them laughing must've been for the rest of the office. Mrs. Paige had perfectly brushed dark hair, stiff clothes, and a reserved face. Yet, she was still eager to join in for a laugh. Meanwhile, Dice had fiery hair, unkempt clothes, and a fresh face. Though, he had more control than Mrs. Paige amid laughter. Among strangers, it would've seemed that they'd mind-swapped.
Mrs. Paige stopped to stare at Dice. She'd noticed him looking around. Caught him thinking. What was she thinking?
"Thank you for conducting that test," Dice said, disallowing emotion into his voice. "Anyway, I have a list of diagnostics I need to run through."

He spun his chair, turning back to his holographic computer screen. His hands swiped along it, becoming little more than a blur of motion. He caught Mrs. Paige's eyes in the reflection of his screen. She blinked. She was lost. To her, and everybody else, it must've even seemed that there was no screen. Names, locations, evidence, computer code, analytics... It was invisible to them. Dice's eyes danced, soaking it all in.
Mrs. Paige gathered herself and cleared her throat. Dice thought he heard her chuckle under her breath, despite herself.
"Dice, we're not done," she said. "There's a reason we've been having you take these tests."
"There's a reason I was hired for this job. And, I intend to do it. So, make it quick."
Mrs. Paige scowled, before resuming her composure.

"I've spoken to my superiors. There are few people who can outmatch the algorithms like you do. Would you be interested in a promotion to a position beyond this clerical work? A position involving higher government? The MDPD?"
Dice's hands slowed, and he collapsed his holographic screen. His chair squealed, coming back to face Mrs. Paige.
"Who in this office wouldn't be interested in that?" Dice said, disinterestedly.
Mrs. Paige closed her eyes and shook her head. "Mr. Raymond... I'm offering you an opportunity of a lifetime. I'm not going to let you walk out of that door without you accepting!"
Dice rested his chin on his hand. He stood from his chair, lifted his briefcase, and walked past Mrs. Paige.
"Alright then," he said.
He made his way toward the door.
"Uh... Mr. Raymond?"
Dice might as well have not heard her.
"Dice?!"
The door slid open as Dice approached it.
"You can finally give Gill my chair," Dice said.
Mrs. Paige rubbed her forehead.
"Is that a yes?"
The door slid shut. Mrs. Paige could vaguely hear Dice's footsteps as he left the building. Then, a whoosh as he entered the tunnel to transport tubes. He was gone.
Somebody gave her a pat on her back, before resting their arm on her shoulder.
"He was a weird one, wasn’t he?"
Indignant, Mrs. Paige looked to see who was talking to her — only to find one of her employees. She opened her mouth to respond.
"Well, I—."
"Also, I don't want that chair. It's the worst one in the office. Send it to the trash mines, or whatever."
The employee gave a smug grin, before returning to their desk.

Dice sunk into his seat and let out a deep sigh of satisfaction. As the transport car closed, the engine kicked on with a hum. After about three seconds, it had accelerated to 300 kilometers per hour. In ten more seconds, that speed tripled to 900. A calm washed over him.

Calmness drained from everyone else. The car was in a vacuum tube, which was known to be deadly in the rare instances when it malfunctioned. Despite there being a crowd in the car, all that could be heard was the steady thrum of the tunnel. Anxiety settled around them. Dice listened as it brushed past people, making them shuffle in their seats. Somebody drew their briefcase closer to their chest. Another person's eyes dodged around.

Dice grinned — it was almost funny. Anxiety had latched onto everybody, except himself. There wasn't any reason to be uncomfortable. The transport tubes had a reliable record. Besides: whenever Dice sat in the car, he always had the cushion of an empty seat on each side of himself. He could never understand why people avoided sitting next to him and gave annoyed glares — perhaps it had something to do with his habit of staring at people — but he appreciated having extra room for his briefcase and legs to rest on. It was the best part of his day.
Actually, it wasn't quite the best part.

Dice's eyes were fixated on the window. The ride was supposed to be a few minutes, but it felt like an hour while the city-scape ran by. Complex high-rises, road-ways and specks of people turned to a blur. Then, it all went black as the car entered a tunnel. The city blinking into darkness was surreal. Something stirred inside him and dragged his eyes to his feet. Was it joy, or was it fear?

The car roared, and Dice was steadily thrust forward. He brought his hand to the dial of his left ear's hearing aid, but the car went mute before he could change it. He shielded his eyes as sunlight dumped on his face. The car had come to a stop. It let out a deep exhale as its door reopened.

After a mess of shoving and tripping, Dice found himself standing on a glossy street. He was caught in a sudden flush of lights and sounds, so overpowering the sky disappeared amidst it all. Though, it would only be a moment before the lights and sounds would also disappear.

Dice turned his hearing aid to its second-lowest setting and took a pause to let his eyes swim around. Feet pounded against the ground, mouths opened to shout, hands tapped along metal railings in impatience, but it all fell on deaf ears. In the silence, Dice could observe with no distractions. It was just him, his eyes, and the world. It provided an hidden barrier — a sanctuary.

He squinted and focused his gaze on a milk elevator. It was just down the street, behind a forest of beams and people. He forced a smile, clutched his briefcase close to his chest, and began his trek through. Immediately, his efforts were greeted with angry elbows and shoulders. Immediately, Dice returned the greeting.
He'd played the game of pushing through crowds for years. While he wasn't any better than when he'd started, he'd learned how to play a different game.

He caught a man's face. The man's shoulders were tense. His fists were clenched — he was clearly high-strung. The man's eyes flitted to the left, and then went toward the sky. He was going to shift right. Dice skimmed over another man's face. Right. A woman's. Left. A man's. Straight.
Left. Left. Straight. Right. Left.
Dice shifted his direction accordingly, taking a smooth pathway around them all. It was a habit so satisfying he'd become addicted to it. It almost made the walk to his apartment worth it. Almost.
As Dice neared the elevator, the rush of people shrunk. A surge of relief rose to his chest.

Dice clutched his shoulder and let out a shout. In a daze, he tried to maintain his sense of balance and direction. He'd been clipped by somebody. Tenderly rubbing his wound, Dice continued his walk toward the elevator. He didn't bother looking back to see who'd clipped him. He didn't need to look. He didn't want to. He already knew who did it. He'd known it a few moments before he'd been hit, when a soft mechanical whir breached his ears. A robot.
Dice put his eye to his elevator's scanner, and furiously punched in the code.
39782. Enter. There was a beep as bold red letters appeared on the scanner.
"Access Denied."

How? He must've put in the wrong passkey. He held back a grimace as he racked his brain, but realized he was too distracted to remember the right one. It was the pain in his shoulder. No... It was the robot.

If only he'd looked back at it and stared into its soul. Yet, he couldn't have. He always had trouble with robots. They weren't like people. Their emotions were buried deep within them, among a weedy undergrowth of wires and transistors. That is, if there were any emotions at all.

Dice pushed the thoughts away and entered a new password. There was a quiet beep. The scanner and keypad rose into the air, along with the milk wall to the elevator. Dice took a step forward, and the wall fell behind him.

The interior of the elevator was an egg. Lining the rounded floor were two plush couches. They ran parallel, starting at the entrance to and ending at the exit. Dice stood in front of the exit, bringing his nose mere centimeters from it.

Turning his hearing aid to the highest setting, a smile spread across his face. He could hear every gear, wire, and motor. He tried piecing each sound to create a working model. A shaky image formed. Though, his thoughts collapsed just as he neared completion.

There were groans and puffs as the capsule's hydraulics came to a halt. The exit door rose. Dice made his way into a long hall. The exit closed, followed by the echo of a second door. The door to his apartment.

Dice's footsteps joined the echoes as they made their way down a platinum hall, decorated with medals and plaques. "Web Developer of the Month". "Repairman of the Month". "Programmer of the Month". "Computer Analyst of the Month". "Volunteer Computer Interface Reviewer of the Month". Last of all, "Paid Computer Interface Reviewer of the Month". They'd all come over the span of a few years, the oldest being dated in 2678, and the most recent in 2683. None of them dated before Dice's professional adult life.
Dice felt a twinge of pride as he skimmed over them. Maybe he should take the time to dust them off and bring back their former sheen. They deserved to be shown off to people.
The pride fled, leaving just a twinge on his face. He looked away and hastened his pace.

Dice's hall led into his room. It was a small space, about 20 square meters. However, it was home. Everything was kept there. On the left wall was a panel that would fold out into a table, two chairs, and a feeding apparatus. On the right, a panel that would fold out into a sleeping-tube. On the floor, one that would fold out into a couch. Opposite from the entrance, a white sphere was anchored into the ground. A holographic computer projector.

On the ceiling was a panel that would open into bathroom — a situation that was particularly annoying. To use it, he had to retreat for the entrance hall to allow the room to rotate into the right position. Maybe things were too small. However, he couldn't afford a new apartment. Not yet.
Dice made a hand motion, prompting his couch to unfold. As he settled down into it, he smiled thinly.
"Five years," he said, under his breath. "It took five years. At least I'm almost there."

He thrust his head back and closed his eyes. He'd jumped through so many hoops to make it where he was. Too many. Suddenly, his chest tightened. It was hard to breathe. He tried taking deep breaths, but only spiraled further.

After a few failed attempts to calm himself down, he sat up and waved his hand in the direction of the holographic computer projector. It blinked, spun around, then locked in place. The room lit up with a soft blue light as a computer screen projected in midair.

Dice's hands returned to their blur of motion, logging into the computer and whipping through pages of documents. "The Map to Climbing the Career Ladder". "How to Influence Mrs. Paige". "How to Reach Peak Efficiency".
Once he'd sifted through every document, Dice rubbed his hands together and leaned back. Everything was in place and accounted for. The shadow of another smile crossed his face.
"Computer! Code: refraction. Activate program: trial simulation delta," Dice said.

The blue light flickered, and the projector whirled around. The holographic screen abandoned its inviting white interface and adopted a cruder format. It was covered in black space, random pixels, and lines of code. Dice's eyes darted across it. He scrunched his brow.
"Finally... A challenge."

He activated the screen's keypad and added in a few lines of binary. The screen flashed and transitioned into another mess of numbers, letters, and pixels. Scrunching his eyebrows again, Dice entered another line of binary. His heart fluttered. The screen flared and transitioned.
He checked the timer in the corner of the screen. Only thirty seconds. He could do better than that.

After ten minutes, he'd shrunk his time to ten seconds. An hour drained by, and he maintained his pace. It was as if time were frozen. The tense furrow on his brow unmoving, Dice flittered his hands about as if he'd just begun.
Two hours went by. No change, except for a creeping twitch in Dice's eye.

Three. Sweat poured through his bodysuit. Steam came off the projector, with it moaning at each turn it made. Though Dice couldn't stop. There was an allure to the game. He could almost feel what the computer was thinking. It could be part of him, if he were to move faster. Think faster.
His head ached. His eyes were on fire. Finally, he blinked. Eyes still closed, he said, "Computer! Code: refraction. Deactivate program: trial simulation delta."
The projector hissed as it slowed its pace and spat smoke into the room. A fit of coughs overcame Dice. He ran toward his entrance hall and tried waving he smoke away.
"Where are the sprinklers?!"

His words were met by a mouthful of water. It poured from panels in the ceiling, making quick work of the smoke. The room was a bath in minutes, but the sprinklers also made quick work of Dice. Their blasts left him sprawled across the floor. He struggled to find a firm grip as he crawled toward the entrance hall.
The water stopped. An alarm made two beeps. A pause. Three beeps. Choking on the water still in his mouth, he scrambled toward the hall.
This was just peachy.

He leaned against a wall with one of his legs in the air as he wrung his pants leg out. Despite his bodysuit being waterproof, he was drenched to the skin. His bodysuit had lost its light blue hue, turning to a dingy gray.
"Great... I'll have to let the dresser-bot change my clothes again."

A glass barrier fell between him and his room. The floor to the room slid away, revealing a black pit. The hall rumbled. Water gripping to the glass barrier streamed down, and the smoke faded away. Dice let out a sigh. The vacuum had started.

Its floor sliding back into place, the room lit up a soft blue. Dice's eyes shot to his computer projector. A new hologram had opened up, displaying a message in bold: "Congratulations on your promotion. Don't use your feeding apparatus tomorrow night. I'd like you to meet me at 17:30, in the Glass Americana. I think you'll like the food there. Sincerely, Professor Cassius."
He went over the message several times, taking care that he didn't miss anything. Professor Cassius? Of all people?

The barrier went up. Dice remained. His gaze was transfixed to the screen. In a certain way, Professor Cassius finding out made sense. Professor Cassius had enough connections. A massive web, really. In fact, Dice should've prepared for this message. It had been practically inevitable.
He read it over one last time. "I'd like you to meet me at 17:30, in the Glass Americana."
Dice brushed himself off.
"Alright then."
A black ooze coiled around Dice's neck. There was a wheeze at his every breath. He closed his eyes. He reopened them. The ooze spread around his wrists and ankles, dragging him backward.

He grunted and tried to wrench his arms free. As his right arm stretched outward, he barely managed to reach something. A wall? Yes. A glass wall. There had to be something to grab. His hand fumbled around. He needed to move quicker.
Not quick enough. Dice's hair raised as his hand squealed against the glass and snapped back. Muscles trembled. Nerves tingled. Shock tore through his body, his back slamming against a wall.
He looked down. The ooze coated his skin. He winced. So cold.
As the ooze covered his face, Dice opened his mouth to scream. No sound came.
Chapter 2
Dice struggled to keep his mouth closed as he viewed the people around him.

Everybody had waiting-bracelets on. Not at all unusual for a restaurant. However, there were more people than he'd ever seen in one place. How were the computerized waiters managing to get everybody to their tables?

He turned his hearing aid down and read the expressions of the faces around him. Most of them were well-groomed. Arrogant. Flustered they weren't quite well-groomed or arrogant enough to get themselves a better spot on the waiting list.
Dice readjusted the cuffs to his red jacket. Although he'd let his dresser-bot put him in his best outfit, it occurred that he was severely underdressed and underprepared.
"Last time I'll trust a dresser-bot," he muttered to himself.
What was taking the restaurant so long to assign him a waiting bracelet? It had already been fifteen minutes.

He shrugged his shoulders. What did he care? If the waiting room was any indication, the restaurant was just an oversized gimmick. Each wall was adorned in red, white and blue ribbons. Star-spangled flags hung down, sweeping the tops of people's heads. The floor and ceiling were constructed of glass, so holographic bald eagles, fireworks, and models of ancient skyscrapers could emerge at a moment's notice.
A bell chirped behind Dice. He turned and watched a few elevators rise. A stream of people filled into them, awaiting their descent back to the streets. Maybe he should—
"Dice! There you are!"

Professor Cassius waltzed toward Dice with his arms outstretched. The corners of Dice's mouth twitched as he smiled and waved. Cassius looked the same as he ever did. His silver coat billowed behind him, his armored black chest-plate was puffed out with pride, and his white hair was styled into a flowing wave down his back.
