Cassius grinned. It was the same knowing grin that had opened and closed lectures in Hawthorne University.
"You still gripping to technology?" asked Dice, monotonously. "Soon enough, you'll go from professor to processor."
Cassius readjusted his belt as he tried to decide if Dice had been joking or serious. Finally, he forced out a chuckle.
"Yes, well— when you're a hundred and fifty, you have no other option but to keep up with the latest technology." Cassius stared into space. "I'm not the most trusting of genetic tampering..."
"Mechanical tampering isn't much better."
Cassius scoffed, and rolled his eyes. He stared at Dice's left ear.
"This is a necessity," Dice said.
Cassius gave a pitying smirk. Dice could only guess what was going through his head.

Cassius was too fond of technology. His left arm, left eye, right leg, and both feet were entirely bionic. Dozens of wires and moving parts were hidden under his thick clothes, to the point where he needed to have a backup generator hooked to his back.
"Anyway, what are you still doing here?" Cassius asked. "I thought I tipped off the waiters to have you at my table thirty minutes ago."
Thirty minutes? But, he'd only been here for ten.
His ears felt hot. He must've arrived twenty minutes late. How could he have let himself miscalculate?

Placing his hand over his mouth to hide his reddening face, he said "Yes, well... It's a crowded place, and you know how these robots work. They can only do their jobs right half the time, if even that."
Professor Cassius put his cold, bionic arm around Dice's shoulder, leading Dice through the crowd and out of the waiting room. A chill ran down Dice's spine at the feel of it.

"Quite a lot of truth in that, my boy," Cassius said, his flesh eye darting about. He pulled his bionic arm behind his back. "These robots... They seem to take every job, and they don't do it half as good as we could. Isn't that right?"

"Exactly. I can work far more efficiently than most of these machines, and yet I've still had to scratch and claw to get a leg up on them. If there were just more sanctions on quantum computing power, and emphasis on our Human Preservation Statutes..."
Cassius' eyes swam around the room as he nodded in agreement. He snatched a glass off a waiter's plate.
"If you don't mind, I'm going to drink this digestive cleanser," he said, turning back to Dice. "I already ate before you arrived."

Cassius stopped to gulp down the liquid. Dice took the time to study the restaurant. The floor and ceiling were covered in the same glass as the waiting room, but the holograms were gaudier. This effect was worsened by the tables and chairs hovering several meters above the ground, leaving every centimeter of floor exposed for the holograms. The only times the tables would ever interfere with the holograms were to let people on or off.
"You like the place?" Cassius asked. He tossed his glass in the air, letting a robotic waiter zoom in to catch it.

The robot zoomed to the aid of another customer while Cassius walked Dice to his table. When the table descended, they each took a seat. Dice tried ignoring the lurch in his stomach as he rose into the air.
"Look down through our table's glass!" Cassius said. "Firework holograms are going off now that we're making our ascent. Isn't that quaint?"
Queasy. That's what it was. Heights always reminded Dice there were things he couldn't control. He closed his eyes and brought his head up.
"So," Dice said, to disguise a deep exhale of air. "Uh... What type of food do they have here?"
The Professor's eyes lit up.

"The finest of American cuisine. Apple pie, donuts, pizza, French fries... Actually, I think that last one might be German. Either way, this place is the perfect encapsulation of American culture. Truly remarkable."
Dice gave a weak nod.

"Still not sure why, but these restaurants are incredibly popular right now," Cassius continued. "Everybody wants to go to these places. Maybe it's the exclusivity? You wouldn't believe what kind of people they turn away from here. The only reason that I'm here is because I — well, I suppose I have 'friends in high places'."
Cassius beamed with pride, but Dice gave a blank stare.
"I'm close friends with the owner," Cassius explained, as his face fell.
"A robot?" Dice asked.
Cassius's eyes lit up again.
"Yes," he said. "He's a really strange fellow, but I've come to find him charming in his own way. How'd you guess?"
"I must've just been lucky..."
A holographic firework went off from the ceiling and projected just over their table. Dice jumped back. He was about to complain, but a waiter hovered over to the table before he could say anything.
"Ah, brilliant!" Cassius said to the waiter. "I love how that effect goes off every time you waiters arrive."
The robot waiter gave a digitized smile.
"Thank you," it said. Two lights turned on in its chest, which then projected holographic menus onto the table. "Now, may I take your order?"
"Why of course. Dice, I'll let you go first."
Dice was supposed to swipe through the holographic menu and choose his meal. Instead, he stared at the waiter through a reflection in the table. The robot was unfit for service, and yet—
"Dice? Are you going to order anything?"
Dice looked up. Cassius was rapping his fingers along the table.
Dice put on a smile.
"You know what Professor Cassius? You've had a chance to get a feel for what's good here. I'll take whatever you're getting."
Cassius gave a brief look of confusion as he tried to study Dice. Rubbing his hands together, he looked up at the waiter.
"Uh... Two apple pies please," he said.
The robot let out a high-pitched ding, and a green check-mark replaced its face.
"Your order is complete. That will be twenty-one radials at the end of the night."
"Just take it out of the account," said Cassius.

The waiter smiled, then flew off. A round of fireworks went off in its wake. Dice's eyes strained to look through them and follow the waiter's neon trail of exhaust. The trail stopped at a metal tube that came through the glass ceiling.
The robots must've been stationed in the floor above them.
"Twenty-one radials?" Dice asked, once finished looking. "That's practically a scam, even for here... You come here often, Professor?"
Cassius gave a sheepish grin and shrugged.
"Often? Not really. But, if I'm being scammed, so be it. The food is good."
Dice felt a pricking annoyance but said nothing.

He honed on the clinks of people setting down glasses, the laughs of people telling jokes, and the chatters of people making lively conversation. There was a leisurely way in which everybody carried themselves, even if their attire maintained a regal air. A part of Dice longed to join in. Just a part. Sitting and observing was still the rational way of conducting himself.
Fireworks went off in front of Dice again. This time, he kept his nerves.
"Your dinner is served," the waiter said in a mechanical warble, before flying back off.
Dice looked at the plate. It was covered in a fist-sized cluster of dry crumbs. His stomach churned. He ignored it and spooned them into his mouth.
"To tell the truth, this is very good," Dice said, with his mouth still full.
He wasn't telling the truth, but it was worth it to keep Cassius happy.
Cassius leaned back in his chair and smiled slyly.
"Very good? Even for food made by a robot?"
Dice raised his hand, as if to signal Cassius had scored a point.
"Yes. Granted, solid food at all isn't exactly my cup of tea..."
Cassius's smile faded, and he scrunched his face.
"You only use your feeding apparatus? Is that what I'm hearing?"
"You know where this food comes from, Professor."
"Renewable materials that help sustain our environment. Yes, I'm aware."
"Stop sugar-coating it."
Dice paused to consider the words he was about to say.

"It's repurposed trash," he said. "Trash that's been processed through various food replicators. I'm not saying there's anything wrong with eating compost, but I prefer to take the liquid supplements that factories produce."
The Professor slammed his metal arm on the table and gave a cold laugh.

"You're another one of those 'supplement purists' aren't you? Never thought I'd ever come across one. Supplements may have helped solve our economic crisis, but they aren't any better for you. Quite the opposite. Tell me that you know that."
"I do. But, I prefer my food made by human factories, rather than partially prepared by robots... Call me eccentric."
"You're eccentric. And, that's coming from me."
Cassius laughed it off as a joke, but his voice had been steel.
Cassius bent down and spooned food into his mouth. Even after he'd started chewing, he took care to keep his face in the food and out of Dice's sight.
It was Dice's move.
"It's been quite some time since I've seen you," he said. He kept his expression reserved and unflinching.
"Indeed, it has," said Cassius, head still bent.

Dice took another good look at the restaurant. Light spilled from every crevice, soft music wafted out of hidden speakers, a rich scent filled the air, and excitement was on everybody's tongue. However, Dice had a greater sense than earlier that he didn't belong. Neither did Cassius. As much as he tried to hide it, he was a tired man. His forehead was matted with wrinkles, wrought from hours of deep thought.
He knew too much to be able to savor the flavor of idleness.
"Why did you bring me here?" Dice asked.
"To have a good meal and a good time."
"Why did you really bring me here?"
Cassius looked up from his plate and gave a dead look into Dice's eyes.
"I have... friends in high places," he said, lowering his voice. "That's how I know about your promotion. I need you to realize that. Now, I'm going to give you advice, and I want you to take it."
Dice nodded and returned the dead look. This was the true Professor — a taste of what he was keeping hidden under his massive cloak, and web of bionic limbs.
The taste left. The Professor closed the dead tunnels in his eyes and leaned back in his chair to resume his carefree persona.
"Waiter," he said, as a robot whizzed by. "I'd like a stimulant injection please. Actually, make that two!"
Cassius watched and laughed as the waiter flew off.

"In the course of my career, I've gained a dislike for quiet people with eyes that wander..." he said. He tried to keep a smile, but his eyes stayed off in the distance. "There's a type of person that succeeds in studying political theory. And, there's a type that fails miserably at it. I saw you as the latter.  You would always sit in the back of my lectures, never saying a word to anybody. You never even took notes. And, you certainly didn't do well on the tests. To be frank, I was concerned you'd prove defective."
"Yes. I suppose I wasn't fit to become a politician."
Cassius raised an eyebrow.
"You failed my class on purpose. I know you did."
Dice didn't say a word.

"I was wrong about you. I marked you off as my failure, forgetting you were your own man. But, I'm glad. Every teacher wants to be proven wrong when it comes to the students — the people — that they underestimate."
Cassius stopped, and looked over Dice. There was almost a glint of envy in his eye. Almost.

"I'm not sure how you've gotten where you are, but you did it Dice. You made it! I congratulate you! Now, going forward, you're going to need guidance. Since you have such a unique and valuable skill-set, I believe that you should go into—."
"I know what I'm going into. As you should know full well, I'm going to be working with the police's facial analytics team."
Cassius chuckled.
"You don't want that. Your abilities could be put to much better use in politics, espionage, or various specialized military positions. Simple police work is a complete waste..."
"I'm going into the police, Professor. That's where I was promoted to by Mrs. Paige, and that's where I'll stay."
Cassius let severity leak into his tone. "I've talked to several legislators and officials, Dice. You're currently in mind for other operations. This is not an opportunity that you want to pass up."
Dice cracked and let out a real smile.
"I'm not interested," he said. "I'm interested in going into a field that will garner respect, and work to help people."
"That's great, but I don't see how the other fields I named off won't garner respect, or help others..."
Dice shrugged his shoulders.

"Did you know that the police force is currently the only branch of government with less than 20% reliance on robotized staff?" he asked. "It's among the few lines of work still placing faith in humans to help other humans. Maybe I'm misguided... But, I believe that making a difference there will work to make a positive difference everywhere."
The Professor nodded, giving his knowing look.
"Alright then. I can respect that."
He rolled his eyes back to look at the ceiling, before bringing them back down.

"But, if you're going to do this Dice, let me give you one piece of advice. For your first police case, you need to request permission to participate in the case code-named 'Hamilton Search-Party'. If you can get the case solved — and I'm sure you will — you'll have a major boost to your career."
"I'm not one for parties. If I'm going to get a boost, I'd rather it be on my own terms."
Cassius smiled grimly.
"Trust me, it's no party."

Dice moved in his chair uncomfortably. He'd caught Cassius hiding his bionic arm behind his back and asserting a false confidence in his voice. He was compensating for something. Dice pressed the descend button on his chair.
"Well look at that!" Dice said, glancing at Cassius' watch. "It's 18:00 already. Professor, I need to be going. I appreciate the offers, but it's just not for me."
"Have a good night!" Cassius said, giving a cheery wave. "Your interview with the police concerning the promotion should be in two days. Try to remember what I told you! Okay?"

As Dice descended, he steadily turned to a small silhouette among a mess of holograms. Cassius continued to watch him through the glass. Even when Dice knew that he was out of sight, he could still feel Cassius watching.
Chapter 3:
Dice adjusted himself in his seat. His back stiffened as he attempted to make himself straight and balanced as possible, but he could still feel himself sinking into the cushion.
His back and neck ached. His eye twitched. It was just his luck that a smart-cushion chair had to be in this waiting room.
He watched the clock floating in front of him. Two more minutes until the interview.
"Are you an hour early to everything you go to? Last I checked, this place doesn't have meetings at six in the morning."
A night guard to Dice's right sneered, before resting his feet on his desk. He had puffy eyes and a five O'clock shadow. Would it have killed him to get a mirror?
"It's a job interview... Besides: it can pay to be early," Dice said.
The guard scoffed.
"I start my shift here at midnight, every night, and it pays scraps..."
Dice kept his eyes on the door. At any moment, it could slide open.
"What's with that stupid stone expression on your face? Is that your resting face, or have you just not gotten enough sleep?"
Dice looked at the guard. There were about a dozen things he could say to wipe the smug grin off his face.
He said nothing.
"So, a job interview, huh?" the guard persisted. "Last time I checked, we're ridiculously overstaffed."
Dice took a moment to close his eyes.
"They're thinking of adding me to their facial analytics team."
The guard took his feet from the desk and gave a look of bemusement.
"Facial analytics? I thought that branch was going almost completely to computers..."
"I was thinking the same thing about night guards," Dice said.
The guard glared and pulled his feet off the desk. He stood from his chair. The door to the meeting room slid open.
"Mr. Raymond?" A man in a black bodysuit peaked his head out of the door.
"That's me."
The man motioned to come in, and Dice rolled from his chair. He was tempted to take one last look behind. He couldn't get the guard's last words out of his mind.
A whole branch, completely to computers?
"And how are you doing this fine morning, Mr. Raymond?"
It was a stern looking woman in a crisp bodysuit of her own. She was sitting behind a table, with two people to her left, and another to her right.
"Good."

The room couldn't have been more than half the size of his apartment. Worse yet, it was split by a glass table that stretched from wall to wall. Though, it was at least well-lit and well-equipped. A row of lights ran along the ceiling, cameras lined the walls, and the table had projectors installed along it.
"Very good," the woman said. "I'm Sally Patters, and we four will be conducting your interview this morning."
Mrs. Patters gestured to the man who'd guided Dice into the room. He nodded, and left through the door he and Dice had entered in.
"Take a seat."

Mrs. Patters kept her eye on Dice until he was settled. He saw the way her eyes glinted. He was a rat in a cage. Though, after staring at her a moment longer, she diverted her eyes. He wasn't the only caged rat in the room. A man to the left's hand was fidgeting. A woman to the right covered her mouth. And, the other man to Mrs. Patters’ left...

His heart stopped. Mrs. Patters was glowering over him again. She'd caught him trying to read everybody. He shifted, trying to make himself comfortable. Maybe the smart-cushion chairs in the waiting room hadn't been so bad after all.
"I apologize in advance if this interview is a bit unorthodox," Mrs. Patters said.
Dice nodded.

"We've taken a second look at your resume. It appears there was a mistake in our system. I'll contend you have a strong skillset, you have a unique background, and your employer, Mrs. Paige, had a lot of excellent things to say. However, your resume suggests that you're somewhat less qualified than we might want..."
A man to her left cleared his throat.
"I'm sorry, but we're not interested in employing you. Your performances on our tests were phenomenal, but it's simply that—."
Mrs. Patters cut him off.

"Here at the Monterey District Police Force, we accept only the highest caliber of individuals. People who've undergone years of rigorous training and proven their mettle. Understand: in our line of work, we're expected to protect the U.R.O from all potential dangers. We need people who are prepared to give us results. I know what you can do, Mr. Raymond... But why should we believe that you are prepared to do it when the cards are down?"

Dice let his muscles relax and pulled himself back in his chair. He took another moment to run his eyes across the people in front of him, paying extra attention to the way that each person was breathing. Sitting. Looking. They might've all been staring at him, but he could stare into them.

"You've been taking neural-stimulants," Dice said, giving a gesture to the man on the far left. "I can tell by the slackening of your jaw, and the slight twitching of your right eye. You seem to have good control over it, though... Have you been up for four hours prior to this meeting?"
The man's face reddened.

"You have a metal lung," Dice continued, to the other man to the left. "Your breathing is uncannily consistent. And, you keep your arms too tight to your chest. You must've had a recent rib injury. I wonder what type of accident led to that..."
Dice swiveled to the woman on the right.

"You spilled oil on top of yourself before coming here," Dice said. "There's a hint of a grease stain on the black of your suit. And, there's only one reason why you'd need oil... Are you harboring illegal electronics?"
Everybody in the room had gone still. The fear in their eyes was palpable.
"And you," Dice said, turning to Mrs. Patters. She stared at him coldly. "I believe that you have your answer."
The corner of Mrs. Patters' lip curved upward.
"Well," she said. "That was certainly impressive. Granted, I'm not sure if it was quite the answer I was looking for."
She took a glance at each of her partners, as if to reaffirm what she was about to say.

"However... You're just as impressive as Mrs. Paige said. I don't believe we can afford to lose you. If you go through a bit more testing, I'm sure we could find a position for you in file organization, computer interface upkeep, and fact-checking. As your history with computer engineering suggests, you'd excel in those positions."
The confidence drained from Dice's chest. Filing? Interface upkeep? Fact checking? That was almost a demotion from his former position.
"That sounds like an idea," Dice said, trying to hide his disappointment.
The curve of Mrs. Patters' lip spread into a smile.
"Yes."
She stared at him. Dice stared back. There was an itch in the back of his mind. She was hiding something. Dangling it right out of his reach. The room spun as he tried to figure it out.
The spinning stopped.
"Mrs. Patters," Dice said, looking at his reflection in the table. "Have you, by any chance, met Professor Cassius?"
He brought his eyes back from his reflection and to Mrs. Patters. She made a sly grin.
"I can't say that I have," she said, cryptically.
Dice tilted his head and mimicked the grin.
"Well, he's close friends with me, and the chief of the Monterey District's police force."
He stopped himself. Did he really want to say what he was about to?
He considered his situation. He was drowning. Professor Cassius must've seen to it that this interview would fail, unless Dice said the right words.

"I know you need somebody working the computer interfaces, but Professor Cassius informed me you needed aid in facial analytics on a new case," Dice said, slowly. "Pardon if I'm misremembering, but I believe it was the 'Hamilton Search Party'?"
Dice measured their reactions. There wasn't a hint of shock on anybody's face. It was as if they'd expected him to bring it up. But then... They had.
"Do you think I would be a good fit for that position?" Dice asked.
Mrs. Patters sifted through files on her monitor, and then clapped her hands.
"Yes, that would be a perfect position. We have that spot open right now, in fact."
Her tone took a complete reversal. Her posture relaxed, her voice was cheery, and her eyes went from sallow to wide.

"I wonder why I hadn't thought of it before," she continued. "We lost our human analyst not even a week ago, and we're in desperate need to have somebody fill their place. Despite the accuracy of our computers, we still face criticism for relying 'too much' on them. I'm not sure if you've seen the recent riots, but there's a certain amount of unrest..."
Dice offered a look of understanding.
"Besides," Mrs. Patters said, "with the Hamilton Search Party case, having a human set of eyes won't just be a benefit. I think it'll be a necessity."
She turned to the interviewers on both sides of her, and they nodded in agreement.
"Yes, he sounds like just the man we need," said a man on the left. "It's been quite some time since I've felt so confident about an interviewee."
"Alright then," Mrs. Patters said. "Congratulations. You have the job."
Dice felt the tension in his muscles lift. He could breathe again.
"Excellent," said Dice. "What's the starting wage, and when will the start date be?"
Mrs. Patters looked straight through Dice.
"Your starting wage will be two radials an hour. We'll have you start in a week," she said.
Dice's eyes widened.
"A week?"
"I apologize for the wait..." said Mrs. Patters. "But, I'm afraid this job switchover won't have the benefit of automated robots. There's more paperwork and hoops for us to go through."
"Pardon me: I can't see how that is. I managed to switch a job within six hours once. I'm a big believer in an efficient work environment."
Mrs. Patters' eyes darted around.

"Well, you'll be a bigger believer in this: we're going to relocate you to Diggle Street so you'll be closer to the lead we have on the Hamilton Search Party. As much as we might like, we simply can't do that for you in less than a week."

Dice felt another itch in the back of his mind. There shouldn't have been any reason to be relocated over a simple facial analytics position, let alone a relocation handled directly by the MDPD. However, Mrs. Patters' expression was blank.
"A week it is," Dice said, with a false smile. He outstretched his hand and shook the hand of each interviewer. "Thanks for the position. I look forward to when I start!"
Dice shook Mrs. Patters' hand last.
"I look forward to having you on our force," Mrs. Patters said.
She stood from her chair and leaned over the table.
"In the next few days, we'll send you the address for your new apartment. In a week, you'll be expected to return here to report to Deputy Haynam."
"I'll be working closely with people?"
Mrs. Patters laughed.
"No. Your personal profile suggests you're better off working alone. You'll just be working with Deputy Haynam... And even that should be constricted to mostly electronic communications."
Dice frowned but said nothing.
"Oh, and one more thing..."

Mrs. Patters pulled a badge out of her sleeve and slid it across the table. It was a thin piece of platinum, formed into the shape of a diamond. There was a wreath stamped into the center of it. Above the wreath were the letters "United Republic of Octavian", and under the wreath were the words "Monterey District Police Department". As Dice flipped it over, he saw an electromagnet lining it so it could attach to any piece of clothing.
"That's a pretty powerful magnet," Dice said.

"It's yours," said Mrs. Patters. "In due time, 'pretty powerful' is something you'll be saying a lot. Call the magnet overkill, but we don't want anybody losing their badges. You'll receive the uniform that goes with it in a week, when you report back to this station."
Dice’s head was brimming with questions. Somehow, he managed to pocket the badge and give an "okay."
"I suppose that concludes our interview," said Mrs. Patters. "I enjoyed having you, Mr. Raymond. Whatever you do, don't fail on me! I expect great things!"
She laughed, but Dice gave a stiff nod.
"I'll make sure I exceed your expectations."

He made a swipe goodbye and sped out the door. However, his pace slowed as he reached the exit. Pulling his hand out of his pocket, he waved his badge in the air. He put the badge back and left with a smug grin.
He didn't need to look back to know the expression on the night guard's face.
Chapter 4:

A beam of sunlight shyly peeked out of the clouds, draping a warm sheen over a donut of a building. Dice hugged his briefcase, taking in the air. It smelled like nature... Trees. There must've been a filtration device tucked in the ground somewhere. He turned his hearing aid up and listened for one. All he picked up was a steady beeping.
It was probably the transport tube going over schedule, to still let people on. It always took forever for transport tubes to fill up. If only they were run more efficiently.

He made his way up a conveyer belt, and toward the row of entrance doors. A holographic banner hung over them — Monterey District Computing Center. Dice smiled. He was finally back in his element. It had been too long since his last trip to the computing center — a place with processing power eclipsing Dice’s wildest dreams.
Granted, the center was generally too crowded and expensive to be worth his trouble. His apartment’s projector was usually sufficient.
Usually...
There was a bigger reason Dice avoided the center: it only had robots on staff. Something about that always crept under his skin.
However, none of that mattered right then. His home computer was dead. Besides: after getting his promotion, he'd earned a trip to the computing facility.
He put his hand to a scanner and waited for the door to open.
"Access Denied."
Dice scowled. It didn't make any sense. It always worked before.
Maybe the scanner misread his handprint.
"Access Denied."
He tried peering through the window of the door, but it was tinted black. He could only make out blurry silhouettes, and even those were questionable.
He rapped on the window a few times. Finally, a door to his left slid open, and a woman's head poked out.
"I'm sorry sir, but we're closing down the computing center for the day," she said.
Her neck was tense. Her hair was wild. Her knuckles turned white as they clutched the edge of the door.
"According to the schedule, you should be letting people in," Dice said, putting on a smile.
"Yes, well... Things come up. I really don't have the time to explain."
This had to happen on the one day he gave himself time to slack off. Just his luck.
There was a crash. A shout. Dice ran toward the woman's door.
"No, no, no," the woman said, raising her hand.
She leaned inward and pressed a button on the inside.  Lunging forward, Dice grabbed the edge of the door just as it was sliding closed.
"Wait," he said.
He whipped his badge out of his pocket. A twinge of guilt shot through his hand as he held it up. However, what was he supposed to do? He couldn't just ignore the chaos, could he?
The woman's face softened.
"Oh, thank god," she said. "Was it one of our staff who called you? Or was it our — customers — who called you?"
"Not sure," said Dice. His eye twitched. "Whoever sent out the message... They masked their identity. They definitely told us to come here though. The rest of my squad will arrive soon."
He rubbed his eye. The MDPD better have been coming.
"So, what's going wrong, exactly?" He strode through the entrance.
"They didn't tell you?"
"Uh... It has something to do with a rogue computer, or something of that kind. Is that correct?"
The woman's eyes widened, and she shook her head.
"It must've been one of our customers who called you," she said.
Her eyes fell to the floor, and she shook her head. Guilt? Retrieving a memory?
"Anyway, the answer to your question is yes... And no."
Both.

"A couple of days ago, one of the robots went rogue. Its circuitry was fried. It went berserk and attacked a customer. U.R.O authorities were eventually called in to dismantle it. I thought that we'd taken care of the problem, but..."
Dice winced. Of course — another story of a malfunctioning robot. What else was new?
"However, today a group of people came to protest. The whole center is being raided."
"That's, uh... That's terrible."
The woman squinted and studied Dice's bodysuit.
"You're prepared to clear up this catastrophe, right?"
It struck Dice he had no weapons of any kind. A lump formed in his throat. His head ached. He was way out of his depth.
A blue light dashed across the wall. A red light. Blue. Red. A siren wailed.
"Well, look at that," Dice said, taking a glance behind. "Backup finally arrived."
He nodded firmly.
"Yes, it seems like everything should be under control. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to go and size up the scene."
Dice ran down the passageway, to the main computing area. The further he went, the louder the crashes. The shouts. He brought his hand to his ear and turned down his hearing aid.

A robot flew into the passageway, ricocheting between the walls. Dice ducked as it rocketed past him and crashed into the ceiling. Plaster flurried, leaving Dice leaning against a dented wall in a fit of coughs. As he regained his footing, a man with bloodshot eyes ran through the passageway. His right hand was clutching the sleeve of his left arm. An oddly shaped left sleeve, at that.
He had a smuggled blaster.
"Stop!" Dice said, holding his badge out.

A blast hurled toward Dice, narrowly missing. Eyes wide, Dice sprinted past the man and down the passageway. Several more people went by, brandishing weapons. Dice didn't stop. This wasn't where he needed to be.
"Hey! Watch it!"
Dice raised his hands and took a step back.
"Sorry, I didn't mean to crash into you. I was just trying to get to—."
The main computing hall. He'd made it.
But... it was entirely alien to how he knew it.

Robots flew everywhere, eyes red with rage. A few of them carried people loosely in their grip, looking as though they'd drop them from the slightest shift. Meanwhile, people on the ground shot illegal blasters at the robots. Others tore at robots with crude metal bars and kicked dents into the computers. Still, others marched in long lines, chanting, "Death to robots. Preserve humanity."
Dice wiped a bead of sweat from his forehead. He looked up. The ceiling glowed orange, a fire lapping at its corners.
Nausea set over him. The situation was already beyond hope.
He turned around. Where was the exit? Everywhere he looked were people and robots. They all had the same expression on their faces: fury.
It was a madhouse. He was part of it.
There was a screech. A holographic flare went off in the air. For a moment, the room gave pause.
"I'm Chief Grisham, of the Monterey District Police Department. I'm going to count to three, and I want everybody to start clearing out! We're not going to give another warning."

The crowd somehow went more vicious than before, scrambling for the exit. At least, that seemed what they were doing. Although everybody was headed to the same place, they ran in different directions.

A robot fell in front of Dice. It was covered in gouges, and several wires were torn out. Though, it still had a blaze in its eye. Without a second thought, Dice grabbed a metal rod from the ground and slammed it down. Despite his hearing aid being low, an ear-piercing shatter resonated as the robot broke into a dozen pieces.
His ears went hot. What had he done?
He studied the parts. A fresh processor. Extra springs. Nuts. Bolts. Fans. Everything going in a robot's body laid out for him, to read without any confusion.
Maybe what he'd done hadn't been so bad after all.
He flipped open his briefcase, scooped up as many parts as he could, and charged for the door.
There was a blur as skyscrapers and people whooshed by. A soft hum. Pitch black. Quiet.

Dice lurched forward, then sat back in his seat. The transport tube came to a stop. Yet, it wasn't followed by the familiar rush of adrenaline. The door opened, prompting him to stand up. It was routine. Tedious.

He hauled himself from his seat, turned his hearing aid down, and trudged through a maze of people. Lights blinked. Robots whizzed overhead. Faces of all kinds streamed by. Dice didn't bother looking at any of it. He needed to get to his apartment's capsule transmitter.

Escaping the crowd and rubbing a fresh bruise on his neck, he turned his hearing aid back up. The elevator’s wall went up. He stepped in. Gears and servos spun as the hydraulics let off steam. His stomach moaned as he was launched into the air.
For some reason, the mechanical language he'd spent so much time trying to understand seemed like gibberish. Maybe it always had been.

The elevator creaked open. It creaked shut. Dice was left to his hall. He felt his face fall. As he passed his wall of trophies, he knocked them down one by one. Each time was followed by the cold clang of metal on metal. Each time, Dice didn't flinch.
Once the trophies were scattered, Dice snapped his fingers. The hall’s lights went out. The trophies were gone. There was only darkness.

He entered his room, where a warm. white glow greeted him. Why was everything suddenly so bland? So barren? The room was just a collection of blank metal walls. Dice stared at them. Maybe he could escape them. Enter a daydream.

As drowsiness set over him, his eyes drifted from the walls. The computer projector remained in the same condition it’d been for the past three days — charred and steaming from overuse. Rewiring it hadn't worked. There were no replacement parts.
He glanced at his briefcase. There had been no replacement parts. Now though?
The briefcase flipped open, and metal parts tumbled out. An eye, a backup generator, a spare arm, a quantum processor. Dice smirked.
Maybe a new processor was all that the projector needed. If he just replaced the old one, the projector might just work good as new...
No. He couldn't push the projector any further.
He tried pulling his eyes away but could practically hear the projector whirring to life and activating the training program. He rubbed his forehead. His shoulders slumped.
He straightened himself, opened a panel in the floor, and pulled out his tools. He slipped on a pair of rubber gloves.

An incision was made in the back of the projector. There were a few minutes of carefully peeling away rusted parts, in a delicate strategy to reach a center. Once he finally had, he removed the processor. Cradling it in his hands and looking it over, it occurred to Dice that this had been its brain. Every thought and input of the projector’s, summed up by this sole object.
It was fried to a crisp.
Dice inserted the new processor.
"Computer! Code: refraction. Activate program: trial simulation delta."

The computer projector fizzled and flickered on. Pupils dilating, Dice clenched his jaw. A virus simulation opened. Dice swiped past it with ease. Several more simulations swiped by, with no difference in difficulty from the first. The projector couldn't compete with him. His mind was too sharp.
The projector groaned from overuse only ten minutes in.
Dice's concentration dissipated. He shut off the projector with a sigh and paced around the room.
He could've sworn he'd accounted for every part. He racked his brain for what else might've gone wrong, but to no avail.
He should've been able to isolate the source of the problems. Another computer could've done it. Why couldn't he?
He took out his badge and smiled thinly. His finger ran over its platinum polish. At least he still had this. It was everything he'd worked for. Everything he'd wanted.
His eyes drifted back to the blank walls.
"I thought that branch was going entirely to computers."
He shook his head, closed his eyes, and ran his hand through his hair. He could've sworn he saw Mrs. Patters' and the night guard's faces staring into him.
"Just the stress getting to you," he muttered. "Worried about the move... That's all."
He rubbed away a bit of ash that had smudged his badge.
"This move isn't going to be so bad. There'll be new people, new things to see, new opportunities... And a new computer."
The projector sparked.
"Now, here's hoping that I don't break the new one too..."
He forced a laugh.
His eyes drifted around the room again. His eyelids became heavy. He placed his hand over his mouth as he held back a yawn.
Walking over to the left wall, he activated a panel. A glass sleep-tube slid out.
Dice popped the top hatch open and rolled himself onto the mattress. As he closed his eyes, he ran his fingers along his badge.
"New beginnings," he whispered
Saying the words aloud should've made them more convincing. They were just as hollow as they'd been in his head. He pocketed his badge and rolled onto his side.
"Computer: set the sleep tube to three days."
The lid closed. The tube returned to its panel in the wall and steamed with a gas. Dice slipped into a deep slumber.
Dice sputtered. He looked down. An oily tube was connected to his stomach, pulsating as it pumped in and out.

He tried to move. He couldn't feel his arms or legs. Only a slight tingle at the tips of his hands and feet. He squinted. There was a red light above his head, burning into him. He clenched his teeth and moaned. His stomach was inside out.
Out. There had to be a way out. Though, everywhere he looked there was only blackness, with a slight hint of metal tinting its edges.
"Help!" Dice shouted.
A pair of eyes flashed in the darkness.
"Help!"
They were gone.
Dice uploaded his computer projector's database to a cloud file and reset it.
He clapped his hands and turned.
His clothes were vacuum sealed in his suitcase. His trophies were in a box to be taken by a moving bot. The damaged projector was scheduled to be removed by a trash bot.
Pretty much everything.
He took in a deep breath and checked the watch on his bodysuit. Four minutes. Good time, but not great.
After a snap of the fingers, he placed his hand on his door's scanner. The lights to his apartment shut off as he entered his elevator.
Dice's heart pounded. He bit his lip. Four minutes should've still left him with enough time to catch the early transport tube.
Right?

The capsule opened. Dice darted his way through a mass of people, while his eyes darted to avoid catching the eyes of anybody. Despite this, he managed to catch somebody with a fastened jaw and heavy scowl.
He sped past them. He couldn't afford to miss his seat on the transport tube. Besides: it was probably nothing.
"Hey, buddy! You look like you're from the Kelvin Union. You smuggle yourself over here?"
Desperate shouts sliced through Dice's ears. He muted his hearing aid.

The doors to the transport tube were just starting to close when Dice stuck his foot in. Chirping, their sensors kicked on and they reopened. There was shoving and grunting from others as he made his way to the back row. The doors closed and the city whizzed by.
He'd finally made it.
"Destination reached: Diggle Street."
Dice narrowed his eyes, while clutching his briefcase and made his way toward the exit. It was dark out. Why was it dark out?
He caught a few people casting pitying looks toward him.
As Dice stepped into the street and the transport tube rushed away, he saw the reason behind the pitying looks.

He couldn't see. A thick steam rose from rows of rusted grates in the ground, shrouding everything. Dice made his way past the grates. The neighborhood was cluttered in heaps of scraps. The crowds of people he'd been accustomed to navigating through were gone. In their place were robots that puttered close to the ground. Dice looked up. The sky had been replaced by a ceiling of crude, iron beams. This had to be a mistake.
Dice wiped the sweat from his forehead. The steam was killing him. He felt his bodysuit cling to his skin.
"A 'calculator cage'... Perfect. Just perfect."

He squinted to read the numbers on each apartment as he walked down the street. The street glared with red lights, which all hung from the iron ceiling. Worse were the glowing lights beneath Dice's feet, no doubt lighting up another calculator cage.
As the numbers drew closer to his apartment's address, holograms crackled in front of him.
"Genetic enhancer!" "Bionic eyes!" "Improved generator at half price!"
Dice was tempted to lift scraps from the ground and use them to smash the hidden projectors.
The holograms stopped once he'd reached his new apartment address: 3000. He inserted his fingerprint and entered his assigned password. Nothing happened.

There was a screech. An elevator descended. Though, it was nothing like the elevator he was used to riding. Rather than being an egg, it was a loosely-built cube. Dice entered to find loose wires and gears hanging out of open cracks. He looked for seat but only found a row of screw-holes in the floor, where seats should've been.
The capsule shrieked as it jerked to a stop. The doors slid open. Dice's jaw slid open. His apartment's entrance was two meters in the air. The capsule must've stalled right before it'd reached it.

He threw his suitcase into his entrance. With a jump, he clung to the entrance's ledge and shimmied his body onto it. Just as he finished, the door to his apartment slammed down.  Dice couldn't tell if he had perfect timing, or if the sensors for the door was dangerously quick.
He didn't want the answer.
The elevator shrieked as it descended toward its next victim.

Dice picked himself up and studied his apartment. The hall and main room were the same as that of his last, but the walls were covered in dents, layers of rust, and grime. The only things of note were his new computer projector, which looked about a decade out of date, and—
"A window," Dice said. "That's something, at least."
Dice peered through it to see the view. His heart sank. There was only a cloud of steam and a penetrating red light.
"Computer: close the window."
A metal panel rumbled, curtaining over the window. Dice unlocked his suitcase, used his foot to open a panel in the floor, and dumped his clothes into it.
"Computer: organize clothing."
"Affirmative. Anything else that you'd like help with, Mr. Raymond Dice?"
Dice made a frown. "No."
The station must've entered his name in backward during the transfer. Was there anything that could go right?
Dice leaned on the wall. Maybe he should open the couch.
No. There was no need. He was fine as he was.
The computer's mechanical arms cranked under his feet as it organized his clothes. Couldn't he have done the job faster himself?
The shriek of the elevator returned. A chill ran down Dice's spine.
"Is the moving bot already here?"

He went over to the door and checked the camera-feed. Nothing. Dice put his fingerprint in his door's scanner and entered the password to unlock it. The door flew open — Dice found himself staring at a tangle of chords and wires. The capsule had stalled just before reaching his floor again.
"Surprise!"
It was a robot. He could tell by the way the voice grated against itself, like a bucket of loose screws. It must've hidden just out of the camera's view.
"What?" Dice asked.
Squinting his eyes, he tried to get a closer look in the gap between his floor and the elevator.
"Surprise! You just moved, didn't you?"
Dice stopped squinting.
"Oh. Yes. Yes, that's me. If you'd like I can crawl into the elevator and collect my belongings."
"What?"
"You're the robot mover, aren't you?" Dice asked.
The robot's voice turned to a high-pitched scrape. "No. Robot movers are low-level labor. Are you insinuating—."
"Then what are you doing here?" Dice asked.
"You are the new neighbor. I came here to welcome you to our neighborhood."
There was a thud as the robot hit the gap between the capsule and the floor.
"If it is no trouble, may I have your assistance?" the robot asked.
Dice brought his hands to the door's keypad and typed his password.
"It's far too much trouble, actually," Dice said. "To be frank, I'm all worn out from welcomes. So many people greeting me, so little time..."
"Understood," the robot said, still flying upward to bash its barrel frame into the ceiling. "Well, welcome. By the way, what is your name? My name is Model 291168..."
"That's great," Dice said, interrupting him again. "My name is—."
Dice didn't finish his sentence. The door shut, the chamber shrieked as it was sent away, and Dice walked back to his room.
"Brilliant," he said to himself. "Hours of work and persistence, and I get relocated to a calculator cage. A calculator cage!"
He chuckled at the insanity of it all.
"I hope that I don't have to see that robot again... Awful machines."
He needed to clear his head.
He went to his computer projector. There were tests that needed to be done.

Dice woke up in a cold sweat. At least, he thought he'd woken up. Yet, no matter where he looked all he could see was black. He tried closing his eyes and reopening them. The blackness was still there.
He winced. Old memories and nightmares flashed before his eyes. This couldn't have been a nightmare though. Could it?
Dice lifted his arms and felt around. He winced. His arms were still sore from his nightly sedative gas and electric muscle-stimulators.
The sleeping tube's glass lid felt the same as normal. He knocked on it. It sounded the same.
He pulled his arms down and stared into the darkness. It didn't make any sense. He'd never woken up in mid-sleep before. He'd never even thought it possible.
There was a noise. It was so slight he'd barely noticed it at first. Dice slowly turned up his hearing aid. The noise became louder. More persistent. More invasive.
It was a sharp hissing. Dice's heart hammered in his chest. He kept listening. About a minute in, he realized what he was hearing.
"The sedative filter..." he said to himself. "It must've popped out of place in my sleep."
Dice's face flushed with relief.
The relief fled. He was still stuck in a tube, in the dark, and couldn't sleep.
Hyperventilating, terrible nightmares came back to him. Terrible, terrible nightmares.

He tried telling himself the tube would open once the night was over, but it was paper-thin reassurance. There was no telling how long it would be before the night would end. He wasn't even sure if the sleeping tube would still be working once it did.
Dice banged on the glass.
"Computer!" he shouted. "Computer, deactivate sleeping tube!"
There was no response.
"Computer, deactivate sleeping tube!"

His face turned blotchy. Sweat formed on his forehead. Fear shot up and down his spine. His hands trembled as they were drawn to the badge in his pocket. He pulled it out and rammed its edge into the glass lid. It didn't even leave a scratch.
"Too strong," he muttered to himself. "Think. Think..."
He hit the roof two more times. Still no difference.

Wasn't there a button in the side of his tube though?  Dice felt around until he found the place where the button would've been. He pressed his badge onto it. He pressed his thumb on the wreath imprinted in the badge's center, turning on the electromagnet.
There was a fizzle from the other side of the glass, followed by a loud beep.
"Error detected," the computer said in a muffled voice. "Sleeping tube offline."

Dice sighed as the tube rumbled out of its panel and onto the floor of the main room. The tube's lid flipped open and light spilled into Dice's eyes. Dice spilled out of the tube. He was groggy eyed, still weak from shock, and disoriented by the latent effects of his sedatives.
He'd never felt so good rolling out of bed before.
"Computer: time," he asked.
"2:33," the computer answered.
Dice put his head in his hands. It was nowhere near time for him to start his day. Though, after taking a second glance at his sleeping tube's mattress, he knew he had no other option.
He entered his password on his door's keypad and listened to the shriek of the capsule as it came to his floor.
"I need to scope the place out anyway..."
The shrieking stopped. Dice's door slid open. Dice felt sick inside. All the breath in his lungs had been sucked out of him. He was suddenly acutely aware of just how weak he really felt.

The capsule had stalled. Perched on top was a woman. She was dressed in a ragged bodysuit, and her hair was a long, black mop. Dice couldn't make much more out, because she sat huddled in the dark corner, shrouded by wires. What was unmistakable though were her eyes. They were unusually large, with fierce gray pupils at the center. When she looked at Dice, he felt as though he were being dissected.

Dice pressed the buttons on the keypad as quickly as he could, but his fingers had turned to rubber. He looked back to the woman, expecting her to say something. She said nothing. Dice tried to look away and found that he couldn't. He was used to being glued to other people's faces, but this time was different. He felt trapped.

When the door finally closed with a clang and the chamber shrieked back to its place, Dice still couldn't get the eyes out of his head. He tried to convince himself it was a dream. No amount of convincing could've worked.
Dice ran to his room and rolled back onto the mattress of his bed. He stared at the ceiling for the rest of the night. All he could see were the eyes.
Chapter 5:
Dice looked at the calendar on his projector. Three days. It had been three days since he'd last left his apartment.
Good. He'd been far too busy and there was still much to do. He hadn't even finished revamping his computer projector.

Still, despite all the things left, he'd managed to get a lot done. He smiled. The sleeping tube was fully functional again, a massage feature had been installed into his couch, and the panels in his floor had been reprogrammed to turn into a giant, digitized chess board.

The chess board was his proudest achievement. He would move from square to square, strategically moving each piece. He could beat most games within a span of fifteen minutes, but the thrill of those fifteen minutes was enough to keep him going for another game. It wasn't as stimulating as working through a computer virus gambit, but it was sufficient enough.
There was hardly a point in leaving his apartment, in his eyes.
Eyes... Gray, piercing eyes.
Dice trembled. His eyes flitted back to his monitor.
It chirped, and a message appeared in the corner: "Report to Deputy Haynam at the Monterey District Police Station."
Just when he thought he'd make it four days.
Begrudgingly, Dice started his daily routine. His body was doused in a disinfecting spray, a fresh pair of clothes was fitted onto him, his unruly hair was tamed, and his mouth was sanitized.

He sat in his kitchen chair and hooked himself up to the respirator of his feeding apparatus. He untangled his arm from the three tubes feeding through it and turned a dial on the side of the mask. The largest of the three tubes pushed itself into his mouth, as a purple paste pumped through it. The two smaller tubes disconnected from the respirator and went into Dice's nostrils, pumping air into his lungs.

Dice closed his eyes, steadily swallowing the paste. His chest rose and fell with the purr of the respirator. The apparatus was in more control of Dice's breathing and swallowing than he was. It was as if he'd entered another sleep-state.
The respirator stopped pumping. Dice turned the dial back. The tubes shifted back in place, and the respirator reeled itself into the apparatus.

Dice went to his door and punched his password into the keypad. His eye twitched. His ears went hot. A shriek wriggled its way from under the door. There was nobody on the capsule transmitter when it came up. There was nobody on it as it came down. Yet, he still glanced to his side every so often, as if he might find somebody standing there. Watching him.
Dice checked his bodysuit's watch as he made his way to the transport tubes. It was still only 6:00 — ahead of schedule.
Dice went stone-faced as he ran through the words that he should say, the things he should do, and the gestures he should make.
He stopped. A robot was blocking his path.
"Excuse me," Dice said.
"Sorry about — wait, you're the new neighbor, aren't you?"
Dice's eyes widened as he looked down. While he wasn't certain, the robot looked identical to the one he'd seen just a few nights ago.
"I have a transport tube to catch," Dice said. "I don't have time to chat."
Dice pushed past it and sped up his pace.
"Why don't you set up a time for when you do?" the robot asked, puttering after him. "I apologize for persisting interruptions, but —"
"Apologies seem to be a theme this morning, don't they?" Dice said, sharply.

"That is certainly a pattern in our interactions," the robot said. "Anyway, homo sapiens are very rare in this sector of the Monterey District. I feel it's my responsibility to ensure that you're properly integrated into our community. How would lunch work?"
"Sorry, but I think I've integrated just fine. Besides: I won't be back until this evening. Too much to do."
There was a rush of air as the transport tube opened. Dice brushed off his bodysuit and hunched down.
"Well, I really need to—"
"This evening then?" the robot interrupted.
"No time then, either," Dice said, stepping into the transport car.
"But, you just said that you'd be back this evening. Logic dictates that you should have plenty of time this evening. This doesn't compute."
"I, umm," Dice said, desperately searching for the right words. People were staring at him. Waiting for him to find a seat. The robot wasn't letting the door close.
"Fine. This evening, I'll go to dinner."
He rushed away to his seat, but the robot still called after him.
"I'll be at your apartment room tonight to pick you up!" it said. "By the way: I still haven't caught your na—."
The transport tube door closed. Tension left Dice's shoulders as he took his seat in the back row.

Sun-drenched skyscrapers crowded the window. At first glance, they were a randomized mess. Though, as Dice studied them, he caught glimpses of delicate archways and tubes linking them all together. They morphed into something calculated. Uniform. He smirked inwardly.
A spire tower loomed ahead of him. It was taller and thinner than the rest, resembling a thimble. Though, its perceived lack of structural integrity made up for by a thick wall hugging its base.
The transport tube slowed, and Dice's eyes widened. It must've been the police station.
There was a jerk as the transport tube stopped.
"At this time, we request you show your authorization for entry and identification. Please remain seated."

A robot hovered through the crowd of people, scanning them and escorting those without authorization through the exit. When the robot reached Dice, he lifted his badge and ID card. The robot gave a smile and flew off. The gate to the police station rumbled, and Dice's seat shuddered as the tube's engine kicked back on.

Dice stepped off into a garage. Dozens of police hover drones lined the walls. Jet-black arrowheads. A memory of one hovering over his apartment building flashed through his mind. Programmed to monitor the district, the drones were semi-sentient machines. They also doubled as modes of transportation for the police.
How hard was it to ride one of them, anyway?

Dice looked one over. The paint didn't have so much as a scratch, the glass was polished smooth, and the exhaust port didn't have a hint of residue on it. Flawless. Had it even been used before? He reached his hand out.
"Don't touch that. How'd you even get in here?"
Dice turned around. A balding man, squeezed into a police bodysuit, walked toward him with his badge held out.
"I said don't touch that: it's police property," the man said, raising his voice.
Dice lifted his own badge from his pocket.
"I believe that I'm police property as well."
The man snickered. A tint of red flushed into his cheeks.
"Sorry. You must be the new guy!" the man said. "Dice... Dice Raymond?"
He held out his hand. Dice took it and gave it a weak shake.
"That's me," Dice said. "And, you are?"
"Oh! I'm Haynam. Deputy Haynam."
He gave a slick grin. Too slick. Dice didn't return it.
"I was tasked to introduce you to the place, and give you your first assignment," Haynam said, before stopping to chuckle. "Well, that was definitely one way to introduce you to the place, huh?"
"Definitely."
Haynam's let his chuckle die off and cleared his throat.
"I guess that'll be your first lesson here. Don't touch the drones. I don't like the idea of anybody scratching my babies up. And now, for your next lesson... Follow me."

Haynam made his way through the garage, whistling and bobbing his head as he went. Dice stayed close behind. As Haynam broke into a subtle step-dance though, Dice's eyes wandered toward people who walked by. They were primarily mechanics and maintenance workers, but there were also a few officers. The officers were what stole his attention. A wariness lined their mouths and weighed down their eyes. Each one moved swiftly as they hopped into their drones and fled through a gaping tunnel in the garage.
Despite their swift movements, their eyes had been half-closed.
"Hey, Raymond."
Haynam whistled.
"Your ass should be over here."
He was already a few meters ahead.
"And close your jaw. This garage is nothing to scoff at."

Dice entered a locker room. Dozens of officers shuffled around, opening and closing their lockers. Some of them were busy adjusting and readjusting their uniforms, while others made a mad scramble toward an exit at the far back.
"Starting my day in the department's locker room," Haynam said, with a laugh. "Just how I like it!"
Haynam sped between several officers. Dice's eyes swam. He squeezed around somebody and ducked as one of the locker doors nearly swung in his face.
Dice gasped once he was back at Haynam's side. Haynam had a wry smirk on his face.
"Lesson two," Haynam said, raising his voice above the raucous. "Show up early every morning. Or else, you'll get caught in this mess."
"I showed up half an hour early."
"Not early enough. Be an hour early. Any later, and you're late in my book."

Haynam's eyes jumped between the numbers of each locker. He stopped when he reached locker number 293 and punched in a code. The door popped open. Haynam reached in, pulled out something, and then threw it at Dice's head. It moved in a blur, but Dice still caught it just in time.
"Nice reflexes," Haynam said, his eyes slightly widening. He blinked. "Now, put it on."

Dice turned it over. It was his police bodysuit, folded into a neat square. Dice held it up by its sleeves, let it unfold, and looked it over. It was a made a dark blue metal mesh. A black strip lined the legs and sleeves. Around the torso there was a thin layer of black armor, with an outline for the badge on the left chest plate.
"Can't stare at it forever, Raymond. This isn't a fashion show."

Dice pulled his badge out of his pocket. He grabbed his suit, pulled his legs through the baggy neck hole, and put his arms through the sleeves. While he spread his arms and legs out, the bodysuits mesh buzzed and tightened. Once it had fit itself snugly around his body, the buzzing stopped. Dice looked himself over. There was one thing missing.
He turned his badge's electromagnet and placed it over the outline in his suit.
"Snazzy, isn't it?" Haynam said.
He turned on his heel, and broke into another speed-walk.

"One of the first things that you'll learn about this place is that it's a glorified sweat-shop," he shouted over his shoulder. "There's nowhere you can go where there won't be some amount of mayhem going on around you. That said, there is one place in here that I consider a sanctuary."
They entered the halls. Only a few people walked past them. The marble floor glowed of a fresh polish, and there was a scent of fresh lemons.
"This the sanctuary?" Dice asked.
Haynam chuckled.
"No. It's usually much busier around here, I swear. This morning though, a good chunk of our force is being dispatched to stop another riot."
"Are robots tearing up downtown again?" Dice asked.
Haynam gave a sardonic smile.
"How'd you guess?"
He sped up his pace as he whipped around a corner. There was the sound of typing. Then, a whoosh.
"Welcome to my office!" Haynam called out. "Move it, Raymond. I can only leave my office door open to the insanity of the department for so long."
Dice broadened his stride, and walked in.

The office was an unremarkable cube, about half the size of his own apartment. The left wall was devoted to a map of the Monterey District and the right to a holographic computer interface. Haynam's desk took up the center. Haynam was already seated.
"Please, take a seat!" said Haynam.
A stool rose in front of the desk. Dice sat down. Pretending to examine the computer on the wall, Dice studied the room through the corners of his eyes. Haynam gave a look.

Haynam wasn't like most people. His ticks weren't kept on his sleeve, so it had taken Dice a bit of picking at Haynam's skin to uncover them. Even then, his ticks were hardly anything notable. The clearest giveaways were that, when under stress, Haynam's eyes were alert and his voice was cutting.
"You like the computer?" Haynam asked, softly.
Dice nodded. "Latest model?"
"Yep. We like to keep things as up to date here as we can." Haynam gestured at the room. "Pretty nice place isn't it?"
"Definitely. You have great taste for décor."
Haynam smiled smugly, and let his shoulders loosen. Dice smiled back.
Perhaps Haynam wasn't as closed a book as he seemed.
"I almost wish that this was my apartment," Dice continued. "I could see myself living in here. It's probably the nicest office I've ever seen."
Haynam laughed.
"You're living the dream, Haynam."
Haynam leaned forward.
"I probably shouldn't be telling you this, but I've slept in here before. Better than sleep in a tube."
"You have the right idea. I can't sleep in those things for the life of me!"
Haynam chuckled.
"Well... I suppose that we should be getting down to business, shouldn't we?"
Haynam clapped his hands, and a computer screen projected in the center of the table.

"It appears that the M.D.P.D doesn't want you working through the department," Haynam said, scrolling through the screen. He winked at Dice. "Don't worry though. I have a feeling that you'll be joining the main team soon."
Dice winked back and laughed softly.

"For now, you'll be working through your apartment," Haynam continued. "They have you assigned to the 'Hamilton Search Party'. The specifics of it are shaky... But, I'll try to tell you what I do know." He cracked his knuckles. "It's a government search that's been delegated to the police. A federal criminal escaped into the Monterey District, and we have reason to believe that they're hiding out in Diggle Street. However, this particular criminal is slippery. They have a history of escaping arrest, so we can't just launch our drones on a street-wide search. We're putting you on the case to locate the criminal, without arousing suspicion."
Dice raised an eyebrow.
"That's all? Are there any descriptions for what type of person that I'm looking for?"
Haynam gave a pitying smile and shook his head.

"That's all. Trust me, I understand your surprise. Our Chief was asking the same questions when we were assigned the case. However: this lack of evidence is the exact reason why you're so valuable to us right now... You're a living lie detector."
"Something like that," Dice said, cautiously.

"That's going to have to be good enough. Here's the deal: nobody on our force has been able to break any ground on the 'Hamilton Search Party', and the clock is ticking. As far as we're aware, our guy could be living anywhere in that calculator cage and could be anybody. Even robots. We've tried assigning this case to facial analytics robots... But, the feds said that they want us to avoid that. This case is apparently too important to risk being compromised. You're the one person that we have right now."
Dice scratched the back of his neck. The only person? That didn't really line up with what he'd been told during his interview.
"I'll be on it," he said. "But, I just want you to be aware: I'm not infallible as a facial analyst. My accuracy has its limits."
A grim shadow came over Haynam.

"You're already 'on it', Raymond. We assigned you to this case a week ago, when you were hired. This isn't a matter of debate. The U.R.O officials are expecting results, and you're the only way to get them. We can deal with complications when and if we get to them."
Dice straightened up, and mimicked Haynam's grim demeanor.
"Understood. You make great points, Haynam. Very... Very apt of you. I'll be on patrol the moment I'm back at my street."
Haynam's brow raised, and then furrowed. He didn't care for the compliments anymore.

"No, you won't be on 'patrol'," said Haynam, raising his voice. "You're undercover, Raymond. Your uniform stays here. Your profession stays here. As far as anybody will be concerned, you'll be on a walk. If anybody asks you what the 'Hamilton Search Party' is, you've 'never known a guy named Hamilton'. And, for the love of god: I don't want to hear you ever call your work a patrol again."
"I won't."

"Good. Now, here are a few guidelines: we want you looking for suspicious persons. If anybody happens to strike you as such, watch them. Shadow them. Determine whether their character is the sort that matches that of a criminal. You'll report back in a week with a list of people, which will have the likeliest suspect at the top."
"And if I'm unsure?"

"You damn well better be sure, Raymond. You need to be able to sum up a person's life in a glance. This is your job now. This is what you signed up for. Besides: you're looking for one very specific person. It can't be that hard."
Dice felt a surge of reassurance rise to his chest.
"Thank you for this, Haynam," he said.
Haynam reached across the desk and shook Dice's hand.
"You're welcome," he said, with another smug grin. "Do your job fast, do it right, and I might have a better position settled for you in the future."
Haynam turned to type into his desk's computer.

"All of our leads have been sent to your personal computer," Haynam said. "Get out of here. Leave your uniform in your locker: the password is 829. And, if this conversation has already gotten your uniform sweaty... Well, burn it."
Chapter 6:

Dice stood at the corner of his apartment building. A headache clutched his temples and sweat streamed down his face. His hand clenched around a nearby lamppost. The street was an oven, but he had to ignore the discomfort.

Squinting through the fog, he stared at everybody that walked by. A robot, carrying a trash incinerator. Another robot, whizzing by with a smile plastered on its face. A man, hauling a scrapped projector. Nobody suspicious.
Or, was he just not being suspicious enough?

There was a robot with a flickering digital face that was both frowning and smiling at the same time. A woman with a mangled briefcase, a few sizes larger than normal ones. Sparks flew as a robot pulled itself forward with its arms, its exhaust barrel grinding against the ground.
Paranoia gnawed at him. Somebody looked in his direction, and a part of him was desperate to interpret it as guilt. His head throbbed as he strained to keep himself in check.
A robot paused in mid-flight to stare at him. Dice made a mental note. Though, had the robot's stare only been out of a passing curiosity?

His hand slapped against the lamppost, making a dull rattle. He needed somebody to follow, but nobody quite had the right look to them. He winced. His intuition was melting into bias, leaving his thoughts muddled.
His chest sunk deeper as he studied a robot that went by: the grooves in its design, the way its arms moved, the way each pixel blinked on its face...
He came up blank.

His fingers ran through his hair. Machines were unreadable. The only thing that he could ever get out of them were their speeds. Some appeared to be in a rush, whereas others would move uncomfortably slow.
Though, how was he going to be able to fulfill the requirements of this case if he couldn't read a robot's emotions?
The ominous thought made his head spin. It was too much. He walked toward his apartment's capsule transmitter and made a mental list of all the people that he'd studied.

When he'd begun making his way through his apartment's hall, he was trying to create perfect images of specific people he'd seen in his head. Though, the images crumbled apart before he even started. Nothing stuck out to him.

He turned on his computer projector. It was seventeen thirty. Dice groaned and rubbed his forehead. Five hours had been spent pacing through the street, and absolutely nothing had come of it. A knot formed in his stomach as he remembered he only had six more days before he needed to report back. The knot tightened when he realized that people would become suspicious if he continued standing in the same spot.
Undoubtedly, they already were.

Dice activated his chess board. It wasn't his fault that he couldn't read these people. He'd never had to do anything like this before. He was used to being one among a crowd of many. He was used to living on a street where there were dozens of people, rather than robots. He hadn't been trained for this.
Perhaps he'd gone in over his head. Perhaps he'd bitten off more than he could chew. Perhaps —
There was a beep. It couldn't have been the chessboard... Could it? He'd never lost a game of chess before.
The beep went off again. There was a short shriek.
The capsule transmitter.
Dice groaned. Walking to the door, Dice prayed it wasn't who he thought it was.
Dice's fingers pressed along the keypad. The door flew open.
"Are you ready to come to dinner?"
It was the robot he'd met in the morning.
"Sure," Dice said.
He winced as he squatted down and slid through the gap in the capsule.
"Hello!"
"'Hell', more like it," Dice muttered, as he looked up.

He almost couldn't recognize the robot at first glance. Rather than hovering in the air, the robot was suspended on a pair of legs loosely screwed into the sides of its barrel. A pair of arm extensions accompanied them. Heat rose to Dice's face. All the limbs were poorly designed, their wire frames being held together by thin rods and springs.
He said nothing. There was no point in shaming the robot. Clearly, it had put the limbs on to impress.
"Are you excited for the night's upcoming proceedings?"
"Well, you set such a high bar. How couldn't I be?"

The robot playfully slapped Dice on the back. Dice's grimaced as something pricked his skin and a chill shot up his spine. His eyes flitted to the side to find that the robot's arm was tipped with knife-like ornaments.
"Well, I suppose that we should be going," the robot said. It pressed the keypad inside the capsule. They were shut into an ear-piercing descent.
"I never have caught your name," the robot said. Dice felt the urge to ignore him, but the robot had raised its voice over the grinding capsule.
"Oh... Me?" Dice asked, with a chuckle. "I'm Dice. Dice Raymond."
"How peculiar."
"You're one to talk... What's your name again?"
"You did not remember my name?"
"I like to think that I have a strong memory. And, as I recall, you never finished telling me your name."
The robot made a harsh clicking sound in its throat — he was trying to laugh.
It rattled as it began listing off the digits to its name. Dice cut it off before it could finish.
"You know what? I'm just going to call you Rob. Is that alright?"
Red light and steam flooded the capsule as the doors slid open, and Dice stepped into the street.
"Why, thank you," Rob said. "No homo sapiens have ever taken the time to give me a nickname before."
"Yeah? Well I made sure to put a real lot of thought into it," Dice said, dryly.
He stopped to look around. Had the street always been this big? Aging structures loomed over his head, and lumbering power generators peppered the street. He was just a speck amidst it all.
"Where are we supposed to go again?" Dice asked.
Rob turned the corner of Dice's apartment building, entering an alleyway. Dice followed, but goosebumps rose on his forearms as they brushed against rusting iron.
Shoulders bumped between the walls — there was less than a meter of space between one building to the next. Several centimeters of water covered the ground, soaking his ankles to the skin.

Dice looked up to find a ceiling where the two buildings converged. Computer processors and an entanglement of wires were strewn along it. Random sparks of electricity randomly arced between them, lighting it up in a blue glow. The only other light in the alley came in the form of straggling red rays that had lost their way from the street.
Dice kept his distance as Rob brought him deeper into the alley. Rob's legs fizzled at each step in the water.

There was a splash. Rob slid forward and gripped the alley walls with his arms. Plaster splattered the water as Rob dislodged his arm. He'd left behind thick gashes — gashes that were only a few among far too many.

A series of horrific images flashed through Dice's head — headlines of robotic kidnappers and murderers. He looked behind, to see the distant shadow of the street. He looked back to Rob. They'd been walking for a while, but Rob gave no indication that they were getting any closer to his home. The alley just didn't seem to end. What if Rob was just leading him along?
Dice's eye broke into a fit of twitching. This was a huge mistake.
"You live down here?" Dice asked. "Must be a long walk."
"Oh, not down here," said Rob, clicking his tin throat. "Only defectives ever bother living down this alley."
Rob kicked at the water, knocking a metal head in the air.
"That's just great..." Dice said. "Where do you live, then?"
"We're almost there."
Dice searched through his list of stock excuses to find one that would give him an out. His stomach sunk. He was too deep in the alley to try turning back now.
"Ah! Here we are."

Rob stopped and stooped over. Dice frowned. The place they'd stopped was indistinguishable from any other spot in the alley. The walls were still covered in gashes, the ceiling was still sparking with molding wires, and the ground was flooded in water.
"I don't see it," Dice said. "Where are we supposed to be going?"
"Under."
"What?"
"I don't live down this alley. I live under it."
"There's really that big of a distinction between the two for you?"

Rob submerged his head and arms. When he reeled himself back up, he held a large metal plate in the air. A whirlpool had formed in the ground. Dice turned up his hearing aid — there was a faint echo of something sloshing as it hit the ground. The whirlpool must've been spilling into a hole.
"Go on," Rob said. "I'll come behind you, and put the plate overtop of us.

Dice squinted into the hole. It was pitch dark and had no bottom in sight. His heart raced. He thought about running. Though, he was painfully aware that Rob was hovering behind him, with a heavy metal plate in hand.
Dice begrudgingly squatted down into the water and slid into the hole.
Water sprayed in his face. His eyes burned. He tried to find direction, but he'd been blinded. Flailing his limbs, he managed to grip onto something. A metal bar.

His arm seared with pain and the bar was slick, but he held on as tight as he could. Jerking half his body to the side, he managed to swing his right arm to the bar. His feet found another row of bars below him.
"A ladder," Dice sputtered. "Thank god."
Despite the downpour, he started down. His feet slid a few times. He nearly fell after missing one bar entirely. However, he somehow managed to make it down on the ground.
The water stopped pouring. There was a clang. Dice rubbed the water from his eyes, looked up, and saw Rob climbing down the ladder.
"Maybe next time I should be the one to put the metal plate down," Dice shouted to him.
"According to my analysis, humans aren't as strong as robots," Rob said. "It's only hospitable that I be the one to handle it."
Dice rolled his eyes.

He shivered. His hair was soaked and he was coated in silt. Dice tried cleaning the grime off his face with his shirt sleeve, but only made it worse. His fingers pinched his soggy bodysuit, peeling some of it off his skin. To no avail.
"Allow me to pull this switch for you," said Rob.
There was a clang, followed by a row of lights blinking to life. Dice squinted as he tried to adjust. A concrete cave stretched around him and shaped into a sort of bowl.

He was standing on a sturdy concrete platform, built into the cave's wall. Though, ahead of him was a bridge suspended over rushing, briny water. Dice craned his neck forward. It was so long. What was even on the other side?
Maybe he wouldn't even have to walk across it. Maybe his platform was all the exploring he'd have to do.
"What do you think of the entrance?" Rob asked.
"I think it looks pretty nice."
Rob steamed as he processed the words. Then, he walked toward the bridge.
"Follow me to the main room."

Dice's muscles quaked. The bridge swayed at each step he took, and the water gurgled below him. It begged for his attention. The cave swung. He had to keep his head up. Whatever he did, he couldn't let himself look down.
Leaning forward, he held to a railing in Rob's back. Somehow, the swinging slowed. The end of the bridge came into focus.
The nausea faded, but everything was still wrong. He took a second look at Rob. He shouldn't have needed his help. He should've been able to get across on his own. It was just a bridge.

Once he'd made it to the other side and regained his balance, he jerked his hand away from Rob's back. Looking down to the watch on his wrist, he sighed. It was only 18:00. How long would it be before he could leave?
"Welcome to my home!" Rob said.
They were in a wide tunnel that stretched on endlessly. It had to at least be five times the width of a transport tube. Dice's mouth went dry.
