"This is where you live?"

"It's where I live, as well as where I work. I maintenance all the plumbing that runs through these tubes. There are constantly leaks and fluctuations, because the water-line wasn't properly designed down here — too many government cutbacks during its construction. Decay doesn't help either..."
Dice nodded.
"How many apartments are you responsible for?"
"About five hundred. However, there are four other water-lines that run parallel to this one, so I'm only 25% responsible for the plumbing in each apartment."
"And you do this job all alone?"
Rob doubled over and squealed through his metal throat.
"No. I have plenty of family to help me," Rob said. "In fact, it's dinner time. Would you like to meet them?"

Dice was frozen. Rob took his silence as a "yes” and led him through the tunnel. They didn't stop until they reached a smaller tunnel that had been burrowed into the concrete. Dice tried to peer in, but all he could see was a pitch blackness.
"Come on," Rob said, entering.
"I don't have the advantage of night-vision like you do," Dice said.

Rob stopped short, and stared Dice in the eye. Dice stared back. An ominous cloud hung between them. Dice wasn't sure how long he stood there, unblinking and unwavering, before he couldn't stand to stand there any longer. However, he knew it had been long enough for something to snap.

As he reluctantly followed Rob into the darkness, he looked back at the ever-shrinking light from the main tunnel. He should've never agreed to come to dinner. All it would've taken was an excuse. Any half-baked excuse.
There was a prolonged scrape. A glaring light flickered on. Wincing, Dice shielded his eyes.
"Say hello to my family," Rob said.
Dice could only make out vague shapes and shadows. He turned up his hearing aid but picked up an overabundance of static.
"Hello," Dice said, as he groped around the room.
"Please, take a seat," said Rob.

Dice's leg jammed into a slab of metal. With a short whimper, he felt around it — it was a chair. He sat down and rubbed the fresh bruise on his leg. A creak and then a thud resounded as Rob sat across from him.
"As is human custom, I believe it's time for us to become acquainted with one another," Rob said. "This is model 2970—."
"That's alright, I can give them my own human nicknames," Dice said, pointing at the blurry figures in front of him. "That's Robby, that's Robert, that's Roberta, and that's... Bob."
"'Bob' is a backup power generator," Rob said, pointing a finger to the left.
Dice gave pause to narrow his eyes in the finger's direction.
"Yes. Yes, he is."
Rob fizzed, and bobbed his head between each of the figures. He must’ve been trying to comprehend all the names.
Once finished, Rob gave a mellow "thank you". Dice returned it with a half-hearted "you're welcome", as he started rubbing his eyes. They were watering.
"Could you please turn the light down," Dice said, still rubbing.
"Why, of course."
Dice winced and adjusted his hearing aid as Rob's arm made an ugly scrape against the wall. There was a smooth snap. The light's intensity decreased and Dice’s vision began to clear.
"Your family is very quiet," Dice said.
"Indeed, they are," Rob said, with a clicking in his throat. There was a ding. "That must be dinner."

Rob walked to a small furnace in the back. A film lingered over Dice’s eyes, but he was finally able to make out more of the room. It was a jagged concrete hole that looked as though it had been chiseled out by Rob himself. There were few items of décor, and the items of décor the room did have were purely practical — a charging station, an assortment of wires, an old filer unit, and an outdated computer projector.

Dice looked back to his table, and his pulse came to a halt. Across from him was a rusted robot with protruding limbs that hung limply and a head that was only held to its torso by a thin rods. Dice thought it must’ve been deactivated for decades. That is, until its eyes managed to flick back and forth. Even as Dice’s vision completely cleared, he couldn't take his eyes off it. The robot couldn’t take its eyes off him. For a moment the robot seemed to look away, and Dice let his gaze wander — but the robot’s eyes shot back the moment he did.
What thoughts were running through the robot’s decaying mind? Why did it stare at him?
"This is your family?" Dice asked, furling his lip.
He couldn’t hide his emotions anymore. This was too much.
"Yes. I informed you of this approximately three minutes ago. Did you forget? I thought you said that you had a strong memory."
Dice warily kept his eyes on the robot across from him. “That doesn't mean there aren't things I'd love forgetting."
There was a slam as Rob shut the furnace. Steam spilled into the room, and Rob raised a platter above his head.
"Sorry," Rob said. "I'd intended to prepare human food, but I couldn't obtain any. If you don't mind, I'll be serving energy packets instead."
Dice eyed the steaming black cubes on the platter. Just putting one in his mouth would send a fatal shock through his body.
“No thanks. I don’t have much of an appetite tonight.”

This had to be some sort of prank. He looked back over his shoulder, to the dim patch of light where the main tunnel had been. It wasn't too late. Yet as he went to stand, something tugged on him and kept him to his chair.
Maybe something would come out of all this. He just needed to wait it out for a little longer.
"Those energy packets look extremely outdated," Dice said, as he watched Rob pass them around the table.
The packets Dice was used to seeing were silver, and had a rainbow tint to their edges when they were hit by light at just the right angle.

"They are," said Rob. "My employer only pays me in reserves, due to my job's perceived ‘low’ stature. But it's no matter. It's better that I'm provided the means survive than not at all. At least I haven't been disposed of due to defectiveness, like more unfortunate robots have been."
"’Unfortunate’ isn't the word that I'd use… Those 'defective' robots are typically responsible for mass catastrophe when they malfunction."

"Point noted. I'll also maintain that there are upsides to being paid in expired energy packets. They oftentimes give processor boosts, when installed at the right temperature. I assume that's why they're Roberta's favorite."
Dice’s eyes swam as he looked for which of Rob’s mangled robots were ‘Roberta’, before giving a defeated nod.
"This seems to be quite the important job" Dice said, as Rob shoved an energy pack in his back. Dice flinched as it crunched. "How were you assigned it, exactly?"
"Like any robot is assigned any job: I was produced for a set purpose and given the job accordingly. My body is most fit for fixing leaks and repairing damage. It's hardwired into me."
"And, in this job, do you ever get to leave? Does it ever get lonely?"
The crunching in Rob's body stopped. Dice smirked. Perhaps there was some amount of vulnerability under the metal shell after all.

"Loneliness is not a feeling that I'm subject to," Rob said. "Even if I were, I have no reason to feel lonely. I have all these robots at my disposal. I'm also able to monitor people's rooms, via a series of pipe barometers: I know how much water each apartment uses per day. I'm even aware of when the apartment owners leave, and when they return. In this way, I'm a part of the lives of everybody in this building without even ‘being in their lives’ at all."
Dice's smile disappeared. His lip quivered. How many other robots knew this much about people?
"So, these robots are all the friends you have?" Dice asked.

"Depending on your definition of the word, yes. I collected them as bits of scraps I've found flowing through the sewage… You wouldn't believe what some people dump down here. Sometimes, full robots. Sometimes, full people. It's truly a tragedy."
Dice’s muscles tensed.
"So, what is your job?" Rob asked. "You never did mention it to me."
Dice tried wiping away the sweat forming on his forehead with his drenched sleeve.
"It's too complicated to understand."
"Nothing is too complicated for my mind to comprehend."
"Yes..." said Dice. He gulped. "But... Well, I never said that it was too complicated for you to understand. It's too complicated for me to understand."
Rob's throat rumbled as he prepared to speak.
"So, I've heard a rumor that you robots are programmed never to come up to the surface while working these types of jobs," Dice said, cutting him off and putting out a fake chuckle. "Is that right?"
Rob nodded and his digitized face formed into a cheery expression.
"That's correct."
Dice's jaw clenched. He readjusted his position in his chair.
"So, then... How is it that you came to my room when I first moved here?"
"I came to meet the new neighbor, of course. There is nothing in protocol prohibiting that."
Dice raised an eyebrow.
"And this morning? How did you run into me?"
"I decided to come above the surface this morning."
"Why? That. Does. Not. Compute."
Rob turned away, and went back to crunching his energy pack.
"Rob, why did you come above ground this morning?"
"I assumed that... I assumed that you had left your room. I wanted to make sure that you were invited to dinner, as I make sure of with all human visitors."
“Convenient assumption.”
“Indeed.”

Dice took another look around the room, with its tattered walls, tangled wires and bits of scraps. He took another look at the rusted robot, which was still staring at him. Dice still hadn't figured out how to tell if a robot was lying or not. He wasn't even sure if a robot was capable of lying. However, he knew one thing: no human had ever ventured down to Rob's cove before.
"Well, thank you for the wonderful meal," Dice said, standing up from his chair. "I’m sorry, but I really need to be going."
The rusted robot's eyes were boring through his head. Rob's head screeched as it turned to face Dice. Dice’s legs were twigs.
"Already?" Rob said.
"It's… human custom to leave early, on the first dinner," Dice explained. "Goodbye."

Rob held out his arm for a handshake. However, Dice only took a glance at the razor-sharp tips of Rob's before walking to the exit. Dice's walk turned into a sprint when he heard Rob get up from the chair and his arms scratch across the walls.

Dice made it through the main tunnel but skidded to a stop at the bridge. He shuddered, and then started across slowly. Though, thinking he heard Rob stalking behind him, Dice let his fear possess him and ran the rest of way across. He climbed up the ladder and tried pushing the lid open. The first two tries, it didn't budge. He shouted when he looked down to find the jagged metal had left cuts in his hands.

In a rush of adrenaline, Dice gave the lid another shove, managing to push it out of its place. He powered through sheets of water until he was sprawled across the pool in the alley. Heart still pounding, he dragged the lid over the entrance to Rob's cove, and broke into another sprint. He didn't stop until the street was in clear view.
"That should've taken care of him," Dice said with a pant, as he doubled over.

He took in several deep breaths. He held his hand to his heart and listened as it slowed back to its normal pace. Grinning, Dice started back into a walk. The end of the alley was only a few meters ahead.

There was a crash. Dice whipped his head around as his heart shot out of his chest. The woman with the silver eyes was just standing in the middle of the alleyway. Staring. Sparks fell from the alley's ceiling, and fell in front of her. She didn't flinch.
A rush of air came back to Dice's lungs. He could've left. He could've ran. He didn't.
"Who are you?" Dice asked. He made an attempt to return the piercing gaze.
The woman didn't respond. Dice tried reading her face, but the darkness of the alley shrouded it from view.
"Answer me," Dice said.
His voice was cold. Metallic. It was a voice that he'd only ever used in the secret of his apartment. Yet, the woman was unfazed.
The woman must've just been deaf, and had just lost her way to her apartment. That was all. He checked the watch on his bodysuit. It was getting too late to keep bothering with her.
Dice walked out of the alley, and went to turn toward his apartment building. However, he couldn't stop himself from taking one last look back at the woman.
She was gone.
A lump formed in Dice's throat. His arms trembled. When he reached his apartment's capsule transmitter, he'd forgotten his password. It took a few tries before he made it to his room.
His mind left in tatters, Dice played a game of chess. He lost. The game must've glitched. That was all.

It was probably from a vestigial part. He bent down and popped open his computer projector. Pulling out a rod that had electric sparks coming off the tip of it, he slid a switch on its side of it to turn it off.
He lifted up the panel where his tools were kept, and placed the rod inside. He'd intended to remove that part at some point anyway.
Dice etched a rod of metal along the glass tube. Ten weeks. Ten weeks since he'd been trying to escape.
How long had he been there though? There was no telling. It felt like eternity. Though, there was no eternity that could've felt hellish as this...
A shout. What was out there? Dice pressed his face against the glass.
Blackness. Only blackness.

Something cold clamped around his shoulders, and pulled him back. He hit the ground, and pain rippled through his back. He looked up. His eyes welled with terror. A metal bowl descended upon him, and then fastened around his scalp. Electricity tore at his skin and made his head ache. A screen lit up in front of him. Suddenly, he was in an entirely new world.
Chapter 7:

Even with the aid of sedatives, Dice couldn't get any sleep for the next few days. He felt trapped inside of his room. Trapped inside of his sleep tube. And, whenever he shut his eyes, trapped inside of himself. His dreams tormented him, sending him through a spiral. He was always walking through the alleyway, never stopping to rest. The water would rise higher, and the sparks would become more ferocious. But, there was no end in sight.

Dice would wake up, only to find that he wasn't truly awake. He was walking through yet another alleyway. He'd wake up again, and finally escape the dream — only to find himself in a living nightmare, lying on the floor of his room in the middle of a game of chess. Staring down his hall and at his door for a long while, Dice felt a fear of somebody or something knocking on it rip through him. Nobody ever did. The mere thought drove Dice insane nonetheless.

Despite his exhaustion, Dice kept at the case. He walked a randomly produced route through his street in the morning, and an equally random route at night. He'd try to catch the faces of as many people as he could, but made sure to never stay in the same place for too long. Even when he caught the eye of a somebody who seemed deserving of being followed, he never found anybody that left nearly as striking an impression on him as he wanted. There was an element of sheer malice he was looking for. A glint in the eye, angled in just the wrong way.

Dice was sitting on his couch in his apartment. His eyes were buried under rows of names and facial descriptions that he'd assembled over the past few days. He only had two days left. Two days to prove if he was a failure, or a success.

Perhaps the man with the twitchy eye could pass as the prime suspect? Or, maybe it was the woman who'd decided to wear three layers of bodysuits? The robot that carried an oversized bag of radials with it whenever heading to work, but never when returning from work?
The woman with the silver eyes?
The thought of her made him tremble.
Not her. Definitely not her.
Dice yawned. He felt his eyelids sink under the weight of it all. He tried opening them. No — he didn't need them open right now. He could afford them just a short rest.

Suddenly, the sky was above his head. The sun was out. Its rays danced across the tops of buildings — tops of buildings that he knew all too well. His old apartment was just ahead of him, and it suddenly occurred to him just how nice it looked. It had a modest dignity to it. His whole street did.
There was a roar as a transport tube whizzed overhead.
A roar.
Dice reopened his eyes, and gave a jump. The capsule transmitter had been making a noise. Somebody was at the door. He checked the time on his computer. It was 1:00.

His balance shorted out on him as he tried to stand, and he leaned on the wall to keep himself steady. His heart skipped a beat as he pressed each button on his keypad. He closed his eyes as his door peeled up. The moment it did, Dice heard something.
A heavy, panicked breathing.
Dice jumped back, and fell onto his side. He grunted, and rubbed his fresh bruises. Cautiously, he opened his eyes.
A jolt tore through him.

Nobody was there. The transmitter capsule wasn't even there. His door had opened up to an empty transmitter shaft. He could hear the transmitter capsule off in the distance, as it screeched in its ascent to his apartment.
Dice panted. Then he let out a sigh of relief. The panicked breathing that he'd thought he heard had been his own.
"Dice, you idiot," he said to himself, pulling himself up from the ground. "Nobody was here. It was all in your head."
He brushed himself off, walked to the edge of the transmitter shaft.
"That's right," Dice shouted down into the shaft. "There's nobody here! It's just me!"

He leaned back on his wall as the screeching of the transmitter capsule loudened. His head dipped into his hands. How could he have let himself scare so easily? His own breathing? It was utterly illogical.
Dice took a look at his computer projector. Then, he took a look at the transmitter capsule. It was awaiting his entry.
"I need a breath of fresh air," Dice said, rationalizing to himself.

He crouched down, and slipped through the gap between the floor and the entrance to the capsule. The capsule gave a whine, and started downward. Dice turned and brought his face to the opposite door. He closed his eyes, and listened to fragmented echoes of motors and wires slowly letting him down. The gears in Dice's mind turned as they tried to find the place of each gear and cog in the capsule. He failed, as was usual. Though, what wasn't usual was that he didn't really care. His head wasn't in the capsule. His eyes were on the door.

The door jammed as it tried to open. A cloud of steam squeezed its way under the crack the door had made. Dice crouched down, grabbed the bottom of the door, and forced it up. As he exited, the steam wrapped around him, traveling through his pores and into his lungs.
The whole world was a blur. Just heat and the color red. Yet, to Dice, this blur was indistinguishable from the blur he felt while sleeping on the floor of his apartment.

His head fuzzy, Dice started down the street. As he made his way around the bend, he noticed how quiet everything really was. It was just him, and the thud of his feet against the ground.  The thud echoed through the grates and calculator cages far below him.

The streetlights were soft, rather than the blinding blaze he was used to. They must've been turned down for the night. He could only see a few meters ahead of him, and what he could see was mostly in the form of billowing steam. He didn't like it.

Dice wasn't sure what he was doing outside. The longer he thought about it, the more he realized that there was no real reason at all. Did there have to be one? Despite the blurry world around him, everything strangely felt so clear.

On his way back to his apartment building, he sat on the ground and rested. He watched the grates high above him. Lights winked at him, and Dice felt calm inside of himself. He brushed the sweaty hair out of his face and prepared to stand up. He never stood up though. Instead, he waited. What for, he didn't know. He waited all the same.
Minutes burned as he stared at the lights. As a doze began overtaking him, he finally got  up and walked to the alleyway. The air thinned. The lights went even dimmer.
The world felt amiss. Something was being masked by the silence.
Clenching his fists and lowering his brow, Dice turned the corner.
The alleyway was empty.
Dice shook his head. It couldn't be. His mind couldn't be playing tricks on him for a second time. He treaded lightly into the alley. Flashes of his nightmares went by, but he ignored them.
"Hello?" Dice called out. "I know that you're here!"
He turned his aid up. Only the sparks overhead responded to his shouts.
"Come out! I know that you're here!"

Still nothing. Yet, for just a moment, Dice thought that he heard something stirring. Dice took a few steps forward, taking care to not make the water slosh. He waited a few seconds. There was more stirring. He snapped his head around, and looked for where it might've been from.
"Who is that?! Who's there!?"
Still no answer. Dice's heart tried to escape his ribcage.
There was a loud clatter. Then, a splatter. A whir.
Dice sprinted toward the noise.
"Who's there?!"
Once again there was no answer, but he saw a faint blue glow off in the distance. It became brighter. Brighter still. The whir loudened.
Dice jumped behind a mound of scraps, and trying to keep as much of his body obscured under the water as he could. The blue light finally whizzed by his head.

It was Rob. Dice squinted in confusion. He wasn't able to look for long though, because Rob stopped to turn around after reaching the end of the alley. Dice dunked his head in the water, and hoped Rob wouldn't be able to see him.
"Dice?" Rob said.
Dice grimaced, and lifted his head. He'd forgotten about Rob's night vision.
"Dice?" Rob said again.
"That's me."
Dice shook his head to rid the water from his hair.
"I was just looking for you!" Rob said.
A twinge went through Dice's chest as he shook his head.
"Just wonderful," Dice muttered. He raised his voice. "What are you doing out here, exactly?"
Rob paused for a moment, and descended closer to the ground. His hover exhaust made ripples in the water underneath him.
"I saw you were out of your room tonight," Rob said. "I'm tasked to study everybody's rooms, to make sure everybody is sleeping properly throughout the night."
Dice wasn't convinced, but stood up and tried walking back to his apartment.
He should've never stayed out. He was wet, tired, cold, and afraid. Worst of all, he was stuck with Rob. Following whatever semblance of intuition that he'd thought he'd felt hadn't been worth it.
"Did your sleep tube happen to short out last night?" Rob asked.
Dice turned around, and raised an eyebrow.
"Why would you ask that?"
"Just curious as to why you were awake is all. Everything is fine?"
"Yes."
Rob's digitized face flashed into a smile.
"Good. I'll see you again, sometime."

Rob's thin blue jet exhaust faded off into the distance, and the alley returned to black. Dice listened as the sparks flickered. He watched the ripples that Rob had left behind in the water, as they steadily disappeared. Dice kept his ear open for another sign of something stirring. Another sign that something was amiss.
Nothing.

He went back up the capsule transmitter, listening to the gears and pulleys as he went. He knew that if he was able to do just a little bit more — if he could just see through walls — he'd be able to tell what was going on. Though, he had limits.
The capsule transmitter had limits. At the time that it was supposed to let off at Dice's apartment, the capsule stalled altogether. Dice banged on the walls, and tried prying the doors open.
Dice looked at the ceiling of the capsule transmitter, where the emergency exit was. He could break open the glass case to the emergency button, and activate it.

As he raised his arm to the glass, the capsule transmitter reactivated, returning to its climb to Dice's apartment. Dice jumped up to the ledge once the door opened, and shimmied his way onto his apartment floor.
"I'm never doing that again," Dice said to himself, resuming his usual calculated demeanor.
He parted his sopping hair from his eyes and wiped some of the dripping water off of his face.
"Computer," Dice said.

He didn't finish. Just as he went to speak, there was soft clang behind him. He turned around. The head of a scrapped robot was laying on top of the capsule. Dice ran toward it, in the hope of looking up the transmitter shaft to see where the head had fallen from.
The door shut just before Dice could reach it.
Chapter 8:

The transport tube moved through the city in a dull crawl. The people chatting around Dice clung to each syllable they uttered. Even the thin clouds in the sky seemed to frozen in place. Dice had hoped he'd be able to get the morning over and done with. Instead, every second held him hostage.
Everybody around him was carefree. Happy. Oblivious. He couldn't help but feel a burning envy rise in his chest. If only they could know what he was about to deal with.

He looked down at his feet, and reviewed the list of people that he'd made. His stomach lurched at the thought of having to turn them in to Haynam. There was no telling how seriously his list of suspects would be taken.

A giddiness rose in his chest, in the pain's place. Once he turned in the list, it would only be a matter of time before he'd make his way to the top of the M.D.P.D's ladder. He'd finally be able to make a difference.

The transport car came to a stop at the wall. Dice raised his badge, and the transport car rolled through the wall's tunnel. As the transport tube let everybody off, Dice made his way through the garage of the police department, and then through the locker room.

The locker room was empty. Quiet. Just as it should've been. Dice had made sure to arrive extra early this morning. He wasn't going to allow himself a single extra error in Haynam's book if he could help it.

Dice slipped into his suit, tightened it, and went to attach his badge to his chest. His thumb slipped, pressing its activation button. The badge ripped out of his right hand. Dice dodged, and the badge bashed into the locker behind him.

Dice took a moment to caress his palm. A sting rippled through the torn muscles in his thumb, and blood seeped from his wound. The locker hadn't fared any better, with a large dent having been left in it by the badge. Dice deactivated it, scanned for peering eyes, and cautiously placed his badge on his chest. It purred as it attached to the mesh fabric. Dice's eyes widened for a split-second as he realized how dangerous it really was. Burying his awe back inside of himself, he went to his locker.

He pulled out a bandage strip out of a first-aid box and placed it over his thumb. As he drizzled a few drops of water over the strip, it dissolved into a bubbling mush. As it dried it grafted with the rest of his skin. Dice let out a soft grunt.
"Lesson number twenty," he said, mimicking Haynam's voice.

The strip let out another bubble as he used his right hand to open the exit door and enter the hall. He clenched his teeth and pinched himself to have a different pain to focus on. The only thing he hated more than heights were tissue replicators.
Dice took a whiff of the lemony scent in the hall. Maybe tissue replicators weren't the only thing.
Dice made it to the door of Haynam's office, and gave it a knock. No response. Dice knocked again. Still no response.

He brought his hand to the keypad, and punched in the combination that he'd remembered seeing Haynam use. Right before Dice pressed enter, he stopped himself. What if Haynam wasn't inside? What if he accidentally walked in on something he was supposed to see?
Dice took his finger off the enter button. There was a rush of air and adrenaline came as the door opened.
"Haynam?" Dice asked, peering his head through the door.

Dice kept on his toes as he walked in and was cautious that the metal mesh of his bodysuit didn't scrape against itself. All of the lights were off, but Dice could hear a quiet breathing just ahead. It was so slight that it almost sounded like the breathing of somebody trying to hide it.
A slam resounded. The door behind Dice had closed. The slice of light from the hall was gone. Dice was left in pitch dark. Even worse, the breathing had stopped.
There was a snore. A thump.
"Wha?" Haynam said, drowsily.
Dice relaxed his shoulders. He walked over to the light switch. Haynam shielded his eyes and let out a moan as the lights flipped on.
"Who’s there? What's going on!?"
Haynam was sitting behind his desk, with his eyes wild and fists out. Dice forced a laugh. It was all he knew to diffuse the situation.
"It's me," he said. "Dice! Dice Raymond? You scheduled for me to have a meeting with you this morning?"
Haynam let out another moan, and sunk back into his chair. It was folded all the way down, into a makeshift bed.
"Damn you, Dice," he said, with a bitter chuckle.
"Sorry about that," said Dice. He attempted to inject as much charisma into his voice as he could.
"Say sorry to yourself."
Haynam sat back up and threw a plasma gun on the table. Webs of red light ran through it. It had been set to kill. Dice wanted to respond, but a part of him had been ripped away in that moment.
"I was this close from blasting you away," Haynam said.
The room grew, towering over Dice. Or, had he shrunk?
"I wasn't aware that an officer could carry a gun," Dice said.
Haynam gave a sly smile. He pulled the plasma gun off from his table, and placed it back in a drawer in his desk.
"Officers can't," he said. "But, deputies can."
Dice gave a firm nod.
Haynam pulled up his chair, and then pressed a button. The stool raised in front of his desk.
"Please, take a seat," Haynam said.
He had a unique way of speaking that enraptured Dice. Cool. Calm. Methodical.
Dice shook his head. He was just tired. That was all.
"I fell asleep in my office again," Haynam said. "I was working overtime. Another riot... Sometimes I wonder why I even bother."
"I suppose that I could say the same thing, sir."
A glimmer flashed in Haynam's eyes.

"Yes, I suspect that you could," he said, with a smile. "That said, like I tell all of my other officers: there's no better working time than overtime! It's during the extra hours you put in that things count the most... You've been working hard on the case?"
"I sent the list to your database just this morning."
"Let's see it then."

Haynam turned on his projector. The list flashed in the center of the table. Haynam scrolled through it, studying all the names and descriptions Dice had gathered. A smile formed in the corner of his lip. Dice's heart skipped a beat
"This — this is a breakthrough on the case."
Heat rose to Dice's face.
"I wouldn't go quite that far," Dice said. "I just threw that together."
Haynam shook his head, continuing to stare at the list.

"No — I'm cross-referencing the names you've gathered," Haynam said. "All of your analyses add up. We need to have you work on more cases. We've sent other officers over there, and we've had our suspicions... But, your list really works to help clear everything up."
"I'm not particularly interested in continuing to do facial analyses."
Haynam looked up from his screen, and gave a fierce glare. His hand slipped under the desk.
Was he fingering his gun's drawer?
"Get interested," Haynam said, bringing his hand to his chin and meeting Dice's eyes. "If not, I'm sure that there are plenty of other facial analytics robots that we can enlist, and sta—."
"No, that's fine. I'm sure that we can work something out."
Haynam returned to his list, and flashed his teeth. How could he be so happy scrolling through the list, determining a person's future on a whim?
"This list just goes on and on..." Haynam said.
"You gave me a week. I used it."
"Definitely looks like that... Who's on the top of the list?"
Dice looked straight into Haynam's eyes. His mouth was dry, but he answered anyway.

"A robot," Dice said. "It works in the sewage department, under my apartment building. I'm not sure of its exact unit number, but I managed to recall that it began with these six numbers: 21168. It also will respond to the name 'Rob', if that helps."
Haynam stopped scrolling through the list of names.
"A sewage bot that works under your apartment?" he asked. "That's the guilty party?"
"According to my facial analytics, which only have been proven to have 60 percent accuracy... Yes."
Haynam's jaw hung open. His pupils expanded. He was clearly shocked. Yet, Dice thought he could detect a hint of pleasure.
"We've been trying to keep tabs on everybody living there, but we never thought... We were never really looking too closely at the low-level robots."
Dice forced a smile.
"Thanks. I'm quite confident that it's him."
He was punched in the gut as he said the words but didn't let on. Haynam grinned and clapped his hands together, oblivious.
"What makes you think that it's him?" Haynam asked.

"There was just something on the robot's face... The way that it acted. I've never liked robots much, but this one was especially hard for me to tolerate. I could tell that it was hiding something, Haynam. It was even studying the activity in people's apartments."
"That's part of the job of sewage bots," Haynam said. The cerebral gleam in his eye dimmed.

"Oh, I'm aware. However, his obsession with it... that wasn't part of his job. He'd document when people would leave and monitor them when they did. Worse, he was collecting outdated bits of technology — clearly a violation of U.R.O protocol. I suppose that would only be a minor violation, on its own... But, he had a strange desire to make the scrapped technology into his friends."
Haynam's eyes pierced through Dice.
"What type of technology was he collecting?"

"Old bits of robot parts, and computer processors. On their own, nothing that would've stood out as significant... However, this robot was still stealing technology and trying to repurpose it into new robots. I've never seen anything quite like it."
Haynam gave Dice a look, and shook his head in disbelief.
"That's definitely our guy," he said.
Dice returned the look.
"I wouldn't be so certain. This robot was suspicious, yes... But—."

"Your descriptions match everything that we've been looking for. I can't believe that we hadn't thought of looking where you looked sooner... The answer had been right under our noses. Literally. Thank you so much for your service Dice. I'll have you assigned to a new case within the next day or so."
A dark shadow came over Haynam's face, and he motioned toward the door. Dice stood up, as he scrambled to find the right words.
"Aren't you at least going to look through the list of other people?" Dice asked. "You can't just convict the robot without further evidence, can you?"
Haynam reached his hand out, and gave a deprecating smile.

"I'll take another look if you feel it's needed, but you did your job and you did it well," he said. "Your analyses, paired with the smuggled technology, should be more than enough to convict this robot. In about a day, we'll have a warrant to search his place and arrest him. The only thing close to 'further evidence' we'll need is your exact testimony to prove the robot's guilt. Though, that's a matter that should be resolved rather quickly..."
Dice slowly walked to the door, but kept his eyes on Haynam.
"And, when would you need to use my testimony to convict the robot?" Dice asked.
"A week, tops," said Haynam. "As I've told you before: we get things done quickly around here. This case in particular can't afford another delay. We'll have the U.R.O breathing down our back..."
Dice's finger spasmed as it pressed enter on the keypad. It could've used about a dozen more delays.
Chapter 9:
Night fell, coating Dice's apartment in darkness. Though, Dice didn't sleep. He didn't move. He sat on his couch, and stared at the wall.

Whenever his eyes closed, his nightmares returned more viciously than ever. He'd find himself in the alley, being chased by a pair of eyes. Harsh, silver eyes. If it wasn't that, it was Haynam pointing his plasma gun at his chest.
Dice's left eye twitched. In an effort to ignore it, he kept staring at the wall. It twitched again.
He put his hand over his eye and rubbed it until the muscles relaxed.
Relaxation was what he needed. His mind was wrecked by the stress of his job. That was all. He just needed to get away from it all.
Yet, the harder he tried pushing his thoughts away, the more agitated they became. His stress had started as a drizzle. Now it was a hurricane.
Why did he sell out Rob?
He knew why: he had to. The evidence of Rob's guilt was perfectly rational. Logical.
Logic couldn't erase guilt though.

There was something odd about Rob. However, there was something odd about every robot Dice had come across. They were machines: it was in their nature to act unnatural. Rob might've been off-putting. That didn't mean he was guilty. Worse yet, the only tool Dice had of determining somebody's guilt couldn't have worked if he'd tried.
Dice rested his chin on his hand. Perhaps Rob had deserved it. Perhaps there was a silver lining in the fact that one more robot was being gotten rid of — even if it was on false grounds.

The woman with silver eyes flashed through Dice's mind. Why hadn't he just turned her in when he had the chance? What was inside of her soul that was worth sparing? He could've at least mentioned a suspicious figure, but he hadn't even been able to do that.

Dice stood from his couch, and opened his window. His face turned to gravel. The fog and red light obscured his view of the street. Yet, while it might've just been an exhaustion-induced hallucination, he could see the alley. It was drawing him in.

Nothing made sense anymore. His world was a mess. There had been too many days without sleep. Too many days of self-doubt. Was it going to be like this at his job from now on? At his own apartment? He wouldn't be able to keep it up. There had to be a way out. A way to leave.
The fog whirled as a mouth opened through it, putting the entrance to the alley in clear view.
His hands clenched into fists. It was time.
Dice opened his toolbox, and pocketed his electric rod. He went down his transmitter capsule.

Dice turned the corner of his apartment, and trudged into the watery alley. He stared at the scraps of dead robots on the ground, and then looked up toward the sparking electricity in the ceiling. He activated his rod, and its own electricity burst out of each end.
His hand trembled as he raised the butt of the rod to his head. He winced. Just a tragic misfire of a spark, and his own spark would be out.

The hairs on his forearm raised as he drew the rod closer to his forehead. Beads of sweat streamed down his face. Fear lumped in his throat. He could anticipate the pain. Yet — some part of him knew that he had to go through with it.
It was time, and he hated being late.
There was a shout of pain. Then a bang.
Dice dropped the rod. He snapped his head around. Somebody was there.  He turned up the dial in his ear. There were more shouts, and more crashes.
Whoever the sounds were from were deep down the alley — just where Rob was supposed to be.

Death could wait. Dice picked his rod up from off a rusted robot. Raising it above his head, he cautiously made his way through the water. The succeeding outbursts of noise were more spread out, but they also grew in volume. Dice was able to discern the shouts — they came from different people each time.
Was Rob being arrested?
Once Dice had made it halfway through the alley, the shouts and crashes stopped altogether. A hush descended over it. Then, a splash. Several splashes. Somebody was running toward him.
Dice pressed himself against the wall. He froze. As his rod sparked, it revealed the person who'd been running: the woman with the silver eyes.

The wind was knocked out of Dice's gut. He'd been hit. He writhed in shock as he was dunked in the cold water, and the pavement made impact with his chest. All the while he tried keeping his rod in the air, hoping it wouldn't make contact with the water.
"Oh god..." somebody groaned. "God... What the hell was that?!"
They groaned again.
"When did robots start going out on evening strolls?"
It was the woman.
Dice stood up, rubbed his back, and pointed his rod in the general area of where he thought she must've been.
"I'm not a robot," Dice said, his voice turning to steel. "I'm armed with a power rod, and I can turn you into a sparking corpse if I want. Explain yourself."
There several splashes. He kicked his foot in their direction, making impact. The woman let out a grunt.
"Great," she said. "I always knew you were one of them..."
Dice closed his eyes and shook his head in confusion.
"One of what?"
The woman said nothing. Dice stepped forward, brandishing his rod. A fountain of electricity spouted from it.
"Tell me your name," Dice said.
Her eyes swam around the alley, and then fixed back on the rod in Dice's hand.
"Stick."
"Your name is stick?"
"Yeah, Stick. Matches— Matches Stick."
Matches had her back against the wall, and her hands were raised over her head. Dice glanced at the foreboding shadow his rod cast on the wall. Was he on the wrong side of the weapon?
"Matches Stick?" Dice repeated, lowering his rod. "Is that supposed to be convincing?"
Matches pulled her hands down and gave a sheepish smile.
"Better than nothing."
"Well, if we're giving out names, mine is Dice Raymond."
Dice was about to offer a handshake, when there was a bang. He snapped his head around. The alleyway quieted back into a hush, but something crept around Dice's gut.
Dice turned to Matches and increased the voltage of his rod.
"Explain to me what's going on."
The smile faded from Matches' face.
"Drop the rod and let me go. I promise: you'll never have to deal with me again."
Blood pumped through Dice's veins as his face as it construed into a scowl.
"That's rich. You'll be back to stalking me by tomorrow night. Now, I'm giving you an ultimatum: either you give up your story, or I give you up to whoever you're running from."
Matches put her hand to her temples and let out a groan. Dice scrunched his face.
"They're coming," Matches said, lowering her hand from her head. "Sorry, Rice: I have to run."
"What? Run?"
Matches pushed past Dice.
"Yeah, run," Matches said. "Ever heard of it?"
Dice's head was spinning. There were shouts and splashes from not far behind him. Dozens of thoughts. Too many.
His eyes widened.
"Wait," Dice said. "I have an idea. We need to head to my apartment. It might not work... But, it'll at least buy you some time."
Matches gave a glare.
"Yeah, no thanks... I've already seen your apartment. The place is empty — nowhere to hide. Not to mention, it's a dump. "
Face turning crimson, Dice shook his head.
"No, you don't understand... I have a way to get out of this."
Dice looked behind and his mouth went dry. The warm red glow of blasters loomed through the darkness.
"I'm trusting you, and you're going to have to trust me," Dice said.
Matches' pupils shrunk as the glow flooded them. Her eyes flitted back to Dice.
"Yeah, alright... I could probably use a bright idea."
The two turned out of the alley, and then to Dice's capsule transmitter. Dice's hands trembled as he pressed each button on his keypad. Despite the humid air, he was chilled to the bone. Numb.
As the transmitter's door slid open for them, there were blasts and screams from the street. Nothing was visible through the steam, though he already could smell the death hanging in the air.
Dice looked at Matches. Her eyes were clouded with terror.
"They know that we're here," Matches said. "They're going to catch us. We don't have enough time."
"We'll make time, then," Dice said. "I'm good with that."
The doors shut, and the transmitter capsule screeched into its ascent. Dice winced. If the pursuers hadn't known where they were already, they certainly knew then.
"Who are the people chasing you?" Dice asked, after a moment of silence.
Matches shuffled to the side.
"Alright then, don't tell me..."
The elevator jittered and slowed. Maybe he'd made a mistake. Why hadn't he called the police and reported her the moment he'd seen her?
It was too late to go back now though. He wasn't in the mood to have a dead body on his conscience.
The screeching of the capsule transmitter stopped and opened to the bottom floor of Dice's room.
"I'm going to need you to climb up there," Dice said.
Matches stared at the wall.
"Come on! Quickly!"
Shaking her head, as if from a trance, Matches went up to the wall and climbed up the ledge. Dice scrambled after her.
"Alright," Dice said. "Head down the hall to the main room. I'll be there in just a minute"

Dice ran to the table of trophies and knocked the trophies to the floor. The table moaned as it was dragged from the wall. Turning the table on his side, Dice slid it across the floor. It hit the capsule transmitter, barricading the gap between his floor and the capsule's narrow opening.
The capsule bounced and then descended down its shaft. The doors to Dice's apartment went to shut but were stopped by the table.
The pursuers must've called the capsule transmitter down. There was only so much time left.
Dice sprinted directly to his computer projector. Tearing its side panel off, he fumbled for the spot to place his power-rod.
"What are you doing?" Matches said.
"Fixing my computer.
"Why?"
"So that I can destroy it."
Matches raised an eyebrow.
"And I thought I was the crazy one..."
Dice kept at the repair. All of the rods were connected. The panel was ready to be put in place. He just needed to reinforce the repaired rod with a screw.
Where was the screw?
Dice paused to look up at Matches. Her hand was pressed back to her temples.
"Everything is going to be fine," Dice said, as he frantically searched around the floor.
It was just one part. Why did it have to go and disappear now, of all times?
"I have no idea what you're doing, but you're not going to finish in time," Matches said. "They're already coming up. I can hear them."
Dice whipped his hand to his ear to turn up his aid. She was right. There was the slightest shriek off in the distance. It was getting louder.
"Well, isn't that exactly what I need to hear right now?" Dice said. "Please, tell me more."
"These are hitmen. They'll easily be able to hack your door. And, if they can't do that, they'll find a way to get it open."
Dice stood up and brushed himself off.
"Now you tell me..."
There was a slight clink, followed by a roll. Dice scanned the ground, until something glinted. The screw. Dice snatched it up and tightened it into the electric rod to the computer.
"Done," Dice said.
He flipped the switch on, activating the computer.
"Computer! Code: refraction. Activate program: trial simulation delta!"
The projector whirred, and the holographic screen filled with dead pixels as it assumed its base format. Dice glanced at the reflection in the corner and watched Matches' jaw drop.
"Did you just activate an illegal virus simulator?" Matches asked.
"What else does it look like?"
Dice swiped through the screen, his eyes flashing through each prompt in a blur. He could hear the computer already starting to squeal. Yet, he wasn't going fast enough.
"Why do you have access to one of those?" Matches persisted. "The only people that I've heard about using them are terrorists."
Dice gave a small frown but tried to keep focused on the screen. The capsule transmitter was in clear earshot.
"You're the one being chased by government hitmen," Dice finally answered, with a strain.
"That doesn't mean you shouldn't be."
Dice glared at Matches.
"I like decoding and disabling complex viruses, okay?" Dice said, with a sigh. "Especially ones that can learn. It keeps my mind sharp."
Matches held a skeptical gaze but kept quiet. All the better. Dice's head was aching as he tried outpacing the projector. No, not just the projector's pace — all of his own former paces.
The capsule transmitter slowed. The screeching stopped. There were thumps from inside the capsule. Time was up.
Dice tried pretending the thumping wasn't there and kept himself in tune with the projector. He just needed to push himself a little harder.
"What are you doing?" Matches said, her voice cracking. "They're here!"
Dice's door slid open. They'd hacked it. The only thing separating the hitmen from the room now was the table that Dice used to obscure the entrance.
It was only going to buy a minute, at most.

There were bangs and shouts for help. The hitmen must've thought that they were trapped in the capsule. Sparks and smoke flared off the projector. They just needed to stay fooled for a little while longer.
"Get off the projector," Matches hissed.
Dice raised his hands and took a step back.
"Done."
Bolts of electricity leaped from the projector and clung to the walls.
"When this thing goes off, I want you to stay in here," Dice said, turning to Matches. "And when you fall, stay in a crouched position."
"When I fall?" Matches asked.
"Also: you're going to need to put that on."

Dice pointed at the feeding apparatus. He jumped away from the projector and ran into the hall. His ears rung as the projector exploded and went up in flames. Dice let out a sigh of relief. The sprinklers turned on, the screen went up between the hall and the room, and the floor slid out to turn into a vacuum.
He looked around for Matches. She was already gone. Had she managed to hook up the ventilator from the feeding apparatus in time?
There was a blast. Dice looked behind him. A gaping hole had been made in his table. A heavily armed hitman was crawling out of it.
No — not a hitman. A soldier.
"Thank God! You firemen arrived just in time!" Dice said, faking a fit of hysterics. "I thought that I was going to die!"

The soldier stood over Dice, glowering. Dice averted his gaze and caught the eyes of several other soldiers crawling through the hole in his table. They were fierce. Focused. Whatever thoughts might've been running through their heads were well hidden under their helmets.
"Funny. There's approximately 1.5 more of you than the usual number in fire responders," Dice said.
He laughed. Nobody laughed with him.
The soldiers lined themselves along the wall. Steam carried out from within the capsule. Then, a grunt. Two hands gripped to the hole in the table. One metal, and one of scarred flesh.
A man crawled out of the hole and brought himself to his full height. He towered over everybody in the hall. Sheer confidence dripped from him.

Dice looked into the man's face. The left half of it was that of a normal man. Stern and worn, but warm at the same time. Though, the right half of his face was metal plate. There was no expression etched onto it. No semblance of humanity. The only ornament it had was a red ball lodged under the slope of the forehead. An eye.
The eye turned down to look at Dice. Dice's intestines turned inside out. As he looked into the eye, there was no soul. Just the glare of a light.
"Take aim," the man said, with a low rumble.

The soldiers lifted their guns and pointed them toward Dice. Though, the guns weren't like the usual plasma guns Dice had been acquainted with. Each one had a luminescent blue funnel attached to its top.
The man smiled and bent down to put himself at eye-level with Dice.
"For firefighters we have pretty odd looking 'water guns', don't we?" the man said, with a chuckle.
A few of the soldiers chuckled with him.
"I'm Captain Knowles," the man said. "Though, my harsher critics have dubbed me 'the knife'. Tell me: do you think that I got that name by fighting a few fires?"
There was a snicker. Knowles' left eye flared with anger.
"You're soldiers?" Dice said, widening his eyes and pretending to be surprised. "I had no idea!"

"Don't get any ideas either," Knowles said, displaying half of a toothy grin. "If you think you can play dumb with me, stay dumb. I know the person we're pursuing followed you here. You can either turn her over, or we'll take her by force. Your choice."
Dice didn't drop his act, despite Knowles trying to bore right through him. Nothing seemed to escape his red eye.
"You're chasing somebody?" Dice asked. "Well, that's exciting. Unfortunately, I can't say I've seen anybody myself."
"'I can't say I've seen anybody myself,'" Knowles parroted.

He smiled and made a dramatic sweep of the arms. Dice winced at the sight of his bionic arm jerking in the air. As he watched Knowles' face, Dice caught a sliver of something cold and detached. Yet, Knowles kept his smile all the same.
"Cadet: you know what to do."

Dice's reflexes kicked in, and he attempted to dodge a soldier running at him. Yet, just as he lunged, a blue film obscured his sight. The nerves up his spine and down his shoulders tingled. He tried to look around, but his eyes were limp. His entire body was.

The film disappeared. Air fled from his nostrils as he received a blow. He sprawled on the ground, with a deep bruise in his side. Dice's arms quivered as he went to push himself back up, but the soldier jabbed his knee into his back. Then, an elbow into the back of his neck.
Dice's cheek squealed as he turned his head to the side. He looked up, to see a fluorescent blue barrel pointed at his head.
"Zero-point energy beams," Knowles said, with a laugh. "You're playing with the U.R.O. With power. Try another move like that, and we'll freeze you again."
"What's going on here?" Dice said. He spread each word out, taking care to avoid exposing his pain.
Knowles walked down the hall, his metal leg leaving a gouge next to Dice's head as he went. His footsteps drew toward the main room. Dice closed his eyes. Had the vacuum and glass screen gone up yet?
Knowles' footsteps quieted and echoed. Dice gave a sigh of relief. It had. All traces of Matches were gone.
"Please let me go," Dice said. "I'm being held against my will. There's no reason to believe I've committed any wrongdoing. I'm an officer, for crying out loud."
Knowles gave a whistle. The soldier pressed his knee down harder on Dice. Dice clenched his teeth and held back a grunt. The soldier shouted, and Dice's back crunched. Dice still didn't grunt.
Knowles' footsteps clanked as he came closer. He let out another chuckle.
"You're knee-deep in a whole world of trouble," Knowles said, projecting his voice with relish. "Literally. Now, I'm not sure where our gal went, but she sure as hell didn't disappear into thin air."
One of the soldiers cleared his throat.
"Sir, it's possible that she hacked this apartment to make it seem like it had a recent visitor — sent off a false signal. It'd explain why his projector exploded."

Knowles kneeled down to Dice's face, and stared him in the eye. Dice could smell the fumes coming off of him. Knowles' face stiffened in a fury that was inhuman. Every muscle of his face, devoted to anger.
"Where is the woman that was running in the alley?"
Dice gave a look of bemusement.
"I don't know what you're talking about," he said, in a voice that rang cold and hollow.
The pressure of the soldier's knee was relieved from his back. Knowles brandished his fingers. They were so close to Dice's face that Dice could read the small serial number imprinted in one of them.
A chill ran down Dice's spine as Knowles' fingers pricked along his back. Their tips were so sharp that they broke through his bodysuit and touched skin.
"Did you know that it takes a certain amount of pressure for something to break through the skin?" Knowles asked.
Dice needed to control his breathing. Just in and out. Keep it steady.
"100 psi," Knowles continued. "Screws, bolts, knives... You can lay on a bed of them and, if you don't hit that amount of pressure, nothing will happen. Go beyond that? Well... Sweet dreams."
The motor in Knowles's arm murmured as his fingers gave a short jab.

"A cold knife riding down a person's skin... A person's skin: it really isn't so different from a person's will, is it? Willpower is a resilient thing but, when pushed hard enough, it will snap. What will it take to break yours? How deep do I have to go?"
The fingers scraped against Dice's back. There was a twinge of pain as a shallow cut was left in their wake.
"I told you," Dice said. "I don't know who this person is, much less where they are. Here I was, thinking my night was awful when my computer exploded... Until you decided to blow my door off."
Knowles removed his fingers from Dice's back.
"My mistake," Knowles said. "I'm sorry."
He walked off. Dice could've stood back up. Though, he stayed in his place. Dice didn't know why, but his muscles remained tense. His ears sharp.
Knowles kneeled back down and grabbed Dice around the jaw.
"I'm sorry I wasn't aware that you were unbelievably stubborn."
Knowles released Dice once more, and walked toward the capsule transmitter.
"Get up," Knowles said.
Dice did. He wanted to drill his eyes into Knowles' face, but Knowles had already turned his back away.

"I know you're hiding her," Knowles said, simply. "I might not know where or how. But, I know that you are. And, I know that you're going to do something stupid with her. I'm going to give you a warning: no matter how clever you think you are, there's no winning. Have fun playing this game while it lasts."
Knowles gave a sideways glance. Dice maintained his dumbfounded expression.
"I'm sorry, but you have the wrong guy," said Dice. "If you think that you can just barge in here, and—."
"That's the spirit," said Knowles.
He whistled to the other soldiers.
"Alright, let's move out."
Each soldier slid through the hole in the table, and into the capsule. Knowles was the last one to pile in.

"We'll have a replacement table sent to you in about a week," he said, sounding chipper. "And, hell: if I'm in a good mood, maybe I'll send you a free meal with it. The food on this street is good, right?"
The transmitter capsule door shut behind him and screeched as it made its descent. Though, for the first time, it left Dice with true terror
Once Dice was sure that they were gone, he called up the capsule with his keypad, and made his own descent.
Dozens of equations ran past Dice's eyes. He struggled to answer each one. Each time he missed one, he received an electric shock that left his hand tingling.
The equations subsided into darkness. His left hand was limp. The darkness flickered, and he watched paragraphs of information speed by his eyes. Then, questions. Too many questions. Too many shocks.
Finally, rows of code streamed by. A firewall to a computer's security... Dice rearranged the code, bypassing it.
He hadn't been fast enough. A crown of electricity lapped at his head.
There was a beep. The bowl on his head unlatched, and he was free to the cold light of his containment tube. The tick-marks on the glass mocked him. How much longer would they get?
Dice's stomach churned. The ground was pulled out from underneath him. He hit the ceiling. The tube must've been turned upside down.
Suddenly, the ceiling was gone as well.
Darkness swallowed Dice. He groped aimlessly at the air. He wheezed as he hit the ground.
Was it the ground? A chasm flared below him in a series of murky green lights. Rows of iron tubes lined it, and a thin metal pathway was paved between them.
He stood up. He was floating in midair. Walking. His eyes followed the green trail. It seemed to go on forever. What was it?
He crouched down and pressed down his hand. His fingers left a streak on the air. His knuckles rapped against it. Glass. Of course. Why hadn't he thought of it before?
He lurched forward as a creak broke through the air. The chasm below him slid away. Or, was he sliding away from it?

There was a snap. Dice looked behind, to see a spotlight hovering over something. A series of spikes were built into a wall, grinding into one another. He recoiled as a chunk of metal fell into it, a screeched as it was torn to pieces.
The shredder was coming closer. No — he was coming closer. The glass was drawing him in.
His legs pumped and his heart pounded. He had to run. His lungs burned and his vision went hazy. No matter what, he couldn't let himself stop. He had to keep going.
Keep running.
Chapter 10:
The capsule shuddered to a stop and bleeped as it demanded a password for entry. Dice tore open the keypad, fiddled with the wires, and then put the keypad back in its place. The door opened.

Dice coughed as he was hit by a wave of smoke. He wafted it away with his arm. Leaving the capsule, he kept his steps soft and his gaze warily darting around. Everything was a matte gray. As his eyes strained, he squinted.

He walked through a narrow platform. Boiling water tanks, fizzling generators, and massive pumps towered around him. Their rotors clicked smoothly as they churned up and down. Dice smacked his lips, and grimaced. The air tasted bitter. A thick smoke rolled from the tops of the generators.
Dice sprinted down the platform and scanned each machine. There was only one that he needed to find.

Steam gushed out of the ceiling. Fire leaped from one machine to another. Dice jerked back when a stream of water dumped onto the floor in front of him. Though, once he made it far enough down the platform, the chaos subsided. He slowed to a stop.
There was a cluster of several high-pressure tanks. Each one was the size of Dice's apartment room, and had a large tube feeding into it from the ceiling. From the vacuums of each apartment.

Dice turned up his aid and put his ear up against them. They each only gave a soft hissing, until Dice reached the fourth one. There was the sound of something rattling against its metal shell. Dice ran to a lever at the end of the row of tanks, yanking it down. The hissing stopped.

Dice went back to the fourth tank. There was a little door in the front of it. Its latch creaked as Dice turned it. The latch jammed. Dice jiggled it, before finally raising his leg and kicking the door open.
"Hello?" Dice shouted into the hole.
Liquified steam plinked from the tank's ceiling and onto its floor. Dice raised his voice.
"Hello?!"
Something glinted inside of the blackness. It came closer. Matches' eyes.
Dice leaned into the hole, pulled Matches out, and ripped the breathing apparatus off of Matches' face. Matches gulped in the smoky air as if it were her first breath in years.

"Are you trying to kill me?" Matches asked with a cough, once she'd regained her balance don the platform. "I felt like I was going to die in there... In fact, I think that I almost broke one of my arms on the way down. My good arm."
"Sorry," Dice said, disgruntled.
"You saved my life. You better be sorry," said Matches.
Matches laughed, and Dice offered a fake laugh in turn.
"Well, thanks for that," Matches said, patting Dice on the back. "Probably would've died tonight without you."

Dice glared at Matches. Matches held her cheery expression, but Dice's thoughts went back to Knowles. There must've been more going on in Matches' head than she was letting on. Dice raised an eyebrow and looked away.
She couldn't possibly be that oblivious to the surrounding danger, could she?
"Glad that I'm out of there," Matches said, rubbing her right arm. "It was cramped in there. Could hardly breathe."
"Tough luck. You weren't the only one," said Dice.
There was a twinge down Dice's back. A phantom knife slid down it. Dice shivered.
Matches frowned.
"What do you mean?"
"What I mean is that I was tackled onto the ground, and nearly arrested. I thought you said those people were supposed to be hitmen?"
Shrugging, Matches sped toward the capsule transmitter.
"Sorry. Should I have called them friends, instead of hitmen?"
"They were U.R.O soldiers," Dice said, his voice raising. "You lied to me."
Matches smirked.
"Tough luck."
Dice blinked and tried to study Matches' face. Matches' head jerked away to avert his gaze. Despite this, Dice caught a hint of worry lining her brow.
"Captain Knowles says that he wants me dead," Dice said. "He wants you dead too. I have the right to know why... Tell me why."
Matches clawed at the controls to the capsule transmitter. She'd said nothing and everything at the same time.
Dice's eye twitched. The case files of the MDPD flashed through his head. His head pounded. He leaned onto a machine and tried controlling his breathing.
"What have I done?"
He looked Matches dead in the face.
"You should be in prison," Dice said.
Matches' eyes widened.
"Excuse me?"

"The government and the MDPD have been looking for a suspicious person living on this street," Dice said. "I was one of the officers responsible for finding them. I convicted a sewage bot who seemed suspicious. But... All this time..."
Matches chuckled, unfazed.
"Look at that: a cop helping out a convict. What are the odds?" Matches chuckled again. "Then again, I guess you won't be a cop for much longer."
Rage rose in Dice's chest. How could she be so indifferent?
"Do you realize what this means?" said Dice. "This is the end of my career. Everything that I've ever worked for."

"Yeah, I think that's what I just said," Matches said, drawing her words out. She paused to bang on the capsule door again. "Enjoy leafing through help wanted ads... If you're not held in a prison first."
Dice's neck tightened, and his fists clenched.

"If it's any consolation, maybe they'll put you in a prison in the Balcombe District," Matches said. "The weather there is a dream, and I've heard the facility is staffed with massage bots. God knows you could use one of them."
Dice scowled as Matches turned around and gave a sheepish grin.
"Anyway, could you help me get this thing open?"
The capsule transmitter stopped at Dice's floor. Matches climbed up the ledge, and through the hole in the table.
"I like what you've done with the place," Matches said.
Dice followed after Matches.

"Glad you like it," Dice said, coldly. "Because, you won't be staying here for much longer. Figure out what you're going to do to get away from these people, and then leave. Our little team-up? It never happened."
Dice stared at Matches, intensely. Matches sat in one of Dice's chairs, keeping her smirk on her face.
"Yeah — not going to happen," Matches said, spinning around. "I do, in fact, have a plan... I'd like to take a vacation across the U.R.O's border, and into the Kelvin Union. Heard about the place?"

Dice swallowed. The name left a fetid stain on his apartment. The Kelvin Union was a hotbed of deplorables. Robots had overrun the nation and driven it into the ground. There were even murmurings that Kelvin was waging a secret war with the U.R.O.
Matches nodded.

"I'll take that as a yes. Anyway, getting there is the teensy problem I've run into. My solution? It involves you and your police job. See, I'm going to need one of those special fighter jets that you guys zip around in."

Dice wanted to retort, but... Couldn't. He couldn't do anything. Matches locked her eyes onto Dice's, and Dice was locked in his place. Something reachid into his mind. It brushed against the walls of his skull and spun the room around. It froze time. It sped it up. Then, it left altogether, and Dice realized that he'd just gone a whole minute without being able to breathe.
Face red, he clutched his throat and took in a deep breath.
"What... Was that?" Dice wheezed. His forehead throbbed as he stroked it.
Matches' face went grim.

"That's a sample of what I can do," she said. "I can break into a person's mind... Ransack it... Turn it to mud. I'll admit though — some minds are very resistant. Yours, for example, kept me from being able to let you breathe."
Dice's heart fluttered, and his stomach churned.
"That's impossible."
"I guess you're going to have to redefine what you consider impossible."
Matches gave Dice a light punch in the arm.
"Don't touch me," Dice said. "I like to keep a bubble of personal space."
Matches laughed.
"I just broke into your mind... And you're upset that I touched you?"
Dice narrowed his eyes.
"Never break into my mind again."
"I don't want to go in your mind again myself. Do you ever clean up in there? That said... If you don't help me? Well... I might just need to."
Smarminess oozed from Matches. It was in her greasy hair, her overused smile, and the false confidence in her posture.
"Is that a threat?" Dice asked.

"It's whatever it needs to be, buddy. I'm just asking for a bit of help to get from point A to point B. If you can't scrounge up the kindness in your heart to give that help, then you've forced my hand."
Dice shook his head as his face furled in disgust. Though, his mind still felt as if had been put in a blender. Did he have much choice?
As it was: would it really be so bad to help?

"You'll be helping somebody who's been royally screwed over," Matches said, as if reading his mind. Was she? "These mind powers? I was born with them. U.R.O officials have known about them for years. Been chasing me, just because I turned out a little different from everybody else. And, once I am in their custody? They intend to turn me into a weapon..."
Pain flashed through her eyes.

Dice's brain swirled from when Matches had reached inside of it. Though, it swirled for a different reason now too. Senses of hatred and sympathy for Matches bashed against one another, leaving everything murky.
Matches let her shoulders relax and leaned back in her chair with a deep exhale. Dice scowled. If only he could feel so easy.
"Fine," Dice said, through clenched teeth. "Not that it was much of my choice in the first place..."

"Good," Matches said, plainly. "Now, before we get started, there's one more thing I'd like to put out there: I think the U.R.O tagged me with a tracker at some point. They never seem to know exactly where I am, but they seem able to pinpoint a rough estimation of my whereabouts."
"You can't shut this tracker off?"

"Don't know where it is, and I don't know how they could've put it on me. It must be some kind of nano-tech. What I know for sure is this: whenever I go anywhere, a U.R.O military squad isn't far off."
Dice bit his lip. As he looked up at the ceiling, he realized just how heavy his eyes were.

The upholstery was rougher than he remembered. The air was stuffy. The walls to the transport car closed against him. The black sheet of night outside the car window compounded on this claustrophobia.
Dice shifted in his seat and looked around. He hid his head in his hands. Everybody was staring at him, lips curled and brows furrowed.
"What's their problem?" Matches mumbled.

Dice elbowed Matches in the gut and offered the passengers a desperate look, as if to apologize. Their faces only twisted from annoyance to revulsion. Dice's head hung to his feet. He couldn't blame them. Matches was dressed in a ragged bodysuit, patterned with grime. It was in sharp contrast with the car's sterile air and bleached carpeting.
The transport tube passed through its third tunnel. Dice's hand hovered over his badge as he leaned into Matches' ear.
"When we get there, don't say anything, don't do anything — don't even think anything. I'll handle it all."

His eye was twitching like mad. He leaned back in his seat and took deep breaths. As the car screeched to a halt, a mischievous grin spread across Matches' face. Hopefully she was just toying with him. That had to be it.

Either way, he had to stay calm. The admissions robot was already screening all of the passengers. He watched as several of them walked off dejectedly. By the time the robot reached him, the car had been entirely emptied.
Muscles in his neck tightening, Dice raised his badge.
"She's with me," Dice said, gesturing to Matches. "She... Umm... She's being brought in for questioning."
The robot nodded stiffly, then whizzed away. The floorboards rumbled as the engine kicked back on. The department's entrance wall opened.
Air poured through the car's door. Dice and Matches stepped out, and into the garage of the police department.

Dice's footsteps made small tremors. He cleared his throat and listened as the sound bounced down the hall. It kept bouncing, reaching beyond the garage's night lights. His eyes widened. Had the garage grown since he'd last been in it?
Matches gawked as she approached a police drone.
"Not yet," Dice said, sprinting toward her.
Dice snapped his finger — though, as he did, his finger rammed into the drone and an alarm went off. Sweat beaded down his face. He sped toward the entrance to the locker rooms.
"Didn't I explicitly say that you couldn't touch anything?" Dice hissed.
"I didn't touch anything."
"Might as well have."
Dice's shoulders tensed and his eyes sagged as he scanned the numbers of the lockers. Even as he turned down his hearing aid, the alarm wailed at his eardrums. Just his luck.
When he reached his locker, he fumbled around through the drawers of his locker until he found a key.
"That looks useful," Matches said.
Dice scoffed.
"That's one word for it."
They sprinted back down the locker room.
"You have flown one of these police drones... Right?" Matches asked.
"Since when was I the one flying it?"
They stopped at the locker exit. Dice tossed the key into Matches' hands.
"This is where you and I split up."
Matches pursed her lips, and her eyes flitted among the lockers. She'd thought that he'd somehow change his mind, hadn't she?
Dice pressed open the locker room entrance. There was a whoosh. The light of the garage spilled into Dice's eyes. Then, streams of electricity.
"Dice Raymond, you're under arrest for committing treason against the U.R.O, attempting to steal government property, and colluding with a convicted felon."

The head of a plasma gun was shoved onto Dice's forehead. Dice looked up and found himself staring into the face of Deputy Haynam. Standing behind Haynam were several officers — accompanied by Professor Cassius.
Haynam clenched his teeth, and made a cruel smile.
"I always suspected that you were secretly a weasel," Haynam said.
"Actually, I'm not so sure about that," Matches said. "My personal theory? He's secretly a robot."
Haynam didn't flinch, and an officer walked behind Dice. Matches made a grunt, undoubtedly from the officer shoving his own plasma gun into her head.
"What do you have to say for yourself, Raymond?" Haynam said.
"I'm thinking that I probably should've dressed better for the occasion," Matches said.
Dice heard the officer behind him knock Matches to the ground.
"Let your friend talk for himself, dammit," Haynam said, eyes unwavering.
Dice wanted to say something. Anything. But, nothing came out.

"Pretty clever of you," Haynam said. "You climbed the ranks of the U.R.O, out of obscurity... Gained a job on a covert government case that hardly anybody knew about... All so that you could ultimately assist the escape of one of the greatest convicts known to the U.R.O."
Haynam laughed and knocked Dice to the ground with the butt of his gun.

"You were almost clever enough to succeed," he continued, voice intensifying. "Unfortunately, you should've played your cards closer to your chest. The robot that you had us imprison? He was suspiciously innocent upon this evening's interrogation session. We had a U.R.O official give him a lookover, and he immediately questioned the legitimacy of this 'prime suspect' that you'd given us... Despite their initial reluctance to do so, the U.R.O sent out a search party for the true culprit. After that? Your whole plan completely unraveled.
"I figured it would only be a matter of time before you showed up here, so I rounded up some officers for your arrest... And, here we are."
Dice wanted to protest, but his mouth was dry.
"I'm sorry, Dice."
Dice flitted his eyes. Professor Cassius' eyes welled with pity. Cassius' apology replayed in Dice's head. Each time, Dice's head ached.
Professor Cassius had been the U.R.O official who'd outed him.
Dice looked away. He didn't want to believe it. He couldn't.
"No need to apologize, Professor," said Haynam. "I think that a decade or two of mental reconfiguration will serve Mr. Raymond very well."
Dice dove deep into Haynam's eyes. Terror clawed at Dice's ribcage. There was no anger, or malice in Haynam. Yet, there was a flicker of courage — the drive to do the right thing.
Courage was more terrifying than anything else could've been.
"Haynam, I never planned for any of this," Dice said. "You know that I wouldn't do anything to betray the U.R.O."
"And yet, you've done everything."

Haynam's hands wrapped around Dice's wrists in an iron grip. Dice flinched as his arms were yanked behind his back and a pair of cuffs cinched around them. Dice fought against them, but felt something jab against his skin. He looked over his shoulder. Knives jutted out from the sides of the cuffs, and were steadily pressing inward.
"I like to call this toy 'the cuffs of life'," Haynam said. "The more that you struggle against it, the harder it gets."
"That's cute. You should become a poet," Matches said.

Haynam released his iron grip. His eyes widened, and his mouth opened to shout. There was a blast. Haynam landed in front of Dice with a thud. His eyes were empty. Soulless. His greasy smirk was gone, leaving his face a cracked mirror of its former self.
"Eh..." Matches said. "I suppose poetic justice is close enough."
Three more blasts. The officers in front of Dice fell. Cassius was the only person who remained. Dice could practically sense Matches' finger on the trigger of the plasma gun, preparing to fire.
"No! Don't!" Dice said.
There was a blast. Then a clang. The cuffs around Dice's wrists released and fell to the ground. Dice gave his arms a stretch in relief. Then he looked at Matches.
Stooping over the body of an officer, she had a wry grin on her face. Dice couldn't stop looking at the officer's face. It was stained purple.
"You really want to spare the old bird?" Matches said, turning to glare at Cassius.
Dice gave her a biting look.
"Alright, alright," Matches said, raising her arms. "Let's just get out of here then."
Matches ran past Cassius, and toward the police drones. However, Dice stayed and stared at the Professor, who stood in the center of the garage with a blank expression.
"Come on, Dice! We have to go!"
Dice didn't look up.
Everything that could've gone wrong had. He'd been caught. People had died. Cassius was disgusted by him.
Nothing could be the same after this. Nothing.
If only turning himself in were still an option.
"You'll have all the time in the world to stand around once you're in the cockpit of the drone. I'm not going to keep waiting for you."
An alarm blared. Matches was already climbing up the side of a drone. She'd be gone in a matter of minutes. Carried by a rush of adrenaline, and Dice sprinted toward her.
"I'm sorry too," Dice said, as he ran past Cassius. Cassius didn't flinch.
Dice's body trembled as he went up the ladder to the drone. He was so high up.
"Thank god!" Matches said, poking her head out of the cockpit. "I was worried that I was going to have to fly this thing myself."
There would be no going back down from this. This was it. His world... Everything he'd worked for...
"You never did answer my question earlier... Can you even fly one of these?"
Dice shook his head.
"There was a reason why I told you that you were going to have to fly it," Dice said.
"Nice. So, either you kill me, or I kill you."
"Well, when you put it that way, being the one to fly the drone doesn't sound half-bad..."

Dice sunk into the seat of the cockpit. A tapestry of panels of buttons and levers spread out in front of him. Trepidation ran through Dice's fingers as they hovered over each one and tried to determine the function. Finally, he came over a button labeled D.I. — Drone Intelligence.

Pressing it, Dice activated a holographic computer interface. He routed it for the U.R.O,'s border and the drone hummed the kick of the ignition.
