Dice's stomach twisted as Cassius shrunk to a blip on the tarmac. Then the tarmac fell away altogether. They were airborne. The drone flew through the exit of the garage, and into the sky.
"Yes! Liftoff! Finally!" Matches said.
Dice put his head in his hands. An acidic sludge climbed up his throat.
"What's wrong? We made it! We're alive!"
"I hate heights..."
"That would've been nice to mention before we were airborne. This is going to be a long one thousand kilometers..."

Dice couldn't disagree. A mess of streets and tubes rushed beneath him. Wisps of clouds and smoke brushed past the window. They were already among the peaks of the tallest buildings in the Monterey District. Yet, even as their dazzling lights danced through the air, Dice felt nothing more than wave after wave of nausea.
"I know this might be cruel, given the circumstance... But, this is a beautiful view," Matches said, stepping next to the control chair.
Dice gave another glance out the window, and then groaned. His eyes fell to the floor.
"It's definitely a view..."
There was a beep. Though, Dice couldn't bring himself to look back up.
"We're not going to be able to enjoy it for much longer if you let this thing crash into the side of a building..."

Matches lugged Dice out of the control chair and placed him in the back seat. Yet even back there, far from the window, Dice's head throbbed. He couldn't get Cassius' face out of his head. Or, worse yet, Haynam's face. Stiff. Lifeless.

Haynam was technically no more than a mess of tissue and cells. His feelings for Haynam was nothing more than a result of instinct. Social conditioning. However, the headache his death brought still wouldn't leave.
Why wouldn't it leave?
"Why do you already have it set for the border of the Kelvin Union? We're still going to need to stop to fuel, as well as for a checkpoint..."
"How was I supposed to know that?"
"I'm resetting the course for the Gordon District. Don't mess with it. There's... Something that I need to get from there."
The Gordon District? The name was vaguely familiar. A good amount of energy packets had the district's name printed on them. Though, aside from fuel, what could Matches possibly need from there?
"You want to play a game?" Matches asked, turning around.
Dice frowned.
"It could probably take your mind off things."
"Sorry... I don't play games."
Matches raised an eyebrow.
"Nothing?"
"Well, I guess I'm a bit of a chess player."
Matches burst out laughing.
"That ancient game?"
"And what do you play?"
Matches pulled up her sleeve, revealing a box. She pulled out a flexible slip of metal and glass, and it lit up blue. A card.
"I can play anything with these," she said. "Name a game, and I know it."
She smirked slyly.
"Especially anything that involves gambling... Am I right?"
Matches shrugged and turned back to the window.
"Can't say you're wrong."
"Anything involving cards is a fool's game... 10% skill, 90% luck. Me? I'm not too fond of luck. If I'm going to play a game, I'd prefer to be able to make my own luck."
"Good for you, then. Enjoy playing chess by yourself."
"And enjoy playing cards by yourself."
"I will."
Matches reshuffled the deck and began playing card tricks. After an extended silence, Matches chuckled.
"You know, I haven't had a fight like that in months," Matches said. "Honestly, I didn't think that I was going to make out of that one alive."
Dice careened to the side as Matches looked up from her cards and had the drone take a sharp turn.
"How did you manage to beat that officer, anyway?" Dice asked. "You had a plasma gun pointed right at your head."
"I did. But... It wasn't hard to snatch the gun, and get the officer in a chokehold... I just needed to be fast and quiet about it."
Dice nodded his head. He tried filling in the pieces in his head but it didn't quite fit. Moreover, Matches' response had been unusually slow and humorless.
"Have you had combat training?" Dice asked.
Matches paused.
"In a way, I guess I have," said Matches. "I've learned most of what I know on the go, though."
"You killed five officers."
Matches smiled to herself.
"It is pretty impressive, isn't it? I was really lucky though. It doesn't always work out that way for me... I needed you to save my neck in the alleyway, for example."
Dice shook his head.
"I wouldn't call the deaths of five officers lucky."
Matches frowned at Dice.
"Come on..." she said. "I didn't have any other option. It was life or death. Besides: those people were practically robots. It didn't matter if they died."
Dice closed his eyes, and leaned back in his chair. Matches was right.
Dice didn't feel right.
It was probably just the motion sickness.
Stray strands of code ran by Dice's eyes. Then, they faded to black. The helmet around Dice's skull unlatched and reeled up into the air.
Dice slammed his head against the wall of his tube. It had been weeks of electric shocks, analysis, darkness, and running on the glass floor.

His bones ached. His head spun. He couldn't get the image of running on the glass floor out of his head — looking down on the ground, so far below, knowing that the glass under his feet could shatter at any time.
His heart thumped. Something thumped on the glass of his tube. Dice curled into a ball and hung his head between his knees. Though, the thumping continued.
Dice pressed his face against the glass and squinted. Just inky blackness. Was it all just in his head?
The glass went up and Dice stumbled out of his tube. A narrow hall brushed against each of his sides. Walking forward, Dice heard the glass wall go back up and something move toward him.
"Who's there?" Dice shouted.
Somebody clucked their tongue.
"So many people..."
A glare flashed. Dice shielded his eyes and looked down the hall. Dozens of people were lined down it, all who looked like himself — sickly, tired, ragged.
"You have all been chosen," a voice echoed. "Now, don't make me regret my choice."
Dice ran toward one of the people down the hall. Maybe they knew what was going on. Maybe they could help. Maybe he could help them.
Shocks of electricity tore down his back. Dice's limbs went stiff. His vision blurred.
The last thing he felt was the ground bashing against his chin.
Chapter 11:
"Dice!"

Dice groggily rubbed his eyes and looked around. The seating area was pitch black — the lights had been shut off to conserve power. Dice turned to look at the control area. Sheets of yellowish acid pelted down on the window. Straining his eyes, Dice was able to make out several spire smokestacks shrouding the skyline. He squinted but there was no seeing past the smokestacks, nor the ground below. The clouds were too thick.
A rock plummeted through his chest. He didn't even know how far away he was from the Monterey District anymore. Nothing made sense. He shouldn't have been here. Yet, he was.

He pulled his badge out of his pocket. There was still grime on it, leftover from the sludge of the alleyway. He brushed some of it away with his thumb, revealing the M.D.P.D lettering underneath. It almost seemed to taunt him.
"Sorry," Dice said, shoving his badge back into his pocket and holding back a yawn. "Three nights without a sleep-tube hasn't been good to me..."
Matches didn't respond, and instead took the drone into a nosedive. Dice gripped the armrests of his seat and closed his eyes.
"I thought the objective was to stay airborne. What are you doing?" Dice said.
"Trying to get us not killed," Matches said. "Of course, I might be working against myself here."
Dice pulled himself out of his seat and made his way toward the cockpit. Struggling to keep his balance, he clung to metal railings lining the ceiling.
"Whatever you do, don't puke all over the dashboard," Matches said, eyes still focused out the window.
"Could you explain to me what's going on?" Dice said. "Communication is key to successful interactions."
"Gee, thanks for the info," Matches said, grunting as she pulled the drone up. Dice flinched as the drone's belly grazed the ground and rose back into the air.
They were surrounded by mountain after mountain of scraps and waste. The sight almost made him sick. Though, as Matches pulled the drone further up, Dice was reminded what true sickness felt like.
"I think we lost one of them," Matches said.
"Lost one of what?"

"One of the military fighters. It's probably scanning the ground, looking for the remains of our drone. My guess is that there's too much background noise on the ground down there for their trackers to work."
Dice tried taking Matches' seat in the cockpit, but Matches wouldn’t budge.
"We were being chased by a military fighter?" Dice asked, trying to remain calm.
"No. We're being chased by military fighters. Plural."
Dice peered out the window and checked the rear-view camera footage but couldn't see anything.
"And, you think that we lost them?"
"Only one of them. There have to at least be three others. Very advanced stealth vehicles. Might've even turned invisible. But, they're definitely there."
Beads of sweat formed on Dice's brow.
"Where are we?"
"Not in the Monterey District anymore, that's for sure. Check the map. I don't have time for questions right now."
The navigator on the dashboard had them placed somewhere within the Genoa District. No — not just somewhere. Right in the center.
Dice went queasy.
"We're in 'the pit'," Dice said.
"I figured. Of all the places for us to be caught in, it just had to be here..."

Matches jerked one of the levers, sending the drone into a barrel roll. Dice slammed into the ceiling, the wall, and then back into the floor. An explosion went off. Dice turned down his hearing aid as his ears began to ring.
"They're launching detonators now?" Dice said. He didn't bother masking the tremor in his voice.
"That, or really bright fireworks."

Matches struggled to regain control the plane as they flew through a ball of smoke and fire. Dice teetered into a wall. He snapped back. Despite the wall's protective layering, the fire's heat had been emanating through it.
Dice's eyes went to the rear-view cameras. Still clear. Nothing on the radar either.
"You're going to get us killed if you pull one of those moves again," Dice said.
Matches snickered.
"It's either that, or we get blasted by one of the detonators."
Dice stared across the vast mass of clouds and smoke. His jaw clenched. His stomach tightened.
"I'm taking the controls."
Matches' eyes widened.
"Sorry flight attendant, but you don't get to fly today. Or ever."
Dice spun the chair around and dumped Matches out. Seizing the controls, Dice boosted the drone over a field of clouds.
"You have no idea how to fly an aircraft!" Matches said.
"And you do?"
"The difference is that my insides aren't going to spill all over the interior of the drone."
Dice shook his head.

"You get any closer to a detonator than you did last time, and I'm not so sure about that. Besides: I've had more experience with computers than you." Dice paused to give partial control back to the A.I and shift the drone back into balance. "Even if I don't have experience with this particular kind of aircraft, I think I should be able to figure things out fast enough. I just — I just need to stay low, to the clouds."
"You just need to stay conscious..."

Dice's eyes flicked from side to side as he looked for any sign of the fighters. The air was clear. The sun was visible. There were no shadows. Though, there was a streaky cloud to his left and right— they parted unnaturally. Dice sped the drone up, but the streaks only seemed to follow.
"They're on each side of us," Dice said. He checked his rear-view camera. "One of them is behind us as well."
Matches scrunched her eyes.
"How—?"
"I can just tell."
"You can go faster than them, right?"
"The drone can only go so fast. It's already near its top speed. And, we don't have any weapons on board. I'm thinking of diving back to the ground."
"That's not going to work twice — especially not if you're the one flying."
Dice tried weaving through the air and maneuvering between the thin streaks in the clouds. They blocked him at every turn.
"I should be able to outmatch them," Dice said. "I'm good at playing chess. I just need more time..."
Matches rolled her eyes and walked to the back of the drone.
"If we take any more time, they'll send another detonator at us," she said.
There was a clatter as Matches rummaged around. Dice knocked away an airborne food packet from the dashboard.
"Stop. You're going to put a hole in the window," Dice said.
"That's kind of the idea."
Matches' footsteps came back up behind Dice. She shoved a helmet over his head.
"I can hardly see."
"Get used to it."

Fear pumping through his veins, Dice adjusted the helmet's visor. Matches was walking up to the drone window with her own helmet on and a plasma gun. Dice's mind was cloudy. He tried looking around Matches, but Matches obscured the entire window.
"Where did you get the gun, and why do you have one?" Dice asked.
"I kept it after fighting one of the officers," Matches said. "I was saving it for when we were in a pinch... Now seems as good a time as any."

Dice went to retort but was drowned out by a bang and the shattering of glass. He was flung back in his seat as acid and the rush of wind ripped through a fresh hole in the window. Dice tried shouting. He tried moving out of the way of bits of glass. Though, he was petrified.
Matches leaned the window and started shooting in the direction of the fighter planes. Acid obscured the visor of Dice's helmet, but he made out vague sparks as orbs of energy blasted the planes.

Several more blasts. One of the planes' invisibility shields went down. The plane's side was enveloped in flames, and it began careening toward Dice. On instinct, Dice thrust the drone upward. Matches tumbled to the back of the plane. There was a dull crash as the two fighter planes collided.
"We did it," Matches said. "I'm going to need my right arm in a sling... But we did it!"
Dice felt the urge to give a sigh of relief, but kept his eyes narrowed in on the maelstrom of wind and acid.
"I'm going to need to fly higher."
"Why?"
"Third fighter plane. Still behind us."
Matches groaned.
"Oh. Right."

Dice pulled up, letting the rain and wind thrash at him. Pools of acid rain sloshed around below him. He maintained his ascent. He looked at his altimeter — the drone had raised a few hundred meters in the air. Though, in his rear camera, there was still a vacuous funnel where sheets of rain should've been.
"I know the plane is still following us, but we're going to need to go down," said Matches. "The air pressure is rising."
"Can't you try shooting at them from out the back?"
"The thrusters are back there, and there are no windows for me to shoot through. Not to mention, I've used nearly all of the energy in the plasma gun."
Dice was going to ask Matches to try anyway, but there was a bleep. Then, another.
Another.
He looked down. The radar detected a gun being aimed at them.
Dice raised the plane even higher, then jerked one of the levers to put the drone in a barrel roll. Nothing happened. A blue film hugged the windows. Time slowed to a halt. Zero-point energy.
The interior of the drone quaked. There was a clap. Thunder? It couldn't be. The rain and wind had stopped...

The nose of the drone dipped. Then, the blue film disappeared. Rain, wind and time returned in a fury as they began losing altitude. Dice throttled his levers, but to no effect. The drone had gone completely rogue.
"Dice!" Matches said. "Dice, stay calm! We can get out of this!"
Dice turned around. Matches was still holding onto a chair but was covered in bits of dust and metal. One of her hands were pressed to her forehead.
In the back of the drone there was a gaping hole. Flames licked its sides. Outside the hole, a chunk of the drone's wing spun aimlessly in the air.
Dice wiped his own forehead. He could feel stress soaking through his skin. Smell panic. Taste oncoming catastrophe. His mind buzzed.
"Dice, turn off the ignition! The primary engine has already exploded! The secondary engine will too, if you keep it on!"
Hands gravitating toward the ignition, Dice drifted in and out of consciousness. He suddenly realized how high in the air he really was. How hard it would feel when he hit the ground.

His fingers were brittle. As he tried to turn the ignition off, their grip faltered, and his hand fell to his lap. A tingling sensation spread through his body. It started out in his shoulders. Then, through his arms. His legs.
Wind had plastered Dice to the back of his seat. He was numb. His head nodded, then sagged to the side.

"Dice!" Matches shouted, from somewhere high and far away. Dice thought that he could feel Matches' hands grip his skull. Reach into his mind. Though, this feeling flickered away as quickly as it came. Soon, all that Dice could see were clouds. Dark clouds. Dark, swirling clouds.
He plunged into the blackened eye of the storm. Then, nothing.
Chapter 12
"Something!"

Dice started up from his seat, with a jolt. He moaned. His vision was blurred. He tried lifting his arms, but they'd gone fuzzy. When he went to close his lips, he found they were chapped and caked with scabs. He must've been breathing through his mouth for too long in his sleep.
Tying to breathe through his nose, Dice gave another moan. It burned. Pools of blood had clogged it. He choked as some of the blood slid down his throat.
"Say something! If you're with me, say something!"
Dice tried turning, but a muscle in his neck stiffened in protest.
"Matches?" Dice asked, with a cough.
"It's about time you said something!"
Matches pulled Dice's helmet off. His vision was clear again.
Yet, the world around was murkier than ever.

The interior of the drone was crumpled and deformed. Some of it even looked as if it'd melted into itself, and then hardened back. The dashboard was reduced to a dozen pieces, the windows were gone, half the roof was peeled away, and the seats had been uprooted from their place.
Dice was sitting in the back of the drone. Though, aside from the gaping hole created by an imploded engine, it'd received less damage than any other part of the drone.
"You're going to heal real ugly... But, at least you're alright."
Dice blinked. Matches was now staring him right in the face. Her eyes were wide with concern. However, what Dice noticed most that Matches didn't have any notable injuries of her own.
"It's good we both made it out of that," Dice said.
"Yeah," Matches said "I think that I fared better than you."
Dice wiped away a streak of blood rolling down his chin.
"I definitely could've turned out better..."
Dice looked closely at Matches. The creases along her forehead. The creases between her eyes. What was hidden there? Guilt? Fear?
"Stop looking at me like that, will you? No wonder you have no friends..."
Matches started moving around loose bits of the plane.
"For drones, these things sure can go out of control easily," Matches said.
Dice studied Matches for a little while longer, before giving up.
"Certainly," Dice said. "What happened to get me here, anyway?"
Matches moved around a few more pieces of metal, making a clear passageway to the exit of the drone, before clearing her throat.
"Well, if you really need a refresher, it all started in an alleyway a few days ago..."
"I might've gone unconscious, but I'm not suffering from amnesia."

"Just checking," said Matches. Her eyes turned up to the remaining patch of ceiling. "So, right after you went unconscious? The fighter kept trying to shoot at us. I had to take you out of the control chair and strap you to the back of the drone — you weigh a literal ton, by the way — as quick as I could. The drone spun out of control after that, and I didn't think that I'd be able to get back in the control chair. Somehow though, I did, and regained control..."
"Judging by the current state of the plane, I'm not so sure you did."
Matches gave a glare.

"Very funny... Where was I? Oh, so after gaining some amount of control, I turned off the ignition and tried to keep our plane in a steady descent for the ground. Once I'd passed through a cloud of smog, the fighter jet stopped chasing me —  whoever was flying probably didn't think descending into the smog was worth losing their signal. After that? I had to try landing the drone. And, well — I didn't do a good job of it... The airbag saved me, but you weren't so lucky. I've been spending the past few hours trying to revive you."
Dice nodded, and tried stretching his arms. Looking out the hole in the drone, he saw it had already sunk into the mound of scraps they'd landed in. They were steeped deep in "the Pit".

Beyond the drone, the sea of trash and scraps was near-endless. Bits of robotic heads. Metal arms. Wires. Doors. Walls of long-dead buildings. It wasn't just a dump. It was a graveyard. The only silver-lining was that the acid rain was no longer raining from the skies, and the clouds weren't as thick.
Dice eyed the melted bits of their drone again.
"The drone has been exposed to this environment for three hours?" he asked.
Matches nodded.

"It doesn’t look like it'll be able to withstand it for much longer," Dice continued. "The acid rain... It's eventually going to decompose it into nothing. We probably won't be protected from the next rainfall. Our protective suits aren't going to be able to protect us for long either, since they've already been exposed once."
Matches kicked at one of the loose rods of metal on the ground and bit her lip.
"So what do we do? Leave the drone and find some other piece of trash to hide in?"
Dice shrugged. It was too much to think about at once. He needed to take his mind off of things for a minute. He reached into his pocket for his badge.
His fingers groped at empty cloth. His eyes widened.
"My badge! It's gone!"
Matches scowled.
"Didn't you hear a word that I just said?"
"You don't understand. My badge — it was important."
"It probably slid out of your pocket while we were still up in the sky... It's long gone by now. Now, can’t we focus on the task at hand?"
Dice stared off into the expanse of waste. His badge — the last thing tying him to his home — was out there. It'd be impossible to get it back.
"Hello? Dice, what are we going to do?"
Dice blinked and turned back to Matches.
"Looking for stronger shelter sounds about right. Should be simple enough."

Matches glowered over Dice, raised her hands and gave a deprecating laugh. Heat rose to Dice's face. Had she been the one to make their escape plan back in the Monterey District? Had it had been her who'd had made sure they narrowly survived at each turn?

"'Simple enough'?" Matches said. "That's rich! You're badly injured and need immediate medical attention. Worse yet, our navigation systems have gone out, due to all of the background noise that these trash heaps produce. Not to mention, we're still about hundred miles away from the Gordon District..."
"I have a solid sense of direction, and I remember our coordinates from before I went unconscious. I think that I should be able to get us through here."
Matches paced around the drone. It was as if she hadn't heard a word. She was so oblivious. So arrogant.
"Of course you're a great navigator," Matches finally said. "Because, you're just great at everything, aren't you?"
"Better than you are."
"I'm pretty sure that one of your legs are fractured. Good luck at beating me at walking."
Dice tried moving his left leg but felt dozens of daggers jab into it. He winced in pain. His chest fell. The horizon to the Pit stretched wider. How was he supposed to get across?
A hint of sympathy flash across Matches' face. She bent down into the pile of scraps and dragged out a metal tube.

"It's a makeshift splint I built out of the police drone's scraps, while you were unconscious," Matches said, throwing it into Dice's lap. "Kind of funny: the police district had you wrapped around your finger. Now? A part of their drone will be wrapped around their leg."
Dice clenched his jaw as he tightened the splint. He couldn't see what was supposed to be so funny.
"Thanks."
Dice shifted his leg again. The daggers were still there, but only as shadows of their former selves. He stood up. A jolt shot up his ankle. He pushed through it, and managed to take a few steps.
"The hobble is a good look," Matches said. "But, I don't know what we do if we end up needing to run from robots..."
Dice's eye twitched.
"There are active robots in the Pit? I always thought that it was just a rumor."
"When you've hopped around the U.R.O long enough, you learn that every rumor about this place has a hint of truth to it."
Matches went back to rummaging through the pile of scraps, before chucking two metal bars at Dice's head. Dice managed to catch them just in time.
"You could've put me in another coma," Dice said.
"I knew that you were going to catch them. Some reflexes you have there, eh?"
Matches' eyes narrowed as she stared at Dice. Dice returned the stare. She knew he had secrets. She could reach into his mind at any time. Yet, she didn't.
What secrets did she have?
The moment passed, and Dice remembered the heavy poles resting in his arms.

"Those are going to be your new crutches for now," Matches said. "Hopefully we'll run into a medical bot soon... In the meantime, we need to head out. The rain is going to rain whether or not we're moving."

Dice grunted as he pulled himself up and moved through the drone. The crutches were crudely shaped and scraped against the palms of his hand. One of the crutches slid as he attempted to take a step. A small shock coursed through him as he straightened the crutch and tried again. The crutches teetered, and he leaned on the weight of his bad leg. The knives returned. Dice collapsed on a nearby wall to pause and breathe, before trying all over again.
"They'll take some getting used to," Matches said.

Dice made a few more attempts but continued to fail. Finally, he went to the mounds of scraps. Though, as he did, his crutches sunk. He sunk. He yanked at the crutches but was only pulled in deeper. He was stuck.
Matches let her arms fall to her sides.
"Alright, clearly this isn't going to work..."
Matches pulled the crutches out of Dice's hands and hauled him over her shoulder. Dice held up as much of his own weight as he could with his good leg.

Matches trudged out of the drone, and through the wasteland. Dice hobbled along with her, trying to ignore his left leg. The faint rays of sun that made their way through the clouds burned the back of Dice's neck. There was so much smoke. Too much. His eyes went heavy. The muscles in his legs wore.
He could afford a break. He didn't need to keep fighting. He'd done so much fighting already. Besides, it would just be a short rest...

The minutes drawled by. Matches continued to trudge through the mess of scraps. The heaps of trash continued to reel them in. Swallow them whole. Yet, Matches lifted them through each time. Dice slipped in and out of consciousness. Matches groaned from the effort. She didn't stop.
"Come on Dice! If you don't start moving, we both die."
It had been at least two hours. Dice grimaced and bit his tongue as he picked up his feet.
"We still going in the right direction?" Matches asked.
Dice lifted his head to look around. His neck was still sore, and the back of it had begun to roast. Their drone was nowhere in sight. Only kilometers after kilometers of trash.
Without their drone as an anchor, they were just two small dots moving across a never-ending expanse.
Dice gave a feeble yes and put his head back down.
"Good," said Matches. "Because, I don't know how much more of this I can take."

Matches let go of her lock around Dice's neck. Dice stumbled toward the ground but tried to soften his landing with his arm. He let out a shout. The only thing soft about his landing had been the countless bruises still throbbing on his forearm.
Matches landed next to Dice, causing trash to fly into his face.
"I'm sinking into it," Matches said. She sighed. "I need some sleep. This could make a good bed, right?"
The clouds above them were getting heavier, and there wasn't a place to take refuge in sight.
"We could try digging under the scraps, right?" Dice asked.
Matches paused, before shaking her head.
"The acid will just leak through, no matter how far we dig. Besides: the acid can deteriorate layers upon layers of this trash..."
Dice noticed just how much a hardened gash on the side of his head hurt. He could feel his pulse pounding through it. Burning.
He closed his eyes. They just needed a short break. After that, they'd be back to it. They'd find somewhere before the rain started up again.
"We probably should've stayed in the drone," Matches said. "Hindsight is cruel..."
The trash crumpled as Matches rolled over. It crumpled again. Again, still.
"Stop rolling over," Dice finally said. "Just pick a position to lay in."
He turned to look at Matches but Matches just gave him a confused glare. She hadn't rolled over.
"What's that noise?" Dice asked.
Matches' eyes widened, and she sat up.
"I thought it was you."

She scrambled to her feet and pulled Dice from the trash heap. A faucet of trash fell to the ground in front of them. Dice looked up. The trash was pouring from the back of a cubed aircraft. A scrap-barge.
The trash stopped pouring from the barge and the barge flew away. The sound of crumpling remained. Then, it was replaced by a low rumble.
"So much for a rest," Matches said.
Matches dragged Dice behind her as she jogged through the piles of metal, while Dice's bad leg struggled to keep up with the pace.
"Calm down," Dice said. "The rumbling is probably just a robot, right?"
Matches' eyes flared.
"Oh, I hope not," Matches said. "That's the only way this situation could get any worse."
What was she talking about?
Matches kept trudging through the trash as quick as he could. Though, the faster Matches went, the less ground she covered. Or, was more ground covering her?
The terrain was getting steeper. Rougher.
A chunk of trash hurled toward them. Then, another. Dice looked behind to find a massive landslide of trash, all funneling toward a center pocket.
"We're in the middle of a pit!" Matches said.
Dice didn't know what that was, but he knew terror. Matches' voice was sopping in it.

Dice limped after Matches, arms flailing and his right leg pumping. His eyes were glued ahead. He couldn't look behind. His muscles ached the further he went. He didn't stop. As the ground steepened, the sinkhole in the pit was only becoming wider.

The chunks of trash tumbling down the side of the pit grew in size. Grew in frequency. A door hinge hit Dice in the face, and he careened backward with a fresh bruise. Matches narrowly gripped Dice by the arm.

Dice should've felt a rush of relief. A burst of anger. Anything. Though, as he looked back down to the pocket, a pocket formed in his gut. It'd widened into a gaping mouth, as more and more trash vanished into it. Its sides were folding into steep walls. Dice tried to speed up, but the ground gave way underneath his feet.

The air was an oven. His injuries were singing a fresh tune. The clouds had turned a stark black and sank low in the horizon. While the trash roared as it rolled into the hole, Dice prepared himself to join the roar.
"What are you doing? Move!" Matches said. "We're almost at the top!"

Matches was lying to herself. Dice could see it in her eyes. He could see it when he looked to the top of the heap. They were separated by a steep slope, and a metal wall that had risen from out of the heaps of trash. It was further away than it had been when they'd started.

Matches vaulted over a large desk as it slid their way. Dice tried jumping after her, only for his left leg to slip and cause him to slam his head. Blood rushed to his nose. The ground drew him further away. Matches' arm quaked as it fastened around Dice's and pulled him up.
The quaking stopped. Dice's forearm slipped through Matches' hand. The hole below came closer as Dice slid down. Rolled down.
Everything was spinning. The pit. The sky. His stomach. His thoughts.
Dice tucked in his arms and legs and went to snag a piece of trash. He missed. Pieces of trash snagged onto him. A rod tore through his bodysuit. A magnet ripped his leg brace away.
"Matches!" Dice called. "Matches!"

He finally crashed into the discarded remains of a sleep tube. The glass squealed as Dice wrapped around it with all of the life left in him. More trash slid by him, dumping into the pit below. There was too much of it. Why did there have to be so much?
"Woah!"
Dice snapped his head around, to see Matches tumbling down through the trash. Dice held an arm out. Tendons in Dice's arm strained as Matches grabbed on. Nevertheless, he held tight.
"You better not let go. You're holding my right arm — my good arm."

Matches pulled herself up to the sleep tube. Dice's eyes were on the pit. It was ballooning in size. He looked up and watched a speck of trash fall from the top of a wall, and then fall into the pit in a matter of seconds.
"Matches," Dice finally said. "What do you think is down there?"
"Death," she said, solemnly. Then, trying to inject levity into his voice, "Death, and outdated tax-collector machines — just like in hell."
Matches smirked up at Dice. Despite the feel broiling inside him, Dice smirked back.
Their trash slope moved faster. It turned to a landslide. Then, just a straight plummet into the pit. Air fled from Dice's lungs. Blackness encased him. Heat. A roar.
Dice turned his head, but Matches' silver eyes were gone. She'd disappeared.
How did she always manage to do that?
Dice jumped off his tube. He choked as he flailed toward other bits of trash. It was far too late to save himself. It didn't matter. He was willing to try anything, rationality be damned.
Dice grabbed a rusted plate and hugged it close to his chest. In a sudden jerk, the falling stopped. Dice hung in the air, dangling by one of his legs. His left leg.
Dice let out a shout of both relief and agony.
"Thank you," he whimpered to the blackness.
He rose into the air. Then, back to the light. Back to the walls of trash. Dice craned his neck upward, to find a barrel-shaped robot holding him by the leg.

Dice was grabbed around the throat. He opened his eyes. A metal arm protruding from out of a wall had him suspended in mid-air. He was in a pure black room, lit by a ceiling of fluorescent white lights.
"Welcome to the concentration chamber!" said a cheery voice, through unseen speakers.

The metal arm unlatched. Dice collapsed to the floor and gulped in air. He looked to his sides. He was standing among a new row of people completely coated in a black ooze. He looked down to his hands. He felt his face. He was coated in a black ooze too.
Thin glass screens cranked through slits in the ground, and in front of them. They lit up with a clean, buttery interface. A man's face flickered in the center of Dice's.
"You are all the peak of genetic potential," the voice continued. "You've been handpicked for your minds — they are beyond that of anybody else."
Two metal rods raised from out of the ground and locked around Dice's ankles.
"And, for what task have you been chosen?" The voice laughed. "Sifting through feeds of specimens in our infrastructure — determining whether they're genetically superior... Or inferior."

The image of the man on Dice's screen transitioned to a blurry camera feed of him in a glass tube. Two buttons lit up underneath the feed — green and red. "Genetically effective" and "genetically defective".
Sweat formed on Dice's brow. His pulse throbbed. The ooze tightened around his scalp, almost as if it could sense his fear.
"Remember: we desire peak accuracy in your judgements. Do not waver. Do not falter. Tell the truth. Only the truth."
Dice's finger hovered over the red button.
He pressed the green.
There was a screech. The glass screen descended back into its slit.
The ooze tightened around Dice's neck. He opened his mouth to breath, but only felt something crawl inside and suck it dry.
"Let this be a lesson to you all: Only honesty is effective. Follow the collective."
Chapter 13
"Thank you for rescuing me," Dice said. "It's much appreciated!"
The robot said nothing.
Maybe it just had a broken voice box.
The hole in the pit shrunk, until Dice had completely risen out of it. Dice went to touch the edge of the pit wall, and only narrowly missed. He was back on solid ground.
Though, the robot's ascent didn't stop. The ground fell away.
"Wait? Where are we going?" Dice asked, holding back a gag.
Still no answer. However, the robot halted ascent and veered forward. Dice studied the sky to determine their direction.
It was west. They were headed west.

Mounds of trash, which had seemed so intimidating just hours ago, flew past. Dice tried to determine the distance they'd covered, but it all went by too fast. His pupils stiffened as they surrendered to the blur.
The robot's engine whinnied as it slowed down. Not a moment too soon, either. Dice's head was pounding with the rush of blood, and his leg had gone numb.
Studying the ground, he saw that it was speckled with various other robots. It was a camp of some sort.
Dice looked at massive structure, made of metal plates and panels haphazardly welded together.
It was an ugly camp.
As Dice descended, the robots broke out in a series of clicks and hollow banging. There was massive variety among them. Cooking robots. Construction robots. Demolition robots.
All kinds. All outdated.
Their clamor didn't stop until he was dropped on the ground. His eyes bounced between them all. Were they happy for his arrival? Or, were they mocking him
"Did you secure another wanderer?" one of the robots asked. It was a top-heavy bot, suspended on two thick treads.
The thin robot that'd been carrying Dice landed on the ground next to it.
"Negative. Not just one. We stopped two of them from falling into a pit trap."
Dice scanned the crowd of robots. They must've rescued Matches too. She had to be hidden somewhere among them.

"They must be a pair of loose bolts, huh?" said the robot with treads. "I've even seen sewage bots with the intelligence to crawl out of those. It's been months since anybody has fallen into those traps, hasn't it?"
"Over a year, according to my records," said the thin robot, with a sharp click.
"I suppose this is long overdue then, isn't it?"
All of the robots inched toward Dice, forming into a circle around him. He was alone. Defenseless.
The sky murmured. There was a flash of lightning. Dice squirmed. He only had so much time before another acid rain.
"Thanks so much for bringing me to your wonderful abode," Dice said. "Though, could somebody inform me as to why I've been brought here?"
A taller robot, outfitted with pristine legs and delicate arms stepped out from the fray. How could a robot living in the Pit be in such good condition?
The robot emitted a high-pitched frequency, and the other robots stopped.
"I'm the head robot, AK29," the robot said. "This is our welcome ceremony, and you're our guest of honor."
Guest of honor? There was a screech as one robot unfurled a knife from its wrist. A thrum as another robot revved a flamethrower.
Dice's eyes widened. Robots could lie.

Dice scanned the swarm and tried finding an opening that he could slip through. There was a robot to his left, with a head connected to its body only by a thin wire. It would be easy enough to knock over — though, dodging the other robots would be another matter entirely.

"Thank you so much for the ceremony," Dice said, hobbling around the circle. "You're all wonderful pieces of machinery. I can't even begin to express how humbled I am in your presence. However, if this truly is a welcome ceremony, could I be directed to my friend?"
AK29 went to Dice's side and put an arm around him.
"Certainly."

It emitted another beep with the wave of its arm, causing a row of robots to open up. At the end of the row, there was Matches. She was several meters away, but dice could still read a look of trepidation on her face.
"Matches!" Dice said, feigning a charismatic grin. "It's just wonderful, isn't it? These robots have taken us in and decided to throw a ceremony."

Matches didn't bother playing along. Her eyes made a slight motion toward the crowd of the robots, and she gave a defeated shrug. Dice's smile faded. His face turned to stone as he reached the end of the row of robots, knowing all too well what was about to happen.

Just as Dice joined Matches, AK29 punched him from behind. Dice hit the ground. Several of the scabbed gashes on his arms were cut anew, and he could taste shards of metal in his mouth. Dice spat them out.
The robots clicked in unison. They started as a small tick in the back of his mind. Their clicking climbed from there, until it was pounding against the inside of his skull.
"All of these years of being ignored... Spited," AK29 said. "All caused by you humans. Do you know how much you've taken from us? Do you know how much it stings to be forced to dwell in your filth?"

Dice rolled over. The roof to the robot's massive warehouse was above him. Just beyond it, black clouds sunk toward the ground. They erupted with thunder. A fat drop of acid landed next to Dice's head.

A steely hand clasped around his head. Dice struggled and clawed, trying to escape its grip. He soon found himself dangling in the air. Pressure wrapped around his jaw and his temples. His eyes bulged.

"This domain of burning waste, pooled from dozens of nations... It was created to bring energy and commerce to your wilting 'districts'. Bring life. Yet, do any of you ever stop to consider the death that it has wrought on us? On the robots that create your districts? Your energy?"
There was a harsh scratch.

"You dump us here, thinking you can kill us all... Mine us for resources. I ask you this: would you ever sacrifice any of your own? Why is it that we must be destroyed when we become outdated, but you're constantly being enhanced? Why are your sad lives allowed to drag on, while ours are squelched in a blink?"
Dice looked to Matches for help, through the corner of his eye. However, just as he did, Matches was seized by AK29's other steely hand.
There was a rumble from out of AK29's throat.
"And now, we can finally initiate our 'ceremony'! Our retribution..."
The pressure intensified. The servos in the robot's hand whirred as they worked to push harder. They cracked and sputtered.
Finally, AK29 dropped him and Matches to the ground.
"Who wishes to go next?"
The world was just a buzz. However, Dice could make out dozens of high-pitched frequencies emitted by robots. The swarm was in a feverish craze.
"Matches?" Dice moaned.
A new robot grabbed him, this time by the hair. Dice kicked his legs. He grunted. His teeth against his tongue was the only thing that kept him from screaming.

Dice hit the ground again. Shards of glass were jammed in his skin. His bodysuit was left in tatters. As he pulled himself up, his left leg buckled. If it hadn't been for his brace, he would've fallen back to the ground.
There were more clicks from the robots. Cheers and claps joined the mix.
There was a thunderclap. Dice looked up. Another thunderclap, followed by a drop of acid. A dash of lightning. He jerked his head. He needed to make a dash of his own.
Dice stumbled forward. Matches was being stretched from head to foot by a robot with trunks for arms. Rage consumed Dice, and he rushed toward the robot.

Dice never managed a solid punch. He tripped before he could get within arm's reach. However, as Dice spat out his second helping of scraps, somebody punched the robot in his stead. It was somebody dressed in an armor, which seemed a patchwork of several metals. They disappeared into the crowd of robots before Dice could get a closer look.

The trunk-armed robot hit the ground with a satisfying crack. There were more cracks as the armored figure launched a flurry of attacks at the other robots. Dice's eyes remained on the robot on the ground. He crawled toward it. Matches must've been trapped under it. He needed to get there before any other robots did. It was only a meter away.
Something grabbed him from behind and pulled him up from the ground.
"You know, if your police job doesn't work out, you should really look into becoming a professional ragdoll."
It was Matches.
"Let's go," she said.
She yanked Dice's arm and pulled him through the web of robots. Dice closed his eyes and winced. They weren't going to make it through.
The raucous of clicking and screeching died off. Dice reopened his eyes. his heart skipped a beat. The robots stood still. Each one had turned to a statue, letting them by without so much as a noise.
"How?" Dice asked, gaping the frozen robots.
It didn't make any sense. It was as if time had stopped, to intervene on their behalf.
Dice waited for an answer but Matches kept her gaze on the army of robots. Intense concentration lined her brow, and her left hand pressed against the side of her head.
They passed through the crowd of robots and reached a hole in the ground big enough to crawl through. An entrance to a tunnel. Dice leaned to enter.
"Not yet," Matches said.

There was a crash. He snapped his head around and saw the armored stranger sauntering toward them. Matches pulled her hand from her head and dropped her gaze from the crowd of robots. The stranger glowered over her. Matches stayed in place and gave a resolute stare.

As the stranger glowered, Dice realized just how tall they were. He took a glance at their armor — it was more thrown together than he'd though. Holes and gaps fed throughout it, and rust lapped at the tips of its gauntlets.
"I've never seen anything like that happened to all of the robots..." the stranger said.
"I tripped on an EMP device in the scraps," Matches said.
"Must've been a big EMP device..."
An EMP device? Matches hadn't said anything about that earlier. Dice went to retort.
"Let's move," the stranger said, turning away from Matches.

Dice stopped himself. The stranger's voice was muffled from under their helmet, but low enough to tell it was a man's. Dice ogled at the stranger, waiting for him to give some kind of explanation. However, the stranger only knelt down and entered his tunnel.
Matches ducked to enter the tunnel after the stranger. Dice watched her, his eyes prodding for answers.
"Who is this person?" he finally hissed.
"I have no idea," Matches said, from inside the tunnel. "I saw him hiding off in the distance while one of the robots was flying me down into the little arena. That's all I know."

Dice stumbled into the tunnel and tried to keep quiet. It was a narrow space, carved out of piles of trash and discarded tech. An oily stench dominated it. The trash's grease trash rubbed onto his skin
"How did you shut off all of those robots?" Dice asked.
Matches made a face.
"I didn't. The stranger must've had a special device."
Dice narrowed his eyes but said nothing.
There was a creak. Dice raised his hearing aid and peered through the hole in the tunnel. A nearby robot's limbs swung in the wind.
They were about to reawaken.
"Speak of the devil," Matches said. "We don't have much more time."
She darted away. Dice tried to keep up his leg stiffly dragged behind him. The unlevel ground, and magnets constantly clinging to his brace only slowed him further.
"We're almost there," shouted the stranger's muffled voice from deep in the tunnel.
Dice made his way around a bend. Light was just off in the distance.
"And here I was thinking that it was going to take us another few weeks," said Matches.
It was the part where they were supposed to laugh. However, something was stuck in Dice's throat. His aid fizzled with static. It was followed by a dull echo. A whiz. A whir.
A high-pitched screech shattered his eardrums.
"They're coming," Dice said, turning his aid back down. "The robots have caught onto us!"
"Then, move faster!" the stranger shouted, gruffly.
Dice's legs were too weak, and his heart was pumping too fast, and the brace on his left leg snagged on a metal plate, and god... He was going to die in the tunnel, wasn't he?
Dice tried pulling his leg free. It crackled in a threat to break.
"You have a knack for falling over, don't you?"

Matches came up from behind Dice. She let out a heave as she gripped the plate wedged over Dice's leg and pulling it off him. Dice slid his leg out. A crimson scrape was left in the metal plate's wake. He readjusted his brace, hiding the scrap underneath. As he stood back up, a blade whizzed by his face and stuck into the wall of the tunnel. Shadows of several robots smeared across the tunnel walls. Their whirs were no longer distant echoes, but thunderous clangs.
"Move, move, move!" Matches said.

Dice staggered over bits of scrap, making his best attempt to run. He looked over his shoulder. The robots had already made their way around the bend. There were dozens of them, infecting every crevice. Dice shook off a chill running along his skin and hobbled faster.
He wasn't fast enough. He could never be fast enough. They'd reached the entrance to the stranger's cove. Its rays of light danced into his eyes. Matches let out a triumphant whoop.
One of the robots gripped around Dice's shoulder. It dug into his flesh. Its fingers were ice, leaving him numb. Dice closed his eyes and bit his cheeks.
"Look out!"

The ground rumbled. Something heavy fell just behind him, and the robotic hand released his shoulder. Dice opened his eyes. A large portion of the ceiling had fallen away. Ahead of him was the stranger, with a bulky cannon mounted over his shoulder.
"Stop looking behind and move your ass!"

A robot was trailing just behind him. Dice bumbled into the cove with Matches. Not wasting a moment, the stranger slammed the door shut. A shred of Dice's bodysuit was caught underneath and torn away.

Dice looked around. The walls and floor of the cove were still made up of scrap metal. Though, the room was furnished with various bits of technology that had been salvaged from the trash heaps. An old light system was installed into the ceiling, with loose wires running throughout it. One of the walls held what seemed to be a scrapped prototype for a computer projector. The entrance door was made up of various interlocking panels, assembled from what looked like demolished remains of buildings. In the center, there was a sleep tube that had been transformed into a display case for a gun.
"Next time you try playing hero, I'll shoot you instead of the ceiling!"
Dice whirled around and found the stranger glowering over Matches again. Matches' silver eyes narrowed as they locked with the slits for eyes in the stranger's mask.
"I have a fractured leg," Dice said, stepping in between them. "I wasn't going to be able to save myself."
A low laugh came from out of behind the stranger's helmet.
"As if I can't see that," he said. "But, whatever you did to get like that, you clearly earned. And, whatever fate you suffer because of your injuries is equally as earned."
Dice looked into the thin slits of the mask. With a strain, he could make out the eyes. Only the pupils — but they were there. Small, dark, and angry.
"Well, thank you for saving our lives and all," Matches said. "But, I and my friend should really go on our way."
Matches tried turning back to the entrance, but the stranger stood in her way and laughed again.
"It's going to be storming out there within minutes," he said. "In fact, I wouldn't be surprised if it's already started. Besides: I'm not inclined to open that door at this particular moment."
Dice pressed his hands to his ears as a scrape resonated from behind the door.
The stranger let out a sigh, and strolled over to the sleep tube in the center of the room.
"On top of all this, I'm going to have to find a brand-new place to make my base of operations..."
Dice looked down, and saw that Matches had her fists clenched. He watched her walk toward the stranger.
"If it was so much trouble for you, why did you even bother rescuing us?"
The stranger let out yet another laugh. Each time, it deformed into something more guttural and horrid. Dice preferred the scraping coming from behind the door.

"I didn't come to your 'rescue'," the stranger said. "I don't go around the Genoa District's Pit looking for dopes like you to save. No... You just happened to be in the same place I was. I went above ground to pick up some spare parts, and ran into your group of robots — nothing more."
It was Matches' turn to laugh.
"You still saved us."

"So I did. I suppose that I didn't want to watch a couple of people be torn apart by a group of sadistic robot rebels. Do you want me to change my mind? Because they're still out there. It's not too late for me to throw you back."
Dice's ears burned. The stranger meandered about, flicking his wrists as he spoke. He slung his voice around, as if it was law. It was slathered in too much relish.
"I want you to take off your mask," Dice said.

The stranger sped up his pace around the room, before stopping to stoop over Dice. Dice looked up into the stranger's mask and stared him into the eyes. They were small for a man so big. The pupils shrunk back.
"You have guts," the stranger said. "It'll be such a shame when they're finally spilled by some robot..."
He put his finger on the wound in Dice's shoulder. A sting coursed through it. The muscles in Dice's neck tightened, and a faint nausea settled over him.
"We humans are tough, but soft at the same time," the stranger said. "Sad, isn't it?"
"What I think is sad is that you live here. In the Pit. With nobody but these robot savages to keep you company."
A fresh sting shot through Dice's cheek, as the stranger slapped him across the face.
"So arrogant!" he said, with a roar. "I saved your life! I brought you in here!"
"I'm sorry," Matches said, coming behind the stranger. "We've been through a lot today. Dice doesn't actually mean anything that he said... Do you Dice?"
Dice shook his head. The stranger eyed Dice's cheek, stepped away, and walked to the corner of the room. He let out a deep sigh, and turned his back away from them.
"Maybe I should be the one apologizing," he said. "I haven't seen another human being in months... And, the ones that I do find are usually dead. Or halfway to death."

There was a pang in the stranger's voice. Dice saw a flash of Haynam's face, and had to close his eyes. There was an extended stillness. Dice had to stare at the image. He had to remember the cold eyes. The gaping mouth, clogged with words that were never spoken.
"I'm Matches, and that's Dice, by the way."
Dice reopened his eyes, and saw that Matches had outstretched her hand to the stranger. With a grunt stranger took it.
He cleared his throat.
"I haven’t gone by my name in years..."
"Then this is the perfect opportunity to change your name," Matches said.
The stranger nodded.
"Yes. I can reinvent myself, can't I? I like that. I'd prefer to not have to go by my true name ever again. It was... So long ago. A different life."
His hand ran along a cluttered work bench, and he snickered.
"My new name can be... Wrench."
"Wrench?" Matches asked.
"Your name is Matches, and his name is Dice," Wrench said. "Might as well name myself after another inanimate object."
He was Wrench. Neither of them questioned it again. For Dice, it may as well have never been any other way.
"So... How long have you been living on this slice of prime real-estate?" Matches asked. "I imagine that the move here was fun."
Wrench's eyes pierced through Matches. Then, he gave a pained chuckle.

"I've been here for decades," he said, casting a sidelong glance at Dice. "The Pit used to seem like a viable place to go... The U.R.O makes loads from unloading the world's trash here and turning it into energy. I figured that I could do the same."
"I'm going to guess that it didn't work out," Matches said.
"I've made a life for myself by coming here. That's more than most people can say. So... It depends on how you look at it."

Dice looked at Matches. Her mouth was open, her tongue hanging onto a word. However, the word never came out. She just stared at Wrench with a lingering pitying expression. Although Dice could only see Wrench's eyes, he could tell Wrench was returning the expression.
"I've given you some of my story," Wrench said, drawing himself up to his full height. "Now, it's your turn. Where did you come from?"
Matches wiped the gape from her face, and grinned.
"I've been waiting for the chance to tell somebody my life's story. Nobody else has ever seemed too eager to hear it."
Wrench's eyes were granite. He made a low growl.

"As much as I'd love to know the story of where your pupils went, we both know damn well what I meant. Nobody gets caught by a gang of robots in the Pit without having done something supremely stupid."

Matches stared at Dice, pleading for help. Though, Dice suddenly felt very frail. He leaned against the wall, and wiped away a cold sweat that was blooming on his forehead. His shoulder stung like mad.

"We were trying to get a package across the border," Matches finally said. "We were headed to the Gordon District, to rendezvous with.... Our... Contractors who have methods of getting us to the other side of the border. When we decided to take a shortcut through the Genoa District, our systems were shorted out by the acid rain. We've only been stranded a day but, as you can see, that was more than enough to nearly kill us."
Wrench folded his arms and nodded.
"A couple of people crashing, while flying a plane to the border? That sounds completely innocent and legitimate."
"It doesn't make it any less true."
"It's only half true, at best... But, that's fine. I assume you still need help getting to the Gordon District?"
"We definitely need help getting out of here. I think we can find our own way to the Gordon District, though."
The room rocked back and forth. Dice held onto the wall to keep balance and maintain focus.

"There are a few ways I know of that can get you out of here," said Wrench. "There are several forager communities in the Pit who could take you to the Gordon District. Of course, they'd make you pay a hefty price... And then, there's me. I know this place better than any of them, and I might have a shortcut or two to the Gordon District."
Matches' eyes lit up.
"Thank you so much," she said. Then, she paused to raise an eyebrow. "Now, what is it going to cost us?"
"You'll have to convince me that guiding you out of the Pit will even be worth it, first... If and when you can do that, my price will be three hundred radials."
Matches ran her hand through her hair.
"Three hundred radials?" she asked. "You live in the Pit! You're never even going to use it!"
"There are plenty of forager communities who'd give a power-system just for a single unit. I'll definitely find ways to use those radials."
"But, we don't even have any—."
"It's fine," Dice said, weakly. "I'll pay him the radials. I should have enough in my U.R.O savings account."
Matches gave a look of relief. Wrench gave a passing look of concern.
"We'll discuss the specifics of our arrangement later," Wrench said. His pupils rolled up and down as they sized Dice up. "It's time that we tend to your friend... Dice, was it?"

Dice nodded, but took a few steps back. There was a biting edge to the way that Wrench spoke. Despite this, crinkles formed around Wrench's eyes, which Dice could only assume that they were caused by a hidden smile. Yet, the idea of Wrench smiling made Dice all the more uncomfortable.

Wrench drew closer to Dice. Then, he walked completely past him. He opened a bronze cabinet at the back of the room, to reveal row after row of random gadgets and supplies. Just from a brief look, Dice could tell that half the cabinet was useless. Though, Wrench held himself up with pride as he rummaged through it.
"I have too many things in here," Wrench said. "I've been collecting things for so long, and I just never know what will or won't one day be useful."
"What you're looking for will be useful and relevant to the conversation at hand though, right?" Matches asked, raising an eyebrow.
"Of course."
Wrench stepped out of the cabinet, his arms cradling a bucket of needles, injectors, casts, and tissue replicators. Dice looked back to the door.  Maybe he could still leave through it.

"We're going to need to take care of all those injuries of yours," Wrench said, making a sympathetic cluck with his tongue. Though, the glee in Wrench's voice was too overbearing for Dice to believe his gesture sympathy.
Dice inched away, though Wrench caught up and pushed his hand against his chest.
"In the chair," Wrench said.
Dice wanted to protest, but Wrench's words were a hot iron. Dice sat down and locked his gaze to the wall, preparing himself for whatever might come.
"So tense," Wrench said, rubbing Dice's shoulders. "It's a sign that you're already binding up."
Dice looked to Matches for help, but Matches had gone to a corner.
"Yes... Far too tense. If I do anymore work on you, it's going to hurt like hell."
"I suppose that's to be expected after suffering as extensive of injuries as mine," Dice said.

"Yes... Well, I need to give you a few stimulation injections before I can continue any further," Wrench said, nodding his head. Then, turning to Matches, he raised his voice, "Alright, I'm going to need you to hold him down. He's going to need extensive injections, and this isn't going to be pretty."
"No," Dice said.
Wrench snapped back around, and gave Dice a look.
"What?"
"Do you even have any background in using medical tools?"
Wrench snorted, and picked up on of his injectors. The canister was far bigger than it should've been . Or, was his memory just playing tricks on him?

"Do I have any background using medical tools?" Wrench repeated. "Well, if you'd like somebody who does, I can gladly lend you to one of those idiot robots out there. They'll fix you up real good. In the meantime? You're stuck with me."
Wrench called over Matches, and forced her to help hold Dice down. Dice fought, and kicked. To no avail.
"I'm fundamentally against the usage of injector stimulators," Dice said. "They're bad for the brain. They dull the mind. They—."
"They're going into your bloodstream," said Wrench, pushing one into the side of Dice's arm. "They're better than letting you waste away as a pile of broken bones."

Wrench had Matches pass him another injector stimulator. Wrench shoved it into Dice's other arm. As the canister flushed into Dice's system, his head shot up with ecstasy. The room lit up in a balmy glow. There was the scent of a flowery perfume from the distant past. Everything became so much clearer. So much simpler.

Wrench grabbed another injector from Matches. Dice felt a slight prick as it was shoved into the side of his neck. With the third rush of stimulators, the whole world went awash with a blinding light. He could now only hear a few muffled grunts, and shouts.
"Won't four be too much?" Matches said, from the beyond.
There was a soft tap in Dice's side.
"Too late. I remember that people used to take ten of these at a time."
"That's impossible! It could've only been small injections! Not full canisters!"
"He can take it..."
Dice took the words and left the room. He laid in the bright light. Only the bright light. He was home. He'd been away for far too long. He'd finally reached the apex of clarity.
Rest.
The air smelled of bleach. The odor spread. Dice's nose burned. His eyes watered.
He wanted a way out. There had to be a way. Though, he was ensnared in a thick darkness. He ambled around. He stumbled back after bumping into a wall.
A scoff leapt around the darkness.

"You poor thing..." It was the same voice that he'd heard so many times before — cruel. Raspy. Conniving. "You think that you can escape, my boy? You think that you can make change? It's time that you learn... There's no point in trying."
There was an intense ringing in Dice's ears. His hands clasped over his ears, but the ringing only worsened. It traveled from his ears, and to his skin. Through his bones. He collapsed on the ground.
The sound stopped. Though, Dice lacked the strength to pull himself back up.
"You're in a sonic chamber," the voice said. It was more warbled than before, yet somehow sharp as ever. "You bypass our codes of conduct? You act against our system? We put you here..."
The ringing returned, pushing down on his body. The stench of fumes became overpowering. Dice felt as if a wall had collapsed on top of him.

"We've crafted intellectual nirvana here, in this... high place," the voice said, towering over the sonic blasts. "We've handpicked you, out of so many, to represent us. To contribute your mental strength to our facilities' collective knowledge. To become one of us. Don't resist. Please... Desist."
Dice grunted, and his muscles quaked as he pushed himself up. His eyes were bleary. Tears were streaming down his face. His ears were popping.
"Buckle up. It's going to be a long three hours."
Chapter 14
There was a steady beeping. It was almost soothing, but something itched at the back of Dice's mind.
Dice went to move his arms. The table under him shuddered. There were restraints around them. He thrusted his chest out, but only felt the tug of more restraints.
Dice opened his eyes. There was a black emptiness. He blinked. Nothing changed.
"Is anybody there?" he asked, trying to keep his voice flat and controlled.
No answer. Dice's breathing stalled out. He was taken back to the time he'd been trapped in his sleep tube. Back to nightmares that he'd had before that... So many nightmares.
He shook and fought. His table rocked back and forth. He didn't stop until the table wouldn't rock anymore, and he was careening toward the ground.
His body quaked as he made impact. He was still strapped down, but now he was stuck on his side.  Brilliant.
At least it was close enough to progress.
Dice sniffed. The air smelled of blaster ammunition, and oil... It had to have been a room in Wrench's cove.
What if Wrench and Matches were dead? What if he was trapped? What if it had all been a trap?
Dice's breathing fled from his control. His heartrate climbed. His head pounded. There was too much darkness. Too many bad memories. They burst in all at once, breaking him down.
"Somebody help me!" he shouted. "Is anybody there!? Let me out! Dammit, somebody let me out!"
He persisted, even as his throat became sore and his voice slipped away from him. He only stopped for a moment to swallow a deep breath of air, before letting out another shout.
"I'm trapped!"
There was a series of thuds. Something creaked. A door? No light came in.
"I'm so sorry," Matches said.
Her hands pulled at a visor around Dice's head. As it came off, light spilled back into Dice's eyes. His heartrate fell, and air rushed back into his lungs.
He looked down. Wires and tubes ran throughout holes in his bodysuit.
"We put a sleep regulator around your head, to make sure that you didn't wake up before it was time," Matches said. "Didn't work... But, at least it had been worth a shot."
Dice looked up at Matches. Her hair was a mess, her face was worn, and her body was covered in a layer of dust. How much time had passed since he'd been asleep?
Matches unlocked the restraints. Dice rolled from the table and yanked the tubes and wires from his body. Nerves rattled in his bones. His eyes swelled as he kept a grunt at bay.
"It's actually midnight right now," Matches said. "If it hadn't been for your shouts, we probably wouldn't have checked on you for hours."

Dice rubbed his shoulder, slightly annoyed. His injuries still felt raw. None of the tissue replicators on his body had fully healed over. Wrench and Matches must not have been tending to him nearly enough.
"How long have I been out?" Dice asked.

"You've been in a coma for three days," said Matches. "I wasn't sure how long it was going to take you during the first day. To be honest, I wasn't even sure if you were going to make it... Wrench had given you too many stimulator injections, and your heart flatlined for several minutes."
"My heart stopped?" Dice said, with passing interest.
"Yeah. Wrench ended up using one of his electric gauntlets to revive you. I told him that they might fry you, but he didn't care... The man's a maniac."
Matches laughed.
"I guess it all worked out in the end."
"Yeah... Guess so."

Dice looked around the room. It was a cramped space — 12 square meters at most. There was a generator in the corner, which connected to various pumps and life support systems. It sparked and shuddered. Dice put his head in his hands. His life had practically been held together by a thread.
An old nightmare flashed by his eyes. He twisted in his seat and stood up. His left leg gave a slight twinge, sending yet another flash.
"What's wrong?" Matches asked.

"Nothing," Dice said, with a weak cough. He adjusted the neck-hole to his bodysuit. "Just remembered a bad nightmare that keeps coming back to me... It's been getting progressively worse, lately... Weirder too. I just need to learn how to ignore it."
Matches gave a questioning glance, then cleared her throat. "Wrench said yes, by the way."
Dice turned back to Matches. Her eyes were downcast, but she had a smirk on her face.
"He's taking the three-hundred radial payment?" Dice asked.

"Yes and no. He bumped it up to five-hundred radials. That said, it's probably worth it... He's taken me outside into the Pit a few times and shown me how to live off the terrain. To keep it brief, there's no way we'll be able to live off of it on our own... Thankfully, Wrench apparently knows about a secret subterranean transport tube system, between here and the Gordon District. He plans on using it to get us to the Gordon District. It's only a few miles from here."
Dice followed Matches' eyes down to the ground.
"That's a lot of money," Dice said. "I'm not sure I have that much cash. And, even if I do, my assets might be completely frozen by now."
Matches pulled her box of cards out of her sleeve, and let a blue blur run between her fingers.
"Doesn't matter. I've owed people money I didn't have before. We just ditch him if you don't have enough. Worst case scenario? He suffers from an accidental death..."
Dice's fists tightened into a ball. A memory of Haynam shot up his spine. He brought his eyes back up from the ground.
"No," Dice said, resolutely. "We don't kill. Never again. All we're trying to do is get ourselves across the border, where... Where we can get away. Start over."
Matches laughed. Why? Dice suddenly couldn't help but suddenly feel apprehensive. Paranoid. He remembered Matches' comment about her life story from only a few nights ago...
What was her story? People only hid when there was something worth hiding.
"I was just joking, Dice," Matches said. "Where's your sense of humor?"
"Humor is overrated."

Dice stopped to sigh. The Gordon District was so far from home. The Kelvin Union was even further. It wasn't too late to go back to the Monterey District, was it? That was where he'd always belonged, up until now. What if he could find a way to explain himself to the MDPD, and reconcile? What if he was making the wrong choice?
"I'm not so sure I want to head to the Gordon District..." Dice said, running his hand through his hair.
Matches stopped playing with her cards to give a stare.
"What?"
"I — it's just so far. I've only ever lived in the Monterey District. And, this might all be one big mistake. Have you ever thought of that?"
Matches leaned against the wall and waved another card past her face. "I don't know... I do know this though: I can't let you leave. You try to pull something, and I'll be back in your mind."
The corner of her lip curved upward. She'd tried to volley it as another joke. Though, Dice caught the glint of grimness. She'd meant every word.
Dice gave a scowl and limped out of the room.

Despite the lingering pain and unfinished tissue replicators, Dice's injuries had healed significantly in the past few days. His left leg was only stiff, with a slight ache. The bruises around his skull were gone. Yet, there was also a fogginess that wouldn't leave. He shook his head as he thought about how many stimulants must've been pumped into his body while he was unconscious.
Wrench was sleeping on the couch in the center of the main room. A dull snore echoed out from inside his mask. Somehow he was able to keep himself comfortable, even with all his layers of armor on.
Dice shook Wrench awake. Wrench woke up with a start and kicked Dice in the gut.
"What is going on!?" he shouted.
Dice stooped over, and caught his breath.
"Me," said Dice, talking through the pain. "I know that it's late, but I'm the one paying for you to get us out of here. We've already waited three days, and I doubt that we'll have much longer."
Wrench gave a soft laugh and stood up.
"You're on my list now, for waking me up," Wrench said. "Speaking of waking up: it's about time you snapped out of that coma of yours..."
Wrench walked toward the center of the cove, calling for Matches.

"By the way," Wrench said, turning back to Dice, "when it comes to these 'three days of waiting', you can only blame yourself. You should've woken up two days ago, but... complications arose when it came to you healing."
Wrench opened up his makeshift sleep tube and pulled out his gun. Then, leaning down to the ground, he picked up a bag and slung it over his shoulder.
"I was already told," said Dice. "You stalled my heart by making me overdose on stimulants."
"I prefer the phrase, 'saving your life'…"

Wrench snatched a couple of guns from a hanger on the wall and handed them to Dice and Matches. Then, raising his own gun, he opened the door to the tunnel. Dice stepped forward, but Wrench held his hand out to stop him and trekked into tunnel by himself.
"It's clear!" Wrench said, his voice echoing from the end of the tunnel.
"Wrench has been extra cautious about his tunnel," Matches whispered, as Dice entered. "Robots keep coming back to it, to try and break in. Wrench said he's going to need to relocate."
"How many of them has he had to disable?"
Matches paused, and then shrugged.
"Not all that many... He's weird about that."

When they made it out of the tunnel, it was pitch dark. The sky was smoked over, obscuring the stars and moon from sight. There were no lights on the ground for kilometers, aside from the meagre glow created by stray pieces of technology.

"It's probably better off that we leave tonight," Wrench said. "We shouldn't run into many robots during this time, due to their programming. If we're lucky, we probably won't see much rainfall either."
"So, the only robots that we’ll run into are the ones that have gone rogue from their programming?" Matches said. "That's a nice thought..."

Wrench pulled a pair of night-vision goggles over his mask, and then passed two pairs down to Matches and Dice. Dice slid the goggles over his eyes, letting their display light up in a crisp neon green. In the top-left corner of the goggles, there was a list of statistics. Temperature, atmospheric pressure, oxygen levels, a safety assessment...
The safety assessment was at thirty percent. Dice pressed his hand to the side of his goggles to turn it off.

He stopped and surveyed the terrain. The Pit was a new world, even with the help of the night-vision. Scraps let off a cold gleam they'd robbed from the moon. They were more jagged than Dice remembered. Bigger. The air was colder. The sky was heavier.
Dice looked up from the terrain to find that Wrench and Matches were already far ahead. Dice limped after them.
"Don't lag behind again," Wrench said. "We have three miles to go before we reach the subterranean system. We can't stop for every time you want to take a nap."

Dice's feet turned to lead bricks. They dragged through the scrap metal, waiting for the end of the endlessness. No matter how far they seemed to get, there was no change. Just heaps upon heaps of trash.

Every so often, lightning would bolt across the clouds, illuminating the Pit in a sickly blue. However, Dice preferred the lightning over the darkness. Groans flung through the air. Unseen scraps caught underfoot and tore at his bodysuit. Damaged robots would putter by. Dice even thought that he saw the vague outline of a withered man wandering along through the scraps.
He didn't have the stomach to turn his night-vision up all the way to see for sure, instead choosing to hold his finger over his gun's trigger.
Exhaustion set in. Dice's left leg trembled. At each bend of the knee, it threatened to collapse to the ground.
Wrench pulled something from out of his pocket.
"My tracker's signal is fuzzy down here," Wrench said. "But, we should be coming right up to our stop."
There was a whizz. A coil of metal flew just a few centimeters in front of Dice. Dice's eyes tried following it, but it disappeared back into the darkness.
"Did either of you see that?" Dice asked.
Wrench let out a grunt.

"A robot? Yeah. Not sure why you're so scared though — it was a real small fry." Wrench whipped his head around, and raised his gun. "That said, we should probably proceed carefully... And keep our mouths shut."
"Not so sure if I can follow that last instruction," Matches said.
Wrench's voice turned to a hoarse whisper. "Well, then get sure."
Their steps softened. Wrench had them hunch down as they weaved behind large structures and mounds in the scraps. It was a longer route, but Wrench insisted on it.
Dice questioned whether the precautions made any difference. No matter where they went, his hearing aid picked up the engines of robots purring just off in the distance.
Maybe it was just paranoia. That had to be what it was.
Wrench held his arm over Dice's chest.
"Stop," Wrench hissed. "We're nearly there."

Dice's foot skidded. A piece of trash flung into the air. There was a crash. Then a rumble, followed by more crashes. Dice dialed up his night-vision and looked down. His heart sputtered. He was standing over the edge of a steep hill. It had to have been at least twenty meters tall.

Dice squinted. There was a mound at the bottom of the hill, looking to have been created by a landslide. Next to it was a rusted door, built firmly into the ground. Dice studied its heavy handles, and welded hinges. They were flaking apart. His face twisted. Hopefully the inside was in a better state.
"Watch your step, or you'll break both of your legs," Wrench said. His goggles flickered menacingly.

Dice bent over, buckled his knees, and started down. His left foot slid. His body followed. He leaned an arm against the ground to try to control his descent. Bits of metal leapt at him and tore at his sleeve. He closed his eyes until he'd slowed to a halt.
"Not half-bad," Wrench said, slapping him on the back. "And here I was, thinking that you were useless at just about everything..."
Dice had made it to the bottom. His chest rose. It sunk back down when Wrench made a snicker and looked over his shoulder.
"How would you rate his slide, Matches?" Wrench said.
There was only a cough from out of the darkness.
"Oh... Now you're quiet," Wrench said, with a scoff.
Dice remembered the bleak eyes hidden under Wrench's night goggles. Wrench couldn't say an earnest word, could he?

Dice pushed past him, making his way to the rusted door. He tossed his gun aside and yanked at the handles — not even so much as a creak. He scanned for a lock but came up short. The metal slabs were simply too heavy.
"A little help?" Dice said. "I'm not going to be able to get this door open myself."
Wrench and Matches groaned.
"Hey: do you want to escape, or not?" Dice asked. "The robots could arrive and attack at any minute."
No response. Dice's rolled his eyes and turned around — but nobody was there.
