"Uh... Guys?"
There was a flicker of green. A row of knives. A choke. Blackness.
Dice's body ruptured with shock as he was thrust back. His night-vision fizzled on and off. Dice dialed it all the way up. A shadow loomed over him.
A robot.

Wiry legs were stitched through scraps, puppeteering the robot's bucket for a body through the air. Dice looked for a head. There wasn't one. Only piercing, spindly limbs. Limbs that were wrapped around Wrench and Matches' necks. They were being strangled.
Dice fumbled along the ground for something. Anything. His tongue was wooden, and his eyes were glazed with terror. He turned to marble, muscles tensing.
"Use... your... gun!" Wrench gargled.
Of course. It was just to his left. Dice dove at it, aimed it at the robot, and fired. There was a blast. A spark.
A metallic shriek. Dice rolled out of the way as the robot jabbed an arm at him. It was more agitated than ever.
Dice took a glance at his gun. He'd left the safety on. Idiot move.

Dice flicked the safety off and aimed the gun once more. He pulled the trigger. There was a satisfying snap. One of the robot's arms cleaved off and wriggled about on the ground. The robot chirped as it recoiled away and dropped Matches and Wrench to the ground. Dice didn't lower his aim until the sound of metal crunching under metal limbs faded to a dull echo.

Dice turned around and took few more blasts into empty space, for extra measure. Then, he lowered his aim to one of the rusted doors and shot off its hinges. The metal grated as Dice pushed the door to the ground.
Hobbling as fast as his bad leg would allow, Dice knelt down to tend to Matches and Wrench. However, Matches already lifting Wrench from the ground.
"You're alright?" Dice asked, incredulously.
"Of course I'm alright. You threw me down an airlock, and I survived. It's Wrench that you should be worried about..."
Wrench already had a bruise swelling around his neck.
"You couldn't have been any faster with the gun?" Wrench said, with a haggard cough.
"Sorry," Dice said. "The robot was so quiet... I didn't even know you two were in danger at first."
Dice went to pull Wrench's mask off, to check the color of his face. Wrench slapped his hand away.

"We don't have enough time," Wrench said, standing himself up. He lifted his bag up from the ground and doddered toward the door. "I'm certain the robot has already sent out a homing signal to its friends... We need to get out of here before more of them start coming.
He ripped Dice's gun away, and started down the ladder into the subterranean-system. Dice listened as a buzzing sound went off in the distance. He shivered, and then followed after Wrench.
Dice's feet thudded as they hit the ground. They were in pitch black. Even with his night-vision, Dice could hardly see a few centimeters in front of himself.
There was a flip of a switch. Everything went up in a blinding light. Dice winced, and ripped his goggles off his face.
"My eyes!" said Matches. "Warn us before you do something like that."
There was a clang. Robots spilled through the doors above them.
"There's your warning," Wrench said, jogging down the tunnel. "Let's move."

They were in a wide, brick tunnel. Dozens of lights dangled from the ceiling overhead. Dice followed them to the back, where they danced on a glass tube. The sides of the tube were streaky, and coated in dust from aging bricks. Hopefully it would be able to make the distance.
Wrench and Matches piled into the tube. Dice tried speeding up, but his leg wrenched. Dice lightened his steps and clenched his teeth as he entered the tube.
"Lagging behind again, Dice?" Wrench asked, scrunching his nose.
He punched the ignition, and the tube's glass flap folded over them. Dice's eyes darted to the window. The robots were still far off in the distance. They were going to make it.

The motor of the transport car sung. A whoosh flapped against their car as the transport tube's vacuum activated. Dice's hands dug into the armrests of his seat as he himself for the coming turbulence.
The car's motor sputtered, and then shriveled to silence.
"The ride is already over?" Matches said. "This thing is faster than I thought."
"Shut up," said Wrench.
"What happened?" asked Dice. "You don't think that the car's motor has rusted out, do you?"
"No," said Wrench. "I tested this thing when I discovered it... It was working then."
"That doesn't make any sense."
"It does if you know how machines work. The battery systems are probably out."
Dice looked back to the window. The robots were gaining ground. They only had so long before they were discovered.
"So, that would mean we need to access the batteries and replenish them, correct?" Dice asked.
Wrench made a cruel laugh, and shook his head.

"This is an older model. The batteries fully rely on the generators to get their charge — which should run underground, perpendicular to our transport car's parking bay. The generators have either been knocked out, or drained of power. We need to go find them, get to them, and recharge them."
He tapped on their car's window, pointing at a passageway across the brick tunnel.
"Step one is already done. Step two will be tricky, but I think we can manage. As for step three? Well..."
Wrench pulled a power rod out of his bag and held it up to his face.

"I can never be too prepared... I got this power rod out of an old mover robot, about a year back. Those bots need a lot of energy, so this thing has quite the kick to it. Hopefully it will be big enough to recharge the system..."
"I could use some recharging myself," Matches said, rubbing her eyes as she reopened the doors to the transport tube. "Would've been nice if we didn't have to run this gambit so late at night..."
Dice looked out the door. A swarm of robots was already crowding the tunnel, and attempting to tear away at their tube. The hair on his arm raised.
"How long do you think we have to get across?" Dice asked.
"I guess we're going to find out, aren't we?" Wrench said.

Wrench handed Matches his gun and ran across the brick tunnel. Leg aching, Dice followed after. There was a clang. Dice turned around to find an oily mass of robots sprawled on the ground, dead. They couldn't have been more than a meter away from him — he could've died and have been none the wiser.
A pulse of energy soared past his head, hitting another cluster of robots.
"You can take cover behind me."
It was Matches.
"Remind me why Wrench gave you the gun, instead of me — the person who could probably use it the most right now," Dice said, as he went behind Matches.

Matches kept blasting away. Dice inched closer to the passageway that Wrench had ran down. Though, Matches wasn't inching with him. Her eyes were dead-set on one of the robots that she'd shot to the ground.
"Matches, come on!" Dice said.
"Matches didn't move. Her eyes were glassy, and her feet were clay. Dice gave Matches a shake.
"Matches, we need to get out of here!"
No change. Dice grabbed her arm and tried dragging her away.
"The gun isn't working!" Matches snapped, yanking her arm away. "I think it's out of ammo."
"And you thought that standing there was going to change that?"

Matches gave a scowl. This wasn't a time to try reasoning with her. Dice picked up his pace — he couldn't move fast enough. Metal razors landed at his feet. An orb of energy hurtled toward his chest, which he only narrowly dodged. Flakes of dust fell from the ceiling, clouding the passageway from view. Coughing, Dice covered his eyes with his arm and powered through.
He leaned against a wall. A hand clasped around his shoulder.
"Took you long enough," Wrench grunted.

The dust cleared. Wrench and Matches were already hiding behind the crack of a vault door. Wrench pulled Dice through, and then rammed his shoulder into the door to force it shut. Though, a robot wedged its arm in the crack just as he did. The door rumbled. More robots were piling on, pushing back against the door.
"Come on!" Wrench shouted. "Help me get this thing shut!"
Dice and Matches rushed to his aid. The robots howled and screamed.
"Push harder!"

The door groaned, and then clicked as it locked into place. Wrench fastened the rest of the door's locks. Wiping away the sweat streaming down his face, Dice let out a deep sigh. However, he didn't allow relief to fully set over himself. He couldn't drive away a question gnawing at his mind — how would they reopen the door?

He left the question at the door and followed Wrench down a winding staircase. Each step made a disgruntled crack. A few bricks sagged and crumbled as Dice walked down them. He tried clinging the railing, but it bowed to the ground. Rows of screws holding up the railing had rusted entirely away.
"Watch your step," said Wrench.
"Watch the steps, more like it..." Matches grumbled.

Dice's hands didn't stop trembling until he could finally see light from around the bend. He walked off the last step and into an expansive chamber. It was dominated by a sprawling cylinder that seemed to stretch on for several hundred meters. It was anchored to the ground by a metal frame and pumps jutting out from all sides of it cylinder. The pumps jittered softly as they fed into the walls, floors, and ceiling. Though, the jittering melted into the background when Dice noticed a faint glow coming off the cylinder. It was a deep crimson. A stark contrast to the drab brown brick walls surrounding it.
Dice reached toward it but snapped back upon a wave of heat.
"All these years riding transport tubes..." Dice said, "… And, I never knew about these old power systems that used to run under them. How did I never know?"
"I guess that even you don't know everything, smart-ass," Wrench said. He leaned down to look under the cylindrical power system. He squinted and wedged off a panel. "Great..."
Dice leaned down. There was nothing worth moaning about. Just the endlessly stretching metal of the power systems' underside. Metallic. Monotone. Mundane nonetheless.
"What?" Dice finally asked.
Wrench jiggled a valve underneath the cylinder. Wrench must've just been complaining for no reason, as usual. Dice stood up, and Matches knelt down. Her eyes widened.
"A parasite bot," said Matches. "It's locked onto the regulator — probably uploaded a virus of some sort, so that it can feed on the energy."
"It's fine, it's fine," Wrench said. There was a spark as the power-chord made contact with the cylinder. Wrench jumped back, smacking his mask on the power system "Shit!"
The room went up with the rattling echoes as the pumps processed a new burst of energy.
"That doesn't sound fine," said Matches.
Dice he ducked under the cylinder. He crouched onto his belly as heat tugged at his skin. Wrench rubbed his head and crawled after him.

"Get out of there," Wrench said. "It's hopeless — we're not going to be able to kill the bot, let alone reprogram the circuit. We can... We can just try the transport tube as it is, and hope that it works this time. Maybe my new surge of power will be enough to fix the problem."
"You know that it won't."

Dice leaned down and looked up into the panel Wrench had torn away. A slug-like bot, about the size of his forearm, twined throughout it. Its metallic skin kneaded in and out, like dough. Its head flickered green as it bit deeper into the power system's control screen.
"I see it!" Dice said.
"Good for you. You want a badge or something? Unless you have some bright idea, we need to be getting out of here. The transport tube upstairs is only going to get more torn apart."

Dice's eye spasmed as his thoughts ran. He'd be able to reprogram the virus the parasite had uploaded. Though, he needed to get rid of the parasite first. How would he be able to goad it away? Dice thought about trying to electrocute it with the power-rod, and then shuddered.
He looked back to Wrench. Then Matches. Dice blinked.
"Matches, get over here," Dice said.
"What?" Matches asked, incredulously.
"You're the only one here who can disable the robot. I'll take care of reprogramming it."
Wrench snorted.
"Dice, have you gone mad? There's no way that —."
"Don't play dumb, Matches," Dice said, cutting him off. "If we want to get out of this, you need to do what you need to do."
Matches glowered at Dice, and reluctantly raised her hand to her forehead. Her face construed into a pained grimace.
The parasite screeched and hissed. It unlatched from the control panel and collapsed onto the ground as a steaming husk.
"What just —?" Wrench began.
"No time for questions right now," Dice said, bringing his hands to the cracked control screen.
Sparks leapt from it as Dice unlocked entered into it. Dice's fingers ran along the keypad as unintelligible blocks of color blotched the screen.
"You just think that you can undo weeks of damage from a virus bot?" Wrench asked.
The blocks of color faded to code. Dice cut a few lines and added several new ones. He hit enter.
"Already did."
Dice rolled out of under the power system as it kicked on with a roar.
"You want to go back under there and try fixing some of the damaged circuits?" Dice asked Wrench.
"No, that should be good enough," said Wrench, eyeing the parasite.
Wrench and Matches started up the passageway. Dice followed after, his head still rolling.
"I thought that parasite bots were banned — only available in black markets."
"Only in the U.R.O," said Wrench.
"But, this is the U.R.O."
"This is the U.R.O's dump. The Pit is where the world's trash goes. As far as I'm concerned, this isn't the U.R.O. Anything goes here..."
Wrench made it up a few more steps before stopping to look Dice in the eye.
"Of course, you'll soon learn that anything goes, anywhere. Let's just hope that it's sooner, rather than later."
Chapter 15:

"When we open this door, we’re going to have an army of robots to deal with," Wrench said. "So, be prepared. We're going to try fighting them off... But, if there's too many of them, run back down to the generator room. I'll try getting the door shut."
He turned back around to look at Matches.
"I'm going my gun back by the way."
"It's broken," Dice said. "All out of ammo, or something."
Wrench gave a bemused look.
"My guns don't break, and they're always fully loaded..."
He snatched the gun anyway from Matches and aimed it at the wall. He pulled the trigger, blasting a hole through it.
"Works just fine for me," he said.
"Just my luck," said Matches, with a chuckle. Though, it was stiffer than usual. Forced. "The trigger must've jammed the moment that I needed it most."
"Isn't how that always is?" said Wrench, grimly.

He went to the door and picked at the locks. Dice's stomach turned, and he shuffled his feet. His ears rang as robots hammered against the door. Wrench stumbled back from their sheer force, before returning to the locks. Dice scanned the door from bottom to top. The hinges were bent, and eight dents had been put in it.
How many robots on the other side of the door? Was opening the door to find out really the best idea?

Dice's hand trembled as Wrench slid the last lock out of place. Dice stepped back. The door left a crater in the wall as it flung open. Dice shielded his face from bits of dust and brick collapsing from the ceiling.
"Move!" Wrench roared. "Move!"

A wave of robots crashed overtop of Wrench. They reeked of smoke. A blood-red aura of heat emanated from them. Steam and metal scraping against brick clouded Dice's ears. He hobbled toward the stairwell. Though, Matches' iron grip pulled him back, bringing him back toward the heap of robots.
"Stop!" Dice shouted. "We need to escape! What are you doing?"
Matches clenched her jaw and said nothing. Her eyes were unwavering, stolen by the horde.  Dice couldn't glean even a flicker of emotion from her face.
Dice looked back to the horde and saw how close it was. He hadn't needed to look, though. He could practically feel its heat. Smell its oil. Taste its rage.
The heat faded. Dice squinted. The robots were shrinking back. Retreating away, down the tunnel.
Matches let go of Dice's wrist and groaned. She pulled her forefinger from her left temple and leaned against the wall.
"Pick up Wrench," said Matches, still rubbing her temples.

Wrench was sprawled across the ground, with his gun still in hand. His armor was covered in deep gashes, but his eyes seemed to twinkle from out of under his mask. Dice pulled Wrench over his left shoulder with a wheeze.
"You fine?" Dice asked.
"Fine enough. My right leg stings... But we have two good legs between us, don't we?"
Was that supposed to be a joke? Dice studied Wrench's eyes, but the twinkle was already gone.
"You went through all of that, and you still managed to keep your mask on?" Matches said, bumbling from the wall.
"Is that's what's giving you that massive headache of yours?"
Matches made a pained laugh through her clenched teeth.
"Yeah, that's it," she said. She cleared her throat.
"Some show those robots put on," Wrench said. His eyes flitted to Matches. "I've never seen that many retreat like that, on a whim... Care to explain what's going on?"
"Pull that mask of yours off, and you got it."
Wrench snickered.
"Alright, we need to move quickly," Matches said, her eyes swimming. "There's no telling when they might try coming back."
"I don't know how 'quickly' that we can move," Wrench said. A dark shadow passed over his eyes. "Look at us... We're limping toward the end goal."
"Well, I guess we need to take extra care to not let our spirits limp."
Dice studied Matches' face. It was still frozen in time. A fractal of itself. Even as Dice quickened his pace, he felt an urge to ask what was going on behind Matches' glazed eyes.

Dice narrowly stopped himself from tripping on a gouge in the ground. Dice's arm slackened as it struggled to hold up Wrench. He looked around. There were gouges all throughout the tunnel. Behind him, there was the soft pattering of water. He craned his neck up. There was a massive hole in the ceiling, letting in a downpour of acid rain.
"We only have one way out now," Dice said. "That recharge from your power-rod better have been enough, Wrench."
"Get to praying," Wrench said.
Dice opened the transport car's door and inhaled the whoosh of air. He hauled Wrench up into a seat. Though, as Dice went to strap Wrench in, Wrench pushed his hands away.
"Last time I checked, you weren't my nurse," Wrench said.
Dice would've retorted, but snapped his head around as he heard a thud.
"Matches!"
She'd hit the ground. Dice limped over, fighting against the searing pain rushing up his bad leg. He knelt down and tried shaking her awake. Though, her eyes were glued closed. She was unresponsive.
"Matches! You need to wake up!"
She didn't. Dice checked for signs of breathing or a pulse. Everything was dead-silent. Dice's own heart skipped a beat. His eyes stung, and became moist.
It must've been the mixture of acid and smoke. Dice could hardly see a thing. Though, he picked up the twittering of robots. They were making their way toward him.
Dice lifted Matches over his shoulder. His tissue replicator crackled. Dice closed his eyes and fought to ignore it.
"Wrench!" Dice shouted. "Wrench, Matches is unconscious!"
Wrench didn't come. He must've still been struggling to get himself out of the car.
The tube was only a few meters away. He could still make it.

Screeches and whirs erupted around him. There were fresh thuds as robots landed to the ground. Dice didn't open his eyes to look. He struggled to get as much out of his left leg as he possibly could. His arm was begging for a rest.
He'd have his rest in due time... Due time.

He reopened his eyes upon reaching the transport tube. Wrench finally stepped out, and hobbled toward Dice. Wrench's eyes looked off in the distance and went wild with terror, but Dice forced himself not to follow them. He couldn't.

Wrench helped Dice lift Matches into the transport car. Then, Dice helped push Wrench back up into the transport car. Spurring the ignition, Wrench held his hand over the button to the door. Dice lifted his leg to enter — though, just before he did, he took a glance behind. The horde of robots were rocketing toward him. They were only a few meters away.

Dice's legs were mortar. Wrench grabbed him by the shoulders, and yanked him in. The transport car's door swooshed shut, and Wrench slammed his fist on the ignition. The transport tube purred. Staring out the window, Dice watched the brick tunnel fly past them in a blur.

"Alright, time to take care of Matches," Wrench said, turning to him. Wrench gave a series of compressions and ventilations. Finally, he went to his pack, pulled out a pair of electric gloves, and pressed them against Matches' chest. Matches jumped awake with a jolt.
"What happened?" Matches asked. "I was thinking about how I needed to get better running shoes, and then... Nothing."

"I'm still wondering what the hell happened too," Wrench said. "Last time I checked, nobody can just 'wish away' an entire hoard of robots. Nobody has a random heart attack either. Care to answer yet? Or, are you still going to leave me in the dark?"
Matches looked away.
"That's odd... You're usually running your mouth," Wrench continued. "Why so quiet all of the sudden?"
The transport car shuddered and moaned. Wrench slapped his hand against the glass. His eyes narrowed.
"I'm risking my life to help you out!" he said. "The least I deserve are some answers!"
Matches looked at Dice, begging for him to create a distraction. However, he couldn't bring himself to. He needed answers. What was Matches trying to keep secret?
Matches turned away to look at Wrench.

"I can go into the minds of people," Matches said, with a heavy exhale. "You know those robot shrinks that you find on the street, claiming that they can see into your brain? I'm like one of them... Only, I actually can."
Wrench brought his hand to his mask.
"Wait..." he said. "Have you been reading the minds of all of us, this whole time?"
Matches shook her head.
"I usually don't go into people's minds unless I absolutely have to. My abilities are... Dangerous. They can kill people if I'm not careful."
Dice looked toward the ground. Something wasn't adding up.
"I thought that you could only go into the mind of one person," Dice said. "How did you go through the minds of all those robots... Twice?"
Matches buried her head in her hands.
"I can go into the minds of many things at once," Matches said. "But, not safely. If I'm not in full control, it drains my mind. I can die."
"Wait — you don't know about any of this either?" Wrench said, turning to Dice.
Dice listened as the car softly plodded through the transport tube. He shifted in his seat, and ran his hand against the leather lining.
"And you — you nearly killed yourself?" Wrench said, his voice rising. "I thought that I made it pretty clear that nobody was supposed to be risking their lives on this trip, except me."
"I wasn't the only one risking my life..." Matches said. "Whenever I control mass amounts of people, or things... Well, my mind can let out bursts."
"What is that supposed to mean?"
"If I die while using my telepathic abilities, there's a chance that everybody in my vicinity can die as well. I could've fried the robots, and you two as well."
Wrench closed his eyes, and bowed his head.
"You haven't done anything like that before, have you?" asked Wrench.
Matches shook her head.
"Not a fan of fried foods."
Wrench leaned back in his seat, and snickered under his breath. He coughed, and then snickered louder.
"You could've killed us all," Wrench said.
He rested his masked chin on his hand.
"But then... If it hadn't been for you, those robots would be chopping us up into their personal trophies."
Dice rubbed his shoulder. Suddenly, its pain seemed insignificant.
"Would've been as close as I've ever gotten to getting a trophy," Matches said.
Laughter filled the air. Dice tried to laugh along. Though, as he looked out the window of the transport tube, he retreated to an old question that had grown into a tumor.
Why did Matches have the abilities that she did? What had happened in her past that had brought her to where she was?

Dice wanted to ask. Though, he couldn't bring himself to breach the light laughter. They'd all reached an agreement to not try unearthing the past. It was unspoken, but Dice could see it written on their faces.
Each person was free to keep their veil on.
Dice swallowed a lump that formed in his throat. He could only hope that the time for them to remove their veils would never come.
"Hey, tight-ass! It's your turn."

Dice tried snatched five cards from the air as they hurled toward his face. However, a stack of ten cards still scattered across the seat of his pants and onto the floor. Dice glared at Wrench as he bent over to pick them up. Wrench and Matches were sitting at a makeshift table they'd made from a bench.
"I'm not playing," Dice said.
Wrench let out a coarse laugh, and slammed the table.
"You don’t play spines?" he said, incredulously. "What type of person are you?"
"There are a lot of things that I don't do," Dice said simply, as he stacked the cards in a neat pile, and placed them on the table. "There are your cards back."
Matches rolled her eyes.
"He doesn't play any cards..." she said. "Apparently chess is the only game he's ever played."
"What's the point in leaving everything up to chance? Besides: I go through intensive computer algorithms for fun, as well..."
Wrench's eyes widened from behind his mask and he muttered something under his breath as he reshuffled the remaining deck of cards.
"Well, we're not going to be able to play spines with only two people," he said. "You're playing."
His voice was stiff and resolute. His eyes lifted from the cards, and bored Dice through the head.
"Too afraid that I'll beat you?" Matches asked.
Dice finally got up from his chair and sat himself at the makeshift table. It was better than having them stare at him constantly.
"How long will it be before we finally arrive at the Gordon District?" Dice asked, as he took his deck of cards.
"Shut up and play the game," Wrench said. "I might've dealt you in, but that doesn't mean I have to deal with you."
Dice counted the cards out. Three. Out of his best cards were a jack, a queen, and a spade. Not an awful draw.
Dice looked at Wrench. His eyes were downcast, and his hand was moving toward the edge of the table. Certainly unlike him.
"Wrench — set down a red."

The game was simple. The object was to be the first to make four matches of the most powerful cards in the draw. This was achieved by making the other player place a card of a certain color down on the table and seeing if it matched one's own card. Though, if the card of the other player didn't match, they could keep their card — leaving one with the choice to concede their turn or draw a new card from the deck.
Dice put down his jack. Wrench put down his card — another jack.
Wrench let out a groan and slid the card toward Dice.
"That's not fair," Wrench said, pulling a new card from the deck. "You can't just jump in, and take my best cards..."
Dice gave a shrug and slipped his card into his deck.

The game went on like this, with Dice taking cards from Wrench and Matches. He was right most of the time — but Matches was a bit harder to read. Her silver eyes would cloud his mind. Was there something to her that was taking him off his edge?
Or, was she cheating?

There was no way of telling. Even more unnerving was the fact that Matches was just as capable of detecting when somebody had the card she wanted. There came a point when Matches began taking just as many cards of Dice's as Dice did of hers.
Finally, Dice slapped down his match of four cards.
"He was looking at my cards," Wrench said. Then, turning to Matches, "And you. You were reading my mind or something, weren't you?"
Matches gave a smug grin but shook her head.
"Maybe," she said. "Or, maybe I'm just that skilled."
Dice scoffed.
"That lucky, more like it," he said.
Matches filtered her cards through her fingers and reshuffled them into the deck.
"I want another round," Wrench said.
"Well, what does it look like I'm doing?" Matches asked.
Matches dealt out the cards, and the game began anew.
"Where did you learn to play cards so well?" Wrench asked angrily, as Matches took another card from him.
"I've lived on random streets," Matches said. "It's pretty easy to win radials while gambling... So, I learned how to play cards as good and fast as I could."
Wrench clicked his tongue and nodded. Dice took his turn, and another one Wrench's cards.
"It's just a stupid game of chance..." Wrench said, slapping his cards down.

"It's a mixture of the luck of the draw, being able to interpret somebody else's facial expressions, and assuming who has what card..." Dice said. He cleared his throat. "Maybe not as much chance as I initially said."
Wrench's eyes widened.
"Oh come on! Not you too..."
"Do you want to play a different game?" Dice asked. "If you have a projector in that pack of yours, we could —."
"Not chess. God... Anything but chess!"
Matches smirked.
"For a guy who hasn't played a game with anyone for decades, you sure complain a lot," she said.
Wrench snorted.

"Decades? Not quite," he said. "I've played quite a few games with the communities in the Pit. I used to head over there whenever I needed to trade for some new batteries, and the like... They were awful to play with, though. Cheaters. Thankfully, it's been months since those rats have had me play a game with them."
Matches rolled her eyes, as she took another one of Wrench's cards.
"I wonder why..."
"I actually thought that I was pretty good. I won most of those games that I played."
Matches ruffled her cards.
"Even if your luck was even twice as good with them as it is with us, I don't see that being the case."
"Hey! I didn't have to deal with either of you punks when I was playing with them... We played the game straight, and casually. Up until the end there, anyway..."
"Oh, I'm sure..."
Dice took one of Matches' cards. Already his third match. A quick game.
"What are the other communities like in the Pit, anyway?" Dice asked.
Wrench's hand froze in midair. Regret sunk into Dice's stomach. A minute drained away, but Wrench still didn't put his card down.

"Most of them are insane, or dead," said Wrench. "Those parasite bots? They're a vice that's rampant throughout the Pit... Though, even more rampant is hatred toward other robots... Other people... Hatred in general, really. It drives people mad."
He set his card down.
"There's a reason why I live alone: I'm the only person who I've found to be worth trusting."
Matches smirked.
"You don't trust anyone? Sounds like you're living the life..."
"You haven't lived in the Pit," said Wrench.
"I've been in worse places."

"Sure you have..." His eyes lifted to the roof of the transport car. "That said: you know better than me what goes on in people's minds. The way we think. Plot. Scheme. How can you know all of that, and still trust people?"
Matches paused. A look of doubt passed over her face.
"Maybe it's because I can read minds that I trust people," Matches finally said.
She pulled out a card. She smiled.
"I guess that's the game," Matches said, splaying her four matched cards across the table.
"You're definitely cheating somehow," said Wrench, with a grumble.
A man's face. Footage of his chamber. His eyes were too docile. His skin was pallid. His body... frail.
Dice's eyes leapt to a brain monitor in the left-hand corner. Neural activity in the frontal lobe was significant, but still insufficient.
Dice pressed reject. The camera feed flickered to black.
Dozens of other genetic specimens wheeled by the screen. Some superior. Some inferior.
There were more who were inferior than not.
The camera footage, brain monitors and pictures flickered away. A barrage of code stormed in its place. Dice danced through it until it had flickered away as well, and his screen turned to glass.

Dice let out a sigh and looked to both sides of him. Nobody else had finished — predictable. Everybody was so slow. Why? Dice couldn’t tell. Discerning the genetic viability of subjects was intuitive. Reviewing code and removing the defects? Even more so.
He waited for his glass screen to descend back into the ground, announcing his success before all the others. Yet, it was locked in its place. Dice nudged the top, hoping it’d make the difference.
His reflection remained.
Dice turned back to each side of him. Other people were starting to finish. The glass screens still weren’t starting down.
He’d been at this for so long, that a time before seemed like a distant blur… However, he’d never seen anything like this.
The sound of fingers tapping against glass ceased. The room stood still. The lingering glass reflection taunted Dice. He wanted to move. Wanted to escape. Yet, he couldn’t.
“Great work,” a voice blared from the ceiling.
Dice winced and turned down his hearing aid. It’d been so long since he’d last needed to hear that voice — the trumpet of hell.
Dice’s screen blinked, opening camera footage on a new chamber. A white capsule. In the left-hand corner was yet another brain monitor. Below it were two buttons: artificial, and biological.
“Your work on genetics and brainwave activity has been instrumental in the progression of our facilities,” the voice continued. “Only the truth is effective. Join the collective.”
“Only the truth is effective,” Dice chanted along with the rest of the room. “Follow the collective.”
There was a slow clap from the speakers.

“Good,” said the voice. “Very good. Now, there’s a new challenge that we’d like to add to your usual analytical work — we need you to determine the difference between a robotic, human android, and a human. Why? Certain androids have infiltrated our facility... Escaped our notice. We need you to be able to pinpoint which is which, in order to protect us."
The room erupted in a series of chants.
"Only the truth is effective. Join the collective."
The voice laughed.

"Settle down... Settle down... The examples we’re going to be giving you today are merely trial subjects. They won't be the truly threatening ones. However, they will still be challenging — technology has increased to the point where differences are miniscule, and tricky to catch. Though, we’re confident that you’ll be able to perform.”
The room went up in tensed sighs and twitches.
“And, if you don’t perform? Well…”
There was a beep as somebody pressed the wrong button. A jolt of electricity. A thud, as they collapsed to the ground.
“That’ll happen, followed by a vacation in the sonic chamber. But, once again — no need to fear. We’re confident in your abilities.”
Dice's eye twitched. He licked his lips.

The person on the screen seemed human in every respect. There was no reason to keep them. Yet, the longer Dice stared, the more off-key they truly seemed. There was something off about the way they blinked. They looked around the room. When he compared these actions with the brain monitors, there seemed to be a shorter delay between neural activity and motor activity than he was used to.
Thuds and jolts erupted all around Dice. Though, Dice didn't waver from pressing "artificial".

The screen went down. Dice looked around himself. Most of the room had fallen to the ground, and were being dragged away by robotic arms to sonic chambers. Dice shuddered as he counted the number of people remaining — six. Including himself.
"To those that survived this test-run — astounding work," said the voice. "However, this is just the beginning. There's so much more ahead of you..."
Chapter 16:

Riding the transport car was a special kind of misery. The temperature was perpetually cold. The car constantly grinded and bumped against the glass walls of its tube, making sleep impossible. The seating areas were cramped. Though, that was to say nothing about the seats themselves: they were built of "smart-cushions" that would sink under Dice's weight, leaving him with the feeling of being smothered. Worse yet, their upholstery was coarse, scraping against his skin whenever he laid down.
Dice spent most of his time staring out the window of the tube. He learned to find solace in the constant stream of dirt, trash, and loose pipes.
Three days of this clung at Dice's face, etching hollows under his eyes. Restlessness flooded his veins. Dreams casted nets at him, leaving him in a domain somewhere between wakefulness and slumber.

Dice swept a strand of hair out of his eyes. It'd been three days — three days of holding himself together. He just needed to maintain it. His eyes lolled into the door. He raised the torn watch on his sleeve to his face.
"How many hours do you think we have left until arrival?"
"Somewhere between six and seven," Wrench said, with a grunt.
It wouldn't be long. Dice jumped between his watch and Wrench, waiting for the hours to drop away. The slight bumps and quakes of their car morphed from a nuisance to a countdown.
Wrench slammed a stack of three plates on their makeshift table. Dice kept his gaze on his watch, pretending to ignore him.
"Fresh grub," Wrench said, proudly. "This is my last ration. After that? We're out of food."
Dice closed his eyes. He listened to Matches get up from her seat and walk to the table.
"I know you're not actually sleeping," said Wrench. "Now, get up and eat. You don't have to like the sludge, but you have to force it down. I can't have you passing out on us once we're there."
Dice clenched his eyes tighter. A stench wafted up his nose — a mixture of smog and rotten cheese. He breathed through his mouth.
"You hear what I said? Get. Up." Wrench gave a clap of the hands. "If you don't? You get the enviable duty of carrying my pack."

With a moan, Dice lugged himself from his chair and went to the table. A greenish sludge waited in his spot. Dice poked it. The texture was lumpy, and rubbery. Yet, he stole a glance of Wrench wolfing it down, his back turned from them.
"This might be the only food we get today," Wrench said, pulling his mask back down and looking over his shoulder. "Eat up."
Dice didn't even take a second look. He wouldn't eat it if it had been the last food on Earth.
"Dice, you don't want to let it get cold do you?" Matches said.

Dice suppressed a gag as he put the food in his mouth. He tried ignoring the rancid taste and swallowed. As the sludge stuck in his throat, Dice snatched Wrench's water dispenser and guzzled it down. A bitter aftertaste remained.
"This is nice," Wrench said.
"The food?" Dice asked, his face construing in disgust.
"No — well, yes. But, also: I've finally gone ten minutes without you asking me for the damn arrival time."
"I've been enjoying your food too much to remember..."
Matches chuckled.
"Truly five-star material right here," she said.
Wrench turned back to face them and set an empty plate down. Pulling a greasy rag out of his pocket, he pretended to clean it.
"I could still turn this thing back around to the Genoa District," Wrench said, his eyes biting. "I'll have you know, happen to have been considered the best chef in my part of the Pit."
"You were the only chef..." Matches said.
"Still..."
"… not impressive."
Wrench snorted.
"I was going to tell you both that we're closer to the Gordon District than I've been leading you on. But, now? Not so much."
Dice shriveled a bit inside. Closer than they thought? How much closer? His eyes weighed down on him again. He needed to know.
"Come one: stop stringing us along," Matches said. "How far away are we from the Gordon District?"
"Half an hour," said Wrench. He pulled his gun out of his bag and toyed with the trigger.
Matches made a fake sniffle.
"I'm going to miss you so much when you're gone..." Matches said, playfully slapping Wrench on the back. "How are we supposed to find a cook as good as you?"
Wrench shifted the gun from safety to kill, stood up and stared out the window of the car.
"I was thinking..." he said.
"Don't you just hate doing that?" said Matches.
Wrench gave Matches a look.

"Well you should know, Mrs. Mind-reader," he said. He cleared his throat before continuing. "Neither of you are familiar with the Gordon District. I'm— I'm familiar with the place. Um... Vaguely. Besides: we all saw what happened when we tried escaping the Pit. We needed each other to survive. I'm thinking you might need me for a little while longer..."
"I think that we should be fine," said Dice.

"No, I insist," Wrench said, putting a hand on Dice's shoulder. Dice brushed it away. "I wouldn't feel right if I didn't make sure that you made it all the way to your destination. Dropping you off — it isn't enough. You hired me as a guide, not a chaperone. Besides... I and the Gordon District have some catching up to do."
More time with Wrench could only be a nightmare. Dice looked to Matches for help. His chest sunk. Matches' eyes were brimming with enthusiasm.
"That's great," said Matches. "I'm not familiar with the ins and outs of the Gordon District, so we could definitely use your help."
Dice shook his head.
"I don't think that we have enough radials to pay you any more than we've already offered."
Wrench kept himself on the window for a moment, before turning to face Dice.
"That should be fine," Wrench said. "I don't need more money. Knowing that I've gone above and beyond in doing my job will be payment enough."
Wrench looked at Matches.
"Now where in the Gordon District are you two supposed to be going to?"
Dice glanced at Matches. It suddenly occurred to him that she'd never told him where they were going in the Gordon District.
"It's a restaurant," Matches said. "The biggest one in the Gordon District. I forget what it's called... Plateau's?"
Wrench nodded.
"I knew that place. It wasn't exactly a 'destination' when I knew it though..."

"I've heard people talk about it all the way back in the Monterey District. It's a major hub for special keys — Omega Keys. They can override any computer system, including the ones that run border wall security between the U.R.O and the Kelvin Union. We absolutely need to go there."
Wrench gave a nod. His pupils shrunk. His posture dipped. His fists clenched.
"Right... the Kelvin Union..." Wrench said. He coughed. "Come to think of it, there is one stipulation that I need before helping you go through with this."
Matches gave a quizzical look.
"What do you need?"
Wrench turned back to the window.

"I've known the sorts of people who try leaving for the Kelvin Union. Never met one that should've. Before I can help you with this, I need to know — what kind of people are you? What is this escapade all about? And... What am I getting into?"
"You're not getting yourself into anything. All we're trying to do is deliver a package. Back me up on this Dice."
"Bullshit!"
Wrench punched the glass of their car. There was a crunch as his fist left a crack. Dice suddenly wanted to be anywhere else.

"Tell me what's going on," Wrench said. "You have those freaky mind powers. And he — there's something off about him, too. We all know that you're not headed to the Kelvin Union to deliver "a package", so don't waste my time with bringing that excuse back up... I want the real reason."
Wrench turned to glare at Matches. After an extended stare-off, Matches let out a sigh.
"We're running from the U.R.O military," Matches said. "We're fugitives. The government wants my abilities, and they want Dice dead for trying to help me."
"You have the U.R.O military after you!?"
Wrench looked down and shook his head.
"And, what tipped the U.R.O off that you were so special in the first place?"
"Hell do I know..."
Wrench held his glare.
"You do know. I can see it in your empty eyes. Are you going to keep lying through your teeth, or are you going to start spilling?"
Matches leaned back. Wrench continued to glare, but to withering effect. Finally, he shifted to Dice.
The fury in Wrench's eyes was palpable. Though, more than that was the fear.
Yet, it was the fear in his eyes that made Dice most afraid.
"Spill," Wrench said.
"I'm a former U.R.O police officer, who got himself wrapped up with the wrong person," Dice said. "As for her? I couldn't tell you more if I wanted to."
Wrench's eyes pressed him further, before finally giving in.
"That's really all you know about her, isn't it?"
Dice nodded.
"Yeah."
Wrench shook his head again and scoffed.
"And that was enough for you?"
Dice nodded again. "None of us know hardly anything about one another... Maybe that's all the more reason to be suspicious. But, maybe it's all the more reason to trust."
Wrench rubbed his hands together.
"Alright then. I'll take it. I hate it, but I'll take it."

"There's one more thing..." said Matches, clearing her throat. "The U.R.O military has a tracker on me. Its signal is drowned out under here, I'm sure. It was drowned out by all of the noise in the Pit as well. But, once we're back above ground? They'll be in the area, and they'll be flipping over buildings looking for us."
"Figures," Wrench said. "Shaping up to be a real party... Anything else I should know before mixing myself in with this suicide-mission?"
"We might die."
"Thanks for the heads up."
Wrench went to the front of the transport car and yanked down several levers on the dashboard. The faint hum of the car rose to a high-pitched screech.
"Prepare yourselves!" Wrench shouted. "We only have a little over twenty minutes now."
Only twenty minutes.
Despite hours of waiting for this moment, Dice suddenly felt a lump form in his throat. He was completely unready.
"I'm glad that Wrench is willing to help us," Dice said. "But, there's one thing that I need to clarify before he comes."
Matches and Wrench turned to look at him.
"You aren't going to be preparing anymore food for us, correct?"
They burst into laughter.
"I wasn't joking."

The transport car's screeching steadily loudened. Dice steadily lowered his hearing aid. He counted down each minute. Though, the closer he felt they were to the end, the longer that the minutes dragged. The seconds. Dice's internal fortitude unraveled to thread.
"We're about to arrive!" Wrench said. "Tighten your seatbelts."
Dice's heart fluttered, and he took in a lengthy breath of satisfaction. The wait for those words had been far too long.

He looked out the window and watched the tunnel fly by. They moved at an increasing speed. The ride was nearly over, after days of waiting. Yet, the lump in Dice's throat remained. Something about it felt all wrong.
"Finally, I won't be stuck between these stuffy seats," Matches said, kicking her legs up to the back of the seat in front of her. "I hate these seats..."
"You're sitting in the best seat in the transport car," Wrench said.
"Still a bad seat."

As Wrench and Matches chuckled, Dice whipped his eyes through the transport car. The car was still increasing in speed. The screeching from the brakes had softened back to something closer to a hum. Dice stood to his feet, and felt g-forces rippling through his skin.
"Aren't we supposed to be coming to a stop?" Dice asked.
"Obviously," Wrench said, with a snort.
He muttered something else under his breath. However, his muttering fell away when the transport car hit a bump, thrusting Wrench into the dashboard. An alarm blared.
"Dammit!" Wrench said. He pulled at several levers on the dashboard. The transport car continued gaining speed. The brick walls outside the window were just a uniform smear.
"Why aren't we slowing down?" Matches asked.

Dice went up to the dashboard. All of the dials were in the proper positions. There shouldn't have been any problems. His eyes gravitated toward the engine thermometer. The temperature was in the red, and climbing.
"It's overworking itself," Dice said, scanning all of the controls on the dashboard.
There was supposed to be an emergency brake. Where was the emergency brake?
"This doesn't make any sense," said Wrench. "We've been slowing down speed for the past two hours... The engine shouldn't be spiking like this."
"Did you have the engine running while we were braking?" Dice asked.
Wrench paused, before finally saying, "Yes."
"You're supposed to shut the engine off when we're in braking mode," Dice said. "The vacuum tube should've been more than enough to keep us on pace."
Wrench whipped his head back and put his hand on his forehead.
"Well, I'm not a master at driving transport tubes," Wrench said.
"Well, you might've gotten us killed," said Dice.
Matches unbuckled herself from her seat and walked toward the dashboard.
"And here I was, thinking it was Wrench's food that would ultimately kill us," Matches said.
She bent down. Dice tried to ignore her and continued searching for the emergency brake. There had to be one somewhere. Was the transport car really that old?

There was a click. Then, an ear-piercing squeal. Dice fell into dashboard, and narrowly stopping himself with his hands. He stood up and looked to his left — Wrench hadn't been so lucky. There was a dent in his mask.
"I think I might've found the emergency brake," Matches said.
"You don't say?" said Wrench.
Dice looked back down at the dashboard. The impact of Wrench's forehead had left a small crater. Sparks flew from empty sockets and mangled knobs.
Dice was jerked backward. He glanced at the engine's thermometer — its screen was illegible static.
"The emergency brakes are shot now..." said Matches. "Just great."
"Even better: the dashboard controls are down," Dice said.
"It's not like they were all that useful in the first place," said Wrench, rubbing the back of his neck.
"Well, they're definitely not useful now."

G-forces hugged Dice's bones and drew at his skin. He looked ahead, and his grip tightened around the edge of the dashboard. A thick wall was at the end of their tube, waiting to greet them. Dice winced. He had about a minute. It wasn't going to be enough. He braced for impact.
There was a crack.
"Great," said Matches.
Dice looked to the window on his left. The dent from Wrench's fist — it was growing.
"That crack is nothing compared to what's about to happen to us," Wrench said, with a huff.
The crack kept Dice's eyes hostage. Despite all of the stress weighing down on him, he let out a sigh of relief.
"Wrench, do you have your gun on you?" Dice asked.
"Yes," said Wrench, unlatching it from his side. "That is, unless you're thinking of shooting yourself."
"With my aim? Might as well be."
Dice snatched the gun from Wrench's hands. He aimed the gun at the crack. A flicker went by his eyes as his finger hovered over the trigger.
A dark ooze... A man's face... Haynam's? No... Somebody else.

Something crept up Dice's throat. He cinched his eyes and pressed the trigger. The window went into a melody as it ruptured. The air fled from Dice's lungs. He opened his eyes, and pressed the trigger again. A hole ripped through the vacuum tube, and the car began to slow.
"Smart," Wrench said, under his breath. His eyes jumped back to the wall that was still ahead of them. "We're still not going to slow down fast enough."
Dice shook his head.
"It's not about slowing the car fast enough," Dice said. "Grab what—."
Dice's voice faded to nothing. He spoke words, but no sound came. He choked. The air in their car was all but gone.

They had ten seconds left, at best. Dice gave Wrench a steely gaze. Wrench's eyes were bloodshot and bewildered. Finally, Wrench went to grab his bag. Dice turned back to the hole in their car. He needed complete focus.
Dice held up three fingers and crouched into a jumping stance. Wrench and Matches came at his side and mimicked his crouch.
The first finger went down. The second finger. The third.
They jumped. Dice pressed the trigger on the gun. Dice closed his eyes as shards of glass rained in his hair. His stomach leapt to his throat. He hit the ground.
"I didn't sign up to become a daredevil," Wrench said with a groan. "Anyway: welcome to the subterranean levels..."
He raised a fist, and promptly dropped it back down.
Dice's left leg was roaring with pain. Bits of glass stuck in his hands as he struggled to stand. He brushed them away, leaving fresh cuts.

There was a crash. A quake. The glass tittered as it flaked onto the ground. Dice floundered forward as he tried to keep his balance. Steadying, he turned back to the brick wall. It had collapsed into a heap of rubble. Their car, into a deformed metal corpse.
That could've been them.
Dice shuddered — it was the latent shock. That was all.

Dice scanned their surroundings. They were still in a tunnel. However, despite it being constructed of primitive brick, it looked younger than the portion of tunnel from the Pit. Signs of corrosion were only slight, and the bricks carried a vibrant reddish hue. If it hadn’t been for a stream of water dripping from the ceiling, Dice might've even been convinced it was only a few years old.
That, and the massive hole their car had put in the wall.
"Have any of those stimulator injectors on you, Wrench?" Matches asked.
Matches had managed to pull herself up from the ground. Wrench hadn't been so lucky. Despite his thick armor, he was still letting out faint moans and grunts.
"I used them all," Wrench said, finally rolling onto his side to push himself up. "After sitting in a car with you two for two weeks, I needed all of the stimulator injections that I could get..."
"Five days," said Matches.
"Three," Dice corrected.
"Might as well have been three lifetimes..."
Wrench readjusted his mask, taking an extra moment to feel around the dent in it.
"He's going to need a new one," said Dice.
"Or, he could just let us see his face," said Matches.
"Or, get a new face entirely."
"Or, maybe he could just keep his mask, even with the dents," said Wrench, taking his gun back from Dice. "Now, if we're done chatting it up, I think that we should probably get out of here."
He blasted a hole in the wall — a stairway cleared out of the rubble. Then he turned around, pointing back at the hole the transport car had put in the wall.
"The structural integrity of this tunnel is compromised," Wrench said. Wrench started in a brisk hobble toward the stairway. "I'm not sure how much longer we have. I'm not in the mood to find out."
"You never seem to be 'in the mood' for anything," Matches said, as they began ascending the stairs.
"Having you shut up for a goddamn minute would be nice."

As they ascended higher in the subterranean levels, Dice was struck by constant graffiti — images of guns, mutilated robots, and torn quantum processors, paired with phrases such as "death to robots". Most of it was crudely done in an oily paint. Vitriol foamed from every stroke, with some of the letters dribbling from jutting brick and onto the floor.
The subterranean levels didn't smell any more appealing than the graffiti looked. Each breath of air was accompanied by sulfur and rot. Where was it coming from?
"Herein lies the death of our oppressors."
On second thought, it probably didn't matter.

"I remember when they started this subterranean tunnel," said Wrench, nostalgia lining his voice. "It was huge — a joint project between the Gordon District and the Genoa District. It was supposed to connect us as a people and provide more wealth. More opportunity."
Wrench paused to scoff.
"It definitely connected us — especially with the crime in the Genoa District. That's why they had to board the tunnel up."
"You only vaguely know the place?" Matches asked.
Wrench shrugged.
"More or less."
There was a crunch as Matches stepped on a disembodied robotic leg. She shuffled away, edging against the wall. Dice and Wrench followed suit.

"I wonder what happened to this place," Wrench said. "But then... I should've known. An inevitability, really. You can always tell when a place is going to fall apart. Its roots — they're always diseased."
Dice nodded, but his eyes he stayed on the walls. How could anybody have predicted what it would become? Despite the bricks being younger, the messages on them were archaic, brimming with death.
"We're only a few flights below the surface," Wrench said. "Trust me: it might not be too pretty down here. But, up there? Nothing like it."
He was unusually chipper. His voice had the sound that could only be replicated by somebody coming back to something they loved. Coming back to their home.
Dice eyed another stream of dripping water. Would the Gordon District be anything like how Wrench seemed to remember it?

Dice couldn't imagine coming back to his home, only to find it in disrepair. Yet — where was his home? When he thought of the Monterey District, did it give him the same feeling that the Gordon District gave to Wrench?
He shook his head to get rid of the thought.
The air filled with a steam, and Dice's bodysuit chafed against his legs. Each flight of stairs was numbered now. First B-4. Then B-3. B-2.

They reached level B-1. Dice immediately took notice of the better upkeep, compared to the floors below. Graffiti was entirely absent. In place of bricks were platinum walls. Even the floor had a smooth metal finish. There wasn't a blemish — it couldn't have been more than a year old.
The steam rose to the ceiling, where the lights illuminated it in a golden glow. Wrench took in a satisfied breath of air.
Chapter 17:
"Yes," Wrench said. "Yes! This is home. It's as if I've never left."
Despite the gloss, Dice wasn't enraptured like Wrench. A few people were curled in the corner, sleeping in heater bags. It simply didn't add up.
"Are there supposed to be a lot of homeless people here?" Dice whispered.
Matches chuckled.
"Clearly you don't know anything about the Gordon District."
Dice's face went red. Though, when he looked into Wrench's eyes, he read shock. Disappointment.
They climbed a ladder in the floor and pushed open a hatch. Blaring light flooded Dice's eyes, making them water. He blinked a few times to adjust.
He found himself staring out into a vast, barren expanse. A few towering buildings took prominence over the landscape, and Dice could only see a few scattered crowds of people off in the distance.
"I'm finally back!" Wrench said, stepping out of the tunnel. As he did, the ground hummed under his feet. Dice went to look down, but Wrench patted him on the back and nudged his chin up.

"Look at those skyscrapers!" Wrench said. "Nothing like those smokestacks all the way back in the Pit! They house millions of people... Millions of dreamers... Millions of meters high. It's a whole world up there. It was — it was my world, once."

Dice looked. These skyscrapers weren't the complex streaks of cubism Dice knew from the Monterey District. Rather, they were immense, sky-high, and compact. Every inch was calculated. Every rod and window was in uniform with the rest. There wasn't a superfluous element. As Dice's eyes attempted to scale their summits, he had to pull them back down. They went too high, and the sun was too bright. Dice wiped away some of the sweat beading on his forehead.
He looked back to the ground. It was made of pearly blue panels for as far as he could see. Wrench's eyes followed, and he let out a laugh.
"Surprised by the solar panels, huh?" Wrench asked. "You honestly haven't heard anything about the Gordon District, have you?"
Dice shook his head.
"I've heard people say that it was an 'energy district' once or twice. But, I never knew it was... Well... This."
"The whole district is covered in solar panels. Centuries back, this was all desert. However, as time progressed, it was realized that this was a perfect spot to harness solar energy."
"That makes sense," said Dice. "I've always wanted to see a district like this — a 'solar city' — like the Brently District. They've always seemed like little more than a dream until now, though."
"The Gordon District is far better than the Brently District. Don't let anybody tell you otherwise."
Wrench chuckled.

"Well, it was... The Gordon District now though? I've never seen it so empty." He clucked his tongue. "I know we used to call this place the 'underground city', but I still remember when we could hardly get people to stop walking across every square inch of our solar panels. God... I wish that I'd been here to see this place fall apart."
Matches' eyes floated off in the distance. She let out a sigh and started through the sea of solar panels.
"No you don't," Matches said. "Trust me. It was a travesty... I travelled here for a couple of days once, while it was going through a major crash. Not smart."
"I don't care what it was like. This place was — was an old friend. And, now it's gone... I never got to say goodbye when it would've meant most."
As Dice and Wrench followed after Matches, Wrench kicked at the ground and let out a wry snort.
"I guess it doesn't matter all that much though," he said. "It was always a dump, even if I never saw it that way."
Dice was at a loss for words. He stared into the barren space. It was disarming. What could it have taken for a city to fall so low?
The glare of the panels burned his eyes. Dice tried shielding them with his hand, but to no avail.
"Wrench — you still have those goggles?"

Wrench handed down a pair, and Dice switched the setting from 'night-vision' to 'shade'. The strain eased from his vision. Though, the heat remained. Dice rolled up the sleeves of his bodysuit and popped a hydration tablet in his mouth. There was never a breeze when he needed one most. Or, was it just that he never noticed how much a good breeze helped until it was already gone?
It had to have been the former.
A group people surged past them.
"We're about there," said Wrench.

They arrived at the foot of one of the scrapers. Crowds of people bustled in and out of the building's doors in a wild rush. Instincts learned in the Monterey District kicked in as Dice read the faces of the people walking by — bloodshot eyes, and a red nose? Probably fired. Hands clutching an unusual lump under a coat? Smuggled energy packets. Baggy eyes, and heavy steps? Overworked.

Dice weaved among them, his eyes remaining anchored on the entrance. Right. Left. Left. Right. Left. Hands resting on the door handle, Dice looked back. Wrench and Matches were still swamped in the waves of people. Dice smirked.
"You know, I think that was worse than the army of killer robots," Matches said, once she and Wrench made it past the crowd.
"It isn't as if I didn't already hear you say that about a dozen times, while you were stepping on my heels," said Wrench.
"Your welcome for getting you through the crowd."
"Is that what that was?"
"Hey: what I did was at least better than weaseling away."
Matches shot Dice a look.
"I was just trying to get to the other side," said Dice. "I figured that you guys could take care of yourselves."
Matches shrugged, and craned her neck up toward the towering building.
"You think too highly of us."
She elbowed Wrench, and then pointed toward the building's top floors.
"So, is the place supposed to be up there?" asked Matches. "Because, if so, that's going to be one hell of a view."
Dice nodded in agreement but trembled inwardly. It would be too much of a view.

"Sorry, but we're not getting the penthouse treatment today," said Wrench, pushing the doors to the open. "The restaurant is underground. In the 'subterranean levels', or the 'ratholes' of the city, if you will."
"Sounds like we're headed to a classy operation," said Matches.
"Something like that."

They entered a lobby lit by fluorescent blue lights. The walls were thick marble slabs, and the floor was a milky surface. People dressed in eye-popping neon outfits and neon robots swarmed the place.
"A trade center," Wrench said, slapping Dice on the back. "This pace is full of them."
Dice didn't have long to absorb it all. Wrench took a sharp right turn into another stairwell. After turning through a series of doors, Wrench took them through one labeled "subterranean levels".
Steam smothered back around Dice. The term 'rathole' was far too generous a title.

They were in a passageway of cheap stone tiling, coated with layers of grime and dirt. Dice bumped into one of the tiles, knocking it to the ground — though, there was no avoiding brushing against the wall. The passageway was cramped, with energy pipes running all throughout it. Even the ceiling was only a few centimeters above his head.
"This doesn't make any sense," Dice said. "Just up there... It was so —."

"So glamorous?" Wrench said. "And down here, it's a travesty? Get used to it. That's what it's like here. See, the Gordon District isn't just a solar city. It's also geothermal — it collects energy from a complex system of heat pumps, built deep into the ground. The geothermal operation though? Not nearly as lauded, for some reason... Oddly enough, people have a hard time respecting those who work in the dirt."
They came to a sealed metal door. Wrench brought his eye to a scanner, and it opened up to another, wider passageway.
"Free storage units! Free energy storage!"
A marketplace.
Wrench turned back to them and winked.
"See? Wouldn't have gotten in here without me. They still remember my eye-scans, after all these years..."
The passageway was just as crowded as the lobby above had been. People were stepping over one another, making trades, cooking food, and sleeping in heater bags.

However, their demeanor was in sharp contrast to that of the people of the lobby. Their hair was disheveled. Their bodysuits were filthy and full of tears. Most of them looked like they hadn't showered in weeks, and smelled like they hadn't showered in months.
It was only when Dice remembered what he was wearing that he stopped staring.
"Is this where you used to live?" Matches asked.
"This place looks exactly like where I used to live," said Wrench. "Same structure. Same buildings. Same cracks in the wall. Even some of the same people. But... It's not where I used to live."
Matches twiddled her thumbs. Dice looked to his feet.

Dodging the glances and shouts of hecklers and hagglers, they made their way deeper through the tunnels. Dice kept his head down, only stopping to give passing glances at holes carved into the walls that were meant to serve as shops, houses, or trade fronts. Every so often, Dice would accidentally catch the eye of somebody. This was always followed by Dice shooting his eyes back down, and quickening his steps. In the eyes of each person, there was immense pain and disillusionment.
It wasn't his pain to bear though. He had to keep reminding himself that, until it was branded in his mind.
They didn't stop until they'd arrived at an especially nice hole in the wall. It was complete with sliding doors, a holographic sign, and a flickering rug that led into the entrance.

"This place used to be a tourist attraction," Wrench said, regret lining his voice. "When it was brand-new, there was nothing quite like it. I remember when they decided to turn it into what it is now though. Chasing radials — it ruins things."
They started toward the entrance, but Dice felt somebody grab him around the waist, and pull him toward a wall.
"Would you like a fresh robot arm? Maybe a head?"

It was a man with wild eyes. Disfigured robot limbs were bundled in his arms. Around his neck was a necklace, with a threatening razor blade hooked in the center. Dice could smell the desperation and rage seeping from under his demeanor.
"I already have all the robot parts that I need," Dice said, trying to push the man aside.
The man was inconsolable. He gnashed his teeth and groped at the razor around his neck. He yanked it closer to Dice's head. Dice continued to push, but he was pinned.
Matches and Wrench came behind him and pulled the man away. Wrench threw the man to the ground, taking a moment to stare him down, before finally walking toward the entrance.
"Radial scavengers," Wrench muttered.
Wrench tugged at the handle, but the door throttled in resistance. Wrench tugged it a few more times, before finally noticing the eye-scanner built into the side of the door.
"Of course," Wrench said. "Plateau's — the nicest place in the subterranean levels, and it needs security now..."
"Not sure if it's so nice anymore..." Matches said, under her breath.
Wrench brought his eye to the scanner. After a moment of pause, the scanner let out a firm beep. The doors slid open, and with it came the sound of music.

Dice turned his hearing aid down. The music vibrated through the floor, despite the floor being made of armored plating. He tried focusing in on the sounds of people laughing and chatting. Though, as he did, he found that to only be more trite and obnoxious than the music.
"My god," Wrench said, ogling at the ceiling. "They kept the lighting system exactly the same, even after all these years. I thought that they would've needed to replace it by now."
Wrench's voice was huskier than it had been before. He was trying to disguise it. But, from who?
Dice followed Wrench's eyes to the ceiling. The lighting system was flickering like mad. It probably had another week, at most.
"You could find a better lighting system than that just lying around in the Pit," Dice said.

Wrench gave Dice a stone-cold glare. Dice suddenly wanted to crawl out of his skin. He backed away from Wrench and followed after Matches. As he did, he surveyed the restaurant. In the back, there was a bar serving alcohol tablets and stimulator injections. Ahead of him, there was a ring of tables. However, nobody sat at them. Instead, they acted as a stage for a couple of singers.
Godawful singers.

Everybody was standing to eat, instead — not that they were really eating. All of the food the restaurant was in the form of food pods. They snugly magnetized onto the side of a person's bodysuit, and had thin, detachable tubes that would pump into a person's mouth. As Dice came past one, he studied it dubiously. It didn't look quite as nice as his old feeding apparatus, and it was unlikely that the food would be much better than Wrench's sludge. The restaurant's deterioration was a testament to that.

As they made it closer to the back of the restaurant, Dice caught notice of two people in slick, pressed bodysuits. A man and a woman. They were sitting at a bar, and a small crowd of people had gathered around them. The two leaned lazily in their chairs as they popped scoops of alcohol tablets into their mouths from out of a bowl. Dice looked at the bartender. He was cheering them on.
"They're getting all of that alcohol for free?" Dice asked. "They'll be dead in an hour."
"And you wonder why they're getting it for free," Matches said. "In all seriousness though, they're just the people that I'm looking for. The gatekeeper twins."
"Who?"
As they approached the crowd, Dice took a look back at Wrench. Though, he'd seemed to have disappeared.
Maybe he was just catching up with some old friends.
"That has to be at least twenty tablets!" somebody shouted.
"Twenty-three from Billard!"

Dice and Matches were now standing among the circle formed around the gatekeeper twins. Dice turned his aid further down. The speakers were just overhead, and the people around him had begun pounding their fists on the counter and stomping their feet on the ground. Dice looked to his side — Matches had joined in.

Dice folded his arms as he observed everybody's slacking jaws, flushed skin-tones, and glazed eyes. As Matches went to grab take an alcohol tablet of his own, Dice gave her a nudge and tried to pull her hand away.
"Not now," Dice said. "We need all of our wits about us."

"Last time I checked, you didn't have any wit," Matches said, popping an alcohol tablet into her mouth. Though, after she'd swallowed it, she raised her other hand — the tablet was still in it. "Sleight of hand."
Dice's eyes narrowed as he backtracked to when he could've missed Matches' trick. Nobody had ever slipped anything passed him before. That wasn't supposed to happen.
"Twenty-eight from Jade!" Matches shouted, joining into the countdown.

Billard's head rolled back as he tried popping a final capsule into his mouth. Despite Billard's attempts to conceal it, Dice knew that he wasn't going to be able to swallow the capsule. Nausea was tugging at the corners of his mouth and eyes. Sure enough, Billard spit the capsule out and raised his hands in surrender.
"Jade wins," Billard said, his lips curdling as he rubbed his stomach.
Half the group around Dice erupted with cheers. The other half grumbled as they gave away their energy packets.
"I would've won, if I'd bet on him just a few hours ago," one of them moaned.
"Sure you would've," Jade said, pumping her fist up in the air. "That'll be a thousand radials to me, by the way!"

Dice remained stoic, fixating his eyes on Billard. Billard drew himself up to his full height and cast a scowl at him. The muscles in Billard's arms bulged. Dice took a second glance at the bowl that in Billard's hands — it was the hollowed-out head of a robot.
Billard stepped out of the light and into shadow, his chestnut hair turning to a shadowy black. Dice struggled to see Billard's eyes from out of under his thick brow.

"And, what have you come here for?" Billard asked, with a hiss. The crowd around Dice went quiet, and a few people slipped away. Billard took a look at Matches, and jumped back to Dice. "I haven't seen either of you around here before... And I know just about everybody in these parts. You're not a radial scavenger, are you? Because, if so, you chose the wrong place to crash."
Billard towered over Dice. However, Dice studied the way that Billard's hands awkwardly clutched at his clothes. The slight wavering in his expression. He was putting on an act.
"No," Dice said, firmly.
Billard stepped back, aghast. Though, Dice wasn't surprised in the slightest — Billard only was able to put on the appearance of rigidity.
Jade came up from behind Billard.
"What's going on here?" she asked. Her arm shifted behind Billard. A concealed gun.
"We're just here to have a good time," Matches said.
"How did you get past our security?"
"Your security must've been on lunch break. All that we had to get past was a door."
Jade raised an eyebrow, and Billard clenched his fists.
"We were actually escorted here by a former resident," Matches continued. "But, his name escapes my mind, at the moment..."
"How convenient."
Jade stepped from behind Billard cocking her gun. Dice raised his hands but Matches remained relaxed. She pulled her deck of cards out of her sleeve and flipped them into the air.
"You and Billard... You run this District, right? The 'twin tornadoes'."
Billard smirked and tilted his chin toward the ceiling.
"That's what some people call us," he said. "As far as we're concerned though? We run an honest business, and 'trade' radials and energy packets for our... services on the side."
Matches slapped her deck of cards on the table.
"Good — because, I've heard a little rumor that you two never lose at your services..." Matches said. "And me? Well, I never lose either."
"That a challenge I'm hearing?"
Matches shrugged.
"From the looks of you two? 'Challenge' isn't quite the word I'd use..."
Jade's face furled in disgust.
"You think you can just come in here and beat us at our game."
"Something like that. I'm putting down ten thousand radials, for a game of spines. You in, or not?"

Billard and Jade's eyes ballooned. Dice's own eyes followed suit. He was almost positive his account was frozen. Even if it wasn't — ten thousand radials would clean him out. There'd be no way of paying Wrench.
Billard chuckled.
"I pity you, but at least you have guts."
"You in or not?" asked Matches.
"We need to verify that you have the funds," said Jade.
Reluctantly, Dice opened his cracked wrist-pad, and put his account on display — ten thousand radials.
Billard rapped his fingers on the table.
"Alright then. How many rounds are we going?"
"One," said Matches, dealing out the cards.
As Billard and Jade took their seats, sweat poured down Dice's face. He gave a glare at Matches and tapped on his wrist pad. She kept her eyes on the cards.
"Reds, Billard?" she said.
Billard forked his finger between his teeth, before setting a card down. Matches smirked and absorbed it into her pile.
"You got lucky," Billard said.

It wasn't the last time he said that. The game whizzed by, with Matches taking cards with ease. The lights over the bar flared in and out. The restaurant heated up. Dice readjusted the neck to his bodysuit.
When Matches spread her four matches down, and Billard pounded a fist on the table.
"I want a rematch," he said.
Matches leaned back.
"I want my ten thousand radials."
Jade sneered, and shook her head.
"Actually, on second thought..." Matches said. "There's something else that I'd like instead. You're called 'the gatekeeper twins' for a reason, right?"
Billard gave a look of bewilderment.
"Do you, by any chance, have Omega Keys?" Matches asked.
"Only those... intimately involved in our business should know about those," said Billard. "How do you—?"
Jade's sneer deepened.
"I knew it!" she shouted. "I had a feeling! Why didn't I trust it... She's Segue!"
Matches smiled and raised her hands.
"Guilty as charged. That's one name I go by," Matches said, laughing. "But, that's unrelated to the matter at hand. I won this cash, fair and square... and I need an Omega Key. Cough it up."
"Who is she?" Billard asked.
Dice's eye twitched, and he rubbed his forehead. He felt just as confused as Billard.
"She's that card-player who was squealing on the U.R.O — sending military forces after every game she played, win or lose," said Jade. "We're ruined."

"No, no, no," said Matches, in a rushed whisper. "That's not true at all. I'm not squealing on the U.R.O. I — I don't have time to explain... I'm headed to the Kelvin Union. I'll be off the backs of all your card-circuits once I'm there. Now, just give me the Omega Key."

"A U.R.O squealer trying to jump ship from the U.R.O, eh?" Billard asked. He balled his hand into a fist, and then relaxed it. "Or, better put: the U.R.O backstabbed a backstabber? Surprise, surprise. Have to admit it though — you did destroy me in that game..."
"You have an Omega Key to get us through the border, or not?" Dice asked.
Billard rolled his eyes.
"We did, but we gave our entire batch away a few days ago. It's going to take a few weeks before our partners send us new shipments..."
Dice looked for a waver. A crack. A flinch. Anything. Though, Billard gave nothing away.
Matches shook her head.
"We don't have a couple of weeks," she said. "You're sure that you don't have any spares? Please: all we need is the key, and the location to use it at. We won't demand any money."
Jade clenched her teeth, and her gun whirred.
"No keys means no keys. You really think you're in the position to be making demands? We could have this whole place turned against you if we wanted. You get out of our restaurant."
Billard shrugged, and motioned for Jade to lower her gun.

"You really think these people can do anything to hurt us?" he asked. "Anyway... We just don't have any. Nothing we can do about that. And giving you the location will be useless, unless you have a key."
Matches' eyes darted around, desperately. Dice's palms were sweaty. His pulse throbbed.
"We can at least get the extra ten thousand radials, right?"
Billard ran his finger through his teeth, then spat at the floor.
"'All we need is the key. We won't demand any money,'" he echoed. "Sorry — great game, but we don't owe you anything."
"That's not fair! You can't just do that!"
Matches ran her hand across her throat. Billard leaned forward, glowering over Dice.

"I've worked for years to accrue wealth and influence. The bottom of this district has fallen to tatters — infested by vermin, and robots. At the top are fat aristocrats, who leech off of what's been spoon-fed to them since they were in incubators. But, me? I'm still here. I've made it. Do you think I got here from caring about what's fair?"
