"'Beauty' is one word for it," he said. "The place works well, alright. For them. But, I'd hesitate to call the beggars from that other square 'beauties' — no offense to the ugly beggars. These robots... They don't care about us. They've cut themselves off from the people. What matters most doesn't matter at all to them."
"Radials?" Matches said, with a smirk on her face.
"The thing that matters the second most."
"Fame?"
"I was going to say family. But, close enough."
Vert's words hung over Dice's head. Everything was smooth. Pristine. Yet, at what cost?

The stairwell thinned out. The air did as well. A filmy layer of smog took place of the clean, filtered air from below. It tore at Dice's throat. He buried his mouth in his elbow and tried smothering his coughs and discomfort. Light from thin lampposts assailed Dice's face. His body trembled, and his face burned. Dice tried burying deeper, when Vert cast him a sidelong glance.
"Too much for you, already?" Vert said, once they'd reached a dead-end. "We still have round two."

Their stairwell ran off into a cliff. The roof was just a few meters above them, but Dice hardly paid it notice. His eyes were fixed beneath the cliff. A maze of lights and flying bots was fifty meters below. As he tried to look away, the maze warped and flashed.
"They definitely didn't build this with humans in mind," Dice said, slurring his words. A pool of saliva flooded his mouth.
"Yeah, they... They definitely didn't make it pretty either," Vert said, craning his neck over the cliff.
There'd been a tinge of discomfort in his voice. Though, what did he have to be afraid of?

Vert whistled. The whistle pattered down the cliff in a soft echo. Once it'd died to silence, Matches jokingly whistled back. However, her echo was stunted as a robot glided down and made a piercing beep. Slats slid from the wall, creating a clean trail to the platform. Vert walked up them. Dice begrudgingly followed. The wind lashed at his face, and world below him groaned. It was so distant, yet somehow still kept grip to his chest. He only hoped it wouldn't manage to pull him down.
"We predicted your arrival," the robot said, its voice grinding.
"And I predicted yours, rust bucket," Vert said, dryly.
"Your Clan has been plastered on quite a few information highways... You're figures of controversy, to say the least."
"What's it to you?" said Vert. His voice had gone soft, but he kept his strides hadn't slowed. He'd already made his way up to the roof.
Clouds wafted by Dice's head. Or, was it smoke? He choked and leaned onto Matches as it penetrated his lungs.
"I know they're literally drones, but you can't sleep just yet," Matches said.
"Me? Asleep? Never. I'm just... Just resting my eyes."
Matches smirked.
"Is that a joke I hear, Dice Raymond?"
Dice shrugged and took a deep breath of the smog. He shuddered.
"Maybe," he said. "This air must be going to my head."

Dice stepped onto the roof. His vision was blurred, and the smoke didn't help. Though, the roof was covered in generators, energy robots, and aircraft. Dice eyed a robot pulling a fluorescent cylinder from a conveyor belt. An energy pack? How could they produce an energy pack, in this environment?

Vert grabbed Dice by the arm and pulled him away. Dice's leg seethed as he tried to keep up. There was a pyramid just up ahead, with an electric rod jutting out of its top. Were they on a signal tower? He stopped to take a closer look but slid away as somebody pushed him from behind.
"Move it! Some of us only have so much time to kill!"

Dice shuffled ahead, and turned to Matches for support. Matches had disappeared. Whipping his head around, Dice saw that Matches had already made her way up to Vert. A robot hovered next to them, guiding toward the pyramid.
"You can't just leave me behind!" Dice shouted after them. "I have no idea where we are."
Matches didn't say a word. A harsh buzzing sound emanated from the robot at her side.
"We have a lot to discuss today," the robot said.
"I appreciate the info," said Vert. "Because, it isn't like the meeting we arranged two weeks ago didn't tip us off... You robots are so perceptive."
Vert snickered under his breath, but the robot gave a genuine thank you. Vert didn't pay notice.
"Have any Clan coordinators arrived yet?" asked Vert. "We'll need to be fully grouped before we can begin discussions."
The robot gave a guttural scrape.
"Negative," it said. "Only two other members of your Clan have arrived, out of a total of seven."
"Sounds like a fun wait," Vert said.
"At least you have this robot to keep you company," said Matches.
"At least there's that."
Dice sped his pace, before skidding to a halt as he reached the pyramid's glass door. He looked for a handle. Nothing. There wasn't even a scanner.

Dice jumped as a cap opened in the robot's chest, followed by a metal rod. A mop of several wires in the rod's tip swung back and forth, before attaching to the glass and climbing up its side. Once they'd gripped around a ridge in the glass, the door rumbled. It folded onto the ground, creating a carpet.
"After you," the robot warbled.
Dice stood still, watching the robot. Who was supposed to go first? Had it been talking to him? Dice waited for a sign. Vert coughed behind him.

Dice walked over the door, and into the pyramid. The glass was soft but firm, compressing slightly under his feet. Dice went to study exactly how the glass was comprised, but his attention was diverted by the architecture of the pyramid's interior. It was elegant in every—.
Dice's breath stopped short as a cold arm wrapped around his neck, yanking him back.
"I wasn't speaking to you."
It was the robot. Dice wanted to glare into its dead eyes but stopped as his face turned red. He turned away, keeping his head down.

"Please excuse my friend's terrible form. He has trouble following executive... Executive command stems," Vert said, catching the right words just as they were tipping off his tongue. "It won't happen again."
The robot rattled as it prepared to give a response.
"Who the hell is your 'friend' anyway?" somebody interrupted.
Eyes flitting to the doorway, Vert flashed a diamond grin.

A woman stood in the doorway. She was dressed in a cheap bodysuit that looked to have been worn ragged but was decorated in dozens of badges. She clearly outranked Vert. Yet, she looked several years younger.
"Speaking of friends," she said, "Thank god you're alive."
"Jackie!" Vert said, running through the doorway. "It's about damn time I saw you!"
Vert went to give her a hug. Jackie gave one begrudgingly, before stepping away and brushing herself off.
"The rest of you may now enter," the robot instructed.
Everybody had already entered.
Chapter 24:
"I thought your stupid plan had gotten you killed!" Jackie said. "All of the reports told us your unit was downed by a U.R.O missile. Are you a dead man walking?"
Vert laughed and gestured to Dice and Matches.
"A bit more complicated than that," he said. "Let's just say that my 'stupid plan' didn't go as planned at all... But, I don't think that I could be happier about that."

Jackie's eyes changed from cheery to somber as she looked over Dice. Then, Matches. Dice squirmed while a crowd of robots filtered past him. He desperately wanted to dip into the crowd and disappear. Instead, he was forced to study Jackie.
Her face was lined from intense scowls. There was heavy scarring on her forehead. Dice rested his hand on his chin. Why hadn't she replaced the scars with clean tissue?
Jackie frowned at Dice, then parted away the hair obscuring her scar, making it more prominent. Dice's eyes lit up. He had his answer. Jackie was proud of the scar. Proud of her intensity.

"Who are these people, again?" Jackie asked. "I thought I gave direct orders that all Clansmen were to be directed to the commerce circuits. This meeting is exclusive to the seven head-coordinators, and myself."
Vert played with his hands and sputtered.

"I — I thought I should bring them along," he said. "They're not Clansmen yet — I ran into them during the siege of Omicron. We need to initiate them. In the meantime, they can replace the two Coordinators we lost."
Jackie drew herself up and squinted her eyes.
"You found random people, and assimilated them into your group?"
Vert fidgeted.
"Trust me: they proved themselves."
Jackie kept squinting, before finally shrugging her shoulders and turning away.
"Alright then. We have more pressing matters to deal with right now."
"When can we get them initiated?" Vert trailed after Jackie.
"We can discuss that later. Right now? We have a debate to prepare for. I have several notes that I need to go over with you..."
Jackie's voice fell to a hush as she listed things off, before fading away entirely. Dice was compelled to follow, but his legs were frozen.
"We just going to stand around here?" Matches asked. "Let's go."

Dice wanted to speak but was mesmerized by a cloud of robots drifting under a window of the pyramid, with holographic computers projecting out of their chests. They must've been conducting the affairs of the city. Filtering through every element. Resolving every flaw.
They blotted out most of the sunlight from view. A flaw in their programming? Dice's eyes narrowed. The robots were covered in solar panels.
His eyes returned to Matches.
"I—," he began.

He couldn't help but jump to the corner of his eye. They were standing in a ring, overhanging a foyer. Hover platforms rose in front of him, then descended back down. Dozens of robots hopped on and off.

What was the platforms' weight limit? One of them teetered as it rose to their level. It didn't have rail guards. Dice flinched — if only there were a safer mode of transportation. A mass of robots darted below, freely.
Trying to count them all, Dice became lost. Whatever happened to robots only living in caves, and forgotten corners? Perhaps he should've stayed in the trade center. Perhaps—.
"Dice?" Matches asked. "Do you want to follow Vert, or not?"
Dice trudged toward the platform.
"So, that's a yes then? You look like a ghost, Dice. Cheer up."
Dice ran his hand through his hair. His gaze followed a platform's descent, before falling into the floor. He couldn't bring himself any closer to the edge.
"You've never ridden on a hover platform before, have you?" asked Matches, patting Dice on the back. "Don't worry. I'm sure we could just get one of these robots to —."
"No, no," Dice said, stepping forward. He bit his lip. The last thing he needed was to be coddled by a robot. "I've ridden these before. I'm fine."
As the platform came back to their level, Dice shrunk back. Matches pushed him forward. The platform swayed. Keeping a firm grip around Dice, Matches helped them regain their balance.
"Sorry," Dice said, clearing his throat. "I'm just a little rusty. That's all."

He pulled away from Matches and brushed himself off, causing the platform to rock. He ignored it. The ride was almost over, with them having already dropped ten meters. There were other things to worry about.

Dice stepped off the platform. Heat, emanating from robotic engines, enveloped around him. He cringed in pain as a robot rammed into his arm. The foyer seemed smaller and more claustrophobic than it'd looked from above, but its buzz was still as intense.
"You're welcome for the help," Matches said.
"Didn't need any."
Matches gave a wry smile. "Sure… Would it kill you to admit a little weakness?"
"I'm sure you'd like that, wouldn't you?"

Matches' face tightened into a scowl. Dice pushed past her, and into a line of robots. The robots moved in a near-perfect unison. Their voices worked as one. Their bodies looked like one. Their minds probably were.

Making his way across the foyer and toward a metal archway, his steps slowed. The crowd of robots thickened, obscuring the pearl floor entirely from view. Dice's neck strained as he attempted to peer over the mechanical mass.
"Hey! There you are! You guys can come up here! I saved you a seat!"
Vert's head poked over the crowd of robots. "Move it, rust-buckets."

He clapped his hands. The metal sea parted, creating a clear pathway toward Vert. Dice squinted. Vert sat in a row of ten pearl chairs, molded into the floor. He was accompanied by Jackie, and several other Clan coordinators.
Dice stepped from out from the crowd, and into the pathway. His back stiffened. Hundreds of robotic eyes rested on him. A clank resounded as Matches stepped out from the crowd and back at his side.
"Don't mind us," Dice said, brushing against a few robots. "Excuse us."

Matches took a seat to the far right. Dice took a seat to the far left, between Vert and Jackie. A chill ran up Dice's spine as he settled in. It had a clammy texture, and several of its garnishes jutted into his back.
"I like sitting and doing nothing as much as the next person — especially in front of a crowd," said Matches, eyes ballooning as they stared into the robots. "But, what are we doing here, exactly?"
"Just smile, and wave," said Vert. "Oh, also — we're talking to the giant robot, so we're going to need you to... not talk. Like, at all."
"The giant wha—?"
"I think I'm right in saying that we're all here now?" said Jackie. She turned her head to each side, summoning nods from the coordinators.
"Let's get this shebang started!" said Vert.

The metal archway bent and churned. A spindly tube shot out of it. Steam followed, as layers of metal fed out from the archway and compounded on the tube. Finally, a hologram flickered at the tube's end — a face. At least, something like it.
The unearthly visage hovered over them, its sharp green eyes vigilant. Dice listened for the slightest sound to expose the machine’s innerworkings. There was only the breath of steam.
"It's a looker, isn't it?" Vert whistled. Vert grinned at Dice, but there was a quiver in Vert's lip.
"Where are the rest of your coordinators?" the robot asked.
Jackie wrapped an arm around Dice. Dice tried pulling away, but Jackie only drew him in closer.
"Mel Traeger, and Alberta Pine? They couldn't make it, on account of being dead," Vert said.
Jackie shot Vert a look.
"They died in action, during our raid on Omicron," she said, puffing herself up. "However, we brought two replacements: Dice, and Matches."
The robot's face floated to look at them, before returning to Jackie.
"No last names?" the robot asked.
Jackie shook her head.
"See to it that there are no more flaws as you conduct this interview," the robot said. "We have little time for mistakes in the Tyler District."
Jackie nodded, and cleared her throat.
"Understood, Prime Terminal," she said. "Now, if it doesn't displease you, we're ready to begin our discourse."
Prime Terminal's eyes blacked out, its face edging closer to Jackie's. Dice thought he heard a slight creak in its joints, but it was too fleeting for certainty.

"As I understand it, your group is requesting temporary refuge and fuel from us. However, our records indicate your Clansmen have been more trouble than usual, as of late — raiding the U.R.O's major bases, and causing havoc among the populace. Specifically, populaces with an abundance of robots. Is this the case?"
Jackie smirked.
"Yes. I'd hope you'd already known. That's the sole purpose of the Clan. We cleanse places that need cleansing."
The floor rumbled as fire streamed down the Prime Terminal's sides. Limbs going numb, Dice turned down his hearing aid. His heart fluttered. His posture faltered.
"You continue to openly defy the U.R.O?" Prime Terminal asked.
Its voice spilled out as icy water. A cold sweat cascaded down Dice's forehead.
"Yes," Jackie said. "We've hit all of the major districts, and our sphere of influence is only going to increase."
The foyer fell subject to anxious clicks and cranks. Prime Terminal's processor must've run thousands of times faster than Dice's own mind — what was it thinking?
"Aren't you impressed?" Vert finally asked. "Every district we've hit instated new laws, to accommodate our demands. There's no other group in the U.R.O quite as effective as us at what we do."
A high-pitched grating fled from the Prime Terminal's bowels. Even with his hearing aid, Dice felt his ears go through a blender.

"Impressed is an insufficient term," Prime Terminal said. "Your motives are honorable, if zealous. Your effectiveness is even harder to dismiss. Though, I am hesitant to support the Clan. The Tyler District believes in peaceful protest, not aggression."
Jackie's smile faded from her face, and she gave a stern glare.

"I'm... I'm gladdened by the fact that you can recognize our prominence," she said. "We worked hard to get where we are — and we won't give up before we've gone the last step. The Clan's goal is the same as your own: to make a difference, which will lead to the betterment of the U.R.O. An alliance between the Clan and the Tyler District, even if brief, would leave a mark on history."

"How can we trust that you will not turn on us, like you have for so many others?"  Prime Terminal asked. "Our goals, while similar, are misaligned. I am sure you have heard rumors that our District has been producing dark matter engines — and, those rumors are correct. Our community's eyes are not set on Earth, but the stars. We aim to become interplanetary, like you humans have tried and failed at so many times — and, we cannot afford the risk of sabotage."
"Don't worry. We come only with peaceful intent."

Jackie swiveled her head and gave a motion down the line. Dice's eyes followed Jackie's, falling on a man who'd stood from his chair. He wore a well-groomed uniform and put his perfect teeth on full display.

"I'm Kevin Sine, head coordinator of the Clan's resources sector," he said. "I concur with Clan Chairwoman, Jackie Pierce. Question our methods if you like, but we make more impact on the U.R.O than the Senate. More impact than you. How can you trust that you have our loyalty? We need your aid — our aircrafts are dangerously low on fuel, our food reserves are practically nonexistent, and there isn't anywhere else we can replenish. Any acts of aggression against your fine district would be suicide."
Sine's plastic grin remained on his face, even as his nose twitched and eyelids flickered.
Dice readjusted in his seat, before bumping into Vert. This felt all wrong. They were in foreign territory, under the thumb of a culture far more hostile than any other he'd seen.

"I know we're asking for a lot, but we'll compensate you in the future," Vert said. "We don't even need star treatment — just stick us in your storehouses. We can use your defective energy packets and consume your scraps. That's all we need to sustain us."
Prime Terminal fizzed, and turned to face Vert.
"We do not keep our low-quality fuel and food in storehouses," Prime Terminal said. "They are deep inside abandoned pipes and tunnels, below us. Not exactly a favorable situation."
Vert shrugged, pretending to be undeterred. However, his fingers danced along his armrest, tensely

"That's fine, prince pixel," Vert said. "We just need the resources — doesn't matter how we get them. Besides, as I understand it, your supply of food and energy is unregulated by the U.R.O. It wouldn't hurt if we shrunk of that surplus supply, rather than reporting it to the U.R.O, now could it?"
Prime Terminal emitted a shrill beep, but Vert remained unwavering.

"Please," he said, staring up at the robot. "I've fought tooth and nail for what I believe. Probably harder than anybody here. You'll be hard-pressed to find another force capable of Omicron, alive. You believe in us. The grounds of our proposal. And, we need help. This decision should be a cakewalk."
"Except, I do not believe in you, or your proposal."
Prime Terminal's words cut through Dice. The row of Coordinators went up in disgruntled moans and shouts.
"What do you mean?" Sine said. "Haven't we more than proven our mettle?"
"Agreed," said Jackie. "What we're offering is not unreasonable."

"It is not reasonable either," said Prime Terminal. "Your Clan's crusade is subject to much controversy throughout the U.R.O. You are worse than the recent plague of parasite bots. Do you wish me to speak on the unspeakable atrocities you've committed?"
Jackie laughed.

"Atrocities?" she asked, dumbfounded. "What happened to robots being objectivists? Clearly, you've been taken in by unsubstantiated rumors, conjured by U.R.O propagandists. Let me assure you: the force we use has always been justified. Our sole goal is overthrowing tyranny and backwards thinking."
A group of robots inched closer to their line, off in the corner of Dice's eye.
"We cling to 'unsubstantiated rumors'?" Prime Terminal asked. "Is that an insult?"
Vert shook his head.
"Not an insult. Just a fact. You people — robots — enjoy facts, don't you?"
"It depends on how you define them."
"Good," Jackie said, pursing her lips. "I put my case out there. Now, will you provide us resources, or not?"
Prime Terminal's face was replaced by a hologram of fire.

"I have already made my position clear," it said. "Associating with you comes with consequences, whether the rumors are true. You have picked a fight with the U.R.O — an establishment we deeply respect — and, as we both know, picking a fight with the U.R.O rarely ends well. Here in the Tyler District, we carefully measure every action we take and don't meddle with chance. Furthermore, if the rumors are true? I could never forgive myself for helping you."
A scowl lined Jackie's brow, but she managed a smile.
"They're not true," she said.

Standing from her chair, she prepared to leave. The Clan Coordinators were livid, but Jackie seemed deaf to them. Though, as she went to step off the archway, she pivoted back to Prime Terminal. There was an empty glint in her eye, as if she'd forgotten something. However, her movements had been too fluid — it must've been rehearsed.
"It's a shame you're unwilling to supply us with resources," said Jackie. "Though, we'll be generous nonetheless: we won't inform the U.R.O of them."
"Much appreciated," said Prime Terminal. "I apologize on the outcome, but it is the only logical decision."
"Very well," said Jackie. "We'll look into help from other districts. However, I do have one request... All the Clan is exhausted. Could you, at the very least, give us some place to sleep tonight?"
Prime Terminal shook its head.
"Giving you a meeting was already generous enough," it said. "You have three hours to gather your Clansmen and leave.
Jackie shrugged. A knowing glimmer clung to her eye.
"Don't you despise the U.R.O and all their unnecessary regulations though?" she asked.
Prime Terminal shook its head profusely.
"Despite what is said about them, we are quite proud of this country," it said. "Could we have created a society like this without their aid?"

"And yet, just on the other side of this border lies the Kelvin Union — a haven, far more receptive to your kind," said Jackie. "I know the Clan has hurt robotic rights... But, we can change that. Wouldn't you prefer to finally reach a place where you're beyond the rest of us humans, and can expand... Unregulated? All I'm asking for is a place to sleep."
There was an extended silence. This time, however, Dice realized Prime Terminal wasn't bluffing. Its eyes flared. It was considering Jackie's proposal.
"You have a solid argument," Prime Terminal said. "I don't support the Kelvin Union, but I sympathize with some of their viewpoints. Robots have been held back for too long."
Jackie gave a thin smile.
"Does that mean you might consider giving us the fuel reserves, after all?"
A clicking formed in the back of Prime Terminal's throat, reverberating throughout the foyer.

"No," said Prime Terminal. "Quite ridiculous. However, I am willing to accommodate you for the night. I am sure we have extra room in the pipe levels. What you have said at this meeting changed my perspective. Perhaps your Clan is not as malicious as we have been led to believe."
Another series of clicks came from the Prime Terminal. The robots throughout the foyer reciprocated the clicks, before ascending to the ceiling in impeccable precision.
"Meeting adjourned," said Prime Terminal. "You'll be escorted to the subterranean levels shortly. In the meantime, exit the House and regroup with your Clansmen."

Prime Terminal folded back up into its archway, its words ricocheting along the walls. Yet, nobody moved. Dice tried catching the eyes of the Coordinators, to measure their weight of disappointment. Though, all their eyes were locked to the ground.
"You heard it," Jackie finally said, breaking the silence. "Let's get going and reunite with our groups."
As the Coordinators filtered out, the sound of shuffling feet was drowned out by moans and grumbles.
"I had a twelve-point argument laid out," one of them said.
"You think you have it bad, Samantha?" said another. "The presentation I prepared was supposed to run a full hour. That meeting couldn't have more than thirty minutes."
Dice took a glance at Jackie and saw the ghost of a smirk resting on her face. Her stride was confident and self-assured. It made no sense.
"Calm down, everybody," Jackie said. "At least we have access to the subterranean levels now. That's what mattered most."
"Am I the only one who's glad we weren't trapped in there for hours?" Vert chuckled.
Matches shook her head. "I don't think I've seen a meeting go so terribly before."
Jackie shrugged.
"Who are these people again?" she whispered into Vert's ear.
Vert cast a furtive glance at Dice and Matches.
"They helped save my life, remember?" Vert said, with a nervous laugh. "We really should initiate them soon, by the way."

Vert's voice trailed off after that. Dice tried reading Vert's lips, but Vert kept his head turned away. Dice turned up his hearing aid. He only managed to catch the words, "...are worthy additions to the Clan, before we take the risk."
Dice couldn't tell if it'd been Vert or Jackie. What did the words even mean? As potential meanings ate away at him, Dice drowned in regret. If only he could just forget.
Vert pulled away from Jackie's ear and they forked apart.
"You two love-birds done whispering yet?" Matches asked.
"Sorry," Vert said, backpedaling between Dice and Matches, and giving a sheepish grin. "We just had business to discuss."

Vert smelled like Jackie now. Soapy, dry, and stale. Vert's confidence had also waned, with only the skeleton remaining. Vert flashed smiles at Coordinators as he walked down the strip, but there was a self-conscious questioning in the corners of his lips. This anxiety bled into Vert's hands and breathing.
Robots flew overhead. Trails of sparks and fireworks ran behind them, to lead Clan Coordinators to an exit. Yet, Vert opted to descend back down the dizzying heights of the pillar.

Metal plates creaking beneath his feet, Dice could sense the entire structure giving away. A shout creeped up his throat. Yet, upon glancing at Vert, Dice buried the fear. There was a curtain of secrecy over Vert's eyes. Could he really be trusted?
"Watch your step," Vert said, sternly. "We’re up really high, and I knew somebody who fell off these before. Let's just say, it didn't end pretty."
Dice's eyes narrowed. Did Vert already know about his fear of heights? How much else might he know? What was he keeping bottled? Would it ever leak out?
"Shouldn't we be following after the rest of the Clansmen?" Matches finally asked.
"I need to recollect my group," said Vert.
"Aren't the rest of the Coordinators just sending out homing signals?"
Vert jumped over a gap in the metal stairway and let out a laugh.
"That's a good point," he said. "But... In this place, I'm not entirely confident in the abilities of technology. Call me paranoid. I'd rather go there on my own terms."
Matches rolled her eyes and turned around.
"Good for you then. I'm headed back."
Vert shook his head and squeezed Matches shoulder.
"At this point, the Coordinators are already gone. Besides: they're pretty antsy, and uptight. I'm sure you'd much rather stick with me."
"Yeah... I'm not in the mood to follow you throughout this city, gathering up your missing sheep. Just tell me how to get to the subterranean levels."
"No can do. You're just going to have to get in the mood."
Vert smiled and threw a playful punch. Despite his smile, his pupils remained firm. Vert cast a look at Dice, and his smile faded entirely
"Anyway, it's too easy to get lost if you're going on your own," Vert forced laugh as he let go of Matches' shoulder. "You'd just be losing time."
"As if you know this place any better than me."
"Trust me: I do. I've studied every centimeter for longer than you can imagine. Besides, you're safest with me. It's surprisingly... dangerous in this place."
Chapter 25:
"Is it just me, or were there way less people when we were all crammed in that aircraft?" Matches asked.
She gestured to the stream of people gathered behind them.

Dice was shocked by the number himself. Though, more shocking was the group’s demeanor. They followed Vert's instructions promptly, and without question. Their steps moved in unison. The same smile was spread along all their faces. Dice scrunched his eyebrows. They couldn't have been the same people from the aircraft, could they?
Vert snickered. "I feel the opposite. This group is finally altogether, working as a unit again — and I was one of those fat cats sitting in the front of the aircraft, where everything was spacious."
He paused to look over his group. His hands rested on his sides, and his face beamed with pride.
"I agree with Vert," Dice said, eyeing Matches. "This group was a zoo earlier."
He'd expected to see Matches flare with anger. Instead, it was Vert's.
"It wasn't awful," Dice said, trying to backtrack. "It's simply that this group was impossible to navigate when we first exited the aircraft. They were clearly out of their element."

"It wasn't their fault," Vert said, scowling at Dice. "We'd hardly escaped the hand of death itself. And, it'd looked as though our mission was about to fail. Now though? Things are looking up. Our plan is actually succeeding."
Matches snorted, and Dice felt the urge to roll his eyes.
"I wouldn't exactly say that things are going as planned," Dice said.
"You don't know the plan," Vert said, with a smug grin on his face. "You're not initiated yet."
He pushed past Dice and let out a guttural shout.
"We've nearly arrived at our destination!" he said. "Look alive, comrades. We need to make a good impression on our hosts."

Their group was tucked in the corner of a barren metal wall, with no host in sight. The robots bustled far above them all. The only sign of use in their corner were dull scratches in the ground, and the hot breath of a computing tower's fan beating down on them.
Uncertain chatters flooded the air. Dice nudged Matches, then followed Vert as he walked closer to the wall.
"You're sure this leads into the lower levels?" Dice asked, arms crossed.
Vert pointed at his sleeve.
"I have a tracker," he said. "Surprisingly, the signal still works down here."
"Well, look at you..." Matches said, elbowing Vert. "Mr. 'I can't trust technology.'"
Vert's face reddened, and he straightened himself up.
"It's a bit of a difference."
Face remaining an empty slate, Dice said, "I agree."
Vert banged on the wall. The wall groaned, then quieted.
"I could've sworn this was the entrance," Vert said.
His voice crumbled. He went to turn on his heel. Though, as his heel squealed along the ground, the wall made a squeal of its own. A thin gap wedged between the ground and wall.
Vert waved his arm toward the crowd of Clansmen. "It's open. Everybody can start entering, single-file."
Vert ducked under the gap and crawled through. Dice and Matches followed.

Dice found himself in an open, dim room. The floor was made of rusted grates, suspended by chords and pulleys. Squinting between the grates, he found a long drop below them. His mind conjured an image of the pulleys snapping. He closed his eyes and winced, before shaking the thought away.

The room was humid and stuffy, despite its openness. Conditions only worsened as Clansmen spilled through the gap in the floor. An engine hanging from a wall, connecting to the pulleys, growled angrily. Heatwaves foamed from its mouth. Pistons gnashed against one another.
Walking under the engine, Dice placed his hands along the wall. He recoiled. The wall was damp, a stream of water running down it. He scanned around to see all the walls glistening with water.
He looked at Vert, but Vert paid no notice. His eyes jumped between his wrist and his Clansmen.
"Is everybody here and accounted for?"
At first Dice had thought that those words had come from Vert. Though, it wasn't Vert's voice. Dice craned his neck to find a robot flying over them.
Vert opened his mouth.

"No need to answer," the robot said. "You've actually brought a touch more people than was predicted. We based our estimates according to the aircraft that you landed in — however, this group is 325.87% over your aircraft's peak carrying capacity.
"326%, to be precise," Vert said, annoyance coating the edges of his voice. "Aren't you glorified calculators supposed to be good at math?"
"I'm positive it's 325.87%. Are you sure that you didn't —?"

"Don't know, don't care. Anyway, yes: this is all of us. We have a lot of people in our group, and access to not-a-lot of aircrafts. Deal with it. Also, you can hit the pulleys. We're prepared for descent."
The robot chirped, then whipped to the wall's engine.
"So, how does this thing work?" Matches asked. "Is it water powered?"
"Used to be," Vert said with a smirk. "That function doesn't work so much anymore though. Instead, it's powered in... Other ways."

The robot plunged an arm into one of the engine's ports. Sparks of electricity shot from it, and the engine puttered with a new life. As the pulleys turned, and Dice's stomach churned. His eyes snapped closed. He could feel the robot's thrusters resting over his head, but he didn't dare open his eyes to look.
The elevator clanged to a stop. It creaked as a door opened. The ground rocked as people shoved past, their hot, sweaty palms leaching through his clothes.
He didn't reopen his eyes until he was sure everybody had left. To his surprise, Vert and Matches stood in front of him. Looking at him. Studying him.
"You falling asleep again?" Matches said patting Dice on the back.
"Just thinking," Dice said.
"Well — well, what about?" Vert asked.

Dice stepped off the grated elevator, and through the rusted door. He missed the stuffy atmosphere of the elevator and its trickling water as he entered a stone passageway, notable only for its lack of decoration.

"That elevator... It was nothing like the old transport capsules from the Monterey District," Dice said. "I'm used to struggling to understand technology. I feel like it's getting too far ahead of us all... Passing us by. This time though? I understood it very well. Too well. I could see all the seams. All the ways that it could break."
"I would think that..." Matches began. "Wouldn't that be more comforting?"
Dice watched as the last people exited the elevator, and the rusted door clamped shut.
"Not necessarily."
Matches smirked. "I don't feel too safe here myself. This whole place seems held together only by nuts and bolts. It's a terrifying contrast to the streamlined city above."
Vert took a turn to laugh.

"The robots aren't as streamlined as they'd like to make themselves out to be," he said. "This whole city of theirs used to be devoted entirely to manufacturing, and harnessing water power. That is, before their riots took it to pieces and turned it to a trade center."
"They made the most out of their changes then, because I wouldn't have been able to guess," Matches said.
"More like the worst out of it." Vert scoffed. "They built a new world but forgot to bury the old one. They've just left it to rot beneath them.
Dice looked over his shoulder for signs of any other robots. "You might want to watch the particular vernacular that you use around these robots. We are relying on them for refuge."
"Calm down officer," said Vert. "They can't hear us in this place. This is just an abandoned pipe system. They're not surveilling this."
Vert's eyes flared with a fire. Dice tried making out the fire’s shape but came up empty.
A jolt ran through his body.
"Sorry," Dice said, pulling away from a person's back.
Matches snorted. "Sometimes I think you have eyes in the back of your head. Other times? I wonder if you even have eyes at all."

Vert's Clansmen were at a dead-stop, having blocked up the tunnel. Searching for a way around the crowd, Matches gaped. Dice fought the compulsion to do the same. It was impossible to see over the crowd, to see what froze them.
"That's some traffic jam," said Matches. "You have some kind of way to get through all of them?"
Vert gave a dismissive scoff and ran his hands along the walls.
"There's a vault at the end of this tunnel," Vert explained. "They'll be sitting ducks until Clansmen on the other side figure out they've arrived."
"Don't you have some way to inform those Clansmen?" Matches asked.
"Yeah. I always carry a blowhorn on me. But, why waste my time trying to do traffic control? No fun. I have something better in mind."
Vert clasped parallel slats in the wall. His eyes darted to two Clansmen at his side, who were watching him.
"You..." he began, softly. Then, with a snap, "Stay where you are. I'm only taking these two."
The Clansmen pleaded at him with lost eyes, before subsiding back into the crowd.

Vert tugged at the slats. The wall grinded as a slab of concrete slid out. Vert let go, letting the slab fall. It never hit the ground. Hanging from the wall on several hinges, the slab acted as an entrance to a passageway. Vert scrambled up.
"Come. Quickly," Vert said. "And shut the door behind you."

Having entered the tunnel after Matches, Dice was left to pull the slab back over the entrance. After a series of grunts, Dice closed it with a crisp click. He gave a kick, to test its strength. There wasn't the slightest shift.

Dice crawled down the passageway, until it fed into a cylindrical shaft. Dice stood and leaned along the wall. Its soft white glow swaddled him in warmth. Dice looked up and saw Vert and Matches scaling rungs along the side of the cylinder. Dice's hand tremored as he grappled one and pulled himself up.
"The door clicked, right?" Vert shouted down.
"Yes," Dice shouted back.
"Good — that means the door locked. The Clan Coordinators unlocked it via hacking the system, so I'm glad it worked."
Dice raised an eyebrow. "You hacked it?" he said. "You sure know a lot about this place."
Vert kept climbing. Dice's eye twitched. The rungs of the ladder slickened the further he went. His palms went sweaty.
"Where are we going?" Matches asked.
Vert shook his head. "Too many questions, too little time."
"I only asked one question."
"One too many. But, since you insist: I have a meeting, and you have an initiation. I know: things are happening in a zip. But, I have a good feeling about them. How about you guys?"

If anybody had given too many questions, it was Vert. What would the meeting consist of? The initiation? Why did it need to be done so fast? Dice gave a half-hearted, "yes" and glanced over to Matches. Had she peered into Vert's mind yet? Was she at least prepared for what they were getting into?

Dice tried clearing the lump in his throat and fixed his eyes to the light emanating around him. Anything to keep his thoughts away from the height. The lump remained, until Vert and Matches hoisted him over a ledge. Even then, he didn't dare look down.
"It's pretty shocking that the robots leave these subterranean structures abandoned," Dice said. "They have so much potential."

"The robots prefer building their structures into the sky, rather than below where nobody can see them," Vert said, leading them down a hall. "It might've been easier to build off these bones — but instead, they were determined on reaching for the sun. That's just how those moron machines work."
Dice rubbed his neck. Despite Vert's disgust, could the results of the robots really be argued with?
"Anyway, we're not in the plumbing shafts anymore, thank god," Vert said. "We're having our meeting in an abandoned pump room."
"And, you know where the pump room is?" Dice asked.
"For the last time: I know where everything is. We didn't want to come here unprepared."
"You seemed unprepared talking to the robots earlier," Matches said, with a laugh. Though, as the laugh carried through the hall, it rang hollow. Vert gave a glare.
"Looks can be..." Vert said, his voice turning harsh. "What's the phrase? Oh, just forget it..."

Dice looked down the hall's wide mouth. Overhanging it was a row of spiked tubes, dipping in and out against the ceiling's clean light. Despite the walls' bleach layering, rust and mold was caked underneath. It was in just as much disrepair as the plumbing shafts had been.

Dice listened for what he thought were voices. Though, it was so soft he couldn't tell if it had been in his head. Even as they drew closer to the hall's dead-end and Vert's strides became surer of themselves, Dice remained unsure.
"Alright people, I'm here!" Vert shouted.

There was a brittle crunch as the dead-end split open. The hall went awash in light. Ahead was a round table, seating the Coordinators. Their heads were held high, carrying heavy pride. Dice's eyes drifted to Jackie. She stood over the table, with one hand on a computer lumbering behind her.
"Come in," she said, wearing her smug half-smile.
Upon entering, the wall boomed shut. Dice stared at Matches. She needed to dig into the minds of these people — figure out what was going on.
She was oblivious.
"Please, take a seat," Jackie said, motioning at three free chairs.
Jackie hawked Dice through the corner of her eye as Dice took a seat. It were as if her offer had been a formality, and she'd expected Dice to stand. Dice pretended not to notice.
"Nice setup you have here," Matches said.
She pushed down on the edge of the table, causing it to wobble and then rebalance itself.
"Hover tech," she said. "Fancy.
Jackie groaned. "Please don't touch the table."
"Why is it even here if we can't touch it?"

Jackie didn't crack a smile. She didn't say a word. Matches' own smile melted from her face. The other Coordinators leaned in, putting her and Dice under a microscope. Dice observed his reflection as his face went hot.
"They're just messing around," Vert said, eyes darting. "I'm sure this all excites them, and — so, what's first on the agenda?"
"Initiation, I suppose," Jackie said, apathetically.
She took in a deep breath and rested her eyes in the corner of the room. Dice glanced over. Was there something over there?
"We going to just cut to the chase? Or, do we go through the whole gambit?" Vert asked.
"Obviously the former," Jackie said. "We'll run through the highlights, so we can resume our meeting. Shall we?"
Her eyes flitted to Dice and Matches. She took a few steps forward and bent the hover table toward herself. A smile flicked past her face.
"I've been watching you two, and you each have potential," she said. "You're not cut out for the best positions in the Clan, yet... But, Vert didn't make a bad choice."

Her voice trailed off. Her lips pursed shut. Dice was left to look into her eyes. Black and vacant. It was like looking into a pool of murky water. There was something at the bottom, but there was no telling what or how far down.
Jackie folded her arms behind her back and spun.

"The Clan is a force devoted to purging the U.R.O of its greatest vices," Jackie said. "We claw and scratch against them, seeking to overthrow the constrictions brought on by their police state. To bring the U.R.O back to its glory days. Do you concur with this position?"
Matches leaned back, before giving a halfhearted yes. Dice gave one as well but couldn't ignore the bitter taste it left on his tongue.
His mind shot back to his time as an officer. To the flurry of emotions he'd felt when he'd first gotten his badge. The joy he felt when he'd been assigned his first case.
The pit of despair when he'd started it. When he ended it and had to watch a man's eyes turn to nothing right in front of him.
If it hadn't been for him abandoning the police, he wouldn't have been in this mess of constant death and turmoil. Was ridding the U.R.O of all governmental structure really the solution to it all?
Jackie gave a clap. The other Coordinators mimicked her, breaking out into applause. However, Dice couldn't even manage a smile.

"Good, we're almost there," Jackie said. "There are two particular forces we fight, fundamentally opposed to the success of the U.R.O. U.R.O leadership, and robots... With their eradication, the world can start anew."
A stone fell through Dice's gut. The words made sense, but still tasted of nonsense.
"Call me crazy," Matches said, raising an eyebrow, "but, I don't think robots are anywhere close to our biggest problem."
Jackie glared at Matches. "You've been misled and misinformed. They're the sole cause of all our problems."
She turned to Dice, hoping to find affirmation. When she didn't, disappointment and pity flooded her eyes. Strangely, Dice felt ashamed. Yet, Jackie was wrong, wasn't she?
"And, what have we been misinformed about?" Dice asked, his voice rising.
The blackness within Jackie's eyes slunk back as she stared into the light and let out a sigh.
"I'm sure you've heard the rumors that we're at war with the Kelvin Union," Jackie said.
Dice and Matches nodded. Though, Matches shifted in her seat, making the chair creak.

"A glorious war, isn't it?" Jackie asked. "The U.R.O, pitted against foreign aggressors who wish to suck us dry of our freedoms... Sounds like just the kind of thing that history is kept for, correct?"

Dice nodded again. "I don't find it particularly interesting who we're at war with though," he said. "It's just a thing that happens. A natural consequence of our power. It's really not the business of the average citizen."
Jackie smirked.

"Yes, of course it isn't," she said. Her fingers pressed lightly on the table, tilting it upward only slightly. "Isn't that what all of the officials always say? 'War isn't the concern of the average person'? Yes... Don't ever question. Don't ever prod. Don't ever wonder."
Matches' head was held down, and she avoided any eye contact. Dice folded his arms and frowned.
"Just tell us what you're getting at."
Jackie sucked in her cheeks and nodded sagely.

"We're at war with a nation that has been overtaken by robots," said Jackie. "You should already know this. What you might not know? They're upset with us for the way that the U.R.O has handled 'robotic rights'..."
She stopped to chuckle to herself.

"They believe we should be giving robots more power," she continued. "That humanity is a sort of sickness that needs to be dealt with. That we need to remove our 'human preservation' statutes. And, unfortunately, I think the U.R.O is going to end up caving... They've already removed 'human preservation' statutes from districts along the border, such as Tyler District. We haven't exactly been winning this war either, since the robots vastly outclass us. Additionally, the world is breathing down our neck, to force us to make peace — most of our trade partners have canceled their scrapping deals with us. And, that's not even the worst of it. The Kelvin Union is plagued with parasite bots... It spread to the U.R.O, among their scrapping operations. It's only going to spread more. When it does, it'll be a catastrophe."
"That's horrible," Dice said. "Though, the U.R.O government and their robots aren't really to blame for that, are they?"

"They're entirely to blame. They're the ones who removed sanctions on robot intelligence two decades ago, thinking they could somehow regulate it. Moreover, their military — despite all the funds and research put into it — has hilariously failed us. If they hadn't been consumed by their own hubris, we wouldn't be here."

"I don't mean to argue — I'm excited about being a Clansman more than anything, and I'm really just playing Devil's advocate — but, if the U.R.O removed 'human preservation' statutes, they could enlist robots rather than crude drones. Wouldn't that help the military? Maybe the U.R.O's choice to accommodate robots would be exactly what we need, after all."
Jackie shook her head. Dice looked to Matches for support, but she still had her head down. Did she not care? Did she not want to hear?

"So naive," said Jackie. "The U.R.O is powerful. But, not even they are powerful enough to control artificial intelligence... Understand: giving artificial intelligence power is exactly how the Kelvin Union crumbled."
Jackie chuckled again. Though, her mouth was stern, and her eyes sallow.

"Our death has already begun," she said. "Robots are everywhere now — taking our jobs, controlling our economy, building new districts. The only way to end any of our problems? By overthrowing the U.R.O from within. By showing the world that the old ways are gone, and they have a new iron fist to contend with. The Clan is that iron fist. We are the solution."
Dice put his head down with Matches, in solidarity.
"We are the solution," Dice said. He bit his tongue.
"We are the solution," said Matches. She raised her head. "So, what do you propose that we do?"
"Follow the order of the Clan," said Jackie, grimly.
She began to hum. A Coordinator stood and walked to the computer behind Jackie. He adjusted its dials. The room's fans roared, and the lights dimmed.
"Do you know what the 'Order of the Clan' is?" Jackie asked.
"No," Matches said. "But, I have a few ideas."
Dice's heart sunk. Matches' upbeat tone had splintered into a depressive drawl.
A serene smile wrapped around Jackie's face. Her eyes closed, leaving Dice to feel as though Jackie had been transported away and replaced by something ethereal.
"Can I trust that your loyalties will be with the Clan, no matter what?" Jackie asked.
Dice nodded. "Yes."
Matches leaned back and placed her hands behind her head. "I don't see any other way for us to quickly get into the Kelvin Union — so yes."
Jackie's face twisted into a scowl.
"She's just joking," said Vert, with a snicker. "They do need to get to the Kelvin Union, but they also support our cause. Isn't that right?"
"Of course." Matches wore a faux smile.
Jackie brushed her shoulders off and resumed her serene demeanor. Though, as she cleared her throat, she cast a sidelong glare at Matches.
"Repeat 'the Order' after me," she said. "Purity can only be achieved through eradicating robots and overtaking the U.R.O."
"Purity can only be achieved through eradicating robots and overtaking the U.R.O," Dice and Matches said. A dark cloud hung over Dice as he said the words. He shook his head. It was nothing.
"We are purity. We will bring things back to glory. We will be the U.R.O's revival."
"We are purity," Dice and Matches said. "We will bring things back to glory. We will be the U.R.O's revival."
An image flashed by Dice's eyes. A dark memory. Dice pinched his eyes closed. He'd gone too long without proper sleep. That was all.
"We are the revolution. We are the Clan."
Dice and Matches repeated the words. Though, Dice struggled not to slur his. All the chanting — it was too much. A nightmare tugged on the reef of his mind.
A whoop lapped around the table.

"Revival!" the Coordinators shouted, pumping their fists. Dice pumped his fist as well, but only mustered a mutter. Matches didn't bother lifting her fist at all, instead placing her hand to her temple. Dice's mind ran. What did Jackie think? More importantly, what did Matches know?

Jackie swung her fist a few more times, prompting more rounds of zealous chanting. Once Jackie's voice wore from the strain, the chanting subsided. Her eyes narrowed on Matches, who remained complacent.

"Congratulations: you're now Clansmen," Jackie said. "In the coming weeks, we'll make sure to host a proper ceremony for you both. Until then, Vert will — he'll be your guardian, keeping an eye out for you."
"Sounds excellent," Dice said.
The corners of Jackie's eyes crinkled, almost in a sort of sympathy. She turned away.

"Alright, now that that's out of the way," Jackie said. "We can begin our strategy meeting. We're going to try keeping this brief and to-the-point, people. We have a lot of work to do, and the less chit-chat the better. First order of business: does everybody still possess their Omega Keys?"
One of the Coordinators raised their hands. "Do our newly recruited members really need to be here for this?"
"It's fine, Gary," said Jackie. "They're fine. Now, everybody: pull out your Omega Keys, please. There should be two for each of you."
Dice turned toward the wall. Maybe and Matches didn't belong in here. Maybe it would be better if they left. Yet, the wall was fastened shut. They were trapped.

There was a series of clanks as the Coordinators set down thin blue strips lined with yellow microchips. Dice suddenly wished he still had access to his old computer-projector. It would've been able to reveal the keys' countless secrets.
"Those are Omega Keys?" Matches said, with a scoff.
Jackie's lips puckered. "Excuse me?"

"Hey, let's all just calm down here," said Vert. He looked at Jackie. "Remember, these people are fugitives for a reason. They've probably gone awhile without authority. Don't worry and be patient. I'll wrangle them in."
"Of course," Jackie said. She turned back to the Omega Keys. "Is that all of them, all accounted for?"
Vert leafed through them.
"Uh... There are supposed to be sixteen," said Vert. "But, I can only count fifteen."
Jackie's eyes pierced through Gary.
"Did you lose one of your Omega Keys?"
"N – No," he stuttered.
"Whatever, it's fine," said Jackie. "We don't have time for that now. We at least didn't lose any others. You can now all now place your Omega Keys back where you had them."
Jackie snapped a finger and pointed at Gary's chair. Gary blushed, before standing from his chair and giving it to Jackie.
"I love it!" Jackie said, sitting down as Gary awkwardly stood behind her. "All of us are here, and united, on the eve of our final crusade in the U.R.O."
Final crusade? Dice tried exchanging a glance with Matches, but Matches' head was back down.
"The Tyler District falls tonight!"
There was applause all around the table.
"Wait? Tonight, tonight? Why wasn't I told about this?" asked Gary.

Jackie shrugged. "Did you even pay attention during our meeting with the Prime Terminal? Tonight is all we have. And, it's now clear this is more urgent than ever... These robots possess dark matter engines. They can build Gideon Rays if they want. My guess? They already have. Sparky, like we discussed: keep an eye out for those."
Gary's face burned a hot red. Dice's face burned with him. Of course the Clan was planning on raiding the Tyler District. How could he have been so oblivious?

“Let’s go through a quick review: I'll be leading the main attack," Jackie said. "Samantha, you're in charge of the planting of underground detonators. You finally have everything in place for that, correct?"
A Coordinator, who Dice assumed was Samantha, nodded their head. Though, Jackie didn't take the time to acknowledge her, continuing to blare out names.
"Mel? You're coordinating navigation through the Tyler District, to ensure that nobody gets lost or sidetracked. Make sure all your assistants are in position and have their communicators online.
"Sparky and Vert? You're handling the ambush attacks. Sparky, I know you like relying on your hacking expertise, but you need to compromise with Vert."
A heavyset man wearing a blue visor gave a begrudging, "yes".
"Rosaria? You're in charge of securing our escape vehicles. I know it's a lot to ask, but you're going to need to get to the aircraft bay with your group before the robots can shut it down.

"Kevin? you're our quality control. Keep a head-count of everybody, keep our medical teams on target, keep track of the other coordinators, and do whatever you can to make sure our head-count is staying bigger than the robot's head-count.
"And, Gary... You'll be in the front-lines of our charge. Try your best to not get shot in the first five minutes."
Jackie lifted her head from her wrist, with an air of pride.
"Does anybody have any questions concerning their roles?"
Nobody said a word. Gary coughed into his arm and shuffled his feet awkwardly. Dice's ears turned hot. He hadn't prepared for this in the slightest
"When do we start?" asked Matches, her voice resuming its chipper tone. She yawned. "Because, I need a cat-nap, and this meeting is exhausting."
"The raid starts within the next few hours," said Jackie, coldly.

She lifted herself from her chair and tugged at her uniform's sleeve. A sword slid out, onto the table. Jackie lifted and swung it, softly scraping the table's surface. Dice winced at the blade's sharp whine. A thick silver tail was gouged in the table before Jackie finally placed the sword behind her back.

"As short notice as 'a few hours' might sound, I've gone through countless hours of training for this moment," she said. "We all have. This is our last hurrah. There isn't a crevice of the Tyler District that we haven't analyzed. Perhaps we should've told you both about this raid sooner — but then, we couldn't take the risk of disloyal followers, now could we?"
Jackie leaned toward Matches. Dice inched away, his heart hammering.
Vert hastily put an arm around Matches.
"Not — not to imply that we think you're disloyal, or anything," Vert said, sputtering. "You're a welcome new addition to the Clan. Right, Jackie?"
Jackie shot Vert a venomous look.
"Of course," she said. "We're more than happy to have you here. Anyway, I think that concludes our meeting... Vert, can you take them to a place where they can have a 'cat-nap'?"
Dice shielded his eyes as a glaring lamp was pulled into his face.
"BL-270 — I'm quite disappointed by your recent actions against the collective," said the voice.
Dice moaned and tried looking around. Blind-spots clouded his vision, and all he could see was blackness. Blackness, and a table. Dice tried to stand up. Tried to move. Though, he was strapped down.
"I'm tired of the collective," Dice said. "I'm tired of going through the same gambit, endlessly... Without rest... Without compensation..."
The voice clucked its tongue.

"You're my prized specimen," it said. "Out of all of them, you've satisfied me the most... Your results? They vastly exceed that of any other. Yet, maybe because of that I've been too hard on you. Maybe it's finally time that I extended my hand outward and explained everything."
The lamp backed from Dice's face and fed back into the ceiling. A man with an artificial left eye leaned in. Dice's heart leapt to his throat.
"My name is Professor Cassius," the man said. "And you, BL-270? You're a clone. Or, as this U.R.O facility calls it, a 'duplicate'."
Dice shook his head.
"No — no, it can't be," he said. "I'm my own person. I'm an individual. You've trapped me here for decades, against my will."

"Only a few years, not decades, my boy," said Cassius, with a chuckle. "And, understand: we haven't kept you here out of some sadistic means... No. Your efforts here have been crucial to the success of the Duplicate Project, and the Hamilton Project."
"The what?"

"You started out as a clump of stem cells. We bred you from that. Monitored you. Trained you to perfection, and then tried figuring out just what made you so successful. Later on? We used your intellect to weed out the failed duplicates of ours, and to study duplicate brain activity.

"Your work on brain activity was especially useful. We transferred your results to the 'Hamilton Project', to help create the first successful batch of androids. Androids with power over mind and machine. They didn't go over as well as we would've liked, choosing to escape their confinement and go rogue... That's why we've had you working especially hard, as of late. We've needed your help to locate them all."
"I work like a slave, because a group of androids went rogue?"

"You work for the benefit of the collective, not as a slave. You've been helping kill androids that might one day kill others. That's your purpose. That's what we've genetically engineered you to do."
Dice's head ached. He stared into the darkness, trying to escape, but the darkness only seemed to draw in and smother him. Too much was going on. Nothing made sense.
"If I'm a duplicate, who am I a duplicate of?"
Professor Cassius coughed.
"Who am I a duplicate of!?" Dice shouted.
"It's utterly random," said Cassius. "I'm sorry. You could be anybody, out of billions."
Tearing at his hair, Dice's eyes bulged. "This isn't fair. None of this is fair. I deserve to have my own life. To be my own person. You can't just keep me as a rat! Do you hear me!?"
"I hear you."
There was a crash. Cassius disappeared. A green light flared on. Dice spun his head, but only found walls of glass, with the words "duplicate" sprawled along them.

"You're right," said Cassius. "Your mind has matured beyond that of any other duplicate. You don't belong here anymore. This chamber you're in? It'll erase all memories of any of this. When you wake up, you'll be a new man, free to live whatever life you choose."
Dice went to retort but was gagged by a black ooze. It coiled around his legs. His torso. His face.
He watched the word "duplicate" on the glass steadily fade away, letter by letter.
"Duplicate."
"D plic te."
"D   lic te."
"D    ic  e."
Chapter 26:
Dice sat up. His head buzzed. Sweat dripped down his face.
He closed his eyes and ran his hands through the coils in his hair. His nightmares couldn't have been true. Could they have? No, it must've just been a fever dream. A hallucination.
He reopened his eyes and scanned around. Maybe Matches triggered the nightmare.
She was nowhere in sight. The entire room was empty, covered in abandoned sleeping bags.
"No," Dice moaned. His eyes and nose stung. He fought back tears. "I don't... It doesn't..."
He choked.
"Everybody, report to their stations," a voice blared through the walls. "You have an hour until the assault."
Dice limped through the exit, back into the plumbing shafts. Streams of Clansmen brushed past.
He had to get out. Find a place of solitude. An entire district was about to be turned to ash, and he would be powerless to stop it. Powerless... Like he'd been all his life.
Discomfort lodged in his soul. Maybe Professor Cassius was right. Maybe he was destined to kill robots.

Dice turned up his hearing aid and looked over his shoulder. He could've sworn he'd heard footsteps trailing after him, echoing his own. However, there were just Clansmen and barren tunnel walls. Paranoia welling up inside, Dice ducked between the crowd and went down a narrow corridor.
The air was dim and cool. A flush of water streamed through a tube overhead. As the corridor thinned more, Dice hunched. Lights flickering along the walls kept him going forward.

Once the lights dropped off and the tunnel began to sandwich him, Dice crouched against a wall. Leaning in, the abrasive rock tore against his skin. A sludge of rust and scraps lapped at his ankles. Dice's shoulders tensed. His lungs deflated.
His entire world had imploded. In less than an hour, the entire Tyler District would do the same. Everything the robots had built would be gone. Was that supposed to be good, or bad?
Dice shuddered. There was no clear answer.

Dice pushed against the walls. They were so close together. Cramped. Compressed. Dice's heart railed against his ribcage. It was as if he was back in the containment tubes from the Duplicate Project. Yet, even that had felt better than this.
"Dice!"

Dice's eyes widened. He peered down the corridor. He wasn't alone. At the end of the tunnel were two silhouettes. He looked away, squinting at where the corridor thinned into a pipe. He would’ve tried pressing through, but he was already as far as he could go.
"Dice-skater!" the voice called again. "Dice the diesel! Spicy Dicey! What are you doing here?"
It was Vert.
"Dice, I know you're there," said Matches. "I'm about to start a game of spines — don't leave me to be stuck playing with this novice."
"How'd you find me?" Dice crawled forward.
Shoulders loosening as he stood, he waddled toward them in a hunch.
"When we saw you were still sleeping, I manually synced up with your wrist’s signature," Vert said.

"We stalked you," Matches said. "Trust me, it's better than it sounds. Actually, maybe not... Anyway, Vert said he'd come back to wake you up, before we started the assault. Looks like you beat him to the punch."
"Do you want to play a game of cards?" Vert asked. "We only have an hour before we launch the attack, and I need to clear my head. I figured we all did."
There was a hazy film around Dice's vision. He just wanted more time alone. More sleep. Could Vert really be trusted?
Vert crouched with a chuckle. He tossed a worn pack of cards in Dice's direction.
"You know how to shuffle?" Vert asked.
Dice didn't hear the words until after Matches had crouched next to Vert.
"Wha — oh, yeah, I know."
"Trust me, Vert," Matches said. "He's great."
"Great. I'll… Trust you, then."
Dice dumped the cards into his lap. As he shuffled them, his fingers turned to bludgeons. The stack was dough in his hands, becoming more misshapen the longer that he held them.
"They don't have any cleaner robots back here?" Matches said, brushing the rust off her hands. "Or, at least a mop?"
Vert burst out laughing.
As the laughter subsided into soft pings in the distance, Vert placed a hand on Dice's wrist. He reached for the cards.
"Why don't I try shuffling those?" Vert flashed a grin.
Once Vert had pulled his hands and the cards away, Dice wiped his wrist off on his bodysuit. Grime had caked onto it. Had it been there all along, or had it come from off Vert's hand?
"Quite the thing we have going, isn't it?" Vert asked. "Don't worry: the Clan only gets worse the longer you're in it."
He snorted. The cards chattered as his fingers glided over their edges. Several of them were left bent.
"In all seriousness, you two will be fine," Vert said. "Sorry if Jackie seems a bit... Intense. She's not usually like this. It's just that the stakes are so high right now, you know?"
"Intensity is just a given in the Clan, isn't it?" Matches asked.
She took a pile of cards and turned them over.

"Exactly!" said Vert, with a smile. "There might be extremes in the Clan. But, these are extremes that need to be taken. The U.R.O must be brought back to its former glory. To stop it from falling, we must make it fall."
Dice took his cards. His fingers throbbed. They were all hot trash. He peered over them. It was almost his turn, and Vert was a dangerous opponent. He had the glint of experience in his eyes.
"You owe me two cards," Vert said. "I always get lucky with my guesses."
He laughed and held his hand to his chest. Dice forced a laugh of his own, to stave off Vert's laugh becoming another perturbing echo.
"Your turn," Vert said, eyeing Dice.
Dice leafed over his cards, before asking for one from Vert. Vert didn't have the card. Dice tossed his card over to Vert and returned to his deck.
"The slightest slip could tarnish the Clan's operation," Dice said. "Why did you ever bother saving us from the Omicron? Why take a risk on us?"
Vert shrugged.
"I saw something in you and — Wrench, was it?" he said. Dice winced at the mention of Wrench. Though, Vert went on as if he hadn't even noticed. "And Matches too, of course."
Vert asked for a card from Dice. The card floated out of Dice's deck, lighting up Vert's face.
"Just make sure that you don't screw up," Vert said, eyeing Matches.
"Wouldn't dream of it," Matches said.
Matches took her turn and ended it with two less cards.
"Sometimes, I try to keep this game lasting forever," Matches said. "I don't think that I'll be able to do that this time though."
Vert snorted. "Like I said earlier, I'm good at what I can do."
Cards slipped out of Dice's and Matches' hands, while Vert's deck kept fattening. Turns went by, with seldom so much as a word. Dice's deck finally thinned to one card.
"Are you guys excited for tonight?" Vert asked.
Dice shrugged. "More afraid, than anything else."
He tossed his last card to Vert and scooted out of the circle.

"Stage-fright?" Vert said, with a grin. He tried injecting sympathy into his voice, but his eyes were set on Dice's card. "Don't worry. Once you're on the battlefield, destroying those robots, you won't even remember how you're feeling right now."
"I wouldn't call this district a 'battlefield'," Matches said, putting down her last card.

"Would the term, 'hellhole' be more accurate? It doesn't matter. What I was going to get at is this: you two are now members of the Clan. The greatest force in the world. You're Clansmen! No matter what anybody does, that can't be taken away from you. Wear your title with pride. Don't forget it."
Matches scooted out of the circle. Vert sat alone with his deck and the stack of cards.
"Report to your station!" A voice blared. "Thirty minutes remaining!"
"Uh... Well," Vert said, standing up. "This was a good talk. Thanks for the game. Now, we really have to go. This Clan isn't going to be able to organize itself."
Vert put the cards back in their box and began walking off. Though, Matches managed to snag them out of his hands.
"I want just one more quick game, between me and Dice," Matches said. "See you in a bit. Don't get killed by any rogue robots."
"I won't," said Vert.
"Don't jinx yourself."

Vert's laughs echoed through the tunnel. Dice considered following after them. Of returning to the crowd of Clansmen, and the mess of orders and instructions among them. He'd be hopelessly lost. However, he would at least have made a choice.
Matches pulled the stack of cards out of the box and shuffled them. She handled them with ease, with them gracefully sliding through her fingers.
She placed the pack of cards down.
"What's wrong?" asked Matches. "Upset you lost another game of cards?"
Keeping his eyes fixated on a pool of water, Dice shook his head.
"I don't think I've ever lost a game of cards before myself," Matches said.
She'd started as a joke but lost her jovial tone halfway through.
"You must've lost against Vert on purpose," Dice said.
Matches managed a halfhearted chuckle.
"Maybe," she said.
Dice kicked at the puddle. He looked for ripples but found none. Darkness absolved the puddle of any detail.
"You going to start the game?" Matches asked. "Or, is the ground that much more interesting?
Dice sighed. Matches placed a hand on Dice's back.
"What's wrong?" Matches asked.
Weathered markings were sprawled along the wall. Were they wear and tear, or graffiti?
"Dice?"
"I — I was wrong about you," Dice said. "Those nightmares I was having... They had nothing to do with you, after all. I'm sorry."
He ran his hand through his hair and closed his eyes.
"I'm sorry too. I should've never interfered," Matches said. "I've had a lot of nightmares myself, lately. Close encounters with Knowles, the death of Wrench, and now this... It's a lot."
Dice shook his head. "My nightmares weren't about any of that."
He clenched his cheeks.

"You’re right. I only saw glimpses of your nightmares," Matches said. "Dark rooms... Cramped spaces... Strange voices... They were some of the most lucid I've ever seen. If you don't want to tell me, you don't have to... But, what were they about?"

Dice's head went numb, and his ears rang. Images flashed in front of his eyes. The tunnel went black and folded around him. A glass wall pressed against him. Pressure bound his eyes as he tried to break free.
"I'm in a cage," he said, with a pant. "A tube. And, I can't... I can't get out. I'm trapped."
Matches' hand was on his forehead.
"It's gone now," she said. "Breathe. Think of something else. It's just a bad dream."
Dice coughed and shook his head.
"No, you don't understand," he said. "I used to think that, but these dreams... They're not just dreams. They're memories. Years' worth of suppressed memories."
Matches pulled her hand away and shook her head.
"That doesn't make any sense."
Dice felt as if he were floating. The walls still pressed against him, but they were so far away.
"I'm artificial. A clone. A duplicate."
Dice choked after letting the words out. Dice wanted to study Matches' face and gauge her reaction. Read her mind. He couldn't bring himself to, in fear of finding horror.
"It's alright," Matches said. “Pretty sure that we’re all misfits, here.”
Matches smiled. It was a thin smile. If Dice hadn't been paying close attention, he would've missed it. Though, unlike many of Matches' other smiles, this one was genuine.
Dice cleared his throat. "My last nightmare cleared things up for me... But, everything is confusing. Remember the man who I kept you from killing in the MDPD? Professor Cassius?"
"Vaguely."

"I don't know how, or for how long... But, he created me. Me, and thousands of other duplicates. We were constantly used in experiments. Some of them, to kill other failed duplicates. Others, to kill failed androids. Our sole purpose was to be killers... We were bred killers."
Matches' eyes were down, watching her fidgeting hands.
"So, what I'm getting out of this is that there's two of you walking around?" Matches asked. "And, I thought one of you was bad enough."
Dice smiled. The smile faded. He shook his head.
"Maybe... Probably. To be honest, I have no idea who I was cloned from. They could be dead. Could be alive. I'm lost."
"Call me crazy, but I don't think there can be anybody else like you."
Dice's eyes jumped to the puddle again. He could've sworn it sloshed. Yet, it remained stagnant under his gaze.
"But, there is," he whispered.
Matches shook her head. "I've heard of clones before. But, I had no idea that there were so many... I had no idea their conditions were so poor."

"I had no idea either, until today. I wish I still had no idea. They put you in capsules that are pitch-black... Cramped. Half the time, you can't move. They numb your nerves and senses, so you can hardly even feel. You live to be connected to a computer, where more knowledge will be uploaded. Where you'll be allowed to sense, and feel... But, you never truly get to sense and feel. Not really."
"Life must've been... Tough once you got out of the capsule."

"You'd think that... But, the further back in my memory I go the blurrier it becomes. I'm not even sure what's real and what's not. For all I know, I was released into the world only a month ago, and everything else is just implanted."
Matches kicked at the water. There was a resounding splash, which climbed up Dice's back as an unnerving chill.
"Yeah..."
"That's just a word people use when they have nothing else to add to conversation."
Matches' expression deepened into a frown, before curling upward in a makeshift smile.

"Yeah..." She straightened herself up. "Anyway, Vert finally isn't snooping around, and seeing as we're revealing things to one another: the Clan isn’t what they say it is. I've been probing people's minds. They want to kill everybody in this district. Not just the robots. The humans too. Sparky's plan is to hijack a Gideon Ray. And, Jackie? She wants Vert to kill us, once this is all over."
Dice snorted. "Figures..."
"Yeah. I'm thinking that we split off from them for an aircraft, first chance we get. I managed to snag an Omega Key while they were bickering in the meeting. We don't need their help anymore."
Matches whipped a blue band out of her pocket and handed it to Dice.
"Matches, you sly dog," Dice said, with a grin. He pocketed the key.
"Guilty as charged."
Dice stared into Matches' silver eyes. "Is there anything else you want to tell me? Any... Any secrets of your own?"
"Other secrets?" Matches asked, her voice collapsing once it had carried passed the puddle rippling under her feet. "I don't have any secrets."
The air was rotten, and musty. It smelled like Dice's old apartment. It had been too long away from there. Away from home.
"I think that's the first joke I’ve heard you make that you haven't laughed at," Dice said, rubbing his eyes.
"I wasn't joking."
"You definitely weren't telling the truth."

Dice studied Matches' face. The longer that he looked at it, more mileage seemed to pile onto it. Dust covered her skin. Her hair was ratty. Her nose was slightly crooked. There were a few scuff marks and scars that certainly hadn't been there before.
Or, had they?
It was the first time he'd noticed it. Whenever Matches smiled, all the wear had slipped by without detection. Now? Everything was peeled back. There were no more fake smiles, or false covers.
Dice shuffled his feet but wasn't met with the familiar sloshing of water. It had all been splashed away, only a coat of rust remaining.
"I don't have much of a story to tell," Matches said. "Not one like yours, that's for sure."
"I doubt that."
Matches gave Dice a fierce glare.
"I don't have a story to tell," she said.
Her face softened.
"I don't have much," she said, sweeping her hair out of her face. "And, what I do have? I'd prefer to keep to myself. Please: just trust me on this."
Matches turned, walking back toward the widening mouth of the tunnel.
"Of course I trust you," Dice said.
The words singed his lips. However, what else could he say? What else could he do?
"Let's go back to the Clan," said Matches.
"Sounds good."
Chapter 27:
"Who is going to eradicate robots?!" Jackie said, in a shrill cry.
Dice's hand jerked to his hearing aid as the room exploded with, "The Clan!"
"And who is going to take over the Tyler District?!" Jackie shouted again.
"The Clan!"
"And, who is going to bring it back to its former glory?!"
"The Clan!"

Smiling smugly, Jackie clasped her hands together. She stood over the crowd, on a platform of deformed robots and scrap-metal. Yet, she might as well have been standing on a cloud. The eyes of every Clansmen brimmed with luster, fully enraptured by her.
"That's right!" Jackie said, puffing herself up. "Now, remember: apart we hold power—"
"Together the Clan wields it!" the crowd cried in unison.
Matches leaned into Dice's ear. "I bet if they were asked how many fingers they had, they would answer the Clan..."
"They would still be right, too," Dice said.
They shared a frail smile.

The Clan had gathered outside a sprawling steel gate, which marked the final separation between the Tyler District's higher and lower levels. A checkered electric barrier guarded it. Dice gave a pitying frown. It would be turned to cardboard in a matter of minutes.
"We are purity. We are the revolution. We are the Clan," Jackie said. "I embolden you: feel no fear. The Clan has not and will not fail. Not yesterday! Not tonight! Not ever!"
The crowd cheered. Jackie raised her hands, drinking it in.
"We've trained for weeks on end! We will win! We will be celebrating tonight for weeks to come!"
Jackie unsheathed her sword, making a few swings at the air.
"The only way we can fail is if we are to believe in failure," Jackie said, lowering her voice and hanging her head. "Focus on your duties, and victory is destiny!"
Jackie pumped her fists, garnering fresh rounds of praise. Dice joined in, ignoring the bitter taste.

As the cheers subsided, Jackie stepped from the platform and walked toward the barrier. She motioned to Clansmen at the front of the crowd, prompting them to follow her. Swift, well-armed, and well-armored, they were distinct from other Clansmen. Their blasters were particularly distinct, being bulkier and brighter than any others.
A guttural shout left Jackie's throat. The Clansmen aimed their blasters at the barrier.
"Fire!"
