Rather than a blast, there was a hum. The electric field buckled. Warped. Steadily swallowing the electric field, the blasters' soft yellow glow was replaced with a blinding red. The barrier sparked and sputtered, before finally being left barren.
A hush fell over the Clan. Dice's eyes bulged in wonder. Yet, the feeling fled upon faint sounds — scrapes and claws, teetering on the edge of his hearing. His gaze focused on the barrier.
"Do you hear that?" Dice asked, with a gulp.
Matches smirked and shook her head. "Still hearing voices?"
Dice put his hand to his hearing aid. It'd been turned down — the sounds must've been a hallucination.
"Guess the nap wasn't enough," he said, faking a yawn.
Jackie gave a sharp whistle, slicing through the silence.
"Aim, and fire on my command!" she shouted.
The Clansmen's arms swung in a jerking motion as they flipped a switch on their blasters. In a growl, the blasters' red lights flickered fiercely.
"Fire!" Jackie shouted.

The room flashed. A boom resounded. The barrier wailing as it fell to the ground, Dice closed his eyes. Anguished screams and cries circled him. His heart pounded, but the pounding of feet drowned it out. Flakes of metal flew into his skin. A gash dashed across his cheek.
The screams settled. Dice's eyes reopened.

Matches was gone. The Clansmen were already moving through a newly-made exit and into the center of the Tyler District. A small army of robots flanked around them. The robots raised their weapons, showing they were fully prepared to attack.
Dice whipped around. Much of the room was buried by the collapsed metal barrier and chunks of the ceiling. Dice's breath stopped short. Limbs jutted from under the rubble.
A hand fell onto Dice's shoulder.
"That was some explosion," Matches said. "It knocked a few years off my life."
Dice grinned. Dust covered Matches, but she was largely unscathed.
"Stay close behind me," Matches said, bringing her hand to her forehead. "Getting through this should be a cakewalk."
Matches jogged toward the crowd of Clansmen. Though, Dice's eyes remained on the rubble. Stragglers were still pulling themselves out.
"Come on Dice," Matches said. "We can't forget what's in front of us."
Reluctantly, Dice hobbled toward her. Gunfire rocketed between the robots and Clansmen. Dice watched each side fall, like dominoes. Yet, the Clan managed to outnumber the robots.
"Where the hell is Vert?" Matches asked.
"No idea. I can't make this battlefield out any better than you."
They pushed past Clansmen, making it further toward the front line, but there was no sign of Vert's ambush. Worse yet, the aircraft hangar was nowhere in sight.
"Probably should've snagged a map while I was snagging that Omega Key," Matches said.
"You think?" Dice said.
"Get back! Get back!"
Dice was shouldered by Jackie. Her eyes were glazed over, and her face red. An explosion went off. Dice hardly noticed it, over Jackie's crazed shouting.
"Pipe down, commander. What's going on?" Matches asked.
Jackie's frantic shouting subsided.

"This wasn't supposed to happen," she said, voice lowering to a hush. "The robots — they were prepared for our attack. We must've tipped them off somehow... They're fading fast, but not fast enough to get us to the aircraft hangar before the detonators go off. Worst of all, Vert and Sparky? They won't pick up."
Jackie turned away, running deeper into the crowd.
"Out of my way!" she shouted, retreating to the barrier's rubble.
"You can't run away! You have the secret weapon!" Matches called after her. "You're the only one here who was smart enough to bring a sword, instead of a gun!"
A pit formed in Dice's stomach.
"We just need to get to the aircraft hangar," Matches said, turning back to Dice. "That's our only goal in this."
Dice ducked and pulled Matches down as a blast flew overhead. Howls erupted behind them. Dice winced. They'd narrowly escaped death.
"That, and staying alive," Dice said.

Matches groaned as she stood. She pressed her hand against her temples, her forehead reddening. A wobbly rift split amid the wall of robots. Meanwhile, the Clansmen were knocking down a path through the robots of their own.
"We made it out of Omicron together, didn't we?" Matches said, forcing a smile.
Dice looked away from Matches. There was no direction. It was all just noise. A crude cacophony of flesh on metal, and nothing more.
"Not all of us," he said.
His eyes burned. His throat went dry. The world went misty. Yet, he kept moving while Matches led the way, throwing robots aside.
"Keep pushing forward," somebody shouted. "We almost have all of them!"
It was a large man wearing a blue visor — Sparky. He was right, too. The robots were whittled down to a slender row.
"Do you have any idea where we're going?" one of the Clansmen asked.
Sparky didn't respond. He didn't need to. The aircraft hangar tower loomed ahead of them. Dice went to look back at the barrier, only to find an insignificant blip.
"What do you think happened to Jackie?"
Matches followed Dice's gaze and nodded.
"Probably dead," said Matches. "Shame, too. She... Well..."
"That's all that you can say for her?"
"I guess she had a nice Omega Key... Glad I stole that from her."

A lone robot coiled between gunfire and blasts. Something crunched under Dice's feet. Dice shuddered. They were walking over fallen robots. Only a handful were still hovering around. Matches let out a sigh of relief and released her hand from her head.
"Keep firing!" Sparky said. "Do you all suddenly have butterfingers? We're supposed to leave no bots alive, if possible!"
"Where's Vert and Jackie?" a Clansman asked. "And who put you in charge?"
"Jackie put me in charge. And Vert is still underground, stalling the detonators and preparing a secondary attack. He'll meet us when he meets us."

Drawing closer to the aircraft hangars, the stream of robots thinned to nothing. There were groans and creaks underfoot. Vert was there, somewhere. However, even under Sparky's stiff direction, Dice questioned whether they'd make it to the hangars. The deeper they went, the more pressing this question became. Dull explosions of detonators went off in the distance, followed by the quake of collapsing structures.
Stenches of oil and smoke made their way up Dice's nose. Dice craned his neck, to see the hangar tower climbing into the sky. There was no tip in sight — just beams of metal, stretching endlessly.
Ahead of them was a pillar, hugged by a wide stairway. Would it be strong enough to support all the Clansmen? Dice swallowed the thought.
A cluster of robots descended. Sparky motioned for the Clansmen to fire, then halted them as a robot emitted a harsh beep.
"We surrender," the robot said. "As pacifists, we don't want things escalating to where we will have to use our Gideon Ray. Please, drop the weapons. We recognize our defeat."
An eerie pang hit Dice's gut. The robots were small in numbers. Unusually small. How long had it been since there had even been any?
There was a blast. The robot hit the ground.
"Sorry," Sparky said, swatting at steam from the barrel of his blaster. "The Clan must live on. Let's keep moving, troops."

More blasts went off, followed by more clangs. Robots wriggled on the ground with electric whines, before finally fizzling out. A shade of sympathy tinted Dice's eyes. He looked away. The robots stunk of smoke and molten metal.
The sound of explosions grew ever closer. Time was running short. He walked toward the pillar, trying to ignore how high they'd have to climb.
Where was Vert? Apart from the Clan, the center was barren.
Dice's eyes widened, and his eyes dipped. Most of the robots must’ve been below ground, fighting Vert's forces over the detonators.
Dice looked over to Matches, who had a perturbed look on her face. She must've been thinking the same thing.
As they ascended the pillar, Dice crossed his fingers and hoped for a sign of Vert. The explosions in the distance stopped. Then, nothing. Silence permeated the center.
Silence, and the clicking of guns. A whir.
The whir.... Where was it coming from?
"Whose gun is malfunctioning?" Sparky barked.
Nobody answered. Sparky's steps slowed. Dice heard the stiff creak of leather in Sparky's bodysuit.
"Everybody, turn your weapons from lethal to silent," Sparky said.
Clicks ran down the row of Clansmen. The whir remained. Hairs on Dice's arm raised.
"Maybe somebody forgot to turn the wind machine off," Matches said.
Nobody laughed.
"Nobody move!"

The voice thundered through the crowd like a hurricane. Sparky let out a shout, and prepared to make a run, but there was a detonation among the Clansmen. Dozens were flung away, a crater left in their wake. Others were ensnared in a net of blue energy, then pulled from the stairwell.
Dice looked up. Three hawk-like aircrafts hovered above. Cannons protruded from their bottoms, a wave of energy distorting their barrels. What type of technology were they utilizing?
Matches' mouth dropped.
"They found us."
The Clansmen broke into a frenzy, half of them running toward the newly-made crater in the stairs, and half of them scrambling down the stairs.
"What type of Clansmen do you want to be?!" Sparky shouted. "We need to fight!"

He grabbed at the Clansmen unfortunate enough to run by him, keeping them in the aircrafts' line of fire. However, a line of Clansmen still managed to group under the aircrafts, and tried shooting them down.
"I'd prefer to be a living Clansman, thanks," Matches said with a huff, helping drag Dice through the crowd.

People took swipes at Dice's bodysuit. His feet dragged as he considered how high they were getting. Though, Matches kept pulling him forward. A secure feeling wrapped over Dice. No matter what happened, he and Matches were in this together.
"It's working! It's working!" Sparky cried.

His voice was already far below them, small and shrill. Dice turned. Several steaming holes had been put through the U.R.O aircrafts, and they were making a descent to the battlefield. With any other force, this would've been a good omen. However, terror took over Dice.
He sped up, his feet tripping over themselves. His breath became heavy. Matches' breath was heavier.
There was a boom, followed by a thud as an aircraft landed. Three more thuds. Screams and shouts. Dice looked down. He was several dozen meters up in the air.
"Stand down," a voice echoed.
There was a whoosh as the door to an aircraft unlatched and descended to the ground. U.R.O soldiers strode out.
"Keep going! Don't look back!" Matches said.
Dice looked back anyway. The aircrafts' turrets aimed at their pillars. Dice could already feel them blasting through. His heart floundered.
"Fancy, meeting you here!" Knowles shouted, stepping from an aircraft and flicking his wrist.

Dice struggled to keep climbing, before finally giving out. He turned up his hearing aid. His eyes were fixated on Knowles, as he prowled around the battlefield. Knowles' eyes darted between Clansmen, comfortably cutting through them.
"I was on a flight to the Kelvin Union and figured I should drop by..." Knowles said. "I didn't expect to meet you guys. It's a small world after all..."
Knowles clutched one of the Clansmen around the throat and tossed them to the ground.
"You people are truly disgusting," Knowles said.
"How did you find us?" asked Sparky.

"We had a tracker on one of your members," Knowles said, dismissively. "A tip from the Tyler District's Prime Terminal also helped... Did you honestly think that we wouldn't find out about this, after your little stunt in Omicron?"
Even as Matches dragged Dice further away from Knowles, Dice could hear Knowles' sharp laughter. Unlike before, it was mixed with a mechanical synthesizer. It was colder. Harsher.
Sparky charged at Knowles but was shot down in crossfire from Knowles' soldiers.

"Look around you," Knowles said. "Look at the corpses of the robots you've destroyed. You're mass-murderers. Do you even feel a semblance of guilt? You supposedly wish to undo the wrongs of the U.R.O. Though, I ask you all: at what cost?"

Knowles snapped a finger, allowing one of the soldiers to shoot through Sparky's head. Sparky collapsed, limply. Dice expected to see a hint of shame or worry in Knowles' eye. Instead, there was only glee.
"Now, can anybody tell—?" Knowles began.
A sinkhole was put in the ground. Knowles gripped to the railing of his aircraft, but several U.R.O soldiers and dozens of Clansmen were lost to blackness. Dice squinted, trying to peer into it.
A swarm of robots emerged, with Clansmen riding atop them. Vert rode at the front of the pack.
"You're not the only hacker in the Clan, Sparky!" Vert said.
"Fire!" Knowles said, taking aim at Vert's robot.
The battlefield was drowned in a tsunami of noise. Watching it unfold, Dice's head ached. He had no idea which side he was for.
With a shout, Matches pushed Dice down. A beam of energy landed into the pillar, above them. Another, below. Their pillar quaked, pieces falling and leaving rows of damaged stairways in their wake.
Dice struggled to his feet. His body trembled and he stumbled forward. He leaned on the wall — the pillar was out of balance.
"I'm confident this pillar will collapse before we make it to the top," Dice wheezed.
"I wouldn't call that confident..." Matches said.
Tilting to the side, they gripped to ridges in the pillar. The pillar groaned, steadily leaning to the side. Dice went to the railing to keep from falling.
"It's about time you were knocked down a peg!"
"But, Sparky... How could you kill Sparky?!"
Dice's eyes snapped down. Vert was trapped under Knowles' stiff metal leg.
"It had to be done!" Knowles shouted. "Anyway, like the new leg? It's courtesy of you, seeing as you shot my good leg off, and whatnot!"
"You thought that was bad?" Vert asked, with a wry chuckle. "Sparky hijacked the Gideon Ray about an hour ago. This district is set to become a crater."
Knowles kicked at Vert's head. Vert whimpered but managed a weak response. Dice couldn't make the words out and was left to watch Vert wriggle in vain.
"Your rebellion is dead," Knowles said. "Now, tell me: where are your stowaways? Where are Dice and Matches?"
Dice looked away and struggled up the pillar's railing. He just needed to get to the opposite side.
His leg slipped and he careened toward the edge. Matches grabbed his hand and pulled him steady.
"You have a suicide streak in you, or what?" Matches asked.
"Or what."
Once they’d climbed to the other side, they leaned their backs against the pillar. Above them, metal and stone rumbled. The pillar split. Dice's arms went numb as he lost altitude.
"At least we get a fun ride out of this," Matches said.
Several Clansmen flew past them, falling to their doom. Dice winced.
"That's one way to put it."
He shimmied to the edge of the pillar and looked behind. The pillar was falling toward the ground. No — toward a neighboring pillar.
The sickness churning in his stomach disappeared. A light went off.
"Matches, we're going to make it," Dice said. "This pillar will collapse into the other. We can walk on the side of this one, to the other one."
Matches smiled for a moment, before letting her face fall.
"We can't hope to hurdle all of these stair ways."
A chunk of rubble broke through the stairways above them, before breaking through their own.
"Looks like we won't have to," Dice said.

Dice's stomach fluttered as their pillar went deeper into its plummet. He no longer felt as if he were leaning, but as though he were laying. Shock ruptured through the pillar, then Dice. Once it'd subsided, Dice scrambled to his feet and looked ahead.
Their pillar had collapsed into the other, making a clear pathway to the top.
"It actually worked!" Matches said, gaping.
"You sound surprised."
"Yeah, that’s about right."
Dice and Matches weaved through the holes left in the pillar's staircases. The top stairwell of the neighboring pillar was nearing into view. They were practically there.
"I think that we're the only people who've made it to the top," Matches said.
Dice let himself smile.
He let himself smell.
A thin layer of smoke came over them. He didn't need to look behind. Coughing, he picked up his feet.
"Duck!" Dice shouted.

Just as they were passing through a gap in the stairwells, Dice pushed Matches over. They were both on their stomachs, hidden behind the cover of the stairwell. A pattering resounded as the stairwell was hit by gunfire.
"Spoke too soon?" Matches said.
"Spoke too soon..."
There was a thud as somebody landed on the pillar. Dice slowly pulled himself up, to see Knowles several meters off.

"I know you're here," Knowles said. His voice had sharpened to the edge of a razor. "It's about damn time that you gave it up! You couldn't even begin to understand the breadth of resources the U.R.O has invested into your capture!"
Matches broke into a sprint. Before Dice knew what was happening, he was stumbling after.
"Maybe it's time to rethink your investments!" Matches said.
Gunfire from the aircraft spread wildly, leaving holes at every angle. Dice tried his best to keep behind cover of the stairwells, knowing all the while that Knowles was closing in
Once he'd made it to the stairwell of the other pillar, Dice shot Matches a dirty look.
"You just ran without me?" he said.
"Sorry. Figured you could keep up. Let's keep moving."
Dice raised an eyebrow, quizzically. How could she have forgotten him? Cautiously, he followed her toward the top.

Dice forgot about how high they were, the blasting gunfire, or the shouts Knowles threw after them. Making it to the hangar was all that mattered. He looked above, at the hangar's grated platform. The entrance door was locked shut.
"What do we do?" Dice asked.
Matches put her hand to her forehead.
"I might be able to break it..."

The door sparked, then flew open. There was a roar as the aircraft accelerated toward them and Knowles sent a blast from his gun. Matches slipped through the entrance. As the aircraft crashed into the pillar, Dice jumped after her and scrambled onto the platform.
With a grunt, Dice stood to his feet. He teetered, his balance lopsided. A crunch resounded. The floor under him bowed, threatening to slide him back down. Matches yanked Dice over to steady ground.
"I think I have a knack for saving you from falling off of things," asked Matches.
Dice shared a laugh. His laugh morphed to a choke. Knowles burst through the entrance. Dice stumbled back. Ears ringing, Dice followed Matches toward a row of aircrafts.
"There!" Matches said, pointing toward an arrowhead for an aircraft. A drone.
"This is pathetic," Knowles said. "You two are cowards. You run from the very group you supposedly supported... Moreover, the group you supported was abominable."
Once they reached the drone, Matches pressed her hand against her forehead. A strained look mapped across her face. "It isn't working... I can't get it open."
Matches banged at the door, to no avail. Dice's fingers ran along its surface trying to find a way to force it open. Yet, the sleek surface left no crevices exposed.
"Cowards!" Knowles repeated.
The words slit Dice's eyes. All he could see was Knowles. Knowles aimed his gun. They were locked in a standstill.
"You think that we support this group, of all people?" Dice said. "Trust me: we're well-aware they're just as bad as you. We don't have allegiance to anybody."
Knowles snickered.
"You were friends with Vert," he said. "The man who led me to kill your friend. The man who shot off one of my legs."

Knowles' stepped closer, his brow twisted in rage. Dice grimaced as he stared into Knowles' eyes. He'd never noticed before, but Knowles' flesh eye was uglier than the robotic. Its whites were bloodshot, its pupil was a murky black, and its eyelids were heavily scarred.

"You have so much fervor when fighting me," Knowles said. "Yet, when it came to taking a stand against these people? You stood idle. You could've done any number of things to try stopping 'the Clan'. And yet... You didn't."
"You could've done any number of things to stop yourself from killing Wrench," Matches said.
Knowles' head rolled back, as if he'd been punched in the face.
"It was an accident," he said, face abating. "I never would've—."
"You killed Vert too, didn't you?" Matches asked.
Knowles' hand fingered the trigger of his gun, making an unnerving click. The menace in his eyes disappeared, only dejection remaining. Dice quivered.
"Did you?" Dice asked.

"Do you know how many people he killed?" said Knowles, voice rising. "How many people his Clan is about to kill? Sometimes, you don't have a choice. You think you're so innocent? Trust me, BL-270: you're not. I know everything about you. You have blood all over your hands, even if you don't remember it."

Dice shook his head. He looked through the grates in their platform to see the battlefield. The landscape was ravaged. There was no telling who'd won. It didn't matter. It was only a matter of time before the Gideon Ray went off.
"Ah..." Knowles said, with a smirk. "So, you finally have your memory! Did Matches help give it back?"

A rush of adrenaline pumped through Dice's head. An orb of energy pumped out of the end of Knowles' gun. Dice fell back, his head in a soft buzz. Yet, the orb never neared him. It hardly grazed his skin, as he sunk out of the way.
Hitting the ground, Dice felt his vision blur. He saw two of everything. Two of Knowles. Two platforms. Two orbs. Two of Matches.
Matches.
There was a crash. A rock formed in Dice's stomach. He didn't want to look.
He looked anyway.
Matches was struggling to stay on her feet. She clutched her right shoulder. Her arm was missing. A lump formed in Dice's throat. In place of the missing arm hung loose wires and gears.
"Matches?" Dice choked.
Matches' eyes went wide.
"You seem surprised."
Knowles dropped his gun and walked toward Dice with clenched teeth.
"All this time..." Knowles said.
He glowered over Dice, pressing a finger into Dice's chest. Dice felt Knowles' steady, hot breath. It didn't smell right. A mixture of soap and oil.
"… And you've still never been told what Matches really is?"
He chuckled a harshly. Dice instinctively dove toward Knowles' gun, and blasted a hole through the door to the drone. He aimed toward Knowles.

"Predictable," Knowles said, unflinching. "Anyway, Matches' name isn't Matches. It isn't Segue. Rather, her 'name' is U-2968. She's an android from the Hamilton Project. You remember that now, don't you? All of those androids the Duplicate Project tasked you weed out, for them to destroy?

"The U.R.O's Hamilton Project created androids as ultimate weapons against the Kelvin Union's robot populace. Capable of manipulating technology and the human mind, their androids could infiltrate the Kelvin Union, control them, and ultimately overthrow them. A rogue mental blast from an android, alone, could kill an army.

"When the androids became a little too smart for their own good? They fought back and broke out, killing hundreds of facility workers. This left us big guns to search for anything that could possibly be an android, send them to you for review, and then destroy them.

"As it turns out? The U.R.O has finally developed blocks for android mind-abilities, making them easier to control. And Matches here is the last android, out of the thousands created. Since we're at war with the Kelvin Union? Securing her is vital."

Dice looked back at Matches. He studied her face. It couldn't have been the face of a robot. It was the face of a human. It had to have been. The way the skin formed — the way the eyes flitted about — was wholly organic. The pupils had a soul buried beneath them. Yet, when Dice whispered, "Is it true?", Matches could only nod.

"Funny isn't it?" Knowles asked. "A man hired to eradicate criminals... A man with a history of hating robots... A man literally created to destroy androids... Ultimately allying himself with an android? With scum? Nobody would've guessed it, Dice. Fate has a good sense of humor."
Dice went to pull the trigger to his gun. Knowles crumpled its barrel with his metal arm and tossed it aside.
"Please, stop," Knowles said, flesh eye going soft. "I don't want to have to hurt you if I don't have to. This is between me and Matches."

The ground rumbled. There was a quake. Dice looked below — a sphere of light encompassed the ground, steadily growing. The Gideon Ray had already started. A fire burned in Dice's chest. He swung his fist but was knocked to the ground by a punch from Knowles. Dice clutched his nose. Waves of pain surged through him. Fireworks went off as Knowles walked away, and toward Matches.

"Did I mention the main reason Matches needs to escape to the Kelvin Union? It's because she's a compulsive gambler," Knowles said. "She was one of the best, always getting into the minds of her opponents. Though, when she finally played against somebody who'd been shadowing her for a while, and become wise to her tricks? They laced a makeshift tracker in her drink, and gave it to U.R.O authorities. Every time she went anywhere, including the illegal casinos she frequented, we weren't far behind. Eventually, she was blacklisted by the gambling community — and, she had us perpetually on her tail."

Dice listened for a defiant objection from Matches. Anything. Though, he only heard shallow breathing. Dice opened his bruised eyes to see hazy figures of Knowles and Matches approaching one another. Matches' arm was still spitting sparks, but she no longer seemed to take notice.

"You've cost me almost my entire body," said Knowles. "I'm going to make sure that you pay. I know where you're going. I know what you're planning. You no longer have anything or anywhere to hide. I have U.R.O reinforcements coming in. You won't be able to stop them."
The platform screeched and shifted. Thunder roamed along it. Matches pressed her hand to her head. Knowles only laughed.
"I had blockers installed against your signals," he said. "The U.R.O is already planning on making them standard issue. Once you're in captivity, you have no shot at getting back out."
"Who said I was going back in?"
Matches lunged at Knowles.
"Dice! Start the plane!"

Dice's thoughts fell under a whirl of confusion. As Knowles and Matches broke into a struggle, Dice blearily stood to his feet. Climbing through the hole he'd left in the plane's door, he stumbled to the front. His fingers ran along the controls. He inserted the Omega Key into the key slot. As the thruster roared on, Dice felt a rush. He was in sync with the machine.
"Hit the acceleration!" Matches shouted.
Dice turned. Matches sprawled across the ground, having barely made it through the hole in the plane's floor. Knowles' metal fingers clung to the edge.
"Dice!" Knowles shouted. "I never did tell you who you were the duplicate of... Did you want to know?"
"I said hit the acceleration!" Matches shouted again.
"You can never outrun yourself, Dice!" Knowles shouted. "You can't outrun your past!"
Dice's head pounded. He slid the throttle forward. His bones rattled as g-forces slammed him to the back of his seat. Matches groaned as she crashed into the back of the plane.

The Tyler District drifted off, the tops of buildings becoming miniscule. There was an implosion. Dice looked up to see the moon winking at him. He looked back down. The Tyler District fell into itself, consumed and contorted by a ball of white light. Yet, rather than terror, Dice felt exhilaration. He leaned back and enjoyed the light-show.

Beeps went off on the radar. There were several incoming aircrafts. Dice amped up the speed to his aircraft, letting the Tyler District's cityscape fade away. As the dots on his radar dropped off, he slowed his speed.
Chapter 28:
Dice snipped the end of a bandage. After rolling it up, he shoved it back in a compartment in the ceiling. He eyed Matches' shoulder. The patch-job was rough, but good enough.
"We made it," Matches said, breaking the silence. She rolled her shoulders. "Granted, I would've liked to do it with my good arm... But, we made it.
"They're still coming after us. When we reach the border, they're going to be there, waiting. And, I'm not so sure we'll be able to do anything."
Matches placed her feet on the dashboard and shrugged.
"We have to get there first, I guess..."
Silence closed back around them.
"I know you must be angry about what happened back there," Matches finally said. "I'm sorry for it. All of it. I should've told you everything awhile ago. I was afraid. I was wrong."
Dice nodded.
"Would've been nice to know you were trying to escape the U.R.O over a gambling addiction," Dice said.
"You've known me long enough. I'm sure that you expected that..."
"Didn't expect that you were a robot."
Matches chuckled. "You're a clone. I'm a robot. I guess that's just our week."
Dice slammed his fist on the dashboard and pushed himself away from the window.
"I can't do this..." he said. "I'm afraid of heights."
"Didn't seem so afraid a moment ago," Matches said, raising an eyebrow.
"A fluke."
Dice ran his hands through his fiery red hair, letting the curls coil around his fingers.
"You... You should've said something. Anything. I've lived all my life hating robots."
"You don't think that I already knew that? You've made it clear just about a million times that you hate robots!" Matches said. "And, we've both had secrets. We started this journey knowing that."
Dice scowled, and stood from his chair.
"The big difference is that I told you as soon as I could. You? You could've told me from the beginning," he said. "That, or back when I asked you. The several times I asked you!"
"I could've told you later," Matches said.
"If it hadn't been for Knowles, I'm sure you would've, wouldn't you?"
The aircraft's engine sputtered. Would it last all the way to the border? How far away was the Kelvin Union, anyway? However far, it was too far from the Monterey District...
Dice sighed. His eyes skimmed over Matches' face. How had he not noticed? How could he not tell the difference?
"I can read people, just by looking at their faces," Dice said, bashfully rubbing the side of his head. "But, when I looked at you, I couldn't. Not in a normal sense. It all makes sense now. Yet..."

Matches looked at him. Her eyes pierced through Dice. As Dice stared into them, he found them impossible to decipher. They could've been scared, sad, angry — or all of the above. Or, none. Dice looked for a place to sit, before leaning on the wall. It had been so long since he'd felt so lost.
Yet, he'd always been this lost. It had only taken him this long to realize it.
"I still can't tell you're a robot," Dice said. "You look… Normal, to me. Like a person. Yet, different all the same."
Matches frowned. Dice's heart skipped a beat. Had she ever frowned before?
"But, I still am person, aren't I?" Matches asked. "Or, am I not one to you?"
Dice's lips formed into words, but his voice went flat. He gave a few incoherent sputters, before managing an, "of course."
"Of course" what, though? Which question was he answering?
Try as he might, he couldn't answer.

He felt along the metal of the aircraft. It was harsh. Cold. Yet, beneath it all, there was still a steady hum. The warm flow of energy. A voice in the dashboard that gave periodic beeps, as it passed by checkpoints.
Dice sat next to Matches. He kept his eyes from the front window, instead listening to the subtle thumps of the plane as waves of wind buoyed it.
Dice wiped sweat off his forehead and rolled up his sleeves. The aircraft had heated up since leaving the Tyler District. They were moving further south.
"I thought things were bad after remembering I was a clone..." Dice said. "And, thinking back on everything we've just been through —."
"It's not so bad?"
Dice put his head in his hands, and let out a stiff laugh.

"I was going to say 'it's worse than I thought,'" Dice said. "But, close enough. You know, for a person who can read minds, you'd think that you'd do a better job at finishing other people's sentences."
Matches chuckled. "I enjoy the guessing game. Reading minds is a strain... It always has been."
Dice nodded and stared out the window. Dark clouds billowed ahead of them, sinking deep into the horizon.
"Always," he repeated.
His eye twitched.
"How long has 'always' been?" he asked, keeping his eyes on the clouds.
"Ten years, roughly," said Matches. "The U.R.O had been developing me for even longer than that, though."
Dice rubbed his eye and took in a deep breath of air.
"And, Knowles was telling the truth — there's not a chance there are more of you?"
Matches shrugged. "Probably not. But, you make the chance of there being more sound like a bad thing."
"One of us is already a clone of somebody else. I don't know if there's room in this cockpit for two."
"Don't worry, I'm one of a kind. Each android was designed to be unique. They wanted it that way, because..."
Matches' voice trailed off. She pulled her legs from the dashboard and crossed her arms. Her brow knitted between her eyes.
"What happened to all of them?" Dice asked.
Matches hung her head.
"Knowles killed them," she said. "We became the very thing that the U.R.O was trying to fight — a rebellious uprising of robots. They couldn't leave a single one of us alive."
She gave a deprecating smile.

"I remember when there were over a thousand of us. Most of us had successfully mastered the mind-manipulation ability. Even more of us were ready to fight. We had so much information loaded into our brains, and so much training put into us... It all amounted to nothing."
Dice closed his eyes.
"I can't imagine," he said. "How did you survive for this long? How long have you been surviving?"
Matches put her hands behind her head and gazed toward the ceiling. She snickered to herself.

"I was one of the cleverer androids. Always figuring out solutions to simulations that the others didn't. The Hamilton Project prized me. Trusted me. That made it easy for me to be one of the first to escape. I've stay escaped ever since."
"Ever since...?"
"Five years. Five years of integrating into the U.R.O, and dodging their forces. I've gone under about ten different identities in that span of time. Have to admit: I had fun with most of them."
"Even this identity?"
Matches smirked. "This one hasn't been half-bad."
Dice looked at the GPS. They were still two hours away.
"One last question," Dice said.
"I was getting worried they wouldn't end."
"How long have you been on the run from Knowles?"
Matches craned her neck back and closed her eyes with a sigh.
"Seven months, about. It's been hard. Everywhere I've gone, he wasn't far behind. Devastation always followed him, too. He's such a pain in the neck..."
Dice winced as he remembered Knowles' hand clinging to the bottom of their aircraft. He winced deeper as his memory trailed back to his first meeting with Knowles.
"That's an understatement," Dice said. He scratched an itch on the back of his hand. "He has to be one of the most terrifying men that I've ever met."
"I wouldn't go that far," Matches said, gingerly sweeping away some hair in her face.
Matches' eyes glazed over and her gaze dodged Dice's. Dice's mouth went dry.
"You're defending him?" Dice asked. "He tried to kill us countless times over!"
"There are things that you don't know about him... He might be cold, but..."
"But what?"

"Knowles used to be the chief of the U.R.O military," Matches said. "He had his own specialized squad of soldiers, devoted to taking down opposing nations. He was incredibly decorated, too. Badges, honors, and awards galore. However, he eventually lost a battle, costing countless lives... He was demoted to monitor the security of the Duplicate and Hamilton Projects.

"He was a good person when I knew him. Bitter, yes. He'd never stop talking about his tragic defeat on enemy lines... But, good nonetheless. He slipped us androids free food or energy packs when he could. He gave us extra privileges. He told us things that he'd been instructed not to. As shocking as it may be, Knowles actually cared about us androids. He was practically one of us...

"The U.R.O ended up getting stricter, as we androids became smarter. Worse yet, the Kelvin Union was making advancements. In all of this, Knowles became harsher... I left around this time. The rest of the androids? They ended up lashing to on him. His entire squad was killed. His body was heavily damaged. The very androids that he'd protected betrayed him at a moment's notice, without a second thought... Including me."
Dice rubbed his brow. A band tightened around his head.
"That can't be true," he said. "Knowles is nothing like that. He's too cruel... Too conniving. You've seen him — how he chases us down, like we're prey. He doesn't see us as people."

"He didn't used to be that way. He had everything... Power, respect, good-health. He lost it all. He wants me, because he blames me — the last android. But, trust me: it's not really me that he's after. There's a good person under there. A better person than me."
Matches put her head in her hands and spun her chair around. A lump formed in Dice's throat.
"Knowles killed Wrench."
"And, I've ruined countless lives while running from the U.R.O," said Matches, her voice scratching. "If he's a bad person, so am I. So are you."
"That's not true," Dice said. "We've had reasons to run from Knowles. Everything that we've done has been justified!"
"And you don’t think Knowles can say the same thing?"
"You aren't being realistic about who Knowles is."
Matches stared Dice in the eye.
"I knew Knowles before he was a shell of a person," she said. "He was one of the kindest people I knew. I still think he is, somewhere under all of that technology..."
"He's a monster."

"People have said the same thing about me. There's a chance they were all even right. But, I think that I'm more than just that. I'd like to think that Knowles is more than that. Maybe we're all just... Lost people."
"Maybe we're not," Dice said, with a smirk. "Maybe we're all monsters, deep down inside..."
He'd meant it as a joke. At least, he thought he had. Yet, as his voice reverberated throughout the room, the more he found himself wondering if what he'd said was true.
The dashboard bleeped. Only a thousand miles left until they reached the border.

The bleeping was drowned out by rain, as it sleeted down their window. Dice's eyes waded through it, to find a canvas of black clouds. Though, on the edge of Dice's sight, the clouds sunk into a bloody horizon. The sun peered from beneath it.  Dice put his hand over his brow, to shield his eyes from its glare. There was a new warmth in his chest.
"I'm sorry," Dice said.
Matches shrugged.
"There's only a thousand kilometers left," she said. "A bit late to be angry with each other at this point, isn't it?"
"Yeah."
Dice groaned.
"A thousand kilometers until we have to see Knowles' face again..."
"Too long?"
"You read my mind."
Chapter 29:
Dice's head ached. He yawned. He stretched. He pinched himself.
"Matches, wake up," said Dice.
"Dammit," Matches groaned. Rubbing her eyes, she pulled herself up in her chair. "Why'd you have to wake me up? I was having such a good..."
Matches stopped herself before she could finish.

Bolts of blue energy arced over their aircraft. The sky was obscured by a fishnet of electricity. Sirens wailed. The dashboard flickered off. Dice squinted ahead. There was an immense wall, built of iron and plasma. The landscape surrounding it was barren desert. Dice looked ahead of the wall, to the Kelvin Union. The only thing that he could see was the sky. A matte painting of gray.
"Illegal vehicle detected," a robot blared. "You will now be escorted to the grounds, for further inspection."
Matches looked over at Dice, with a dry smirk.
"We made it," she said. "I was asleep half the time... But, still: we made it."
"I'm not convinced that it's going to matter for much," said Dice. "If the Kelvin Union looks anything like this place..."
"We'll just go on a vacation somewhere else," Matches said, with a shrug. "Nothing stopping us from breaking past another frontier, after we break past this one."
Dice nodded. Though, as they dropped to the ground, his eyes dropped. Could they really be so sure that they'd make it across? He could already see them easily being stopped by the guards.
"At least you're confident about this," Dice said, with unease.

"You're not?" asked Matches. "Most U.R.O officials are weasels. That, or easily led drones. Either way, it'll just take a blast from my mind to get past whoever is there. Then, we hijack the security to the wall with our Omega Key. We can do this in our sleep."
"I think you're forgetting how hard it was to it was to get here in the first place..."
"You're forgetting that we made it over every hurdle up until now, no matter how hard."
Dice counted grains of sand as they drew nearer. An officer stood by a control building, accompanied by a robot. His foot hastily tapped against the ground.
Matches leaned back and pointed up. Dice followed. A transport tube was suspended high above them. A car rumbled through it, riding directly through the wall's plasma shield.
"That's our ticket out of here," Matches said. "We take down the wall and walk along the tube. It's going to be hard for anybody to catch us."
Dice checked the rear window. There was still no sign of Knowles, but Dice could taste his presence in the air. Precious seconds dripped away.

Dice's head rattled as their aircraft hit the ground. Their dashboard flickered back on, and the fishnet of electricity dissipated from their window. Dice went to restart the engine. It coughed, then went dead. Dice stared helplessly while the officer strode toward their window. Matches pulled the Omega Key out of the dashboard. Walking to the back, she opened the exit platform.
"Come on," said Matches. "We don’t want to leave the officer waiting. We interrupted his lunch break."

Dice followed her out. The sun's rays pierced Dice's eyes while it passed through the clouds. Dice's bodysuit clung to his skin from the humidity. The air buzzed, as if taunting him. He lowered his hearing aid.

"What are you two doing all the way out here?" the officer demanded, walking toward them. A sick feeling turned in Dice's gut turned as he looked at the badge. Looking the officer in the eye, Dice felt his tongue turn to a slab of wood.
"We were just going for a joyride," Matches said. "I didn't realize how far we'd flown, until we were caught in your zero-point energy net."
The officer smirked, and stroked his mustache.
"The big-ass wall didn't tip you off that you were heading toward the border?" he said.
"I thought it was a robot outpost, or something," Matches said. "I'm a sucker for tourist attractions. Guess this turned out to be more of a tourist trap, though..."
"It's private government property," said the officer. "Not a tourist trap."
Matches let out a moan and put her hand over the bandage where her arm had been blasted off.
"Sorry..." Matches said. "My arm — I had it amputated a few days ago. I just haven't been thinking straight."
A flicker of empathy passed over the officer's face. However, it was snatched away when the robot let out a harsh alarm. The officer glanced at his wrist-pad, and scowled.
"Cut the crap," he said. "My robot just alerted me this aircraft isn't even yours. In fact... From the scans, this aircraft has been blacklisted. The U.R.O is in an active search as we speak."
"Your robot must be malfunctioning," said Matches. "Wouldn't be the first time a robot malfunctioned, am I right?"
The officer sneered.
"You'd like that, wouldn't you?" he said.
He brandished the interface on his wrist, before expanding it into a hologram. Dice shriveled when he saw his own face in it.

"What next? Am I supposed to believe these people are perfect clones of you?" he asked, pulling out two pairs of cuffs. They spit sparks from their tips as he unlocked him. The robot took one. Dice quivered.
"That sounds about right," said Matches, smirking.
"Look at that... We have a joker on our hands," the officer said, rolling his eyes. "Put your hands over your head. Both of you."
Matches grinned. "Actually, I only have one hand... Amputee, remember?"
"Shut it. You're under arrest. I'll be contacting the U.R.O officials shortly."
Dice put his hands over his head. Matches pressed her hand on her head. Her face twisted. She grunted.
"I said for you to place your hands over your head," the officer said. "If you don't—.
He gave a hoarse choke. A foggy pressure rested on Dice's scalp. Eyes bulging and face turning purple, the officer finally collapsed to the ground. The robots burst apart. The pressure lifted.
Dice took in a deep breath of air. His lungs burned, his eyes watered, and he was on his knees. The trance felt as though it had only been a minute. Yet, his surroundings suggested otherwise.
Dice picked himself up and looked over to Matches. She was hobbling toward him, a tired look in her eye. Dice stepped forward, but the world tipped back and forth.
"That was a lot tougher than I thought it'd be," said Matches, as she rubbed her forehead. "They must hire the strongest-willed guards for this place, or something. That took a lot out of me."
"It took a lot out of me too," said Dice. "Those abilities of yours... So disorienting."
"It's part of the charm," said Matches, making her way toward the wall's entrance. "Just be glad that I didn't accidentally kill anybody with them."

Dice sheepishly rubbed the back of his neck and made a weak chuckle. He was about to follow after when he heard a spark. His head snapped around. He crouched and picked up a pair of the officer's handcuffs. His eyes narrowed, studying the way the cuffs mechanisms turned.
"What are you doing?" Matches said, turning back around. "We need to get past the wall security."
"Coming," Dice said, still looking at the cuffs.
He stood up and picked up his pace, ignoring the stings of sand flinging on his skin.
"What, were you going to put the cuffs on the officer, or something?" asked Matches.
"I don't have that much of a sense of irony," said Dice. "You know that. I just thought that the cuffs looked interesting..."
Matches patted Dice on the back.
"You really miss being an officer, don't you?"
Dice's ears flared hot.
"Those days are behind me," he said. He hooked the cuffs onto a latch in his bodysuit.
There was a howl. Wind? It couldn't be. Tension rose in Dice's chest.
Matches broke into a sprint. Dice limped after. The muddling cloud caused by Matches still weighed down on his mind.
They reached the entrance to the wall. Matches ripped the keycard out of her pocket, causing the door to swiftly open for them.
"Here."
Matches tossed the Omega Key. Dice's reflexes kicked in, snatching it out of the air.
"You take the shields down, through the wall's mainframe. I'll look for the entrance to the elevator," said Matches.
"Why do I feel like one of those things is harder than the other?" asked Dice.
"Just because my brain is a computer doesn't mean I'm any good with them," said Matches.
Dice snorted. Scanning the room, he found a large computer parked in the center. Its motor purred softly. His gaze drew toward the monitor, covered in pulsating lights.

Striding up to it, he inserted the Omega Key and waved his hand. He waved again. After an extended pause, a hologram of a keyboard materialized in front of him. Why did computers always slow to a snail's pace in the most desperate of times?
He whipped through the computer's files until he reached the controls for the wall's plasma gates. He hit, "override".
There was a groan from the computer's engine as it processed the information. Then a bleep. Dice looked out the window. The plasma shields folded down.
He looked off in the distance. There were three black specks. He huffed and removed the Omega Key. Of course, the U.R.O had to arrive at the worst of times.
"Matches!" Dice said, tottering down the hall. "Matches, I disabled the shields! We need to get going, now!"
There was a squeal. Matches sprinted around a corner.
"That was faster than I thought," she said. "Anyway, I found the elevator."
"Then, what took you so long to come back?" Dice asked. "Were you just sitting there?"
"I figured that I'd file my taxes while you were handling the shields," said Matches. "So, no: I was being productive."
"Fair enough."
Dice arrived at a door with a keypad on its side, and a "warning" sign plastered overtop it. He handed Matches the Omega Key, staring at the warning sign.
"Do you know how high that thing is going to take us?" Dice asked.
"Yes. A quarter kilometer."
Matches swiped the Omega Key on the scanner, then handed it back to Dice.
"Do you know how long the ride is going to be?" asked Dice, pocketing it.
"Yes. Three minutes."
The scanner chirped. After a moment of buffering, the elevator doors reluctantly drew open.
"Did you know that Knowles' strike team is already here?"
Dice and Matches stepped inside the elevator. As the doors closed, Matches gave a final halfhearted, "yes."

The motors whined as they pulled up. Dice looked at the walls. They were made of a smooth, black glass. However, as the elevator rose, the blackness fell away and light spilled through on all sides. The walls were windows. Dice watched the ground. A rolling sea of sand.

"We're already halfway," said Matches. Her eyes stared on the gap in the border wall, where the shields had been brought down, as if her stare could somehow keep them down. Dice stared with her. It was better than watching U.R.O ships pull ashore.
"Still feels like there's a kilometer to go," Dice said, with a choke.

There was a buzzing. Dice put his hand to his ear — it couldn't be his hearing aid. His eyes jumped from the floor to the ceiling. It couldn't have been from inside the elevator either. It had to be coming from outside.
Dice's eyes shifted back to the floor. It was filthy. Unmaintained. His eyes twitched — the elevator shaft must've been in the same state.

The walls narrowed. Dice's bodysuit tightened around his neck. He pressed his face against the glass. A stench of oil permeated from the shaft. Dice coughed. His nose burned. He would've killed to smell the lemon scent from the old police station.
The police station...
Dice slid his thumb around the rim of his cuffs and let out a sigh.
"Only a quarter of the way left," said Matches.
She swept her hand across her face.
"You don't sound too confident," said Dice.
"You're not looking out the window, are you?"
"Now, why would I do that?"
Matches gave a grim look.
Dice turned. The aircrafts were in full view, their large slicing through the air, and their boosters rippling through the sand. They could've only been a couple kilometers away.
"They're so close," Dice said. "And... We're so high."
"Didn't scare you before," said Matches. "Doesn't have to scare you now. Maybe we'll speed up, and they'll slow down. That happens, right?"
A beam of light glared in Dice's eye. The sun? Dice covered his left eye and squinted. Hurtling toward the elevator shaft was a blast of energy.
"You don't think they're actually about to destroy the elevator and the wall, do you?" Dice asked.
"Just to stop little old us?" Matches said.
The beam of energy passed out of view. There was a dull thud. The ground quaked. Dice looked below, glimpsing flittering glass. Despite the damage, the elevator kept moving.
Dice looked back to the aircrafts. They'd arrived. Two more blasts launched.
Dice stepped back. There had to be a door or escape hatch somewhere. A square of creases was in the ceiling. Jumping, he pounded at it.
"It's jammed," said Matches. "Besides: We don't need to resort to the emergency escape just yet. The elevator is still moving."
The elevator shuddered. Dice was flung into a wall. He turned to see a steaming dent in the wall and the control panel breaking out in a fever of sparks and static.
"Forget what I just said," said Matches. "I'm pretty sure we're screwed."
Dice went over to the control panel but recoiled when a spark leapt at him.
"Have you tried using your mind to take out the aircrafts?" asked Dice.
Matches shook her head.
"It's no use. I think one of the crafts are blocking my signals. Besides — my head is pounding like hell."
Dice looked out the window. They were still at the same height.
"We really could've used a damn blaster right about now..." said Matches.
The aircrafts were so close they grazed the wall. Dice's heart skipped a beat — he could've sworn he saw Knowles' red eye flash beneath the windows of one of the aircrafts.
The aircrafts split up. One flew toward the transport tube, another flew toward the wall's base, and one hovered in front of them.
"I'm not sure how helpful a blaster would be," Dice said. "But, we have something else that might be useful..."
Dice pulled the Omega Key from his pocket, then wedged its edge between the Control Panel. The panel popped off, revealing the quantum motherboard underneath.
"Dice, what are you doing?" asked Matches.

"One of the aircrafts is already at the base of the wall," he said, slipping the Omega Key in a slot to the mother board. "They're about to access to the wall's security and override our elevator. Might as well beat them to it."

He studied the way certain transistors shifted and coiled. The labyrinth of wires. He unplugged the ends of two of the wires from the hanging panel. Which one was he supposed to hook up to his wrist? He took in a deep breath. The motherboard was a being unto itself.
"They're here," Matches said.
Dice's elbow bumped into the wall, rattling the motherboard. A bolt of electricity shot from its side.
"Thanks for the tip," Dice said. "I nearly ruined that."
He glanced out the window. His ears were suddenly on fire. Knowles stood in the window to the aircraft, waving. Smiling. The aircraft's glared with a hot light.
Dice turned back to the wires and hooked one to his wrist. The cracked screen flickered on, with a crude interface.
"I'm almost there," Dice said, swiping through it. "Just have to find the right controls.
"Sounds good," said Matches. "Because, so is their laser. It's about to fire."
"Please — don't update me again until they're gone," said Dice.
There were dozens of controls. A cluttered, homogenous web. It was impossible to tell what was the right one.

Dice bit his lip and took his best guess. There was a fizz. A buzzing. The elevator heated up, then rumbled. Dice's eyes flitted to the window, to find the aircraft's laser shooting through it. A portion of the glass had already melted away.
"This better wor—."
The aircraft and the laser fell away. Dice's stomach lurched. The sky turned to a blur. Dice turned to the wall behind, to find a deep gash left by the laser.
"Did you double the elevator's speed?" Matches asked.
"I guess," said Dice. "To be honest, I'm not sure what I did... I just know it worked."
As he unplugged the wires from his wrist, Knowles' aircraft flew to the transport tube. As it landed, there was a flash. Plasma unfurled along the wall's edges.
"They turned the shields back on," Dice said swatting at the spots in his vision. "What's the plan from here?"
Matches shook her head.
"It takes a while for the shields to come back up. We still have a few minutes to get across..."
"Knowles is sitting the transport tube. He'll catch us."
Matches shrugged. "Our goal was to reach the Kelvin Union. Even if we only have a few moments, before Knowles catches us... At least we can say we made it."
The elevator shuddered, and its door slid open. Dice found himself standing on an archway over the transport tube.
"On second thought, maybe we've been going about this all wrong," Matches said.
Dice suppressed a gag as he caught glimpse of the ground below. A slight slip spelled death.
"Yeah? How so?"
"What's with all this walking we're doing? Flying... It's ten times faster."
Matches smirked and waved down Knowles' aircraft.
"Hey Knowles!" Matches shouted. "I like the new jet!"
Dice shook his head. "You have to be insane."
"That was established a long time ago."
Chapter 30:
Matches vaulted over the edge of the archway, landing on the transport tube with a thud. After a jerk of hesitation, Dice jumped after her.
"God!" Dice shouted.
His knees buckled from the impact, planting him in the glass. He winced as his sweat streaked across it, then sizzled. The sun had turned the transport tube to a stove.
"I'd give that landing a solid ten," Matches said, picking Dice up.
"Out of what?" Dice moaned. "A hundred?"
"You bet."

Rubbing his bruised knees, Dice watched the drawbridge to Knowles' aircraft lower. The other aircrafts circled over them, like vultures. Knowles sauntered down the drawbridge, his coat billowing behind him.
"Stay in position," Knowles announced. "This is between me and her."
He brandished his teeth in a fake smile. A knife held in his right hand glinted.

"When I started this search mission, I never thought we'd actually make it here," said Knowles, turning to Matches. "The U.R.O always told me they wanted you, dead or alive... I was never keen on bringing you in dead. However, now?"
Knowles flipped his knife, then snatched it by the handle.
"I suppose that I really don't have any other choice, do I?"
Matches stepped toward Knowles, but Dice pushed her aside.
"You want me?" Dice asked. "Come and get me!"
Knowles snickered.
"No. I don't want you."
Knowles creeped closer.
"You don't have to do this," said Dice. "I know you've been through a lot. Your... Your old crew. They all died, didn't they?"
There wasn't a flicker of change in Knowles' face.
"I don't get your point."
"You — you were changed," Dice said, groping for the right words. "You became jaded."
Matches put her hand on Dice's shoulder to pull him back, but Dice yanked himself away.
"You've put too much stock in your friend's... Assessment of my pathology," Knowles said.
Knowles glowered over Dice, with a fierce scowl. Dice felt the heat of Knowles' breath on his face.
"You're a good man, deep under there," Dice said. "This isn't who you are."
Knowles patted Dice on the shoulder.

"I'm not already a good man?" Knowles asked. "Therein lies your greatest misconception. All I've ever done is work to protect the U.R.O. If you just surrendered kindly, we would've averted all conflict some time ago."
"You killed Wrench."
Knowles winced.

"You'll never let me forget that, will you? I don't kill who I don't have to. You two, on the other hand? Look at how many deaths you've inadvertently caused. How long will it take to realize you're on the wrong side of this?"

Knowles grabbed Dice around the wrists, pinning them behind his back. Knowles hands were ice. Dice wanted to fight. Though, Knowles was right. Too many people had died in their run from the U.R.O — all just so he could attain freedom.
Dice stiffened as Knowles' arm lit up, sending a rod of electricity down his forearms. The nerves down his back spasmed. He went to talk, but his jaw turned to marble.

"It's about time you were back in the U.R.O's possession," said Knowles. "Professor Cassius was always so convinced you deserved freedom... That you somehow had 'more potential' than any of the other clones. Personally, I think he just saw too much of himself in you — his ego turned you into his self-insert. Made him think you were more than you are."
Knowles gripped Dice by the chin.
"He was hilariously wrong..." Knowles said. "You couldn't even follow through on the 'Hamilton Search Party' assignment. Pathetic."
Knowles' hand tightened around Dice's neck. Dice choked, his lungs going numb.

"Oh yes, I forgot to tell you... Professor Cassius? You're his clone. Despite the multiple warnings, he put himself in his own experiment. Put you in the experiment. So... Now you know the answer to that mystery."

Dice's eyes watered. The world had flipped on its side. How could he not have seen it? Professor Cassius' constant involvement in his life... His obsession. The involvement in his experiments. It all made sense.
Yet, it made no sense at all. Why had Professor Cassius done it? Why put him through all this? Hadn't the Professor cared?
Knowles stepped toward Matches, dragging Dice with him. Matches' eyes narrowed in disgust.
"I know who you were," she said. "You can lie to the rest of the world. But, you can't lie to me."
Knowles raised his knife at Matches. Its gleam had all but left, with only a bleak glare left hanging to its tip.

"You're so used to reading everybody's thoughts, you think you know mine," said Knowles. "This time though? My aircraft has a blocker. You're alone, Matches. You have to face all the travesties you've wrought on people — to face yourself."
Knowles' hand tightened deeper around Dice's neck. The world was suddenly dark and muffled.
"I remember when you worked at the Hamilton Project," said Matches. "You were a different person then."
The corner of Knowles' lip twitched.

"It was a different world, then," he said. "It was all an act. We were putting on a show, to keep you androids under control. Once you left our control? Our act left. We aren't who we pretend to be, Matches... You should know this. You're a gambler. It's only when the chips are down that people become who they are."
Matches raised her arm as Knowles' knife neared her face.
"And, what are we?" she asked.
"Broken. Maybe I'm a little broken too."
The wind wailed. Knowles' feet screeched against the glass, while Dice's feet slipped along the tube's sides. He stared into the cuts left in the glass.

"I have to take you in," Knowles said. "You have to be fixed — even if being fixed means destroying what you are. We don't live in a world where robots like you can run amuck, mucking things up. It's not a nice reality. But, it is what it is."
"Is it?"

Matches leapt forward. Knowles threw his knife. The sharp blur narrowly missed Matches, clanging on the glass. Dice didn't have the time to see where it went. He fell back as Matches knocked Knowles away from him.
His hands were free. He cast a sidelong glance toward Matches and Knowles, who were caught in a tussle.
Dice's eyes returned to the gashes in the ground. Where was the knife?
"You can't win this," Matches said. "The person who's really alone in this fight is you. You could've brought all your soldiers down — but, your pride stopped you."
The tube reverberated as Matches punched the ground. "In the end, it's all about you."
The knife was a meter away, wobbling on the edge of the tube. Dice scrambled toward it.
Knowles grunted, and kicked Matches forward.

"It's not about me," he said. "It never will be. That's the reason why I haven't brought my men down. I'm not letting another person be torn apart by a robot, if I don't have to. I'd rather be torn apart by you, than have you tear apart my crew."
The knife slid off the edge of the tube. The world slowed as Dice's hand whipped toward it, his fingers outstretched. He narrowly grabbed the handle of the knife.
"Even if you tear me apart, you still don't win. My crew will blast this tube apart if they have to. This is it. You lose to me, or you die. You can't escape fate."
Breaths heavy, Dice crawled to the gouges in the glass. He flitted his eyes to Knowles — he was still distracted by Matches. Dice lifted the knife into the air.
"You don't have to do this," Matches said. "I don't have to."
Matches yanked Knowles' arm behind his back, tearing it off. Knowles laughed.
"You're telling me there's a world where you don't try to fight me to the death? A world where you don't try to run away from your problems? "

Dice drove the knife into the glass. There was a dull ping. The knife slid across the surface, leaving only a shallow scratch. Dice sputtered. He drove it in again, deepening the scratch. A little bit more time was all he needed.
Glancing over, he saw Knowles pin Matches to the ground. Unease gnawed at Dice's mind. He stared at the drawbridge to the aircraft. Knowles could walk up it at any time, and escape.
Dice's teeth clenched. He gave a grunt as he mustered all his strength. His arms raised above his head. He dove toward the glass.

With a crack, a fine line split down the glass. There was a wheezing — the vacuum was open. Cracks spreading, Dice bit his lip and prepared to drive the knife a last time. There was a blast. Dice looked up to see an orb pass over his head. His eyes jumped to the aircrafts. Their cannons took aim at him.
"Stop!" Knowles said.
He push Matches away.

"And if I don't, what will you do?" Dice asked, holding the knife closer to the glass. In the corner of his eye, Matches staggered onto the aircraft's drawbridge."You've tarnished my reputation and sent the entire U.R.O after me... I have nothing left."
"None of this is worth it!" Knowles shouted. "You have a choice! You have a choice to be better!"

He pulled a gun out of his pocket and aimed for Matches. Knowles fired, but was drowned out by the firing of the other two aircrafts. Dice took in a deep breath. Shoving the knife down, the glass shattered into large chunks. As it rippled, Dice rolled off the transport tube. His stomach leapt into his throat. His muscles went limp. The ground clutched him by the neck, pulling him closer.

Peering back to the tube, Dice watched Knowles fall into it. Knowles shrunk, floating away. Yet, Dice could still see the glare of Knowles eyes. The disappointment. Knowles mouthed something. Dice squinted, reading his lips.
"My blood is on your hands."
Knowles' neck tensed. His eyes bulged. They went empty. Dice watched for a flicker of life, but none came. A chill ran down Dice's spine as he remembered the last time he'd seen such empty eyes.
Knowles was dead.
It was on his hands.
Looking down, Dice's vision was hugged by sand. Yet, he felt nothing. It felt... Right. He deserved it. None of this had been worth it. It never would be.
Blasts above his head became louder. One of the aircrafts exploded. The engine in another went dead. A third aircraft's engine roared, coming ever closer.
The world dimmed. Dice's chest was tightened. The ground tightened. Dice could count the grains of sand. He tried, then stopped.
Perhaps it didn't matter if any of this had been "worth it". Helping Matches — the journey — it'd meant something. Something that was immeasurable.
A blue film wrapped around Dice's vision. Wind retreating, Dice's descent stopped. His body froze. The ground fell. Or, was he somehow falling... Up?
The final aircraft came into view. Dice neared its open drawbridge. He was pulled in. The blue film disappeared, and Dice collapsed on the aircraft's floor.
"You really need to work on sticking those landings," Matches said.
Her voice came from speakers in the ceiling, warbled. Almost mechanical. Dice cautiously pulled himself up, and walked toward the cockpit of the aircraft.
"I thought you were going to die," said Matches. "We got really lucky."
Dice felt his chest lighten.
"I can't believe it either," he said.

He made it into the cockpit room. The ceiling was torn apart. Wires hung loosely, and sparks of electricity soared past his face. The ground was covered in the bodies of unconscious U.R.O soldiers. Dice shuddered. The shudder turned to trembling when he glanced at the pilot seat. Matches sat there, a massive hole put in her chest.
"Matches!" Dice said.
Matches raised her hand.
"I — I'm fine," she sputtered. "The course of the aircraft is set for Tucker. It's a big city in the Kelvin Union... Not far from here. I should be able to replace my parts there. I'll be fine."
Dice nodded. Matches' eyes darted around the room, and her fingers twitched as she spoke.
"How did you take out the other aircrafts?" Dice asked.
"I knocked out the inhibitor," said Matches. "I destroyed the functions of the two other ships afterward."
Dice eyed the hole in Matches' chest. It was a crater, filled with melted metal and snapped rotors.
"Tucker... What do we do once you're fixed, and we're there?"
Matches fidgeted, before a smile formed on her face.
"You'll start a new life," she said. "And I'll... I'll gamble mine away."
Dice grinned.
"That sounds about right."
He stepped over the body of a soldier.
"Are — are they still alive?" Dice asked.
"Yes" Matches said, her gears crunching as she stood from her cockpit chair. "I put them all in a coma after shutting down the inhibitor. Trust me: I couldn't bring myself to kill them..."
Dice smirked as he walked toward a rack of parachutes. "So, you do have a heart."
Matches looked down to the hole in her chest. "Did."
Dice chuckled and began pulling parachutes from the rack.
"Well, we should probably do something about them," Dice said, gesturing toward the soldiers.
Dice knelt and strapped a few soldiers in parachutes. Matches followed suit, bumbling as she went.

Dice studied Matches' face. It had lost its natural flow. It was in the jerky way her lips moved. The uneven delay when her eyes blinked. Despite this, Dice couldn't abandon his image of Matches. Different as she was, she still felt the same.
Dice rubbed a twitch from his eye. Was he letting emotions cloud his judgement?

The question hung in the back of his mind while he dragged the soldiers to the drawbridge. It remained even as he opened the soldiers' parachutes, and left them to the sky. They turned to a red cloud of cloth in the horizon, then red specks flying fast apart,
Dice pulled up the drawbridge. He drank in the last bits of sunlight before the aircraft turned back to black.
"How long until we get to the city?" Dice asked.
"An hour or two," Matches said, walking to the cockpit.
She paused to run her hand through her hair. Dice stayed by the closed drawbridge, leaning on the wall.
"We really did make a big mess of all of this, didn't we?" Matches said.
"Definitely," Dice said, shocking himself as the words came out. "But... but, hey: it was a fun ride."
Matches managed a smile. Her eyes dipped to her hands.
"All of the people who've died," Matches said. "It was over me... It all lands on me. I caused all of this. And, it's only going to get worse."
Dice's eyes widened. He limped up to Matches and put his hand on her shoulder.
"Don't blame yourself," Dice said. "This is not your fault."
Matches shook her head.
"Then, why do I see Knowles' face everywhere I look? He was right. Robots... We only destroy the world around us. It's in our design."
Dice grimaced.

"No," he said. "In the end, I killed Knowles. Everything that's happened... So much of it was out of our hands. You couldn't control it. Besides... We were together on this. We still are. Things will... They should get better."
"You're right," Matches said, coughing as she gave a laugh. "Only a few weeks ago, I was running for my life. Now, look where we are."
Only a few weeks? It'd felt like a lifetime. Dice thought back to his time as a police officer. The first day he saw Matches.

"Yeah," said Dice. "We've gone far, haven't we? When... When I first saw you, I knew you were be trouble. It was written all over your face. I wanted to report you. Now, though? I'm glad I didn't follow my gut."
Matches nodded. "It's a good thing we can't sum up people in a single glance. If we could, life would be far less interesting."

Dice snorted. "Not just glances. You can stare at a person for hours, and still not know a thing about them. Professor Cassius... I thought I knew him. That I could trust him. But, all that time, he'd been leading me on. He was a monster. He was... Me."
Matches looked over her shoulder, to the cockpit window.
"You're not one... Neither am I," she said. "We can't control who or where we come from... We can only control where we go."
They walked up to the cockpit. In the distance, the silhouette of skyscrapers penetrated the horizon. The moon dimly glowed in a corner of sky. However, things somehow looked brighter than ever.
"There's something that I need to give you," said Matches.
She pulled out a piece of cloth, and handed it to Dice. Dice squinted, then unwrapped it. A silver piece of metal peeked out. His badge.
"How... How did you?" Dice stammered.

"I recovered it after it fell out of your pocket, back in the Genoa District," said Matches. "I should've given it back when I first found it. But I just... Didn't. I think you should have it now though... Officer Raymond."

Dice's head ached. The badge was dented and grimy. The lettering and insignia had worn away, and the magnet in the back was peeled halfway off. It disgusted him. Despite this, when his reflection glinted off the badge, a smile rested there.
"Thank you," Dice said. He unlatched his handcuffs from his bodysuit. "But, that chapter? It's over."
He walked toward the back of the aircraft. Matches's footsteps followed after him, but he didn't wait for her. The drawbridge murmured as he yanked the lever down for it to open.
"You're not leaving, are you?" asked Matches.
Dice tossed the badge and cuffs off the drawbridge. Their gleaming silver edges were swallowed by the stars.
"Part of me is," Dice said.
He sat on the edge of the drawbridge. Matches sat next to him. The stars twinkled. Almost as if they were making music. Dice brought his hand to his ear. If only he could hear it.
"It's gorgeous," said Matches.
"The stars?" Dice asked. "Yeah..."
The hole in Matches' chest fizzed, but she smiled.
"No — no," she stuttered. "The skyline."
Dice scrunched his face. The only thing off in the skyline were twisted spires of metal.
"You're talking about the city over there?" Dice said.
Matches nodded.
"It can't really compete with the stars, though," said Dice.
"But, it does anyway."
Dice's face tingled as the wind softly brushed against it. The stars continued to gleam, but his eyes remained on the city. Only when his eyes watered from the glare did he turn away.
Chapter 31:

Black dust crowded Dice's view. He careened to the left, trying to turn his aircraft from a swath of robots. His face slammed into the dashboard. As blood rushed to his face, the alarm in the cockpit blared. A holographic monitor lit up in front of his face. He looked out the window to see a hail of rubble.
"You crashed into a building," Matches said.
"Yep. I'm not exactly a master-class pilot here."
He took another glance at the holographic monitor. He bit his lip.
"Our left wing is down!"

He fumbled at the controls, desperately trying to redirect them. His face smacked back into the dashboard. The aircraft thrashed. There was the sound of breaking glass. Dice's bones turned to gelatin. Pulling his head back up from the dashboard, he broke into a fit of coughs. His face stung.
"The landing could've been worse," Matches warbled.
Dice's arm swung limply when he went to unbuckle himself. Flakes of dust and bits of plaster flew into lungs. He sneezed.

Walking up to the dashboard, Matches started down a hole in the window. A jolt ran through Dice — Matches had only gotten worse in the hours since her injury. Her face was pale and metallic. Her expressions were fading out. The energy in her movements had dissipated.

Struggling to keep balance, Dice slid down the crushed nose of their aircraft and into a narrow, metal street. The surrounding buildings were disorienting. Almost alien. Most were rigid black boxes, covered with charging stations in place of windows and doors. If not that, they looked to be oversized computers, complete with fans and projecting holograms.
Nonetheless, Dice leaned along a row of buildings. Discarded technology littered the entire street.

He turned around to give their aircraft a look goodbye. A crater was in the building they'd crashed into, and a pile of rubble was left in its wake. Despite this, it was hardly noticeable, blending with the street seamlessly.
"This isn't so bad," said Matches.
Dice scoffed.
"I hope that's a joke."
"It's not."
Dice shot Matches a look.
"Just, tell me where we're supposed to go."
Matches gave a blank stare.
"This city was supposed to be full of life," she said. "But, it's... Empty. Sorry, but I'm completely lost."
Dice glanced at their aircraft. It wasn't too late to go back, was it?
His eyes flitted to the buildings ahead. An oversized supercomputer pulsed and glowed, beckoning him to enter.
"That one," Dice said. "Let's head there."
Matches' pupils dilated and her lips quivered, but she said nothing. Unease dug into Dice's heels, weighing down his steps. Yet, Matches straggled behind him. She'd slowed to a crawl.
A robot whizzed by, nearly running into Dice. Dice brushed himself off. Grabbing Matches by the arm to pull her along, he hastened his pace.
The air thrummed. Oil shot up Dice's nostrils. On the edge of the vision, there was a flash of red. A glint of metal. Robots were following them.

Dice went to take sharp turn into a corner, when something lashed at his arm. He stumbled back. Biting his lips, Dice watched a narrow stream of red puncture his bodysuit. He looked behind. A group of robots was flying toward them.
"Halt."
Dice jerked around to find another robot. He kicked at it, knocking it away.
"You're a foreign human," the robot buzzed, as it bounced against the ground. "You don't belong here."

Muscles tensing, he turned into a tight alleyway. He scanned around. There had to be somewhere to hide. However, looking along the walls, he found nothing. He kicked at trash on the ground as he went. There had to be something useful.
"Matches, right about now would be a good time to short-circuit all of those robots."
Matches rubbed her head, and moaned. Dice looked into her eyes. They were vacuums. He placed his hand on Matches' forehead, then flinched back. Her head was burning.
"Don't worry, we're almost out of here," Dice said. "I'll find something to fix you. Don't worry."
He arrived at a fork in the alleyways. The robots' cold thrum coming back up behind him, he turned left.
"We just need to avoid them long enough, and we should lose them," Dice said.

Dice tripped over a piece of scrap. He lost grip of Matches. The skin on his face screamed as he slid against the concrete. He tried pulling himself up. His muscles gave out. His bones ached. There was a twinge in his arm, still leftover from the Genoa District. His lungs burned from him hyperventilating. His heart was on fire.
A blare trickled into Dice's ears. A robot. His arms were shoved behind his back. He was forced up, and back onto his legs. It was too late... He was caught.
His arms were released.
"Follow me."

Dice's eyes rolled to the side. Pain was still clawed at his face, and his vision was hazy. Yet, he was able to make out a robot, accompanied by a human. The robot was slender in design, loose rods making up its torso and limbs, and a thin head balancing atop them. The man next to it was gaunt and ragged. He had a fierce scowl on his face.
"Who are you two?" Dice mumbled.
"We saw your aircraft crash here," the man said. "We have a safehouse, but we need to move fast."
Dice was swimming in questions, but the pair was already walking away, Matches in arm. Warily, Dice limped forward. He tried ignoring the ringing in his ear and the blood dripping down his face.

They turned several corners, turning the world to a carousel. The further they went, the more war-torn the landscape was. There were fallen buildings, strewn bodies, and parasite-infested remains of robots.
"What happened here?" Dice said. "How'd they all die?"
"This place is a police state," the man said. "They died fighting law enforcement."
"If that's true, where are all their weapons?"
"The police collect them," the man said, matter-of–fact. "They don't care much for the bodies though..."
They finally stopped at a heavily dented wall.
"It looks like somebody crashed into here," Dice said.
"Wow. Perceptive," said the man.
The robot punched a panel of metal in the wall. It popped inward, causing a section of wall to fall to the ground. Dice's eyes widened.
"Move it," the man said, shoving Dice from behind.
