“You said they were chasing you over a card?” Maddy asked. Mitchell nodded. “Could I see it?”
Mitchell dug in his pocket and handed the “Iceblaster” card over.
Maddy looked it at it, and chuckled. Then, the last of the blue faded from Maddy’s fingertips. It leapt into the card. She handed it back.
“See that glow?” Maddy asked.
“Yeah. It’s awesome.”
“If anybody asks, tell them the truth: you spoke with me, a ghost. I cursed the card. Nobody will want to mess with that. They won’t want to mess with you, either.”
Turning over the card, Mitchell gave a smile. He looked up. “Is there any way that you can also haunt Barney? It doesn’t have to be a month or anything. Just, like, a week?”
Maddy shook her head. “Even if I could, I really can’t.”
She waved one of her hands in the air. Yet, even as she did, the hand disappeared. Her legs were gone. The fade was making its way up her body.
“I thought — I thought that you were stuck here.”
Maddy shook her head. “Only until I could prove whether there are still good men in this world. Looks like there are.”
Mitchell’s chest swelled. Then, it dropped. “Technically I’m only twelve, though. Do I really count?”
Maddy smirked. “The afterlife doesn’t care about technicalities.”
With that, she was gone. The only trace remaining was the unearthly glow, in Mitchell’s playing card.
He laughed and walked toward the house’s main entrance. He couldn’t wait to see the look on Barney’s face.
End

title: God of the Past
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
I was whispering to God, when I finally heard him whisper back.
Some people don’t like to listen to me. I don’t understand why nobody ever listens to me. It’s not fair, how I fare. But, I don’t care. No… I heard the whisper of God.
God.

I searched so long for meaning, hunched over my papers with a stolid gaze. My eyes locked. Jaw slacked. Back racked with pain. It aches to look back and think about all the time spent. Lost. So little gained, if any. Though, no matter.

The lab I joined was meant to study the past. Specifically, the Jurassic era; days bursting with life, since covered by dust. We secretly sought evidence of something more, though. Our ulterior ambitions came about after we discovered “Vetera” in a desert — that’s what Dr. Florin insisted on calling him. He… He was a weird fossil, to say the least. Not buried that deep, but clearly ancient. Clearly not like anything ever uncovered.
Dr. Florin decided we make a case for an era between the Jurassic and Cretaceous. If only he knew that we were thinking too small — that in our research we might find… Find the divine.

A snowstorm was bleating at the window, bleeding out the lab’s heat. My intern had turned in for the night. All my peers had left too. They apparently had families to attend to. Wives. Children. Siblings. Parents. The holidays are funny. Everybody loses themselves, reverting to a primitive state. They return to places they’ve promised themselves to abandon, thinking something has changed. Yet, nothing has. Not even they.
Holidays have never been my forte.

I was poring over new feedback on Vetera through radioactive isotopes, a struggling flicker of light as my only company. I probably should have gone home. My head and nose were stuffy. Nauseous. The data was noxious.
My nose ran. My mind ran, then slowed. Slurred. Glazing over, my eyes were dragged down by an anvil. Probably the Advil I’d been taking, making me sleepy. Odd side-effect.

I couldn’t go home, though. I’d already promised Dr. Florin I’d have the data sifted by morning. Home had shown its back to me; Megan wasn’t happy, and I didn’t have the time to deal with her. There’s never any point in picking at a wound, before it’s had time to scar over.

Besides, the lab had a nifty new dating machine. Top of the line. It was even featured in the papers. The head technician claimed that it was accurate within a century. Keeping an eye on it throughout the night and learning its ins and outs would surely give me a higher position in the lab. At least, I hoped.

Though, there was an obnoxious tick to the machine. Every several minutes, it would breathe heavily, before receding back into breathlessness. Listening to it too closely was suffocating. An itch wore at me, eroding my focus. Eventually I crumbled and pushed my chair from my desk.
There must’ve been ear-plugs around the lab somewhere.

Drawers flew open. Cabinets shuddered and fluttered. Baskets spilled out. Though, the ear-plugs remained hidden. A tightness surrounded at my chest, and my face sagged. The ticking wouldn’t stop. My clothes were damp with sweat, my face was blotchy — and the lab was inexplicably colder.
A thick puff of snow rattled against the window. The ticking of the machine became clamorous. Corrosive. Close.
I was slapped in the face, by a jagged fist. There was a crash. I jumped back.
“Great...”

The fist had been Vetera’s. I’d stumbled into him. He’d been knocked off his pedestal, limp. Every bone, from his lithe legs to magnificent cranium, lay cracked on the linoleum. Perhaps I should have picked him up. Yet, if I did, the ground’s filth would spread to me. Furthermore, I didn’t want my fingerprints on Vetera. It was bad enough to have him knocked down on my watch, as it was. Perhaps I could find an excuse.
“Dr. Florin is going to kill me.”

I placed my head in my hands. This night was a wreck — not just for me, but for a fossil that had endured countless millennia. I placed my hands over my ears. It was the ticking sound’s fault. That was what was to blame. Yes. The sound poked at my head, teasing me. It knew. It thought it was funny.
“For the love of God, shut up! Shut up! Shut up!”
I clamped my hand over my mouth. I needed to keep calm. Keep control. Maybe if I just explained the situation to Dr. Florin, he would be fine.
“And why should I shut up? Up until now, I’d say I’ve been remarkably… Closed off.”
The voice was shrill and frail, but pointed.
My heart shriveled. Perhaps my senses had been deceiving me. Indeed, as I scanned the room, there was only row after row of cluttered desks.

Admittedly, my eyes were limited by the lamplight of my own desk. I glanced at the lab’s light switch. Though, upon thinking of turning it on, my spirits receded. There was no point. Nothing was there. The voice was just a mirage, induced by stressors and sleeplessness.
“By the way,” the voice said, “I’d like you to stop studying all of that data, if you could.”
My brow furrowed. “Please stop.”
“I asked you to stop first.”
I nodded dejectedly, before spinning around in my chair. They had a point, whoever they were. Wherever they were.
“But, you’re not real,” I said, with a smirk. “Just a dream.”
“Not quite a dream,” they said. Something pricked me on the back of my neck. I turned around, only to be met by blank space. “Better put, not a dream at all.”
Furtively edging along the wall, my hands groped for the lab’s phone.
“Whoever you are,” I said with a snort, “you’re wasting your time. You need to get out of here.”

The phone blipped as it was ripped from its stand, and the “emergency call” button was pressed. The intruder merely laughed. Fizzing, the phone’s screen went dark. A hush entered the lab, as the blizzard outside was belittled to a breeze.
“Dr. DeGrom,” they said, “you might want to think twice before making threats. I’m only here for two things: to make your acquaintance.”

There was a cluck of the tongue, followed by a squall. The bulb in my desk’s lamp shattered, pulling a curtain of black over the lab. I waited for the intruder to give their second “thing”. It never came.

My pulse lapped at my ears, burning them red-hot. Instinct overrunning me, I sprinted to my desk. I needed to protect the data. As I ruffled through the papers, my eyes narrowed. There must’ve been something in the data that I missed — something of importance. Though, darkness had left the papers an indecipherable soup.
The squall returned, digging into my skin as a scalpel. I grabbed at a fistful of my hair to muddle the pain, but to no avail.
“You’re getting warmer,” the intruder said, their voice cracking a nearby window. Frost dribbled through. “Though, you aren’t there yet.”

I ambled about the lab, before stumbling into my chair. Tripped up, I failed to keep balance and hit the ground. There was a crunch. There were broken bones. Thankfully, not my bones. Though, a double take told me it would’ve been better if they had been mine.
I’d fallen on Vetera. Dr. Florin was going to kill me. Twice, if I’m keeping score.
“Yes,” the intruder hissed.
“You happy about all this?” I said, with a moan. Raw bruises covered my body.
“Only that you haven’t figured it out.”
“Haven’t figured what out? Out with it!” I shouted. I wobbled to my feet. My fists pumped with fervor. “Out! Just give it out!”

They gave another laugh. “The fossil you have… Dr. Florin was right. It’s part of an era that nobody has recognized. Though, as your data proves, the era was between the Triassic and Jurassic — not the Jurassic and Cretaceous.”
“My — my data proves that?”
“Correct. Clearly you weren’t reading it closely enough. No matter… As I’m sure you’ve figured out by now, Vetera is no normal fossil.”
“Yes… He reminds me of a Neanderthal. Though, not quite, you know? The structure doesn’t quite line up…”
“Neanderthal?” They snorted, and the lab quaked a bit. “So naïve. ‘Vetera’ is nothing of the sort. He’s so much more. Which is why… I can’t let you, or your lab, keep him.”
The storm and my breaths had converged, entering a rhythmic melody. I caught myself as I leaned my head against the wall. I was being lulled. Pulled, from my work.
Clutching my papers closer to my chest, I shouted, “Who are you!? What are you!?”

“Not quite sure, anymore. I’ve been for as long as I remember. Watching, observing. You should really watch your tone by the way, DeGrom. It’s no wonder Megan is so displeased with you, with you carrying yourself that way. You’re a short-tempered primate, truly.”
“You know Megan?”

“I know everything about you, DeGrom. You hate taking walks in the park, because it’s always too crowded. You hate public bathrooms, because of the nerves the ‘germs’ give you. You hate birds in the morning, because they’re too noisy. You hate mornings. Though, you like cleaning your house — the feeling of control systemization gives you. You like late nights. You like liquor. Especially on late nights, when—.”
“That’s enough! Enough!”
I was clawing at my face and hair. Somehow, I was back on the ground, writhing. The intruder’s voice was an incessant pest. It seemed to come from nowhere and everywhere, all at once.
“I just want you to leave,” I whimpered.
Vetera’s bones shifted, appearing to hover for just a moment. They collapsed shortly after.
Just a trick of the senses. It had to be.

“I will leave when I can. When I’m done. Though, it will never happen soon enough. I suppose that’s the curse of being me — of existing, for so long. I’m sure you can understand, even if you’ve existed for not even a fraction of how long I have.”
I sat up. “What do you mean?”
“I mean that I’ve been around for thousands of millennia. Ever since the beginning. And, now I’m here. Chatting with you. Because, I want your fossil.”
A smirk crossed my face. “If you wanted the fossil so bad, it sounds like you could’ve skipped a few of those steps.”
“I could’ve. But then… It would’ve been less fun.”
“How so?”
“Have you ever wondered what it might be like to be around, for as long as I have? To see the Earth’s beginnings, and then see it fade?”
“Can’t say it’s ever crossed my mind, no.”
“I read your old paper on the importance of archeology… ‘Why Remembering the Past is Imperative’. Glad to hear you could forget.”
A lump formed in my throat, as a revelation hit me. “Are you God?”
“It depends on your definition.”
The words were branded in my head. There they remain, to this day.

“DeGrom,” the intruder continued, voice lowering. “I know everything about everyone. Almost everyone, anyway. My head is everywhere, eating up knowledge. Though, never going anywhere. Always staying put, leaving things to be as they are. Does that make me God, in your eyes? Is that godhood’s nature?”
“Yes.”
I knew the answer before it left my lips. I knew it was the wrong answer, the moment it had. Yet, it was also the true answer.
The intruder scoffed. “I figured as much.”

A hum swung through the air. Vetera swung with it, crackling as he hovered above the linoleum. Crunching, as his bones came closer together. He was pushed further in, further up, until he was a ball high in the air. Then, he was gone.
“Why?” I wailed. “Why? That… Vetera was Dr. Florin’s life’s work! My life’s work!”
“And now, he’s been made quick work of,” said the intruder. “Such is the state of life. I suppose it’s finally time I revealed myself… Gave you answers.”

The room rumbled. Lights twitched, winking on and off. It stung to watch it. Then, all but one of the lights died out. The remaining light left a meek circle of luminescence in the center of the lab. A claw clutched the spotlight’s edge. No — a talon. An entire figure emerged from tar-black darkness.
“Impressed?” the intruder asked.

Their legs were wiry and coated with sharp feathers. Their entire body was comprised of feathers, in fact. There was an oily texture to them. They had knives for wings. An oversized beak made up their face.
Their beady eyes bore through me. I wish I could call them soulless. Yet, there was a shred of humanity in them. The eyes darted about with a keen awareness. Consciousness.
“You,” I managed. My lips were rubber.
“Look familiar?” they finished for me, scraping their wingtip along the ground. “Yes. I suppose you could call me a… Relative, to that dried up specimen of yours.”
Lifting my chair and jutting my jaw, I gave a snarl. “Are you an alien?”
“You’re more alien than me. You rookie primates, asserting yourselves as the dominant race, never ceases to bemuse me.”
“Get back,” I shouted, edging near them. “This is your last warning!”
They sped toward me, before knocking me to the ground. A crash resounded as my chair hit the floor behind me. I struggled against the terrible wings, but my muscles were drowsy.
“Lose yourself, for one minute,” they said, their beak clacking at each utterance. “I’m here to give you warning. For a scientist, aren’t you curious? Don’t you wonder what I know? What I am?”
I threw my head back in surrender.
“Have you ever thought it strange,” they continued, “that, out of all the species that archeology has uncovered, humanity remains the sole race to have achieved civilization?”
I shrugged. “Humans are the only intelligent ones.”

“On the contrary. Humanity is the only race too stupid to realize the toxicity of civilization. Every other species that has come before you… They realized the folly in ‘intelligence’. In community. They tore it down and burned everything of it, before it came too far.”
Their eyes went fierce, and their wings became tighter.

“I’m from one of those species. In an age long before your own, we ruled the world. Its skies, its land, its oceans… They were ours. And, we squandered it. Life was trampled in our wake. We finally came awake. And, we ended it, before we ended everything.”
I squinted. “Then, where are the rest of you?”
“Gone,” they said, their face going haggard. “I’m the sole survivor. I erased everything of us from the fossil record, after our demise… At least, I’ve done my best.”
They paused to take a glance at my datasheets, before turning back to face me.
“Since then, I’ve stopped every other intelligent species that’s arisen from completing their attempt at civilization.”
“You haven’t stopped us.”
A part of me wanted to smile. They beat me to it, with a smile of their own.
“You may think you have civilization… But, you’re only close. You haven’t ruined things completely, just yet. When you do? I’ll be there, to end you all.”
With a screech, it unlatched its wings and floated into the darkness.
“And what good is that to me?” I shouted. “You’ve left me with no evidence! You’ve left me with nothing!”

“Life will never learn,” they said from the dark. “I’ve tried hiding everything, to see if a species can divorce itself from ego, on its own… If it can rise above its nature. So far, I’ve been disappointed. I’m giving you a warning: change, or change will be forced upon you.”
There was a final screech. After, only silence to answer my cries.

Thereafter, only ever silence. Nobody has ever listened. Nobody ever wants to listen. All I know is the cold, now. People say I’m a fraud. That I lied. That I stole the fossil. Yet, it was God that I spoke to. He took the fossil. He told me how we save ourselves from being fossils.
I’ve only told the truth. I’ve only chased knowledge and given it. So, why doesn’t anybody believe me? Why am I so alone?
We are not alone.
End

title: Grasp Your Fate to Grasp Your Future
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
Today, I’m in tomorrow. Or do I have it wrong? Is today actually yesterday? Thus, am I in today?

Trying to figure it out always gives me a headache. All I know for certain is that my head is somewhere, and that somewhere is not here. On a positive note, at least my headache hurts better than it usually does. Granted, it would hurt best if it didn’t hurt at all.
I clench my teeth. I can’t let myself lose my train of thought. I need to focus.

I’m sitting in my living room. A boxy television set is ahead of me, the corners of its screen bubbling with static. I’m lounging on a wisp of air, my eyes transfixed at the screen’s center. At any moment, the news station should be reporting my upcoming streaming service. Yet — nothing comes. Instead, the reporter’s tinny voice merely drones on about another tax increase. Damn the tax increase. I want to see my face on the screen.
I take a deep breath. Meditating on inner peace is the only way to succeed in life. Losing oneself should never be permitted. The mind is a sanctuary that must be defended.
Screw it. I slam my head into my hands. The vision fades, and I’m back backstage. This is wonderful. I’m in my element, surrounded by a crowd of people — by people who love me.

Who am I kidding? My vision just failed on me. It doesn’t make any sense. I’ve always been able to control my visions, and they’ve always shown me what I need out of the past or future. Why couldn’t they cooperate now?
“What was that about?”
I pull my head from my hands, and look up to see my manager, Tanner. He’s holding a clipboard in his hand, because of course he is. Doesn’t he have anything better to do, than constantly hawk me?
I’m being harsh. Tanner is a nice guy, who’s loyal to his job. He’s driven. He’s motivated. There’s no point in talking about him negatively. So, why do I feel so negative?
“Oh my god, you’re sweating buckets!” Tanner says.
“I’m having so much stage-fright,” I say. “Is there any way to call this entire thing off? Because, if we can, that would be just great.”
Chuck’s eyes narrow into a look of bemusement.
“What? Now? Why? You — you can do this. You’ve been at tens of dozens of other conferences, and you’ve never had stage-fright before. There’s no reason to start having it now.”
“Well, tonight is different, okay?”

I bite my lip, and look to the door. Any minute, I’ll have to go out there. I know exactly what I’m supposed to say. I’ve recited it in my head a million times. Yet, now, I’m not so sure I’m supposed to say them. My future looks so shaky. Nothing makes sense.
“Are the other speakers here?” I ask. “Loretta Cormac? Roger Briggs?”
“Yes. Of course they’re here. But, you shouldn’t be focusing on that yet. Later. For right now: you’re Brent-freaking-Irving. There’s nobody —.”
“Yeah, okay. Thanks. I think we’re done here.”
I stand to my feet. My hands tread through the wrinkles in my suit, brushing them out. I pat a finger on my hairline, to see if the gel is holding steady. I nudge a delinquent strand back into place.
The door yawns open, and I walk down the hall. Screams and cheers lap at my ears. As I draw nearer to the stage, shouts of my name trip over one another.
“How are you doing today, Mr. Irving?” asks a stage-hand.
I put on a false smile.
“Wonderful! Just wonderful.”
My steps quicken, and I brush past. Yet, another stage-hand comes up to me.
“Your ear-pieces and teleprompter are all in sync, and ready to go,” she says. “You should be good!”
Shooting a thumb up, I grin.
“Just amazing. It’s like I always say: preparation marks the path to elation!”

She smiles at me, clearly taken up by my words of praise. However, I’m not here. My head dives back into the stream of time. After taking a few strokes, I’m on the stage and listen as I give my speech. Yet, nobody in the audience responds. My delivery is wooden. Each joke I give flounders. The profound lines I’ve prepared come off subtle as a bludgeon. I need to do something to bring life into the auditorium. However, it’s already too late. My speech is dead.

I’m warped back to the backstage. My body is crammed in a tight elevator, about to be hoisted onto the stage. However, I can’t get my mind off the visions. They must be right. However, I’ve never had my visions act out in such a way before. What’s happened to my control? Why is everything spiraling?
“Break a leg, Mr. Irving!” the elevator technician says, his teeth glinting as he grins at me.
“Save a leg, you mean,” I say back, with a wink. “Remember: positivity is power.”
Eyes widening, the technician nods. “Very true. You’re just amazing! How do you get all of your ideas?”
I shrug as I’m raised from the ground. “I guess they just come to me. I’ve always been lucky, in that way.”

Disappearing into the abyss between the stage and its underside, I shed my skin. My face falls, and my heart dunks into a pit. “Luck” is certainly one place to attribute my success. However, I prefer the term “cheating”. If it hadn’t been for me going into that alley, all those nights ago —.
My head throbs, as it tries to trail back. I slap myself. I can’t let it trail back. I need to focus on the future. I need to focus on the now.

Grunting, I let my visions guide me through the numerous opening lines I could give, upon entering the stage. I ask to be brought to the best opening line — yet, I’m dragged through a myriad of mediocrity. As I fumble for something that might work, my platform creaks. The visions fade. I’m nearly to the stage. A crack opens in the ceiling, dumping light into my shaft. Screams and shouts rip at my eardrums. I readjust my earpiece, and clear my throat.
I’ll be fine on the stage. I’m the best. I just need to keep telling myself that, and I’ll be fine. Yet, my chest still tightens. Everything is uncertain.
I grin — at least my uncertainty is certain. It’s not a strong silver-lining, but it works. Finding the silver-lining in things always works.
“And now, I’d like to introduce our next speaker,” an announcer begins.
“Brent Irving,” I say, finishing for him.

The platform clicks to a stop as I finally reach the stage, and a thin fog clears. There’s a resounding applause, but I give a restrained wave. There’s a flash in the corner of my eye, as the teleprompter activates. I turn from it and look out into the sea of faces filling the auditorium.
“Simmer down, simmer down,” I say. “It’s just me.”

There’s a peppering of chuckles. It’s not enough, but it will have to do. At least it’s not as if nobody laughed. Besides: even if everybody had laughed, the laughs would’ve only come from a crowd of nobodies.
This is supposed to comfort me. Yet, somehow, I feel smaller. Countless eyes are on me. Can feeling small ever be spun into a good thing?
“So, how are you guys all doing at this year’s Motive-Con?” I grin. “As an aside, I personally always thought this event should be called, ‘Motive-Pro’... But, for some reason my name never stuck.”
I laugh. My laughs fade into echoes. Sweat blooms on my brow. Clearing my throat, I continue.
“I’ve seen a ton of great speakers here today. Coming up here, I thought to myself, ‘I don’t envy the poor soul who has to go up last’. And that was when I remembered...”
My eyes drop, sending a jolt of life back through the crowd. I’m doing better. Though, upon glancing at the time on the teleprompter, I realize that I’m not even a quarter of the way through.
“Alright,” I say, slapping my hands together. “I’ve procrastinated for long enough. And procrastination is a cardinal sin, in my book. Literally.”

I rummage through my mind, peeking at potential futures. I cross my fingers, praying for an escape — though to no avail. In most of the futures, I’m frozen with fright. In others, I cave and read from the teleprompter. The only future where I manage to break away from stage-fright and say something, has me doing so to no reaction. That said, the thing I say is at least something. I’ll take it.

“So, I’m sure you all know why I’m here and why you’re here,” I say. I pause, and wait for more words to come. “Or, at least, I hope you do. I’m a former business advisor. I'm also author of the book — small title, not sure if you’ve heard of it — ‘Grasp Your Mind to Grasp Your Future’. It topped the bestseller lists within a week of release, and remains a strong seller. Though, I... After amassing my fortune, I’ve tried making a name for myself beyond that. The book isn’t what I try to promote, these days. Rather, my mission is to promote the key ideas I pushed in that book. Particularly, the ‘Irving Axioms’.”
I stride along the stage, locking my eyes with random members of the audience.

“Success is a product of the small choices we make in our lives. It could be from something as simple as remembering to do your laundry in the morning. I know — it sounds ridiculous. But, I’m speaking from experience.”
I’m speaking from future experience. My head is still swimming in and out of the present, presenting me with previews.

“I grew up in a bad neighborhood as an only child, with parents who both had to work to keep things afloat. I wasn’t at the best school, and I wasn’t the best at school either. By all accounts, I should’ve fallen on my face. And... Well, I did. It was only after I took a long look in the mirror that I decided to pull myself together, and make myself into the person I am today. I built a moral system for myself, which still carries me to this day.”

The auditorium is brimming with amazement, and my sight blurs from eager cameras and spotlights. Though, my stomach petrifies. My tongue turns to wood. I can taste the lies on my lips. Why can’t anybody else?

“The Irving Axioms are a trinity of what I believe are foundational principles: perfection, perception, and persistence. To be more specific: they’re the desire to attain perfection in your goals, the perception to conceptualize them, and the persistence to try achieving them. To get what we want out of tomorrow, we must start by blueprinting tomorrow today.”

I watch the audience’s eyes widen to drink up every word that I say. Despite my guilt, a smile forms on my face. The audience might not know any better than to believe me — but then, isn’t the lie I tell them worth it? If they’re better off for believing, was it ever a lie in the first place?

My face flinches as I glimpse another future. I’m speaking with my peers in a closed room, and they’re unimpressed with my presentation. They don’t want to work with me. I haven’t done enough — I need to change something. Asking my visions to show me the way out, like they always have, I only discover them to be mute.

“These Axioms were especially critical when I started pursuing business,” I say, floundering for another point to jump to. “I remember the first time I went to give business advice to one of my superiors. I’d been crunching our numbers for our last quarter, and realized that it would’ve been more lucrative to...”

As I start to ramble, the curtain behind me parts. Tanner is giving me a glare, his eyes having turned to marbles. Keeping my back to him, I raise my voice and stand taller. Meanwhile, a fuzzy hand creeps to the back of my neck. It grips my spine, pulling it like a chord. I’m sucked down a drain, and spill into a cold alley.

Rain spatters on pavement, before mixing with trash and turning to slop. I drag my feet through it. My hair droops from my head, drenched. I pull an empty bag from my pocket, and toss it aside. Remnants of a white powder blow back, but I ignore it and trudge on.
“Nothing ever works.”

A chilling wind runs over me. Despite the thick gloves on my hands, I still rub them together in hope of extra warmth. I tighten the collar of my coat. Nearing the street, I count the number of headlights that pass by. Would one of them be willing to give me a ride, out of the city? Doubtful. Besides, they’d still find me. And, there was no way I’d have enough money to cover my latest gambling debt.
“I’m alive, so that’s something,” I say. “But I have no future, and that’s nothing.”
I turn and run back into the alley. I stop. My fist pounds against brick, and a scream rises in my throat.

“All I want is a good tomorrow,” I say. “If I could just see the way to make this all work... I could make it happen. Everything would be easier. Everything would be better. I just need a chance! I just need a way out! Why isn’t there a way out!?”
The rain bursts into a downpour. There’s a flash of lightning, and the roar of thunder. I look down, and stare at a puddle’s thin reflection of my eyes.
“If anybody is out there, please,” I say, “give me control over time. Let me see, so that I can finally do what needs to be done.”
My eyes squint deeper into my reflection.
“Bloody Mary!” I shout. “Bloody Mary! Bloody Mary!”

The reflection shifts, my eyes smearing into a deep red. There’s an ear-piercing rend. I’m flung backward, and a dark shadow fills out the corners of my vision. There’s a leer in its eyes. I try to glance at it, but it constantly flees to the corner.
“You talk a good deal,” it says. “I’ll grant you your desire, on one condition: that you follow through on setting things right.”
I nod, and clamber to my knees.
“Thank you,” I say, cupping my hands. “But, what if I can’t? What If I don’t?”
The storm starts to subside, and the shadow disappears. I scan the alley for it, but it might as well have never been there.

The vision flutters away, and my head hurtles back to the stage. I can still feel my tongue hanging onto the last word I'd been uttering, before the vision. I glance at my timer — not a moment has passed.
Not a moment.
There's no way I'll be able to last the twenty minutes. I won't even be able to last the ten. I need to end things, now.

"— and, that's how you find direction!" I say, making a heel-turn from my last line. I grope for a killer closer, but know that I won't get one. "And, once you find direction? You will find... Success. Some might claim that success is an overrated enterprise. Though, I'll tell you this: once you've reached it, there's no feeling like it. Make the changes you need to. Put in the effort."
I've given up. The audience shifts in their seats, unengaged and disgruntled. I don't blame them.
"Thank you," I say. My body feels as though it's locked under a microscope. Isn't it though?

I give a meager bow, and exit the stage. My teleprompter is still rolling, and I only garner a few scraps of applause. Yet, there's not much I can do. Heart thudding against my ribcage, I slip behind the curtain.
"What the hell was all of that?" Tanner's goatee wags as he shakes with fury. The edge of his glasses glint sharply.
"It was something, right?" I say, giving a sheepish grin.
"Your teleprompter was just off in the corner, right in plain view! All you had to do was read the thing. Didn't you see it?"
I nodded, and pushed past him. Snatching a water bottle from a table, I pop open the cap and take deep gulps.
"And you can still read, can't you?"

"Shut up, Tanner. I just didn't feel it, okay? Everything up there... It was too calculated, and forced. Anyway, I'm feeling really sick, and I'm thinking about throwing in the towel on this whole thing."
Several minor speakers walk by and cast me sidelong glances. Suddenly, Tanner's demeanor turns desperate.
"Brent, baby... What's gotten into you? We can always make these things work, remember? Take some of your own advice. Besides, tonight is very important, with that big meeting and all."
I smirk. He's not wrong. Though, he can't see what I can. The next twenty minutes are a desolate wasteland. I'm on my own.
"You have no idea how many hoops I've had to jump through," Tanner continues, pacing. "So many people who said no. And, of the people who said yes? Well, most of them —."
"Fine," I say. "I'll go through with the meeting, or whatever."
"Thank god. I'll lead you to the room. It's just down—."
"I know where it is."
"But, the center's faculty just told me where we could have it, an hour ago."
"I have my ways of finding out."

My feet plod ahead, down a narrow corridor and then out of the backstage. I'm in a cold, marble hallway. Streams of people surround me, passing by without giving a second look. Do they not recognize me? Do they just not care?
I don't care.
Skimming over the numbers of several doors, I finally find the one I'm looking for. I turn the latch, and enter.

It's packed full of people. However, that isn't saying much — the room just barely surpasses the size of a closet. Bumping into a whiteboard hung along the wall, I stand over the round table at the center.
"Take a seat," a woman says. Marsha Walters — easily one of the most provocative speakers I know of.
Seeing that all the seats are occupied, I drag a stool from the corner and hunch onto it.

"So, what are we doing here exactly?" Roger Briggs says, with a yawn. He unbuttons his jacket, and stretches his arms. "I've been up for the past twenty hours for this event. Anything that'll shorten the time between me leaving here and me getting into my hotel's bed would be nice."

The eyes of the other speakers shoot at me, seemingly agreeing with him. I wish that I can leave my skin, and let one of my potential selves take over. Yet, at this point, I know there's no point in even trying. Winging it is the best option I have.
Clearing my throat, I make an aggrandizing sweep toward all them.
"I'm here to make a proposal," I say.
"I'd damn well hope," scoffs a speaker I don't recognize — Tanner must've been desperate to get this room full. "I only came here because I knew you'd be here. Well, that, and the cookies."
I glance at an empty tray, at the center of the table. Tanner had been very desperate.

"We've all made sizeable names for ourselves in the motivational speaking and self-help circuits," I continue. "However, I've hit a sort of brick wall. For some reason, it’s like I’m not all there. It's been getting harder to come out to these things. And, ‘creating content’ for my blogs and such? It just doesn't mean the same thing anymore."

"Yeah, I think we could gather that from your recent performance," says Loretta Cormac. She gives a roll of her eyes. "Seriously... All that speaking talent, and it suddenly goes to waste. Did your ghost writer quit on you, or something?"
My face turning hot, I shake my head.
"Ghost writer? No — I'd never... Everything that I create is a hundred percent my own work."
I bite my tongue. It's only half the truth. Though, why should they know?

"It's alright to admit that you have a ghost writer," says Briggs, clearing his throat. "Most of us use them, at least once in a while... It's ridiculous to expect ourselves to constantly be working behind the camera, while also constantly mugging for the camera. Am I right?"
He looks around the room, and collects a series of nods.

I stop myself from gaping, and clap my hands. "That’s exactly what I was getting to. We all have so much on our plates, and so little time. Wouldn't it be nice if we had just one platform, where we could center all of our motivational efforts?"
“Just one?” Briggs asks, raising an eyebrow.
I nod, with a grin.
"Everything about your plan sounds great... Except for the part where we're pigeonholed into one platform," one of the speakers say.
"Well, it wouldn't exactly be that..."
My face is burning, and my muscles tense. The air in the room shifts, stifling my lungs.
"What is this thing called? And how exactly would it affect me?"
I readjust my tie, and try putting on a genial face. My skin stretches, and I know I look something like a mannequin. Though, I have to power through. This meeting has been in my head for months.

"It's called the, 'Irving Network'. It'll be a streaming-based application, accessible on almost every device for a monthly fee. My plan is to produce and direct web-series with you guys, concerning motivation and self-help. Obviously, we'd need a few trial brainstorming sessions to see if our ideas gel, before we officially partner up. But, if I choose you to headline a show, you'll be offered a several year contract and a tidy salary."
"Several year contract?" says Marsha. "Would that mean I can't take my work anywhere else during that time?"
I shrug. "Yes. But, it's for good reason. If you—."
"Let me guess," says Briggs. "While all of our work is constricted your app, you'll still be allowed to branch out on other platforms."
"Well, yes... Since I'll technically own the company, I—."

Loretta Cormac stands from her chair, her eyes sawing through my forehead. "You'll get to slap your name and face all over the thing, and take credit for all of our work. And you think we're supposed to be on board for this? I presume you get to take in most of the profits, as well?"
"Once again yes. But, that's only if this thing is even profitable."
"You're Brent Irving. It shouldn't be, but we all know it will be."

There's an itch in the back of my mind. I want to close my eyes and fuse my head with the table. This idea had seemed so brilliant, just a few hours ago. Besides, everything is already in place — I have production crews at the ready, a team of writers, and even the application is in its finishing stages. How could it suddenly seem so stupid? Moreover, how am I going to make up for all of this?
The room goes up in murmurs as people make their exit. I try maintaining eye contact with the few speakers that remain, but even they look livid.
"So..."  I say.
"God, you're a hypocrite," says Briggs. "You claim to want to help others. But, the only person your work has ever helped is yourself. Some self-help..."
He stands from his chair, and leaves.

Marsha Walters bites her lip. "You've worked in this circuit for years, with a ‘holier than thou’ attitude. It looks like it's finally caught up to you. Instead of constantly looking out for your own relevancy, maybe you should've been making connections before pulling this stunt."
The room goes barren. Somebody shuts the light off as they head out, leaving me in darkness.

I want to believe that fate has betrayed me. Maybe it has. Though, peering through my memories, all I see is myself at the center. I wince, remembering times that I’d outright stolen stage time from other speakers.

Everything I've done has been with the goal to reach success. Yet, my success hasn't been earned. Every step of the way, I’ve been told the exact way to go. The mystery of one's future is elusive to me. Each breath is preordained to go a certain way. Millions of people follow me, latching onto my every word. Yet, at what cost? What weight do my words even hold?
A slight screech erupts, followed by the voice of an announcer. "This year's Motivation Conference will be closing in thirty minutes. Please exit the building, and have a great night."

I remain in my seat, and stare into the blackness. My head plunges, traveling hours ahead — several days ahead. I watch my life unfold, and my prominence peel away. Today will leave a blemish on my career. As I go ever deeper, I see myself slip into a docile state. I lose everything.
My vision of the future slips away, leaving me to look at clouds of ash and soot.
Everything I am soon won't be. Everything I've thought counted will cease to count on me. What's the point? What was ever the point?

I stare ahead until my eyes burn. I blink and then stare again. There's no telling how long I sit, but I eventually hear a knock on the door. The handle jiggles. Light spills through a crack, and it creaks open.
"Sir? The center has closed. What are you still doing in here?"
It's a janitor. His face is stolid and alert. Though, after he flips on the light, his face softens.
"Is something wrong, sir?" he asks. He pauses, to study my face. "Wait... Aren't you one of those speaker people?"
I nod.
"Then, what are you sitting in here for?"
Sighing, I put my head in my hands. I wait for him to leave. Though, he stands there, watching me. He takes a step closer.

"It's funny," I say. "I've spent half my life telling people how to live their lives. And, they've listened. Yet, I I've never said what I really need to say. Somehow, I feel like nobody has ever been willing to listen to me at all."
Silence returns. Then, the janitor drops his mop and takes a seat.
"I'll listen."
The future remains empty. However, maybe that's fine. Maybe the future is never meant to be filled in.
Presently, I fill in the present. That's all I need.
End

title: Independence day
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth

Hope’s shoes were immaculate. So was her outfit. Though, her hair — there were a few strands shifted out of place. It created a stinging in my stomach. Come to think of it, it still does. Couldn’t she have had hair that frizzed a little less? It is such a little thing to fix.

Nonetheless, my head held high. I kept my wits about me about as much as I could. Everybody that walked by had a gleam in their eye. A few even waved. No doubt, they were all enamored by my outfit. I was decked out in my best business suit. The fact that I kept my watch on my sleeve probably didn’t hurt.

The cart’s wheels screeched as we pulled into the peanut butter aisle. Scanning the aisle for incomers, I put my arm over Hope’s shoulder and drew her close. With any luck, my display of affection would distract from our annoying cart.
“Honey, do you think that they’ll want the chunky peanut butter, or the smooth peanut butter?” I asked.

I grabbed the smooth peanut butter. The question had been a formality, really. The thought of chunky peanut butter was revolting. All that goop mixed with solid matter — something was the matter with whoever ate that trash.
Hope slipped out from under my arm and studied the jam. As she did, she gave an exaggerated sweep across her shoulder. She made a huff.
“I don’t know why you insisted on wearing that thing Avery,” she said. “The cuffs feel like sandpaper.”
“It’s my best business suit. Why wouldn’t I be wearing it? Don’t you want me to dress my best?”
“Not sure if a family gathering is the best fit, but…”
She grabbed a bottle of jam from the shelf.
“This look good to you?” she asked.

She went to put it in the cart. I would’ve taken it from her — it was an inferior jam, chock full of artificial sweeteners and preservatives — but I wasn’t in the mood to argue. It was a small miracle that I’d managed to get the cart full of as many of the correct items as I had.

My grocery list gave off a glow as my pen scratched off the last item. I’d gotten everything. It was the perfect combination of items. I had accounted for the food preferences of every member in Hope’s family, while simultaneously accounting for mine. It was going to be a hit. I was sure of it.

The store’s music picked up in a triumphant thrum as we left the aisle and made our way for the checkout line. All the while, people’s heads turned as they continued to check me out. They loved me, didn’t they?
“Mission accomplished,” I said, flashing my patented smile.
“You always need to say that?” Hope said, flashing one right back.
Her smile looked duller then than when I’d first met her. No doubt, Hope’s looks were beginning to lose their luster.
“When the mission is accomplished, yeah,” I said.
“But are you sure we shouldn’t get some Mayor Houck pins before we leave?”
She grabbed a baggy of bright pins from off a shelf and looked at me despairingly.
Suddenly, the walkway toward the checkout lane was too bright. Intrusive colors were everywhere, blasting my brain for attention. I wanted to ignore it all.
Waving the pins in my face, she continued. “Please? It’ll make for such cute pictures.”
I wanted to ignore her. My heartrate rose, and my lip was curling. Why could she bring that out of me?
“Today isn’t about Mayor Houck,” I said, coolly. “We got all the things that we need.”
“He was a colleague of yours though, wasn’t he? Or, at least a —.”
“Please, I never even talked to the guy for his entire time in office,” I said. I felt my voice raise. It shouldn’t have felt good.

“But it does help to remember Thomas Jefferson and John Adams died on July 4th.” I was level again. Control is never out of reach. “And I don’t see anybody making a big hoopla about that. Mayor Houck was just a guy, honey. He’s a year gone. Who cares?”

A few people were giving me dirty looks. I swear of it. I swerved into the checkout lane and tossed our items onto the belt. Getting out of the cursed store was the priority. I was already beginning to see cracks in the place.

Grime covered the floors, there was a relentless squeal in the conveyor belt, the tiles were loose, and my head was getting noisy. So annoying, how problems swarm like that. Face warming, I readjusted my collar and shot a grin at the cashier.
“How are you doing today?” the cashier said. He picked at a pimple, hardly looking up from his screen.
People pay the runts so freaking much, and they can’t even bother pretending to be excited. My entire cart was on the belt before he even scanned an item.
After scanning a few items through, he shot me a look. He looked away. “I swear, I’ve seen you somewhere before. On TV or something, maybe?”
I chuckled and gave Hope a nudge. Of course, she just rolled her eyes. It was impossible to impress her.
He took a second look.
“Wait… You’re the guy on all those signs and billboards. You running for mayor or something?”
“Avery McNider, and treasurer’s office, actually,” I said. “Being the mayor… Such a waste of time, really. No money in it.”
My eyes went to my watch, then to the clock in their walls. The tick on their clock was off by a second. If only clockmakers could get everything to run smoothly. There’d be no need to check.
“Are you using debt, for credit?” the cashier asked.
“Come again?” I said.
He’d been making a sly jab. It was thanks to me that our town’s debt was almost gone — and here he was, acting like I was wrong for taking credit.
“Debit or credit?” he said, spacing his words cautiously.
He knew that he’d set off a button. He’d known what he was doing. Yet, he dared to play ignorant. The gall on some people is simply astounding.

I was going to tell him debit and insert my card. Though, the plush animals by the checkout stared at me. Particularly, a stuffed bear. Its beady eyes pried at me, attempting to break into my soft tissues. Its furry face feigned innocence, but I knew better. I could see the pure fury broiling beneath the surface.
“How much is that plushy?” Hope asked.
The cashier chuckled. “The Sir Stuffs-a-Lot? 5 bucks. You seen the cartoon?”

Hope snatched up the plushy, without bothering answering him. She’d been paying attention to my gaze the whole time. Don’t ask me how, but she’d caught onto the fact that the plushy had been taunting me. She was trying to join in.
To think that I once considered her a partner. That goes to show how naive we can be, even with our best preparations.
“Hope, we already purchase all of our items for the day,” I said. “Remember the list?”

She smirked as she pulled the stuffed bear down on the conveyor belt. She remembered. I’d hammered home the idea into her a million times, until my face shone beet red. Meanwhile, the bear’s fur on the belt glinted a blood maroon.
“Come on Avery,” she said, with a pout. “It’s fourth of July! Can’t you just make an exception to your stupid rule?”

I looked at the price tag. Twenty dollars. That was way beyond what I was willing to spend. I looked at the bear. I’d turned my back for one moment, and it’d become a sight that sent shivers down my spine.

The bear was animated. Not cartoon animation — no. Living. Pulsing. Palpable. Its chest undulated inward and outward, as though it had breath. It gave me a toothy grin, jagged teeth being prominent. They had a cold glow, like light bordering an event horizon.

I wanted to shout, “Are you seeing this?” but my throat was parched. Something was choking me. Worse, time had stopped. I scanned Hope, then the cashier. Their faces were frozen with looks of contempt.
It’s funny — they’d been pretending to be so happy around me. Yet, the stopping of time had locked them in micro-expressions, and their true feelings were clear as day.
“Hello,” said the stuffed bear.
I ignored him, and tried shoving my debit card in the machine. Though, it didn’t respond.
“That’s rude,” said the bear. “How would you feel if somebody didn’t respond to you when you talked?”
“I stopped talking to stuffed animals when I was five,” I said. “Maybe earlier. Now, if you don’t want the stuffing knocked out of you, I’d knock it off.”
The bear leaned from its place on the conveyor belt and patted me on the shoulder.
“So much power, going to so much waste,” it said. “I hope you treasure your position as treasurer. Because, I have an inkling you’re not going to have it for much longer.”

By that point, there was no ignoring the thing. It’s true that, by acknowledging it, I was playing exactly into its fuzzy paws. Though, what was I to do? The world was still moving in slow motion, and a buzz was growing in my head. Furthermore, there was a relief that came with talking to the bear.
An anger beat beneath its little chest. It held a solidarity with my rage at the universe. Something about that was soothing.
“What’s your game, exactly?” I asked.
“Sir Stuffs-a-Lot is the name, playtime is the game,” it said. He gave a little squeak. “And, believe me: it’s playtime.”
The lights to the store flickered, before coming back on with a clinical hue. As colors desaturated, my skin saturated with sweat.
I whipped my blackberry out of my pocket.
“Hope, I think there was something in that stupid breakfast sandwich you bought me,” I said. She remained contrapposto. “If anybody has anything to do with this freak show, reveal yourselves now!”
I pressed the phone’s power button in a blitzkrieg, but the screen was locked bleach white.
“I love a good feast,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot.
“You’re not getting a lick of my groceries,” I said.
“Who was talking about the groceries?”
I grabbed the bear by the throat. It bit me on the wrist, then wriggled its way back to the conveyor belt. It’d left a bite mark in my skin. Worse, there were scuff marks on my watch.
“Screw you!” I said.
“Right back at you,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot said. “You choked me first.”
“Well, you’ve been giving me the creeps.”
“And that’s my fault? Can’t a bear taunt a guy about killing him, in peace?”
My lips puckered. There was no way that the bear had just said what I’d thought it said.
“Way to go, with your embezzling,” Sir Stuffs-A-Lot said. “God, I hate politics… I didn’t want to have to kill you either, really. But, I mean, you leave me know choice.”
My hand edged near a packet of lighters. Mind you, I do not support incinerating one’s enemies in the slightest. But desperate times sometimes call for that.
“It’s fourth of July,” I said. “Can’t we just let bygones be bygones?”
“Sounds lame,” Sir Stuffs-A-Lot said. He jumped past the conveyor belt and began rubbing his fuzzy butt in my groceries. “Fourth of July is the perfect day for vengeance.”
“Hey, stop that!”

It was too late. My groceries were floating in the air now, moving back toward their shelves. I was going to need to shop for things all over again. My eyes went to my list for a sense of reassurance, only to watch it turn to dust.
“What the hell are you?” I asked.
“Your penance,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot. “I emerge election year or so, to destroy blood-sucking politicians.”
“You choose to be a care bear?”
Sir Stuffs-A-Lot shrugged. “Suck it.”
This had been shaping up to be a perfect day, up until now. It was all the bear’s fault. The weird things always happen to me.
“Strange that I’ve never heard anything about you, until today. You just think you can storm in, and take over?”
“The same things can be said about you. You just tried to take over the town, with an iron fist.”
“Only the money. And, I’ve given back to the community too!” I said.
“How?”
I stood still for a moment. Stress shot through me. Pop quizzes should’ve ended back in middle school.
“I — I care about these people?” I said, trying to gauge the bear’s reaction.
I leaned over at the cashier and pinched his cheeks.
“Like this guy! He’s awesome!”
I glanced at my bags. There were holes in some of them. Clearly, he was awful. Though, then, that would’ve ruined my point.
“Do you want to know what happened to Mayor Houck?” asked Sir Stuffs-A-Lot.
“He died while choking on some frozen yogurt,” I said. “Well, on the toppings to his frozen yogurt, if you want to get technical…”

“Precisely. I orchestrated all of that. From the moment Mayor Houck had entered the frozen yogurt bar, I’d been watching in the wings, manipulating the environment. He was doomed to die, before he ever took a bite.”
“Always hated that guy,” I said, suppressing a laugh. “Super glad that you offed him. He wanted to raze the treasurer’s office and run it himself.”
“He was pretty awful,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot. “The history of this town is littered with bad politicians, in fact. Ever notice how many of the bad politicians die?”
“All politicians in this town die.”
“That’s been me.”
I nodded. It all added up.
“What’s with all of the politicians in this town who’ve died from heart attacks?” I asked. “If you’re going to kill a bunch of politicians, might as well get creative about it.”
“The plastic faces politicians put on are hideous. And, the faces they make when they have a heart attack are downright hilarious,” Sir Stuffs-A-Lot said. He was wheezing more than a leaking balloon.
“But, what about me? I’m not a bad person,” I said.
I’m not sure how, but Sir Stuffs-A-Lot made the store more dead than it already had been.
“You’re just the worst,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot, breaking the silence. “You don’t even have a tortured past or anything. You’re a plain old asshole.”

He touched me in the center of my forehead, and my life flashed before my eyes. I was flung from my perfect childhood, to my perfect education, to my perfect adulthood. He had a point, perhaps. Most of my life had been spent checking my status, gossiping about the status of others, or working to attain status.
“In my defense, I was given anything and everything I possibly could’ve needed to succeed in life,” I said. “Am I really to be blamed for turning out to be incredibly greedy and selfish?”
Sir Stuffs-A-Lot was on my face now, using his stubby arms to compress each side of my skull.
“I blame the system,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot.
“Oh, thank God.”
“Unfortunately, you are the system.”

The pressure grew. I tore at the bear and my hair, hoping something would give. More images fluttered by, of instances when I’d manipulated things to get my way. Personally, I don’t see what the issue was. Nonetheless, a heat emanated from the bear, and it was only getting hotter.
“Please, give me mercy! There are too many things I want to do with my life!”
Tears were rolling down my face now. I would’ve given anything for time to resume, and to hear Hope’s voice again.

“I sense an inherent goodness in your heart,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot. “I must’ve misjudged. I will relieve you, on the condition that you change your ways. You must clean up this town — make it better.”
“Yeah, yeah! Just don’t kill me!”
Inherent goodness? Fat chance. I think that he was sensing the guitar tattoo I’d gotten over my chest when I was 17. Nonetheless, when the pain receded, I wasn’t going to correct him.
“Thank you,” I said, panting to catch my breath.
I leaned my body against the conveyor belt.
“Also, give me your watch,” said Sir Stuffs-A-Lot.
“Why?”
It gave me its cutest puppy-dog eyes. “Because, you parasite.”

Gingerly, I unlatched the watch from around my wrist. Stooping, I fastened it around Sir Stuffs-A-Lot’s. It barely fit, making Sir Stuffs-A-Lot’s body sag. Hatred swept through me. The only thing that quelled my wrath was that the bear had spared my life.
“You better take good care of it, Sir Stuffs-A-Lot!” I said. “You have no idea how many people I screwed over, to pay for that thing. That watch is a work of god. Priceless. Priceless!”
The cashier cleared his throat, then began filling my cart with our bags.
“You okay?” Hope asked, raising an eyebrow.
The lights to the store flickered back to their full brightness. My phone flickered on and off half a dozen times.
“Yes,” I said, drawing myself back to my full height.

I picked up Sir Stuffs-A-Lot, dangling him in front of me. The watch was still latched to his arm. Yet, everything else had returned to as it was, as though my conversation with Sir Stuffs-A-Lot had never occurred.
“So, you like him?” asked Hope.
“If we’re going to give him to your family as a gift, might as well toss in my watch. Keep it classy.”
“They’ll just adore him, honey!” Hope said.
I readjusted my collar and wiped a bead of sweat from my forehead. “Dear, I hope so.”
We walked out of the store with all eyes remaining on us. I’m still not sure if the store was appalled or enamored. I like to think both. I’ve always thought myself quite the show.
Hope’s family hated the bear’s guts. They also hated me, as it happens. Oh, and the day went up in fireworks.
The family left early — they didn’t want to hear about how I was about to turn a new leaf and stop being corrupt, for some reason. We didn’t even get to see the actual town fireworks. Go figure.

Once election day rolled around, I won my position as treasurer. Unfortunately, I can’t really bring myself to do anything corrupt anymore. Thus, my money has dried up. I was kind of freaked out by Sir Stuffs-A-Lot. As a little addendum, the new mayor has a strong stance against corruption, and watches me like a hawk.
I keep Sir Stuffs-A-Lot around. He’s always watching, from my desk. He’s a nice reminder of something; I’m just not sure what. I guess I don’t want him to ruin my heart.
Did I mention that Hope left me? The balls on that bitch…
Peanut butter sandwiches are healthy for the heart, I’ve heard. Especially with jam. I make sure to make them without error. In due time, I’ll have impeccable health.
Once I’ve achieved that, I can work on improving the town’s economy. Right now, I just don’t care.
I suppose that Sir Stuffs-A-Lot taught me a lot, after all.
End

title: Life Drones On
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth (Writing as Benjamin Vale)
"I think I'm in love," I say.
"It's just one logo," Bradley tells me. "There are still the dozen others that we have to go through."
He awkwardly swipes the tablet in his desk, brushing through several more graphics.
"No, man," I say. "Go back to the original. That was totally the best one."
Bradley lets out an annoyed huff.
"You seriously just want to go with the first one? I spent my past week working on these," he mumbles.

A twinge of regret shoots through my chest. Had I wasted Bradley's time? He's such a valuable asset, and I can't afford to lose him. I give him an apologetic grin. Hopefully he understands that I understand.
"Stop!" I shout. Who am I kidding? Bradley is a pest. "Swipe back."
Bradley complies. My mouth waters, and my eyes bulge. I lean forward and squint, to soak in the full image.
"Wait — no, that one is bonkers. Sorry, scratch what I said a sec ago. That is the logo that we have to go with."

It's an image of two flaming letters — a "D" and an "O". I can practically feel the heat emanating off of them. The "D" also has such a sharp design, which makes great contrast with the sleek curvature of the "O". The "O" also reminds me of a donut. In fact, it looks exactly like the flaming donut I'd had just a week ago, at my friend's party... What was his name again?

It doesn't matter. Suddenly, I'm starving. I scan Bradley's glass desk. It’s empty, save for three touch-pens, and the tablet at the center. I suppose it doesn't matter, since I can't eat anything... That said — there’s not even a glass of water?
I take another look. A bottled water rests in Bradley's lap. My eyebrows arch. I spend way too much on the water bill for this office, for Bradley to just be drinking his own bottled waters.
Wait — have I paid the water bill yet? I'll need to check with my secretary. What was her name again?
"Vick are you kidding me?" Bradley says, shooting me a glare. "Sorry, I — I don't mean to be... Uh, brash. But you just told me that you wanted to go with the first one!"
"First one sucks," I say, stretching my arms behind my head. "Go with this one."

I'd almost lost my train of thought for a second there. Probably hadn't had enough sleep the night before. Last night had been pretty crazy. I'm not sure if I've ever been at a party that lasted so long. Jake Lavin really knows how to throw those bashes right. Does he have some sort of party planner? Maybe I should look into getting one for my own upcoming party. It’d certainly help Alex out.

Bradley clears his throat. "Are you even sure you want to go with any of these? Our logo has served us pretty well over the past three years. Don't get me wrong: I'd love for you to go with one of my designs. But, I feel like we should be taking things a bit —."
"No. Go. That logo. Now. Take it to the marketing department, or whatever. I need this ball rolling, stat."
"Yeah, ok... But, you haven't even seen what Adam designed yet!"
"Don't need to. Already know what I'm doing. Enough with the chit-chat: do what I said. It's a Direct Order."
"Dear god... That's so bad."
"Never gets old!" I say, with a smirk.

Bradley rolls his eyes, trudging from his desk and down the aisle. I follow suit, drifting from the graphic design department and toward the accounting department. I pause to spin 360° and soak in the office. Windows sprawl along the walls, stretching from floor to ceiling. Sunlight sprays through, soaking the office in a warm glow. I grin. The entire office is sheet white — flooring, walling, furniture, tools. The only exception is my employees, who wear informal t-shirts and jeans. Well, everybody except Bradley.
Screw Bradley.

Anyway, it's an absolute dream. While growing up, I’d always imagined creating an office like this. It beats the stuffy morgues most people have to go to. How could anybody live like that? Waking up each morning, just to put themselves in a personal animal pen... Why are cubicles so small, anyway? Why are they cubes, for that matter? For a culture that believes so strongly in "thinking outside the box", we certainly spend a lot of time thinking inside the box.
I snicker, eyes still roving around. Not me though. Not —.
"Gee, so are you just going to keep standing there? Or, are we going to finally get to business?"
I ogle to my left. My right.
"Over here."
I look straight ahead. Of course — accounting. How could I have forgotten?
"If I'm not mistaken, we were supposed to meet... A full five minutes ago," I say, glancing in the corner of my screen.
"We were," Sherry says. "And I've been sitting here, waiting."
"So have... So have I! I was just checking a few diagnostics. Want to make sure that this place is in tip-top shape. To be awesome, things have to work awesome!"

"Yep, yep," says Sherry. She gives a double-take at the tablet in her desk. Then, she hands me a stack of papers. "There's my report. I guess you can plug it in to... Wherever the hell you need to plug it, and do what you need to do."
"That's it?"
"You're a busy guy. I figured that condensing things into a report would be best — for your sake."
She purses her lips, gives me a nod, and then gestures behind herself. I tilt my head and give a quizzical look. It hits me — I'm supposed to be talking to the head of my code department.

Coding is my favorite skill that I don’t have. True story: I once tried learning coding in high school. I sucked at it, though. My teacher said it had something to do I had trouble with grasping the material? I could never quite understand what she was getting at... It doesn't matter. I hated high school, anyway. And college, for that matter.
Is it fair to say that education is overrated?
"Why, hello, hello! What do you have for the old CEO?" I say, whipping to the desk of Gary — the head of the coding department.

"Not much, really," said Gary. "I patched a few bugs on our website... Also, I talked to the crew about the suggestions you made. Honestly? I don't think it's such a smart idea to add a feature where people can post their purchases on social media. Logistically, it's just not feasible for our small team to do. More than that, wouldn't it be crossing a few lines? We’d need agreements with the social media companies."
"Relevant, Gary. That's what we're trying to be. That's what we need to stay on top of the competition. We can make this work. We have to. Ever heard the term 'chillax'?"
"Do I really have to answer that?"
"I've been talking with my people —”
“What people?”
“— and they think this new feature would be the boost that Direct Order needs."
"You're asking for a lot."
"Man, I don't really..."
A buzz goes off. I glance at the corner of my screen.

"I really have to go, Gary. I still have to talk to... Talk to analytics! Also, that was my alarm for an important summit with the board of directors, in five minutes. But hey, maybe we should go get a sandwich sometime. Oh yeah... And also: figure this thing out."
Mouth gaping, Gary tries to say something — but I'm already zooming away, toward the analytics department.

So many things to do, so little time. The slightest drawn-out conversation can send me spiraling off schedule. It reminds me of an old game I used to play. Jenga, was it? Yeah, that was it. I used to play it all the time with my sister. Actually, it's been awhile since we'd last talked. Had I remembered to send her invitations?
Remember... I need to talk to analytics. I can't forget. I walk down the aisle, to the analytics section.
"Hey Lucy, what's happening?" I say.

I eye a dipping bird on her desk, as it makes its perpetual motion. I should probably get one for my desk. It's strange I don't have a desk toy. Wait a minute — aren’t desk toys against Direct Order guidelines?
"Not much," Lucy says with a sigh. "I assume you want a report?"

"I'm fine without the papers, to be honest. I'm not a big fan of reading. Just tell me about the biggest updates, if you can. Also, how has your day been going? Mine has been going great. Just this morning, I—."

"People are buzzing about the announcement you made," says Lucy. "'We have something extraordinary that we're keeping under wraps'… Really good choice of words. Right now, the announcement has garnered an average of 30% engagement across your social media platforms."
"And that's good?"
"That's great."
"Great!"
Another buzz goes off — only two minutes until the summit with my board of directors.
"Well... Uh... Keep the campaign going!" I say. "If our base is happy, I'm happy."

I give a whistle as I head across the office and toward the meeting room. Heads turn as I fly over rows upon rows of desks. I smile to myself. My employees see me every day, yet they still gawk at me with a look of wonder in their eyes. I wonder what they all think of me.
I stop at the door to the meeting room, and let it scan the tag on my metal hood. It beeps, then slides open. As I enter, it shuts behind me.
"Vick Mobley! Welcome!"

I scan the room. A row of businesspeople are seated at a long table. I hover to the chair at the very end, and my eye shoots to a business man in the corner — he’s new, but he looks familiar. Have I seen him somewhere?
"Sorry for being late," I say. "Keeping tabs on this company... It's a nightmare. I miss the days when Direct Order was still running out of my garage."

Davis chuckles. "Yes, well... So do I. It's fine though. I've been handling things here, while you were busy. You do a brilliant job steering this ship. Your unique leadership style really makes the place."
"Thanks," I say, echoing his chuckle.

Though, I can't help but seethe under my breath. There's a palpable hunger in Davis' eyes. He wants my job. He's always wanted it. Yet, he's also the only person on this board I can trust. The rest of the suits — they’re vultures, who didn’t invest in my company until the instant it could serve them. If anything were to happen to Direct Order, I see them leaving just as quickly.
"Unfortunately, fellas," I say, "I'm almost done for the day. I only have about five minutes to give this conversation — after that, you guys are stuck talking to my looping interface."
"That's fine," says Davis. "Like I said: I’ve been handling things. If you want, I can just give you the big details, and send you on your way. Is that alright, everybody?"
The board nods and looks to the man in the corner.
"This is Mark Bridges," says Davis. "He's the current chairman of 'Ship-It'. He came here with a proposal."
I scoff. Bridges has unkempt hair, a visible stubble, and his suit is slightly wrinkled.
"I hear dozens of proposals, every day..." I say, skeptically. "This another attempt at a buy-out?"
Davis smiles, serenely. "Yes. That's exactly what this is."
I give Davis a look. "Then, this is a flat no. Meeting over. Right?"
The board rustles uncomfortably, and averts eye contact.
"Not this time," says Davis. "Vick: they're offering us three billion dollars."
I nod dismissively. Yet, I feel a punch to the gut.
"We need to come to a decision in a week," says Davis. "But Bridges has been giving us his pitch and, honestly, I'm leaning toward a yes."
I nod dumbly. "Well, that's great. I, uh — I'm going to need to hear this pitch for myself, but..."

"Direct Order would largely operate the same it does now," says Bridges. "We'd simply be acquiring the company. Granted, there will be a few redundant positions to trim — but, I hardly see that being a problem."

"I guess not," I say. "But what about projections for how this will affect our company, long-term? Do you have a strategy for how to integrate our companies? Would this acquisition hurt this year’s sales? What about our infrastructure? Besides... We're still a very young company. Would this be the best for our image?"

"It's fine, Vick," Davis says. "We've discussed all of it. Bridges has a comprehensive, 10 step initiative. So long as we follow it, Direct Order will triple in sales by the end of next year. And both of us? We'll be filthy rich. I can send you all of the notes to read through, if you'd like."

I squint, and my eyes swim around. Everybody on the board seems pleased with themselves. Too pleased. I haven't seen them like this since I proposed that we double our charges for shipping, and that'd been an absolute disaster.
"No, no need. I hate to read. It all sounds... Good," I say, measuring my words carefully. "Ship-It is a good company. I could definitely see this working. When do we have to vote?"

A bitter taste floods my mouth. Ship-It is an awful company. For years, their service has been inferior and their prices have been terrible. Yet they've somehow managed to make us struggle. I've even created a nickname for them, which has become popular among my office — Shit-Shit.
Pretty clever.
There's another buzz in the corner of my screen. Three minutes until my painting session.
"I need answers fast," I say. "I have to be somewhere, soon."
Davis stretches his arms, then gestures toward Bridges.

"Bridges was hoping we could hold the vote next week, on the 13th." Davis pauses to give me a sly grin, then chuckles. "That seems to be the only date all of us can make it. That shouldn't be a problem for you... Should it, Vick?"
I nod my head yes, but say, "No. Of course not."
Davis' smile fades, and his eyes go wide. He presses a thumb against his lips.
"You sure, Vick? After all, I know that it's the same day you have your we—."
"I'll be fine," I say firmly. "I've never missed a meeting before, and don't plan on starting now. I have time. I always have ti—."

My session at Direct Order's offices times out. I blink into a maple room. A fan swings lazily overhead, and water burbles from a stone fountain. I take in a whiff of air, to no avail. If only I could smell my surroundings. I remember the last time I was physically outdoors, and smelled something. It was burnt steak. I was at a trendy new restaurant with Shawna. The food was awful. The night was amazing.
"Glad to see that you could make it," says Isabelle. "Or, at least, some of you."
Her back is turned to me, as she works at her easel. Vague, golden shapes smear across it. Trees? Fenceposts? It's impossible to tell.
"It's been a crazy day," I say. "So many things going on. I know that I've said Direct Order can’t get any busier... But, I was wrong. I'm about to explode."
"Good," says Isabelle in a monotone.
"See, this is why I love coming to you. You're so understanding."
"Any progress on your painting yet?" she asks.

"God... No. Sorry, but I just haven't had the time to work on it. Today was — I don't even want to talk about it. And yesterday I was cleaning up a complete mess in Direct Order's software... You wouldn't believe it. While updating our software, somebody somehow mixed up the —."
"I wasn't asking for me," Isabelle says. "I was asking for you. Your painting is already on its easel, in your corner."
My eyes dart toward it.
"Passive aggressive much?" I ask, with a chuckle. "Why ask me if you already know the answer?"
"I don't. Only you know the answer. Progress on a painting doesn't start on paper, Vick... It starts in the psyche. Focus your emotions."
"Yeah, ok, whatever. Go make a fortune cookie or something."
I hover to my painting and extend a metal arm to grab a paintbrush. I give it a dab of blue, then glide it across the easel.
My easel is a wash of reds, greens and browns. I mean to depict the ground during Autumn, but it could use a shade of blue. The sky is just as important as the ground. I can't let myself ignore it.

As I slather blue above the brown and orange, I smile inwardly. It's brilliant. Isabelle has told me several times that I'm an “artistic genius" just waiting to break out. For once, I believe those words.

She's an artistic genius herself, having won dozens of awards and I pay her good money. However, I usually can't help but feel that she merely tolerates me. She probably only calls me "genius" so I'll keep paying her money. Something she’s also told me several times is that I can't drag my brush across the paper and pretend that it's art — that I need focus and structure, rather than dumping on several paints all at once.
I only call her "genius" so that she'll keep letting me use her studio.
There's another buzz. Two minutes remaining.
"I'm going to have to pop out of here soon," I say. "I'm due at a five-star restaurant in Los Angeles."
"You can leave whenever you want," says Isabelle. "Though, I suggest that you set aside some time in the coming weeks to try finishing your painting. I really want you to get a feel for it."
"Sounds like a plan," I say. "But, honestly, I'm not really feeling this ‘painting thing’ anymore. Maybe it’s not me? I have so much going on. I'm sure you already know about the—."
"Ah, yes," Isabelle says, with an annoyed huff. "Thanks so much for remembering to invite me, by the way..."
I give her a bemused look.
"Remembering to invite you?" I repeat, weighing the words on my tongue. "Really? That's funny. I could've sworn that I..."
Isabelle's jaw clenches, and she nods her head. I simply force a smile and give a nod of my own.

"Anyway, I'm not letting you drop my class if I can help it," Isabelle says. "I will break the true artist out of you, Mobley. Today, next week: I want us to have a full session. None of these 'five minute' paltry sessions."
"That sounds great," I say. "But, that's actually the same date as —."
Everything fades to black. A soft candle slowly fills the darkness. As my eyes adjust, I realize I'm at a table. I’m at a table, surrounded by several other tables.
I look up. Cold starlight shines through a glass roof, bathing me and the rest of the restaurant. I look back down. Shawna is seated across from me, looking beautiful as ever.
"I'm here," I say.

I wait for her to crack a smile. Instead, she stares daggers through me. I look at what she's wearing — a silver dress, and a pearl necklace. Had I bought her those? I'd bought her so many things — it was impossible to remember.
"So, what food are we getting?" I ask.
Shawna's brow arches, and her face tightens. "I already ate."
"Oh, God," I say, slapping myself — my drone — in the face. "Don't tell me — I messed up the scheduling again. I was supposed to be here an hour ago, wasn't I?"
Shawna twirls a fork in her finger and shakes her head.
"No. I guess you could say you 'came right on time'."
I smile, relief flushing through me. "Great. Excellent. So... Why did you already eat then?"  I chuckle. "Do you have a surprise event planned for tonight, or something?"
"No," she says. "I came early. And, I was hungry. So, I ate."
I look around. This has to be some kind of prank. Yet, all I see are couples casually enjoying themselves. Why don't we look like that?
"That's funny, because I'm starving too," I say. I pat my stomach.
Shawna offers half a smile. "Alright then. Order something."
Her fingers rap against the table. Sweat beads down my forehead.
"Well... There's no point really, is there? I, uh... Well, I already have food."

I unhook my motion sensors, swivel from my computer monitor, and go to my small fridge. My mouth watering, I pop it open and pull out a slice of pizza. Finally, I turn back to the computer and wave the pizza in the camera.
"See?" I say. "Already taken care of."
I take a large bite. I make a face.
"God, that's spicy! In hindsight, I probably shouldn't have ordered so many jalopies..."
"Jalapenos?"
"Gesundheit."
Shawna suppresses a smile. I casually lean back in my chair and take another large bite. I make another odd face. I have terrible taste.
"Well it's nice that you have food, all the way over there," she says. She looks down at the table and raps her fingers again.
I reattach my motion sensors to lean my drone's screen toward her.

"It really is. All I have to do is press a button on the side of my screen, and the butler sends anything I need down here. There's this high-tech dumbwaiter I had installed — it takes food right to me. I hardly even have to move. I guess the dumbwaiter isn't so dumb after all. Come to think of it... Why do we even call 'dumbwaiters' dumbwaiters? I mean, considering how much planning goes into them, it's hardly an accurate name."
"Vick..."
"Come to think of it, the more I say the name, it doesn't even sound like a real name. A real word, even. Dumbwaiter..."
A waiter strides up to us, flushed in the face.
"May I help you?" he asks, lips puckered.
Shawna shoots me a glare. I look at the waiter — his eyes are a bottomless pit. What's everybody's problem, tonight?
"No thank you," I say, giving a wide smile. "But, I really appreciate you checking up on us!"
The waiter's lip furls and eyes narrow. "Yes. Of course. Anything for the... lovely couple."
As he stalks off, he mutters something. I consider turning up my drone's hearing sensors. Though, it doesn't really matter, does it? I turn to look back to Shawna. She's what matters.
