"I guess we can start talking about the wedding preparations," I say.

Shawna stares through me. Odd. I look around, hoping to find support among the sea of faces. Finally, my eyes wander to the window in the ceiling — toward the twinkling tail of the milky way. I look back to Shawna, and gesture toward it. "By the way, it's a gorgeous night, isn't it?"
She blinks, letting me hold my arm in the air.  Finally, she looks up. She clucks her tongue.
"Oh. Yeah. Really nice."
I feel my face go hot. Maybe it's the jalopies. Yet, it can't be that. No — I usually only ever feel this way during conversations with Davis. My face twists into a false smile.
"Alright, what's your problem?" I say, leaning over the table and extending my drone's arm to poke her in the arm.
Disgruntled, Shawna rubs the spot I touched. "I don't have a problem."
"You seem like you have a problem."
"You're the one with the problem. Did you see the way the waiter was looking at you?"
I put my pizza own. "Come on, Shawna. You can't pretend with me."
She gives a huff. "Well, you sure think you can pretend with me..."
I give her a bemused look. "What are you talking about?"
"You told me you'd actually be here tonight."
"I told you the truth. I am here."
"No, you're not. You're hiding out in your trillion-dollar cave."
I laugh. "It's a highly advanced control chamber. Trust me, if you just understood the power of this computer...
I watch her face. It's on fire. I'm losing her.
"Today was just so... I didn't have time to fly out there today, okay? It — today was a day where I had tons of things to do today. "
"Oh yeah? What things?"
"Well, I had to—."
"Are those things more important to you than our wedding?"
"Well, I mean... Well, it's not like th—."
She claps her hands.

"Alright, let's hear it. What are all of these things that are so much more important than being here? What's your excuse for dumping this entire wedding on me, while you can hardly be bothered to even remember our wedding's date?"
A buzzing goes off.
"What was that?" Shawna snaps.
"My buzzer. I have a meeting with Harris in... Three minutes."
"Who? You mean Alex?"
"No. I'll talk to him at the bachelor party. Save the best man for last. No — I'm talking about Harris. You don't remember him? He's my nephew..."
Shawna stares at me blankly.

"Scruffy hair? Spotty beard...? He's the one who's constantly asking me for money. No? Anyway, he just got out of business school. Just like I did, twelve years ago. The kid really reminds me of me, actually... Do you think Harris would make I good director of social marketing?"
"I honestly think—."

"—he would? Yeah, that's what I was thinking too. I was just reading this article the other day about young people, in the marketing sector. Particularly on social media. They're little geniuses at making cash! And social media is ripe with money, for people who know how to play it right. Sort of like... Like how a guitar is an amazing instrument, if you just know how to play it right. Come to think of it, I never did get a hang of the —."
Shawna clenches her teeth, lowering her voice to a hush.
"Vick. Stop."
Deep inside, I know that Shawna is hundreds of miles away. Why do I still feel like she's about to kill me?
"Yes?"
She makes her fork skate across her empty plate.
"I have something I need to say, and you can't butt in."
I bite my tongue. "Al— alright then."

Shawna clears her throat. "I'm starting to wonder if it's... Maybe cutting it too close? I know that this is going to feel like a slap in the face, but it's just — you're hardly ever here. And, even when you are, you... Well, you aren't. What if this isn't right? What if we're making a mistake? What if we're doing this too fast?"
She puts down her fork and looks at me. "Alright. You can talk now."
My eyes go wide. Did she really say what I think she said? She couldn't have. I look down, soaking in the gravity of her words.
I take a bite of my pizza. After I've gulped it down, I burst into a laugh.

"Too fast? Shawna... You're... Uh... You're the love of my life. This is destiny." Shawna's eyes go wide. Her face seems to glow. "Besides: despite all our hiccups, we've managed to stay together for these past four years."
"Two years."
I shrug. "Same difference."

Shawna doesn't seem convinced. Something broils inside of me. Where it comes from, I don't know, but I suddenly find myself saying, "Besides, it's too late to back out now. I've poured almost two million into this thing. Everybody is going to be there. Prestige celebrities, the press, the president..."

Shawna puts her hand on her forehead. She moans something, but I can hardly make it out. Finally, she looks up. Bags are under her eyes. Deep lines surround her mouth. She suddenly looks exhausted. Older, even.

"Look, Vick: I need you to promise that you're going to actually be there on the 13th. This — this is supposed to be the rest of our lives." She manages a weak smile. "No tricks. No games. When it's time for me to walk down the aisle, your ass better be standing at the altar."
"Well... Look, I have a lot—."
"Vick."
I try to swallow, but my mouth is a desert. "I'll be there."
I'm gone.

I'm standing in the middle of an open field. Frisbees whiz by my drone. Laughs reach my hearing sensors. A child ogles at me, then runs off. I hover down, to the pier of a lake. A lanky man with a mop of hair stands there. He turns around and embraces me, with outstretched arms and an awkward grin.
What's so awkward about the grin? I think it's the nose. I really shouldn't have let Harris get that nose job of his.
"How's my favorite uncle doing?" Harris asks.
"Great," I say. "I just got off a meeting discussing my upcoming wedding, and whatnot. Pretty exciting stuff."
Harris slaps my drone on the back. "You have a wedding coming up? Why didn't you tell anybody? Wait... Am I the first person you've told?"
I give a befuddled look. "No. People have known about the wedding for months. You ca—"
"Oh — yeah, I'm just messing with you, Uncle Vick."
He chuckles, and I chuckle along. He couldn't be more oblivious. I guess he really is my sister's son.
Harris scoops a rock from the ground and chucks it across the water. There's a dull plunk.
"Dammit," he says. "I'm never able to get it to skip along the water, just right."

"You need to use an incredibly flat and dull rock," I say. "But, personally? I've never found skipping rocks to be worth the time. The rocks that are perfect for skipping are also perfectly boring. Granted, it's hard to find rocks that aren't boring. Anyway, where was I? Oh, yes: I didn't have us come here so we could skip rocks. There's something I need to talk to you about."
"Finally need a buddy for one of your vacations, after three years?" he asks. "Because, if you do... No need to even ask. I can leave right now."

I shake my head. "No, actually. See, my company has an opening in its social marketing department. Specifically for the position of director. I've been looking for somebody to fill the vacancy, and I realized... You've been out of a job for quite some time, haven't you?"

"Just a year," says Harris. He sticks his tongue in the corner of his mouth as he picks up another rock and tries focusing his aim. "I manage to squeak on by though. Conventional jobs just aren't my speed."
I sigh. "Look, Harris... You and your mom — we aren't on the best of terms. You know that. I really feel like you taking this job would get things back together."
"I love you Vick. But, I don't see how this spat concerns me. Honestly, if you want to mend your relationship with her so much, you should try meeting her in person."
I squint. "The position will pay in the six figures. And it has the potential to rise a couple figures from there, if you can do your job right."
Harris' jaw falls and he looks right through me. "You serious?"
"I remember what it's like. I just want to help get you on your feet."
"I can't even begin to... I had no idea that you... Seriously, Vick, this is just amazing."
I smirk. "It’s nothing, really. However — I will need you to get in a plane flight to Direct Order's HQ the 11th. From there, we can discuss your job, and the exact responsibilities it would entail."
Harris scratches his forehead and shuffles his feet. "Yeah, about the 11th — I kind of have a band thing going on that night. Can't really swing going all the way out to Silicon Valley that day."
"We're talking about a six-figure —."
"Can't do it."
"The 12th?"
"Nope."
"The... The 14th?"
"I could make the 13th... That's the only day I have open for the next two weeks, though."
I shake my head. "Alright. The 13th it is, then. I can make that work. I — I want you there by 1:00, sharp."
"I can do that, easily."
Harris grins, then tosses a rock into the lake. "This is going to be great. Thanks again, Uncle Vick. You're a great man."
I nod gratefully, but can't help feeling a sickness in my gut. A buzz goes off on my sensors.
"Well, would you look at that?" I say. "Looks like I'm going to have to go now. I'll see you soon, Harris."
"See you soon, Vick. Love ya."

The park blinks out of existence. I'm back in my control room. I pull off my sensors and turn off the computer. As its processor winds down, I hear a dull hum. I don't care. It gives me a sort of calm. I need it to help myself sleep tonight.
Reclining my chair, I let its memory foam swallow me. It's been only 16 hours since I've last slept, but it feels like it's been years.
Closing my eyes, the muscles in my body tense. My head is a rock. There's no way I'm going to be able to make the 13th work. Yet, I'm going to have to.

My mind runs through all my responsibilities. I need to make it to the bachelor party on the night of the 12th, and reconnect with Alex. And I need to be at my wedding on the 13th. That's an indisputable fact. However, I'm also going to have to find a way to get to the boardroom meeting and the painting class. And, Harris... How am I going to handle Harris?

Suddenly, it hits me. If I fly to my Los Angeles mansion, I should be able to access the experimental control room from in there. I can conduct all of my business operations — and then, once those are done, I can head to my wedding. It'll all work out.

The only problem is that the experimental control room in Los Angeles isn't entirely finished, the chair will be far less comfortable, and the dumbwaiter won't function to the same level as my current one. Though, what does it matter? That's all a small price.
I can make this all work. I'm going to. I have to.
Page Break
Part 2:

With a yawn, I roll out of my chair and look around the control room. It's far shabbier than the one in Silicon Valley. Sunlight bleeds through the cracks. Rods and plaster crudely jut through the metal plating. The air is suffocating. Worst of all, it's smaller.
It reminds me of this old summer house my family used to take me and my sister to, when I was growing up. It was on some mountainside, overlooking a gushing river. It was a horrendous experience.

Speaking of horrendous experiences, I have somewhere to be. I turn on my computer and attach my sensors. I'm now hovering over a caramel floor, speckled with various blots of colors. I've teleported to Isabelle's art studio.
I never get a break, do I?
An easel is just ahead of me. Isabelle is hunched over it, clearly hard at work. Cautiously, I approach her.
"Hello," she says.
"Wait — you heard me?"
"Your hover-blades. I could hear those things from a mile away."
I look at her painting. It's an image of the sun kissing the horizon of an ocean. I marvel at the way in which her brush can make the water twinkle to life.
Unfortunately, I can hardly think of a more generic subject for a painting.
"Are you going to keep staring at my work, or are you going to finally go out and do your own work?" she asks.
I snort. "Well, that's the thing... I have good news and bad news for you, today.
She drops her paintbrush. "What's the bad news?"
"Don't you want to hear the good, first?"
"With you, there's never any good..."
I wince. That's harsh. It's true... But, still.

"Alright, look," I say, "I'm quitting your class today. But, before I do that, I want to finish my painting. Unfortunately, I have to use auto-pilot for my painting. I have a meeting in approximately —." I glance at the timer in the corner of my screen. "Two minutes."

Isabelle keeps her back turned to me, but her cheeks turn upward in a smile. I smile to myself. Perhaps my bad news wasn't so bad, after all. I've learned the skill of breaking bad news to people over the years. Whenever I had to show my parents my report card, for example, it always ended with us playing a game, or going out to eat ice cream, or something. We had the best ice cream place nearby, back then, too. Hippy's, or something?
"You're abandoning my class just like that, huh?"

"I try to do as much of everything as I can. But, this? I just can't. There's so much going on in my life right now... Besides: I was a terrible fit for your class. You know that. I know that. We all do."
"I don't know many things, Vick. But, I do know this: you never put in the effort."
"I am putting in the effort. I'm here. Right now. To finish my painting. You have no idea how many things that I have to do today, or how many things I've put off to come here."
Isabelle shrugged. "I don't. Yet, something tells me that I don't need to. If you really cared, you wouldn't be done."
"I'm not done yet."
"Then go finish your painting and get out."
"Yeah... About that. I'll be back, later."
A buzzer goes off in the corner of my screen. I'm back in the Silicon Valley office to Direct Order, with Harris staring me in the face.
"So..." he says, stuffing his hands in his pockets. "This is where you work?"
He leans on the coffee machine, then dips his hand in the cereal dispenser. He pulls out a handful of cereal and shoves it in his mouth.
"Nice place. Awful food."
He takes a mug, takes some coffee, then takes a swig.
There's a nervous laugh at my side. "This is the man that you're considering for Director of Social Marketing?"
I look over, and it's Bradley. He's wearing his usual stiff business suit, and is shoving his glasses ever deeper into his stupid face.
"Yes Bradley, this is who I'm considering," I say. "Do you have a problem with that? Because, if you do, I have a problem with that."

Bradley brushes away his combover and a patch of sweat. "Well, it's just... Even though he has a degree in business, he hardly has the work experience. He's untested. From my knowledge, he hasn't held a job in two years."
"Three," says Harris, before bumping into a stack of paper cups. He steps away as they roll onto the floor, and then he irons out the wrinkles in his t-shirt.
"Sorry," he says, "I have a bit of jet-lag. Anyway, yeah: never had a big need for corporate jobs. They're stuffy. They pigeon-hole people pretty easily too.
Bradley nods, before shooting me a glare. "I know that he's your nephew, Vick... But honestly. For the good of the company, you should at least pick somebody who’s qualified."
I brush him off and put my hand on Harris' shoulder. "Do you want the job Harris?"
Harris looks up, and sighs. "I don't know. Kind of?"
I give Bradley a smug grin. "He's qualified." I look back to Harris. "And, you've got the job."
Bradley's jaw hits the floor, but I ignore him and walk Harris through the office.

"We'll be paying you somewhere around 200,000 dollars," I say. "The position will be rigorous... But, there's a bit of fun involved as well, so don't worry too much. As leader of social marketing, you'll mostly be... Social marketing? I'm sure you know social media pretty well, so you'll be a good fit."
"I guess," says Harris. He stops, and looks at a desk. "Hey, is that globe hovering?"
He points at a knick-knack. My eyes narrow.
"Yes, I think it is," I say. "Pretty cool, right? If you work here, you get to have a desk, just like that."
I pull Harris away. He can get distracted even worse than me.
A buzz goes off. I check the corner of my screen — I have two minutes, before I need to leave for the wedding.

I look into Harris' eyes, and smile. He has a look to him — the same look I once had. I've always told myself that it's the look a man gives when they've learned the greater meaning in life. It comes when they've finally discovered their ambitions.
Harris rubs his eyes.
"So... When do you want me to start?"
"I was thinking that you should start —."
"Stop!" It's Davis.

He stomps toward me, his jaw stiff and his stride rigid. I've told him many times to purchase shoes that would give him better arch support, to keep him in a better mood. Though, as usual, he clearly hasn't listened to me. Davis never listens.
"What do you think you're doing," Davis says, cocking his head, and leaning on a desk.
"I was hiring in a new recruit. You're looking at the new director of social marketing."
Davis' lips tighten. "Yes. Great. Except no, I'm not.."
Harris' mouth twists. "Wait... I was just promised a job. And now I don't have one?"
"Didn't you get the memo that I sent out the other day?" Davis says to me, ignoring Harris.
I smirk. "Davis, you know that I don't read the memos. I have so many things to attend to... Infographics are easier."
"I'm supposed to be in charge of hiring the director of social marketing. Not you. You completely went over my head!"

"Yeah, well you don't understand: this is my nephew, and he's getting this job. Capeesh? Besides, do you really want to fight me on this? Because it's not like you haven't been stepping my toes, lately..."
Davis sputters.
"We'll have to finish hashing this out in ten minutes," I say, glancing at the corner of my screen. "I'm set to transition in a few minutes. Wait, actually... Seconds."
"We can't let our company run off nepotism!" Davis shouts.
"See ya!"
Davis looks as though he's about to burst. The screen goes black.
"Hello, Vick. It's about time you showed your face... Oh wait — you really haven't, have you?"

I'm hovering in the center of my wedding’s dressing room. Forcing a chuckle, I hang a robotic hand in the air for a high-five. It's only given an awkward shake. Alex Hooper gives me a frown. I frown, back. He looks different than usual. His mop of auburn hair is neatly brushed back and gelled. His beard has been shaved. He's dressed in a formal black suit. Most strange of all, a sullen look sullies his face.
Despite looking his best, he's at his worst, which is the worst thing to see in your best man.
"What's going on?" I say.
"Not much," says Alex, rolling his tongue between his cheeks. "Just trying to keep everybody from going absolutely nuts..."
"What do you mean?"
"What do I mean? Vick, you're not here! The wedding starts in twenty minutes!"
I choke and look at the corner of my screen. I must've miscalculated the times... I could've sworn that it wasn't supposed to start for three hours.
"Don't worry," I say. "I'm on my way right now."
"No you’re not! What? You think I can't tell that you're still using your stupid control base?"
"I'm not that far..."
"Vick, wake up! It'll take you an hour and a half to get here, by helicopter... And by car? Forget it."
"Yeah, about the helicopter thing... I loaned it to Jeff."
Alex shakes his head, and paces around the room. "Who?"
"What?"
"You don't know who your friends are. That's what."
"Jeff is a friend."
"If he took your helicopter, I'm sure he's a leech."
"Same difference..."
"And now you don't even have a way to get here!"
"You're my best friend, Alex. We've, uh... We've been through a ton of stuff together. We can figure this one out, just like we always have. Remember that time when —."

"No. You didn't even come to your bachelor's party, last night. This is supposed to be one of the best days of your life, but I somehow get the impression you don't care one bit about what's going on."
"Yes. I care about everybody here."
"Name one person."
"Uh... You? Thought we already established that."
"We haven't talked in four months, Vick."
I let out a sigh, and hover toward the mirror. I see a blurry image of myself reflected in the screen. It's me, isn't it? Why doesn't anybody realize it's still me?
"Have the caterers arrived?" I ask, snapping a finger.
"Yes, they've come. Everybody has come, Vick."
"Nice. Because, I'm in the mood for a drink right about now. I made sure to get that one wine you really like..."
"Good luck drinking, while you're sitting in your cave."
"Guess you can drink mine for me then."
I wink. Alex scowls.

"We can't just cancel," he says. "Besides, I've been telling everybody that you're here. You've made everybody expect that you're going to be here. Even Shawna almost seems convinced that you finally made it. Do you realize what a mess this is going to be?"
"Speaking of messes, remember that one time when we —."
"Do you even hear a word I'm saying?"

My fingers press against my computer desk. I look to the ceiling and count the drips of water that fall from a hole. I stare at the stain that the drips leave in the ground. The plumbers did a botched job, only finishing half the pipe. Would it have killed them to finish?

"Yes," I finally say. I've taken too long to respond. Though, maybe it's time that I started answering slow. Growing up, my teachers and parents always told me to slow down — told me that I was moving too fast. I always thought they were wrong.
"I was wrong," I say. "I shouldn't have messed up the times. If I'd just remembered, none of this would've happened."

Alex's face contorts. For a moment, he reminds me of my father whenever he was trying to help me with my math homework. I could never follow a word he was saying, even though he always tried his best. Despite being fast, I never do a good job at keeping up with things.

Letting out a moan, Alex buries his face in his hands. "This — I don't think I'm ever going to be able to forgive you for this. Seriously, out of all the buddies you could've chosen to dump this on, it had to be me?"
"I have a plan," I say. A buzz drowns out my words, and I check the corner of my screen. Great — I only have two minutes left.
“All your other 'plans' have blown up in your face. Can you, by any chance, tell me what this brilliant plan of yours is?"
"You're going to dress my drone in a suit and tie and take it to the altar. I'm going to perform the ceremony with the drone."
Alex looks shell-shocked. Then, he bursts out laughing.
"What?” I say. “That's what I'm going to do."
Alex nods. "Oh, I know. That's definitely what you're going to do. It sounds just like you. Doesn't make it any less stupid, though."
"It'll be just like old times!"
"You're getting married today, Vick. If that didn't tip you off that ‘old times’ are over, I honestly don't know what will..."
I feel like I've been punched in the face. Alex looks like he wants to punch me in the face, too. Though, what can I do except smile sheepishly, and hope the moment will pass?
"By the way," I say, "I have to go in a few seconds."
Alex forces a smile. "I know. That's exactly like you too. But, when you're back: we have a lot to talk about."
"Hopefully not."

I'm back in the studio, in front of my painting. That is, what was my painting underneath a new painting that my drone made on auto-pilot. My eyes bulge, devouring the piece. It's a luscious array of dark reds and greens, culminating into an image of a tree trunk. I study the layers of shadow and shading. It's spectacular — far better than anything I could've conceived.
"You're back," says Isabelle.
"How could you tell?"
"The fact that your screen isn't repeating the same three expressions over and over tipped me off... You're not holding the paintbrush correctly anymore either, which helps too."
I nod. The drone's head nods with me. Glancing over to her, I try mimicking the way she's holding her brush. My brush fumbles out of my hand, splattering paint as it lands on the floor.
"Some painting that you made," she says.
A grin forms on my face. "Definitely. It's diverged a bit from what my initial idea was... But, it's really great."
There's a scrape as Isabelle gives a sharp swipe to her canvas.
"How does that work, anyway? You station your drone up in my office, and it can just keep painting on its own...?"
"The drone is me," I say, with a chuckle. "Anyway, I have a crack team of programmers who help me out, whenever I need a drone to do something."
"Oh. So, the programmers do all the art, and you steal the credit for it?"
"I'm the vessel that carries things out."
"Doesn't sound like much of a job to me. This art... It's not really you."
"But it is me. I thought of the idea to come up with the painting. 'I think therefore I am', right?"
"You think, therefore there's something. But, it's not necessarily you."
I leer at her. "Not in a good mood today, are you?"
"I just lost my biggest client."
I laugh. "Didn't realize I was paying you the most out of everybody."
"You aren't. I was referring to your ego."
Another buzz. I only have a minute. Why does the buzzer always have to go off at the worst times?
“Well, I have to go soon,” I say, “I only have a minute.”
“You might as well just go now.”
“But, my art project... You insisted that I had it done.”
She frowns, her lip slitting away a dimple in her cheek. “It’s already done.”
Running my hand through my hair, I crack the camera of my drone.
“Great,”  I mutter. “Anyway, I can’t just... Do that. I’ve never overridden the timing protocols on the drone before.”
“Maybe it’s about time that you did. After all, your drone — sorry, you — can just finish the painting for you, even when you’re gone.

I look back at my painting. It's dazzling. I can already see it being put up in my favorite art shop, or a museum. I chuckle to myself — the art in museums rarely even broaches the skill that’s gone into my painting.
Jerking my neck in Isabelle’s direction, I give her a salute.
“Alright. Looks like this is it. Sorry for the rushed exit, but hey: I’ll send you a gift basket or something, in a week. Do you like chocolate?”
Isabelle opens her mouth to respond, but I’m already hunched over my keyboard, overriding my drone’s settings. I punch in a passkey and select Direct Order’s headquarters as my next destination.

“Good,” I say, as the art studio flickers away, “because, you might end up having a truckload of it. Worst comes to worst, you can find a way to make the excess into a painting, or something. You’re welcome.”

I drip into an empty meeting room. Light saws through my eyes. Blinking, I sling my gaze around the room. Where is everybody? I could’ve sworn that the meeting with Ship-It was supposed to start ten minutes ago.
“Nice to see that you could make it.”
My eyes finally land on Davis, who’s sitting in a far corner.

“Oh, hey,” I say. “Sorry about our fight, earlier. I’m not sure what got into me. Really busy day. Speaking of being busy, where the hell is everybody? Did I miss something? I would’ve at least expected Garth to be in here to take notes.”
“Well, I don’t know how to tell you this, but —.”
“Did they cancel on us? Too afraid to make the plunge on our deal?”
“You know...”
“Not a surprise. I always knew they were assholes.”
I laugh and listen to my synthesized voice echo across the empty walls. I sound so weird. Is that really my voice? It must be. Pretty eerie — I should probably have that fixed.
“Vick, we made the deal without you. The board voted to have the meeting early... You didn’t get the email? We pushed the meeting back a full hour.”

A thin smile forms on Davis’ face. He leans over and presses his hand to a tablet in the table. Footage leaps up. Small voices, lined with static, flow from it. I recoil as I listen to the words, and my hand hovers over my drone's mute button.
“I never received an email,” I say. “You’re dead wrong. My intern would’ve told me. My robot would’ve alerted me... Something.”

Though, I know the words aren’t true. I’d flown to Los Angeles for the wedding, just the night before. My drone's alerts would’ve been disabled, and my intern wouldn’t have been able to reach me. How could I have been so stupid as to forget checking my email?
Though, I already know how — every time I open my email, it's a spaghetti of random words and phrases. It's all too easy for me to get lost — to forget where I was, where I am, and what I was doing.
I shake my head, and the meeting room tilts. I feel sick. Everything is moving too fast.
“So fast... How could you have gone through the meeting so fast? And, without me?”
Davis chuckles. “We had all of the nitty-gritty ironed out about a week in advance. Today, we were just putting the ink to paper.”
“Without my vote?”
Davis’ fingers gallop long the table, and he bites his lip. Very strange — I’m used to only seeing his lips puckered.

“I don’t think your vote would’ve meant much,” he says, clucking his tongue. “You already signed the papers a week ago. You know — the notes I sent you? And, besides — even if you hadn’t, we had enough votes to make this decision without you. Especially since this company is... Well... Moving on, without you.”
I scrunch my brow. “Wait, what?”
Davis claps his hands and rubs them together. “I knew it. You didn’t read the fine print, did you?”
I go to put my metallic arm on Davis’ shoulder. He sidesteps away.

“Vick... In the process of this merger, your position as CEO has become defunct. Add to that your erratic behavior around our offices, and your clashes with me, and many of our shareholders felt it best that we — well — let you go.”
Shrieking glass meets my ear, as I run my drone’s arm along the table. I stare at the tail my arm gouged. I stare through it and to the floor.

“This can’t be happening,” I say, my voice turning rough. It’s been forever since I’ve heard my voice get like that. “We created this thing together, Davis. I didn’t even want this merger to happen. And now you’re letting me go? Do you know how much revenue I bring to the company? Without my leadership, we'd be broke. This merger would’ve never even happened!”
Davis’ arms cross, and he sucks in his cheeks. He presses himself back against the wall, stance unwavering. I raise my drone to the ceiling, hovering over him.

“And to think that you decided to pull this stunt on my wedding day, of all days. You realize that I had to work around about a dozen different obligations, don’t you? I shouldn’t be here right now. And yet, here I am!”
Davis brushes a strand of hair out of his face. I hate when he does that. He looks like one of those annoying jocks on the sitcoms I used to watch.

“I’m not completely dropping you by the wayside, Vick. We’re giving you a severance package of 50 million dollars, as well as 10 million in stocks. And, your nephew — we’ll still give him some position in social marketing, and try working around him for as long as we can. I figure that it’s the least I can do, after all of this.”
I scowl. “No. You can’t just toss me overboard, and sail away like everything is fine. This is my ship, and you don’t get to give it to Ship-It!”
“But, you agreed—.”

“I agree to a lot of stupid things, Davis. One time I agreed to buy an orangutan from the zoo, just because I thought he looked cute. God, that was a bad idea. But, my bad ideas are not always... As bad as your bad idea, to get rid of me! I do so much for this place. You don’t even know the half of it. I'm half of this company!”

“That’s exactly why we needed to let you go, Vick. You run around here like a chicken with its head cut off. You do too much, and everybody can see it wearing on you. Honestly: how often are you having to live your life from that drone apparatus? However long it is, it’s too much.”
“I need the drone to keep things stable.”

“Don’t you see what’s happened to you? With everything going on in your life, from the marriage, to the new house, to your eccentric hobbies... A break is something you inevitably needed. Maybe that’s not something you’re willing to admit. However, I think you’re going to eventually end up thanking me.”

He lets out a deep exhale and then smiles, clearly pleased with himself for having said his piece. He's finally locked the door on me, sealing me away from his precious company. He has a point, too — I have dozens of things going on in my life. Maybe I should be looking at this as an opportunity to refocus. Though, I can only focus on Davis’ smarmy face. I notice the fake tan on his skin, and the rich embroidery of his business suit. Back when I’d first met him, he wouldn’t have bothered to wear more than a greasy t-shirt and sweatpants. So much has changed since then.
Why couldn’t things go back to how they were? Why all the backstabbing?
I blink. Davis’ hand is outstretched toward my drone, for a handshake.
“Thanks,” I say, “... for nothing. See you around.”
I pull my drone away. Davis merely rolls his eyes and strolls toward the door. I don’t care. I’m preoccupied with overriding the controls to my computer, to leave this dump.
“I didn’t want it to end like this,” Davis says, unlocking the door to the meeting room. “But, it had to be done. Merging both of these businesses just made sense. It’s... Just business.”

I keep my mouth shut. Though, inwardly, I know that this is personal. It always has been. One by one, Davis has picked away all the people that’d built Direct Order into what it was. He’s all that’s left.
One. Two. Three.
I’ve left. I’m back in the tight dressing room. I can already hear the ceremony's music playing.
Alex jumps in front of my screen. “Thank god you’re back! I wasn’t sure that I’d be able to stall for another half hour.”
“Nice how everything works out that way, right?” I say.
“It depends on what you mean by ‘everything working out’.”

Alex bites his lip, and gestures to the mirror. My suit dangles from my drone on a hanger. My face is on the screen, unkempt and unshaven. I look like I've crawled out of the sewer. Oh well — nobody would be able to smell that I hadn’t showered. Right?
My vision swings as Alex places his arm around my drone.
“I shouldn’t have expected anything else but this, I guess,” he says. “Problems aside, at least you’ve made it. You’re finally at the greatest day of your life.”
I swallow, and hover toward the exit. I want to believe what he says. Yet, after losing my job? My livelihood? How could this day possibly be considered "great"?

Everything rushes by. My mind wades through a fog. I let it wrap around my eyes, and lock me to my computer chair. Suddenly, my drone is floating at the altar. I catch the countless gawking eyes of an expectant crowd. Cannons shoot confetti down the aisle. An orchestra plays.

“Whatever you do, don’t stress,” Alex says, leaning into my drone. “Just be yourself and you’ll ace — actually, don’t think about not stressing. While you’re at it, don’t think about me telling you not to think about being stressed.”
He cups his hands, and straightens up. “Wow... I’m some help, aren’t I?”

Suddenly, Shawna walks through a cloud of confetti. My fog fades, and the room sharpens.  Her eyes pierce through mine, like a knife. I wonder for a moment how I could’ve thought that anything else mattered. This — this was everything.
Traces of a scowl line her face. Her eyes cut to the ground. They cut back into my eyes. Their blade twists.

When she stands beside me on the altar, we go through our vows. Yet, my lips are raw. I place a ring on Shawna's finger. She places her ring on mine. The room drops away, my perception plunging underwater.
“I do,” I answer, to a warbled question.

I hear the words “you may now kiss the bride". My drone leans in, and Shawna pecks a kiss on its camera. Yet, something feels wrong. There’s a pit in my chest. Even as applause resounds, I can’t help but shrivel inside.
“I love you,” Shawna says.
She doesn’t mean it. I want to say something back. I won’t mean it either. I pull off my headgear and look around my cave. I’m not there. I’m here.
Why am I here?
“Computer,” I whisper. “Shut off the feed. I want out.”
Lines of code flash along the screen, warning against my action. Suddenly, I want nothing more than for my computer to spontaneously fail. My fingers thrum against my keys, bypassing the system.
“That was a direct order.”
End

title: Misanthropy from Entropy
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth (Writing as Benjamin Vale)
Day 0:
This is Cade Carver reporting.

I’m in my sleeping quarters for the night. It’s the last night before the launch. Despite my complaints about these cramped quarters, I have to admit I’m going to miss them. It’s been a long two years building up to this, and the routine has become strangely comforting.

I figured now was as good a time as any to start a new log. The old one was getting bloated, and I wanted a clean slate before my life completely changes. The Emerald Project is going to alter the world. I’m going to be the face of America. I need to be prepared.

I know I shouldn’t be using this chintzy voice recorder for this — the boys tried getting me to use one of their cameras. They want things “cutting edge”. But, that just doesn’t cut it, for me. What’s the point in operating a bulky camera, when my recorder and cassettes work just fine?
My mother once told me, “if you cut off your foot to make a shoe fit, you’re one step away from falling over.”
I think she was joking? I’m not.

I’m going to try taking the recorder and tapes in the containment unit with me. Hopefully I can sneak it by the scientists. My stash of tapes is hidden just outside the sterilization chamber. I should be able to grab it from there, before I enter the unit. Boyle won’t care, and our security will be too occupied with the press and equipment to bother double-checking me. It’ll work great!
But, the press… That’s something else I have on my mind. They’ve scrutinized the Emerald Project ever since I was brought on board.

I should be fine. Most journalists are good people, with a natural sense of... Good-nature. Some of them are a bit too curmudgeon for my tastes, but I think they’re going to be on my side tomorrow. The public is in support, even if the media is skeptical.
Huh. What else to talk about? Oh.

Earlier today, the team had me go through their protocols again. Nothing I haven’t done a million times. To be frank though, I underperformed compared to my personal best. The team told me it was good enough. Said it was just performance anxiety. Me? Not buying it. You don’t go through ten years of military service without having anxiety stamped out of you. Truth is, I didn’t try hard enough during training. Couldn’t have. I need to try harder. When I enter that containment unit tomorrow, I can’t give anything less than my best. Everybody is counting on me to get this right. Failure is no option.

On a lighter note, Dr. Boyle was ecstatic when he spoke to me today. Our nuclear reactor’s output is optimal, all the transistors are operating smoothly, the computers are computing, the wires are wiring — to be honest, I couldn’t follow him on everything that he told me. Dr. Boyle’s mind is far smarter than mine.

He… He’s cracked String Theory, apparently. He’s been using Seattle’s nuclear power plant to make doorways into a fifth dimension — a dimension beyond length, height depth, or time. So far, his doorways have been no bigger than the tip of a needle. But, he’s going to make a bigger one. Far bigger.

Apparently, we can use the fifth dimension to test for the origins of the universe or something. Though, more importantly, it’ll transform warfare as we know it. With the ability to send things into a fifth dimension, we could intercept missiles, erase armies, and even swallow nations whole.
All this power… And, I’ll be the first human to enter this dimension.

It sounds good to me. My only hang-up is that it almost feels like we’re playing God. Knowing the beginning of the universe is a lot. Maybe too much knowledge? My friends and folks told me as much. But, Dr. Boyle has made some good points: if we don’t secure this technology now, the Soviets might figure out its secret. America will be decimated, and our weapons will be useless to stop them. Besides, if this power is safe in the hands of anybody, it’s us.
Still, I can’t help but wonder what’ll happen when I’m hogtied in that capsule and shunted away. What will I see? Will I see anything? Will I even survive?

We haven’t been able to test any other animals, before this. The capsule needs to be manned from inside the fifth dimension for the experiment to work — otherwise, it won’t be able to open from the other side. Besides, it would’ve been hard to convince the American Government to fund a twenty-billion-dollar experiment for a guinea pig. They wanted a person as the face of their mission.

The boys in the lab have done their best to future proof things. There’s no telling how the laws… The laws of science might work in the fifth dimension. An artificial atmosphere was constructed for my capsule, to recycle oxygen and water supplies. It’s also outfitted with dozens of experimental pills, to provide me sustenance.

Dr. Boyle has told me a few “postulations” on what I might experience, but they’re not much beyond guesswork. Nobody really knows what’s going to happen, least of all, me. Boyle hopes to have me out of the dimension in an hour, but it might be a day.
He also warned me that an hour might feel like an eternity. I wasn’t too happy about that, but it is what it is.
I hope things work for the best.
But… Hope isn’t a small thing, isn’t it? When the lights go out and the sun goes down, hope is all we really have.
Day 1:
Cade Carver reporting.
Today has been an adrenaline rush.
At 5:00 sharp, my trainers rushed me to the reaction room.
Not sure what I was doing, still sleeping at 5:00... Dreaming, probably. I should’ve already been up. Though, in my defense: even Neil Armstrong needs rest.

Anyhow, it was a madhouse, getting down to that reactor. Scientists spilled out of every corner, every one of them running somewhere — everywhere. The whole place had gone chicken. I used to get lost, during chaos like that. Yet, this morning, there was something reaffirming about it all. This was it.
Once at the heart of the reactor, I noticed it was noisier than usual. It wasn’t the scientists, either. I turned around: outside the reactor’s windows were dozens of journalists and spectators.
I guess I knew that there would be a turnout — we’re changing the future. But, that? That many? I wasn’t expecting that.
Though, that wasn’t anything, in hindsight. While the medical crew was taking my blood samples, somebody bumped into me.
That somebody happened to be President Ronald Reagan.

He said something… Something like, “Hey there, Pilot Carver.” A grin was fixed to his face, perfect as pearls. His hand shot out. “I heard you were going to do a thing for me, today. Going to make America proud for me. Do this thing, and beat the Soviets. That true?”
Something like that.

I knew I had to say something, say something smart, but something I didn’t know was what something I should say. But, I knew I couldn’t just stand there. Not with the President staring me in the face, glowing like a lightning bug. In a snap, I took his hand and gave a firm, ”Yes, Mr. President, sir.”
Have to say, I didn’t do half bad.
The conversation picked up from there. The President discussed the specifics of my training routine, and then told me about a few potential future missions for me.
“Whatever you do, Mr. President,” I said, trying to stay steady, “make sure you don’t stick me underwater, in a submarine. If there’s one thing I hate, it's a submarine.”
We shared a laugh, and he went to talk with the science guys.
Yet, even with him gone, I couldn’t get past the fact that I, of all people, had the privilege of speaking with him.

The staff led me into a chamber, to slip on my containment suit. It was made of a real shiny latex that bearhugged me. Once it was smooching every inch of my skin, I put on my goggles and helmet — my helmet only being slightly better than the visor of a hazmat suit. Then, all the staff left. Fumes poured from vents in the chamber, and the sterilization process began.
Not sure how long I was there for. I’ve never been best at keeping track of time. This is extra true when my head is feeling chatty.
Let’s just say, my head has never felt chattier.

Dr Boyle came in when it was finished. He took his time looking me over. Immediately, my head carted me back to boot camp, where a drill sergeant’s eye scorched every inch of me. A huff pulled me back —Boyle was pulling a thin, blonde strand of hair from my shoulder.
“We somehow missed this,” he said, waving the hair under his thin mustache.

Couldn’t help but smile to myself. Wasn’t the only thing he missed. When I left the sterilization room, I put my hidden stash of recorders and cassettes in a pouch strapped to the back of my suit. The pouch is supposed to store extra batteries, in case of an emergency power outage in the capsule. But, I’ll never need to use the batteries. The Emerald Project has considered nearly every possibility.

After going from my stash, I went to a hangar above the main reactor. Computers lined the walls, towering to the ceiling. At the center of the room was a soda can of a containment capsule. Dr. Boyle patted me down, double checked my vitals, and then had me strapped me in. The staff ran to the corner of the room, and the capsule’s door slid over me. Peering through my window, I watched a trap-door collapse beneath my capsule. I descended, becoming suspended over the reactor chamber.

Since then, that’s where I’ve been sitting — just above a bushel of the reactor’s lasers. Dr. Boyle has been running like nuts, triple checking everything. He has a funny look I’ve never really seen before. It’s intense. Concerned.

Hopefully the crew can’t tell I’m talking into my recorder, up here. This capsule is sound proof, and my helmet obscures my mouth pretty well. But, if they can tell what I’m saying, I want to let them know: they can calm down a few notches. Matter of fact, they can’t just “can”: they need to calm down. That’s the only way I’ll be getting through this.
Anyhow, in a few minutes the capsule is set to put me in a state of hyper sleep. It’ll keep my metabolism low over the next hour, as I’m placed in the bubble. This is going to be one hell of a ride.
At least I know it’ll be more than worth it.
Cade Carver, signing out.
Cade Carver, signing back in.
I’m confused. Ecstatic, but confused.

My straps are off. I woke up a few minutes ago. At least, it feels like it was a few minutes ago... It’s impossible to tell. I guess this means the experiment was a success? Good thing — I was worried I was dead, for a bit there.

My memory is a bit fuzzy on what happened, since I last signed out. I remember things becoming mighty busy, down there. Some alarm went off. Dr. Boyle went into a frenzy, lips lashing at some of the crew. Couldn’t really tell what was being said — my capsule was sound-proof, after all, and somebody shut off my audio feed.

Whatever was said, it must’ve been bad. Dr. Boyle had some of the scientists taken away by security. Then, he went on with the experiment. The lasers started lasering, hitting my capsule. The lab went up in a sweltering flare. It gave a little tear, getting all paper-like. Then, things got real warbled. The capsule’s gas tubes activated, and I went unconscious.
How long have I been unconscious? Hard to say. I think it’s only been an hour. But, there’s no telling for sure.
Out my window, there’s a ton of empty. It reminds me of my pond in the winter, back home — murky, oily, cold.
Soft flecks float about. Things burst and swim to the back of my eye, then back into the empty. Below me, stars merge into a whirlpool. Are they stars? Or, are they something else? Can’t really tell.
I wish Dr. Boyle were here. But, he’s... out there. In the real world.
So odd to say that, now that I think about it. I’m still in the real world, aren’t I? I definitely don’t feel — not real. Is that the right word? Or, is it unreal? Not sure. Probably not.

Thankfully, I’m not completely cut off. Just on the edge of the empty, there’s this cut of light. I’m using my goggles to zoom in on it. Yes. I can make out something blurry. The lab? It looks like it’s been put in front of a funhouse mirror. Except, I’m having a hard time finding the fun.

Dr. Boyle is there. He’s slightly out of sorts. Papers are all over. Ash, too. The lasers used to push me in here are singed. Dozens of scientists are rushing by. I can’t really tell where to. What’s going on? It looks like the media is pressing against the glass walls to the lab. They’re trying to break in. They’re moving, frantic. Desperate.
Odd. I’m used to seeing more calm. Something must’ve happened. Hopefully they know I’m fine, and wide awake.
Wait — that’s right. I’m supposed to activate my capsule’s beam, to reopen the portal. Where has my head been at? It must be the air. Just a minute — if minutes count for anything, anymore.
Wow. This is — okay, that must... Yeah. Alright. There we go.

Well, might as well get the bad news out of the way first: my control panel had a power surge. It’s fizzled out on me. Good news is, I did a bit of tinkering and was able to make it kind of responsive. The return beam should be turning on, any moment here. Nothing to be worried about.
Huh — actually, more bad news. The beam hasn’t turned on. There’s smoke coming off the panel. I’m going to have to shut off the main power and initiate the PSM — Power Saving Mode.
If there’s one thing the Emerald Project needs to get better at, it’s acronyms.
And, apparently, control panels.
Okay, done with that. Everything is good now.

Except, it isn’t. At all. I’m watching the lab, and things have gotten worse. A computer in the back is in flames. The lights have gone out. People are falling over. What in the — wait — there’s a crack in the reactor. That's not right, is it? Dr. Boyle couldn’t have made a mistake, could he have?
The glass windows are breaking. People just jumped out, wearing gas masks — firefighters. They’re scooping up the President and rushing him out.
More firefighters came in. More people are being dragged out. Dr. Boyle, too. His eyes are bloodshot, and he’s — he’s… He tried to punch one of the firefighters.
I’ve never seen Dr. Boyle look like that. This is ugly. How could the experiment have gone so wrong?
Sorry — I went quiet for a while there, didn’t I? On the sunny side, at least everybody was evacuated alive. This might’ve been a catastrophe, but it worked out fine.
Everybody is fine.
Alright, I turned off my goggles. Can’t really bring myself to look up there anymore. I’d prefer to watch the empty, right now.
Feeling very tired, suddenly. I want to sleep. I need to sleep.
Cade Carver, signing out.
Day 4:
Cade Carver reporting.
Sorry for the absence. It’s been a few days at least, hasn’t it? Who am I kidding? It’s impossible to say.

I wish I could say I’ve been busy. I’d be lying. Nothing happens here, among nothing — the empty. But, at least this empty isn’t absolute. I see sparking particles, still. Once or twice, the capsule was even caught in a whirl of energy. Yet, all these flickers only flicker. My flickers of energy? Same case.

Motivation is hard to come by. The conditions here aren’t nice, putting it nicely. Food goes down sluggish, it goes out worse, and sleep is uneasy. I’ve tried all I can to find a way out of here. After a day straight of reworking the capsule’s systems to find the way, I started realizing there isn’t one. Sleep is my new occupation. That, and chatting — mainly with myself. When not, with Mr. Grimsby and his pals.

Heh. Gee… That must sound confusing. See, I’ve been trying to pass time by listening to old radio recordings I brought with me. It’s comforting to hear the tinny voices, talking about outdated world events and urging me on. I know they can’t hear me — but, when I’m talking, that never seems to cross my mind. They’re the closest things to human contact I have.
If this makes me crazy, so be it. But, I like to think we all need a rope to reality. Otherwise, it’s too easy to lose a sense of meaning. Feeling that now more than ever.
If I wasn’t, I probably wouldn’t have made this update. It would’ve felt wrong. The world needs more optimism than the reverse.

About an hour ago, I activated my goggles to peer through the slit in the empty. I saw Dr. Boyle. He was working in the lab, his face mortar. He tinkered with a few of the computers and reassembled a few loose bits of technology, before finally leaving the place. I’m not sure what he’s doing. Yet, I like to think he’s planning to break me out. Planning to make things better.
That better be what he’s doing.
Cade Caver, signing out.
Day 5:
Cade Carver reporting.
It’s been another day — guessing. Guess I don’t have many things to report. Yet, some things are better than no things.

Nothing should’ve made me felt as good as Dr. Boyle showing back up in the slit. But, I’m starting to think something is wrong with him. I’m used to seeing a pleasant, easygoing manner about him. Now? His clothes are disheveled, and an edge is in his eye. He’s had a few outbursts. I want to believe he has some wits about him, but I’m not so convinced. I half wonder if Boyle’s brain crawled out and his body is a living carcass.
I want to believe the best, anyhow. Still, I can’t ignore. I’ve been in here for a while and haven’t lost my grip yet. What excuse does Dr. Boyle have?
I keep listening to the tapes, but I’ve already eaten twenty hours of them. I only have ten hours left.
Oh well — I’m tired. Ready to pass out. Despite no time passing here, sleep makes passes at me faster than it should.
The old horizon will greet me soon. Boyle is hard at work, trying to get me out of here.
Cade Carver, signing out.
Good night.
Day 10:
Bad day. This has been a very bad day.
Sorry… Cade Carver reporting.

Dr. Boyle rebuilt his lasers and then reactivated them. Normally, I’d be pleased. Though, his reassembly sent a massive shockwave of energy into the empty. My pod was kicked back. I was slammed to the back. After getting my feet and my balance, I looked at the slit. Except, it was no longer a slit. It was a gaping hole.

I flailed my arms. I screamed. I beat at the windows. Boyle couldn’t have been less aware. A smile creased his face, before going decrepit. Distressed, he went to the back of his lab to toy with more wires.

The empty’s slit kept spreading, growing to massive proportions. Its film mapped across the nothing as a ghoulish gash. It hadn’t been until then that I’d noticed a gray tint to it. It isn’t quite the black-and-white in old movies. But, it’s close. The empty seems to sap its color away, flashes of neon perforating the slit’s edges.

Yet, enough with the talk about the slit. More disturbing was Boyle’s speed. After going to the back of the lab, his arms moved at twice their normal pace. At first, I thought it was merely from his urgency. It couldn’t have been. His pace didn’t stay doubled. It tripled.
It kept rolling from there, with him pinballing across the room.
Ever since, I’ve been watching. Right now, Boyle is still going. His face is relaxed. He has no idea. I should turn away and distract myself. Though, I’m mesmerized.
I want to help him — to enter the slit, and finally escape this abyss. The slit is close, and only comes closer as I speak. Though, I know I’m trapped. My capsule can’t move. I can’t leave.
I’ll just keep watching for now, waiting for Boyle to slow down.
Boy, I hope he gets me out of here.
Day 11:
Cade Carver reporting.

Boyle goes in and out of the lab more often, moving ever faster. Yet, he isn’t just moving fast. He’s… He’s aging fast, too. The frontline of his hair has retreated. A silver streak runs through. Age lines and crow-feet, which were once subtle wisps, have whipped deep into his skin.
I question whether he really is moving fast. What if I’m moving slower? What if the flow of time is damned up to me?
Damn it.
It’ll be okay. Boyle isn’t going to abandon me. He’s pushing himself to the limit, working tirelessly.
Besides, the world couldn’t have forgotten me. I’m the pioneer of another dimension. I’ve crossed a threshold no others have dared.
I’m going to hold out for them, because I know they’re holding out for me.
They must be.
Day 12:
Cade Carver reporting.
Is it wrong that I missed the feeling of grogginess this morning, while forcing down my breakfast?

I should’ve never left my last recording. So much has changed. The lab decayed, with moss and mold eating the walls away. Most of the plaster peeled, leaving exposed brick. The computers have blown or been replaced. Boyle doesn’t look so good, either. I swear he’s shrunk three inches in the past three hours. He moves with a hobble now, his posture has eroded to a hunch, and his face is haggard.
Wait — he’s… Oh god. Oh no. No!
He’s — he’s not getting up. Why isn’t he getting up? When will he…?
Dr. Boyle! You need to get up! Get up Boyle!
Get up!
Day 17:
Cade Carver.
Hi. It’s been awhile.
My food rations are dwindling. Only have about a week left. It’s fine. The slit in the empty grows. It’s mapped its way across my entire window. I just need it to get closer now.
It’ll be fine. I still have time to kill.
Speaking of killing time, outside of the empty? Time is dead.
It took half an hour before somebody eventually discovered Dr. Boyle. At least, half an hour for me. For the outside? It might’ve been half a year.
After that, I spent the better half of my day staring at the walls of the lab.
You don’t want to know the worse half.
I had the tapes to listen to, though. Besides — watching mold slowly eat up the lab was interesting, at least.

After another day, the lab was emptied by a construction crew. All the lab equipment that possibly could’ve saved me? Gone. Then, the crew brought in cranes and wrecking balls. Every crevice to the lab was defiled, deforming to dust.
It’s not all bad. I was at least given another change in scenery. Seattle’s skyline was opened to me — a silver band, specked with shimmering scrapers and streets.
At first, I thought the city’s glow was in my head — that it’d been too long since I’d last seen it. I soon realized how wrong I was. It hadn’t been too long.
I’d been too long. I was sitting still. The world was flying past me.

Since, I’ve watched buildings expand and stretch for the clouds. I’ve seen buildings expire and curdle. Streets have been torn up. New ones have been paved in their place. Old towers have been revamped or stamped out. Now, the city winks at me. Yet, it’s all an act.
As I speak, the empty’s slit yawns ever deeper. It must be taunting me, as it still hasn’t reached my capsule. I doubt it ever will.
People walk by. They erect monuments. They sit content. Then, they spit at their monuments. They adopt new systems. New technology. Their eyes turn from their structures, and into themselves.
Steps going heavy, their visits become sparser. They wither. New monuments are put in place of the ones once known, and another crowd of people comes with them. Cycle repeating, the days go awash.
The present is sand on the beach, constantly betraying itself for the whims of winds and waves.
Day 18:
If my grasp of time doesn’t fail me, I’ve been here for eighteen days. I’d say that’s nineteen days too many.
I finally destroyed the tapes I’ve been listening to — after weeks of being stuck with them, I couldn’t take it anymore. The voices were grating. My interest? Abating.
The outside remains oblivious to my existence. However, it’s for the best. The world faces oblivion.

Everything is in turmoil. Technology has progressed far beyond my grasp — I watched people go from staring into miniature televisions, to staring into goggles, to walking within holographic bubbles. Their utopia wasn’t to last.
Earth shook, the Sun shook with it, and the sky shifted red. In the distance, bits of the skyline fell. Admittedly, it gave me pause. Yet, it wasn’t as disturbing as what I’m watching right now.

Divorced from their bubbles, people look to the sky. Their bodies tremble. Their eyes go dusky. I wish I could say I don’t share their fear. However, I’m looking to the sky too. A fire blazes, but it’s not the Sun. I’d be pressed to call it a falling star, but a trail of fog tails its descent.
It’s drawing in. It disappeared. At least, I think it has. I must’ve lost it. I must’ve —
A light surges. The warmth of its glow seeps through the slit and into my chamber, brushing my skin. However, I — I’m shivering. Why am I shivering?

Hearth’s ash settles on Seattle, a fresh crater having gouged its heart. Rows of corpses line the ground. I’m trying to find a sign of life, somewhere. Though, I can hardly move. There’s hardly movement.

Time is still moving by. The bodies are already beginning to rot. A tank roves in, scooping the bodies and dragging them away. However, they aren’t American tanks. Their sides are branded with a terrible symbol.
The Soviets. They’ve taken Seattle.

The carnage has been swept away. New flags are raised. Buildings that only had holes in them are patched up. The buildings that aren’t patched are dispatched wholesale. People stream back in, taking the buildings. All their faces are foreign to the cheer I’ve known. An overall gloom overhauls their demeanor, docility resting on their faces.
Wait — one of them broke into a fight with another. Now, three. It’s a full-on riot.
Soldiers have come out to quell the riots. They’re gone. They soldiers have taken the threats away. Seattle sleeps easy once more.
Yet, is it really Seattle? I’m still watching it morph… But, it can’t be. Factories tear through the ground. People labor in front of me, anguished.
The Seattle I once knew? It’s been vanquished.
I suppose this is it. All along, I’ve thought myself trapped in here. However, they’re more trapped out there.
Day 19:

Seattle is deteriorating. Couldn’t say why if I tried. Though, the buildings have been all but torn away, with only a few stragglers straining for sky. The rest of Seattle is a barren plain, shrouded in smog and soot. I wish it was blasted by a missile one more time, so it could finally roll over dead. However, it’s stubborn. It refuses to fall. It won’t grant me mercy, instead choosing to torture me with its presence.
In most cities, people are born, they live, and they die. This hellscape skips a step and adds another. People are born, they die, and they die again.

I want to turn away, but I can hardly bring myself to. There’s a void in my chest, which only seems satisfied by observing the void of another. My hope is that there aren’t more cities like Seattle — cities overrun and overseen by despots. Seattle is a diseased corpse now, infecting anybody unfortunate enough to step in it. I thought America would’ve been strong enough to win. However, muscle is useless if the body is starved.
How America fell to the Soviets will always eat at me. Yet, maybe it was inevitable. Somebody at the top must’ve stopped caring. Then, they all did.
I guess that’s the function of life. People come, they go, and those they used to know forgo the leftover memories. None of us matter. If we did, I wouldn’t be in my current state of matter.
Wait… A week just flitted by. The Sun is eclipsed by something big. Is it the moon? It can’t be. It’s getting bigger.
People are running through the streets, their eyes wild. The military is nowhere to be found.
The blot isn’t getting bigger. It’s getting closer. And, it’s not a blot. It’s a rock. A big rock. A meteor.
It just met the Earth. I — I can’t believe it. The ground’s been grounded to a powder. Streets ripple. They’ve disappeared. They’re replaced by bedrock.
The empty’s slit stretches around my pod. Though, it still hasn’t reached me.
The rocky breach protrudes over the city. It steamrolls the clouds, expanding far beyond my scope of vision. The sky has practically disappeared. All I’ve ever known…
There’s not a person in sight. Not even an animal. Months seem to pass by, but there’s still nothing. Nothing, but stillness.
Snow fell just a second ago, then melted. Spring springs up, then withers to the winter weather once again. And again. A minute looks like years. Decades. Yet, Seattle remains empty.

Finally! Plants are growing on the rock. Except, they’re alien to me. They possess a darker shade of green. Some of them have already bloomed. They’ve already died. There are new ones. Now there aren’t.

Either way, the flowers are larger and thornier than I’m used to seeing. Their petals glare with harsh oranges and yellows. At night, the petals pucker like the lips of a rearing cat. Yet, there’s an undeniable allure. Part of me wants to reach out and touch them.
Another part wishes they’d left the rubble undisturbed.
Plants keep growing and dying. I’m not sure how many years have gone by, but no people have ventured to the crater. At this point, I’m wondering if years are still a thing people use
Worse yet, I wonder if there are there still people to use them.
Something rustled through the flowers. It’s —.

It’s not there anymore. It’s everywhere. That is, they’re everywhere. Beasts. They roam among the vegetation, and they’re noting like I’ve ever seen. Bone spurs spurt from the spine of one. Another has a coat of scales, and eyes that extend from its head on antennas. Still, there’s an especially grotesque creature writhing along the ground on its stomach, with a needle of a nose nosing it along. A black ooze flows beneath it — yet the ooze pales in comparison to the charred skin comprising its body. The closest I can liken the creature to is a mixture of a slug and a mosquito, but the size is unexplainable.
I can’t look. Its nose has punctured another animal. My head feels fuzzy.

The moment has fled. The monster is dead. Most of the beasts are, in fact. The longer I sit here, the more they shift and alter shape. Old ones go, new ones take their place. It all repeats, as a never ending flow.

I want it all to end though. I have nothing left but this recorder, and I’m running out of tape. Meanwhile, the world? It’s never going to run out. I’m trapped, left to watch eternity tap-dance for its own enjoyment. Not mine. What is mine? The bliss to exist…? It’s faded. Become trist. I can never touch the world. I can’t experience it for my own sake. My own sanity.
I’m only an observer, now.
The world is blind to me. It’s broken its bind with me.
Why can’t it just unwind with me?
Day 20:

The slit nearly breathes on the window to my capsule. I’ve considered breaking the window and jumping out, to try reuniting with reality. Yet, it’s probably still too far away. Besides: reality has become too harsh to face.

At the start of my day, wave after wave of species rose and fell. With these waves came droughts, floods, disease, earthquakes, hurricanes, and more asteroid strikes. I wish I could say I felt as threatened by the fifth asteroid impact as I did the first. Yet, I can’t. I’ve watched several species build up civilizations, only to become just as much a blip as humanity. Life climbs nature’s ladder, until nature forces it off. I sit complacent, only wondering why life ever thinks it could achieve anything beyond its nature.
Things live only to stop living. To pretend otherwise is to lie.

However, the world is more concerning than ever. The landscape ahead of me? It’s populated by creatures that broil with anger, and tear at each other’s throats out without compunction. At first glance, they’re no different than any of the other creatures I’ve seen. Centuries pass by, without them making a shift to their tendencies. However, they’re not nearly as brainless as normal creatures. Rather, they’re dressed in fine clothing. Their green and red faces possess intricate systems of opening and closing, as if for communication. They fight like animals but think like humans.
I know why they fight. The ground is patchier, flora fleeing. Cracks coat the soil, and thorns shoot through various plants and cacti. The Sun is swelling.
Just swell.
I never thought I’d say this, but… I’m more comforted by my prison than the idea of being free. At least my prison is warm, and full of food. It offers peace, in a world of despair.
Day 21:
My mother once told me, “We don’t even know what we don’t know.”
At least we know we don’t know it.

Life has finally evaporated from the Earth, dust taking over. I’d hoped life would’ve lasted longer… Maybe it could’ve found a way to continue somewhere beyond this planet. Though, I guess the secret of perpetual existence remains known only to me.

Then again, do I exist? I observe — that’s undeniable. Yet, I feel denied. I hunger to reach out and touch the world. To feel fresh air on my face. To sift the dust through my fingers. To have the Sun’s rays settle on my skin.
I’d give both my eyes to feel real again.
The Sun is a fat blister on the desert’s skin. Its rays penetrate everywhere, and everything. It’s inflating.
It keeps going. It settles into the soil. The soil sizzles, going molten. Everything is melting. I — I see red everywhere. It’s so bright. It’s overpowering.
Sorry… My body is shaking like mad. My muscles have gone weak. This is nothing — like — the Earth is gone. There’s no more ground. The Sun has taken up my entire field of vision.
I’m terrified. Petrified. But I’m numb. For some reason, none of this feels…
It’s not quite right.
Day 22:
The Sun is confetti.
It’s exploded everywhere. Massive chunks of plasma, the size of planets, whizzing by and then fizzling bye.
The entire solar system. Gone.
That’s that.
Ahead of me, the empty’s slit seems only a yard from my window. If I opened the capsule’s door and jumped through, maybe I could finally get back.

I don’t want to get back. There’s nothing to go back to. Everything I ever knew has been overturned. Moreover, time is overclocked. Already, stars are flickering out, like the headlights to my old pickup.
It was a nice truck. It got me around. Was pretty pretty, too. I miss it.
The consolation of the constellations has abandoned me. Maybe it’s all in my head, but it feels as though they’re all spreading apart.

It’s not in my head. I blinked a second ago, and half the universe blinked away with me. This isn’t right. The universe — it’s supposed to sandwich back in on itself. The Big… The Big Crunch, was it? Wasn’t that what Boyle said? That’s the order of it all. But, it hasn’t done that.
There was supposed to be order. A clean, well-oiled machine. God was supposed maintenance this all, wasn’t he? Play his part?
It’s apart. Darkness pervades everything. The brightness of reality that the slit once offered me has dimmed to nothing. The empty is better than it.
Countless years… Amounting to a dull null.
God.
God?

Guess it’s just you and me, at this point… So, might as well pop the question: why have you abandoned me? All I ever wanted to do was explore. To see things. The secrets. I wanted to push the limits. To test the boundaries. Did I really deserve this?
Am I out of my mind to wonder why chasing after your mind was so wrong?
I was wrong. I was wrong about you. You betrayed me! If you even cared, I wouldn’t have… You wouldn’t have made me wait, endlessly, for…

Wait. Something happened. The darkness has — I don’t know how to explain it. It’s folding into itself. Space has become an origami of white. It’s getting bigger. I can hardly see. It’s beautiful. Coming closer.
The walls to my capsule have been eaten up. My eyes — they burn. Might as well be melted.
But, I want to feel. I’m going in.
Cade Carver, signing out.
End

title: Pill of perfection
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
Jonah’s face was flushed. A tension lapped at him. His bones throbbed. He wished there was some way to leave his skull.
He went to take a sip of his beer, only for it to pour all over his clothes.
“I can’t begin to describe all the ways that I’m an idiot,” Jonah said, trying to wipe the dribbles up with his sleeve. “Okay Larry?”
“Hey, just count your blessings,” Larry said. “You still have your girlfriend, right? You have a nice place. And hey, there’s always me.”
Jonah shook his head. “Yeah, here’s the thing: girlfriend dipped, and I’m way behind on rent. I’ll probably be evicted soon.”
Larry snickered, rocking his leather chair back and forth, face glowing in the light of the fireplace. A halo had been put around him.
“Woo boy, that’s a tough spot Jonah.”
“It’s not fair! Why does everything—.”
Jonah was interrupted as the backing to his chair flung backward. Irritation itching at him, he fought to pull the mechanism back in place.
“You’ve just gotta calm down,” Larry said, swiping his locks of red hair from his eyes. “Everybody always said that I was the idiot between us and look at where I am now!”

A snide smile made its way across Jonah’s face. He scoffed. There was a time when people thought that Jonah had more potential than Larry. Though, that was when they were both twelve. Puberty flipped the conversation ever after. Larry was royalty in high school. He was a king in college. From there, everything always went his way.
Ten years had come and gone, since they’d been in the same dorm. Jonah’s tether was wearing out. Larry hadn’t aged a day.
Larry launched his phone ten feet into the air, while Jonah winced. The phone didn’t come close to touching Larry’s living room’s ceiling, before falling back into Larry’s grasp.
“You lost a job opportunity...” Larry said rolling the phone in his hand. It was the latest model. “So what? More will come your way.”
Jonah shook his head. “You just don’t understand. This job was key for me. I had worked for months to get my foot in the door. And then… They just drop me, for somebody else.”
“You get good gigs all the time. You’ll get more. You’re a great musician, Jonah.”

The words went through Jonah’s ears, but he didn’t hear them. He didn’t want to. “Great musician.” Larry hadn’t bothered hiring Jonah for any of his business events or parties, let alone his upcoming wedding.
Worse, maybe Larry was justified in that. Generally, Jonah’s gigs weren’t more than playing at a kid’s birthday party. It was possible that he sucked, much as he didn’t want to believe it.
He pursed his lips and studied his bottle of beer. His fingerprints along it were grotesque, under the firelight.
“You thought about becoming a music teacher?” Larry asked. “I think the school is looking for a new one.”

“Those who can’t do teach. I went through all those years trying to leave education system, and you think I should just plop right back in?” Jonah raised his hands over his head. “Besides, I’m supposed to be an artist, Larry. I’m not like you — I can’t stuff myself in a suit every day, take a paycheck, and live with myself. I need to stay true to who I am.”
Larry shrugged his shoulders and gave his phone another flip. “Being successful and making money feels good to me. But hey, to each their own.”

The swipe stung. Larry had been part of a band with Jonah, an eon ago. It was a pitiful band, that didn’t survive their teens. Yet, for a short time, Larry believed in Jonah. They’d thought they’d wind up rocking the world together.
Larry chuckled to himself and took a swig of his beer. He had a fifty-watt smile. How could somebody have so much achievement, for so little effort?

Jonah thought back to all the nights spent in his room, tirelessly working at his piano, and modulating his sound via his computer. Every note of his compositions were crafted and performed to precision. Not an iota was left to random chance. That is, except the compositions’ success. If reality were in his favor, he could’ve seen fame and fortune too. It was just an unlucky roll of the die. It had to be.
“Larry, have you ever wondered why everything always goes this way for us?” Jonah asked.
Larry gave Jonah a glare. “What do you mean? I haven’t done anything.”
Jonah’s nostrils flared. That was it. His bottle of beer fell from his hand, shattering on Larry’s marble floor.

“You know exactly what I’m talking about. I spend months trying to get land a job interview and get rejected after days of preparation— you walk into your interviews ten minutes late and underdressed, but still schmooze your way to the position.” Jonah chuckled, but his chest brimmed with hate. “I spend weeks pining after a girl, who you wind up taking out after a minute’s talk. I spend a week writing a research paper — you punch it out the night before, and wind up with the better grade. I spend years working on my useless degree, only for you to drop out and become ridiculously more successful. Now here you are, with a killer job, all the friends in the world, and an upcoming wedding.”
“What can I say?” Larry said, hooding his eyes beneath his hair. “I’m good at gaming opportunity, and markets.”
“No kidding. Even compared to Buffett, your list of successes is a buffet. Buffett, Larry. And to think, back in high school people thought I was the numbers guy… Can’t count on anything, can I?”
Larry put a hand over his eyes and let out a groan. “I have initiative, Jonah. That’s a big part of the difference between us. Things get hard, and… You’re down for the count.”
Jonah stood from his chair and grabbed his coat. “And since when was anything hard for you? Huh? When was the last time that you had to scrape and claw for something?”
Jonah made his way for the door, only to slip on the spilled beer he’d left on the floor. He landed on his back with a heavy thud.
“Jonah, you alright?”
Larry bounded from his chair and helped Jonah back up from the ground.
“Thanks,” Jonah said, weakly.
Nervous ruptures went up and down his back. He rubbed the tender spot where he’d landed. No doubt, it would be bruised there in the morning.
Larry gave Jonah a pat on the shoulder, before grasping tight and holding there.
“I have to level with you about something, Jonah… But you’re not going to like it.”

Jonah looked into Larry’s eyes. There was a guilt there. Yet, for what, Jonah couldn’t tell. Half of him was overjoyed Larry might’ve been seeing his side of things. The other half was infuriated that Larry wasn’t giving him the usual pep talk.
Larry’s hand went into his pocket. There was a rattle. He pulled out a bottle of pills.
“These pills…” Larry said. “They’re the reason why I’m where I am.”
Jonah’s anger faded. “You’ve been taking antidepressants?”
Eyes widening, Jonah offered Larry a pat on the shoulder. Larry pushed it away.
Bringing his hands to his chest, he burst into laughter. “Oh, god no.”
Jonah’s mind and sympathies hit a wall. “What then? Some type of drug? Are you addicted to those things?”
Larry shook his head. “Jonah, these aren’t normal pills.”
He popped the cap and handed one to Jonah. It was a clear gel pill. Utterly mundane. Jonah squinted, and drew it closer. At the center of the pill, a rainbow glinted.
“Are they sugar pills then?” Jonah asked.
“They’re perfect pills.”
“Okay, but what do they do?”
“That’s what they do, Jonah. They make your life perfect. Not a single flaw, for an entire day.”
Insanity? A prank? Or, was it true? It couldn’t be.
Jonah snorted. “You’re telling me that all this good fortune you’ve attained is because of a pill?”
Rolling his eyes, Larry pocketed the pills. He took a step back. “You don’t believe me.”
“I believe that those pills are doing something to you, Larry. But, not what you think.”

Larry paced around the room, running his fingers along his walls. Every few seconds, his fingers would run over a trophy or token that Larry had collected over the years. Each one was from something frivolous Larry had done; donating to charity, winning the championship, getting the business contract signed. Could it all have really been done by one man?
“You wanted to know the difference between you and me,” Larry said. “This is it. Every morning, you work your ass off. Day in and day out, until your brain is about to pop. Me? I just pop this pill…”
