A glint of light shot from the pill and into Jonah’s eye. He looked down and gawked. It were as though it had been prodding at him. Begging him to swallow it.

“I know this’ll make me sound like a prick, but I’m tired of them,” Larry said. “Tired of hiding them, anyway. The medals around one’s neck feel good, for a time. But now? I feel guilty, Jonah. I’ve never shared them with anyone. I’m disgusting. I’m perfect, but I’m disgusting.”

Larry’s fingers leapt from the wall and pulled down on the skin beneath his cheekbones. He’d always had such angelic features. For a fleeting glimpse though, Jonah could see the age lines mapping their way throughout his face. There were chinks in the armor.
“How’d you get these?” Jonah asked. It took all his will to keep from putting the pill in his mouth.

“See, that’s the part nobody ever wants to believe. One morning, I’d had a bad day… I cried out that I wanted my life to be better — I wished that everything would start to go right, just for once. Perfection, for just one day.” He smirked to himself. “Just one of those dumb things you say, right? But then, I woke up… And the pills were by my bed. Unbelievable. Ever since? The bottle is always full, every morning. And things always go perfect throughout my day, so long as I take one.”
“I believe it.”
Jonah laughed, and he wasn’t sure why.
“Then take them,” Larry said. His eyes were wild. He whipped the pills out of the pocket and brought them to Jonah’s face. “Take them, and don’t bring them back. They should be yours.”
“These better not be some sort of heroin,” Jonah said, inspecting them.

“They’re better. They’re a dream. Every great dream you’ve ever had, rolled into one. If you want to say no to perfection, that’s fine. But you’re always going to wonder what would have happened if you’d tried to have it.”
“And what about you? Why are you giving this to me?”
Larry turned his back and stumbled toward the stairway. Jonah told himself Larry was just drunk, but it looked as if he was fighting some magnetic force.
“I’ve had perfection handed to me, for years,” Larry slurred. “I don’t want to live another day without knowing how I’d do without it.”
Larry was nuts. He had to be. Nonetheless, Jonah popped a pill, pocketed the bottle, and told Larry good night. He headed home.
His car sounded like garbage, like usual. Though, the ride — for once, that was okay.
“You know, the other day I really thought this music sounded like shit…”

Marcus Rex gave a hearty laugh and adjusted his jacket. It was a hot red and tailored to fit Rex’s trim body. Jonah had seen several producers in similar garb. Was there a store that they all shopped at?
“You told me that it had potential though,” Jonah said, giving back the laugh.
He leaned on Rex’s couch and took in a deep breath. The room smelled of lavender; Jonah’s favorite scent.
“We just tell everybody that so that they never feel bad,” said Rex, with a wink.

A small ping went at Jonah’s chest. However, Rex already whipped his pen across a contract, into the form of his signature. Jonah tried glimpsing the contract’s details from over the knickknacks on Rex’s desk, to no avail.
“There’s no way you’ll say no,” Rex said, grinning to himself. “This is the thrill ride of contracts. You won’t see it get higher than this.”

Rex had said the same thing on the phone, while Jonah was having breakfast. It was the only reason that Jonah had dropped his waffles right then and driven over to Rex’s office complex. Well, perhaps not the only reason. That morning had gone well. Almost impossibly well.

When he rolled out of bed, his hair was perfectly combed, without a single strand out of place. He went to put his socks on, and they slipped on with ease. There hadn’t been any lint to pick off on his shirt. His toothpaste came right out of the bottle, without any effort. The water in his shower was at a perfect temperature, with no adjustment needed. There wasn’t a bit of grogginess in his head, or puffiness in his face.
His coffee tasted like heaven. His waffles? Like the heaven that comes after heaven. There was a heaven after heaven, right?
It was when Jonah opened his email on his phone, to find a flood of new job offers, that Rex’s phone call came in. Rex’s demand for an immediate meeting was impossible to refuse.
That was fifteen minutes ago. Jonah hadn’t wasted a breath getting into Rex’s office, and Rex hadn’t wasted a breath getting things in place.
Rex cleared his throat. “I can’t believe this is happening!” he said.
Jonah raised an eyebrow. The words sounded odd, not coming from his mouth. “What do you mean?”
“A talent like you? You’re a one in a million thing, man. That music you made… Just dynamite!”

Adrenaline zapped through Jonah’s body, making his body tingle and his pupils dilate. Rex’s words were refreshing, after endlessly having producers tell him he was a moron. He hadn’t felt this way before. Ever. Yet, he could get used to it.
“Here you go, Rockstar,” Rex said.

Jonah looked down at the contract. It was a deal for an entire album of his music. Three hundred thousand dollars, over the course of a year, plus 20% royalties on sales. He’d also be going on a statewide tour, upon the album’s release.

Jonah flipped through the pages, reading the legal minutiae. Normally, he would’ve been utterly lost. Yet, there was a newfound sense of clarity as Jonah read through it. The terms were hilariously simple; he’d be idiotic to pass the offer up.
Nonetheless, Jonah said, “I’ll need my agent to look this over. I don’t feel comfortable signing this just yet.”

Rex nodded, understandingly. “Of course, take your time. I slapped this all together in a frenzy last night, so there might be a mistake in there or two.” He gave a nervous chuckle. “Just, don’t take too long: we don’t want anybody else snatching you up. Actually…”
Rex looked over his shoulder, as though someone were watching him. Then he pulled a check out of his pocket and wrote a number that was followed by several zeroes. He handed it over.
“Also, here: take some lunch money. On me. Just an incentive.”
“Seriously?” Jonah said, incredulously.
Rex’s brow furrowed in concern. “Sorry. Is it not enough?”
Jonah pocketed the contract and check, trying to maintain composure.
“It — it’s plenty good,” Jonah said.

He burst out of the office and into the hallway, whooping like mad. Strangely, he received no odd looks. After a few minutes, everybody in the office had joined in. A few people pulled confetti cannons from their drawers, leaving Jonah a walking pinata.
Arriving at the elevator, the door opened as clockwork. A man strode out, giving a whoop.
“I don’t know why I’m cheering, but it feels good!” the man said. He gave another whoop and went on his way.
In the lobby, the secretary gave him an excited wave goodbye. “Would you like a mint?” she asked.
“Don’t mind if I do.”
A whole bowl was shoved into his arms.
“Here, just take all of them. Take the whole thing!”

Her face leaned into his, and a radiant smile moved between them. Jonah could’ve kissed her. He shoveled a handful of mints into his mouth instead, taking the bowl with him. Who could say no to free mints?
He stepped out into the parking lot and went to his car. It was parked right at the front of the lot, in the perfect spot. With a chuckle, he pressed the unlock button. The car gave a crisp beep.
There was a honk.
“Hey, you!” somebody said.
Jonah turned to see a man jumping out of a bright red sports car, keys in hand.
“Do you want to trade cars?” the man said.
Jonah’s mouth hung agape.
“I’d — I’d like a lot of things,” Jonah said. “But, everything has a cost, am I right? Now, I’ll just be on my way…”
The man stood in Jonah’s way. “No really, you can have it,” he said. He showed Jonah his keys.
Jonah grabbed the keys. He looked at the car. It was dazzling in the daylight, not a single flaw on it.
A smirk formed on Jonah’s face.

The wind rushed through Jonah’s hair, as the sports car’s engine roared down the highway. He was singing his favorite song at the top of his lungs. Every element of the atmosphere held concert in that moment, to give Jonah adulation. A breeze lapped at Jonah’s skin, the sun danced in his eyes, the car seat gave a massage. His mind filled with a clarity, as possibility shot through it.

He could go anywhere. He could do anything. The notes to his next composition were already forming in his head. No — he would write a whole album of compositions. It would be brilliant. Gorgeous. Nothing like it had ever been thought of before, let alone heard.
Reality was a mountain. Somehow, he’d found his summit. Nothing was ever going to bring him down.
Jonah’s phone rang, and he brought it to his ear.
“Jonah?”
It was his ex-girlfriend, Marcy.
“I want you back,” she said, in a rushed breath. “I miss you. I really miss you.”
Jonah laughed, and let the phone fall out of his hand.
“Jonah? Jonah?” she asked.
All she could hear was a growing roar.
“Have you checked the premises for any crazed fans?” Jonah asked.
Jonah’s security guard gave a laugh.
“You have some of the most well-behaved fans I’ve ever seen, Jonah,” he said, adjusting his shades. “Honestly, I often wonder whether you even needed to hire me.”
“I don’t need a lot of things,” Jonah said. “But then… If you have the resources for something, you might as well throw them at it. And, resources are not exactly a problem for me.”

The security guard gave another laugh. Jonah simply leaned back behind his desk and absorbed the room. He was in a retro music store. The ceiling was aglow with neon lights, and posters of random artists were scattered throughout. He smiled. An airbrushed photo of his face was bound to join them.
“This is going to be a smashing success,” Rex said. He put a hand on his shoulder.
“Agreed.” It was the husky voice of another man — Spud. “I mean, there hasn’t been a collection of compositions like this in decades. Honestly, you’re giving Beethoven a run for his money.”
Spud and he became best buds, as of a day ago. Rex had introduced them.
“Tell me the story of how you put it together, again?” Rex asked.
He’d shoved Spud away to flash his signature smile.
Jonah shrugged. “One night, it just flowed out of me. My brain just lasered in, and… Yeah.”
“Lasered in… Brilliant!” Rex shouted. “That quote is platinum. We need to print it out and slap it under your logo.”

Rex kept talking after that, but his voice faded out. He was a phantom. The whole room was a dreamlike place. It’d been a month since the day Jonah began taking the pills. Observing the people surrounding him, he realized he was in a whole new world. How had so little time done so much? Was it that everything was moving hyper fast, or had he just taken the rest of his life hyper slow?
“Do you guys think I have a chance among the greats?” Jonah asked.

There was a round of head nods and reassuring praise. Basking in it, Jonah looked back to all the artists. None of them had hit the record highs he had, in their first months. Something special had to be in him — he was something unlike what anybody else had done.
The world changed, for the better. After a lifetime of being dunked on, Jonah’s mark was being made.
“Send them in,” Jonah said.

His security guards opened the door, releasing a stream of people. By the dozens, Jonah signed albums, shook hands, and told stories. He’d never felt a bliss quite like it. People saw him. More bogglingly, they wanted to. Their eyes were wide, as they hung onto his every word.
“Your work saved me,” one of his fans said, clutching his album tight to their chest.

Along with this statement came rounds of people announcing his fame, genius, and purity. If only his old roommates could see him now. That, and all the people who he’d grown up with. God, the look on their faces would’ve been priceless.
A haggard man with a scraggly beard came to Jonah’s desk. Jonah crinkled his nose — the man stank of beer and fish.
“Jonah, it’s me, Larry.”
Jonah’s eyes widened. “Oh yeah! I remember you.” He twirled his pen on the desk. “Do you have anything for me to sign, or anything?”
Larry forced a grin. There was desperation beneath his eyes. Jonah squinted. There was also a chunk of bread tangled beneath Larry’s beard.
“I just wanted to chat with an old pal,” Larry said. “Talk about how things are going.”
He patted Jonah on the back.
“Aww, that’s nice,” said Jonah. “Also, did you wash your hands before coming here?”
Larry rubbed his hands on a pant leg, then nodded. “So, I heard you made a new album.”
Jonah turned his head to both sides of the room, then shrugged. “Yep. Just announced today. I also sold an album, a month back. It was a bit of a hit.”
“So I heard! Yeah, you’re everywhere right now!”
“And how’s your life going?”
Larry bit his lip, then placed his hand on the table. The muscles along his hand tightened.
“It’s going,” he said. “Is there any way that we can talk privately? Out of here?”
“No. In fact, I’m going to leave you with thirty more seconds. I have a line here, and we need to keep it going.”
“Jonah, we’re friends, remember? Can’t you just invite me over to your house, or something? Think about all the times that I helped you out, over the years. Did I ever give up on you?”

The words cut deep, but Jonah’s mind went back to the pills. That thought cut deeper. There was a chance that Larry was plotting to take the pills back. After years of not having them, hadn’t Jonah earned the right to his pills? Wasn’t it his turn, now?

“Look, life is going terrible, Jonah,” said Larry. “I lost my job. All my assets dried up. I had to sell all my stock, to try paying off my debt — but, I still wound up going bankrupt. My wedding was also a disaster…”
“Oh yeah… Your wedding! Sorry that I didn’t attend. Had a recording scheduled that I couldn’t miss.”
Larry’s eyes turned sharp and his lips trembled, as though he were a wounded dog.

“We wound up breaking it off,” Larry said, suppressing a choke. “I have a proposition, and you’re going to hate it, okay? But what if we give me a pill every morning? There are tons of extra pills in that bottle, each morning. It wouldn’t hurt to help, would it?”

Jonah winced. “Big problem there: what if it stops replenishing, and I start to run out? You’ve only ever taken out one pill a day, correct? Same with me. No point in risking what works. Hard to fight with perfection, am I right?”
Larry’s eyes darting around the room, he wiped his brow. He was a rat in a trap, searching for a way out.
“Maybe we could alternate? You give me the pills one day, and I give them back the next…”

Jonah raised his head, tilting his chin to the ceiling. “No, that doesn’t work.” He cleared his throat and raised his voice. “Thanks for coming. You’re awesome! Believe in yourself, and make sure to check out my new album when it releases.”
A series of swoons swept the crowd. Amid the showering, Jonah stood to bow and gave a wave.
“Come on, Jonah,” Larry begged, putting his hand near Jonah’s. Jonah pulled his hand away. “I just need one more day of good fortune. I gave you the world. The least you can do is share it.”

“I spent years scraping and clawing for a chance at luck in life,” Jonah said, as much to the crowd as to Larry. “Years. And look at me now! I have the world! There’s nothing I could trade this away for.”

Larry shook his head. “You put on your little outfit and wear a smile deeper than your pockets. Perfection sounds great. But, to live a life where you never do a bad thing, and a bad thing never happens… That doesn’t make you a perfect person, does it? You just have perfect circumstances.”

What Larry was saying didn’t make any sense. He should’ve been praising Jonah, and admiring his genius, like everybody else. That’s what the pill did to people, didn’t it? What made Larry so different?
Jonah’s voice lowered back to a whisper. “I need you to leave.”

Larry backed away, giving cautious looks to the security guards on each side of him. “Your life is perfect. But what about for those around you? What use is it to be perfect…? Unmarred…?” Larry snorted. “What mark is something unmarred supposed to leave? Perfect lives aren’t real. In any case, they’re not meant to be. We’re human. Living in a world that that is unreal is unrealistic. Toxic.”
“What did you come here to ask me for, again?”
“Help, from a friend.”

Larry opened the door to leave the building. Yet, when he looked up to Jonah, Jonah stretched and checked his watch. An aura of auspiciousness returned to him. He had already signed the albums of three more fans.

Jonah’s fingers raced along the piano keys, hitting each note impeccably. Sounds lilted at his ear and reverberated throughout the auditorium. It were as though the only sounds in the universe were his fingers along the keys, and the music they made.

He turned to look out at the crowd. It sparkled under stage light and swayed in tune with the stroke of each key. A wave of peace washed over Jonah’s body, as he was transported to another plane. It were as though some force had taken over him. It wasn’t him who was playing, but something inspired.

His fingers moved ever faster as the notes hit a crescendo. The composition hit its most powerful note, and he finally came to a stop. Applause erupted. His masterwork was complete. Though, there wasn’t an ounce of sweat on him. His muscles were as spry as they’d been at the start. He could’ve gone on forever if he’d wanted.
“Encore, encore!” the audience shouted.
Jonah stood from his piano and gave the bow he’d given a hundred times. The crowd’s excitement ballooned.
“Keep going,” Rex said, through a speaker in Jonah’s ear. “You haven’t even gotten through half the track, yet. Plus, they’re loving you.”
Jonah didn’t want to go on. The crowd was screaming for his music, but they weren’t screaming for him. Not really.
He gave a random thrust of his hand onto the piano, and a brilliant series of notes came out. There was a round of cheers. Yet, the notes had all been accidental. They hadn’t been his.

Jonah attempted to play a series of ugly notes. As he did, the muscles in his hand spasmed, and his fingers landed on different keys than he’d intended. Once again, something brilliant resulted. It felt dull though.

Jonah thought back to his composition. Had it really been his composition? The sounds in his new music didn’t carry any of his signature. His musical abilities had exceeded anything that he’d used to be able to achieve before the pill. It was invigorating to hear sounds that were so divine. However, at the core of it, was the music his to claim?
A din formed in his heart. The sounds he was praised for playing couldn’t be his.
“Give us more!” the crowd shouted. “We love you!”
“Well, screw you,” Jonah wanted to say. It was the sort of thing he would’ve been able to say, only a month ago. However, those words never left his mouth. Instead he said, “I love you too.”
It sounded like he meant it. The words weren’t from him.
He turned from the crowd and made his way backstage.
“It’ll be a moment, people,” he said. “When I come back, prepare to have your minds blown.”

He had no intention of coming back out. He was done for the night. He’d accomplished so much in the past few weeks — constant concerts and signings. Achievement and admiration became intimate friends. Perhaps too intimate.

At the beginning of his tour, every performance came with exhilaration, and a rush of adrenaline greater than the last. To some extent, that still held true. However, there was a writhing creature growing inside Jonah. It wriggled about, trying to break free. The constant success didn’t feel right. It wasn’t him.
He’d lived his whole life as a failure. It was fundamental. That could never really change, could it?

Jonah put his face into a bowl of ice, to cool his head. It was soothing. It was too soothing. Irritation rising, he tried wiping his face on a nearby towel. The towel was soft, to an unnerving extent.

Worse, as Jonah’s frustrations rose, he could feel no physical manifestations of them. His heartrate remained steady, his body temperature kept the same, and his body maintained its posture. He fought for a burst of aggression, but this desire was tied town. His emotions were captive, unallowed to escape.
“Great job out there, Jonah,” said Rex, giving Jonah a slap on the back. “Your music is incredibly moving. I felt tears rolling down my cheeks. Tears! Can you believe it?”

Jonah nodded. When had been the last time he’d been able to cry? Was he still able to cry? Grinning, he studied Rex’s outfit. It was the same fiery red, as always. Jonah wanted to ask Rex why he wore it so much but stopped himself when he remembered he was wearing the same thing.
“Rex, I think I’m going to call it a night,” said Jonah.
Rex checked his gold watch, then shrugged. “Sounds good to me. It’s been a long night anyway, and you’ve done plenty. The crowd should already be satisfied with what they’ve gotten.”
“Isn’t this the part where you’re supposed to encourage me to keep going? People paid good money to get tickets and come here.”
Rex laughed. “Very funny joke. Yeah, if you want to keep going, by all means! You’re on the top of your game, and the night is still young.”
“I thought you’d just said it’s been a long night…”
“The night is always long, and it’s always young. Do whatever you feel is right. You can do no wrong.”
“Maybe I don’t know what’s right.”
“Then, do nothing. That’s just as fine as anything else. You certainly can’t screw up doing nothing, am I right?”
He gave Jonah a playful ribbing, then put on his shades.
“Rex,” Jonah said. “Do you ever feel like a fraud?”
Rex did a heel turn, then readjusted the cuffs to his thousand-dollar suit. “Of course. I’m a complete poser. But hey: fake it till you make it, right?”
“Yeah, sure… But, is it worth being fake once you’ve made it?”
“If it’s worth it, then of course it’s worth it. And if it’s not, at least you’ll have a good time.”
“I’m a fraud, Rex.”
Rex’s eyes were saucers. His mouth twisted, and his cheeks puffed out. Finally, a laugh escaped as leaking gas.
“You? You’re a modern Mozart, Jonah. There’s nobody like you.”
“That’s because I’m not me. You don’t get it… Everything I’ve done? Everything you see and hear? It’s an act. It’s the product of something else. Someone else.”
“All creativity is derivative of something. That doesn’t mean you’re not a wunderkind.”
A small crowd had formed around them. Everybody was looking at Jonah in a bewildered awe. They thought he was being humble. Jonah wanted to puke.
“If you had the power to change the world, in whatever way you saw fit…” Jonah said, measuring his words carefully. “To make life match your dream life… How would you use it?”
Rex snickered. “I mean, look around you. We’re rolling in success, man. I think I’m already in a dream.”
“No, really. If you could do anything. If you just used that ability to better yourself, and only yourself, would that be wrong? Or, would you be obligated to give yourself to the world?”
“Isn’t that what you’re doing? Sharing your gifts with the world? Think of all the people you’ve changed, in this short span of time.”

Jonah had to smile. Nonetheless, his head flashed with images of countless people he could’ve helped. Nothing was stopping him from trying to cure disease, end hunger, or create world peace. If he tried, it would’ve worked. He hadn’t. He wasn’t going to either. The mere thought of an attempt was daunting.
“I want to call it a night. I’m sleepy.” In truth, Jonah hadn’t felt sleepy in weeks. “Can you take me to where Larry is?”
“Larry who? There are a lot of them.”
“Take a lucky guess. I get the feeling you’ll be able to figure out which one.”
A cloud of dust permeated the air. The ceiling fan croaked as it wobbled into a spin. The lights buzzed, threatening to short out.
Jonah took in a deep breath. Somehow, the air seemed just as clear as it would have been outdoors. If only the same could have been said for his mind.
“Had a change of heart?” Larry asked.
He was sitting in a beanbag, by his apartment’s radiator.
“Larry, I don’t think I know what I had,” Jonah said. “All I know is this: so long as you know I have these pills, my life is torture.”

Jonah pulled the bottle out of his pocket and rattled it. The rainbow light was missing from the center of the pills, with them now being completely clear. Yet, the pills still winked at Jonah beneath the light, as though he’d just met them for the first time.
Larry twirled his phone in his hand. It had a ghastly crack along the screen. “You call living every day in intense bliss torture?”
“Come on, Larry. You know what I mean. You think I’m the worst, for not sharing these pills with you. And I — I really can’t stand the pain of it all, honestly. It’s eating at me.”
“So, what do you want?”
Jonah looked around. He shook his pills again. It’d been awhile since he’d taken one. However, there was no way for him to take one. Not during this.
“I want you to apologize,” said Jonah. “I want you to say that you understand what I’m doing.”

“You’re not going to change my mind.” A derisive chuckle left Larry’s lips. “Walk out on the street, and you won’t find a person who doesn’t adore you. But there’s me, one person — just one — who has a problem with what you’re doing, and you can’t even live with that?

A muscle of Jonah’s twitched. It was just a slight twitch, in a muscle along his left hand. He desperately wanted to switch the twitch into a full clench. He would ball his fingers into a fist and punch Larry in the face.
“It’s not fair,” said Jonah. “I’ve done nothing wrong, Larry! Nothing!”
“Doing nothing wrong doesn’t mean you’ve done anything right.”
“You had your chance to have chance be in your favor. When you gave me the pills, did you really think I was just going to waste them?”
“Doesn’t matter whether I did, you definitely have. All you’ve used them for is to make some popular music. Big deal.”
“It is a big deal! I’m the biggest thing going on in culture, right now!”
Larry walked to his minifridge and fished for a beer. “Last I checked, popular culture is trash… I can’t say I’ve seen an exception.”
He studied Jonah’s face, waiting for a reaction.

“You don’t think my music is flawless?” Jonah said, incredulously. He began pacing in a circle. “It’s calculated to be so.  It’s an equal amount of chaos, and order. It’s both fluid, and solid. It’s classical, but modern.”

“It’s rubbish. But, why does it matter what I think? We’ve known each other for years Jonah and gone our separate ways. You’re more wildly successful than I even was, with those pills. Are you really going to live your life pining after what one person thinks?”
The cap shot from Larry’s beer, and past Jonah’s face. Foam bubbled over from the top of the bottle. Larry took a long sip and smacked his lips. Jonah grimaced.

“Perfection can’t be perfection if the world isn’t in complete and utter agreement about it,” Jonah said, his voice turning to a rasp. “Don’t you get it? So long as you hate me, I’m not there yet. My life can’t be perfect!”
Larry’s eyes narrowed. “I never said I hated you, Jonah. I just hate your music.”
Jonah kicked at the wall, leaving a dent in the flimsy plaster. The pill was wearing off, but Jonah didn’t care.
“How did you get these pills?” Jonah shouted.
The lights flickered off for a moment, a shadow creeping over Larry’s face. “I already told you the truth.”
“How did you get them? These things are a curse!”
Larry stared at Jonah, his face granite and unrelenting. Jonah punched at the air in a fit of rage, then collapsed on the floor. He shouted, until the floorboards creaked.
Somehow, there was more relief in his fury than a month of everything going right.

“I spend each day waiting for the hammer to drop,” Jonah said, through sobs. “Everything is perfect, but it’s too perfect… Something is supposed to give, and it never does. And I want to help others, but I’m too afraid to. If I were to share my luck, what if that means I push my luck into losing it all? In trying to solve all the world’s problems, I might create my own undoing.”
“Have you ever tried though?” Larry said, a mix of pity and judgement on his face.

“I’m not going to be a savior,” said Jonah. “It’s a trap. It always ends in death. Always. And, I’ve thought hard about what happens if I die… I don’t want to. Suppose these pills kill me, for example — it’s terrifying. Do I go to hell, after what I’ve done? Worse… Would I go to heaven, and live eternity as a fraud?”
“The pills won’t kill you. I’m not even sure if you can die, taking them.”

“But what if I still do?” asked Jonah. “You’ve lived with these pills — don’t pretend these thoughts don’t come to your head. When there are no problems, the mind creates them somehow. Otherwise, the world is just so… Vapid.”
Layers of dust had settled on Jonah. His head ached. There was a scratching at his mind, begging him to take a pill.

“Then give them to me,” Larry said. “Look at you. I thought the pills would benefit you more than anyone, but clearly not. You have every reason to be happy. But you’re worse than you were before any of this. I know that this might not seem right, but… Maybe people are meant to experience hardship. Maybe they’re meant to suffer.”
Waving the pills in Larry’s face, Jonah snarled. “Yeah, you’d like that, wouldn’t you? I’m sure you’re just desperate to have these back — to have the success you used to have.”
Larry’s face went red, and he shrugged. “Hey, it’s just a suggestion.”
“Just a suggestion… Just a suggestion! I’ve lived my whole life trying to meet suggestions.”

A rush pounded through Jonah’s skull. Jonah ran toward the sink and dumped his pills down the drain. He flipped the switch to the disposal and listened to the crunch of the pills being ground into powder. As Jonah turned it off, the sink belched.
There was a gulp.
Larry’s face was aghast. “What did you just…”
He paused. He took a sip of beer. Then, he slapped his knees, and let out a laugh.
“You actually did it!” he said. “I have to be honest Jonah… Before now, I never thought you had it in you to destroy those things. I definitely never would’ve been able to do it myself.”
Jonah stared down the disposal. Larry was at his side. Yet, somehow, Jonah was emptier inside than ever.
“Yeah,” Jonah said, keeping his eyes to the ground. “I definitely did it.”

Larry outstretched his hand. “It’s going to be rough. But, trust me: everybody is going to be better for this. What you’ve done… It’s just incredible. Now, hopefully you can keep all that success you have.”
“Don’t worry,” said Jonah. He took Larry’s hand and gave a firm handshake. “I think I’ll figure it out. I always figure some way out of things.”
Larry snickered. “That you do. That you do. Also… I just want to say, I’m sorry about what I said about your music. I really do like it.”
“I’m sorry too.”
Their eyes locked. There was a connection. An unspoken trade of trust. In that moment, Jonah knew he had Larry. They were on solid terms again.
“Goodnight!” said Jonah.
Larry opened his mouth to say something, but Jonah had already made his way to the door. Jonah took care to close it softly behind him.
He hopped into his car, peeling down the highway and into the night.
There was a rattling in Jonah’s cupholder. Reaching in, he pulled out a bottle of pills.
At the center of each one, there was the familiar glint of a rainbow.
“Just where I left you,” he said. “Finally, the real deal.”
He popped a pill in his mouth. Then, he laughed.
End

title: Sticky-Note
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
A breeze laps at my face. The sun gives an embrace. The road bends. There’s a crack. A snap.

I give the wheel a nudge, but it doesn’t move. My chest shoots with pain. Strength faltering, I veer to the side. I'm flying off. The mouth of a dark lake looms beneath me. I’m drawn in. Goosebumps rise. If I could just get away...

I slam my brakes. Though, gravity doesn’t stop for them. There’s a spray of ooze. Mud cakes on the windshield. I rev my engine, only to receive another splash of mud. My vision blurring, I check my mirror.
"Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear."
A crash. A splash. Mud washes. I'm nauseous. The car shakes and sways. The engine delays. It is dead.
So am I.
I open an eye.
I let out a pant and clutched my heart. I felt my forehead. It was dewy.
It was a dream. Just a dream. I rolled over — a picture of a crashed car was scrawled along a notepad. I raised an eyebrow. Where'd it come from?
A blare railed at my ears. Teeth chattering, I groped around until my hand finally slammed "snooze" on my alarm. Silence.
A gasp. My eyes widened.

Monday mornings are hell. But, rolling out of bed on a Tuesday, to find an alarm reading "8:30", when you were supposed to be rolling out of the driveway at 7:00 and into your work-desk at 7:30, and knowing you'll probably be fired, which will then leave you broke, and eventually on the streets, marking you a perpetual failure for the entire world to scoff at...?
It makes Mondays... Look a little... They look a little less like hell.
If only I hadn't stayed up so late the night before. I'd been such an idiot. An idiot!

My legs numb, I stumbled toward the bathroom. A crash resounded as I hit the ground, and a pang shot through me. Looking back, I winced. I'd tripped over a stack of old VHS tapes. Self-improvement tapes, now all tangled in a web of black film.

"Step Up to Bat to Make a Better You". I grabbed the cassette in a jerk of pure instinct. I couldn't help myself. I couldn't put it down. Even as I combed my hair, I fumbled with the cassette. It was tied into a terrible knot. I'm terrible with knots.

My hair was in a terrible knot of its own. This came as a shock, too — my hair was so thin and greasy that I should've been far beyond the days of knots. Yet, there was no denying: the knot was not... Not. Rather, it was.
Trying to undo it, I felt strands of my hair fall out.
"Ouch!"
I'd clamped my finger in the top of the VHS. I tossed the cassette to the ground. A whimper fled my throat. I drowned it with mouthwash. With a gurgle, I spat the wash out. It tasted like dog.
Breakfast was no better — a handful of granola shoved into my mouth. It might as well have been dog kibble.

I hate dogs. They're sweaty, ugly, chaotic... Come to think of it, they're everything that I am. My body trembles just at the thought of them — they always put me in a state. Considering the state of the world, I doubt we need much more of dogs — of me — running around.
As I rushed to the door, my hand gravitated to my head. My hat... Where was my hat?
I sprinted back to my room, my eyes ferreting to the floor. To my bed-post. Nothing. My cheeks flushed. I must've put my hat in my closet. How could I have been so stupid?

My legs turned to lead as I approached my closet. My hand gripping my doorknob, I closed my eyes. With a gulp, I unlatched the door. Mounds of sticky-notes, covered in sprawls of ink, poured out. I waded through them. Bullets of sweat shot down my face. I just had to ignore the notes — the words written on them. They were nothing. Their pull was all in my head.

Grasping the wool rim of my fedora, I stepped from my closet and slammed the door. My arm stiffened, fogging with pins and needles. I let out a grunt. The door had clipped my ulnar nerve — the "funny bone". Funnily enough though, the pain was just noise. I was still left in a daze by the notes. Everything they'd said — there'd been so much I just wanted to forget.

I remained in a daze as I unlocked my door and stepped into a downpour of rain. I shivered. Of course, it was raining. Why hadn't I just checked the weather forecasts from the day before? I should've at least brought my umbrella.

I turned back to my door. It'd already clicked shut. I jiggled the knob. Already locked. I slapped my forehead — I'd locked it from the inside, so I couldn't forget. Brilliant — there was no time to try unlocking it. Nearly twenty keys were hooked to my keychain, and I was on a time crunch.

Unlocking my car was practically impossible. Water soaking through my clothes, I spit a spurt of water from my mouth. The neighbors must've thought me a ridiculous sight: an oaf standing in the rain, hunching over his keys. Hopefully they wouldn't talk. I'd taken great care to ensure they knew as little about me, so they couldn't. They couldn't have possibly known my name, could they? Hopefully they hadn't read my name from my mail...
Could they have been reading my mail from my mailbox? It wasn't implausible. God, I hoped it wasn't so. If only the mailman hadn't kept me from putting a lock on my mailbox.
Still fumbling with my keys, I glanced at my watch. Its hands were frozen, a pool of water filling through a crack in the glass.

A key shoving into its ignition, my car stammered and revved on. Some might’ve called my car a 'lemon'. I was too much of a cheapskate to buy anything better, but I probably should've. Tremors overtook me each time it revved on, out of fear of the engine exploding. Though, maybe... Maybe I was just shivering because of the rain.
Yes, that was it.

I slammed the gas, while my heart slammed against my ribcage. In addition to dogs, I hate machines. They're unreliable and tend to break down at the worst times. I've documented dozens of instances of technology breaking down sporadically and betraying me, on various sticky-notes. Sometimes, I think technology outright hates me. Actually, it does. It's for this reason I don't buy technology from after the year 2000. Upon the turn of the millennium, everything went to crap. Old TV sets and VHS players from garage sales are all I need to coast by. Nothing else can be trusted.

My car's clock turned to 8:41. There was no hope of making it to work on time. I wiped my forehead. Would I be fired? Hopefully not. If only I'd put more thought into everything. Mr. Crowley was always telling me I needed to "work more efficiently." He was right. I did. Why couldn't I?

I turned on a street slick with rain, then clutched my elbow. The pins and needles had died off, but I still felt a raw throbbing. It's odd — usually, I enjoy the sensation of pins and needles. Paresthesia. I'll purposely sit in awkward positions to induce it. The numbness, followed by the tingle of life, is a rare comfort. Yet, the sensation induced by my ulnar nerve only offered discomfort.
With the turn of a dial, my radio blared on. A glib voice filtered through the speakers.
"I love the rain. Such beautiful weather," it said. "The perfect time to be indoors, and get some things done around the house."

The dial turned back off. Biting my lip, I thought back to what I'd been doing in my condo — creating countless clutter. I tried thinking of other things I might've been doing but came up empty. It was as if there were gaps in my memory. Perhaps it was time for me to pick up a hobby, but I somehow didn't have a handle on anything.
I never seem to have a handle on anything.

There was a screech as my tires came to a halt and meandered into a parking lot. My office. It was only three miles away from my condo. I'd strategized it this way, so that I'd never have an excuse to be late. Somehow, I still managed.

I listened to the putter of the engine as it counted down the seconds. I scanned around, but cars occupied the entire lot. Hands trembling, I pulled up a few more feet and sandwiched myself between a pickup truck and Mr. Crowley's Corvette. If only I had a Corvette. That said, I was a terrible driver. Deathly terrified every time I'd go on the open road. Just pulling up next to Crowley's Corvette filled me with fear of scratching it.

Glancing at my clock, I felt my mouth run dry. It was already 8:45. It couldn't be true — yet, it was. I shoved open my car door and heard a thump — I'd hit the pickup truck. My head thumped. I shut the door, and my feet thumped. They took me toward my office building. An oversized brick, sitting on a hill of charcoal.
My car door had left a thin scratch along the side of the truck. Just a thin one. Yet, it was a blemish, nonetheless. Thank god it wasn't Crowley's Corvette.

The gold-lettering on the building's door shimmered as I clasped the latch. "Murrish Bank". Many a time, my co-workers jokingly called it "Mush Bank". I think they nicknamed it because "the work turns your brain to mush." Was it Joe who named it that? He always had something clever to say. Much cleverer than myself. But, I might be misremembering. Anyhow, that's not the reason that I call it "Mush Bank". For me, it's a reminder that I must "mush" while working there.
I'm very bad at taking my own advice.

The door grunted shut, and the carpet wore against my feet. My eyes flitted to a row of punitively puny desks, then landed on my own. They flitted back. A fan breathed down my back as a counter loomed ahead of me. Heat rushed to my face. I faced a glass bowl of peppermint — a mix of sheet-white and blood-red. My reflection in the glass was a mix of that, that is — not the peppermints.
"Melvin Happer."
Blood draining from my face, I jumped. Shuddered.

"Yes sir," I mumbled, eyeing a man in a crisp, black suit. Mr. Crowley. He was an inch or two shorter than me, but I still felt as though he could knock me over. His piercing eyes gave him all the presence he needed.
"Did you file those papers this morning like I told you to, good buddy?" Mr. Crowley said, hands abating into one another. They were so prim. He was so trim — ten times the man I was. Maybe more.
"No," I said, inching toward the counter.
My hands swept along my suit, brushing off bits of lint. I adjusted my tie. Was it cinching my neck? My feet tripped on a bit of carpet, as the laces to my shoes undid.
"It's fine. How about that expense report I needed you to do? Did you get that filed?"
"Well... Uh... As — as it happens..."
"As what happens, Happer?"
"I didn't get that done either."
The corner of his lip twitched. His brow contorted.
"The bank notes?" he asked.
I shook my head.
"Drawer count?"
I shook again.

Mr. Crowley gave a cold chuckle. "Happer. I appreciate you, good buddy...  But, those papers we needed filed? Your flub just cost us $2,000 dollars. I was counting on you to do your job, and you blew it. You left early last night, didn't you? And you were late again, weren't you?"
I went to speak, but glue slathered my lips. I rubbed my ear. There had to be something to say, but all words slid away. I'd utterly failed.

Some people work best under stress. Others, at the very least, find that stress builds their character. For me, stress is the great enemy. There is no winning with it. No reasoning with it. There is only utter defeat.
"I might've been late, but I really can't be sure," I said. "I have a terrible memory. Sorry."
Mr. Crowley gawked. His hand rested on his chin.
"I heard the door open a moment ago, but I don't see anybody in here. Do you know if somebody might've come in?"
I shrunk. I shrugged.
"It — it's possible. You know my eyesight though. Very nearsighted."
"It's okay, Happer. I know you were late."
He put his hand on my shoulder. I flinched.

"Really?" I said, feigning relief. I shot a look of desperation at Jack, from across the counter. Tara. Bill. Somebody needed to come to my aid. Yet, nothing came. "That... that's so good. Very nice. It won't happen again at all, so long as I can help it. I'll try to make sure of it."
The building rumbled as rain pelted on the roof. There was a crash of thunder. Lights flickered.

In one of my self-help books, I'd read that you must hold steadfast during uncomfortable scenarios. That you can't allow yourself to show signs of weakness, and instead must look for the light at the end of the tunnel. However, what do you do when you're already at the end, and there is no light?
"Sorry... Again," I said, running my hand through my hair. My left foot twisted behind my back, as if I were about to curtsy.
"'So long as I can help it'?" Mr. Crowley said, curtly. "I've heard you apologize so many times. I agree with you: it won't happen again. But... Not in the way that you might like."
"Wha — wait. Are... Are you suggesting that you're going to fee — fire me?"
I gulped. My eyes darted back to Tara and Jack. Their heads were buried in their work. I was invisible.

"You're not giving me much of a choice here, Happer, good buddy," Mr. Crowley said. "Murrish Bank is an establishment devoted to quality work. Unfortunately, you just haven't been offering us that. You're always late. You look exhausted. You're terrible with our customers... I don't know how you've been spending your time outside of the building, but it clearly hasn't been any help."
"You... You're right," I said, "I guess I really don't deserve a second chance, at this point."
"Wrong. I've given you plenty of second chances. You've just wasted all of them. You're a good person, Happer. I like you, I really do. But, I can't keep you on board, in good conscience."

My head slumped. This was all entirely on me. If only I hadn't been staying up throughout the nights. If I'd just been a little bit better at my job. A little bit smarter. If I wasn't a pitiable person, maybe I could've done better.
I rubbed another piece of lint off my pants. I studied the palm of my hand — a bit of the skin had grazed off, leaving it raw. I must've been rubbing too abrasively. Rushing.

I turned around, toward the door. Toward the rain. As my posture sunk deeper, my mind trailed back. Toward the lists of failures and mistakes I'd made. All of the pratfalls. The pitfalls. Today was supposed to have been a good day — my mood-graph had predicted it.  Yet, this was just my luck of the draw. Since childhood, I'd been the klutz. The screw-up.
"Now, you can't go just yet. I'm going to need you to collect your things."

My feet turned to ice. I'd never be able to come back from this. I had no other prospects. This job was all I had. And, who would I turn to? My parents? My brother? I'd be the laughing stock of the family. They'd been right about me going to art school. Such a waste of time and money. I was such a waste. I sighed, my face flushing purple. This was everything I'd ever had nightmares about.
My fists clenched. I turned back around.
"Excuse me?"

A fury burned in my chest. I'm not quite sure what came over me, in that moment. Though, it wasn't me. I swear, it wasn't me. It'd been like walking in a dream. I'd lost all control. My legs. My arms. My hands. As a fist carried into Mr. Crowley's face, all I could feel was shock and horror. Something had possessed me.
It wasn't me.
Mr. Crowley stumbled back and let out a cough. His hand covered his nose, streaks of red leaking between the cracks.
"Happer! Happer!" he said, raising his other hand.
Somebody on the other side of the counter gasped. I didn't care. I don't care.
I glide through the air. The room dims. My arm carries me. The wind howls in horror as and I give a shout, and my fist meets skin.
There's a smattering of red. A buzzing. A flurry.
"Security!" Mr. Crowley said. "Somebody call security!"
The daze dips — dipped away.
"I — I'm so sorry, Mr. Crowley," I said, meekly. "I have no idea what came over me. There's absolutely no excuse for my behavior. Please, forgive me."

I bent down to give Mr. Crowley a hand. He sneered and pushed it away. Spite inhabited his eyes. I backed away. I'd never seen such rage in somebody before. Such malice. It didn't seem right. A sort of relief rushed through me — perhaps it was for the better that I was being let go by somebody volatile as him.
"Can I still have a second chance?" I asked Mr. Crowley.
Or, at least, it'd been something like that. I'm actually not quite sure.
Mr. Crowley spat at my feet, his face still contorted into a scowl. "You have five minutes to collect your things, or I'm calling the police."

The police? I shuddered. There are few things I fear more than them. One night, I was driving on the main road a bit slower than usual. I'd detected a slight palpitation in my heart, and a tremor in my car's engine. Slowing my speed was the only way to avert disaster. At least, until the blare of a police car and the bark of their dogs nudged me off the road, and gifted me a ticket.

In another experience, I ended up pinned to the ground, with the hot breath of an enraged officer on my face. My memory is slightly hazy as to what led to those events — yet, it was undoubtedly another instance of injustice.
"I'm so sorry! Please forgive me! I tripped! I swear!"
Upon my attempt to wipe away the blood from his face, Mr. Crowley let out a yelp.
"Stay away and collect your things. You're lucky that the police aren't on their way, right now."

My face softened, trying to dig past Mr. Crowley's granite features. He didn't even offer a flicker of understanding. I turned to my co-workers, but their faces only morphed to that of disgust. I was shut out by all of them. Stranded. An outcast.

Heat bloomed on my cheeks. My eyes clouded, and my nose burned. The floor oscillated as I stumbled forward, ambling toward my desk. A drought plagued my throat. The windows to the building shuddered, wind ramming against them.

Papers fluttered between my hands, my fingers quaking. I clutched my stapler. My hourglass. Time was up. Perhaps I'd had too little for breakfast — that must've been it. One small mistake had compromised me, entirely.  If I'd just gotten up earlier, and eaten right, none of this would've happened. That was all.
Hugging a bushel of office supplies, I made my way toward the door.
"I hope that we can make amends after this," I said. "We can still be friends, right?"
Mr. Crowley's jaw was clenched, a frown fixed to his face.
"I don't hold grudges, preferring to mend broken ties," he said, bringing his left sleeve to his mouth. "But... You broke my nose. Get out of my building."
"But... But, that's not right," I stuttered. "That — that's unprofessional. We should still be friends, regardless of what might've happened today. People are supposed to be friendly."
Mr. Crowley winced in disgust. Or, was it embarrassment? He was embarrassed by me, wasn't he? I shouldn't have said what I said, should I have? Classic... Just classic.
"Happer, you're really pushing it."

I outstretched my hand to give a handshake. Mr. Crowley gestured toward the exit. I stepped forward, then stopped, standing my ground — albeit, slightly off-balance. Mr. Crowley stared me in the eye. He licked his lips. He outstretched his own hand. However, as I went to take it, my stapler fell from my pile and landed on Mr. Crowley's arm. He let out a shriek.
"Happer!"

I stumbled out the door, for my car. There was a pounding of feet and the bleep of buttons as Mr. Crowley went to the phone. No doubt, he was dialing the police. That, or an ambulance. Yet, I didn't look back. Rain drenching me to the skin, I shoved my stuff in my trunk and peeled out of the parking lot. I didn't bother monitoring my speed. I couldn't afford to let police catch me.

My condo was littered in work supplies and muddy footprints. Yet, I laid on my bed, eyes glued to the ceiling. I kicked the self-help books and cassettes off my bed. Useless —they were all useless. Despite all their advice, I was still wet, and unemployed.
At least I've been worse things.

My eyes darted back to the image of the car scrawled across my notepad. It was so odd... I had no recollection of drawing it. Yet, there it was. This wasn't the first time an image had manifested on my bedside, either. Over the past several months, I'd built up a collection of images that corresponded with my nightmares. My bad memories.
Bad memories...
My head was set adrift, traveling back to my conversation with Mr. Crowley. The words he'd said. The words I'd said.
"We should still be friends... People are supposed to be friendly..."

I winced. How could I have said something so stupid? The memory hammered at me. I thrust my head into my bed. I gave my forehead a slap. However, the flashes of memory only became more intense, with me reliving every detail. The way in which Mr. Crowley had smiled. The way his facial muscles flicked in disgust. The way his eyes bored through me.
I must've looked and sounded pathetic. No — I must've been pathetic. I could already hear my voice tinging through my head, as a small squeak.
"Yes," I said. "I messed that up."

I moaned, and more memories flashed by. The looks on the faces of my friends. The way they'd abandoned me, like I was nothing. I was nothing, wasn't I? I'd flinched and groveled at my boss's behest. I'd let my eyes warily dart about, like a squirrel's. It was only too obvious what a mess I was.
"I get it!" I said, tugging at my hair. "I don't need to think about it anymore. I just need a break. I'm sorry!"
"You can't forget!" a voice boomed. "No matter how much you try! No matter where you go, it’ll follow you!"
The thoughts sharpened, making my head ache. Heart pounding, I grabbed a marker and sticky-note and ran down my hall, into the bathroom. I needed to escape.
"I'm sorry!" I whimpered. "I'm sorry... I'm sorry..."
I shut the bathroom door and turned the lock. I brought the marker to the notepad.
"You fool," the voice boomed, throttling the room. "You can't escape your author."
A whirlpool of terrible memories gushed into the room. My hand went limp and slammed the marker against the mirror, leaving a dark mark. I went to scream but was drowned out by the growl of thunder.
"You can't!" the voice said. "You’re scum! A social deviant! Stop! This is all your fault!"
There was a squeal as my marker whipped around the glass. My eyes glazed over, and my chest tensed. The world was blinking...
… Blinks out of existence. My burden of guilt is dead. A new person has taken control. I know what must be done. I don’t want to do it… But, it’s where things have come to.

I come to — came to. I shook my head. I couldn't let myself lose control. Yanking my hand away from the glass, I brought the marker back to the paper. There was a thump as it hit the counter, but I ignored it. I needed to get the words jotted down.
"You'll still always be a failure!" the voice cried. I groaned as it tore through my body, leaving my body trembling and my throat sore.
Nothing else mattered. I honed in on my flashes of memories, grappling to the most painful ones.  I wrote each one down on the notepad, and then tore them away for a new piece.
"Saying something indescribably cruel to Mr. Crowley."
"Tripping over myself."
"Punching Mr. Crowley."

Once finished, I dropped the marker and collapsed to the floor. My breathing was shallow, and my face flushed red. Though, as I listened for the booming voice, silence settled. The room steadied. The storm calmed. I was just an unemployed man, sitting in a room, hunched over a clutter of papers. Squinting to read one of them, I jerked my head away. The papers were in an incoherent sprawl, but the mere thought of them left me with flashes. Eyes locked to the mirror, I scooped the papers up, opened the bathroom door, and headed to the hall. Once in my room, I opened the closet. Papers spilled out and I struggled to ignore them. Finally, I jumped away and slammed the door shut.
Yet, whispers managed to slink out from under the door. Past nightmares. Mistakes. Things that couldn't be undone or unsaid. So many things...

A clump of hair fell into my hand. I raced down the hall, shaking my head. Almost everything had been taken care of — erased. Though, it all somehow still felt hollow. For once, I'd gone to a place here there was little hope of turning back.

I'm not sure when I started putting my bad memories down on sticky-notes. I must've been around ten years old? I had a streak of bad luck at that time, so it would've only been natural. I'd also gotten a pack of sticky-notes with my school supplies and had just begun learning how to use them. I must've realized I could write bad experiences on the notes, then throwing them away. The process had an effect on me — the memories of the experiences would flush away, as if they'd never occurred.
I can't remember the memory that'd led me to starting this process. Though... I suppose it means the process worked?

Unfortunately, after a litany of screw-ups, I realized I couldn't keep throwing the memories away. After all, if I couldn't remember the bad memories, what was stopping me from repeating them? There was also the unfortunate fact that I had holes in my memory, and the people around me didn't understand how. So, I took it upon myself to hide the notes away in my closet. At the time it'd seemed genius. Any time that I needed to remember a bad experience, I could just go in there.
Since then, I've realized how stupid I was to put the notes in my closet. Come to think of it, maybe I should write that down as a bad memory: "stupidly decided to put notes in closet."

I digress. Over the decades, the notes have reached a point where I can no longer navigate them. Every time I open the closet, I run the risk of collapsing in terror, and never coming back out. In fact... I think it might've happened already before? My memory fails me on that, as well.
I snapped from my place on the wall, with a gasp. I scanned around. I'd practically been drowning. Being pulled down a whirlpool of inky nothingness.
Inky nothingness... I peered down the hall, through the open bathroom door. The mirror was still a mess. Somebody needed to clean it off.
I was that somebody.

Taking each step lightly, I entered the bathroom and pulled a spray and a roll of paper towel from under the sink. My eyes watered at the sight of the spray bottle. I have a very weak sense of smell, but cleaning supplies always cause my sinuses to flare up
I doused the mirror in the suds, the world blurring. There was a squeal as I wiped the paper towel along the mirror. A squeal...
The layers of suds peel. A face emerges in the mirror. My face.
"Hello," I say.
"Oh god," I whimper.
My face contorts. A snouted creature assumes its place. I back away, but its eyes chase me. Beady. Soulless.
"Tonight, Happer dies."
Thunder claps. A corner of the mirror cracks. I turn to the door, but it clamps shut. My head bobs around. There must be a way out.
The tile floor burbles, turning to lava.
"Where do you think you’re going?"
I stare at its jagged ears, and matted fur. It's an oversized beast. A monstrous wolf. A curse.
"Cat have your tongue"
"How — what — who are you?"
"Well, I'm your reflection."
It grins, its eyes gaining a glint. It preens its fur, then tilts toward me.
"My reflection? What do you mean?"
It chuckles. The mirror's glass bends. It shatters. My hands jump to my ears.
"I'm in your head," it twitters.
Glass douses my hair. Head succumbing to haze, I try to brush the glass away. Yet, my hands run crimson.
A snicker. A flicker. A crash of thunder.
"You, stamp! Slop! Stop!"
"Me, stop? You sad thing. You little bother... Anyway, the fun is just beginning. And for once, you can't escape. Can’t forget."
I sputter. "I don't understand."
"I'm your nightmares, incarnate. Your locked away cries, fears, rage. I hail from another realm, of fire and brimstone. For years, you've suppressed me. But no longer!"
I run my hands through my hair. Everything becomes hazy. My lungs threaten to collapse.
"What is your goal?"
"To fix you. You see, my friend... You’ve been defeated. Your life has lost all direction. It's time for your rebirth. The place that destroyed you? It will meet my fiery vengeance."

The door rips away. A gust of wind calls me. A sticky-note flutters to my skin. Fear floods my marrow, as a whirlwind of sticky-notes follows. They all cling to me. Each one reminds me of a different mistake. Hundreds of traumatic flashes. The bathroom starts to fade. The notes continue to shower, and I fall toward the ground.
Just black.
Heart attack.

My hand remained on my chest as I sat from my car seat and panted for breath. I tried to ignore the pang. It couldn't have been a heart attack. It was just in my head. A result of running thoughts, that had gotten out of hand.

I looked out my window. A thin drizzle coated it, leaving me with a smudged image of my driveway. My eyes flitted to the sky. The rain had receded, but a coat of gray remained. A harbinger of another storm to come. A murmur rolled from the deep.

Was it daylight still, or evening? If only there were a way to see past the thick shrouds of clouds. I could use some deep sleep. How long had I been in here? I could've sworn that I'd gone inside and to my bed, right after pulling in the driveway...
"You swear? Please… You know what really brought you here."
My hands trembled. Locking them into each other, I glanced at my radio. It was dialed off. My eyes jumped to the yards of my neighbors. All empty. There was nobody around — and yet I'd heard a sound.
"You heard me right. Stop trying to fight me."

My eyes widened, going wild. My thoughts went back to my younger years — back when my older brother used to play pranks on me. I'll still never forget the time that he told me a dollar bill was in the dryer and tried shoving me in there. Or the time he managed to lock me in a shed, on a sweltering summer's day, under the pretense he was just trying to "play".
"You look like a clown."
I looked up.
"Look down."
A chill sliced down my spine. All along my skin were bits of sticky-notes. Each one chocked with scarring memories. Things I'd done. Things I'd said.
"Look at you — an absolute imbecile. A psycho. A murderer."
"Wha— what?" I asked, shrilly. "I'm not trying to kill anybody!"
"Then why do you have a gun in your hand? Just admit the truth."

My tongue turned to cardboard. The voice had been right — a gun was in my hand. My stomach churned. I felt sick. How did I even have a gun? I hadn't seen anything like one since I was younger, when my brother was aiming his BB gun at a couple of quails. A couple of quails, and then me.
"A little bird, trapped in a cage. Speeding through the streets."
My arms became weak, and my head fluttered. Somehow, my driveway had disappeared. My foot was on the gas, my hands were on the steering wheel, and I was speeding toward Murrish Bank.
"I don't understand!" I said. I spat at a sticky-note hanging over my lip. "I swear, I'm not doing this."
"Look over here. Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear."
I tried to keep my eyes on the road. I jerked my wheel, trying to steer away. To head back home. Back to my bed, where everything made sense. Yet, my eyes burned and compelled me to look up.
"You’re under my control now."

My eyes were torn from the road and pulled into the gaze of my mirror. Back to the monster I'd seen in my bathroom. It snarled at me, its tongue flaring between its teeth. I shuddered. The teeth were like knives, jutting from its mouth. Trying to escape, I let out a moan. My car swerved and shuddered. There was another thunderclap, followed by a spray of rain.
The monster chuckled, then reached its claws toward me. I glanced in the back of my mirror, to the backward street-lamps and road signs. I was nearly there, now. I gave my wheel a jerk. Nothing.
The monster growled. Its claws clenched shut. My heart shriveled to a raisin, and blood drained from my face.
"You've always thought you could get ahead. Though, your nature is to be kept asleep. To be forgotten. To let me dominate."
The monster laughed, then flew toward me. I thrust my head back, ramming it into my headrest. My eyes shot back to the road.

I scanned around for the monster. A relieved sigh fled my throat. I was back in control. My hands shifted the wheel, attempting to turn around. Yet, my hands turned in the opposite direction. My car jostled, then swerved, pulling into my work's parking lot. There was a twang. My muscles stiffened. Air sifted away, then thinned. Hair raised. An empty parking spot came into view. There was a shriek as I pulled in, and a neighboring car was shunted.
An alien laugh rumbled through my chest. Lightning dashed among the clouds. My eyes dropped to my hands — to the fingers of my right hand, curling around the trigger of my gun.
"We're ready, locked and loaded. Fully prepared to finally bring on the finale."
Prying my left hand from the wheel, I bashed myself in the head.
"Get out!" I shouted. "Get out of me! I beg of you: don't do this!"
"And exactly what is 'this'?"

My left hand gravitated toward my right. My fingers looped into one another, as I tried clasping around the gun. Yet, to no avail. A surge of adrenaline pumped through my right arm. The fingers tightened. The trigger jiggled. Clicked. My eyes clenched. A bang. Another shattering of glass. I wanted to believe that I was still in my bathroom. That the shattering had been in my head. I opened my eyes. I couldn't believe.
"Yes! Yes!"
My gut turned into itself. I hadn't just shot through my window, but the window of the car next to me. A Corvette.
The world turning in on itself, I squinted. It was Mr. Crowley's Corvette.
"Great," I moaned. "Just great..."

There was the rustling of sticky notes as I stood from my seat. A hand pulled the latch to my door, and a leg kicked it open. I was sucked out, and into the parking lot. I tried to get a better look of Crowley's damaged Corvette. Yet, my eyes were locked to the building. My mind, held hostage. My body, lost to the control of another.

I stopped in front of the glass door to the building. There was a harsh chuckle as I was forced to look over the reflection — a man, feathered in endless sticky-notes. Despite the words on the sticky-notes being backward, I still suppressed a gag upon an onslaught of bad memories. I was covered, head to toe. Yet, I felt naked. Exposed.
"There you are, in all your glory."
The door opened. A bell chirped as I entered the bank. As rank scents entered my nostrils. As titters entered my ears.

The titters were tainted as shatters whisked through. I glanced at my gun. Smoke and the stench of sulfur wafted from its barrel. I glanced up. Rain and lingering shards of glass fell through open windows. Bank tellers dove to the ground, fear crowning their brows.
"Somebody, call the police!" a familiar voice yelped. Mr. Crowley. He was running toward me. Though, he was hardly recognizable. Fear was wrapped around his face as a gauze.
"Crow your cry," I shouted, tilting my gun toward him. "It’ll be your last!"
Mr. Crowley sputtered.
"Happer? Good buddy? Is that you? What the hell are you doing?"
I strode toward him. Pressed the barrel of my gun against his head.
"Ending this... thing," I said. "I'm no longer your slave."
My gun jostled. Trembled. Was it from Mr. Crowley's head? No. He didn't move a muscle. It was my arm, trembling. My finger slipped from the trigger.
"I always thought you a good employee, Happer. Just... Not what we were looking for," said Mr. Crowley.
"Re — really?" I said. "Would you take me back?"
"Sure... Just take the... Take the gun away. My god!"

I took in a deep breath of air and raised myself back up. Resumed my composure. I couldn't let Mr. Crowley get to me. Though, despite all my efforts, I couldn't bring myself to pull the trigger either. I remained locked with Mr. Crowley. Stuck under his thumb, once more. His eyes skimmed over me. A smile flicked past his face.
"All these notes on your body — your past embarrassments?" Mr. Crowley said. "Why bother documenting those? Why force yourself to relive those past moments, with such intensity?"

I couldn't answer. Couldn't think. My jaw slackened. Though, the gun remained pressed on Crowley's forehead. We remained locked, until a flash of blue passed through the room. A flash of red. A wail of thunder. A siren.
I swear that it hadn't… been me that'd compelled me to do these things.
You might think that I'm trying to play your heartstrings. Yet, I swear, I'd been controlled by something that wasn’t me. Something I can't quite piece together.

Some say I was overtaken by ego. I disagree with them, fundamentally. They simply don't understand me. The thing I did is a thing I regret. If I could forget it, I would. Yet, it remains upon the crust of my consciousness, tormenting me. Thus, how could one believe I did this on purpose?
No, people blame me to deny what is within us all: a cliff. A monster.
We're all just a few missteps away from being what I've become.
Th — though, maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I’m just being an idiot.
End

title: The Charity Case
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
Sunshine showers the wicked and the just, just the same.

Microphones whine. Cameras flash, outdoing the daylight. People congregate in stacks. The arid weather doesn’t deter them. They’re rolled up in tasteless tweed suits, eating at each other’s heels. They chomp at the bit to catch a glimpse of Danner Percy. Though, it’s all in vain. Danner hovers above them all, behind a podium and a throng of bodyguards.
A cutthroat boom shears the raucous in half.
“So, you’ve shown up,” Danner says. “Good.”
Shadows line the corners of Danner’s eyes and lips. A few reporters laugh with the smile that belongs there, but never takes form.
“As you all know, you have no idea what I’m about to announce. That is, other than that my announcement will be something.”
His eyes wander away. Bits of dust kick up, before collapsing back into the chapped earth. A lone cactus stands in the distance.
“Forgive me if this is all a bit… Prickly. But it’s something that I got to get off my chest, alright?”
Murmurs mist over the crowd. A handler scrambles to Danner’s ear, and points to a teleprompter. Danner gives a scoff and readjusts his tie.
“I was always taught to be honest, growing up. Guess I should stick by that teaching. Just going to rip off the bandage: cancer.”
Danner’s eyes squint. They burn, as the sun goes more intense.
Suppressing a choke, Danner continues, “I have cancer. Cancer in the skin, cancer in the liver, cancer in the lungs… Cancer up the ass.”
The crowd going up in a frenzy, Danner’s bodyguards struggle to keep the press back. Cameras click, tasers spark, and Danner takes a step forward. His jaw is firm, and his face sardonic.

“You load of bandwagoners. You get hit with a juicy story, and you go nuts. Only, my cancer isn’t the story I’m here to give. Not by a longshot. I’ve made my life’s work off my oil business, not getting sympathy from tabloids…”
Ravenous hunger still hangs in the air, but Danner has the mob’s attention. He pulls a remote from his pocket and flicks it on. A screen with two logos dancing across it ascends behind him.

“That’s right: I’m on the verge of changing the world. Percy Oil? We’re buying up the non-profit company, ‘Dream Labs’. They’re the current leaders in cancer-treating technologies. I’m pouring three billion into their efforts, as well as into charity for families in need. Also, as of today? Dream Labs is no longer a non-profit. It’s public!”
Applause resounds. The screen flashes through images of waterfalls, canyons, birds, and cheery people. A rapturous score overtakes the imagery, and narration begins.
“Our world is a beautiful, delicate place. It needs our protection. Our intervention. We’re about to make that intervention.”
Danner joins in.
“We have the chance to end cancer. To bring hope to millions.”
“Suckers,” Danner said, slamming the door of his limo shut.
He lit a cigarette and shoved it in his mouth. Taking a deep inhale and leaning back, he said, “Bliss. God, I needed this.”
He cocked his head to the left. A man in a lab coat sat there, his head tucked into his chest. He locked his hands into a lopsided pyramid.
“So, fatty,” Danner said, rubbing his hands together. “What did you think?”
“It — it was definitely something sir,” the man said. He gave a feeble gesture to the nametag on his chest. “Also, it’s… It’s not fatty.”
Danner slapped his knees, and his cigarette nearly flew from his mouth. “Yeah, and I’m Madonna reincarnate. You are what you are, not what you aren’t. Get over it.”
“I’m Dr. Malden.”
“Dr. Mandy? Ha! That has to be the gayest name I’ve heard in some time.”
“Malden.”
“Whatever.”
Danner faked a yawn. A twinge of irritation rose in Dr. Malden’s chest. He opened his mouth. He pursed his lips.

“I’m going to rake in so much cash over this,” Danner continued. He made several punches at the air before landing a punch on his tinted window. “I mean, a cancer foundation that actually works for profit? It’s genius. I can’t believe that nobody thought of it sooner.”
Dr. Malden shrank in his seat. He swept away the thin hair from his forehead and dabbed himself with a handkerchief. Had the limo gotten hotter? It felt so.
His throat spasmed as he was slapped in the back.
“Come on, you’re in a limo with the biggest billionaire in Texas! This is supposed to be a hoot. Isn’t this supposed to be a hoot, Jeeves?”
Danner tossed his cigarette, gave a whistle, and unrolled the driver’s dividing screen. “You’ve been to my casino, right Jeeves? It’s killer, right?”
The driver gave a knowing nod and rolled the window back up. Turning back to Dr. Malden, Danner had a hearty laugh. Dr. Malden’s pulse skipped a beat. The car seemed to gyrate.
“We’re going to a casino?”
“We are now. It’s my casino, so it’s great. The dumbest people alive blow all sorts of cash there. At poker, you can beat just about any of them.”
He would’ve continued but was hit by a coughing fit. His pupils went small, if for but a moment, before he pulled himself back.
With a wheeze, Danner mustered a, “Sorry…  Sorry.”
The tension in Dr. Malden’s chest released a bit. A smile grew in the corner of the mouth. His hand wiped it away. What was he thinking? Smiling was bad. Wrong. The man was in pain.
Though, the man was a pain…
Dr. Malden stared at the ceiling. He needed to get control over himself and the situation, that was all. Putting out his arm, he gave Danner a pat on the back.
“I want to know why you really brought me here,” Dr. Malden said. “Be — because, I don’t think you just want to take me to a casino.”
Danner smirked. A flash of fury erupted in his eyes. Danner smacked Dr. Malden’s hand away.
“No crap. You really think I give a damn about you?”

Danner fell back in his seat. His gaze was lost to the air. Dr. Malden clutched his briefcase, his muscles tensing. There wasn’t any restraint to this man. Just pure, animalistic impulse. Pitiful, truly.

“I’m sorry if I’ve invoked anger,” Dr. Malden said, measuring his words. One wrong word, and he could lose his job. “I’m just trying to get to the root of this interaction, is all. If you could just—.”
Danner scoffed and gave a loose twirl of his hand. “You can cut it out, kay? I’ve been sober for an hour, so I’m not in the mood to play verbal chess… I know why you’re here. You know too.”
“I do?”
“What? Are you suddenly a… A bigger idiot than I thought, or something? I told you to bring the cure thingy for a reason.”

A rock fell through Dr. Malden’s chest. Of course, this meeting was about the cure. He should’ve known. There was no hope at a promotion. There were no business secrets to be exchanged. Just pure talk. At least Danner had been blunt.
The briefcase leapt to Dr. Malden’s lap. He unclipped it, and it snapped open. A faint glow lapped at Dr. Malden’s face.
“How wonderful,” said Danner, his words slurring into one. “You have a light show set up for it, and everything.”
“It’s UV radiation, in order to preserve the —.”
“Yeah, whatever. Hand it over. You’re getting paid to know the science stuff, not to explain it to me, alright?”

Danner snatched the briefcase before Dr. Malden could even lift it. A glint skimmed Danner’s eye as his hands grubbed through the case. A black lump of metal lifted out and crawled along Danner’s hand.
“Stop that,” Dr. Malden said. “It’s dangerous. You need to keep it on the regulators, or it could go rogue — you could get us both killed.”
Danner sneered. “How does this thing work, eh doc?”

Dr. Malden’s mind was pure blank space. Restraining a quiver, he said, “It — it’s nanotechnology. It’s designed to read the cell receptors of every cell and identify the ones that are cancerous. At least, that’s the idea. We’re still in very early stages though. If you let that thing crawl around you, it might consume all your cells. And mine. It — it’s not tested enough, yet.”
Danner chuckled as the metal crawled over his skin. “Sorry, but this stuff is too fun for me to give two damns about that.”
“It’s killed all of our lab rats during every test we’ve performed with it.”
“Yeah, and cancer kills too. Your point?”
“This kills faster. Much faster.”

Danner eyed Dr. Malden. His face went gaunt. It wasn’t until Dr. Malden blinked that Danner turned away, and Dr. Malden could breathe again. Danner must have been testing him. That, or Danner was insane.
In any case, Danner removed the glob of metal from his wrist, and shoved it back in the case.
“That came off easier than I thought,” Danner said with a grin.
“Like I was trying to say before, the case emits a UV radiation signature that renders the nanobots inert.”
Danner nodded, but ran his fingers along the edges of his watch.

“You’re the leader of this project. How long do you think you dweebs would need to get this thing operational?” Danner asked. “Mind you, I’m about to pour three billion bucks into the company. That can all go toward your project, if need be. I’m even willing to make the number bigger. Money is no object.”

“Thank you for the gesture. Though, this nanotech project is a side-venture to Dream Corp… Just a fairy tale, really. There are countless kinks we need to refine, before we could even consider calling it a success. Honestly? Dream Corp has considered scrapping this whole thing.”
“Tell me the time.”
“Huh?”
Danner’s eyes lasered in.
Dr. Malden swallowed. “It depends on what you mean. That’s a very packed question. If you want —.”
“Tell. Me. The time!”
“Give us two years, and we might have a prototype that’s ready for human testing.”
Danner put his head in his hands. “Holy hell…”
Dr. Malden’s chest was crushed under an anvil. He gave himself a makeshift massage on the shoulder.
“Of course, two years is assuming we get the proper funding, the proper staff, and that everything goes according to plan… I’m really sorry but — but...”
“Sorry but what?”

The words came out as ice. The limo halted. The red glow of a traffic light cast across Danner’s face. Danner’s fist pounded into the window. He went to Dr. Malden’s throat. His hand was sandpaper against Dr. Malden’s skin.

Danner bared his teeth, the gold ones giving a glare. “Sorry… but I already spoke to Dream Corps’ executives. Sorry, but I was told you guys can get closer than two years. Sorry, but you need to have this cure ready in six months. Sorry, but that’s all the time I have. Sorry, but if you don’t do this, you’re screwed.”
Danner loosened his grip and leaned back in his seat. Purple drained from Dr. Malden’s face, air rushing back to him. The limo’s engine kicked back into a thrum.
Danner lit another cigarette and gave a wry grin. “So, how much do you feel like gambling, tonight? Me? I’m going all in.”

The storm lashed at Dr. Malden. Clothes drenched to the skin, Dr. Malden grimaced. He kicked at a puddle of mud. A chill overcame his muscles, leaving them quaking. They stiffened. His eyes went to his watch, then to the sign behind him. “San Antonio Texas Airport.”

“It’s going to be easy, this time” Danner had said. “I won’t need to fly you out to Dallas. You just need to head to San Antonio Texas Airport. It should only be about twenty minutes from where you’re at. They have an airstrip, for private planes. Show them your I.D. and they’ll let you in. My flight will be there by 12:00, sharp.”
So much for that. By “12:00”, had Danner meant midnight? At this point, anything was possible.
“There you are, chunk-o!”

Dr. Malden squinted. Danner was up ahead, if far off. He’d finally arrived — albeit, surrounded by an entourage that carried a canopy over him.
