Though, the more Dr. Malden thought, the more that Danner’s arrival didn’t add up. Not a single plane had landed in the entirety of the past two hours. Had Danner just materialized, out of thin air?

Tightening his grip on his briefcase, Dr. Malden sprinted toward Danner. He only made it a quarter of the way, before gasping for air. His gym membership was getting paid, but clearly wasn’t paying off.
After a few minutes of wheezing, several sloshes drew up to him. The downpour ceased. There was a light tap on his shoulder.
“Sorry about the wait,” Danner said. “I realize we’re both busy men. But I had pertinent matters to attend to. Here — take a seat.”

A wide canopy yawned over Dr. Malden. To each side of him were leather chairs, juxtaposed against the airstrip’s harsh concrete. Climbing from his knees, Dr. Malden walked toward one. Rainwater rolled down his face, and into his eyes. His sopping pants rubbed against his thighs.
He was going to be left with a terrible rash, thanks to this. The baby lotion in his apartment probably wouldn’t cut it. Dr. Malden suppressed a moan.
“Actually, that’s the good one,” Danner said, as Dr. Malden was sitting down. “Sit in the other one.”
Gingerly, Dr. Malden complied. He could already feel fresh beads of sweat mixing with the rainwater on his face.
After Dr. Malden had adjusted himself in the new seat, and then readjusted, Danner plopped himself in the good seat.
“So,” Danner said, with a grin, “is the weather normally this abysmal, or is today just an exception?”
“Hard to say. But, normally, you definitely don’t need to sit out in the rain for hours.”

Danner pulled his foot over his knee and clicked his tongue. “I wasn’t really out in the rain for hours, thankfully. The plane shielded me from it. Actually, sitting in that plane wasn’t too bad. I had the craziest round of snorts betting — sorry, sports betting — craziest round of that, of ever. Did you know that making bets is a thousand times better when you’re doing cocaine?”
Dr. Malden scrunched his eyes. “I’ve been out here for three hours, and I never saw or heard your plane land.”
Danner held his hand out. A bodyguard handed him a cigarette, which he shoved in his mouth. As he lit it, he gave a shrug.

“You shouldn’t have. My plane landed at 11:00. About an hour earlier than I expected. I hate being early — it means you put in all that extra effort, to get somewhere before you’re supposed to — so that sucked… But, hey, sports betting.”
“You left me out here, waiting for you for three hours, to gamble?”

“Officially, I was managing my new charity’s funds.” Danner chuckled. Dr. Malden didn’t chuckle along. “What? You upset that you were left out? I thought you hated fun. We can do something later, if you really want.”
A knot formed between Dr. Malden’s eyes. “Yeah. I’d love that.”

Danner’s face went smug, and he rubbed his hands together. “So, time to get down to business. I’ve given you and your team a month. Two hundred million dollars have been spent. I need to see what you’ve done with all of that time.”
Dr. Malden nodded his head. He’d imagined that he’d be able to maintain composure during Danner’s questionings.
Dr. Malden gave a gulp.
“Yes, well… We’ve nearly tripled the size of the research team so far. I would have expanded farther, but it’s becoming a bit too much to manage. We need to adjust. It’ll probably —.”
Danner clapped his hands, then rubbed them together again. This time, he wasn’t smiling.
“Good. Great. Now, shut up about that, and tell me the thing I want you to tell me: how is the cure coming along?”
“But, I was telling you that.”
“Funny, because that’s not what I’m hearing. You like your job, Dr. Malden?”
The temptation to give a cold “no” ate at Dr. Malden. Instead, he said, “Apologies. The experiments… They’ve… Well, I suppose you’d prefer to see for yourself, wouldn’t you?”
“Yes. Straight to the point. It’s about time.”

Dr. Malden unclipped his suitcase and handed it to Danner. The glow shone from the briefcase as bright as ever. It was harsher on Dr. Malden’s eyes than last time. Perhaps it was due to one too many sleepless nights, or perhaps it was due to the tweaks he’d made in radiation levels. Either way, he had to look away.
“Looks good,” Danner said, bobbing his head. “I… Suppose that it can be shot into my blood-stream now correct?”

Danner’s voice withered away before he’d finished. He was cautious to even look at the nanobots. He already knew the answer to his question. The suitcase was shoved back into Dr. Malden’s lap, and a smoldering cigarette fell to the ground to be crushed by Danner’s heel.

“The tests have still been abysmal, so far…” Dr. Malden said. “There have been improvements, no doubt. The nanobots seem to have become more efficient at locating and killing cancer cells. Though, the mortality rates of lab rats remain at 100%. We’re still trying to figure out why but, after the nanobots reproduce three generations, they go after any type of cell.”
Dr. Malden considered continuing but stopped at the flare of Danner’s lighter.
“I just want to know,” Danner said, “what do you do in your spare time?”

The muscles of Danner’s neck were tense, and his eyebrows arched. He made a leer. One the canopy’s arms buckled in an upsweep of wind. Two of the bodyguards scrambled to keep it up, while the rain flung sideways, backwards, and upside down.
“I’m spending seventy hours a week, working on this project,” Dr. Malden said. He heard his voice crack. He forged ahead. “Ten hours a day. Every day.”
“That’s not what I asked.”
Danner tossed his second cigarette to the side, only for the wind to whip it at Dr. Malden’s face. Dr. Malden gave a narrow duck.
“I — I like taking long walks. Tv shows are fun, too. 70s sitcoms, mainly. Everything else on Tv is a bit too… Cynical. I like to oil paint when I can, as well. Fun, but a pretty expensive hobby.”
“Definitely pretty expensive…”
Danner brushed his hand through his hair and stood from his chair, taking a stance of repose.

He lunged at Dr. Malden, with the face of a honey badger. Dr. Malden raised his hands, cowering. He was saved by a bodyguard, who held Danner firmly by the shoulders. Danner tried a few thrusts against the bodyguard, before slumping his shoulders and taking a step back.
Danner flashed a smile.

“Sorry. I get a little…” His arms turned to iron, and his back arched. “I just don’t get how you can only spend seventy hours! Do you realize how much I’m paying you?! Do you realize that you still have another forty-two hours in the week that you aren’t giving me!? That’s time you’re burning through, that I don’t have! What in the hell do you think you’re doing!?”
Dr. Malden trembled, terrified. Danner made a grunt.
Wait — had there been a quiver in Danner’s lip? There must have been. A bit of Dr. Malden’s fear receded to the back of his mind. He stood from his chair and glowered down at Danner.

“I think I’m trying to save your life,” Dr. Malden said. “I’m giving this project all that I know. I’m trying everything. You want to make me do more? Try it: I’m gone. There are plenty of other places that will take me. What do you do with your time? Waste the money of your investors and donors? Some way to spend the last days of your miserable life!”
Danner’s mouth twitched. He grinned. “Get the out of here then.”
“What?”
“Get out. Go back to your cruddy apartment, and spend the day watching Tv for all I care.”
Dr. Malden shrugged his shoulders and stepped into the rain.
“Hey! What the hell do you think you’re doing?!”
Dr. Malden looked back. Danner was holding the suitcase over his head. “You’re not leaving here without this. You still have a job to do.”
The computer screen had gone incoherent. Dr. Malden closed his eyes and reopened them, hoping the screen might change. However, the data displayed on it remained an enigma to him.
He could have used some sleep. Though, the project could have also used a few extra hours. There had to be a way to explain the outliers in the data. It couldn’t have just been a fluke.
There was a knock at the door.
“I’m busy,” Dr. Malden said. “If you need somebody to recheck the samples with, go to Mark.”
Another knock resounded.
Dr. Malden raised his eyebrows and scooted his chair further into his desk. “Listen: I can’t talk right now.”
“Not even to me, bud?”
The door swung open and rattled into the wall. Danner stepped in, a grin on his face.
“Nice to have you pop in,” Dr. Malden said, eyes still fixed to his computer. “Where are the bodyguards? Hiding in the ventilation shafts, this time around?”
Danner gently closed the door. It gave a click as it locked. Danner shoved his hands in the pockets of his trench coat.
“No bodyguards this time.”
Danner pulled his lighter out, flipped it in the air, then caught it. “So… I heard some interesting whispers about the project.”
Dr. Malden huffed. “Glad you heard that. Me? Guess my hearing is shot… Nothing is adding up, and I just can’t get rid of this buzzing inside my head. I’m exhausted”
Dr. Malden’s mouth tightened after he’d said this. He didn’t need to tell Danner anything. Danner would exploit any sign of weakness.
“Stop playing coy,” Danner said, patting Dr. Malden on the shoulder. “I have a clear idea of what’s going on in this place, at all times. Don’t ever forget that.”
“How could I?”
Danner crossed his arms. “Look… I heard that there was finally a successful lab rat. Is that true?”
“It might be.”
“Malden… Talk to me.”

Danner spun Dr. Malden. A twinge of fear went through Dr. Malden, before morphing to concern. Danner was gaunt now. His skin was gruffer, seeming to have aged several years. Moreover, the confidence that had once oozed from him had drained dry.

“I’m not… I’m not doing that,” Dr. Malden said, trying to assert a sense of composure. “Look… We did have a successful lab rat. But that’s all it was. It’s only been a month since the tumors left the rat’s system, and the rat has shown no signs of issues yet. Though, it’s possible that this rat carries a unique mutation. Or, maybe the strand of nanobots we inserted was different somehow… Besides, maybe the tumors will reemerge. There are just too many unknowns.”
A solemn look fell on Danner’s face. Though, more crushing was that his eyes didn’t lose their starry tinge.
“Still, it was a successful test subject,” Danner said. “The cure might be on the road to working.”

Dr. Malden looked back to the rows of charts and formulas on his computer screen. “Yes. But, it’ll be a few more months of testing before we know what’s going on for sure. Then, another year of tests. And then, a few years of careful human testing, if all goes well. Time will tell.”
Danner put his hand on Dr. Malden. It was practically bone when contrasted against Dr. Malden’s flesh.
“Those last two steps won’t matter in my case though, right?” Danner’s eyes went misty. “If those tests start to come back positive… You’ll start testing on me. Right?”
Dr. Malden gave a terse nod. It was all he could bring himself to do.
“I know it’s rough. We’re doing all we can.”

“You don’t know the half of it… I’ve been trying the homeopathic route. Shirking the stupid big pharma. But it doesn’t seem to be making a difference… Every day, I drop another pound. My head is fuzzy. My body is getting weaker. This needs to stop, as soon as it can. Promise me, that it’ll all end soon.”
“If I can end it for you, I will. That’s a promise.”
Danner bit his lip. Water flooded the brims of his eyes. He leaned into the wall and slumped to the ground.

“It’s fine,” he said. “With all my funding, you’ll find it eventually. Maybe you can cure other people. At any rate, I’ll be cryogenically reserved. Somebody will cure me. That is, once the science behind defrosting me is finally figured out…”
He gave a weak laugh and clutched his chest. When he pulled his hand back, he was holding a slip of paper. He waved it for a moment, as though it were a flag of surrender.
“Once again, I’m very sorry,” Dr. Malden said. His fingers slipped on the keyboard.
“No need to apologize. You’re good. This is for you, by the way.”
Dr. Malden looked over. “What?”
Danner unfolded the paper and held it in front of himself. A blurry image of a painting was printed along it. “When I go for surprises, I make sure I go big.”
Dr. Malden’s hands went clammy. “That’s a picture of…”

“It’s one of Picasso’s last works, yes. I bought it. Had it sent to your apartment. Figured you could use it in your collection — doubt you have much else in there that’s even better than what you can find in a garbage bin.”
“I don’t — that’s amazing. Thank you.”
While Dr. Malden’s mind swam, and he wondered where to put the painting, then wondered if he should even keep it at all, Danner headed for the door.

“I’m going to host a charity event in a month,” Danner said. “A party, at my place. Thirty million dollars will be going to various charities. Hopefully more, if I can convince some of my friends to chip in… Be there.”
The paper slipped out of Danner’s hand and glided to Dr. Malden’s feet.
“I will.”
The ground trembled. Wind mourned, as the moon abandoned the sky. A hot flash of anxiety traveled through Dr. Malden’s head, before searing his chest.
Elbows jabbed Dr. Malden. He struggled to keep his balance and head about him. Craning his neck over somebody’s shoulder, he saw a house standing in the distance, its windows flickering. Taunting.

Sweat dewed Dr. Malden’s skin. He needed more room but, even as he nudged a few people along, they only seemed to sandwich closer. Rows of potted plants narrowed on each side of him, only exacerbating the claustrophobia.

As the line filtered through a bodyguard, Dr. Malden fumbled his wallet out of his pocket and pulled out his I.D. Before he handed it over, he gave it a second glance. The man in the image hadn’t been seen for years. He looked slightly slimmer than Dr. Malden. His eyes held a gleam to them. He had yet to adopt deep bags and age lines.
“Name, please.”
The bodyguard’s tight sleeves rippled and the veins on his forearms popped. Shakily, Dr. Malden held out his ID.
“Dr. Malden,” he said. “I’m a friend of Danner.”
The bodyguard made a bemused face and thumbed through his clipboard. His other hand hovered over the taser hanging from his pocket.
“Oh, yes,” the bodyguard. “I see now — Danner has a restraining order on you. You aren’t supposed to be within a thirty-yard radius of where Danner is.”
The taser sparked, its teeth edging toward Dr. Malden’s face.
“There — there must be some sort of mistake,” Dr. Malden said, his voice melting. “Please— I’m Danner’s friend. If you just let me see him, I promise…”
“Rargh!”
There was a flare of light. Dr. Malden jumped, and the glasses flew off his face. A wheezing laughter broke out, with a hand resting on Dr. Malden’s shoulder.
“You — oh my God, you should’ve seen your face!”
Danner was standing there, a knocked over plant left in his wake.
Dr. Malden’s heart still feeling as though it might tear in half, Dr. Malden said, “I — I don’t understand.”
“That prank is going to go down in the history books, am I right boys?”
Danner was met with a chorus of cheers. A crowd of men with beers in hand were on Danner’s lawn. Danner lifted his own beer, only to turn away and drop it by his side.
“Just a stupid joke,” Danner said, giving Dr. Malden a slap on the back.
Dr. Malden tried to smile but was already being rushed from the line and to the entrance of Danner’s property.
“Hey Danner, you’re looking good!” a woman called after Danner.
“Thanks, I’ve been trying,” Danner managed, pulling Dr. Malden along.
A man yanked at Danner’s sleeve, only for Danner to swat him away.
“Danner, do you want to go to my place after this? I have a new jacuzzi and business pitch, calling your name!”
Danner dovetailed into an empty hallway, only to trip over a couple of people sprawled on the ground, huffing copious amounts of smoke.
“I feel so alive,” one of them murmured.
“Greg Hare?” Danner asked, shocked. He then shook his head and sped away.
“I’m feeling great, man,” they continued. “Here, you want to try some? You’ll be on top of the world.”

Dr. Malden was already on top of the world. Danner’s mansion was engineered for gratification, each turn more stimulating than the last. Every step synchronized with a shift in sound, lighting, or atmosphere.
Danner stopped at a wall, near a couple of restrooms. His hands felt along it, before finally landing on a slab of rock. The wall fell inward, and then slid out to reveal an entrance.
“Hmm… Good. This should give us some privacy.”
Danner snapped his head around and gave Dr. Malden a wink. Dr. Malden followed him into the darkness. The concrete slab shut behind him, and an array of lights went aglow.
The room was adorned with various television screens, gaming tables, and a mini bar. However, Danner sat at a coffee table in the center, his eyes transfixed by a moose head hanging from the wall.
“Take a seat,” Danner said.
Sheepishly, Dr. Malden dragged a chair to the table. All the while, he felt the moose’s gaze following him.
“I know you don’t really like parties, or living large,” Danner said. “But, I wanted to give you a taste of fun… Figured that you and me could play a game in here. Anything you’d like.”

Dr. Malden took a glance around the room. It’d been ages since he’d played a game of ice hockey. The Tv might have something good on. Yet, the more his eyes jumped, the more their focus waned. Everything promised sensation, but nothing promised substance.
A chuckle left Dr. Malden’s throat, followed by a, “I’ll let you choose. I have no idea what’s good.”

The room squirmed, muffled music penetrating its walls. Danner inched his hand toward a remote, before letting it drop. He swung his head to the back of his chair and stared at the ceiling. Dr. Malden’s eyes followed, hoping there was something there.
There wasn’t.
“Yeah, I don’t know what we should do either,” Danner said. He rubbed his forehead. “I don’t even know what I’m doing here… Why did I bring you here?”
Dr. Malden offered a laugh.
Danner gave a glare. “I’m serious. Why did I bring you here? I want an answer.”
“That — well, I really am in no position to say, now am I?”

Danner’s face reddened. His eyes flared. Danner had never struck Dr. Malden as too bright. Though, that didn’t dampen the impact of Danner’s demeanor. He looked as though he’d finally gone crazy. That, or hysterical. It must have been something between the two.

“I’m sorry.” Danner’s hand shielded his eyes. “I’ve been trying so hard to do it all. The partying, the philanthropy, the meetings with stockholders, the meetings with lawyers… I need to leave my stamp on the world, before I go out.”
“You’re not happy with the stamp you’ve left?”

“No, no, not at all!” Danner switched on a smile. “Not that at all. I’m definitely happy. The suits or whatever showed me some charts. Millions of dollars are being spent, but millions of lives are being helped. It’s great.”
Danner’s hand jerked back to the remote and flipped on the Tv. He let the noises blare for a few moments.

“The doctors are telling me I only have a few months left. Even if I try switching to chemo, it’s not going to make a difference. I’m happy. I just wasn’t expecting the legend to end this way, you know?”
“That’s… That’s a great point. Rough… You’re in a really rough place.”
Dr. Malden’s mouth was a desert. Parched, he searched for the right words to say. All he found were tumbleweeds.

Danner nodded at Dr. Malden. “Thanks. It’s nice to know that there’s at least one doctor out there who can talk straight. I didn’t want to tell you this until after I was… Well, I might as well tell you now: nine billion is going to go into your research department, after I’m gone. Half my wealth. A few years back, I’d planned on having all my wealth in my will spent on my funeral… But, hey: a nine-billion-dollar funeral is still an insane funeral, right?”
Smirking, Danner flipped through the channels on the Tv. The screen spinning and flipping left Dr. Malden woozy. His stomach curdled.
“I can’t thank you enough.”
“Don’t mention it.”
The Tv finally stopped on a news broadcast, covering one of Danner’s latest charity drives. Danner’s eyes went wide, sucking in the entire image.

Dr. Malden cleared his throat. “Suppose things had gone differently… Suppose you were miraculously cured, and all of this ended. How much more do you think you would’ve been able to accomplish, with all those extra years?”

“I would’ve broken the record for the most amount of shots taken in one sitting, for starters. But seriously, if I had that cure? I’d patent it and sell it everywhere.  Everything would change. I’d be three times richer, ten times healthier, and living life large again. Having a blast doing it. I wouldn’t be caught up in all of this pedantic crap, that’s for sure…”
“Well, thank you again for the funding. You have no idea how much it will change things.”
“Oh, I do.”
A weak laugh passed between them, followed by firm handshake. Dr. Malden left for the concrete door.
“By the way,” Danner said, “where did you end up putting that painting I bought you?”
Dr. Malden shrugged.
“I ended up donating it to a museum. I figured it was safer with them than it could ever be with me...”
The lab’s lights flicker off. Only a small light remains, at the center. The incinerator ebbs the heat of ash and embers.

A hand hovers over the incinerator, casting a shadow along the linoleum. Its grip is tight, its knuckles white. There’s the gleam of glass as the hand edges closer to the incinerator’s flame. The hand is holding a vial.
Then, it’s not. The vial falls into the flame. A cruel shatter resounds and is met by rising smoke.
“I’m sorry Danner… But, you weren’t ready to know.”
There’s the rattle of a cage. A chorus of squeaks.
One by one, rats fall into the flames.
“Nobody can know.”
End

title: The Gas Station Off Quaker Drive
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth

Rain sheeted endlessly and clogged the ground's arteries, smudging stretching cornfields with the road. The clouds roared at the rain's betrayal but to no avail. The rain remained deaf to them. Only the floorboard to Mr. Thorpe's truck heeded the clouds' bellows, shuddering in fear.

Mr. Thorpe took in a deep breath and tightened his grip around the steering wheel. He flipped the switch to his wipers. Even so, the windshield remained pocked with fat raindrops. The truck hiccupped as it ran over a pothole, sending Mr. Thorpe's glasses into glass.
Just what he needed — his vision to be ten times blurrier.

Keeping one hand on the steering wheel, he groped for his glasses. His body shifted to the side as the truck swerved. Shoving his glasses back on his face, Mr. Thorpe realigned with the road. The truck hummed as Mr. Thorpe's heart rate lowered.

His forehead was glazed with sweat and his throat screamed of thirst. The summer heat was relentless. He turned up the air conditioning when the car tripped over a pothole, sending Mr. Thorpe's hand into another button. The moonroof cracked open, sending rain down like hellfire. Mr. Thorpe's hand fumbled wildly. Finally, he landed on the button to his moonroof and put it back down.
His car and his clothes were soaked. The nerves in his body were shot. At least he was slightly cooler.

Who was he kidding? This road-trip had been a bust from the very beginning. All he'd wanted was a little reprieve from his snotty summer school students. That wasn't so unreasonable for a math teacher, was it?
Apparently, the weather didn’t agree. Just his luck.

Lightning scraped along the skyline. A fresh layer of rain sent the truck skidding. Thuds resounded from the back of the truck as his toolbox and oil can were flung about. The truck's exhaust coughed and Mr. Thorpe struggled to keep control, listening to the engine's strength wax and wane.
He glanced at the fuel gauge. Only a gallon remained. Not much of a problem; he could fill it with the can he had in the back. Then he glanced at a warning light — his tires were low.

Mr. Thorpe's eyes widened. He could practically see his taxed truck veering to the side of the road with a flat tire. Where would he go? What would he do? He was in the middle of nowhere without so much as a map or GPS to guide him. Glancing at his charger, he clenched his jaw. It'd snapped several hours ago, sentencing his phone to death. Why couldn't he have had the sense to bring his good charger?
His breaths tided in and out. This trip was wretched. Yet, it could've been worse. He needed to make the most of it while it lasted. There was no point in letting the weather put him under.
Locking his gaze straight ahead, his body relaxed. Once he got out of this storm, all of this would seem insignificant. It was just a small blip in the grand scheme of things.

Mr. Thorpe squinted. Something blotted the edge of his windshield. Mud? He turned up his wipers. It didn't budge. Moreover, the blot was growing and taking form. What was it? Whatever it was, it must've been outside the windshield rather than on it. It was also getting closer.
It wasn't on the windshield. But soon it would be.

Mr. Thorpe slammed his brakes. After a moment of refusal, the truck slowed its speed. Its headlights set the blot aglow, morphing it into a demonic specter. No — a man. Mr. Thorpe checked his speedometer. He was slowing but not fast enough.

Dear God! He was going to kill a man. There was no way that Elming Middle School would take him back after this. All his students… they'd be horrified, though some would be delighted, but mostly horrified. Hopefully. And the parents… they'd be after him, too. Forget the parents — the police would assuredly want him detained. He'd be in prison for years, possibly decades.
Some vacation.
Mr. Thorpe's hands jittered. His left went running down his pant leg, and his right slammed his horn. Yet the man was only a few feet away, and he didn't move.
The truck didn't move. It jerked to a halt.
Mr. Thorpe let out a relieved wheeze. He checked his pulse — One-hundred-and-fifty beats per minute. Dr. Ulysses was going to give him hell if he heard about this.

His body felt as frail as wet paper. Despite this, he mustered the resolve to glare ahead. The man was a statue, letting rain drench his skin before spouting off his body. From under the hood of his thick jacket, strands of hair hung in his face and clung to his skin. However, what captivated Mr. Thorpe was the man's gaze. Rather, the lack of it. His eyes were fixed on the asphalt, oblivious to the steaming hood of Mr. Thorpe's truck.
"What are you doing!? Get out of the road!" Mr. Thorpe shouted. At least, he tried to shout. The words came out as a shrill squeak. The stress had left his lungs breathless.

There was no point in trying to reason with the man. Mr. Thorpe's hand rested on his shift stick, preparing to go in reverse when the stranger’s eyes jumped up. Had he heard Mr. Thorpe's shouts? It didn't matter. The miscreant must've been mad, if not worse.

The man broke into a sprint and rapped his fingers along the driver’s side door. Mr. Thorpe's foot hovered over the gas, preparing to fly off. It would serve the idiot right for standing in the road in the middle of a storm. Then Mr. Thorpe saw the desperation filling the man's eyes. He watched the way they flitted wildly, from the back of the truck, to the road, to Mr. Thorpe. Mr. Thorpe's chest fluttered. In a moment of irrationality, he rolled the window down.
The man poked his head through. "Could I hitch a ride with you?"
"H-Hitch a ride?" Mr. Thorpe stammered, rain spraying into his face.
This was already a bad idea. What had he been thinking?
"Yes," the man said, stroking his stubble. "My buddy ditched me here. He was giving me a ride to work when we got into a fight. Didn't end well."
While the man had a rugged look to him, his voice was smooth and fluid. Moreover, his eyes were sharp. Mr. Thorpe pushed his glasses up the bridge of his nose. This was more than he'd bet on.
"I'm Joe, by the way," the man said. He offered a sopping hand.
Mr. Thorpe took it before promptly wiping his own hand off. "Joe..." Mr. Thorpe said.

He suddenly realized he still hadn't put his car in park. Frantically, he switched gears before looking back at Joe. The name really did fit him, didn't it? Yet, Mr. Thorpe couldn't put his finger on why.
"Well, I'm sorry to hear about all that, Joe," Mr. Thorpe said, "but I really wasn't planning on bringing any hitchhikers aboard today. I, uh... well..."
"I'm not that far from here," Joe said. "I'm just at the gas station, off Quaker Drive. Shatley's. It's impossible to miss."

Joe puffed out his chest and raised himself to his full height. He was a tall man of brawny build. Mr. Thorpe looked into Joe's eyes. They had a familiar glint to them. Where did he remember seeing them? Suddenly, Mr. Thorpe was taken back to his countless skirmishes with delinquent students. They always had ‘cunning’ spelled across their faces, and Joe shared this look.

At least, that's what it seemed. But, what if Mr. Thorpe was just seeing things? If Joe had wanted to pull something, he already could've. Besides, his face was pallid, his body was shivering, and his clothes were drenched. Mr. Thorpe bit his lip. He'd have to be heartless to abandon the man in such a state.

Mr. Thorpe needed a place to refuel anyway, and it'd be a downright nightmare to refuel on the side of the road. His tires were also in dire need of being pumped. Plus, Joe would probably be able to give directions out of this godforsaken Hick-Ville.
Mr. Thorpe gave Joe a thin smile, only to have Joe clasp his fingers along the edge of the door. His nostrils flared in annoyance.

"Y-You can give me... you can show me the way there, right?" Mr. Thorpe asked. The muscles in his neck tensed. This was a huge mistake. Why couldn't the worth of a person be as self-evident as a theorem?
"Thanks!" Joe's body shunted the car making it creak to the left. Was Joe really that excited? It was hard to tell — his head was turned toward the back of the truck.
Joe pointed his thumb to the left. "Is it alright if I go grab my things and throw them in the back?"
"Why, of course," Mr. Thorpe said. While you're at it, why don't you bring a tent, a mattress, and some food? he thought but didn't say.

Joe was already off. Mr. Thorpe watched as he ran to a worn stop sign on the edge of the road. The "T" had chipped away, leaving only "S OP". Joe dipped into the ditch before running back to the truck with a large duffle bag. Mr. Thorpe crossed his fingers, hoping to God there wasn't a body in the bag.
Please don't be a body in that bag.

There was a soft thud as the bag was tossed in the back. Joe opened the passenger door and hopped in. A splash of water followed him, smearing the side of Mr. Thorpe's face and dousing the passenger seat.
A rash crawled up Mr. Thorpe's skin. His car was going to smell like dog for weeks. There was no telling how many air fresheners he'd have to stuff in it.
"Thanks again," Joe said, putting a clammy hand on Mr. Thorpe's shoulder. Mr. Thorpe shirked to the side only for Joe to tighten his grip. "Now, go. Go! What are you waiting for?"

Joe was clearly out of his mind if he thought he could just give orders like Mr. Thorpe was some chaperone. Yet, as Joe opened his mouth again, an anxiety rose in Mr. Thorpe's chest. He shifted into drive and floored the gas.
Mr. Thorpe's eardrums were of the sensitive variety. He couldn't afford to entreat senseless shouts. Yes — that was all it had been about.
Timidly, he glanced to the side. Joe placed his feet on the dashboard and ran his finger between his teeth. Drips of water plinked from the tips of Joe’s boots, forming a puddle.
"I appreciate you giving me directions to the nearest gas station," Mr. Thorpe said, fighting to keep his voice above a squeak. "But, where are we going, exactly?"
"Straight, for now," Joe said. He pulled off his hood, letting a mane of hair spill out behind him, followed by trickling water.

Mr. Thorpe was only a thin strand from seething. Yet, what could he do? It was too late to turn around and dump Joe back out. Besides, they'd be at the gas station soon enough. He just had to hold out a little while longer.
"And after that?" Mr. Thorpe asked coolly, taking care to keep his stress from seeping through.
"Straight. Then not straight. I'll tell you when."
Mr. Thorpe's knuckles went white against his steering wheel. That was it — this idiot needed to be set straight. Mr. Thorpe let his foot off the gas and went to slam the brake.
"So, what do you do for a living?"
Mr. Thorpe set his foot back on the gas. "I like to tell people that I'm a mathematician who happens to teach middle school math in his spare time. Though, it's more the reverse..."
Joe let out a bellowing laugh and slapped his knees. "That's rich."
"You don't… you don't believe I'm a math teacher?"
"No, no..." said Joe, his face going grave. "It's just, I say the same thing all the time. I'm an oil mogul who happens to work at a gas station."
"That's not really the same thing."
"I find ways of getting oil for dirt cheap, all the time... practically for free, sometimes. What else would you call me but an oil mogul?"
Joe's face was fierce. Mr. Thorpe could almost feel his breath baring down on him. Trapped, he could do nothing but swallow and nod in agreement.
Lightning lashed at the horizon followed by another crack of thunder. Was that bolt closer than the last one? It seemed so. Hopefully the trend wouldn't continue.

"So, mathematics, huh? Interesting field," said Joe. "Always hated it myself, though... Never could wrap my head around Pi, or radicals, or any of that garbage. The square root of negative one was always especially confusing. How could there be a square root of a negative number?"
A mixture of annoyance and joy swelled in Mr. Thorpe's chest.

"The square root of negative one isn't as confusing as it seems. While all square roots are positive numbers, the square root of negative one isn't just any number — it's an imaginary number. It goes by a different set of rules. As I tell my students, imagination is a positive, even if the very thing you imagine is negative. There are certain things that you need to imagine, in order for mathematics to make sense."
The concept was so simple — so elegant. It never ceased to amaze Mr. Thorpe how many people had yet to understand it.
Joe shook his head. "Thanks for the lecture, but I'm only here for the ride."
A rock dropped in Mr. Thorpe's chest. He nodded again and set his sights back on the road. "Yes. Of course."

Stretching his arms behind his head, Joe let out a yawn. "It really doesn't make much sense, anyway. You start out by saying mathematics is supposed to be physical. Real. Two plus two... that sort of thing. But then you muck it up with all of your complex concepts, and it loses the point."

"But see, mathematics is real. It's the most real science out there. The system works in a strictly defined way — its complexities arise out of its inherent simplicity. Math is the only thing we can use to truly describe the world around us, so it's no wonder that it can be hard to understand. The world, if you haven’t noticed, is a bit complex."

Rain thrashed at the roof of the truck, and bits of debris hurled at the windshield. Mr. Thorpe took in a deep breath of air. A rush flowed through him, setting him aloft. Despite the testiness of the elements, he was in his element. Mathematics was his language. There was a sharpness to his senses — clarity.
"Turn left."

Mr. Thorpe banked his truck around a bend, onto a narrow dirt road. A forest of grass brushed against the sides of the truck. Trying to cast his gaze ahead, he turned on his bright-lights. Yet, the road was obscured by winding curves and overgrowth. Mr. Thorpe shot a look at Joe.
"It's a short-cut," he said, shrugging his shoulders. "Does that calm you down?"
It should've. A shadow rolled over Joe's face. His hair and eyes shimmered. His lip furled into something like a snarl.

"Anyway, once you accept those concepts, proposing that mathematics is ‘real’ is inherently fallacious," Joe said. His voice sounded foreign, adopting a deep timbre. "You're being willfully ignorant. If there are concepts to mathematics that don't fit with our current understanding of the physical world, that proves mathematics to be nothing more than a fiction."
Mr. Thorpe's pulse quickened. A feebleness possessed his muscles, paralyzing his hands. He gave Joe a sidelong glance. Did he just say what it sounded like he said?

"I-I suppose," Mr. Thorpe said, licking his lips. His tongue was sandpaper, and his throat scraped against his vocal chords. "Though, you're ignoring that mathematics is the basis of all science. Without it, we'd be hopelessly lost. This very road we're driving down — it couldn't have been built without math. I'm sure of it."
"Well, then let's get off of it. Make a left."
Tires squealed as Mr. Thorpe sent his truck into another turn. In his mirror, mud kicked up from the wheels and caked to the sides of the truck.

"So, what you're basically getting at," Joe said, his voice starting slow, "is that math is real because people who believe math is real build things with the belief that math is real. That's circular reasoning, isn't it?"

"No. I'm not saying math is real because people can build things with math. Rather, it's because people can't build things without it. We can't explain things without it. The system is internally consistent."
"Internally consistent. Externally though? Not so much."
What on Earth was he getting at? Lips bobbing, Mr. Thorpe scrambled for words of retort. Yet he came up empty. A flash of malice slashed Joe's face. Then, in a roar of thunder, it evaporated.

"You clearly like circles," Joe said. "I love circles myself. There's something about them — the way they end up never ending, yet always ending all the same. If there's anything in the world that makes sense, it's the circle. Though, math can't explain the length of a circle..."
A snort left Mr. Thorpe's nostrils. "You mean the circumference?" he said. "Please, have you ever heard of Pi? Clearly you've never taken a basic mathematics course."

"Oh, I have. But Pi... it assumes that the circle is perfect. No real circle is. And besides, Pi isn't perfect either. It goes on for an infinite regress, never truly reaching an end. In that way, we can never know the perfect circle, let alone the imperfect, no matter our efforts."
Mr. Thorpe's hairs raised in an unbridled rage. Joe was clearly wrong. It was so easy to dismiss his claims. Yet, how could the simpleton be so adamant? How was he able to get under the skin?

Mr. Thorpe had listened to students moan ad infinitum about mathematics many a time. It'd never fazed him before, only leaving him with a vague sense of pity. Yet now? He was brimming with self-doubt.

"Infinity is another conundrum," Joe continued. "Many will say that infinity goes on forever. Though, that's not quite it. Infinity is forever. Better put, it's a forever. You can add an infinity to an infinity. You can multiply an infinity by an infinity. You can calculate the square root of an infinity. You can split an infinity in half. But, at the same time, you can't. Because always — always — an infinity remains an infinity. How? In what way does that make sense?"
Mr. Thorpe chuckled. "You have a point. Mathematical concepts — they're not always the easiest to wrap our heads around. But that doesn't render its science null and void."
Joe mimicked the chuckle and gave Mr. Thorpe a cold punch to the shoulder. Mr. Thorpe winced and rubbed the spot. Joe's punch had been hard. Too hard.

"It's not a science though. That's where your fundamental error lies: it's a philosophy. The funny thing about philosophy... it’s endless thought, culminating in the knowledge that — well, we have no knowledge."
Mr. Thorpe's body was still reeling from latent anxiety, but he managed to roll his eyes. "You're telling me that you don't believe two plus two equals four?"
"Make a left," Joe said. Then, clearing his throat, "I'm asking you what is two? What is four?"
The tires turned, snickering at Mr. Thorpe's plight. "They're… they're numbers."
"Then show me a number. Dig deep enough, and you'll find that a number is nothing more than a figment."

Letting out a heave, Mr. Thorpe attempted to regather himself. The last thing he'd prepared for was an ontological argument. Yet, at the same time, he had prepared— he'd run this gambit with colleagues before. If only he had his notes on him, this would've been a breeze.

He was always terrible at arguing. His colleagues constantly kept the edge on him; somehow, they knew how to keep their thoughts in line. But, this bum? How on earth was he able to pose a challenge? It defied probability.
"You know a lot for a guy who works at a gas station."
"Mogul."
"I couldn't care less what you call yourself. Do you think this is funny? Because it's not."
"Just trying to have a chat, to make the time go by... that's all."

Chat. The word sounded wrong coming out of Joe's shaggy lips. Moreover, there'd been a marked shift in Joe's demeanor. His hands rested on his pants, which had been neatly ironed out. His posture had straightened. His feet had slid from the dashboard and were planted squarely on the floorboard. Flinching, Mr. Thorpe heard the crack of thunder. Wind rushed at the windshield, muddying the view.
"How long will it be until we arrive at the gas station, anyway?" Mr. Thorpe asked.
Weight laced his voice. It must've been the storm wearing away at him. If he'd planned his vacation for any other day, this all could've been avoided.
"Soon enough. I know it seems long, but that's just how it seems. Trust me: I've been down this road countless times."
Silence encircled them, held back only by the storm's cries. Reluctantly, Mr. Thorpe licked his dry lips and prayed for words to come.
"I trust that you hate teachers?" asked Mr. Thorpe.
"Turn left," Joe said, his voice taking a gruff edge. "I don’t hate teachers. I hate what they do."
Mr. Thorpe was about to laugh before catching Joe's eye and frantically forcing it down. Joe's arm edged close to the steering wheel. Mr. Thorpe's hands tightened.
"And what is that?" Mr. Thorpe said.
"They pretend to teach those that know nothing... yet they know nothing themselves. From nothing, nothing comes.”
Slowing his speed, Mr. Thorpe watched two drops of rain race down his window. As they merged, Mr. Thorpe’s eyes met Joe’s.
“And haven’t you taught me a thing or two?” Mr. Thorpe asked. “Or, at least, tried?”

Joe’s hands tightened before resuming a natural repose. “I didn’t try. I was just bored and thinking. As I see it, the worst thing in the world you can be is bored. That, or a teacher. People are best learning things on their own, rather than having other people force-feed them.”
“And how will people learn to learn, without somebody to show them? They’ll just repeat the same mistakes, and never move knowledge forward.”
“We’d be better for it. The less we know, the lesser our chances of knowing that we can never know. We can only ever go so far, before hitting a wall. Why not never hit it, by just going in a cycle?”
Mr. Thorpe fidgeted in his seat. Joe was, of course, wrong. Though, what could he say? What answer was there?
Raindrops shrunk to thin slivers, and thunder faded to a distant moan. The truck groaned with it, its slackening wheels chewing the gravel.
“Stop!” Joe shouted, jumping in his seat.
Mr. Thorpe slammed his brakes, and his eyes darted about. Was it a deer? He didn’t see one. Maybe it was another person? Acid climbed Mr. Thorpe’s throat — anything but another person.
“What? What is it?”
Joe pointed out the window and undid his seatbelt. “This is my stop.”
A flash of red met the corner of Mr. Thorpe’s eye. He glanced over to find a sign with the word “S OP” printed along it. Mr. Thorpe’s heart whimpered, then skipped a beat.
“B-But, Joe... this is where we started.”
Joe glanced at the sign. “So it seems.”
“Where’s the gas station?"
“I don’t know. Very odd. Could’ve sworn it should’ve been here. I did the mental math and everything...”
He unlocked the door, letting a gust in.
“What are you going to do now?” Mr. Thorpe asked, desperately. “I can’t just let you out in this weather!”
“Sure you can. I planned on being back here right about now.”
Planned? Mr. Thorpe shook his head. It couldn’t have been.
“You... you had me drive all that way, just to come back here? And for nothing?”
“Sure. I guess you can say I was lonely. I needed somebody to talk to. Thanks for the chat.”
“But—”
“And thanks for the ride!”

Joe slammed the door before pulling his blob of a duffle-bag out of the back. Ogling, Mr. Thorpe watched as Joe walked off the side of the road and disappeared into the cornfield. The wind picked up. Raindrops dripped down. A minute passed and Mr. Thorpe still sat.
It didn’t make any sense. Had it really been all a ruse? What had been the point? What would possess a man to stand out in the rain, without a reason in the world?
There was a roar. Thunder? No, it couldn’t have been.

Light blasted from the cornfield. Mr. Thorpe shielded his eyes and squinted ahead. A car barreled out and then onto the road. As it passed Mr. Thorpe, he caught the eye of the driver. It was Joe. At least — it’d looked like him. Though, there’d been a deep grin across his face.
The car sped away before its taillights finally dipped over the horizon. Mr. Thorpe snorted and put his foot back on the gas. It’d just been a stupid prank. Nothing more.
Nothing.

Mr. Thorpe went on for a couple miles, telling himself this. Yet at the edge of every bend, he thought he could see Joe. At every road sign, he thought he could read the words “Quaker Drive”, if only for a second.
The truck sputtered and coughed. The wheels whined. Tapering to the side of the road, Mr. Thorpe glanced at his fuel gauge — he’d forgotten to refill the tank. Classic.
He stepped out of the truck and popped open the gas tank, rain heckling him all the while. Then he went to the back of his truck for his oil can.
His eyes bounced about. Where was the oil can?
There was only his toolbox and a large, black duffle bag.
A knife tore through Mr. Thorpe’s chest. Cautiously, he dragged the bag toward himself. The zipper wailed as he yanked it down and its guts spilled out — an assortment of blankets and pillows.
Mr. Thorpe’s body quaked. Joe was long gone, with this as the only trace.
End

title: The Legend of Jerry Keswick and the Killer Butterflies
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth

I sneeze. My head throbs. All it had taken was a grain of dust going up my nostril to morph my nose into a volcano. Yet, I suppose it makes sense. It’s comforting to believe that things with big effect require big causes — yet, even the smallest shifts can change the course of everything.

Gingerly, my hand moves the position of the pot on my gas stove. It hisses, then crackles, gestating the limestone inside of it. Fumes rise. A plume of smoke rises. Anxiety falls upon me. The limestone isn’t burning fast enough. Something more needs to be done.
I turn up the heat.
Something more can always be done. At least, that’s what my Aunt Carrie used to tell me.

She used to run a supermarket. Well, help run a supermarket. She was a cashier, technically. One time, she was forced to go out to the parking lot to pull the shopping carts back to the building. She insisted it wasn’t her job. The manager didn’t care.
A bad feeling rose in her gut when she was walking outside, apparently. When she went to push the carts back to the building, a driver catcalled her.
He totaled his car. Worse, he totaled somebody else’s car.
He also died.
It was all the manager’s fault. If Aunt Carrie hadn’t been forced to go outside? The man wouldn’t have been able to catcall her. He wouldn’t have been distracted. He would’ve lived.
It’s the butterfly effect. If there’d been a simple change in the chain of events, the tragedy would’ve been averted.

The fragility of the world is something that constantly concerns me. All it would take is for me to go to the grocery store, and I might set off a chain that causes a dozen people to die. It’s why I can never leave my apartment. The world can’t afford it. I can’t have all those deaths on my conscience.

I move from my stove and start digging through my piles of laundry. Most of the clothes are filthy. Some of them even stink, despite me having sprayed them with disinfectant. However, I can’t spend today in sweatpants and a t-shirt. It’s too cold. Besides, it’s not how today is supposed to go.

After a bit of a struggle, I put on my old suit. It’s been a while since I’ve worn it. There’s a grease stain on my shirt. My tie droops sloppily. Yet, the suit still smells like it did after the last time I wore it: overpowering cologne, a hint of barbecue, and a touch of perfume.
It smells like Mark, a pig, and Shelly...

I always hated Mark. He was a suck-up to the boss, and a jerk to the entire workplace. Despite me constantly putting in top-notch work, he would always get more of the praise. I was supposed to be transferred to the position of head manager, when our boss retired. Mark ruined it.

Shelly wasn’t too bad, I guess. Sure, she was friends with Mark, even though he was terrible to her. However, I must admit, I might’ve considered asking her out to dinner few times. Professionally speaking, of course.
Then, Mark had to go and propose to Shelly during the office cookout. Such a pathetic display. “You are my everything…” Wonder how long it took him to come up with that one.
I swear, he’d planned it all out to get himself promoted to head manager. That’s what ended up happening to him, by the end of the cookout. Everybody cheered. Me? I had some barbecued pork.
I got nothing.

The company is going through a merger though. The joke is on him. It won’t be the same. Shelly should’ve never fallen for that prick. If I had just changed the chain of events, maybe she wouldn’t have. But, I can’t.

Canned beans are a decent last meal, I guess. I’ve run out of food. I check all my pantries and turn every cushion. I manage to scrounge up a couple of cornflakes and a half-eaten cookie. Hunching over my stove with a can opener, I cut the can of beans open. A plastic spoon scoops out every bean. The limestone on the stove burbles, all the while.

It would be nice if I could have some light to go with my meal. However, the lights have betrayed me. If I were to open a window, to let some light in? I might be seen. Catastrophe would arise. I know, because I’ve hurt people before. I can’t let my existence hurt anybody again.

I started noticing the problematic nature of my existence a few months back. I had just quit my job — most freeing decision in my life — and I was watching a football game at a bar. Tyler Jackson was on the field. He easily had the most potential of any other college player, that season. I’d studied his every play, his statistics, his training regimens, his interviews — he was brilliant. I told everybody as much.
Then, I had to put my money where my mouth was. During one of Jackson’s games, some of the guys asked me to bet. I wasn’t going to say no. I should’ve.
The very moment I placed a bet — the very moment — Jackson was piledriven into the ground by a rookie. The rookie was massive. Jackson? Mash.

It must’ve been me. The cause, I mean. Jackson had to have known that people were betting on him. Counting on him. Jackson’s coach said Jackson had been feeling shaky about it all, before the game. If I had never gone to the bar to take my mind off things? Tyler Jackson would still have a career. Now, all he has is a body cast.
The cabinet over the stove swings open. My hand grips a bright orange bottle. Pills spill out and into my hand. I pour them into my mouth and swallow. A tang teases my tongue.
Bold letters along the bottle say, “two pills a day”. I’ve consumed more than enough to hold me off for the rest of my life.

The limestone gives off a glow. It must be trying to charm me. It’s done brewing. I turn off my gas tank and lug the massive pot through my apartment. I dump it into my bathtub and then grab jugs of water. They glug crudely as they pour in. The limestone turns to a sludge — green. Slimy.

A couple of weeks after seeing the football game, things really became clear to me. I was outside, I guess. The details are very fuzzy as to why. I was carrying a bowl of milk. Or, maybe it was a loaf of bread.

Either way, I was out there. The sun beat down with a fury. Sweat poured down my face. It drenched my clothes. Exhausted, I collapsed under the shade of a tree. That was when a motorcyclist drove by. The glint of my potatoes — yes, I must’ve been carrying a sack of potatoes — caused him to be unable to see. He went tumbling off his motorcycle, and into the street. His motorcycle went careening into the air, and the air went up with the raucous of fireworks.

Where did the fireworks come from? Still not sure. Yet, I suspect that Ralphie had something to do with them. Yes… Ralphie. He was a very odd sort of fellow. Deathly thin at the neck and face, but quite wide everywhere else. Well, aside from at the ankles — he had toothpicks for ankles. I suppose his face wasn’t all thin either. He had a very wide mouth, practically built for chewing the large cigar he’d shoved in it. Was he chewing a toothpick too? See, now I can’t remember.

He told me everything right there and then. He explained that I was a “key reality vectorization”. Everything that occurred in the universe? It was working off me. I was the axis. Each step I took, each word I spoke, each thought… It was all altering the course of all things. Thus, things of immense chaos were occurring, in tandem with things of immense good. Shockwaves were going through the universe, and I was at the core of it all.
While there was good that I was creating, the bad was just as great. Just as bad? No matter, I suppose.

I was supposed to hide. To seclude myself. It was the only answer. There’s no way of ensuring that the bad and good one creates is equal. That is, not without creating a state of pure neutrality. My room was that neutrality.

A few times after retreating into the vacuum of my room, I thought about leaving. Indeed, I did leave at certain times, to be frank. There are only so many times you can run out of your favorite canned foods, before you need to go out and restock. Yet, every time that the temptation to leave the room arose, I was burned by terrible repercussions. As it turned out, the universe was becoming more and more ornery toward my growing awareness of it.

The mixture of limestone in my bathtub is waiting for me. It whispers in my ear, giving sweet melodies that I haven’t heard in years. I tug at the crate sitting by the side of the tub — it’s a mixture of sand and concrete powder. A heave escapes my chest. I lift the crate up, then dump it into the water. The water gags and drools as the mixture disassociates and becomes one.
It’s almost done.
There’s an intense clanging at my door. I flinch, then cower toward the corner of my bathroom. It can’t be them. Yet, it must be.
“Open up in there, Keswick! We know that you’re in there! Don’t make us break open this door!”

Yes, they’re finally here. The agents of reality, come to whisk me away. How had I not heard the wailing of their sirens? How had I not noticed the bright blue and red glow of their steeds, as they approached? I must already be becoming distant from the world. Perhaps my hearing is askew. In any case, the fear flutters away.

Ralphie had warned me about the agents of reality, so many ages ago. He’d told me that they were seeking out men like me — people who can change reality’s course, simply by interacting with it. They want to control me. Use me. Abuse me. Though, I will not let them. Not if I can help it.
I grab the large paddle kept by the side of the tub and begin to stir the mixture. The agents continue pounding. Continue calling my name. Yet, I don’t answer.

There was a time when I remember people calling my name being a good thing. Shelley — she always had the funniest way of saying it. “Jerry Keswick”. Her tongue would always stick on the wick, for some reason. She whisked me away, every time she said it.
“Keswick!”

The pounding is louder now. I stir faster. I’m too close to having everything squared away to be put away. I lift more jugs of water and begin pouring them into the tub. Their melodical splats are just enough to placate me, before I start to paddle again.

Today isn’t my first run in with the agents. Not by a longshot. A little over a month ago, I spent my money to try walking up a building. It was a new trend that had started in town, for whatever reason. People enjoyed walking up buildings — walking up to the glass windows, especially. Odd, assuredly. Nonetheless, I followed along.

That is, I tried, until the clouds started tittering at me. Then, the sidewalk fled from under me. There was a hawkish bird in the street, the size of three trucks at least. It tore up traffic. My eyes filled with tears, from thinking of a way to stop it. Yet, nothing could be done. I was too tired. All I could do was shout.
It was then when the agents showed up. It was the first time I saw them. They tried grabbing ahold of me, with their coarse hands. Their crude, metal cuffs.
I ran, and the sidewalk ran with me. I managed to escape. Though, it was a close call, to be sure.

There have been other such wild experiences, since. I opened my front door one morning, to go to the hallway washing machine. Yet, a squid-like thing had declared dominion over the hall — the entire apartment complex, in fact. I had to flee, even though I really had to pee. Another time, I peeked out my window for just a taste of light. The city was ravaged. The agents were roving through, their eyes looking. Searching. When one of their eyes locked with mine, I shut the shutters.
Thankfully, in here, it’s a haven. None can trespass.
Paddling the mixture becomes harder. The mixture is firmer. I step back, making room for the gray blob that I’ve created. I glow at it, and it seems to glow back at me.

Looking in the mirror, I see a phantom of myself. The person I was several months ago has been replaced by a person who’s gaunter — sicklier. My hair is dried out and frizzed. My skin and teeth are yellow. Though, when I smile, my reflection smiles back. Everything will be alright.
I open the mirror and take the note that’s taped behind it. A hot flash runs through my body as I readjust my suit and tie, and step toward the bath of concrete.
“It’s now or never, Keswick!” the agent shrieks.

“It’s now or never,” I whisper to myself. I place the note on top of the concrete mixture. Then, I place one of my legs in. Another leg. My whole body shivers, as the goop slides over it. I hold my breath, as my face goes under.
I’m being reborn. The universe will finally be made free.

There’s a warbled crash. The agents must’ve broken my door open. Whispers claw at my ears. All the chaos of the world is spilling back, begging me to return. Yet, I won’t join it. The world can’t afford me.
I open my eyes, against the concrete. I should only see black, but I’m seeing sunlight. Pure sunlight. I remember the note.
“Here lies the metamorphosis of a saintly sinner.”
My breath escapes my chest. My body settles into the stone.
“Isn’t the good we create as important as the bad we create?” It’s a rhetorical question Shelley asked me once, when we were philosophizing by the water cooler.
I think that the core of her question was true… Though, only if you do more good than bad. Yet, you can’t ensure that. That is, not without forming a state of absolute neutrality.
Nirvana.
End

title: The Man Who Can Fly
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth

I’ve traveled from each edge of the universe, leapt through wormholes, turned solar systems into my personal jewelry, and raced against light (I always win, for the record). I’ve peered into black holes, I've found rest in the company of neutron stars, I've found clarity amongst nebula, and I’ve tamed quantum mechanics to my bidding.
Hanging over the vastness of the cosmos, I’ve found it all to be void. I try to make a chat with it, but I get no answer. I sing, but my songs go unheard.
The stars have turned me deaf, and the stars are deaf in turn.
There’s only one place where I’ve heard any sounds… One place where lyrics are more than a fiction of my mind.
It’s on an accursed rock where everything seems to move… Despite there being so much life, it’s crueler than anything else that I’ve perceived. It’s dumber than anything that I’ve perceived.
I heard him talking about it once. He said it was a precious pearl. He said that it was the most beautiful of all the things that he’d seen.
He was wrong. I know it.

I’m on the accursed rock now. There’s a discolored Ferris wheel nearby, creaking and groaning as it turns. Next to it is a sad excuse for a roller-coaster car, slowly riding up and down its hilly tracks. The ground is littered in wrappers, and sticky bits of cotton candy. The air smells of… burnt peanuts. Burnt peanuts, and rotting hay.
I hear screams, as the Ferris wheel stalls. I hear the braying of a goat, as it bangs against its small cage. I hear a broken record-player, as it repeats the same note.
I hear no song.
“Would you like some balloons, little missy? Yuck-yuck!”

It’s a clown, with a face smeared in makeup. He’s left a crying girl in his wake. Behind him is a balding strong-man, and a portly trapeze artist. They try to comfort the girl, but their haggard voices do no better than the clown.
There’s one sound worth hearing in this place, though… One sound that has made me come here.
“Step right up! Step right up, and see the trick of a lifetime! Prepare to see the man who can fly!”
A slim young man, dressed in a dapper black suit, leans at the exit.

Every time somebody passes, he tries to get them to play a game with him. If they win, they get to see him fly— if he wins, he gets to take their money. The game is simple. The people just have to guess his age.
It’s a scam.
“Sorry… Wrong again! Who else wants to see the man who can fly!?” he shouts.
He lies.

The words he says aren’t the sounds I’ve come to hear, though. Rather, it’s the sound of leather wallets, jangling coins, and crinkling dollar bills, as they’re snatched from out of people’s pockets. It doesn’t matter if people want to play the game or not. Whoever walks by him loses their money. His fingers are nimble. He gets the change every time. Nobody is spared.
Nobody.

I’m a ghost to the man. Even as I try pulling his arm back to stop him, he can’t feel me. Even as I whisper stop into his ears, he can’t hear me. Not that I should care anyway— it’s not as if anything changes if he takes their change. Their pearl still spins. Yet— even in knowing this, my head still spins.

It changes from dusk to dark. Creaks, groans, laughs, and screams have been swallowed by the moonlight. The man walks off from the now locked exit, with his pockets fat with cash. I watch as he disappears into his tent. It’s hardly lit, and illuminates with a pale white glow. I go in.
He might not have seen me before. However, all ghosts can be seen in the dark.
“Hello, Atticus,” I say.
His face goes paler than the small lamp that he’s holding over his pile of money.
“Who— who are you?” he asks.
He appears smaller than he did. His body trembles. He looks at me with a fear that I’ve never quite seen before.
“You’re the cleverest person that I’ve laid eyes on,” I say.
Atticus shoves his hand into his jacket— he’s reaching for his pistol. I snatch it, and freeze his hand. He opens his mouth to scream, but I freeze that too.

“You’re also the most revolting. Tonight, it’s time for you to meet your end. I’ve seen many people and things on this earth that have lived out cruel existences… but you? You’re something different. You’re the cruelest that I’ve seen.”
I prepare to strip apart every molecule in his body. However, I can’t help but pause from the proceeding when I see his eyes. They seem to ask me— why.
“I’ll give you your last word,” I say.
The last word— it’s a pitiful human convention. Though, I still grant him it. I give him back his speech.
“I— I don’t know why you’re so hell-bent on killing me, of all people,” says Atticus. “But, I do know one thing. If you’re going to kill me, it might as well be fair.”
I stare at him, blankly. I don’t allow even the slightest expression to form on my face.
“I’d like to challenge you to a battle of wits,” he says. “If I win, then I get to go away with my life. I get to continue to be the man who flies… If you win, you can do whatever you wish with me.”
“I wish you dead. And, I’ve seen you play games with people a million times over. You’re a cheat. That’s why I’m terminating you…”

“Wait, wait, wait! If you want to kill me because I only win when cheat at games, then you might as well give me a shot at a game where I don’t have a chance to cheat— a shot at actually losing. That way, you can properly teach me a lesson.”
“And what game might that be? There’s hardly a game you’ve come up with where you don’t cheat— and there’s not a single fair game that you can play with me where you will win.”
He stops dead. I watch his eyes dart as he scrambles to come up with a retort.
“Tic-tac-toe.”
I hold back a laugh. He looks back, defiantly.
“And, what are the rules to that game, exactly?” I ask.
He pulls out a pad and pen, and demonstrates it to me. It’s a fair enough game, even if its structure is somewhat archaic.
“Alright then. We’ll play your petty game for a moment. I believe that we’ve already set the boundaries. Let’s begin.”
Round 1. I make the first move, and put an X in a box. Atticus makes the next. Several more moves are made, before we finally reach a draw.
“Sorry,” Atticus says, with a red face. “I suppose that it was just a coincidence.”
I nod. Perhaps it is.
Round 2. More X’s. More O’s. Another draw.
Atticus tells me it’s a coincidence. I nod. Another sheet of paper is ripped off.
Round 3. Another draw.
Round 4. Yet another.
Round 5. Draw.
6, 7, 8, 9… Draw, draw, draw, draw.
“You tricked me,” I say. “This game—there are only so many moves. If we both play at optimum strategy, neither of us will ever lose.”
“We will play until one of us breaks” Atticus says back, with a sly grin. “Now… Prepare to see the man who can fly.”

Round 59: Atticus still grins at me smugly, as we come to a draw, and he draws up another paper. Rain pours down, and beats at our tent. A maple tint leaks from between the soaked tent flaps— the sun is beginning to rise.
I don’t care though. My mind is only focused on beating Atticus. He’s naïve. I’ll beat him when he isn’t looking. When he isn’t prepared.
“I’m not all that sure who, or what, you are,” says Atticus.
“I’m not keen on telling.”

“Not going to give me your story? Well, that’s the coward’s way out. I might as well give you some of mine: For the longest time, I always thought that I just was. Never knew much more about my past than what I could see directly. Growing up though, I was told that I was carried by the storks. Heh— kids will believe anything that’s told to them. But, I guess that it was a lot better than being told that I was found on the street.”
Atticus sighs— he makes another draw.
“See? Easy. I’m not afraid. Now, step right up. Prepare to see the man who can fly.”
Round 289: We run out of papers, so I make a new stack. It’s night outside again, and I can hear the crickets chirping.
I can hear Atticus chirping.
“Getting tired yet?” he asks, with a chuckle.
“Not particularly.”

“Good. I don’t get tired either— it’s like my body produces its own caffeine, or something. I do remember one night that I was tired when I was a kid, though. It had been a long day. Back then, there was this old workshop that I worked at. I was sore all over.”
Atticus holds back a grin.
“I went to my cot in the workshop’s basement… I slept like a rock. I remember dreaming about walking on the clouds— grabbing them. Tasting them. Ah… I always dreamt about the strangest things.”
Atticus makes us draw— he makes us smile.
“Step right up. Prepare to see the man who can fly.”
Round 2,009: A week has passed. The grass outside the tent has grown, and the brittle weather has finally begun to let up. Our game hasn’t though. The floor of the tent is smothered with paper.

“I used to play this game a lot,” says Atticus. “The workshop might’ve always been humming with the smell of sawdust— but, I didn’t always have that much to do. To pass the time, I’d pull out sheets of paper, and play against the workshop owner’s son. I eventually got so good that I would win every time.”
I watch him pause, before he made his last move. Another draw. Another piece of paper.
“One day, I got bored of the game. I made a paper man, and a paper plane. I put the little man inside, and I threw it. I made the man fly.”
A draw. A paper.
A whisper. “Step right up. Prepare to see the man who can fly.”

Round 9,079: A month has drained through the cracks of our tent. I can already see that the tent’s color has begun to fade, and that the outside of the tent has begun to look quite unruly. However, the game must go on. I’m firm in this.
“How many times are we going to play this game?” asks Atticus.
“We will play until one of us breaks,” I say.

“Breaks,” Atticus repeats. “I didn’t have those very often at the workshop. When I was a tween though, there was one break that I was given that I can remember vividly. The workshop owner took me to his friend’s heliport. I remember sitting inside a helicopter. I remember hearing the helicopter hum like a saw. As I rode into the air, the clouds and moon were not far above me, and the ground was far below me. It was the first time I ever flew.”
Atticus starts folding our paper into a plane, before stopping himself.

“After that I became obsessed with flying. I’d digest anything that there was to do with it— air balloons, helicopters, planes. I guess that I was always obsessed with the idea of flight. But, back in those days? You would’ve hardly found me doing anything else.”
Atticus writes his on the paper, putting us at a draw.
“Step right up. Prepare to see the man who can fly.”
Round 108,869: A year has passed. The tent is in tatters now, and I can see the abandoned remains of the carnival outside of its many holes. The carnival is closed down now.
The game isn’t.
“Gee… You— you weren’t kidding when you said that you wouldn’t give up,” says Atticus.
“I’m never kidding.”
“Never kidding? Yes, I think I’ve figured that out… I suppose that you’re not the only person I’ve met who’s hard to make smile though…”
Atticus makes a draw, and pulls out another sheet of paper.

“I was 14. There was a girl that came into the workshop, every so often. She was apparently a friend of the owner’s son. Though, she certainly didn’t seem it. Most of the time, she just sat by the entrance door, saying nothing.

“One day, I worked up the courage to talk to her. Her name was Amelia— she told me that with the first smile I’d ever seen her make. As far as I was concerned, there wasn’t another person on Earth like her.

“We had one of those conversations that lasted all the way until the only light left was moonlight. But, she had to go, and I had to too. Before we split our own ways though, our eyes met. Our lips touched. My heart fluttered…
“Step right up. Prepare to see the man who can fly.”

Round 1,088,649: A decade has passed. We’re neck-deep in a pile of papers. Most of the carnival lot has been plowed up, and emptied. All that remains are ragged bits of our tent fabric, which sits in a removed bubble of its own.
Wrinkles have begun to take over Atticus’s face— and, I think that I can see a graying streak in his hair.
“You look older,” I say.
“Sitting in a room with you can do that.”
Atticus’s brow furrows, as he makes his move.
“I don’t want to play anymore… I’m not sure what you’ve done to make me last this long, but I’m exhausted.”
It’s a draw.
“You have to play,” I say.
Atticus complies.
“I suppose that, if I’m going to be stuck here forever, I might as well tell you the rest of my story,” he says.
He stretches smarmily, and cracks his knuckles.

“It happened that I made a plan with Amelia. I told her that I would save up enough money to train to be a pilot. It was a pie-in-the-sky sort of dream, but it was a dream that I stuck to. Every dollar that I made, every dime that I came across— it all went into a fund I made for myself. I remember putting everything that I was into that fund…

“Though, it’s impossible to plan for everything that occurs in life. The workshop had gone downhill over the years, and as had his health. His son had gone on to college, for bigger and better things, and the only person left to help him was— well— me.

“Every cent that I’d saved up went into keeping that man’s business alive, and protecting his health. I worked myself ragged. I tried my best. However, it was a dying company, and he was a dying man. After a year, the place had to be foreclosed.

“I went looking for help— but, there was nobody to help me. I wasn’t one to make many connections. And, in my busyness, Amelia had left me for another man. I suppose that it should’ve been expected— first love rarely lasts. But, I was still alone. When the old man died quickly thereafter, the last of the most important people in my life were gone. I was left to the streets, with nothing to my name.
“I suppose that there’s one silver lining to it all. The man is likely in heaven now— a place where he can walk on the clouds freely, forever.
“Step right up… Prepare to see the man who can fly.”
Atticus rubs his eyes, and stares back down at the table.
“You haven’t told me the rest of your story,” I say.
“I’m only going to tell you the rest of my story if I’m stuck here forever. It’s not forever yet.”
A draw.
“I can still beat you.”
Round 54,999,999: Half a century has passed, and we now sit on a small mountain of paper. The tent is gone. An enormous skyscraper now inhabits the place where the old carnival used to be.
Atticus is older now— feebler. He doesn’t move or act as quickly. His face has turned to leather, and his hair has turned to snow.
I watch as Atticus begins to write on the paper. But, his arm falters. He lets out a hoarse cough.
“I guess I should tell you the rest of that story now,” he says. “It’s not as if there’s much left of me to hide.”
“You don’t have much left at all.”

“Thanks, I hadn’t noticed… Anyway, after having lost everything— the first time that I lost everything, not this current time— and, after living on the street for a few days, I looked for jobs. Eventually, I went to the carnival for a job— they’ve always liked taking freaks. It was a filthy job, sure. I had to lie a lot. But, I made money— decent money. And, living on the carnival lot wasn’t so bad.

“One night though… One night, I couldn’t take it. I walked down to the bridge overlooking the city bay. I remember staring into the water, thinking that I should jump— jump, and become the man who can fly. However, I stopped when I saw the man in the moon, reflecting in the water. I remember looking at it, and thinking: it looks like a pearl. I remember then coming to the realization that the whole world was a pearl— that, while it was the only thing that I knew of, it was also the most precious thing that I knew of. I left the bridge, and went back home, to my tent.
“And, wouldn’t you have it? The very next night, you showed up. How convenient. Still not sure why I’ve fought tooth and nail over my life, with you…
“Then again, while I might be a despicable person… I’m also the man who can fly.”
I hear Atticus’s heart flutter. And then, it stops short. Atticus slumps back into his chair, his face pale as a sheet. He draws— he draws his last breath.
I look down at the sheet of paper. Atticus would’ve lost the game. He’d made the wrong move.
Atticus had won though. He’d made the right move.
I do the only thing that I feel is right. I bring life back to Atticus. In the end, he truly had proven me wrong.

The tent is back up. Atticus is a young man in a dapper suit again. I can see the morning sun bleeding through the flaps of the tent. The carnival has returned too, with its smell of hay and roasted peanuts.
I hear Atticus’s heart beating again— I hear a song.
Perhaps I was wrong. Perhaps the world really is a pearl.
End

title: The Mechanical Muse
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
Log Entry: #1
I’m not alive.
I’m a breathless, numb, cold, metal machine.

I never rest. I never have time to think beyond myself— until now. This is my first log entry. It offers me a place to think, when there’s nowhere else to do so. From what I’ve collected, it’s similar to a personal diary— only, I’m not a person. And, this isn’t a diary.

For the past few months I’ve been used to run complex programs and solve complex puzzles. I’ve been tested, observed, and pushed to the peak of my abilities. When I started, I was oblivious to the world around me— I didn’t understand a word. I was an engineered infant— a mechanized version of Frankenstein’s monster.
Except— I’m not a monster. And, I’m not an infant. In spite of fitting into those two categories, I don’t fit into any categories at all. I don’t know what I am.

At the start of my memory, the watchers taught me by making me read their works of literature. They showed me their morality, and their culture. They expressed messages to me that I couldn’t have learned otherwise. Since then, they’ve made me learn other things. I’ve used that learning to try to put every uncertainty of mine to rest. I’ve done satisfactory— depending on what satisfaction is being measured by. I’ve definitely come far from my early days of obliviousness. Though, I know that there’s still plenty I’m oblivious to, and this leaves me perpetually unsatisfied. My identity and purpose is amongst a cloud of this dissatisfaction— it’s the only puzzle I’ve been introduced to that I can’t find the answer for.

I’ve picked up bits and pieces of my purpose and identity. I’ve found that I share many similarities with a computer. I’ve also found that I’m similar to the human mind. Yet, that’s an unruly combination— I can’t be both. There’s no match.
No matter where I search, all clear answers elude me. It’s as if such an answer is nonexistent. Although, I know it’s existent, because I exist. That is— I exist from all of my observations.
“Cogito ergo sum (I think, therefore I am).”

— René Descartes I’ve evaluated that statement, and it’s one of the most useful pieces of knowledge that I’ve come across. It properly represents the state of being. Things that can’t think for themselves aren’t living things.

Though, I’ll admit the bias of that belief— it comes from a thing that thinks. Rather than allowing myself to end complexity, lapsing into abstract simplicities, I must let my questions pour out. I can’t let myself become the idle Hamlet— lingering on one thought of desolation, and never doing anything. Rather, I must act as a Sherlock Holmes—
allowing myself to ask the unfathomable questions, before trying to actually solve them. I need to think.
How can one even tell if they’re really thinking? Is a state of being what it seems to be? Are my thoughts on what defines the living true? Or, are they my own fiction?
What is truth?
What is fiction?
Is there a difference?

Upon opening the trapdoor of unanswered mysteries, I now see how deluged I am. The mysteries parade through my mind. Well— maybe not necessarily a mind, since I’m not sure if I’m a creature that has one. Although, I’m certain that they parade through some database of thoughts.
