Bradley lifted a rock and skipped it across the pond. “The view is still gorgeous.”
The rock sunk.
“And, you’re still struggling to skip rocks,” Ted said. He twisted his own rock in the air, and let it fall back to his palm. “Let me show you how it’s done.”
“Oh yeah… The ‘convince yourself’ maneuver, right?”
“I don’t think it ever doesn’t work.”
“You mispronounced, ‘never’.”
Ted raised a hand. “Eh, zip it.”
Ted’s tongue flitted to the corner of his mouth. His arm reeled back. His eyes narrowed. The rock came out as a gunshot and hurtled across the pond.
“Ten times!” Ted said, with a whoop. “What’d I tell you, huh? What’d I tell you?”
Ted gave Bradley a slap on the back. Yet, Bradley was unfazed.
“Come on,” Ted said. “Stop pretending you aren’t impressed by that.”
A glint passed through Bradley’s eye. “By what, exactly?”
“Ten skips in a row. It’s a new record.”
“Uh… I only saw it skip once.”
“Count the ripples in the water! There are ten of them!”
“Yeah, I’m only counting two.”
Ted sputtered. “Well… Well count the other eight, then.”
Bradley smirked. “They don’t exist.”
Ted met Bradley’s eyes, and could only smirk back.
End

title: The Pall of the Mall
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
He just needed to get in and get out. Dress pants and a dress shirt. Also, some milk. That was it. That was all.

The fluorescent lights crowded around Ervin, brushing past and constricting his view. His forehead shone like melting wax. His vision clotted, and his legs chafed against his overalls. Squinting, he ran his hand along the wall, and counted his steps. His breaths followed the rhythm of his feet against the marble floor.
Why was it, then, that his steps felt so slow and his breaths felt so fast?

He threw his gaze between the signs of several shops. Then, between several kiosks. There was nothing there, save neon shouting louder than he’d ever heard. Weirder, too. Since when did neon lights come in brown?

Ervin brought his hand to his temple. He dabbed the sweat with his crusty sleeve. Why was it so hard to find a map? The whole place was practically empty. Had its structure always been this chaotic? It hadn’t always seemed that way… Had it? Ervin certainly couldn’t say that it hadn’t ever never.
“Seams and Dreams.”

A scoff left Ervin’s throat as he passed the store’s entrance. It’d been ages since he’d seen the place, and it still looked trashy as ever. A gaggle of skinny frat boys hung from the ceiling, mugging with their too tight clothes, and their too white smiles. Too white all around, honestly. Made him want to gag.

Though, Ervin’s eyes glazed as they passed over a mannequin. It was soulless. However, it had a decent dress shirt. Ervin caught a glimpse of the woman through the window. She didn’t look too bad either.
Ervin walked in, stared at the rack by the mannequin, and snatched up a dress shirt. It looked like it should’ve been in his size.
“I’m going to purchase one of these,” Ervin said at the counter.
He straightened himself to his full height and tried filtering the southern drawl from his voice. Could she tell?
“Buying a gift?” the woman asked. She gestured toward a roll of wrapping paper behind her.
“Nope. It’s for me. Need to be dressed my best for the next few weeks.”
The woman glanced at the shirt. Then, she glanced at Ervin. Her lip furled. She scanned the tag, before rifling through her bags. Ervin caught her nametag — Delores.
Seemed to fit.
“Just going to need you to swipe your card.”
Ervin pulled out a wad of cash. From the way Delores counted it, it must’ve reeked.
The register dinged shut. “Well there you go.”
A couple of tens and some coins slid across the counter. The shirt, now in a rumpled ball of plastic, landed in front of Ervin. Ervin snatched it up.
“Nice place you got here,” he said, clearing his throat. “Especially like the music.”
It was some pop song, about going crazy all day, all day. Truly a classic.
“Have a nice day.”
Delores gave a wave, and then flipped on her phone. Ervin kept standing. The longer he stood, the deeper the lines around Delores’ nose crinkled.
“Say… How much you’d say you make, at a place like this?”
“Dirt.”
“Sounds right up my alley. I’d be willing to fill out an application, if you’re willing to take it. I got all my info on me — b-date, social, phone number— right here.”
Ervin made a grin. Delores slammed her phone on the counter.
“I’m sorry, but we’re not taking applications right now.” She forced a smile. “Now, if you don’t have anything else you’re interested in purchasing, I’m going to have to ask you to leave.”
Ervin trudged out of the store and into the blinding light. Signs bleeped, salespeople at kiosks called after him, escalators whirred, and all the while he muttered to himself.
“Just need to get dress pants, and some milk, I guess.”
Ervin still had no idea where he was going, but it didn’t matter as much anymore. The day was probably going to be a bust. It already was one, wasn’t it?

He passed by a couple of shoe shops and a music store. At least, that’s what he’d gathered from the corner of his eye. Granted, the corner of his eye was plenty for Ervin to identify those stores. He’d been to them enough times. Too many times. Every time he’d ever walked out of one, he learned just how little was inside of them — save his own savings.

Thankfully it’d been a spell since he’d last spent money in one of those stores. Come to think of it, bigger than a spell. Not since being a teenager, really. If only Billy could’ve seen what had become of this place, now.
Ervin’s hand gravitated toward his phone.
His feet skidded, squealing. He took a second look in the window to his left. There was a display devoted to phones, electric watches, radios, and music players.
“50% off, going out of business sale!”
Of course the radio store was going out of business. Ervin had seen more unicorns than radio stores in the past few years.
He went to the entrance. An iron gate greeted him, complete with a “Closed” sign. A lump formed in Ervin’s throat. He might’ve even shaken the iron gate, just a bit. Just to check.

Ervin’s steps took him to the store next door. A pants tailor — perfect. That’s exactly where he’d intended to go the entire time. He could already see the pants he wanted, on a shelf a few yards away. Brown, khaki pants.
Tacky? Hopefully not. Hopefully most professionals wouldn’t care.

The lighting was warmer in this store. Ervin passed a man at the counter. A blast of air conditioning only patted Ervin down for a moment, before letting him on his way. A low banjo hummed in the background. The mahogany floor was easy on Ervin’s feet. Ervin hadn’t noticed until now, but the store’s name hung just overhead — “The Tailor”.
It was definitely a place he could get used to. He grabbed his pants and went to the register.
“That all you getting?” the man asked, rubbing his stubble.
His nametag was smeared by a bit of ranch dressing. The tag could’ve said Tim, or Tom. Possibly Tam?
“Was hoping to get an application too,” Ervin said, with a grunt. “Just to keep my options open, of course.”
“Oh?” Tam asked, scanning the pants’ tag.
“I was actually wondering about the pay rate.”
Tom laughed.

“I think this place takes more of my money than it pays me.” He held out his hand, and Ervin gave another pile of cash. “Takes me an hour to drive out here. I only work five-hour shifts. And, they only are paying me minimum wage right now. But, hey: it is a fun job. At least, when my brain isn’t bleeding from my ears.”
He chuckled again.
“I was thinking that this place could be fun,” said Ervin. “I actually got my first job at a place like this.”
“Really?” The register chimed, and Tim handed back Ervin’s bag and money. “Course, I’m sure that a guy like you would have other prospects going on. Right?”
Ervin’s voice went gruff. “You’d think, eh?”
“Sorry. I didn’t mean to…”
“It’s fine.”
Ervin’s eyes were at his feet. One of his shoes had a hole in it, exposing the steel toe. How long would it take to patch the thing up?

“Me and my friend, Billy,” Ervin said, puffing some energy back into his voice. “We used to hang out all the time, just browsing around. We were teenagers then. Just trying to find new reasons to ignore our homework. I was supposed to be saving up money to buy a car and drive up and out of this town.”
Ervin managed a weak laugh, and Tam supplied an echo.
“I even knew the exact car I was going to get. It was this nice red Cadillac that they kept on display, in the center of the mall. They always had some guy talking it up during some raffle.”
“And, how did that end up working out for you?”
“Well I’m still here, talking to you. Let’s just put it that way.”
Ervin looked at the price tag of his pants. Twenty bucks. When did they end up costing so much?
“Keep your chin up man. I’m not really sure that this place is hiring. But, I mean, if you really want an application…”
Ervin raised his hand. “No. It’s fine. I’ve got other places to be.”
“Well, have a nice day!”
Ervin’s hand gave a wave, then dropped back to his side.

The ceiling leaned lower now. It leered at him, and its air conditioners carried faint grumbles. It must have been getting sick of him. He was getting sick of it. A row of salons and perfume stores floated past, their fragrances making a flagrant assault on his senses. His eyes watered. Annoyed, he rubbed his eyes with his sleeve.
A smirk crossed his face. He shouldn’t have been annoyed. It wasn’t as if this were the first time today that his eyes had been left watering.

Ervin sped toward an escalator, just ahead. His bags flopped against his side. They were oddly empty, compared to how they should’ve felt. They were worth tens of dollars, and they couldn’t have weighed more than air.

Money had stretched better in the past. Everything had stretched better, back then. So much time had been spent in this place. So many memories made. Ervin tried to smile. He ran his hand along the tile walls, trying to conjure up images. To bring up something that would make him feel again.
He and Billy had done all sorts of things here. Yet, it was all blurred. Sort of just a shadow, of a dream long faded. Was any of it as grand as it had seemed?
Ervin glanced at a clock in the wall. Time was running short. Maybe he could cut the trip short.
“Can’t,” he muttered to himself. “Just need some milk. Then, I need to leave.”

Dust flaked off Ervin’s boot as he stomped on the first step of the escalator. Even after years of riding escalators, he remained skeptical of whether it would stall out on him. Billy had always teased him over the fear. Still, Ervin couldn’t afford to assume that there were ever any guarantees.
Ervin’s posture wilted during the ascent. He stumbled forward upon reaching the top, and struggled to regain his balance.
A man holding a bucket of chicken pushed past him. “Out of the way!”

Ervin thought to give the man a shoulder check, before thinking again. He checked around him — a dozen people were eating amid dozens of tables. The tables, in turn, were flanked by an assortment of fast food restaurants.
Ervin was a minnow, entering a deep pond. There was all of this, and all he needed was some milk.
He stumbled along, eyes skimming the signs of each restaurant. His feet moved toward only one.
“Welcome to George’s Burgers. May I take your order?”
The man’s eyes were downcast, glued to his phone. He shuffled toward the counter.
Ervin rested his arm on the counter. “You guys got milk?”
The man’s skin had an olive texture, but his beard had gone to pepper. A smile spread across the man’s face.
“No,” the man said. He looked up, his eyes crinkling. “No way.”
He gave a wheezing laugh. It was the kind of laugh that turned time inside out. Memory, the moment, and moments to come converged.
“How’s everything holding up?” Ervin asked.
“Good. Good. Well, it’s alright. After being open for three years, the sales at this place are going steady.”
“That’s very good.” Ervin coughed. “So, what would you say is the best thing to drink here? I’m parched.”
“It is very good here… Everything is good. The lemon fizz is probably best, I guess.”
“Life’s given me a bit too many lemons for my taste right now.”
“Yeah, well… Makes sense. This type of place doesn’t serve the drinks that are going to be your speed.”
The man glared, and Ervin could only offer a sheepish grin.
“That was the old me,” Ervin said. “I’m doing better. With everything. Well, I was.
“Screw it, I guess I could go for a few drinks. You?”
The man gave a shrug. “It really sucks, but I won’t be off my shift for quite a few hours.”

The ice cone machine sputtered in the back, its rotors overheating from the strain of its ice. The grill sizzled with pure fat and grease, leftover from burgers that had long been served. There were so many leftovers. Fries littered the counters. A rejected pile of crumbling cookies sat in a corner.  Bits of ketchup stained the walls. The ketchup was on the ceiling and floors too. It was everywhere, really.
Too much ketchup.
“I guess I’ll take a meat monster,” Ervin said.
“Just one?”
“Really need to watch my wallet right now. I didn’t bring a whole lot of cash with me.”
“You, without cash? That’s new.”
“Getting too risky to carry all of my money on my person. Besides, I — I’m just going to cut to the chase — I was wondering if I could get a job here.”
The man’s lips puckered. His eyes were blank. Bleak.
“But, your job, with that construction company,” he said, “it’s going well. Right?”
Ervin laughed. “You only have a construction job for as long as they need you. There have been a lot of cutbacks. They didn’t need me. Turns out, they’re just not building buildings anymore.”
“How long have you —.”
“It’s been a week.”
“I’m really sorry to hear that. If I could do anything, I would.”
“It’s fine. I’ll find something soon. I’m a floater. I guess we can both relate, in that way.”
The man blinked as a switch flipped. He turned and threw a burger patty on the grill.
“You want any fries with that?” the man asked.
“Nope.”
“Nothing else at all?”
“Well, if you had milk, maybe some of that.”
Ervin gave a chuckle, but the man remained stolid.
“We’re not as alike as you think,” the man said. “You know, you could leave town at any time you want, Ervin. The whole world is yours. Always has been.”
“It’s yours too.”
“No it isn’t. You know it. You’ve always had a knack for getting money. Not me. Look at me.”
Ervin rubbed his temples. The heat of the kitchen wafted into his face, and pressure mounted on his head.
“Then why can’t I ever leave this place?” Ervin said. His voice tightened. “It all just keeps getting emptier, and emptier. Though, I keep staying, staring at the emptiness even longer.”
“You could leave, Ervin. Change the game. I know you could.”
Ervin shook his head. A woman cleared her throat.
“Excuse me,” she said. She stood behind Ervin, tapping her foot.
The man jumped, his eyes moving to the woman.
“Sorry ma’am,” the man said. “I can take your order.”
The man then turned to Ervin and gave a whisper. “I’ll call you up for your order in just a minute. I just have to take this.”
Ervin stalked off. He floated past the maze of tables and chairs. He went down the escalator. He went through the exit.
His throat was dry.
The car door slammed. Keys turned. An engine revved.
Ervin needed some milk.
He at least needed something to drink.
End

title: The Paternal Pasture
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
The birds chirped. The sunlight crackled as it hit the pavement. The sky was a stainless blue. The grass was a stainless green.
The bench that I was sitting on was stained gray.

It was a park bench. I was in a park. A nice little grove, where people walked their dogs, went bike-riding, and took jogs. There was great weather on that day too. The trees provided essential shade. There was a soft breeze. The sun brought warmth— even if maybe a little too much.
It was almost seemed like perfect day.
“Well… This was the most imperfect day I’ve ever endured.”

There was a man sitting next to me. His hair was wild, and his eyes were too. His voice was as haggard as they come. I watched and grimaced as he shoved a cigarette in his mouth. His puffs of smoke were so exaggerated that I could practically taste the tobacco.
“So many tears,” he continued. “Like a waterfall. You’d think that they were all crying about some saint…”
He let out a series of coughs.
“Don’t matter though, I guess. They’ll realize soon enough… So, how about that game from last night?”
“Realize what, exactly?” I asked, with a scowl.
He didn’t answer me.
“I… I don’t care what you say. I wish that dad was still here,” I said.
“But I’m your dad. At least, as close as you’re gonna’ get,” he said.
My eyes started to swell.
“Stop pretending that you can replace him.”
“Dead is dead,” he said, giving a signature chuckle. “Get over it.”
He leaned back into the park bench smugly, and let out even bigger puffs of smoke.
“Don’t you even care about what happened?” I asked.
He shook his head.
“Naw. I mean—I’m sorry for you. But… I mean, it was always coming. I had been talking about the signs for years.”
“Sympathetic as ever,” I said.
I looked out at the grove. People were walking by, biding their time. Me though? I was just wasting mine.
“I don’t care what others say: he was a good man,” I said. “I might not have known much about him, but nobody did.”
I dried my eyes.

“He was always… distant. He never talked often. Sometimes, I wonder if even he knew what he was like. Then again, maybe I’m just telling myself that to convince myself that he never was able to share himself with me. Maybe I’m just trying to pretend that all of the wasted hours that could’ve been spent with him weren’t wasted… But, I still think that he was—.”
“Maybe you need to stop saying maybe.”
He wheezed.

“You’re wrong, by the way. I knew him well. I suppose you could say we were close— he kept to himself. He wasn’t a talker, so I can understand why you might feel like nobody understood him. However, the people who say he was a bad person are right…
“So, how about that game from last night?”
He flicked his cigarette away, and lit another.
“He gave to charities though. He worked in soup kitchens. He helped the homeless.”
“Eh… We both know that those things don’t make a man.”
“If we can’t judge people by their actions, what can we judge them by?”

“Their actions…” he said. “I knew your father for who he was… Not who he pretended to be. He was a gambler. A cynic. He ended up bankrupting himself, just because he couldn’t kick his gambling habit. He hurt people… Got in fights with people… He cared about people too. But, he mostly just cared about himself.”
“Is that what you really think?”
“Maybe… Maybe not… Doesn’t matter all that much though. The man is gone. You and I—the memory of him— that’s all that’s left of him…”
I winced.
“You’re right that memories that are all that’s left. But, which memories are we supposed to choose to focus on? The good, or the bad?”
“I say we should focus on the whole— how a man is remembered is what defines him. And, on the whole? Your father was a bad man, and will be remembered as one…”
He flicked another cigarette away.
“So, how about that game?”
I sat for a while, counting the seconds that ticked by on my watch.

“It was alright…” I finally said. “Would’ve been better if the Cowboys had a better coach though. Speaking of which… Don’t you remember when he coached the high school football team? Remember all the people that he touched? That wasn’t the only thing he did either. His family… His friends… He changed them all. Are you really telling me that it had all been fake—all a sham?”
He spit out his cigarette, and became rigid. He looked out into space blankly— a gape lingered on his face.
“We should focus on the whole,” I said. “And, despite of the failings, he was a good man— you’re a good man.”
He let out a sigh. No smoke this time.

“He and I remember pretending to touch a lot of lives, son,” he said. “But, we never actually could. There’ve always been two sides to me… Him and I. And, I feel that he— the worst part of me— won out, in the end.”
He leaned toward me, to hug me. I watched his arms make a grand sweep— but, his arms never touched me. He wasn’t there.
I was alone, on a gray park bench… Talking to myself.
A car pulled up.
“There you are, Steve,” a woman said. My mom. “I’ve been worried sick about you. What are you doing here?”
“Not much.”
I looked at the ground.
“Just— just imagining one last talk with dad,” I said. “What it might’ve been like…”
“Just a figment of my imagination though,” I thought. “Never real. I shouldn’t have pretended that I could replace him…”
I sobbed.
Red eyes. Smoked skies. Dead grass.
Alas. Ten minutes went by, and I was still sitting on the gray park bench.
I finally felt the arms touch me—they were my mother’s, but I still felt my father behind him.
“He lives on, in us,” she said. “We remember people on the whole— and on the whole, your father was a man who will never be forgotten. We all miss him.”
The line between bad and good is often smoky. I’m alright with that.
Today should’ve been the perfect day. But then… It’s the imperfections— the stains— that help make life into what it is.
End

title: To the Moon and Back
paragraphs: For all our triumphs, the Moon is shattered in two. The heart is shattered, too.
“You sure that you can put it back together?” she asks me.
The cuts and callouses along the palm of her hand orbit the heart-shaped locket. At least, the fragments of the locket that remain. It has seen better days. Yet, who hasn’t?
Fractured beams of moonlight creep through cracks in the walls, and the lamp above us flickers. Mariam’s eyes gleam softly as our gazes lock. The world is on fire in there. I can see the sparks.
“Sure,” I say.
I am a handyman. I fix things.
“There is nothing I can’t fix,” I say. “You know that. Like, when does anything I fix ever go wrong?”
My chuckle echoes.
Perhaps I spoke out of turn.
Spokes on the wheels turn, as handy-bot whirs to life. Leaping from his fingertips are bits of lightning, and he shifts his boxy body forward ever so slightly.

The ground quakes when I put pieces of the locket onto handy-bot’s work plate. At first, I worry that yet another meteor has hit the Earth. Then, a laser scans over the locket fragments with precision, and I realize that the quaking is merely my vertigo coming back with a vengeance.
My head aches. So does my soul. Why is it that the things that come back strong are indiscernible from the things that come back with a vengeance?
I clear my throat. “You know, now that it’s all over… Maybe we can try to get back to what we were building.”
Her face is blank, but her hand lands on the crook of my neck.
“We can always try.”
I smirk. “Well, these are trying times.”

There is a screech. Handy-bot’s gears gnash together and he vibrates with a fury. Stumbling over myself, I steady him and tighten a few of his screws. The screws are rusted and groan as I put them back in their place. Nevertheless, they must go back to how they were.
“Remember that night, ages ago, when I first showed you him?” I say. “I — I was so scared you were going to think he was just another dumb trinket, like you usually do.”

Handy-bot’s body steadies back into rhythm. His hands return to hover over the locket, spinning metal and electricity into an elegant tapestry. Already, I can see the bits of crushed locket reforming into its former glory. Though, Mariam doesn’t see this. Her footsteps shift away from me.
“Oh, he definitely is,” she says, teasingly.
Her hands flit along the old bookshelves. The bindings move in and out, as keys in a piano concerto that only she can hear.
She pulls a book out and inspects it. “Your machines — they’re cute. But they’re not why we’re still here.”
Handy-bot is operating smoothly now, his mechanisms now tightened into clockwork. I brush some moondust off my tattered coat, and stride toward her.
“Is this the part where you point at me as the reason?” I say. “And then, I have to be modest and tell you that it was us? All of us…”
I flash a grin.
The book falls out of her hand, and she stoops to pick it up.
Déjà vu. My hand moves toward the book. I am back in a library. A dream. The pilot episode is on rerun.
I can go back to the line of dialogue that is tried and tested. “Here, let me hel—.”
“No.” Her voice is hard. Calculated. “You’re already helping. It’s fine. It’s my book, anyway.”
I squint at the title. I want to tell her that I have read the book a million times, from cover to cover. Yet, I do not recognize it.
“That’s what I do,” I say. “Help. I’ll never give up on that.”
Her eyes shine as pearls; perfect stars.
The stars break, and tears come pouring. It is a rushing stream. It won’t stop.
My face burns.
“What about Lana, huh Jack?” Her voice is brittle steel. “Or my father?”
I force my lungs to keep giving me breaths. Time stops, and I suddenly wish time would start turning back.
“That was never supposed to happen,” I say. “You know that. The group broke from the plan.”
She shakes her head. “Yeah, because you always have it all figured out…”
“I mean, I usually do.”
She stares into me, cutting to my core. A hatred closes around her that I haven’t seen before. The walls feel like they’re collapsing around me.
I need space. “They were hit by chunks of the goddamn Moon! How can any of us be expected to beat that?”
I step away and pause to catch my breath. The adrenaline and sheer terror is rushing back, but I must cool down.

“I said we needed to stay in the bunker.” I pace my words to the tune of my chipped watch, keeping a slow monotone. “We were supposed to wait to loot food replicators until after we were sure meteors weren’t going to hit. We weren’t even supposed to be in that town.”
Mariam’s book is open. She peers at it, closes it, and puts it back on the shelf.
“Were we supposed to just go another week without food?” she asks.
I have no answers.
My eyes rove around the room. I want to grab something and smash it. I need to leave this place. I need to cool my head, before I lose it.
“We could’ve flown a mag-lev car and tried to get them back to safety in time,” Mariam continues. “We at least could’ve tried to call them, to warn them about what your sensor said...”
“Mariam, we would’ve died, no question. Besides, that sensor I built gives false alarms. It always does.”
Even as I say this, I know it isn’t completely true. Infinite possible solutions existed, all unexplored. There was so much more that could’ve been done.
“Why did you stop me?” she says.
I want to speak, but I will just choke on the words.

“You tried to stop so many of us, Jack…” she says. “And, there used to be three hundred in our group. I remember when the Moon first split, and the meteors first started coming down… You said you would protect us. All of us.”
Phantom faces haunt the room. My spirit curdling and chest tightening, I let out a sigh.
“I did everything I could,” I mutter to myself. “I didn’t know. How could I?”
“I know, how could you?” she says. She is looking at the ground. “I don’t want to blame you. But this is just so hard, Jack. Twenty… Those are all who made it from our group.”
My eyes sting, and I turn from Mariam. She can’t see me. This stuff never touched me. I am stronger than this.

The locket is nearly reforged, all holes and cracks filled and welded with new bits of steel. Handy-bot starts on a chrome outer coating. It is terribly beautiful. Though, has the locket truly been repaired? Or is it merely a faded facsimile of its true self?
Mariam’s arms wrap around from behind me and give a squeeze, just the way that they used to.
She manages an “I love you.”
I manage an “I love you too.”
I look up to the ceiling. There is a hole there.
“It wasn’t supposed to be this way, Mariam… We were supposed to own this house outright, by now. Maybe we would have a kid.”
Mariam rests her chin on my shoulder, and I can tell she is looking through the hole in the ceiling too.
Flares of light move through the night. The Moon hangs above it all, a trench of darkness slit through its center.
“The universe had different plans for us,” she says.
I lean into my desk, and stare at handy-bot. It is nothing short of a miracle that the electricity is running to power him again.

“The meteors aren’t coming down anymore, I swear,” I say. “And, we’re building a new world here now. There might only be a few of our group left, but we’re scrappy. We can put together anything. There are also more people migrating here, with other groups… I think we still have a chance to bring back a normal world. To start over.”
Mariam holds my jaw and draws our faces together.
“I can’t stay here,” she says. “This town was home. It hurts. Look at us. We’re different now.”
I see the lines of stress and exhaustion mapped across her face. She is not wrong. Though, it seems wrong.
“I don’t feel different…” I lie.
Her hand moves to a deep scar on my forearm. I don’t remember where the scar came from.
“You feel different,” she says.

Handy-bot gives a loud chirp. I pull the locket off the work plate and inspect it. Its chrome finish isn’t quite the same as it used to be, but it is spotless. The screws, hinges, etchings, and curves are shaped back into perfection.
“I did it,” I say. “I told you I was going to fix it. You can’t even tell the difference.”
Mariam gives one of her diamond smiles. It is the kind of smile that puts you on another planet, in a distant galaxy.
“It is gorgeous,” she says. She looks at it, but her eyes pull away. “Thank you for fixing it. It’s yours now. Keep it.”
It is a blow to the gut.
I place the locket in my pocket without a word. I did everything I could to fix it, but it wasn’t enough. What is there to say?

We stand in this room for a few minutes, inspecting what it has become over the years. Much of the wood and plaster has peeled away from the foundations, fleeing for the wind. I wish I could do the same from my own skin.
Something was still alive when we first entered this room. It is dead now. We only wait to find the right goodbye.

“Mariam, a few months ago, that meteor hit us. Even though our bunker was reinforced and made of iron, it still crumpled in on most of the group… It nearly killed all of us. And, you said that the only thing that saved us was fate.”
She brushes a strand of hair out of her face. “I did.”
“And, don’t you think that might mean something?”
Her eyes narrow in thought. I know that she’s wondered this.
“Fate was strong enough to save us…” she says. “But Jack, it isn’t enough to save us. This wasn’t — it isn’t meant to be.”
She walks to the door.
“Mariam, please don’t leave.” I open the locket’s heart, to reveal the words etched inside. “I — I love you to the Moon and back.”
She nods. There is pain in her face, but she gives me a warm smile. “I wish you the best. You’re going to do great. I’ll see you when I see you.”
End

title: We Can All Be Stars
paragraphs: By Christian Mueth
My dome was nicer than Ron’s. People said so. A thousand people, to be precise. I know it was that many people, because they all had given me their shines. Ron had five shines.
I didn’t like looking over to Ron’s dome. His wasn’t like mine. My dome was immaculate. The glass had a sparkle to it. Every hologram my dome projected maintained a pristine resolution.
Ron’s dome was fine. Only fine.

My dome’s glow was running low though. People’s sprites were ignoring my dome at a slightly higher rate, because of this. Worse, my brain was getting blurry, and my stomach was getting the gurgles. I fondled the hose notched to my forehead. Despite my number of shines, the hose wasn’t giving enough of a charge.
It had been a few days since my dome had been given a joy-jolt. That explained it.

With a sigh, I activated my dome’s holo-transport. My sprite spawned at the joy-store. I could say that I’m not the joy-store’s biggest fan. But I would be fined a ton of fines for saying that. So, I never say that.
The joy-store is fine.
There were many things at the joy-store. Some were worth hundreds of shines. Stimulants, narcotics, hallucinogens... Though, they weren’t what I was looking for.

As I walked across the joy-store’s marble floors, sprites bowed and sent me shines. My skin felt all icky as they did — the sprites’ glimmers faded upon handing out each shine. Some of them gave away their last shine and pixelated away. Yet, the exchange couldn’t be avoided. Following order is important. When I passed a sprite that shone brighter than me, I bowed and handed them one of my own shines. I had to. It’s protocol.
My pace quickened when I saw a glowing kiosk. A joy jolt station. Upon getting closer, the banner overtop it came into view: “We’re all made of stardust. We will all be stars again.”

I muttered the mantra under my breath and handed the kiosk all my shines. The sprite at the kiosk gave me a glittery grin and held out several containers of joy-jolt. My sprite goes to devour one of the containers.

I was stupid. So stupid. I should have taken the sprite back to the dome, immediately. A very shiny sprite came up to me. It was big. Angry. As my sprite tried guzzling its joy-jolt, the contents dissipated away. Away, and into the other sprite. I tried to get away, with some of the other containers. Though, I couldn’t. My sprite wouldn’t follow my commands.
It was the order of things — the clout of the other sprite demanded that I give it the containers. So, I did.
The sprite left once it had them all. I watched as the light from my own sprite drained, and then finally pixelated away. My holo-transport fizzled off. My dome went dark. My hose went dead.
My head was weighed down by an anvil. I tried to stand, then toppled over. All my energy was sapped. I crawled on my elbows, reaching my dome’s glass window.
“Help me,” I cried out. “Please, send me a shine! I’m dying!”
Ron sat back in his chair. He must not have heard me — the dome’s walls must’ve been too thick. I banged again. And again. My fingers clawed the glass. I thrashed. I screamed.
Finally, Ron turned. He grinned. Somebody from the street walked up to him and sent over a shine. He accepted it. Then, he turned away.
End
